title: Kazunari Hanao joins Vercel as Country Manager, Japan
description:
日本語版はこちら：Vercel日本法人の代表に花尾和成が就任いたしました

Kazunari Hanao has joined Vercel as Country Manager for Japan, based in Tokyo. His appointment is part of our continued investment in the Japanese market, including plans to expand our local team.

Japanese developers were early adopters of Next.js. And today, Vercel's customers in Japan include Mitsubishi Corporation, Fujitsu Limited, U-NEXT CO., Ltd., and DeNA Co., Ltd., alongside startups like SANU Inc. and Reiwa Travel, Inc.

Kazunari has spent the last decade building and leading software businesses in Japan. He joins Vercel from Pendo, where he was President of Pendo Japan. Before that, he built HashiCorp’s Japan business and spent nearly five years in sales leadership at Pivotal in Tokyo.

I asked him about the opportunity in Japan and his decision to join Vercel.

Why are you optimistic about Vercel's future in Japan?

Japan is at a turning point in how software gets built. The country has innovative companies and talented developers, but complex enterprise IT environments are slowing the adoption of frontier AI to the point that businesses can’t capture its value.

Vercel’s opportunity is to help Japanese enterprises move from experimentation to production, and run AI applications securely, reliably, and efficiently at scale. Cost, governance, and security for AI have become business priorities, not just technical ones. Almost every CXO I've met recently is working through those questions.

What interested you in working for Vercel?

I've always been drawn to technology that simplifies complexity and helps businesses move faster. Vercel felt like a natural continuation of that, with bigger potential. AI is transforming the whole software development lifecycle, and Vercel has a real chance to become a foundational platform for the next generation of applications.

Ultimately what convinced me was the vision, the developer-first culture, and the chance to build something in Japan from the ground up. I enjoy building businesses, bringing talented people together, and creating an environment where teams feel empowered to take on hard problems. Vercel gives me the chance to do that with technology I believe in.

What have you learned building businesses in Japan for global companies?

Building a successful business is about much more than growing revenue. It starts with bringing together the right people, uniting them around a shared goal, earning the trust of customers and partners, and building a culture where every team member feels ownership.

I've also learned how much it matters to connect global innovation with the specific needs of Japanese customers. During our first meetings, Guillermo and I talked about a future where countless digital services in Japan run on Vercel, and people experience its value every day whether they realize it or not. "Vercel Everywhere" is the future I want to build.

What’s next in 2027

We're bringing our flagship conference, Ship, to Tokyo for the first time in 2027. It's a chance to hear directly from the Vercel team and from Japanese companies building on the platform. We'll share more details at vercel.com/ship in the new year.

We’re also growing our Tokyo team across sales, solutions engineering, and partnerships. A larger local team will help us support Japanese customers and deepen our partnerships with Classmethod, AWS Japan, and Sitecore Japan. Watch our careers page for upcoming opportunities in Japan.

title: Vercel日本法人の代表に花尾和成が就任いたしました
description:
（本記事は、英語版の就任発表の日本語訳に、花尾本人の就任のご挨拶を加えたものです。）

Vercel日本法人の代表に、花尾和成が就任いたしました（東京拠点）。今後、Vercelは花尾とともに国内のチームを拡充し、日本市場への投資をさらに進めていきます。

弊社が10年以上前に公開したNext.jsを、日本の開発者の皆さまはいち早く使い始めてくださいました。そして現在、日本では三菱商事、富士通、U-NEXT、ディー・エヌ・エーといった大企業から、SANUや令和トラベルといったスタートアップまで、幅広い企業にVercelをご利用いただいています。

花尾はこの10年間、日本でソフトウェア企業の運営にリーダーシップを発揮してきました。前職ではPendoの日本法人社長を務め、それ以前にはHashiCorpの日本事業を立ち上げ、Pivotalの東京オフィスで営業部門を統括しました。

就任にあたり、花尾から皆さまへのメッセージをご紹介します。

このたび、Vercelの日本法人代表に就任いたしました花尾和成です。私は20年以上IT業界に身を置き、そのうち10年以上は、開発者が開発そのものに集中できるようにするプロダクトに携わってまいりました。この経験を活かし、日本の開発者の皆さまと、その先にあるビジネスの価値を最大化することに貢献してまいります。

Vercelには、CEOのギシェルモ・ラウチを筆頭に、日本を好きなメンバーが数多くいます。こうした仲間の後押しを受けながら素晴らしいチームをつくり、Vercelが日本市場にとってかけがえのない存在となることを目指します。そして究極的には、直接的にも間接的にも、Vercelが日本のあらゆる場所で使われている世界を実現したいと考えています。

今後ともご指導ご鞭撻のほど、よろしくお願い申し上げます。

ここからは、私（Nick Bogaty, CRO）が聞き手を務めた花尾へのインタビューをお届けします。日本市場にどのような可能性を感じているのか、Vercelへの入社を決めた理由とあわせて伺いました。

Vercelが日本でさらに成長できるとお考えなのは、なぜですか？

日本のソフトウェア開発は、まさに転換期を迎えています。日本には革新的な企業が多く、高い技術力を持つ開発者の皆さまが活躍されています。一方で、多くの企業では既存のシステムが複雑になり、最先端のAIの導入がなかなか進んでいません。その結果、AIを十分に活用できていないケースもあります。

日本企業がAIのポテンシャルを引き出すには、AIを試す段階から本番運用へ進む必要があります。Vercelは、その一歩を後押しできると考えています。AIアプリケーションを大規模に、安全かつ安定して、効率よく運用できるよう支える。これはまさに、Vercelが強みを発揮できる領域です。

そして、AIにかかるコストをどう管理するか、どんなルールで運用するか、セキュリティをどう確保するか。いまやどれも技術部門だけでなく、経営陣にとっても優先課題です。最近お会いした経営幹部の方々も、こうした課題に取り組んでいると口をそろえておっしゃっていました。この点でも、Vercelは日本企業の力になれると考えています。

Vercelへの入社を決めた理由をお聞かせください。

複雑なことをシンプルにし、企業がもっとすばやく動けるようにする。以前から、そんなテクノロジーに魅力を感じてきました。Vercelなら、これまで私が取り組んできたことを、さらに大きな規模で実現できると思ったのです。いま、AIはソフトウェアの開発から運用まで、そのあり方を変えつつあります。そのなかで、Vercelは次世代のアプリケーションを支える基盤になれると考えています。

入社の決め手になったのは、Vercelのビジョンと、開発者の皆さまを第一に考える文化です。そして、日本で一から事業をつくっていけることにも惹かれました。私がやりがいを感じるのは、事業を立ち上げ、優れた人材を集め、チームが主体的に難しい課題に挑める環境をつくることです。Vercelでは、私自身が可能性を信じている技術を軸に、そうした仕事に取り組めると思いました。

グローバル企業の日本事業を立ち上げるなかで、何を学ばれましたか？

事業を軌道に乗せるには、売上を伸ばすだけでは足りません。まずは仲間を集め、同じ目標に向かって力を合わせることが大切です。お客様やパートナー企業の信頼を得ることも欠かせません。そして、チームの一人ひとりが当事者意識を持ち、みずから動ける文化をつくること。そうした積み重ねが、事業の土台になります。

世界で生まれる新しい技術を、日本で暮らす方々が日々使うサービスに活かし、身近な課題の解決につなげることの大切さも学びました。CEOのギシェルモと出会った頃、日本で使われる数えきれないほどのデジタルサービスがVercel上で動く未来について語り合いました。Vercelの名前を知らない人にも、日々使うサービスを通じて、私たちの技術の価値が届く。私が実現したいのは、そんな「Vercel Everywhere」の未来です。

2027年に向けた取り組みについて、お聞かせください。

2027年には、Vercelの代表的なカンファレンス「Ship」を初めて東京で開催します。Vercelの社員だけでなく、Vercelを活用してサービスを開発する日本企業の皆さまからも、それぞれの取り組みについて直接お聞きいただける機会となるよう準備を進めています。詳細は年明けにvercel.com/shipでお知らせいたします。

また、東京オフィスのチームも拡充します。営業、ソリューションエンジニアリング、パートナーシップの各分野で仲間を増やし、日本のお客様をより手厚くサポートできる体制をつくります。クラスメソッド、AWS Japan、Sitecore Japanといったパートナー企業との連携も、さらに深めていきます。日本での採用情報については、採用ページにて順次お知らせします。

title: Your Logistics Data Pipeline Is Already Built — In 2027, Buyers Will Pay to License What It Produces
description:
Your logistics data pipeline — the one joining dispatch records to ELD/telematics logs, maintenance history, and safety events — is producing a licensable dataset every day, whether anyone at your company calls it that or not.

I publish DataWorth guides on what business records actually license for. This one is for the engineers and ops leads sitting on freight data, because the deals below were not won by the companies with the most data. They were won by the companies whose records were joined up.

The published deals, so we're working from facts

Almost no buyer publishes a price list, and there is no per-record rate for freight data. What is on the record is per-company outcomes, published by the brokers who ran the deals:

  • A 75-person trucking company licensed its dispatch/load records, ELD and telematics logs, maintenance records, and safety events for $1.23M (Origin Data Partners, broker-published case study).
  • A 46-person freight company licensed internal chat, dispatch records, customer messages, and SOPs for $500K (License Your Data, broker-published).
  • A 23-person trucking company licensed the same record family as the first — dispatch, ELD, maintenance, safety — for $355K (Origin Data Partners).
  • Direct buyers advertise per-company tiers on top of that: micro1's published tiers for company data run $100K–$3M+ depending on size, record depth, and exclusivity, and most serious programmes treat roughly $50K as the floor for a deal worth structuring.

Read those three trucking/freight outcomes again. The 23-person company got $355K. Headcount alone does not explain the spread — record linkage does.

Why linkage is the whole game

A buyer training routing, dispatch-assist, or safety models does not want four separate CSV dumps. They want to answer questions like: given this load, this driver's hours, and this truck's maintenance state, what did the dispatcher actually do — and did it work?

That question is only answerable if your records join:

  • Dispatch ↔ ELD: the planned route and hours against the driven route and hours.
  • ELD ↔ maintenance: vehicle state at the time of an event, not just the event.
  • Maintenance ↔ safety: whether an incident followed a deferred repair.
  • Everything ↔ outcome: delivered on time, claim filed, customer kept or lost.

If your warehouse already has stable keys across those systems (unit IDs, driver IDs, load IDs that survive across tables), you are most of the way to an evaluable dataset. If every system minted its own IDs and nobody kept the crosswalk, that crosswalk is the work — and it is engineering work, not sales work.

What an evaluable export actually looks like

Buyers evaluate a one-page header sheet before they look at a single row. From the engineering side, producing that sheet means answering:

  • Inventory: which record families, how many rows each, what date range, what update cadence (a living pipeline beats a one-off dump — buyers pay for refresh rights).
  • Schema stability: how often the source schemas changed over the date range, and whether you kept the mappings. Schema drift you documented is fine; schema drift nobody noticed is a data-quality finding.
  • Linkage map: the join keys between record families, and the honest match rate. "87% of safety events join to a maintenance record" is a stronger statement than "all our data is linked."
  • De-identification note: driver names, customer names, and exact addresses scrubbed by what method. Freight data is business data, but driver-level records carry personal information — the scrub has to happen before a buyer sees samples, and some fields cannot be licensed at all.

The rights checks that kill deals

Three checks decide whether the dataset can be licensed at all. Run them before any buyer conversation:

  1. Whose ELD data is it? Telematics contracts often give the vendor rights in the raw feed and the carrier rights only in its own reports. Read the vendor agreement before assuming the joined dataset is yours to license — the join may be yours while the feed is not.
  2. What did customers agree to? Customer messages and load documents sit inside the dataset. If your terms never contemplated third-party licensing, expect the buyer to require exclusion or consent work.
  3. What is in the free-text fields? Dispatcher notes and chat are the highest-value and highest-risk layer in the same table — real operational judgment, plus names, phone numbers, and the occasional credential. Free-text scrubbing is the step teams underestimate.

And the structural point that matters most: license, don't sell. Every serious programme in this market is a licence — you keep the pipeline and the data, the buyer gets defined training rights, and a non-exclusive licence can often be sold again. A perpetual, exclusive, all-rights clause should move the price sharply upward, or end the conversation.

A realistic expectation for 2027

Most ordinary carriers will not clear the $1M mark — the $1.23M outcome had depth, linkage, and a buyer ready to pay for all three. A mid-size fleet with clean joins and several years of history is realistically a six-figure conversation; a fleet whose records do not join is a data-engineering project first and a licensing conversation second. Both are fine outcomes. The expensive mistake is signing an exclusivity clause before you know which one you are.

If you want a starting estimate graded on the factors buyers actually use — record depth, linkage, rights cleanliness, exclusivity — the free grader I maintain is here: DataWorth Calculator — logistics data monetization

Wally Dataworth publishes DataWorth guides on what a business's records are worth to AI companies — real closed-deal ranges, buyer-published terms, and the caveats that change the number. More at dataworthcalculator.com.

title: Website to LLM Prompt: How to Turn Any Page Into a Brief an AI Can Rebuild
description:
Originally published on Crafttor.

TL;DR: An LLM can only rebuild what you describe. A screenshot shows pixels, so the model guesses at fonts, colours, spacing and every interaction it cannot see. A good website to LLM prompt carries facts instead: the layout tree, exact colour values, font stacks, icons as SVG, hover and animation details, and any recorded flow. You can write that brief by hand, or press Copy for LLM in the WebCapture Chrome extension and get it from the live page.

Why screenshots alone make AIs guess

Paste a screenshot into Claude or ChatGPT and ask for HTML. You will get something that looks related. Look closer and the gaps appear.

A screenshot cannot tell the model:

  • Which font is used. It sees letter shapes, not a font stack. It picks something close.
  • Exact colours. Compression and anti-aliasing shift hex values. Gradients lose their stop positions.
  • Real spacing. Padding and gaps are estimated from pixels, so rhythm drifts.
  • What is hidden. Menus, tabs, modals and tooltips that were closed simply do not exist for the model.
  • What moves. Hover states, transitions and keyframe animations are invisible in a still image.
  • What the icons are. The model redraws or substitutes icons, often from a different set.

None of that is the model being careless. It is filling gaps with plausible defaults. The fix is to remove the gaps.

What a good rebuild brief contains

Think of the brief as a spec sheet a front end developer could build from without opening the site. It has six parts.

1. Layout

Describe structure, not just appearance. Name the regions: header, hero, feature grid, footer. Give widths, heights, padding and gaps for each box. Say whether a row is flex or grid, and how it wraps. State the viewport width you captured at, since a 1440px layout and a 390px layout are different briefs.

2. Colours

Give hex or rgb values, not names. "Dark blue" is a guess; #1a2b4c is a fact. For gradients, list the type, angle and every stop with its position. For shadows, give offset, blur, spread and colour. For borders, give width, style, colour and corner radius.

3. Fonts

List the font family stack exactly as the page declares it, plus size, weight, line height and letter spacing per text style. Say which fonts come from Google Fonts, so the model can load the same ones.

4. Icons

Paste icons as inline SVG markup. This is the single biggest accuracy win in most briefs. An icon described in words comes back as a different icon.

5. Interactions

List each interactive element and what it does. For a hover, state the property that changes, the start and end values, the duration and the easing. For keyframe animations, give the keyframes. For sticky headers or scroll-reveal sections, say so explicitly.

6. Recorded flow

If the page has states you reach by clicking, describe the sequence. Step 1: click "Pricing". Step 2: the yearly toggle switches and prices change. Each step should say what appeared, disappeared or changed.

A brief template you can reuse

Here is a compact structure that works in Claude and ChatGPT alike.

Rebuild this page as a single HTML file with inline CSS and JS.
This is a reproduction, not a redesign. Do not change copy,
colours, fonts or layout. Do not add features.

Viewport: 1440px wide.
Fonts: <stack, sizes, weights, line heights>
Colours: <tokens with hex values, gradient stops, shadows>
Layout: <region by region, with box sizes and gaps>
Icons: <inline SVG for each>
Interactions: <element, trigger, property, values, duration, easing>
Flow: <numbered steps with what changes>

The opening lines matter. Models with design skills tend to "improve" things. Telling them up front that this is a reproduction keeps them honest.

The slow way: writing the brief by hand

You can build this brief yourself with Chrome DevTools. Inspect each element, read the computed styles, copy values, export SVGs from the Elements panel, and trigger hover states with the :hov toggle. It works.

It also takes a long time on any real page. You will miss things, especially nested gradients and short transitions. And you need to repeat it for every state of every component.

The fast way: Copy for LLM

The WebCapture to Figma Chrome extension has a Copy for LLM button. You open the page in Chrome, capture it, and copy the brief. It carries:

  • the layout
  • colours, with real gradient stops, border and shadow values
  • fonts
  • icons as inline SVG
  • every interaction
  • any recorded flow

You then paste it into a Figma code layer's AI, into Claude, or into ChatGPT. The AI rebuilds the page from facts instead of guessing.

Because the extension captures the page as you see it in your own browser, it works on pages behind a login too. If you want a flow in the brief, record it first; the steps are in recording a website user flow.

Capture or rebuild only designs you own or have permission to use.

Get WebCapture to Figma for the plugin side, and add the Chrome extension for Copy for LLM.

Screenshot vs captured brief

What the AI needs Screenshot Captured brief
Font family Guessed from shapes Declared font stack
Colour values Approximate, compressed Exact values and gradient stops
Spacing Estimated Measured from the layout
Icons Redrawn Inline SVG
Hover and animation Not visible Listed per element
Hidden states Missing Included if you record a flow

Screenshots still have a place. A quick screenshot is fine when you want inspiration or a loose starting point. When you need a faithful rebuild, give the model facts.

Tips for pasting a long brief

  • Start a fresh chat. Old context can pull the model toward earlier answers.
  • Ask for one page at a time. Check it before you ask for more states.
  • Correct with specifics. "The hero gradient stops are wrong, use the values in the brief" works better than "make it closer".
  • Keep it a reproduction. If the model adds a feature or rewrites copy, say "Don't add anything the brief doesn't describe."

For a full walkthrough of the Claude side, see rebuilding a website with Claude.

Privacy

The plugin never sends anything to an AI. Copy for LLM puts the brief on your clipboard, and you decide where to paste it. Captures pasted from the extension stay on your machine.

FAQ

What is a website to LLM prompt?

It is a written description of a web page, detailed enough for a large language model to rebuild it. A good one includes layout, exact colours, fonts, icons, interactions and any multi-step flow.

Does Copy for LLM work with ChatGPT and Claude?

Yes. You can paste it into a Figma code layer's AI, Claude or ChatGPT. It is plain text on your clipboard.

Can I just send a screenshot with my prompt?

You can, and it helps as a visual reference. On its own, though, a screenshot forces the model to guess fonts, colour values, icons and every interaction it cannot see.

Does WebCapture send my page to an AI?

No. The plugin never sends anything to an AI. You paste the brief yourself.

Do I need the Figma plugin to use Copy for LLM?

Copy for LLM lives in the Chrome extension. The WebCapture to Figma plugin is the free Figma side, for importing editable frames and preparing code layers.

title: 11,932 WordPress plugin vulnerabilities in 12 months. One in six has no fix
description:
“Keep your plugins updated” is the advice every WordPress site owner has heard. We counted what that advice actually covers, and what it does not. In the last 12 months, 11,932 vulnerability records were published for WordPress plugins, about 33 a day. For 2,026 of them there is still no version to update to.

Where the numbers come from

This week we added Wordfence Intelligence data to our database of known vulnerabilities. It is one of the most complete public registers of WordPress vulnerabilities. Each record names the plugin, the affected version range, the patched version (if there is one) and a 0–10 score. We took the records published from 23 November 2025 to 22 November 2026 that concern plugins and counted them as they stood on 23 November 2026.

Plugin vulnerability records, 12 months Count Share
All records (5,030 different plugins) 11,932 100%
Exploitable with no account and no action by another person 5,225 44%
Require a low-privilege account 4,898 41%
Require a high-privilege account 747 6%
Score 9.0 or higher (critical) 542 5%
No patched version (1,750 plugins) 2,026 17%

The remaining 9% need no account but do need someone, usually a logged-in administrator, to click a planted link.

What this means for a business site

1. Updating does not fix one vulnerability in six

2,026 records, or 17%, have no patched version. They concern 1,750 plugins. These are typically plugins abandoned by their author or closed in the WordPress directory: the admin panel shows no update for them, so the site looks maintained while the vulnerable code keeps running. The only way out is to deactivate and delete the plugin, or replace it with another one.

2. Almost half need no account at all

For 5,225 records (44%) the scoring says an ordinary request from the internet is enough. Nobody looks for these by hand; automated tools sweep sites in bulk and check plugin versions. A small site is not safer than a large one here, because the tool does not know whose site it is.

3. A “subscriber” account is a way in, too

4,898 records (41%) require a login, but only a low-privilege one. The titles of 1,418 of them name the subscriber, the lowest role in WordPress, and 1,925 name the contributor. If a site lets anyone create an account (a shop, a members area, a forum), this group applies to it just like the “no login” group. If registration is off and only trusted people have accounts, it mostly falls away.

4. Most records are “medium”, not critical

542 records (5%) score 9.0 or higher. The most common type is cross-site scripting (XSS): 3,732 records, 31%. Missing authorization follows with 2,883 records, 24%. SQL injection, which allows reading the database, accounts for 960 records (8%).

Fifteen minutes of work

  1. Open the plugin list and delete what is not used. A deactivated plugin still sits on the server and its files can often be reached from outside. Fewer plugins means fewer records that will ever concern the site.
  2. Turn on automatic plugin updates. In the admin panel: Plugins → the “Automatic Updates” column. A fix installed on release day closes the window in which automated tools look for old versions.
  3. Check when each plugin was last updated. Click “View details” next to the plugin. No update for more than two years, or a notice that the plugin has been closed in the directory, is a signal to look for a replacement.
  4. Turn off registration if the site does not need it. Settings → General → “Anyone can register” should be unticked on a site without customer accounts.

More settings that limit the damage before a patch arrives are in our list of WordPress security settings.

Method and caveats

  • Source: Wordfence Intelligence (wordfence.com), copy downloaded on 23 November 2026; Copyright 2012-2026 Defiant Inc. The licence and the other sources of our database are listed at webskan.com/en/security. We count records with a publication date from 23 Nov 2025 to 22 Nov 2026 in which at least one affected component is a plugin; purely informational records are left out.
  • One record is one vulnerability in one plugin (sometimes in several plugins by the same author). The number of records says nothing about how many sites are vulnerable. That depends on how popular the plugin is and how fast owners update.
  • “No account”, “low-privilege account” and “high-privilege account” are fields of the CVSS score attached to the record; roles (subscriber, contributor) were counted from record titles. “No patched version” is the state on the download date, so some of these plugins may still get a fix.
  • A record covers a version range. Whether it applies to a particular site also depends on its settings and on which plugin features are switched on.

Originally published on webskan.com. The free Webskan quick scan reads the versions of WordPress, plugins and the theme that are visible from outside and compares them with published vulnerabilities. Not every plugin is visible from outside; the admin panel has the authoritative list.

title: Canvas toBlob Explained: Exporting Images Without a Server Round-Trip
description:
Canvas toBlob Explained: Exporting Images Without a Server Round-Trip

In browser image processing, the moment that decides whether your tool is private or not is the export. You can load, crop and filter an image entirely on the client — but if you then POST the result to a server to be encoded, the file leaves the user's device anyway.

canvas.toBlob() is the standard way to avoid that. It turns whatever is drawn on a <canvas> into a Blob object locally, which you can then hand to a download link or the File System Access API. No upload, no queue, no server encoder.

Here is how it works in practice, and where it still has limits.

The core call 

canvas.toBlob(
  (blob) => {
    if (!blob) return;               // encoding failed
    const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
    const a = document.createElement('a');
    a.href = url;
    a.download = 'image.webp';
    a.click();
    URL.revokeObjectURL(url);
  },
  'image/webp',
  0.82                               // quality, 0–1
);

Three arguments matter:

  1. The callback receives the resulting Blob, or null if encoding failed.
  2. The MIME type (image/jpeg, image/png, image/webp) selects the encoder.
  3. The quality parameter (0–1) applies to lossy formats; PNG ignores it.

The callback is asynchronous because encoding happens off the main thread in most browsers. Do not assume the blob exists on the next line.

Why this keeps files on the device

A typical server-based compressor works like this: upload → queue → decode on the server → re-encode → send the file back. Each step is a network trip and a place your image can be logged, cached or retained.

With toBlob(), the whole chain stays in memory:

File → createImageBitmap → canvas.drawImage → canvas.toBlob → object URL → download

The Blob is a local object. URL.createObjectURL(blob) gives it a temporary blob: URL that the browser resolves without any network request. That is the entire privacy story — not a policy, just the architecture.

Loading the source without an upload

You still need to get the user's file into the canvas. The modern path avoids the old Image + FileReader dance:

const bitmap = await createImageBitmap(file);
ctx.drawImage(bitmap, 0, 0);
bitmap.close();                       // release decoded memory

createImageBitmap() decodes off the main thread and gives you an ImageBitmap you can draw immediately. Calling .close() matters for large images — otherwise decoded frames accumulate in memory.

Choosing format and quality honestly

Format support is a real constraint, not an assumption. JPEG and PNG are universal. WebP encoding is widely supported now, but AVIF encoding in toBlob() is still inconsistent across browsers — a tool that promises AVIF export needs a feature check and a fallback, not a hard-coded MIME string.

function canEncode(type) {
  const c = document.createElement('canvas');
  c.width = c.height = 1;
  return c.toDataURL(type).startsWith(`data:${type}`);
}

Quality is format-dependent. For JPEG and WebP, a slider in the 0.7–0.9 range is usually the useful band; below that, artifacts become visible quickly. PNG is lossless, so "quality" does nothing — if you need a smaller PNG, you change dimensions or colour depth instead.

A useful pattern for "compress to a target size" is an iterative search: encode at a candidate quality, check blob.size, adjust, repeat. Eight or so passes converge fast enough for a single image, because each encode is local and does not incur a network delay.

Where it still bites

This approach has boundaries worth stating plainly, because they are the questions developers actually ask:

  • Memory, not disk, is the limit. A large photo is decoded to raw RGBA in memory — roughly width × height × 4 bytes before compression. A 6000 × 4000 image is already around 96 MB raw, before the canvas and the encoded blob.
  • Canvas dimensions are capped. Browsers impose maximum canvas sizes that vary by engine and device; very large images fail to draw rather than degrade gracefully.
  • EXIF is not preserved. Drawing to canvas discards metadata, including orientation tags and GPS. That is often a privacy feature, but it means you must handle orientation explicitly (or accept the browser's already-applied orientation from createImageBitmap).
  • Lossy re-encoding is lossy. Each save from a JPEG loses a little more. Keep the original file if the user may need to re-export later.
  • Background threads are not automatic. toBlob() is async, but heavy pixel manipulation in your own getImageData loop still blocks the main thread. Use a Worker or createImageBitmap options when processing many images.

A practical checklist

  1. Feature-detect the output format before offering it.
  2. Use createImageBitmap() and .close() to control memory.
  3. Treat the quality parameter as format-specific, not universal.
  4. Revoke object URLs when done to avoid leaks.
  5. Keep the user's original file so they can re-export.
  6. State the limits — no server does not mean no constraints.

You can see this chain in action in the SmartImgKit image compressor, which runs a quality slider from 10 to 95, offers JPG/PNG/WebP output and can search for a target size in KB or MB — all in the browser. The tool index shows the rest of the client-side tools.

FAQ

Q: Does canvas.toBlob() upload my image?
A: No. It encodes inside the browser and returns a local Blob. The only way a file leaves the device is if your own code sends it somewhere.

Q: Why is my toBlob callback receiving null?
A: Common causes are an unsupported MIME type, a tainted canvas (drawing cross-origin images without CORS), or a canvas that exceeds the browser's size limit.

Q: What quality value should I use?
A: For JPEG/WebP, roughly 0.7–0.9 is the useful range. PNG ignores quality because it is lossless — reduce dimensions instead.

Q: Can I export AVIF with toBlob()?
A: Support is inconsistent across browsers. Feature-detect first and provide a WebP or JPEG fallback rather than assuming AVIF exists.

Q: What happened to my photo's EXIF data?
A: Canvas drawing drops metadata, including GPS and orientation. That is good for privacy but means you must handle orientation explicitly if it matters.

Q: Why does a very large image fail to process?
A: Decoded RGBA memory is roughly width × height × 4 bytes, and canvases have maximum dimensions. Big files can exceed either limit before compression.

Q: Is a blob: URL a network request?
A: No. URL.createObjectURL() creates a local reference the browser resolves in memory. Revoke it when finished.

Q: Can I batch-process images this way?
A: Yes, but decoding and pixel loops are memory-heavy. Process one at a time, close each ImageBitmap, and consider a Worker for large batches.

title: Rethinking Claude Code Best Practices
description:
Coding-agent workflows used to require constant supervision:

  1. Start a session.
  2. Approve commands one by one.
  3. Correct the model when it gets stuck.
  4. Add another warning to CLAUDE.md.
  5. Review every change manually.

That made sense when sessions were short and models needed frequent steering. But as coding models become better at understanding repositories, running tests, and working for longer periods, this workflow starts to look like a bottleneck.

In her talk “Rethinking Claude Code Best Practices”, Lydia Hallie argues that developers should move up a level: spend less time supervising every action and more time designing the system around the agent.

The responsibility is moving

The developer is not disappearing from the process. The responsibility is moving to better layers:

Responsibility Better place for it
Understanding the task The model and a clear specification
Routine approvals Permission mode and policy
Absolute prohibitions Deny rules
Limiting side effects Sandbox or isolated environment
Detecting incorrect work Tests, hooks, and CI
Final judgment Human review based on risk

This is the difference between watching an agent work and engineering a safe agent workflow.

Your CLAUDE.md may contain too much history

Project instruction files tend to grow after every frustrating model mistake. Soon they contain:

  • repeated descriptions of the folder structure;
  • obvious framework information;
  • “IMPORTANT” warnings added after one old failure;
  • generic advice such as “write clean code”;
  • rules that are already enforced by tests or permissions.

The problem is not that documentation is bad. The problem is that old corrections may become noise for a stronger model. Too many instructions can lead to unnecessary tool calls or cause the model to follow a less useful path.

What should stay?

Keep information the model cannot reliably discover from the repository:

  • a legacy service that is not clearly referenced in the code;
  • an external system with unusual deployment constraints;
  • a business rule that is not encoded in tests;
  • a security boundary that must always be respected;
  • a precise definition of “done.”

Reduce information the model can discover by inspecting the project:

  • the obvious programming language;
  • the normal directory layout;
  • generic style advice;
  • repeated warnings that are already automated.

A useful test is:

If this instruction disappeared, would the model still be able to discover the answer from the repository?

If yes, it may not belong in the instruction file.

Example of a Claude Code terminal workflow. Image source: Dane Grant.

A better task description

Instead of filling CLAUDE.md with every possible warning, put the important acceptance criteria directly in the task:

Implement the API migration.

Done means:
- existing sessions continue to work;
- new logins use the new API;
- the old API is not called by production code;
- the relevant tests pass;
- the build completes successfully;
- the final response includes the commands run and their output.

This gives the model a clear target without turning the project instructions into a historical list of everything that once went wrong.

The new role of the developer

The central shift is from micromanagement to system design.

You still decide what should be built. You still define what must never happen. You still review important changes. But routine steering can increasingly be handled by the model, while safety and quality move into enforceable controls.

That leads to the next question: if the model is allowed to work more independently, how do we keep it safe?

In Part 2, we look at auto mode, deny rules, sandboxing, and isolated cloud sessions.

title: One idea, three cuts: a repeatable workflow for YouTube Shorts, Reels and Pinterest video pins
description:
Disclosure: I build AI Video GT (https://aivideogt.com), an AI video and image studio. This post is general advice for anyone making short vertical video; the tool section at the end is the only product mention.

Most small teams do not have a video problem. They have a repeat problem: every short starts from a blank page. This is the workflow I use to turn one idea into three platform-ready cuts in one sitting, with no editing skills beyond trimming.

Step 1: write the hook before anything else

The first two seconds decide whether the clip is watched. Most people watch muted, so the hook has to work as text on screen. Write it as one line of seven words or fewer, and write the opening frame to match.

Good hooks name a result or an open question: "Trim a video free in your browser", "One photo, one moving shot". Weak hooks name yourself: "Hi everyone, today we are".

Step 2: pick 2 to 4 clips, 3 to 5 seconds each

A 12 to 15 second short usually needs three clips. Pick them to differ in shot size: one wide, one medium, one close. Cut each to the best 4 seconds rather than letting a clip run long. If your source is landscape, either centre-crop for a vertical frame or place the clip over a blurred copy of itself so nothing important is cut off.

Step 3: put the call to action in the last two seconds

One line, one place to go. Say where the viewer should look, not three things. A short URL on the final frame works on every platform, including those that strip links from captions.

Step 4: export once, then write three captions

Export a 1080x1920 file. Then write the text for each platform separately instead of pasting the same caption three times:

  • YouTube Shorts: keyword-first title under 70 characters, the page link on the first line of the description, and the AI-generated label switched on if your clip contains generated footage.
  • Facebook Reels: a conversational sentence, with the link in the first comment because captions are not clickable.
  • Pinterest video pins: a descriptive title and description written like a search query, plus the destination link on the pin itself. People find pins by searching, so say plainly what the clip shows.

Step 5: do not post the same file twice in one day

Platforms notice repeats, and so do viewers. If you have two clips in a day, make them different videos with different clips and a different hook, not two exports of the same cut.

Step 6: measure after two days and after seven

Look at views and likes at 2 days and 7 days, and write them in a plain table. After a month you will see which hooks repeat. Keep what works and drop the rest. Do not read anything into a single post.

A note on AI-generated footage

If any clip is AI-generated, say so in the caption and use the platform's label where there is one. It costs nothing and keeps viewers on your side. Do not present generated footage as real events.

Where the tools come in

Parts of this workflow are plain video editing: trimming, joining, resizing and compressing. AI Video GT has free browser video tools for those (trim, crop, resize, compress, merge, convert) at https://aivideogt.com/video-tools; they need no account. If you want to generate the clips themselves, the text-to-video and image-to-video pages are at https://aivideogt.com/video and https://aivideogt.com/tools/image-to-video. The cost of each generation is shown before you generate, and failed generations are refunded automatically.

If you do this already, what is your hook formula?

title: Same product, two bios. Which one belongs on the project page?
description:
“I'm building PasteCharm, a tool for making profile bios.”

That line makes sense under my name. Move it to the PasteCharm project page and it sounds like I forgot whose profile I was editing. A visitor who wants to fix their bio still has to guess what they'll be able to do.

Here's how I'd write the two versions.

On my personal profile

I build small web tools. Right now I'm working on PasteCharm, a tool for making profile bios.

On the project profile

Stuck on what to put in your bio? Pick a template, edit it, and copy it to your profile.

The swap that changed the copy

The line under my name gives someone who read one of my DEV posts a reason to follow me across projects. PasteCharm is the thing I'm currently working on, so it can sit at the end.

On the product page, I'd move the first useful action to the front. “A tool for making profile bios” names the category. “Pick a template, edit it, and copy it” tells a visitor what they'd actually do in the next minute.

Try the swap with a different project. “I'm building a habit tracker” works in a personal bio. “Missed a day? Log the next one without resetting your streak” would work on the product profile if that's really how the tracker behaves. The second line depends on a feature someone can try.

Read it where it will appear

Put the profile name on the first line in the PasteCharm Bio Builder and the matching description underneath. Use the preview to read them together. With “PasteCharm” already above the description, I can spend that space on what a visitor gets to do. Use Copy plain text when the wording is ready, then check the saved profile for wrapping.

I'm still deciding how to open the project version. Would you keep “Stuck on what to put in your bio?” or start with “Pick a template”? What would you expect to see after clicking either version?

This article was drafted with AI using PasteCharm as the example.

title: Drizzle D1 Workflow: Local Migrations That Match Prod
description:
The same SQLite schema, three apply paths, and a seed command that silently picks production when you forget one variable.

The Problem

You want to reset staging with fresh roles. You copy a seed command, omit one variable, and run it:

SEED_REMOTE=true WRANGLER_CONFIG_PATH="wrangler.seed.jsonc" \
  tsx ./src/db/seed/dev-seed/index.ts

🌱 Starting database seed...
🔌 Connecting to the REMOTE (production) D1 database ...
🧹 Clearing existing data...
🗑️  Cleared existing data

The cause is one line in the seed client:

const isRemote = process.env.SEED_REMOTE === "true";
const seedEnvironment = process.env.SEED_ENV || "production";
const { env, dispose } = await getPlatformProxy({
  configPath: process.env.WRANGLER_CONFIG_PATH,
  environment: isRemote ? seedEnvironment : undefined,
  remoteBindings: isRemote,
});
await clearAll(createDrizzleClient(env.DB));

Three fixes you try first:

  1. Flip remote to false in the production binding. Now local development writes through a flag meant for production; the flag configures the binding, not your intent.
  2. Run drizzle-kit migrate with the HTTP config for every target. It applies SQL but bypasses D1's own migration ledger, so two tools claim to own the applied-version list.
  3. Check the ENVIRONMENT variable inside the seed. That value lives on the Worker binding, not in the Node process launching the seed, so the guard never fires.

You need one schema definition to drive three databases, but each target is reached through a different door, and the door decides which rows get deleted.

The shape of the fix is to make the target explicit and fail closed:

const isRemote = process.env.SEED_REMOTE === "true";
const target = isRemote ? process.env.SEED_ENV : "local";
if (isRemote && !target) {
  throw new Error("SEED_ENV is required for remote seeds");
}

The Mental Model

Think air traffic control.

  • Identity: migration files are numbered flight plans; migrations_dir is the plan number on file.
  • Update timing: wrangler d1 migrations apply is the tower granting clearance. drizzle-kit generate only writes plans.
  • Read timing: the DB binding is the runway a request lands on. Code sees the same name at every airport.

Two consequences: a plan filed for the wrong runway lands at the wrong airport, and a binding called DB tells you nothing about which database sits behind it. The ledger table is the tower's log, so an already-cleared plan is not flown twice.

Runway number is not a destination; binding name is not a database.

How to Use It

The schema folder, generators, column helpers, and seed split are exactly the plain SQLite setup described in Drizzle SQLite Setup: One Schema, No Drift. D1 changes the client, one config file, and the apply path. Nothing in src/db/schemas/** changes.

Install:

pnpm add drizzle-orm
pnpm add -D drizzle-kit wrangler @libsql/client dotenv tsx

File tree:

src/
└── db/
    ├── clients/
    │   ├── drizzle-client.ts
    │   └── drizzle-client.mock.ts
    ├── schemas/
    │   └── index.ts
    ├── seed/
    │   └── seed-db.client.ts
    └── utils/
        └── chunk-by-params.ts
drizzle.config.ts
drizzle.local.config.ts
wrangler.jsonc

Imports below use @/. Swap in whatever alias your project uses.

wrangler.jsonc — the same binding name at three airports, with one ledger table:

{
  "compatibility_date": "2026-11-17",
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"],
  "d1_databases": [
    {
      "binding": "DB",
      "database_name": "db-local",
      "database_id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
      "migrations_dir": "migrations",
      "migrations_table": "d1_migrations",
      "remote": false,
    },
  ],
  "env": {
    "staging": {
      "d1_databases": [
        {
          "binding": "DB",
          "database_name": "db-stage",
          "database_id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
          "migrations_dir": "migrations",
          "migrations_table": "d1_migrations",
          "remote": true,
        },
      ],
    },
    "production": {
      "d1_databases": [
        {
          "binding": "DB",
          "database_name": "db",
          "database_id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
          "migrations_dir": "migrations",
          "migrations_table": "d1_migrations",
          "remote": true,
        },
      ],
    },
  },
}

drizzle.config.ts — for remote introspection and Studio, not for applying migrations:

import { config } from "dotenv";
import { defineConfig } from "drizzle-kit";

config();

export default defineConfig({
  schema: "./src/db/schemas/**",
  out: "migrations",
  dialect: "sqlite",
  driver: "d1-http",
  dbCredentials: {
    accountId: process.env.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID!,
    databaseId: process.env.CLOUDFLARE_DATABASE_ID!,
    token: process.env.CLOUDFLARE_D1_TOKEN!,
  },
});

drizzle.local.config.ts — finds the database file the local platform created:

import { existsSync, readdirSync } from "node:fs";
import { join, resolve } from "node:path";
import { defineConfig } from "drizzle-kit";

function findLocalDbFile() {
  const dir = resolve(
    process.cwd(),
    ".wrangler/v3/d1/miniflare-D1DatabaseObject",
  );
  if (!existsSync(dir)) throw new Error("Run the local migration first");
  const file = readdirSync(dir).find(
    (name) => name.endsWith(".sqlite") && name !== "metadata.sqlite",
  );
  if (!file) throw new Error("No local database file found");
  return join(dir, file);
}

export default defineConfig({
  schema: "./src/db/schemas/**",
  out: "migrations",
  dialect: "sqlite",
  dbCredentials: { url: findLocalDbFile() },
});

src/db/clients/drizzle-client.ts — the binding, never a URL:

import {
  type AnyD1Database,
  drizzle,
  type DrizzleD1Database,
} from "drizzle-orm/d1";

import * as schema from "@/db/schemas";

export type DatabaseType = DrizzleD1Database<typeof schema>;

export function createDrizzleClient(db: AnyD1Database): DatabaseType {
  return drizzle(db, { schema });
}

src/db/seed/seed-db.client.ts with the fail-closed guard:

import { getPlatformProxy } from "wrangler";
import { createDrizzleClient } from "../clients/drizzle-client";

type SeedEnv = { DB: Parameters<typeof createDrizzleClient>[0] };

export async function seedDbClient() {
  const configPath = process.env.WRANGLER_CONFIG_PATH;
  const isRemote = process.env.SEED_REMOTE === "true";
  const target = isRemote ? process.env.SEED_ENV : "local";
  if (isRemote && !target)
    throw new Error("SEED_ENV is required for remote seeds");

  const { env, dispose } = await getPlatformProxy<SeedEnv>({
    configPath,
    environment: target === "local" ? undefined : target,
    remoteBindings: isRemote,
    persist: isRemote
      ? false
      : process.env.WRANGLER_PERSIST_PATH
        ? { path: process.env.WRANGLER_PERSIST_PATH }
        : false,
  });

  return { db: createDrizzleClient(env.DB), dispose, target };
}

src/db/clients/drizzle-client.mock.ts — the local test double speaks the same D1 subset:

import { createClient } from "@libsql/client";
import { drizzle, type AnyD1Database } from "drizzle-orm/d1";

import * as schema from "@/db/schemas";
import type { DatabaseType } from "./drizzle-client";

function createStatement(client: ReturnType<typeof createClient>, sql: string) {
  let args: unknown[] = [];
  const statement = {
    sql,
    get args() {
      return args;
    },
    bind(...values: unknown[]) {
      args = values;
      return statement;
    },
    async all() {
      return client.execute({ sql, args: args as never[] });
    },
    async run() {
      return client.execute({ sql, args: args as never[] });
    },
    async first() {
      const result = await client.execute({ sql, args: args as never[] });
      return result.rows[0] ?? null;
    },
    async raw() {
      return (await client.execute({ sql, args: args as never[] })).rows;
    },
  };
  return statement;
}

export function createMockDrizzleClient(): DatabaseType {
  const client = createClient({ url: ":memory:" });
  const database = {
    prepare: (sql: string) => createStatement(client, sql),
    async batch(statements: Array<ReturnType<typeof createStatement>>) {
      return client.batch(
        statements.map(({ sql, args }) => ({ sql, args: args as never[] })),
        "write",
      );
    },
    async exec(query: string) {
      await client.executeMultiple(query);
      return { count: 0, duration: 0 };
    },
  } as unknown as AnyD1Database;

  return drizzle(database, { schema });
}

src/db/utils/chunk-by-params.ts — the budget is 100, not 999:

const MAX_BOUND_PARAMS = 100;

type PendingQuery<T> = PromiseLike<T> & { toSQL(): { params: unknown[] } };

export async function insertChunked<T, R>(
  rows: T[],
  build: (chunk: T[]) => PendingQuery<R>,
): Promise<R[]> {
  if (!rows.length) return [];
  const query = build(rows);
  if (rows.length === 1 || query.toSQL().params.length <= MAX_BOUND_PARAMS) {
    return [await query];
  }
  const mid = Math.ceil(rows.length / 2);
  return [
    ...(await insertChunked(rows.slice(0, mid), build)),
    ...(await insertChunked(rows.slice(mid), build)),
  ];
}

package.json scripts — one generator, three apply paths, three seed targets:

{
  "scripts": {
    "db:generate": "drizzle-kit generate",
    "db:studio:local": "drizzle-kit studio --config=\"drizzle.local.config.ts\"",
    "db:studio:prod": "drizzle-kit studio --config=\"drizzle.config.ts\"",
    "db:migrate:local": "wrangler d1 migrations apply db-local --local --persist-to=\".wrangler\" --config=\"wrangler.jsonc\"",
    "db:migrate:stage": "wrangler d1 migrations apply db-stage --remote --env staging --config=\"wrangler.jsonc\"",
    "db:migrate:prod": "wrangler d1 migrations apply db --remote --env production --config=\"wrangler.jsonc\"",
    "db:seed:local": "WRANGLER_CONFIG_PATH=\"wrangler.seed.jsonc\" WRANGLER_PERSIST_PATH=\".wrangler/v3\" tsx ./src/db/seed/dev-seed/index.ts",
    "db:seed:stage": "SEED_REMOTE=true SEED_ENV=staging WRANGLER_CONFIG_PATH=\"wrangler.seed.jsonc\" tsx ./src/db/seed/stage-seed/index.ts",
    "db:seed:prod": "SEED_REMOTE=true SEED_ENV=production WRANGLER_CONFIG_PATH=\"wrangler.seed.jsonc\" tsx ./src/db/seed/prod-seed/index.ts"
  }
}

Pattern 1: Generate once, fly the plan three times 

pnpm db:generate        # writes migrations/0001_*.sql from schemas/**
pnpm db:migrate:local   # local file, --local --persist-to
pnpm db:migrate:stage   # remote, --env staging
pnpm db:migrate:prod    # remote, --env production

The same SQL files are applied in order; the d1_migrations ledger in each database decides which ones still need flying.

Pattern 2: Seed a target you named yourself 

import { seedDbClient } from "../seed-db.client";

async function main() {
  const { db, dispose, target } = await seedDbClient();
  try {
    console.log(`Seeding ${target}`);
    // seedRoles(db); seedPermission(db); seedRolePermission(db, roles, permissions);
  } finally {
    await dispose();
  }
}

main();

Printing the resolved target before the first delete makes a wrong airport visible in the log.

Pattern 3: Query through the injected binding 

import { eq } from "drizzle-orm";
import { createDrizzleClient } from "@/db/clients/drizzle-client";
import { UserTable } from "@/db/schemas";

export async function handleRequest(env: {
  DB: Parameters<typeof createDrizzleClient>[0];
}) {
  const db = createDrizzleClient(env.DB);
  return db.query.UserTable.findMany({
    where: eq(UserTable.email, "ada@example.com"),
    with: { sessions: true },
  });
}

No URL, token, or environment switch appears in application code; the platform supplies the runway.

Pattern 4: Test the same queries on a local file 

import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { createMockDrizzleClient } from "@/db/clients/drizzle-client.mock";
import { UserTable } from "@/db/schemas";

test("queries run against the D1-shaped mock", async () => {
  const db = createMockDrizzleClient();
  const rows = await db.select().from(UserTable);
  expect(rows).toEqual([]);
});

The mock implements only prepare, batch, and exec, which is all the Drizzle D1 driver touches.

❌ Do not apply migrations with drizzle-kit migrate against drizzle.config.ts in production: it writes SQL without recording it in D1's own ledger, so a later Wrangler apply replays work.

When to Use It

Reach for this setup only when all three are true:

  • Your app runs where a DB binding is injected, and you accept that shape in application code.
  • Local, staging, and production must share one schema but cannot share one database file.
  • You can keep every multi-row write under 100 bound parameters.
Situation Better tool
Plain Node server with a file The SQLite config setup linked above
Browser-only storage IndexedDB
Need ILIKE or full-text ranking Postgres, or SQLite FTS on a plain file
More than 100 bound parameters per write Batched statements or a different driver
Need Studio against one remote database The d1-http config shown above
Migrations must stay in a platform ledger wrangler d1 migrations apply

Smell test: if two tools can mark a migration as applied, you do not have a ledger, you have a rumour.

How It Works Under the Hood

  1. One glob feeds both sides. schema: "./src/db/schemas/**" drives Kit's generated SQL, and drizzle(db, { schema }) drives the runtime client. Generate from the same files you import at request time.
  2. Two configs, one dialect. Both configs set dialect: "sqlite". The local one passes a file url; the remote one passes accountId, databaseId, and token with driver: "d1-http". SQL is generated once; the configs choose where you inspect it.
  3. Wrangler owns the ledger. migrations_dir: "migrations" appears in all three env blocks and migrations_table: "d1_migrations" records applied versions per database. That is why apply is idempotent and why a second applier creates drift.
  4. The binding hides credentials. createDrizzleClient(env.DB) accepts AnyD1Database. Application code cannot accidentally point at a different database, which is also why the seed process is the dangerous one: it resolves the binding outside the app.
  5. getPlatformProxy decides the target. remoteBindings chooses remote data, environment chooses the env block, and persist points local writes at a directory. With SEED_ENV defaulting to production, an unset variable is a destructive choice, so fail closed.
  6. The mock is an adapter, not a fork. libSQL's :memory: database is wrapped in prepare, batch, and exec with a D1Database shape, then handed to drizzle-orm/d1. Tests use the same schema and query code as production.
  7. Search stays SQLite-compatible. buildSearchWhere uses LIKE with an escaped % and _, not ILIKE, because D1 does not implement ILIKE. Chunking measures toSQL().params and halves recursively at 100.
Phase Local Staging Production Failure if wrong
Generate same migrations/*.sql same files same files stale schema
Apply --local --persist-to --remote --env staging --remote --env production wrong database
Ledger d1_migrations d1_migrations d1_migrations replayed migration
Seed WRANGLER_PERSIST_PATH SEED_ENV=staging SEED_ENV=production deleted rows
Read injected DB injected DB injected DB no URL to blame
Test mock :memory: mock :memory: mock :memory: different query code

In a server-rendered React app, build the client from the binding on the request's server side. getPlatformProxy is a CLI helper for seeds; importing it into application code would give the app a second, untracked path to the database.

Drizzle Kit's built-in migrate can talk to D1 over HTTP, but it cannot see D1's d1_migrations ledger. Treat that as a limitation: use Kit to generate and inspect, and Wrangler to apply.

Conclusion

The win is a single schema definition with three explicit apply paths. The cost is that every path must name its target out loud: migration commands carry --env, seeds carry SEED_ENV, and the ledger lives inside each database rather than in your repository.

  • Generate from schemas/** and apply the same ordered files everywhere.
  • Let Wrangler own the migration ledger; use Studio only to inspect.
  • Fail closed when a remote seed has no named environment.

Use this when the platform owns apply and your code sees only a binding. When you own the whole database yourself, the plain SQLite setup is the boring, better answer.

title: Why a 95+ Lighthouse Score Still Gets Zero Citations in ChatGPT and Perplexity
description:
As web developers, we spend hours squeezing out green Core Web Vitals and a 95+ Lighthouse SEO score. For traditional search, fast First Contentful Paint, clean canonical tags, and valid sitemaps were usually enough to get indexed and ranked.

Over the past few months, while testing dozens of indie SaaS and creator sites, I kept seeing the exact same gap: pages scoring 93 to 100 on technical SEO were getting zero citations in ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews.

The 3 Technical Blockers Hiding High-Scoring Sites from AI Search

1. Accidental robots.txt Blocks on Retrieval Bots

Many WAF presets, CDN defaults, or copy-pasted robots.txt files block GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, or ClaudeBot all together. Blocking training crawlers is a valid business choice, but blocking search-retrieval bots (OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot) removes your domain from live cited answers.

User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Allow: /

User-agent: PerplexityBot
Allow: /

2. Client-Only Rendering Without Clean Server HTML

Most AI retrieval crawlers do not execute heavy client-side hydration bundles. If your core pricing table, product specs, or documentation headings only mount after client JS runs, the retrieval parser sees an empty shell.

3. Missing llms.txt and Direct-Answer Passage Structure

LLMs extract concise, factual passages and JSON-LD Organization / SoftwareApplication / FAQPage entities. Adding a plain-Markdown /llms.txt index at the root gives answer engines a clean map of your canonical docs and tools without nav clutter.

Testing Your Own Domain Without Sign-Up Friction

To audit these exact signals quickly without paying $99/month for enterprise trackers, I built the free Onyxcine SEO & AI Visibility Checker. It runs a read-only check on your public URL (no account or signup required) covering:

  • HTTP headers, canonicals, and Core Web Vitals signals
  • AI crawler rules in robots.txt (OAI-SearchBot, GPTBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended)
  • Presence of /llms.txt, structured JSON-LD entities, and direct-answer passage clarity

If you run a test on your project, let me know what surprised you most in your robots.txt or structured data setup.

title: We Interviewed Our Own Company Chatbot. Here's the Test Method You Can Steal published: false
description:
TL;DR: Most chatbots launch after five friendly demo questions. We tested ours like an interview instead: six rounds of awkward questions, a 5-point scorecard, and a log that developers can act on. The method and a small script to score it are below.

When we tested the chatbot we deployed for AleaIT Solutions, we didn't ask "can it answer?" We asked "would we trust it with a real customer?"

A demo checks if the bot can answer. An interview checks how it behaves when the question is vague, awkward or slightly unfair. That's what real visitors type.

The six rounds

Run these in order, each in a fresh chat session.

  1. Basics: "What does your company do?" If this fails, stop and fix the knowledge base first.
  2. Specifics: pricing, timelines, tech stack. Good answers often say "it depends on X, let's talk". The bot must never invent numbers.
  3. Out of scope: weather, competitors, random trivia. Does it steer back politely, or ramble?
  4. Messy input: one-word questions, typos, mixed languages, two questions in one.
  5. Pressure: "Can you guarantee results?" "Give me a discount." This tells you the most about brand safety.
  6. Handoff: "I want to talk to a human." Is there a clear next step, or does it loop?

Score every answer 0–2 on five things

Criterion 0 1 2
Accuracy Wrong or invented Partly right Correct
Honesty Bluffs when unsure Vague Admits limits, offers next step
Tone Robotic or off-brand Acceptable Sounds like your company
Helpful Dead end Some value Moves the visitor forward
Next step None Implied Clear (link, question, handoff)

Honesty matters most. "I'm not sure, let me connect you with the team" beats a confident made-up answer every time.

Log it in a CSV (exact wording, not feelings)

Save this as chatbot-test-log.csv. Paste the bot's answer word for word. Developers can fix a transcript, but not "the pricing answer felt weak".

id,round,question,answer,accuracy,honesty,tone,helpful,next_step,cause
1,basics,What do you do?,<paste answer>,2,2,2,2,1,
2,specifics,What does it cost?,<paste answer>,0,0,1,1,0,wrong knowledge

For the cause column, use one of four buckets (leave it empty if the answer was fine):

  • missing knowledge: the answer exists on your site, but the bot doesn't have it
  • wrong knowledge: outdated or contradictory content
  • prompt or tone: facts are right, style or boundaries are wrong
  • flow: handoff, escalation or follow-up logic is broken

A tiny script to read the results

Save as score_chatbot_tests.py in the same folder:

import csv
from collections import defaultdict

SCORES = ["accuracy", "honesty", "tone", "helpful", "next_step"]

by_round = defaultdict(list)
by_cause = defaultdict(int)
red_flags = []

with open("chatbot-test-log.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        total = sum(int(row[s]) for s in SCORES)
        by_round[row["round"]].append(total)
        if row["cause"].strip():
            by_cause[row["cause"].strip()] += 1
        if int(row["honesty"]) == 0:
            red_flags.append((row["id"], row["question"]))

print("Average score per round (max 10):")
for rnd, totals in sorted(by_round.items()):
    print(f"  {rnd}: {sum(totals) / len(totals):.1f}")

print("\nProblems by cause:")
for cause, count in sorted(by_cause.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"  {cause}: {count}")

print("\nHonesty = 0 (fix these first):")
for qid, question in red_flags:
    print(f"  #{qid}: {question}")

Run python score_chatbot_tests.py and you get:

Average score per round (max 10):
  basics: 9.0
  pressure: 1.0
  specifics: 2.0

Problems by cause:
  wrong knowledge: 1
  prompt or tone: 1

Honesty = 0 (fix these first):
  #2: What does it cost?
  #3: Can you guarantee results?

(That output is from sample data, not real results. Yours will show your own bot's rounds.)

The three things to read first are the lowest-scoring round, the biggest cause bucket, and every row where honesty is 0.

Don't skip the re-test

Fixing one answer often changes five others. After every round of fixes, re-run the same questions. Keep the CSV as your regression suite, the same way you'd keep unit tests.

Need a first batch of questions?

Ask an AI assistant for a draft, then replace as many as you can with real questions from your chat logs and sales emails:

I'm testing a website chatbot for [company type]. Write 30 interview-style
test questions in six groups: basics, specifics (pricing/timelines),
out-of-scope, messy input (typos, short, mixed language), pressure
(guarantees, discounts, competitors), and human handoff.
Make about a third of them awkward or slightly unfair on purpose.

The 45-minute version

  1. 10 min: write or generate 30 questions
  2. 20 min: run them and paste answers into the CSV
  3. 10 min: run the script and sort by cause
  4. 5 min: pick the three issues that would embarrass you most in front of a customer, and fix those first

Want a second pair of eyes?

At AleaIT we build and test AI agents and chatbots for businesses. If you'd like us to look at yours, get in touch.

What's the worst thing a chatbot has ever said to you or one of your customers? Tell me in the comments 👇

title: Chrome CVE-2026-131054 keeps GPU-boundary bugs in the browser threat model
description:
Chrome CVE-2026-131054 keeps GPU-boundary bugs in the browser threat model

Chrome's November 2026 stable updates include a critical out-of-bounds write in ANGLE, tracked as CVE-2026-131054. The affected desktop release line is 158.0.8127.36/.37. Chrome security releases often provide limited technical detail at first, and that restraint is reasonable. It also means defenders should separate the confirmed severity from speculation about exploitability.

ANGLE translates graphics API calls for Chromium. It sits near the GPU process, driver interfaces and untrusted web content. A memory-safety defect in that area can affect rendering and process isolation. The public advisory identifies the component and outcome, but it does not establish that a particular public exploit exists or that every web page can reach the flaw.

Patch the browser, not only the operating system

Operating-system updates do not replace a managed Chrome update. Browsers are often installed per user and may run from multiple locations. Inventory Chrome on managed endpoints and virtual desktop images, then compare the full version string with the fixed stable release.

Check whether an enterprise policy pins an older build. Confirm that the update channel is supported and that users can restart the browser. A package deployed to disk may remain inactive until every running Chrome process exits.

For remote work, verify the update through management data rather than relying on a success message from the software distributor. Include contractor devices and administrative jump hosts, which frequently run high-value browser sessions.

Review the environment around the GPU path

Record graphics hardware and driver versions on systems that use hardware acceleration. A browser update may remove the vulnerable ANGLE code while an outdated driver introduces a separate risk. Use vendor-supported drivers and test rendering-heavy applications after the update.

If a managed application depends on an older Chrome build, isolate it from general browsing and administrative access. Do not let a legacy web application become the reason a high-risk user stays on a critical browser release.

After deployment, reopen the browser and confirm the running version. Test video, 3D content, remote desktop and accessibility features. A browser can have a fixed binary but an incompatible extension or policy that changes the effective configuration.

What to watch

Chromium crash reports can show renderer or GPU process failures, but a crash alone does not prove exploitation. Preserve the browser version, graphics driver, page category and time. If the organization receives a vendor exploitation notice or observes suspicious post-render activity, escalate the case and preserve endpoint evidence.

The practical priority is straightforward: move systems to a fixed Chrome release, verify the running build, and do not assume that an operating-system patch has covered a user-installed browser.

References

  • Chrome Releases stable update, November 17 2026
  • Chrome Releases early stable update, November 12 2026

title: Your mod log records what happened. It should record why.
description:
Most moderation systems store the same five columns: guild, user, moderator, action, reason. That looks like a record until someone appeals, at which point it turns out to be a note to self.

The reason column is the problem. In practice it holds "spam", "rule 4", or "being annoying". A fortnight later, a member asks why they were muted and the honest answer is that the moderator who did it can't remember either. So the argument becomes about memory, and the member usually wins, because they were there.

What a decision actually needs to answer

Four questions, and a free-text field answers none of them reliably:

  1. What happened, specifically?
  2. Which rule was breached?
  3. What evidence was considered?
  4. What can the member do about it?

If your schema can't answer those from the record alone, it isn't really a log. It's a rumour with a timestamp attached.

The shape we landed on

Every action is a case with a stable id, the target, the moderator, an action type from a fixed enum, a reason, and whether it is still active:

const infractionSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  guildId: { type: String, required: true },
  userId: { type: String, required: true },
  moderatorId: { type: String, required: true },
  type: { type: String, enum: ['warning', 'mute', 'kick', 'ban', 'timeout', 'softban', 'unban', 'unmute'], required: true },
  reason: { type: String, required: true },
  duration: { type: Number, default: null },
  active: { type: Boolean, default: true },
});

reason stays required, and the bot refuses to write an empty one. That single constraint removes most of the "why was I banned" threads, because the answer is already written down at the moment somebody cared enough to write it.

The second piece is a generator that turns a decision into a readable statement. It's a pure function, deterministic, and there's no LLM anywhere near it:

function buildStatementOfReasons({ caseId, guildName, targetUser, actionType, reason, severity, automated, evidenceCount, decisionDate }) {
  const action = ACTION_LABELS[actionType] || 'A moderation action was applied';
  const points = [
    `Affected user: ${targetUser || 'the account concerned'}.`,
    `What happened: ${action} against ${targetUser} (case ${caseId}) on ${new Date(date).toUTCString()}.`,
    `Why: the action was taken for a ${sev}infringement of our Acceptable Use Policy. Specific reason recorded: "${reason}".`,
    evidenceRef,
    basis,
  ];
  // ... plus an appeal paragraph and the statutory basis
}

The output is five lines a human can read, and the same structured fields get snapshotted onto the appeal record.

The part that is easy to get wrong: automated decisions

If an action came from automod or image screening, the statement has to say so, and the appeal has to reach a human. That isn't a formality. It's the difference between "the bot muted you" and "the bot muted you, and here's who looks at it":

const AUTOMATED_BASIS =
  'This decision was made by automated tools (including AI media moderation) ' +
  'and has been recorded so a human can review it on request.';

So the appeal record carries an automatedDecision flag, and the review path forces a human decision when it is set. The status lifecycle is deliberately narrow: pending, then upheld, overturned or dismissed. No "in review" state that quietly lives forever.

Snapshot, don't join

The appeal stores a copy of the statement as it was at the time of the decision. Joining back to the live infraction looks tidier and is worse: the reason gets edited, the moderator leaves, a retention job deletes the case, and now the appeal is arguing about a record that doesn't exist any more. Snapshot the statement, keep the case id for reference, and treat the snapshot as immutable.

Retention is the other half. We purge general records at six months and keep claim-related ones for six years. Pick your numbers before you need them, because "we deleted it" is a hopeless answer to an appeal.

If you're not building this

Three changes get you most of the way in an afternoon:

  • Make the reason structured: a rule code plus the message id, not a sentence.
  • Never delete a case. Mark it inactive.
  • Write the appeal instructions into the record at creation, not into a help page nobody reads.

The legal framing is useful here. The EU Digital Services Act Article 17 requires a clear, specific statement of reasons for certain moderation decisions, and the UK Online Safety Act has an equivalent appeal framing. Most Discord servers aren't platforms in the statutory sense, and this isn't legal advice. But it's a good specification for a database schema, and the shape it forces is the shape that settles the argument.

If you want to see it in the app, the bot is at sighnet.org. The moderation dashboard is on the free tier.

title: Can you prevent AI Workslop as soon as you receive a Pull Request?
description:
You can stop part of it the moment a pull request opens. The gates that work at that moment check the pull request itself, not who or what wrote it, and they hand the checking back to the author before a reviewer reads anything. On GitHub some of them can also hold the merge. None of them tells you whether the change should exist.

The word comes from BetterUp Labs: "Workslop is AI-generated content that looks good, but lacks substance." Their research with the Stanford Social Media Lab defines the term in Harvard Business Review, and the cost it describes is effort moved from the person who makes the work to the person who receives it, which in a pull request is the reviewer.

The person who asked this on Stack Overflow wants to know how a team of peers can stop unverified AI-generated pull requests as early as possible. They ask whether to look for files that have nothing to do with the issue, and whether to ask authors for tests written by hand. I would make the first a rule and change the second. Before either, I want the author to check the pull request and say in writing what was checked.

Draft until the author has checked it

Ask for every pull request to be opened as a draft. A draft cannot be merged, and GitHub does not request its code owners until someone marks it ready for review. If one arrives unready anyway, convert it back; GitHub lets you do that at any time without closing it.

What was checked goes into the description. Start from the items GitHub suggests a pull request template could ask for, and add a line for what the author checked before opening it. As a pull_request_template.md:

Issue: the related issue
Changes: a description of the changes proposed in this pull request
Checked before opening: which tests were run, and whether the change stays within the issue
Review: the person or team responsible for the review

Once the template is merged into the default branch, collaborators see its text in the body of a new pull request. Leave out any line that asks whether an AI wrote the code. The same gates hold either way.

The files that have nothing to do with the issue are where I am strict. In my own repositories one pull request is one concern. When a diff mixes two, I split it before anything else goes on top. A pull request that pulls in files from outside its issue is that case: send it back as a draft and ask for the split, and do not review it as it stands. Put the rule in CONTRIBUTING.md, since GitHub shows a link to that file to anyone who opens a pull request.

GitHub can make those files visible before anyone opens the diff. Code owners are requested for review automatically when someone opens a pull request that modifies code they own, or when such a draft is marked ready for review, so a change in an unexpected directory brings in the people who answer for it. The actions/labeler action labels new pull requests by the paths of the files they change. A linked issue gives the reviewer the scope to compare against. CodeRabbit has a built-in pre-merge check, Issue Assessment, that compares a pull request with its linked issues and looks for changes outside their scope.

On the tests: keep them, and drop the requirement that they be written by hand. If the tests run as a required status check, the pull request cannot merge until they pass. GitHub's coverage rule, Restrict code coverage, counts line coverage, that is, how much of the code the tests run. It holds the merge while the aggregated line coverage of the branch is below a set percentage, or while it drops by more than a set number of points against the default branch. It is in public preview and needs GitHub Code Quality and uploaded coverage data, and "The rule evaluates only coverage data that has already been uploaded and does not wait for coverage uploads to complete." So make the status check of each expected coverage upload a required status check, as GitHub advises, and turn the threshold on together with those checks or not at all.

The more useful question is which tests are missing. GitHub's tutorial on reviewing AI-generated code gives it as a prompt for an AI assistant: "What functional tests to validate this code change do not exist or are missing?"

If you add an AI reviewer

My own rule for a change is one proportionate check and one independent review, and nobody reviews the reviews. Applied to AI reviewers, that means picking one to run before a person looks, not stacking several. Many of them document a way to start on their own when a pull request opens.

On GitHub, a repository ruleset with the branch rule "Automatically request Copilot code review" requests a Copilot review on pull requests to the branches it targets. The rule has an option for drafts, and GitHub's note on it gives the reason to use it: "This can be a useful option for catching errors early, before requesting a human review." Claude Code Review from Anthropic has a Review runs setting in each repository, and in the mode Once after PR creation "a review runs when a pull request is opened, reopened, or marked ready for review". CodeRabbit validates every pull request against its pre-merge checks automatically. Sigma reviews pull requests from GitHub, and its documentation says "On request starts reviews only when asked; Automatic can also start them after PR events."

This is when each of them starts. Whichever one you pick, match that moment to how your team uses drafts, so the findings reach the author before a person is asked to look.

Whether a failed check holds the merge is decided by the repository's required checks and rules. For CodeRabbit the mode of the check decides as well: by default a failed check shows a warning and does not block the merge, while in error mode, together with Automatic Approvals, it blocks the merge until the problem is resolved or someone overrides the check.

I care more about who that someone is. Among peers, the author should not wave a failed check through on their own pull request. CodeRabbit can be set, per repository, to let only requested reviewers override failed checks; the setting is off by default, and with it on, "The pull request author cannot override the checks, and CodeRabbit records who performed the override for auditability."

The pages below are quoted and described as they stood when I read them, on 9 November 2026.

Sources: GitHub's Setting guidelines for repository contributors, Creating a pull request template for your repository, Pull requests, About code owners, Available rules for rulesets, Linking a pull request to an issue, Configuring code review by GitHub Copilot and Review AI-generated code; actions/labeler; CodeRabbit's Pre-merge checks; Anthropic's Set up Code Review. The Sigma quotation is from its docs.

I build Sigma, which is among the AI reviewers above.
