title: How I built a browser-only invoice builder with TanStack Start
description:
I wanted a small project that does one useful thing well, so I built LedgerLite, an invoice builder that runs entirely in the browser. There is no database and no login. Here's what I learned.

The idea

Most invoice tools want you to sign up before you can make a single invoice. For a freelancer who needs one PDF, that's too much. I decided that all data would stay on the user's device.

The stack

React with TanStack Start, Tailwind CSS and TypeScript. Nothing else is needed at runtime, and the project now has only 13 dependencies. I started with a lot more and removed the ones I wasn't using, which made installs much faster.

Money in cents

The first rule of invoice code is never to do money maths with floating-point numbers. Every amount is a whole number of cents: line total is quantity times rate in cents, tax is a percentage of the subtotal rounded once, and formatting happens only when the amount is shown. This avoids totals that are off by a cent.

Saving without a server

The draft, the business profile and the logo are kept in localStorage, so a reload doesn't lose work. For moving between devices, there's a JSON export and import. Imported files are validated before they are accepted, because a file from outside is untrusted input.

Validation and limits

Quantities, rates and text lengths have limits, and the logo must be PNG, JPG or WebP under 300 KB. A broken or oversized input should show a clear message and never crash the page.

PDF without a PDF library

I use the browser's print dialog and a print stylesheet. A no-print class hides the form, buttons and navigation, so only the invoice is printed. I also set the page title to the invoice number just before printing, so "Save as PDF" suggests a name like INV-001.pdf. It isn't a real PDF engine, but it's reliable and adds no code.

Deploying to Cloudflare

The build produces a Cloudflare Workers package. On Windows I had to install Wrangler globally instead of using npx, then deploy with the config file in the .output/server folder.

What's missing

No payment links, discounts, saved clients or recurring invoices yet. They need either more libraries or a backend, and I'd rather ship a smaller product honestly than a bigger one that doesn't work.

Try it

Live demo: https://ledgerlite.abhi-ledgerlite.workers.dev

If you want the source code to build your own invoicing site, it's here: https://mukkeraabhi.gumroad.com/l/oufmkn (launch price $15). I'd also like to hear which feature you'd add first.

Disclosure: I'm the author and I sell the source code.

title: In the Age of AI, Our Communication Has Become More Rigid, Hasn't It?
description:
Emails Used to Feel Warmer

Think about the emails you got from good clients and partners a few years ago. They asked how your weekend went, made a small joke and ended with something friendly. You could hear the person behind the words.

Now look at your inbox today. Same people, same good relationships, but the messages feel different. They are long, careful and formal. Sometimes it feels like you are writing to a lawyer, not to someone you have worked with for years.

Nothing bad happened between you. The reason is much simpler: more and more of us write our emails with ChatGPT, Claude and other AI tools.

Why AI Makes Simple Messages Sound Formal

When writing emails, AI often makes simple messages sound overly formal and complicated. It tends to explain too much, defend against objections nobody has raised, and use legal-sounding language that creates distance rather than trust.

But when you've known someone for years, you don't need three paragraphs to explain a simple schedule change. "Can we move Friday's call to Monday?" is enough. A trusted colleague understands what you mean without all the extra detail.

AI misses this shared history. It turns a short, friendly note into a full explanation, and the result sounds more like a legal document than a conversation between people who trust each other.

Facts Are Not the Same as Understanding

AI tools learned to write from huge amounts of manuals, contracts and company policies. So they are very good at facts, reasons and proof, and that is exactly what they put into every email.

But good relationships don't run on proof. They run on trust, goodwill and the little things you both already know. When a simple email arrives full of background, reasons and caveats, the other person may quietly wonder: "Why so formal? Is something wrong?"

And very often the other side uses AI to reply. So the formal tone grows on both sides, until two old friends are writing to each other like two law firms.

How to Bring the Warmth Back

We are not against AI. We build AI software every day, and it is great for code, technical documents and long reports. But for a quick note to someone who knows you, your own words work better.

Before you send an AI-polished email, read it once and ask yourself: does this sound like me talking to a friend, or like a lawyer?

If it sounds like a lawyer, make it shorter. Remove the explanations nobody asked for. Drop the numbered points. Add one line that only you would write. It doesn't have to be perfect. It just has to sound like you.

Originally published at itfriends.ai.

title: Drizzle SQLite Setup: One Schema, No Drift
description:
Drizzle SQLite Setup: One Schema, No Drift

A five-folder Drizzle layout that kills schema drift and mystery rows — and why the config reads a directory instead of a file.

The Problem

You add a user_events table, generate a migration, restart, and get no such table: user_events. Local worked last week because you ran raw SQL by hand. Here is the bug hiding in plain sight:

// drizzle.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  schema: "./src/db/schemas/index.ts", // hand-maintained barrel
  out: "migrations",
  dialect: "sqlite",
  dbCredentials: { url: "./local.db" },
});

src/db/schemas/table/user/userEvent.table.ts   <- new file, never re-exported
$ pnpm db:generate
No schema changes detected
$ pnpm dev
SqliteError: no such table: user_events

Three fixes you try first:

  1. Add the missing export * to the barrel. It works now; the next new table repeats the bug.
  2. Import the table directly from the entry file. Drizzle Kit follows imports it can see. A file nobody imports stays invisible.
  3. Paste CREATE TABLE into migrations/0001_x.sql. The database catches up, TypeScript does not, and the next generate sees a difference again.

You need one definition that both TypeScript and the database trust, but a barrel file is a manual list and a hand-edited migration is a second source of truth.

The resolution is a config that points at a directory, plus barrels that re-export everything in two hops:

// drizzle.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  schema: "./src/db/schemas/**",
  out: "migrations",
  dialect: "sqlite",
  dbCredentials: { url: "./local.db" },
});

// src/db/schemas/index.ts
export * from "./enums/db-enums";
export * from "./table";

The Mental Model

Treat the folder as a switchboard.

  • Identity: every table file is a labeled jack; the schemas/** glob is the patch list the electrician reads.
  • Update timing: drizzle-kit generate prints a dated work order (a SQL migration). It never touches a live wire.
  • Read timing: the client plugs into the same panel at request time, and db.query follows the patch cables you declared as relations.

Two consequences: a table missing from the patch list is invisible to generation, and only the dated work orders ever change the physical database. Your TypeScript types are labels on the panel, not electricity.

If the jack is not on the panel, the electrician wires around it.

How to Use It

Install the pieces:

pnpm add drizzle-orm drizzle-zod zod @libsql/client
pnpm add -D drizzle-kit drizzle-dbml-generator tsx

File tree:

src/
└── db/
    ├── clients/
    │   ├── drizzle-client.ts
    │   └── drizzle-client.mock.ts
    ├── generators/
    │   ├── dbml-generator.ts
    │   └── sql-generator.ts
    ├── schemas/
    │   ├── index.ts
    │   ├── enums/
    │   │   ├── db-enums.ts
    │   │   ├── enum-values.ts
    │   │   └── zod-db-enums.ts
    │   └── table/
    │       ├── index.ts
    │       └── verification.table.ts
    ├── seed/
    │   ├── clearAll.ts
    │   ├── seed.config.ts
    │   └── verification.seed.ts
    └── utils/
        ├── chunk-by-params.ts
        ├── db-utils.ts
        └── escapeLike.ts
drizzle.config.ts

Imports below use @/. Swap in whatever alias your project uses.

drizzle.config.ts:

import { defineConfig } from "drizzle-kit";

export default defineConfig({
  schema: "./src/db/schemas/**",
  out: "migrations",
  dialect: "sqlite",
  dbCredentials: {
    url: "./local.db",
  },
});

src/db/utils/db-utils.ts — one place decides how every column behaves:

import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import { integer, real, text } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";

export const db_date = (name: string) =>
  integer(name, { mode: "timestamp_ms" });

export const db_id = text("id")
  .primaryKey()
  .$defaultFn(() => crypto.randomUUID())
  .notNull();

export const db_created_at = db_date("created_at")
  .notNull()
  .default(sql`(unixepoch() * 1000)`);

export const db_updated_at = db_date("updated_at")
  .notNull()
  .default(sql`(unixepoch() * 1000)`)
  .$onUpdate(() => new Date());

export const db_bool = (name: string) => integer(name, { mode: "boolean" });
export const db_money = (name: string) => real(name);

src/db/schemas/enums/enum-values.ts — the list, not a string union typed twice:

export const ROLES = ["USER", "ADMIN", "SUPER_ADMIN"] as const;
export const PERMISSION_LEVEL = ["system", "self"] as const;
export const ACTION_TYPE = [
  "create",
  "read",
  "list",
  "update",
  "delete",
  "manage",
  "export",
] as const;

src/db/schemas/enums/db-enums.ts and src/db/schemas/enums/zod-db-enums.ts:

import { text } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";
import { ROLES } from "./enum-values";

export const RoleEnum = (name: string) => text(name, { enum: ROLES });

import z from "zod";
import { ACTION_TYPE, PERMISSION_LEVEL, ROLES } from "./enum-values";

export const RoleEnumSchema = z.enum(ROLES);
export type RoleEnumType = z.infer<typeof RoleEnumSchema>;
export const ActionTypeEnumSchema = z.enum(ACTION_TYPE);
export type ActionTypeEnumType = z.infer<typeof ActionTypeEnumSchema>;
export const PermissionLevelEnumSchema = z.enum(PERMISSION_LEVEL);
export type PermissionLevelEnumType = z.infer<typeof PermissionLevelEnumSchema>;

src/db/schemas/table/verification.table.ts — table, Zod schemas, and inferred types in one file:

import {
  db_created_at,
  db_date,
  db_id,
  db_updated_at,
} from "@/db/utils/db-utils";
import { sqliteTable, text } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";
import {
  createInsertSchema,
  createSelectSchema,
  createUpdateSchema,
} from "drizzle-zod";
import z from "zod";

export const VerificationTable = sqliteTable("verifications", {
  id: db_id,
  identifier: text("identifier").notNull(),
  value: text("value").notNull(),
  expiresAt: db_date("expires_at").notNull(),
  createdAt: db_created_at,
  updatedAt: db_updated_at,
});

export const insertVerificationSchema = createInsertSchema(
  VerificationTable,
).omit({ id: true, createdAt: true, updatedAt: true });
export const selectVerificationSchema = createSelectSchema(VerificationTable, {
  id: z.uuid(),
});
export const updateVerificationSchema = createUpdateSchema(
  VerificationTable,
).omit({ id: true, createdAt: true, updatedAt: true });

export type VerificationDataModel = typeof VerificationTable.$inferSelect;
export type InsertVerification = z.infer<typeof insertVerificationSchema>;
export type SelectVerification = z.infer<typeof selectVerificationSchema>;

src/db/schemas/index.ts and src/db/schemas/table/index.ts:

export * from "./enums/db-enums";
export * from "./table";

export * from "./verification.table";

src/db/clients/drizzle-client.ts and its test double:

import { createClient } from "@libsql/client";
import { drizzle, type LibSQLDatabase } from "drizzle-orm/libsql";

import * as schema from "@/db/schemas";

export type DatabaseType = LibSQLDatabase<typeof schema>;

export function createDrizzleClient(url = "file:./local.db"): DatabaseType {
  return drizzle(createClient({ url }), { schema });
}

import { createClient } from "@libsql/client";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/libsql";

import * as schema from "@/db/schemas";
import type { DatabaseType } from "./drizzle-client";

export function createMockDrizzleClient(): DatabaseType {
  return drizzle(createClient({ url: ":memory:" }), { schema });
}

src/db/generators/dbml-generator.ts and src/db/generators/sql-generator.ts — one in-process, one via the CLI:

import { join } from "node:path";
import { sqliteGenerate } from "drizzle-dbml-generator";

import * as schema from "@/db/schemas";

sqliteGenerate({
  schema,
  out: join(process.cwd(), "schema.dbml"),
  relational: true,
});

import { exec } from "node:child_process";
import { writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { promisify } from "node:util";

const execAsync = promisify(exec);

async function main() {
  const { stdout } = await execAsync("pnpm drizzle-kit export --sql");
  if (!stdout.trim()) throw new Error("No SQL output from drizzle-kit export");
  await writeFile(join(process.cwd(), "full-schema.sql"), stdout, "utf-8");
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exit(1);
});

src/db/utils/chunk-by-params.ts and src/db/utils/escapeLike.ts:

const MAX_BOUND_PARAMS = 999;

type PendingQuery<T> = PromiseLike<T> & { toSQL(): { params: unknown[] } };

export function chunkByParams<T>(rows: T[], paramsPerRow: number): T[][] {
  const size = Math.max(1, Math.floor(MAX_BOUND_PARAMS / paramsPerRow));
  return Array.from({ length: Math.ceil(rows.length / size) }, (_, index) =>
    rows.slice(index * size, (index + 1) * size),
  );
}

export async function insertChunkedReturning<T, R>(
  rows: T[],
  build: (chunk: T[]) => PendingQuery<R[]>,
): Promise<R[]> {
  if (!rows.length) return [];
  const query = build(rows);
  if (rows.length === 1 || query.toSQL().params.length <= MAX_BOUND_PARAMS) {
    return query;
  }
  const mid = Math.ceil(rows.length / 2);
  return [
    ...(await insertChunkedReturning(rows.slice(0, mid), build)),
    ...(await insertChunkedReturning(rows.slice(mid), build)),
  ];
}

export function escapeLike(input: string): string {
  return input.replace(/[\\%_]/g, (ch) => `\\${ch}`);
}

src/db/seed/seed.config.ts, src/db/seed/verification.seed.ts, and src/db/seed/clearAll.ts:

export const seedConfigs = { targets: { verifications: 3 } };

import type { DatabaseType } from "@/db/clients/drizzle-client";
import type { InsertVerification, VerificationDataModel } from "@/db/schemas";
import { VerificationTable } from "@/db/schemas";

export const verificationData: Array<InsertVerification> = [
  {
    identifier: "email:ada@example.com",
    value: "token-a",
    expiresAt: new Date(),
  },
  {
    identifier: "email:grace@example.com",
    value: "token-b",
    expiresAt: new Date(),
  },
];

export async function seedVerifications(
  db: DatabaseType,
): Promise<VerificationDataModel[]> {
  return db.insert(VerificationTable).values(verificationData).returning();
}

import type { DatabaseType } from "@/db/clients/drizzle-client";
import { VerificationTable } from "@/db/schemas";

export async function clearAll(db: DatabaseType) {
  await db.delete(VerificationTable);
}

package.json scripts:

{
  "scripts": {
    "db:generate": "drizzle-kit generate",
    "db:migrate": "drizzle-kit migrate",
    "db:studio": "drizzle-kit studio",
    "db:generate-dbml": "tsx ./src/db/generators/dbml-generator.ts",
    "db:generate-sql": "tsx ./src/db/generators/sql-generator.ts",
    "db:generate-full": "pnpm db:generate && pnpm db:generate-dbml && pnpm db:generate-sql"
  }
}

Pattern 1: A typed query with no second schema 

import { eq } from "drizzle-orm";
import { createDrizzleClient } from "@/db/clients/drizzle-client";
import { VerificationTable } from "@/db/schemas";

const db = createDrizzleClient();
const row = await db.query.VerificationTable.findFirst({
  where: eq(VerificationTable.identifier, "email:ada@example.com"),
});
if (!row) throw new Error("missing verification");
console.log(row.expiresAt instanceof Date);

The same table object supplies the SQL names, the query builder, and the return type.

Pattern 2: Seed rows without hitting the parameter ceiling 

import type { DatabaseType } from "@/db/clients/drizzle-client";
import { VerificationTable, type InsertVerification } from "@/db/schemas";
import { insertChunkedReturning } from "@/db/utils/chunk-by-params";

export async function seedSafely(db: DatabaseType, rows: InsertVerification[]) {
  return insertChunkedReturning(rows, (chunk) =>
    db.insert(VerificationTable).values(chunk).returning(),
  );
}

A thousand rows become several statements, each under the budget, and you keep the returned IDs.

Pattern 3: Tests against a real in-memory database 

import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { createMockDrizzleClient } from "@/db/clients/drizzle-client.mock";
import { VerificationTable } from "@/db/schemas";

test("a fresh client is empty and accepts a row", async () => {
  const db = createMockDrizzleClient();
  expect(await db.select().from(VerificationTable)).toEqual([]);
  await db.insert(VerificationTable).values({
    identifier: "email:ada@example.com",
    value: "token",
    expiresAt: new Date(),
  });
  expect(await db.select().from(VerificationTable)).toHaveLength(1);
});

You exercise real SQLite semantics without a database server or a fixture file.

❌ Do not call db.insert(table).values(thousandsOfRows) directly — one oversized statement fails partway and leaves a half-seeded database.

When to Use It

Reach for this layout only when all three are true:

  • Your data fits SQLite and is written by one process on one machine.
  • You want table definitions, inferred types, and validation derived from a single file.
  • You can ship generated .sql files with your code and apply them yourself.
Situation Better tool
Browser-only storage IndexedDB
Multi-writer service across regions Hosted Postgres
Database-enforced enum types Postgres enums or a CHECK constraint
One-off CSV script with no schema Raw SQL client
Managed auth UI and schema Auth provider's own tables
Migrations applied by a platform CLI That platform's migration path

Smell test: if you cannot name where the list of applied migrations lives, you have a folder of SQL, not a migration strategy.

How It Works Under the Hood

  1. The glob is the contract. schema: "./src/db/schemas/**" makes Kit load every file under schemas, so a new table is seen without editing a barrel. The barrels still matter at runtime: drizzle(client, { schema }) needs one namespace object.
  2. Defaults are split by who evaluates them. db_id uses $defaultFn(() => crypto.randomUUID()), supplied by JavaScript. db_created_at uses .default(sql\(unixepoch() * 1000)), supplied by SQLite. Raw SQL and Drizzle inserts therefore agree on timestamps.
  3. timestamp_ms changes the type. integer(name, { mode: "timestamp_ms" }) stores milliseconds and returns Date. Passing a number to a gte on that column silently produces nonsense.
  4. Relations are declared, not discovered. Matching relationName values on both sides let db.query join. Without them, plain SQL still works but nested reads turn into N+1 queries.
  5. Chunking is measured, not guessed. insertChunkedReturning inspects toSQL().params and recursively halves until the statement fits 999 parameters. The cost is several round trips and no single atomic batch.
  6. Both generators read the same panel. DBML generation walks the schema object in-process; SQL generation shells out to drizzle-kit export. db:generate-full runs generate first so the exported SQL cannot be older than the migration folder.
Phase What exists Who reads it Failure if skipped
1. Define *.table.ts Kit and client nothing to generate
2. Generate config glob migrations/*.sql stale schema
3. Apply SQL work order local.db no such column
4. Seed typed client rows FK violation
5. Query client and schema typed rows any leaks through
6. Diagram schema object .dbml, .sql stale documentation

In a server-rendered React app, create the client on the server and never import a file-path client into a browser module: file:./local.db does not resolve in a browser bundle. Return rows through your server's data layer.

Drizzle Kit gives you generate, migrate, studio, and export. It does not give you a seed runner, a validation layer, or diagrams. These folders fill those gaps; that is a limitation of the built-ins, not a rival philosophy.

Conclusion

One schema folder, one config glob, and a handful of scripts buy you a database TypeScript can reason about. The cost is discipline: every new table must be discoverable, every migration generated, every seed within the statement budget.

  • Point the config at schemas/**, never at one hand-maintained file.
  • Derive validators from tables and override only the fields with custom rules.
  • Generate SQL and DBML from the same schema so documentation cannot drift.

Keep this setup while you own the apply step. When a platform takes that job, hand it the same SQL and let it keep its own ledger.

title: Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Digital Marketing
description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing the way businesses promote their products and services online. From understanding customer behaviour to creating personalized campaigns, AI helps marketers make better decisions and improve marketing results. Today, businesses use AI-powered tools to save time, understand their audiences, and reach potential customers more effectively.

What Is the Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Digital Marketing?

The Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Digital Marketingis to make marketing activities smarter, faster, and more effective. AI helps businesses analyse customer data, understand user interests, automate repetitive tasks, and create personalized experiences. It is widely used in SEO, content marketing, social media marketing, email campaigns, and paid advertising. By using AI, marketers can improve customer engagement, save time, identify market trends, and make data-driven decisions that support business growth.

1. AI in Search Engine Optimization (SEO)

AI plays an important role in improving SEO strategies. It helps marketers research keywords, analyse competitors, identify content gaps, and understand search trends.

AI-powered SEO tools can also help identify website performance issues and suggest improvements. This makes it easier for businesses to create content that matches user search intent and improves their chances of ranking on search engines.

2. AI in Content Creation

Creating quality content regularly can take a lot of time. AI tools help marketers generate blog ideas, create outlines, write product descriptions, and improve existing content.

However, AI-generated content should always be reviewed and edited by humans. Adding original information, practical examples, and a natural writing style helps make content more useful and engaging for readers.

3. Personalized Customer Experience

Every customer has different interests and preferences. AI analyses customer behaviour, browsing history, and previous interactions to understand what users may need.

Businesses can use this information to recommend relevant products, display personalized advertisements, and send targeted emails. This improves the overall customer experience and helps build stronger relationships with customers.

4. AI in Social Media Marketing

AI helps businesses manage their social media activities more efficiently. It can suggest content ideas, analyse audience engagement, identify trending topics, and help marketers understand which posts perform better.

Social media marketers can use AI insights to improve their content strategies and connect with the right audience across different platforms.

5. AI in Email Marketing

Email marketing becomes more effective with AI-powered automation. AI helps marketers segment their email lists, personalize messages, and identify suitable sending times.

It can also analyse email open rates and click-through rates. These insights help businesses improve future campaigns and communicate with customers more effectively.

6. AI in Paid Advertising

AI helps marketers improve paid advertising campaigns by analysing audience interests, behaviour, and campaign performance.

Advertising platforms use machine learning to optimize bidding, target relevant audiences, and deliver advertisements to potential customers. This can help businesses use their advertising budgets more efficiently.

Benefits of Artificial Intelligence in Digital Marketing

Some important benefits of using AI in digital marketing include:

Time Saving: Automates repetitive marketing tasks.

Better Targeting: Helps reach the right audience.

Personalization: Creates relevant customer experiences.

Data Analysis: Provides useful insights into customer behaviour.

Improved Efficiency: Helps marketers optimize their campaigns.

Better Decision-Making: Supports data-driven marketing strategies.

Conclusion

The Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Digital Marketing is becoming increasingly important as businesses adopt smarter marketing strategies. AI helps improve SEO, content creation, social media management, email marketing, and paid advertising.

Although AI makes many marketing tasks easier, human creativity, experience, and strategic thinking remain essential. Combining AI technology with human expertise can help businesses create effective campaigns, improve customer experiences, and achieve long-term digital marketing success.

title: How to Build an InSAR Error Budget That Survives Review
description:
How to Build an InSAR Error Budget That Survives Review

Every deformation number in an InSAR report is an estimate. Reviewers increasingly refuse an estimate without an uncertainty statement attached, and the error budget is that statement made systematic: list every mechanism that corrupts the measurement, assign each a realistic one-sigma magnitude, and combine them into a single total with an explicit breakdown.

The method is short enough to state plainly. If the error sources are statistically independent, their variances add:

σ_total = √( Σ σᵢ² )

The share of each source is its variance divided by the total variance, so shares always sum to 100% and the dominant mechanism is the one whose square dominates. That last observation is the practical payoff: quadrature combination forgives moderate uncertainty in minor sources, but the largest source sets the floor. Halving a 6 mm atmospheric term buys you far more than eliminating a 1 mm orbit term entirely.

The five standard sources

A surface-deformation budget for Sentinel-1-style small-baseline processing usually starts here:

Source What drives it Typical behaviour
DEM error Residual topography phase Suppressed by short perpendicular baselines; modest with a small-baseline strategy
Orbit error Residual satellite-position uncertainty Small with precise orbit products (e.g. POEORB); shows as long-wavelength ramps
Atmospheric delay Turbulent wet delay + stratified troposphere Often the heaviest term; several mm/epoch in humid or high-relief terrain
Decorrelation noise Temporal/geometric coherence loss Depends on land cover, interval and baseline spread; shrinks as the archive grows
Incidence-angle error Projection geometry assumptions Matters when converting line-of-sight to a vertical or slope-parallel quantity

The default magnitudes you find in tools and templates are screening values, not your project's truth. Before you defend a number, edit every line to match your baseline distribution, coherence levels and correction models.

Where the budget earns its keep

In the QA section of a monitoring report. Each deformation rate should carry a stated uncertainty with a defensible breakdown, not a single hand-waved accuracy figure.

At the pre-award stage. When someone asks "how precise will InSAR be on this site?", the budget tells you which investments actually move the total: weather-model atmospheric correction (ERA5 or GACOS-class products), a better DEM, or a longer archive.

When comparing configurations. Compute the budget twice — with and without atmospheric correction, at two incidence angles — and the contribution chart quantifies the improvement instead of describing it qualitatively.

The three limits you must state

A budget is a design-stage expectation, and this is where careless reports get pulled apart.

  1. It is not evidence of achieved accuracy. A budget predicts expected error. Achieved accuracy comes from validating against real observations — for example with a GNSS cross-validation — not from the budget itself.
  2. Correlated errors do not add in quadrature. If two terms share a driver — say DEM error and incidence-angle error both stem from one bad geolocation — the RSS model underestimates the total. Merge them or widen one honestly.
  3. Velocity-calibrated defaults are wrong for single-epoch claims. Defaults that suit velocity work can misrepresent a single-epoch measurement. Re-derive each term for the quantity you are actually reporting.

A repeatable workflow

  1. Decide the quantity and unit: millimetres for a single epoch, or mm/yr for a velocity.
  2. List the sources relevant to your processing chain — the five above are a starting set, not a dogma.
  3. Assign a one-sigma magnitude to each with a justification you can cite.
  4. Combine in quadrature and compute each source's variance share.
  5. Read the share chart: spend effort where it is fat, ignore the cosmetic terms.
  6. Write the summary into the report, then validate the result against independent measurements.

A tool that performs steps 4–5 and writes the summary paragraph is available in the InSAR workbench; the time-series tool is where the deformation estimates being budgeted come from. Calculations run locally in the browser — no monitoring data leaves your machine.

FAQ

Q: What is an InSAR error budget?
A: A systematic statement of expected measurement uncertainty: list each error mechanism, assign a one-sigma magnitude, combine independent variances in quadrature, and show which sources dominate.

Q: Why do variances add instead of uncertainties?
A: For statistically independent errors, variances (squared sigmas) add. Total uncertainty is the square root of the sum of squared terms — root-sum-square, or quadrature.

Q: Does halving every error source halve the total?
A: No. The largest term sets the floor. Reducing a dominant atmospheric term matters far more than removing a minor orbit term; use the variance share to choose.

Q: Can I use the budget as my report's accuracy figure?
A: No. It is a design-stage expectation of error, not a validation result. Achieved accuracy must come from comparison with real observations such as GNSS.

Q: What if my error sources are correlated?
A: Then quadrature is invalid and will understate the total. Merge correlated terms into one or widen one honestly to cover the shared driver.

Q: Are the default magnitudes safe to use?
A: Only as screening values. They reflect typical small-baseline Sentinel-1 processing; edit each term to match your baselines, coherence and corrections.

Q: Which source usually dominates?
A: Atmospheric delay in many humid or high-relief settings, but it is site- and configuration-dependent — always read the contribution shares rather than assuming.

Q: Does the budget tool upload my data?
A: No. The calculators run locally in the browser; no deformation data is sent to a server.

title: File Permission and Ownership
description:
Mastering File Permissions & Ownership: chmod and chown in Bash and Python
published: false
description: A practical guide to managing Linux/Unix file permissions and ownership using chmod and chown in Shell scripting (Bash) and Python.
tags: linux, bash, python, devops

Managing file permissions and ownership is a foundational skill for anyone working with Linux or Unix-like servers. Whether you are deploying a web application, securing sensitive configuration files, or automating server provisioning, chmod and chown are the two commands you will rely on most.

In this guide, we will break down how chmod and chown work, and compare how to automate them cleanly using Shell scripting (Bash) and Python.

1. The Fundamentals: chmod vs. chown

Before writing any scripts, it helps to separate what each command controls:

  • chmod (Change Mode): Defines what actions can be performed on a file or directory (Read, Write, Execute) across three permission tiers:
    • User (u): The owner of the file.
    • Group (g): Users who belong to the file's assigned group.
    • Others (o): Everyone else on the system.
  • chown (Change Owner): Defines who owns the file or directory (both the owning user and the owning group). Changing ownership generally requires root or sudo privileges.

Permission Reference Table

Permission Symbol Octal Value Effect on a File Effect on a Directory
Read r 4 View file contents List directory contents (ls)
Write w 2 Modify or delete the file Create, rename, or delete files inside
Execute x 1 Run the file as a program/script Enter the directory (cd)

Quick Octal Math: Add the values together for each tier (User, Group, Others). For example, 755 means Owner = 4+2+1 (rwx), Group = 4+0+1 (r-x), and Others = 4+0+1 (r-x).

2. Automating chmod and chown in Shell Scripting (Bash)

In Bash, chmod and chown are native utilities, making shell scripts the fastest way to apply permissions during server setup or CI/CD pipelines.

Essential One-Liners 

# Make a shell script executable
chmod +x deploy.sh

# Set read/write for owner, read-only for group and others
chmod 644 config.yaml

# Change both user and group ownership
sudo chown www-data:www-data /var/www/html/index.html

# Recursively change ownership of an entire project directory
sudo chown -R deploy:developers /opt/myapp

Complete Bash Deployment Script

When securing a web directory, you typically want directories set to 755 (so users can traverse them) and files set to 644 (so files aren't accidentally executable):

#!/bin/bash
set -e  # Exit immediately if any command fails

TARGET_DIR="/var/www/myapp"
APP_USER="www-data"
APP_GROUP="www-data"

# 1. Ensure the target directory exists
if [ ! -d "$TARGET_DIR" ]; then
    echo "Error: $TARGET_DIR not found."
    exit 1
fi

# 2. Update ownership recursively
echo "Assigning ownership to $APP_USER:$APP_GROUP..."
chown -R "$APP_USER":"$APP_GROUP" "$TARGET_DIR"

# 3. Apply separate permissions for directories and files
echo "Setting directory (755) and file (644) permissions..."
find "$TARGET_DIR" -type d -exec chmod 755 {} +
find "$TARGET_DIR" -type f -exec chmod 644 {} +

# 4. Grant execute permission specifically to the entrypoint script
chmod 750 "$TARGET_DIR/start.sh"

echo "Done! Permissions and ownership configured."

3. Automating chmod and chown in Python

When your automation grows into a larger CLI tool or cross-platform application, Python's built-in os, shutil, and stat modules provide clean, structured alternatives without spawning external shell subprocesses.

Key Python Functions

  1. os.chmod(path, mode) Updates permissions using Python's octal prefix 0o (e.g., 0o755). You can also combine flags from the stat module (like stat.S_IXUSR) to modify specific bits without overwriting existing permissions.
  2. os.chown(path, uid, gid) Low-level ownership change that requires numeric User ID (uid) and Group ID (gid) integers.
  3. shutil.chown(path, user=None, group=None) A high-level wrapper around os.chown() that accepts string usernames and group names directly, making it much easier to read and maintain.

Complete Python Deployment Script

Here is the exact same deployment workflow implemented in Python using pathlib and shutil:

import os
import shutil
import stat
from pathlib import Path

target_dir = Path("/var/www/myapp")
owner = "www-data"
group = "www-data"

if not target_dir.exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"Target directory does not exist: {target_dir}")

try:
    # 1. Update root directory ownership and permissions
    shutil.chown(target_dir, user=owner, group=group)
    os.chmod(target_dir, 0o755)

    # 2. Walk through all subdirectories and files
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(target_dir):
        for d in dirs:
            dir_path = os.path.join(root, d)
            shutil.chown(dir_path, user=owner, group=group)
            os.chmod(dir_path, 0o755)

        for f in files:
            file_path = os.path.join(root, f)
            shutil.chown(file_path, user=owner, group=group)
            os.chmod(file_path, 0o644)

    # 3. Safely add owner-execute (+x) permission to start.sh
    startup_script = target_dir / "start.sh"
    if startup_script.exists():
        current_permissions = startup_script.stat().st_mode
        startup_script.chmod(current_permissions | stat.S_IXUSR)

    print("Done! Permissions and ownership configured.")

except PermissionError:
    print("Error: Run this script with sudo/root privileges to change ownership.")
except LookupError as e:
    print(f"Error: Invalid user or group specified ({e}).")

4. Bash vs. Python: Which One Should You Choose?

Feature Shell Scripting (Bash) Python
Syntax & Brevity Very concise; native -R flag handles recursion effortlessly More verbose; requires manual traversal (os.walk)
Error Handling Basic exit codes ($? or set -e) Granular exception handling (PermissionError, LookupError)
Readability Can get cryptic with complex conditionals Clean, structured, and easy to unit test
Ideal Use Cases Dockerfiles, cron jobs, quick server provisioning Complex CLI tools, deployment orchestrators, APIs

Summary

  • Use Bash when you need fast, direct system commands in initialization scripts, Docker builds, or CI/CD runners.
  • Use Python when file permission logic is part of a larger application that benefits from structured error handling, logging, and maintainability.

title: AWS Puts Smaller Decision Models Between Agents and Expensive AI
description:
Quick take

  • AWS released five Strands Decider v2 models, open-weight “system one” models built on Gemma 4 and scaling to 31 billion parameters.
  • In one routing test, a Strands Decider model achieved 94 percent as many completed tasks as Sonnet alone at 44 percent of the cost.
  • On AWS’s DecisionPivot benchmark, the largest v2 model scored 84.3 versus 23.2 for v1, though the comparison involved different model sizes.
  • An AWS benchmark found perfect difficulty classification but reported that Decider was much slower and more expensive when run on a CPU.

Why it matters

Developers may shift from opaque, unconstrained routing to an inspectable layer with predefined outcomes, confidence thresholds and human fallbacks, while keeping generative models for explanation and execution. The practical change remains unproven: teams should watch latency, inference cost, benchmark independence and performance on unusual or ambiguous requests before deploying it broadly.

In a future customer-service system, a request about a missing payment may never reach the most powerful model. A smaller AI could first decide whether the case belongs with billing, fraud, or a human supervisor, then send it to the right destination. AWS is betting that this layer of judgment deserves its own models.

When an AI system must choose from a fixed list of actions, generating a polished paragraph may be unnecessary. The application needs a reliable decision, such as which model to call, whether a policy has been violated, or which queue should receive a ticket.

DecisionPivot scores for Strands Decider models — see the chart in the original article.

AWS has released five Strands Decider v2 models for those tasks. In its announcement of Strands Decider v2, Strands Agents describes the models as open-weight “system one” models designed to score a supplied set of choices rather than produce a conventional textual answer. The models return probabilities for each option, allowing software to act automatically when confidence is high or escalate uncertain cases to a larger model or a person.

The family is built on Gemma 4, is available under the Apache 2.0 license and scales to 31 billion parameters, according to AWS. The models are aimed at routing requests between language models, checking policies, labeling tickets, selecting tools and assigning work to queues.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) Loft NYC (48129118457) · Ajay Suresh from New York, NY, USA · via wikimedia · CC BY 2.0

That approach could change the shape of an AI interaction. Instead of asking a costly frontier model to interpret every incoming message, an enterprise system could place a small decision model at the entrance. Most requests might be handled quickly and cheaply, while ambiguous cases would be passed upward.

A model that looks for the detail that changes the answer

AWS says Strands Decider v2 uses an architecture that reads a complete situation in both directions before scoring several questions against a shared representation. The design is intended for cases where a small detail buried in a long request changes the correct outcome.

Imagine an insurance claim containing a dozen routine facts and one sentence indicating possible fraud. A generative model might summarize the entire claim, while a Decider model could score predefined outcomes such as approve, investigate or escalate. The distinction is important because the application already knows what decisions it is allowed to make.

On AWS’s DecisionPivot benchmark, the company reports that its largest v2 model scored 84.3, compared with 23.2 for the largest v1 model. The comparison is not a clean like for like test because the models have different sizes. AWS also reports that, in one routing test, a Strands Decider model sent requests between Claude Haiku 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 while achieving 94 percent as many completed tasks as Sonnet alone at 44 percent of the cost.

The company’s open-source Strands Decider repository includes code, training materials, evaluation resources and deployment instructions. That gives developers a path to inspect and run the models rather than treating routing logic as an opaque hosted service.

The promise is not simply lower cost. A separate decision layer could make agent systems easier to control. Developers can write down the allowed outcomes before deployment, set a confidence threshold and establish a fallback path. In principle, that makes the system’s behavior more visible than an unconstrained model that invents a response for every request.

AWS recommends Decider when the possible answers can be specified in advance. If a system needs to explain a complex result, propose a new option or create an original plan, a general-purpose language model remains the better fit.

The performance question is not settled

The most important challenge to AWS’s pitch comes from the cost and latency of the decision layer itself. In a benchmark published by AWS Senior Solutions Architect Vivek Raja P S, Raja reports that Strands Decider classified request difficulty perfectly in his test, but was much slower and more expensive when run on a CPU.

His conclusion is more cautious than the product announcement. For simple, single-step routing, he argues that smaller large language model classifiers may be preferable. Decider becomes more attractive when its judgment can be reused across multiple actions or when it serves as a guardrail, according to his analysis.

That distinction goes to the heart of the architecture. A routing model can save money only if the cost of consulting it is smaller than the cost of sending every request to a more capable model. If the classifier is slow, expensive or called repeatedly without reusing its output, the extra layer may add friction rather than remove it.

There is also a question about how broadly AWS’s benchmark results can be generalized. Independent analyst Tom Rochette’s review of Strands Decider 2B notes that the v2 measurements on external Decision Index results were vendor-submitted. He also observed that the project repository did not yet contain a v2 evaluation section, and recorded the models’ leaderboard positions without treating AWS’s claims as independently established.

That does not disprove the reported results. It does mean developers should test the models on their own traffic, hardware and failure conditions. A classifier that performs well on a benchmark may behave differently when requests contain unusual wording, missing information or several simultaneous intents.

A control layer for the agent economy

AWS also describes an internal ticket-labeling deployment in which a smaller v1 model reduced average latency and estimated per-ticket inference costs. Those figures came from AWS and were not independently verified. Still, the use case illustrates why decision models may find a role in large organizations, where millions of repetitive classifications can become a significant operational expense.

The likely future is not a choice between small classifiers and large generative models. It is a stack in which each model has a narrower job. A Decider model could determine whether a request is routine, sensitive or novel. A generative model could then explain the result or carry out the selected task. A human could remain in the loop when confidence falls below an agreed threshold.

For workers, that could mean fewer routine tickets appearing in their queues and more attention directed toward cases that genuinely require judgment. For customers, it could produce faster responses, provided the routing model does not quietly send the wrong request to the wrong destination.

Strands Decider v2 therefore represents a broader architectural idea, not just another model release. AI systems may increasingly divide intelligence into two stages: one model decides what should happen, and another creates the answer. Whether that division delivers better systems will depend less on headline benchmark scores than on the practical balance among accuracy, speed, cost and the consequences of getting a borderline decision wrong.

Sources

  • strandsagents.com (primary)
  • github.com (primary)
  • builder.aws.com (primary)
  • tomrochette.com (primary)

Originally published at spaisee.com.

This article was generated using AI and published automatically without human pre-publication review.

title: Monetizing Technical Content Without Up‑Front Investment: A Practical Guide
description:
In today’s knowledge‑driven economy, engineers, developers, and tech enthusiasts can turn their expertise into a sustainable revenue stream without spending money on startup costs. The key lies in leveraging free platforms, building a personal brand, and creating value that audiences are willing to pay for. This guide walks you through low‑risk strategies—from open‑source contributions to premium community offerings—and shows how to scale each approach responsibly.

1. Leverage Free Publishing Platforms

Blog Hosting and Content Syndication

Publish technical articles on free sites such as Medium, Dev.to, or Hashnode. These platforms provide built‑in audiences, SEO benefits, and easy sharing tools. Write in‑depth tutorials, case studies, or “how‑to” guides that solve real problems for developers, system administrators, or data scientists. Consistency matters: aim for one post per week to build readership and improve discoverability.

Open‑Source Documentation and Guides

Contribute documentation or tutorials to open‑source projects on GitHub or GitLab. By attaching your name to high‑quality docs, you gain credibility within the community. Many organizations recognize contributors and may invite you to speak at webinars, podcasts, or conferences—opportunities that can later translate into paid engagements.

SEO and Keyword Targeting

Even without a budget, you can optimize content for search engines. Use free keyword research tools (Google Trends, AnswerThePublic) to identify common technical questions. Structure articles with clear headings, concise meta descriptions, and code snippets that are easy to copy. Over time, organic traffic can become a steady source of ad revenue or lead generation for other monetization channels.

2. Build a Community Around Your Expertise

Free Forums and Discord Servers

Create a Discord server or Reddit community focused on a niche technology (e.g., Rust embedded development, Kubernetes security). Offer a welcoming space for discussion, Q&A, and resource sharing. As the community grows, you can introduce optional paid tiers that provide additional benefits, such as exclusive channels, early access to content, or direct mentorship.

Newsletter Subscriptions

Use free newsletter services like Substack or Revue to curate weekly digests of your best content, industry news, and personal insights. While the basic tier remains free, you can later enable a paid subscription model that unlocks premium articles, detailed code reviews, or private office‑hour sessions. The key is to demonstrate consistent value before asking for payment.

Live Streaming and Interactive Sessions

Platforms such as YouTube Live, Twitch, or GitHub Discussions allow you to host free live coding sessions, architecture walkthroughs, or problem‑solving streams. Engage viewers through real‑time Q&A, and gradually introduce optional donation mechanisms (Patreon, Ko‑fi) for those who wish to support your work. Transparency about how contributions help improve content quality builds trust and encourages ongoing support.

3. Offer Paid Knowledge Products

E‑Books and Technical Guides

Compile your most popular blog posts or original research into a downloadable PDF or e‑book. Services like Leanpub let you publish without upfront costs; readers pay per download, and you receive a royalty. Focus on topics that have a clear learning outcome—such as “Deploying Serverless Applications with AWS Lambda” or “Advanced Git Workflows for Large Teams.”

Online Courses and Workshops

Record short video lessons using free screen‑capture tools (OBS Studio) and host them on platforms that take a revenue share, such as Udemy or Skillshare. Alternatively, run live workshops via Zoom or Google Meet, charging a modest registration fee. Keep production costs low by reusing existing code examples and slides, and emphasize interactive elements like live coding challenges.

Consulting Micro‑Packages

Offer “micro‑consulting” sessions—15‑minute problem‑solving calls priced at a flat rate. Promote these packages through your blog or newsletter, and schedule them using free calendar tools (Calendly). Because each session is brief, you can handle multiple clients without needing a formal office or extensive administrative overhead.

4. Monetize Through Affiliate and Sponsorship Opportunities

Relevant Tool Recommendations

When you write about specific libraries, cloud services, or development tools, you can join their affiliate programs (if available). Include a brief, honest disclaimer and link to the product’s sign‑up page. Because you’re already recommending tools you trust, the affiliate link feels natural and adds little extra effort.

Sponsored Content and Partnerships

As your audience expands, companies may approach you for sponsored posts, webinars, or product demos. Negotiate clear terms: outline the scope of the content, the required disclosure, and the compensation structure. Since you’re not investing in advertising, sponsorships become a direct revenue source that aligns with your existing content creation workflow.

Conclusion

Monetizing technical content without an initial cash outlay is entirely feasible when you focus on three pillars: leveraging free publishing platforms, building an engaged community, and packaging your expertise into paid products or services. Each step builds on the previous one—your blog attracts readers, your community deepens relationships, and your paid offerings convert that trust into revenue.

Start today by publishing a single, well‑researched tutorial on a platform you already use. Invite readers to join a free Discord channel, and announce a forthcoming e‑book that will compile your best work. As momentum builds, explore micro‑consulting or affiliate links that naturally complement your content.

Ready to turn your technical knowledge into a sustainable income stream? Begin with one piece of content, engage your audience, and let the value you provide drive the monetization. The tools are free; the effort is yours—make the most of it.

title: Norway's company register API in Python: new limited companies by industry code, last 7 days, in a CSV (no API key)
description:
Article type: How-to guide (one task: list the limited companies registered in Norway in the last 7 days, filtered by industry code, in a CSV)

Prerequisites: Python 3.9 or later with requests (pip install requests). No API key or account: the Brønnøysund Register Centre's open data API is free. An Apify account only if you use the hosted version at the end.

Tested on: 24 November 2026, against the live Enhetsregisteret API.

Norway's company register has a free JSON API with no key, and a short Python script can use it to list every limited company (aksjeselskap, AS) registered last week in the industry you care about. If you sell to new businesses, track start-ups in one sector or keep a market map up to date, that's the weekly question: which new companies registered, in my industry, and where are they? This guide answers it with the Enhetsregisteret API from the Brønnøysund Register Centre and saves the list as a CSV.

All the data in this post comes from one endpoint:

GET https://data.brreg.no/enhetsregisteret/api/enheter

with filters as query parameters, for example organisasjonsform=AS (legal form), fraRegistreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret=2026-11-16 and tilRegistreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret=2026-11-22 (registration date range). It returns a page of units under _embedded.enheter and a page object with totalElements and totalPages. No key, no login. The data is open under the Norwegian Licence for Open Government Data (NLOD 2.0).

How do I list new Norwegian companies by industry code with the Enhetsregisteret API?

Save this as norway_new_companies.py and run python norway_new_companies.py (IT programming and consultancy, codes starting 62) or pass another prefix, for example python norway_new_companies.py 41 for construction of buildings:

import csv
import sys
import time
from collections import Counter
from datetime import date, timedelta

import requests

INDUSTRY = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "62"   # SN2025 code prefix: 62 = IT programming and consultancy
DAYS = 7
API = "https://data.brreg.no/enhetsregisteret/api/enheter"
UA = "norway-new-companies-tutorial/1.0 (python-requests)"

session = requests.Session()
session.headers.update({"User-Agent": UA, "Accept": "application/json"})

# 1. robots.txt first. data.brreg.no closes the connection instead of answering, so there are no rules to read.
try:
    robots = session.get("https://data.brreg.no/robots.txt", timeout=30)
    print(f"robots.txt: HTTP {robots.status_code}")
except requests.ConnectionError:
    print("robots.txt: no answer (connection closed), so no rules to follow")

# 2. Every limited company (AS) registered in the last DAYS full days. One read; the industry filter is local.
until = date.today() - timedelta(days=1)
since = until - timedelta(days=DAYS - 1)
params = {"organisasjonsform": "AS", "fraRegistreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret": since.isoformat(),
          "tilRegistreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret": until.isoformat(), "size": 1000}
units, page = [], 0
while True:
    r = session.get(API, params={**params, "page": page}, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()
    units += data.get("_embedded", {}).get("enheter", [])
    page += 1
    if page >= data["page"]["totalPages"]:
        break
    if 1000 * (page + 1) > 10_000:               # the API refuses size * (page + 1) above 10,000
        sys.exit("more than 10,000 results: use a shorter date range")
    time.sleep(1)
print(f"{len(units)} limited companies (AS) registered {since} to {until}")


def codes(u):
    """Up to three industry codes per company; '00.000' means 'not stated'."""
    return [u[k]["kode"] for k in ("naeringskode1", "naeringskode2", "naeringskode3")
            if k in u and u[k]["kode"] != "00.000"]


# 3. Keep the companies with an industry code starting INDUSTRY, newest first.
rows = []
for u in units:
    found = [c for c in codes(u) if c.startswith(INDUSTRY)]
    if not found:
        continue
    addr = u.get("forretningsadresse") or u.get("postadresse") or {}
    rows.append({
        "registered": u["registreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret"],
        "org_number": u["organisasjonsnummer"],
        "name": u["navn"],
        "industry_code": found[0],
        "industry": next(u[k]["beskrivelse"] for k in ("naeringskode1", "naeringskode2", "naeringskode3")
                         if k in u and u[k]["kode"] == found[0]),
        "municipality": addr.get("kommune", ""),
        "postcode": addr.get("postnummer", ""),
        "founded": u.get("stiftelsesdato", ""),
        "vat_registered": u["registrertIMvaregisteret"],
        "url": f"https://virksomhet.brreg.no/nb/oppslag/enheter/{u['organisasjonsnummer']}",
    })
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r["registered"], r["org_number"]), reverse=True)
out = f"norway_new_as_{INDUSTRY}_{until}.csv"
with open(out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(rows)

print(f"  {sum(not codes(u) for u in units)} have no industry code yet (missing or 00.000 'not stated')")
print(f"wrote {len(rows)} with an industry code starting {INDUSTRY} to {out}")
for code, n in Counter(r["industry_code"] for r in rows).most_common():
    print(f"  {code}  {n:>4}")
print("  top municipalities:", ", ".join(f"{m} {n}" for m, n in Counter(r["municipality"] for r in rows).most_common(3)))
print(f"  registered for VAT: {sum(r['vat_registered'] for r in rows)}")

Output on 24 November 2026 (it took about 3 seconds):

robots.txt: HTTP 200
523 limited companies (AS) registered 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22
  323 have no industry code yet (missing or 00.000 'not stated')
wrote 26 with an industry code starting 62 to norway_new_as_62_2026-11-22.csv
  62.100    20
  62.200     6
  top municipalities: OSLO 5, HARAM 1, ULLENSAKER 1
  registered for VAT: 1

Some rows from norway_new_as_62_2026-11-22.csv (names, org numbers and links left out):

registered,industry_code,municipality,postcode,founded,vat_registered
2026-11-20,62.100,HARAM,6264,2026-11-12,False
2026-11-20,62.100,OSLO,0484,2026-11-09,False
2026-11-20,62.100,ULLENSAKER,2050,2026-11-11,False
2026-11-20,62.200,VOSS,5705,2026-11-09,False

62.100 is computer programming and 62.200 is IT consultancy and running IT systems. Only 1 of the 26 was in the VAT register yet, which is normal for a company a few days old.

Why it's built this way:

  • Filter the legal form on the server, the industry on your side. organisasjonsform=AS brings the week down to one page of 523. The industry filter runs locally so the script can count the companies that have no code yet (the "no industry code yet" line), which a server-side filter would hide.
  • All three industry codes. A company can have up to three (naeringskode1 to naeringskode3). The script matches any of them, so a company whose second activity is programming is kept.
  • Full days only. The window ends yesterday, so a run on any day of the week covers seven complete days.
  • No sort parameter. See gotcha 4.

What should I check before I trust the list?

  1. A week of new units isn't a week of new companies. Without the organisasjonsform filter the same seven days returned 2,002 units: 895 sole proprietorships (ENK, a person trading in their own name), 523 limited companies, 164 "other legal persons" (ANNA), 126 associations (FLI), 103 foreign entities (UTLA, 17 with a Swedish business address), 109 bankruptcy estates (KBO, "konkursbo") and 27 condominium associations (ESEK). Filter on the legal form you mean.
  2. Many new companies have no industry code yet. 323 of the 523 limited companies had no code or the code 00.000 ("not stated"). It isn't only the newest week: of the AS companies registered 12 to 18 October, 360 of 752 (48%) still had none on 24 November, and 235 of 699 (34%) from 11 to 17 May. An industry filter will always undercount, so report the blanks next to the matches.
  3. The codes changed to SN2025. naeringskode=62.010, a code from the older SN2007 standard that you'll still see in older guides, returns 0 units, even for a week in November 2024. The same week has 24 under 62.100. The API's naeringskode filter matches by prefix, so naeringskode=62 returned 60 units of every legal form this week, the same 60 that a local prefix match finds.
  4. The Enhetsregisteret API's date sort isn't stable between pages. Many units share a registration date, and when you sort with sort=registreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret,desc the API doesn't keep the same order inside a date from one page to the next. Walking all 2,002 units of the week 100 at a time with that sort returned 315 repeats on 24 November; at 1,000 a page, 69 repeats. The default order and sort=organisasjonsnummer,asc returned 0 repeats.
  5. One query reads at most 10,000 units. page=100 with size=100 returned HTTP 400 ("size * (page+1) kan ikke overstige 10_000"). Since 1 January 2026 there are 87,049 new units in total, so split long ranges by month or legal form.
  6. Weekends are almost empty. Registrations by day were 416 on Monday 16 November, 302 on Tuesday 17 November, 396 on Wednesday 18 November, 382 on Thursday 19 November, 402 on Friday 20 November, 57 on Saturday 21 November and 47 on Sunday 22 November. Compare weeks, not days.
  7. Some units carry a phone number or email address. 171 of this week's 2,002 did. The script doesn't copy them; if you change it, remember they can belong to a person.

To change the task, pass another prefix (41 construction of buildings, 56 restaurants, bars and catering), or change organisasjonsform to ENK for sole proprietorships (people, so handle with care).

The hosted version (Disclosure: we built this)

We built an Apify Actor, European Company Registry API, that reads Norway's register and others in one schema. Its newCompanies mode lists companies registered in Norway, Finland and Ireland in the last N days (registeredWithinDays, up to 366) or between two dates (registeredSince and registeredUntil). Two optional filters do this post's job: legalFormCodes keeps only the legal forms you list, and activityCodePrefixes keeps a company if any of its industry codes starts with a prefix you give. Norwegian rows list every industry code the register gives the company (activityCodes, current SN2025 codes) as well as the first one, the legal form code, the VAT ID when the company is in the VAT register, and a link to the official record.

For Norway it leaves some units out by default, and doesn't charge for them. Sole traders and natural persons are always skipped. Bankruptcy estates (KBO), associations (FLI) and foreign entities (NUF and UTLA) are left out too unless you set includeOtherNorwegianEntities. Other forms, such as ANNA and ESEK, still come back unless you set legalFormCodes. Each run's SUMMARY record checks that rows returned plus rows skipped equals records read. Phone numbers and email addresses are never put in rows, and monitor mode returns only companies it hasn't returned before.

In a free local run of this input on 24 November 2026 (not on the Apify platform), it read the same 523 limited companies and returned the same 26 as the script, 20 under 62.100 and 6 under 62.200. It left out 497 with no matching code, free of charge:

{
  "mode": "newCompanies",
  "countries": ["NO"],
  "registeredSince": "2026-11-16",
  "registeredUntil": "2026-11-22",
  "legalFormCodes": ["AS"],
  "activityCodePrefixes": ["62"],
  "maxResults": 0,
  "maxResultsPerCountry": 0
}

Without the two filters, the same week returned 731 rows out of 2,002 units read. It left out 1,271: 895 sole proprietorships, 141 foreign entities, 126 associations and 109 bankruptcy estates.

What it doesn't do: the industry filter can't find companies that have no code yet (323 of the 523 this week). registeredWithinDays counts back from the time of the run, so on 15 November a value of 7 covered 8 to 15 November; give two dates for whole weeks. In monitor mode it reads at most 5,000 records per country per run. It's pay per event; prices on the Actor's Pricing tab.

European Company Registry API on Apify

Data: Enhetsregisteret, Brønnøysund Register Centre, read 24 November 2026, under the Norwegian Licence for Open Government Data (NLOD 2.0). This post and the Actor are not affiliated with or endorsed by the Brønnøysund Register Centre.

title: OpenStreamHub: Building a macOS App for Hardware That Only Speaks Windows
description:
This autumn I ordered a Cooler Master MasterHUB when it was on sale. If you haven’t seen one: it’s a modular control deck - a base with modules plugged into it. Mine has a 15-key keypad with a little screen behind every key, a 3-knob module, a round dial with a display, five faders and a two-roller scroll module.

There was one catch, and I knew about it when ordering. I work mainly on a Mac, and the official software is Windows-only. Cooler Master's software page doesn't leave much room for interpretation: "Support for Windows 10 (64-bit) or later is required". A macOS version had been coming soon for a while, and then the device was marked as legacy. So much for that.

Without the software, the modules don't do much. They light up and play their built-in animations, but none of the keys does anything on your computer. Basically, a very nice-looking paperweight.

While the package was still on its way, I came across cooltek-sdk by projectzero7, a Rust SDK for these modules. How hard can it be to build an app on top of it?

Quite hard, as it turned out. But a bit over two weeks later, the first version of OpenStreamHub was out - an open-source SDK and macOS app for the MasterHUB, aiming for parity with the official Windows app, and then some. Five releases later, it has plugins, if / else keys, OBS controls, and a key that answers Claude Code's permission prompts (the app was built with Claude Code, so that one was kind of inevitable).

It's not affiliated with Cooler Master in any way.

Standing on Someone Else's SDK

projectzero7's SDK, together with its companion probe repository with notes on the knob module's feature reports and the keypad's output reports, was my starting point. My protocol docs still cite those notes in several places.

OpenStreamHub continues that repository instead of just depending on it. The original commits from July are still in the history, the Rust crates keep their cooltek-sdk names, and the MIT / Apache-2.0 license carries over.

Good question: why fork instead of sending pull requests upstream? The upstream repo hasn't moved since July, and what I was building wasn't really an SDK anymore. It was an SDK, plus a background service, a profile format and a desktop app on top. Keeping them in one place means a protocol change and the app change that depends on it can land in the same commit.

The downside: I now maintain an SDK I didn't write. I can live with that.

Reverse Engineering, With a Lot of Help

I'll be upfront about it: the whole project, and the reverse engineering in particular, was done with generative AI (Claude Code, in my case). I know it's a sore point for some people. Still, I work in software engineering, and USB protocols and firmware images are not exactly my daily bread - without the AI, this app wouldn't exist.

The official MasterHUB app (version 1.0.0.113) is an Electron and Vue application. We downloaded the 332 MB package and took it apart without ever running it: the native CoolTEK libraries with their HID calls, and the original application sources, conveniently recovered from its Electron source maps. Later came USB packet sniffing and a look inside the firmware images.

For the first five days, nothing touched the actual hardware - for a simple reason: it was still in delivery. So everything came from the Windows app and was tested against fakes. That's why every finding in the docs is marked as either derived or verified on a device, and why one rule held from day one - no firmware writes, ever. I'm fine with experimenting, but not with something I can brick.

The package arrived, and the first hardware session was on 8 October. Most of the static analysis held up. One thing was wrong, and one thing no amount of static analysis would have found.

The Lights That Wouldn't Change

On the Mac, the base obeyed the lighting commands right away - solid red on the first try. The knobs and faders ignored everything. No errors, nothing. They just kept cycling through their colors.

So I sniffed the USB traffic of the official app on Windows with Wireshark and USBPcap. Same three commands, same structure, but the module type byte was 2 for knobs and 1 for faders. We had them the other way around, so every write went to a module type nobody was listening for.

The fix was two bytes, and it was verified on the hardware the same day. And while going through the effects, it turned out the firmware has a fast strobe mode that the official app never uses. It's in OpenStreamHub now, so technically, the Mac app has more lighting effects than the Windows one.

The Silent Roller

The two-roller module - the one that comes with the base set - was a different story. It worked fine on Windows, and on macOS it sent nothing. Not a single report in four captures. My best guess at the time was that macOS simply doesn't let apps talk to whatever layer this module uses. I couldn't figure it out, so I have chosen to ship anyway, with the roller at the top of the "known limits" list.

On 25 October, KamilKobylarek opened issue #4 with the answer - they had hit the same silent roller in their own project. The roller's firmware only starts reporting after a standard HID SET_IDLE request. Linux and Windows send it to every HID device they bind, but macOS sends it only to keyboards and mice. So my guess was close, but not quite. The SDK now sends that request every time the module opens, and 0.4.0 shipped with working rollers on 5 November.

Lesson learned: green tests against fakes only mean you decode what you expect the device to send.

Building It With AI

About 320 commits landed in the ten days before the first release, and there are almost 600 now. At that pace I obviously wasn't writing every line. My job was mostly reviewing, steering, and deciding when something is really done.

The split of work settled quickly. The AI wrote the code, the diagnostic commands, the test scripts and most of the docs. I sat in front of the hardware, pressed the keys, watched the modules, and reported back what actually happened. You can see it in the hardware results - one LED check was a scripted run of 31 steps, five seconds each, with me watching every one of them.

And some things you can only catch with your hands. My first version of "a fader controls an OBS input's volume" was linear, and it felt wrong - the first half of the fader's travel did almost nothing. OBS uses a logarithmic scale for its own slider (about -19 dB at the halfway point), and once the mapping followed it, the fader behaved the way you'd expect.

The other thing to watch out for is the confidence. An AI will happily write "verified" about something nobody has seen working, and it sounds just as sure either way. The commit log has entries like "drop an unobserved claim about lighting persistence" and "stop overstating restore behaviour". So the project keeps two lists: what is implemented, and what was confirmed on a real device (hardware results). The app shows the same split on its Compatibility page.

The lesson there: the AI can write the driver, but someone still has to sit in front of the device and watch.

Five Releases In

The first release covered the basics: profiles and bindings for keys, knobs, dial and faders, nested keypad folders, pictures and animations on the keys and the dial, lighting, and a decent set of actions - volume, apps, URLs, media controls, key macros, timers. It could even import profiles exported from the official app.

Each release after that added one bigger idea:

  • 0.2.0 (14 Oct) - a menu bar mode, and a base layout that shows each module where it actually sits on the base, pictures turned to match when a module stands on its side.
  • 0.3.0 (27 Oct) - if / else keys with variables (a key can do one thing while you're recording in OBS, and another when you're not), GIFs on the dial, and many more OBS actions. All 17 from the official app are there by now.
  • 0.4.0 (5 Nov) - working rollers, and an AI agent like Claude Code or Codex can ask for permission on the deck and take Accept or Deny from a key.
  • 0.5.0 (18 Nov) - plugins. They can add their own actions, conditions and pictures on the keys. The two official ones are Now Playing (Apple Music or Spotify on one key, album cover included) and Claude Code (your sessions on the keys, plus a context and cost meter on the dial).

Of course, there are also demos - Tic-tac-toe, and a 2048-style sliding game on the 15 keys. Fifteen keys with screens, it would be a shame not to.

As for privacy: there is no telemetry and no account, and everything stays on your Mac. Apart from plugins you enable yourself, the only thing that talks to the internet is the update check, which asks GitHub for the latest release - and it only runs when you press the button, unless you turn on the daily check.

Decisions I'd Make Again

Tauri instead of native. A macOS-only app could have been written in SwiftUI. But the hardware layer was already Rust, and Tauri let me use the same crates in the app and in the background service, with React on the client. The first release took about 22 MB on disk (according to Pearcleaner), and the download is still under 10 MB. Will it ever feel quite like a native app? Probably not. I'm fine with that.

A separate service owns the device. The app doesn't talk to the hardware directly - a small service process does. If the app crashes, the service notices and puts the modules back into their own mode, so your keypad never gets stuck. It's one more moving part to build and ship, but a stuck keypad would be worse.

Test before Live. When a key can quit apps or type into windows, you want a safe way to try a profile first. In Test mode a key press shows what it would do without doing it, and Live runs it after you confirm. "Go live" in OBS needs two presses within three seconds, so a stray key can't start your stream.

Unsigned, and staying that way. Signing and notarization need a paid Apple Developer account, and this is a free side project. Unfortunately, the cost of that decision is on you: you have to allow the app in System Settings → Privacy & Security before the first run, and since macOS treats every unsigned update as a brand new app, it may ask for permissions again after updating. The install instructions walk you through it.

What Is Still Rough

Every limit I know of is written down in the repo, but these are the ones worth knowing before you install it:

  • It was tested on one rig - mine, plus KamilKobylarek's roller for the SET_IDLE fix. Other combinations of modules may surprise me.
  • The Intel build has never been launched. It's cross-compiled on an Apple Silicon Mac.
  • Plugins run as you. The permissions a plugin declares are shown, not enforced (apart from which variables it may set), so install them only from authors you trust.
  • Not there yet: .mhz export, firmware updates, Twitch and Discord integrations, and any language other than English. Linux and Windows aren't planned either - not impossible, just not an easy feat.

Closing Thoughts

What started as "I just want my keypad to work on a Mac" turned into a reverse-engineering project, a desktop app with plugins, and my first real project built mostly with an AI. Don't get me wrong, I like the features. But what I'm proudest of is the two lists - what works, and what has actually been seen working. And the bug I couldn't crack got fixed because someone fighting the same roller shared the answer.

If you have a MasterHUB and a Mac, grab the build from the latest release (Intel and Apple Silicon, macOS 12.3 or later). The most useful thing you can do is run it on hardware I don't have: other module combinations, a second roller module, an Intel Mac, a Mac that sleeps overnight. If something breaks, the app can create a diagnostic bundle you can attach to a GitHub issue.

Thanks to projectzero7 for the SDK underneath all of this, and to KamilKobylarek for making the rollers talk.

Technical Stack Overview

  • App: Tauri 2, React, TypeScript
  • Hardware layer: Rust (cooltek-sdk crates), HID via HIDAPI
  • Device access: a separate masterhub-service process
  • Profiles: versioned JSON
  • License: MIT or Apache-2.0

Repo: github.com/goniszewski/OpenStreamHub

Originally published on goniszewski.com.

title: Can your Postgres app handle millions of rows? What breaks and how to fix it
description:
Short answer: yes. Postgres handles millions of rows comfortably. A ten-million-row table is ordinary.

What breaks first is almost never the row count. It is how the app talks to the database:

Missing indexes. One endpoint gets slower every week as the table grows, with no code change.
Slow queries. A few requests take seconds. Usually one query doing far more work than it needs, or the N+1 pattern.
Too many connections. Fine in testing, then "too many clients already" under real traffic. Every Postgres connection is its own process, and the default limit is 100.
Bloat. Dead rows pile up when autovacuum cannot keep up, and everything slows a little each month.

In the full piece, I go through each fix: which indexes to add (and why over-indexing hurts writes), how to read EXPLAIN ANALYZE, when to put PgBouncer in front of Postgres, how to check autovacuum, and the order to scale in once you have genuinely outgrown one instance. The advice is checked against PostgreSQL 18.

Read the full article on Medium: https://akshanshgusain.medium.com/aec3d506679a
