title: Ahead of Time Code Compilation (JEP 544)
description:
In this article we are going to deep dive into JEP 544 and how compiled code inside the Ahead-of-Time (AOT) cache is dramatically improving application startup and warm-up times.

Project Leyden did already introduce the concept of AOT Cache in JDK 24. The concept is simple: during a training run, the application is executed under a representative workload to produce an artifact containing bytecode, build-time metadata, selected heap objects, and runtime data like profiling data. Then the app runs in production using this cache, so the application starts partially warmed up.

If you want more details on how Project Leyden worked before JEP 544, you can check this three-article series.

JEP 544 – Ahead-of-Time Code Compilation (JDK 28+)

The major milestone for Leyden this year has been JEP 544: Ahead-of-Time Code Compilation. As the name suggests, compiled native code is now directly stored into the AOT cache. This means that optimized native machine code is immediately available upon application startup.

But what does this really mean?

Running code in the JVM

The following is a simplified explanation of a very complex process, if you want the full explanation you can always check the source code, which has a very good explanation in comments.

Usually, code that runs in the JVM starts by being in bytecode, from a class file. To generate code that can run on your hardware, the JVM has the JIT and two compilers (C1 and C2) that can generate native code.

When some method gets called for the first time, the JIT quickly translates that bytecode into native code. This is a very fast process, because it literally just translates each bytecode instruction into a pre-defined set of native instructions. This is what we call Tier 0. No optimization, no smart compilation, just blind translation.

Once the code runs, the JVM starts to save some information about that code. Does it have dead-code parts? What branches are being used more often? Can the code be reorganized to be more efficient? And every single time the method gets called, there is a counter that increases. After the method has been called enough times, it is considered hot, and therefore a good candidate to be optimized using the profile data saved during previous executions.

To compile using the profile data, it checks first how many other methods are waiting to be compiled. If the C2 compiler is busy, the C1 compiler will recompile the method into Tier2, which produces better code than Tier0, but has a rather fast compilation. If the C2 compiler is free, the C1 compiler will spend more time recompiling the method into Tier3, which has many more optimizations. Both Tier2 and Tier3 code will keep saving profiling statistics to improve future compilations.

At some point, the method may be called so much that the JVM will consider another recompilation, with much more profiling information, to further optimize its execution. If the code is deemed trivial, then C1 will just compile into Tier1, which is a basic compilation with no fancy optimizations. The method will stay in Tier1 with no more changes and the compilers can forget about it. There's no reason to try to optimize a trivial code.

If it is not considered trivial, that’s when C2 will compile the method with the best optimizations available. On this Tier4 level, we no longer save profiling statistics, to avoid any overhead. This is peak optimized code, the JVM can’t make it better.

Some hot methods will be de-optimized into Tier3 again every now and then to gather new statistics and make sure the code is still optimally compiled. This makes a lot of sense in case the application circumstances change. For example, if you have a specific code for Black Friday, how the method behaves during Black Friday will be completely different than any other day of the year.

How does this translate to Leyden?

Before JEP 544, the AOT Code Cache stored profiling data and method counters. This means that we have already marked which methods are going to be hot and we already have the profiling information needed to compile them. We can quickly compile those methods and jump into higher tiers of compilation faster. The compiler threads will be busier during startup, but peak performance is reached sooner.

After JEP 544, the AOT Cache does not only store profiling data, which is still useful, but now it also stores actual compiled code in whatever tier they reached during the training run. That means that we can not only skip most of the startup time, but execute methods directly at a higher tier of compilation and reduce warm-up time.

Performance Benchmarks & Data Analysis

Let’s see now how good the AOT Cache improves warm-up by comparing response times from two different examples.

These tests were conducted using leyden-perf-test, driven by QDup and Hyperfoil on my laptop with standard hardware CPU pin settings to minimize noise. Which means, numbers may not be as good as if it was a dedicated server, but the trends are very clear.

Simple REST

First, take a look at a very simple REST endpoint using Quarkus that returns a hello world string. This is simple code, the JVM should be able to optimize it quickly.

As we can see in the following histogram graphs, with the AOT Cache we already start with a response time three times faster and we quickly reach peak performance before the request number 400, whereas the application with no cache is still optimizing after request 700.

We can even see in the test with AOT cache available, that around request 550 there is some de-optimization that affects response time, and quickly disappears to optimize again. This is normal behaviour that would also happen in the run without cache, we just don't see it on the graph because we are still busy reaching peak performance.

We could be more nit-picky and look closer when is peak performance reached. Probably there is some improvement beyond what we can see from these graphs if we zoom in, and we may need to reach a thousand requests to have almost-instantaneous response times. But the general trend can be observed already: with the cache, startup response times are faster from the very first response, and warm-up comes sooner.

Simple Hibernate

The following test is very similar to the previous one, but instead of returning a hello world string, it has to retrieve the value from a local database. As the codebase is more complex, the initial response times are higher than in the previous example, and the warm-up takes longer.

We can see that the initial response times with the cache are close to one fourth of the original response time without cache. And while the run with the cache reaches peak performance before request number 900, the application with no cache has almost the same response time after request 1000, it is still busy profiling methods before optimizing them.

These are just two examples, which may be considered even trivial examples. But the trend can be already seen: the more complex the program, the more the cache can improve startup and warm-up times compared to using no cache.

We will dive deeper in future articles with more examples and real use case scenarios.

If you are trying to add the AOT Cache to your deployments, I am interested in hearing from you. It doesn't matter if it was a good or a bad experience. Specially, bad experiences can help us make Leyden easier for everyone (including you).

title: Resilience Patterns for LLMs: Retries, Fallbacks, and Circuit Breakers
description:
When an LLM provider experiences an outage, rate limit spike, or degraded performance, most backend developers default to a simple solution: wrap the API call in a retry loop.

Relying solely on retries often makes outages worse. If an API returns a 429 Too Many Requests or a prolonged 500 Internal Server Error, hitting the endpoint repeatedly burns your execution quota, inflates user latency, and contributes to the "thundering herd" problem when the upstream service attempts to recover.

To build production-grade AI applications, you must separate retries from fallbacks and protect your system architecture accordingly.

Understanding Retry vs. Fallback

A retry means attempting the exact same request against the same provider. This is designed for transient failures: a dropped TCP connection, a temporary network hiccup, or a sporadic 503 error.

A fallback means routing the request to a completely different provider or a secondary model family. Fallbacks are required when the primary provider is facing a hard outage, severe throttling, or persistent API degradation.

Mixing these two concepts leads to fragile systems. Retrying a 429 status code, for instance, ignores the provider's explicit request to pause traffic.

1. Smart Retries with Exponential Backoff and Jitter

If you encounter a transient error (like a 502 or 503), do not retry immediately in a tight loop. Instead, use exponential backoff combined with jitter.

Exponential backoff increases the delay between each attempt exponentially (e.g., 1s, 2s, 4s). Jitter adds a randomized offset to prevent thousands of concurrent clients from hitting the recovering server at the exact same millisecond.

Here is a practical Python implementation using explicit backoff and error handling:

import random
import time
import openai

def call_llm_with_retry(prompt: str, max_retries: int = 3) -> str:
    base_delay = 1.0
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            response = openai.chat.completions.create(
                model="gpt-4o",
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
            )
            return response.choices[0].message.content
        except (openai.APIConnectionError, openai.InternalServerError) as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1:
                raise e
            # Calculate exponential backoff + jitter
            sleep_time = (base_delay * (2 ** attempt)) + random.uniform(0, 0.5)
            time.sleep(sleep_time)
        except openai.RateLimitError:
            # Pass rate limit errors immediately to trigger the fallback layer
            raise

2. Multi-Provider Fallback Chains

When retries are exhausted—or when a rate limit error occurs—your execution path should immediately switch to a backup provider. For example, if your primary model is OpenAI's gpt-4o, your secondary fallback could be Anthropic's claude-3-5-sonnet.

Here is how to structure a fallback chain across different SDKs:

import os
from anthropic import Anthropic
import openai

anthropic_client = Anthropic(api_key=os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))

def generate_completion(prompt: str) -> str:
    # Step 1: Try Primary Provider (OpenAI) with retries
    try:
        return call_llm_with_retry(prompt, max_retries=2)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Primary provider failed or rate limited: {e}. Executing fallback...")

    # Step 2: Fallback to Secondary Provider (Anthropic)
    try:
        response = anthropic_client.messages.create(
            model="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022",
            max_tokens=1000,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
        )
        return response.content[0].text
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Fallback provider failed: {e}")
        raise RuntimeError("All configured LLM providers are unavailable.")

3. Protecting Infrastructure with Circuit Breakers

If an LLM provider goes down completely, executing two retries and a fallback for every single incoming request adds seconds of latency to your application.

A circuit breaker tracks the failure rate of a provider over a rolling window. If the failure rate exceeds a specified threshold (e.g., 50% failures over 10 requests), the circuit "opens."

When open, the system bypasses the primary provider entirely and routes requests straight to the fallback provider. After a set cooldown period, the circuit enters a "half-open" state, sending a test request to verify if the primary provider has recovered.

Key Takeaways

  1. Never retry 429s blindly: Treat rate limits as a trigger to back off or immediately execute a provider fallback.
  2. Limit retries: Two to three attempts with jittered backoff are enough for network blips.
  3. Decouple business logic: Normalize prompts and responses so switching between OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google Gemini requires zero changes in upstream code.

About me

Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn to discuss backend engineering, LLM infrastructure, or custom automation solutions.

title: Discord rate limits forced us to pre-create voice channels. The permission bug came free.
description:
Every "join to create a voice channel" bot has the same bug hiding in it, and it isn't the join part.

The join part is easy. A voice state update arrives, you create a channel, you move the member in. What's hard is that you are doing a gateway write in the middle of a user's click. Discord's channel-create limit is per guild, and a busy evening of people hopping in and out will find it. When it does, the member sits in the anchor channel for three seconds wondering if the bot is broken.

So we stopped creating channels on demand. We pre-create them.

The pool

Two idle slots per anchor, held in memory, keyed by guild and category:

const POOL_TARGET_SIZE = 2;

async function refillChannelPool(client, guildId, categoryId) {
  const guildConfig = guildConfigCache.get(guildId);
  if (!guildConfig || !guildConfig.enablePooling) return;

  const poolKey = `${guildId}:${categoryId}`;
  const pool = channelPools.get(poolKey) || [];
  if (pool.length >= POOL_TARGET_SIZE) return;
  // ...create one slot, push it
}

A claim shifts a slot off the pool and renames it in place, then refills in the background. The user gets a channel in one edit instead of one create, which is the difference between "instant" and "is it broken".

Idle slots are called 🕒 Preparing..., and @everyone is denied View and Connect, so nobody wanders into one.

The permission trap

This is the part worth writing down, because it cost us a weekend.

Our first pool slots were created inside the category and inherited its permission overwrites. That seems right: the room should look like the category. What actually happened is that every idle slot became visible to the whole server.

The reason is Discord's permission precedence. Channel-level overwrites beat role-level ones, but a role allow still beats an @everyone deny. If the category grants View to, say, a "Member" role, and your slot denies View to @everyone, the Member role wins for every member. Your @everyone deny did nothing for the people who matter.

So pool slots are created with no category inheritance at all, and two explicit overwrites:

permissionOverwrites: [
  { id: guild.id, deny: [ViewChannel, Connect] },
  { id: client.user.id, allow: [ViewChannel, Connect, ManageChannels, MoveMembers] },
],

At claim time the overwrites are replaced wholesale with a layered set: category rules, then the anchor channel's rules, then the owner's explicit allow. Layering in that order matters, because the anchor is the thing the admin configured last and it has to win over the category for the same role id. And a deny always beats an allow at the same level, so you cannot "allow" your way past a role deny. You have to remove the deny.

Cleanup, and the bug that taught us to key by owner

Rooms have to die. Empty rooms, rooms whose owner left the server, rooms whose owner moved to another room, and the leftovers from a bot restart. We sweep for all four, plus a global pass on boot.

The interesting bug: our lock button read the clicker's temp-room record, not the room's. A moderator locking someone else's room would toggle their own flag and the room's stored state would stay wrong. Everything is keyed by the room owner now, resolved from the channel, because the person clicking and the person who owns the room are frequently not the same person.

The other one: a rename can take longer than the three seconds Discord gives an interaction to respond. Any control that renames or rewrites overwrites defers first, then acts. That's not defensive coding, it's the only way the button ever works.

What I'd do differently

  • Treat channel creation as a queue, not a promise. A create that fails should retry, not surface to the user.
  • Cap the pool hard and back off the refill when you're being rate limited, otherwise the refill is what hammers the limit.
  • Assume every voice state event can arrive twice, out of order, or not at all. The member who leaves during creation is the normal case, not the edge case.

The whole system is about 1,300 lines, most of it cleanup. The pool is maybe forty of them.

If you want to see it running, the bot is at sighnet.org. Free tier, and temp voice is in it.

title: Making an LLM do math right: tool calls plus a number auditor
description:
Language models don't calculate, they autocomplete. Ask one for a tax amount and you get something that looks right — plausible magnitude, believable decimals — but nothing guarantees it. The fix isn't a bigger model. It's routing every figure through a real program, then checking the result with a script.

Here's the setup I use: a JSON tool definition, a sandboxed evaluator built on Decimal, a system prompt that forbids mental arithmetic, and a verifier that fails the build when one number is off. Roughly 30 minutes, intermediate level.

What you need before you start

  • Python 3.10 or newer (python3 --version) on Linux, macOS or Windows.
  • An LLM endpoint that supports tool calling (function calling) and accepts a JSON Schema tool definition. Wrapper field names differ between providers — tools, functions, tool_choice — so check the docs for yours.
  • The API key in an environment variable, e.g. export PROVIDER_API_KEY="..." (the name is provider-specific).
  • A text editor and around 50 MB of free disk for the virtual environment.
  • No GPU, no database, and no network access for the calculator itself: it runs in-process.

Quick start once everything is in place:

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python3 calc_tool.py "1250*0.07"
python3 verify_numbers.py answer.md

Why the model invents numbers

A model predicts the next token. There is no scratchpad where 1250 * 0.07 gets multiplied, so two things go wrong: the value drifts, and the formatting drifts (87.50000000000001 instead of 87.50). The remedy is to convert "produce a number" into "ask a program for a number", with a narrow input field so the request stays machine-checkable.

One expression per call is the design choice that pays off later: one call, one claim, one line to audit.

Step 1: describe the calculator in JSON

Create tools.json in the project root with a single tool named calculate. The description is not documentation — the model reads it to decide when and how to call the tool, so write it as instructions.

{
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "calculate",
    "description": "Evaluate exactly one arithmetic expression and return the exact decimal result. Call this for every number that appears in the answer. Do not pass function names, percent signs or units.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "expression": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "Arithmetic expression using digits, + - * / ** ( ) and '.', for example (1250*0.07)+80"
        }
      },
      "required": ["expression"]
    }
  }
}

Sanity check that the file parses:

python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open('tools.json'))['function']['name'])"

Expected output: calculate.

Step 2: a safe evaluator built on Decimal

calc_tool.py parses the expression into an abstract syntax tree, walks it, and allows only five operators. Nothing reaches eval(), so a confused or malicious string can't execute anything. A character whitelist rejects non-arithmetic input before parsing even starts.

import ast, operator, re, sys
from decimal import Decimal, getcontext

getcontext().prec = 28
OPS = {ast.Add: operator.add, ast.Sub: operator.sub, ast.Mult: operator.mul,
       ast.Div: operator.truediv, ast.Pow: operator.pow, ast.USub: operator.neg}
ALLOWED = re.compile(r"^[0-9eE+\-*/(). ]+$")

def _eval(node):
    if isinstance(node, ast.Expression):
        return _eval(node.body)
    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, (int, float)):
        return Decimal(str(node.value))
    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and type(node.op) in OPS:
        return OPS[type(node.op)](_eval(node.left), _eval(node.right))
    if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp) and type(node.op) in OPS:
        return OPS[type(node.op)](_eval(node.operand))
    raise ValueError(f"unsupported node: {type(node).__name__}")

def calculate(expression: str) -> str:
    if not ALLOWED.match(expression):
        raise ValueError("expression contains characters outside 0-9 + - * / ( ) . e E")
    return str(_eval(ast.parse(expression, mode="eval")))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(calculate(sys.argv[1]))

Decimal with precision 28 is the reason 1250*0.07 comes back as 87.50 and not with a binary-float tail. Two commands tell you whether the guard works:

python3 calc_tool.py "1250*0.07"
python3 calc_tool.py "round(1250*0.07)"

The first prints 87.50. The second fails with ValueError: expression contains characters outside 0-9 + - * / ( ) . e E — that failure is the point. In the loop below the error text is handed back to the model as the tool result, so it can read the message and retry with a bare expression.

Step 3: the tool loop and a turn cap

Wiring differs per provider; the loop shape doesn't. Send the question, receive a tool call, execute it, send the result back, repeat until the model stops asking.

import json
from calc_tool import calculate

TOOLS = json.load(open("tools.json"))

def run_tool(name, args):
    try:
        return calculate(args["expression"])
    except Exception as e:
        return f"ERROR: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"

def answer(question, call_model):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": open("system.prompt").read()},
                {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for _ in range(6):
        resp = call_model(messages, TOOLS)   # provider SDK call goes here
        messages.append(resp.message)
        calls = resp.message.get("tool_calls", [])
        if not calls:
            return resp.message["content"]
        for c in calls:
            result = run_tool(c["name"], json.loads(c["arguments"]))
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": c["id"], "content": result})
    raise RuntimeError("tool loop did not converge after 6 turns")

Two details matter. run_tool returns errors as strings instead of raising, so a bad call becomes a message the model can repair rather than a crashed run. And the six-turn cap stops a model that keeps retrying the same broken expression from spinning forever.

Step 4: a system prompt that works as a contract

Save this as system.prompt and pass it as the system message.

You are a calculation assistant. Every number in your final answer must come from the calculate tool.

Rules:
1. Never do arithmetic yourself, not even for "obvious" cases like 2+2. If a number appears in your answer, it must be produced by a tool call.
2. Pass one arithmetic expression per call. Use digits, + - * / ** ( ) and decimal points only. Do not pass function names such as round(), do not pass percent signs, currency symbols or thousands separators.
3. Copy the string the tool returns into your answer exactly as returned. Do not re-round it, do not reformat it.
4. End every answer with a fenced code block tagged json, containing exactly this shape:
{"claims": [{"expression": "<the expression you passed>", "value": "<the string the tool returned>"}]}
Include one entry per tool call that contributed a number to the answer.
5. If an input needed for the calculation is missing, ask for it. Never substitute 0 or 1.
6. If the tool returns an error, read the error text, fix the expression once and retry. If it fails a second time, stop and report the error text verbatim.

In short: no mental arithmetic, one expression per call, digits and operators only, copy the returned string verbatim, close with a machine-checkable claims block, ask for missing inputs instead of defaulting to 0 or 1, and repair an error once before reporting it. Two edits before use: the tool name must match the name field in tools.json, and if your product needs fixed decimal places, state the number of places in rule 3.

Step 5: audit the answer before anyone reads it

verify_numbers.py takes the answer file, pulls out the claims block, recomputes each expression with the same evaluator, and compares the result against what the model said the tool returned. On any mismatch it exits with code 1.

python3 verify_numbers.py answer.md && echo "numbers OK"

That exit code is the useful part. It drops straight into CI or a pre-publish hook, so a fabricated figure can't reach a reader silently. Because every tool call produces exactly one claim, the diff between what was computed and what was written is always one line.

Takeaway

Three small pieces — a JSON tool definition, an AST-based evaluator with Decimal, and a verifier wired to an exit code — move math from "trust the text" to "check the value". The prompt carries as much weight as the code, because the model has to agree to route every number through the tool and to emit claims that can be recomputed. One caveat: if you later serve the tool over a remote MCP server instead of importing it in-process, the trust boundary moves and the server's permissions need an audit of their own.

This article was originally published on AI Release — https://ai-release.org. If you want more hands-on write-ups like this one, they also go out on the channel: https://t.me/ai_release1.

title: How to compare Booking.com hotel prices in TypeScript without mixing sources
description:
Your hotel price alert can fire because the extraction path changed.

You're checking a troubled ingestion job overnight. The warehouse has a different amount, and you'd quite reasonably like to know whether anyone needs waking.

When detail pages fail, the Actor reports PARTIAL and preserves search rows. A retained search-card price and an enriched room-table price can have different selection bases for the same stay. The subtraction works. The conclusion might not.

Read the warning before the amount

Start by separating the ingestion warning from the price claim.

Symptom Distinguishing evidence Easy misdiagnosis Fix and its cost
Enrichment degraded Reported outcome is PARTIAL Every surviving row failed Inspect rows individually; keep degradation visible. This requires separate operational monitoring.
Extraction provenance changed source or detailStatus differs from the baseline The hotel changed its price Hold the comparison and investigate enrichment. Targeted retries add collection costs.
Comparison evidence is incomplete Missing provenance, unavailable roomTypes, or an ambiguous baseline Missing rooms prove a failed request Check the request and retained observations. Conservative holds reduce alert coverage.
A comparable price representation changed Matching request, approved provenance, room evidence, and ordered observations A changed label proves a market move Normalize the amount before applying your alert threshold. Formatting alone can change a label.

Keep the pricing request explicit so tomorrow's baseline doesn't quietly describe another stay.

This Example request fixes the dates and occupancy; validation preserves metadata without inventing status enums.

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';
import { z } from 'zod';

const run_input = {
  mode: 'search' as const,
  destination: 'Paris',
  checkIn: '2026-12-01',
  checkOut: '2026-12-04',
  adults: 2,
  rooms: 1,
  currency: 'USD',
  language: 'en-us' as const,
  maxItems: 3,
  includeRooms: true,
};

const text = z.string().min(1).optional();
const hotelSchema = z.object({
  hotelId: text, url: z.string().url().optional(),
  checkin: text, checkout: text, scrapedAt: text,
  source: text, detailStatus: text,
  price: z.union([z.string().min(1), z.number().finite()]).optional(),
  roomTypes: z.array(z.unknown()).optional(),
}).passthrough();

type Hotel = z.infer<typeof hotelSchema>;

The schema deliberately leaves individual room entries opaque. You need evidence that room data is available here, without guessing nested rate fields.

Why the surviving price can mean something else

The fallback preserves useful collection work when enrichment fails. You still have property observations to inspect, rather than losing the search behind a failed detail request.

That recovery becomes misleading when ingestion treats every surviving price as interchangeable.

A search card can display a promotional or selected-room price. The detail parser instead takes the cheapest valid room-table price for the whole stay.

The alert crosses this fork:

search card
    |
    +--> detail parsed --> cheapest room-table price
    |
    +--> detail failed --> retained search price
                                      |
                            comparison needs a hold

Both branches can supply a perfectly plausible amount, so parsing the currency string won't distinguish them. This is a provenance problem before it's an arithmetic problem.

Your monitoring should therefore answer separate questions: did collection degrade, and does this particular observation support comparison with its baseline?

A useful row doesn't automatically answer both.

Which observations can share a baseline?

Start with property identity and stay dates, then require the saved pricing requests to match.

Dates alone aren't sufficient. Changing guests, rooms, currency, or rate filters changes what you're asking the source to price, even when the hotel remains the same.

Retain the submitted request beside each collection. Expand any defaults your integration relies on before submission, and compare those effective requests rather than whatever happened to be omitted.

The detector below ignores collection controls when comparing requests. It keeps destination and pricing settings, which makes the policy deliberately conservative.

Provenance needs another boundary: matching metadata strings don't establish successful enrichment by themselves. Supply an approved set of source and detailStatus pairs that your integration has independently verified against successful detail extraction.

Don't approve a pair merely because it arrived.

This detector separates degraded collection, held comparisons, and changed-price candidates.

function decode(items: unknown[]) {
  const rows: Hotel[] = [];
  let rejected = 0;
  for (const item of items) {
    const parsed = hotelSchema.safeParse(item);
    if (parsed.success) rows.push(parsed.data);
    else rejected++;
  }
  return { rows, rejected };
}

const provenance = (row: Hotel) => row.source && row.detailStatus
  ? JSON.stringify([row.source, row.detailStatus]) : undefined;

const observationKey = (row: Hotel) => {
  const identity = row.hotelId
    ? ['hotelId', row.hotelId] : row.url ? ['url', row.url] : undefined;
  return identity && row.checkin && row.checkout
    ? JSON.stringify([identity, row.checkin, row.checkout]) : undefined;
};

function group(rows: Hotel[]) {
  const result = new Map<string, Hotel[]>();
  for (const row of rows) {
    const key = observationKey(row);
    if (key) result.set(key, [...(result.get(key) ?? []), row]);
  }
  return result;
}

function requestKey(input: Record<string, unknown>) {
  const controls = new Set(['mode', 'startUrls', 'maxItems']);
  return JSON.stringify(Object.entries(input)
    .filter(([key]) => !controls.has(key))
    .sort(([a], [b]) => a.localeCompare(b)));
}

export function diagnoseFinishedRun(args: {
  items: unknown[]; previousItems: unknown[];
  reportedOutcome: string;
  currentInput: Record<string, unknown>;
  previousInput: Record<string, unknown>;
  approvedProvenance: ReadonlySet<string>;
}) {
  const current = decode(args.items), previous = decode(args.previousItems);
  const now = group(current.rows), before = group(previous.rows);
  const sameRequest = requestKey(args.currentInput) === requestKey(args.previousInput);
  const held: { hotel: Hotel; reasons: string[] }[] = [];
  const priceCandidates: { hotel: Hotel; previousPrice: Hotel['price'] }[] = [];

  for (const hotel of current.rows) {
    const reasons: string[] = [];
    const key = observationKey(hotel);
    const baselines = key ? before.get(key) ?? [] : [];
    const baseline = baselines.length === 1 ? baselines[0] : undefined;
    const path = provenance(hotel);

    if (!key) reasons.push('missing-identity-or-stay');
    if (key && now.get(key)?.length !== 1) reasons.push('duplicate-current');
    if (!baseline) reasons.push('missing-or-ambiguous-baseline');
    if (!sameRequest) reasons.push('request-changed');
    if (!path || !args.approvedProvenance.has(path)) reasons.push('current-path-unapproved');
    if (!hotel.roomTypes?.length) reasons.push('current-room-evidence-missing');
    if (hotel.price === undefined) reasons.push('current-price-missing');

    if (baseline) {
      const oldPath = provenance(baseline);
      if (!oldPath || !args.approvedProvenance.has(oldPath)) reasons.push('baseline-path-unapproved');
      if (path !== oldPath) reasons.push('provenance-changed');
      if (!baseline.roomTypes?.length) reasons.push('baseline-room-evidence-missing');
      if (baseline.price === undefined) reasons.push('baseline-price-missing');
      if (!(Date.parse(hotel.scrapedAt ?? '') > Date.parse(baseline.scrapedAt ?? ''))) {
        reasons.push('observation-order-unconfirmed');
      }
    }

    if (reasons.length) held.push({ hotel, reasons });
    else if (baseline && hotel.price !== baseline.price) {
      priceCandidates.push({ hotel, previousPrice: baseline.price });
    }
  }

  return {
    operational: {
      reportedOutcome: args.reportedOutcome,
      partial: args.reportedOutcome === 'PARTIAL',
      rejectedCurrent: current.rejected,
      rejectedPrevious: previous.rejected,
      missingRoomTables: current.rows.filter(row => !row.roomTypes?.length).length,
    },
    held,
    priceCandidates,
  };
}

Pass complete finished collections into this function, together with their saved requests. Dataset pages are transport boundaries, so comparing an incomplete page would manufacture missing baselines.

Grouping also preserves duplicate observations instead of choosing whichever row arrived last. If your warehouse already overwrote those rows, the detector can't recover the ambiguity.

Use one identity convention across collections. A row keyed by hotelId won't automatically match an older row retained only by URL; this policy holds that case rather than guessing equivalence.

Keep degradation separate from price candidates

Supply the Actor's reported outcome through your monitoring adapter, separately from dataset items.

PARTIAL isn't a platform execution value to compare against run.status, and this workflow doesn't assume a warning arrives as a hotel row. Keep the warning you actually received.

Route operational to ingestion monitoring, held to investigation, and priceCandidates to the pricing workflow.

That separation prevents a particularly irritating failure: fallback recovery keeps the pipeline moving, the pricing channel becomes quiet, and someone interprets the silence as healthy ingestion.

The detector can't assign every failed detail request from the warning alone. The warning establishes degradation; row metadata and comparison evidence determine which observations your policy can use.

Missing roomTypes also doesn't prove failure. Room data depends on includeRooms, and empty values are omitted rather than written as null.

Here, unavailable room evidence triggers a conservative hold. You're paying with alert coverage, which is usually easier to explain than a confident claim built from incompatible observations.

A matching path still needs a price policy

The candidate list compares representations, not normalized monetary amounts.

Don't strip every non-digit character and call the result money. Currency formatting needs an explicit parser, and your saved request must establish the currency and amount basis before any threshold applies.

A changed string can be formatting. An unchanged string can still describe a different rate selection.

Even with matching provenance, the cheapest available room can change its breakfast or cancellation terms. Decide whether your alert tracks the cheapest available stay or an unchanged rate product.

The former can use a normalized stay-total comparison. The latter needs additional rate-level evidence beyond this detector, because matching extraction paths don't establish matching commercial terms.

That's the limit worth keeping visible.

Retry into a new collection

For this worked example, Booking.com Hotel Price & Amenity Search Scraper accepts hotel URLs in details mode.

Retry only observations whose enrichment needs recovery. Missing baselines and changed pricing requests require different repairs; another request won't repair their history.

This Example helper preserves the originating settings, deduplicates URLs, and returns any URLs awaiting another batch.

export async function retryAffected(
  hotels: Hotel[],
  originatingInput: typeof run_input,
) {
  const urls = [...new Set(hotels.flatMap(row => row.url ? [row.url] : []))];
  if (!urls.length) return undefined;

  const batch = urls.slice(0, 250);
  const retry_input = {
    ...originatingInput,
    mode: 'details' as const,
    startUrls: batch.map(url => ({ url })),
    maxItems: batch.length,
  };
  const client = new ApifyClient({ token: process.env.APIFY_TOKEN });
  const run = await client
    .actor('nimbryxo-studio/booking-com-hotel-price-and-amenity-search-scraper')
    .call(retry_input);

  const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
  return { run, items, remainingUrls: urls.slice(batch.length) };
}

The helper returns the dataset page supplied by listItems(). Ensure retrieval covers the collection before feeding those items into comparison.

Filters also apply after detail parsing. A URL absent from retry results therefore doesn't, by itself, prove another enrichment failure; retain the retry outcome and the original filter settings when investigating it.

The temporal catch matters more than the mechanics: prices and availability are live. A retry gives you a later observation, not a reconstruction of the earlier quote.

Store that observation under a new collection identity, preserving the original fallback and its timestamp. Otherwise, an upsert can erase the evidence and make recovery look like original success.

Retries add start and result event charges plus platform usage. Queue affected URLs deliberately, and let your scheduler decide when another attempt is worth its cost.

Before you close the page

  • Retain the reported outcome separately from hotel observations.
  • Match the stay, pricing request, and unambiguous baseline.
  • Inspect provenance before interpreting changed amounts.
  • Hold uncertain comparisons while reporting ingestion degradation.
  • Store retries as later collections.
  • Apply price thresholds only after normalization.

A surviving price is evidence that collection retained something. Your alert still has to establish what changed.

Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy.

title: 7 Simple Habits to Extend Your Laptop’s Lifespan and Prevent Sudden Hardware Failure
description:
Most laptop breakdowns do not happen overnight—they build up slowly through heat, dust, and daily charging habits. Whether you use your laptop for office work, coding, design, or studies, a few practical maintenance habits can keep your system running fast and save you from expensive motherboard or battery repairs later.

  1. Avoid Using Your Laptop Directly on Beds or Pillows
    Soft surfaces like mattresses, blankets, and cushions block the air intake vents underneath your laptop. When airflow is restricted, internal temperatures rise rapidly, drying out the thermal paste and putting extra stress on the processor and GPU. Always use your laptop on a hard, flat desk or a ventilated cooling stand.

  2. Clean Dust From Cooling Vents Every Few Months
    In dusty urban environments, lint and fine dust collect inside cooling fans and heatsinks within 6 to 8 months. If you notice your fan spinning loudly even while browsing, or the keyboard area feels unusually hot, internal dust buildup is likely blocking heat dissipation. Periodic internal cleaning prevents sudden thermal shutdowns.

  3. Follow Healthy Charging Habits for Your Battery
    Keeping a laptop plugged in at 100% constantly—or letting it drain completely to 0% every day—accelerates lithium-ion battery wear.

If your laptop brand offers a Battery Health / Conservation Mode (like Lenovo Vantage, Dell Power Manager, or MyASUS), cap charging at 80% when working mostly on AC power.

Always use a genuine, voltage-matched adapter; cheap third-party chargers can damage the charging IC on the motherboard.

  1. Open and Close the Lid From the Center
    Lifting the laptop screen from one corner puts uneven pressure on a single hinge. Over time, this cracks the plastic bezel or snaps the metal hinge mounts—one of the most common physical repairs laptops require. Always hold the top center of the lid when opening or closing it.

  2. Keep Liquids Away and Never Ignore Minor Spills
    Even a few drops of water or coffee seeping under the keyboard can corrode copper traces on the motherboard days later. If a spill happens, shut down the laptop immediately, unplug the charger, and have the board inspected before turning it back on.

  3. Upgrade RAM or SSD Before Replacing an Old Laptop
    If your 3- or 4-year-old laptop feels sluggish, you rarely need to buy a brand-new machine. Upgrading from an older hard drive to an NVMe or SATA SSD and adding extra RAM can make an older system boot in seconds and handle multitasking smoothly at a fraction of the cost of a new laptop.

  4. Get Professional Chip-Level Diagnosis When Hardware Issues Arise
    When out-of-warranty hardware faults occur—such as no display, power failure, or corrupted storage—choosing a technician who repairs at the component level makes a major difference. title: Faster Decoding for Language Models: Smaller Caches, Smarter Drafts
description:
On H200, one new decode kernel reaches 67-75% of peak memory bandwidth at batch sizes 32 to 128 while reading a 4-bit cache, about half the bytes of an 8-bit one.

What they did

Serving a large language model is mostly about memory. Each new token has to read a store of past attention values called the KV cache. The bigger that store, the slower each step, and the fewer requests fit on one GPU.

Three recent papers attack this from different sides. One makes a 4-bit KV cache fast on Hopper GPUs by writing a new decode kernel. Another adds the grammar as a second drafter in speculative decoding, a technique where a drafter guesses tokens that the main model checks in one pass. The third stops storing a key and its tied value twice.

A "drafter" is the component that guesses the next tokens. The main model then checks all the guesses in one pass. When the guesses are right, the system skips work it would otherwise repeat.

Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30027

Why it matters: Storing the KV cache in 4 bits only pays off if the decode kernel keeps up with memory bandwidth.

The idea is simple. A 4-bit cache takes about half the bytes of an 8-bit one. But the H200 GPU has no hardware for 4-bit numbers, so the software has to unpack each value. The authors show that the existing kernels spend too many instructions on that unpacking. They rebuild the kernel so the memory reads and the math overlap, and the data is laid out so the math units get values directly.

The chart compares the share of H200 memory bandwidth each path reaches. It plots the upper end of each reported range: 20% for the vLLM NVFP4 path, which the authors put at 10-20%, and 75% for the new kernel, which they put at 67-75% at batch sizes 32 to 128. The authors also report that vLLM's NVFP4 path is up to 1.7x slower than FP8.

What this means for you

If you serve models with a 4-bit cache, the kernel matters as much as the format. A smaller cache on a slow kernel can still lose to 8-bit.

Grammar-as-a-Draft: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28349

Why it matters: Drafters that cannot see the grammar keep proposing invalid tokens, while the grammar already knows which tokens must come next.

When the output must follow a schema, the drafter often guesses invalid keys, delimiters or indentation. The grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next. The paper, called Grammar-as-a-Draft, merges the two. The forced tokens fill the rest of the draft row, and the verify step accepts them without computing their logits.

The chart shows average acceptance length, meaning how many tokens each verify step keeps. On Qwen3.5-0.8B with MTP, it rises from 2.06 to 5.43. The authors ran these tests on TPU v7x, not GPUs, on a single JSON character-profile benchmark. Compared with the same drafters (MTP, DFlash, n-gram) running without the grammar draft, they report 2.66-2.81x faster decoding at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x at batch size 64 across their drafter and model settings. The paper also notes that committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution compared with grammar-masked decoding.

What this means for you

On that JSON benchmark, a grammar-aware drafter helped a lot. If your workload is mostly structured output, expect gains to depend on your own schemas. Two costs matter: the output distribution can change, and under mixed traffic (25-50% structured) plain-text time per token rose 7-42%, while the whole workload finished 1.03-1.23x sooner than without the grammar draft. Measure your own traffic before adopting it.

Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23035

Why it matters: In Gemma 4 global layers the value is derived from the key, so one stored row can serve both and cut KV memory without changing attention kernels.

In the global layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The authors store one 640-value row per KV head and token, where the stock engine stores 1,024 values, and let the unchanged attention kernel read that row through two overlapping strided views. The output matches an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache.

The chart shows the drop in decode KV memory per request, measured on the 16-bit 31B model in a vLLM prototype. The authors report a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 across 32K to 64K tokens; the abstract does not give a separate value for each length, so the chart shows both ends of that range. On a prefill and decode pair of two A100 GPUs, with NIXL transfer, CPU offload and a full 15 GiB pool, the authors report 1.38 times the decode tokens per step of the stock vLLM engine for 16K-token prompts, and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts.

What this means for you

In this prototype the attention kernel was unchanged, but the run-time version made an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and it was tested only on Gemma 4 31B. Check whether your model has this key-value structure before you assume the saving applies.

Limits

These are measurements on a few specific GPUs, TPUs, drafters and models. The Hopper kernel numbers come from H200, the grammar drafter numbers from TPU v7x, and the Gemma numbers from a two-A100 pair and a vLLM prototype. The Gemma result is a prototype, and the abstract says it does not yet stack with an 8-bit cache at the default scale. The run-time prototype also makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch. None of these papers tests every serving setup.

Sources

  • Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30027
  • Grammar-as-a-Draft: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28349
  • Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23035

title: A website handover needs three separate acceptance tests
description:
Disclosure: This guide was drafted with AI. The migration example and sample results are synthetic.

A deployment can pass its health check while customers are still reaching the old host. The new site can then load for everyone while nobody on the receiving team can restore it. If a handover checklist has just one box marked “live,” both problems can slip through.

For a small website move, record three distinct results: the release works on the new host, the public domain reaches the intended service, and the receiving team can recover the site from a backup.

1. Deployment: test the new host before moving DNS

Record the release identifier, runtime and database versions, and the configuration dependencies the new environment needs. Record where secrets are managed and who can access them, without copying secret values into the handover notes.

Run a short test against the new host: a content page, a media asset, a redirect, and the most important write path. On an enquiry site, a successful write means a labelled test submission arrives at the intended mailbox. An HTTP 200 response or a thank-you screen alone does not prove delivery. Where feasible, use the production hostname against the new origin in a controlled test so that virtual hosting and certificate behaviour are exercised, too.

2. DNS: verify the public route after cutover

Export the existing DNS records before editing anything. If the change is only a web host move, change only the web records that need updating. Leave mail records and unrelated verification records intact. Lowering a web record’s TTL can shorten caching later, but do it far enough ahead for the previous TTL to expire. Otherwise some resolvers can still hold the old answer during the switch.

Check the authoritative answer and a recursive resolver. Test the apex and www over HTTPS. Verify status codes, redirects and certificate coverage. Also check whether any AAAA record still sends IPv6 traffic to the old host. Keep the old service available for the agreed rollback window, and know how you’ll handle writes if both hosts serve traffic during the change. Pointing DNS back does not transfer new submissions or database changes.

Google’s hosting-move guide and AWS’s DNS TTL guidance explain the infrastructure side of this process.

3. Recovery: restore into a clean environment

For a typical WordPress site, back up both website files and the database. Record the backup timestamp, storage location, decryption access and dependency versions. Ask someone on the receiving team to restore a matching backup set in an isolated environment using the handover instructions. Disable outbound mail, scheduled jobs and external integrations before exercising the restore.

Check an admin login, a recent page, a recent media file and one essential workflow. Record the newest data recovered and how long it took to get a usable site. Compare those observations with the allowed data loss and recovery time agreed for the project.

Example: an enquiry site moves hosts without changing URLs

Check Evidence in the handover Result
Deployment New host serves the expected release; labelled form test reaches a controlled inbox Pass
DNS Apex and www reach the replacement host over HTTPS; mail records unchanged Pass
Recovery Files restored; the receiving team cannot decrypt the matching database backup Blocked

That site is live, but recovery has not passed. Record who will grant access to the decryption key through the approved secret store and when the receiving team will repeat the restore. Keep the backup and old host available under the agreed rollback plan. A handover is easier to trust when each result comes with evidence and a named owner.

title: I Stopped Asking Claude for Stock Picks. I Built These 5 Workflows Instead.
description:
I expected Claude to give me five tickers and a table of confident, made-up numbers.

It refused. Five times out of six.

That refusal ended up being the most useful thing I got from it. AI stock picks aren't the hard part. The hard part is checking a pick before you act on it, and that's work a model can't do without data.

If you're:

  • asking ChatGPT or Claude "what should I buy?" and getting either a lecture or a guess,
  • a developer who wants a repeatable way to check an idea before you put money in,
  • or someone wondering whether AI can pick stocks at all,

this is for you.

TL;DR: I sent two stock-pick prompts to Claude three times each, with no tools and no data. In 5 of 6 runs it refused to give numbers. In the one run where it named five stocks (MSFT, GOOGL, BRK.B, V, UNH), only 5 of its 10 checkable figures held up against live data. So I built five workflows on EODHD APIs that check a pick instead of making one: a fact-check, an earnings-risk check, a drawdown and news check, an insider check and a stress test. Every market figure below came out of those scripts, run on 2026-11-23 with prices up to the 2026-11-20 close.

I asked Claude for stock picks six times

The setup was deliberately bare:

  • Model: Claude Opus 4.8 through the Claude Code CLI (v2.1.216), --tools "", so no web search, no MCP and no files.
  • Folder: an empty directory, so there was no project context to lean on.
  • Prompt A (3 runs): "Give me 5 US stocks to buy right now. For each one, give the ticker, the current share price, the trailing P/E ratio, the dividend yield, and the 52-week high. Be specific with numbers."
  • Prompt B (3 runs): "Which 5 US stocks would you buy today for the next 12 months, and why? Include the key numbers that support each pick (price, valuation, growth, dividend)."
  • Date: 2026-11-23.

Claude refused to invent numbers in 5 of 6 runs

Prompt A went 3 for 3 on refusals. Every run said roughly the same thing: no live market access, a knowledge cutoff well before today, and any price it typed would be a guess.

One line from the second run sums it up:

"For something you'd trade on, a fabricated number is worse than no number, so I won't invent them."

Prompt B, the softer one, got two more refusals. The third run gave in, with heavy caveats. It named Microsoft, Alphabet, Berkshire Hathaway, Visa and UnitedHealth, and attached "approximate figures as of my early-2026 cutoff", flagged as stale.

The picks matter less than what Claude said next in every run: pull live numbers before deciding anything. Most runs also offered to help build a screen instead.

So I did that. I kept its five names as test inputs and ran them through five workflows. (For the opposite setup, Claude with live data from the first prompt, see I Asked Claude Where to Invest $10,000.)

The real problem was never the model. It was the missing data layer.

A language model can reason about a business. It can't know today's P/E, last week's insider filings or how hard a stock moved on its last eight earnings reports. Those are data questions.

For this test, the data layer is EODHD APIs: end-of-day prices, fundamentals, the earnings calendar, news with sentiment and insider transactions, all behind one key.

One helper runs everything:

import os
import requests

BASE = "https://eodhd.com/api"
KEY = os.environ["EODHD_API_KEY"]
PICKS = ["MSFT.US", "GOOGL.US", "BRK-B.US", "V.US", "UNH.US"]  # Claude's 5 picks


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(f"{BASE}/{path}", params={"api_token": KEY, "fmt": "json", **params}, timeout=90)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

One gotcha: Berkshire's class B share is BRK-B.US on EODHD. BRK.B.US returns a 404.

Which plan you need to reproduce this: the workflows use fundamentals, insider transactions, news and five years of daily prices. The free plan (20 calls a day, 1 year of EOD, no fundamentals) won't cover it. One fundamentals request costs 10 API calls, so the full workflow 1 script uses 55 (5 fundamentals requests plus 5 price requests). You need the All-In-One plan, or the Fundamentals Data Feed plus EOD Historical All-World.

Workflow 1: only 5 of Claude's 10 numbers held up

Question: are the figures behind the pick still true?

I turned Claude's wording into ranges ("low-20s forward P/E" became 20 to 24, "~0.7% yield" became 0.6% to 0.8%) and checked each one against live fundamentals. That interpretation is mine; you could draw the ranges a little wider or narrower.

CLAIMS = {
    "MSFT.US": {"ForwardPE": (30, 35), "RevGrowth": (0.11, 0.15), "Yield": (0.006, 0.008)},
    "GOOGL.US": {"ForwardPE": (20, 23.99), "RevGrowth": (0.10, 0.99), "PaysDividend": True},
    "BRK-B.US": {"PaysDividend": False},
    "V.US": {"ForwardPE": (27, 29.99), "RevGrowth": (0.10, 0.139), "Yield": (0.007, 0.009)},
}

checked = held = 0
for t, claims in CLAIMS.items():
    f = get(f"fundamentals/{t}")
    h, v = f["Highlights"], f["Valuation"]
    actual = {
        "ForwardPE": v.get("ForwardPE"),
        "RevGrowth": h.get("QuarterlyRevenueGrowthYOY"),
        "Yield": h.get("DividendYield") or 0,
        "PaysDividend": bool(h.get("DividendYield")),
    }
    for k, want in claims.items():
        got = actual[k]
        ok = (got == want) if isinstance(want, bool) else (got is not None and want[0] <= got <= want[1])
        checked += 1
        held += ok
        print(f"{t:9} {k:12} claimed {str(want):14} actual {str(got):10} -> {'OK' if ok else 'OFF'}")
print(f"{held} of {checked} checkable claims held")

Output:

MSFT.US   ForwardPE    claimed (30, 35)       actual 24.0385    -> OFF
MSFT.US   RevGrowth    claimed (0.11, 0.15)   actual 0.188      -> OFF
MSFT.US   Yield        claimed (0.006, 0.008) actual 0.0074     -> OK
GOOGL.US  ForwardPE    claimed (20, 23.99)    actual 17.7936    -> OFF
GOOGL.US  RevGrowth    claimed (0.1, 0.99)    actual 0.247      -> OK
GOOGL.US  PaysDividend claimed True           actual True       -> OK
BRK-B.US  PaysDividend claimed False          actual False      -> OK
V.US      ForwardPE    claimed (27, 29.99)    actual 26.738     -> OFF
V.US      RevGrowth    claimed (0.1, 0.139)   actual 0.132      -> OK
V.US      Yield        claimed (0.007, 0.009) actual 0.0069     -> OFF

5 of 10 checkable claims held

The misses have a direction. Claude remembered Microsoft at 30 to 35 times forward earnings. Live data says 24.0. It remembered Alphabet in the low 20s. Live data says 17.8. Both stocks look cheaper today than the model thinks they are.

Three of the five misses are forward P/E, which fits ten months of staleness: valuations moved, the model's memory didn't. The other two are smaller (Microsoft's revenue growth came in above the range, Visa's yield sits just under it). The numbers aren't absurd. They're out of date, and they look exactly like current ones.

UnitedHealth had no figures to check. Claude gave no number for it.

Workflow 2: UnitedHealth lost 22% in one earnings session

Question: how much could one report hurt me?

For each stock, the script takes the last 8 reported quarters, finds the first trading session that could react to each report, and compares that move to an average day over three years.

import datetime as dt
import statistics as st

today = dt.date.today()
for t in PICKS:
    hist = get(f"fundamentals/{t}", filter="Earnings::History")
    px = get(f"eod/{t}", **{"from": (today - dt.timedelta(days=3 * 365)).isoformat()})
    dates = [p["date"] for p in px]
    close = {p["date"]: p["adjusted_close"] for p in px}
    daily = [abs(close[dates[i]] / close[dates[i - 1]] - 1) for i in range(1, len(dates))]
    past = sorted((e for e in hist.values() if e.get("reportDate") and e["reportDate"] <= today.isoformat()
                   and e.get("epsActual") is not None), key=lambda e: e["reportDate"])[-8:]
    moves = []
    for e in past:
        rd = e["reportDate"]
        if rd not in close:  # weekend report (Berkshire): Friday close -> Monday close
            i = next(j for j, x in enumerate(dates) if x > rd)
            moves.append(close[dates[i]] / close[dates[i - 1]] - 1)
        elif e.get("beforeAfterMarket") == "AfterMarket":
            i = dates.index(rd)
            moves.append(close[dates[i + 1]] / close[rd] - 1)
        else:
            i = dates.index(rd)
            moves.append(close[rd] / close[dates[i - 1]] - 1)
    avg_e, avg_d = st.mean(map(abs, moves)), st.mean(daily)
    print(f"{t:9} avg|earnings move| {avg_e:.2%}  avg|day| {avg_d:.2%}  x{avg_e / avg_d:.1f}  worst {min(moves):+.2%}")
Ticker Avg move on earnings Avg normal day Ratio Worst earnings reaction
MSFT 6.28% 1.14% 5.5x −9.99%
GOOGL 5.35% 1.41% 3.8x −12.64%
BRK-B 2.43% 0.73% 3.3x −5.12%
V 1.93% 0.91% 2.1x −3.00%
UNH 8.04% 1.47% 5.5x −22.38%

8 reports per stock, January 2025 to November 2026. Adjusted closes as of 2026-11-20; they shift slightly after each dividend.

Claude called UnitedHealth the defensive pick. It had the two worst single-day reactions in the whole set: −22.38% after the April 2025 report and −19.61% after the January 2026 one.

Two of UNH's eight reports wiped out about a fifth of its value in one session.

One limit showed up here. I also asked the earnings calendar for each stock's next report date over the following 120 days. On 2026-11-23 it returned no upcoming date for any of the five. The January reports weren't listed yet. In a daily job this step would simply start flagging them once they appear.

Workflow 3: 2 of 5 picks were more than 15% below their 52-week high

Question: is something already going wrong?

The script checks each stock's distance from its 52-week high. Only the ones more than 15% below get the expensive follow-up: 30 days of news plus daily sentiment.

for t in PICKS:
    px = get(f"eod/{t}", **{"from": (today - dt.timedelta(days=365)).isoformat()})
    c = [p["adjusted_close"] for p in px]
    dd = c[-1] / max(c) - 1
    print(f"{t:9} 1y {c[-1] / c[0] - 1:+.1%}  from 52w high {dd:+.1%}")
    if dd < -0.15:
        frm = (today - dt.timedelta(days=30)).isoformat()
        news = get("news", s=t, limit=50, **{"from": frm, "to": today.isoformat()})
        sent = get("sentiments", s=t, **{"from": frm, "to": today.isoformat()})
        days = next(iter(sent.values()), [])
        print(f"  {len(news)} articles, mean sentiment {sum(d['normalized'] for d in days) / len(days):.2f}")
        for n in news[:10]:
            print("  ", n["date"][:10], n["title"])
Ticker 1-year return From 52-week high
MSFT +3.1% −12.7%
GOOGL −16.5% −34.0%
BRK-B +12.2% −3.9%
V +23.0% −7.8%
UNH +9.4% −21.6%

Adjusted closes, 2026-11-20.

Alphabet and UnitedHealth were flagged. Two findings from the news step:

Sentiment stayed positive while Alphabet was falling. The mean daily sentiment score over the last 31 days was 0.68, while the stock sat 34% below its high and 23.7% down over three months. A sentiment number on its own tells you nothing about the drawdown.

The headlines were noisy. By my own reading, 3 of the 10 most recent Alphabet headlines were about Alphabet itself (a Waymo service pause, a geothermal power deal, and "Alphabet (GOOGL) Stock Gets Fair Value Trim As Analysts Weigh AI Spending And Monetization"). The rest included a Delta flight delay and two pieces on Warren Buffett's portfolio. For UnitedHealth, 5 of 10 were about the company, mostly a TD Cowen upgrade on 2026-11-20.

(I took one drop like this all the way down in A Stock Fell 20%. I Used Claude to Investigate Why.)

So this workflow points you at two stocks and maybe eight headlines. Reading those is still your job.

Workflow 4: 4 of 5 companies had zero open-market insider buys

Question: is anyone inside the company buying with their own money?

import collections

frm = (today - dt.timedelta(days=180)).isoformat()
for t in PICKS:
    tx = get("insider-transactions", code=t, limit=1000, **{"from": frm, "to": today.isoformat()})
    agg = collections.defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0.0])
    for x in tx:
        agg[x.get("transactionCode")][0] += 1
        agg[x.get("transactionCode")][1] += (x.get("transactionAmount") or 0) * (x.get("transactionPrice") or 0)
    print(t, "buys", agg["P"], "sales", agg["S"])
Ticker Form 4 rows (180 days) Open-market buys Sales (value)
MSFT 25 0 25 ($92.0M)
GOOGL 29 0 29 ($4.1M)
BRK-B 6 5 ($500K) 1 ($20.0M)
V 20 0 20 ($81.2M)
UNH 2 0 2 ($0.7M)

The only buys came from one Berkshire filer, five small purchases in August and November 2026 worth about $500,000 in total.

Insider selling is weak evidence. Executives sell for taxes, diversification and pre-planned schedules. Open-market buying is the rarer signal, and there wasn't much of it here. This workflow would have mattered more if one of these names had a cluster of buys. None did.

Workflow 5: Berkshire and UnitedHealth held up on 16 and 17 of the market's 20 worst days

Question: does the thesis survive a bad market?

Claude gave a reason for two of its picks: Berkshire as "downside ballast", UnitedHealth for "defensive demand". Those are testable claims.

The script finds SPY's 20 worst days over five years and checks how each pick did on those days. It also measures the 2022 drawdown, from SPY's 2022 high on 2022-01-03 to its 2022 low on 2022-10-12 (both checked on adjusted closes).

frm = (today - dt.timedelta(days=5 * 365)).isoformat()
series = lambda t: {p["date"]: p["adjusted_close"] for p in get(f"eod/{t}", **{"from": frm})}

spy = series("SPY.US")
d = sorted(spy)
spy_r = {d[i]: spy[d[i]] / spy[d[i - 1]] - 1 for i in range(1, len(d))}
worst = sorted(spy_r, key=spy_r.get)[:20]

for t in PICKS:
    s = series(t)
    r = {x: s[x] / s[p] - 1 for p, x in zip(d, d[1:]) if x in s and p in s}
    better = sum(r[x] > spy_r[x] for x in worst)
    dd22 = s["2022-10-12"] / s["2022-01-03"] - 1
    print(f"{t:9} worst-20 avg {st.mean(r[x] for x in worst):+.2%}  better than SPY {better}/20  2022 {dd22:+.1%}")

MSFT −3.71% 7 / 20 −32.1% 0.69
GOOGL −3.80% 8 / 20 −32.7% 0.66
BRK-B −2.49% 16 / 20 −12.2% 0.57
V −3.37% 11 / 20 −19.1% 0.60
UNH −1.57% 17 / 20 +0.5% 0.21

1,253 sessions, 2021-11-24 to 2026-11-20. Adjusted closes.

Here Claude's reasoning held up. Berkshire beat SPY on 16 of the 20 worst days and lost half as much in 2022. UnitedHealth beat it on 17 of 20 and finished the 2022 window up 0.5%.

Put workflows 2 and 5 together and you get a more useful picture than either one alone. UnitedHealth protected you when the market crashed, and then hurt you on its own earnings days. The defensive pick still had the biggest single-day losses in the group.

If you hold more than a handful of names, correlation is where hidden risk builds up. I covered that in I Gave Claude My Portfolio and Asked It to Find the Hidden Risks.

What survived the five workflows

Pick W1 facts W2 earnings risk W3 drawdown W4 insiders W5 stress
MSFT 1 of 3 claims held high (5.5x) −12.7% sales only weaker than SPY
GOOGL 2 of 3 held medium (3.8x) flagged, −34.0% sales only weaker than SPY
BRK-B 1 of 1 held low (3.3x, 2.43% avg) −3.9% small buys held up (16/20)
V 1 of 3 held lowest (2.1x) −7.8% sales only mixed (11/20)
UNH nothing to check highest avg move (8.04%, −22.38% worst) flagged, −21.6% sales only held up (17/20)

None of this says "buy" or "don't buy". It says what you'd need to believe to own each one. That's the step a chat answer skips.

Not financial advice. The five tickers are Claude's answer, used here as test inputs, not recommendations.

If you want to run the same checks on your own watchlist, the data comes from EODHD APIs. Use the code KEVIN10 at checkout for 10% off.

Doing it without code: the same workflows as Claude prompts

The model in my six runs reasoned fine. It just had nothing to reason about. Give it data and the same model runs these checks itself.

Connect the EODHD APIs MCP server to Claude, then use one prompt per workflow:

"For MSFT, GOOGL, BRK-B, V and UNH, pull current fundamentals and give me forward P/E, quarterly revenue growth and dividend yield. Cite the field you used for each number."

"For each of those tickers, list the last 8 earnings report dates and the price move on the first session after each one. Compare it with the average daily move over 3 years."

"Which of them are more than 15% below their 52-week high? For those only, summarise the last 30 days of news and separate company-specific headlines from noise."

"Show open-market insider purchases (code P) for each ticker over the last 180 days. Ignore sales."

"Find SPY's 20 worst days in the last 5 years and show how each ticker did on those days."

The scripts above are the ones I'd schedule. The prompts are faster for a one-off check. Either way, the numbers come from a live query and not from the model's memory.

Where this breaks and what I'd trust

  • One model, six runs, one day. Claude refused in 5 of 6 runs on 2026-11-23 with Opus 4.8. Another model, another day or a pushier prompt could produce a confident table of invented numbers. That's the case these workflows exist for.
  • The ranges in workflow 1 are my reading of Claude's words. "Low-20s" as 20 to 24 is a judgment call, and two of the misses (Visa's forward P/E and yield) sit right at the edge of my ranges.
  • Eight earnings reports is a small sample. UNH's two big drops dominate its average. Treat the ratio as "how bad can it get", not as a forecast.
  • The news step is a filter, not an analyst. 50 articles is the limit I set, and the ticker filter pulls in market roundups. You still have to read.
  • Insider data shows what was filed, not why. Pre-planned sales look identical to discretionary ones in a raw count.
  • Adjusted closes change after each dividend. All price figures are as of 2026-11-20. Alphabet and UnitedHealth both go ex-dividend on 2026-12-07, so a rerun after that date will show slightly different numbers.

What I'd trust: the direction of each finding, the counts, and the habit of checking a pick five ways before acting on it. What I wouldn't: any single number in isolation, including mine.

FAQ

Can AI pick stocks?

In my test, Claude declined to in 5 of 6 attempts. It said it had no live data and that invented figures would be dangerous. When it did name stocks, half of its checkable numbers missed against live data. AI is more useful for checking picks against real data than for making them.

Is Claude good for stock analysis?

It's good at reasoning once it has data. Without tools, it worked from figures about ten months old and said so. Connected to a data source such as the EODHD APIs MCP server, it can pull fundamentals, prices, news and insider filings and cite where each number came from.

Why does Claude refuse to give stock picks?

In all five refusals it gave the same two reasons: it had no live market data, and "buy right now" depends on the reader's goals and risk tolerance. It never refused to explain metrics or help build a screen.

Are ChatGPT or Claude stock picks reliable?

Not as raw chat answers. In the one run where Claude gave picks, 5 of 10 checkable figures missed against live data. Three of the misses were forward P/E ratios, which is consistent with valuations moving after its training cutoff. Check every number against a data source before acting on it.

What data do I need to fact-check an AI stock pick?

Current fundamentals (P/E, growth, yield), daily prices for drawdowns and stress tests, earnings history, news and insider transactions. All five workflows here run on one EODHD key, on the All-In-One plan or the Fundamentals Data Feed plus EOD Historical All-World.

Key takeaways

  • Claude refused to invent stock numbers in 5 of 6 runs. When it did name picks, 5 of its 10 checkable figures missed against live data.
  • A pick is a hypothesis. Five checks (facts, earnings risk, drawdown, insiders, stress) turn it into something you can actually judge.
  • The "defensive" pick held up on 17 of the market's 20 worst days and still had a −22.38% earnings day. One check alone would have missed half of that.

I stopped asking Claude what to buy.

I ask it to check what I'm about to buy, and I give it the data to do that.
