title: Files, paths and environment variables: what you touch every day
description:
A script reads a hundred-megabyte log file with readFile, takes 58 milliseconds and works. In production the file is two gigabytes, the process eats two gigabytes of memory and the service dies of OOM. Same code.

It isn't a speed problem: readFile isn't slow, it just loads everything. And loading everything is fine until it isn't. This lesson is about that, about the paths that break on Windows, and about the configuration that should stop a server from starting wrong.

fs/promises: the module you want

Node has two faces of the file system. The callback one (node:fs) and the promise one (node:fs/promises). Use the second: import readFile from the callback module by mistake and this is the error.

TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "cb" argument must be of type function. Received undefined

Mixing the two is the first stumble. With the right one:

import { readFile, readdir, writeFile, appendFile, mkdir } from "node:fs/promises";

console.log("read:", JSON.stringify((await readFile("./data/one.txt", "utf8")).trim()));

await appendFile("./data/one.txt", "another line\n");
console.log("after append:", JSON.stringify(await readFile("./data/one.txt", "utf8")));

await writeFile("./data/new.txt", "created\n");
await mkdir("./data/c/d", { recursive: true });
console.log("recursive readdir:", (await readdir("./data", { recursive: true })).sort());

read: "hola"
after append: "hola\nanother line\n"
recursive readdir: [ 'a', 'a/b', 'c', 'c/d', 'new.txt', 'one.txt' ]

Four operations you always need. appendFile adds without erasing; writeFile overwrites the whole file, it doesn't edit it; mkdir with { recursive: true } creates the whole hierarchy and doesn't fail if it's already there. And readdir with recursive gives you the full tree, which is how you walk a directory without writing a recursive function by hand.

Two warnings about writeFile: it overwrites without asking, so one distracted call empties a file that took you an hour to generate; and { flag: "wx" } is how you write only when the file doesn't exist, which is how you avoid trampling a datum by accident.

Writing without leaving the file half-done

writeFile isn't atomic: if the process dies halfway, it leaves a truncated file. And a truncated config file is worse than no file, because whoever reads it can't tell it's incomplete.

The pattern that avoids it is two lines: write to a temporary file and rename.

import { writeFile, rename, readFile, stat } from "node:fs/promises";

const target = "./config.json";
await writeFile(`${target}.tmp`, JSON.stringify({ port: 3001 }, null, 2));
await rename(`${target}.tmp`, target);

const info = await stat(target);
console.log("after rename:", (await readFile(target, "utf8")).replace(/\s+/g, " "));
console.log("is a file:", info.isFile(), "· bytes:", info.size);

after rename: { "port": 3001 }
is a file: true · bytes: 18

rename replaces the target without asking and, within the same file system, is atomic: whoever reads config.json sees the old version or the new one, never half. If you write the temporary file to /tmp and the target lives on another file system, the rename copies and stops being atomic; that's why the temporary file goes next to the target.

That stat is the other module you're missing: it gives you size, dates and whether it's a file or a directory. info.isFile(), info.size, info.mtime. Everything you need to decide without opening anything.

File errors can be handled, and they have names

A file error isn't a black box: it carries a code you can compare.

import { readFile, mkdir } from "node:fs/promises";

for (const [label, fn] of [
  ["missing", () => readFile("./nope.txt", "utf8")],
  ["already there", () => mkdir("./data")],
]) {
  try {
    await fn();
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(label, "→", error.code, "·", error.message);
  }
}

missing → ENOENT · ENOENT: no such file or directory, open './nope.txt'
already there → EEXIST · EEXIST: file already exists, mkdir './data'

ENOENT is "not there", EEXIST is "already there", EACCES is "no permission". With the code you can decide: if the config file doesn't exist, use defaults and warn; if you lack permissions, that's a deployment error and it has to fail. Comparing message text is fragile; comparing code isn't.

Don't check whether it exists: try it

There's an existsSync in Node and it's a trap. Between your check and your read there's a window where the file can disappear: checking and then using is a race, even if it lasts microseconds. The correct pattern is to try and handle ENOENT.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

async function readIfExists(path) {
  try {
    return await readFile(path, "utf8");
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.code === "ENOENT") return null;
    throw error;
  }
}

console.log("config.json:", await readIfExists("./config.json"));
console.log("missing.json:", await readIfExists("./missing.json"));

config.json: {
  "port": 3001
}
missing.json: null

One operation instead of two, and no window. The throw on the last line is the important half: only "not there" becomes null; an EACCES keeps going up, because lacking permission isn't the same as lacking a file.

Big files: reading everything is a bug

Here's the claim from the introduction, measured. A 96 MB file, two ways to read it, process memory afterwards:

Way Resident memory Time
readFile 176 MB 58 ms
for await over a stream 102 MB 141 ms

We started at 81 MB, so readFile added about 95 — the whole file — and the stream added about 21, the size of one chunk. Note the second column too: the stream takes more than twice as long. It isn't magic, it's a trade, and on a server memory runs out before time does.

The two rows are two separate runs, and that's the point: in the same process the readFile buffer is still alive when you start streaming, so the comparison is worthless.

// read-all.mjs
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const mb = (n) => Math.round(n / 1024 / 1024) + " MB";
const t0 = performance.now();
const content = await readFile("./big.log");

console.log(
  "readFile →",
  mb(process.memoryUsage().rss),
  "·",
  Math.round(performance.now() - t0),
  "ms · read",
  mb(content.length),
);

readFile → 176 MB · 54 ms · read 95 MB

// in-chunks.mjs
import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";

const mb = (n) => Math.round(n / 1024 / 1024) + " MB";
const t0 = performance.now();
let total = 0;
for await (const chunk of createReadStream("./big.log")) total += chunk.length;

console.log("stream →", mb(process.memoryUsage().rss), "·", Math.round(performance.now() - t0), "ms · read", mb(total));

stream → 100 MB · 142 ms · read 95 MB

A stream hands you chunks of a fixed size and doesn't ask for the next one until you're done with the previous. That's backpressure: if your consumer is slow, the read slows down instead of piling up in memory. And for await...of — the one you learned with events.on — is the shortest way to consume it.

For the usual case, copying a stream into a file, there's a function that handles everything:

import { createReadStream, createWriteStream, statSync } from "node:fs";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";
import { createGzip } from "node:zlib";

await pipeline(createReadStream("./big.log"), createGzip(), createWriteStream("./big.log.gz"));

const mb = (bytes) => Math.round(bytes / 1e6) + " MB";
const kb = (bytes) => Math.round(bytes / 1e3) + " KB";
console.log("compressed:", mb(statSync("./big.log").size), "→", kb(statSync("./big.log.gz").size));

compressed: 100 MB → 97 KB

pipeline connects the three pieces, propagates errors and closes what it opened. Chaining .pipe() by hand does the same until something fails, and then it leaves files open and promises hanging.

And for the specific case of a log — many lines, none of them huge — there's a piece that turns the stream into lines:

import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";
import { createInterface } from "node:readline";

const rl = createInterface({ input: createReadStream("./log.txt"), crlfDelay: Infinity });

let n = 0;
for await (const line of rl) {
  console.log(++n, line);
}

1 line one
2 line two
3 line three

readline splits on newlines without loading the file and is consumed with the same for await as everything else. Processing a two-gigabyte log line by line is exactly this; split("\n") on the whole content is exactly the bug from the introduction.

Cancelling a read

In the async lesson you met AbortController. Here it gets its first real use: readFile accepts { signal } and can be interrupted.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const control = new AbortController();
control.abort();

try {
  await readFile("./big.log", { signal: control.signal });
  console.log("this should not run");
} catch (error) {
  console.log("read cancelled →", error.name + ": " + error.message);
}

read cancelled → AbortError: The operation was aborted

It looks trivial with the controller already aborted, and it's exactly what you need in production: when the shutdown signal arrives, you abort the controller and every read in flight cuts itself off.

Paths: join concatenates, resolve decides

Two functions that look the same and aren't.

import { join, resolve, dirname, basename, extname } from "node:path";

console.log("join relative:", join("data", "a", "..", "one.txt"));
console.log("resolve relative:", resolve("data", "one.txt"));
console.log(
  "dirname:",
  dirname("/var/log/app/error.log"),
  "· basename:",
  basename("/var/log/app/error.log"),
  "· extname:",
  extname("/var/log/app/error.log"),
);

join relative: data/one.txt
resolve relative: /tmp/l8e/data/one.txt
dirname: /var/log/app · basename: error.log · extname: .log

join joins and normalises: it eats the .. and returns a relative path if you gave it relative pieces. resolve does the same and also turns it absolute against the working directory. That's the whole difference, and it's the one that makes join predictable and resolve depend on where you launched the process.

The rule: to build paths inside your project, join. To get an absolute path for something the user gave you, resolve. And never concatenate with +.

The other three split a path: dirname keeps the folder, basename the name, extname the extension. They're for renaming photo.jpeg to photo.webp, for pulling a slug out of a URL turned into a filename, for checking that an uploaded file is what it claims.

And Windows: writing "folders/file.txt" by hand works on Linux and macOS, and on Windows almost always too, because Windows accepts forward slashes. Until it doesn't. Use join and let the module pick the separator; it saves you the bug that only shows up on a colleague's machine.

If you come from Python, path is your pathlib with less sugar: no Path objects, just functions that take strings and return strings. The useful comparison is that resolve does what Path.resolve() does, and join what the / operator does.

Environment variables

process.env is an object with the process's environment variables, and everything is a string. No numbers, no booleans, no validation.

console.log("PORT:", process.env.PORT, "· type:", typeof process.env.PORT);

PORT: undefined · type: undefined

It isn't there, and nothing happens. That's the problem: undefined travels down until something fails three layers below with a message that never mentions configuration.

To load a .env without installing anything, the runtime has shipped it for a couple of versions:

node --env-file=.env env.mjs

PORT: 3001 · type: string
APP_NAME: node-course

--env-file errors if the file doesn't exist, which is right in production; --env-file-if-exists doesn't, which is what you want locally. And if you see dotenv in a project, it's the old way of doing the same thing: still works, no longer needed.

Two rules that aren't negotiable:

  • The .env is never committed. It holds secrets. What gets committed is .env.example, with the same keys and fake values, which is the contract: whoever clones the repo knows what it needs.
  • Configuration is validated at startup. If DATABASE_URL is missing, the process must die at the beginning, not on the third request. 
const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port < 1 || port > 65535) {
  console.error("invalid PORT:", process.env.PORT);
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log("starting on port", port);

invalid PORT: undefined

That exit(1) is the only place process.exit is justified: before there's anything to break. Past that point, you close in an orderly way.

Common problems

The process runs out of memory reading a file

readFile loads everything. If the size isn't bounded, use createReadStream with for await, or pipeline.

ENOENT on a file that exists

A relative path resolved against cwd(), not against your module. Use join(import.meta.dirname, ...).

Works on Linux, fails on Windows

Paths concatenated by hand. join picks the separator; you don't.

readFile gives me a Buffer and the text looks odd

Without the second argument ("utf8") you get bytes. With it, text.

process.env.PORT is "3000" and + 1 gives "30001"

Everything is a string. Convert with Number() and validate the result.

The server starts with incomplete configuration and fails later

You didn't validate at startup. Fail early, with a message naming the missing variable.

What you take from this lesson

  • node:fs/promises for everything; the callback module is the other face.
  • readFile loads the whole file: 95 MB of memory for a 95 MB file.
  • Streams read in chunks, with backpressure, and cost a little more time.
  • pipeline connects and closes for you; for await consumes a stream without ceremony.
  • readFile accepts { signal }: the AbortController from the previous lesson cuts reads.
  • join concatenates and normalises; resolve also makes it absolute against cwd().
  • process.env is all strings: convert and validate.
  • --env-file replaces dotenv; .env isn't committed, .env.example is.
  • Configuration is validated at startup and the process dies there when it's wrong.

You now know how to read and write on the system without breaking it, and how to start with sane configuration. What comes next is the reason you're here: an HTTP server, first with the bare http module and then with a framework, so you understand what each one does.

Never stop coding!

title: Why moving a Python diff parser to Rust made it 3.1x slower while one Git fix made it 4x faster
description:
I have been building Athena, an offline Python tool that scans Git history to find broken callers across a codebase before you merge a pull request. On small repositories it felt instant. Once I pointed it at 1,000+ commits and thousands of files, a single cold scan took 30 to 45 seconds.

My first instinct was the usual one: rewrite the whole thing in Rust. After profiling the actual bottlenecks, I realized a full rewrite would throw away Python's rock-solid ast module and make contributing much harder. So I kept Python as the core and tried fixing only what the profiler flagged.

1. The biggest early win had nothing to do with Rust

Before writing any Rust code, I looked at where time was actually going. Our Git inspector was spawning a new git cat-file -s and git show subprocess for every changed file. Across hundreds of commits, OS process startup overhead dominated the whole runtime.

Switching to a single batched binary git cat-file --batch stream fixed it immediately:

Before: 1 subprocess per file (git show / cat-file -s) -> 12.74s
After:  1 batched git cat-file --batch stream          ->  3.17s (4.02x faster)

No language rewrite needed. Just fewer processes.

2. When porting Python to Rust actually makes it slower

Next, I ported our unified diff parser (parse_unified_diff_raw) to Rust via PyO3. Every test passed and all 229 recorded inputs matched Python identically. Then I ran the benchmark:

  • Pure Python: 1.6 ms
  • Rust (PyO3): 4.8 ms (3.1x slower)

Why did Rust lose? When Python calls a Rust function through PyO3, strings and lists have to cross the Foreign Function Interface (FFI) boundary. Parsing a unified diff is mostly lightweight string slicing, so converting and allocating those strings across Python and Rust cost more than the parsing work itself. I deleted that Rust port and kept diff parsing in Python.

3. Where Rust actually crushed Python

Rust paid off big on tight CPU loops where compute far outweighed FFI copying. Four hot kernels passed strict equivalence checks and stayed enabled (with FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 available anytime to toggle back to pure Python):

Kernel Speedup Parity Checks
redact_secrets 41x (237.3us -> 5.8us) 776/776 identical
score_graph_trigrams 8.8x (37.3ms -> 4.2ms) 330/330 identical
compute_community_assignments 3.5x (9.6ms -> 2.7ms) 206/206 identical
extract_structural_symbols_raw 1.9x (16.2us -> 8.6us) 800/800 identical

4. Verifying zero quality loss across 1,000+ commits

Speed means nothing if native ports silently change results, so I audited pure Python against the hybrid Rust build across three large public repositories over 1,000+ commits each:

Repository Commits Graph Build (Python -> Rust) Parity
google/flatbuffers 1,000 43.39s -> 1.62s (26.73x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical
NVIDIA/cuvs 1,472 29.89s -> 1.33s (22.48x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical
microsoft/playwright-python 1,000 45.78s -> 12.22s (3.75x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical

playwright-python saw a smaller jump because it is mostly Python files (where ast.parse stays in Python) and still iterates 100k+ edges in Python during queries.

Takeaway

If you have a slow Python CLI or developer tool, resist rewriting the whole codebase on day one. Batch your subprocess calls first, measure FFI copy costs carefully and only move the hot loops that actually benchmark faster.

All code, tests and benchmark scripts are open source under Apache-2.0 here: https://github.com/aaryanrwt/athena

title: How I Built an Open Online Typing Game Platform with Real-Time 1v1 Multiplayer in React
description:
How I Built an Open Online Typing Game Platform with Real-Time 1v1 Multiplayer in React

Over the past few months, I set out to build TypingGame.in (https://typinggame.in) — an interactive, completely free online typing academy and arcade game portal.

While platforms like Monkeytype and TypeRacer dominate the market, I wanted to build something that blended educational touch-typing curriculums, real-time 1v1 PvP racing, and arcade gameplay (car racing, bubble popping, and zombie defense) into a single cohesive web application.

Here is a breakdown of how the architecture works, how WPM is calculated accurately, and how real-time 1v1 sync is handled.

  1. Calculating Standardized WPM & Accuracy in Real-Time

A common issue in novice typing tests is treating each space-separated word as a single unit. In professional and government certification standards (such as SSC CGL and RRB), typing speed is universally standardized to 5 keystrokes = 1 standard word.

Here is the exact formula implemented in the speed test engine:

Gross WPM = (Total Characters Typed / 5) / Time Elapsed in Minutes

Net WPM = max(0, (Correct Characters / 5) / Time Elapsed in Minutes)

Accuracy % = (Correct Characters / Total Characters Typed) * 100

By evaluating velocity against Date.now() timestamps rather than relying on setInterval tick counts, the speedometer remains immune to browser background throttling or tab switches.

  1. Dual-Engine Architecture: Desktop Keyboard vs. Mobile Virtual Keyboards

One of the trickiest challenges when building an interactive typing game online (https://typinggame.in/) is handling smartphone virtual keyboards (like Android Gboard or iOS Safari).

On desktop keyboards, pressing any key fires a standard KeyboardEvent with e.key.length === 1. On mobile devices, however, virtual keyboards use Input Method Editors (IME) with predictive composition, which often emit e.key = 'Unidentified' and keyCode: 229.

To support both seamlessly:

  • We track keystrokes via direct input interception overlaying the paragraph stage.
  • If a desktop single-character keydown fires, sound effects and velocity update immediately.
  • If a mobile virtual keyboard inserts characters via input / onChange, the engine compares the delta between userInput and targetText on the fly, starting the wall-clock timer automatically.

You can try the live test on mobile or desktop at TypingGame.in Speed Test (https://typinggame.in/typing-test)

  1. Real-Time 1v1 Multiplayer Racing

For the competitive arena at TypingGame.in/multiplayer, players can generate a 6-digit room code and race side-by-side.

Every keystroke emits a lightweight telemetry payload:

  • Current character index
  • Live WPM
  • Accuracy percentage
  • Progress completion ratio

A lightweight WebSocket relay synchronizes player cars on the track with interpolation, providing that nail-biting arcade racing sensation without heavy server overhead.

  1. Lessons Learned & What's Next

  • Pre-rendering matters: Static pre-rendering of 250 routes allowed the site to load in under 500ms with 0 Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

  • Accessible inputs: Transparent focus interception provides a distraction-free experience while preserving native screen reader support.

Feel free to play a few rounds on TypingGame.in (https://typinggame.in) and share your fastest WPM score! If you have suggestions or questions about the architecture, let's discuss in the comments below!

title: What the Three Colors in GVR Sync Results Actually Tell You
description:
GVR (GBase Visio Rsynctool) is GBASE's visual active-active synchronization tool for clusters running the GBase 8a analytical database. When a sync job finishes, the UI summarizes the result with colored counters, where the number is the task count:

  • Green: completed
  • Orange: skipped
  • Red: error

This post walks through what each color means and how to investigate it, using a sync of a single table t1 as the example.

Successful Tasks

Opening the task detail shows the sync result for table t1 as success.

Skipped Tasks

A skipped (orange) task usually comes down to one of three reasons:

  • The target table does not exist, and the "auto-create table on standby" option is not enabled.
  • The target table structure differs from the source, and the "table overwrite" option is not enabled.
  • Source and target are completely identical — same table structure and same data (SCN), so there is nothing to sync.

Failed Tasks

A red task means the underlying sync job had already started but hit a problem partway through and could not finish — for example, a node crashing suddenly or a network failure. The task log pinpoints the cause; in the example here, the log showed the connection to the target database dropping mid-run, which caused the failure.

The Entire Sync Fails

When the whole job fails rather than individual tables, the problem was usually found during the preparation phase, before any underlying sync task started — for example:

  • A service is offline
  • A network fault
  • A password was changed

Again, use the task log view to analyze what went wrong.

How to React to Each Color

Each color maps to a different next action. Green needs nothing. Orange means reading the skip reason first, then deciding whether to enable auto-create or table overwrite. Red — and a whole-job failure — means going into the task log and separating a mid-run fault from a preparation-phase one. In every case, after you fix the underlying issue, simply run the sync again against the gbase database, and the counters should turn green.

title: JSONB or typed classes: what the PostgreSQL planner sees
description:
Franck Pachot's JSONB example on our server and the same question in redb Pro: plans, row estimates and plain figures.

Franck Pachot recently took apart a simple case on dev.to (JSONB performance: declare access patterns to PostgreSQL query planner). A table holds 100,000 measurements, each in a JSONB column. The query counts the measurements where three values are zero and groups them by lab. ANALYZE collects statistics for the JSONB column as a whole, not for the keys inside the document. For a condition like (record->>'value_1')::INT = 0, with no index and no statistics on that expression, the planner has nothing to go on: it takes the default equality selectivity, 0.5%, for each of the three conditions and multiplies them. 100,000 × 0.005³ is a hundredth of a row, so the estimate becomes one row. In fact about 12,500 rows match, and the plan comes out wrong. The cure is to declare the access pattern: expression indexes, a compound expression index or extended statistics.

We ran his example on our server and asked redb the same question, where the data has C# classes and every field has a type. Below are the plans, the row estimates and the times. The result first: on this query JSONB with a hand-made index is faster than redb. What typing buys for that is further down.

His case on our server

The table measurements(tick BIGSERIAL, record JSONB), 100,000 rows, with value_1, value_2, value_3 (0 or 1) and scientist_id in the document. A lookup table scientist_labs with 10,000 scientists and three lab names. The query:

SELECT s.lab_name, COUNT(*)
FROM measurements m
JOIN scientist_labs s ON s.scientist_id = (m.record->>'scientist_id')::BIGINT
WHERE (m.record->>'value_1')::INT = 0
  AND (m.record->>'value_2')::INT = 0
  AND (m.record->>'value_3')::INT = 0
GROUP BY s.lab_name
ORDER BY s.lab_name

PostgreSQL 18.6, jit = off. The time is a plain run of the statement, the median of three warm runs (why not EXPLAIN ANALYZE is explained at the end):

Variant Estimated / actual rows Join ms
no index 1 / 12,491 Nested Loop 29.7
three expression indexes 12,589 / 12,491 Hash Join 25.9
compound index on the three expressions 12,481 / 12,491 Hash Join 11.1
extended statistics only 7,263 × 2 / 6,245 × 2 Hash Join 26.5

The one-row estimate reproduces. The best variant, as in his article, is the compound index: 11.1 ms.

The same data in redb

In redb, data is described by a class. Pachot's document is closest to a class with a nested class: the values and the lab details live in the measurement itself.

public class LabInfo { public string LabName { get; set; } = ""; }

[RedbScheme("pachot_measurement_nested")]
public class NestedMeasurementProps
{
    public int Value1 { get; set; }
    public int Value2 { get; set; }
    public int Value3 { get; set; }
    public LabInfo? Lab { get; set; }
}

One difference from his schema is worth naming at once. His document holds scientist_id, and the lab name comes from the lookup table. Here the lab name lives in the measurement as a field of the nested class, so the query needs no lookup. The distributions are the same: the values 0 and 1 are equally likely and independent, the lab is picked uniformly out of 10,000, the name by (i % 3) + 1. The data is seeded with a fixed seed.

The question is the same, and it is one query:

var groups = await redb.Query<NestedMeasurementProps>()
    .Where(m => m.Value1 == 0 && m.Value2 == 0 && m.Value3 == 0)
    .GroupBy(m => m.Lab!.LabName)
    .SelectAsync(g => new { g.Key, Count = Agg.Count(g) });

The compiler checks the field names and their types. Value1 is an int here and is compared with an int. There is no ::INT cast in the query, because in the database it is a number, not text inside a document.

What the planner sees

redb Pro turns this query into one SQL statement:

SELECT COALESCE(json_agg(row_to_json(t))::text, '[]') FROM (SELECT
  pvt."Lab.LabName" AS "LabName",
  COUNT(*) AS "Count"
FROM (
  SELECT o_src._id AS _id_object, f0._string AS "Lab.LabName", o_src._dv AS "Value1", f2._long AS "Value2", f3._long AS "Value3"
  FROM (SELECT dv._id_object AS _id, dv._long AS _dv FROM _values dv WHERE (dv._id_structure = '1000016' AND dv._long = '0') AND dv._array_index IS NULL AND dv._id_object NOT IN (SELECT t._id FROM _objects t WHERE t._id_scheme = -10)) o_src
  LEFT JOIN _values f0 ON f0._id_object = o_src._id AND f0._id_structure = '1000020' AND f0._array_index IS NULL
  LEFT JOIN _values f2 ON f2._id_object = o_src._id AND f2._id_structure = '1000017' AND f2._array_index IS NULL
  LEFT JOIN _values f3 ON f3._id_object = o_src._id AND f3._id_structure = '1000018' AND f3._array_index IS NULL
) pvt
WHERE ((pvt."Value1" = '0' AND pvt."Value2" = '0') AND pvt."Value3" = '0')
GROUP BY pvt."Lab.LabName"
) t

The outer json_agg is the transport of the grouped result: the three group rows go to .NET as one JSON. The query itself is inside.

Each field is stored as a row of the values table: _id_structure says which field it is, and the value sits in the column of its type. Integers go to _long, strings to _string. To the planner, the condition Value1 = 0 is _id_structure = X AND _long = 0, a plain comparison of two columns that have statistics. There are no expressions to declare.

We created no index for this query. The system index IX__values__structure_long_object does the work, one index for every int field of every class in the database. Add another int field to the class tomorrow and filter on it, and the index is already there.

The source of the query is built from the first condition: the o_src subquery reads only the Value1 = 0 rows, about 50,000, not all 100,000 objects. The other conditions and the lab name are joined to that set, and GROUP BY gets only the 12,459 matching objects.

The plan: a parallel Hash Join of two index-only scans for Value1 = 0 and Value2 = 0, then an index-only lookup of Value3 = 0 per row, then a lookup of the lab name per match, a sort and a grouping.

Where the estimates go wrong

redb has its own statistics weakness, and the same plan shows it:

Node Estimated Actual
Value1 = 0 rows about 18,000 49,969
after Value2 864 per worker 24,863
after Value3 101 per worker 12,459
groups 3 3

The planner estimates one field reasonably well. But three fields of one object are three rows of the values table, and when it joins them by _id_object the planner treats them as independent. Each further condition multiplies the error, and by the end the estimate is 51 times below the actual count. Extended statistics cannot help here: they work on columns of one row, and these fields sit in different rows.

This time the error cost little: the low estimate chose an index lookup per row, and each such lookup is one index probe.

The figures

Variant Steps ms
JSONB, no index 1 29.7
JSONB, compound expression index 1 11.1
redb Pro, nested class, one GroupBy 1 50.5
redb Pro, tree, grouping by parent 2 67.6

Every redb variant returns the same answer, and it matches a count over the seeded data in .NET: California Scientific 4192, Industrial Labs 4179, Western Science People 4088.

The tree row is the same task in another model: the lab is the parent, its measurements are child objects. The first step groups the matching measurements by parent in one statement (GroupByRedb(m => m.ParentId), 49.6 ms); the second reads the lab names in two statements (17.5 ms). With a few small service statements, the server total is 67.6 ms.

On Pachot's question, a JSONB document with an index made by hand for this query is two to five times faster than redb: 11.1 and 29.7 ms against 50.5. Through the redb API, with the result parsed in .NET, it is 53.5 ms.

What types and foreign keys buy for that price

Pachot writes that with JSONB you declare the access paths to the planner yourself: which expressions, which index, which statistics. That is work done for every query that has to be fast, and redone when the query changes.

In redb, data has a type and relations from the start:

  • a field is declared in a C# class, and a query on it is checked by the compiler instead of failing on a typo in the string 'value_1';
  • an int is stored as a number, with no cast from text in every condition;
  • the indexes on the values tables are the same for every class; a new query does not add any;
  • a new field in a class needs neither a table migration nor a new index;
  • relations are held by foreign keys. Every value is tied to its object and to the definition of its field; the parent in a tree is a foreign key to an object, and so is a reference field to another object (RedbObject<T>). In Pachot's document, scientist_id is just a number inside JSON: the database will not check that such a scientist exists, and will not stop you from deleting a scientist the measurements refer to.

The price in our measurement: 50 ms where JSONB with a hand-made index answers in 11. If there is one hot query, the compound expression index wins. If there are many queries and they change along with the code, typing spares you a declaration for each of them.

How we measured

  • PostgreSQL 18.6 in a container, AMD Ryzen 5 5500U, jit = off, work_mem = 64MB, shared_buffers = 4GB, random_page_cost = 1.1. A separate database; nothing else ran on the server meanwhile.
  • redb Pro from the development branch, query planner on, default configuration.
  • Each figure is the median of three warm runs after one warm-up run.
  • Times are from plain runs. This server's kernel reads time through hpet (tsc is not offered), and one clock read costs 1.2 µs. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) reads the clock for every row at every node, which here inflates the time 5 to 19 times. So the tables show the plain execution time of the statement, while the plans and row estimates come from EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). For comparison, with timing on, the compound index showed 102 ms and the redb nested class 280 ms. For the same reason our figures cannot be compared with those in his article, only with each other.
  • The JSONB data was seeded with random(), as in his article, and gave 12,491 matching rows. The redb data was seeded from new Random(20261124) and gave 12,459.

Franck, if you read this: we would like your view on how the planner handles fields that live in different rows of one table, and what could be done better there.

Code and documentation: github.com/redbase-app/redb, articles: redbase.app/articles.

If this was useful, a ⭐ on GitHub helps others find it.

title: Jensen Huang Is Back: Why Nvidia Stock Jumped 31.5%, and the AI Failover Lesson Every Developer Should Learn
description:
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and the stock jumped 31.5%. Here's what that says about single points of failure, plus a Node.js AI inference failover you can test without a GPU.

Cover: Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO, and Nvidia stock jumps 31.5% in one session.

By Syed Zubair Hussain Shah · November 24, 2026

Eleven days after Huang resigned, Nvidia brought him back. The stock rallied, and the board's reversal raised a harder question about how much the company depends on one person.

Nvidia's board said it wouldn't bring Jensen Huang back. Less than a week later, it did.

On November 23, Nvidia reinstated Huang as president, CEO, and a board member. The stock closed 31.5% higher, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value in one session, according to Reuters. Even after that jump, shares were still below where they'd been before his November 12 resignation. Nvidia's announcement · Reuters on Huang's return and the stock move

Why did Nvidia stock jump when Jensen Huang returned?

Nvidia said its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after speaking with him and receiving input from senior U.S. government officials. Reuters reported that President Donald Trump intervened to help bring him back. That abrupt reversal raised questions about the board's independence. Some investors welcomed Huang's return while still questioning how the board handled his departure and reinstatement. Nvidia's announcement · Reuters on the reinstatement · Reuters on investor reactions

My read is that investors were more comfortable with Huang running Nvidia through its next phase of AI expansion than with the uncertainty of a leadership change. The broader market was also bouncing back from an AI selloff. Both help explain the rally. The figure that gives me pause is that Nvidia still hadn't made back all the ground it lost after Huang resigned. A huge one-day gain and lingering uncertainty can easily coexist. Reuters' closing market report · Reuters on Nvidia's remaining losses

The question I'd take into my next AI build

When I want to find out what a system depends on, I take one piece away and see what stops. As a full-stack developer, the dependency I can test is the endpoint that runs the model.

Say your React app calls a Node API for a one-paragraph summary. The API sends the request to one model endpoint. If that endpoint stalls, your UI can still load and your database can still respond. The one action the user came for is stuck.

I'd put the fallback in the Node API. That gives the browser one request to track and lets the backend decide when a second call is worth the money. For a read-only task like summarization, I'd give the primary 1.2 seconds, give an independent backup up to 1.8 seconds, and surface an error if both fail. Those are demo budgets. In an actual product I'd set them using measured latency and what a user can reasonably wait for.

A JavaScript fallback you can test without a GPU

This example expects two HTTP endpoints that accept { "text": "..." } and return { "summary": "..." }. Use it in a Node backend with a primary and backup that implement the same response contract.

const retryableStatuses = new Set([429, 502, 503, 504]);
const retryableNetworkErrors = new Set([
  'ECONNREFUSED', 'ECONNRESET', 'EPIPE', 'UND_ERR_SOCKET',
]);

async function requestSummary(url, text, timeoutMs) {
  const signal = AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs);

  try {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ text }),
      signal,
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      await response.body?.cancel();
      throw Object.assign(new Error(`Inference returned HTTP ${response.status}`), {
        status: response.status,
      });
    }

    const result = await response.json();
    if (typeof result?.summary !== 'string' || !result.summary.trim()) {
      throw new Error('Inference returned a missing or empty summary');
    }

    return result.summary;
  } catch (error) {
    signal.throwIfAborted();
    throw error;
  }
}

export async function summarize(text, { primary, backup }) {
  try {
    const summary = await requestSummary(primary, text, 1200);
    return { summary, route: 'primary' };
  } catch (error) {
    const canFailOver = error.name === 'TimeoutError' ||
      retryableStatuses.has(error.status) ||
      retryableNetworkErrors.has(error.cause?.code);
    if (!canFailOver) throw error;
  }

  const summary = await requestSummary(backup, text, 1800);
  return { summary, route: 'backup' };
}

To see it fail over, save the code above as inference.mjs, then put this file next to it and run node demo.mjs using Node.js 22 or newer. The primary deliberately leaves the connection open without sending a response. The backup returns a canned result.

// demo.mjs
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
import { once } from 'node:events';
import { summarize } from './inference.mjs';

async function start(handler) {
  const server = createServer(handler);
  server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1');
  await once(server, 'listening');
  return { server, url: `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}` };
}

const primary = await start(() => {});
const backup = await start((_req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'application/json' });
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ summary: 'The request survived the timeout.' }));
});

try {
  console.log(await summarize('Summarize this note.', {
    primary: primary.url,
    backup: backup.url,
  }));
} finally {
  for (const { server } of [primary, backup]) {
    server.close();
    server.closeAllConnections();
  }
}

The result says route: 'backup' after roughly 1.2 seconds on a local machine. An HTTP 401 or 400 surfaces immediately. That's deliberate. A bad credential or request body is worth fixing where it originated.


Node.js inference failover: the primary GPU endpoint stalls, and at 1,200 ms the request moves to the backup.

The part I'd show a client

I'd run the happy path once, then take the primary endpoint out of the demo. I'd show the summary still arriving and the logs identifying which route served it. After that, I'd take both endpoints down so the client can see what their users would see when the feature is unavailable.

Before calling this production-ready, I'd check whether the two endpoints share a GPU pool or account quota, and compare their output on the same evaluation cases. I'd also record fallback rate, end-to-end p95 latency, and cost per accepted summary. If the primary times out after the server has already started generating, the provider may still bill for that attempt. It's easy to miss that cost when all you see in the browser is a successful response.

Nvidia's comeback made me think about dependencies I take for granted. In my own apps, I can at least test one of them before a customer does. I'd pick the AI feature people use most, take its inference endpoint offline, and look at the app from their side of the screen.

Wanna work with me? I build full-stack apps and AI integrations. If your AI demo works and you're figuring out how to put it in front of customers, let's talk. zubairhussain.xyz

title: Five resampling filters on one product photo: 5.4x on edge error, and sharpening makes it worse
description:
Six posts in this series have pointed measurement at cutout edges: the original geometry check, colour contamination, the edge-hue test, its blind spot, a coverage matrix, and seven rembg models. All of them are about the matte.

This one is about what happens to the pixels after the matte, in the step nobody chooses. Image.resize() defaults to BICUBIC. cv2.resize() defaults to INTER_LINEAR. Most export pipelines call one of them with no filter argument, once per marketplace preset, and the person who signed off on the pipeline has never seen the difference.

So I measured it. Same photo as the rest of the series, five PIL filters, three reduction ratios, one sharpening sweep, and an enlargement case. The result is not "use LANCZOS". It's that the filter is worth 5.4x on edge error while looking like nothing at all on the whole-frame average — and that sharpening, the tool everyone reaches for after a resize, moves the edge in the direction that looks right and the error in the direction that hurts.

The setup

One image, unchanged from the series: a 1200×800 Unsplash photo of a white ceramic mug. One edge: the left silhouette, where the mug's body at luminance 206 meets a background at 254. That's a 48-level step, vertical over rows 470–580, sitting at x ≈ 152.

That edge is the easiest thing I could have chosen. High contrast, nothing behind it, straight for 110 rows. Whatever the filters cost here, they cost more on a soft shadow or a rounded shoulder. Treat the numbers as a floor.

Three instruments, and each one gets checked against a case with a known answer before it is allowed to say anything:

  • rise — the 10–90% distance across the edge, in output pixels, by linear interpolation between the two samples that bracket each level. On a Gaussian-blurred step this equals 2.563σ, so synthetic blurs of known σ are a ground truth.
  • overshoot — the worst excursion past the plateaus, as a fraction of the step height. This is ringing: the halo a viewer reads as "sharp". Plateaus are sampled from the outer fifth of a window twice as wide as the rise window, so the ringing cannot poison the level it is measured against.
  • RMSE — distance from the master, over the whole frame and over edge pixels only (2,114 pixels where |∇L| > 8 in the master).

The rise check, on synthetic steps:

σ 2.563σ expected (quadrature) measured error
0.5 1.28 1.51 1.30 13.9%
1.0 2.56 2.68 2.67 0.7%
1.5 3.84 3.93 4.05 3.1%
2.0 5.13 5.19 5.17 0.4%
3.0 7.69 7.73 7.91 2.3%

"Expected" is the generator's own 0.80 px floor combined with 2.563σ in quadrature, because the synthetic step is not infinitely sharp. Worst error is 13.9%, at the smallest blur where the floor dominates. That is the error bar for everything below: differences smaller than about 15% of a rise measurement are not differences. Overshoot on the same synthetic steps reads 0.0% at every σ, which is the other half of the check — a clean step has no halo, and the instrument agrees.

The master itself: rise 4.07 px, overshoot 4.3%. That 4.3% is the photo's own edge, produced by whatever the camera and the JPEG encoder did, and it sets a baseline that no filter below should be praised for beating.

Roundtrip: down, then back up

A downscale has no ground truth at the smaller size — nothing to compare against. So each case here goes master → 1/s → back to 1200 px, and is scored against the master. What comes back is not the master; the difference is what the filter destroyed, measured at a scale where the comparison is fair.

ratio filter RMSE edge RMSE rise overshoot
1/2 NEAREST 1.23 12.80 4.33 4.3%
1/2 BOX 0.92 8.34 4.42 4.3%
1/2 BILINEAR 0.80 5.75 5.25 4.3%
1/2 BICUBIC 0.56 3.35 4.32 4.3%
1/2 LANCZOS 0.51 2.38 4.03 4.3%
1/4 NEAREST 2.01 19.33 4.62 4.1%
1/4 BOX 1.75 14.61 4.66 4.2%
1/4 BILINEAR 1.51 10.82 7.17 4.2%
1/4 BICUBIC 1.17 8.06 5.87 6.2%
1/4 LANCZOS 1.06 6.86 5.27 8.3%
1/8 NEAREST 3.23 26.23 7.89 4.0%
1/8 BOX 2.88 19.84 8.42 3.2%
1/8 BILINEAR 2.69 17.70 12.84 3.1%
1/8 BICUBIC 2.26 14.38 9.73 6.2%
1/8 LANCZOS 2.11 12.95 8.27 8.4%

Four things in that table are worth more than the ranking.

The ranking never moves. NEAREST, BOX, BILINEAR, BICUBIC, LANCZOS, worst to best, at all three ratios. If you pick a filter once you can stop thinking about it, and the pick is LANCZOS.

The spread collapses with the ratio, and that is not good news. At 1/2, edge error runs 12.80 to 2.38 — 5.4x. At 1/8 it runs 26.23 to 12.95 — 2.0x. The filters converge because every one of them has lost the same detail by then; they are all equally wrong. A small table of test images resized to thumbnails will make any two filters look similar, for this reason.

Whole-frame RMSE is nearly blind here. At 1/2, NEAREST scores 1.23 out of 255, which is 0.5%. If your quality gate averages over the frame, every filter in this table passes, including the one that turns a straight edge into a staircase. The edge is 2,114 pixels out of 960,000 — 0.2% of the image — and it is the part anyone looking at a product photo sees first. Restricting to those pixels changes the spread from 2.4x to 5.4x.

Ringing arrives with the ratio, not with the filter. At 1/2 no filter exceeds the master's own 4.3%, including LANCZOS, which has negative lobes and therefore can ring. At 1/4 it reads 8.3%, at 1/8 8.4%. NEAREST stays at 4.0% all the way down, because a box footprint never overshoots — it can't ring, it can only staircase. So "LANCZOS rings" is true only past a certain ratio, and "NEAREST is safe" is true only if you don't care about the staircase.

There is a contradiction buried in the 1/8 block. LANCZOS has the best RMSE by 2x and a wider 10–90% edge than NEAREST — 8.27 px against 7.89. Both are correct. RMSE sums a slight halo against a lot of staircase and prefers the halo. The rise measures one property and sees only the ramp. Neither number is the answer; a real acceptance test would need both, and most don't have either.

Sharpening buys sharpness with fidelity

ImageFilter.UnsharpMask(radius, percent, threshold) subtracts a blurred copy of the image from itself. It does not know what an edge is. Applied to the 1/2 LANCZOS roundtrip — the best case in the table above — ten settings:

radius amount RMSE edge RMSE rise overshoot
— none 0.51 2.38 4.03 4.3%
1.0 50% 0.52 2.31 3.86 4.3%
1.0 100% 0.60 3.06 3.52 4.3%
1.0 150% 0.69 4.01 3.39 5.8%
1.5 50% 0.59 2.94 3.44 5.2%
1.5 100% 0.83 5.32 2.88 6.2%
1.5 150% 1.08 7.75 2.62 7.7%
2.0 50% 0.70 3.90 3.12 6.2%
2.0 100% 1.11 7.68 2.53 10.6%
2.0 150% 1.51 11.28 2.23 14.9%

The last row takes 45% off the rise and triples the whole-frame error. Edge error goes from 2.38 to 11.28 — 4.7x — and overshoot from 4.3% to 14.9%, which is 7 luminance levels of halo on a 48-level step. Sharpening did not restore anything the filter destroyed. It moved the 10–90% crossings closer together by bending the curve, and the bending is the error.

The first row of the sweep is the interesting one, because it's free: radius 1 at 50% changes edge RMSE from 2.38 to 2.31 and whole-frame RMSE from 0.51 to 0.52. Both are inside the instrument's noise. A light pass at a small radius is not a trade, and if that is what your pipeline does, this post is not about you. The post is about the slider that goes to 150%.

Sharpen before the resize, or after?

Four ways to put the same sharpening in the same 1/2 LANCZOS pipeline. Radius 1.5 at 100%, and one variant where the radius is scaled to match:

where RMSE edge RMSE rise overshoot
sharpen the master, then resize 0.79 5.13 2.91 6.0%
resize, then sharpen 0.83 5.32 2.88 6.2%
resize, sharpen at half size, radius 1.5 1.54 11.15 2.34 17.0%
resize, sharpen at half size, radius 0.75 0.78 4.93 2.91 6.2%

The first two are a tie. Order, on its own, does not matter. What matters is that radius is in output pixels: the same 1.5 at half resolution covers twice the image distance once you scale back up, which is why the third row is a different, much worse operation than the second, and why the fourth row — same effect, correct number — comes back to the tie.

That's the trap worth remembering. If you chain resize and sharpen, either sharpen at output size, or scale the radius by the ratio. Keeping the number and changing the resolution is not the same filter.

Enlargement: nothing is recovered, and one thing is faked

The other direction, because half of these pipelines exist to hit a 2000×2000 minimum from whatever the seller uploaded. A 600×400 export of the master, blown up to 2000×1333 with each filter:

filter rise gradient energy
NEAREST 6.57 0.1541
BOX 6.57 0.1541
BILINEAR 8.00 0.1513
BICUBIC 7.25 0.1577
LANCZOS 6.82 0.1639
LANCZOS + unsharp r2 150% 4.92 0.1740

BOX and NEAREST come out within 0.05 px of each other on every edge number in the table, which is not a coincidence: above a ratio of 1, an output pixel's box footprint almost never spans two source pixels, so there is almost nothing to average. They are not literally the same image — 0.055% of pixels differ, by up to 59 levels where a box lands on a sliver of the neighbouring pixel — but on a photo, the difference is invisible. If you have both in a filter switch, one of them is dead code.

BILINEAR is 1.2 px wider than LANCZOS and has lower gradient energy: that is blur the filter added. Blur is honest — it doesn't claim to be detail.

The last row is not. The photo's own edge is 4.07 px at 1200 px wide, so at 2000 px it would be 6.79 px; LANCZOS lands at 6.82, which is as close to the floor as this instrument can resolve. Sharpening a 600 px file pushed to 2000 px takes it to 4.92 px, 27% narrower than the original photo's edge. No filter can make a copy sharper than the thing it copied. A 10–90% rise measurement cannot tell that it happened — it just returns a smaller number, which is exactly what a reviewer would call "sharper".

One more detail from the same row: radius 1 at 100% on that enlargement leaves the rise at 6.82, unchanged, while raising gradient energy from 0.1639 to 0.1646. A radius has to approach the width of the ramp before it bends it. On a 3.33x enlargement the ramp is ~7 px, and a 1 px radius is a rounding error on it.

What I'd put in the pipeline

  • One filter, everywhere. LANCZOS, and stop overriding it. It wins at every ratio in the table, and the alternative in most codebases is the library default rather than a decision.
  • Chaining is a tie only if your filter is good. I measured master → 1/8 in one pass against master → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8. LANCZOS: 12.95 edge RMSE direct, 12.90 chained — a tie. NEAREST: 26.23 direct, 32.55 chained, 24% worse. The "resize in steps" advice exists because cheap filters have small support; give it a filter with proper support and the extra passes buy nothing but time.
  • Keep each reduction at 4x or less. At 1/2 nothing rings; at 1/4 LANCZOS is already at 8.3% and at 1/8 it stays there. A 3000 px master exported to 2000×2000 is a 1.5x, nowhere near the region where any of this matters.
  • Sharpen at output size, at radius 1, at 50–100%, if you sharpen at all. Past that, the table says you're buying something.
  • Never sharpen an upscale. It cannot add detail, and it narrows the ramp below what the source supports. The instrument that a QA step would use cannot see the difference.
  • Score edge pixels, not the frame. A 1.23 RMSE average passes a staircase.

The measurement is small enough to keep as a test. This is the whole rise instrument, minus the interpolation helper:

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

def rise_px(img, rows, win):
    a = np.array(img.convert("L"), dtype=float)
    vals = []
    for y in range(*rows):
        seg = a[y, win[0]:win[1]]
        pad = max(int(len(seg) * 0.15), 3)
        lo, hi = np.median(seg[:pad]), np.median(seg[-pad:])
        if hi - lo < 20:
            continue
        x10 = cross(seg, lo + 0.1 * (hi - lo))
        x90 = cross(seg, lo + 0.9 * (hi - lo))
        if x10 is not None and x90 is not None and x90 > x10:
            vals.append(x90 - x10)
    return float(np.median(vals))

Point it at a ten-row strip across any known edge in a test fixture, and you have a resize regression test that catches a filter change, a library upgrade that moves a default, or somebody's sharpening pass — which is how I found most of this.

What this doesn't cover

One photo, one edge, one polarity. A dark subject on a light background. A light subject on dark would flip the sign of the ringing and, at these magnitudes, could look different to a viewer even where the numbers match.

A JPEG master that already rings. The 4.3% baseline overshoot is the photo's, not the filters'. A clean PNG master would show filter ringing more clearly, especially at 1/2 where everything here sits at the baseline.

A roundtrip is not a downscale. Going down and back up costs each filter twice and can flatter the ones that ring, because the upscale re-smooths the halo. A single downscale, scored at the small size against a downsampled master, would give different absolute numbers — probably smaller gaps, same order.

Luminance only. Resizing also desaturates edge pixels, and the series has the chroma instruments to test that; I didn't run them here. A colour edge would not necessarily behave like a grey one.

sRGB, not linear. PIL resizes in the file's own encoding, which for a product photo is sRGB, so the filtering happens on gamma-encoded values. Doing it in linear light changes both the edge brightness and the ringing amplitude, and that is its own measurement, which I have not run. This post is about what the libraries do, not what they ought to do.

The rise instrument is good to ~15%. Don't quote the difference between 2.31 and 2.38 as a finding. I did, once, and had to walk it back.

I work on PicViva, an editor whose resize for marketplaces exists to hit five platforms' size rules from one master, and whose clarity enhancement is the sharpening pass described above with the slider exposed. The reason this got measured instead of guessed is that the two features disagree: the resize wants to be gentle and the sharpen wants to be visible, and shipping both with per-marketplace presets means I had to know which one was allowed to move first — and what to do when a seller turns the sharpening up because the exported thumbnail "looks soft".

If you've measured this on your own photos: does LANCZOS come out ahead for you too, or does your subject break the ranking?

title: Stop Letting AI Agents Approve Their Own Code: Two-Repo Split, Cross-Model Review, and a $40 Cloud Test VM
description:
I run up to 4 AI coding agents in parallel on a 16 GB MacBook. Whenever two of them launched full pytest runs at the same time, macOS hit swap immediately and froze. Worse, when I let the same agent edit code, run tests, and report success, it sometimes relaxed assertions to make a failing test pass or returned an exit 0 from stale artifacts left in a shared directory.

Telling an LLM in a prompt to "be careful" or "don't touch unrelated files" stops working once the context window fills up. I replaced prompt-based discipline with hard repository boundaries, cross-model code review, and a shared cloud test runner. This setup currently backs my personal quantitative research codebase with nearly 7,000 tests, and every piece of it works just as well for any Python or backend project.

1. Split the Repo in Two: Scheduling vs. Computation

When all my code lived in one repository, an agent fixing a data loader bug could casually edit the task scheduler or read out-of-sample validation data from an exploratory script. No amount of Markdown instructions stopped that reliably.

I split the system into two separate Git repositories:

  • Control repo (task_manager): Handles the task queue, state machine, budgets, out-of-sample data locks, and an append-only run ledger. It never runs numerical calculations.
  • Execution repo (quantation_factor_database): Handles market data, metrics, and artifact exports. It only exposes a narrow CLI (tools.agent_harness.cli) and has zero scheduling privileges.

Approach Risk of Cross-Module Edits Concurrent Merge Conflicts Trade-Off You Accept
Single repo + prompt rules High after long sessions High Constant manual cleanup
Monorepo with folder rules Medium (direct imports still work) Medium Painful to split out public code later
Two separate Git repos Low (process and repo boundary) Low (independent test suites) Must maintain a strict CLI and JSON contract

Splitting into two repos does add overhead. Every cross-repo change requires updating the CLI flags and JSON schema on both sides, and we use Copybara to export allowlisted parts of the execution repo to our public open-source project GSX-Eis/jq-factor-lab. In return, an agent working on computation can never touch scheduling rules.

2. Never Let the Same Model Write and Review Code

Letting one model write a patch and verify it is an easy way to get false positives. A single model has blind spots around its own assumptions, and when a test fails, it often tries to work around the failure by loosening an assertion or returning a default value so the process exits with 0.

I also ran into silent cache bugs where a script exited 0 after writing an empty file, or a wrapper read an old report left behind in a shared output folder.

To stop both failure modes, I split work across four steps and different model families:

  1. Leader scopes the task: A coordinating agent checks the read-only baseline, breaks work into non-overlapping tasks, and lists the exact files each task may touch. Multica gives each task its own Git worktree, so 4 agents never overwrite each other's files.
  2. Builder implements: The builder works only inside its worktree, runs commands through tools.agent_harness.cli instead of raw internal scripts, and runs changed tests in the cloud before submitting.
  3. A different model reviews: A reviewer from another model family reads the diff line by line. It specifically looks for weakened assertions, missing error handling, and unclosed locks, sending the branch back if negative tests are missing.
  4. Temp-tree merge and full regression: The leader merges via --no-ff in a temporary worktree and runs the full 12-shard suite before closing the task.

Resolving Doc Conflicts

When human planning docs and code disagree, agents often copy stale commands from an outdated README. I added a strict precedence rule in AGENTS.md at the repo root:

  1. Live CLI --help output (highest authority)
  2. Runtime config files and typed schemas (schemas/)
  3. Operator flows in README.md
  4. Historical planning notes (.planning/, background only, never copy commands from here)

Exit Code 0 Is Not Enough

Our CLI wrapper separates "the subprocess didn't crash" from "the output is valid." Every invocation gets a fresh execution_id, writes to attempts/<execution_id>/result.json, and checks the SHA-256 hash of the source config. If the file is missing or the hash doesn't match, the wrapper blocks the run with exit code 4 even if the child process returned 0:

EXIT_SUCCESS = 0       # Process exited 0 and schema + SHA-256 checks passed
EXIT_PRECONDITION = 2  # Missing config or boundary violation before start
EXIT_EXECUTION = 3     # Subprocess crashed, timed out, or killed by signal
EXIT_QUALITY_GATE = 4  # Subprocess returned 0, but output is missing or tampered

def verify_bound_result(result_path: Path, expected_run_id: str, config_sha256: str) -> dict:
    # Read only from this invocation's execution_id folder to avoid stale artifacts
    payload = read_json_strict(result_path)
    if payload.get("run_id") != expected_run_id:
        raise ContractGateError("run_id mismatch: refusing stale artifact", code=EXIT_QUALITY_GATE)
    if payload.get("source_config_sha256") != config_sha256:
        raise ContractGateError("config hash mismatch: evidence tampered", code=EXIT_QUALITY_GATE)
    return payload

3. Moving 418 Test Files Off a 16GB Laptop Onto a $40/mo Spot VM

Once the execution repo grew to 418 test files across 12 shards (nearly 7,000 tests), running suites locally on a 16 GB MacBook became unusable. I banned local pytest runs completely and moved all unit, shard, and full regression runs to a single GCP Spot VM (8 vCPU / 32 GiB RAM / 100 GB disk) with a hard $40/month budget.

Why Not GitHub Actions or One VM Per Agent

  • GitHub Actions: Some frozen test fixtures and private samples don't belong on hosted CI, and cold-starting Numba, DuckDB, and PyArrow on every run was too slow.
  • One VM per agent: Blows past the $40 monthly budget and creates environment drift across machines.

Sharing one Spot VM behind a lock queue means only one full regression runs at a time, and concurrent worktrees either wait or exit with code 75 to retry. In exchange, the environment stays identical and cheap.

Two-Layer Locking and Thread Caps

Before syncing code, the local runner acquires quantation-gcp.lock across worktrees. On the VM, every run goes through /usr/local/bin/cloud-test-lease-run.sh (a kernel flock lease) and locks numerical libraries to a single thread so 6 pytest-xdist workers don't oversubscribe 8 vCPUs:

REMOTE_THREAD_ENV = {
    "OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS": "1",
    "OMP_NUM_THREADS": "1",
    "VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS": "1",
    "MKL_NUM_THREADS": "1",
    "NUMBA_NUM_THREADS": "1",
}

def build_leased_remote_cmd(lease_cmd: str, lease_id: str, target_cmd: str) -> str:
    # Keep fd 8 open for stdin (such as rsync filter rules) when the lease wrapper backgrounds
    restore_stdin = "exec \"$@\" <&8"
    return f"exec 8<&0; exec {lease_cmd} {lease_id} -- sh -c '{restore_stdin}' sh {target_cmd}"

Two Real Pitfalls on the Cloud VM

  • Idle auto-shutdown colliding with SSH: To stay under $40/month, quant-idle.timer checks active leases and SSH sessions every 5 minutes and powers off the VM after 20 minutes of idle time (agents are forbidden from running manual shutdown commands). Twice, a merge run hit SSH timeouts because the VM happened to be shutting down right as the job started. We fixed this in CloudRunner by checking instance state first and calling gcloud compute instances start when the VM is TERMINATED.
  • Six xdist workers crashing Numba on dcor: Turning up concurrency to 6 workers caused random collection-phase aborts when multiple workers imported dcor at the same time and raced on the Numba/LLVM cache. Warming up dcor serially once inside the lease before launching xdist fixed it cleanly.

4. Deleting SQLite So Agents Can't Pick the Wrong Database

Humans leave fallback code around for backwards compatibility, but fallback paths give AI agents extra ways to fail. When SQLite and DuckDB coexisted in our repo, agents occasionally wrote results to the wrong backend inside an exception handler.

I removed SQLAlchemy, SQLite loaders, and automatic auto backend detection completely, leaving DuckDB + Parquet as the only storage path, guarded by static contract tests that fail if anyone re-imports old database drivers.

On the scheduling side, quality_gate.sh runs a 10-step check before every merge, including Ruff, type checks, package boundary linting, and an isolated contract check in a temporary directory:

# Hard gate: verify package boundaries and run contract checks in an isolated temp dir
"$python_bin" -m task_manager.tools.arch_linter --boundary --json || GATE_FAILED=1

"$python_bin" - <<'PY'
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

# Test schema contracts in an OS temp dir so we never touch the live workspace state/
with TemporaryDirectory(prefix="contract_gate_") as tmp_dir:
    root = Path(tmp_dir).resolve()
    init_schema(sqlite3.connect(root / "state.db"))
    raise SystemExit(run_cli(["--task-root", str(root), "--json", "check", "contracts"]))
PY

5. Current Numbers, Six Hard Rules, and Open Problems

Here's where both repositories stand on our latest verified runs:

  • Execution repo (GCP Spot, all 12 shards / 418 files): 6,884 passed, 32 existing baseline failures, 11 skipped, 0 collection errors in 749.25 seconds (~12.5 minutes). Daily --changed --fast runs finish in 1 to 2 minutes.
  • Control repo (quality_gate.sh): 2,954 passed, 43 existing failures, 36 skipped, 0 collection errors, ~80% coverage on core modules, and 0 boundary violations.
Failure Mode Prompt-Only Fix (Fails) Engineering Constraint (Works) Cost You Pay
Agents edit unrelated core modules "Don't touch other files" Two separate repos + arch_linter Must maintain CLI/JSON contract
Same model loosens test assertions "Check edge cases carefully" Separate author and reviewer models Extra review turn and tokens
exit 0 returned from empty/stale files Trust process exit code Fresh execution_id dir + config SHA-256 Extra schema check in wrapper
Concurrent pytest freezes 16GB Mac Ask agents to run sequentially Ban local pytest, route to Spot VM Must maintain rsync filter rules
Worktrees overwrite remote workspace Coordinate manually in chat Local lock + remote flock lease One heavy suite runs at a time
Agents pick stale docs or wrong DB Patch the prompt repeatedly Strict doc order + delete SQLite path Must clean up legacy fallbacks

Two limitations remain open. First, as I spin up more concurrent branches, queue wait times on a single 8-vCPU Spot VM may become a bottleneck. Second, both repos still carry pre-existing test failures (43 in control, 32 in execution) that we gate on "zero new failures" while paying down the backlog.

When you run multiple AI coding agents in parallel, what breaks first in your workflow: stale context, tests passing on weak assertions, or agents stepping on each other's environments?

Disclosure: I built and run this system myself, verified every command, exit code, and test count against the actual repositories, and used AI tools to help draft and tighten the English prose.

title: HTML Sémantique : Pourquoi arrêter d'utiliser des <div> partout
description:
Si vous avez déjà inspecté le code source d'un site web moderne, vous êtes probablement tombé sur ce que les développeurs appellent affectueusement la « soupe de <div> » (div soup). Des dizaines de balises

imbriquées les unes dans les autres, sans aucune indication sur leur rôle réel.

Visuellement, avec un bon fichier CSS, une page construite uniquement avec des <div> et des <span> peut ressembler à s'y méprendre à un site parfaitement structuré. Alors, pourquoi s'embêter à apprendre et utiliser d'autres balises ?

La sémantique HTML n'est pas un caprice de puriste. C'est le socle invisible qui détermine la qualité de votre référencement, l'accessibilité de votre site et la maintenabilité de votre code.

1. Qu'est-ce que le HTML sémantique ?

Une balise sémantique est une balise qui décrit clairement le sens du contenu qu'elle renferme, tant pour le navigateur que pour le développeur.

  • Balises non sémantiques : <div> et <span>. Elles ne donnent aucune information sur leur contenu. Ce sont des boîtes génériques utilisées uniquement pour la mise en page ou le style.

  • Balises sémantiques : <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <footer>, ou encore . Dès qu'on lit la balise, on comprend immédiatement sa fonction dans la page.

2. Les 3 impacts concrets sur vos projets

Passer d'une « soupe de <div> » à un HTML sémantique transforme radicalement le comportement de votre page web sur trois plans essentiels.

1. L'accessibilité (A11y) : Ouvrir le web à tous

C'est l'argument numéro un. Les personnes malvoyantes ou aveugles naviguent sur le web grâce à des lecteurs d'écran (comme NVDA, JAWS ou VoiceOver). Ces outils ne « voient » pas votre CSS ; ils lisent votre arbre HTML.

• Avec des <div>, le lecteur d'écran lit tout le texte à la suite, sans repères. L'utilisateur ne sait pas où commence le menu ni où se trouve le contenu principal.

• Avec des balises sémantiques, le lecteur d'écran annonce : « Navigation », « Contenu principal », « Pied de page ». L'utilisateur peut sauter directement d'une section à l'autre grâce aux raccourcis clavier.

Le piège classique du bouton : Créer un bouton avec <div class="btn" onclick="...">Valider</div> est une erreur majeure. Contrairement à une vraie balise <button> , une <div> n'est pas focalisable au clavier (touche Tab), ne réagit pas à la touche Entrée et n'est pas reconnue comme interactive par les technologies d'assistance.

2. Le référencement naturel (SEO)

Les moteurs de recherche comme Google envoient des robots (crawlers) pour analyser et indexer vos pages. Ces robots utilisent la structure HTML pour hiérarchiser l'information.

• Le contenu placé dans une balise <main> ou <article> est considéré comme le cœur du sujet de votre page.
• Le contenu placé dans <nav> ou <footer> est identifié comme secondaire ou répétitif.

En utilisant les bonnes balises, vous facilitez le travail des algorithmes de recherche et améliorez vos chances d'apparaître dans les résultats enrichis (rich snippets).

*3. La lisibilité et la maintenabilité du code
*
Imaginez devoir reprendre le code d'un collègue (ou le vôtre, six mois plus tard) et tomber sur ceci :

<!-- ❌ Difficile à lire et à maintenir -->
<div class="top-bar">
  <div class="menu">...</div>
</div>
<div class="wrapper">
  <div class="left-col">
    <div class="post">...</div>
  </div>
  <div class="right-col">...</div>
</div>
<div class="bottom">...</div>

Comparez maintenant avec la version sémantique :

<!-- ✅ Clair, explicite et standardisé -->
<header>
  <nav>...</nav>
</header>
<main>
  <article>...</article>
  <aside>...</aside>
</main>
<footer>...</footer>

Le code est immédiatement compréhensible. Vous n'avez même plus besoin de commentaires pour indiquer où se ferme la balise principale : </main> parle de lui-même.

3. Les balises essentielles à adopter dès aujourd'hui

Vous n'avez pas besoin de mémoriser les plus de 100 balises HTML existantes pour bien démarrer. Maîtriser ces 7 balises de structure couvre 90 % des besoins d'une page web :

  • <header> L'en-tête de la page ou d'une section (contient souvent le logo, le titre principal et la navigation).

  • <nav> Un bloc contenant les liens de navigation principaux du site.

  • <main> Le contenu principal et unique de la page. Attention : il ne doit y en avoir qu'un seul par page.

  • <article> Un contenu autonome et réutilisable (un article de blog, une fiche produit, un commentaire).

  • <section> Un regroupement thématique de contenu, généralement introduit par un titre (<h2>, <h3>).

  • <aside> Un contenu indirectement lié au contenu principal (une barre latérale, des articles similaires, une publicité).

  • <footer> Le pied de page (mentions légales, copyright, liens secondaires, coordonnées).

4. Faut-il bannir totalement la balise <div> ?

Absolument pas ! La balise <div> reste parfaitement légitime lorsqu'elle est utilisée pour ce pour quoi elle a été créée : être un conteneur purement visuel.

Si vous avez besoin d'envelopper deux éléments uniquement pour leur appliquer une grille CSS (display: grid), un alignement Flexbox ou une bordure décorative, sans qu'il n'y ait de sens particulier derrière ce regroupement, la

est l'outil idéal.

La règle d'or: Posez-vous toujours la question : « Existe-t-il une balise HTML qui décrit ce que cet élément est ? » Si la réponse est non, utilisez une <div>.

Conclusion

Écrire du HTML sémantique ne prend pas plus de temps que d'écrire des <div>. C'est simplement une habitude à prendre dès l'intégration de vos maquettes. En adoptant ces réflexes, vous rendez le web plus inclusif, vous optimisez votre SEO gratuitement et vous gagnez un temps précieux lors de la maintenance de vos projets.

title: Hosting AI Agents in Production: Serverless, Containers, or VPS?
description:
When developers build their first AI agent, they usually deploy it the exact same way they deploy a standard REST API. They wrap the agent framework in a FastAPI or Express endpoint and push it to AWS Lambda, Vercel, or Serverless Functions.

Then the performance and reliability issues begin.

A standard REST API is completely stateless. A client sends a request, the server executes business logic, returns a JSON payload, and destroys the execution context.

An AI agent does not work this way. Agents maintain memory across conversation turns, execute multi-step tool calls, wait on third-party APIs, and rely on warm execution environments to avoid costly re-initialization steps.

Deploying agents without considering these execution lifecycles leads to broken context, timeout errors, and unnecessary cloud spend.

The Serverless Trap: Cold Starts and Lost Memory

Serverless platforms are engineered to scale to zero. When a request hits a serverless function, the infrastructure spins up a micro-container, processes the request, and tears down the container when idle.

If your agent needs to maintain in-memory context or run complex multi-step workflows, serverless introduces three major bottlenecks:

  1. Cold Starts: Re-instantiating heavy framework objects, vector store connections, and LLM clients on every cold request adds seconds of user-perceived latency.
  2. Execution Limits: Most serverless platforms cap single request execution times (e.g., AWS Lambda's 15-minute hard limit or default web host timeouts of 15–30 seconds). An agent looping through multiple tool calls can easily hit these limits.
  3. State Hydration Overhead: To maintain state across turns, every single invocation must fetch full conversation history and vector embeddings from external databases, re-hydrate the agent's memory, execute one step, and persist the state back.

Here is what state re-hydration looks like in a serverless context:

from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, AIMessage
from my_agent import AgentRunner
import db

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    session_id = event["session_id"]
    user_input = event["message"]

    # Must re-fetch and re-build agent state on EVERY request
    history = db.get_chat_history(session_id)
    agent = AgentRunner(model="gpt-4o")
    agent.load_memory(history)

    # Execution can time out if the agent loops through multiple tools
    response = agent.run(user_input)

    db.save_chat_history(session_id, agent.memory)
    return {"statusCode": 200, "body": response}

While this architecture works fine for single-turn Q&A bots, complex multi-turn workflows quickly become slow, fragile, and difficult to debug.

Containers and VPS: Keeping Context Warm

If your agent executes multi-step workflows, runs background tasks, or maintains persistent connections, long-running processes are superior. This means using containers (Docker via AWS ECS, GCP Cloud Run with allocated instances, or Kubernetes) or a Virtual Private Server (VPS).

In a containerized or VPS environment, the process stays alive between requests. You can hold short-term session state in memory, stream responses over WebSockets or Server-Sent Events (SSE), and execute long-running background tasks without strict request timeout limits.

Here is how an agent runner operates inside a persistent process model:

from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket
from my_agent import AgentRunner

app = FastAPI()
# Agent instances stay warm in memory across requests
active_agents = {}

@app.websocket("/ws/agent/{session_id}")
async def agent_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket, session_id: str):
    await websocket.accept()

    if session_id not in active_agents:
        active_agents[session_id] = AgentRunner(session_id=session_id)

    agent = active_agents[session_id]

    while True:
        user_message = await websocket.receive_text()
        # Stream response back immediately without re-initializing tools
        async for chunk in agent.stream_response(user_message):
            await websocket.send_text(chunk)

With this setup, connection overhead is minimized, context remains warm, and streaming responses back to the client requires zero architectural workarounds.

The trade-off is infrastructure management. You now own scaling policies, process restarts, health checks, and resource monitoring.

How to Choose: A Practical Framework

The decision comes down to execution duration, state requirements, and operational overhead:

  • Serverless (AWS Lambda, Vercel): Best for single-turn agents, simple prompt-in/response-out APIs, or tasks guaranteed to finish under 30 seconds without complex context retention.
  • Containers (AWS ECS, GCP Cloud Run, Kubernetes): Best for production enterprise applications needing automatic horizontal scaling, isolated environments per tenant, and long-running multi-step tool execution.
  • VPS (Hetzner, DigitalOcean): Best for early-stage products, fixed-cost predictable workloads, and agents requiring local disk storage or local background queues like Celery.

The goal isn't to pick the cheapest or trendiest stack. It's to deploy on a platform that respects the stateful, iterative nature of AI agents.

About Me

Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. Invite readers to connect on LinkedIn to discuss agent architecture or custom automation builds.
