title: Separate the Job, the Run, and the Worker Claim
description:
The previous tutorial ended with a completed job. A reader tried the next thing: put that job back in the queue.

Ace Meridian's comment found a useful boundary in the example. Its completions table had job_id as the primary key. Manually changing a completed job back to ready let a worker claim it again, but inserting its second completion collided with the first.

A local reproduction confirmed the collision. The completion transaction rolled back, leaving the manually reopened job ready, claimed, and without a new result. The old example had no requeue API: completion was terminal. Adding requeue means changing that model.

This follow-up separates three identities:

Identity Meaning When it changes
job_id The report we can run again When we create a different job
run_id One intentionally requested execution When we request another run
generation The worker claim within that run When another worker takes over

The important distinction is between retrying an existing run and requesting another run. Those operations need different behavior even when their input happens to look the same.

Keep the completed run

Suppose report-1 finishes as run-1. We then explicitly request run-2:

report-1
  run-1: done, result = "first"
  run-2: ready, generation = 0  <-- current

Starting the next run inserts a new row and moves jobs.current_run_id in one database transaction. It does not clear the old result or change the completed row back to ready.

An expired worker claim is different. A takeover keeps the same run_id and increments its generation. It is still trying to finish the same requested execution.

Carry the issued claim all the way to completion

In the lease tutorial, completion checked the worker and its generation. Here it also checks the run identity and the job's current-run pointer.

That matters when two runs both issue generation 1 to worker-a. Matching the worker name and generation alone does not identify the same execution. A late completion carrying run-1 must not become a completion of run-2.

The worker keeps the exact claim returned by claim(). It must not read the latest row and construct a replacement claim from someone else's current ownership fields. These plain Python values are a trusted fixture contract, not signed capabilities or an authentication layer.

Retry the request to start a run

There is another lost-response boundary: the server commits run-2, but the caller never receives the acknowledgement.

Generating run-3 on that retry would express a different intent. The caller instead persists new_run_id before its first request and reuses that ID on retry. In a real API it also needs to scope that identifier to the authenticated caller or tenant.

start_next_run() first checks whether that job/run pair already exists:

  • Same parent: return the already accepted run ID. Do not reset its claim, result, or current-run pointer.
  • Different parent: refuse reuse of the ID with a different meaning.
  • No existing row: require the expected parent to be current and done, then insert the new run and move the pointer atomically.

A particularly useful test replays the old request after run-3 is current. The response still identifies run-2; the job remains on run-3. A successful replay is not an instruction to make an old run current again.

AWS's idempotent API design article explains the underlying client-intent distinction and why parameter mismatches and identifier retention need explicit contracts. This fixture has only a parent ID to compare. A configurable report would also need to bind the accepted run to its original parameters.

Runnable example

Save the complete file below as job_runs.py and run it with Python 3.12 or later:

python job_runs.py

It uses only the standard library and temporary SQLite files. The test clock is deterministic. Work happens outside the database transaction; only claim, completion, and starting the next run acquire the write transaction.

SQLite permits one write transaction at a time. BEGIN IMMEDIATE acquires that transaction before the fixture reads and updates its state; it can still fail when another writer remains busy. See SQLite's transaction documentation. The two concurrent tests use separate connections and a barrier, without timing sleeps.

"""Job/run/claim fixture. Python 3.12+, standard library, local database only.
Run: python job_runs.py
"""
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from contextlib import closing, contextmanager
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from threading import Barrier
import sqlite3
import tempfile
import unittest


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Lease:
    job_id: str
    run_id: str
    owner: str
    generation: int


class Conflict(Exception):
    pass


class LeaseLost(Exception):
    pass


class Clock:
    def __init__(self, now=0):
        self.now = now

    def __call__(self):
        return self.now


def connect(path):
    db = sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=5, autocommit=True)
    db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return db


def one(db, sql, args=()):
    with closing(db.execute(sql, args)) as cursor:
        return cursor.fetchone()


@contextmanager
def transaction(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        try:
            db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE").close()
            yield db
            db.execute("COMMIT").close()
        except BaseException:
            if db.in_transaction:
                db.execute("ROLLBACK").close()
            raise


def initialize(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        db.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE jobs (
            job_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            current_run_id TEXT NOT NULL
        );
        CREATE TABLE runs (
            job_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            run_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            parent_run_id TEXT,
            generation INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
            owner TEXT, lease_until INTEGER,
            state TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ready'
                CHECK (state IN ('ready', 'done')),
            result TEXT,
            PRIMARY KEY (job_id, run_id)
        );
        INSERT INTO jobs VALUES ('report-1', 'run-1');
        INSERT INTO runs (job_id, run_id) VALUES ('report-1', 'run-1');
        """).close()


def claim(path, job_id, run_id, owner, clock, ttl=10):
    if type(ttl) is not int or ttl not in range(1, 3601):
        raise ValueError("TTL must be an integer in 1..3600")
    if not isinstance(owner, str) or not owner:
        raise ValueError("owner must be non-empty")
    with transaction(path) as db:
        now = clock()
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE runs
            SET generation = generation + 1, owner = ?, lease_until = ?
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ? AND state = 'ready'
              AND (owner IS NULL OR lease_until <= ?)
              AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM jobs
                WHERE jobs.job_id = runs.job_id
                  AND jobs.current_run_id = runs.run_id)""",
                (owner, now + ttl, job_id, run_id, now))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                return None
        generation = one(db, """SELECT generation FROM runs
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?""", (job_id, run_id))[0]
        return Lease(job_id, run_id, owner, generation)


def complete(path, lease, result, clock):
    with transaction(path) as db:
        now = clock()
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE runs
            SET state = 'done', result = ?, owner = NULL, lease_until = NULL
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ? AND owner = ? AND generation = ?
              AND state = 'ready' AND lease_until > ?
              AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM jobs
                WHERE jobs.job_id = runs.job_id
                  AND jobs.current_run_id = runs.run_id)""",
                (result, lease.job_id, lease.run_id, lease.owner,
                 lease.generation, now))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                raise LeaseLost("completion refused")
    return result


def start_next_run(path, job_id, expected_run_id, new_run_id):
    """Persist new_run_id before calling; reuse it for retries of this intent."""
    if not isinstance(new_run_id, str) or not new_run_id:
        raise ValueError("new_run_id must be non-empty")
    with transaction(path) as db:
        existing = one(db, """SELECT parent_run_id FROM runs
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?""", (job_id, new_run_id))
        if existing is not None:
            if existing[0] != expected_run_id:
                raise Conflict("run ID reused with a different parent")
            return new_run_id  # Replay acceptance, never reset the run.
        current = one(db, """SELECT runs.state FROM jobs JOIN runs
            ON runs.job_id = jobs.job_id AND runs.run_id = jobs.current_run_id
            WHERE jobs.job_id = ? AND jobs.current_run_id = ?""",
            (job_id, expected_run_id))
        if current is None or current[0] != 'done':
            raise Conflict("expected run must be current and completed")
        db.execute("""INSERT INTO runs (job_id, run_id, parent_run_id)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?)""", (job_id, new_run_id, expected_run_id)).close()
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE jobs SET current_run_id = ?
            WHERE job_id = ? AND current_run_id = ?""",
                (new_run_id, job_id, expected_run_id))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                raise Conflict("current run changed")
    return new_run_id


def snapshot(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        current = one(db, "SELECT current_run_id FROM jobs WHERE job_id = ?",
                      ('report-1',))[0]
        with closing(db.execute("SELECT * FROM runs ORDER BY run_id")) as cur:
            return current, [dict(row) for row in cur.fetchall()]


class RunTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        base = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'test-db'
        base.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        self.temp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='runs-', dir=base)
        assert Path(self.temp.name).resolve().is_relative_to(base.resolve())
        self.addCleanup(self.temp.cleanup)
        self.path = Path(self.temp.name) / 'jobs.sqlite'
        self.clock = Clock()
        initialize(self.path)

    def claim(self, run='run-1', owner='worker-a'):
        return claim(self.path, 'report-1', run, owner, self.clock)

    def finish(self, run='run-1', result='first'):
        token = self.claim(run)
        complete(self.path, token, result, self.clock)
        return token

    def next(self, parent='run-1', new='run-2'):
        return start_next_run(self.path, 'report-1', parent, new)

    def test_new_run_preserves_both_results(self):
        self.finish()
        self.next()
        self.finish('run-2', 'second')
        current, rows = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertEqual(current, 'run-2')
        self.assertEqual([(r['state'], r['result']) for r in rows],
                         [('done', 'first'), ('done', 'second')])

    def test_old_run_refused_even_when_owner_and_generation_match(self):
        old = self.finish()
        self.next()
        new = self.claim('run-2')
        self.assertEqual((old.owner, old.generation), (new.owner, new.generation))
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(LeaseLost):
            complete(self.path, old, 'late old result', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)
        complete(self.path, new, 'second', self.clock)

    def test_requeue_retry_does_not_reset_running_claim(self):
        self.finish()
        self.next()  # Pretend this response was lost.
        token = self.claim('run-2')
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertEqual(self.next(), 'run-2')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)
        complete(self.path, token, 'second', self.clock)

    def test_historical_retry_does_not_move_current_pointer_back(self):
        self.finish()
        self.next()
        self.finish('run-2', 'second')
        self.next('run-2', 'run-3')
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertEqual(self.next(), 'run-2')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)
        self.assertEqual(before[0], 'run-3')

    def race(self, ids):
        barrier = Barrier(2)
        def attempt(new_id):
            barrier.wait(timeout=5)
            try:
                return ('accepted', self.next(new=new_id))
            except Conflict:
                return ('conflict', new_id)
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
            return list(pool.map(attempt, ids))

    def test_competing_new_intents_only_one_wins(self):
        self.finish()
        outcomes = self.race(['run-2a', 'run-2b'])
        self.assertEqual(sorted(x[0] for x in outcomes), ['accepted', 'conflict'])
        self.assertEqual(len(snapshot(self.path)[1]), 2)

    def test_concurrent_duplicate_intent_returns_same_run(self):
        self.finish()
        self.assertEqual(self.race(['run-2', 'run-2']),
                         [('accepted', 'run-2'), ('accepted', 'run-2')])
        self.assertEqual(len(snapshot(self.path)[1]), 2)

    def test_unfinished_run_cannot_be_requeued(self):
        self.claim()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(Conflict):
            self.next()
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_run_id_reuse_with_different_parent_is_rejected(self):
        self.finish()
        self.next()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(Conflict):
            self.next('another-parent', 'run-2')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_pointer_failure_rolls_back_insert(self):
        self.finish()
        with closing(connect(self.path)) as db:
            db.execute("""CREATE TRIGGER reject_pointer BEFORE UPDATE ON jobs
                BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'injected failure'); END""").close()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(sqlite3.IntegrityError):
            self.next()
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_takeover_changes_claim_not_run_identity(self):
        first = self.claim()
        self.clock.now = 10
        second = self.claim(owner='worker-b')
        self.assertEqual((second.run_id, second.generation), ('run-1', 2))
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(LeaseLost):
            complete(self.path, first, 'stale', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)
        complete(self.path, second, 'winner', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(len(snapshot(self.path)[1]), 1)

    def test_expired_claim_refused_without_takeover(self):
        token = self.claim()
        self.clock.now = 10
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(LeaseLost):
            complete(self.path, token, 'late', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_wrong_job_and_old_run_cannot_claim_new_run(self):
        self.finish()
        self.next()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertIsNone(self.claim('run-1'))
        self.assertIsNone(claim(self.path, 'another-job', 'run-2',
                                'worker-a', self.clock))
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

What the tests establish

The local run passed 12 tests, including:

  • Two completed runs retain their separate results.
  • An old completion is refused even when the new claim has the same worker name and generation.
  • Replaying an accepted start request does not reset an active worker or move the current pointer backward.
  • Two competing new intents have one winner; two concurrent copies of the same intent return the same run ID.
  • A failure while updating the current pointer rolls back the new run insert.
  • Takeover increments a claim generation within one run, while an expired claim remains unable to complete.

These are checks of this local database contract. They do not establish delivery or cancellation guarantees for a remote queue, file store, webhook, or email provider.

Where the boundary ends

The fixture deliberately keeps every run. Deleting old rows would also delete the record used to recognize a late retry, so production retention needs a defined retry window and, where necessary, durable tombstones. A new run ID should never be recycled within that contract.

It does not implement renewal, cancel, scheduling, tenant authorization, or a durable audit log of refusals. SQL constraints and restricted write paths would need to protect the state model from arbitrary administrative updates. The claim values are supplied by trusted workers; copying a current claim out of the database is outside that trust boundary.

An external artifact can be staged under an immutable key containing both run ID and claim generation, then published through an accepted completion pointer. Keep artifacts still referenced by historical completed runs; garbage collection also needs to account for work still in flight. A database refusal cannot undo an external side effect that already happened.

For an MCP tool or a background-job API, the useful contract is small: retry carries the same run identity, a deliberate rerun gets a new one, and completion carries the claim originally issued to that worker.

How does your system distinguish a delivery retry from an intentional rerun? If you have a requeue, retention, or late-completion case this example misses, leave it in the comments. The reader's requeue experiment is exactly why this follow-up exists.

title: No Night Watchman For Partitions
description:
The cage is built when the resident arrives, not by a watchman who walks the zoo at night counting whether there are enough cages for tomorrow.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

Partitions at write time are built into the shared library; four services use the package. I describe the mechanism, not a measurement of its cost on a busy table.

This is part 8 of the series on what a shared platform does for every service, told as a zoo. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

In real life

Biscuit has a night job. With a lamp, every night, he walks the zoo and counts the empty cages: are there enough for tomorrow's arrivals? "Enough cages for tomorrow? Again..." It is the most boring job in the zoo, and Biscuit does it with exactly the enthusiasm it deserves.

One night he oversleeps. A new resident arrives in the morning, and there is no cage. Pickle finds it standing on the path with its parcel: "A new resident and no cage!"

Pip's answer is to fire the night shift. A cage is built when a resident arrives - at that moment, for that resident, not ahead of time by someone guessing. And Nora adds the rule that keeps the register honest: the cage goes into the book only when it actually stands. Not when someone started building it.

A partition per time range

Some of our tables are partitioned by time: one partition per day, per month, per year. A row must land in a partition that covers its timestamp. The classic way to make sure that partition exists is a scheduled job that creates the next few partitions ahead of time - the night watchman. Before this package, the library had exactly one such watchman, and it knew exactly one table: the audit journal.

The night watchman fails in the boring ways. It runs on a schedule, so it guesses how far ahead to go. It oversleeps when the scheduler is down. It knows only the tables someone told it about. And a row for a range nobody guessed - a late event, a timestamp in the future - finds no cage.

The cage comes with the resident

The partition package does the opposite. At the moment of a write, it makes sure the partition for that row's range exists, creates it if it does not, and only then lets the row in. In the library's own words: partitions are created at the moment of writing, there is no default step, the name is remembered only after the creating transaction commits, and there are no background scanners.

As a form - the names are illustrative:

partition:
  table: <schema.table>
  key: created_at
  step: Month              # Day | Week | Month | Year | Every(d); no default
# on write: no partition for the row's range -> create it, then insert
# the name is remembered only after the creating transaction commits

In PostgreSQL terms, the first row of a new month does roughly this - a form, the naming is illustrative:

-- the row's range has no partition yet
CREATE TABLE <table>_<range> PARTITION OF <table>
    FOR VALUES FROM ('<range start>') TO ('<range end>');
INSERT INTO <table> (...) VALUES (...);
-- every later row of that range goes straight to the INSERT

Three decisions in that form carry the design.

No default step. The application chooses Day, Week, Month, Year or an arbitrary period, and the package refuses to guess. A default would be right for some tables and silently wrong for others.

Remembered after commit. The package caches the names of partitions it knows exist, so it does not ask the database on every write. It adds a name to that cache only after the transaction that created the partition commits. If the transaction rolls back, the partition does not exist, and a cache that remembered it anyway would let the next row in through a door that is not there. That is Nora's rule: into the book only when the cage stands.

No scanner at all. Nothing walks the tables in the background. The only time a partition is created is when a row needs it.

Night watchman At write time
when a partition appears on a schedule, ahead when a row needs it
a row for an unguessed range no partition, failed write its partition is created
which tables the one it knew any table that declares a step
the cache of known names — filled only after commit

Who asked for it

The package came from a request: the admin service wanted a partitioned journal of console calls, and the only partition helper the library had was the one built for its own audit journal. Instead of a second watchman for a second table, the library got a package any table can use. Four services use it today - the admin service, the identity service, the security service and the project data service.

What went wrong

The failure this answers is a design one, not an incident I can point to: a scheduled partition creator is a second moving part that must be right for a write to succeed, and it is only right as long as its guess about the future is right. Every table that wanted partitions would have needed its own watchman or its own entry in the one that existed.

The quieter lesson is in the cache. Remembering a partition before its transaction commits is the kind of bug that never shows up in a test - until a rollback happens in exactly the wrong place. Writing "only after commit" into the package's own description is how we keep that rule from being optimised away.

What I do not claim

  • Not a measurement of the cost of the check on a busy table. It is built, not benchmarked here.
  • Not that every partitioned table has moved to the package. Four services use it.
  • Not that a night watchman is never right. It is not needed here.
  • Not the exact settings format. The form above shows the shape.
  • Not the exact statements the package runs. The SQL above is a form of the idea.

What of this is method

  • Create the cage when the resident arrives. Not ahead, by guessing.
  • Remember only what committed. A cache filled before commit lies after a rollback.
  • No default where defaults differ. The application chooses the step.

Zoo keeping, built in - Part 8. Next: Same "Seat Taken", Before And After The Race.

If you partition by time, who creates the next partition - a job or the write? If your job oversleeps, what happens to the first row of the new month? If you cache partition names, when exactly do you add one? Who walks your zoo with a lamp at night?

title: Automating Nightly Builds for Node Projects: A Practical Guide
description:
Automating Nightly Builds for Node Projects

Nightly builds are a powerful way to surface integration problems before they reach a release. They give you a fresh, clean run of your entire pipeline every day, catching regressions that might slip past PR checks. This guide shows you how to add a robust nightly build to any Node.js repository in roughly an hour, using only tools that are already part of the ecosystem.

Why Nightly Builds Matter

  • Early detection: If a dependency update or a refactor introduces a subtle bug, the nightly job will surface it immediately.
  • Consistent environment: The job runs on a clean machine each time, so you avoid the “works on my machine” problem.
  • Team confidence: Developers can push changes knowing that a full integration test will run the next morning.

The key to a successful nightly job is not just the CI configuration—it’s the foundation you lay in the repository. A sloppy project will produce flaky nightly builds regardless of how well you configure GitHub Actions or GitLab CI.

1. Project Audit Checklist

Before adding any CI configuration, run the following audit. It’s a quick 10‑minute pass that saves hours of debugging later.

1️⃣ Pin the Node version 

"engines": { "node": ">=18.16.0 <19.0.0" }

Add the line to package.json or create a .nvmrc file. This guarantees the CI runner uses the same runtime as local developers.

1️⃣ Commit the lock file

Make sure yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml is in the repository. The lock file ensures the exact dependency tree is reproduced on every build.

1️⃣ Run a security audit 

npm audit --audit-level=moderate

Fail the CI if any vulnerabilities are found. Nightly builds are a good place to surface security issues early.

1️⃣ Check for duplicate packages 

npm ls lodash

Duplicate copies of a library can inflate bundle size and cause runtime errors. If you see duplicate trees, investigate and dedupe.

2. Build Scripts Must Be Idempotent

A nightly job should be able to run on a clean checkout without side effects. That means your build scripts must clean before they build.

"scripts": {
  "clean": "rimraf dist",
  "build": "npm run clean && tsc"
}

Prebuild Checks

Add a small shell script that validates required environment variables before the build starts. For example:

# prebuild.sh
if [ -z "$NODE_ENV" ]; then
  echo "NODE_ENV is missing"
  exit 1
fi

Then reference it in your CI job.

Type‑check Only

If your nightly job only needs type safety, use tsc --noEmit to skip generating JavaScript files:

"scripts": { "type-check": "tsc --noEmit" }

3. Linting and Formatting

Code quality should never be an afterthought. Nightly builds are an excellent place to enforce linting rules.

npx eslint . --ext .js,.ts --max-warnings 0

Treat warnings as failures to keep the codebase clean.

Add a formatting check:

"scripts": {
  "format:check": "prettier --check .",
  "format": "prettier --write ."
}

Fail the build if format:check returns a non‑zero exit code.

4. Deterministic Tests

Nightly builds run tests on a clean machine. If your tests depend on shared state or external services, they will become flaky.

Fresh Database or Mocks

If you use a database, spin up a fresh instance or use an in‑memory mock. For example, with PostgreSQL:

docker run --rm -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pass -p 5433:5432 postgres

Detect Open Handles

Jest can hang if async operations are not cleaned up. Enable --detectOpenHandles:

"scripts": { "test:ci": "jest --detectOpenHandles" }

Coverage Thresholds

Keep new code tested. Add a global threshold:

npx jest --coverage --coverageThreshold={ "global": { "branches": 80, "functions": 80, "lines": 80, "statements": 80 } }

5. Environment Configuration

Never commit real secrets. Create a .env.example that lists all required keys.

# .env.example
API_KEY=xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
DB_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/db

Use dotenv in scripts to load the variables:

require('dotenv').config();

In CI, use the secrets feature of the platform to inject the real values.

6. Putting It All Together in GitHub Actions

Here’s a minimal nightly.yml that ties everything together:

name: Nightly Build
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'  # 2 AM UTC
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Use Node.js 18
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Lint
        run: npx eslint . --ext .js,.ts --max-warnings 0
      - name: Format check
        run: npm run format:check
      - name: Type check
        run: npm run type-check
      - name: Build
        run: npm run build
      - name: Tests
        env:
          NODE_ENV: test
          DB_URL: ${{ secrets.DB_URL }}
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
        run: npm run test:ci

This workflow:

  1. Runs at 2 AM UTC every day.
  2. Installs dependencies with npm ci to guarantee a clean install.
  3. Lints, checks formatting, type‑checks, builds, and runs tests.
  4. Fails early if any step fails.

7. Common Pitfalls and Fixes

Problem Symptom Fix
Lock file missing Dependency tree changes between runs Commit the lock file
Global node_modules cache Flaky builds due to stale packages Use npm ci in CI
Tests share state Random failures Use fresh DB or mocks
Linting only on PRs Nightly builds silently degrade Add lint step to nightly job
Secrets in repo Security breach Use platform secrets and a .env.example

8. Running Nightly Builds Locally

Sometimes you want to test the nightly workflow before pushing. Use act to run GitHub Actions locally:

act -j build --env-file .env.example

This runs the build job with the same steps as in CI, allowing you to debug failures quickly.

9. Extending the Workflow

Once you have the basic pipeline, you can add more features:

  • Static analysis: Add tsc --noEmit or eslint --max-warnings 0.
  • Performance benchmarks: Run a script that measures build time.
  • Artifact upload: Save the built bundle to a storage bucket for later inspection.
  • Slack notifications: Send a message if the nightly build fails.

Each extension should be added incrementally, ensuring that the core pipeline remains stable.

10. Summary

By following the audit checklist and configuring a minimal yet comprehensive GitHub Actions workflow, you can achieve reliable nightly builds in under an hour. The process emphasizes clean environments, deterministic tests, and strict linting—all of which reduce the risk of hidden bugs slipping into production.

If you’d like a ready‑to‑use bundle that sets up the entire nightly build automation for Node projects, it’s available at https://heracles-store.pages.dev/p/nightly-build-automation-bundle-for-node-projects/.

Written with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy before publishing.

title: Improve Developer Experience using AI tools
description:
Introduction

In this article, I want to present a case where AI-assisted development seemed particularly relevant to me.

Context

I'm a front-end developer, currently working on a front-end application built with VueJS.
To manage the application's translations, we use POEditor, which lets us add "terms to translate" and gives translators a dedicated tool to work with.
On the development side, we have an internal tool that extracts the translations from POEditor into a package (translations-provider). Then, we have an NPM script that consumes this package and updates the translation files in the application.

This setup is convenient for managing translations, but the developer experience isn't great, because developing a new feature involves several manual steps.

Currently, adding a translation for a new feature takes four steps:

sequenceDiagram
    actor Dev as Developer
    participant PO as POEditor
    participant TP as translations-provider (CI)
    participant Front as Front-end app

    Dev->>PO: 1. Creates the translations
    Dev->>TP: 2. Generates the translations export (via a manual pipeline)
    TP-->>Dev: Pipeline finished
    Dev->>Front: 3. Runs the import script
    Dev->>Front: 4. Cleans up the translations

The last step is the most tedious: since POEditor isn't versioned, the export contains every translation present at that moment, including those added by other developers for features still in progress. So you have to sort through the diff of the translation files by hand to keep only what relates to your branch.

The need

In a world where development is increasingly AI-assisted, the goal is to get rid of this manual step and to integrate POEditor into an AI-assisted development workflow (with Claude Code, for example).

Here is the target workflow:

sequenceDiagram
    actor Dev as Developer
    participant Claude as Claude Code
    participant Jira
    participant PO as POEditor
    participant Front as Front-end app

    Dev->>Claude: 1. Asks to implement a ticket
    Claude->>Jira: 2. Reads the ticket
    Claude-->>Dev: 3. Proposes a plan
    Dev-->>Claude: Approves the plan
    par Implementation
        Claude->>Front: 4. Implements the feature
    and Translations
        Claude->>PO: 4. Creates the required translations
    end

Conveniently, POEditor has released an MCP server that lets an AI interact with it!

An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server exposes, through a standard protocol, the tools and data of an external service to an AI assistant (here: reading and creating terms and translations in POEditor).

On the Jira side, the tooling relies on the Atlassian MCP server to read tickets. It's a prerequisite, but it's not what I want to talk about today.

Implementation

This use case lets me illustrate what I did to automate these tasks and integrate them into my development workflow.
The exact content doesn't matter much; what matters is the tools and the reasons for using them.

To bring a lasting solution to my development workflow and improve my developer experience, the most important thing, in my opinion, is to clearly separate what is deterministic from what isn't. In our case:

Deterministic Non-deterministic
Run a new translations-provider pipeline (translations export) Determine when to create translations
Run the translations import once the pipeline has finished Extract the translations from a ticket
Clean up the received translations to keep only what we need Interact with the MCP server to create the translations

On top of that, it's important to have guardrails on what my tooling will do. Letting a model do whatever it wants with the tools at its disposal is out of the question. For me, this is a key point of any AI tooling setup in our development workflow, in order to stay in control of the work being done.

In my case, I want to:

  • Limit the actions on the POEditor MCP (creating new terms and adding translations only)
  • POEditor organizes translations into projects. I want to allow access only to the project linked to my front-end application
  • Create new translations in POEditor only after explicit approval from the user
  • Stick to what the tooling is designed for. Stop and inform the user when leaving the nominal case. Never try to reach the goal through workarounds
  • Never invent translations. Whatever is created must come only from a ticket or from user input

Architecture

Here is what's in place:

flowchart TB
    Skill["`**SKILL poeditor-translations**
        Conductor: orchestrates the creation of translations.
        Uses the available tools (read ticket / create translations / import translations)`"]

    Skill --> Jira[("`**Atlassian MCP server**
        Jira access
        *prerequisite, already in place*`")]
    Skill --> Agent["`**poeditor subagent**
        The only one talking to POEditor:
        detects duplicates, creates approved terms`"]
    Skill --> Sync["`**sync-translations-from-poeditor.sh**
        Runs the translations-provider pipeline,
        waits for it to finish, imports the translations`"]
    Skill --> Keep["`**keep-only-keys.sh**
        Keeps only the ticket's translations`"]

    Agent -->|"MCP tool call"| Guard
    Guard -->|"allowed project"| MCP[("`**POEditor MCP server**
        Reads and creates terms
        and their translations`")]

    subgraph sgGuards["Guardrails"]
        Settings["`**settings.json**
        Reads allowed, writes on approval,
        everything else denied; declares the hook`"]
        Guard["`**poeditor-guard.sh hook**
        Blocks any call outside the allowlist`"]
        Projects["`**projects.json**
        Allowlist of POEditor projects
        (name → ID)`"]
    end

    Settings -.->|"declares"| Guard
    Projects -.->|"read by"| Guard
    Sync --> Locales[("Locale files")]
    Keep --> Locales

    classDef central fill:#ffd966,stroke:#b8860b,stroke-width:2px,color:#000
    classDef prereq stroke-dasharray:5 5
    class Skill central
    class Jira prereq

The skill is the single entry point: it handles the non-deterministic part (reading a ticket, extracting labels from it, talking with the developer) and delegates everything else. Access to POEditor goes through a subagent with a deliberately narrow scope, while the deterministic steps (pipeline, import, cleanup) are handed over to scripts. Finally, the guardrails don't rely on the model's goodwill: settings.json and the hook are enforced by Claude Code itself, whatever the prompt. This makes the guardrails truly deterministic.

Guardrails in detail

A rule written in SKILL.md is only an instruction: the model interprets it, and may misunderstand it or drift away from it. For critical rules (write only to the authorized POEditor project, create nothing without approval, delete nothing), that's not enough.

These rules are therefore enforced by Claude Code itself, whatever the prompt: the permissions in settings.json restrict which MCP tools can be used and require approval before every write, and the poeditor-guard.sh hook blocks any call targeting a project outside the allowlist.

A dedicated subagent

The poeditor subagent has a single role: talking to POEditor. Its definition file restricts the tools it can access (reading terms, adding terms and translations, nothing else) and sets the model it uses: Sonnet, which is cheaper, is more than enough for such a well-scoped task. Its context is isolated from the main session's: it receives a list of terms and returns a report.

What AI brings on top

The tooling doesn't just automate the manual steps: the subagent also checks the quality of the translations before creating them. For each new term, it reports:

  • a key that already exists in the POEditor project;
  • a prefix conflict: if profiles.role already exists and profiles.role.label is requested, the generated JSON file would be broken (the same key can't be both a string and an object);
  • an EN or FR value that already exists, in the target project or in another project: it may be a label to reuse rather than duplicate;
  • a duplicate within the requested list itself.

In my opinion, this is the real value of AI-assisted development and of all the tooling that can come with it: on top of improving the developer experience and automating tedious tasks, we can improve the quality of our work by flagging what a developer might have missed.

Sharing the tooling with the development team

To make this tooling available to the whole development team, the skill, the scripts and the settings are project-scoped, with an AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md) file at the root to declare the skill.

The SKILL.md itself states when it should be invoked. In my case, the nominal use is when developing a feature from a Jira ticket that contains translations. You can also invoke the skill "manually", telling it which ticket to use to extract the desired translations.

Sharing is done simply through a project-level merge request. There is of course developer documentation explaining the purpose and how it works.

Here is an overview of what the merge request contains:

.
├── .claude/
│   ├── agents/
│   │   └── poeditor.md                  # Subagent: sole access to POEditor (duplicate checks, creation of approved terms)
│   ├── hooks/
│   │   └── poeditor-guard.sh            # PreToolUse hook: blocks any POEditor MCP call outside the allowlist
│   ├── poeditor/
│   │   └── projects.json                # Allowlist of authorized POEditor projects (name → ID)
│   ├── skills/
│   │   └── poeditor-translations/
│   │       ├── SKILL.md                 # Skill: orchestrates the workflow, from the Jira ticket to the locale files
│   │       └── scripts/
│   │           ├── keep-only-keys.sh    # Keeps only the ticket's keys in the locale files
│   │           └── sync-translations-from-poeditor.sh   # Runs the translations-provider pipeline, waits for it to finish, imports the translations
│   └── settings.json                    # Permissions for the POEditor MCP tools (allow / ask / deny) and hook declaration
├── docs/
│   └── poeditor-translations.md         # Developer documentation: setup, usage, manual procedure
├── .gitignore                           # Ignores .claude/settings.local.json (personal settings)
├── .mcp.json                            # Declares the POEditor MCP server (OAuth, no secret committed)
└── AGENTS.md                            # Updated i18n rule: the skill becomes the recommended path

Conclusion

In this article, I mainly focused on presenting the setup rather than the content.
That's intentional: content is easy to generate for one's specific needs.
What I wanted to share here is my take on an AI-assisted development workflow.
If I had to sum up, here is what matters:

  • Separate what is deterministic from what isn't. No need to spend tokens if a Bash script can do the job (and it gives more certainty about the result, too)
  • The skill is mainly a task scheduler. That's where I say what to do, in what order and how. There are also a few guardrails in its instructions, but they're not the most important ones
  • For a well-identified task, a subagent matters: it isolates its context so that it does only one thing, but does it well. Here, my subagent only talks to POEditor (through the MCP server)
  • The configuration in settings.json is essential to specify what models are allowed to do (blocking key deletion in POEditor, for example)

Improving your developer experience with AI doesn't mean blindly handing everything over to it: it means choosing what you delegate to the model, setting the conditions under which it acts, and keeping control over what matters most.

Cover image generated by AI.

AI was also used to proofread and translate this article.

title: How to build a REST API with JWT authentication in Node.js with NestJS (2026)
description:
"Build me a REST API with JWT auth" is probably the most common backend task there is. The happy path is an afternoon in any framework. The parts that make it production-ready are the ones that don't show up in a demo: refresh tokens that can be stolen, a sign-in endpoint that tells an attacker which emails are registered, a PATCH that turns a null into a 500, a second instance that doesn't see the first one's tokens.

This is how I'd build that API with NestJS today, every file of it, from the first nest new to the tests and a production checklist. If your picture of Nest is from a few years ago (a module file, a DTO class and a controller for every resource, @nestjs/passport plus @nestjs/jwt wired by hand), a lot has changed in Nest 12, and most of it makes the small end lighter. You'll see that in the first step, which is one file.

The same application is in the docs as Build a REST API with JWT authentication in Node.js.

What "production-ready" means here

The API stores personal notes, and the list of what it has to do is the same for any resource:

  • Validate every body, query string and route parameter, and type the handlers from the same rules.
  • Hash passwords properly, issue short-lived access tokens and long-lived refresh tokens, and rotate the refresh tokens.
  • Keep users, data and refresh tokens in PostgreSQL, so restarts and extra instances don't sign anyone out.
  • Refuse to start with a missing or malformed configuration.
  • Rate-limit password guessing.
  • Send security headers, and let only your own web app call it from a browser.
  • Describe itself in OpenAPI.
  • Answer liveness and readiness probes, and shut down cleanly on SIGTERM.
  • Write JSON logs in production, with passwords and tokens masked.
  • Have tests that don't need a database server for the common case.

In Nest, every item on that list is a first-party package or a built-in, so the work is in putting them together, not in choosing between five libraries for each.

Here are the routes the API ends up with, by the section that adds them:

  • Notes: GET /notes, GET /notes/:id, POST /notes, PATCH /notes/:id, DELETE /notes/:id.
  • Accounts and tokens: POST /auth/sign-up, POST /auth/token, POST /auth/token/refresh, POST /auth/token/revoke, GET /me.
  • The OpenAPI document and Swagger UI: GET /docs.
  • Health checks: GET /health/live, GET /health/ready.

You'll need Node.js 22 or later. From the second step onwards you also need PostgreSQL; I run it in a Docker container.

It starts as one file

Create the project with the Nest CLI. The --minimal flag generates an application whose code is a single file, src/main.ts (see One-file projects):

$ npm i -g @nestjs/cli
$ nest new notes-api --minimal
$ cd notes-api

Two packages go in, and two come out. The Node adapter runs Nest directly on node:http, and it's the fastest of Nest's three adapters, so the Express adapter that the CLI installed isn't needed. Zod is for validation:

$ npm i --save @nestjs/platform-node zod
$ npm uninstall @nestjs/platform-express @types/express

Now replace src/main.ts with the first version of the API. Notes live in a Map for now, so they're gone on every restart, but every route, every validation rule and the shape of every response is already the real one:

// src/main.ts
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import {
  Body,
  Controller,
  Delete,
  Get,
  HttpCode,
  Injectable,
  NotFoundException,
  Param,
  Patch,
  Post,
  StandardSchemaValidationPipe,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NodeAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-node';
import { z } from 'zod';

const title = z.string().trim().min(1).max(200);
const body = z.string().max(10_000);

const createNoteSchema = z.object({ title, body: body.default('') });
type CreateNoteDto = z.infer<typeof createNoteSchema>;

// Every field optional, none nullable: a null title is a 400.
const updateNoteSchema = z.object({ title, body }).partial();
type UpdateNoteDto = z.infer<typeof updateNoteSchema>;

interface Note {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  body: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
}

@Injectable()
class NotesService {
  private readonly notes = new Map<string, Note>();

  findAll(): Note[] {
    return [...this.notes.values()];
  }

  findOne(id: string): Note {
    const note = this.notes.get(id);
    if (!note) {
      throw new NotFoundException();
    }
    return note;
  }

  create(dto: CreateNoteDto): Note {
    const now = new Date();
    const note: Note = { id: randomUUID(), ...dto, createdAt: now, updatedAt: now };
    this.notes.set(note.id, note);
    return note;
  }

  update(id: string, dto: UpdateNoteDto): Note {
    const note = this.findOne(id);
    Object.assign(note, dto, { updatedAt: new Date() });
    return note;
  }

  remove(id: string): void {
    if (!this.notes.delete(id)) {
      throw new NotFoundException();
    }
  }
}

const noteId = { schema: z.uuid() };

@Controller('notes')
class NotesController {
  constructor(private readonly notesService: NotesService) {}

  @Get()
  findAll() {
    return this.notesService.findAll();
  }

  @Get(':id')
  findOne(@Param('id', noteId) id: string) {
    return this.notesService.findOne(id);
  }

  @Post()
  create(@Body({ schema: createNoteSchema }) dto: CreateNoteDto) {
    return this.notesService.create(dto);
  }

  @Patch(':id')
  update(@Param('id', noteId) id: string, @Body({ schema: updateNoteSchema }) dto: UpdateNoteDto) {
    return this.notesService.update(id, dto);
  }

  @Delete(':id')
  @HttpCode(204)
  remove(@Param('id', noteId) id: string) {
    this.notesService.remove(id);
  }
}

const app = await NestFactory.create(
  {
    controllers: [NotesController],
    providers: [NotesService],
  },
  new NodeAdapter(),
);
app.useGlobalPipes(new StandardSchemaValidationPipe());
await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

A few things in there are new enough that you may not have seen them.

There's no module class. NestFactory.create() accepts the root module's metadata directly, as a plain object (see Root module from metadata). It's still a full Nest application, with dependency injection and the usual decorators. The class comes back in the next step, as soon as there are other modules to import.

Validation takes any Standard Schema. @Body({ schema }), @Param('id', { schema }) and, later, @Query({ schema }) accept a Zod schema, or one from any other Standard Schema library. StandardSchemaValidationPipe validates every parameter that declares one, and hands the handler the schema's output, not the raw input: title arrives trimmed and a missing body arrives as an empty string. The parameter's type is inferred from the same schema, so there are no DTO classes to keep in sync with the rules (see Schema-based validation).

Two details in the update schema are easy to get wrong, in any framework. The first: it isn't createNoteSchema.partial(). Zod still applies a .default() inside partial(), so a PATCH that only renames a note would quietly reset its body to an empty string. Building both schemas from the same field schemas avoids that. The second: the fields are optional but not nullable. A PATCH with {"title": null} gets a 400 right here, instead of travelling all the way to the database's NOT NULL constraint and coming back as a 500.

Start the app in watch mode:

$ npm run start:dev

From another terminal, create a note, then send a few requests that should fail validation. (--json needs curl 7.82 or later; it sends a POST with a JSON body.)

$ curl localhost:3000/notes --json '{"title":"Buy milk"}'
{"id":"d90a31d3-2df2-447d-8d5e-c2b2e241a8eb","title":"Buy milk","body":"","createdAt":"2026-11-19T19:42:46.765Z","updatedAt":"2026-11-19T19:42:46.765Z"}
$ curl localhost:3000/notes --json '{"title":""}'
{"message":["title: Too small: expected string to have >=1 characters"],"error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}
$ curl -X PATCH localhost:3000/notes/d90a31d3-2df2-447d-8d5e-c2b2e241a8eb --json '{"title":null}'
{"message":["title: Invalid input: expected string, received null"],"error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}
$ curl localhost:3000/notes/not-a-uuid
{"message":["Invalid UUID"],"error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}

The empty title, the null and the malformed id are all 400s, each with a message that says what was wrong.

Store notes in PostgreSQL

A Map doesn't survive a restart, so the notes move to PostgreSQL through @nestjs/drizzle. At the same time the database URL moves into the environment, read with @nestjs/config:

$ npm i --save @nestjs/config @nestjs/drizzle drizzle-orm@rc pg
$ npm i --save-dev drizzle-kit@rc @types/pg

For local development, a container is all the database you need:

$ docker run -d --name notes-db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=notes -e POSTGRES_DB=notes -p 5432:5432 postgres:17

Its URL goes in a .env file in the project's root directory. ConfigModule loads that file at startup, and drizzle-kit reads it too:

DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:notes@localhost:5432/notes

One file was fine for the first version, but it's about to get long, so this is where the app gets some structure. Each part moves to a file of its own under src/:

  • database/schema.ts
  • notes/notes.controller.ts, notes/notes.module.ts, notes/notes.schemas.ts and notes/notes.service.ts
  • app.module.ts, config.ts and main.ts

By the end of the article, auth/, users/ and health/ folders join them, and the tests live in test/.

Validate the configuration at startup

I want a bad configuration to stop the process before it serves a single request, which is exactly what you want during a rolling deploy: the new version never takes traffic, and the old one keeps running. So the environment is a Zod schema too. ConfigModule validates it at startup and serves the values the schema returns, which means PORT comes out as a number, not a string:

// src/config.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const envSchema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']).default('development'),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().default(3000),
  DATABASE_URL: z.url(),
});

export type Env = z.infer<typeof envSchema>;

The notes table

This is the table, in Drizzle's schema language. The small at() helper keeps every timestamp column the same: with a time zone, read as a JavaScript Date:

// src/database/schema.ts
import { pgTable, text, timestamp, uuid } from 'drizzle-orm/pg-core';

const at = (name: string) => timestamp(name, { withTimezone: true, mode: 'date' });

export const notes = pgTable('notes', {
  id: uuid('id').primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
  title: text('title').notNull(),
  body: text('body').notNull(),
  createdAt: at('created_at').notNull().defaultNow(),
  updatedAt: at('updated_at').notNull().defaultNow(),
});

export type Note = typeof notes.$inferSelect;

Request schemas, now with pagination

The schemas from the first version move to their own file. There's one addition: the list takes a page size and an offset, with a default and a cap, so no request can read the whole table:

// src/notes/notes.schemas.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

const title = z.string().trim().min(1).max(200);
const body = z.string().max(10_000);

export const createNoteSchema = z.object({ title, body: body.default('') });
export type CreateNoteDto = z.infer<typeof createNoteSchema>;

// Every field optional, none nullable: a null title is a 400.
// Not createNoteSchema.partial(): the default would reset `body` on every update.
export const updateNoteSchema = z.object({ title, body }).partial();
export type UpdateNoteDto = z.infer<typeof updateNoteSchema>;

export const listNotesQuerySchema = z.object({
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
  offset: z.coerce.number().int().min(0).default(0),
});
export type ListNotesQuery = z.infer<typeof listNotesQuerySchema>;

z.coerce.number() is there because query strings are always strings: ?limit=50 arrives as "50", and the schema turns it into 50 before the handler sees it.

Why every write is one statement

The service now talks to the database, which @InjectDrizzle() injects:

// src/notes/notes.service.ts
import { Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDrizzle } from '@nestjs/drizzle';
import { desc, eq } from 'drizzle-orm';
import type { NodePgDatabase } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { notes, type Note } from '../database/schema.js';
import type { CreateNoteDto, ListNotesQuery, UpdateNoteDto } from './notes.schemas.js';

@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  constructor(@InjectDrizzle() private readonly db: NodePgDatabase) {}

  findAll({ limit, offset }: ListNotesQuery): Promise<Note[]> {
    return this.db
      .select()
      .from(notes)
      .orderBy(desc(notes.createdAt), desc(notes.id))
      .limit(limit)
      .offset(offset);
  }

  async findOne(id: string): Promise<Note> {
    const [note] = await this.db.select().from(notes).where(eq(notes.id, id));
    return note ?? notFound();
  }

  async create(dto: CreateNoteDto): Promise<Note> {
    const [note] = await this.db.insert(notes).values(dto).returning();
    return note;
  }

  async update(id: string, dto: UpdateNoteDto): Promise<Note> {
    // One statement, no read before the write: a concurrent DELETE can't be undone.
    const [note] = await this.db
      .update(notes)
      .set({ ...dto, updatedAt: new Date() })
      .where(eq(notes.id, id))
      .returning();
    return note ?? notFound();
  }

  async remove(id: string): Promise<void> {
    const deleted = await this.db.delete(notes).where(eq(notes.id, id)).returning({ id: notes.id });
    if (deleted.length === 0) {
      notFound();
    }
  }
}

function notFound(): never {
  throw new NotFoundException('Note not found');
}

The part I'd point at in this file is how update() and remove() are written. A very common way to update a row is to load it, change it and save it. Between the load and the save there's a gap, and another request can delete the note in that gap; the save then writes it back, and the delete is undone. Here, each of them is a single statement with returning(), and the service learns whether the note existed from what that statement changed. No rows back means a 404. The list sorts by createdAt and then by id, so two notes created in the same millisecond still come back in a stable order from page to page.

The controller and the module

The controller is the same as in the one-file version, plus the query schema on the list:

// src/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Delete, Get, HttpCode, Param, Patch, Post, Query } from '@nestjs/common';
import { z } from 'zod';
import {
  createNoteSchema,
  listNotesQuerySchema,
  updateNoteSchema,
  type CreateNoteDto,
  type ListNotesQuery,
  type UpdateNoteDto,
} from './notes.schemas.js';
import { NotesService } from './notes.service.js';

const noteId = { schema: z.uuid() };

@Controller('notes')
export class NotesController {
  constructor(private readonly notesService: NotesService) {}

  @Get()
  findAll(@Query({ schema: listNotesQuerySchema }) query: ListNotesQuery) {
    return this.notesService.findAll(query);
  }

  @Get(':id')
  findOne(@Param('id', noteId) id: string) {
    return this.notesService.findOne(id);
  }

  @Post()
  create(@Body({ schema: createNoteSchema }) dto: CreateNoteDto) {
    return this.notesService.create(dto);
  }

  @Patch(':id')
  update(@Param('id', noteId) id: string, @Body({ schema: updateNoteSchema }) dto: UpdateNoteDto) {
    return this.notesService.update(id, dto);
  }

  @Delete(':id')
  @HttpCode(204)
  remove(@Param('id', noteId) id: string) {
    return this.notesService.remove(id);
  }
}

The notes module registers the two:

// src/notes/notes.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { NotesController } from './notes.controller.js';
import { NotesService } from './notes.service.js';

@Module({
  controllers: [NotesController],
  providers: [NotesService],
})
export class NotesModule {}

The root module and main.ts

The root module is a class again, because now it imports other modules: the configuration, the database and the notes. DrizzleModule.forRootAsync() reads the URL from ConfigService, opens a pg pool, and closes it when the application shuts down:

// src/app.module.ts
import { Module, StandardSchemaValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { APP_PIPE } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { DrizzleModule } from '@nestjs/drizzle';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { envSchema, type Env } from './config.js';
import { NotesModule } from './notes/notes.module.js';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({ isGlobal: true, validationSchema: envSchema }),
    DrizzleModule.forRootAsync({
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService<Env, true>) => ({
        drizzle,
        connection: config.get('DATABASE_URL', { infer: true }),
      }),
    }),
    NotesModule,
  ],
  providers: [{ provide: APP_PIPE, useClass: StandardSchemaValidationPipe }],
})
export class AppModule {}

The validation pipe moved too, from app.useGlobalPipes() in main.ts to an APP_PIPE provider. It still applies to every route. The difference is that it's now part of AppModule, so the end-to-end tests at the end get it for free when they boot the module, without repeating anything from main.ts.

With the setup in the module, main.ts is short. It creates the app, turns on shutdown hooks and listens on the configured port:

// src/main.ts
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NodeAdapter, type NestNodeApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-node';
import { AppModule } from './app.module.js';
import type { Env } from './config.js';

const app = await NestFactory.create<NestNodeApplication>(AppModule, new NodeAdapter());
app.enableShutdownHooks();

const config = app.get<ConfigService<Env, true>>(ConfigService);
await app.listen(config.get('PORT', { infer: true }));

enableShutdownHooks() is one line that's easy to leave out. A container platform sends SIGTERM on every deploy. With shutdown hooks on, the application closes properly when it gets one: the HTTP server stops accepting connections and the database pool is closed. Without them, the process just ends.

Run the first migration

drizzle-kit needs a configuration file in the project's root directory, saying where the schema is and where the migrations go:

// drizzle.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'drizzle-kit';

export default defineConfig({
  dialect: 'postgresql',
  schema: './src/database/schema.ts',
  out: './drizzle',
  dbCredentials: {
    url: process.env.DATABASE_URL!,
  },
});

Generate the first migration from the schema, then apply it (the Migrations section of the Drizzle chapter has the details):

$ npx drizzle-kit generate --name=notes
$ npx drizzle-kit migrate

Restart the app, and the notes survive restarts. To see the configuration check at work, start it with a broken URL. It stops before serving anything:

$ DATABASE_URL=not-a-url npm run start
ERROR [ExceptionHandler] Error: Config validation error: DATABASE_URL: Invalid URL

Add JWT authentication: what not to write yourself

Right now anyone can read and change every note. Next, users sign up, sign in for tokens, and see only their own notes.

Here's where most JWT tutorials hand you jsonwebtoken, bcrypt and a guard to write. Nest has a first-party package for it now, @nestjs/authentication, and I'd use it rather than write sign-in by hand, because the hand-written version is where the subtle bugs live. Three of them:

  • Timing. The natural sign-in code is "find the user; if there's none, return early; otherwise compare the password". An unknown email then gets its answer much sooner than a wrong password, because hashing is slow on purpose, and anyone can tell from the response time which emails have accounts.
  • Refresh-token reuse. A refresh token that can be used forever is a password that never expires. Tokens have to rotate, and a spent token that comes back has to be treated as theft.
  • The race inside rotation. Rotation only works if "spend this token" happens exactly once, even when two requests try at the same moment.

The package does the security-sensitive parts: hashing passwords, signing and verifying tokens, rotating refresh tokens. It also registers a global guard, so every route requires a signed-in user unless you mark it public. Your code supplies the users, the database and the configuration:

$ npm i --save @nestjs/authentication

The access tokens are signed with a secret, which goes in .env. It must be at least 32 bytes:

# Generate with: openssl rand -base64 32
JWT_SECRET=

The configuration schema makes it required, so the app won't start without it, or with a short one:

// src/config.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const envSchema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']).default('development'),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().default(3000),
  DATABASE_URL: z.url(),
  // Signs the access tokens: at least 32 bytes.
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32),
});

export type Env = z.infer<typeof envSchema>;

Users, refresh tokens and note owners in PostgreSQL

The schema grows by two tables and one column: the users, a refresh_tokens table where the package's refresh tokens are kept, and an owner on every note:

// src/database/schema.ts
import { boolean, index, jsonb, pgTable, text, timestamp, uuid } from 'drizzle-orm/pg-core';

const at = (name: string) => timestamp(name, { withTimezone: true, mode: 'date' });

export const users = pgTable('users', {
  id: uuid('id').primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
  email: text('email').notNull().unique(),
  passwordHash: text('password_hash').notNull(),
  createdAt: at('created_at').notNull().defaultNow(),
});

export const notes = pgTable(
  'notes',
  {
    id: uuid('id').primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    ownerId: uuid('owner_id')
      .notNull()
      .references(() => users.id, { onDelete: 'cascade' }),
    title: text('title').notNull(),
    body: text('body').notNull(),
    createdAt: at('created_at').notNull().defaultNow(),
    updatedAt: at('updated_at').notNull().defaultNow(),
  },
  (table) => [index('notes_owner_id_created_at_idx').on(table.ownerId, table.createdAt)],
);

// What @nestjs/authentication keeps for refresh tokens, stored by their SHA-256.
export const refreshTokens = pgTable(
  'refresh_tokens',
  {
    id: text('id').primaryKey(),
    familyId: text('family_id').notNull(),
    userId: text('user_id').notNull(),
    createdAt: at('created_at').notNull(),
    expiresAt: at('expires_at').notNull(),
    familyExpiresAt: at('family_expires_at').notNull(),
    usedAt: at('used_at'),
    // A family is revoked when any of its tokens is.
    revoked: boolean('revoked').notNull().default(false),
    claims: jsonb('claims').$type<Record<string, unknown>>(),
  },
  (table) => [
    index('refresh_tokens_family_id_idx').on(table.familyId),
    index('refresh_tokens_user_id_idx').on(table.userId),
    index('refresh_tokens_family_expires_at_idx').on(table.familyExpiresAt),
  ],
);

export type Note = typeof notes.$inferSelect;

A few choices in there: email is unique in the database, which is what actually prevents two accounts with one address. Deleting a user deletes their notes (onDelete: 'cascade'). The index on the owner and the creation time matches the list query once it filters by owner. And a refresh token's id is the SHA-256 of the token, never the token itself, so a copy of this table isn't a copy of anyone's session.

Now the migration. owner_id is required, and the notes from the previous step have no owner, so in development, empty the table first:

$ docker exec notes-db psql -U postgres -d notes -c "TRUNCATE notes"
$ npx drizzle-kit generate --name=users
$ npx drizzle-kit migrate

drizzle-kit writes the migration as plain SQL under drizzle/, in a folder named after a timestamp and users. It's worth reading before you apply it, since it's what will run against production too:

CREATE TABLE "refresh_tokens" (
    "id" text PRIMARY KEY,
    "family_id" text NOT NULL,
    "user_id" text NOT NULL,
    "created_at" timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,
    "expires_at" timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,
    "family_expires_at" timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,
    "used_at" timestamp with time zone,
    "revoked" boolean DEFAULT false NOT NULL,
    "claims" jsonb
);
--> statement-breakpoint
CREATE TABLE "users" (
    "id" uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    "email" text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    "password_hash" text NOT NULL,
    "created_at" timestamp with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL
);
--> statement-breakpoint
ALTER TABLE "notes" ADD COLUMN "owner_id" uuid NOT NULL;--> statement-breakpoint
CREATE INDEX "notes_owner_id_created_at_idx" ON "notes" ("owner_id","created_at");--> statement-breakpoint
CREATE INDEX "refresh_tokens_family_id_idx" ON "refresh_tokens" ("family_id");--> statement-breakpoint
CREATE INDEX "refresh_tokens_user_id_idx" ON "refresh_tokens" ("user_id");--> statement-breakpoint
CREATE INDEX "refresh_tokens_family_expires_at_idx" ON "refresh_tokens" ("family_expires_at");--> statement-breakpoint
ALTER TABLE "notes" ADD CONSTRAINT "notes_owner_id_users_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY ("owner_id") REFERENCES "users"("id") ON DELETE CASCADE;

The ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN "owner_id" uuid NOT NULL line is why the TRUNCATE came first: PostgreSQL can't add a required column with no default to a table that has rows in it.

Users

The package never reads your users table. It asks your code for a user, and your code decides what a user is. Here, it's three fields, and deliberately no password hash:

// src/users/user.ts
export interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  createdAt: Date;
}

The repository is the only code in the app that ever sees a password hash. Everything it returns is a User without one, so a user can be returned from a route or written to a log without leaking the hash:

// src/users/users.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDrizzle } from '@nestjs/drizzle';
import { eq } from 'drizzle-orm';
import type { NodePgDatabase } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { users } from '../database/schema.js';
import type { User } from './user.js';

const columns = { id: users.id, email: users.email, createdAt: users.createdAt };

/** Only `User` objects leave this class: password hashes stay inside. */
@Injectable()
export class UsersRepository {
  constructor(@InjectDrizzle() private readonly db: NodePgDatabase) {}

  /** The new user, or `null` when the email is taken. */
  async create(email: string, passwordHash: string): Promise<User | null> {
    // One statement: two sign-ups with the same email can't both succeed.
    const [user] = await this.db
      .insert(users)
      .values({ email: normalize(email), passwordHash })
      .onConflictDoNothing({ target: users.email })
      .returning(columns);
    return user ?? null;
  }

  async findById(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
    const [user] = await this.db.select(columns).from(users).where(eq(users.id, id));
    return user ?? null;
  }

  /** For password sign-in only. */
  async findCredentials(email: string): Promise<{ user: User; passwordHash: string } | null> {
    const [row] = await this.db.select().from(users).where(eq(users.email, normalize(email)));
    if (!row) {
      return null;
    }
    const { passwordHash, ...user } = row;
    return { user, passwordHash };
  }

  async updatePasswordHash(id: string, passwordHash: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.db.update(users).set({ passwordHash }).where(eq(users.id, id));
  }
}

const normalize = (email: string) => email.trim().normalize('NFC').toLowerCase();

create() follows the same rule as the notes service: one statement. "Check whether the email is taken, then insert" has a gap where two sign-ups with the same address both pass the check. onConflictDoNothing() leans on the unique index instead, and an empty result means the email was taken. Every email is also normalized (trimmed, Unicode NFC, lowercased) on the way in and on the way to a lookup, so Ada@Example.com and ada@example.com are one account.

GET /me returns the signed-in user. @CurrentUser() injects the user that the authentication guard loaded for this request:

// src/users/me.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CurrentUser } from '@nestjs/authentication';
import type { User } from './user.js';

@Controller('me')
export class MeController {
  @Get()
  me(@CurrentUser() user: User) {
    return user;
  }
}

The users module registers the controller and the repository, and exports the repository, because the authentication code needs it:

// src/users/users.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { MeController } from './me.controller.js';
import { UsersRepository } from './users.repository.js';

@Module({
  controllers: [MeController],
  providers: [UsersRepository],
  exports: [UsersRepository],
})
export class UsersModule {}

One more small file tells the package your user type, once. After that, @CurrentUser('id') accepts only keys of User, and a typo is a compile error:

// src/auth/auth-types.ts
import type { User } from '../users/user.js';

declare module '@nestjs/authentication' {
  interface AuthenticationTypes {
    user: User;
  }
}

Hash passwords without leaking which emails exist

PasswordHasher hashes passwords with scrypt from node:crypto, at the parameters OWASP recommends, and runs it on the libuv thread pool so it doesn't block the event loop. A small service wraps the two things the controller needs, registering and verifying:

// src/auth/credentials.service.ts
import { ConflictException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PasswordHasher } from '@nestjs/authentication';
import type { User } from '../users/user.js';
import { UsersRepository } from '../users/users.repository.js';

@Injectable()
export class CredentialsService {
  constructor(
    private readonly usersRepository: UsersRepository,
    private readonly passwordHasher: PasswordHasher,
  ) {}

  async register(email: string, password: string): Promise<User> {
    const user = await this.usersRepository.create(email, await this.passwordHasher.hash(password));
    if (!user) {
      throw new ConflictException('Email already registered');
    }
    return user;
  }

  /** The user, or `null` when the email or the password is wrong. */
  async verify(email: string, password: string): Promise<User | null> {
    const found = await this.usersRepository.findCredentials(email);
    // With no account, verify() checks a dummy hash, so the response
    // time doesn't reveal which emails are registered.
    const valid = await this.passwordHasher.verify(password, found?.passwordHash);
    if (!valid || !found) {
      return null;
    }
    if (this.passwordHasher.needsRehash(found.passwordHash)) {
      await this.usersRepository.updatePasswordHash(found.user.id, await this.passwordHasher.hash(password));
    }
    return found.user;
  }
}

This is the timing bug from the list above, handled. verify() calls passwordHasher.verify() every time, even when there's no such user: it takes the stored hash or undefined, and with undefined it checks a dummy hash at the same cost. A hash at the default cost takes a few hundred milliseconds. If an unknown email returned early instead, it would come back far sooner than a wrong password, and the difference would tell anyone with a stopwatch which emails have accounts. The needsRehash() branch is for the future: when the recommended parameters go up, every user's hash is upgraded the next time they sign in, while their plain password is in hand.

Verify JWT access tokens

A credential provider turns a request into a user. JwtBearerProvider reads the Authorization header, checks the token's signature, exp, iss and aud, and passes the verified claims to your validate(), which loads the user:

// src/auth/jwt-auth.provider.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthenticationRegistry, JwtBearerProvider, type JwtClaims } from '@nestjs/authentication';
import type { User } from '../users/user.js';
import { UsersRepository } from '../users/users.repository.js';

@Injectable()
export class JwtAuth extends JwtBearerProvider<User> {
  constructor(
    private readonly usersRepository: UsersRepository,
    registry: AuthenticationRegistry,
  ) {
    // The key, issuer and audience come from the `accessToken` options.
    super({ realm: 'notes' });
    registry.registerProvider(this);
  }

  // Called once the signature, `exp`, `iss` and `aud` checked out.
  // Returning null (the user was deleted) rejects the token.
  validate({ sub }: JwtClaims) {
    return sub ? this.usersRepository.findById(sub) : null;
  }
}

Loading the user on every request costs one indexed query, and buys something: a deleted user's access token stops working on their next request, rather than when it expires.

The sign-up and sign-in routes

These are the request bodies of the four auth routes:

// src/auth/auth.schemas.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const signUpSchema = z.object({
  email: z.email(),
  password: z.string().min(12).max(128),
});
export type SignUpDto = z.infer<typeof signUpSchema>;

// No minimum here: a password set under an older rule still signs in.
export const signInSchema = z.object({
  email: z.email(),
  password: z.string().max(128),
});
export type SignInDto = z.infer<typeof signInSchema>;

export const refreshTokenSchema = z.object({
  refreshToken: z.string().min(1),
});
export type RefreshTokenDto = z.infer<typeof refreshTokenSchema>;

The minimum length applies at sign-up only. If you raise it next year, users with older, shorter passwords can still sign in. The maximum applies everywhere, so nobody can make the server hash a megabyte of password.

The controller verifies credentials with the service above, and issues tokens with the package's TokenService:

// src/auth/auth.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Post, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Public, TokenService } from '@nestjs/authentication';
import {
  refreshTokenSchema,
  signInSchema,
  signUpSchema,
  type RefreshTokenDto,
  type SignInDto,
  type SignUpDto,
} from './auth.schemas.js';
import { CredentialsService } from './credentials.service.js';

@Public()
@Controller('auth')
export class AuthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly credentialsService: CredentialsService,
    private readonly tokenService: TokenService,
  ) {}

  @Post('sign-up')
  async signUp(@Body({ schema: signUpSchema }) body: SignUpDto) {
    const user = await this.credentialsService.register(body.email, body.password);
    return this.tokenService.issue(user.id, { method: 'password', claims: { amr: ['pwd'] } });
  }

  @Post('token')
  @HttpCode(200)
  async token(@Body({ schema: signInSchema }) body: SignInDto) {
    const user = await this.credentialsService.verify(body.email, body.password);
    if (!user) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid email or password');
    }
    return this.tokenService.issue(user.id, { method: 'password', claims: { amr: ['pwd'] } });
  }

  // An unknown, expired or reused refresh token gets a 401.
  @Post('token/refresh')
  @HttpCode(200)
  refresh(@Body({ schema: refreshTokenSchema }) body: RefreshTokenDto) {
    return this.tokenService.refresh(body.refreshToken);
  }

  // Signs this device out. Unknown tokens get the same answer, as in RFC 7009.
  @Post('token/revoke')
  @HttpCode(204)
  async revoke(@Body({ schema: refreshTokenSchema }) body: RefreshTokenDto) {
    await this.tokenService.revoke(body.refreshToken);
  }
}

There's more going on in that file than its length suggests:

  • @Public() on the class skips authentication for these four routes. Every other route of the application requires a valid access token, because the guard is global. That matters more than it looks. With a guard per controller, the one controller where somebody forgets the decorator is public, and nothing tells you. Deny-by-default flips that: the mistake you can make is forgetting @Public(), and that one shows up as a 401 the first time you try the route.
  • @HttpCode(200) on token and refresh. POST routes answer 201 Created by default, and issuing tokens for an existing account creates nothing.
