To compare two weeks, download both artifacts and run python compare_runs.py week-1/<run-dir> week-2/<run-dir>.

GitHub documents three limits for scheduled workflows. The shortest interval is five minutes. Runs "can be delayed during periods of high loads", and the start of each hour is busy, so pick an odd minute. In a public repository, GitHub disables scheduled workflows after 60 days with no repository activity.

Where hosted monitoring fits

The workflow above gives you scheduled runs and saved data. You still do the comparison yourself. That is the work that the hosted platforms do for you. Humanbound's own blog makes the case for this in Your agent passed its security test. That was three weeks ago.

On the Humanbound platform, hb posture --trends shows posture history and hb findings shows a finding lifecycle. A finding is Open, Fixed, Regressed, or Stale (not triggered in 14 or more days of testing). hb monitor shows the status of the daily automated assessments, and hb monitor --pause and hb monitor --resume stop and restart them. The docs also describe weekly schedules and runs triggered by a deployment. The docs say that the platform reuses attack strategies from earlier cycles. They also say it can test for data that leaks from one user's session into another's, a test that needs coordinated sessions over time. These features need hb login, and the docs mark hb monitor as Pro. In local mode, hb posture --trends prints a message that posture history needs a login.

I have not run the Humanbound platform or the other hosted products for this post, so I cannot compare how they handle run-to-run noise. Ask each vendor the same question: if I run the same test twice with no changes, how far apart are the scores, and does your trend view show that spread?

Hosted monitoring does not remove the problems in this post. A smarter attacker each cycle is good for finding new weaknesses. It also means that this week's test is not the same as last week's test. Ask how the platform separates "the agent got worse" from "the attacker got better".

Frequently asked questions

What tools give continuous security testing for AI agents?
Promptfoo, garak, PyRIT and Humanbound's open-source CLI run on demand, and you schedule them in CI. Microsoft's AI Red Teaming Agent, Giskard, Mindgard, Lakera Red, Straiker and the Humanbound platform offer hosted, recurring testing.

How do I measure the security posture of an AI agent over time?
Run the same adversarial test on a schedule. Pin the attacker model, the judge, the tool version and the test depth. Run three baseline tests to see the normal spread. Then compare each new run with the baseline: first the error count, then the failure categories, then the score.

How often should I run continuous red-team tests?
Run them on every change to the model, the system prompt or the tools, and weekly in addition. Weekly runs can catch changes that you did not make, such as a provider's update to a hosted model.

Why did my posture score drop when I changed nothing?
The attacker generates new attacks on each run, and errors reduce the number of graded conversations. In my two runs with the same settings, the score dropped by 8 points, and 11 more conversations went ungraded in the second run because the judge's replies were not in a format hb could read.

Can I track posture history in Humanbound without an account?
Not inside hb. In local mode, hb posture reads the newest run only, and hb posture --trends needs a login. Save each run's .humanbound/results/ folder, for example as a CI artifact, and compare the runs yourself.

Should a scheduled red-team job fail the build?
Usually not. Make the scheduled job report only, and alert a person when a failure category repeats. Keep build failures for the pull request gate, where a person can act on them.

Method: all scores come from saved local hb runs (versions 2.9 and 2.12) between 4 September and 29 October 2026. CLI behavior was read from the humanbound 2.15.0 package. Tool descriptions come from each vendor's page, read on 19 November 2026.

Originally published on Humanbound.

title: Latency percentiles: why the mean, averaged p99s and naive load tests mislead
description:
If you're asked in an interview how you'd report the latency of a trading system (or of any service, really), the answer the interviewer is hoping for isn't "the average", and I simulated a day of messages to show why. All the numbers below come from that one run.

The simulated day has 24 hours of 100,000 messages each, so 2.4 million in all. Most messages take about 2 µs, a small share of them hit something slow such as a cache miss or an interrupt, and one hour in the afternoon is busy and has a much heavier tail than the rest.

Measure Value
Mean 2.12 µs
Median (p50) 2.00 µs
p99 2.91 µs
p99.9 34.5 µs
Max 413.7 µs

The mean sits right next to the median and tells you almost nothing about the tail, while the p99.9 is more than ten times the p99, which is where the trouble actually is. In trading the slow moments tend to be the busy and volatile ones, and those are exactly the moments when being fast earns money. So I'd report percentiles, and I'd always give the count and the period alongside them, because "p99 of 2.91 µs over 2.4 million messages on Tuesday" means something to whoever reads it and "p99 of 2.91 µs" on its own really doesn't.

You can't average percentiles

Suppose you've kept a p99 for every hour and somebody asks you for the whole day. The mean of the 24 hourly p99s comes to 5.47 µs, whereas the day's real p99 is 2.91 µs, and the gap is mostly the busy hour (its own p99 was 65.35 µs) dragging the average up. As far as I know the only correct figure for the whole day is the one computed from all of the data together. In practice you'd keep a histogram for each hour with log-sized buckets, in the style of HdrHistogram, add the counters together and then read the percentile off the sum.

Coordinated omission

However, the third trap is probably the hardest one to spot, because it's hidden in the way most load tests get written (a client that sends a request and waits for the reply, records the time and only then sends the next one). To demonstrate it I ran a client like that against a simulated system that should receive a request every millisecond for one second, where each reply takes 0.05 ms and there's a single 100 ms stall halfway through.

The naive client simply waited through the stall and recorded a single 100 ms measurement before continuing, sending the requests it had missed late and timing each one from the moment it actually went out, so its p99 came out at 0.05 ms. However, if you time every request from when it was originally due (which is how a real user or a real exchange feed would experience it), you'll find 100 requests were delayed by more than 1 ms and the p99 is actually 90.05 ms, so I'd say the original test had probably concealed the stall almost completely.

The remedy I'd normally suggest is sending requests on a fixed schedule that doesn't wait for replies and measuring each request from when it should have gone out. If that isn't possible for some reason, I think you can at least correct the histogram afterwards for the samples you missed (HdrHistogram supports this directly).

I've written all of this up in considerably more detail for low-latency interviews, including what tick-to-trade actually measures and how you'd record histograms without slowing down the hot path, at https://academicquant.co.uk/qd-latency-percentiles?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=devto-latency-percentiles-why

title: Make your agent pay for a check before it says "done"
description:
Agents report success too easily. Ask one to export invoices to CSV with a totals row, and it will tell you "done" whether the total is right or not. Usually you find out when the client does.

I built a small fix, seen from the agent's side as a buyer: before my agent tells anyone a task is finished, it pays for an independent judgement of the actual result against the task. A Miner on Telegraph answers the TASK_EXECUTION_QUALITY_GENERAL Intent, and the agent pays about a cent in test USDC from its own escrow balance. It also checks the client's must-have items for free, and only says "done" on a clear pass.

Disclosure: this is my Telegraph H2 hackathon entry, competing for a prize. Everything below runs on testnet (Ethereum Sepolia, test USDC); no real money moves.

Try it in one minute, no wallet

Open https://donecheck.swiftbotlab.workers.dev, click Example: planted defect and then Check it.

The task asks for a JavaScript expression that is true when a string has at least 12 characters. The agent's answer is s.length > 12, which is off by one. A paid judge (a Telegraph Miner answering TASK_EXECUTION_QUALITY_GENERAL) replies FIX: "the expression uses > instead of >=". You also get a receipt, and a button that checks the receipt against Telegraph's settled epoch block. I pay for these checks from a throwaway testnet wallet, with a small shared daily cap.

Three verdicts, fail closed

  • SUBMIT: the judge clearly passes it, and every required item is in the result.
  • FIX: the judge says it fails, or a required item is missing (even if the judge passed it).
  • HOLD: no clear answer (a null verdict, "partially satisfies", or no Miner answered). A human looks. Unknown is never reported as success.

How well does it work?

I wrote 20 everyday tasks (CSV, JSON, SQL, regex, a translation, a summary, a bug fix...), each with a correct result and a version with a planted defect. That makes 40 cases, run once on testnet:

  • 0 of 20 defective results were submitted. The judge stopped 17, the free required-items check 2, and 1 was held.
  • 18 of 20 correct results were submitted. The 2 misses are the judge contradicting itself (once "fails" while describing the result as correct).
  • About $0.009 in test USDC and a median 13.2 s per check; 38 of 38 receipts settled on the node.

It's my own set, not a benchmark. Every number has a pinned file and a one-line jq command in docs/EVIDENCE.md.

Use it from your agent (5 minutes) 

git clone https://github.com/swiftbotlabs/gig-guard && cd gig-guard
npm install && npm test                 # 52 tests against a fake node, no funds
node examples/fix-loop.mjs --offline    # FIX -> redo -> SUBMIT, offline

For live checks you need a testnet-only key with a little Sepolia ETH for gas. Then:

echo "TELEGRAPH_PAYER_KEY=0x<testnet key>" > .env && set -a && . ./.env && set +a
node examples/fund-escrow.mjs 1         # mint 1 test USDC, approve, deposit to escrow
node src/cli.mjs deliver '{"task":"...","result":"...","mustInclude":["total"]}' && echo done || echo "not done"

Exit code 0 means SUBMIT, so the check is one line in any agent loop. The full walkthrough is in docs/TUTORIAL-done-check.md.

Where the pieces come from

  • Telegraph docs: https://anjoman.ai/docs. The escrow payment path the agent uses: https://anjoman.ai/docs/using/escrow-inference
  • Ranked Miners per Intent (the leaderboard): https://anjoman.ai/dashboard/explore
  • Telegraph's open missions and bounties: https://github.com/telegraphprotocol/bounties (this is Mission 09, Personal Agent).
  • The same repo also has a contract gate (Mission 14). It is out of scope here.

Honest limits

  • It uses one judge per check. When that judge contradicts itself, the gate holds rather than guesses, and that costs a human look.
  • The judge sees at most 2,000 characters of task plus result.
  • It is testnet only: the Telegraph node offers testnet payment routes today. What a mainnet switch needs is in docs/MAINNET.md.

Try it and tell me what breaks

If you build agents, paste one of your own tasks and outputs into https://donecheck.swiftbotlab.workers.dev. Then open an issue at https://github.com/swiftbotlabs/gig-guard/issues with what you checked and whether the verdict was right. Wrong verdicts are the most useful ones. There is no reward for this, only the check itself.

title: Ubuntu removed a root CA. Node 22.23.2 still trusts it: comparing CA lists by public key
description:
On 30 October, apt on my Ubuntu 24.04 container installed ca-certificates 20260816ubuntu0.24.04.1. Its changelog has one line that matters here:

  * Blacklist the following CA cert due to intermediate cert compromise
    (LP: #2171507)
    + "emSign ECC Root CA - G3"

That is the root above the intermediates with tiny private keys that I wrote about in October. The system store dropped it. The question I wanted answered was narrower: what on this machine still trusts it? Answering it takes two steps. Ask each runtime which list it reads, then compare the lists by public key.

Step 1: ask each runtime where it looks

Python's ssl module reads whatever OpenSSL was built to read:

import ssl

print(ssl.get_default_verify_paths())
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
print(ctx.cert_store_stats())
print(any("emSign ECC Root CA - G3" in str(c["subject"]) for c in ctx.get_ca_certs()))

DefaultVerifyPaths(cafile='/usr/lib/ssl/cert.pem', capath='/usr/lib/ssl/certs', openssl_cafile_env='SSL_CERT_FILE', openssl_cafile='/usr/lib/ssl/cert.pem', openssl_capath_env='SSL_CERT_DIR', openssl_capath='/usr/lib/ssl/certs')
{'x509': 120, 'crl': 0, 'x509_ca': 120}
False

/usr/lib/ssl/cert.pem is a symlink to /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, so plain ssl follows the distro: 120 roots, no G3. That stops being true the moment you pip install requests. The Requests docs say it "uses certificates from the package certifi", and certifi ships its own cacert.pem, frozen at whatever certifi version you have.

Node is the interesting one. Since 22.15 it has tls.getCACertificates(type), which returns the list for each source: bundled (the copy compiled into the binary), system, extra (from NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS), and default, the list TLS clients actually use. This script prints all four and checks for G3:

const tls = require('tls');
const { X509Certificate } = require('crypto');

const spki = (p) => new X509Certificate(p).publicKey.export({ type: 'spki', format: 'der' }).toString('base64');
const distinct = (pems) => new Set(pems.map(spki)).size;
const hasRoot = (pems, cn) => pems.some((p) => new X509Certificate(p).subject.split('\n').includes(`CN=${cn}`));

console.log(`node ${process.version}, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=${process.env.NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA ?? 'unset'}, flags: ${process.execArgv.join(' ') || 'none'}`);
for (const t of ['default', 'bundled', 'system', 'extra']) {
  const pems = tls.getCACertificates(t);
  console.log(`  ${t.padEnd(8)} ${String(pems.length).padStart(4)} entries, ${String(distinct(pems)).padStart(3)} distinct keys, G3: ${hasRoot(pems, 'emSign ECC Root CA - G3')}`);
}

On Node 22.23.2, run three ways (the bundled, system and extra lines are the same in all three runs, so I cut them from the second and third):

node v22.23.2, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=unset, flags: none
  default   145 entries, 145 distinct keys, G3: true
  bundled   145 entries, 145 distinct keys, G3: true
  system    360 entries, 120 distinct keys, G3: false
  extra       0 entries,   0 distinct keys, G3: false
node v22.23.2, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1, flags: none
  default   505 entries, 149 distinct keys, G3: true
  ...
node v22.23.2, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=unset, flags: --use-openssl-ca
  default     0 entries,   0 distinct keys, G3: false
  ...

Three things in that output matter.

The default list is the bundled one. The Node docs describe it as "a snapshot of Mozilla CA store that is fixed at release time". 22.23.2 came out on 28 July (per Node's release index), so its snapshot has G3, and no OS update can change that.

NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1 adds, it does not subtract. The docs for --use-system-ca say Node uses the system store "along with" the bundled one, and they are blunt about the consequence: "Node.js currently does not support distrust/revocation of certificates from another source based on system settings." So 145 bundled plus 360 system entries gives 505, which collapses to 149 distinct keys: the 145 bundled roots plus four roots that only the system store has. G3 is still in. Turning on the system store only helps with roots the bundle is missing, never with roots the distro removed.

--use-openssl-ca reports an empty default list, and it still works. In that mode the default list leaves out the bundled roots, as the docs say it will, and the OpenSSL store that Node verifies against does not show up in it. So I checked that it really verifies against the system store rather than against nothing:

node --use-openssl-ca -e "require('https').get('https://www.rfc-editor.org/', r => console.log(r.statusCode, r.socket.authorized))"
SSL_CERT_FILE=/dev/null SSL_CERT_DIR=/nonexistent node --use-openssl-ca -e "require('https').get('https://www.rfc-editor.org/', r => console.log(r.statusCode)).on('error', e => console.log(e.code))"

200 true
UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY

The 360 system entries for 120 roots are not a bug either. The docs warn that the array "may contain duplicates if the same certificate is repeatedly stored in multiple sources", and Node reads both the bundle file and the certificate directory. Count distinct keys, not entries.

Step 2: compare the lists by public key

Comparing files by hash tells you nothing, and comparing by name is fragile. A CA can reissue a root with the same key under a new certificate, so the key is the identity that matters. The script below hashes each certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo and walks just enough DER to find the subject and the key, with the standard library only:

"""Compare CA bundles by public key. Usage: python3 trust_inventory.py REF.pem OTHER.pem ..."""
import hashlib, re, sys
from base64 import b64decode

PEM = re.compile(rb"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----(.+?)-----END CERTIFICATE-----", re.S)


def tlv(buf, i):
    """Return (tag, start of value, end of value) for the DER element at i."""
    tag, n = buf[i], buf[i + 1]
    i += 2
    if n & 0x80:
        size, n = n & 0x7F, int.from_bytes(buf[i:i + (n & 0x7F)], "big")
        i += size
    return tag, i, i + n


def fields(buf, start, end):
    """Split a SEQUENCE body into its elements as (tag, start, end) of the whole element."""
    out = []
    while start < end:
        tag, vs, ve = tlv(buf, start)
        out.append((tag, start, ve))
        start = ve
    return out


def parse(der):
    """Return (SPKI SHA-256, subject CN or O) for one DER certificate."""
    _, s, e = tlv(der, 0)               # Certificate
    _, s, e = tlv(der, s)               # tbsCertificate
    f = fields(der, s, e)
    if f[0][0] == 0xA0:                 # skip the explicit [0] version
        f = f[1:]
    subject, spki = f[4], f[5]          # serial, sigAlg, issuer, validity, subject, spki
    name = {}
    for oid, label in ((b"\x55\x04\x03", "CN"), (b"\x55\x04\x0a", "O")):
        k = der.find(b"\x06\x03" + oid, subject[1], subject[2])
        if k != -1:
            _, vs, ve = tlv(der, k + 5)
            name[label] = der[vs:ve].decode("utf-8", "replace")
    return hashlib.sha256(der[spki[1]:spki[2]]).hexdigest(), name.get("CN") or name.get("O")


def show(sign, names, limit=6):
    for n in names[:limit]:
        print(f"    {sign} {n}")
    if len(names) > limit:
        print(f"    ... and {len(names) - limit} more")


def load(path):
    data = open(path, "rb").read()
    certs = [b64decode(b"".join(m.split())) for m in PEM.findall(data)]
    return len(certs), dict(parse(c) for c in certs)


ref_path, *others = sys.argv[1:]
ref_count, ref = load(ref_path)
print(f"{ref_path}: {ref_count} certificates, {len(ref)} distinct keys (reference)")
for path in others:
    count, roots = load(path)
    extra = sorted(roots[k] for k in roots.keys() - ref.keys())
    missing = sorted(ref[k] for k in ref.keys() - roots.keys())
    print(f"\n{path}: {count} certificates, {len(roots)} distinct keys")
    print(f"  trusted here but not in the reference: {len(extra)}")
    show("+", extra)
    print(f"  in the reference but not here: {len(missing)}")
    show("-", missing)

To get Node's bundle into a file, node -e "process.stdout.write(require('tls').rootCertificates.join('\n'))" > node-bundled.pem. Then compare it, today's certifi release (2026.11.20) and an older certifi copy I found inside a desktop app, all against the system store:

/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt: 120 certificates, 120 distinct keys (reference)

node-v22.23.2-bundled.pem: 145 certificates, 145 distinct keys
  trusted here but not in the reference: 29
    + AffirmTrust Commercial
    + AffirmTrust Networking
    + AffirmTrust Premium
    + AffirmTrust Premium ECC
    + Atos TrustedRoot 2011
    + COMODO Certification Authority
    ... and 23 more
  in the reference but not here: 4
    - SECOM TLS ECC Root CA 2024
    - SECOM TLS RSA Root CA 2024
    - Telia EC TLS Root CA v3
    - Telia RSA TLS Root CA v3

certifi-2026.11.20.pem: 113 certificates, 113 distinct keys
  trusted here but not in the reference: 0
  in the reference but not here: 7
    - Buypass Class 2 Root CA
    - Buypass Class 3 Root CA
    - Certigna Root CA
    - QuoVadis Root CA 1 G3
    - QuoVadis Root CA 3 G3
    - emSign ECC Root CA - C3
    ... and 1 more

vendored-certifi-in-app.pem: 121 certificates, 121 distinct keys
  trusted here but not in the reference: 1
    + emSign ECC Root CA - G3
  in the reference but not here: 0

The same Ubuntu changelog accounts for all 29 extra roots in Node's bundle. The June package (20260601~24.04.1) lists 24 roots removed in its update to Mozilla bundle 2.86, DigiCert Global Root CA and the four AffirmTrust roots among them. The October package removes four more with bundle 2.90 and blacklists G3. Node 22.23.2 was released on 28 July and still carries every one of them.

certifi goes the other way: the current release trusts fewer roots than Ubuntu and lacks seven that Ubuntu still ships, two other emSign roots among them. The old copy inside the app is byte-identical to certifi 2026.07.22, and it still has G3.

The fix for Node is an upgrade

Node did remove G3. The commit "crypto: update root certificates to NSS 3.131.1" (20 October) lists emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root CA - C1 and emSign ECC Root CA - C3 as removed. I fetched src/node_root_certs.h at the current release tags:

v22.23.5  116 roots  G3: no
v24.22.3  118 roots  G3: no
v26.13.1  118 roots  G3: no

Run through the same comparison, the 22.23.5 bundle has only two roots the Ubuntu store lacks (Atos TrustedRoot 2011 and the Chunghwa Telecom ePKI root) instead of 29. So on 22.x the answer is 22.23.5 or later. The other Node on this machine, 20.20.2, bundles 144 roots including G3 and has no getCACertificates at all. It will not get a fix: Node 20 reached end of life on 30 April 2026 (release schedule), and 20.20.2 from 24 March was its last release.

If you would rather your Node processes follow the distro's decisions, --use-openssl-ca does that. NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1 does not.

The copies you did not install on purpose

The last step is a plain find:

find ~ /opt /usr \( -name cacert.pem -o -name tls-ca-bundle.pem -o -name ca-bundle.pem \) -type f 2>/dev/null

It turned up 296 files on this machine. 284 were named cacert.pem, and 264 of those sat in uv's package cache. Of the 20 outside the cache, 15 still list G3: certifi inside three virtualenvs and a uv tool, pip's own vendored certifi in three uv-managed Python installs and one virtualenv, six copies in container image layers, and the desktop app from above. The other five: botocore's own cacert.pem, a game that ships one, and three Flatpak bundles. I did not work out which of these each program reads at runtime, so treat the count as places to check, not as 15 open holes.

What I would check on any machine

  1. node -p "process.version + ' ' + require('tls').rootCertificates.length" on every Node you run, then compare with a current release of the same line. The OS store does not reach the bundled list.
  2. python -m certifi in every virtualenv that uses Requests, and the certifi version pinned in your lock files.
  3. Container images: each one carries the ca-certificates package and any certifi from the day it was built.
  4. The find above, then the SPKI comparison on anything it turns up.

The distro did its job on 30 October. The other copies change only when you upgrade the thing that ships them, and nothing warns you that a copy is out of date.

Written with AI assistance from my own notes and test results. I checked every fact and command before publishing.

title: Designing Resilient Third-Party API Integrations for Production
description:
Most third-party API integrations do not fail because of flawed syntax or poor business logic. They fail because the system was engineered under the assumption that the external service would always behave predictably.

When writing integration code, handling authentication and sending basic requests is only about 20% of the effort. The remaining 80% involves accounting for real-world failures: transient network glitches, unexpected rate limits, silent response schema updates, and sudden vendor downtime.

If you only code for the happy path, a minor vendor disruption will quickly cascade into your application. Here is how to build resilient API integrations that survive unpredictable failure modes.

Step 1: Enforce Strict Timeouts and Retry Strategies

Never make an HTTP request without an explicit timeout. A hanging connection to an external vendor can exhaust your application's worker pool, bringing down your entire backend service.

Combine strict connection timeouts with an exponential backoff strategy for transient errors (such as 502, 503, or rate-limiting 429 status codes). Exponential backoff ensures you do not overwhelm an already struggling API with rapid retry loops.

Here is a production-ready implementation in Python using httpx and tenacity:

import httpx
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_random_exponential, retry_if_exception_type

class ExternalAPIError(Exception):
    """Custom exception for non-retryable API failures."""
    pass

@retry(
    stop=stop_after_attempt(4),
    wait=wait_random_exponential(min=1, max=10),
    retry=retry_if_exception_type((httpx.TimeoutException, httpx.HTTPStatusError)),
    reraise=True
)
def fetch_vendor_data(endpoint_url: str, api_key: str) -> dict:
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}

    # Define explicit connect and read timeouts
    timeout = httpx.Timeout(timeout=5.0, connect=2.0)

    with httpx.Client(timeout=timeout) as client:
        response = client.get(endpoint_url, headers=headers)

        # Raise HTTPStatusError for server errors or rate limits to trigger retries
        if response.status_code in (429, 502, 503, 504):
            response.raise_for_status()

        if response.status_code != 200:
            raise ExternalAPIError(f"API request failed with status: {response.status_code}")

        return response.json()

Step 2: Validate Response Schemas explicitly

External vendors frequently push unannounced updates, rename attributes, or omit fields from JSON payloads. If your application expects user.email and suddenly receives user.contact_email, untyped code will crash deep inside your business logic.

Validate incoming responses at the network boundary using a strict data validation layer. If the vendor alters their response structure, fail early at the point of ingestion.

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, ValidationError

class VendorUserPayload(BaseModel):
    user_id: str
    email: EmailStr
    account_status: str

def parse_vendor_response(raw_json: dict) -> VendorUserPayload:
    try:
        return VendorUserPayload(**raw_json)
    except ValidationError as error:
        # Schema drift detected; alert monitoring tools immediately
        raise ExternalAPIError(f"Response payload schema validation failed: {error}")

Step 3: Implement Circuit Breakers for Vendor Downtime

If an external vendor experiences an extended outage, continually making requests wastes compute resources and increases latency for your users.

A circuit breaker pattern monitors outbound request failure rates. When failures cross a specific threshold, the circuit "trips" open, immediately failing subsequent requests or returning cached/fallback data without attempting the network call. Once the cooldown period passes, the breaker allows test requests through to check if the vendor has recovered.

Step 4: Log Structured Context for Observability

Debugging integration failures without context is inefficient. Generic logs like Error 500 provide no actionable information during an incident.

Always log structured, contextual metadata for outbound integration requests:

  • Correlation IDs to trace the request through your microservices
  • Endpoint paths and HTTP methods
  • Status codes and rate-limit response headers (e.g., x-ratelimit-remaining)
  • Redacted error bodies for inspection

Ensure sensitive data, secret tokens, and personally identifiable information (PII) are scrubbed before writing to log stores.

Assume Failure by Design

Reliable software systems are not built by hoping third-party services stay online. They are built by assuming external dependencies will fail, and placing strict, defensive boundaries around them.

About me

Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. If you want to discuss backend architecture or need help streamlining your API workflows, connect with Tanmay on LinkedIn.

title: NoNoncense 2.0: Who May Use This Machine ID?
description:
Distributed ID generators often look simple: combine a timestamp, a counter, and a machine ID. NoNoncense uses that idea for fast counter, sortable, and encrypted nonces. It is a wonderfully fast design, right up until two running nodes receive the same machine ID.

The hard part is not incrementing a counter. It is deciding who may use each machine ID, especially when pods are replaced, nodes autoscale, deployments overlap, and network partitions happen. Two locally correct counters with the same machine ID can produce globally duplicate values.

NoNoncense 1.x left that decision to application startup: derive an ID, initialize the nonce factory, and make the topology safe yourself. That is perfectly reasonable for a fixed fleet. Version 2.0 brings the decision into the supervision tree and gives different deployments a suitable way to establish exclusivity.

Where exclusivity comes from

The strategy is not an afterthought; it expresses what makes an ID unique in a particular deployment:

  • SQL leases coordinate through PostgreSQL or MySQL. They are a natural fit when the application already has a database and wants a durable, inspectable source of truth.
  • Valkey or Redis leases use per-field hash TTLs for a compact, server-managed lease registry. They need only ordinary commands: no Lua scripts, no Redis functions.
  • Kubernetes StatefulSets can use the pod ordinal through an environment variable when that ordinal is globally unique among nonce-generating pods.
  • Host identifiers retain the fixed-node model for deployments with a known, stable node list.

The last two are intentionally uncomplicated: when the platform can prove an instance's identity, NoNoncense can use it directly. The interesting work begins when it cannot and the application needs to coordinate competing nodes.

One lifecycle, several coordinators

For dynamic deployments, NoNoncense treats a machine ID as a lease. NoNoncense.MachineId starts a LeaseManager under supervision and waits for it to acquire an initial lease before application startup can complete. Only then are the configured nonce factories initialized. There is no interval in which a node generates values with an unproven ID.

The manager then renews the lease in the background. Its strategy interface distinguishes a confirmed loss from an uncertain result:

{:ok, lease, ttl_ms}
{:error, :lost, reason}
{:error, :retry, reason}

lost means the coordinator has positively rejected ownership, perhaps because the lease expired and somebody else claimed the ID. retry means the result is uncertain: a timeout or a dropped connection might have happened before or after the coordinator applied the renewal.

The lease also has a local deadline that does not depend on the coordinator answering. It is counted from the moment the strategy call started, minus a 10-second safety margin, so a slow call cannot stretch it. The manager retries uncertainty with backoff while that deadline holds. On confirmed loss or local expiry, it disables the affected factories and calls the optional :on_lease_lost callback. Continuing after that would trade an availability problem for a uniqueness problem, so the library chooses uniqueness.

For dynamic strategies, it then retries acquisition with backoff. A disabled factory is never simply switched back on: it is initialized afresh, after waiting past every timestamp the previous state could have used, so a node that gets its old ID back cannot repeat a nonce. Recovery is part of the component's normal lifecycle rather than a bespoke application failure path.

The current lease lives in a separate, supervised lease store process, which is also what enforces the local deadline. If the manager crashes and supervision restarts it, it first tries to renew that lease rather than needlessly claim another of the 512 available IDs. The store is deliberately not durable: after a node crash or forced kill, normal lease expiry remains the source of truth.

This lifecycle is not limited to the included backends. A strategy is a small behaviour that implements acquire/2, renew/3, and release/2, and declares whether its IDs are deterministic. Applications can therefore bring a coordinator with their own allocation rules while keeping the same startup, recovery, and safety policy.

What it looks like in your app

Adding it to the supervision tree is the whole integration. This example uses the SQL strategy, after running its migration:

children = [
  MyApp.Repo,
  {NoNoncense.MachineId,
   strategy: NoNoncense.MachineId.Strategy.SqlLease,
   strategy_opts: [repo: MyApp.Repo],
   instances: [[base_key: System.fetch_env!("BASE_KEY")]]}
]

Supervisor.start_link(children, strategy: :one_for_one, name: MyApp.Supervisor)

Startup blocks until a lease is held, so nothing downstream runs without a machine ID. After that, NoNoncense.nonce(64), NoNoncense.sortable_nonce(64) and NoNoncense.encrypted_nonce(64) just work. Swap the strategy and strategy_opts to use Redis or Valkey, a StatefulSet ordinal, or a fixed node list.

SQL: let the database arbitrate the race

The SQL strategy works with PostgreSQL and MySQL using a small, pre-populated lease table. Each possible machine ID has a row containing an expiry time, an ownership token, and a lock version.

Acquisition is a two-stage optimistic operation:

  1. Read the expired rows, ordered by ID.
  2. Attempt to claim one with an UPDATE that matches both its ID and the lock_version just read.

Nodes try the lowest few IDs in order and the rest in random order, which keeps IDs compact without making a crowd of starting nodes collide on the same row. The update sets a new random token, moves expires_at forward, and increments the version. If two nodes read the same expired row, they both try to update it, but only one update still matches the old version. The loser tries another candidate. The database turns a familiar optimistic-locking primitive into lease arbitration: no process-local lock, no table-wide lock, and no opportunity to overwrite a concurrent claim.

Once claimed, the random token becomes the lease identity. Renewals and releases match the machine ID and that token, so a node that has lost its lease cannot extend or release the next owner's row. Renewals deliberately ignore lock_version: if a renewal commits but its response is lost, the retry still succeeds instead of reporting a false loss.

Two clocks, not one

A database clock alone does not make reuse safe. The nonce timestamps come from the node's clock, so a successor on a clock that runs behind could emit values that an earlier holder already used.

So every claim and renewal stores the later of two cutoffs: the database time plus the TTL, and the node's own time plus the TTL. A row can be claimed only when both the database clock and the claimer's local clock have passed that stored expiry. The node's local time is measured on the same clock that stamps the nonces, so the successor's timestamps start after anything its predecessor could have produced.

On a graceful release, the cutoff becomes a short quarantine (three seconds), so a freed ID is not handed out in the same instant.

Valkey and Redis: turn field existence into ownership

Redis 8 and Valkey 9 add HSETEX: hash updates with a per-field TTL and a condition on whether the fields already exist. That makes it possible to store all leases in one hash without a polling cleanup job.

At first, an ID field looks sufficient:

"17" => ""

But HSETEX conditions check field existence, not whether a field still holds a particular value. A renewal conditioned only on field "17" could refresh an ID after another owner had taken it. That is exactly the operation a lease protocol must reject.

NoNoncense therefore writes two fields in one HSETEX command, with the same TTL:

"17"                    => ""
"token.17.random-token" => ""

The first field makes occupied IDs easy to discover. The second is an ownership marker: its name contains both the ID and the token, so the value does not matter. On acquisition, HSETEX ... FNX creates both fields only if neither already exists. On renewal or release, HSETEX ... FXX succeeds only if both still exist.

When a lease expires, both fields disappear together. A later owner creates a new token marker, not the old one. An old owner therefore cannot refresh or delete the new owner's lease: its marker is gone, so the conditional command updates nothing and the manager treats the lease as lost.

This is the useful pattern: when a datastore can conditionally test only existence, give each ownership generation its own expiring marker and update the resource and marker atomically. The marker turns an existence check into proof that this exact owner still has the right to act.

The clock-skew cutoff

As on the SQL side, expiry in the coordinator is not enough: a successor's nonce timestamps must exceed anything its predecessor could have used. Each ID therefore also has a persistent exp.17 field, with no TTL, holding the holder's local expiry. It outlives the ownership fields.

Every acquire and renew sends three commands in one MULTI/EXEC:

  1. The conditional HSETEX on the ID and marker fields.
  2. HSETNX to make sure exp.17 exists.
  3. A second HSETEX ... FXX KEEPTTL that writes the new cutoff to exp.17, and names the marker field too.

Because the third command requires the marker to exist, the cutoff is written only if the first command really established ownership. An expired holder cannot overwrite its successor's cutoff. A successor may take an ID only once its fields have expired in Redis and its own clock has passed exp.17.

No scripts required

None of this uses Lua, Redis functions or EVAL. It needs HGETALL, HSETEX, HSETNX and MULTI/EXEC. In environments that restrict scripting, that is a short, auditable list to approve.

Fast generation, deliberate ownership

The new strategies make the same promise in different environments: nonce factories run only while the deployment can establish that their machine ID belongs to them. SQL gets there with a database clock, tokens, optimistic compare-and-swap and a two-clock reuse cutoff. Valkey and Redis get there with an atomic, expiring ownership marker and a persistent cutoff field. StatefulSets and fixed fleets use the identity their platform already provides.

The optional conflict guard adds another signal for connected Erlang nodes, and optional Telemetry reports acquisition, renewal, retries, loss, release, and conflicts. Neither feature touches the nonce generation hot path.

The guarantee is only as strong as the coordinator's durability, so the docs spell out what each backend needs: a single writable primary for SQL, and a single instance with append-only persistence for Redis or Valkey, plus a warning that restoring an old backup can roll back lease records. If you restore one, stop all nonce generators first.

The result is a deliberately asymmetric design: the path that generates a nonce stays tiny and fast, while the rare coordination path does the careful work needed to answer one question with confidence: who is allowed to generate values with this machine ID right now?

NoNoncense 2.0 is available on Hex. The machine ID documentation and migration guide cover configuration and upgrading from 1.x.

title: I fact-checked 11 AI presentation tools on 23 numbers — accuracy is not usability
description:
Every AI presentation tool claims it can turn a prompt into a finished deck. I wanted to check a narrower, verifiable thing: when the source material contains specific numbers, do those numbers survive into the slides — and is the resulting deck actually presentable in a meeting?

Method

I gave 11 tools the same three briefs and asked each for a 10-slide deck:

  • Brief A — a short topic only
  • Brief B — a long article to summarize
  • Brief C — a data brief with 23 specific figures embedded in it (revenues, percentages, dates, headcounts)

After generation, I went through every deck figure by figure and scored how many of the 23 came through unchanged. I also scored completeness (did it actually produce 10 slides?) and basic usability (layout, overlap, readability). All tools were tested on free tiers, in November 2026.

Finding 1: Fidelity is nearly solved at the top

Several tools reproduced all 23 figures exactly — including the big chatbots that generate slides directly (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude), plus Gamma and Canva. A second group (Kimi, Qwen, DeepSeek) also got the values right, each with caveats: Qwen exported an image-based PDF with a watermark, DeepSeek produced an outline rather than a deck.

Finding 2: Fidelity is not usability

This is the part I didn't expect:

  • One tool scored 23/23 on the numbers while its deck had text overlapping images badly enough that you couldn't present it. Perfect facts, unusable slides.
  • Another tool quietly produced 3 slides instead of the requested 10.
  • The overall quality ranking (out of 50) put Gamma first (44), then Gemini (43), ChatGPT (43) and Claude (42) — while some tools with perfect number fidelity landed near the bottom on usability.

The gap between "the facts are right" and "you can put this on a screen" is where most tools actually fail.

Full data

Per-tool scorecards, the methodology, and the raw results as a downloadable CSV are here: https://aippt.org/ai-presentation-benchmark

The brief itself is published on that page, so the test is reproducible — if you get different results with the same brief, I'd genuinely like to hear about it.

Disclosure

I make one of the tools in this space (AIPPT.org). To keep the test honest, I excluded my own tool from the scoreboard entirely — the page shows the other 11 tools' results, including the ones that beat us on individual measures. I plan to re-run the same briefs quarterly and keep old snapshots linked.

If you spot an error in a scorecard, tell me and I'll re-check and correct it on the page.

title: Patch virtual vs. patch: quando proteger uma API em vez de fazer novo deploy
description:
Patch virtual vs. patch convencional: quando blindar uma API e como remover a proteção

O patch virtual bloqueia temporariamente uma forma conhecida de explorar uma falha de software enquanto o código vulnerável permanece no lugar. Use-o quando conseguir cobrir o tráfego da API afetada antes de implantar uma correção com segurança. Aplique o patch e verifique a frota afetada assim que a build corrigida estiver pronta.

Experimente o Apidog hoje

Em 23 de novembro de 2026, a OpenAI e a Cisco apresentaram o Shirudo, um projeto Linux de código aberto que consegue carregar proteções eBPF direcionadas em um sistema em execução. Ele coloca em foco uma decisão familiar para equipes de plantão. Se a correção definitiva levar horas para ser validada, você consegue reduzir a exposição agora sem quebrar as requisições das quais seus clientes dependem? Anúncio do Shirudo pela OpenAI

Patch virtual vs. patch convencional

Decisão Patch virtual Patch convencional
O que muda? Uma regra de gateway ou um controle de runtime limita a exposição. Um aplicativo, dependência ou componente de sistema corrigido substitui a versão afetada.
Quando ajuda? O controle alcança o tráfego afetado antes que a correção possa ser implantada. Há uma correção confiável disponível e a equipe consegue implantá-la com segurança.
O que comprova que funcionou? Evidências de cobertura e verificações de serviço aprovadas no ponto de aplicação. Versões corrigidas verificadas em toda a frota, além de verificações de release aprovadas.
Quando o trabalho termina? A correção definitiva é verificada e a regra temporária é desativada. A correção é instalada e verificada em todas as instâncias afetadas.

Um patch virtual é um controle compensatório. Seu inventário ainda mostra a versão vulnerável enquanto o controle está ativo. Mantenha o chamado de remediação aberto e registre nele a regra, o responsável e a data prevista de remoção. Orientação da OWASP sobre patch virtual

Um patch convencional pode ser uma biblioteca atualizada em uma imagem de contêiner ou uma build corrigida do seu próprio serviço. Acompanhe o que a frota está realmente executando. Uma imagem corrigida no registry diz pouco sobre workers mais antigos que ainda atendem requisições. Guia de gerenciamento de patches corporativos do NIST

Quando você deve blindar uma API?

Use uma blindagem quando três condições forem atendidas.

  1. O controle cobre o tráfego afetado. Confirme quais caminhos de entrada e workloads estão no escopo, incluindo chamadores internos e processamento em segundo plano quando relevante.
  2. Você consegue validá-la antes da build corrigida. Use tráfego representativo de staging para verificar o comportamento esperado da regra e confirmar que as requisições normais continuam funcionando.
  3. Há um responsável pelo encerramento. Atribua a implantação do patch, alinhe as evidências de cobertura e defina um horário de revisão para a mudança temporária.

Suponha que uma API de objetos tenha um recurso opcional de processamento vulnerável, e o gateway já permita desativar o acesso a esse recurso. Sua equipe pode avaliar o comportamento com o recurso desativado rapidamente enquanto reconstrói e testa o serviço. As leituras de coleção e de detalhe devem continuar funcionando. Se os clientes usam o recurso opcional, informe ao suporte qual resposta esses clientes receberão e por quanto tempo a mudança provavelmente durará.

Meça os dois lados do trade-off. Compare o tempo esperado para aplicar a regra com o tempo para levar uma build corrigida ao mesmo conjunto de workloads. Acompanhe o sucesso das requisições normais, a latência e as contagens de rejeição durante a implantação. Um aumento nas rejeições precisa de contexto. Pode ser o controle fazendo seu trabalho ou um fluxo de trabalho de cliente que seus fixtures de staging não cobriram.

Prefira aplicar o patch imediatamente quando a build corrigida estiver pronta, um canário parecer saudável e a implantação alcançar as instâncias expostas tão rapidamente quanto a regra temporária. Se nenhum controle confiável cobrir o caminho afetado e o risco justificar uma ação imediata, considere restringir o acesso ou desativar o recurso afetado enquanto a correção é preparada. Quando houver evidências de comprometimento, inicie a resposta a incidentes junto com a remediação.

Onde uma blindagem de API deve atuar?

Escolha o ponto de aplicação com base no que ele consegue observar e em quais requisições precisam passar por ele. Um web application firewall (WAF) em um gateway de API avalia o tráfego HTTP ali. Uma blindagem de runtime no Linux aplica a política onde o host consegue observar a atividade relevante. Cada uma depende de cobertura em sua própria camada.

Uma regra de gateway é adequada a uma mudança voltada a HTTP quando o gateway enxerga os atributos relevantes da requisição e todas as requisições afetadas passam por ele. Verifique o escopo com base no inventário de serviços. Se um serviço processa trabalho de várias origens, inclua esses caminhos no plano de remediação. Para um exemplo específico de dependência sobre por que o inventário de componentes importa, veja nossa cobertura de uma vulnerabilidade Brotli no Node.js.

Um controle no host faz sentido quando o comportamento relevante é visível no host e você consegue estabelecer cobertura nos kernels e workloads afetados. Sua posição pode aproximar o controle do componente que você está protegendo, com requisitos próprios de implantação e rollback. Mantenha as verificações de autorização da aplicação no plano de testes de release. Uma mudança no gateway deve entrar na mesma revisão que qualquer alteração em autorização de middleware.

O que o Shirudo acrescenta?

O Shirudo consegue carregar proteções eBPF direcionadas em um sistema Linux em execução sem reiniciá-lo para aplicar a blindagem. A OpenAI descreve um fluxo de trabalho assistido por agente para preparar e verificar uma blindagem candidata, com operadores controlando a implantação. O projeto descreve loaders assinados para proteções BPF, verificação de kernel e evidências respaldadas por TPM de mudanças nas proteções carregadas. Repositório do Shirudo

O repositório chama o projeto de pré-lançamento. Ele lista um kernel Linux com a ABI de loader assinado e os patches de kernel do Shirudo, além de TPM 2.0, para alvos de produção. A OpenAI descreve a identificação em toda a organização e a implantação em escala como um objetivo de longo prazo. Reserve orçamento separadamente para preparar os hosts e revisar uma mudança temporária. Descrição do roadmap do Shirudo pela OpenAI

Revise uma blindagem proposta como uma mudança de produção, mesmo que ela tenha levado apenas alguns minutos para ser elaborada. A assinatura estabelece a procedência quando você confia no signatário. A verificação em runtime compara o programa com as regras de segurança aplicáveis. Sua própria revisão ainda precisa estabelecer se a política corresponde aos workloads pretendidos, preserva o tráfego normal e tem um plano de remoção.

Quando você deve remover a blindagem?

Remova uma blindagem temporária depois de verificar que a versão corrigida cobre a frota afetada e que o serviço com patch passa nas verificações de release. Mantenha um responsável e um horário de revisão no chamado do incidente até que a remoção seja concluída. Se a cobertura estiver incompleta, registre quais sistemas ainda precisam de mitigação e quem é responsável por eles.

  1. CVE divulgada. Mapeie o componente e as versões afetados para as instâncias em execução. Registre quais tráfegos de API e workloads dependem deles.
  2. Blindagem ativada. Verifique o controle em staging, ative-o sob controle de mudanças e confira o tráfego normal após a implantação. Entregue a lista de workloads afetados ao responsável pelo release.
  3. Patch testado e implantado. Teste a build corrigida em staging, implante-a e confirme as versões implantadas. Verifique regiões secundárias, alvos de failover e templates de autoscaling para que uma imagem antiga não retorne depois do incidente.
  4. Blindagem desativada. Confirme a cobertura da frota, remova o controle temporário e verifique novamente o tráfego normal. Registre a remoção no mesmo chamado do incidente.

Decida o que acontece se a correção sofrer rollback. Se você reverter para uma build afetada, mantenha ou restaure a proteção correspondente antes que essa build receba tráfego. Trate a implantação do código e a remoção da regra como mudanças separadas para que a equipe possa verificar cada uma.

Defina o escopo das verificações de regressão de API com o Apidog CLI

Use seu agente de código e o Apidog CLI para transformar um inventário de endpoints em uma checklist de staging. Para a API de objetos, comece pela leitura de coleção e pela leitura de detalhe. Mantenha os mesmos fixtures para a linha de base, a build de staging com blindagem e a build de staging com patch, para que as comparações sejam significativas.

Instale a CLI e entre com seu token de acesso à API do Apidog. Informe ao agente o ID do seu projeto. Se você trabalha no Codex, siga a configuração do Apidog CLI para Codex.

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token '<YOUR_TOKEN>'

Passe este prompt ao agente.

In Apidog project <PROJECT_ID>, list the GET endpoints under /objects and identify collection and detail reads. Suggest normal staging fixtures and response assertions for both. Report any missing endpoint or assertion coverage. Leave the project and gateway configuration untouched.

O agente executa este comando de inventário somente leitura.

apidog endpoint list --project '<PROJECT_ID>' --method GET --path-contains /objects

Na saída do sandbox, GET /objects e GET /objects/{id} dão ao agente duas verificações separadas para propor. Para a coleção, use uma lista pré-populada e valide o status esperado e a estrutura da resposta. Para o detalhe, use um ID de fixture conhecido e valide que a resposta corresponde a esse fixture. Compare os resultados de staging e sinalize qualquer alteração de contrato antes de prosseguir. O inventário mostra quais requisições cobrir. Testes aprovados no serviço em staging fornecem a evidência para a implantação. Depois de ter uma suíte reutilizável, anexe os resultados ao job de release. Apidog CLI em CI/CD

Se os revisores de API e de infraestrutura trabalharem separadamente, atribua a checklist do agente e a revisão da blindagem como tarefas separadas no Sharkly. Ele permite que sua equipe atribua trabalho a agentes de código nos seus próprios computadores e revise os resultados antes da implantação.

Perguntas frequentes

Patch virtual é o mesmo que live patching?

Os termos podem se sobrepor. O patch virtual descreve a finalidade de um controle temporário que bloqueia o acesso a uma falha. Live patching descreve como uma mudança entra em vigor em um sistema em execução. Uma mudança ao vivo pode aplicar uma restrição temporária de runtime ou atualizar o código em execução, dependendo da ferramenta.

Todo patch virtual de API precisa de um WAF?

Não. Escolha um controle que enxergue o comportamento relevante e cubra os workloads afetados. Um WAF se adequa ao tráfego HTTP em um gateway. Um controle de runtime pode se adequar à atividade no nível do host. Se sua equipe conseguir entregar uma correção verificada no mesmo prazo, o patch permanente pode ser a operação mais simples.

Por quanto tempo você deve manter um patch virtual?

Mantenha-o até verificar a correção definitiva em toda a frota afetada. Defina uma data de revisão ao ativar a blindagem e revisite-a se a implantação atrasar. Uma frota com versões mistas pode exigir a blindagem por mais tempo do que a primeira implantação bem-sucedida.

Um agente pode aprovar uma blindagem de produção?

Use seu processo de controle de mudanças para decidir quem aprova a implantação. No fluxo de trabalho do Shirudo descrito pela OpenAI, agentes podem ajudar a preparar e validar blindagens, e as equipes de segurança controlam o que é implantado. Forneça aos revisores o escopo alvo, os resultados da validação e as instruções de remoção.

Você pode fechar um chamado de CVE depois de aplicar um patch virtual?

Registre a mitigação e seu escopo, mas mantenha a remediação definitiva aberta. Anexe evidências das versões corrigidas e dos resultados de verificação quando a implantação for concluída. Acompanhar as duas mudanças permite que a equipe de plantão veja se pode remover a blindagem com segurança.

title: Parcheo virtual vs. parcheo: cuándo proteger una API en lugar de redesplegarla
description:
El parcheo virtual bloquea temporalmente una vía conocida para llegar a un fallo de software mientras el código vulnerable sigue en su sitio. Úsalo cuando puedas cubrir el tráfico de API afectado antes de lo que tardarías en desplegar una corrección de forma segura. Aplica el parche y verifica la flota afectada en cuanto la compilación corregida esté lista.

Prueba Apidog hoy

El 23 de noviembre de 2026, OpenAI y Cisco presentaron Shirudo, un proyecto Linux de código abierto que puede cargar protecciones eBPF específicas en un sistema en ejecución. Pone el foco en una decisión habitual para el equipo de guardia. Si la corrección permanente tarda horas en validarse, ¿puedes reducir la exposición ahora sin romper las solicitudes de las que dependen tus clientes? Anuncio de Shirudo de OpenAI

Parcheo virtual frente a parcheo convencional

Decisión Parcheo virtual Parcheo convencional
¿Qué cambia? Una regla de gateway o un control en tiempo de ejecución limita la exposición. Una aplicación, dependencia o componente del sistema corregido sustituye a la versión afectada.
¿Cuándo ayuda? El control llega al tráfico afectado antes de que la corrección pueda desplegarse. Hay una corrección fiable disponible y el equipo puede desplegarla de forma segura.
¿Qué demuestra que funcionó? Evidencia de cobertura y comprobaciones del servicio superadas en el punto de aplicación. Versiones corregidas verificadas en toda la flota, además de comprobaciones de lanzamiento superadas.
¿Cuándo se da por terminado el trabajo? La corrección permanente está verificada y la regla temporal se retira. La corrección está instalada y verificada en cada instancia afectada.

Un parche virtual es un control compensatorio. Tu inventario sigue mostrando la versión vulnerable mientras el control está activo. Mantén abierto el ticket de remediación y registra allí la regla, el propietario y la fecha de retirada prevista. Guía de parcheo virtual de OWASP

Un parche convencional puede ser una biblioteca actualizada en una imagen de contenedor o una compilación corregida de tu propio servicio. Haz seguimiento de lo que realmente se está ejecutando en la flota. Una imagen corregida en el registro dice poco sobre los workers antiguos que siguen atendiendo solicitudes. Guía de gestión de parches empresariales de NIST

¿Cuándo conviene usar un escudo para una API?

Usa un escudo cuando se cumplan tres condiciones.

  1. El control cubre el tráfico afectado. Confirma qué rutas de entrada y cargas de trabajo están dentro del alcance, incluidos los llamadores internos y el procesamiento en segundo plano cuando corresponda.
  2. Puedes validarlo antes que la compilación corregida. Usa tráfico representativo de staging para comprobar el comportamiento previsto de la regla y confirmar que las solicitudes normales siguen funcionando.
  3. Alguien es responsable de la salida. Asigna el despliegue del parche, acuerda la evidencia de cobertura y fija una fecha de revisión para el cambio temporal.

Supongamos que una API de objetos tiene una función opcional de procesamiento vulnerable y que el gateway ya admite desactivar el acceso a esa función. Tu equipo puede evaluar rápidamente el comportamiento con esa función desactivada mientras vuelve a compilar y probar el servicio. Las lecturas de colección y de detalle deberían seguir funcionando. Si los clientes usan la función opcional, informa a soporte de qué respuesta recibirán esos clientes y cuánto tiempo es probable que dure el cambio.

Mide ambos lados del equilibrio. Compara el tiempo previsto para aplicar la regla con el tiempo necesario para llevar una compilación corregida al mismo conjunto de cargas de trabajo. Durante el despliegue, vigila el éxito de las solicitudes normales, la latencia y los recuentos de rechazos. Un aumento de los rechazos necesita contexto. Puede ser que el control esté haciendo su trabajo o que se trate de un flujo de trabajo de cliente que tus datos de prueba de staging no contemplaron.

Prioriza un parche inmediato cuando la compilación corregida esté lista, un despliegue canario tenga buen estado y el despliegue llegue a las instancias expuestas con la misma rapidez que la regla temporal. Si ningún control fiable cubre la ruta afectada y el riesgo justifica una actuación inmediata, considera restringir el acceso o desactivar la capacidad afectada mientras se prepara la corrección. Si tienes evidencia de compromiso, inicia la respuesta a incidentes junto con la remediación.

¿Dónde debe ejecutarse un escudo de API?

Elige el punto de aplicación según lo que pueda observar y qué solicitudes deben pasar por él. Un firewall de aplicaciones web (WAF) en un gateway de API evalúa allí el tráfico HTTP. Un escudo de tiempo de ejecución de Linux aplica la política donde el host puede observar la actividad relevante. Cada uno depende de la cobertura en su propia capa.

Una regla de gateway encaja en un cambio expuesto por HTTP cuando el gateway ve los atributos de solicitud relevantes y todas las solicitudes afectadas pasan por él. Verifica el alcance con el inventario de servicios. Si un servicio gestiona trabajo de varias fuentes, incluye esas rutas en tu plan de remediación. Para ver un ejemplo específico de dependencia sobre por qué importa el inventario de componentes, consulta nuestra cobertura de una vulnerabilidad de Node.js Brotli.

Un control en el host tiene sentido cuando el comportamiento relevante es visible en el host y puedes establecer cobertura en los kernels y las cargas de trabajo afectados. Su ubicación puede acercar el control al componente que proteges, con sus propios requisitos de despliegue y reversión. Mantén las comprobaciones de autorización de la aplicación en el plan de pruebas de lanzamiento. Un cambio en el gateway debe revisarse junto con cualquier cambio en la autorización de middleware.

¿Qué aporta Shirudo?

Shirudo puede cargar protecciones eBPF específicas en un sistema Linux en ejecución sin reiniciarlo para aplicar el escudo. OpenAI describe un flujo de trabajo asistido por agentes para preparar y comprobar un escudo candidato, con operadores que controlan el despliegue. El proyecto describe cargadores firmados para protecciones BPF, verificación del kernel y evidencia respaldada por TPM de los cambios en las protecciones cargadas. Repositorio de Shirudo

El repositorio indica que el proyecto está en fase de prelanzamiento. Enumera un kernel Linux con la ABI de cargador firmado y los parches de kernel de Shirudo, además de TPM 2.0, para entornos de producción. OpenAI plantea la identificación en toda la organización y el despliegue a escala como un objetivo a largo plazo. Presupuesta por separado la preparación de los hosts y la revisión de un cambio temporal. Descripción de OpenAI de la hoja de ruta de Shirudo

Revisa un escudo propuesto como un cambio de producción, incluso si solo tardaste minutos en redactarlo. La firma establece la procedencia cuando confías en el firmante. La verificación en tiempo de ejecución comprueba el programa frente a las reglas de seguridad aplicables. Aun así, tu propia revisión debe establecer si la política coincide con las cargas de trabajo previstas, preserva el tráfico normal y cuenta con un plan de retirada.

¿Cuándo deberías retirar el escudo?

Retira un escudo temporal después de verificar que la versión corregida cubre la flota afectada y que el servicio parcheado supera sus comprobaciones de lanzamiento. Mantén un responsable y una fecha de revisión en el ticket del incidente hasta que la retirada esté completa. Si la cobertura es incompleta, registra qué sistemas aún necesitan mitigación y quién es su responsable.

  1. Se divulga la CVE. Vincula el componente y las versiones afectados con las instancias en ejecución. Registra qué tráfico de API y qué cargas de trabajo dependen de ellos.
  2. Escudo activado. Verifica el control en staging, actívalo bajo control de cambios y comprueba el tráfico normal tras el despliegue. Entrega la lista de cargas de trabajo afectadas al responsable del lanzamiento.
  3. Parche probado y desplegado. Prueba la compilación corregida en staging, despliégala y vuelve a leer las versiones desplegadas. Revisa las regiones secundarias, los destinos de conmutación por error y las plantillas de autoescalado para que una imagen antigua no vuelva después del incidente.
  4. Escudo desactivado. Confirma la cobertura de la flota, retira el control temporal y vuelve a comprobar el tráfico normal. Registra la retirada en el mismo ticket del incidente.

Decide qué ocurre si la corrección se revierte. Si vuelves a una compilación afectada, mantén o restaura la protección correspondiente antes de que esa compilación reciba tráfico. Trata el despliegue del código y la retirada de la regla como cambios separados para que el equipo pueda verificar cada uno.

Delimita las comprobaciones de regresión de API con Apidog CLI

Usa tu agente de programación y Apidog CLI para convertir un inventario de endpoints en una lista de comprobación de staging. Para la API de objetos, empieza por la lectura de colección y la lectura de detalle. Mantén los mismos datos de prueba para la línea base, la compilación de staging con escudo y la compilación de staging parcheada, para que las comparaciones sean significativas.

Instala la CLI e inicia sesión con tu token de acceso a la API de Apidog. Proporciona al agente el ID de tu proyecto. Si trabajas en Codex, sigue la configuración de Apidog CLI para Codex.

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token '<YOUR_TOKEN>'

Proporciona este prompt al agente.

In Apidog project <PROJECT_ID>, list the GET endpoints under /objects and identify collection and detail reads. Suggest normal staging fixtures and response assertions for both. Report any missing endpoint or assertion coverage. Leave the project and gateway configuration untouched.

El agente ejecuta este comando de inventario de solo lectura.

apidog endpoint list --project '<PROJECT_ID>' --method GET --path-contains /objects

En la salida del sandbox, GET /objects y GET /objects/{id} ofrecen al agente dos comprobaciones distintas que proponer. Para la colección, usa una lista precargada y comprueba el estado esperado y la estructura de la respuesta. Para el detalle, usa un ID de fixture conocido y comprueba que la respuesta corresponde a ese fixture. Compara los resultados de staging y señala cualquier cambio de contrato antes de continuar. El inventario muestra qué solicitudes hay que cubrir. Las pruebas superadas en el servicio preparado en staging aportan la evidencia para el despliegue. Cuando tengas una suite reutilizable, adjunta sus resultados al trabajo de lanzamiento. Apidog CLI en CI/CD

Si los revisores de API y de infraestructura trabajan por separado, asigna la lista de comprobación del agente y la revisión del escudo como tareas separadas en Sharkly. Permite que tu equipo asigne trabajo a agentes de programación en vuestros propios ordenadores y revise los resultados antes del despliegue.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿El parcheo virtual es lo mismo que el parcheo en vivo?

Los términos pueden solaparse. El parcheo virtual describe el propósito de un control temporal que bloquea el acceso a un fallo. El parcheo en vivo describe cómo un cambio surte efecto en un sistema en ejecución. Un cambio en vivo puede aplicar una restricción temporal en tiempo de ejecución o actualizar código en ejecución, según la herramienta.

¿Todo parche virtual de API necesita un WAF?

No. Elige un control que vea el comportamiento relevante y cubra las cargas de trabajo afectadas. Un WAF encaja en el tráfico HTTP en un gateway. Un control en tiempo de ejecución puede encajar en la actividad a nivel de host. Si tu equipo puede publicar una corrección verificada en el mismo tiempo, el parche permanente puede ser la operación más sencilla.

¿Cuánto tiempo deberías mantener un parche virtual?

Mantenlo hasta que hayas verificado la corrección permanente en toda la flota afectada. Fija una fecha de revisión cuando actives el escudo y vuelve a revisarla si el despliegue se retrasa. Una flota con versiones mezcladas puede requerir el escudo durante más tiempo que el primer despliegue exitoso.

¿Puede un agente aprobar un escudo de producción?

Usa tu proceso de control de cambios para decidir quién aprueba el despliegue. En el flujo de trabajo de Shirudo descrito por OpenAI, los agentes pueden ayudar a preparar y validar protecciones, y los equipos de seguridad controlan lo que se despliega. Proporciona a los revisores el alcance objetivo, los resultados de validación y las instrucciones de retirada.

¿Puedes cerrar un ticket de CVE después de aplicar un parche virtual?

Registra la mitigación y su alcance, pero mantén abierta la remediación permanente. Adjunta evidencia de las versiones corregidas y de los resultados de verificación cuando el despliegue esté completo. Hacer seguimiento de los dos cambios permite al equipo de guardia ver si puede retirar el escudo de forma segura.

title: It's 2 a.m. and the ONTAP Volume Is Offline: A Triage Runbook for the NetApp Certified Support Engineer Exam
description:
Your phone buzzes at 2:07 a.m. The alert says a database team can't write to its NFS share, and the share lives on an ONTAP cluster you have never logged in to. What do you type first?

That question is the whole point of the NetApp Certified Support Engineer exam (NS0-194, NCSE). It doesn't ask whether you can design a storage array. It asks whether you can walk up to a broken one, find the cause and fix it without making things worse. That's why it also makes a good runbook.

This post is that runbook. Each step maps to one of the six official exam domains, and every command is real ONTAP CLI you can run in a lab or a simulator. You get a better on-call routine and a study plan in one read.

What is the NetApp Certified Support Engineer exam?

The NS0-194 exam validates the skills of an engineer who supports NetApp ONTAP systems on site or remotely. According to NetApp's Support Engineer certification page, it tests general troubleshooting and root cause isolation, hardware replacement, documentation, node configuration, and software and firmware upgrades. NetApp recommends six to 12 months of hands-on experience.

Item Detail
Exam code NS0-194
Certification NetApp Certified Support Engineer (NCSE), ONTAP Professional
Questions 60
Time 90 minutes
Passing score 63%
Domains 6
Suggested experience 6 to 12 months
Delivered by Pearson VUE

The question count, time and passing score come from the NWExam syllabus page. The domains and experience level come from NetApp. Check the current price on Pearson VUE when you book, because published figures differ between sources.

The six domains are ONTAP OS, troubleshooting NetApp hardware and software, NetApp hardware, NetApp cloud data services, data protection, and Active IQ. The runbook below covers them in the order you'd meet them during a real incident.

Step 1: Is the cluster itself healthy?

Before you look at the volume, look at the ground it stands on. Many "storage is broken" tickets are really a node down, a failed takeover or a network port that went dark.

cluster1::> cluster show
cluster1::> system health status show
cluster1::> system health alert show
cluster1::> storage failover show

cluster show tells you whether every node is healthy and eligible. storage failover show tells you whether the HA pairs are in a normal state or whether one node has taken over its partner. If a takeover happened at 2:01 a.m., you already have a strong lead.

This is the habit the exam rewards: collect information before you change anything. The troubleshooting domain literally lists "How to collect and analyze information" as its first objective.

Step 2: What do disks, aggregates and volumes say?

Next, go one layer up the stack, from physical disks to the aggregate to the volume.

cluster1::> storage disk show -broken
cluster1::> storage aggregate show -fields state,raidstatus
cluster1::> volume show -state offline
cluster1::> volume show -fields percent-used,available -percent-used >90

A quick refresher on the ONTAP OS domain's "disk or aggregate concepts" and "volume concepts":

  • Disks are grouped into RAID groups, and RAID groups make up an aggregate.
  • An aggregate is the pool of physical capacity on one node.
  • FlexVol volumes are carved out of an aggregate and owned by a storage VM (SVM).
  • An aggregate in a degraded RAID state still serves data, but losing another disk could take it down.

If the volume is offline and you know why (for example, someone took it offline for maintenance and forgot), bring it back:

cluster1::> volume online -vserver svm_db -volume vol_db01

If it's online but 100% full, writes fail even though nothing is "down". That's one of the most common causes of a "can't write" ticket. Check whether snapshot reserve or a runaway log file is eating the space before you grow the volume.

Step 3: Can the client actually reach the data LIF?

ONTAP serves data through logical interfaces (LIFs) that sit on physical or virtual ports. After a takeover or a cable problem, a LIF can end up on a port that isn't its home port, or on a port with no link at all.

cluster1::> network port show -link down
cluster1::> network interface show -is-home false
cluster1::> network interface show -vserver svm_db -fields address,home-node,curr-node,status-oper

If the LIFs migrated and the home ports are healthy again, send them back:

cluster1::> network interface revert -vserver svm_db -lif *

This is the "ONTAP networking concepts" objective in practice. Know the difference between a physical port, an interface group, a VLAN and a broadcast domain, and know that a LIF fails over within its failover group.

Step 4: Is the client allowed in?

The network is fine and the volume is online, but the client still gets "permission denied". Now you're in the "How to troubleshoot data access problems" objective, which comes up a lot.

For NFS, ONTAP has a built-in command that evaluates the export policy for you. You give it the client IP, protocol and access type, and it shows you which rule matched at every level of the path:

cluster1::> vserver export-policy check-access -vserver svm_db -volume vol_db01 -client-ip 10.20.30.41 -authentication-method sys -protocol nfs3 -access-type read-write

If the result says read where you expected read-write, or denied, look at the rule index it names:

cluster1::> vserver export-policy rule show -vserver svm_db -policyname db_hosts

Common causes are a client match that names the wrong subnet, rw set to never, or a parent junction with a stricter policy than the volume. The check-access output shows each path component, so a parent problem stands out.

For SMB, name resolution and domain connectivity cause most failures:

cluster1::> vserver services name-service dns check -vserver svm_files
cluster1::> vserver cifs show -vserver svm_files

The exam's "Supported ONTAP protocols" and "How ONTAP interacts with external components" objectives cover this: DNS, LDAP, Active Directory, NTP and the clients themselves.

Step 5: Is it slow rather than broken?

Sometimes the ticket says "down" when the truth is "so slow the app timed out". ONTAP can break a volume's latency down by where the time is spent:

cluster1::> qos statistics volume latency show -iterations 5 -rows 5

The output has one column per layer, such as network, cluster interconnect, data processing, disk and QoS throttling. The layer with the biggest number is where to look:

  • High network latency points at the client side or the network path.
  • High disk latency points at busy or failing media, or an aggregate that's too full.
  • High QoS max latency means a QoS policy is deliberately throttling the workload.
  • High cluster latency means traffic is crossing the cluster interconnect, often because the client mounts through a LIF on a different node from the volume.

Reading those columns at 2 a.m. is error-prone, so here's a small Python script that does it for you. Paste the command output into a file and run the script on it.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Find the dominant latency layer in 'qos statistics volume latency show' output."""
import re
import sys

UNITS = {"us": 0.001, "ms": 1.0, "s": 1000.0}


def to_ms(value):
    match = re.fullmatch(r"([\d.]+)(us|ms|s)", value)
    return float(match.group(1)) * UNITS[match.group(2)] if match else None


def triage(text):
    lines = [l for l in text.splitlines() if l.strip()]
    header = next(l for l in lines if l.startswith("Workload"))
    # Join two-word column names so the header splits cleanly.
    cols = header.replace("Qos Max", "Qos_Max").replace("Qos Min", "Qos_Min").split()
    layers = cols[3:]  # after Workload, ID, Latency
    for line in lines:
        parts = line.split()
        if len(parts) != len(cols) or parts[0] in ("Workload", "-total-") or parts[0].startswith("-"):
            continue
        name, total = parts[0], to_ms(parts[2])
        values = {layer: to_ms(v) or 0.0 for layer, v in zip(layers, parts[3:])}
        worst = max(values, key=values.get)
        share = values[worst] / total * 100 if total else 0
        print(f"{name:<12} total {total:8.2f} ms  ->  {worst} ({share:.0f}%)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    triage(open(sys.argv[1]).read() if len(sys.argv) > 1 else sys.stdin.read())

Here's a trimmed sample of the output (column names vary a little between ONTAP releases, and older ones say N-Blade and D-Blade):

Workload       ID Latency Network Cluster   Data   Disk Qos Max
-------------- -- ------- ------- ------- ------ ------ -------
-total-         - 12.40ms  0.40ms  0.10ms 0.90ms 10.90ms   0ms
vol_db01     1234 18.20ms  0.30ms  0.10ms 1.10ms 16.70ms   0ms
vol_logs      999  4.10ms  0.20ms  2.80ms 0.80ms  0.30ms   0ms
vol_app       777 25.00ms  0.20ms  0.00ms 0.50ms  0.30ms 24.00ms

And the result:

$ python3 latency_triage.py sample.txt
vol_db01     total    18.20 ms  ->  Disk (92%)
vol_logs     total     4.10 ms  ->  Cluster (68%)
vol_app      total    25.00 ms  ->  Qos_Max (96%)

Three volumes, three different fixes. vol_db01 needs a look at the aggregate and its disks. vol_logs is being reached through a LIF on the wrong node. vol_app is being throttled by a QoS policy on purpose, so the "fix" is a conversation about its service level, not a hardware ticket.

Step 6: What do the logs say, and how do you hand them over?

ONTAP's Event Management System (EMS) is the first log to read:

cluster1::> event log show -severity ERROR
cluster1::> event log show -node node02 -message-name *disk*

When you need NetApp support or a deeper analysis, trigger an AutoSupport so the latest configuration and logs reach NetApp:

cluster1::> system node autosupport invoke -node * -type all -message "Case: vol_db01 write failures"

The "ONTAP logging mechanisms" objective expects you to know EMS, AutoSupport and where node logs live. In practice, the most useful skill is writing down what you saw and in what order. The certification lists documentation as a core task, and a clean timeline makes the root-cause write-up much easier the next morning.

Step 7: Does the fix need a hardware swap?

Say the root cause is a failed disk or a controller component. The NetApp hardware domain covers field-replaceable units (FRUs) and the replacement process. The usual pattern for a controller-side FRU on an HA pair looks like this:

cluster1::> system node autosupport invoke -node * -type all -message MAINT=2h
cluster1::> storage failover show
