cluster1::> storage failover takeover -ofnode node02
# replace the part on node02, following the FRU procedure for your platform
cluster1::> storage failover giveback -ofnode node02
cluster1::> storage failover show
cluster1::> system node autosupport invoke -node * -type all -message MAINT=END

The MAINT=2h AutoSupport message suppresses automatic case creation during the maintenance window. The takeover moves the partner's storage and LIFs to the surviving node, so clients keep working while you change parts. For a failed disk you usually don't need any of this: the disk is hot-swappable and ONTAP rebuilds onto a spare.

Exam questions in this domain test the order of operations. They want to know what you check before you pull anything, when a takeover is required, and how you confirm that giveback completed. Learn the procedure for at least one current FAS or AFF platform from NetApp's documentation.

Step 8: Is the data protected, and is it in the cloud?

Once service is restored, check that you haven't lost your safety net. The data protection domain covers Snapshot copies and SnapMirror replication:

cluster1::> volume snapshot show -vserver svm_db -volume vol_db01
cluster1::> snapmirror show -fields state,status,lag-time,healthy
cluster1::> snapmirror show -healthy false

A SnapMirror relationship that stopped updating during the incident is easy to miss and painful to discover a week later. If the lag time jumped, run a manual snapmirror update once the source is stable.

The cloud data services domain asks how ONTAP extends into the public cloud. Know these at a concept level:

  • Cloud Volumes ONTAP runs ONTAP as a virtual machine in AWS, Azure or Google Cloud.
  • Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and Azure NetApp Files are managed services built on ONTAP technology.
  • FabricPool tiers cold blocks from an on-premises aggregate to object storage. You can see it with storage aggregate object-store show and volume show -fields tiering-policy.

If an on-premises volume uses FabricPool, slow reads of cold data might be an object-store problem rather than a disk problem. That's exactly the kind of cross-domain question that shows up on support exams.

Where does Active IQ fit in?

Active IQ is NetApp's AutoSupport-driven analytics portal. NetApp now brands it as Digital Advisor, but the exam blueprint still calls it Active IQ. It takes the AutoSupport data your cluster sends and turns it into health checks, risk alerts, upgrade recommendations and capacity forecasts.

In a support workflow it does two jobs. Before an incident, it flags known risks such as firmware with a known bug, a misconfigured HA pair or an aggregate trending toward full. After an incident, it gives you the configuration history so you can see what changed. Make sure you know how to find a system, read its risk list and act on a recommendation.

How does the runbook map to the exam?

Runbook step Exam domain
1. Cluster and HA health Troubleshooting NetApp hardware and software
2. Disks, aggregates, volumes ONTAP OS
3. Ports and LIFs ONTAP OS (networking)
4. Export policies, DNS, SMB Troubleshooting (data access), ONTAP OS (protocols)
5. Latency breakdown Troubleshooting (performance)
6. EMS and AutoSupport ONTAP OS (logging)
7. FRU replacement NetApp hardware
8. Snapshot, SnapMirror, cloud Data protection, NetApp cloud data services
Risk and history review Active IQ

How should you study for NS0-194?

A two-week plan works if you already handle ONTAP day to day:

  1. Days 1 to 3: build a lab. The ONTAP simulator or a trial Cloud Volumes ONTAP instance is enough. Create an SVM, a volume, an export policy and an SMB share.
  2. Days 4 to 7: break it on purpose. Take a volume offline, fill a volume to 100%, change an export rule, move a LIF off its home port. Then fix each one using only the commands above.
  3. Days 8 to 10: read the hardware replacement and HA procedures for one platform, and set up a SnapMirror relationship between two SVMs.
  4. Days 11 to 14: practice questions. Start with NetApp's official NS0-194 practice test, then work through the NS0-194 sample questions on NWExam. Note which domain each wrong answer belongs to and go back to the lab for it.

Keep the full NS0-194 syllabus open while you study, so you can tick off each objective as you cover it in the lab.

FAQ

How many questions are on the NetApp NS0-194 exam?

There are 60 questions, and you have 90 minutes. The passing score is 63%.

Do I need another certification before NS0-194?

No certification is strictly required. NetApp suggests the Cloud Native Associate and Hybrid Cloud Associate accreditations as useful preparation, plus six to 12 months of experience.

Is NS0-194 only about ONTAP?

Mostly, yes. ONTAP OS and troubleshooting carry most of the content, but you also need hardware replacement, cloud data services, data protection and Active IQ.

What's the best hands-on preparation?

Break and fix a lab cluster. Being able to explain why a command's output points at one layer and not another is what the scenario questions test.

Is Active IQ the same as Digital Advisor?

Yes. Digital Advisor is the current name of the Active IQ portal. The exam objectives still use the older name.

Back to 2:07 a.m.

The next time that alert fires, you won't start by guessing. You'll check the cluster, then the storage, then the path, then permissions, then performance, and you'll write down each answer as you go. That order is how good support engineers work, and it's the order the NetApp Certified Support Engineer exam expects you to think in.

title: RTL bugs in Arabic and English websites, and how to fix each one
description:
Building a site in Arabic and English is not "flip it and translate". These are six RTL bugs we have hit in real projects, including on this very site, and what fixed them.

1. The page scrolls sideways in Arabic only

Symptom: on a phone, the Arabic page can be dragged left and shows empty space.

Cause: something sits outside the screen on the "start" side. We found a hidden anti-spam form field positioned with left: -9999px. In English it hid harmlessly to the left; in Arabic the page grew ten thousand pixels wide.

Fix: hide things without moving them, and clip the page as a safety net.

.visually-hidden { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%); }
html, body { overflow-x: clip; }

2. Margins on the wrong side

Cause: margin-left, padding-right and left: are physical directions.

Fix: use logical properties, which follow the reading direction.

.card { margin-inline-start: 16px; padding-inline-end: 12px; inset-inline-end: 0; }

3. Numbers, emails and code get scrambled

Symptom: +966 53 000 0000 shows up as 0000 000 53 966+, or an email jumps around inside an Arabic sentence.

Fix: isolate left-to-right runs.

<span dir="ltr">+966 53 000 0000</span>

.phone, code { direction: ltr; unicode-bidi: isolate; }

4. Icons that should flip, and icons that shouldn't

Arrows for "next" and "back" should mirror in Arabic. Play buttons, checkmarks and logos should not. Mirror selectively:

[dir="rtl"] .icon-arrow { transform: scaleX(-1); }

5. Arabic looks squeezed

Cause: a Latin font with fallback Arabic glyphs, and Latin line height.

Fix: set a real Arabic font for :lang(ar) and give it more line height.

:root[lang="ar"] body { font-family: "Noto Naskh Arabic", serif; line-height: 1.9; }

6. Search engines see one language

Fix: give each language its own URL, tell Google they are translations of each other, and set lang and dir on the html element.

<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/post">
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="ar" href="https://example.com/ar/post">

FAQ

Should I build two separate sites?

No. One codebase with logical CSS and translated content is easier to keep in sync. Separate URLs per language are what matter for search.

Does Tailwind support RTL?

Yes. Use the logical utilities (ms-*, me-*, ps-*, pe-*, start-*, end-*) instead of left and right.

Building a bilingual site? Ask the editor on ahmed-adil.com.

Originally published on The Supplement, Ahmed Adil's blog.

title: JavaScript Explained for Beginners: How Websites Respond to Your Clicks, Searches, and Actions
description:
Have you ever visited a website, clicked a button, and watched something happen instantly?

Perhaps a dropdown menu opened. Maybe a message appeared after you submitted a form. You might have searched for a product and watched matching results appear on the screen.

These interactions may seem ordinary because we experience them almost every day. However, there is usually some programming logic working behind the scenes to make them happen.

One of the technologies responsible for many of these interactive experiences is JavaScript.

If you're new to web development or have never written a line of code, don't worry. You don't need to understand complicated programming concepts to grasp what JavaScript does.

Let's start with something familiar: the websites you already use.

  1. What Is JavaScript?

JavaScript is a programming language commonly used to make websites interactive and dynamic.

In simple terms, JavaScript allows developers to write instructions that tell a webpage how to respond when users interact with it or when certain conditions are met.

For example, a developer can use JavaScript to:

Display a message when someone clicks a button.

Open and close a navigation menu.

Check whether required form fields have been completed.

Filter products based on a search term.

Switch between different content tabs.

Update information displayed on a webpage.

Retrieve information from an external service through an API.

Think of JavaScript as the technology that helps a webpage respond to different situations.

A webpage doesn't always have to remain static. With JavaScript, developers can create experiences that react to user input and update content without necessarily reloading the entire page.

  1. Understanding JavaScript Through Everyday Website Examples

The easiest way to understand JavaScript is to look at things you probably already do online.

Example 1: Clicking a Button

Imagine visiting a website with a button labelled "Learn More."

You click it, and additional information appears below the button.

What happened?

The browser detected your click, and JavaScript executed instructions to display the additional information.

A simplified example looks like this:

Welcome!

Click Me

const button = document.getElementById("myButton");
const message = document.getElementById("message");

button.addEventListener("click", function() {
message.textContent = "Thanks for clicking!";
});

Let's understand what the code does:

getElementById() finds an HTML element using its ID.

addEventListener() tells JavaScript to listen for a particular event.

"click" specifies the event being monitored.

textContent changes the text displayed inside the heading.

When someone clicks the button, the heading changes.

That's a simple example of JavaScript making a webpage interactive.

Example 2: Opening a Dropdown Menu

Imagine visiting an online store.

You see a menu icon. When you click it, a list of navigation options appears.

You click it again, and the menu closes.

JavaScript can control this behaviour by responding to clicks and changing the visibility or state of the menu.

This is useful for navigation menus, mobile interfaces, account options, and other interactive website elements.

Example 3: Checking a Form Before Submission

Imagine filling out a registration form.

You enter your name but forget to provide your email address. When you attempt to submit the form, a message appears asking you to complete the missing field.

JavaScript can help validate form inputs and provide immediate feedback.

For example:

const email = "";

if (email === "") {
alert("Please enter your email address.");
}

Here's what's happening:

JavaScript checks whether the email variable contains a value.

The if statement evaluates the condition.

If the email is empty, an alert message appears.

This is an example of a programming condition.

However, client-side validation alone is not enough to secure a form. Important information must also be validated on the server because browser-side checks can be bypassed.

Example 4: Searching for Products

Imagine visiting an e-commerce website with hundreds of products.

Instead of scrolling through everything, you type "sneakers" into the search box.

The website displays products that match your search.

JavaScript can help process the search input, compare it with available product information, and update the displayed results.

For larger applications, the search may also involve a backend server and database.

This is one reason JavaScript is useful for creating responsive shopping experiences.

Example 5: Switching Between Tabs

Have you ever visited a website with tabs labelled:

Description

Reviews

Specifications

When you select a tab, a different section of information appears.

JavaScript can control which content panel is displayed when a user selects a particular tab.

This helps developers organise information without displaying every section at the same time.

Example 6: Displaying Notifications

Imagine adding an item to your shopping cart.

A small message appears:

"Product added successfully!"

JavaScript can display this notification after a user performs a particular action.

These messages help users understand what is happening on a website.

  1. How JavaScript Works With HTML and CSS

To understand JavaScript properly, you also need to understand its relationship with HTML and CSS.

These three technologies work together to create many of the websites we use today.

HTML: The Structure

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.

It defines the content and structure of a webpage.

For example, HTML creates:

Headings

Paragraphs

Images

Links

Buttons

Forms

Navigation sections

Think of HTML as the foundation and structure of a building.

CSS: The Presentation

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.

It controls how HTML elements look and how they are arranged on a webpage.

CSS handles things such as:

Colours

Fonts

Spacing

Borders

Alignment

Layouts

Responsive presentation

Think of CSS as the paint, decoration, and visual arrangement of a building.

JavaScript: The Behaviour

JavaScript adds behaviour and interactivity.

It allows developers to define what should happen when users click, type, select, submit, or interact with webpage elements.

Think of JavaScript as the system that makes certain things happen in response to different actions.

Here's a simple way to remember their responsibilities:

HTML = Structure

CSS = Presentation and Layout

JavaScript = Behaviour and Interactivity

For example, imagine building a product page.

HTML displays the product image, name, price, description, and purchase button.

CSS controls the appearance of those elements.

JavaScript can respond when a customer clicks "Add to Cart" and update the cart information displayed on the page.

A complete shopping cart, however, also needs backend logic and data storage to handle things such as persistent cart contents, inventory, and checkout securely.

Each technology has a different responsibility, but they can work together to create a complete experience.

  1. Important JavaScript Concepts Every Beginner Should Understand

You don't need to master every JavaScript concept immediately.

However, there are a few fundamentals worth understanding as you begin learning.

A. Variables

Variables allow you to store information that your program can use.

For example:

let username = "Amaka";
let age = 25;

Here, username stores a name, while age stores a number.

JavaScript also provides const for variables that shouldn't be reassigned.

B. Functions

A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a particular task.

For example:

function greetUser() {
alert("Welcome to my website!");
}

Whenever the function is called, the instructions inside it are executed.

Functions help developers organise code and avoid repeating the same instructions unnecessarily.

C. Conditions

Conditions allow a program to make decisions.

For example:

let age = 20;

if (age >= 18) {
console.log("Access granted");
} else {
console.log("Access denied");
}

JavaScript checks the condition and executes the appropriate block of code.

D. Events

Events are actions or occurrences that JavaScript can respond to.

Examples include:

Clicking a button.

Typing into a text field.

Submitting a form.

Changing a dropdown selection.

Loading a webpage.

Developers use event listeners to make their applications respond to these events.

E. The DOM

DOM stands for Document Object Model.

It is the browser's structured representation of an HTML document.

JavaScript can interact with the DOM to access, modify, add, or remove webpage elements.

For example, a developer can use JavaScript to change a heading, update a paragraph, or display a new section of content.

Understanding the DOM is particularly important when learning how JavaScript interacts with webpages.

  1. Does Every Website Need JavaScript?

Here's something beginners should understand: not every website needs JavaScript.

A simple website containing information about a business, its services, contact details, and location may work perfectly well with HTML and CSS.

Some interactions can also be achieved using HTML and CSS alone, while other tasks can be handled through server-side processing.

JavaScript becomes especially useful when a website needs more dynamic client-side interactions.

For example:

Interactive dashboards.

Product filtering.

Dynamic forms.

Real-time interface updates.

Interactive navigation.

Browser-based applications.

The goal isn't to add JavaScript to every webpage simply because it is available.

The goal is to understand when it provides value and how to use it appropriately.

  1. How to Start Learning JavaScript as a Complete Beginner

If you've never coded before, JavaScript might look intimidating at first.

You may see unfamiliar words, symbols, brackets, and instructions.

That's normal.

The best approach is to learn progressively and practise what you learn.

Here is a simple learning path.

Step 1: Understand HTML

Before focusing on JavaScript, learn how webpages are structured.

Practise creating headings, paragraphs, links, images, buttons, and forms.

Step 2: Learn Basic CSS

Understand how to style your HTML elements.

Practise changing colours, font sizes, spacing, borders, and layouts.

Step 3: Learn JavaScript Fundamentals

Start with:

Variables.

Data types.

Operators.

Functions.

Conditions.

Loops.

Arrays.

Objects.

Don't rush through these concepts. Take time to understand how they work.

Step 4: Learn DOM Manipulation

Practise selecting HTML elements and changing their content or appearance using JavaScript.

Step 5: Understand Events

Learn how to respond to clicks, typing, form submissions, and other user interactions.

Step 6: Build Small Projects

This is where your knowledge begins to come together.

Try building:

A button that changes text.

A simple counter.

A dropdown menu.

A basic calculator.

A form with validation.

A simple to-do list.

You don't have to build everything at once.

Complete one small project, understand how it works, and then move to another.

  1. Common Mistakes Beginners Should Avoid

As you start learning JavaScript, watch out for these common mistakes.

  1. Trying to memorise everything

Programming is not simply about memorising code. Focus on understanding concepts and learning how to apply them.

  1. Copying code without understanding it

Copying examples can help you get started, but take time to understand what each instruction does.

  1. Ignoring error messages

Errors are part of programming. Learn to read them, investigate their causes, and correct your code.

  1. Skipping the fundamentals

Jumping straight into complicated frameworks without understanding basic JavaScript can make learning unnecessarily difficult.

  1. Giving up when your code doesn't work

Your first attempt won't always produce the expected result. Test your code, identify the problem, make adjustments, and try again.

Every debugging experience can teach you something valuable.

Conclusion: Start With One Small Interaction

JavaScript becomes easier to understand when you connect programming concepts to things you already experience online.

A button that responds to a click, a form that checks user input, a menu that opens, or a search box that filters products can all introduce you to important programming concepts.

You don't need to begin by building a complicated web application.

Start with a simple HTML page. Add a button. Write a few lines of JavaScript. Make something happen when someone clicks it.

Then explore another interaction.

Gradually, you'll begin to understand variables, functions, conditions, events, and how JavaScript communicates with webpage elements.

Remember:

HTML gives a webpage its structure. CSS controls its presentation. JavaScript brings behaviour and interactivity to the experience.

The best way to learn JavaScript isn't just to read about it.

It's to write code, experiment, build small projects, and keep practising.

Your journey into programming can begin with one button and a few lines of code.

Now, here's a question for you:

If you could build your first interactive website feature today, what would you choose?

A dropdown navigation menu.

A contact form with validation.

A shopping cart.

A live product search feature.

Share your choice in the comments!

About Amik Digital

At Amik Digital, we explore web development, programming concepts, and practical digital knowledge to help beginners and aspiring developers understand how technology works.

Follow along for more beginner-friendly insights into the world of web development.

title: gitai: a Git server built for AI agents
description:
gitai

Git was not built for hundreds of agents landing changes on the same repository at once. Anthropic built Scion for that, but Scion is internal and not available to the public. gitai is an independent open source implementation of the design Anthropic published: a Git server that moves the work to the server, rebases each change onto the tip of main, and lands it with a compare and swap, so there is no merge queue and no push, rebase, retry loop. If the new tip fails tests, a bundled verifier can bisect and revert the culprit. It is early, at v0.4.2, and the author marks his own acceptance test as failed on latency, so test it before you trust it.

What you get

  • A server side Git workflow built for agent fleets, written mostly in Go.
  • Changes rebased onto the tip of main and landed atomically, with no merge queue to babysit.
  • A bundled verifier that bisects and reverts the change that breaks the tip.
  • An independent project in the spirit of Anthropic's Scion, not affiliated with Anthropic.

Test it on a side repository first, and check the latency on your own workload before you trust it with your main branch.

Repo: https://github.com/feder-cr/git-ai

Quick poll

What would you use gitai for first?

  • Landing agent changes on a shared repo
  • Testing it on a side project first
  • Reading the docs and the Scion design first
  • Watching it for now

Vote in the comments.

If you found gitai interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: Manual Git via Excel & 5-Minute WebSphere Boots: The Reality of Legacy Enterprise Java
description:
Before Git and instant cloud deployments, there was SVN, red strikethroughs in Excel for "version control," and 5-minute waits just to boot localhost.

If you've ever maintained a legacy enterprise Java system, you already know the unique joy of navigating a 40-page runbook just to configure a single JDBC data source—or timing your restroom and convenience store breaks around IBM WebSphere startup cycles.

Transcript

Totolis: Alright, I'll show you how to update the Excel design spec. First, grab a lock in SVN.

Alex: Okay, locked and opened. Still zero actual coding today, I guess...

Totolis: Good. Now open the Process Logic tab.

Totolis: When you modify a cell, never delete the old text. Turn it red and put a strikethrough on it.

Alex: ... Come again?

Totolis: Then, outside the print area on the right, type '2026-10-26 ALEX DEL Ticket XXXX'.

Alex: Hold on. This file is already tracked in SVN, right...?

Alex: Why are we manually typing commit logs directly into spreadsheet cells...?

Totolis: The revision history tab isn't enough.

Totolis: The client needs to see what changed at a glance during the in-person printout review.

Alex: ...

Totolis: Keep it like that until it passes UAT. Only do a hard delete right before final delivery.

Alex: So we're doing soft deletes... on Excel cells now...?

Totolis: Exactly.

Totolis: By the way, same rule applies to the Java code.

Alex: ... Huh?

Totolis: Just comment out the deleted lines and tag them with the date and ticket number, just like the spec.

Alex: ... Good one, Totolis-san. You almost had me there.

Totolis: A joke? Do I look like I have a sense of humor to you?

Totolis: Next, you'll spin up the local web app.

Totolis: The base install is already done. Just follow the runbook for the initial config.

Alex: Got it.

Alex: ... Um, Totolis-san. Can I ask you something?

Totolis: What.

Alex: Why does configuring a single JDBC data source require a forty-page runbook...?
