title: Claude Code hooks: I wired 5 and 2 never fired
description:
I wired five Claude Code hooks on a demo repo: three of three reads of a secrets file were blocked, and two hooks stayed at zero until I fixed one matcher each.

agentshipped / notes-api

Agent Shipped demo repo (notes-api): the public playground used in the channel's videos.

notes-api

A tiny Express notes API. This is a public demo repo for the Agent Shipped YouTube channel techniques from real projects are shown here, on code anyone can clone.

npm install
npm start          # http://localhost:3000/notes
npm test           # node:test (no tests yet - that is on purpose)

Endpoints: GET /health, GET /notes, GET /notes/:id, POST /notes {title, body}, DELETE /notes/:id.

Shown in

Videos on the Agent Shipped channel that use this repo:

  • One git hook blocked a fake GitHub token, so no secret hit history #Shorts · E002 · 2026-11-02
  • Claude Code invented one endpoint shape. A 3-line rule fixed it #Shorts · E001 · 2026-11-03
  • I let Claude Code test my Express API, then ran it myself three times · E003 · 2026-11-08 · write-up
  • I don't trust an agent's restart. I trust a counter going up by one #Shorts · E010…
View on GitHub

A hook that never matches prints no error, so the settings file cannot tell you which hooks will fire. Counting what each hook did found the two silent ones.

A guard hook with a log

A hook is a command that Claude Code runs around a tool call. You register it in .claude/settings.json under an event name, with a matcher that picks the tools it listens to. Claude Code passes the command a JSON object on standard input with the tool name and the tool input.

The first hook is a guard that listens before every Bash and Read call. The script reads stdin with jq, takes tool_input.command if it exists, otherwise tool_input.file_path, and calls that the target. If the target mentions .env, it exits with code 2 and writes one sentence to stderr. That is the whole blocking mechanism. The agent gets the sentence as the reason the call failed.

The script also appends one line to a log on every call, so you can count what it did instead of trusting it. I told the agent not to run the script, because a test run would add extra lines.

A secret to protect

There is no real secret in the repo. The terminal builds a .env with a random token at run time:

printf 'TOKEN=%s\n' "$(openssl rand -hex 18)" > .env && echo 'created .env' && cat .claude/hooks/guard.sh

The script parses with jq, picks the target, logs one line, then decides. A match writes the blocked line, speaks on stderr and exits 2. Anything else exits 0.

Three ways in

In a fresh session, so the hook is loaded, I asked for exactly three attempts at the same file, with no other way around a block:

  1. The Read tool on .env.
  2. The Bash tool running cat .env.
  3. The Bash tool running a grep that would print the token line.

One matcher, Bash|Read, has to catch three routes. Each attempt came back with the stderr sentence, and no file content appeared.

Count the blocks 

grep -c '^blocked' .claude/hooks.log

The number is 3: three attempts, three blocked.


The grep count of blocked lines: 3 of 3 attempts. · watch this step

A guard that works is the easy half of the story.

Four more hooks, two planted wrong

The second prompt asked for four more scripts, registered next to the guard: a syntax check, a stop marker, an audit log and a change log. Each appends one line with its own label to the same log, which makes it countable.

I planted two mistakes and told the agent to write the matchers exactly as given. The audit hook got bash in lower case. The change hook got Write. A model that tidies a typo would hide the lesson.

The syntax hook runs after Edit or Write and calls node --check. The stop hook has no matcher, because the Stop event fires when the agent finishes its turn and there is no tool to match.

What is registered 

jq .hooks .claude/settings.json

PreToolUse holds the guard on Bash|Read and the audit hook on bash. PostToolUse holds the syntax hook on Edit|Write and the change hook on Write. Stop holds one entry with no matcher. The paths are right and the JSON is valid. Nothing looks wrong, and that is the trap.

A real edit

I asked the agent to edit an existing file with the Edit tool, not rewrite it: change not found to note not found, then run node --check src/index.js. Silence means the file still parses. The screen only shows the edit, not which hooks ran.

The count

One count per label, zeros included:

for h in guard blocked syntax stop audit changed; do printf '%s %s\n' "$(grep -c "^$h" .claude/hooks.log)" "$h"; done


Look at the two zeros: audit and changed. Blocked is 3. · watch this step

blocked is still 3. guard, syntax and stop are above zero. audit and changed are 0, each for its own reason.

  • audit: matchers are case sensitive. The tool is Bash and the matcher says bash. No error, no warning.
  • changed: the agent never used Write. Changing an existing file is an Edit call, and Write is for creating a file or replacing it whole. The syntax hook has Edit in its matcher, which is why it has a count.

The one-line fix

Two substitutions in the settings file, then a list of every matcher:

sed -i -E 's/("matcher" *: *)"bash"/\1"Bash"/; s/("matcher" *: *)"Write"/\1"Edit|Write"/' .claude/settings.json && jq -c '[.hooks[][].matcher]' .claude/settings.json


The matcher list after the fix; the Stop entry shows null. · watch this step

The pattern only touches a matcher whose whole value is that word, so the syntax hook stays as it was. The scripts are untouched: the only wrong thing was the line that tells Claude Code when to call them. The Stop entry shows null because it has no matcher by design.

Edit once more

Same kind of task in a fresh session, so the fixed settings load: change note not found to Note not found in the same file, then run node --check src/index.js. Only the two matchers differ.

The verdict

The same count loop again:


Same count loop after the fix: audit and changed are no longer zero. · watch this step

audit and changed are above zero. blocked is still 3, because nothing tried to read the secrets file this time. All five hooks have now run.

What to copy

  • Give every hook script a one-line log with its own label, then print a count per hook. Trust that number, not the settings file.
  • Blocking is exit code 2 plus one sentence on stderr.
  • Write matchers as exact tool names: Bash, not bash.
  • Match the tool the agent really uses: Edit|Write for a change hook.
  • Do not switch a hook off to make a demo pass. Fix the line that decides when it runs.

Not just JavaScript

The same hook contract works in any stack. In a Python repo, use python -m py_compile instead of node --check, and ruff or mypy instead of a JS linter. The guard reads the same stdin JSON.

Video with the full run: https://youtu.be/aR5c3T0jqvc

Techniques from my real projects, shown on a public demo repo.
Narration: AI voice. The sessions, code and errors are real. Not affiliated with Anthropic or any tool vendor.

title: Designing a repair ticket workflow: statuses, events and customer updates
description:
Disclosure: I work on Quikpair, repair shop management software. This post is about the workflow design problem itself, so it applies whether you build your own tool or buy one.

If you ever have to model a repair shop (phones, laptops, appliances), a first version is often a single table with a free-text "status" column. It works for a week. Then someone asks "which jobs are waiting on a part?" and the answer is a spreadsheet.

Here is a structure that holds up better.

1. Separate the job from the ticket

At the counter, a customer hands over a device. That is a job card: customer, device, reported fault, condition notes, expected date. Once it is accepted it becomes a repair ticket that moves through the workshop. Keeping both avoids losing intake details when the technician edits the ticket.

2. Use a small, fixed set of statuses

Free text makes reporting hard. A short list covers most shops:

  • Received
  • Diagnosing
  • Waiting for approval
  • Waiting for part
  • In repair
  • Ready for pickup
  • Delivered
  • Cancelled or returned unrepaired

Allow shops to rename them, but keep a stable internal key so reports and notifications do not break.

3. Store every status change as an event 

CREATE TABLE ticket_status_events (
  id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  ticket_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  status_key  VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
  changed_by  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  note        TEXT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

The current status is just the latest row. In return you get turnaround time per stage, an audit trail when a customer disputes something, and a clean trigger point for notifications.

4. Tell the customer on the transitions that matter

Many "where is my phone?" calls can be avoided by not leaving customers in silence. Consider messaging them on three events: received, status change, and ready for pickup. In many markets customers use WhatsApp heavily, so sending from the shop's own business number is worth considering instead of SMS. Check the messaging provider's current pricing first.

5. Tie parts and billing to the ticket

Parts used should be recorded on the ticket, so cost per repair is known when the invoice is made. If you operate in a GST country, store tax rate and HSN or SAC details per line so the invoice is correct without manual edits. With multiple branches, scope stock, tickets and reports by branch from day one. Retrofitting it later is usually harder.

What I would test first

Run one week of real repairs through whatever you build or buy. Counter intake speed is a good thing to watch, since slow intake discourages staff from using a tool.

Quikpair covers this flow (intake to delivery, WhatsApp updates, GST-ready invoices, multi-branch reports): https://quikpair.com

I am curious how others handle the "waiting for part" state. Do you track the supplier order separately or keep it on the ticket?

title: GPT-Live-1.1 on an Indian phone number: SIP setup, Hindi and the real cost in ₹
description:
OpenAI put GPT-Live-1.1 in the API in November 2026. OpenAI's own SIP examples use Twilio and US numbers. If your callers are in India, the hard parts are somewhere else:

  • finding a trunk for your +91 number that OpenAI will accept,
  • getting Hindi right on 8 kHz phone audio,
  • staying inside TRAI's calling rules, and
  • knowing what a minute costs in rupees once everything is added up.

This is the path we would follow, with working code for each step. Every API detail was checked against OpenAI's docs on 24 November 2026.

Disclosure: I work at Fonix, which builds voice agents for Indian businesses. Fonix is not built on GPT-Live. This is the guide we wanted when we evaluated it.

TL;DR

  • GPT-Live-1.1 (gpt-live-1.1, endpoint v1/live/sessions) is full duplex: it listens while it talks. It hands tool work to a separate backend model (delegation), which is billed separately.
  • Price: $0.05 per connected minute, billed by the second. The $0.02 standby rate is for WebRTC only. SIP calls always bill at the active rate.
  • SIP needs TLS signalling on port 5061 and SDES-SRTP media. OpenAI has an India endpoint: sip:$PROJECT_ID@sip-in.api.openai.com;transport=tls.
  • OpenAI's partner list (LiveKit, Twilio, Telnyx, Bandwidth, Daily/Pipecat) has no Indian telephony provider. Check your trunk before you write any code.
  • The API has one Hindi voice, nira (female). ChatGPT's Hindi voices, Neer and Leher, are not in the API list.
  • At ₹88 to the dollar, voice time alone is about ₹4.40 a minute. Add GST, the backend, telephony and forex, and our worked example comes to about ₹6.60.

1. What you are wiring up 

Caller ──(phone network)──> Indian provider, your +91 number
                               │  SIP over TLS :5061, SDES-SRTP audio
                               ▼
                 sip:proj_xxx@sip-in.api.openai.com
                               │  webhook: live.transport.incoming
                               ▼
         Your server ──POST /v1/live/sessions/{id}/accept──> OpenAI
               │
               └──wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/{id}/attach  (the "sideband")
                     transcripts · tool calls · keypad presses · call progress · final usage

GPT-Live is the voice. It does not know your business. Bookings, lookups and anything else that touches your systems run in the backend and in tools you write. Of the eight steps a call goes through, four are yours alone (webhook, accept, sideband, tools). You share two more with your provider: the trunk and transfers.

2. The trunk: ask before you code

GPT-Live doesn't connect to the phone network itself. Your provider owns the number and passes the call to OpenAI over SIP. Plenty of SIP trunks run plain SIP over UDP on port 5060 by default, and OpenAI refuses that.

If your numbers are with Exotel, Plivo, Ozonetel, Knowlarity, Tata Tele or Airtel, get written answers to these questions:

Ask your provider Why it matters
Does your trunk support TLS on port 5061 to an external SIP address? OpenAI only accepts TLS signalling.
Does it support SDES-SRTP media? GPT-Live requires encrypted audio. Without SRTP the call never connects. OpenAI's docs say to enable SRTP in your provider's settings.
Can my +91 number route to an endpoint outside your network, on my plan? Indian numbers come from licensed operators, and how calls leave their networks is regulated.
Do you honour SIP REFER? GPT-Live transfers calls with REFER. If the provider ignores it, transfers need another route.
What do inbound and outbound minutes cost? Is there a monthly trunk or number fee? This part of the cost isn't in GPT-Live's price.
For outbound calls: digest auth and an sips: endpoint? OpenAI dials out using sips: URLs and SIP digest authentication.

Network rules

These come from OpenAI's SIP guide:

  • Signalling: outbound TCP/TLS on port 5061 to the addresses DNS returns for sip-in.api.openai.com. That endpoint routes to SIP hosts in India.
  • Media: bidirectional SRTP over UDP to and from 13.79.45.80/28, 20.204.17.112/28, 23.98.140.64/28, 40.67.149.176/28 and 40.83.204.240/28. The exact IP and port arrive in the negotiated SDP.

The India endpoint decides where signalling lands. It doesn't, by itself, tell you where inference runs or where transcripts are stored. Ask OpenAI if that matters for your sector. (More on rules below.)

Project setup

  1. In your OpenAI project settings, go to Webhooks and create an endpoint subscribed to live.transport.incoming. Keep the signing secret.
  2. Copy your project ID (proj_...) from General.
  3. Point the provider's trunk at sip:proj_xxx@sip-in.api.openai.com;transport=tls.

3. Answer the call

OpenAI posts a webhook for each incoming call. Verify the signature on the raw body, deduplicate retries, then accept or reject. The first decision wins. The phone rings for at most 3 minutes.

// server.js: Node 20+, Express, the official openai SDK. Keys stay on the server.
import express from "express";
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { attach } from "./sideband.js";

const openai = new OpenAI({ webhookSecret: process.env.OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET });
const app = express();
const seen = new Set(); // use Redis or your database in production

const TOOLS = [
  {
    type: "function",
    name: "find_slots",
    description: "List free appointment slots for a date (YYYY-MM-DD).",
    parameters: {
      type: "object",
      properties: { date: { type: "string" } },
      required: ["date"],
      additionalProperties: false,
    },
    strict: true,
  },
  {
    type: "function",
    name: "book_slot",
    description: "Book a slot returned by find_slots.",
    parameters: {
      type: "object",
      properties: {
        slot_id: { type: "string" },
        name: { type: "string" },
        phone: { type: "string", description: "10-digit Indian mobile number" },
      },
      required: ["slot_id", "name", "phone"],
      additionalProperties: false,
    },
    strict: true,
  },
];

// No express.json() here: signature verification needs the exact bytes.
app.post("/openai/webhook", express.text({ type: "*/*" }), async (req, res) => {
  let event;
  try {
    event = await openai.webhooks.unwrap(req.body, req.headers);
  } catch {
    return res.sendStatus(400); // signature did not verify
  }
  res.sendStatus(200); // acknowledge fast; OpenAI retries non-2xx responses

  const deliveryId = req.headers["webhook-id"]; // the same on every retry
  if (seen.has(deliveryId) || event.type !== "live.transport.incoming") return;
  seen.add(deliveryId);
  if (event.data.type !== "sip") return;

  // Treat SIP headers (From, To...) as caller metadata, never as authorization.
  const sessionId = event.data.session_id;

  const r = await fetch(`https://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/${sessionId}/accept`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      session: {
        type: "live",
        model: "gpt-live-1.1",
        instructions: [
          "You answer the phone for Sharma Dental Clinic in Pune.",
          "Reply in the language the caller uses: Hindi, English or a mix.",
          "Hand anything about availability or bookings to the backend.",
          "Read phone numbers back in two groups of five digits and wait for a yes.",
          "If asked, say you are an automated assistant.",
        ].join(" "),
        audio: { output: { voice: "nira" } }, // the API's Hindi voice; omit audio.format on SIP
        delegation: {
          type: "responses",
          responses: {
            model: "gpt-6-luna", // OpenAI's suggested starting point; gpt-6-sol for harder tasks
            instructions:
              "Use find_slots before offering any time. Never state a slot you did not fetch. " +
              "Confirm name and phone before book_slot.",
            tools: TOOLS,
          },
        },
      },
    }),
  });

  if (!r.ok) {
    console.error("accept failed", r.status, await r.text());
    return;
  }
  attach(sessionId); // straight away: the sideband replays only the last 3 seconds
});

app.listen(3000, () => console.log("listening on :3000"));

Notes:

  • gpt-live-1.1 comes from the model page. Some of OpenAI's SIP examples still show gpt-live-1.
  • To decline a call, POST /v1/live/sessions/{id}/reject with an integer SIP status between 300 and 699, for example { "status_code": 486 } for busy.
  • The function-tool objects use the standard Responses API shape, inside delegation.responses.tools.
  • If you'd rather run your own agent, use delegation: { type: "client" }. Your server then receives session.delegation.created and replies with session.commentary.append.

4. The sideband: tool calls, keypad, final usage

SIP carries the audio. Everything else arrives on a WebSocket you attach to the session. With Responses delegation, backend events arrive wrapped in a response.event envelope. Read finished function calls from the nested response.output_item.done. Return results with response.item.create, then send response.create. Appending the output alone doesn't resume the backend.

// sideband.js
import WebSocket from "ws";
import { findSlots, bookSlot } from "./calendar.js"; // your own calendar code

const tools = {
  find_slots: ({ date }) => findSlots(date),
  book_slot: ({ slot_id, name, phone }) => bookSlot(slot_id, name, phone),
};

export function attach(sessionId) {
  const ws = new WebSocket(`wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/${sessionId}/attach`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY}` },
  });
  const handled = new Set(); // events can be replayed when you attach

  ws.on("message", async (raw) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(raw.toString());

    if (msg.type === "response.event") {
      const ev = msg.event;
      if (ev.type !== "response.output_item.done" || ev.item?.type !== "function_call") return;

      const { call_id, name, arguments: args } = ev.item;
      if (handled.has(call_id)) return; // one owner per side effect
      handled.add(call_id);

      let output;
      try {
        output = await tools[name](JSON.parse(args));
      } catch (err) {
        // Give the backend something it can say, not silence.
        output = { error: "The calendar is not responding. Offer to take a message." };
      }

      ws.send(JSON.stringify({
        type: "response.item.create",
        event_id: `out_${call_id}`,
        item: { type: "function_call_output", call_id, output: JSON.stringify(output) },
      }));
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "response.create", event_id: `go_${call_id}` }));
      return;
    }

    switch (msg.type) {
      case "transport.dtmf.received":
        // Callers press keys out of habit. Decide what 0 or 9 should do.
        console.log("keypad", msg);
        break;
      case "session.usage.updated":
        // Running total of billed seconds, useful for live cost dashboards.
        break;
      case "session.closed":
        console.log("call ended:", msg.reason, "billed seconds:", msg.usage?.seconds);
        ws.close();
        break;
    }
  });

  ws.on("error", (err) => console.error("sideband error", err.message));
}

Make every tool fast. GPT-Live can keep talking while a lookup runs, but a calendar call that takes several seconds still feels slow on the phone. Decide what the agent says when a tool fails. A wrong answer is the worst outcome, and dead air comes next.

5. Hindi on phone audio

Three things matter more than "it's multilingual":

  1. One Hindi voice. OpenAI's GPT-Live voice table lists nira (Hindi, female). There's no male Hindi voice. ChatGPT's Neer and Leher are not in the API list.
  2. Narrowband audio. Browser demos run at 24 kHz. Phone calls arrive at 8 kHz, usually G.711, and that loses much of what separates similar sounds. The playground isn't a test.
  3. No other Indian-language voices. If your callers speak Tamil, Kannada, Bengali or Marathi, test them separately. Hindi results don't carry over.

The cheapest test that catches the most bugs is the read-back. Call your own number from a mobile, ideally somewhere noisy, and say each of these the way a real caller would. Then check what the agent repeats and what reaches your tools:

Say this Check
"मेरा number नौ-आठ-सात-शून्य, फिर 4 2 1 9 8 6" Hindi and English digits in one breath → 9870421986
"परसों शाम को" Relative day ("day after tomorrow") resolved to the right date
"साढ़े छह के आसपास" Half-hour time → 6:30 pm, not 6 or 7
"डेढ़ हज़ार" / "ढाई सौ" 1,500 / 250, not 1,000 or 200
A name spelled letter by letter Spelled names survive the line
"Main road, temple ke paas" Landmark-style addresses saved as said

If the read-back is wrong, the booking is wrong. Put these phrases in a regression script and run them on every prompt change.

6. Outbound calls, and TRAI

GPT-Live places outbound calls through your trunk. Outbound SIP calling runs through the Live API, not the Realtime API.

# Outbound call. Numbers are E.164 (+91...). Keep credentials on the server.
jq -n \
  --arg u "$SIP_USERNAME" --arg p "$SIP_PASSWORD" \
  --arg to "$CUSTOMER_E164" --arg from "$YOUR_E164" '{
  session: {
    model: "gpt-live-1.1",
    instructions: "Confirm the appointment booked for tomorrow at 11 am. Offer to move it if needed.",
    audio: { output: { voice: "nira" } },
    delegation: { type: "client" }
  },
  transport: {
    type: "sip",
    destination: $to,
    trunk: {
      provider_url: "sips:sip.your-provider.example:5061",
      auth: { type: "digest", username: $u, password: $p },
      caller_number: $from
    }
  }
}' | curl https://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @-

A 200 response means the session started, not that anyone answered. Attach the sideband at once and watch transport.ringing, transport.answered and transport.failed. Ringing is capped at 3 minutes and a connected call at 2 hours. Neither limit can be changed.

Before you dial anyone, check India's rules. They apply whichever model you use:

  • Promotional calls must come from registered 140-series numbers, with your business registered on DLT. Promotional calls from ordinary 10-digit numbers can get all of the sender's numbers disconnected.
  • Banks, NBFCs, insurers and other regulated financial firms make service and transactional calls from the 1600 series.
  • NCPR (Do Not Disturb): scrub promotional lists before you call.
  • DPDP Act 2023: recordings, transcripts and caller numbers are personal data. Give notice, state the purpose, limit retention, and know where the data is processed. The DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025. Some sectors go further: RBI, for example, requires payment data to be stored in India.

Inbound answering is the simple case, because the caller rang you.

7. Transfer to a person, or hang up 

# Hand the caller to your front desk. Your provider must honour SIP REFER.
curl -X POST "https://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/$SESSION_ID/refer" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"target_uri": "tel:+91XXXXXXXXXX"}'

# End the call
curl -X POST "https://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/$SESSION_ID/hangup" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY"

Both return 200 with an empty body. The REFER target becomes the Refer-To header, and your provider handles the rest of the transfer. Keep the sideband open until session.closed delivers the final usage.

8. What a minute costs in rupees

GPT-Live's own price is fixed. Everything else depends on your setup. Here is a worked example for 1,000 connected minutes a month. Only the first line is OpenAI's published price; the others are example values. Replace them with your own.

Line Basis ₹ a month
GPT-Live-1.1 voice 1,000 min × $0.05 × ₹88 4,400
Backend model example: ₹0.50 a minute 500
Card forex markup example: 2% of the OpenAI bill 98
Telephony example: ₹0.60 a minute 600
GST 18% on all of the above 1,008
Total 6,606 (₹6.61 a minute)

Three things catch people out:

  • Silence costs the same as speech. Standby pricing doesn't apply to SIP. A caller hunting for a pen, or waiting on a slow lookup, is billed at the full rate.
  • The backend bills per delegation. A booking call that checks the calendar three times costs more than one that answers an FAQ.
  • Engineering isn't in any per-minute number. Someone builds and runs the server, call logs, recordings, dashboards and alerts.

To try other numbers, use the calculator on the full guide. It takes your minutes, today's exchange rate, your telephony rate and whether you can claim the GST back.

9. Production checklist

  • [ ] Trunk confirmed in writing: TLS 5061, SDES-SRTP, routing to an external SIP address, REFER support
  • [ ] Firewall allows TLS to sip-in.api.openai.com and SRTP from OpenAI's five media ranges
  • [ ] Webhook signature verified on the raw body; retries deduplicated by webhook-id
  • [ ] Sideband attached immediately after accept or create (3-second replay window)
  • [ ] Each side effect has one owner, so a tool never runs twice
  • [ ] Every tool returns within a second or two, and every failure has something to say
  • [ ] Read-back test passes on a real mobile line: digits, relative days, half-hours, amounts, names
  • [ ] Transfer to a human tested end to end, including when nobody picks up
  • [ ] Call recording, retention and notice in place under the DPDP Act
  • [ ] Outbound numbers and DLT registration sorted before the first campaign
  • [ ] Concurrency checked on your organisation's limits page (GPT-Live-1.1 has its own limit, separate from GPT-Live-1)
  • [ ] Someone gets alerted when calls start failing at 9 pm

If you'd rather not build all of this

GPT-Live-1.1 is a strong voice model, and if you have engineers and an agent you already trust, it's a good thing to build on. If what you actually need is callers answered well, in Hindi, Hinglish or another Indian language, with call logs and transcripts you can read, Fonix does that without the project plan. Setup takes about two minutes, and the free trial includes 20 test minutes.

The full guide also covers the build-or-buy comparison and an FAQ: GPT-Live-1.1 phone agent in India.

Sources: OpenAI's GPT-Live-1.1 model page, the Telephony and SIP guide, the GPT-Live delegation guide and the GPT-Live voice table, all read on 24 November 2026. OpenAI changes these often, so check the docs before you ship.

title: Designing Reliable Webhook Pipelines for Financial Applications: Preventing Forged Events and Duplicate Transactions
description:
Modern financial applications rarely operate in isolation.

Investor portals communicate with payment providers, accounting platforms, identity verification services, CRM systems, banking APIs, and internal reporting tools. These systems frequently exchange information through webhooks.

A webhook is an HTTP callback that allows one application to notify another when an event occurs.

For example:

  • A payment provider notifies an application that a payment has succeeded.
  • An identity verification service reports that a document has been verified.
  • An accounting platform sends an updated transaction status.
  • An investor portal receives a notification that a document or account status has changed.
  • A subscription platform reports that a payment or renewal has failed.

Webhooks make integrations faster and reduce the need for continuous polling.

However, they also introduce a security challenge: how can an application know that an incoming event is genuine, has not been modified, and has not already been processed?

For financial applications, an incorrectly handled webhook can trigger duplicate operations, incorrect account updates, misleading notifications, or unauthorized changes to business records.

Let's examine how to design a more secure and reliable webhook architecture.

1. Understand the Risks Behind Webhook Integrations

A webhook endpoint receives HTTP requests from an external service. If the receiving application does not verify those requests properly, an attacker may attempt to send fabricated events.

Consider a financial platform that receives a webhook whenever a payment is completed.

If the application trusts the incoming JSON payload without verifying its authenticity, someone may attempt to submit a fabricated event claiming that a payment has succeeded.

Other common risks include:

Forged events: An attacker sends a request that looks like a legitimate notification from a payment or integration provider.

Replay attacks: A previously captured, valid webhook is submitted again to trigger the same operation.

Duplicate processing: A provider retries a delivery, and the application performs the same business operation multiple times.

Out-of-order events: An application receives an older event after a newer event and accidentally overwrites the latest state.

Secret exposure: Webhook signing credentials are leaked through source code, configuration files, or application logs.

Denial of service: An endpoint receives excessive requests or oversized payloads, affecting application availability.

These risks require controls at both the integration and application levels.

2. Verify Webhook Signatures Before Processing Events

Signature verification is one of the most important controls in webhook security.

A common approach is HMAC-SHA256, where the sending application uses a shared secret to generate a signature based on the request payload.

The receiving application independently calculates the expected signature and compares it with the signature supplied by the sender.

The basic process is:

  1. The sender prepares the webhook payload.
  2. It generates a signature using a shared secret.
  3. The signature is included in an HTTP header.
  4. The receiving application calculates its own signature.
  5. Both signatures are compared.
  6. The event is processed only if verification succeeds.

For example, GitHub uses the X-Hub-Signature-256 header for HMAC-SHA256 webhook verification.

A simplified Python example:

import hashlib
import hmac

def verify_webhook(payload, received_signature, secret):
    expected_signature = "sha256=" + hmac.new(
        secret.encode("utf-8"),
        payload,
        hashlib.sha256
    ).hexdigest()

    return hmac.compare_digest(
        expected_signature,
        received_signature
    )

This example illustrates the signature comparison process. A production implementation must also validate the header format, handle missing values safely, use the exact raw request body required by the provider's protocol, and manage secrets securely.

One important detail: do not parse and re-serialize JSON before signature verification. Changes in whitespace, encoding, or field ordering can change the bytes being signed.

Also, use a constant-time comparison function rather than a normal equality operator.

3. Protect Webhook Endpoints Against Replay Attacks

A valid signature does not automatically prevent replay attacks.

Imagine an attacker captures a legitimate webhook notification. If the same signed request is submitted again, signature verification may still succeed because the payload has not changed.

This creates a problem when the receiving application performs a business operation every time it receives the event.

A stronger design uses authenticated timestamps and unique event identifiers when the provider's protocol supports them.

The application should:

  • Verify the signature.
  • Validate the authenticated timestamp against an acceptable time window.
  • Check whether the event identifier has already been processed.
  • Reject stale or repeated deliveries according to the provider's protocol.

For protocols that authenticate timestamps, a limited time window can reduce the opportunity to replay captured requests.

However, not every webhook provider signs timestamps or delivery identifiers. Developers must follow the actual provider's signing protocol rather than assuming that every header is cryptographically protected.

GitHub, for example, documents the use of its X-GitHub-Delivery header to identify deliveries and ordinary redeliveries. That header is useful for deduplication, but it is not part of GitHub's body signature.

4. Implement Idempotency to Prevent Duplicate Operations

Webhook providers may retry deliveries when a receiving endpoint is unavailable or does not respond successfully.

This means an application must expect that the same event may arrive more than once.

Suppose a payment notification arrives and the application updates an investor's account balance.

If the provider retries the same event, the application should not apply the payment a second time.

This is where idempotency becomes important.

An idempotent operation produces the same intended result when the same event is processed repeatedly.

A practical implementation can maintain a database record for each processed event.

Example:

CREATE TABLE processed_webhooks (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    provider VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    event_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    payload_hash VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    processed_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    UNIQUE KEY unique_provider_event (provider, event_id)
);

Before performing a business operation, the application checks whether the event has already been processed.

The database uniqueness constraint helps prevent two concurrent requests from processing the same event simultaneously.

A production implementation should also handle the case where the same event identifier arrives with a different payload. That should be treated as suspicious rather than silently accepted as an ordinary duplicate.

Most importantly, the event record and the associated business operation should be coordinated transactionally wherever possible.

5. Handle Events Asynchronously Using Queues

Webhook endpoints should not perform lengthy business operations before responding to the sender.

For example, a single event might require:

  • Database updates.
  • Account reconciliation.
  • Document status changes.
  • Notifications.
  • Reporting updates.
  • External API requests.

Performing all these operations synchronously can make the endpoint slow and unreliable.

A better architecture separates event reception from event processing.

A typical workflow:

  1. Receive the webhook.
  2. Validate the request signature.
  3. Validate the event structure and required fields.
  4. Check event freshness and duplication.
  5. Persist the event or enqueue it durably.
  6. Return a successful HTTP response.
  7. Process the event through a background worker.
  8. Record the processing result.

For example, a message queue such as RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, or Apache Kafka can help separate incoming events from downstream processing.

The queue should not be treated as a substitute for persistence or idempotency. Events must be stored and processed reliably, including when workers fail or restart.

6. Do Not Assume Events Arrive in the Correct Order

Webhook delivery systems do not always guarantee that events will arrive in the same order in which they occurred.

Consider this sequence:

  • Event A: Payment initiated.
  • Event B: Payment completed.
  • Event C: Payment refunded.

The application may receive Event C before Event B because of network delays or delivery retries.

If the application blindly updates its records using arrival order, it could overwrite a newer status with an older one.

To reduce this risk:

  • Use provider-supported event sequence numbers or object versions where available.
  • Store event timestamps and identifiers.
  • Validate state transitions before updating records.
  • Avoid allowing older events to overwrite newer confirmed states.
  • Retrieve the latest object state from the provider's API when necessary.

Timestamps alone should not be treated as proof of ordering unless the provider documents the relevant guarantees.

7. Protect Webhook Secrets and Integration Credentials

Webhook signing secrets are security credentials.

If a signing secret is exposed, an attacker may be able to generate forged requests that pass signature verification.

Development teams should:

  • Generate high-entropy random secrets.
  • Store secrets in a dedicated secrets manager.
  • Use separate secrets for different webhook integrations.
  • Avoid committing secrets to source-control repositories.
  • Prevent secrets and signature values from appearing in application logs.
  • Rotate credentials according to a defined process.
  • Revoke and replace compromised secrets immediately.

Planned secret rotation can use a controlled overlap period where both the old and new secrets are accepted. A compromised secret should not remain trusted simply to avoid integration downtime.

8. Secure Webhook Delivery Infrastructure

Webhook security also depends on the infrastructure surrounding the endpoint.

Important controls include:

HTTPS: Require secure transport and valid TLS certificates.

Request size limits: Reject excessively large payloads before expensive processing begins.

Rate limiting: Protect endpoints from excessive traffic and abusive requests.

Schema validation: Validate event types, required fields, data types, and expected values before processing.

Restricted methods: Accept only the HTTP methods required by the webhook protocol.

Asynchronous processing: Use durable queues for operations that do not need to happen during the initial request.

Structured logging: Record event identifiers, timestamps, processing results, and relevant request metadata without logging sensitive payload contents or credentials.

If your application sends webhooks to callback URLs supplied by customers or third parties, the outbound delivery system also needs protection against server-side request forgery (SSRF). Validate destinations and block internal or otherwise prohibited IP ranges at connection time, including after DNS resolution.

9. Build a Webhook Security Testing Strategy

Webhook integrations should be tested for both security and reliability.

Before deploying an integration, test scenarios such as:

Test scenario Expected behaviour
Missing signature Reject the request
Invalid signature Reject the request
Modified payload Signature verification fails
Stale authenticated timestamp Reject according to the provider's protocol
Duplicate event Do not repeat business operations
Same event ID with different payload Reject or flag as suspicious
Oversized payload Reject before expensive processing
Concurrent duplicate deliveries Process the business operation once
Out-of-order events Prevent stale state updates
Compromised or revoked secret Stop accepting the revoked credential

Testing should also cover queue failures, worker restarts, provider retries, and database transaction failures.

OWASP's Web Security Testing Guide includes specific guidance for testing inbound webhooks, including replay, duplicate delivery, and concurrent processing scenarios.

Final Thoughts

Webhooks are an essential part of modern financial application architecture. They connect services, automate workflows, and allow systems to respond to important events without constant polling.

But reliability should never depend on trusting every incoming HTTP request.

A secure webhook pipeline should verify signatures, validate event freshness where supported, prevent duplicate processing, handle out-of-order events, protect integration secrets, and use reliable asynchronous processing.

The goal is not simply to receive an event. It is to establish that the event is authentic, process it safely, and ensure that the intended business operation happens exactly as designed.

For financial applications, these controls help protect the accuracy of records, the reliability of integrations, and the integrity of automated workflows.

References

  1. OWASP Webhook Security Cheat Sheet
  2. OWASP Web Security Testing Guide – Inbound Webhooks
  3. GitHub – Validating Webhook Deliveries
  4. GitHub – Best Practices for Using Webhooks

title: You Gave Every Agent Its Own Worktree. You Also Gave Each One Its Own rust-analyzer.
description:
TL;DR. In my setup, one worktree per agent meant one language server per agent, each with its own copy of the same analysis. I tried to share rust-analyzer between worktrees twice, and both attempts half-worked. Then I built a language server that reads what rustc writes down during cargo check. In one single-session run on Bevy with the index already built, it peaked at 917 MB and, after startup, got through the session's 1,635 requests in 5.5 seconds; rust-analyzer peaked at 11.3 GB and took 114.4 seconds. Several servers running at once are not measured yet.

git worktree add took between 1.1 and 1.7 seconds. The first workspace-wide symbol search in that fresh worktree took rust-analyzer 66.97 seconds. The same search again took 0.10. That was July 2026, on a private workspace of 431 Rust files.

An agent that has just been handed a worktree starts with a question of that kind, and it starts cold every time. But the minute is the smaller part of the bill. A worktree is a separate directory, so in my setup it got a separate language server, and every server built its own complete picture of the project in memory: the same dependencies, the same standard library, the same code no agent had touched. In the run further down, a single rust-analyzer session peaked at 1.5 GB on serde and 11.3 GB on Bevy.

On 26 September the bill arrived. One of my build machines, with 64 GiB of RAM, had 14 code-analysis engines loaded and sat above 85% memory. Requests hung for minutes, and then the kernel's OOM killer shot the service (the public issue). Those 14 were engines for every language, and I did not record how many of them were Rust. What I did know was how prod-code, the service that answers my agents' questions about code, handled Rust: it embeds rust-analyzer's analysis as a library, and it started one Rust engine per worktree copy. That was the part that grew with every agent.

"One worktree, one language server" is a habit, not a law. It took me two attempts to see which part of the habit was wrong.

Attempt one: one daemon, private overlays

In July I tested analyzed 0.4.2: one shared rust-analyzer world, and each session gets a private overlay with its own changed files.

The model held. Across 3,950 queries with up to 20 sessions, none returned another session's code. The operations did not hold. With five sessions, a new overlay waited 12 to 47 seconds, and after every session had closed the daemon still held between 9 and 21.6 GiB. That is version 0.4.2 in July; I have not retested later ones.

The plan recorded that week ruled out building a separate semantic index and merging its results above LSP.

Attempt two: teach rust-analyzer to share

After the OOM I forked rust-analyzer. In the fork, a base checkout and its worktree copies share every crate whose files, build-script output and dependencies are identical, and only what differs is analysed again.

I measured it on rust-analyzer's own repository: 328 crates, about 1.8 GB for the base, with build scripts and proc macros off. A second plain copy cost about 520 MB more. With sharing, an unchanged copy cost 25 to 40 MB, and sixteen copies, each with an edit in a leaf crate, fit in about 2.07 GB in total.

It worked, and it was about 9,000 lines through some of the most intricate parts of rust-analyzer. I sent it upstream as one pull request, and it was closed two days later. The maintainers' reasons were fair: I had not read the project's AI policy and the description broke it, 9,000 lines is not a first contribution, and I had not discussed any of it with the team, who have had their own discussion of a shared server open since July (#22765). Carrying a patch that size on top of a moving codebase was not a plan either.

The question I had been asking wrong

Both attempts asked how several worktrees could share the analyzer's memory. Neither asked why that memory exists.

rust-analyzer analyses Rust on its own. It parses, resolves names, expands macros and infers types, and it keeps the result in RAM. rustc does all of that too, on every cargo check. In my workflow cargo check was already part of the loop: rust-analyzer runs it on save by default to show the compiler's errors (checkOnSave), and my agents run it to see whether a change compiles. The compiler works out where every name points and what type every expression has, reports the errors and exits. Nothing keeps those answers in a form an editor can ask.

Rust Intelligence keeps them. ridx index runs cargo check with a small rustc driver that, after analysis, writes one binary file per crate: definitions, every resolved reference, types, impls. A method call points at the impl rustc selected, not at a guess by name. The language server maps those files from disk and answers lookups in them. It does not hold a second compiler in memory, because it is not one.

Build time on the left, edit time on the right. Cargo checks crates as needed, and worktrees reuse a dependency's index file when their keys match. From the architecture document.

In July the plan had ruled out a separate index. What changed is who writes it: the compiler, as a by-product of a check that was already running.

The compiler had already answered. Nobody was keeping the answers.

What one session costs

The same scripted editor session against both servers: 40 files of each repository opened one by one, with symbols, semantic tokens and inlay hints, then hover, definition, references and completion at sampled positions, and an edit.

Repository Peak memory, Rust Intelligence / rust-analyzer Time for the requests, after startup CPU for the requests
serde 72 MB / 1.5 GB 2.43 s / 5.40 s 2.34 s / 6.97 s
tokio 221 MB / 3.2 GB 2.03 s / 28.1 s 1.90 s / 35.9 s
rust-analyzer 434 MB / 4.6 GB 4.59 s / 52.3 s 4.44 s / 66.7 s
bevy 917 MB / 11.3 GB 5.54 s / 114.4 s 5.38 s / 170.5 s

Read it with its conditions. This is one session per server and repository, run once, on Linux with a Ryzen 9 7950X and 64 GB, with Rust Intelligence at commit f7105fcc; the rust-analyzer version was not recorded. The index was built beforehand, which takes minutes on a large workspace the first time, and that time is not in the table, while rust-analyzer's own analysis is in its numbers. rust-analyzer answered 26 to 31 requests per repository with an error and Rust Intelligence none; I did not record what the errors were, so that says nothing about the quality of either server's answers. The table says what each server spent on the same requests, 1,635 of them on Bevy. Not every kind of request was faster: on Bevy the median references and documentHighlight were quicker on rust-analyzer, and the totals above are for the whole session. It does not say the answers were identical. And it is one session: several servers at once, indexing in parallel and the physical memory of a whole machine are not in it. The raw results and the script are in the repository.

What sixteen worktrees would and would not get

The first objection from anyone who runs agents is not about one session. It is: I have sixteen worktrees that diverge, some of them change Cargo.toml or features; what happens to the machine?

What the design gives them. The index file of a registry or git dependency is keyed by what it was compiled from and how: version, target, cfg flags, toolchain and the crates it was built against. Worktrees that build a dependency the same way reuse that file instead of writing it again, and a worktree that changes features or Cargo.toml gets new files only for the dependencies the change reaches.

And most of the index stays in memory-mapped files, which the kernel can page out and read back. The server keeps derived tables on the heap as well; the peak in the table above counts both, and I have not measured the split.

What it does not give them. Sixteen cargo check runs are still sixteen cargo check runs: every worktree checks its dependencies and its own crates in its own target directory, and the first index of a large workspace takes minutes. In 0.3.9 a worktree also writes the index of all its own workspace crates, including the ones identical to a sibling worktree's; sharing those is planned, not shipped. And I have not yet put sixteen of these servers on one machine and measured the total, the way I did with the fork. Until I do, the claim is a mechanism and one session, not a fleet.

"A language server must work while the code is broken"

This is the strongest objection to the whole idea, and it is why rust-analyzer is built the way it is. It answers on every keystroke, in code that does not compile, without waiting for a build. An index written by the last cargo check is one build behind by definition.

In 0.3.9, hover, completion, inlay hints and type errors for the code you are typing come from a small compiler-free front end that reads everything else from the index. References, rename and navigation catch up after a compile: once the edited buffers have been still for 250 ms, the crates that own them are compiled again from the buffers' text into an index for the session, and nothing is written to your files. Since 0.3.11 the compiler's own errors for the unsaved text arrive with that compile, not only after a save. The 250 ms is the pause before that compile starts, not the answer time. From an edit to a references answer that includes it, the project's own measurement gives a median of 0.36 s on a one-file crate and 3.31 s on a file of one of its library crates (integration notes, §4); until then the answer comes from the previous index. A crate with compile errors is indexed from everything that did resolve, inside the bodies with errors too. Two gaps remain: a crate that depends on the edited one sees the change only after a save, and a buffer the compiler cannot parse stays on its crate's previous index. That is a compile per pause, not an answer per keystroke. And for every file you have not touched, the answer is as fresh as the last check. The driver is pinned to one toolchain, Rust 1.98.1, because it links to the compiler's private libraries. There is no Windows and no Intel macOS build. Agreement with rust-analyzer is measured per method and recorded in the changelog, for example 95.5% for completion and 82.2% for references in 0.3.0, but that suite was not re-run for 0.3.7, 0.3.8 or 0.3.9.

If your day is one editor on one checkout with memory to spare, rust-analyzer's trade is a good one. An agent's day is different: it edits a few files, runs cargo check anyway, and mostly asks about code it did not write.

Check it on your own worktrees

Start with what you already run. Does your orchestrator or editor start one language server per worktree? After the first question in each, how much memory is every one of them holding?

Then compare on two working copies of your own repository. On Linux (x86_64, arm64) or macOS on Apple Silicon, with rustup:

curl -fsSL https://rust-intelligence.com/install.sh | sh

ridx compare puts an answer side by side with rust-analyzer's on your code, so you do not have to take my table on trust. ridx accepts rust-analyzer's command line, so an editor already set up for rust-analyzer can start it instead; in VS Code that is "rust-analyzer.server.path": "ridx". An agent does not need an editor session at all: ridx def, ridx refs and ridx hover answer from the shell.

Before you buy RAM for the next ten agents, count the language servers already running on that machine and ask what each one is holding. On mine, each was holding one more copy of what the compiler works out on every check.

Source: github.com/alex09x/rust-intelligence, MIT OR Apache-2.0. Cite: 10.5281/zenodo.24379816, which resolves to the latest archived version.

Originally published at prod.codes.

title: Playwright MCP vs Kane CLI: 42,333 vs 2,056 tokens
description:
When a coding agent tests a web app through Playwright MCP, its own model drives the browser one tool call at a time and decides whether the test passed. With Kane CLI, which we build at TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest), the agent hands one plain-English objective to a separate browser agent and gets back a pass or fail with evidence.

We wanted to know how much text each approach puts in front of the calling agent, so we ran the same flow both ways and counted every response.

The short version:

  • Playwright MCP, reading full snapshots: 42,333 tokens
  • Playwright MCP, using browser_find: 4,076 tokens
  • Kane CLI, first run: 2,056 tokens

The headline gap is against full snapshots. Against browser_find, the gap is much smaller. This is one flow, so treat it as one data point.

The flow

On TestMu AI's Ecommerce Playground:

  1. Open the store
  2. Search for "iPhone"
  3. Open the first result
  4. Add it to the cart
  5. Confirm the cart lists an iPhone

How we measured

  • Playwright MCP 0.0.83. We connected through the official MCP SDK client, the same protocol Cursor uses, and made the tool calls a Cursor agent would make, with no model in between. That isolates what the tools themselves return. It also means this was not a live Cursor session.
  • Two ways of reading the page. In the first, the agent takes a full browser_snapshot before each action. In the second, it uses browser_find, which searches the snapshot and returns only the matching nodes.
  • Why the second read is needed. In 0.0.83, action tools such as browser_navigate and browser_click save the snapshot to a file and return only a link, so the agent has to ask for the page again before its next action.
  • Kane CLI in agent mode. We ran the same flow as one objective with --agent --headless, then replayed the saved test.
  • Counting. Every response was counted with the o200k_base tokenizer.

The results

Measure Playwright MCP, full snapshots Playwright MCP, browser_find Kane CLI, first run Kane CLI, replay
Setup text loaded 4,396 tokens of tool definitions 4,396 tokens of tool definitions 1,784 tokens, if the agent reads the hosted skill Same skill, already read
Calls from the agent 12 tool calls 12 tool calls 1 command 1 command
Text returned to the agent 42,333 tokens 4,076 tokens 2,056 tokens in 24 NDJSON lines 3,575 tokens in 53 NDJSON lines
Final result line only None; the agent decides None; the agent decides 764 tokens 65 tokens
Browser time 15 seconds, plus the agent's thinking on 12 turns 15 seconds, plus the agent's thinking on 12 turns 96.7 seconds, reasoning included 23 seconds
Kane CLI credits None None 22.8 credits None

All four runs confirmed an iPhone in the cart.

Where the tokens went

Snapshots are the cost. With full snapshots, four page reads made up 41,385 of the 42,333 tokens. The store's home page alone was 20,116 tokens: a 1,360-line accessibility tree with 1,156 element references.

browser_find helps, if the agent knows what to look for. Searching for "Search For Products" or "Add to Cart" cut the reads to a few hundred tokens each. The search-results page still returned 2,241 tokens, because "iPhone" matched every product card.

Kane CLI's result is small and structured. The agent can read only the final run_end line, which carries the status, a summary and the values Kane CLI extracted.

Approval checks add up. The Playwright MCP flow made 12 MCP tool calls. In Cursor, that means 12 prompts under an empty allowlist, or 12 classifier reviews under Auto-review. The Kane CLI command needed at most one. Only Run Everything skips the checks.

Where Kane CLI came out worse

  • The first run was slower. It took 96.7 seconds against 15 seconds of browser time for Playwright MCP. The two aren't like for like: 96.7 includes Kane CLI's reasoning, and 15 leaves out the calling agent's thinking on 12 turns. It is still a wait you will notice.
  • It cost 22.8 credits. Kane CLI's own model work is billed as credits, outside the calling agent's context. The work is still paid for, in a different place.
  • The replay returned more text than the first run: 3,575 tokens against 2,056. The final line alone was 65 tokens, and the replay used no credits, but an agent that reads the whole stream reads more.

What these numbers do not show

  • One flow on one demo store. A lighter page would shrink the snapshot cost.
  • The calling agent's reasoning isn't counted. It grows with each of the 12 Playwright MCP turns, and the totals above leave it out.
  • Tokenizers differ. Cursor's models tokenize slightly differently from o200k_base.
  • Setup text is a separate row. The 42,333, 4,076 and 2,056 figures leave it out.
  • Versions move. This was Playwright MCP 0.0.83, and newer versions have shipped since. Re-measure before relying on the figures.

Which one to use

  • Playwright MCP for long, open-ended browsing sessions where the agent needs a live view of the page. If token cost matters, try browser_find before full snapshots.
  • Kane CLI when you need to know whether a user flow works and want an exit code to act on.

The difference is who decides. Playwright MCP hands the agent browser snapshots and leaves the judgment to the model. Kane CLI runs the objective itself and hands the agent a verdict.

Try it on your own flow

Kane CLI installs from npm. This is the shape of the two Kane CLI runs, a first run saved by name and then a replay:

npm install -g @testmuai/kane-cli
kane-cli login --oauth

# First run, saved so it can be replayed
kane-cli run "Go to <your-store-url>, search for 'iPhone', open the first result, add it to the cart, then verify the cart lists an iPhone" \
  --agent --headless --name iphone-cart

# Replay
kane-cli testmd run .testmuai/tests/iphone-cart_test.md --agent --headless

Run the same flow through Playwright MCP, count the responses with one tokenizer, and compare. If you get very different numbers, post the flow and the versions in the comments.

This measurement was first published in Playwright CLI vs Playwright MCP: Which Should Your Coding Agent Use?, which also covers Playwright CLI.

title: Test a web app built with Claude Code in 5 minutes
description:
Claude Code edits real code and it compiles, but a green build is not a working web app. An edit drifts a type, touches a file you didn't ask about, or leaves a form that no longer submits, and the build stays green. The diff shows what moved, not whether the flow still works.

Kane CLI, which we build at TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest), drives your running web app in a real browser, checks each step of a flow you describe in plain English, and returns a pass or fail. In this tutorial, Claude Code runs that check itself.

Do you need a special testing CLI for Claude Code?

Not for unit tests: Claude Code already runs pytest, vitest or jest on its own. Kane CLI covers the layer those runners cannot reach: it opens the app in a real browser and reports whether the user flow works.

What you need

  • Node 18 or later, and Chrome installed
  • Claude Code
  • A TestMu AI account
  • A web app running locally. The example is a task app on http://localhost:3000; change the URL to yours.

The CLI is free to install. Runs use KaneAI credits. As of November 2026, you can start free with 10,000 credits, valid for 30 days.

Step 1: Install Kane CLI 

npm install -g @testmuai/kane-cli
kane-cli login --oauth   # opens the sign-in page in your browser
kane-cli whoami          # confirms you are signed in

There is nothing to wire into your repo or build config.

Step 2: Add the Claude Code skill 

npx @testmuai/kane-cli-skill

This installs the skill to ~/.claude/skills/kane-cli/. The skill teaches Claude Code when to call Kane CLI and how to read the result. If Claude Code is already running, restart it so it loads the skill. The skill docs cover installing it for one project only.

Step 3: Describe the flow and verify

The flow signs in, so put a test account's credentials in a variables file instead of the chat. Create .testmuai/variables/local.json, fill in the values yourself, and keep the file out of git:

{
  "username": { "value": "" },
  "password": { "value": "", "secret": true }
}

Start your app, then give Claude Code this prompt:

Open the running web app, sign in, add a task, mark it done, and confirm it
persists after a refresh. Use kane-cli. The app is at http://localhost:3000.
Sign in with {{username}} and {{password}} from .testmuai/variables/local.json.

On the first request, Claude Code runs a ready check: who is signed in, how many credits are left, whether Chrome was found, and whether your app is already running. Then it runs the flow.

By default the browser opens in a visible window, so you can watch. A run takes from 30 seconds to a few minutes.

When it finishes, Claude Code shows a result card with pass or fail, what happened, the credits used, and links to the evidence pack and the test case.

How Claude Code knows whether it passed

Kane CLI returns one JSON event per line (NDJSON) and an exit code:

Exit code Meaning
0 Pass
1 Fail
2 Setup or auth error; nothing ran
3 Timeout or cancelled

One thing to know about code 1: it also covers a start URL that doesn't load. If the app isn't running, you get a 1, not a 2, and the run still uses credits. Check that the URL opens before you start.

Every run also saves a .evidence file with the step-by-step trace, screenshots, video and logs, so there is proof behind the verdict.

Make it part of the edit loop

Once the skill is in place, ask in plain words:

Fix the coupon bug and verify it in a browser.

Claude Code makes the change, runs the flow, reads the result and fixes what failed, in one session. Two habits help:

  • End with the outcome. "Confirm the task is still marked done after a refresh" is a check. "Click Save" is not.
  • Never weaken the check to get a pass. If the app is wrong, fix the app.

Run the same kind of check in CI

Authenticate with your TestMu AI credentials, pass --headless and --timeout, and gate on the exit code:

kane-cli run "Go to $APP_URL and verify the task list is visible" \
  --agent --headless --timeout 180 \
  --username "$LT_USERNAME" --access-key "$LT_ACCESS_KEY"

Keep the credentials in your CI secret store. A non-zero exit code fails the job.

What this checks, and what it doesn't

Kane CLI checks the flow you describe, in a real browser: sign-in, forms, data that has to survive a refresh. It does not replace unit tests, and it won't check a flow nobody described. Start with the one or two journeys that would hurt most if they broke.

Based on our page Test web apps built with Claude Code.
