title: So schützen Sie einen API-Server mit Shirudo vor einer ungepatchten CVE
description:
So funktioniert Shirudo, kurz gesagt: Starten Sie ein Zielsystem, auf dem Shirudo läuft, wählen oder schreiben Sie ein Schutzschild (Shirudo nennt es upatch) für die CVE, signieren Sie es auf Ihrem Operator-Rechner, veröffentlichen Sie es in einem signierten Tree und lassen Sie das Zielsystem es abrufen. Das Schutzschild blockiert den Exploit-Pfad auf dem laufenden Server, und Sie löschen es aus dem Tree, sobald der echte Patch ausgeliefert wird.

Probieren Sie Apidog heute aus

Diese Anleitung führt genau diesen Kreislauf auf einem Java-API-Server durch, der CVE-2026-114938 ausgesetzt ist – der Schwachstelle im JDK-Base64-Decoder – und verwendet dabei das Schutzschild, das im Shirudo-Repository mitgeliefert wird. Alle Befehle stammen aus der Dokumentation des Projekts. Shirudo befindet sich in der Vorabversion und benötigt einen gepatchten Kernel sowie ein TPM. Betrachten Sie dies daher als Lab-Walkthrough.

Was ist Shirudo?

Shirudo ist eine Open-Source-Sicherheitslaufzeitumgebung auf BPF-Basis für Linux von OpenAI und Cisco. Operator bringen kleine signierte Micropatches aus – sogenannte Upatches –, die einen verwundbaren Codepfad auf einem laufenden System blockieren: an Kernel-Hooks (BPF-Upatches) oder innerhalb der JVM (Java-Agent-Upatches). Jedes Laden wird in das TPM eingemessen, sodass Sie nachweisen können, was auf einem Zielsystem läuft.

Der Name bedeutet auf Japanisch „Schild“. Für ein API-Team sind vier Eigenschaften entscheidend:

  • Signiert oder abgelehnt. Der Kernel lädt BPF nur über Loader, die mit einem Schlüssel in einem versiegelten .bpf-Keyring signiert sind. Selbst root auf dem Zielsystem kann also kein unsigniertes Schutzschild laden.
  • Eingemessen. Jedes Laden und Entladen erweitert ein TPM-Register; shirudo attest liefert einen Nachweis, den Sie offline verifizieren können.
  • Abgerufen. Ziele folgen einem signierten „Upatch-Tree“ in einer OCI-Registry und synchronisieren ihn in zeitlichen Abständen.
  • Temporär. Eine weitere signierte Operation entfernt ein Schutzschild, sobald der Fix ausgerollt ist.

Hintergrundinformationen dazu, warum Live-Kernel-Kontrollen zum Thema für API-Server geworden sind, finden Sie in unserer Analyse zu OpenAIs 948 Linux-Root-Exploits.

Welches Shirudo-Schutzschild passt zu Ihrem API-Server?

Shirudo kennt zwei Upatch-Typen, und nur einer davon reicht in Ihre Anwendung hinein. Bringen Sie das Schutzschild vor der Planung mit Ihrem Stack in Einklang:

Ihr API-Server Schutzschild-Typ Was heute möglich ist
Java (Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut) Java-Agent-Upatch Schützt eine JDK- oder App-Methode im Prozess, z. B. java-base64, java-sql-inj
Jeder Stack, Kernel-CVE auf dem Host BPF-Upatch an einem LSM-Hook Verweigert den Kernel-Pfad des Exploits, z. B. den AF_ALG-Splice-Block für CVE-2026-31431
Node.js-, Python-, Go-, PHP-App-Bug BPF-app-sandbox-Upatch Begrenzt, was ein Exploit als Nächstes tun kann: exec, ausgehende Verbindungen, Dateischreibvorgänge

Die letzte Zeile zeigt die ehrliche Grenze. Für einen Node.js-Bug wie die Node.js-Brotli-RCE gibt es keinen In-Process-Upatch-Typ. Die README zu app-sandbox im Repository besagt, dass die Sandbox „das Loch nicht schließt“: Sie verhindert, dass der Code des Angreifers Programme startet, Dateien schreibt oder ausgehende Verbindungen aufbaut. Die Laufzeitumgebung müssen Sie trotzdem aktualisieren.

Ein Hinweis zu Java: Eine JVM liest JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS beim Start, daher benötigt Ihr API-Prozess einen Neustart (kein JDK-Upgrade). Bei einer JVM in einem Container kann das java-base64-Jar mit java -jar java-base64.jar <pid> an den laufenden Prozess angehängt werden.

Schritt 1: Ein Shirudo-Testziel booten

Der Shirudo-Quickstart bootet eine QEMU-VM, die die Produktionsrichtlinie mit einem Software-TPM durchsetzt. Sie benötigen einen Linux-Host mit KVM (Lima auf einem Mac), clang und LLVM 23, OpenSSL 3.5+, Docker oder Podman und ulimit -l unlimited. Wenn Sie die Installation überspringen möchten, verwenden Sie das Online-Getting-Started-Lab.

git clone https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo && cd shirudo
testing/vm/kernel-artifact.sh fetch          # CI kernel with the signed-loader ABI
make && make shirudo-build                    # target binary + operator signing helper
export PATH="$PWD:$PWD/tools/shirudo-build:$PATH"

make stack-up && make vm VM_NAME=quickstart   # local registry/backend + test target
. build/test-vm/stack/env
make vm-enroll VM_NAME=quickstart
make vm-ssh VM_NAME=quickstart                # root shell on the target

Auf dem Zielsystem sollte shirudo status den Wert Status: ok ausgeben, wobei jede Bedingung OK ist. Skripte lesen shirudo status --json; --check beendet sich mit Exit-Code 1 bei tampered.

Der Signiercode liegt ausschließlich im Operator-Helfer shirudo-build, niemals auf einem Zielsystem. Diese Trennung macht „der Agent entwirft, Sie genehmigen“ zur Realität.

Schritt 2: Die CVE auf dem Zielsystem reproduzieren

Beweisen Sie die Exposition, bevor Sie sie abschirmen. Der Live-Patching-Leitfaden baut ein kleines Programm, das dem JDK-Base64-Decoder die präparierte Eingabe zuführt:

operator$ upatches/test/build.sh
target#   sh /workspace/shirudo/testing/end2end/guarded-jvm.sh \
            /workspace/shirudo/upatches/test/badDecoder.jar
badDecoder: no guard, the JDK refused: Last unit does not have enough valid bits
status 1

Die JDK der Test-VM lehnt die Eingabe von sich aus ab; eine verwundbare x86-64-JDK auf dem AVX-512-Pfad schreibt über das Zielarray hinaus. In Ihrer API betrifft das jeden Endpoint, der Base64 aus einer Anfrage decodiert: Uploads, Bildfelder, Webhook-Signaturen.

Schritt 3: Ihren Coding-Agenten das Schutzschild entwerfen lassen

Das Repository liefert Agent-Skills in .agents/skills/ mit, die Codex direkt und Claude Code über den Link .claude/skills liest. Der Skill upatch deckt das Schreiben, Bauen, Verpacken und Laden eines Upatch auf einem Testziel ab. Für eine CVE, die das Repository bereits abdeckt, verwenden Sie das mitgelieferte Schutzschild. Für die nächste geben Sie Ihrem Agenten einen klar abgegrenzten Prompt:

Use the upatch skill in this repo. Write a Java agent upatch named
java-base64-api that rejects the input shape behind CVE-2026-114938 in
java.util.Base64$Decoder before it writes, modeled on upatches/java-base64.
Build it with the test VM's throwaway keys only, load it on the quickstart
target, and show me badDecoder.jar refused and a valid Base64 payload
accepted. Do not touch my production keys or the production tree.

Der Agent baut und testet mit dem Wegwerf-Schlüssel der VM. Nur Ihr Produktionsschlüssel fügt dem Tree, dem Ihre Flotte folgt, eine Operation hinzu. Prüfen Sie den Guard wie jeden Patch: Er sollte ausschließlich die Exploit-Form ablehnen und ohne die Eingabebytes zu protokollieren, so wie es der mitgelieferte Agent tut.

Schritt 4: Das Schutzschild signieren, veröffentlichen und anhängen

Sobald Sie den Code genehmigt haben, signieren und veröffentlichen Sie vom Operator-Host aus. tools/put-shields führt shirudo bpm build und shirudo bpm push aus und erstellt einen Katalog mit dem Manifest-Digest:

KEYS=/tmp/shirudo-test-vm-private-$(id -u)/operator-keys/keys
tools/put-shields --version 1.0.0 --keys-dir "$KEYS" \
  --catalog build/tutorial/shields.json \
  --new-index oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching upatches/java-base64

JAVA_DIGEST=$(jq -r 'first(.shields[] | select(.package == "java-base64")).manifest_digest' build/tutorial/shields.json)

shirudo bpm tree append oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching/java-base64:1.0.0 \
  --package-digest "$JAVA_DIGEST" "$TREE" --tree-id local-tree --keys-dir "$KEYS"

Die Beefile deklariert fixes = ["CVE-2026-114938"] und wählt nur x86_64-Ziele aus. Ein Paket erreicht ein Ziel ausschließlich über den Tree.

Schritt 5: Bestätigen, dass der Endpoint erreichbar bleibt

Innerhalb eines Sync-Zyklus (auf der Test-VM höchstens 10 Sekunden) ruft shirudo-bpm-tree-sync.timer auf dem Zielsystem den Tree ab, verifiziert seine Signatur gegen den versiegelten Keyring und lädt das Schutzschild. Auf dem Zielsystem führen Sie nichts aus:

target# shirudo upatch list
  NAME          LOADED  TYPE  KIND  PAYLOAD
  java-base64   yes     load  java  fea9e483dd384ec7..

target# sh /workspace/shirudo/testing/end2end/guarded-jvm.sh \
          /workspace/shirudo/upatches/test/badDecoder.jar
Base64 guard installed on java.util.Base64$Decoder.decode0
Base64 guard rejected candidate: length=66, padding=1, remainder=2, alphabet=standard
badDecoder: refused by the guard
status 0

Der Guard weist die Eingabe ab, bevor der Decoder sie sieht; JDK und Anwendungs-Jar bleiben unverändert. Ein blockierter Aufruf löst eine IllegalArgumentException aus, sodass Ihre API ihren normalen Fehler bei ungültigen Eingaben zurückgibt. Beweisen Sie nun, dass legitimer Verkehr weiterhin funktioniert.

Lassen Sie Ihren Coding-Agenten die API mit der Apidog-CLI als Regressionstest prüfen

Ein Schutzschild, der auch echte Uploads kaputt macht, ist ein Ausfall, den Sie selbst verursacht haben. Lassen Sie nach dem Laden Claude Code oder Codex Ihre API-Tests über die Apidog-CLI ausführen.

Die Einrichtung besteht aus einer Installation und einem Login: npm install -g apidog-cli, dann apidog auth login. Danach geben Sie Ihrem Agenten einen Prompt:

The java-base64 Shirudo shield just loaded on staging. List the POST
endpoints in my Apidog project, run the regression scenario against the
Testing environment, and tell me which requests that carry Base64 bodies
failed. Upload the report.

apidog run arbeitet ausschließlich mit Flags: -t wählt das Szenario, -e die Umgebung, -r die Reporter, und --upload-report sendet die Übersicht an Apidog für Ihr Team:

apidog endpoint list --project 1314366 --method post
apidog run -t <scenarioId> --project 1314366 -e 6334890 -r cli,json --upload-report

Wenn eine gültige Payload jetzt fehlschlägt, ist der Guard zu weit gefasst: Schicken Sie die fehlgeschlagene Anfrage zurück an den Agenten aus Schritt 3 und bauen Sie neu. Unsere Anleitungen zu Apidog-CLI in Claude Code und Apidog-CLI in Codex beschreiben die Agent-Einrichtung im Detail.

Sobald ein Team diesen Kreislauf bei jeder CVE durchläuft, vervielfacht sich die Agentenarbeit: ein Agent entwirft das Schutzschild, ein anderer führt die Regressionssuite aus, ein Mensch signiert. Sharkly ist ein Board, auf dem Sie diese Läufe als Aufgaben an die Coding-Agenten auf Ihren eigenen Computern (Claude Code, Codex und andere) verteilen und die Ergebnisse prüfen, bevor irgendetwas ausgeliefert wird. Der Einstieg ist kostenlos.

Schritt 6: Das Schutzschild nach dem Patch zurücknehmen

Schutzschilder sind temporär. Sobald die gepatchte JDK ausgerollt und Ihre API darauf neu gestartet ist, hängen Sie eine Löschoperation an:

shirudo bpm tree append oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching/java-base64:1.0.0 \
  --package-digest "$JAVA_DIGEST" "$TREE" --tree-id local-tree \
  --keys-dir "$KEYS" --op delete

Der Tree wächst nur: Das Löschen ist eine weitere signierte Operation, während das Hinzufügen weiterhin aufgezeichnet bleibt. Nach dem nächsten Sync gibt shirudo upatch list den Wert none aus, und das Entladen wird wie das Laden in das TPM eingemessen.

Was Shirudo nicht für Sie erledigt

Seien Sie sich der Grenzen bewusst, bevor Sie das Ihrem Plattformteam vorstellen:

  • Heute ist ein eigener Kernel nötig. Produktionsziele benötigen einen Kernel mit der Signed-Loader-ABI und Shirudos Kernel-Patches sowie TPM 2.0. Ein unverändertes Distributions-Image auf Ihrer Cloud-VM läuft noch nicht damit. Siehe die Systemanforderungen.
  • Es behebt keine App-Logikfehler. Eine Auth-Bypass-Schwachstelle wie der Next.js-Middleware-Bypass ist ein Logikfehler in Ihrem Code; ein Schutzschild kann nicht wissen, welche Anfragen hätten abgelehnt werden müssen.
  • Von Agenten geschriebener Kernel-Code muss geprüft werden. Die Kritik an Live-Kernel-Kontrollen von Agenten war erheblich. Die Signaturtrennung hilft nur, wenn ein Mensch den Upatch liest.

FAQ

Ist Shirudo kostenlos? Ja. Es ist Open Source unter BSD-2-Clause, wobei die BPF-Programme dual unter BSD/GPL lizenziert sind. Es befindet sich in der Vorabversion, rechnen Sie also mit Änderungen.

Erfordert Shirudo einen Neustart, um ein Schutzschild anzuwenden? Bei BPF-Upatches ist kein Neustart nötig: Das Zielsystem lädt sie in den laufenden Kernel. Java-Upatches erreichen JVMs, die nach dem Laden gestartet werden, daher benötigt Ihr API-Prozess einen Neustart – oder Sie hängen das Agent-Jar an den laufenden Prozess an.

Können KI-Agenten Shirudo-Schutzschilder schreiben? Ja. Das Repository liefert einen upatch-Skill mit, den Codex und Claude Code lesen. Der Agent kann mit Wegwerf-Schlüsseln bauen und testen; nur Ihr Operator-Schlüssel veröffentlicht im Tree, dem die Ziele folgen.

Funktioniert Shirudo mit Node.js- oder Python-API-Servern? Nicht prozessintern. Sie können BPF-Upatches für Kernel-CVEs auf dem Host verwenden und den app-sandbox-Upatch einsetzen, um zu begrenzen, was ein Exploit als Nächstes tut. Die Laufzeitumgebung müssen Sie dennoch aktualisieren.

Ersetzt Shirudo das Patchen? Nein. Ein Schutzschild gewinnt Zeit, während Sie den echten Fix testen und ausrollen. Sobald der Fix live ist, hängen Sie eine Löschoperation an, und das Schutzschild wird entfernt.

Fazit

Shirudo verwandelt „wir können erst am Donnerstag patchen“ in ein signiertes, eingemessenes, entfernbares Schutzschild. Für eine Java-API, die CVE-2026-114938 ausgesetzt ist: Laden Sie das mitgelieferte java-base64-Schutzschild über den Tree, beweisen Sie, dass der Exploit abgewiesen und legitimer Verkehr zugelassen wird, und löschen Sie es dann, wenn die gepatchte JDK verfügbar ist. Lassen Sie Ihren Agenten das nächste Schutzschild entwerfen; der Signaturschlüssel bleibt bei einem Menschen.

title: Como usar o Shirudo para proteger um servidor de API de uma CVE não corrigida
description:
Como usar o Shirudo em um servidor de API: shields assinados para uma CVE do JDK

Como usar o Shirudo, em resumo: inicie um alvo que execute o Shirudo, escolha ou escreva um shield (o Shirudo chama isso de upatch) para a CVE, assine-o na sua máquina de operação, publique-o em uma árvore assinada e deixe o alvo fazer o pull. O shield bloqueia o caminho do exploit no servidor em execução, e você o remove da árvore quando o patch real for lançado.

Experimente o Apidog hoje

Este guia percorre esse ciclo em um servidor de API Java exposto à CVE-2026-114938, a falha do decodificador Base64 do JDK, usando o shield que vem no repositório do Shirudo. Todos os comandos vêm da documentação do projeto. O Shirudo está em pré-lançamento e exige um kernel com patches e um TPM, então encare isto como um tutorial de laboratório.

O que é o Shirudo?

O Shirudo é um runtime de segurança open-source baseado em BPF para Linux, da OpenAI e da Cisco. Os operadores distribuem pequenos micropatches assinados, chamados upatches, que bloqueiam um caminho de código vulnerável em um sistema em execução: em hooks do kernel (upatches BPF) ou dentro da JVM (upatches de agente Java). Cada carregamento é medido no TPM, então você pode provar o que um alvo executa.

O nome significa “escudo” em japonês. Quatro propriedades importam para uma equipe de API:

  • Assinado ou recusado. O kernel só carrega BPF por meio de loaders assinados por uma chave em um keyring .bpf selado, então o root no alvo não consegue carregar um shield não assinado.
  • Medido. Cada carregamento e descarregamento estende um registro do TPM; shirudo attest retorna evidências que você verifica offline.
  • Puxado (pull). Os alvos seguem uma “árvore de upatches” assinada em um registry OCI e a sincronizam periodicamente.
  • Temporário. Mais uma operação assinada remove um shield quando a correção já foi distribuída.

Para entender o contexto de por que controles de kernel em tempo real se tornaram um assunto para servidores de API, leia nossa análise sobre as 948 exploits de root no Linux da OpenAI.

Qual shield do Shirudo se encaixa no seu servidor de API?

O Shirudo tem dois tipos de upatch, e apenas um deles alcança o interior da sua aplicação. Combine o shield com a sua stack antes de planejar qualquer coisa:

Seu servidor de API Tipo de shield O que ele pode fazer hoje
Java (Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut) Upatch de agente Java Protege um método do JDK ou da aplicação no próprio processo, ex.: java-base64, java-sql-inj
Qualquer stack, CVE de kernel no host Upatch BPF em um hook LSM Recusa o caminho do exploit no kernel, ex.: o bloqueio de splice em AF_ALG para a CVE-2026-31431
Bug de aplicação em Node.js, Python, Go, PHP Upatch BPF app-sandbox Limita o que o exploit faz depois: exec, conexões de saída, gravações em arquivo

Essa última linha é o limite honesto. Para um bug em Node.js como o RCE de brotli no Node.js, não existe um tipo de upatch no próprio processo. O README do app-sandbox no repositório diz que a sandbox “não fecha o buraco”: ela impede que o código do atacante inicie programas, grave arquivos ou faça conexões de saída. Você ainda precisa atualizar o runtime.

Uma ressalva sobre Java: a JVM lê JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS na inicialização, então o seu processo de API precisa de um restart (não de uma atualização do JDK). Para uma JVM em contêiner, o jar java-base64 pode se anexar ao processo em execução com java -jar java-base64.jar <pid>.

Passo 1: inicie um alvo de teste do Shirudo

O quickstart do Shirudo inicia uma VM QEMU que aplica a política de produção com um TPM de software. Você precisa de um host Linux com KVM (Lima em um Mac), clang e LLVM 23, OpenSSL 3.5+, Docker ou Podman, e ulimit -l unlimited. Para pular a instalação, use o laboratório online de primeiros passos.

git clone https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo && cd shirudo
testing/vm/kernel-artifact.sh fetch          # CI kernel with the signed-loader ABI
make && make shirudo-build                    # target binary + operator signing helper
export PATH="$PWD:$PWD/tools/shirudo-build:$PATH"

make stack-up && make vm VM_NAME=quickstart   # local registry/backend + test target
. build/test-vm/stack/env
make vm-enroll VM_NAME=quickstart
make vm-ssh VM_NAME=quickstart                # root shell on the target

No alvo, shirudo status deve exibir Status: ok com todas as condições OK. Scripts leem shirudo status --json; --check retorna código 1 em caso de tampered.

O código de assinatura fica apenas no helper de operação shirudo-build, nunca em um alvo. Essa separação é o que torna real o “o agente redige, você aprova”.

Passo 2: reproduza a CVE no alvo

Comprove a exposição antes de protegê-la. O guia de live patching cria um pequeno programa que alimenta o decodificador Base64 do JDK com a entrada maliciosa:

operator$ upatches/test/build.sh
target#   sh /workspace/shirudo/testing/end2end/guarded-jvm.sh \
            /workspace/shirudo/upatches/test/badDecoder.jar
badDecoder: no guard, the JDK refused: Last unit does not have enough valid bits
status 1

O JDK da VM de teste recusa a entrada por conta própria; um JDK x86-64 vulnerável no caminho AVX-512 grava além do array de destino. Na sua API, isso vale para qualquer endpoint que decodifique Base64 de uma requisição: uploads, campos de imagem, assinaturas de webhook.

Passo 3: deixe seu agente de código redigir o shield

O repositório inclui skills para agentes em .agents/skills/, que o Codex lê diretamente e o Claude Code lê por meio do link .claude/skills. A skill upatch cobre como escrever, compilar, empacotar e carregar um upatch em um alvo de teste. Para uma CVE que o repositório já cobre, use o shield fornecido. Para a próxima, dê ao seu agente um prompt bem delimitado:

Use the upatch skill in this repo. Write a Java agent upatch named
java-base64-api that rejects the input shape behind CVE-2026-114938 in
java.util.Base64$Decoder before it writes, modeled on upatches/java-base64.
Build it with the test VM's throwaway keys only, load it on the quickstart
target, and show me badDecoder.jar refused and a valid Base64 payload
accepted. Do not touch my production keys or the production tree.

O agente compila e testa com a chave descartável da VM. Apenas a sua chave de produção adiciona uma operação à árvore que a sua frota segue. Revise a proteção como faria com qualquer patch: ela deve rejeitar apenas o formato do exploit e registrar logs sem os bytes de entrada, como faz o agente fornecido.

Passo 4: assine, publique e anexe o shield

Depois de aprovar o código, assine e publique a partir do host de operação. O tools/put-shields executa shirudo bpm build e shirudo bpm push e grava um catálogo com o digest do manifesto:

KEYS=/tmp/shirudo-test-vm-private-$(id -u)/operator-keys/keys
tools/put-shields --version 1.0.0 --keys-dir "$KEYS" \
  --catalog build/tutorial/shields.json \
  --new-index oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching upatches/java-base64

JAVA_DIGEST=$(jq -r 'first(.shields[] | select(.package == "java-base64")).manifest_digest' build/tutorial/shields.json)

shirudo bpm tree append oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching/java-base64:1.0.0 \
  --package-digest "$JAVA_DIGEST" "$TREE" --tree-id local-tree --keys-dir "$KEYS"

O Beefile declara fixes = ["CVE-2026-114938"] e seleciona apenas alvos x86_64. Um pacote só chega a um alvo por meio da árvore.

Passo 5: confirme que o endpoint continua no ar

Dentro de um ciclo de sincronização (no máximo 10 segundos na VM de teste), o shirudo-bpm-tree-sync.timer do alvo busca a árvore, verifica a assinatura dela contra o keyring selado e carrega o shield. Você não executa nada no alvo:

target# shirudo upatch list
  NAME          LOADED  TYPE  KIND  PAYLOAD
  java-base64   yes     load  java  fea9e483dd384ec7..

target# sh /workspace/shirudo/testing/end2end/guarded-jvm.sh \
          /workspace/shirudo/upatches/test/badDecoder.jar
Base64 guard installed on java.util.Base64$Decoder.decode0
Base64 guard rejected candidate: length=66, padding=1, remainder=2, alphabet=standard
badDecoder: refused by the guard
status 0

A proteção recusa a entrada antes que o decodificador a veja; o JDK e o jar da aplicação permanecem inalterados. Uma chamada bloqueada lança IllegalArgumentException, então a sua API retorna o erro normal de entrada inválida. Agora comprove que o tráfego legítimo continua funcionando.

Deixe seu agente de código testar a API com o Apidog CLI

Um shield que também quebra uploads reais é uma indisponibilidade que você mesmo causou. Depois que ele carregar, peça ao Claude Code ou ao Codex para executar seus testes de API pelo Apidog CLI.

A configuração é uma instalação e um login: npm install -g apidog-cli, depois apidog auth login. Em seguida, dê ao seu agente um único prompt:

The java-base64 Shirudo shield just loaded on staging. List the POST
endpoints in my Apidog project, run the regression scenario against the
Testing environment, and tell me which requests that carry Base64 bodies
failed. Upload the report.

O apidog run funciona apenas com flags: -t escolhe o cenário, -e o ambiente, -r os reporters, e --upload-report envia a visão geral para o Apidog, para a sua equipe:

apidog endpoint list --project 1314366 --method post
apidog run -t <scenarioId> --project 1314366 -e 6334890 -r cli,json --upload-report

Se um payload válido passar a falhar, a proteção está ampla demais: envie a requisição que falhou de volta ao agente do Passo 3 e recompile. Nossos guias sobre Apidog CLI no Claude Code e Apidog CLI no Codex cobrem a configuração do agente em detalhes.

Quando uma equipe passa a rodar esse ciclo em cada CVE, o trabalho dos agentes se multiplica: um agente redige o shield, outro executa a suíte de regressão, um humano assina. O Sharkly é um board onde você distribui essas execuções como tarefas para os agentes de código nos seus próprios computadores (Claude Code, Codex e outros) e revisa o que eles produzem antes de qualquer coisa ir para produção. É grátis para começar.

Passo 6: remova o shield depois do patch

Shields são temporários. Assim que o JDK corrigido for distribuído e sua API reiniciar nele, anexe uma exclusão:

shirudo bpm tree append oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching/java-base64:1.0.0 \
  --package-digest "$JAVA_DIGEST" "$TREE" --tree-id local-tree \
  --keys-dir "$KEYS" --op delete

A árvore só cresce: a exclusão é mais uma operação assinada, com a adição ainda registrada. Depois da próxima sincronização, shirudo upatch list exibe none, e o descarregamento é medido no TPM como o carregamento.

O que o Shirudo não faz por você

Seja realista quanto aos limites antes de apresentar isso ao time de plataforma:

  • Hoje ele exige um kernel customizado. Alvos de produção precisam de um kernel com a ABI de loader assinado e os patches de kernel do Shirudo, além de TPM 2.0. Uma imagem de distro padrão na sua VM de nuvem ainda não vai rodá-lo. Veja os requisitos de sistema.
  • Ele não corrige bugs de lógica da aplicação. Um bypass de autenticação como o bypass de middleware do Next.js é uma falha de lógica no seu código; um shield não tem como saber quais requisições deveriam ter sido rejeitadas.
  • Código de kernel escrito por agente precisa de revisão. As críticas ao lançamento se concentraram em agentes escrevendo controles de kernel em tempo real. A separação da assinatura só ajuda se um humano ler o upatch.

Perguntas frequentes

O Shirudo é gratuito? Sim. É open source sob a licença BSD-2-Clause, com os programas BPF em licença dupla BSD/GPL. Está em pré-lançamento, então espere mudanças.

O Shirudo exige reinicialização para aplicar um shield? Não há reboot para upatches BPF: o alvo os carrega no kernel em execução. Upaches Java alcançam JVMs iniciadas depois do carregamento, então o seu processo de API precisa de um restart, ou você anexa o jar do agente ao processo em execução.

Agentes de IA conseguem escrever shields do Shirudo? Sim. O repositório inclui uma skill upatch que o Codex e o Claude Code leem. O agente pode compilar e testar com chaves descartáveis; apenas a sua chave de operação publica na árvore que os alvos seguem.

O Shirudo funciona com servidores de API em Node.js ou Python? Não no próprio processo. Você pode usar upatches BPF para CVEs de kernel no host e o upatch app-sandbox para limitar o que o exploit faz depois, mas ainda precisa atualizar o runtime.

O Shirudo substitui a aplicação de patches? Não. Um shield ganha tempo enquanto você testa e distribui a correção real. Quando a correção está em produção, você anexa uma exclusão e o shield sai.

Conclusão

O Shirudo transforma “não conseguimos aplicar o patch até quinta” em um shield assinado, medido e removível. Para uma API Java exposta à CVE-2026-114938: carregue o shield java-base64 fornecido por meio da árvore, comprove que o exploit é recusado e que o tráfego real passa, e então remova-o quando o JDK corrigido chegar. Deixe seu agente redigir o próximo shield; mantenha a chave de assinatura com um humano.

title: How to Use Shirudo to Shield an API Server From an Unpatched CVE
description:
How to use Shirudo, in short: boot a target that runs Shirudo, pick or write a shield (Shirudo calls it a upatch) for the CVE, sign it on your operator machine, publish it to a signed tree, and let the target pull it. The shield blocks the exploit path on the running server, and you delete it from the tree once the real patch ships.

Try Apidog today

This guide runs that loop on a Java API server exposed to CVE-2026-114938, the JDK Base64 decoder flaw, using the shield that ships in the Shirudo repository. Every command comes from the project's docs. Shirudo is pre-release and needs a patched kernel and a TPM, so treat this as a lab walkthrough.

What is Shirudo?

Shirudo is an open-source, BPF-based security runtime for Linux from OpenAI and Cisco. Operators ship small signed micropatches, called upatches, that block a vulnerable code path on a running system: at kernel hooks (BPF upatches) or inside the JVM (Java agent upatches). Each load is measured into the TPM, so you can prove what a target runs.

The name is Japanese for "shield". Four properties matter for an API team:

  • Signed or refused. The kernel loads BPF only through loaders signed by a key in a sealed .bpf keyring, so root on the target can't load an unsigned shield.
  • Measured. Every load and unload extends a TPM register; shirudo attest returns evidence you verify offline.
  • Pulled. Targets follow a signed "upatch tree" in an OCI registry and sync it on a timer.
  • Temporary. One more signed operation removes a shield once the fix is rolled out.

For background on why live kernel controls became an API-server topic, read our breakdown of OpenAI's 948 Linux root exploits.

Which Shirudo shield fits your API server?

Shirudo has two upatch types, and only one of them reaches inside your application. Match the shield to your stack before you plan anything:

Your API server Shield type What it can do today
Java (Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut) Java agent upatch Guards a JDK or app method in-process, e.g. java-base64, java-sql-inj
Any stack, kernel CVE on the host BPF upatch at an LSM hook Refuses the exploit's kernel path, e.g. the AF_ALG splice block for CVE-2026-31431
Node.js, Python, Go, PHP app bug BPF app-sandbox upatch Limits what an exploit does next: exec, outbound connections, file writes

That last row is the honest limit. For a Node.js bug like the Node.js brotli RCE, there's no in-process upatch type. The repo's app-sandbox README says the sandbox "does not close the hole": it stops the attacker's code from starting programs, writing files or connecting out. You still upgrade the runtime.

One Java caveat: a JVM reads JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS at start, so your API process needs one restart (not a JDK upgrade). For a JVM in a container, the java-base64 jar can attach to the running process with java -jar java-base64.jar <pid>.

Step 1: Boot a Shirudo test target

The Shirudo quickstart boots a QEMU VM that enforces the production policy with a software TPM. You need a Linux host with KVM (Lima on a Mac), clang and LLVM 23, OpenSSL 3.5+, Docker or Podman, and ulimit -l unlimited. To skip the install, use the online getting-started lab.

git clone https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo && cd shirudo
testing/vm/kernel-artifact.sh fetch          # CI kernel with the signed-loader ABI
make && make shirudo-build                    # target binary + operator signing helper
export PATH="$PWD:$PWD/tools/shirudo-build:$PATH"

make stack-up && make vm VM_NAME=quickstart   # local registry/backend + test target
. build/test-vm/stack/env
make vm-enroll VM_NAME=quickstart
make vm-ssh VM_NAME=quickstart                # root shell on the target

On the target, shirudo status should print Status: ok with every condition OK. Scripts read shirudo status --json; --check exits 1 on tampered.

Signing code lives only in the operator helper shirudo-build, never on a target. That split makes "the agent drafts, you approve" real.

Step 2: Reproduce the CVE on the target

Prove the exposure before you shield it. The live-patching guide builds a small program that feeds the JDK Base64 decoder the crafted input:

operator$ upatches/test/build.sh
target#   sh /workspace/shirudo/testing/end2end/guarded-jvm.sh \
            /workspace/shirudo/upatches/test/badDecoder.jar
badDecoder: no guard, the JDK refused: Last unit does not have enough valid bits
status 1

The test VM's JDK refuses the input itself; a vulnerable x86-64 JDK on the AVX-512 path writes past the destination array. In your API, that's any endpoint that decodes Base64 from a request: uploads, image fields, webhook signatures.

Step 3: Let your coding agent draft the shield

The repo ships agent skills in .agents/skills/, which Codex reads directly and Claude Code reads through the .claude/skills link. The upatch skill covers writing, building, packaging and loading a upatch on a test target. For a CVE the repo already covers, use the shipped shield. For the next one, give your agent a scoped prompt:

Use the upatch skill in this repo. Write a Java agent upatch named
java-base64-api that rejects the input shape behind CVE-2026-114938 in
java.util.Base64$Decoder before it writes, modeled on upatches/java-base64.
Build it with the test VM's throwaway keys only, load it on the quickstart
target, and show me badDecoder.jar refused and a valid Base64 payload
accepted. Do not touch my production keys or the production tree.

The agent builds and tests with the VM's throwaway key. Only your production key adds an operation to the tree your fleet follows. Review the guard like any patch: it should reject the exploit shape only and log without the input bytes, as the shipped agent does.

Step 4: Sign, publish and append the shield

Once you approve the code, sign and publish from the operator host. tools/put-shields runs shirudo bpm build and shirudo bpm push and writes a catalog with the manifest digest:

KEYS=/tmp/shirudo-test-vm-private-$(id -u)/operator-keys/keys
tools/put-shields --version 1.0.0 --keys-dir "$KEYS" \
  --catalog build/tutorial/shields.json \
  --new-index oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching upatches/java-base64

JAVA_DIGEST=$(jq -r 'first(.shields[] | select(.package == "java-base64")).manifest_digest' build/tutorial/shields.json)

shirudo bpm tree append oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching/java-base64:1.0.0 \
  --package-digest "$JAVA_DIGEST" "$TREE" --tree-id local-tree --keys-dir "$KEYS"

The Beefile declares fixes = ["CVE-2026-114938"] and selects x86_64 targets only. A package reaches a target only through the tree.

Step 5: Confirm the endpoint stays up

Within one sync (at most 10 seconds on the test VM), the target's shirudo-bpm-tree-sync.timer fetches the tree, verifies its signature against the sealed keyring and loads the shield. You run nothing on the target:

target# shirudo upatch list
  NAME          LOADED  TYPE  KIND  PAYLOAD
  java-base64   yes     load  java  fea9e483dd384ec7..

target# sh /workspace/shirudo/testing/end2end/guarded-jvm.sh \
          /workspace/shirudo/upatches/test/badDecoder.jar
Base64 guard installed on java.util.Base64$Decoder.decode0
Base64 guard rejected candidate: length=66, padding=1, remainder=2, alphabet=standard
badDecoder: refused by the guard
status 0

The guard refuses the input before the decoder sees it; the JDK and application jar stay unchanged. A blocked call throws IllegalArgumentException, so your API returns its normal bad-input error. Now prove legitimate traffic still works.

Let your coding agent regression-test the API with Apidog CLI

A shield that also breaks real uploads is an outage you caused. After it loads, have Claude Code or Codex run your API tests through Apidog CLI.

Setup is one install and a login: npm install -g apidog-cli, then apidog auth login. Then give your agent one prompt:

The java-base64 Shirudo shield just loaded on staging. List the POST
endpoints in my Apidog project, run the regression scenario against the
Testing environment, and tell me which requests that carry Base64 bodies
failed. Upload the report.

apidog run is flag-only: -t picks the scenario, -e the environment, -r the reporters, and --upload-report sends the overview to Apidog for your team:

apidog endpoint list --project 1314366 --method post
apidog run -t <scenarioId> --project 1314366 -e 6334890 -r cli,json --upload-report

If a valid payload now fails, the guard is too broad: send the failing request back to the Step 3 agent and rebuild. Our guides to Apidog CLI in Claude Code and Apidog CLI in Codex cover the agent setup in detail.

Once a team runs this loop on every CVE, the agent work multiplies: one agent drafting the shield, one running the regression suite, a human signing. Sharkly is a board where you hand those runs out as tasks to the coding agents on your own computers (Claude Code, Codex and others) and review what they produce before anything ships. It's free to start.

Step 6: Take the shield back after the patch

Shields are temporary. Once the patched JDK is rolled out and your API restarted on it, append a delete:

shirudo bpm tree append oci://127.0.0.1:15444/live-patching/java-base64:1.0.0 \
  --package-digest "$JAVA_DIGEST" "$TREE" --tree-id local-tree \
  --keys-dir "$KEYS" --op delete

The tree only grows: the delete is one more signed operation, with the add still on record. After the next sync, shirudo upatch list prints none, and the unload is measured into the TPM like the load.

What Shirudo won't do for you

Be clear-eyed about the limits before you pitch this to your platform team:

  • It needs a custom kernel today. Production targets need a kernel with the signed-loader ABI and Shirudo's kernel patches, plus TPM 2.0. A stock distro image on your cloud VM won't run it yet. See the system requirements.
  • It doesn't fix app-logic bugs. An auth bypass such as the Next.js middleware bypass is a logic flaw in your code; a shield can't know which requests should have been rejected.
  • Agent-written kernel code needs review. Launch pushback centred on agents writing live kernel controls. The signing split helps only if a human reads the upatch.

FAQ

Is Shirudo free to use? Yes. It's open source under BSD-2-Clause, with BPF programs dual-licensed BSD/GPL. It's pre-release, so expect changes.

Does Shirudo require a reboot to apply a shield? No reboot for BPF upatches: the target loads them on the running kernel. Java upatches reach JVMs started after the load, so your API process needs one restart, or you attach the agent jar to the running process.

Can AI agents write Shirudo shields? Yes. The repo ships an upatch skill that Codex and Claude Code read. The agent can build and test with throwaway keys; only your operator key publishes to the tree targets follow.

Does Shirudo work with Node.js or Python API servers? Not in-process. You can use BPF upatches for kernel CVEs on the host, and the app-sandbox upatch to limit what an exploit does next, but you still need to upgrade the runtime.

Is Shirudo a replacement for patching? No. A shield buys time while you test and roll out the real fix. Once the fix is live, you append a delete and the shield comes off.

Conclusion

Shirudo turns "we can't patch until Thursday" into a signed, measured, removable shield. For a Java API exposed to CVE-2026-114938: load the shipped java-base64 shield through the tree, prove the exploit is refused and real traffic passes, then delete it when the patched JDK lands. Let your agent draft the next shield; keep the signing key with a human.

title: CSS revert-rule: undo one rule, not the whole layer
description:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

CSS now has a way to say "pretend this rule didn't set this property": the revert-rule keyword. It has been Baseline Newly available since September 2026, and it's the missing piece between revert and revert-layer, which both throw away much more than you usually want.

The demo above is a small cascade lab. The card is a real element with real CSS: an inline style, two rules in a theme layer, one rule in a base layer and the browser default. Change the value of a level to revert-rule, revert-layer or revert and the stack shows which declaration ends up winning, while the browser paints the result.

The three ways to roll back the cascade

Until now we had two "undo" keywords, and both work on big groups of declarations:

  • revert rolls back to the previous origin. Inside your own styles, that means falling all the way back to the browser's default styles.
  • revert-layer rolls back to the previous cascade layer. Every other rule in the same layer is ignored too.
  • revert-rule rolls back only the current style rule. Other rules in the same layer still apply.

The specification puts it precisely: the cascaded value is rolled back "as if the current style rule had not been present at all." Then the cascade simply picks the next declaration in line: another rule in the same layer, an earlier layer, another origin, or the inherited or initial value.

Try it in the demo. With .chip.hot { background: revert-rule } the card turns teal, because the plain .chip rule in the same layer takes over. Switch to revert-layer and the whole theme layer is skipped, so you get the dark base background. With revert you lose all your author styles for that property and end up with a transparent card.

The code

This is the stylesheet the demo writes into a <style> element. JavaScript only swaps the value of each declaration, so the browser does the actual cascade:

@layer base, theme;

@layer base {
  .chip { background: var(--g-base); border-radius: 18px; }
}

@layer theme {
  .chip     { background: var(--g-chip); border-radius: 28px; }
  .chip.hot {
    background: revert-rule; /* act as if this rule didn't set background */
    border-radius: if(style(--shape: sharp): 4px; else: revert-rule);
  }
}

The background: revert-rule line on its own is a teaching example. If you always want the previous rule to win, you can just delete the line. The keyword earns its place in two situations.

Inside if(). This is the use case both the specification and Chromium's intent to ship highlight. if() returns a value depending on a condition, but if you wanted the else branch to keep what another rule set, you had to copy that rule's value into it. With revert-rule the else branch can mean "do nothing here". In the demo, tick --shape: sharp: the corner becomes 4px. Untick it and the declaration steps aside, so the 28px from .chip comes back. The .chip.hot rule doesn't need to know what that radius is.

In the style attribute. MDN notes that the style attribute counts as its own style rule, so style="color: revert-rule" falls back to whatever your stylesheet says. The demo's top level lets you check this: an inline revert-rule hands control back to .chip.hot.

Two more details from MDN that the demo confirms. You can chain them: if .chip.hot and .chip both say revert-rule, the cascade skips both and lands on the base layer. It also works on any property, including the all shorthand.

Browser support and gotchas

According to webstatus.dev and MDN's compatibility data, revert-rule shipped in Firefox 150, Chrome and Edge 148, and Safari 27. That made it Baseline Newly available in September 2026. I ran the demo in current Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and in all three the computed background matched the expected winner in every combination.

Things to keep in mind:

  • Old browsers drop the declaration. An unknown keyword makes the whole declaration invalid, and invalid declarations are ignored. For a plain background: revert-rule that happens to give the same result, which is why the demo still makes sense there. Don't rely on that once if() or anything else is in the value. To detect support, use @supports (color: revert-rule) or CSS.supports('color', 'revert-rule'), as the demo does.
  • if() is not Baseline. MDN lists it as limited availability. Its compatibility data has it in Chrome and Edge 137 and Safari 27.3, but not in Firefox. In the demo, Firefox shows a warning and the corner stays rounded. Treat if() with revert-rule as progressive enhancement and make sure the result you get without it is acceptable.
  • Animations are a special case. The specification says that inside the animation origin, revert-rule behaves like revert-layer.
  • It isn't a specificity tool. revert-rule doesn't make a rule lose to anything. It removes that one declaration from the competition, and only for the element the rule matches.

What to keep an eye on

  • if() reaching Firefox. That's when the if(...; else: revert-rule) pattern becomes safe for core styles rather than just enhancements.
  • Design systems. A component rule that only applies a token under a condition, and otherwise leaves the value to whoever set it before, is exactly what this keyword allows. I expect it to replace a fair number of "re-declare the default" overrides.
  • The spec is still a draft. CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5 is an Editor's Draft, so the edge cases could still be refined.

Sources

  • revert-rule - CSS | MDN
  • CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5: the revert-rule keyword
  • Intent to Ship: The revert-rule Keyword (blink-dev)
  • revert-rule on webstatus.dev
  • if() - CSS | MDN

Originally published at richi.codes.

title: Importing an Existing GBase 8a Cluster into GDOM
description:
GDOM (GBase Database Operation Manager) is the operations and management platform GBASE ships for its GBase 8a MPP analytical database. A freshly installed GDOM contains no cluster information at all. This post walks through importing an existing gbase cluster into GDOM, including the first-login scenario after a clean installation.

Adding the Cluster

From the top menu, open Clusters, choose Cluster Management on the left, click Add, enter a name and description, and confirm to create the cluster entry.

On first use there are two options:

  • Install a new cluster: GDOM deploys a brand-new cluster (covered in separate documentation).
  • Import an existing cluster: bring a cluster already running in production under management — the path this post follows.

Importing an Existing Cluster

Fill in the Connection Information

Enter the cluster connection information and let GDOM fetch the cluster details. Careful: the dba user and password here are the OS user that installed the cluster, not a database account — this is the step people most often get wrong.

Select the Cluster Version

If the cluster version is not in the list, upload the version package first, then pick the correct one. Next, enter the database username and password, and the tool runs a parameter check.

Deployment Plan

The deployment plan is single-instance in most cases. You set the agent installation directory and port. For the network topology, the example uses a single-plane setup (business and data traffic share the same IP). Another parameter check follows.

Confirm and Import

After confirming everything is correct, the import starts. If anything looks wrong, you can go back one step and fix it. The wizard then moves through the import progress view to completion.

After the Import

Once the import finishes, the cluster status takes a few minutes to refresh — typically 1–2 minutes before it shows a healthy state. The GDOM home page also picks up the cluster's information.

Going forward, keep in mind why this path matters: for a cluster already carrying production workloads, importing it into management is far safer than rebuilding. GDOM only collects information and deploys its agents into the existing gbase database environment — it never touches the data inside the cluster.

title: كيف تختبر قصّ صور المنتجات في بطاقات متجرك على الجوال؟
description:
افتح شبكة المنتجات على جوال بعرض 320 بكسل ثم 390 بكسل، وانظر إلى أصغر تفصيل يحتاجه العميل لتمييز المنتج. إذا اختفى في البطاقة وظهر عند فتح الصورة الأصلية، جرّب object-fit: contain على بطاقة واحدة. ظهور التفصيل بعد التغيير يعني أن إطار البطاقة قصّه. بعدها تستطيع تعديل طريقة العرض أو تجهيز صورة للبطاقة بنسبة إطارها.

غطاء واحد يكشف المشكلة

لديك متجر يبيع عبوات ماء بغطاءين. إحداهما مزوّدة بحلقة برتقالية يمكن الإمساك بها. في صفحة المنتج تظهر الحلقة مع الغطاء، لكن في شبكة المنتجات يملأ جسم العبوة معظم البطاقة، وقد يبدو الخياران متشابهين من أول نظرة.

جرّبت العرض بصورة العبوة نفسها على خلفيات بثلاث نسب. ارتفاع الملف في الحالات الثلاث 600 بكسل، والعبوة بقيت في الموضع نفسه. إطار البطاقة أعرض من ارتفاعه بنسبة 4:3.

ملف الصورة ما يبقى رأسيًا مع cover في منتصف الإطار
عمودي 400×600 300 بكسل من أصل 600
مربع 600×600 450 بكسل من أصل 600
أفقي 800×600 600 بكسل من أصل 600

في الملف العمودي، يحتاج cover إلى تكبير الصورة حتى تملأ العرض. عند التوسيط تسقط 150 بكسل من أعلى و150 من أسفل. في هذا الاختبار اختفى الغطاء من البطاقة ولم يبقَ من الحلقة سوى طرفها. حافظ contain على الصورة كاملة وترك مساحة عند الجانبين. إذا بقيت نسبة إطار البطاقة 4:3، فالجزء المقتطع من الملف نفسه عند العرضين. جرّب الجوالين لأن بعض القوالب تغيّر نسبة الإطار عند الانتقال بين أحجام الشاشات.

جرّبها بصورتك

احفظ الكود في ملف crop-test.html، وضع بجانبه صورة طولية باسم product-portrait.jpg. افتح الملف في المتصفح وجرّب عرضَي 320 و390 بكسل من محاكي الجوال. تبدأ البطاقتان من الصورة نفسها ونسبة الإطار نفسها. الفرق بينهما هو طريقة ملء الإطار.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>اختبار قصّ صورة المنتج</title>
<style>
  .grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
    gap: 12px;
    max-width: 480px;
    margin-inline: auto;
  }

  figure { margin: 0; }

  .frame {
    aspect-ratio: 4 / 3;
    overflow: hidden;
    background: #eef2f5;
  }

  .frame img {
    display: block;
    width: 100%;
    height: 100%;
    object-fit: cover;
    object-position: center;
  }

  .show-all img { object-fit: contain; }
</style>
<main class="grid">
  <figure>
    <div class="frame">
      <img src="product-portrait.jpg" alt="عبوة ماء زرقاء بحلقة برتقالية">
    </div>
    <figcaption><code dir="ltr">cover</code></figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure>
    <div class="frame show-all">
      <img src="product-portrait.jpg" alt="عبوة ماء زرقاء بحلقة برتقالية">
    </div>
    <figcaption><code dir="ltr">contain</code></figcaption>
  </figure>
</main>
</html>

لتجربة صورة ثانية، غيّر مسار الملف في البطاقتين معًا. ولتكرار الفحص على قالب متجرك، انسخ نسبة إطار الصورة من القالب وضعها مكان 4 / 3. إذا بقي الغطاء ظاهرًا في صورة المنتج الأصلية واحتجت أن يظهر أعلى البطاقة، جرّب object-position: center top مع cover. افحص القاعدة بعد ذلك، لأن نقل القص إلى الأسفل قد يخفي شكلها.

متى تغيّر طريقة العرض ومتى تطلب صورة جديدة؟

إذا كانت مجموعة المنتجات تعتمد على تفاصيل قريبة من الحواف، مثل حلقات العبوات أو مقابض الأكواب، ابدأ بـcontain. بعد ذلك افتح صفًّا فيه عدة منتجات وتأكد أن المنتج بقي بحجم يمكن تمييزه داخل البطاقة. إذا احتجت مساحة الصورة كاملة مع cover، جهّز للبطاقة صورة مستقلة بنسبة إطارها، واترك مسافة حول الحلقة والقاعدة قبل التصدير.

قد تجد أن الحلقة غائبة حتى عن الملف الأصلي. هنا تحتاج لقطة تبيّن طريقة حمل العبوة، قبل تجربة مزيد من إعدادات CSS. راجع دليل صور المنتجات في بالعرب لاختيار الصور التي تجيب عن سؤال العميل قبل أن يشتري.

ابدأ بمنتج واحد من المجموعة. بعد أن يظهر التفصيل المطلوب على الجوال، احفظ نسبة البطاقة ولقطة مرجعية مع طلب إعداد صور بقية المنتجات.

أُعدّ هذا المقال بمساعدة الذكاء الاصطناعي. شُغّل المثال في Chrome للتحقق من نتيجته.

title: SaaS: mide el onboarding más allá del email
description:
Cuando alguien se registra en un SaaS, solemos celebrar el email de verificación como si fuera la activación. Es una señal útil, pero no demuestra que la persona haya entendido el producto ni que haya encontrado su primer valor.

En un proyecto reciente, mirar solo ese clic nos hacía pensar que el onboarding funcionaba. Sin embargo, varias personas confirmaban la dirección y no volvían a abrir la aplicación. La solución no fue añadir más mensajes. Fue definir mejor qué significa empezar a usar el producto y medirlo con señales de frontend y backend.

El problema de medir onboarding con un solo clic

El email divide el flujo en dos estados muy simples: enviado y confirmado. Un SaaS real tiene más pasos:

  1. La persona crea una cuenta.
  2. Confirma su dirección.
  3. Completa una acción importante.
  4. Obtiene un resultado que puede reconocer.
  5. Regresa y repite ese resultado.

Si el tablero solo cuenta el segundo paso, mezcla registros curiosos, usuarios que se equivocaron de correo y clientes que todavía no encuentran un motivo para quedarse. Eso produce decisiones con una base un poco fragil.

También conviene recordar que las bandejas temporales o los datos de prueba pueden representar escenarios legítimos de QA. Una cuenta asociada a tempmailso, por ejemplo, puede servir para comprobar un flujo, pero no debería contarse automáticamente como cliente activado.

Define el primer valor antes de elegir eventos

Antes de instrumentar diez eventos, escribe una frase concreta:

Un usuario está activado cuando consigue ___ sin ayuda y puede repetirlo en ___ minutos.

Para una herramienta de facturación, el primer valor podría ser crear una factura y verla en estado enviado. Para un producto de colaboración, puede ser invitar a un compañero y completar una tarea compartida.

La frase ayuda a separar actividad de progreso. login_completed es actividad. first_invoice_sent puede ser progreso. No todo evento merece ser métrica principal, aunque sea facil de capturar.

Una definición pequeña también hace más fácil discutir con producto y soporte. Si cada equipo tiene una idea distinta de activación, el dashboard termina siendo una lista de números que nadie usa mucho.

Construye un embudo con eventos de producto y backend

Un embudo inicial no necesita una plataforma compleja. Puede empezar con una tabla de eventos y cuatro nombres consistentes:

account_created
email_verified
workspace_configured
first_value_completed

El frontend registra la intención y el backend confirma el resultado. Esta diferencia es importante. Un botón puede emitir first_value_clicked, pero solo el servidor sabe si la operación terminó bien, si hubo un error de permisos o si el objeto se guardó dos veces.

Un evento útil debería tener al menos:

{
  "name": "first_value_completed",
  "user_id": "u_123",
  "workspace_id": "w_456",
  "occurred_at": "2026-11-24T08:00:00Z",
  "source": "api",
  "schema_version": 1
}

No guardes contenido privado que no necesitas. Para el análisis suele bastar con un identificador interno, el tipo de acción y una marca de tiempo. El backend debe rechazar eventos imposibles, como una activación antes de crear la cuenta.

Si el formulario es parte importante del onboarding, merece la pena revisar también formularios de email sin perder el foco. Un campo que salta de posición puede reducir la finalización, aunque los eventos de API parezcan normales.

Prueba una cohorte pequeña sin cambiar todo el producto

Empieza con una cohorte semanal. Compara a las personas que se registraron durante esos siete días y sigue tres conversiones:

  • registro a verificación;
  • verificación a primer valor;
  • primer valor a una segunda sesión dentro de un plazo razonable.

No hace falta escoger un plazo perfecto al principio. Elige uno que tenga sentido para el producto y escríbelo junto al reporte. Luego puedes cambiarlo, pero sabrás qué definición produjo cada número.

Una consulta conceptual podría verse así:

SELECT
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE email_verified_at IS NOT NULL) AS verified,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE first_value_at IS NOT NULL) AS activated,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE second_session_at IS NOT NULL) AS retained
FROM onboarding_cohort
WHERE created_at >= :start_date
  AND created_at < :end_date;

No mezcles cohortes en el mismo porcentaje. Si cambias la pantalla de bienvenida el martes, el resultado de esa semana puede ser dificil de comparar con la anterior. Anota el cambio junto al dato; los datos tambien necesitan contexto.

Para pruebas automatizadas, define el contrato de los eventos antes de llenar el dashboard. Esta guía sobre aislar las pruebas de email con un contrato explica una idea aplicable aquí: una prueba debe comprobar la señal que importa, no solo que una llamada no lanzó error.

Errores comunes al interpretar la activación

Confundir entrega con valor. Que el mensaje haya llegado no significa que el producto haya resuelto un problema.

Cambiar varias cosas a la vez. Si rediseñas el formulario, cambias el email y modificas el precio, no sabrás qué funcionó.

Ignorar los fallos silenciosos. Un 200 OK puede ocultar una operación que quedó pendiente. Confirma el resultado desde el backend.

Tratar todas las cuentas como iguales. Una prueba interna, una cuenta de equipo y un cliente de pago pueden necesitar cohortes diferentes.

Perseguir búsquedas en lugar de necesidades. Frases como “fake e mail com” o “tamp mail com” pueden aparecer en los datos de búsqueda, pero no son una definición de activación ni un motivo para añadir enlaces sin contexto.

Q&A: dudas prácticas sobre métricas de onboarding

¿Debo eliminar el email de verificación del embudo?

No. Déjalo como señal de salud del canal, pero añade el evento de primer valor. Así puedes detectar si el problema está en la entrega o en la experiencia posterior.

¿Cuántos eventos necesito al empezar?

Los mínimos que expliquen el camino: cuenta creada, verificación, primer valor y retorno. Es mejor tener cuatro eventos confiables que treinta eventos que nadie revisa.

¿Qué hago si la muestra es pequeña?

No presentes una diferencia pequeña como una verdad definitiva. Observa tendencias, revisa sesiones cualitativas y espera otra cohorte. A veces el equipo miran un porcentaje y olvida cuantas personas hay detrás.

Recapitulación y siguiente experimento

Medir onboarding más allá del email consiste en conectar una promesa de producto con una acción verificable. Define el primer valor, registra señales desde el backend, separa cohortes y documenta cada cambio.

Como siguiente paso, escogería una sola fricción: por ejemplo, el tiempo entre confirmar la dirección y completar la primera acción. Mide la mediana, revisa cinco sesiones y prueba una mejora pequeña. Despues compara con una cohorte equivalente.

El objetivo no es crear el dashboard más grande. Es aprender qué ayuda a una persona nueva a llegar a su primer resultado, y hacer ese camino un poco más claro cada semana.

title: SQL Server Management on Windows, Mac & Linux with VisuaLeaf
description:
A column definition, a query, an execution plan, and a migration job each describe the same data from a different angle. In SQL Server work, you usually need all four open at once. This article walks through one SQL Server database in VisuaLeaf to show where its workspace helps.

VisuaLeaf brings these tasks into a desktop workspace with a SQL editor, visual query builder, table management, schema diagrams, profiling, data transfer, comparison, and charts. The screenshots here illustrate those workflows from SQL Server testing.

Establish the connection and permission boundary

A connection needs a server address, port, database, and supported authentication method. The selected database and schema also determine which objects your queries reference.

The connection dialog exposes the following authentication options.

Authentication family Options shown in the dialog
SQL Server SQL Server login
Windows NTLM with domain credentials, Kerberos, or this computer's login
Microsoft Entra user sign-in Password or sign in with browser
Microsoft Entra workload identity Service principal or managed identity
Microsoft Entra default Default credentials, including the Azure CLI or environment configuration

VisuaLeaf’s connection dialog for SQL Server

Or you can choose different sign-in methods:

The connection dialog lists SQL Server logins, Windows authentication, and several Microsoft Entra sign-in methods.

The completed connection test used a SQL Server login. Validate Windows authentication against your domain and Microsoft Entra authentication against your tenant, including its MFA requirements.

SQL Server permissions govern access to objects and operations. A reporting account can receive access to selected tables or views through database roles and grants. A client-side read-only setting adds an application control on top of those grants.

Inspect tables, constraints, and relationships

A column's data type is only part of its definition. Before changing a table or writing data, inspect the properties that SQL Server uses to validate each operation.

VisuaLeaf's Table Management exposes column definitions, keys, indexes, and constraints, with generated DDL available for inspection. Read the generated statement when changing a definition so you can see the database operation behind the form.

An ER diagram provides the relationship view. Primary and foreign keys show how tables connect and which joins follow declared constraints. Indexes need separate inspection. SQL Server does not automatically create an index on the referencing columns when you add a foreign key.

An ER diagram exposes primary keys, foreign keys, column types, and relationships across a SQL Server schema.

Build queries visually and retain access to T-SQL

The visual query builder represents tables, join conditions, selected columns, filters, aggregates, and sorting on a canvas. Generated SQL changes with those settings, making the resulting statement available for review.

Join cardinality still matters. A one-to-many join can repeat a parent row before aggregation. Review the join columns and the unit being counted when adding another table.

Joins drawn along a foreign key also depend on indexing. SQL Server doesn’t create an index on the referencing columns, so a join that looks right on the canvas can still scan the whole child table:

ALTER TABLE dbo.OrderLine
  ADD CONSTRAINT FK_OrderLine_Order
  FOREIGN KEY (OrderId) REFERENCES dbo.[Order] (OrderId);

-- The constraint does not create this index. Add it yourself:
CREATE INDEX IX_OrderLine_OrderId ON dbo.OrderLine (OrderId);

A table can also supply a filter or join condition without contributing a selected output column. Its presence in the query graph can therefore remain necessary even when its field list is empty.

Use the SQL editor for CTEs, window functions, multi-statement scripts, and other T-SQL that needs direct editing. The tested workflow confirmed SQL generation from the visual builder. Start visually, then switch to the editor when the query needs more than the canvas can express.

Build joins, filters, and aggregations visually while reviewing the generated T-SQL.

Understand how row editing identifies and changes data

Before a grid can update a row, it needs a reliable way to find that row in the table. VisuaLeaf uses the primary key: a table with a key opens as editable, while a result that can’t be traced back to a single table and key opens read-only.

*Note:* Inline edits are written to the database as soon as you confirm them. For changes you may need to roll back, write the UPDATE in the SQL editor and check its auto-commit and transaction settings first.

Identity columns are handled for you. The Insert Row form marks them *AI* (auto-increment) and leaves them as Auto-generated, so SQL Server assigns the value. The AI badge is the useful signal here: a key icon only tells you a column is the primary key, not that SQL Server generates its value. If you insert an explicit value through T-SQL instead, SQL Server rejects it with Msg 544 unless IDENTITY_INSERT is turned on.

The Insert Row form marks the identity column as auto-generated, so SQL Server assigns its value.

For more control, Open in SQL Editor moves the insert into the editor, where you can review the statement and run it inside a transaction.

Work with SQL Server features in their database context

T-SQL work can involve views, stored procedures, functions, and triggers as well as tables. Their definitions can contain filters, calculations, and write behavior that matter when reviewing an application database. VisuaLeaf lets you Server objects and edit their source alongside its query tools.

System-versioned temporal tables introduce another distinction. SQL Server maintains validity periods and row history through generated datetime2 columns and system versioning. A temporal query can return several versions of one logical record.

The temporal test displayed those versions with their validity periods. Review the system-time interval and UTC timestamps when interpreting history results, and distinguish the current row from its recorded versions.

Inspect the Open, In Progress, and Closed versions of a request using SQL Server’s temporal-table history.

Connect profiling statistics to execution plans

Profiling and execution plans answer different questions. Statement statistics show execution frequency and accumulated resource use. A plan describes the operators SQL Server uses to access and process rows.

VisuaLeaf's profiler presents statement-level execution statistics and lets you inspect a selected statement. Total time, average duration, execution count, and maximum duration each show a different view of the workload. Match the displayed statement to the query you intend to investigate, since catalog and monitoring queries can also appear in the list.

The graphical plan makes scans, seeks, joins, sorts, aggregates, and spools easier to trace. Identify whether you are viewing an estimated or actual plan. Estimated costs describe optimizer estimates. Actual plans add runtime information that can help explain differences in row counts and execution behavior.

For SQL Server's cached statement statistics, the lifetime of the counters is tied to the cached plan. Plan eviction can remove the corresponding statistics. In the tested profiler, the Runs tab reported aggregate totals, and chart intervals reflected activity between refreshes. Interpret the time window and counter lifetime before comparing measurements.

The profiler combines statement-level statistics with a graphical execution plan for the selected query.

Move data between engines and verify the result

Cross-database transfer requires explicit source, target, field, and type mappings. SQL Server types such as smallint and nvarchar need compatible target definitions. Review numeric ranges, text lengths, nullability, and generated-value behavior alongside the column names.

VisuaLeaf's transfer editor exposes source and target configuration, field mapping, transformations, and handling of existing rows. The SQL Server-to-PostgreSQL test completed a lookup-table transfer and displayed the target rows beside the job.

Use a stable key for the subsequent comparison. Match logical records by their identifying columns, then inspect changed values and rows present on only one side. Verify both row counts and content. Review schema objects such as indexes, defaults, foreign keys, and temporal definitions separately when planning a full migration.

A completed SQL Server-to-PostgreSQL transfer is displayed beside the target table for inspection.

Create charts from query results

The Chart Builder maps SQL result columns to categories, numeric measures, and other visual dimensions. This keeps the query's joins, filters, and aggregation attached to the result being presented.

Check the aggregation at both stages. If SQL already returns a count per category, the chart should use that numeric count as its measure. Counting the returned result rows would measure the number of categories instead.

Also check the denominator behind percentages. A chart built from a limited result set describes that selected set. Its title and labels should make the scope clear.

The chart uses a SQL query result, with categories mapped to slices and an aggregated numeric column mapped to size.

Make VisuaLeaf your SQL Server workspace

VisuaLeaf brings SQL Server querying, schema inspection, data editing, performance investigation, reporting, and cross-database work into one visual workspace. You don’t have to switch between tools: you can write a query, inspect its plan, chart the result, and move the data to PostgreSQL in the same place.

It also runs where your team works. VisuaLeaf has Windows, macOS, and Linux clients, so everyone gets the same interface, whatever system they use. SSMS runs only on Windows, so macOS and Linux users need another tool.

This review focused on day-to-day development and analysis. Server administration, such as backup and restore, SQL Server Agent jobs, and Microsoft Entra sign-in with MFA, wasn’t part of the testing. If your work depends on those, try them against your own server during setup.

For writing queries, understanding schemas, tuning statements, and moving data between engines, VisuaLeaf gives you a single cross-platform workspace with the SQL always visible behind the visual tools.

*Download VisuaLeaf* and connect it to your SQL Server database to try it.

title: We open-sourced our e-signature app: one sealed PDF anyone can verify, with Aadhaar eSign
description:
Short answer: Codevibe Sign is an open-source e-signature app. You upload a PDF, place the boxes and send it. People sign in the browser on any phone or laptop, with no account. You get back one sealed PDF with a one-page certificate and an audit trail, and anyone can check that file later, even offline, without asking our server. When a document needs a signature in the legal sense, Aadhaar eSign runs through Leegality, a licensed eSign provider.

You can use it three ways:

  • Cloud: a free workspace at sign.codevibe.in (10 envelopes a month, no card).
  • Self-host: the whole web app with Docker, free and with no limits.
  • Libraries: npm i codevibe-sign for the API client, PDF tools, core rules, React components and a CLI, all Apache-2.0.

Here is the 3-minute demo:

Why did we build another e-signature tool?

Because we kept paying per seat for something our clients needed in their own products. We are a software development agency in Gurugram, and offer letters, NDAs and client agreements come up in almost every project we build. The hosted tools work, but they charge per user, keep the documents on their servers, and are hard to embed in your own app.

We wanted three things:

  1. A signed file that proves itself. Not a link to someone's dashboard, a PDF you can keep for ten years.
  2. Code we could run on our own server, or inside a client's product.
  3. Aadhaar eSign for the Indian documents that need it, without building a separate flow.

So we built it, used it ourselves, and opened the code.

What do you get back after everyone signs?

One PDF, sealed, with a certificate page at the end. When the last person signs, the server:

  • draws every field value onto the pages, so nothing is left as an editable form field;
  • appends a one-page certificate: who signed, how they were checked, when, the document fingerprint and a QR code to a public record;
  • applies a PAdES seal (SHA-256, RSA 3072) that covers the whole file.

Change one byte after that and the seal breaks. The QR code opens a public record page with the seal status, signers, fingerprints and audit trail, never the document itself. You can turn that page off per envelope or per workspace.

PDFs that are already signed are refused on upload, so earlier signatures are never wiped by a new seal.

How does anyone check a signed PDF?

Four ways, and none of them need an account.

Where How What you get
QR code Scan it from the certificate page The public record: seal status, signers, audit trail
Web Drop the file on sign.codevibe.in/verify Valid or not, who signed and when. The file is checked in memory and dropped
API POST /v1/verify or GET /v1/verify/{sha256} The same answer as JSON, no API key
CLI npx codevibe-sign verify signed.pdf An offline check of the seal

The seal certificate for sign.codevibe.in is public on purpose, with its SHA-256 fingerprint in the README. It holds only the public key, so publishing it lets anyone check a seal without being able to make one. If you self-host, your files are sealed with your own certificate.

How does signing work for the person who signs?

They open a link, confirm a code and press one button until it says Finish.

  • Every signer confirms a six-digit code from their email by default. SMS codes or a plain email link are options.
  • One button reads Start, then Next, and Finish when nothing is left, with a progress bar.
  • Signatures can be drawn, typed or uploaded. The signer's name and signing time are printed under each one.
  • Names in Devanagari, Bengali, Gurmukhi, Gujarati, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Arabic are drawn correctly on the signed PDF, with bundled Noto Sans fonts.

Senders get sequential or parallel routing, reminders, expiry, templates, bulk send from a CSV, workspaces with their own address and time zone, signed webhooks and an HTTP API with an OpenAPI description.

When do you need Aadhaar eSign instead?

When a law asks for an electronic signature in the statutory sense, not just agreement. Under Indian law, a contract formed by electronic means is valid (IT Act 2000, section 10A), and for most offer letters, NDAs and business agreements the built-in flow and its audit trail are the evidence. Where a law requires a signature listed in the IT Act's Second Schedule, you need Aadhaar eSign or a DSC.

In Codevibe Sign you pick Aadhaar eSign for one signer in the send flow. They confirm with an OTP on Leegality's page. Codevibe Sign never sees or stores their Aadhaar number. You get back the signed PDF with their Aadhaar signature and the seal, plus a separate certificate and audit trail PDF.

An eSign costs ₹35 on the Free plan and ₹25 on Cloud, plus GST, from prepaid credits, and only a completed eSign is charged. On Cloud you can connect your own Leegality account instead.

Some documents still cannot be signed electronically at all: wills, trust deeds, most powers of attorney and most negotiable instruments. The README lists the current exclusions. This is not legal advice.

How do you add it to your own app?

Install one package, or run the server next to your app. The fastest way to see it work:

npx @codevibe_technology/sign-server start --memory

That runs the server with everything in memory: a generated seal certificate, emails and codes printed to the terminal, and a fresh API key. Send it a PDF with the curl command it prints, sign through the link, then check the file:

npx codevibe-sign verify signed.pdf

In your own backend, the typed client creates and sends envelopes:

import { createSignClient } from 'codevibe-sign/client';

const sign = createSignClient({ baseUrl: 'https://sign.example.com', apiKey });
await sign.envelopes.create({ title: 'Offer letter', send: true, documents, recipients, fields });

And codevibe-sign/react has an unstyled SigningView, signature pad and field placer that you theme with CSS variables. It needs Node.js 22 or newer.

Is it free, and what is the licence?

The libraries are Apache-2.0 and the server and web app are AGPL-3.0, kept apart on purpose. npm i codevibe-sign only ever installs Apache-2.0 code, so you can use it in a closed-source product. Running the AGPL server as its own service and calling its API does not make your product AGPL either.

Plan Price What you get
Free ₹0 1 workspace, 10 envelopes a month, 2 members
Cloud ₹999 a month or ₹9,990 a year, plus GST Unlimited workspaces and envelopes, 25 members included
Self-hosted Free Everything, no limits, on your own server

The cloud runs the same code you can download. Nothing is held back for a paid edition.

What is next?

  • eMudhra as a second eSign provider, behind the same interface.
  • More than one Aadhaar signer in an envelope.
  • Translations of the signing pages and emails.

It is a pre-release, so APIs may change before 1.0. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

FAQ

Do the people who sign need an account?
No. They open the link in their email and sign in the browser, with no app to install.

Can I self-host it for free?
Yes. The whole web app runs with Docker Compose and PostgreSQL, with no limits on envelopes, members or storage. Your documents never leave your server.

Is it safe that the seal certificate is public?
Yes. It holds only the public key, which lets people check a seal. Making one needs the private key, which stays on the server.

Is an electronic signature valid in India?
For most business documents, yes, under section 10A of the IT Act. Where a law requires a signature in the statutory sense, use Aadhaar eSign or a DSC.

Can I use it in a closed-source product?
Yes. The libraries are Apache-2.0, and calling the AGPL server over its API keeps your product under any licence you choose.

  • Try it: sign.codevibe.in
  • Code: github.com/codevibe-technology/codevibe-sign
  • npm: codevibe-sign

Built by Codevibe, a software development agency in Gurugram, India.

title: Removing echo from a live call in Rust: keeping two audio streams in step
description:
I maintain NexQ, an open source app that transcribes calls. It records two streams: your microphone ("You") and whatever the computer is playing ("Them"). With headphones that works well. With speakers, the microphone also hears the other person, and the transcript says every sentence twice, once under each name.

This is how the echo gets removed before the audio reaches speech to text. The code was written by Plus Chen, a contributor, in two pull requests: #83 and #104. The second one is the interesting one.

The easy half

WebRTC already has a good echo canceller, AEC3. There is a pure Rust port called sonora, so no C++ build is needed. You give it two signals:

  • the reference, what the speakers are playing
  • the capture, what the microphone heard

It learns the path from speaker to microphone and subtracts it. Both streams here are 16 kHz mono, and AEC3 works on 10 ms frames, so 160 samples at a time:

let _ = self.apm.process_render_i16(&reference, &mut unused);
if self.apm.process_capture_i16(frame, cleaned).is_err() {
    cleaned.copy_from_slice(frame);
}

If the canceller fails on a frame, the original microphone audio goes through. Losing your voice would be worse than an echo.

The hard half: keeping two streams in step

AEC3 needs the reference before the microphone audio that contains its echo, and it can only find the echo within about half a second of it. Two separate devices don't promise you that:

  • WASAPI loopback sends nothing while the output is silent. Not zeros, nothing.
  • One device's clock runs a little faster than the other's.
  • Sometimes a chunk gets dropped.

The first version also had a drift of our own making. Every capture chunk was resampled to 16 kHz separately, and the length was rounded up. On a MacBook, a 512-frame chunk at 48 kHz became 171 samples when the right answer is 170.67. A 953-frame chunk at 96 kHz became 159 and not 158.8. Both streams ran fast, by different amounts, so they drifted apart by almost half a millisecond every second. Within a minute or two AEC3 was looking at the wrong moment, and the echo was back.

The fix for that part is one resampler per stream that lives across chunks, so each stream comes out at exactly 16 kHz whatever the chunk size. For the rest, the canceller keeps a small queue and corrects itself.

Hold the microphone back. Mic audio waits 80 ms before it is processed. That way the matching reference has time to arrive.

Keep a cushion. Four reference frames (40 ms) stay queued ahead of the mic frame being cleaned, to absorb uneven chunk timing.

When the reference runs out, use silence until the cushion is full again. On Windows this happens at every pause in the other person's speech, so it is normal and not an error:

if queued == 0 {
    self.refilling = true;
} else if self.refilling && queued >= CUSHION {
    self.refilling = false;
}

When too much piles up, drop the extra. Every half second it looks at the fewest frames that were queued in that time. If even the minimum was above the cushion plus three, the reference is running ahead and the excess is removed:

if !self.refilling && self.fewest_queued > TOO_MANY {
    let excess = (self.fewest_queued - CUSHION) * FRAME;
    self.reference.drain(..excess);
}

Looking at the minimum and not the current value is what makes this safe. A burst of chunks raises the current value for a moment. Only real drift raises the minimum.

Both corrections bring the queue back to the same place, where AEC3 already expects the echo.

Testing it without a room

The tests build a fake room. The speaker signal is noise shaped like syllables, and the microphone gets it 30 ms later, quieter, with one reflection.
