The two streams are fed in chunks of different sizes, with gaps where loopback would send nothing. One test asserts that after four seconds the echo is down by more than 20 dB. Another checks that your own voice is still there.

Where it stops working

It holds with the two clocks up to 300 ppm apart. At about 1000 ppm the delay moves faster than AEC3 can follow, and the echo comes back. Fixing that would mean resampling the reference to the microphone's clock.

The code is in echo_cancel.rs and resampler.rs.

If you have solved clock drift between two audio devices in a simpler way, I'd like to read about it.

This article was written with the help of AI, from the code and tests linked above.

title: Managing TanStack Start/Router Head Tags Without Duplicate Canonicals
description:
A small head factory that kills duplicated canonical links and stale social tags — and the surprising part is that the URL must be stamped by the route, not the root.

The Problem

The root head gives every page a title, description, and canonical. The about page adds its own title and Open Graph tags. Both look correct alone.

// src/routes/__root.tsx
export const Route = createRootRoute({
  head: () => ({
    meta: [
      { title: "Atlas" },
      { name: "description", content: "Field notes for hikers" },
      { property: "og:title", content: "Atlas" },
      { property: "og:url", content: "https://atlas.test" },
    ],
    links: [{ rel: "canonical", href: "https://atlas.test" }],
  }),
});

// src/routes/about.tsx
export const Route = createFileRoute("/about")({
  head: () => ({
    meta: [
      { title: "About | Atlas" },
      { property: "og:title", content: "About | Atlas" },
      { property: "og:url", content: "https://atlas.test/about" },
    ],
    links: [{ rel: "canonical", href: "https://atlas.test/about" }],
  }),
});

What ships:

<head>
  <title>About | Atlas</title>
  <meta property="og:title" content="About | Atlas">
  <meta property="og:url" content="https://atlas.test/about">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://atlas.test">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://atlas.test/about">
</head>

TanStack Router dedupes title and meta by last nested occurrence, but not links. Two canonical links survive, and crawlers get conflicting answers about the authoritative URL.

Fix one: compute the canonical in the root from the browser location.

links: [{ rel: "canonical", href: `https://atlas.test${window.location.pathname}` }],

It works in the browser but not during SSR, where window does not exist. Crawlers get no reliable canonical.

Fix two: delete the root canonical and put one in every leaf route.

// root
links: []; // the canonical lives in each route now

Routes without a head get none; a nested route that adds one recreates the duplicate.

Fix three: keep the leaf route but build the URL by concatenation.

head: ({ match }) => ({
  links: [{ rel: "canonical", href: `https://atlas.test/${match.pathname}` }],
});

match.pathname already starts with /, so you get https://atlas.test//about; a trailing slash gives the page a second URL.

You need one canonical identity per URL, present everywhere, but only the leaf route knows the path and only the root knows the site.

A head factory closes over site facts once and takes page facts as arguments:

export function buildHead(config: BuildHeadConfig) {
  const ctx = createHeadContext(config);
  const urlFor = (path: string) => createCanonicalUrl(ctx.baseUrl, path);
  return {
    globalHead: () => ({
      meta: buildHeadMeta(ctx, {
        title: ctx.defaultTitle,
        description: ctx.defaultDescription,
        url: urlFor("/"),
      }),
      links: buildHeadLinks(ctx.stylesheets),
    }),
    head: (options: HeadPageOptions) => {
      const url = urlFor(options.pathname);
      return {
        meta: buildHeadMeta(ctx, {
          title: resolveTitle(ctx.titleTemplate, options),
          description: options.description ?? ctx.defaultDescription,
          url,
        }),
        links: [...buildHeadLinks(ctx.stylesheets, url), ...buildAlternateLinks(url)],
      };
    },
  };
}

The Mental Model

Treat the module as a printing press with two plates: a master plate for site facts, a page plate for path and title. It prints one sheet; <HeadContent /> hands it to the browser.

  • Identity: buildHead(config) sets the press once. Normalized base URL, title template, robots, theme color, OG image, and stylesheets live in a closure for the life of the app.
  • Update timing: each route match calls head() with a pathname and title. The press prints a fresh sheet at match time. No effect, state, or subscription schedules the work.
  • Read timing: <HeadContent /> reads the sheets for the matched route tree during SSR and again on client navigation. The router merges them; leaf meta entries win by name or property.

Server and client print the same sheet because nothing reads the DOM. A new config means a new press; you cannot reconfigure one mid-flight.

The press stamps the address once, on the sheet that actually goes out.

How to Use It

Setup 

src/
├── lib/
│   ├── head/
│   │   ├── buildHead.ts
│   │   ├── index.ts
│   │   ├── links.ts
│   │   ├── meta.ts
│   │   ├── og.ts
│   │   ├── types.ts
│   │   └── url.ts
│   └── site-config.ts
├── routes/
│   ├── __root.tsx
│   └── about.tsx
└── utils/
    └── url.ts

A minimal generic stand-in for config values your app already has. Replace the strings with your own.

// src/lib/site-config.ts
export const siteConfig = {
  appName: "Atlas",
  siteUrl: "https://atlas.test",
  defaultTitle: "Atlas",
  titleTemplate: "%s | Atlas",
  defaultDescription: "Field notes for hikers",
  themeColor: "#0f172a",
  robots: "index, follow",
  social: true,
  stylesheets: ["/styles.css"],
  ogImagePath: "/opengraph-image.jpg",
};

The two URL normalizers:

// src/utils/url.ts
export function normalizeUrl(urlValue: string): string {
  return urlValue.replace(/\/+$/, "");
}

export function normalizePathname(pathname: string): string {
  const trimmed = pathname.replace(/^\/+|\/+$/g, "").replace(/\/{2,}/g, "/");

  return trimmed === "" ? "/" : `/${trimmed}`;
}

Every type used below:

// src/lib/head/types.ts
export interface HeadMeta {
  charSet?: string;
  name?: string;
  property?: string;
  content?: string;
  title?: string;
}

export interface HeadLink {
  rel: string;
  href?: string;
  hrefLang?: string;
  type?: string;
  sizes?: string;
}

export interface HeadResult {
  meta: HeadMeta[];
  links: HeadLink[];
}

export interface BuildHeadConfig {
  appName: string;
  siteUrl: string;
  defaultTitle: string;
  titleTemplate: string;
  defaultDescription: string;
  themeColor: string;
  robots?: string;
  stylesheets?: ReadonlyArray<string>;
  ogImagePath?: string;
  social?: boolean;
}

export type HeadPageOptions = {
  pathname: string;
  description?: string;
} & (
  | { title: string; titleByTemplate?: never }
  | { titleByTemplate: string; title?: never }
);

URL construction:

// src/lib/head/url.ts
import { normalizePathname, normalizeUrl } from "@/utils/url";

export function createCanonicalUrl(baseUrl: string, pathname: string): string {
  const normalized = normalizePathname(pathname);

  return normalized === "/" ? baseUrl : `${baseUrl}${normalized}`;
}

export function createAssetUrl(baseUrl: string, path: string): string {
  return `${baseUrl}/${path.replace(/^\/+/, "")}`;
}

Links, with the canonical added only when a page URL is supplied:

// src/lib/head/links.ts
import type { HeadLink } from "./types";

function buildFaviconLinks(): HeadLink[] {
  return [
    {
      rel: "icon",
      type: "image/png",
      href: "/favicon-96x96.png",
      sizes: "96x96",
    },
    { rel: "icon", type: "image/svg+xml", href: "/favicon.svg" },
    { rel: "shortcut icon", href: "/favicon.ico" },
    {
      rel: "apple-touch-icon",
      href: "/apple-touch-icon.png",
      sizes: "180x180",
      type: "image/png",
    },
  ];
}

function buildWebmanifest(): HeadLink[] {
  return [
    {
      rel: "manifest",
      href: "/site.webmanifest",
    },
  ];
}

export function buildHeadLinks(
  stylesheets: ReadonlyArray<string>,
  canonicalUrl?: string
): HeadLink[] {
  return [
    ...stylesheets.map((href) => ({ rel: "stylesheet", href })),
    ...buildFaviconLinks(),
    ...buildWebmanifest(),
    ...(canonicalUrl ? [{ rel: "canonical", href: canonicalUrl }] : []),
  ];
}

export function buildAlternateLinks(url: string): HeadLink[] {
  return [{ rel: "alternate", hrefLang: "x-default", href: url }];
}

Social tags, all keyed consistently so nested-route dedupe works:

// src/lib/head/og.ts
import type { HeadMeta } from "./types";

export interface OgMetaOptions {
  appName: string;
  title: string;
  description: string;
  url: string;
  imageUrl: string;
}

export function buildOgMeta(options: OgMetaOptions): HeadMeta[] {
  const { appName, title, description, url, imageUrl } = options;

  return [
    { property: "og:title", content: title },
    { property: "og:description", content: description },
    { property: "og:site_name", content: appName },
    { property: "og:type", content: "website" },
    { property: "og:url", content: url },
    { property: "og:image", content: imageUrl },
    { property: "og:image:width", content: "1200" },
    { property: "og:image:height", content: "630" },
    { property: "og:image:alt", content: appName },
    { name: "twitter:card", content: "summary_large_image" },
    { name: "twitter:title", content: title },
    { name: "twitter:description", content: description },
    { name: "twitter:image", content: imageUrl },
    { name: "twitter:image:alt", content: appName },
  ];
}

The base meta set and the title resolver:

// src/lib/head/meta.ts
import { buildOgMeta } from "./og";
import type { HeadMeta, HeadPageOptions } from "./types";

export interface HeadMetaContext {
  appName: string;
  themeColor: string;
  robots: string;
  googlebot: string;
  social: boolean;
  ogImage: string;
}

export interface HeadPageMeta {
  title: string;
  description: string;
  url: string;
}

export function resolveTitle(
  titleTemplate: string,
  options: HeadPageOptions
): string {
  return options.titleByTemplate === undefined
    ? options.title
    : titleTemplate.replace("%s", () => options.titleByTemplate);
}

export function buildHeadMeta(
  context: HeadMetaContext,
  page: HeadPageMeta
): HeadMeta[] {
  const { appName, themeColor, robots, googlebot, social, ogImage } = context;
  const { title, description, url } = page;

  const meta: HeadMeta[] = [
    { charSet: "utf-8" },
    { name: "viewport", content: "width=device-width, initial-scale=1" },
    { name: "theme-color", content: themeColor },
    { title },
    { name: "description", content: description },
    { name: "robots", content: robots },
    { name: "googlebot", content: googlebot },
    { name: "format-detection", content: "telephone=no" },
    { name: "mobile-web-app-capable", content: "yes" },
    { name: "apple-mobile-web-app-title", content: appName },
    {
      name: "apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style",
      content: "black-translucent",
    },
  ];

  if (social) {
    meta.push(
      ...buildOgMeta({
        appName,
        title,
        description,
        url,
        imageUrl: ogImage,
      })
    );
  }

  return meta;
}

The press itself:

// src/lib/head/buildHead.ts
import { normalizeUrl } from "@/utils/url";

import { buildAlternateLinks, buildHeadLinks } from "./links";
import { buildHeadMeta, resolveTitle } from "./meta";
import type { BuildHeadConfig, HeadPageOptions, HeadResult } from "./types";
import { createAssetUrl, createCanonicalUrl } from "./url";

export type { BuildHeadConfig, HeadPageOptions, HeadResult } from "./types";

const GOOGLEBOT_DEFAULT =
  "index, follow, max-video-preview:-1, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1";

interface HeadContext {
  appName: string;
  baseUrl: string;
  defaultTitle: string;
  titleTemplate: string;
  defaultDescription: string;
  themeColor: string;
  robots: string;
  googlebot: string;
  stylesheets: ReadonlyArray<string>;
  ogImage: string;
  social: boolean;
}

function createHeadContext(config: BuildHeadConfig): HeadContext {
  const {
    appName,
    siteUrl,
    defaultTitle,
    titleTemplate,
    defaultDescription,
    themeColor,
    robots = "index, follow",
    stylesheets = [],
    ogImagePath = "/opengraph-image.jpg",
    social = true,
  } = config;

  if (!titleTemplate.includes("%s")) {
    throw new Error('buildHead: titleTemplate must contain "%s"');
  }

  const baseUrl = normalizeUrl(siteUrl);

  return {
    appName,
    baseUrl,
    defaultTitle,
    titleTemplate,
    defaultDescription,
    themeColor,
    robots,
    googlebot: robots.includes("noindex") ? robots : GOOGLEBOT_DEFAULT,
    stylesheets,
    ogImage: createAssetUrl(baseUrl, ogImagePath),
    social,
  };
}

export function buildHead(config: BuildHeadConfig) {
  const context = createHeadContext(config);

  const globalHead = (): HeadResult => ({
    meta: buildHeadMeta(context, {
      title: context.defaultTitle,
      description: context.defaultDescription,
      url: createCanonicalUrl(context.baseUrl, "/"),
    }),
    links: buildHeadLinks(context.stylesheets),
  });

  const head = (options: HeadPageOptions): HeadResult => {
    const url = createCanonicalUrl(context.baseUrl, options.pathname);

    return {
      meta: buildHeadMeta(context, {
        title: resolveTitle(context.titleTemplate, options),
        description: options.description ?? context.defaultDescription,
        url,
      }),
      links: [
        ...buildHeadLinks(context.stylesheets, url),
        ...buildAlternateLinks(url),
      ],
    };
  };

  return { globalHead, head };
}

Set the plates up once:

// src/lib/head/index.ts
import { siteConfig } from "@/lib/site-config";

import { buildHead } from "./buildHead";

export const { globalHead, head } = buildHead(siteConfig);

Import with import { globalHead, head } from "@/lib/head"; swap @/ for your alias, or use relative paths. The config object is a stand-in for your own constants and environment values.

Install the shared sheet in the root 

import { globalHead } from "@/lib/head";
import { HeadContent, Scripts, createRootRoute } from "@tanstack/react-router";

export const Route = createRootRoute({
  head: () => globalHead(),
  shellComponent: RootDocument,
});

function RootDocument({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <head>
        <HeadContent />
      </head>
      <body>
        {children}
        <Scripts />
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

Defaults print once, and the root emits no page canonical. HeadContent must live in the root <head>.

Stamp a page identity from the match 

import { head } from "@/lib/head";
import { createFileRoute } from "@tanstack/react-router";

export const Route = createFileRoute("/about")({
  head: ({ match }) =>
    head({ pathname: match.pathname, titleByTemplate: "About" }),
  component: () => <div>About</div>,
});

Canonical, og:url, and alternate link derive from one pathname, so they cannot drift.

Handle dynamic segments 

import { head } from "@/lib/head";
import { createFileRoute } from "@tanstack/react-router";

export const Route = createFileRoute("/posts/$postId")({
  head: ({ match }) =>
    head({
      pathname: `/posts/${match.params.postId}`,
      titleByTemplate: "Post",
      description: "A field note",
    }),
  component: () => <div>Post</div>,
});

Route params become a canonical URL without touching the browser.

❌ Do not pass window.location.pathname into head(). It is absent during SSR, and the router already hands you the authoritative path via match.

When to Use It

  • Every page has a stable URL derivable from match.pathname or route params.
  • You want identical defaults: title template, robots, OG image, stylesheets, icons.
  • Your head is pure data, not component state or browser values.
Situation Better tool
Title needs fetched data Route loader plus head reading match.loaderData
Head must follow client-only state A component effect that writes document.title
One route needs a different theme color An extra meta entry in that route's own head
Multiple languages or regions Route-specific hrefLang alternate links
You need head scripts The route scripts option
A single static page with no shared data An inline head object in that route

Smell test: writing window inside head means the URL should come from the match.

How It Works Under the Hood

  1. The plate is fixed at setup. createHeadContext(config) strips trailing slashes from siteUrl, checks the template for %s, and precomputes the OG image URL. A bad template throws at load.

  2. The template handles one placeholder. resolveTitle uses titleTemplate.replace("%s", () => options.titleByTemplate), which replaces only the first %s. The HeadPageOptions union forbids passing both title and titleByTemplate.

  3. Canonicals are normalized, not concatenated. normalizePathname strips leading and trailing slashes and collapses repeats; createCanonicalUrl returns the bare base URL for /. Naive concatenation yields https://atlas.test//about and a trailing-slash variant.

  4. Only the page sheet carries a canonical. globalHead() calls buildHeadLinks(context.stylesheets) with no URL; head() adds one canonical and one alternate. Router dedupe covers nested title and meta, not links. The cost: the root sheet has no canonical, so / needs its own head() entry if it wants one.

  5. The cost is small. Each head() call allocates arrays and objects, and the closure retains config for the app's life. There are no DOM writes or effects. googlebot is derived once: robots containing noindex is reused verbatim, otherwise a verbose default applies.

Phase Work performed Canonical value
Module evaluation buildHead(siteConfig) normalizes and stores context none, no sheet printed
Route match on the server About route calls head() with match.pathname https://atlas.test/about
SSR render HeadContent emits the merged head one canonical link
Discarded render A redirect wins before HTML is sent; the sheet is dropped printed, never shipped
HTML on the wire Browser parses the head one canonical link
Hydration No head recompute, no effect writes to the DOM unchanged
Client navigation to / Leaf sheet unloads; root sheet has no canonical none unless / defines its own

Server rendering note: head functions run on the server and again on client navigation. They must be pure: no window, document, or component state, so the same config and match produce the same head in both places.

Router dedupe does not normalize a bad URL or apply a title template, and head is not a hook, so useLocation() is unavailable; pass match.pathname.

Conclusion

You give up per-page improvisation and get one predictable sheet per URL. The root owns site facts, the leaf owns page facts, and the factory joins them before HTML exists.

  • Keep site-wide values in one config so they cannot drift between routes.
  • Pass match.pathname to every page head; let normalization handle the edges.
  • globalHead() omits canonical links; a home route needing one calls head().

Use this press when many routes share one identity. For one static page, the boring inline head object wins.

title: Que fait le navigateur entre l'adresse que tu tapes et la page que tu vois
description:
Tu tapes une adresse dans ton navigateur, tu appuies sur Entrée et, quelques secondes plus tard, une page apparaît à l'écran.

On a tendance à penser que le navigateur affiche simplement le contenu envoyé par le serveur. En réalité, plusieurs opérations se déroulent entre le moment où tu saisis l'adresse et celui où tu peux commencer à utiliser la page.

C'est notamment pour cette raison que, lorsque la connexion est lente, tu peux voir le texte apparaître avant certaines images ou constater qu'une page met du temps à devenir interactive.

Comprendre ces étapes permet de mieux savoir ce qui se passe derrière une page web et, surtout, de comprendre certaines décisions que l'on prend lorsqu'on développe un site.

Voici donc les étapes qui se passent avant l'affichage :

1.Le serveur envoie du HTML

Lorsque tu demandes une page, le navigateur contacte le serveur qui héberge le site. Le serveur traite la requête et renvoie une réponse contenant généralement un document HTML.

Pour t'en rendre compte, ouvre un site dans ton navigateur et utilise le raccourci Ctrl + U. Tu verras son code source.

Ce que tu obtiens est essentiellement du texte contenant des balises et du contenu. Tu ne retrouves pas encore la présentation habituelle du site avec ses couleurs, ses espacements et ses images.

Le navigateur doit justement interpréter ce document pour construire la page que tu vois.

2.Le HTML devient une structure : le DOM

Le navigateur ne se contente pas de lire le HTML comme un simple texte. Il l'analyse et transforme les éléments en une structure organisée appelée DOM (Document Object Model).

Pour comprendre, prenons cet exemple :

<body>
  <h1>Bonjour</h1>
  <p>Un <strong>petit</strong> texte</p>
</body>

Le navigateur construit une sorte d'arbre dans lequel chaque élément occupe une place.

Ici, body contient h1 et p. À son tour, p contient strong(Inutile d'expliquer encore que signifie ce terme).

Cette organisation permet notamment à JavaScript d'accéder aux éléments de la page et de les modifier.

Par exemple :

const paragraphe = document.querySelector("p");

paragraphe.textContent = "Mon premier changement avec JavaScript";

Avec querySelector(), tu demandes au navigateur de retrouver le premier paragraphe dans le DOM. Ensuite, JavaScript modifie son contenu.

C'est ce qui permet de rendre une page interactive sans devoir réécrire tout le document HTML.

3.Le CSS donne une apparence aux éléments

Le navigateur analyse également les feuilles de style CSS. Elles lui indiquent comment présenter les éléments : couleurs, tailles, polices, marges, espacements et positionnement.

Prenons un exemple assez simple, mais intéressant à comprendre : la différence entre display: none et visibility: hidden.

.cache1 {
  display: none;
}

.cache2 {
  visibility: hidden;
}

Les deux propriétés permettent de rendre un élément invisible, mais elles ne produisent pas le même résultat.

Avec display: none, l'élément est retiré de la disposition de la page. Il ne prend donc plus de place.

Avec visibility: hidden, l'élément devient invisible, mais l'espace qu'il occupait est conservé.

Tu peux facilement vérifier cette différence en appliquant ces deux propriétés à deux paragraphes placés entre d'autres éléments.

C'est un petit détail du CSS, mais il peut avoir des conséquences sur la disposition d'une page.

4.Le navigateur calcule les positions avant de dessiner

À ce stade, le navigateur dispose des éléments HTML et des informations nécessaires pour connaître leur apparence.

Il doit maintenant déterminer précisément où chaque élément sera placé et quelle place il occupera.

Cette opération s'appelle le layout(d’ailleurs je suis en train d'écrire un article sur mon blog concernant les layouts et que je vais vous partager le lien d'ici peu).

Par exemple, il doit calculer la largeur d'un paragraphe, la hauteur d'une image, l'espace entre deux blocs et leur position dans la page.

Une fois ces informations calculées, le navigateur passe au rendu graphique : il dessine les différents éléments pour produire l'image que tu vois à l'écran.

Il faut toutefois retenir que ce travail ne se fait pas nécessairement une seule fois.

Imagine que tu utilises JavaScript pour augmenter la hauteur d'un bloc. Si ce changement modifie la disposition des autres éléments, le navigateur doit recalculer les positions concernées.

Lorsque les modifications sont nombreuses et mal organisées, elles peuvent provoquer des ralentissements.

C'est une des raisons pour lesquelles les développeurs doivent faire attention à la manière dont ils modifient les éléments d'une page surtout avec le JavaScript sans utiliser l'ASYNC.

5.JavaScript peut ralentir la construction de la page

Voici une autre chose importante à comprendre lorsqu'on commence à travailler avec JavaScript.

Lorsqu'un navigateur analyse le HTML et rencontre une balise <script> classique, il interrompt généralement l'analyse du document(HTML) pour récupérer le fichier JavaScript et l'exécuter.

Pendant ce temps, la construction du DOM est mise en pause.

Prenons deux exemples :

Première version :

<script src="app.js"></script>

Deuxième version :

<script src="app.js" defer></script>

La différence se trouve dans l'attribut defer.

Dans le premier cas, le navigateur met en pause l'analyse du HTML pour charger et exécuter le script externe.

Dans le deuxième cas, le téléchargement du fichier JavaScript se fait en parallèle de l'analyse du HTML. Son exécution est ensuite reportée jusqu'à ce que le document HTML soit entièrement analysé.

C'est particulièrement utile lorsque ton JavaScript doit manipuler des éléments qui se trouvent dans le HTML.

Par exemple, si ton fichier app.js contient :

const titre = document.querySelector("h1");

titre.textContent = "Bienvenue sur mon site";

Il faut que le navigateur ait déjà créé l'élément h1 dans le DOM lorsque ce code s'exécute.

Avec defer, tu peux éviter le problème lié à un script externe exécuté trop tôt dans le chargement du document.

Attention toutefois : defer s'applique aux scripts externes classiques. Il n'a pas le même comportement avec les scripts JavaScript écrits directement dans la page.

===> Comment vérifier ce comportement dans son navigateur ?

Tu peux faire une petite expérience sans installer quoi que ce soit.

Crée un fichier index.html :

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>Test du chargement JavaScript</title>
</head>
<body>

  <h1>Chargement de la page</h1>

  <script src="app.js"></script>

  <p>Ce paragraphe se trouve après le script.</p>

</body>
</html>

Crée ensuite un fichier app.js :

console.log("Le fichier JavaScript est exécuté");

Ouvre la page dans ton navigateur et appuie sur F12 pour accéder aux outils de développement(Accessible aussi en faisant un Clic droit et souvent la dernière option "Inspecter").

Dans l'onglet Network, tu peux observer les ressources demandées par le navigateur, notamment le fichier JavaScript.

Tu peux également activer l'option de limitation du réseau (Throttling), par exemple avec une connexion Fast 3G, pour mieux observer les différences de chargement.

Fais ensuite une deuxième expérience en ajoutant defer à la balise script.

Tu constateras que les deux versions ne suivent pas le même ordre d'exécution : sans defer, le navigateur attend le chargement et l'exécution du script avant de poursuivre l'analyse du HTML. Avec defer, il poursuit cette analyse pendant le téléchargement du fichier.

Pour observer la différence, regarde aussi l'ordre des messages dans la console en ajoutant un console.log() avant et après la balise script dans le HTML.

L'objectif n'est pas simplement de connaître un attribut HTML de plus, mais de comprendre pourquoi son utilisation peut améliorer le chargement d'une page.

6.Ce que vous devez retenir

Avant de vous intéresser à ces mécanismes, je pense que voyiez surtout le résultat final : une page qui s'affiche dans le navigateur. Maintenant, tu comprends mieux le travail qui se déroule derrière cet affichage.

*Recommandations *

Quand vous écrirez vos prochaines pages, je faites davantage attention à la manière dont vos scripts sont chargés et au moment où ils manipulent les éléments HTML. Ce sont des détails qui peuvent sembler secondaires au début, mais qui comptent lorsqu'on veut construire un site propre et réactif selon les normes.

C'est aussi ce qui est bon dans le développement web : derrière quelque chose d'aussi simple qu'une page qui s'affiche, il y a plusieurs mécanismes qu'on apprend progressivement à maîtriser.

Avez-vous appris quelque chose par ce post ?

title: Right-Sizing Cloud Servers: Stop Paying for Idle Infrastructure
description:
Provisioning cloud infrastructure for peak traffic is standard practice. However, when those peak-allocated servers run 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, you end up paying full price for capacity that sits unused at 3 AM.

This is the quiet tax of "just in case" infrastructure. Teams lift and shift workloads to cloud providers like AWS, promise themselves they will optimize the setup later, and then move on to new feature requests. The result is bloated monthly bills driven by idle compute instances.

Right-sizing your servers is not a one-time project—it is a continuous operational practice. Here is how to audit your workloads and systematically strip away idle capacity.

Step 1: Collect 2 to 4 Weeks of Metric Data

Never resize or terminate a server based on a single day's performance snapshot. Weekly batch jobs, end-of-month processing, or unexpected traffic bursts can skew short-term data. Pull at least 2 to 4 weeks of CPU and memory usage data before making any infrastructure changes.

Using the AWS SDK for Python (boto3), you can programmatically flag instances whose peak CPU usage remains consistently low over a 14-day window.

import boto3
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def find_underutilized_instances():
    cloudwatch = boto3.client('cloudwatch')
    ec2 = boto3.client('ec2')

    # Fetch all running EC2 instances
    instances = ec2.describe_instances(
        Filters=[{'Name': 'instance-state-name', 'Values': ['running']}]
    )

    end_time = datetime.utcnow()
    start_time = end_time - timedelta(days=14)

    for reservation in instances['Reservations']:
        for instance in reservation['Instances']:
            instance_id = instance['InstanceId']

            # Query maximum CPU utilization over the last 14 days
            stats = cloudwatch.get_metric_statistics(
                Namespace='AWS/EC2',
                MetricName='CPUUtilization',
                Dimensions=[{'Name': 'InstanceId', 'Value': instance_id}],
                StartTime=start_time,
                EndTime=end_time,
                Period=86400,
                Statistics=['Maximum']
            )

            datapoints = stats.get('Datapoints', [])
            if datapoints:
                max_cpu = max(dp['Maximum'] for dp in datapoints)
                if max_cpu < 40.0:
                    print(f"Downsize candidate: {instance_id} | Peak CPU: {max_cpu:.2f}%")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    find_underutilized_instances()

Step 2: Establish Downsizing and Cleanup Thresholds

Once you have your baseline metrics, apply clear operational rules:

  • Downsize: If an instance's peak CPU utilization stays below 40% across a full two-to-four-week cycle, it can likely be moved to a smaller instance family or size.
  • Stop or Terminate: If a server shows near-zero traffic or utilization for two consecutive weeks, stop it. If it remains stopped for another two weeks without causing dependency issues, terminate it and back up any attached volumes if needed.

The smallest instance type that reliably meets your SLA and performance targets is the correct instance.

Step 3: Automate Off-Peak Shutdowns for Non-Production

Development and staging environments rarely need to run overnight or on weekends. Leaving non-production servers active 168 hours a week when they are only utilized during 40 working hours accounts for significant unnecessary spend.

You can automate instance shutdowns outside business hours using scheduled scripts or serverless automation workflows.

import boto3

def stop_non_prod_instances():
    ec2 = boto3.client('ec2')

    # Query instances tagged for development or staging
    response = ec2.describe_instances(
        Filters=[
            {'Name': 'tag:Environment', 'Values': ['dev', 'staging']},
            {'Name': 'instance-state-name', 'Values': ['running']}
        ]
    )

    instance_ids = [
        instance['InstanceId']
        for reservation in response['Reservations']
        for instance in reservation['Instances']
    ]

    if instance_ids:
        ec2.stop_instances(InstanceIds=instance_ids)
        print(f"Stopped off-peak instances: {instance_ids}")
    else:
        print("No active dev/staging instances found to stop.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    stop_non_prod_instances()

By connecting a function like this to a scheduled trigger (such as AWS EventBridge), you automatically eliminate idle server hours every evening and weekend.

Step 4: Adopt Flexible Infrastructure Models

For workloads that are stateless, fault-tolerant, or batch-driven, static server allocation is rarely optimal. Incorporating Spot instances or auto-scaling groups tied to actual demand lets your system handle traffic spikes without keeping over-provisioned servers alive around the clock.

Make Right-Sizing a Habit

Cloud cost optimization is not a one-off task after a major migration. Workloads evolve, feature requirements change, and unused resources accumulate over time. Revisit your CPU, memory, and network metrics on a monthly schedule, build automated cleanup guards, and make sure your provisioned infrastructure matches your actual daily usage.

About me

Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. Feel free to connect with Tanmay on LinkedIn.

title: One Design for the Space Radar Map and Every Site: Bigger Targets, Clearer Choices
description:
For developers: this is the user-facing write-up of a refactor that replaced about fourteen button styles in a three.js app with one stylesheet shared by five sites, enforced by tests. The markup and rules are linked at the end. Originally published at blog.spaceradar.ai.

The Space Radar map and its four sites, the journal, games, models and video, now share one design. Every button, choice, menu, slider, close button and panel comes from one small set of controls, so they look and behave the same wherever you meet them. On a phone every control is big enough for a finger, on a keyboard you can always see where you are, with reduced motion turned on nothing slides, and on every view one orange button shows the main thing to do.

It was overdue. The map grew one feature at a time, and each feature brought its own buttons. By November it had about fourteen different button looks, four menus that a phone showed unstyled, eleven different ways to close a panel, and little orange corner brackets to mark what was selected. Each was fine on its own. Together they made you learn the app again in every panel.


Before: the browser’s own radios, a plain menu and no section labels. The cover picture is the same panel after the change.

Easy to hit with a finger

On a touch screen every control is at least 44 pixels tall, the size accessibility guidelines recommend for a fingertip. The regular buttons grow from 40 to 44. The small ones, and the round close button, keep their look but get an invisible hit area of 44 pixels round them, so a tap just beside the cross still closes the panel. Menus use 16-pixel text on touch, so an iPhone does not zoom the page when you open one. Sliders are 44 pixels tall on touch and still let the panel scroll.

Easy to follow with a keyboard

Every control draws the same 2-pixel blue ring when it has the keyboard’s focus, so you can always see where Tab has taken you. What is selected is now read from the same attribute a screen reader is told, pressed, checked or selected, so what is drawn on screen and what is spoken cannot disagree. Radios and checkboxes are the browser’s own inputs, drawn over: the keyboard and the screen reader work on them as they do everywhere else.

One orange button

Orange now means one thing: the main action of what you are looking at. Start recording in the Record panel, Fly to it on an object’s card, Subscribe in the email form. There is one per view, never two. Blue means links, the focus ring and whatever is selected, and everything else is a quiet grey pill. The orange corner brackets are gone; a selected choice wears the same blue wash everywhere.


The Moon’s card: Fly to it is the one orange action; the rest are quiet.


What to show: drawn checkboxes and the same rows as every other list.

Calm when you ask for calm

If your system asks for reduced motion, nothing in the control set transitions. The rule elsewhere is that nothing loops, bounces or glows, with two exceptions, and both stay still under reduced motion: the Games button and the Buy Me a Coffee cup.

Games used to sit in the head of the side panel, where its wordmark wrapped onto two lines. It is now an icon on the tool rail at the right of the map, with a soft blue glow that breathes once every 3.6 seconds and pauses whenever the rail is out of sight. On a phone, Games is a row of the More menu.

The same on every site

The set is one stylesheet. The map uses it, and the kit that builds the journal, games.spaceradar.ai, models.spaceradar.ai and video.spaceradar.ai carries the same file, byte for byte. A search box, a filter pill or a Subscribe button is the same thing on all of them, in the same dark look, with the same type. If you learn it once, you know it everywhere.


Every control in the set, in every state, on one specimen page.

Keeping it that way is the hard part, so it is written down and tested. The project’s tests refuse a menu, radio, checkbox, slider or close button built without the set, and a cross typed as text, and the design principles say that a control the set lacks is added to the set, never beside it. If you build on Space Radar, the control set is documented with its markup, its rules and before and after pictures.

None of this adds a feature. It makes the features there are easier to find, to reach and to trust. Open any card on the map and try it with your thumb, or with Tab.

Try it: Open the space station’s card and try the controls. Free, in your browser, no account.

Questions people ask

Is the Space Radar map easy to use on a phone?
Every control on the map grows to at least 44 pixels on a touch screen, the size accessibility guidelines recommend for a finger. Small buttons and close buttons keep their look and get an invisible hit area of that size, and selects use 16 px text on touch so the phone does not zoom in.

Can I use Space Radar with a keyboard?
The design rules ask for everything to be reachable by keyboard, and every control in the shared set draws the same visible 2 px blue focus ring, so you can always see where you are. Keyboard shortcuts leave text fields alone.

Does Space Radar respect reduced motion?
Yes. With reduced motion turned on in your system, nothing in the control set transitions, and the two small decorations that move, the glow on the Games button and the coffee cup in the corner, stay still.

Why is only one button orange?
Orange marks the one main action of whatever you are looking at, such as Start recording or Fly to it. Blue marks links, the focus ring and whatever is selected. Everything else is a quiet grey pill.

Where did the Games button go?
It moved from the top of the side panel to the tool rail on the right of the map, as an icon with a slow, soft glow. On a phone it is in the More menu.

Sources

  • UI components: the control set (docs/UI_COMPONENTS.md)
  • Design principles (docs/DESIGN_PRINCIPLES.md)
  • The control set’s stylesheet (site/css/controls.css)
  • WCAG 2.2: Target Size (Enhanced), success criterion 2.5.5
  • WCAG 2.2: Focus Visible, success criterion 2.4.7

title: Abstraction of MongoDB
description:
I have a question. Why is everyone in tech obsessed with abstraction?

Almost everything is an abstraction over some complex or repetitive task.

Some abstractions remove repetitive tasks, while others hide complexity and provide simpler ways to do that work.

But this abstraction comes with some cost. We'll discuss that cost some other day.

MongoDB is also an abstraction that provides a simpler way to store and work with data.

And this abstraction starts with its core concept: documents.

What does that mean? Don't be confused.

It means you can store user data in one document, product data in another document, and if you need to store other details, like orders, you can store them in separate documents.

You don't need to worry about how MongoDB stores this data at the physical or low level. MongoDB manages how the data is stored internally. This gives you the document abstraction.

Now, the second main abstraction is tables and relationships.

Think in terms of a relational database. Assume you need to store details of a user, like their address. What would you do?

Ummmmmmm 🤔🤔

We first create a user table and then connect it with an address table.

Here, we need to manually define relationships between these tables.

But MongoDB allows you to store this information in one document.

One disclaimer: neither model is perfect. It depends on the use case.

This gives you an abstraction over managing relationships between data.

Now, the next abstraction MongoDB provides is operations.

We can query documents and collections to retrieve useful information.

Using commands, you tell MongoDB what you want to find or change. Now, MongoDB determines how to execute that operation using its query engine, indexes, and storage mechanisms.

And that's how MongoDB makes working with data simpler through abstraction.

title: Supabase vs. Business Application Platforms: An Honest Capability Matrix
description:
Disclosure: This post compares INFORMAT, a business application platform we build, with Supabase. Every Supabase limitation below is linked to Supabase's own documentation so the claims can be checked instead of trusted. There is also a section on where Supabase is clearly better than INFORMAT, and it ended up longer than expected.

The comparison nobody sets up correctly

Most "X vs. Supabase" posts make the same mistake: they compare feature lists.

That is the wrong axis. Supabase is a backend platform. It gives you primitives — a database, auth, storage, functions, realtime — and assumes you are the application. A business application platform is a different genre: it assumes the platform is the application, and you are configuring it.

Concretely: with Supabase, "an employee requests time off, their manager approves it, finance gets notified, and the request appears in a monthly report" means you write the schema, the API calls, the approval state machine, the notification pipeline, the permission checks, and the UI. With an aPaaS, that sentence is roughly a form, a flow diagram, and a report.

Neither is wrong. They are different products for different buyers, and the confusion costs people real time. So here is the honest matrix — plus the four places where the difference actually bites.

TL;DR

Supabase INFORMAT
Category Backend-as-a-Service Business application platform (aPaaS)
Core primitive Postgres + auto-generated APIs Application + workflow + org model
Primary user Developers writing an app Teams configuring an app
Data model Standard Postgres tables, fully portable Metadata-driven business objects
Best at Custom product development, fast Internal systems with process and permissions
Licensing Apache-2.0, 100k+ GitHub stars Commercial, on-prem license
If you are a three-person startup Supabase, without hesitation Probably overkill
If you deploy to an air-gapped government intranet Different conversation This is the conversation

Now the parts that matter.

Where Supabase is genuinely better

Starting here, because a comparison that opens with "we win" is not a comparison.

1. Data portability is unmatched. Supabase is a real Postgres database. pg_dump works. Any DBA can connect with psql. Any ORM, migration tool, or BI tool works against it. That is an enormous, underrated feature: the exit door is always open. Platforms that abstract the database away — including INFORMAT, to a degree — cannot say that as cleanly. If an organization's biggest fear is lock-in, that settles the argument.

2. The SDKs are real. Official clients for JavaScript, Flutter, Python, Swift, Kotlin, C#. A developer who has never seen Supabase is productive in an afternoon. INFORMAT does not have that yet; more on this below.

3. Local development is a solved problem. The supabase CLI spins up the entire stack locally: database, auth, storage, and functions on a laptop in one command. That is the single biggest developer-experience advantage in this entire comparison, and it is not close.

4. Branching is a genuinely good idea. Each pull request can get its own isolated environment with its own credentials, spun up as a clone of the base project, with the schema rebuilt from migrations. Merging runs an ordered deploy: Clone → Pull → Health → Configure → Migrate → Seed → Deploy. For a team that ships database changes through code review, that workflow is excellent.

5. The ecosystem compounds. 100k+ GitHub stars means Stack Overflow answers, hiring pools, tutorial coverage, and third-party integrations. A closed commercial platform cannot manufacture that.

6. The primitives are complete and composable. Data API (REST and GraphQL), Realtime, Storage with transformations, Edge Functions on Deno, plus Vector, Cron, and Queues as first-class modules. Assembling a backend from parts is a supported path, not an adventure.

For a consumer app, a SaaS product, or anything where the team owns the UI and the business logic and nobody answers to a compliance officer, Supabase is very likely the right call. It gets recommended here without reservation.

Where the genre difference actually bites

Four gaps show up repeatedly when the target is an enterprise internal system rather than a product. All four are about things a BaaS deliberately leaves to you.

1. Edge Functions are not a workflow engine

A leave-approval flow can legitimately wait three days for a manager. A purchase order can sit in review for a week. A contract can loop back for revision four times.

Edge Functions have hard boundaries, and they are documented rather than hidden (supabase.com/docs/guides/functions/limits):

  • 2 seconds of CPU time per worker (async I/O excluded)
  • 400 seconds wall clock on paid plans, 150s on free
  • 256 MB memory
  • 150-second idle timeout → 504

These are sane, well-chosen limits for a serverless edge runtime, and they are exactly why it is not a workflow engine. Durable, long-running, resumable business processes need state that survives the request: who is holding the task, what the SLA clock says, what happens when the approver is on vacation, how a rejection re-enters the flow.

That is what a BPMN engine provides. INFORMAT embeds Flowable, a full BPMN 2.0 engine with a visual process designer, so the process is the data model rather than a chain of function calls whose state has to be reconstructed. A task node waits on an assignee for as long as it takes; that wait is a row, not a suspended invocation.

If the process is "resize this image," use an Edge Function. If the process is "this requisition needs three signatures and escalates after 48 hours," you want an engine, whichever platform it lives on. Adding Temporal or Inngest to Supabase is a legitimate path to the same shape — it just means integrating a fifth system.

2. Row-level security is not an org chart

RLS is excellent, and it solves the hard multi-tenant SaaS problem: tenant_id = auth.jwt() ->> 'tenant' on every table and the job is done. Supabase deserves credit for making that the default mental model.

Enterprise internal permissions are shaped differently. The questions are not "can this row be seen" but:

  • Can a department manager edit records for their subtree only?
  • Can an HR admin see the salary field while a team lead sees the record without it?
  • Does an acting approver inherit the real approver's permissions for two weeks?
  • When someone changes departments, does historical access follow the old org or the new one?

Those are questions about an organizational graph, not a row predicate. Some of them can be expressed in RLS policies — people do, and it works — but the policy SQL grows into a shadow org model maintained by hand, in a language the HR system does not speak.

This is INFORMAT's closest thing to a genuine architectural advantage: the permission model is bound to a first-class department/role/member directory and evaluated as a chain from user to role to data scope to field rule, so "manager of a subtree" is a primitive rather than a clever policy.

And the honest flip side: because those permissions live in the application layer, they cannot be bypassed — but the data also cannot be reached without going through the platform. Supabase puts the guard inside the database, which is a stronger, more auditable boundary. If INFORMAT ever handed out raw database connections, that model would leak. This is a real design tradeoff, not a win.

3. Self-hosted Supabase is single-project

This is the finding that surprised the most, and it comes straight from Supabase's self-hosting page (supabase.com/docs/guides/self-hosting):

"Self-hosted Supabase runs as a single project, which means that Studio doesn't support multiple organizations or projects."

And:

"Some features of the managed platform aren't available when self-hosting: branching, advanced metrics beyond logs, managed backups and PITR, analytics and vector buckets, ETL, and the Management API."

Self-hosters also take on the operational surface: provisioning, hardening, service configuration, Postgres maintenance, high availability, backups and disaster recovery, monitoring and uptime. The Kubernetes route is community-maintained (supabase-community/supabase-kubernetes) rather than official, and the CLI's local stack is explicitly not a production deployment: "not hardened for production and must not be exposed to external traffic."

None of that is a scandal. Self-hosting a full backend platform is genuinely hard, and Supabase is unusually honest about the tradeoffs. It matters only when the deployment shape is:

  • Ten business units, each with its own apps, on one installation behind the corporate firewall
  • An air-gapped network where "managed backups" and "the Management API" are not options anyone can buy
  • A database that has to be on an approved list

That last one is where the two products are structurally different. One INFORMAT instance hosts many applications over one identity and one org directory, ships as an on-prem package with license and machine binding, and runs against domestic databases (Kingbase, SAP HANA) and TongWeb. That is not a feature list; it is a deployment genre.

For a team in the EU or US happily on managed cloud, this entire section is irrelevant. Fair.

4. Realtime is broadcast; collaboration is a model

Supabase Realtime is good at what it does: subscribe to changes and broadcast them. For chat, live cursors, or a dashboard that refreshes itself, it is the right tool.

Multi-user editing of a business record is a different problem — field-level merge, optimistic locking, who is editing what right now, what happens when two people change the same field within the same second. Broadcast gives you the transport; the model is still yours to build.

INFORMAT has the transport too (a WebSocket push channel with cluster-aware routing and per-principal filtering) and is still building the model. Neither platform has this finished. It is mentioned here because it is the next thing every buyer will ask for, and pretending otherwise would be exactly the kind of claim this post argues against.

The capability matrix

Capability Supabase INFORMAT Who is ahead
Relational database Postgres (portable, direct psql access) Metadata-driven objects over PG Supabase
Auto-generated API REST + GraphQL, typed clients Reserved RPC-style endpoints Supabase
Official SDKs 6+ languages None public yet Supabase
One-command local dev supabase start Manual Maven + DB setup Supabase
PR preview environments Branching, Vercel integration Versioned SQL + manual envs Supabase
Open source / community Apache-2.0, 100k+ stars Commercial, private Supabase
BPMN workflow engine Bring your own Flowable, visual designer INFORMAT
Org model (dept/role/member) Build it yourself First-class INFORMAT
Permission model RLS (row-level, in-database) App-layer, org-bound Split — see §2
Form / table / dashboard designers Build it yourself Built in INFORMAT
Multi-app on one install 1 project (self-hosted) Many apps, shared identity INFORMAT
Auth providers Email, phone, OAuth, SAML, MFA, passkeys Google, WeChat, DingTalk, Feishu, WeCom Supabase (breadth)
Storage S3 + CDN + transformations Local / COS / S3 Supabase
Realtime Table-change subscriptions Internal push channel Supabase
Serverless functions Deno edge functions Code studio, not edge Supabase
Vector search pgvector module pgvector inside RAG Supabase (as a product)
Scheduled jobs / queues Cron + Queues modules Automation, async, MQ Tie
AI agent layer Vectors + MCP examples Agent framework, skills, MCP server endpoint INFORMAT
Domestic DB / regulated stacks Not offered Kingbase, SAP HANA, TongWeb INFORMAT
On-prem license + machine binding Community Docker Commercial on-prem INFORMAT
IM and payment integrations Build it yourself DingTalk, Feishu, WeCom, Stripe, Alipay, WeChat Pay INFORMAT
Multi-language UI i18n in your app 6 locales built in INFORMAT

Count the rows: roughly 10–11 go to Supabase, 10–11 to INFORMAT. That is the point. Anyone claiming a clean sweep is selling, not comparing.

What INFORMAT is still missing

A comparison post from a vendor that lists no weaknesses is a brochure. Here are the real gaps, in priority order:

  1. No auto-generated API contract. Supabase's biggest practical win is that creating a table creates a typed API. INFORMAT's business objects already know their own schema and should be emitting OpenAPI from them. They do not. That is the top roadmap item, and the one to fix first.
  2. No public SDKs. Integration today means reading API docs by hand. For an agent-first platform that is an obvious hole.
  3. No one-command local environment. No container image, no Compose file. Every trial and every partner onboarding starts with setup work that should not exist in 2026.
  4. Thin public documentation. The internal docs directory is full of design notes — useful internally, not useful to an evaluator. Supabase's documentation is half its product; INFORMAT's is not there yet.

This list is published on purpose. The alternative is having an evaluator discover it in week one of a trial and conclude the platform was hiding something.

So which one?

Pick Supabase if: you are building a product, your team writes the UI, you are on managed cloud, your permissions are tenant-shaped, and data portability is a board-level concern. That is most readers.

Pick a platform like INFORMAT if: you are delivering internal systems — approvals, master data, equipment, quality, HR — where process and org structure are the hard part, the buyer is IT rather than engineering, and it has to run inside your own network against an approved database.

Be honest with yourself if: you started with Supabase for an internal system and the backlog now contains "add an approval flow," "restrict this field by department," and "same thing for four more business units." Those three items are a platform decision wearing a feature request's clothes.

The most expensive mistake in this space is not picking the wrong tool. It is picking a tool whose genre does not match the problem, and only finding out eighteen months in, when the workaround has become the architecture.

Sources

  • Self-hosting shape and feature list: supabase.com/docs/guides/self-hosting
  • Edge Function CPU, wall-clock, and memory limits: supabase.com/docs/guides/functions/limits

title: How to Check Color Contrast for Accessibility (WCAG AA)
description:
You pick a nice grey for body text, it looks fine on your monitor, and an audit later flags every paragraph on the site. If you want to know how to check color contrast for accessibility before that happens, the good news is that it is one formula and a few rules. The bad news is that most mistakes happen in the rules, not the formula.

This guide shows the WCAG numbers, how to calculate a ratio yourself, how to check it in Chrome DevTools, and the traps that make a "passing" pair fail.

Why color contrast matters

Low contrast text is hard to read for people with low vision or colour vision deficiencies, and for everyone reading a phone in sunlight. It is also the most common accessibility failure on the web. Chrome's own DevTools documentation calls low contrast text "the top accessibility issue on the web", citing WebAIM's Million report.

WCAG covers it in Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum), which is the level AA requirement most laws and policies point to.

The WCAG contrast ratios you need to know

What you are checking AA AAA
Normal text 4.5:1 7:1
Large text (18pt / 24px, or 14pt / about 18.66px bold) 3:1 4.5:1
UI components and meaningful graphics (SC 1.4.11) 3:1 none

Two exceptions are easy to miss. Text in a disabled control, pure decoration, or text that is part of a logo has no contrast requirement. Everything else does, including placeholder text, captions and the small print under a form.

How to check color contrast by hand

The ratio compares the relative luminance of the two colours: (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the lighter colour. Luminance comes from the sRGB channels after you convert them to linear light, as defined in the W3C relative luminance definition.

Here is the whole thing in Python, no libraries:

def lin(c):
    c = c / 255
    return c / 12.92 if c <= 0.04045 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4

def luminance(hex_color):
    h = hex_color.lstrip("#")
    r, g, b = (int(h[i:i+2], 16) for i in (0, 2, 4))
    return 0.2126 * lin(r) + 0.7152 * lin(g) + 0.0722 * lin(b)

def ratio(fg, bg):
    l1, l2 = sorted((luminance(fg), luminance(bg)), reverse=True)
    return (l1 + 0.05) / (l2 + 0.05)

for fg, bg in [("#767676", "#ffffff"), ("#777777", "#ffffff"),
               ("#ffffff", "#3b82f6"), ("#ffffff", "#2563eb")]:
    print(f"{fg} on {bg}: {ratio(fg, bg):.4f}:1")

We ran it, and this is the output:

#767676 on #ffffff: 4.5422:1
#777777 on #ffffff: 4.4781:1
#ffffff on #3b82f6: 3.6779:1
#ffffff on #2563eb: 5.1686:1

Look at the first two lines. #767676 and #777777 are one step apart, and they land on opposite sides of 4.5:1. The W3C Understanding document is explicit that the ratios are thresholds and must not be rounded: 4.499:1 does not meet 4.5:1. So a tool that shows "4.5" for #777777 and a green tick is giving you the wrong answer.

The third line is a very common case: white text on a mid blue button (#3b82f6, the Tailwind blue-500). At 3.68:1 it fails for normal text but passes for large text and for the button's outline as a UI component. Moving one shade darker to #2563eb gets you to 5.17:1 and the problem is gone.

How to check color contrast in Chrome DevTools

You do not need an extension for a quick check:

  1. Right-click the text and choose Inspect.
  2. Hover the element with the inspect tool. The tooltip shows a Contrast value, with a warning sign if it is too low.
  3. In the Styles pane, click the colour swatch next to color. The colour picker has a Contrast ratio section that shows the AA and AAA lines and can suggest a passing colour.

For a whole page, the Lighthouse accessibility audit and the CSS Overview panel list every low contrast element. The Chrome DevTools contrast guide walks through each of these.

Check it with a free contrast checker

When you are choosing colours rather than auditing a live page, a dedicated checker is faster. We built MyToolStudio, and its free WCAG color contrast checker runs in your browser with no sign up.

We put the failing button pair from above into it: text #ffffff, background #3b82f6. It reports 3.68:1, the same number as the script, with AA normal text marked as a fail and large text and UI components as a pass. A few things that save time:

  • Font size and bold controls. Set the real size of your text and the tool tells you whether it counts as normal or large, so you know which threshold applies.
  • Opacity. Semi-transparent text is measured as it actually appears on the background (more on that below).
  • Suggested fixes. For our pair it offered #0d70e1 as a background that keeps white text and reaches 4.75:1.
  • Contrast grid. Paste up to 12 colours and every text and background pair is checked at once, which is handy for a whole palette.

If a palette fails everywhere, the accessible color palette generator starts from passing pairs, and the color blindness simulator shows how the result looks with different types of colour vision.

Common mistakes when checking contrast

Rounding up. Covered above, and worth repeating: 4.48:1 is a fail.

Ignoring opacity. color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5) on white looks like a dark grey in your CSS, but on screen it blends to roughly #808080. Our script gives 3.95:1 after rounding the blended channel, and the checker reports 3.98:1 because it does not round it first. Either way it fails for normal text. Always measure the blended colour, not the CSS value.

Testing one state only. Hover, focus, visited and disabled styles all have their own colours. A link can pass at rest and fail on hover. Placeholder text is not exempt either.

Text over images and gradients. One check against the "average" colour proves nothing. W3C lists this as a known failure (F83). Check the lightest part of the image behind the text, or add a solid or semi-opaque layer under it.

Treating large text as "anything that looks big". Large means at least 24px regular or about 18.66px bold. A 20px regular heading is still normal text and needs 4.5:1.

FAQ

What is a good color contrast ratio?
For WCAG AA, at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and UI parts. If you can reach 7:1 for body text, you also meet AAA.

Does WCAG 2.2 change the contrast rules?
No. WCAG 2.2 keeps 1.4.3, 1.4.6 and 1.4.11 the same as 2.1. APCA, the new contrast method for WCAG 3, is still a draft, so treat its Lc score as extra information and keep using the 2.x ratios for compliance.

Do logos and disabled buttons need to meet contrast?
No. Text that is part of a logo, pure decoration, and inactive controls are exempt from 1.4.3. Everything a user needs to read or operate is not.

Wrapping up

Checking contrast is quick once you know the rules: use the real blended colours, match the threshold to the text size, check every state, and never round up. If you are working through other web checks, our earlier guides on testing a robots.txt file and decoding a JWT safely follow the same hands-on approach.

You can find the rest of our free developer, SEO and accessibility utilities on the MyToolStudio tools page. For the official wording of the criterion, read the W3C Understanding page for SC 1.4.3.
