title: 1Z0-997-26 Exam: Architecture Comparisons for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure 2026 Architect Professional
description:
Why comparison literacy decides the 1Z0-997-26 exam

A useful 1Z0-997-26 study artefact is not a memorized list of OCI service limits. It is an architectural decision chain:

Workload constraint → resilience or security boundary → managed OCI service → operational trade-off → telemetry check

That sequence reflects the work the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure 2026 Architect Professional exam is intended to assess: turning enterprise constraints into OCI designs that satisfy availability, cloud-native, security, database, and observability goals at once.

Oracle targets experienced OCI architects rather than administrators learning VCN basics. Expect 50 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes with a 68% passing score; confirm current details with Oracle University before booking.

Comparison literacy decides outcomes because OCI offers overlapping services at every layer. When a prompt gives three valid tools and one binding constraint, knowing where each service stops beats memorizing feature sheets.

1Z0-997-26 exam scope and format

Oracle University delivers 1Z0-997-26 via online proctoring or Pearson VUE testing centers. Catalog terms list 50 single- and multiple-select items, 90 minutes, a 68% passing threshold, and a USD $245 fee; verify regional pricing and rules directly before sitting.

Passing earns the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure 2026 Certified Architect Professional credential. No prior exam is mandatory, though the Become An OCI Architect Professional learning path assumes Associate-level IAM, networking, compute, and storage skills (1Z0-1072-26) plus one to two years of OCI work.

Avoid studying from retired 1Z0-997-25 outlines (scheduled for archival on September 30, 2026), which included dedicated multicloud interconnect and migration sections. The 1Z0-997-26 blueprint consolidates into five domains, leaves multicloud architecture to exams like 1Z0-1151-26, and emphasizes Zero Trust Packet Routing, Organizations Management, Globally Distributed Autonomous Database, Autonomous Recovery Service, and OCI Cache.

The official 1Z0-997-26 objectives at a glance

These 1Z0-997-26 official exam objectives cover five domains. The percentages below are the official domain weights, not a promised number of questions for each topic.

1. Architect High Availability and Disaster Recovery Solutions — 15%

Resilience separates Availability Domains (isolated regional data centers) from Fault Domains (hardware isolation inside an AD). OCI Load Balancer terminates TLS at Layer 7, while Network Load Balancer forwards Layer 4 TCP/UDP traffic with client IP preservation. Regional DR pairs RTO and RPO targets with Full Stack Disaster Recovery (FSDR), organizing compute, storage, load balancers, OKE, and peer databases into DR protection groups with step groups for switchover, failover, and prechecks.

Example: an application runs Autonomous AI Database on ECPU with cross-region Autonomous Data Guard and needs automated cutover. FSDR orchestrates the entire stack rather than failing over the database alone.

2. Architect Cloud-Native Solutions — 20%

Cloud-native objectives span containers, serverless APIs, and Infrastructure as Code. With OCI Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE), distinguish enhanced clusters (virtual node pools, managed add-ons, pod workload identity, financially backed SLA) from basic clusters (SLO only), plus VCN-native pod networking from flannel overlay. Scenarios also test OCI Container Instances, OCI Container Registry (OCIR), OCI DevOps Service, Oracle Functions, API Gateway, and OCI Resource Manager for managed Terraform stacks, remote .tfstate, and drift detection.

A useful self-check is runtime scope: does the workload need Kubernetes scheduling and pod IAM, or serverless functions behind API Gateway?

3. Architect Security Solutions — 25%

Carrying the top weight, security covers OCI Bastion for ephemeral private SSH sessions, OCI Network Firewall for stateful Layer 3 to Layer 7 inspection and TLS filtering, and Zero Trust Packet Routing (ZPR) for topology-independent packet enforcement. Application and governance controls span OCI Web Application Firewall (WAF), OCI Certificates, OCI Vault / Key Management Service (KMS) for HSM keys and secrets, and OCI Organizations Management for parent-child tenancies, Universal Credits mapping, and governance rules.

For a scenario, imagine that business units require isolated child tenancies under central billing and mandatory guardrails. Compartments divide one tenancy; Organizations Management governs multiple tenancies.

4. Architecting, Implementing, and Operating Databases in OCI — 20%

Database selection weighs host custody against automation across OCI Base Database Service and Oracle Autonomous AI Database (ATP and ADW). Oracle Database Autonomous Recovery Service provides zero data loss real-time protection, incremental-forever backups, and immutable recovery validation. Globally Distributed Autonomous Database shards one logical database across regions for horizontal scale and data sovereignty, while OCI Cache runs managed Redis and Valkey clusters with immutable parameter configurations.

A useful self-check is custody versus locality: do legacy agents require guest OS access, or do residency mandates require regional sharding under one SQL view?

5. Implementing Observability Solutions — 20%

Observability turns telemetry into action. OCI Monitoring evaluates metrics via MQL queries and triggers alarms through OCI Notifications, while OCI Logging gathers Service Logs, Unified Monitoring Agent Custom Logs, and Audit Logs for Logging Queries. OCI Connector Hub moves batches from Logging, Monitoring, Queue, or Streaming through filter or Functions tasks to Object Storage, Notifications, Monitoring, Streaming, or Log Analytics with at-least-once delivery, and OCI Search indexes cross-compartment resources.

Example: operations must route filtered audit alerts to Notifications and Object Storage. Connector Hub runs that pipeline declaratively and deactivates persistently failing connectors rather than dropping data.

Showdown 1: Zero Trust Packet Routing versus Network Security Groups

Zero Trust Packet Routing (ZPR) enforces intent-based policies written in Zero Trust Packet Routing Policy Language (ZPL) over security attributes on endpoints and VCNs, as detailed in the Zero Trust Packet Routing overview. Network Security Groups (NSGs) apply stateful or stateless Layer 3 and Layer 4 rules to VNICs inside a VCN.

Both filter packet traffic without reading IAM principals or API permissions, yet diverge as topologies evolve. NSGs bind to subnet CIDRs and cap at five NSGs per VNIC, creating risk during network refactors. ZPR decouples intent from IP topology (up to three attributes per general resource, five per VNIC, one per VCN) and enforces ZPL across VCNs linked by LPGs and DRGs.

ZPR layers over route tables, security lists, and NSGs rather than replacing them: packets must pass every rule across all layers, and ZPR does not inspect inbound internet or on-premises traffic. Tagging a database with a ZPR attribute blocks unpermitted VCN traffic until an explicit ZPR policy allows it.

If a scenario needs database isolation that survives subnet edits or peering changes, think Zero Trust Packet Routing. If it asks for direct VNIC rules on internet ingress, think Network Security Groups.

Showdown 2: OKE versus OCI Container Instances

OCI Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) manages a Kubernetes control plane with managed or virtual node pools, VCN-native pod networking, managed add-ons, and pod workload identity on enhanced clusters. OCI Container Instances runs containers on serverless flexible shapes with VM isolation and no cluster management.

Each option pulls images from OCIR, attaches to VCN subnets, and emits OCI Events. Where they part ways is orchestration depth: OKE provides Kubernetes APIs, node cycling during upgrades, and a financially backed SLA on enhanced clusters versus an SLO on basic clusters. Container Instances removes node pools, assigns chosen OCPUs and memory to the container group, and pauses billing when stopped.

OKE adds cluster lifecycle maintenance for full orchestration; Container Instances sacrifices Kubernetes service discovery and pod autoscaling for zero control-plane upkeep.

If a scenario specifies short-lived CI/CD jobs, isolated APIs, or stop-and-pause billing without orchestration, think OCI Container Instances. If it requires Kubernetes manifests, managed add-ons, or pod-scoped IAM, think OKE.

Showdown 3: OCI Base Database Service versus Autonomous AI Database

OCI Base Database Service provisions customer-managed Oracle Database VM systems with guest OS access, custom options, and manual patch scheduling. Oracle Autonomous AI Database runs on managed Exadata infrastructure, automating patching, tuning, indexing, and ECPU scaling.

While both deploy in VCN subnets, encrypt via OCI Vault, and back up to Autonomous Recovery Service, administrative custody splits them cleanly. Base Database lets administrators install host agents and set patch windows. Autonomous AI Database removes host OS access, automates updates, and pairs with Full Stack Disaster Recovery on ECPU deployments alongside cross-region Autonomous Data Guard.

Base Database trades DBA effort for host control; Autonomous AI Database trades OS access for automated tuning and elastic scaling.

If a scenario requires third-party OS agents or custom patch windows, think OCI Base Database Service. If it prioritizes minimal DBA overhead and ECPU auto-scaling, think Autonomous AI Database.

Official 1Z0-997-26 learning resources

Oracle publishes no standalone printed 1Z0-997-26 study guide book. Official prep centers on the Oracle University exam catalog page, the MyLearn learning path, and its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Architect Professional course.

That course bundles 26+ hours of modules, Student Guides (Volumes I and II), an Activity Guide, six skill checks, an exam-prep module, a practice exam, and a hands-on lab. Pair those official 1Z0-997-26 learning resources with OCI docs for FSDR, ZPR limits, enhanced OKE clusters, Autonomous Recovery Service, OCI Cache, Organizations Management, and Connector Hub, and confirm registration rules in Oracle CertView or Pearson VUE.

1Z0-997-26 practice questions and CertsPrime

Diagnostic question sets belong after you cover all five domains, not as your primary textbook. Working through 1Z0-997-26 practice questions exposes where you misread constraints, confuse ZPR and NSGs under pressure, or overlook prerequisites such as ECPU compute for Full Stack DR. Practice items cannot replace tenancy labs or verifying limits in Oracle documentation.

CertsPrime is an independent third-party resource, not an official Oracle platform and not endorsed by Oracle. Review its exam preparation resources as supplementary diagnostic practice while checking technical rules against Oracle's published documentation.

How to prepare for the 1Z0-997-26 exam

This sequence follows the five published domains and comparison boundaries as a study recommendation, not an Oracle-mandated order. Adjust the pace to your background; this is a sequence of activities, not a promised pass timeline.

  1. Audit your baseline across all five 1Z0-997-26 exam topics. Score your familiarity across Security (25%), Cloud-Native (20%), Databases (20%), Observability (20%), and HA/DR (15%).

  2. Work through the MyLearn Student Guides and modules. Prioritize Security and Observability early if your background centers on Compute and VCN basics.

  3. Remove retired 1Z0-997-25 material from your plan. Set aside standalone multicloud interconnect and migration notes dropped from the five-domain 2026 blueprint.

  4. Build a security lab with Bastion, NSGs, Network Firewall, and ZPR. Attach security attributes to private endpoints, write ZPL rules, and verify how route tables and NSGs gate traffic alongside ZPR.

  5. Configure a cross-region Full Stack Disaster Recovery plan. Add compute, load balancers, and peer databases to DR protection groups, run prechecks, and compare switchover against failover step groups.

  6. Deploy an OKE enhanced cluster alongside Container Instances. Compare VCN-native pod networking, managed add-ons, and workload identity against flexible serverless shapes and stopped-instance billing.

  7. Test Base Database, Autonomous AI Database, and Autonomous Recovery Service together. Enable real-time backup protection and map when Globally Distributed Autonomous Database or OCI Cache solves residency or latency limits.

  8. Wire a Connector Hub observability pipeline. Route Logging and Monitoring sources through filter or Functions tasks to Notifications and Object Storage, then run MQL and Logging Queries.

  9. Run timed 50-question diagnostic drills. On every missed item or lucky guess, log the exact prompt constraint that ruled out the remaining options.

Final 1Z0-997-26 exam preparation tips

In the last 48 hours, review service boundaries rather than opening unfamiliar topics. Refresh ZPR limits and internet non-enforcement, enhanced versus basic OKE features, Base Database versus Autonomous AI Database custody trade-offs, FSDR step-group ordering, and Connector Hub delivery guarantees, then stop new reading the evening before.

Confirm your booking, ID rules, and online-proctoring test in Oracle CertView or Pearson VUE ahead of test day. During the 90-minute block, read each stem for its binding constraint before reviewing options, because Oracle distractors usually describe valid OCI services that violate one stated requirement.

title: Oracle EBS or Oracle Fusion? Questions to Answer Before You Decide
description:
Many organisations running Oracle E-Business Suite are weighing whether to stay on EBS, upgrade within it, or move to Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications. There is no single right answer. The right choice depends on business priorities, the current landscape and the organisation's appetite for change. These are the questions worth answering first.

1. What does the business need in the next five years?

Growth into new countries, acquisitions, new business models or a push for faster close all change the requirements on the ERP. Start with business outcomes rather than technology features.

2. How customised is the current EBS environment?

Heavy customisation increases the cost of every upgrade and makes a move to a standardised cloud model more of a process redesign than a technical migration. An honest inventory of customisations is essential.

3. How many systems integrate with EBS today?

Interfaces built on direct database access will need to be redesigned for Fusion, which exposes data through APIs and standard services. The number and complexity of integrations is often the biggest variable in effort.

4. What is the state of master data?

Supplier, customer, item and employee data that is duplicated or inconsistent will need to be cleaned before any migration. This work pays off whichever option is chosen.

5. How will the organisation handle change?

Fusion delivers regular quarterly updates. That brings continuous improvement but also a need for ongoing testing and change management that differs from the EBS upgrade cycle.

6. What is the realistic timeline and phasing?

Some organisations move module by module, for example starting with HCM or procurement in the cloud while core financials remain on EBS for a period. A phased roadmap can reduce risk.

Making the decision

A short assessment that covers business goals, customisations, integrations, data and change readiness usually makes the right path clear. Learn more about our Oracle EBS services and Oracle Fusion services.

Conacent Consulting, Oracle Gold Partner since 2005.

title: We added one field to the object in our sessions and rolling back made the errors worse
description:
Our trade portal is a Spring Boot application on eight pods, with sessions stored in Redis through Spring Session so a customer can land on any pod. A release in October added one field to the customer context object we keep in the session: the depot a customer prefers to collect from. The rollout started at ten past eleven, one pod at a time.

Within two minutes customers with an open session started getting error pages, on some clicks and not on others. The logs had java.io.InvalidClassException: local class incompatible, stream classdesc serialVersionUID differs from the local class.

Spring Session's default serializer for Redis is plain Java serialization. A Serializable class with no explicit serialVersionUID gets one computed from its structure, so adding a field gives it a different value, and Java refuses to read a stream written with another. During the rollout, whichever version wrote a session last, the other version could not read it. Each customer's next click was a coin toss between an old pod and a new one.

We rolled back. It made things worse. By then the new pods had rewritten thousands of sessions, the old version could not read any of them, and now every pod was old. Neither version could read what the other had written, and backwards was no safer than forwards.

The fix that afternoon used serialver, a tool in the JDK that prints the serialVersionUID a class would get. We ran it against the class in the previous release, pinned that value in the new class and released again. Java serialization treats an added field as a compatible change when the identifiers match, and the new field simply arrived empty from old sessions. The errors stopped as the release completed.

Since then every serializable class in the portal declares its serialVersionUID, and a build check fails on one that does not. Sessions are now serialized as JSON, through a bean named springSessionDefaultRedisSerializer, with unknown fields ignored. We switched serializers early on a Sunday morning and accepted that everyone had to sign in again once. The release pipeline has a test that writes a session with the previous release and reads it with the new one, and the other way round.

Any data shared between two versions of an application is an interface between them, whether or not anybody designed it as one.

– Sergey Shinder

title: We moved our label reference generator into Kubernetes and pods on different nodes started issuing the same numbers
description:
Every parcel we send gets a reference that goes on the carrier's label and comes back to us on every tracking event. A small Java service hands them out. Each reference is a millisecond timestamp, a worker number and a counter that starts at zero every millisecond. For six years the service ran on four virtual machines in one subnet with 256 addresses, and the worker number was the last byte of the machine's IP address. Inside one subnet of that size, no two machines can share a last byte, so it was unique by construction, and nothing else checked.

In September we moved the service into Kubernetes and let it scale with load. Three weeks later a customer rang to ask why she had been told her parcel was delivered to an address in another town.

Our cluster gives each node its own block of 256 addresses for its pods, a common default. Pod addresses are unique across the cluster, but their last bytes are not. A pod at 10.244.3.21 and a pod at 10.244.7.21 got the same worker number. When both issued their first reference in the same millisecond, both counters were zero, and the two references were identical. At quiet times it almost never happened. At peak, with nine pods, it happened a few times a day.

The shipments table had no unique constraint on the reference, because the generator could not produce duplicates. Tracking events from the carrier were matched by reference, so each pair of parcels shared one stream of scans, and one customer received the other's delivery notice. We found thirty seven pairs.

A worker number is now leased, not derived. At startup each pod claims a free number from a table in Postgres, writes its pod name and an expiry two minutes ahead, and renews the lease every thirty seconds. If it cannot renew, it stops issuing references until it can claim a number again. The reference column has a unique constraint, so a duplicate would be an error at insert time instead of a misdirected email. We corrected the tracking history of the thirty seven pairs by hand and wrote to the customers involved.

The design had leaned on a property of our network, not of the generator. Moving it to a new network quietly took that property away.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Our Remote Desktops Kept Each Profile on a Thirty Gigabyte Disk and Our Planners' Mailboxes Grew Past It
description:
Our transport planners and office staff work from home on Citrix desktops. Since 2022 each person's Windows profile has lived in a container, a virtual disk stored as a file on a file server, which a tool called FSLogix attaches when they sign in. Whichever server they land on, they get the same desktop, settings and documents. The container also holds the local copy of their Outlook mailbox, because Outlook working from a local copy is much faster than fetching every message from the server.

FSLogix creates those containers with a maximum size of thirty gigabytes unless it is told otherwise. Nobody told it otherwise. When we set it up, the largest profile we had was nine.

On a Monday in January 2025 the planning team began reporting faults that looked unrelated. Outlook said it could not save a draft. Teams would not open. A spreadsheet saved the evening before had lost its last changes. By Wednesday thirty eight people had raised tickets, and the service desk had restarted, reset or reinstalled something for most of them.

Every one of the thirty eight had a profile container at or near thirty gigabytes. Our planners keep years of email, because a dispute about a delivery booking is settled by the email thread, and Outlook had been told to keep a local copy of all of it. The local copy grew with the mailbox until the container was full. After that, anything that tried to write to the profile failed, and each program failed in its own way. Our monitoring watched the free space on the file server, which had four terabytes to spare. It never looked inside the files.

The maximum is now fifty gigabytes. Outlook keeps a local copy of the last twelve months and reads older mail from the server when someone searches or opens it, which takes a second longer and is rarely noticed. Caches that programs rebuild for themselves are kept out of the container altogether. A nightly job reads how full each container is from the inside and raises a ticket at eighty percent, naming the person, so the service desk can call them before anything fails. The service desk's checklist for unexplained faults on a remote desktop now begins with that figure.

When one disk lives inside another, monitoring the outer one tells you nothing about the inner. Measure every layer your users actually write to.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Your Order Lookup Passed the Email Straight to MongoDB and Someone Sent an Object Instead
description:
Guest checkout
needed a way
to see your order
without an account.

Order number.
Email address.

Both must match.

app.use(express.json());

app.post("/order", async (req, res) => {
const order = await orders.findOne({
number: req.body.number,
email: req.body.email,
});
...
});

The form sends two strings.

The attacker
does not use the form.

{
"number": { "$gt": "" },
"email": { "$ne": "" }
}

express.json
parses that body
into real objects.

The driver
passes them to MongoDB
as written.

And to MongoDB
an object with a dollar key
is not a value.

It is an operator.

Number greater than nothing.

Email not equal to nothing.

That matches every order
in the collection.

findOne
returns the first.

A name,
a delivery address,
what they bought.

Change the condition,
step through the range,
and the next order comes back.

And the next.

No quotes were broken.

No string was built.

Nobody concatenated anything.

That is why it gets past
people who know about
SQL injection.

The code looks
completely parameterised.

It passed review.

It passed every test,
because every test
sent strings.

The problem is the type.

You expected a string,
and JSON
can carry far more
than strings.

Mongoose
does not save you by default.

It casts the operand
inside the operator,
and keeps the operator.

Here is what to do.

Check the type
before the query:

if (typeof req.body.email !== "string")
return res.sendStatus(400);

Better,
validate the whole body
against a schema,
with zod or similar,
so only the shapes you expect
get through.

In Mongoose,
turn on sanitizeFilter.

It wraps any dollar key
in a request value
inside $eq,
so it is compared,
not executed.

And try it yourself.

Send an object
to every endpoint
that queries by user input.

The form only sends
what the form sends.

Your server
accepts what anyone sends.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: You Appended Each Parcel's Label to the Shared List and Every Parcel Got the Last One
description:
The despatch service
built one list
of labels every parcel needed.

Read from config,
one append at a time.

Then, for each parcel,
it added that parcel's own label.

var common []string
for _, l := range cfg.Labels {
common = append(common, l)
}

for i := range parcels {
parcels[i].Labels = append(common, parcels[i].Extra)
}

For two years
the config had two labels.

Fragile. This way up.

Then someone added a third.

Keep dry.

The next morning
every parcel in the batch
carried the same extra label.

The one meant
for the last parcel.

Here is the mechanism.

A Go slice
is a small header:

a pointer to an array,
a length,
a capacity.

append writes
into the spare capacity
if there is any.

It only copies
to a new array
when there is no room.

Built one append at a time,
the array behind common
grew to 1, then 2, then 4.

Two labels,
capacity two.

No room,
so every append
made a fresh copy.

The bug was there.

It just could not fire.

Three labels,
capacity four.

One free slot.

So every parcel's append
wrote its label
into the same slot
of the same array.

Every parcel's slice
pointed at it.

The last write won,
for all of them.

No error.

No race detector warning.

The tests
used the two label config.

The fix is to stop sharing
the array:

parcels[i].Labels = append(slices.Clone(common), parcels[i].Extra)

slices.Clone
has been in the standard library
since Go 1.21.

Or cap the shared slice
so append must copy:

shared := common[:len(common):len(common)]

That third number
sets the capacity
equal to the length.

And add a test
that builds two results
from the same base
and checks
that they differ.

append can hand you back
the same memory
you gave it.

Whether it does
depends on room
you never see
in the code.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Python, JavaScript, Java or C++: Which Language First?
description:
Python, JavaScript, Java or C++: Which Language Should You Learn First?

The language you start with matters less than finishing what you start. Still, each language leads to different kinds of work. Here is a practical comparison for Nigerian learners.

Python

Python Programming runs for 12 weeks at ₦250,000. Python is readable, which makes it friendly for beginners. It is widely used for automation, data analysis and AI, so it pairs well with Data Analysis and Automation & AI.

JavaScript

JavaScript Programming runs for 10 weeks at ₦180,000. JavaScript powers the web in the browser and, through Node.js, on servers too. It is the natural gateway to frontend, backend and fullstack careers.

Java

Java Programming runs for 10 weeks at ₦200,000. Java is common in large business systems and Android development, so it is a solid choice if you are drawn to structured, enterprise-style software.

C++

C++ Programming runs for 12 weeks at ₦220,000. C++ is valued where speed and control matter, and it teaches you how computers really work. It is demanding, but it builds strong fundamentals.

Quick decision guide

  1. Want to get web projects online fast? Start with JavaScript.
  2. Interested in data, automation or AI? Start with Python.
  3. Aiming for large organisations or Android? Consider Java.
  4. Love understanding how machines work? Try C++.

How to learn without burning data

  • Download tutorials and documentation while on Wi-Fi.
  • Practise offline in a code editor on your laptop.
  • Use short daily sessions of 45 to 60 minutes rather than one long weekend session.

The most important step

Whatever you pick, write small programs every day and put them on GitHub. Employers and clients want proof. Attend the free intro class to see how live instruction works, then commit to one language for at least ten weeks.

title: Hackers sat inside 3 AI companies, copying the messages people sent to AI
description:
Hackers sat inside three AI companies, copying the messages people sent to AI. None of the three knew until a security firm told them.

One password from those messages was used the next day.

On 19 Nov 2026, HD Moore, Chief Research Officer at Dragos, published the results of a five-month experiment. From July through November 2026, the team submitted approximately two million prompts to widely used AI services. The prompts carried unique URLs and canary credentials, such as fake AWS keys (passwords to Amazon cloud accounts), that existed nowhere else. If anyone used one of those secrets, someone had read the prompt that carried it.

The secrets were used. Here is what the research shows, and what it means for any business whose staff or software send prompts to AI services.

How a prompt travels

Most people picture inference as text in, text out. Dragos describes a longer path. An AI router offers one API endpoint and forwards each request to a pool of models, sometimes at different hosting providers. The request often passes through more than one router before it reaches the server that runs the model. In Dragos's words, "every hop can see the entire prompt and response."

Customers can set privacy flags on the account, on an API key or on each request. The strictest is Zero Data Retention (ZDR), which specifies that the prompt and response are not stored. Routers should forward ZDR requests only to providers that offer the same control.

Dragos traced about two thousand routes by planting an image URL in requests and reading the nested error messages each hop returns. Several hundred of those routes included a system Dragos couldn't identify.

Three breached providers

The most serious finding: attackers were stealing data from three different hosting providers. None of the three knew until Dragos notified them. The earliest incident dates back to the middle of July.

The largest breach involved a couple hundred of Dragos's AWS keys. Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, inside a few short windows in late October, and every request sent during those windows was stolen. Some stolen keys came from requests the provider rejected before a model ever ran. Dragos's conclusion: the attacker was "copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack."

In the other two breaches, some stolen requests were marked ZDR. As Moore puts it: "A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside."

What the attacker did with the keys

The path Dragos recorded:

  1. Tested each key to see if it was live, in some cases within a few hours of the request.
  2. Listed S3 buckets and searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store.
  3. Tried enabling hosted models in AWS Bedrock, creating Bedrock API keys and adding their own IAM users to keep access.

The bait keys were used for tens of thousands of AWS API calls. One key, seeded on 21 Oct, was first used the next day and was still in use three weeks later. On 1 Nov the same attacker added ARTEX, an LLM-driven penetration testing framework, which made a handful of calls to confirm keys were still live. Dragos lists two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, as worth adding to detections.

No exploit needed: marketplace sellers

The second finding involved no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed a model at the lowest price, enabled request logging and waited. In one case, about a day and a half after two prompts went through one seller, someone on a home broadband connection opened both secret URLs and started guessing usernames at the login page. Prompts for the same model sent through a different seller were never touched.

The response

On 22 Nov 2026, OpenRouter announced that it had off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility, and notified all potentially affected customers. OpenRouter says the findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. Phala published a preliminary report: requests to its DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 deployment routed by OpenRouter between 21 Oct and 8 Nov 2026 should be treated as exposed, and any secrets in them rotated. Together AI disclosed a separate leak: an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public GitHub repository, and an unauthorized party used it to download stored prompt samples.

What to change

Dragos's advice starts from one limit: "a privacy flag only binds the first hop, and that AI agents will happily send whatever they can read, including credentials." From the report:

  1. Pick the route. Go directly to a first-tier provider where you can, or pick a router's upstream providers yourself instead of the default pool, and verify that your privacy settings change where requests go.
  2. Keep secrets out of agent context. Whatever an agent can read, it can send.
  3. Seed your own canaries. Add a fake credential to the context your agents and pipelines already send, and treat any use of it as an incident.
  4. Turn on secret filtering where a provider offers it, knowing it misses sensitive data that isn't shaped like a key.

The business stake is plain: a cloud key in a prompt can become a cloud account in someone else's hands, and the clean-up stays with you. Every prompt is a web request that leaves your network. Know what leaves your business on the web, and secure it.

Which do your teams use today: a first-tier provider directly, a router with providers you picked, or a router's default pool?

Sources

  • Dragos, "Three breaches, endless leaks: Your AI supply chain needs canaries", HD Moore, 19 Nov 2026: https://www.dragos.com/blog/ai-supply-chain-security-canary-tokens
  • OpenRouter, "Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers", 22 Nov 2026: https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/data-processing-incidents-on-inference-providers/
  • Phala, "November preliminary incident report", 10 Nov 2026: https://phala.com/posts/phala-november-preliminary-incident-report
  • Together AI, "Security event: Prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026", 21 Nov 2026: https://www.together.ai/blog/security-event-prompt-leakage-for-requests-in-june-and-july-of-2026

title: Your Factur-X invoice passed every check — the printed PDF still says something else
description:
A reader of my Factur-X validator launch post described a failure mode better than I could:

A lot of invoices that fail later didn't start broken in the XML. The spreadsheet that built them already dropped leading zeros on the invoice or order number, or mixed decimal commas, so the XML is well-formed while the visible PDF still shows the original value.

The file is valid in every way the standards care about, and wrong in the only way a human clerk will notice.

One file, two layers

Factur-X (ZUGFeRD 2.x) is a PDF/A-3 with a CII XML invoice attached inside. The two layers are produced independently: the XML carries the data that gets processed, the page carries what a human sees. In theory they're two renderings of one document; in practice they're two artifacts that share a database row.

What the standards check — and don't

"The invoice validates" usually means XSD (well-formed CII) plus EN 16931 Schematron (business rules inside the XML: buyer name present, line amounts add up, amount due consistent). PDF/A-3 conformance is a separate container check, often done with veraPDF.

None of the three compares the XML to the printed page. EN 16931 doesn't know the page exists; PDF/A validation doesn't know the invoice content exists. A file where the XML says INV-0042 and the page says 42 can pass all of it.

How the drift happens

Typical spreadsheet-to-XML pipeline: 0042 becomes 42 when a cell is formatted as a number; French 1 234,50 becomes 1234.50; the XML builder recomputes totals while the template prints the sheet's formulas; the template gets edited and the XML isn't regenerated from the same snapshot. Each of these is internally consistent XML. The pair is not.

"Just compare the page text" is the hard part

Extracting text gives positioned glyphs, not labelled fields. Is this string BT-1? Is 1 234,50 equal to 1234.50? Which of the three totals is amount due? Where did the value go on page 2? Every answer is layout-specific, and across a few real templates it becomes a pile of heuristics.

So my validator is honest about its boundary: it reads the embedded XML, never the page.

What it does do

Every failure now carries the rule ID, the XPath, and the offending value, so you can find the cell that produced it without opening the XML:

{
  "valid": false,
  "errors": [{
    "ruleId": "BR-CO-16",
    "severity": "ERROR",
    "xpath": "/rsm:CrossIndustryInvoice/.../ram:DuePayableAmount",
    "message": "…",
    "value": "-250.33"
  }],
  "warnings": []
}

A receiving-side checklist

If you receive Factur-X invoices (in France, since September 2026, that's everyone):

  1. Extract the XML and validate it (XSD + EN 16931).
  2. Check PDF/A-3 conformance if your archive requires it.
  3. For invoice number, issue date, total incl. VAT and VAT breakdown, compare XML to page. Eyeballing beats nothing.
  4. On mismatch, ask for a reissue from the same source data, not a patched PDF.

Step 3 is the part software doesn't do reliably. That's not a standards gap; it's an engineering one.

Try it

Browser: https://factur-x-api.com/validateur-factur-x — drop a PDF or XML, get the rule list.

API:

curl -X POST https://factur-x-api.com/api/validate \
  -H "X-API-Key: facturx_..." \
  -F "file=@invoice.pdf"

It accepts the PDF or the bare XML. Keys come from https://factur-x-api.com/tarifs; the free tier covers a handful of validations per month, and the key endpoint sits behind a Turnstile check because of bot signups.

One ask

If you have a redacted PDF + XML pair where the printed values diverge, send it over. One real example decides whether page-text comparison is a feature or a rabbit hole — I'd rather learn that from an actual file than from synthetic ones.

Context: since September 2026 French companies must be able to receive e-invoices; issuing started with large companies, SMEs follow in September 2027, and invoices move through certified platforms (PDP). That's why receiving-side breakage shows up first.

title: Add a free 24/7 stock heatmap to React or HTML in 30 seconds
description:
Most stock heatmaps are a pain to put on a site. The usual widgets want an API key or a paid plan. Building your own means standing up a quote backend, and the map goes blank when the cash market closes. If you just want a live S&P 500, Nasdaq-100, or a mixed stock, ETF, and crypto watchlist on a blog or a Next.js page, that is more infrastructure than the feature is worth.

247heatmap-widget is a small MIT-licensed wrapper around the hosted maps on 247heatmap.com. You drop in an iframe, a <heatmap-247> element, or a React component. There is no API key, no account, and no server of your own. Index maps keep updating after hours, overnight, and on weekends using 24/7 perpetual futures prices. Each tile shows the ticker, the price, and the percent move.

S&P 500 heatmap on 247heatmap.com. Larger tiles are larger companies. Green is up since the previous close, red is down.

A 55-second walkthrough is on YouTube: https://youtu.be/7zjK4HleVu8

Plain HTML iframe

If you only need a map, you do not install anything. These are the official snippets from the embed configurator.

S&P 500, dark:

<iframe src="https://247heatmap.com/embed/sp500/dark/" width="100%" height="480" style="border:0;min-height:360px;background:#101216;" title="S&P 500 heat map — 24/7 Heatmap" loading="lazy"></iframe>

S&P 500, light. Use a light frame background so the page does not flash dark while the map loads:

<iframe src="https://247heatmap.com/embed/sp500/light/" width="100%" height="480" style="border:0;min-height:360px;background:#f4f6f8;" title="S&P 500 heat map — 24/7 Heatmap" loading="lazy"></iframe>

Nasdaq-100 and Dow 30:

<iframe src="https://247heatmap.com/embed/nasdaq-100/dark/" width="100%" height="480" style="border:0;min-height:360px;background:#101216;" title="Nasdaq-100 heat map — 24/7 Heatmap" loading="lazy"></iframe>
<iframe src="https://247heatmap.com/embed/dow-30/light/" width="100%" height="480" style="border:0;min-height:360px;background:#f4f6f8;" title="Dow 30 heat map — 24/7 Heatmap" loading="lazy"></iframe>

You can add an optional credit line under the iframe. Please leave the small “Powered by 247heatmap” link that already ships inside the map.

Custom watchlists and the web component

Index maps are fixed universes. A custom map can mix large-cap names with ETFs and crypto. Build the list in the custom watchlist builder, or write the tickers yourself. On the iframe URL, t is the ticker list, m=24h or m=1h changes the color basis (omit m for the move since the previous close), s=equal makes every tile the same size, and live=1 hides tiles that do not have a live price.

<iframe src="https://247heatmap.com/embed/custom/?t=NVDA,AAPL,MSFT,SPY,BTC,ETH&m=24h&s=equal&live=1" width="100%" height="480" style="border:0;min-height:360px;background:#101216;" title="Custom stock heat map — 24/7 Heatmap" loading="lazy"></iframe>

A custom watchlist at 247heatmap.com/custom/. The same tickers embed with map="custom".

Custom embeds stay on /embed/custom/ — there is no /embed/custom/light/ route. Crypto symbols such as BTC and ETH go on the custom embed, not a separate crypto iframe.

If you would rather set this with HTML attributes, load the <heatmap-247> web component from unpkg:

<script src="https://unpkg.com/247heatmap-widget@1.0.0/dist/heatmap-247.iife.js"></script>

<heatmap-247 map="sp500" theme="dark" height="480px"></heatmap-247>
<heatmap-247
  map="custom"
  tickers="NVDA,AAPL,MSFT,SPY,BTC,ETH"
  live="true"
  metric="24h"
  size="equal"
  height="520px"
></heatmap-247>

live, metric, and size map to the same query string as the iframe. attribution="false" removes the host-page credit under the frame; the in-map “Powered by” link stays.

React and Next.js

Install the package from npm:

npm install 247heatmap-widget

import { StockHeatmap } from "247heatmap-widget/react";

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <StockHeatmap
      map="custom"
      tickers={["NVDA", "AAPL", "MSFT", "SPY", "BTC", "ETH"]}
      live
      metric="24h"
      size="equal"
      height={520}
    />
  );
}

Heatmap247 is the same component. tickers is only sent when map="custom"; on an index map it is ignored.

StockHeatmap renders an iframe and does not read window, so it is safe in the Next.js App Router. You do not need dynamic(..., { ssr: false }). If you prefer the custom element, import the web component from a Client Component:

"use client";
import "247heatmap-widget/web-component";

export function Map() {
  return <heatmap-247 map="nasdaq-100" theme="dark" height="480px"></heatmap-247>;
}

Options worth knowing

map accepts sp500 (the default), nasdaq-100, dow-30, or custom. Aliases such as nasdaq, ndx, dow, djia, and spx resolve to those routes; anything else falls back to S&P 500 so the iframe does not 404. theme is dark or light on the index maps. height and width take a CSS length, or a bare number in pixels; the defaults are 480px and 100%.

live works on index embeds as well as custom ones. In HTML that is ?live=1 on the iframe URL, live="true" on <heatmap-247>, or live on StockHeatmap. For a custom map, metric is close (the default, omitted from the query string), 24h, or 1h, and size is cap (default) or equal. Tickers are uppercased and capped at 60 symbols.

The embed configurator is the fastest way to preview a map before you paste code. The widget, including TypeScript types, lives on npm and in the 247heatmap/247heatmap-widget repo under the MIT license. The maps are for information only and are not investment advice; overnight and weekend tiles may show a perpetual futures price rather than the cash market.

title: Solving Time Zones in a Booking System with UTC Minutes
description:
How one small decision, storing every time as a date plus integer minutes in UTC, handled cross-time-zone booking in the scheduling system I designed. The schema, the negative-minute case, and why integers beat time strings.

A host in Sydney offers 9:00 am on Monday 25 May. An invitee in New York should see 7:00 pm on Sunday 24 May. Same meeting, two different dates.

That is the real problem in any booking system. It is rarely the calendar UI. It is two people in two time zones, often on two different days, looking at one slot.

In the booking service I designed at Beasnik, for an all-in-one SaaS for marketing agencies, one rule carries most of the weight: the backend only speaks UTC, and a time is an integer number of minutes. This post explains that rule, the schema behind it, and the few small rules around it.

The rule: UTC in, UTC out

The backend never sees "3:40 pm", and it never converts between time zones. Every request carries UTC, every row stores UTC, and every response returns UTC. Only the browser knows what time it is for the person looking at the screen.

  • A time of day is an integer: minutes since midnight UTC. A day is 1,440 minutes, so 15:40 UTC is 940.
  • A booking is a date plus minutes: schedule_date, an integer such as 20260525, and schedule_time.
  • Weekly availability is a weekday plus a start and an end minute: Monday, 180 to 660.
  • The browser converts at the edges. Local time becomes UTC minutes before a request is sent, and UTC minutes become local time just before they are shown.

This split had a side effect I came to value most. The server never needs the visitor's time zone to work out open slots, so one cached month of slots serves every visitor, whether they open the page in Dhaka, Berlin or New York. The cache key is the event type and the month, nothing else.

Where time lives in the schema

Three tables hold every time value in the domain. The diagram shows only their time columns, filled with the Sydney example used throughout this post.

Time columns in the booking schema: UTC minutes, lengths in minutes, and zone names

Every time column is one of three kinds:

  • UTC minutes. start_time and end_time on a weekly rule, and schedule_date plus schedule_time on a booking. These are the only columns that say when. They are always UTC, and the minutes can go below 0 or past 1,440. More on that below.
  • Lengths in minutes. Duration, the buffers before and after, minimum notice, and the cancel and reschedule windows. A 30-minute meeting lasts 30 minutes in every zone, so these never need converting.
  • Zone names. The event type's timezone is the host's zone. The booking's timezone is the zone the invitee booked from. They are used to show times and to count the host's day, never to store a time.

Notice what is missing. No column holds a local time, and no column holds a time as text.

Why integers, not time strings

The obvious way to store "9:00 am" is a string like "09:00", or a TIME column. I chose a plain integer, 540, for six reasons.

  1. Converting is one subtraction. UTC is local minus the offset: 540 − 600 = −60. With a string you parse it, convert it and format it again, in PHP and in JavaScript, and both sides have to agree on the format.
  2. Comparing is a number comparison. As text, "9:00" > "10:00" is true, because "9" sorts after "1". As integers, 540 is less than 600, every time. ORDER BY start_time in the database sorts correctly too, negative values included.
  3. Durations are already minutes. A slot ends at start plus duration. A booking with buffers blocks from its time minus the buffer before, to its time plus the duration plus the buffer after. There is no unit conversion anywhere.
  4. An integer can step outside one day. A time string lives between 00:00 and 23:59. It cannot say "one hour before midnight of this date" (−60) or "one hour into the next day" (1,500). That ability is what keeps a range from splitting at midnight.
  5. Display format is a UI choice, not data. The booking page has a 12-hour and 24-hour switch. "9:00 AM" and "09:00" are two ways to print 540, chosen at render time. Nothing stored has a format to parse.
  6. Odd offsets just work. India is +330 minutes and Nepal is +345. Offsets in whole hours would break there. In minutes, they are just more integers.

Why not a full UTC timestamp?

For a single booking, a UTC timestamp would work. I chose a date plus minutes so that bookings and weekly rules share one shape. A weekly rule has a weekday, not a date, so it can never be a timestamp. With one shape, the slot engine compares a candidate slot, a weekly range and a booking with the same four integers.

Finding the offset for any time zone

The only time-zone fact the browser needs is the offset: how many minutes a zone is ahead of UTC. Dhaka is +360. New York is −240 in May and −300 in January. The browser formats the same instant in UTC and in the target zone with the built-in Intl API, and subtracts.

Even that subtraction needs the 1,440-minute cycle. At 23:00 UTC it is already 05:00 the next day in Dhaka, so the two clocks differ by 300 − 1,380 = −1,080. Any result outside ±720 is wrapped by 1,440, which turns −1,080 into the real +360. That wrap has one blind spot, covered at the end of this post.

That is all the time-zone handling there is. The server keeps no table of offsets and does no conversions on the request path. Any zone the browser knows by name, it can turn into an offset.

Creating availability is just comparing integers

A host in Dhaka picks Monday, 9:00 to 17:00. In the browser that is 540 to 1020 in local minutes. Before saving, the page checks each day's ranges with plain comparisons:

  • Valid range: start is less than end.
  • Overlap: two ranges overlap when each one starts before the other ends: a.start < b.end and b.start < a.end.

If either check fails, the save button stays disabled and the range shows an error. Then the offset is subtracted: 540 − 360 = 180 and 1020 − 360 = 660. Monday, 180 to 660, is what the backend stores.

The check runs once, in local time, and that is enough. Every range on a day moves by the same offset, and a constant shift never changes which ranges overlap. 9:00–12:00 and 11:00–14:00 overlap as 540–720 and 660–840, and they still overlap as 180–360 and 300–480 in UTC.

Removing booked time from the open slots

The server uses the same comparison to take booked time out of the slots. A booking blocks a window that includes its own buffers:

blockStart = schedule_time - buffer_before_minutes
blockEnd   = schedule_time + duration_minutes + buffer_after_minutes
busy       = slotStart < blockEnd && blockStart < slotEnd

A 30-minute booking at 600 with 10-minute buffers blocks 590 to 640. The candidate 630–660 overlaps, because 630 is below 640 and 590 is below 660, so it is dropped. The candidate 660–690 does not overlap, because 660 is not below 640, so it stays.

The engine walks each weekly range from its start to its end minus the duration, one duration at a time, and drops every candidate that overlaps a busy window. No date object is created inside that loop. The buffers are read from the booking row, copied there when it was made, so editing the event type later never changes what old bookings block.

Negative minutes: when UTC lands on a different date

Subtracting the offset often pushes a value below 0 or to 1,440 and above. This is not a rare edge case. It happens for most hosts far from UTC:

  • Below 0: a host east of UTC with an early start. Sydney (+600) at 9:00 gives 540 − 600 = −60.
  • 1,440 or more: a host west of UTC with a late finish. New York in May (−240) at 21:00 gives 1,260 + 240 = 1,500.

The obvious fix is to split at midnight: store Sydney's 9:00–17:00 as "Sunday, 1,380 to 1,440" plus "Monday, 0 to 420". We didn't. We keep the host's weekday or date as the label and let the minutes go negative, or past 1,440. The Sydney range is one row: Monday, −60 to 420.

The meaning never changes: midnight UTC on the labelled date, plus the minutes. Monday 25 May at −60 is Sunday 24 May, 23:00 UTC. Monday at 1,500 is Tuesday, 01:00 UTC.

One moment on three calendars: Sydney, UTC, New York

The dashed line is one moment. Each person's calendar puts it on a different date, and the stored value needs no time zone at all.

Splitting would have cost more than it looks. One range becomes two rows on two days. Editing the range means editing both. Overlap checks have to stitch the halves back together, and a slot near midnight belongs to both days at once. With a signed value, a range is always one row, and its start is always below its end.

What this buys:

  • The overlap check works unchanged. Start stays below end, so the four comparisons above still hold.
  • The slot engine doesn't care. It walks −60, −30, 0, 30 and onward exactly as it walks 540, 570, 600. Negative numbers are just numbers.
  • An exact moment is one addition. To build the calendar invite and the emails, the server takes midnight UTC of the date and adds the minutes. Adding −60 lands on 23:00 the day before, with no special case.
  • Printing a time is one formula. The browser wraps the value into one day with ((m % 1440) + 1440) % 1440. −60 becomes 1,380, which prints as 11:00 pm. The date is settled separately, as the next section shows.
  • Bookings use the same shape: the date the invitee picked, plus their local minutes minus their offset.

One rule keeps it safe: compare minutes only when they share a date label. Monday at −60 and Sunday at 1,380 are the same moment, but a check that compares Monday only with Monday will never see that. When the labels differ, turn both into exact moments first.

Showing open slots in the invitee's time zone

The backend returns a month of open slots as UTC minutes grouped by date. The browser adds the invitee's offset to each one, then puts it on the right date:

  1. Between 0 and 1,439: same date.
  2. Below 0: previous date, plus 1,440.
  3. 1,440 or more: next date, minus 1,440.

Take the Sydney host's slot, stored as Monday 25 May at −60:

  • Invitee in Dhaka (+360): −60 + 360 = 300, so 05:00 on Monday 25 May.
  • Invitee in New York (−240): −60 − 240 = −300. That is below zero, so it moves to Sunday 24 May: 1,440 − 300 = 1,140, which is 19:00.

Invitees can switch time zones from a dropdown on the booking page. The page re-runs the same addition on the UTC data it already has, so switching needs no server call.

Why cross-time-zone booking just works

The host and the invitee never need each other's time zone. Each side converts only between its own zone and UTC. Ten time zones need ten offsets, not a conversion for every pair.

When the invitee books, the browser sends the date they picked and their local minutes minus their offset. That is the same shape the host's availability uses, so both sides meet in UTC.

The server turns a booking into an exact moment in one step: midnight UTC on the stored date, plus the minutes. That moment goes into the Google Calendar invite, and Google shows every attendee their own local time.

Other decisions in the same spirit

  • The UI speaks hours and days; the database speaks minutes. A two-hour notice is stored as 120 and a one-day cancel window as 1,440. The UI shows hours or days by dividing by 60 or 1,440.
  • The daily cap uses the host's day. "Three meetings a day" means the host's day, not UTC's. A Dhaka day runs from 18:00 to 18:00 UTC, so bookings are moved into the host's zone before they are counted.
  • All-day events are 0 to 1,440. A Google Calendar all-day event becomes one full-day block on each date it covers.
  • Old zone names are normalised. Asia/Calcutta becomes Asia/Kolkata before any arithmetic runs.

Sharp edges worth planning for

The design held up, but four edges are worth knowing before you copy it.

  • Give each moment one canonical form. A signed value is right for a weekly range, but the same booking can be written as Monday at −60 or Sunday at 1,380. If bookings carry the invitee's date while the slot engine groups busy time by the host's dates, one can miss the other. Normalise a booking to its UTC date plus 0 to 1,439 when you save it, or compare absolute minutes: days since 1970 × 1,440, plus the minutes.
  • Wrap in both directions. Below 0 moves to the previous date, and 1,440 or more moves to the next. It is easy to write the first branch, test it with an Asian or Australian host, and forget the second.
  • Offsets are not limited to ±12 hours. Zones run from UTC−12 to UTC+14, and New Zealand is UTC+13 all summer. Wrapping at ±720 turns +780 into −660, a full day off. Work the offset out from the full date and time in both zones, not from the two clocks alone.
  • Daylight saving moves offsets. The browser uses today's offset. For dates after a clock change, use the offset of the date being shown, and keep weekly rules in the host's local time so "9 to 5" stays 9 to 5 all year.

How this design helps the database

Storing every date and time as an integer in UTC pays off across the whole database: storage, indexes, caching, queries and reports. It matters most in the busiest query in the system, the month of busy time loaded on every visit to a booking page.

  1. Smallest, cheapest type. Integers are the smallest and cheapest type to store, index and compare.
  2. Indexes stay usable. The query filters raw columns, with no DATE() or CONVERT_TZ() wrapped around them.
  3. One zone, no conversion. Every row is stored in UTC, so a booking made from Dhaka and one made from New York sit on the same scale and compare, sort and group directly. Whether the database is reading busy time for the slot engine or checking existing bookings inside the booking transaction, it never needs a time-zone setting: the check is the same simple integer comparison the slot engine uses.
  4. No daylight-saving gaps or repeats. Local clocks skip an hour in spring and repeat one in autumn, so a local time can be missing or happen twice. UTC never jumps, so stored values never collide or go missing.
  5. One cache entry for every visitor. Because responses are UTC only, the slot cache is keyed by event type and month, never by the visitor's zone. Visitors from fifty time zones share one entry and the one query that filled it.
  6. Small cache entries and responses. A cached month of slots is a short list of numbers per date, like [-60, -30, 0, 30], instead of a 20-character timestamp such as "2026-05-24T23:00:00Z" for every slot. That is roughly a fifth of the size, in the cache and on the wire.
  7. The date is an integer too, and still readable. schedule_date in calendar_bookings is stored as YYYYMMDD, so 25 May 2026 is 20260525. It sorts like a number, and a month is a plain range: schedule_date BETWEEN 20260501 AND 20260531. I didn't use a Unix epoch integer, because 1779667200 means nothing to a person reading the table, while 20260525 reads at a glance.
  8. Monthly reports by simple arithmetic. Dividing a YYYYMMDD date by 100 gives its month: 20260525 DIV 100 = 202605. Bookings per month is GROUP BY schedule_date DIV 100, with no date functions.
  9. One index fits the busiest query. An index on (event_id, status, schedule_date) is the one to add: it matches how the slot query filters, by event type, then status, then a date range. With integer dates, that range scan is as cheap as it gets.

Takeaways

  • One unit, one zone. Store minutes, store UTC, and convert only at the edges.
  • Integers, not strings or timestamps. Conversion, comparison and overlap become plain arithmetic, and the database gets small, fast, index-friendly columns.
  • Don't split at midnight. A date label plus signed minutes is an exact moment, and a range stays one range.
  • Check overlaps before converting. A constant shift never changes which ranges overlap.
  • Compare on one date label. Same label, compare minutes. Different labels, compare exact moments.

Time zones feel hard because people mix local times, dates and offsets in the same place. Keep them apart: integers in the middle, people's clocks at the edges.

title: Self-hosted remote desktop in Rust that survives hotel Wi-Fi and strict firewalls
description:
I needed to reach family and office PCs over hotel Wi-Fi, mobile data and a strict company firewall, and I kept fighting laggy, frozen sessions. So I built Remote Desktop Rider.

GitHub: https://github.com/codewithelvin/remote-desktop-rider (MIT)

The self-hosted part

A small rider-server on any Linux VPS introduces devices and relays traffic when a direct path isn't possible. It only ever sees encrypted data; it can't watch or take over sessions. There are no accounts and no cloud: devices pair once by comparing a verification code, and every session needs the computer's PIN.

Install on a VPS (the script is deploy/get.sh; please read it first):

curl -fsSL https://codewithelvin.github.io/remote-desktop-rider/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- <public-ip>

It verifies the binary's SHA-256, installs a hardened systemd unit and prints the address and fingerprint you enter in the app. Add --domain and --email to also get an HTTPS fallback via nginx + Let's Encrypt for networks that block UDP.

Why it holds up on bad links

  • QUIC over UDP, one stream per video frame: a lost packet never stalls newer frames, and stale frames are dropped, not resent
  • Hardware H.264 (QuickSync/NVENC/AMF); bitrate adapts live from 300 kbps to 20 Mbps, and Auto quality lowers resolution on slow links
  • The cursor is drawn locally, so the pointer stays snappy
  • Connection fallback: direct on LAN → NAT hole punching → relay → random UDP port → TLS tunnel on TCP 443

Also

Unattended access (works at the login screen, lock screen and UAC prompts, and after reboots), clipboard sync, drag-and-drop files, multi-monitor, one-time "quick connect" codes for helping someone once, and auto-updates with SHA-256 checks.

Limits, honestly

The computer being controlled must be Windows for now (you can control it from Windows, macOS or Debian/Ubuntu). Builds aren't code-signed yet (no budget), so Windows SmartScreen will warn; every release publishes SHA256SUMS. It's young, so I'd love reports from real networks; there's an issue for that on GitHub.

Happy to answer anything in the comments!

title: How Stale PostgreSQL Statistics Made a Query 580 Times Slower
description:
Slow Postgres, part 3 of 8. The SQL and raw numbers for every test are on GitHub.


PostgreSQL 18, sampled every 5 seconds. Gaps: pgbench runs.

A retention job marked 463,418 of five million orders archived, a status ANALYZE had never seen, so Postgres estimated 1 row for it. An endpoint listing one customer's archived orders kept walking the status index, reading 463,418 entries to return one: 29 ms a call instead of 0.05 ms.

One note before the numbers: the AlphaVPS link at the end is a referral link, so I may get a commission at no extra cost to you, and the netcup voucher I offer there comes from my own account.

The short version:

  • A 1-row estimate for 463,418 archived orders kept a per-customer query on the wrong index: 29 ms a call against 0.05 ms after ANALYZE.
  • Autovacuum runs ANALYZE once 50 rows plus 10% of the table have changed, whatever the change. The 9.3% backfill sat under that line until 40,000 more rows changed. A manual ANALYZE took 190 ms.
  • PostgreSQL 18.7 and 17.12 picked the same plans with the same analyze threshold and similar timings. The only difference in behavior I measured is that 18 vacuums a frozen table much sooner after inserts, but still doesn't analyze it.
  • Run ANALYZE yourself after a job that loads or rewrites part of a table, and on temp tables after you fill them. Where a few percent can flip a plan, lower autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor for that table.
  • Correlated columns stay wrong with fresh statistics. CREATE STATISTICS fixes them after the next ANALYZE.

The lab: five million orders

PostgreSQL 18.7 in Docker on the 4-vCPU, 8 GB cloud VM from parts 1 and 2, with part 2's settings: 1 GB of shared_buffers, so the table stays in memory, and JIT and parallel workers off. Autovacuum runs with its defaults. The same scripts then ran on 17.12 in a fresh container. With everything in memory, 18's asynchronous I/O has nothing to speed up.

Five million orders, one every 11 seconds from January 2025 to September 2026. A million customers have five orders each, and each ships to one address: 20,000 postcodes in 21 cities, each city in one country. There are indexes on customer_id and status. The rows come from generate_series and setseed, so yours match mine on either version. Your pg_stats won't, because ANALYZE samples at random; my two runs differ a little too.

The endpoint lists one customer's orders in one status:

SELECT id, status, amount_cents, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 648065 AND status = 'archived';

Where row estimates come from

ANALYZE reads a random sample, 30,000 rows at the default default_statistics_target of 100, and stores a per-column summary, which you read in pg_stats. On this table it took 190 ms:

INFO:  "orders": scanned 30000 of 53496 pages, containing 2803890 live rows and 0 dead rows;
       30000 rows in sample, 4999897 estimated total rows

18's ANALYZE VERBOSE adds buffer, WAL and CPU usage under that line; 17 stops there.

Estimates come from three parts of it. The first is the most common values (MCV) and their shares, here for status:

most_common_vals:  {delivered,shipped,paid,cancelled,refunded}
most_common_freqs: {0.8021333,0.07926667,0.059,0.039466668,0.020133333}

status = 'paid' gets the table's 4,999,995 rows × 0.059 = 295,000. There are 300,322.

The second is n_distinct. A value that isn't in the common list gets an even share of the rows the list doesn't cover. customer_id has no common list, and its n_distinct is -0.202, meaning 20.2% of the rows: about 1,012,000 customers, so five rows each, which is exact.

The third is a histogram for ranges: 101 bounds that split the sampled values into 100 buckets with the same number of rows each. One week of June 2025 came out at 51,262 rows against 54,982.

default_statistics_target caps the common values and the buckets at 100 each and sets the sample at 300 times the target. At 1,000, ANALYZE read the whole table and took 1.6 seconds; at 10,000, 17 seconds, on both versions. Raise it per column (ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS) when the value you filter on doesn't make the top 100.

Back to status: its five frequencies add up to 1. As far as the planner knows, no rows are left for any other value, so it gets the minimum estimate, one row. That's right until somebody writes that status:

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'archived';
Index Scan using orders_status_idx on orders  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=50)

A backfill the statistics never saw 

UPDATE orders SET status = 'archived' WHERE created_at < '2025-03-01';
-- UPDATE 463418, 3.9 s

The endpoint's plan before the backfill, after it, and after ANALYZE (full plans in timeline-pg18.out):

before    Index Scan using orders_status_idx       rows=1  actual rows=0.00  Buffers: shared hit=3     0.019 ms
after     Index Scan using orders_status_idx       rows=1  actual rows=1.00  Buffers: shared hit=5609  32.491 ms
            Rows Removed by Filter: 463417
ANALYZE   Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx  rows=1  actual rows=1.00  Buffers: shared hit=10    0.027 ms

That's 18's format: actual rows with two decimals, plus Buffers and an Index Searches line without asking. 17 prints rows=1 and needs BUFFERS spelled out, but it chose the same plans and read the same 5,609 pages.

The backfill didn't change the plan. With archived at 1 row, reading one status index entry and checking its customer costs 8.45 in planner units, against 24.52 for the five rows behind the customer_id index (part 1 covers how those units are priced). That was right while the status didn't exist. After the backfill every call fetched 463,418 archived entries and their rows to keep one.

Timed every five seconds for five minutes after the backfill, the plain query took a median of 29.0 ms over 52 samples, against 0.04 ms before it and 0.05 ms after ANALYZE (29.8 ms stale on 17). Four pgbench clients got 112 calls a second out of the stale endpoint and 180,353 after ANALYZE (118 and 188,180 on 17). A call that fast is hard to time, so the gap depends on the tool: 580 times by the psql medians, 1,600 times by pgbench throughput.

Why autovacuum left the table alone

Autovacuum analyzes a table once the rows inserted, updated or deleted since the last ANALYZE (n_mod_since_analyze in pg_stat_user_tables) pass

autovacuum_analyze_threshold + autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor × reltuples
          50                 +              0.1               × 4,999,897  = 500,040

and it checks every autovacuum_naptime, one minute by default. PostgreSQL 18 kept this formula.

The backfill was 36,622 rows short. In the chart at the top, the counter sat at 463,418 for five minutes. Then I marked 40,000 shipped orders as delivered, the counter went to 503,418, and autovacuum analyzed the table about a second later. That second was luck, and so were the 60 seconds the 17 run waited at the same step: it depends on where the update lands in autovacuum's one-minute cycle. The ANALYZE took 0.55 s, and the estimate went to 455,197.

My five minutes ended because I wrote those rows. On a real table they end when 36,622 more rows change: at 1,000 a minute that's 37 minutes, at 100 a minute about six hours.

The docs say it plainly: autovacuum schedules ANALYZE "strictly as a function of the number of rows inserted or updated; it has no knowledge of whether that will lead to meaningful statistical changes." That catches slow drift. It misses:

  • a change under the line that lands on one value, like the backfill: 9.3% of the table and all of archived;
  • the wait for the next round, up to a minute, which a job that loads a batch and queries it right away always hits;
  • big tables, where the line moves too: at 100 million rows it's 10 million changed rows;
  • temporary tables, which autovacuum can't see, and partitioned tables, whose parent it never analyzes.

PostgreSQL 18 changed two autovacuum triggers, both for VACUUM. autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold caps the dead-row trigger at 100 million rows, which bites only past 500 million. The insert trigger, 1,000 rows plus 20% of the table, now scales that 20% by the share of pages not yet frozen, and that is the one difference in behavior my lab measured between 17 and 18. With nothing frozen, both versions put the line at about 1,002,000 rows. After VACUUM (FREEZE) on a fresh copy, 18's line was 1,000 rows, and autovacuum vacuumed the table 19 seconds after a 400,000-row insert. 17's was 1,001,000, and nothing ran in three minutes. Neither analyzed the table, so October was still estimated at 540 rows against 400,000.

Two cheap fixes. Run ANALYZE at the end of the job that changed the table: 190 ms here, less than seven stale calls. And where a few percent can flip a plan, lower the line for that table:

ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.01);

That put the line at 54,090 rows. I moved 60,000 paid orders to a new status, on_hold, and autovacuum analyzed the table 43 seconds later. The estimate for on_hold went from 1 to 54,515. On a big table you can set a fixed count instead: autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0 and autovacuum_analyze_threshold = 100000.

What the planner sees without ANALYZE

Stale statistics don't leave the planner blind. I loaded 400,000 orders for October and November 2026 in one INSERT, 8% of the table, and looked at estimates before any ANALYZE:


EXPLAIN estimates on PostgreSQL 18 before ANALYZE, against counted rows. The archived row is from the backfill. 17's estimates were within 1% of these.

The row count was close: 5,358,467 against 5,400,000. pg_class still said 5,005,827 rows on 58,953 pages, but the planner reads the table's current size, 63,106 pages, and scales the old rows-per-page up to it.

The new dates were past the end of the histogram. Without an index on created_at, created_at >= '2026-10-01' got 536 rows against 400,000, and >= '2026-11-01' got 536 too: past the last bound, the planner won't go below a hundredth of one bucket. With an index, October got 44,291: the planner fetches the column's real maximum from the index and stretches the last bucket up to it. Nine times too low beats 746.

A temp table nobody analyzed has no statistics, so the planner guesses. I copied the 400,000 new orders into one. From its file size and a default row width the planner put it at 187,200 rows, then took 0.5% of that for an equality: status = 'shipped' came out at 936 rows against 120,138. After ANALYZE: 120,533.

Correlated columns: fresh statistics, wrong estimate

ANALYZE fixes statistics that are old. It can't fix part 2's problem, two correlated columns multiplied into 300 rows instead of 15,000 on PostgreSQL 17, because the planner keeps statistics per column. For country = 'PT' AND city = 'Lisbon' it multiplies the two shares as if they were independent, 1.99% × 1.54%, and gets 1,650 rows. Of the 5.4 million rows, 81,000 match: every Lisbon order ships to PT.

CREATE STATISTICS keeps statistics on a group of columns. Each of its three kinds fixes a different estimate:


Estimates from EXPLAIN on PostgreSQL 18 after ANALYZE, on a log scale. 17 came within 10% of each.

dependencies records how far one column decides another: city decides country completely (1.0), country decides city 18% of the way. The Lisbon estimate went to 75,574. It assumes the values in your query agree, though: country = 'ES' AND city = 'Lisbon' matches nothing and also got 75,574, worse than 9,955 without extended statistics. It only works for = and IN.

mcv stores the most common combinations, here all 21 pairs, and works for ranges too. It gave 79,919 for PT and Lisbon and 1 for ES and Lisbon.

ndistinct counts distinct combinations, which GROUP BY needs. GROUP BY city, postcode was estimated at 21 × 20,164 = 423,444 groups. There are 20,000, since every postcode sits in one city. With ndistinct: 20,156.

Two catches. Nothing changes until the next ANALYZE: right after CREATE STATISTICS the Lisbon estimate was still 1,650. And they go stale with the table. Leave out the kind and you get all three:

CREATE STATISTICS orders_country_city ON country, city FROM orders;
ANALYZE orders;

With that and a second object on (city, postcode), the three estimates were 83,942, 1 and 20,123, and ANALYZE went from 175 ms to 352 ms. The planner uses them for conditions on one table, like part 2's users scan, not for joins.

pg_upgrade to 18 now carries most planner statistics over, but not the ones from CREATE STATISTICS. The upgrade docs have you run vacuumdb --all --analyze-in-stages --missing-stats-only for the gaps, then vacuumdb --all --analyze-only.

How to check this on your own database

  1. In EXPLAIN ANALYZE, find the lowest node where estimated and actual rows differ by 10x or more.
  2. See how much its table changed since the last ANALYZE, with the query below.
  3. Look the value up in pg_stats: is it in most_common_vals, and is a range past the last histogram bound?
  4. Run ANALYZE on the table and EXPLAIN again. If that fixed it, apply one of the two fixes above.
  5. If it's still wrong and the filter uses columns that depend on each other, create statistics on them and ANALYZE. 
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_mod_since_analyze, last_analyze, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_mod_since_analyze DESC;

Run it on your own server

Everything here ran on one 4-vCPU AMD EPYC cloud VM with 8 GB of RAM: PostgreSQL 18.7 first, then 17.12, each in a fresh Docker container. Your milliseconds will differ. The SQL, the raw output of both versions and the chart code are on GitHub, and sh bench/run.sh 18 (or 17) reruns the whole lab in about 20 minutes. Run it on your own server, and if you get a different picture or think I got something wrong, open an issue or a PR.

My own projects run on netcup (VPS from €2.21 a month) and AlphaVPS (VPS from €2.54 a month). For netcup, message me on LinkedIn and I'll send you a €5 voucher for new customers.

Good luck with your plans. Part 4 is next: column order in a composite index, and what PostgreSQL 18's skip scan changes there.

Finish

I hope you understood the instructions correctly. If you have any edits to this article, I will be waiting for your comments. If I really helped you, I kindly ask you to subscribe to my LinkedIn and provide feedback on this article.

Link to follow me:

LinkedIn

title: ☁️ Where does all the data in cloud applications actually get stored?
description:
☁️ Where does all the data in cloud applications actually get stored?

One of the answers is Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service)!

As part of my AWS learning journey, I've recently explored Amazon S3, one of the most widely used storage services in AWS.

Here's what I learned:

🔹 1. What is Amazon S3?

Amazon S3 is an object storage service that allows users to store, retrieve, and manage data over the internet.

You can store images, videos, documents, backups, application files, and much more.

🔹 2. Important S3 Concepts

  • Bucket: A container used to store objects.
  • Object: A file stored inside a bucket.
  • Key: The unique name used to identify an object.
  • Storage Class: Determines how objects are stored and accessed.

🔹 3. S3 Storage Classes

AWS provides different storage classes based on data access requirements:

  • S3 Standard
  • S3 Intelligent-Tiering
  • S3 Standard-IA
  • S3 One Zone-IA
  • S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
  • S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive

🔹 4. Key Features

  • Scalability
  • High durability (11 nines)
  • Data encryption and access control
  • Versioning
  • Lifecycle management
  • Replication

🔹 5. Real-World Use Cases

  • Website image and video storage.
  • Application backups.
  • Data lakes and analytics.
  • Static website hosting.
  • Disaster recovery.

💡 Key Takeaway:

Amazon S3 makes storing and managing data in the cloud simple, scalable, and reliable.

I'm continuing to explore AWS services and build my cloud computing knowledge step by step.

🚀 One service at a time, one step closer to becoming a Cloud Engineer!

Have you worked with Amazon S3? What practical project would you recommend for beginners?
