title: Designing Payment History UI for Pending, Reversed, and Failed Transactions
description:
Payment history should show what happened to each transaction and whether the result is final. To build a reliable interface, developers need a consistent status model, clear timestamps, and separate handling for payment errors and display errors.

1. Normalize Transaction Statuses

Payment providers use different status names. Map them to a shared internal model before displaying them in the UI.
A basic model might include:

  • Pending: the transaction is still being processed.
  • Completed: the payment has succeeded.
  • Failed: the payment attempt failed.
  • Canceled: the payment was canceled.
  • Reversed: a previously completed transaction was reversed.

These labels need precise definitions. For example, a reversal is not the same as a failed payment. A reversal changes the outcome of an earlier transaction, so the interface should preserve that history.
Keep the provider's original status in the backend. Map it to a user-facing label based on the provider's documentation and the type of operation. Some providers have additional states that require separate handling.

2. Separate Authorization from Capture

Authorization and capture represent different stages of a card payment.
An authorization may reserve funds before the merchant captures them. The interface should reflect that distinction. If the payment is authorized but not captured, avoid labeling it as a completed charge.
The exact wording depends on the payment flow. A short explanation such as “Funds authorized” or “Payment processing” can help users understand the current state. Avoid promising when reserved funds will become available unless the provider confirms the timing.

3. Show the Details Users Need

Each transaction row should answer three questions: what was the payment, when did it happen, and what is its current status?

Include:

  • Amount and currency
  • Merchant or recipient
  • Transaction date
  • Current status
  • A short explanation when the status needs clarification

For transactions that change state, show the latest update time when it helps explain a delay. Keep the transaction ID available for support requests, even if it appears only in the details view.
When a payment is reversed, make the reversal clear. Do not silently rename the original transaction as failed or remove it from the history.

4. Handle Errors and Delays Correctly

Several situations need distinct UI behavior:

  • Pending: show that processing is ongoing. Do not imply that the payment has succeeded.
  • Failed: explain the failure when reliable information is available. Offer a retry only if the payment flow supports it.
  • Reversed: show that the transaction was reversed and preserve the original record.
  • Empty history: explain that no transactions are available yet.
  • History loading error: tell the user that the transaction list could not be loaded.

A failure to load payment history does not mean the payment failed. Likewise, a timeout does not prove that a transaction was rejected. Check the transaction's actual state before suggesting another payment, or users may pay twice.

5. Make Statuses Accessible

Use text labels alongside color and icons. For example, do not rely on a red indicator alone to communicate a failed payment.

Make status changes available to assistive technologies where appropriate, and avoid announcing every routine update if it would create unnecessary interruptions. The W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide provides guidance on accessible interface patterns.

6. Test Status Transitions

Test the full payment lifecycle, including:

  • Delayed confirmation
  • Authorization without capture
  • Cancellation and reversal
  • Failed attempts and retries
  • Missing transaction details
  • Stale status data
  • API errors when loading history

Check both the stored state and the displayed label after every transition. A status change should update the existing transaction record rather than create a duplicate entry.

A reliable payment history uses consistent labels, preserves transaction events, and distinguishes an unresolved payment from a confirmed failure. That gives users an accurate view of their transactions and helps support teams investigate problems.

title: Why setCount(count + 1) Three Times Only Adds 1 (React Stale State)
description:
This click handler calls setCount(count + 1) three times:

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function handleClick() {
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);
  }

  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{count}</button>;
}

Click it once, and the counter shows 1, not 3.

It's not a React bug. It's how state works, and the same idea explains stuck timers and callbacks that read old values. I rendered every example below with React 19.3 (react-dom + jsdom) and recorded the actual results.

Video version:

Why: state is a snapshot

count isn't a live variable. It's a constant for the current render. Inside this click, count is 0 and stays 0:

setCount(0 + 1);   // "set it to 1"
setCount(0 + 1);   // "set it to 1"
setCount(0 + 1);   // "set it to 1"

React batches the three updates and re-renders once, with 1.

Fix: updater functions 

setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1);

React queues updater functions and runs them in order, each receiving the latest pending state: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. One click, 3.

Rule of thumb: if the next state depends on the previous state, pass a function.

Bug 2: "setState didn't work!" 

function handleClick() {
  setCount(count + 1);
  console.log(count);
}
Click Logged On screen
1 0 1
2 1 2

The update worked. The new value just arrives in the next render. If you need it immediately, compute it first:

const next = count + 1;
setCount(next);
console.log(next);

Bug 3: the interval that stops at 1 

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    setSeconds(seconds + 1);
  }, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);

The effect runs once, so the interval callback captured seconds from the first render: 0, forever. Every tick sets it to 0 + 1. After ~5 seconds in my test, the screen still showed 1.

setSeconds(s => s + 1);   // after ~5 s: 5

The updater doesn't read the captured variable, so it always works from the latest state. (Adding seconds to the dependency array also "works", but it tears down and recreates the interval on every tick.)

Bug 4: async callbacks see old values 

function handleClick() {
  setCount(count + 1);
  setTimeout(() => {
    report(count);
  }, 1000);
}

Click three times quickly: the screen shows 3, but the three timeouts report 0, 1, 2. Each callback closed over the count from the render it was created in.

If a callback really needs the latest value, keep it in a ref:

const countRef = useRef(count);
useEffect(() => { countRef.current = count; }, [count]);

function handleClick() {
  setCount(count + 1);
  setTimeout(() => report(countRef.current), 1000);
}

Same three clicks: the timeouts report 3, 3, 3.

Cheat sheet

  • State is a snapshot: constant for each render.
  • New state depends on old? Use setX(x => x + 1).
  • console.log right after setX shows the old value (by design).
  • Effects and intervals capture values: use updaters.
  • Async callbacks that need the latest value: use useRef.

Which of these have you hit? 👇

I post one tested coding tip every day on YouTube at Refactorly. The 30-second version of this one is here.

title: Attribute Routing Comes to Go's ServeMux, in Struct Tags
description:
The HTTP services post in this series gave routing a section called "The Weak Spot", showed four lines of the Go 1.22 mux, and moved on to chi, gorilla and gin. This post covers what that section left out: the pattern language set against attribute routing, and the things ASP.NET Core does around its router that Go's mux does not attempt. It then fills most of that list with a small library I wrote for the purpose, mapget. Every snippet and every response below was run on go1.27.3.

What you had in C 

[ApiController]
[Route("orders")]
public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("{id:int}")]
    public ActionResult<Order> Get(int id, [FromQuery] string[] expand) { ... }

    [HttpPost]
    public ActionResult<Order> Create(NewOrder body)
    {
        ...
        return CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get), new { id = order.Id }, order);
    }
}

That controller uses six separate features. The route template is matched. :int is a constraint, so /orders/abc is a 404 before the action runs. id and expand are bound from the path and the query string and converted. NewOrder is bound from the JSON body, and a body that fails is answered with a 400 ValidationProblemDetails that the action never sees. CreatedAtAction generates the new order's address from the route table. And the whole controller can be described as OpenAPI from what is already written there.

Only the first of those is routing in the narrow sense. Go's mux does the first and stops there.

What the mux matches 

mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc("GET /orders", listOrders)
mux.HandleFunc("POST /orders", createOrder)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /orders/{id}", getOrder)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /orders/latest", latestOrder)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /files/{path...}", getFile)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /docs/", docs)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /{$}", home)

A pattern is [METHOD ][HOST]/[PATH]. I registered those seven and sent requests at them:

Request Answer Why
GET /orders/42 getOrder, r.PathValue("id") is "42" {id} matches one segment
GET /orders/latest latestOrder The most specific pattern wins, whatever order they were registered in
HEAD /orders/42 getOrder A GET pattern also matches HEAD
DELETE /orders/42 405, Allow: GET, HEAD The path matched and the method did not
PUT /orders 405, Allow: GET, HEAD, POST
GET /files/a/b/c.txt getFile, path is "a/b/c.txt" {path...} takes the rest
GET /docs/a/b docs A trailing slash is an anonymous ...
GET /docs 307 to /docs/
GET / home {$} matches the end of the path only. Without it, / matches everything
GET /orders//42 307 to /orders/42 The path is cleaned first
GET /Orders/42 404 Literals are case-sensitive. ASP.NET Core's are not
GET /orders/42/ 404 No pattern has that trailing slash

Precedence is the part I like most. ASP.NET Core orders candidates by how literal each segment is, with Order to override it, and when two endpoints still tie it throws AmbiguousMatchException on the request that hits both. The mux has one rule: a pattern beats another if it matches a strict subset of the other's requests. If neither does and they overlap, registering the second one panics, and the message says why with examples:

pattern "GET /a/b/{y}" conflicts with pattern "GET /a/{x}/c":
GET /a/b/{y} and GET /a/{x}/c both match some paths, like "/a/b/c".
But neither is more specific than the other.
GET /a/b/{y} matches "/a/b/y", but GET /a/{x}/c doesn't.
GET /a/{x}/c matches "/a/x/c", but GET /a/b/{y} doesn't.

That is the mux's message with the file positions trimmed. An ambiguous route table stops the program at startup, where ASP.NET Core's surfaces on the first request that hits both endpoints.

What it leaves to you

I tried the things a C# developer reaches for next.

mux.HandleFunc("GET /items/{id:int}", h)   // panic: bad wildcard name "id:int"
mux.HandleFunc("GET /items/item-{id}", h)  // panic: bad wildcard segment (must start with '{')

There are no constraints, and a wildcard is a whole segment or nothing, so report-{year}.{ext} cannot be written either. GET /orders/abc reaches getOrder with id set to "abc", and the handler decides what that means.

r.PathValue("idd") on a pattern with {id} compiles, runs and returns "". Nothing connects the name in the pattern to the name in the handler.

The rest of the list:

  • Binding. Path values are strings. The query string, headers and body are yours to read and convert.
  • Error bodies. The mux's own 404 and 405 are text/plain. Anything for a bad parameter is whatever each handler writes.
  • Link generation. There are no route names, and no equivalent of LinkGenerator or CreatedAtAction. Addresses are built with fmt.Sprintf in a second place.
  • Groups. There is no MapGroup. A sub-mux behind http.StripPrefix works, and the patterns inside it then no longer say where they live.
  • A list of routes. The mux cannot be asked what it holds, so there is nothing to print at startup and nothing to build an OpenAPI document from.

Here is one endpoint with an integer id, a page parameter that defaults to 1 and a search term, written against the mux with care:

func getOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    id, err := strconv.Atoi(r.PathValue("id"))
    if err != nil {
        http.NotFound(w, r)
        return
    }
    q := r.URL.Query()
    page := 1
    if s := q.Get("page"); s != "" {
        if page, err = strconv.Atoi(s); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "page must be an integer", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
    }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(find(id, page, q.Get("q")))
}

That is thirteen lines before any work is done, none of them routing, and each endpoint will write them slightly differently.

Putting the route on the request type

Go has no attributes. It does have struct tags, which encoding/json already uses to say where a field comes from. mapget uses them for the whole request, route included:

type GetOrder struct {
    mapget.Route `route:"GET /orders/{id}"`
    ID     int      `path:"id"`
    Expand []string `query:"expand"`
}

func (s *Service) GetOrder(ctx context.Context, in GetOrder) (Order, error) {
    o, ok := s.orders[in.ID]
    if !ok {
        return Order{}, mapget.NotFound("there is no order with that id")
    }
    return o, nil
}

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    app := mapget.New(mux)
    mapget.Handle(app, svc.GetOrder)
    http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux)
}

Handle reads the tags once, registers GET /orders/{id} on the mux you gave it, and wraps the function in an http.Handler that binds, calls and writes. The mux still does all the matching, so every row of the table above still holds. The handler is a plain function of a context and a value, and a test calls it without building a request.

If you prefer the pattern at the registration, in the style of app.MapGet, mapget.HandleAt(app, "GET /orders/{id}", svc.GetOrder) does that with an untagged type.

The field's type is the constraint

ID is an int, so there is nothing to add to the pattern. These are from the example service in the repository:

$ curl -s localhost:8080/api/orders/abc
{"status":404,"title":"Not Found"}

$ curl -s 'localhost:8080/api/orders?status=open&limit=abc'
{"errors":{"limit":["must be an integer"]},"status":400,"title":"One or more validation errors occurred."}

$ curl -s --json '{"customer":5}' localhost:8080/api/orders
{"errors":{"customer":["must be a string"]},"status":400,"title":"One or more validation errors occurred."}

A path value that does not parse is a 404, which is what {id:int} does. A query value, header or cookie that does not parse is a 400, and every failing field is reported in one answer. The bodies are RFC 9457 problem details, with the title, status and errors members that ASP.NET Core's ValidationProblemDetails has.

Fields can be strings, booleans, integers, floats, time.Duration, or anything that implements encoding.TextUnmarshaler, which covers time.Time, netip.Addr and the UUID packages. A narrower constraint is a type of your own whose UnmarshalText rejects what it should. There are header, cookie and body:"json" tags beside path and query, a ,required option and a default tag.

Rules go in tags too

DataAnnotations ([Range], [StringLength], [RegularExpression]) have a counterpart in tags named after the JSON Schema keywords: minimum, maximum, minLength, maxLength, pattern, enum, minItems and maxItems. They go on parameters and on any field inside a JSON body:

type ListOrders struct {
    mapget.Route `route:"GET /orders"`
    Status string `query:"status" enum:"open,shipped"`
    Limit  int    `query:"limit" default:"20" minimum:"1" maximum:"100"`
}

type NewOrder struct {
    Customer string `json:"customer" minLength:"1" maxLength:"80"`
    Lines    []Line `json:"lines" minItems:"1" maxItems:"50"`
}

type Line struct {
    SKU string `json:"sku" pattern:"^[A-Z]{2,6}-[0-9]+$"`
    Qty int    `json:"qty" minimum:"1"`
}

$ curl -s 'localhost:8080/api/orders?status=lost&limit=500'
{"errors":{"limit":["must be at most 100"],"status":["must be one of open, shipped"]},"status":400,"title":"One or more validation errors occurred."}

$ curl -s --json '{"customer":"","lines":[{"sku":"tile","qty":0}]}' localhost:8080/api/orders
{"errors":{"customer":["must be at least 1 character"],"lines[0].qty":["must be at least 1"],"lines[0].sku":["must match the pattern ^[A-Z]{2,6}-[0-9]+$"]},"status":400,"title":"One or more validation errors occurred."}

On a path field a rule is a route constraint: ID int tagged path:"id" minimum:"1" answers 404 for /orders/0, as {id:int:min(1)} does. The same tags are written into the OpenAPI schemas. A rule that a tag cannot state, such as one comparing two fields, goes in a Validate() error method on the request type, which runs after the tags have passed.

Mistakes are found at startup

The pattern and the fields are checked against each other when the route is registered, and a mismatch panics, as a conflicting pattern does in the mux:

mapget: main.GetOrder.ID reads path value "idd", which is not in the pattern "GET /orders/{id}"
mapget: pattern "GET /orders/{id}/{rev}" has the wildcard {rev} and main.GetOrder has no field tagged path:"rev"
mapget: main.ListOrders.Page: default "one" is not an integer

A link is a value of the request type

Url.Action and LinkGenerator take names and an object of route values, and return null at run time when the two do not fit. Here the type that declares the route also builds its address:

app.Path(GetOrder{ID: 42})                             // "/orders/42"
app.Path(GetOrder{ID: 42, Expand: []string{"lines"}})  // "/orders/42?expand=lines"

Rename the field, change its type or move the route under a prefix, and every link either follows or stops compiling. The create handler in the example uses it for its Location header:

func (s *service) create(_ context.Context, in CreateOrder) (mapget.Created[Order], error) {
    // ... store the order as o ...
    o.Self = s.links.MustPath(GetOrder{ID: o.ID})
    return mapget.Created[Order]{Location: o.Self, Body: *o}, nil
}

$ curl -si --json '{"customer":"Ada","lines":[{"sku":"TILE-4","qty":12}]}' localhost:8080/api/orders
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /api/orders/2

Groups, the route table and OpenAPI 

app := mapget.New(mux)
api := app.Group("/api", logging)

mapget.Handle(api, s.list)
mapget.Handle(api, s.get)
mapget.Handle(api, s.create)
mapget.Handle(api, s.ship)

app.Handle("GET /openapi.json", app.OpenAPI(mapget.Info{Title: "Orders", Version: "1.0.0"}))
app.WriteRoutes(os.Stdout)

Group is MapGroup: a prefix and some ordinary func(http.Handler) http.Handler middleware. Because registration goes through mapget, it knows what the mux holds and can print it:

GET   /api/orders            main.ListOrders   []main.Order
POST  /api/orders            main.CreateOrder  mapget.Created[main.Order]
GET   /api/orders/{id}       main.GetOrder     main.Order
POST  /api/orders/{id}/ship  main.ShipOrder    mapget.NoContent
GET   /openapi.json          -                 -

The same table, with the tags and the Go types, is enough for an OpenAPI 3.1 document: parameters from the path and query tags, schemas from the types as encoding/json reads them, 201 and 204 from Created and NoContent, and a problem details response on every operation. This is the operation for GET /api/orders/{id}, trimmed of its error response:

{
  "operationId": "getOrder",
  "summary": "Fetch one order",
  "tags": ["orders"],
  "parameters": [
    { "name": "id", "in": "path", "required": true,
      "schema": { "type": "integer", "format": "int64" } }
  ],
  "responses": {
    "200": {
      "description": "OK",
      "content": { "application/json": { "schema": { "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Order" } } }
    }
  }
}

What it costs

The tags are read with reflect at registration. Per request, the wrapper sets a few struct fields through reflect on top of the parsing the hand-written handler does anyway. I benchmarked the hand-written handler above against the mapget version of the same endpoint, both through a real ServeMux:

go1.27.3, Apple M4 Max Time Allocated Allocations
By hand 371 ns 528 B 8
mapget 417 ns 560 B 9

Those are medians of five runs of go test -bench. The difference is 46 nanoseconds and one allocation a request.

What the fuzz test found in the mux

Path and binding are meant to be inverses: whatever address Path writes for a value, a request for it should bind to the same value. That is a property, so I gave it to go test -fuzz with a real ServeMux in the loop. It found two things, both in the mux.

On go1.27.3, a path segment that is exactly %2F matches no {wildcard}:

Request to GET /trip/{name}/{n} Answer
/trip/a%2Fb/1 200, name is "a/b"
/trip/%2Fa/1 200, name is "/a"
/trip/%2F%2F/1 200, name is "//"
/trip/%2F/1 404

The mux unescapes each segment before matching and uses the string "/" internally to mean a trailing slash, which single wildcards are written to skip (routing_tree.go, if seg != "/"). A segment that unescapes to exactly "/" is skipped with it. Path now returns an error for a path value of "/".

The second turned up in CI, on the oldest Go I had said I supported. On go1.22.12, r.PathValue("rest") for the pattern /trip/{name}/{n}/{rest...} and the request /trip/0/-83/* panics with an index out of range. Go 1.23 returns "*". Go 1.22 has been out of support since February 2025, so mapget asks for 1.23 and the fuzz test runs in CI on both ends of the range.

Since then the fuzz test has run more than fifteen million round trips on 1.23 and 1.27 without another failure.

When a router package is still worth it

  • You need matching the mux cannot express. chi takes a regular expression in the pattern and wildcards inside a segment. I checked both on chi v5.5.0: /orders/{id:[0-9]+} answers 404 for /orders/abc, and /files/report-{year}.{ext} matches report-2026.csv. If your addresses look like that and cannot change, use chi.
  • You want a framework. gin and echo bring their own context type, binding, rendering and a large set of middleware written against that context. That is a different decision from routing, closer to choosing MVC over minimal APIs, and it is a reasonable one for a team that wants the conventions decided for it.
  • You need case-insensitive paths. The mux will not do it, and lowercasing in middleware means redirecting or rewriting every request.

If none of those apply, the standard mux is enough. Binding, error bodies, links and the OpenAPI document are separate from matching, and mapget adds them without replacing it.

Huma already does most of this

Most of mapget exists already. Huma has typed handlers, path and query struct tags, problem details and an OpenAPI 3.1 document. It runs on the standard mux through an adapter, validates from tags (minimum, maxLength, pattern), and has adapters for chi, gin, echo and others. I ran the same endpoint on Huma v2.41.0: /orders/42 binds, /orders/abc is a 422 where mapget answers 404, and the document is served at /openapi.json. If you want this for work, use Huma.

I wrote mapget anyway, for fun and to learn, and it may not deserve to exist beside Huma. I wanted to know how much of ASP.NET Core's routing could be rebuilt from struct tags on the standard mux, and writing a library is a good way to find out what one has to decide. The two parts I have not seen elsewhere are the route on the request type and the link built from that same type.

Whether a route belongs on a type is a fair question in Go. The habit there is to register every route in one visible place and to be sparing with reflection, and a route in a struct tag goes against the first of those. HandleAt keeps the pattern at the registration for anyone who prefers that. The rest is in keeping with the standard library: it is reflection over struct tags, as encoding/json is, and it panics at registration on a mistake, as the mux does.

What mapget does not do

It has no constraint syntax in the pattern and no partial-segment wildcards, because the mux has neither. A regular expression constraint is written as a type whose UnmarshalText rejects everything else, and the README has an example. It has no dependency injection: handlers are methods on a struct that holds what they need. It reads JSON bodies only, so a form or an upload takes a *http.Request field or a plain handler registered beside the typed ones. Authentication is middleware. The OpenAPI document carries the rules written as tags and knows nothing of the ones in a Validate method.

It is at version 0.2 and was written for this post: about 2,150 lines with no dependencies outside the standard library. The API may still change before 1.0.

go get github.com/AndyCross/mapget

The source, the fuzz test and an example service with Swagger UI over its generated document are at github.com/AndyCross/mapget, and the reference is on pkg.go.dev.

title: Ecoasis AgTech Park Proposes Colorado Data Center with Up to 160 Acres of Greenhouses
description:
Ecoasis AgTech Park has outlined plans for a data center campus in Pueblo, Colorado, that would sit alongside up to 160 acres of greenhouses. The proposed development covers 272 acres in total, with the data center limited to 10 percent of the site.

Waste Heat Directed to On-Site Growing Operations
Under the proposal, the campus would house a compact data center designed to channel waste heat to the surrounding greenhouses, supporting year-round agricultural operations while improving overall energy efficiency. The facility would rely on a closed-loop cooling system, with water recirculated through the greenhouses' irrigation infrastructure to minimize additional water consumption.

The proposed development reflects an emerging sustainability trend across data center projects in the United States, where developers are exploring innovative approaches to energy efficiency, heat recovery, and responsible water management. By integrating digital infrastructure with agricultural operations, Ecoasis aims to turn excess heat generated by computing equipment into a useful resource for greenhouse heating.

The proposed 272-acre Ecoasis AgTech Park in Pueblo, Colorado, could include up to 160 acres of greenhouses, with the data center component limited to 10% of the overall property. The project is being developed through a partnership involving greenhouse design firm Thomas Larssen and real estate developer Gill van der Drift.

Ecoasis said the unit development application is still in progress, with final cooling and water specifications subject to county review. Construction is targeted to begin in spring 2027, with initial operations projected for the first half of 2028. If approved and completed, the development could demonstrate how future data center projects in the United States can combine digital infrastructure with agricultural applications and resource-efficient operations.

The project stems from a partnership between Thomas Larssen, a greenhouse design firm, and real estate company Gill van der Drift. The campus would be sited at Interstate 25 and Greenhorn Drive, on land the pair acquired.

Spring 2027 Start Targeted with Phased Build-Out
According to the companies, construction is slated to begin at the site in spring 2027, with first operations projected for some point in the first half of 2028.

The campus is expected to be delivered in phases across a four-year period. The Pueblo proposal would place the data center and the agricultural operation on the same property, with the greenhouse acreage accounting for the large majority of the 272-acre site and the computing footprint held to a tenth of the land.

Heat Reuse Remains Uncommon in the United States
The project is a rarity for the US market, which has not seen the spread of data center waste heat reuse that Europe has.
The Nordic countries in particular have become a center for heat reuse schemes, supported by large legacy district heating networks.
One example is Microsoft's partnership with Finnish utility Fortum to supply waste heat from two facilities it has planned in the country. Once completed, those facilities are expected to provide around 40 percent of the district heating needs of Espoo, Kauniainen, and Kirkkonummi.

Ecoasis is also not the first to pursue a link between data center heat and greenhouse operations. Digital Energy has pioneered a model in which it co-locates compute at greenhouse sites, using existing grid connections and selling the waste heat to the greenhouse operator.

Site and Specifications at a Glance
The Ecoasis AgTech Park campus would occupy land at Interstate 25 and Greenhorn Drive in Pueblo, Colorado, spanning 272 acres.
The data center component would be capped at 10 percent of the property, and waste heat from the facility would be directed to up to 160 acres of greenhouses. Cooling would use closed-loop systems, with water recirculated through the greenhouses' irrigation system.
Final cooling and water specifications remain subject to county review as the unit development application proceeds. The partnership behind the project combines greenhouse design expertise through Thomas Larssen with real estate development through Gill van der Drift.
Construction is planned to begin in spring 2027, with first operations projected in the first half of 2028, and the campus built in phases over four years.

title: Kineticons: every icon moves like the thing it pictures
description:
Kineticons: every icon moves like the thing it pictures

Icons are usually the stillest things on a page. They sit there, frozen, while everything around them animates. Kineticons asks a simple question: what if each icon moved the way its object does?

That's the whole idea. A bell swings. A padlock shuts. A battery fills. Each of the 2,850 open-source icons has its own motion, drawn from the thing it pictures — not a generic wobble pasted onto every shape, but movement that belongs to that icon.

2,850 icons, 20 categories

The library has grown to 2,850 icons across 20 categories: the original 2,083 icons plus 767 brand icons. Every one of them is animated. It's a large set, but the point isn't the count — it's that the motion is part of each icon's design, not an afterthought bolted on later.

One drawing, three styles

Every icon comes from a single drawing, rendered in three styles: outline, duotone, and filled. You pick the style that fits your interface, and the motion comes with it. There's no separate animated variant to hunt for and no second asset to keep in sync — the drawing and its movement are one thing.

Motion is plain CSS

The animation isn't a JavaScript library or a video file. Each icon's motion is plain CSS, with triggers you control: hover, focus, manual, or loop. The icon moves when you want it to, and stays still when you don't.

And when a user has asked their system to reduce motion, the icons respect that. The animation steps aside instead of ignoring the preference — which is how motion on the web should work.

Why motion, and why this kind

Motion in interfaces usually does one of two jobs: it tells you something happened, or it makes something feel alive. Most icon libraries leave both jobs to you — the icon is a static picture, and any movement is something you add yourself, on top, with your own animation code.

Kineticons puts the movement inside the icon, where it belongs. The motion is part of the icon's identity: the bell doesn't just look like a bell, it rings like one. That means the feedback is there by default, in every place the icon appears, without extra work in each component that uses it. And because the motion is plain CSS with triggers you control, it stays cheap and predictable — no animation library to load, no JavaScript running on every frame.

Use it anywhere

Kineticons ships packages for the frameworks people actually use: React 18 and 19, including Server Components, Vue 3 and Nuxt, and Svelte 5. If you don't want a framework at all, there's static SVG and a CDN.

That breadth matters because icons are one of the few things every part of a product shares — the marketing site, the app, the docs, the extensions. One library that works in all of those places means one set of icons to learn and one style to keep consistent, instead of a different set per stack.

Install it with:

npm install kineticons

It's also on JSR as @kineticons/core, there's a VS Code extension (fabwaseem.kineticons) that puts the icons where you work, and a Figma Community file for the design side. MIT licensed, so it's free to use anywhere.

Try it

If your interface has icons that just sit there, give one of them a reason to move — the bell is a really good place to start, and the padlock is a close second.

  • Site: https://kineticons.fabwaseem.com
  • GitHub: https://github.com/fabwaseem/kineticons

title: The day a CEO delivered the first unit himself
description:
In August 2016, a CEO did not ship the first unit. He took it there himself.

Jensen Huang, founder and chief executive of NVIDIA, hand-delivered the first production DGX-1 to OpenAI's office in San Francisco. NVIDIA announced the delivery on Monday, 15 August, and said it had happened the previous week. Elon Musk, then a cofounder of OpenAI, was there to receive it. A photograph released with the announcement shows Huang and Musk with the machine.

This needs to be stated carefully, because the shorthand is often wrong. The DGX-1 was not NVIDIA's first product, and Musk was not NVIDIA's first customer. What is true, and worth keeping precise, is narrower: the first DGX-1, NVIDIA's first dedicated AI supercomputer in a box, went to OpenAI, and Musk was there when Huang handed it over.

Huang signed the machine. Fortune reported the inscription: "To Elon and the OpenAI Team! To the future of computing and humanity. I present you the world's first DGX-1!"

On 9 August 2016, Musk posted a public thank-you: "Would like to thank @nvidia and Jensen for donating the first DGX-1 AI supercomputer to @OpenAI in support of democratizing AI technology." Fortune quoted that post in its report the following week. NVIDIA's announcement described a hand delivery of the first production unit. I am not going to pretend I have seen the commercial terms. The public record is the delivery, the inscription, and Musk's thanks. TOP500, writing the same day as NVIDIA's announcement, noted that the system listed at $129,000 and that it was not clear whether OpenAI had paid for it or come to some other arrangement.

I have no relationship with NVIDIA, with Jensen Huang, or with Elon Musk. I run a small engineering company in Coimbatore called MigrateForge. I am writing about this day because of what the delivery itself shows about founders, first systems, and long bets.

What the machine was

NVIDIA had unveiled the DGX-1 on 5 April 2016 at its GPU Technology Conference. The company's own newsroom said the system offered "up to 170 teraflops of half-precision (FP16) peak performance." TOP500, covering the OpenAI delivery in August, described the same figure as 170 teraflops at FP16 (half precision). Each system held eight Tesla P100 GPUs, linked with NVIDIA's NVLink interconnect.

The launch announcement also made a throughput claim that is easy to overstate if the wording is loosened. NVIDIA said the DGX-1 delivered "the equivalent throughput of 250 x86 servers." It tied that comparison, in a footnote, to Caffe training of AlexNet on the ILSVRC-2012 dataset, against a cluster of two-socket Intel Xeon E5-2697 v3 systems with InfiniBand. That is NVIDIA's published comparison, not a general statement that one box replaced 250 unspecified servers in every workload. The distinction is the sort of thing engineering readers will notice, so it should stay in the sentence.

Huang, speaking about the work behind the machine, was quoted by Jon Peddie in GfxSpeak three days after the delivery announcement. "Building DGX-1 took 3,000 people working for three years," Huang explained. "So if this is the only one ever shipped, this project would cost $2 billion." The same wording appears in the NVIDIA announcement as carried by WebWire on 15 August 2016.

He also said why this first system went where it did: "I thought it was incredibly appropriate that the world's first supercomputer dedicated to artificial intelligence would go to the laboratory that was dedicated to open artificial intelligence."

What OpenAI said it would do with it

OpenAI's researchers were already clear about the constraint they were trying to remove: time and compute.

"The DGX-1 is a huge advance," said Ilya Sutskever, then an OpenAI research scientist, in NVIDIA's announcement. "It will allow us to explore problems that were completely unexplored before, and it will allow us to achieve levels of performance that weren't achievable." In the same announcement he added that advances depended on GPUs being fast: "Speed of our computers is, in some sense, the lifeblood of deep learning."

Andrej Karpathy, then also an OpenAI research scientist, put the same point in terms of scale. Tom's Hardware quoted him on the day of the announcement: "One very easy way of always getting our models to work better is to just scale the amount of compute. So right now, if we're training on, say, a month of conversations on Reddit, we can, instead, train on entire years of conversations of people talking to each other on all of Reddit. And then we can get much more data in terms of how people interact with each other. And, eventually, we'll use that to talk to computers, just like we talk to each other."

That was 2016. The public statements from that week are about compute, language, and experiments that had been out of reach. I will leave later origin stories about what followed at OpenAI to the people who were there. The fact that holds without embroidery is that Huang put the first of these machines into the hands of a small lab, in person, and that the lab's researchers said they would use it to train larger models than they could train before.

Nine years later, in October 2025, NVIDIA quoted Huang looking back on that delivery: "In 2016, we built DGX-1 to give AI researchers their own supercomputer. I hand-delivered the first system to Elon at a small startup called OpenAI." The company said he hand-delivered one of the first units of a later system, DGX Spark, to Musk at SpaceX in Starbase, Texas, and called the exchange a connection to the 2016 origins. I note that only as a bookend. The 2016 delivery is the one that still teaches the lesson.

Show up for the first system

The part of the story that stays with me as a founder is not the specification sheet. It is that the CEO packed the first unit and went to San Francisco.

A first system is a fragile moment. The product is new. The buyer is taking a risk on something the market does not yet understand. A freight delivery would have been easier, and a press release would still have been written. Huang went anyway. He signed the box. He stood for the photograph. He put his name next to the first customer for that machine.

That is a founder habit. Long engineering bets do not close themselves. They need someone who will still be there when the first unit leaves the building, and who treats that moment as part of the work, not as a ceremony after the work is done.

I am looking for our first paying client at MigrateForge. I will not compare that search to the delivery of a DGX-1. The scale is different, and the companies are different. The only honest parallel is a smaller one: a first customer is a serious moment, and it deserves to be treated as part of the engineering, not as a press event after the fact.

The first cutover deserves the same attention

Most mid-market engineering organisations are not founder-led, and their long bets are more exposed when leadership changes. The hardest technical decision on the books is often a legacy migration. Often that means a production PHP or CodeIgniter 3 application that has run the business for years, been changed by many hands, and is understood in full by very few people.

When a CEO, founder or long-tenured CTO is leaving, arriving, or under review, that migration is usually the first thing to stop. The phrase is some version of "let's wait until leadership settles." The logic is understandable. Who signs off on leaving PHP? Who owns the outcome if a cutover goes wrong? If the person who approved the work might not be there when it goes live, waiting looks careful.

Waiting is not free. The application keeps taking changes. The people who understand its edge cases move on. A later migration has more surface to prove and fewer people who can say whether a behaviour is a bug or an old workaround. A quarter becomes a year.

A leadership change should be allowed to redirect strategy. It should not freeze the evidence-gathering that makes a first cutover safe. The first time you move a production PHP system onto a new stack, someone accountable should be in the room, and the go-live bar should already be written down. That bar should not depend on who is in the chair that week. It should depend on whether the new system behaves like the old one under the journeys the business already runs.

That is the work we do at MigrateForge. We convert plain PHP and CodeIgniter 3 applications to Java 21 / Spring Boot. Laravel is not supported yet; it is next.

The method is straightforward:

  1. Record real user journeys on the existing PHP application.
  2. Prove the PHP application can replay its own recording at 99.5% or better. If the original system cannot reproduce itself to that bar, the recording is not yet reliable enough to judge a conversion.
  3. Convert the application to Java 21 / Spring Boot.
  4. Replay the same journeys against the converted system, comparing HTTP responses, database writes and outgoing calls.
  5. Keep cutover blocked until they match.

If leadership changes in the middle of that programme, the bar does not move. The recorded journeys are still the recorded journeys. The comparison is still HTTP responses, database writes and outgoing calls. The new leader inherits a test, not an opinion.

These figures are from our own runs. On two benchmarks, WA Blast Pro and InvoicePlane, 858 fixtures reached 100% parity. Those are benchmarks, not client systems, and they are not a promise about any particular codebase. On the first pass of one conversion wave, we reached 82%, with 9.7 hand fixes per 1,000 lines. I include that number because it is not 100%. A first pass is not the finish line. Engineers still have to close the gap, and the replay comparison tells them where it is. We do not have paying clients yet. We are looking for our first.

A first cutover, like a first system, is not a ceremony. It is the moment you find out whether the work holds. The people who made the bet should be there, and the test should already be in place.

You can read more about our approach at migrateforge.com.

CTOs: when the first cutover of your PHP system comes, will you be in the room, and will the replay bar already be written down?

Sources

  • NVIDIA Newsroom, "NVIDIA Launches World's First Deep Learning Supercomputer," 5 April 2016. Launch specifications, including "up to 170 teraflops of half-precision (FP16) peak performance," eight Tesla P100 GPUs, NVLink, and the claim of "the equivalent throughput of 250 x86 servers," with the Caffe/AlexNet footnote. https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-launches-world-s-first-deep-learning-supercomputer
  • WebWire reprint of NVIDIA's 15 August 2016 announcement, "NVIDIA CEO Delivers World's First AI Supercomputer in a Box to OpenAI." Hand delivery "last week" to OpenAI in San Francisco; first production DGX-1; Huang's "incredibly appropriate" remark; the 3,000 people / three years and "$2 billion" remarks; Sutskever quotes. https://www.webwire.com/ViewPressRel.asp?aId=204723
  • TOP500, Michael Feldman, "NVIDIA Delivers DGX-1 Supercomputer in a Box to OpenAI," 15 August 2016. Hand delivery by Huang; Musk identified as an OpenAI cofounder; 170 teraflops (half precision, FP16); eight P100 GPUs; NVLink; list price $129,000; terms of the transfer not clear. https://top500.org/news/nvidia-delivers-dgx-1-supercomputer-in-a-box-to-openai/
  • Fortune, Jonathan Vanian, 15 August 2016. Personal delivery to OpenAI's San Francisco office the previous week; the signed inscription; Musk's 9 August 2016 thank-you post. https://fortune.com/2016/08/15/elon-musk-artificial-intelligence-openai-nvidia-supercomputer/
  • GfxSpeak, Jon Peddie, 18 August 2016. Direct quotation of Huang: "Building DGX-1 took 3,000 people working for three years." "So if this is the only one ever shipped, this project would cost $2 billion." https://gfxspeak.com/archives/enables-openai-tflops/
  • Tom's Hardware, Lucian Armasu, 15 August 2016. Karpathy quotation on scaling compute and training on years of Reddit conversations. https://www.tomshardware.com/news/openai-nvidia-dgx-1-ai-supercomputer,32476.html
  • NVIDIA Newsroom, "NVIDIA DGX Spark Arrives for World's AI Developers," 13 October 2025. Huang: "In 2016, we built DGX-1 to give AI researchers their own supercomputer. I hand-delivered the first system to Elon at a small startup called OpenAI." Later hand delivery of a DGX Spark unit to Musk at SpaceX, described as a connection to the 2016 origins. https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-dgx-spark-arrives-for-worlds-ai-developers

title: Next.js on a container versus Vercel: where the Hobby plan stops fitting
description:
TL;DR: Vercel's Hobby plan is the right home for a non-commercial Next.js site, and nothing in a container tier beats that deal. The line is commercial hobby projects, WebSockets and long requests. Past it, a standalone-output Dockerfile builds a small image, and this post lists what changes without Vercel's platform features, with measured memory and CPU and the two kinds of environment variables.

Vercel is where Next.js is designed to run, and for a personal project its free Hobby plan is hard to argue with. This is not an argument against it. It is a map of the line where a Next.js app stops fitting a serverless free tier and starts fitting a container, with the real limits on both sides and a Dockerfile that produces a small image.

What Vercel's Hobby plan actually gives you

  • Free, with one condition that matters: personal, non-commercial use only. A side project that takes payments, shows ads or belongs to a company is outside the terms; the next plan is Pro at $20 per member per month.
  • 100 GB of fast data transfer, 1 million function invocations, 4 hours of active CPU and 360 GB-hours of provisioned memory a month.
  • Functions run up to 60 seconds. No overage billing on Hobby: when a limit is hit, the resource is unavailable until the next cycle.
  • Preview deployments per pull request, the global CDN, image optimization and Incremental Static Regeneration, all wired in without configuration.

If your app is a static or mostly static site, a portfolio, docs, or a blog, and it is non-commercial, stop reading and use Vercel. Nothing in a container tier beats that deal for that shape.

Where a container fits better

  • Commercial hobby projects. A small SaaS with three paying users is "commercial". On a container free tier the question is not asked; the trade is that the container sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic and takes about a minute to wake.
  • A real server. WebSockets, long-lived connections, an in-process job queue, a custom server.js, or a request that legitimately takes longer than a minute. Serverless functions end; a container process does not.
  • No per-invocation ceiling. A container has no invocation, CPU-second or memory-hour budgets, only the box it runs in: 512 MB and 0.25 vCPU on the free tier, and 100 container-hours a month.
  • Everything in one place. A Next.js front end next to a Python API and a managed Postgres, in the same dashboard, with environment variables you set once.

The Dockerfile: standalone output

Next.js can emit a self-contained server with only the files it needs. Turn it on in next.config.js:

/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = { output: 'standalone' };
module.exports = nextConfig;

FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
ENV NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/public ./public
USER app
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

The standalone folder contains server.js and a pruned node_modules, so the final image is the Node runtime plus what the app really uses, typically well under 200 MB rather than the 500 MB+ you get by copying the whole project. HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 matters: the standalone server binds to localhost by default, which the platform cannot reach.

Why your own Dockerfile rather than the generated one: SnapDeploy's generated Node.js Dockerfile builds on a Node 18 base image. Next.js 15 still runs there, but recent releases require Node 20 or newer, and the standalone layout above is not something a generic generator knows about.

With a Dockerfile in the repository, SnapDeploy uses it and reads the port from EXPOSE. If your pages use next/image, install sharp as a dependency; it is compiled during npm ci on the Alpine image without extra steps.

What changes without Vercel's platform features

Feature On Vercel In a container
Static assets and CDN Global edge cache automatically Served by the Node process; put a CDN in front if traffic is global. On SnapDeploy every container URL is already behind Cloudflare.
Incremental Static Regeneration Shared cache across functions Works; the cache lives in .next/cache inside the container and is rebuilt after a restart or a wake.
Image optimization Built in Done by the server with sharp; CPU-bound on a quarter vCPU, so pre-size images or use an external loader.
Preview per pull request Automatic Manual: deploy a branch to a second container (the free tier has four).
Cold start Function cold starts, usually well under a second None while awake; about 60 seconds to wake a free container that slept, none on Always-On ($12/month).

Memory and CPU, measured

A standalone Next.js server with the App Router idles around 100 to 150 MB and stays under 300 MB serving a typical page mix, so 512 MB works. The constraint is CPU: server rendering a heavy page on 0.25 vCPU takes several times longer than on your laptop. Static generation at build time (generateStaticParams, ISR with a long revalidate) moves that work to the build, where it belongs, and the container mostly serves files.

Deploying

  1. Add output: 'standalone' and the Dockerfile; commit a .dockerignore with node_modules, .next and .env*.
  2. Push. Containers → Deploy from GitHub → pick the repository. Port 3000.
  3. Add environment variables. NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are baked in at build time, so set them before the first build.
  4. Deploy. Builds take a few minutes (the npm run build step dominates). Test the container URL, then the same page after 20 idle minutes to see the wake page once.

Check the image before you push 

docker build -t site .
docker images site --format "{{.Size}}"
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 site
curl -I http://localhost:3000/

If the size is several hundred megabytes, the standalone folder was not used (check next.config.js) or node_modules is being copied in. If the page renders but images are broken, public/ or .next/static was not copied into the runtime stage. If the container starts but nothing answers on port 3000, HOSTNAME is missing and the server is bound to localhost.

Environment variables: two kinds

Next.js treats NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables as build-time constants: they are inlined into the client bundle when npm run build runs, so they must be present during the build, and changing one means a rebuild. Everything else (database URLs, API keys, secrets) is read at runtime by server components, route handlers and middleware, and can be changed in the container settings followed by a restart. A common mistake is putting a secret in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ name; it ends up in the JavaScript you ship to every browser.

Where free stops

  • The container sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic; the first visitor afterwards waits about a minute on a wake page. Vercel has no equivalent wait.
  • 100 container-hours a month across four containers, counted while awake. A site visited a few times a day is fine; one that is pinged to stay up is not.
  • Custom domains need Always-On ($12/month). Vercel's Hobby plan includes them.
  • No built-in analytics, speed insights or per-branch previews; the free tier's four containers are what you have for previews.

Numbers used: Vercel Hobby limits from Vercel's plan and limits pages as of September 2026; SnapDeploy free tier from the free tier docs (4 containers, 512 MB, 0.25 vCPU, 100 container-hours a month, sleeps after 15 minutes, no card).

title: Finding a site's brand color from the console, and why painted area points the wrong way
description:
If you want to match a site's look, the first color you need is its brand color: the one on the main button, the links, the logo. Finding it by eye is usually easy. Finding it with code is where I went wrong twice, so here is what I measured on three fictional demo sites I built (Northwind Roasters, a coffee shop; Ledgerline, fintech; Afterhours, a dark developer tool) and the snippet I ended up with.

The obvious approach, and what it got wrong

My first try summed up the area of every element with an opaque background-color, grouped by color. On Northwind it said the top color was #f6eadb at 49%, then white at 45%. On Afterhours, #17141f at 97%.

Both are wrong, for two reasons:

  • Nested boxes count twice. A card inside a section inside a wrapper adds its area three times if all three have a background. The totals mean nothing.
  • The page background was missing. I looped over document.body.querySelectorAll('*'), which skips <body> and <html>, and that's where most sites set the page color. Northwind's real background, #fffaf3, didn't even make the top three.

Sampling what is actually painted

The fix is to ask the browser what's on top at each point, then walk up to the first ancestor that paints a background. The snippet scrolls through the page one screen at a time and samples a grid every 16px:

async function brandColor(step = 16) {
  const lin = (c) => (c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4);
  const chroma = ([r, g, b]) => { // OKLCH chroma
    [r, g, b] = [r, g, b].map((v) => lin(v / 255));
    const l = Math.cbrt(0.4122214708 * r + 0.5363325363 * g + 0.0514459929 * b);
    const m = Math.cbrt(0.2119034982 * r + 0.6806995451 * g + 0.1073969566 * b);
    const s = Math.cbrt(0.0883024619 * r + 0.2817188376 * g + 0.6299787005 * b);
    return Math.hypot(1.9779984951 * l - 2.428592205 * m + 0.4505937099 * s,
      0.0259040371 * l + 0.7827717662 * m - 0.808675766 * s);
  };
  const rgb = (c) => { const m = c.match(/rgba?\(([\d.]+), ([\d.]+), ([\d.]+)(?:, ([\d.]+))?\)/); return m && (m[4] ?? 1) > 0.5 ? [+m[1], +m[2], +m[3]] : null; };
  const hex = (c) => '#' + c.map((v) => Math.round(v).toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join('');
  const paintedBg = (el) => { // first ancestor with an opaque background
    for (; el; el = el.parentElement) { const c = rgb(getComputedStyle(el).backgroundColor); if (c) return c; }
    return [255, 255, 255]; // the canvas default
  };
  const seen = new Map(), clicks = new Map();
  const add = (m, k) => m.set(k, (m.get(k) || 0) + 1);
  for (let y = 0; y < document.documentElement.scrollHeight; y += innerHeight) {
    scrollTo(0, y); await new Promise(requestAnimationFrame);
    for (let py = 0; py < innerHeight; py += step) for (let px = 0; px < innerWidth; px += step) {
      const el = document.elementFromPoint(px, py);
      if (el) add(seen, hex(paintedBg(el)));
    }
  }
  scrollTo(0, 0);
  for (const el of document.querySelectorAll('a, button, [role=button]')) {
    if (!el.getClientRects().length) continue;
    const cs = getComputedStyle(el);
    for (const c of [rgb(cs.backgroundColor), rgb(cs.color)]) if (c && chroma(c) > 0.05) add(clicks, hex(c)); // skip greys
  }
  const total = [...seen.values()].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const top = (m) => [...m].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, 4);
  console.log('Painted background:', top(seen).map(([h, n]) => `${h} ${(100 * n / total).toFixed(1)}%`).join(', '));
  console.log('Saturated colors on links and buttons:', top(clicks).map(([h, n]) => `${h} x${n}`).join(', '));
}
brandColor();

The second loop is the part that finds the brand color: it collects the background and text colors of links and buttons, keeping only saturated ones (OKLCH chroma above 0.05, so greys, black and white drop out).

What it found

At 1280px wide:

Site Painted background (share of samples) Saturated colors on links and buttons
Northwind #fffaf3 64.1%, #ffffff 21.4%, #f6eadb 12.0%, #c2410c 1.5% #c2410c ×3, #4d7c5a ×1
Ledgerline #ffffff 87.7%, #f1f5f9 10.9%, #1d4ed8 1.0%, #ecfccb 0.4% #1d4ed8 ×2
Afterhours #0c0a14 75.9%, #17141f 23.5%, #8b5cf6 0.5% #8b5cf6 ×1

At 390px the shares move a little (the brand color goes up to 2.1% on Northwind and 1.5% on Afterhours, because buttons take more of a narrow screen) and the clickable colors are the same.

Three things stand out:

  1. The brand color is a tiny share of the paint. 0.5% to 2.1% across the three sites. Any approach that ranks colors by how much of the page they cover will put it fourth or lower, behind the background and surfaces.
  2. The painted ranking is still useful, just for different roles. First is the page background, second the surface (cards, panels, alternating sections). That matches how I built the sites.
  3. Clickable elements name the brand color every time. On all three, the most common saturated color on links and buttons is the one I chose as primary. On Northwind the second one, the sage green #4d7c5a, is the accent.

Where this will fail

My demo pages have only a few buttons each, so the counts are small. On real sites, check these before you trust the result:

  • Default link blue. A site that never styled its links will show #0000ee as a clickable color. If it shows up, ignore it.
  • Image buttons and gradients. A button painted with a background image or gradient has a transparent background-color, so the snippet only sees its text color.
  • Accent colors that aren't clickable. Ledgerline's lime accent #65a30d is used for small highlights, not links, so it doesn't appear in the clickable list. The #ecfccb in its painted list is a pale tint of it.

For a quick answer the snippet is enough: first painted color is the background, second is the surface, top clickable saturated color is the brand.

I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that does this kind of role guessing for the whole palette (plus fonts and spacing) and exports it as CSS variables or a Tailwind theme; the guide is here: extract the colors from any website, with roles.

Written with help from an AI assistant. Every number comes from running the snippet on the three demo pages in headless Chromium.

title: Why iPhone Focus Mode Still Lets You Open Distracting Apps
description:
You’re writing an email. Work Focus is on. No banner appears, no notification sounds, and your hand still opens a feed between two awkward sentences. From a user’s point of view, “I was distracted” describes both a notification and a reflex tap. From a developer’s point of view, they’re two different events.

Start with what happened on the device

Apple’s Focus settings let you decide whose notifications and which apps’ alerts can reach you. That is useful when a banner from the group chat takes you out of your draft. But the phone can be perfectly silent when you tap a social app yourself. Changing which notifications are delivered doesn’t, on its own, give that app’s icon a different behavior.

A session-based blocker has a different job. Apple’s Family Controls picker lets a person select apps or categories. Managed Settings can apply a shield to the selected tokens. The person decides which apps belong on that list. That matters when the course PDF, class chat and distracting feed all live on the same device.

Treat a pause as a real product decision

In Focusgotchi, the free timer pairs a task with a pixel pet that grows through focused minutes. The optional Pro blocker adds a rule to a running focus session. Consider a student who needs to send a reference to a teammate. They pause the session. Leaving a shield up at that point makes the pause button feel broken, even if the countdown itself stopped perfectly.

Here’s a small acceptance test for that interface. Pick one feed to shield and one notes app to leave open. Start focus and try both. Pause and try the feed. Resume and try it again. Finally end the session early and reopen the feed. The expected sequence for the selected feed is shielded, available, shielded, available. The notes app should open throughout.

Why would someone turn the blocker on again tomorrow?

A shield only helps once you choose to start a session. In Focusgotchi, you’ve hatched a pet, and studying with it is how you keep it well. Your selected Gotchi gets sick after three full days without focus together and dies after seven full days away. Fifteen focused minutes before then can help a sick pet recover. Opening your notes for a few minutes can feel worth doing even on a day when the deadline is a long way off.

Over three hours of focus the starter grows from its shell into an adult. Those sessions can also earn the 180 focus coins it costs to hatch Sunny. Your first pet stays in your collection.

Ask one question before adding a stricter setting

“What happened the last time you got interrupted?” If the answer is “a message popped up,” tune the notification rules. If it’s “I opened the feed myself,” look at what should happen on that tap. And if it’s “I finished one paragraph and didn’t know what to do next,” a clearer task label might do more than either setting. Three people can ask for better focus and need three different things from the interface.

Technical references: Apple’s iPhone User Guide, “Allow or silence notifications for a Focus on iPhone,” and Apple Developer Documentation for FamilyActivitySelection and ShieldSettings.
