title: AWS Activate Credits: Founders vs Portfolio, Eligibility and How to Apply
description:
AWS Activate gives eligible startups promotional AWS credits through two main tiers: Activate Founders for self-funded startups (starting at $1,000, with up to $5,000 for select participants) and Activate Portfolio for startups backed by an Activate Provider such as an accelerator or investor (up to $200,000). You apply with an AWS Builder ID, choose your tier, describe your company and link an AWS account. AWS says you should hear back within 5 to 10 business days.

This article walks through the tiers, the eligibility rules, the application, what the credits cannot pay for, and what to set up after approval so credits are used well and nothing is billed unexpectedly. Amounts below are as listed by AWS on 2026-11-24 and AWS changes startup offers often, so read the current page before you apply.

Who this guide is for

This guide is for founders, first-time cloud buyers and technical leads at early-stage startups in the US, India and elsewhere who are deciding whether and how to apply for AWS Activate. By the end you will know which tier fits you, what information to prepare, what reviewers can reject you for, and how to protect yourself from a surprise bill once credits are in your account.

If you are comparing AWS with other clouds, see Azure Free Account in 2026 and Google Cloud Free Tier. For an AI-focused program, see Claude for Startups credits and eligibility.

Activate tiers at a glance

AWS's startup credits page lists the following programs. All amounts are in USD.

Activate Founders Activate Portfolio AWS Credits for AI Startups
Who it is for Self-funded, bootstrapped startups applying directly Startups backed by an Activate Provider Invite-only, offered after Activate Portfolio
Amount listed Starts at $1,000; select participants may qualify for up to $5,000 Up to $200,000 $200,000+, scaling with workload
Organization ID Not needed Required, from your Activate Provider Invitation
Funding stage Pre-Series B Pre-Series B Not applicable

An Activate Provider is an organization such as an accelerator, angel investor or venture capital firm that is part of the Activate network. The Organization ID comes from that provider. AWS describes it as a code tied to your relationship with the provider, not a promotional code you can look up, so do not share it publicly.

AWS also lists Kiro Startup Credits for eligible startups that do not currently hold Activate credits. That is a separate program with its own terms.

Which tier should you choose?

  • No outside backer yet: apply for Founders. You do not need an Organization ID.
  • In an accelerator or backed by an investor that is an Activate Provider: ask the provider for your Organization ID and apply for Portfolio. If you are unsure whether your provider participates, ask them before you apply, because only the provider can issue the ID.
  • Already received credits: you can apply only if you are requesting more credits than you previously received.

Eligibility requirements

The credits page lists these requirements for Activate:

  • Pre-Series B funding stage.
  • Founded within the last 10 years.
  • An AWS account on the paid tier plan.
  • New to Activate credits, or requesting more credits than previously received.

AWS's "everything you need to know" guide adds detail by tier:

  • Founders: new to Activate credits, self-funded, a working company website, founded within the past 10 years.
  • Portfolio: affiliated with an Activate Provider and holding an Organization ID, no prior credits of equal or greater value, pre-Series B with any recent funding round within 12 months, a working website, founded within 10 years.

AWS does not publish a list of rejection reasons, so treat each requirement above as a possible reason for a denial.

Prerequisites before you apply

Prepare these items first so the form takes a few minutes:

  1. A professional email address on your company domain, rather than a personal mailbox, for your AWS Builder ID.
  2. A working company website or product page that describes what you build.
  3. Your funding stage and, for Portfolio, the Organization ID from your provider.
  4. An AWS account you control. Eligibility requires the paid tier plan, so if you opened a new account on a free plan, check in the console how to switch to the paid plan before you apply.
  5. A short description of your product and your expected AWS use, in case the form asks for it.

How to apply, step by step

The AWS startup credits page gives the process in four steps.

Step 1: Create or sign in to an AWS Builder ID

Open the AWS startup credits page and start the application. Create an AWS Builder ID with your professional email, or sign in if you already have one.

Step 2: Choose your tier

Choose Founders if you are self-funded. Choose Portfolio if you are backed by an Activate Provider, and enter the Organization ID that provider gave you.

Step 3: Describe your company

Provide details about your product, your funding stage and your company profile. Keep these consistent with your website. A mismatch between the form and what a reviewer can see online is the kind of inconsistency that can lead to a denial.

Step 4: Link or create your AWS account and submit

Link your existing AWS account or create one, then submit. AWS says you will "hear back within 5-10 business days" and that you are emailed whether you were approved or not.

What the credits can and cannot pay for

AWS says Activate credits can be used on over 200 eligible AWS services, including compute, databases, storage and networking, and that they also apply to third-party models on Amazon Bedrock.

The AWS Promotional Credit Terms list what is not covered. Read the terms yourself, since they are the binding document. They include:

Not covered by credits Source note
Amazon Mechanical Turk Excluded unless AWS authorizes otherwise
AWS Managed Services, AWS Professional Services, AWS Training and Certification Named in both the Activate guide and the terms
AWS Marketplace Listed in the terms
Route 53 domain registration or transfer Listed in the terms
Upfront fees such as Savings Plans and Reserved Instances Listed in the terms
Cryptocurrency mining Listed in the terms
Enterprise Support, Unified Operations, Enterprise On-Ramp, Partner-Led Support Listed in the terms
Sales, use and similar taxes Section 7 of the terms

AWS's Activate guide says credits can be applied toward eligible AWS Support plans, but it does not name which plans. Check the terms and your Billing console before assuming a specific support plan is covered.

How credits are applied to your bill

Per AWS's guide and terms:

  • Credits apply monthly to new usage charges on eligible services. They do not retroactively cover past bills.
  • You cannot choose which services the credits go toward. They apply automatically until used or expired.
  • Charges beyond the available credit balance are billed to your account.
  • Each promotional credit code can be redeemed once and only on one AWS account, and credit cannot be sold, rented or transferred.
  • Credit cannot be combined with other AWS promotional offers unless AWS authorizes it.

How long credits last

AWS says Activate credits "usually expire within 1-2 years depending on the package." The terms say credit cannot be redeemed after its expiration date, failure to redeem it before then results in forfeiture, and expired or cancelled credit is not refundable. AWS may cancel credit at any time. Your approved credits and expiration dates appear in the Billing and Cost Management console.

After approval: avoid surprise bills

Credits do not make usage free once they run out. Set up alerts the day the credits arrive.

Step 1: Check the balance and expiry

Open the Billing and Cost Management console and find your credits and their expiration dates. Put the expiration date in your team calendar.

Step 2: Create a budget from a template

  1. Open the Billing and Cost Management console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/.
  2. In the navigation pane, choose Budgets.
  3. At the top of the page, choose Create budget.
  4. Under Budget setup, choose Use a template (simplified).
  5. Under Templates, choose Monthly cost budget, which notifies you if you exceed, or are forecasted to exceed, the budget amount. The Zero spend budget template notifies you after spending exceeds AWS Free Tier limits, which is a different trigger.
  6. Update the details, then choose Create budget.

For the full walk-through, including email recipients and verification, see AWS Budgets and billing alerts setup.

Step 3: Plan what to spend credits on

Because credits apply automatically and expire, decide early which workloads use them. Avoid starting long-running resources you do not need only to burn credit, because anything that continues after the credits end is billed to you.

Troubleshooting

Problem What to check
Application denied Confirm every requirement: pre-Series B, founded within 10 years, working website, paid tier account, and that you are new to credits or asking for more than before. Fix the gap, then reapply
No response after 10 business days AWS says to expect an answer in 5 to 10 business days by email. Check the spam folder and the Builder ID email address
Portfolio form rejects the Organization ID Only the Activate Provider can issue it. Ask the provider to confirm the exact ID and that it is active
Credits not showing Check the Billing and Cost Management console for the account you linked, not another account
Charges still appear after approval Credits cover eligible services only and new usage only. Check the exclusions table and the date the credits were applied
Credit amount lower than expected The amounts shown are caps or starting values. AWS does not publish how it decides amounts above the starting figure

What we checked

  • Opened the AWS startup credits page on aws.amazon.com on 2026-11-24. It lists Activate Founders at "up to $5,000", starting at $1,000, Activate Portfolio at "up to $200,000", and an invite-only AI startups tier with $200,000+.
  • Cross-checked those amounts against AWS's "everything you need to know about AWS Activate credits" guide on 2026-11-24: Founders $1,000 with up to $5,000 over time, Portfolio up to $200,000. Both pages agree. A search result summary for another AWS page mentioned $100,000 for Portfolio, which we could not confirm, so we use the credits page figure and tell you to confirm it.
  • Compared eligibility on the credits page (pre-Series B, founded within 10 years, paid tier account) with the guide's per-tier lists on 2026-11-24. The guide adds the 12-month recent-round condition for Portfolio.
  • Read the AWS Promotional Credit Terms at aws.amazon.com/awscredits on 2026-11-24 for expiry, forfeiture, non-transferability, taxes and the list of ineligible services.
  • Opened the AWS Budgets template page on docs.aws.amazon.com on 2026-11-24 and copied the template names and the console steps exactly: Budgets, Create budget, Use a template (simplified), Monthly cost budget, Zero spend budget.
  • The credits page does not state credit duration or rejection reasons. The 1 to 2 year duration comes from the Activate guide, and we found no official list of rejection reasons.
  • Not checked hands-on: we did not submit an application or open an AWS account, so the form wording may differ from the steps above. Steps follow AWS's documentation as of 2026-11-24.

Last tested: 2026-11-24

References

  • AWS startup credits (Activate)
  • Everything you need to know about AWS Activate credits
  • AWS Promotional Credit Terms
  • Creating a budget (AWS Billing and Cost Management)
  • Using a budget template (simplified)

This guide was researched and drafted with AI assistance and checked against the vendor documentation listed in its References. Read the maintained version and related guides on EpiFive.

title: Mega Menu SEO: Your Dropdown Links May Not Be in the HTML
description:
A mega menu can look perfect, open on hover, pass every accessibility check, and still give Google zero links. If the dropdown is built in React and only renders its panel when it opens, the links aren't in the HTML your server sends, and Googlebot never opens the menu to make them appear. I found this on my own site this week: the header listed nine service pages, and the live home page linked none of them from the header.

This post covers how to check your own menu in 30 seconds, which popular React menu components behave this way (I tested Radix, shadcn/ui's base and Headless UI), and the fix I shipped, with its real cost in DOM size.

The short answer

  • Does Google crawl mega menu links? Only if they're real <a href> links in the page's HTML. Google renders JavaScript, but it doesn't hover or click, so a panel that renders only on hover or click never appears for it.
  • Which menus are affected? In my test, the closed state of Radix NavigationMenu, Radix DropdownMenu, Headless UI Menu, Popover and Disclosure, and any {open && <ul>} pattern, all rendered 0 of 2 links.
  • The fix: keep the links in the HTML while the menu is closed. Use forceMount (Radix), unmount={false} (Headless UI), a CSS-hidden panel, or a hidden list of plain links.

What I found on my own site

knowledgemarkg.com runs on Next.js. In November I replaced the header with a mega menu: Services, Free Tools and Blog, each with a two-column dropdown. The label is a link to the section page, and a chevron button opens the panel. It works well for people.

While checking why a few service pages were slow to get indexed, I fetched the live home page with curl and counted the links to /services/. There were 4, all from the footer and the page body. The header's dropdown links to the nine service pages weren't in the HTML at all, because the component rendered the panel like this:

// The pattern most hand-rolled menus use
export function MegaMenu({ menu }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  return (
    <div onMouseEnter={() => setOpen(true)} onMouseLeave={() => setOpen(false)}>
      <Link href={menu.href}>{menu.label}</Link>
      <button aria-expanded={open} onClick={() => setOpen(!open)}>▾</button>
      {open ? <Panel menu={menu} /> : null}   {/* closed = nothing in the HTML */}
    </div>
  );
}

When the panel is closed, React renders null. That's the state the server renders, so that's the HTML Google gets.

Check your own menu in 30 seconds

Don't use the browser's Elements panel for this. By the time you look, you've probably hovered the menu, and DevTools shows the live DOM, not what the server sent. Use View Source (Ctrl+U), or curl:

# What the server actually sends (no JavaScript run, no clicks)
curl -s -A "Mozilla/5.0" https://example.com/ | grep -o 'href="/services/[^"]*"' | sort -u

# Count them
curl -s -A "Mozilla/5.0" https://example.com/ | grep -o 'href="/services/[^"]*"' | sort -u | wc -l

Swap /services/ for any path your menu links to. If a page in your dropdown doesn't show up, it isn't in the server HTML. Two more checks are useful:

  • Search Console → URL Inspection → View crawled page → HTML. That's the HTML after Google rendered it. If the links aren't there either, Google didn't see them.
  • Compare with the sitemap. A page that is in your sitemap but linked from nowhere visible to a crawler often ends up in "Discovered - currently not indexed". I wrote about the difference in Crawled vs Discovered - currently not indexed.

Why Google doesn't see links in a closed menu

Two parts of Google's documentation explain it:

  • Google's crawlable-links guide says it can generally crawl a link only if it's an <a> element with an href. Links inserted with JavaScript count too, as long as they end up as that same markup.
  • Its lazy-loading guide says plainly that Google Search does not interact with your page: no scrolling, no clicking. Hover is not mentioned at all.

So rendering isn't the issue. Google does run your JavaScript. The issue is that nothing ever sets open to true during rendering. Content that waits for a user action never exists for the crawler.

This is different from content that's on the page but hidden with CSS, like a collapsed accordion. Those links are in the HTML. The question for an accordion is how much weight hidden text gets. For a conditionally rendered menu, there's nothing there to weigh.

I tested the popular React menu components

To see whether this is just my hand-rolled menu, I rendered each component on the server with React's renderToString, closed, with the same two <a href="/services/..."> links inside, and counted the links in the output. Versions: React 19.3.1, @radix-ui/react-navigation-menu 1.4.1, @radix-ui/react-dropdown-menu 2.2.1, @headlessui/react 2.2.10.

Component (closed) Links in server HTML
Radix NavigationMenu 0 of 2
Radix NavigationMenu, Content forceMount 2 of 2
Radix DropdownMenu 0 of 2
Headless UI Menu 0 of 2
Headless UI Popover 0 of 2
Headless UI Popover, unmount={false} 2 of 2
Headless UI Disclosure 0 of 2
Hand-rolled {open && <ul>} 0 of 2
Native <details><summary> 2 of 2
Panel always rendered, hidden with CSS 2 of 2

The test was just this, once per component:

const { renderToString } = require("react-dom/server");
// ...build each menu closed, with two <a href="/services/..."> inside...
const html = renderToString(menu);
console.log((html.match(/href="\/services/g) || []).length, "/ 2");

shadcn/ui's Navigation Menu and Dropdown Menu are built on these Radix components, so I'd expect the same result, but I tested the Radix packages, not the shadcn copies. Server-rendering the closed state like this is a fair stand-in for the first HTML a crawler gets, but it isn't Googlebot itself. Use the URL Inspection check above to confirm what Google saw on your site.

None of this is a bug in those libraries. Unmounting closed popups is a sensible default for dropdowns full of actions like "Delete" or "Sign out". It just isn't what you want for site navigation.

Four ways to fix it

1. Keep the panel mounted (library option)

If you use a library, it probably already has a switch:

// Radix NavigationMenu (and shadcn/ui's NavigationMenu, which wraps it)
<NavigationMenu.Content forceMount>
  {links}
</NavigationMenu.Content>

// Headless UI v2
<PopoverPanel unmount={false}>
  {links}
</PopoverPanel>

With Headless UI, unmount={false} renders the panel with hidden and display:none, and the links are in the HTML. This is the smallest change if your panel is light.

Radix is different, and my first version of this post missed it (a reader caught it): forceMount keeps the closed panel in the HTML but does not hide it. In NavigationMenu 1.4.1 the closed Content renders as a plain div with data-state="closed" and pointer-events:none, with no hidden attribute and no display:none, so the server HTML paints every panel open. Add your own rule, scoped to your menu panels, such as [data-state="closed"] { display: none }.

2. Always render the panel, hide it with CSS

Render the panel every time and toggle visibility with a class (hidden / group-hover:block, or visibility plus opacity for a transition). It's simple, but every icon, description and decoration in the panel is now in every page's DOM, multiplied by the number of dropdowns. On a mega menu that adds up.

3. Render a light, hidden list of the same links (what I did)

My panels have an icon tile and a description per link, plus gradient decorations. Rendering all three menus fully on every page would have added a few hundred elements, and keeping the home page's DOM small was something I'd already worked on. So the closed state renders one plain link per destination inside a hidden element, and the full panel still only renders when opened:

{open ? (
  <Panel menu={menu} />
) : (
  // Closed: the same destinations as plain links, so they are in the server HTML.
  // One element per link - the heavy panel (icons, descriptions) still renders only when opened.
  <div id={`nav-panel-${menu.key}`} hidden>
    {menu.items.map((item) => (
      <Link key={item.href} href={item.href} prefetch={false}>
        {item.label}
      </Link>
    ))}
  </div>
)}

The id matches the button's aria-controls, so the button always points at a real element. prefetch={false} stops Next.js from trying to prefetch these links, which matters less for hidden links, but there's no reason to load them.

The result: the live home page went from 4 to 11 unique links to /services/, and its body grew from 1,122 to 1,159 elements (counted from the served HTML, scripts excluded). That's 37 elements for every link in three menus.

These hidden links go to exactly the same pages a visitor gets by opening the menu. That's the line to stay on: don't add destinations or keyword-stuffed anchor text that people can't reach.

4. Use <details>, or make the parent link do the work

A native <details><summary> keeps its content in the HTML when closed and needs no JavaScript. It works well for mobile menus. Whatever you choose, make the top-level label a real link to a hub page (/services, /tools) that links to every child page in plain HTML. Then even a fully JavaScript-only menu leaves a crawl path.

What the fix did, and didn't do

On the day I deployed, I checked the six service pages that had been slow to index, using Search Console's URL Inspection. Five were already indexed, before Google could have seen the fix. Google had found them through the footer and the sitemap. One, website redesign, is "Crawled - currently not indexed", which means Google fetched it and decided not to index it. A missing link can't explain that, so the next step for that page is better content, not more links.

So I'm not claiming this fix got pages indexed. What it does is make the header links real for every crawler. On a site with nine service pages, that's nine links from every page instead of zero. That's the main way a small site tells Google which pages matter. If the menu is the only place a page is linked, it's the difference between being found and not.

Quick checklist

  1. curl your home page (or Ctrl+U) and grep for a path that only your dropdown links to.
  2. Missing? Find where the panel renders null or {open && ...} when it's closed.
  3. Fix it with forceMount / unmount={false}, a CSS-hidden panel, or a light hidden list of the same links.
  4. Check the DOM size before and after. Lighthouse flags very large DOMs.
  5. Confirm in Search Console: URL Inspection → View crawled page → HTML.
  6. Make sure every top-level menu label links to a hub page that lists its children.

Related reading from my site's own clean-up: PageSpeed 100 on mobile with Next.js: what worked and reducing unused JavaScript in Next.js. If you'd rather have someone check your site's crawlability, the free website audit looks at links, speed and indexing in one pass.

FAQ

Does Google crawl links in a mega menu or dropdown menu?

Yes, if they are real <a href> links in the page's HTML. If the menu only renders its panel after a hover or click, the links don't exist for Google, because Google renders JavaScript but doesn't interact with the page. Check with View Source or curl, not the DevTools Elements panel.

Are mega menus bad for SEO?

Not by themselves. The common problem is technical: many React and JavaScript menus don't render their links until they are opened, so crawlers get no links at all. A menu whose links are in the HTML is a normal, crawlable navigation.

Does Radix or shadcn/ui NavigationMenu render links for SEO?

In my test (Radix NavigationMenu 1.4.1, server-rendered with React 19), the closed menu rendered 0 of 2 links. Adding forceMount to NavigationMenu.Content rendered both, but it does not hide the closed panel, so add CSS such as [data-state="closed"] { display: none }. shadcn/ui's Navigation Menu wraps the same Radix component.

Does Headless UI render menu items when closed?

Not by default. In my test, Headless UI 2.2.10 Menu, Popover and Disclosure all rendered 0 of 2 links when closed. PopoverPanel with unmount={false} rendered both, hidden with display:none.

Does Google index links hidden with CSS or the hidden attribute?

Links hidden with CSS or the hidden attribute are still in the HTML, so Google can read them; that's the difference from a menu that isn't rendered at all. Keep hidden links to the same destinations users reach by opening the menu.

How do I check if Googlebot can see my menu links?

Fetch the page without a browser (curl, or Ctrl+U for View Source) and search for a URL only your dropdown links to. Then confirm in Google Search Console with URL Inspection, View crawled page, HTML, which shows the HTML after Google rendered it.

Will adding hidden menu links make my page slower?

Slightly, so keep them light. On my home page, a plain hidden link per destination for three menus took the body from 1,122 to 1,159 elements. Rendering the full panels with icons and descriptions would have cost much more.

Originally published on knowledgemarkg.com.

title: I built a lightweight Spotify client, then talked myself out of it
description:
Not affiliated with or endorsed by Spotify. Dorion is a separate open-source project by SpikeHD; it's what inspired me.

I just archived a project I was excited about. This is the story of how it
started, the moment I realized my own numbers were lying to me, and why stopping
felt like the right call.

It started with Dorion

I came across Dorion, an alternative
Discord client built with Rust and Tauri. The idea hooked me immediately: instead
of shipping a whole browser inside the app, it uses the one your operating
system already has. The result is a client that's small and made for lower-spec
machines, with themes and plugins on top
(README, LinuxLinks).

I first saw it in an Instagram Reel that compared the performance of the two
apps side by side, with the main features intact. That combination, a big
difference without giving anything up, is what stuck with me.

And I thought: I want this for Spotify. The official app also carries a
browser around. Why couldn't it be tiny too?

First try: do it properly

I started the ambitious way. My own interface, my own login flow, talking to
Spotify's APIs directly. It worked, in the sense that it was a real client. But
every hour I spent on it was an hour spent rebuilding things Spotify had already
built, for a project whose entire promise was being small.

So I did what Dorion does: I threw most of it away. The new version was just a
native window pointed at open.spotify.com. No login code, no API keys, nothing
to maintain. The whole app came down to a 3 MB file.

That was a good day. I felt hopeful. It looked like a promising idea, so I
started measuring it against the real app.

The first benchmark made me very happy

To prove it was lightweight, I built a small benchmark to compare my app against
the official one on my own machine. The first results came in and they were
spectacular. My app was using almost nothing.

Then I looked closer. My app was using 24 MB. For something that was
displaying a full Spotify web player.

That looked strange to me, so I stopped to work out the best way to isolate the
app's execution, so I'd be measuring the app and nothing else. That's how I got
to the real answer: the benchmark was only measuring one process out of nine. The
rest of the app, the part that actually does the work, was invisible to it.

When your measuring tool is the problem

That was the first of several bugs in my own benchmark, and each one was a little
humbling:

  • It wasn't counting most of the app.
  • It was so aggressive at cleaning up between runs that it would have shut down every web view on my machine, including ones belonging to other apps.
  • On my computer, a decimal comma turned 968,2 into 9682, so some numbers came out ten times too big.

The uncomfortable part is that the first, wrong numbers looked great. If I had
stopped there, I'd have published a triumphant article about a result that
wasn't real.

The honest numbers

After fixing everything, I ran it again. This time I trusted it.

My app Official Spotify
Size on disk 3 MB 436 MB
Time to open 229 ms 1031 ms
Memory, idle ~968 MB ~954 MB
CPU, idle ~5% ~0.2%

Two clear wins, one tie, and one loss.

My app was a fraction of the size and opened several times faster. That part was
real, and it felt good. But the memory was the same, and sitting idle it used
about ten times more CPU. For an app you leave open all day, that's the number
that matters.

The reason was simple once I saw it. The weight of Spotify isn't in the frame
around it. It's in the web player itself. My app removed the installer, not the
work.

It also made sense once I looked at how the official app is built. According to
Spotify's own engineering team, the desktop client is a native application that
uses the Chromium Embedded Framework (CEF) to display a web-based interface, and
since 2021 it shares a single TypeScript UI with the web player
(Spotify Engineering, InfoQ).
So I was never replacing a heavy native app with a light one. Both run the same
kind of web interface on a Chromium engine. I swapped the engine, not the work
the interface does.

Deciding to stop

I had ideas to improve it. I could make it back off when minimized, trim
processes, tweak flags. But I could see where that road went: a lot of effort, a
risky amount of testing so the music wouldn't break, and an uncertain payoff. And
it all depended on a website I don't control, which could change something on a
Tuesday and break my media keys.

So I stopped. In the end, the results were too close to the official app. I tried
to look at it as a user would: there was no good reason to pick my version over
the real one as an alternative. The effort wouldn't have paid off for anyone.

I archived the project and wrote down what I'd learned, so the work wouldn't
just vanish.

What I'd tell myself at the start

  1. Decide what "success" means before you build. If I'd written "idle CPU must be close to the official app" on day one, I'd have known within an hour that I was going to lose.
  2. Don't trust a result because you like it. The wrong numbers were the good-looking ones. Be most suspicious when it all seems to go your way.
  3. Know where the cost really lives. I assumed the browser shell was the heavy part. It wasn't.
  4. Stopping isn't failing. I finished with a working app, honest data, a documented decision, and a much better sense of how to evaluate the next idea.

There are things I never measured, like memory while music is actually playing,
and I'd be the first to say those numbers could change the picture. But the gap
in idle CPU was large and consistent, and I was comfortable stopping on that.

The code, raw data and notes are here:
https://github.com/lucasheartcliff/litespot.

title: How to validate a Mexican CURP: regex, birth date and check digit in Python, JavaScript and Go
description:
A CURP (Clave Única de Registro de Población) is the 18-character ID that RENAPO, Mexico's population registry, assigns to every citizen and resident. If your signup form, payroll import or onboarding flow takes one, you can check three things without calling anyone:

  1. The shape. Each position only admits certain characters.
  2. The birth date inside it is a real calendar date.
  3. The check digit in the last position matches the other 17 characters.

What you cannot check offline is whether the CURP exists or who it belongs to. More on that at the end.

If you only came for the regex, here it is:

^[A-Z][AEIOUX][A-Z]{2}[0-9]{6}[HMX](?:AS|BC|BS|CC|CH|CL|CM|CS|DF|DG|GR|GT|HG|JC|MC|MN|MS|NE|NL|NT|OC|PL|QR|QT|SL|SP|SR|TC|TL|TS|VZ|YN|ZS)[B-DF-HJ-NP-TV-Z]{3}[0-9A-J][0-9]$

It is stricter than most of the ones that get copy-pasted around, and looser in one place where they are wrong. The rest of the article explains each piece, adds the date and the check digit, and ends with tested code in Python, JavaScript and Go.

What is inside a CURP

The layout comes from the Instructivo Normativo para la asignación de la CURP, published in Mexico's official gazette (DOF) in 2018. Its own example is a woman named Concepción Salgado Briseño, born on 26 June 1956 in the Distrito Federal:

SABC 560626 M DF LRN 0 1
Position What it holds In the example
1 First letter of the first surname S (Salgado)
2 First internal vowel of the first surname A
3 First letter of the second surname B (Briseño)
4 First letter of the given name C (Concepción)
5-10 Birth date as YYMMDD 560626
11 Sex M (mujer)
12-13 State of birth DF
14-16 First internal consonant of the first surname, the second surname and the given name L, R, N
17 Differentiator for people who share the first 16 characters. It also tells you the century 0
18 Check digit 1

One warning about that example. The Instructivo prints the key as SABC560626MDFLRN09, and with the check digit algorithm described below the last digit comes out as 1, not 9. Every real CURP we have tested follows the algorithm, so treat the printed key as a picture of the layout and do not use it as a test case.

The regex, piece by piece

Normalize first. Trim the input and upper-case it before matching, and store the normalized value.

Positions 1-4: [A-Z][AEIOUX][A-Z]{2}. Position 2 is a vowel or an X. The X is the wildcard of the whole system. RENAPO's rules for assigning the CURP (2021) list the cases, with examples:

  • An Ñ becomes X: Alberto Ñando Rodríguez starts with XARA.
  • A first surname with no internal vowel gets X in position 2.
  • A person with a single surname gets X in position 3: Margarita Zaro starts with ZAXM.
  • A person registered with no surnames gets XXX: XXXJ for a Juan.
  • When the four letters spell a word from RENAPO's catalog of offensive words, the second letter is replaced: Ofelia Pedrero Domínguez gets PXDO.

So a CURP never contains an Ñ, and an X can show up almost anywhere.

Positions 5-10: [0-9]{6}. Only the format at this stage. Write [0-9], not \d. In Python, \d on a str matches any Unicode digit, so full-width digits like ０４ pass the regex, and int("０４") happily returns 4. In JavaScript and Go \d is ASCII-only, but an explicit class behaves the same everywhere.

Position 11: [HMX]. H is hombre (male) and M is mujer (female). The table in the Instructivo stops there, and so do most regexes. But RENAPO has issued CURPs with an X in this position for non-binary people, following court rulings. An INE report from January 2023 records it: the X goes «en lugar de la “H” o “M”» (in place of the H or M). A validator with [HM] rejects those people. That includes python-stdnum 2.2.

Positions 12-13: the state. Thirty-two states plus NE (nacido en el extranjero) for people born abroad:

AS Aguascalientes, BC Baja California, BS Baja California Sur, CC Campeche, CH Chihuahua, CL Coahuila, CM Colima, CS Chiapas, DF Ciudad de México, DG Durango, GR Guerrero, GT Guanajuato, HG Hidalgo, JC Jalisco, MC Estado de México, MN Michoacán, MS Morelos, NL Nuevo León, NT Nayarit, OC Oaxaca, PL Puebla, QR Quintana Roo, QT Querétaro, SL Sinaloa, SP San Luis Potosí, SR Sonora, TC Tabasco, TL Tlaxcala, TS Tamaulipas, VZ Veracruz, YN Yucatán, ZS Zacatecas.

The official catalog is Annex 3 of RENAPO's rules, and the published PDF lists the annex without including it. The codes above are the ones python-stdnum ships.

Positions 14-16: [B-DF-HJ-NP-TV-Z]{3}. Three consonants. X is in the class, and it is used here too: when a name has no internal consonant, when that consonant is an Ñ, and in position 15 when there is only one surname.

Position 17: [0-9A-J]. RENAPO assigns it to tell apart two people whose first 16 characters are identical. Both official documents give the same range: 0-9 for people born up to 31 December 1999 and A-J for people born from 1 January 2000. Many regexes use [0-9A-Z] here.

Position 18: [0-9]. The check digit.

Anchors. In Python use fullmatch. With re.match and $, a trailing newline still matches: re.match(r"^[0-9]{2}$", "04\n") succeeds.

About the offensive-word rule: python-stdnum carries a list of 81 such words and rejects any CURP that starts with one. We do not, because the official catalog (Annex 1 of the same rules) is not in the published PDF, and rejecting a genuine key is worse than letting a malformed one reach the next check.

The birth date

Six digits with a two-digit year. Position 17 resolves the century: a digit means 19xx and a letter means 20xx. Then build the date and make sure it exists.

Leap years make good test cases:

  • WUKQ000229HNEQWKA3 has a letter in position 17, so it is 29 February 2000. Valid.
  • WUKQ000229HNEQWK03 has a digit, so it is 29 February 1900. That year was not a leap year. Invalid.

Two things to watch:

  • JavaScript's Date and Go's time.Date do not reject impossible dates. They roll them over, so 30 February quietly becomes 1 or 2 March. Build the date and read the month and day back. Python's date() raises ValueError, which is what you want.
  • A birth date in the future is not a valid CURP either. SABC560626MDFLRNA1 passes the regex and the check digit, but the letter in position 17 makes it 2056.

The check digit

Neither the Instructivo nor RENAPO's rules print the algorithm. They only say that position 18 is assigned by an algorithm. The one below is what open source validators such as python-stdnum implement, and it matches the real CURPs we have tried. Run it on your own CURP.

  1. Give each character a value: its index in 0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNÑOPQRSTUVWXYZ. That is 37 symbols, with the Ñ between N and O.
  2. Multiply the first 17 values by the weights 18, 17, 16 ... 2, from left to right.
  3. Add everything up.
  4. The digit is (10 - sum % 10) % 10.

For SABC560626MDFLRN0:

Char S A B C 5 6 0 6 2 6 M D F L R N 0
Value 29 10 11 12 5 6 0 6 2 6 22 13 15 21 28 23 0
Weight 18 17 16 15 14 13 12 11 10 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2
Product 522 170 176 180 70 78 0 66 20 54 176 91 90 105 112 69 0

The sum is 1979. 1979 % 10 is 9, and (10 - 9) % 10 is 1.

Three things about this algorithm:

  • The Ñ is in the table even though it never appears in a CURP. Leave it out and every letter from O to Z is worth one less. For the key above, a 36-symbol table gives 3 instead of 1. The bug hides well, because any CURP without letters from O to Z still validates.
  • In Go, Ñ takes two bytes. If you look characters up in that string by byte offset, everything from O onwards is off by one. The Go version below computes the value with arithmetic instead.
  • It does not catch every typo. The ninth character (the first digit of the day) has weight 10, so it adds a multiple of 10 and never changes the result. Positions 4 and 14 have weights 15 and 5, so about half of the possible substitutions there go unnoticed. The date check covers part of that gap. The check digit will not.

The code

Each version returns which of the three checks failed, so you can show a useful message.

Python 

"""Structural validation of a Mexican CURP: format, real birth date, check digit.

This does not tell you whether the CURP exists in RENAPO's registry.
"""
import re
from datetime import date

STATES = (
    "AS|BC|BS|CC|CH|CL|CM|CS|DF|DG|GR|GT|HG|JC|MC|MN|MS|NE|NL|NT|OC|"
    "PL|QR|QT|SL|SP|SR|TC|TL|TS|VZ|YN|ZS"
)

CURP_RE = re.compile(
    r"[A-Z][AEIOUX][A-Z]{2}"          # 1-4   letters taken from the names
    r"([0-9]{2})([0-9]{2})([0-9]{2})"  # 5-10  birth date, YYMMDD
    r"[HMX]"                           # 11    sex
    rf"(?:{STATES})"                   # 12-13 state of birth, NE = born abroad
    r"[B-DF-HJ-NP-TV-Z]{3}"            # 14-16 internal consonants
    r"([0-9A-J])"                      # 17    homonym / century differentiator
    r"([0-9])"                         # 18    check digit
)

# 37 symbols: the Ñ sits between N and O even though it never appears in a CURP.
ALPHABET = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNÑOPQRSTUVWXYZ"


def check_digit(curp17: str) -> int:
    """Check digit for the first 17 characters of a CURP."""
    total = sum(ALPHABET.index(c) * (18 - i) for i, c in enumerate(curp17[:17]))
    return (10 - total % 10) % 10


def validate_curp(value, today=None):
    """Return (True, "ok") or (False, reason).

    reason is one of "format", "date", "check_digit".
    """
    if not isinstance(value, str):
        return False, "format"
    curp = value.strip().upper()

    m = CURP_RE.fullmatch(curp)
    if not m:
        return False, "format"
    yy, mm, dd, differentiator, digit = m.groups()

    # Position 17 carries the century: 0-9 = born up to 1999, A-J = 2000 onwards.
    century = 1900 if differentiator.isdigit() else 2000
    try:
        born = date(century + int(yy), int(mm), int(dd))
    except ValueError:
        return False, "date"
    if born > (today or date.today()):
        return False, "date"

    if check_digit(curp) != int(digit):
        return False, "check_digit"
    return True, "ok"

JavaScript 

// Structural validation of a Mexican CURP: format, real birth date, check digit.
// This does not tell you whether the CURP exists in RENAPO's registry.

const STATES =
  "AS|BC|BS|CC|CH|CL|CM|CS|DF|DG|GR|GT|HG|JC|MC|MN|MS|NE|NL|NT|OC|" +
  "PL|QR|QT|SL|SP|SR|TC|TL|TS|VZ|YN|ZS";

const CURP_RE = new RegExp(
  "^[A-Z][AEIOUX][A-Z]{2}" +           // 1-4   letters taken from the names
    "([0-9]{2})([0-9]{2})([0-9]{2})" + // 5-10  birth date, YYMMDD
    "[HMX]" +                          // 11    sex
    `(?:${STATES})` +                  // 12-13 state of birth, NE = born abroad
    "[B-DF-HJ-NP-TV-Z]{3}" +           // 14-16 internal consonants
    "([0-9A-J])" +                     // 17    homonym / century differentiator
    "([0-9])$"                         // 18    check digit
);

// 37 symbols: the Ñ sits between N and O even though it never appears in a CURP.
const ALPHABET = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNÑOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

/** Check digit for the first 17 characters of a CURP. */
export function checkDigit(curp17) {
  let total = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 17; i++) {
    total += ALPHABET.indexOf(curp17[i]) * (18 - i);
  }
  return (10 - (total % 10)) % 10;
}

/** Returns { ok: true } or { ok: false, reason: "format" | "date" | "check_digit" }. */
export function validateCurp(value, today = new Date()) {
  if (typeof value !== "string") return { ok: false, reason: "format" };
  const curp = value.trim().toUpperCase();

  const m = CURP_RE.exec(curp);
  if (!m) return { ok: false, reason: "format" };
  const [, yy, mm, dd, differentiator, digit] = m;

  // Position 17 carries the century: 0-9 = born up to 1999, A-J = 2000 onwards.
  const century = differentiator <= "9" ? 1900 : 2000;
  const year = century + Number(yy);
  const month = Number(mm);
  const day = Number(dd);
  // Date rolls invalid dates over (Feb 30 becomes Mar 2), so read it back.
  const born = new Date(Date.UTC(year, month - 1, day));
  if (born.getUTCMonth() !== month - 1 || born.getUTCDate() !== day) {
    return { ok: false, reason: "date" };
  }
  if (born.getTime() > today.getTime()) return { ok: false, reason: "date" };

  if (checkDigit(curp) !== Number(digit)) {
    return { ok: false, reason: "check_digit" };
  }
  return { ok: true };
}

Go 

// Package curp validates the structure of a Mexican CURP: format, real birth
// date and check digit. It does not tell you whether the CURP exists in
// RENAPO's registry.
package curp

import (
    "errors"
    "regexp"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var (
    ErrFormat     = errors.New("curp: invalid format")
    ErrDate       = errors.New("curp: invalid birth date")
    ErrCheckDigit = errors.New("curp: check digit mismatch")
)

const states = "AS|BC|BS|CC|CH|CL|CM|CS|DF|DG|GR|GT|HG|JC|MC|MN|MS|NE|NL|NT|OC|" +
    "PL|QR|QT|SL|SP|SR|TC|TL|TS|VZ|YN|ZS"

var curpRe = regexp.MustCompile(
    `^[A-Z][AEIOUX][A-Z]{2}` + // 1-4   letters taken from the names
        `([0-9]{2})([0-9]{2})([0-9]{2})` + // 5-10  birth date, YYMMDD
        `[HMX]` + // 11    sex
        `(?:` + states + `)` + // 12-13 state of birth, NE = born abroad
        `[B-DF-HJ-NP-TV-Z]{3}` + // 14-16 internal consonants
        `([0-9A-J])` + // 17    homonym / century differentiator
        `([0-9])$`, // 18    check digit
)

// charValue is the position of c in "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNÑOPQRSTUVWXYZ".
// It is computed instead of looked up because Ñ takes two bytes in UTF-8, so
// strings.IndexByte on that literal would be off by one from O onwards.
func charValue(c byte) int {
    switch {
    case c >= '0' && c <= '9':
        return int(c - '0')
    case c >= 'A' && c <= 'N':
        return int(c-'A') + 10
    default: // O-Z, after the slot that belongs to Ñ
        return int(c-'A') + 11
    }
}

// CheckDigit returns the check digit for the first 17 characters of a CURP.
func CheckDigit(curp17 string) int {
    total := 0
    for i := 0; i < 17; i++ {
        total += charValue(curp17[i]) * (18 - i)
    }
    return (10 - total%10) % 10
}

// Validate returns nil when value is a structurally valid CURP, or one of
// ErrFormat, ErrDate, ErrCheckDigit.
func Validate(value string) error {
    return validateAt(value, time.Now())
}

func validateAt(value string, today time.Time) error {
    curp := strings.ToUpper(strings.TrimSpace(value))

    m := curpRe.FindStringSubmatch(curp)
    if m == nil {
        return ErrFormat
    }
    yy, _ := strconv.Atoi(m[1])
    mm, _ := strconv.Atoi(m[2])
    dd, _ := strconv.Atoi(m[3])
    differentiator, digit := m[4][0], int(m[5][0]-'0')

    // Position 17 carries the century: 0-9 = born up to 1999, A-J = 2000 onwards.
    century := 2000
    if differentiator <= '9' {
        century = 1900
    }
    // time.Date rolls invalid dates over (Feb 30 becomes Mar 2), so read it back.
    born := time.Date(century+yy, time.Month(mm), dd, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    if int(born.Month()) != mm || born.Day() != dd {
        return ErrDate
    }
    if born.After(today) {
        return ErrDate
    }

    if CheckDigit(curp) != digit {
        return ErrCheckDigit
    }
    return nil
}

Test vectors

Use these to test your own port. The first key is the example in python-stdnum's documentation, the SABC ones derive from the example in the Instructivo, and the rest are synthetic.

Input Result Why
BOXW310820HNERXN09 ok Born abroad (NE)
SABC560626MDFLRN01 ok The Instructivo's example with the digit the algorithm gives
SABC560626MDFLRN09 check digit The same key as printed
WUKQ040229HNEQWKA1 ok 29 Feb 2004
WUKQ000229HNEQWKA3 ok 29 Feb 2000
WUKQ000229HNEQWK03 date 29 Feb 1900 does not exist
WUKQ990431HNEQWK00 date 31 April
SABC560626MDFLRNA1 date Letter in position 17 means 2056
SABC560626XDFLRN05 ok X as sex
PXDO850714MOCDMF00 ok X in position 2
ZAXM750301MSLRXR08 ok Single surname
XXXJ800101HNEXXN03 ok No surnames
WUKQ040229HNEQWKK1 format K is outside A-J
WUKQ040229ZNEQWKA1 format Sex is not H, M or X
WUKQ０４０２２９HNEQWKA1 format Full-width digits

How this was tested: 36 vectors run against the three implementations, 200,000 random inputs (valid keys, wrong digits, impossible dates, stray characters) gave the same verdict in all three, and the check digit matched python-stdnum on 200,000 random keys.

What a valid structure does not tell you

A key that passes all three checks is well formed. That is all. It can still be a CURP that was never assigned, one that belongs to somebody else, or one that RENAPO has since deactivated. Only the registry can answer that.

Offline validation is still worth having as the first step: it rejects typos and junk before you spend a lookup on them, and it lets you tell the user which part is wrong.

Rebuilding the first four letters from a person's name is possible too, but the rules are long: compound names, María and José, particles such as DE LA. They are all in RENAPO's rules, linked below.

Disclosure: this article is published by the team behind OrigoID, an identity verification API for Mexico. The registry lookup is the part we do for a living, and it is described here. Nothing above depends on it.

Sources

  • Instructivo Normativo para la asignación de la Clave Única de Registro de Población, Diario Oficial de la Federación, 18 June 2018. Layout of the 18 positions and the range for position 17.
  • Reglas para la ejecución de los procedimientos para la asignación de la CURP, RENAPO, 22 October 2021. Special cases for positions 1-4 and 14-16.
  • Informe sobre la viabilidad de incorporar en la Credencial para Votar el dato que reconozca a las personas no binarias, INE, January 2023. The X in the sex position.
  • python-stdnum, stdnum.mx.curp. Reference implementation of the check digit.

title: Amazon Buys Decart's AI Optimization Tech to Make Inference Cheaper on Its Own Chips
description:
Amazon is buying deeper into the most expensive layer of the AI stack. On November 23 it announced a signed agreement to acquire the proprietary technology behind the Decart Optimization Stack, and to hire Decart AI's three co-founders — Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf — along with a team of researchers and engineers.

The target is not a model. It's the machinery that makes models affordable to run: methods for getting more work out of hardware and software together, aimed at faster, cheaper training and inference on Amazon's own custom silicon.

Two caveats matter. This is a signed agreement, not a done deal — closing is still subject to conditions. And Amazon disclosed no price and no closing date. What's public is the deal and the intent, not a measured performance gain or a new product.

Why does inference cost deserve this much attention? Because serving cost decides what ships. Throughput depends on memory movement, kernels, compilation, scheduling, batching and hardware — not just parameter count. A model that benchmarks well can still be too expensive to serve, and a cheaper serving stack can make a mid-tier model the practical pick.

What to watch: which parts of the stack get integrated, how measured gains compare with baselines on identical workloads, whether developers see new interfaces, and when the deal closes. Until then, keep benchmarking your own serving stack instead of assuming the gains transfer.

Read the full story at rohantechofficial.com.

title: What is useFetch in React?
description:
useFetch is a Custom Hook in React. It is used to fetch data from an API and reuse the fetching logic in multiple components.
useFetch is not a built-in React Hook. We create it ourselves using built-in hooks like useState and useEffect.

Let's fetch user data from an API.

Create useFetch.js:

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

function useFetch(url) {
const [data, setData] = useState([]);
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
const [error, setError] = useState(null);

useEffect(() => {
    async function fetchData() {
        try {
            setLoading(true);

            const response = await fetch(url);

            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error("Something went wrong");
            }

            const result = await response.json();

            setData(result);
        } catch (err) {
            setError(err.message);
        } finally {
            setLoading(false);
        }
    }

    fetchData();

}, [url]);

return { data, loading, error };

}

export default useFetch;

Use the Custom Hook in App.jsx:

import React from "react";
import useFetch from "./useFetch";

function App() {

const { data, loading, error } =
    useFetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users");

if (loading) {
    return <h2>Loading...</h2>;
}

if (error) {
    return <h2>Error: {error}</h2>;
}

return (
    <div>
        <h2>User Details</h2>

        {data.map((user) => (
            <div key={user.id}>
                <h3>{user.name}</h3>
                <p>{user.email}</p>
            </div>
        ))}
    </div>
);

}

export default App;

title: From 67 to 95: What Was Really Slowing Down Our Next.js Homepage
description:
We sell website speed. So when our own redesigned homepage went live with a mobile PageSpeed score of 67, it stung.

The design itself wasn't the problem. Three details were: decoration we had added on purpose and never measured, a framework setting meant to make pages faster, and one line of CSS on the headline. Fixing them took the homepage to 95-99 on mobile, with the main content showing in 1.3-1.7 seconds instead of about 5.

This post walks through all three, with the numbers, the code, and what we'd check on any site.

Who this is for: engineers working on Next.js (or any framework that renders on the server and hydrates in the browser), and owners who want to know why a site that looks fine on their laptop scores badly on Google's phone test.

The short version

If you are… Here's the headline
Business / product The page was carrying far more than it showed: hundreds of tiny animations and three copies of the same styling. Removing the duplicates made it lighter and let the headline appear first. Nothing visible changed.
Engineering 762 individually animated SVG paths were serialized into both the HTML and the RSC payload; we merged them into 50. Then experimental.inlineCss put an 84 KB stylesheet in the <head> and Next copied it twice more into the RSC payload; turning it off took the compressed homepage from 123 KB to 74 KB. Finally, the hero headline faded in from opacity: 0, so it couldn't count as the LCP element.

How we measured

All the "live" numbers below come from Google's PageSpeed Insights on the production homepage, phone mode. A single run can swing by several points, so we ran three and compared them.

The metric that matters most here is Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): how long until the biggest piece of content in view, usually the headline or hero image, is shown. Google treats under 2.5 seconds as good.

Problem 1: 762 animations nobody counted

The redesign has a "garden" theme. Root systems grow down from the top of some sections and into the footer, drawn by code so they look organic but render the same every time.

Each root was its own animated SVG <path>. The homepage had 502 of them in one section, and the footer added 231 more, on every page. Each one also had to be serialized twice: once into the HTML and once into the data React uses to take over the page in the browser (the RSC payload).

PageSpeed's verdict on launch day:

  • 762 non-composited animated elements
  • 4.4 seconds of main-thread work on a throttled phone
  • Homepage HTML: 800 KB
  • Mobile performance: 67

The fix

The roots didn't need to be individual elements to look individual. We now draw one combined path per depth and stroke width, plus one for the tips, and reveal the whole network with a single clip-path transition from the top down. The geometry is identical, so the footer roots still meet the seedlings above them.

Before After
SVG paths 917 234
Animated elements 762 50
Homepage HTML 800 KB 590 KB

The lesson: decorative motion has a cost per element, not per effect. Ten thousand pixels of animation in one element is cheap. The same picture split into hundreds of animated pieces is not, and on a server-rendered page you pay for it twice.

It helped, but it wasn't the whole story. A month later the score was in the high 70s and the main content still took 4.8-5.0 seconds to appear on Google's phone test, and our own free website check put "slower than it should be on phones" at the top of our list. Being flagged by your own tool is a good motivator.

Problem 2: the stylesheet, three times

Next.js has an experimental setting, inlineCss, that puts your stylesheet directly in each page instead of in a separate file. The idea is sound: the browser can paint without waiting on a second, render-blocking request. We had turned it on for exactly that reason.

// next.config.ts (before)
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    // Ship the stylesheet inside the HTML, so first paint doesn't wait
    // on a separate render-blocking request.
    inlineCss: true,
  },
};

What we hadn't checked was what it did to the page's size. Looking at the raw HTML, the 84 KB Tailwind stylesheet appeared in the <head> as expected, and then twice more inside the RSC payload that Next.js streams with the page. Every page carried the same CSS three times, about 40% of the homepage. On a phone, all of it downloads before the headline can appear.

The fix

We turned the setting off. The CSS goes back to being one separate file, which the browser downloads once and reuses on every other page.

// next.config.ts (after)
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  // No experimental.inlineCss: it put the 84 KB stylesheet in every page and
  // Next also copied it twice into the RSC payload. A separate, cached
  // stylesheet is lighter.
};

The compressed homepage went from 123 KB to 74 KB, and every other page got the same saving.

The lesson: "inline the critical CSS" is good advice when the CSS is small and appears once. Check what your framework actually sends. View the page source, search for a distinctive class name, and count how many times it shows up.

Problem 3: the headline that wasn't there yet

The last issue was the smallest change and the most interesting cause.

The hero headline had an entrance animation: it rose into place while fading in from fully transparent.

/* before */
@keyframes hero-rise {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(26px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

It looked nice. But an element at opacity: 0 can't count as the page's largest content. When the browser looked for the LCP element, the headline was invisible, so it picked the next biggest thing: our small logo. PageSpeed then charged all the page's early JavaScript work to that logo, and reported a long "render delay" for the page's main content.

The fix

The headline still moves; it just never disappears. It settles into place from a few pixels lower, fully visible from the first frame.

/* after: the LCP element is never invisible */
@keyframes hero-settle {
  from { transform: translateY(14px); }
  to   { transform: translateY(0); }
}

Visitors who ask their device for reduced motion get no animation at all, as before.

The lesson: never fade in your LCP element. Animate the decoration around it, or animate position only.

The result

PageSpeed Insights on the live homepage, phone mode, three runs:

Launch day A month later Now
Mobile performance 67 high 70s 95, 95, 99
Main content shown (LCP) n/a 4.8-5.0 s 1.7, 1.7, 1.3 s
Accessibility, Best Practices, SEO 100

The page looks exactly as it did on launch day. It just stopped carrying things nobody could see.

A checklist for your own site

  1. Run PageSpeed Insights three times on mobile and look at the middle result, not the best one.
  2. Find your LCP element (PageSpeed names it). If it isn't your headline or hero image, ask why.
  3. Never fade in that element. Animate position, or animate something else.
  4. View the page source and search for one of your CSS class names. If it appears more than once, you're shipping duplicates.
  5. Count animated elements, not animations. Hundreds of small animated SVG pieces cost far more than one larger one.
  6. Re-measure on the live site after every fix. Local Lighthouse runs a different version and a different network, so treat it as direction, not the final word.

If you'd rather not do this by hand, our free website check runs Google's test three times, names the element holding your page back, and tells you what to fix first. It's the same check that flagged ours.

Originally published on cusicdigital.com.

title: What is a Custom Hook in React?
description:
A Custom Hook is a JavaScript function that allows us to reuse stateful logic (React Hooks logic) in multiple components.

Create a counter Custom Hook.

import { useState } from "react";

function useCounter() {
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

const increment = () => {
    setCount(count + 1);
};

const decrement = () => {
    setCount(count - 1);
};

return { count, increment, decrement };

}

export default useCounter;

Use the Custom Hook in App.jsx:

import React from "react";
import useCounter from "./useCounter";

function App() {

const { count, increment, decrement } = useCounter();

return (
    <div>
        <h2>Counter: {count}</h2>

        <button onClick={increment}>Increment</button>

        <button onClick={decrement}>Decrement</button>
    </div>
);

}

export default App;

Examples:

  • useCounter()
  • useFetch()
  • useLocalStorage()
  • useWindowSize()

title: I Decomposed a 3,000-Line God Screen Into 11 Modular Composables — Here's How
description:
In modern Android development with Jetpack Compose, UI code is declarative, concise, and elegant.

Until it isn't.

If you don't enforce strict architectural boundaries, Jetpack Compose screens have a notorious tendency to metastasize into God Objects.

Nowhere is this temptation stronger than the Settings Screen.

Whenever a new feature is built, it needs a toggle, a dialog, or a configuration slider:

  • Added biometric lock? Add a toggle to Settings.
  • Added SMS transaction parsing? Add bank selection chips to Settings.
  • Added CSV export and Google Drive backup? Add file pickers to Settings.
  • Added secret vault geofencing? Add a map radius slider to Settings.

Before we knew it, FinLedger's SettingsScreen.kt had bloated into a staggering 3,140-line monolithic file.

During Hardening Sprint H8, we performed major surgery on this screen, decomposing it into 11 modular, single-responsibility units.

Here is why Compose god screens destroy app performance, and how we refactored the screen into a clean, reactive architecture.

The Architectural Costs of a 3,000-Line Composable

A 3,000-line composable file is not just an aesthetic eyesore; it introduces severe technical liabilities:

flowchart TD
    subgraph GodScreenNightmare["The Recomposition Cascade in a God Screen"]
        User["User Toggles Dark Theme Switch"] --> State["SettingsUiState Emits Update"]

        State --> MonoScreen["SettingsScreen (3,140 Lines of Compose):
        Observes monolithic SettingsUiState holding 40+ properties!"]

        MonoScreen --> RecompCascade["Unnecessary Recomposition Cascades:
        - Recomposes SMS Bank Checkboxes
        - Recomposes Biometric Auth State
        - Recomposes Backup Progress Indicators
        - Recomposes Geofence Map Sliders"]

        RecompCascade --> FrameJank["Severe Main-Thread Frame Drops:
        Switch toggle animation stutters!"]
    end

1. Recomposition Cascades and UI Jank

When a single screen composable observes a massive SettingsUiState data class containing 40 different properties, any state change—such as toggling dark mode or updating a reminder time—forces Compose's runtime to evaluate dozens of unrelated child composables. This causes dropped frames and micro-stutter during animations.

2. Constructor Bloat in ViewModels

To support all 40 settings, SettingsViewModel required 14 different repository and manager dependencies injected into its constructor: SecurityManager, BackupRestoreManager, SmsInboxScanner, VaultRepository, PreferencesRepository, and more. Testing such a ViewModel required writing hundreds of lines of mock boilerplate.

3. The Android Studio Preview Breakdown

An oversized Compose file completely breaks Android Studio's @Preview tooling. Rendering a preview for a small toggle button required the IDE to compile 3,000 lines of complex UI, resulting in frequent IDE crashes and ten-second preview refresh latencies.

The 11-Unit Modular Architecture

In Sprint H8, we broke the monolithic screen into 7 domain setting cards and 4 isolated dialog modules:

flowchart TD
    subgraph DecomposedArchitecture["The 11-Unit Modular Architecture"]
        direction TB
        SettingsScreen["SettingsScreen.kt (Scaffold & TopBar: < 120 Lines)"]

        SettingsScreen --> C1["1. SecuritySettingsCard.kt:
        PIN, Biometrics, Dynamic FLAG_SECURE"]
        SettingsScreen --> C2["2. DataManagementCard.kt:
        Backup Vaults, CSV Export, Restore Checkpoints"]
        SettingsScreen --> C3["3. SmsAutomationCard.kt:
        Sender Header Filters, Historical Inbox Scanner"]
        SettingsScreen --> C4["4. PreferencesCard.kt:
        Currency Symbol, Theme, Number Formatting"]
        SettingsScreen --> C5["5. VaultSettingsCard.kt:
        Auto-Lock Inactivity Timer, Geofence Radius"]
        SettingsScreen --> C6["6. NotificationSettingsCard.kt:
        Daily Review Reminders, Budget Alerts"]
        SettingsScreen --> C7["7. AboutCard.kt:
        App Version, Build Number, Open Source Licenses"]

        C1 -.-> D1["Dialog 1: PinSetupDialog.kt"]
        C2 -.-> D2["Dialog 2: BackupRestoreDialog.kt"]
        C5 -.-> D3["Dialog 3: GeofenceRadiusDialog.kt"]
        C2 -.-> D4["Dialog 4: ResetWipeDialog.kt"]
    end

Let's examine the rules that govern this new architecture:

Rule 1: Granular, Immutable State Sub-Models

Instead of a single god-state class, SettingsUiState was refactored into focused sub-interfaces:

  • SecurityUiState (only PIN, biometric, and screen lock properties)
  • BackupUiState (only export paths, last backup date, and progress)
  • SmsAutomationUiState (only permission statuses and scanned counts)

When the user toggles dark mode, only PreferencesCard recomposes. The biometric cards, SMS filters, and backup buttons are skipped completely by the Compose compiler (Skipped Recomposition).

Rule 2: Event Hoisting to Scoped Lambdas

Setting cards do not talk directly to ViewModels.

Each modular card accepts only plain Kotlin data classes and emits plain lambdas:

  • SecuritySettingsCard(state = securityState, onToggleBiometrics = { ... }, onOpenPinDialog = { ... }) This allows each card to have its own instantaneous @Preview in Android Studio with zero mocks or Hilt dependencies required.

Rule 3: Isolated Ephemeral Dialogs

Dialogs are notoriously heavy in Compose. If a dialog composable is defined inside the parent screen body, its internal state lingers in memory even when closed.

We extracted dialogs into dedicated standalone files (PinSetupDialog.kt, BackupRestoreDialog.kt). The dialog composables are only composed into the composition tree when their explicit boolean flags evaluate to true, and they are completely unmounted and garbage-collected the moment they are dismissed.

Real-World Performance Improvements

Measuring the screen before and after Sprint H8 on an entry-level physical Android test device showed dramatic gains:

Dimension Monolithic Settings (Pre-Audit) Modular Architecture (Post-H8)
File Line Count 3,140 lines (1 file) < 280 lines per file (11 files)
Compose Recomposition Time 18.4 ms (Dropped frames) < 1.8 ms (Zero frame drops)
Android Studio Preview Time 9.2 seconds / Crashes 0.6 seconds (Instant)
ViewModel Injected Dependencies 14 God-Dependencies Decoupled into 3 domain use cases

Key Takeaway

In Jetpack Compose, modularity is not just an organization preference; it is a performance necessity.

Decomposing a 3,000-line god composable into isolated domain cards and ephemeral dialogs restores 60 FPS fluidity, enables instant IDE previews, and ensures that adding new configuration options never drags down the responsiveness of your app.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

Explore FinLedger on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.devanshufinance.app

title: HTML email templates that work in Outlook and dark mode
description:
After more than 200 hours coding newsletters for one client, I’ve learned that email HTML has its own rules. Here’s what makes templates hold up across inboxes.

Why Outlook breaks layouts

Desktop Outlook on Windows renders HTML with Microsoft Word’s engine. Flexbox, grid, many CSS properties and background images don’t work the way they do in browsers.

  • Use tables for layout, with fixed widths for columns
  • Inline important styles; some clients strip style blocks
  • Use conditional comments for Outlook-only fixes
  • Keep the main width around 600–640px

Surviving dark mode

Some email apps invert colours automatically. A dark logo on a transparent background can disappear completely.

  • Add a subtle light outline or padding behind dark logos
  • Avoid pure black on pure white; slightly softer colours invert more gracefully
  • Use dark-mode media queries where supported for full control
  • Test in both modes before every send

Build once, reuse forever

A modular template with reusable blocks (header, article, product grid, CTA, footer) turns each new newsletter into an assembly job instead of a new build, and keeps every issue consistent.

title: Concert 🎸 v1.0.0 Release Notes
description:
September 20th 2026 — Andrei Merlescu publishes the first commit for concert 🎸, a FIFO waiting room written in Go built for the web. Open Source.

andreimerlescu / concert

Concert is a Reverse Proxy for Room

Concert

A FIFO waiting room reverse proxy. Put Concert in front of any HTTP origin, such as a PHP site, a WordPress install, or a legacy app that falls over under load. When traffic exceeds what the origin can handle, visitors wait in an orderly queue with a live position instead of getting 502s and timeouts. Admitted visitors load their page's assets through a separate tier that queued and denied visitors can't reach, and clients that misbehave are blocked for an escalating cooldown.

Concert is a single Go binary built on:

  • room, a FIFO waiting room middleware for Gin
  • sema, a resizable semaphore
  • the ess package of naddr, which tells the admin portal who owns every address it shows: country flag, ASN, network, and the IPv4, IPv6 and IPv8 forms

Why

A PHP-FPM pool has a fixed number of workers (pm.max_children). When every worker is…

View on GitHub

This article was not written by an AI. You're hearing directly from the horse's hands through the screen. 👋 hey 🤩

A Turning Point

I have spent decades managing nginx, httpd | apache2, caddy and haproxy. They're great technologies. In 2026 I reached a turning point where I wanted to build concert 🎸, a first in, first out waiting room that I could place in front of my websites running on small hosts.

What started as a single binary called concert, the project has become four now.

  1. concert remains and it's been enhanced further (keep reading)
  2. concert-bench is a benchmark utility to keep the system healthy
  3. econcert is an enterprise compliant concert
  4. wpconcert is a multi-site server with Concertfile support, safe for WordPress.

The concert application went from only serving a waiting room for small hosts to a full fledged enterprise ready drop in replacement to Caddy or nginx or apache.

All three binaries were built in collaboration with Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Neon by a computer engineer guiding the process.

Three Editions, One Code Base

The concert code base contains the source for each of the binaries. The binaries use a subset of the source that each require to operate correctly.

🥇 concert is the primary edition that serves a waiting room reverse proxy
🥈 wpconcert is a WordPress specific edition that serves a waiting room built for WordPress and *cgi applications in general.
🥉 econcert is the full edition that serves an enterprise waiting room reverse proxy

Both the 🥇 base and 🥈 editions are free and open source software under the Apache 2.0 license.

The 🥉 Enterprise edition is a licensed service. The enterprise-only packages in the concert repository is copyright AGPL-3.0 where the concert and wpconcert binaries are copyleft Apache 2.0.

The 🥉 Enterprise edition will require a valid license key to operate. It's priced based on sum of all the rooms capacity. If they deploy a 50-node cluster of concert that serves 100K room capacity, that'll need a sales call. Book a time on my cal.com/andreimerlescu

More Than Just One Package

The concert binary and its compliments are built on top of other open source technology written by others and myself included. Specifically, it depends on room, which also depends on sema. Both of which I built specifically to serve this larger purpose, but divide the work across the respective domains.

Faster Waiting Room Core

Concert is built on room which is built on sema, two other Go packages that I published on my GitHub.

sema got upgraded to v1.3.0 which added PrioritySemaphore —introducing four O(1) priority admission tiers (PriorityLow through PriorityCritical, strict FIFO per tier) alongside a lock-free HighestWaitingPriority() contention signal, while keeping Semaphore 100% backward-compatible.

room upgraded to non-draining capacity shrinking, O(log N) treap-backed queue storage with parallel RLock polling, lazy-heap reaping, and post-spike compaction, and stateless Ed25519 signed rm1 passes and leases (with verify-only split mode, fail-closed Validate(), and EventTokenRejected hooks).

Replacing O(N) queue scans and write-locked status checks with O(log N) treaps, parallel RLock polling, O(1) bitmask priority dispatch, and zero-Redis local Ed25519 verification cuts lock contention and keeps queue latency flat even under massive traffic spikes.

The Concertfile

A Concertfile is Concert's declarative configuration file (with a strict .json alternative) loaded via -config to run multiple virtual hosts behind a single :443/:80 listener.

A global { ... } block configures shared settings like TLS, HTTP/3, and the Admin Portal, while each hostname block defines its own isolated waiting room, upstream (http:// or fcgi+unix://), os.Root static root, micro-cache, and security policies.

It acts as the single source of truth for your deployment, supporting zero-downtime hot reloads via SIGHUP or the Admin Portal with automatic rollback if any syntax or validation check fails.

# /etc/concert/Concertfile
{
    listen :443
    http_listen :80
    tls_email ops@example.com
    tls_cache /var/lib/concert/acme
    hsts_max_age 31536000
    http3 on
    data_dir /var/lib/concert/data
    portal_listen 127.0.0.1:8081
    portal_allow 127.0.0.1/32, ::1/128
    body_read_idle_timeout 30s
    max_upload_time 10m
}

shop.example.com, www.shop.example.com {
    preset wordpress
    root /var/www/shop
    upstream fcgi+unix:///run/php/php8.3-fpm.sock
    cap 12
    priority_cap 4
    micro_cache 15s
    secure_cookie on
    ban_paths /xmlrpc.php, /.env, /.git/*
}

api.example.com {
    upstream http://127.0.0.1:3000, http://127.0.0.1:3001
    root /var/www/api-static
    assets /static/*
    bypass /healthz
    cap 40
    priority_cap 10
    max_queue 1000
    secure_cookie on
}

Run it with wpconcert -config /etc/concert/Concertfile (or econcert), and hot-reload changes with zero downtime via kill -HUP $(pidof wpconcert) or the Admin Portal's Reload config button.

Built for WordPress & Multi-Site Hosts

Keeps your site up during traffic spikes—without Nginx or Apache:

wpconcert talks directly to PHP-FPM, serves images/CSS/JS straight from disk, and places extra visitors in an orderly waiting room sized to your PHP workers so your server doesn't crash with 502/504 errors.

Instant caching that doesn't breaks logins or WooCommerce carts:

A built-in short-lived micro-cache absorbs sudden bursts of anonymous visitors in under a millisecond while automatically bypassing logged-in users, /wp-admin, and active WooCommerce carts so checkouts stay fresh and private.

One-command setup with WordPress security turned on by default:

wpconcert init and wpconcert doctor inspect your PHP-FPM pool and generate a properly sized Concertfile, automatically blocking /wp-config.php, uploaded .php webshells in /wp-content/uploads/, and /xmlrpc.php scanners before PHP ever wakes up.

Some PHP scripts can take a long time to execute and that's normal. wpconcert is built for that utility of the language and the way services use PHP. The WP is a dad-joke level alternative acryonym called Why PHP not WordPress. Why? Indeed. 😂

Enterprise Mesh & Zero-Downtime Fast-Lane (econcert)

Active-active edges now get traffic-weighted leaf capacity shares, native leaf mTLS, and live drained re-benchmarking.

Fast-Lane adds online settlement reconciliation, 80%/95% journal alerts, and audited receipt archival.

Traffic-Weighted Multi-Edge Mesh & Live Re-Benchmarking:

Active-active edge nodes report live queue demand so leaf hosts split capacity proportionally to real traffic (with alert deduplication), and admins can recalibrate any leaf live via drained re-benchmarking—with a built-in 409 guard that refuses to drain the last healthy leaf.

Native Leaf mTLS & Single-Use Hop Replay Defense:

Leaves verify edge client certificates directly on their main TLS listener (-hop-require-mtls) while still accepting direct public browsers on the same port, and protects every Concert-Hop claim with single-use nonces backed by a 256-shard O(1) replay cache that fails closed under -enterprise-hardened.

Fast-Lane Payment Operations:

Reconciles pending or unresolved x402 settlements live from the Admin Portal or API without restarting, receives automatic warning/critical alerts at 80% and 95% receipt-journal capacity, and safely compacts old expired receipts with the audited econcert archive-receipts command.

Conclusion

concert 🎸 is a big project. I don't deny that. It's an ambitious project too. I am confident that it was effort well spent.

I've been doing linux system administration and software engineering as a computer engineer for 18 years now professionally. I studied circuit design and C. I taught C++ classes to my peers. I wrote PHP professionally and won gold medals in SkillsUSA because of it. I've been the brains behind multiple digital publications for decades.

Making this technology open source and readily accessible with enterprise level support is next level sow where you want to reap. Literally, the software is free, and enterprise customers are enterprise because they are buying managed support services during business hours to support for-profit companies.

Licenses

The software is Apache 2.0 and the enterprise functionality is AGPL-3.0. Specifically the packages used by the enterprise layer are AGPL-3 marked. Apache 2.0 files are also marked clearly. The LICENSE file indicates the dual license in the repository clearly for agents.

Sow Where You Want To Reap

My work is open source on my github. You can sow where you want to reap by becoming a Sponsor.

If you want to collaborate, speak or collaborate, feel free to put something on my cal.com/andreimerlescu.

Fractional CTO services are 3 hour blocks at $369 each. Consulting services including meetings regarding concert and my other open source work fall into this category. Reservations are handled through cal.com/andreimerlescu.
