This is where you have an enhancement to something, or a new idea, or you want to change something I built, this give you the chance to sow where you want to reap. It gives the project a $369 budget where paywall can be considered approachable to accomplish the project. Meaning. If we use AI, then we have usage credits for a given project. With Gemini 4 Neon Extra High on a Max subscription, the 35M tokens a day upgrade from 5M day on Claude Pro has been a dramatic 7x upgrade in my utilization of frontier AI models. I'll consider adjusting this given Neon's capabilities. Frankly speaking, it was priced for Claude's tax.

I can help you integrate what I built into your company. Use the time for Q & A if you have tech chops yourself.

If you want more functionality added to it upstream but don't want to invest the energy into it, sponsor a hackathon and the results will get published open source.

Using Concert 🎸

There are dozens of websites in the wild that currently use concert in its pre v0.3.0 release, which is why I am publishing this article announcing the completed release before releasing it.

Before releasing econcert and wpconcert I am going to put them through a production test of my own stuff first. Before subjecting you. Any AI can say that this code is ready to go, but concert v0.2.0 has been stable in production for a long time, but removing nginx and haproxy itself in a multi-node setup was a major undertaking.

To date, I haven't been able to capture the full token consumption of the project (hence what toktail's purpose is) but I estimate that between Claude and Gemini 4 Neon, I've been billed for over 1B tokens for this one project over the last few months since I released it the day before Fall 2026 began. title: Multi-account failover for Claude Code & Codex without losing your session (TernaryCode v0.3.5)
description:
If you run Claude Code or Codex across several projects every day, two things interrupt flow more than anything else:

  1. Not knowing which terminal pane stopped waiting for your approval.
  2. Hitting a 5-hour or weekly usage limit mid-task, having to log out, log into a second account, and losing your active session.

In TernaryCode v0.3.5 (free, MIT, written in Rust for macOS, Windows, and Linux), I built isolated multi-account management with failover directly into the workspace alongside hook-backed status tracking.

How isolated accounts work under the hood

Instead of overwriting your global ~/.claude or ~/.codex directories, TernaryCode gives each registered account its own isolated config directory:

  • Claude Code: launches with a per-account CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR
  • Codex: launches with a per-account CODEX_HOME

Everything stays local on your machine (~/Library/Application Support/ternarycode on macOS, %APPDATA%\ternarycode on Windows, ~/.local/share/ternarycode on Linux). There is no cloud account and no telemetry.

Real 5-hour & weekly usage + conversation-preserving failover

Each account reports real server-side 5-hour and weekly usage percentages along with reset times. You drag accounts into your preferred failover order in Settings → Accounts.

When a running pane hits a usage limit:

  • The pane flags the rate-limit state immediately in the Inbox and pane notice.
  • With one click (or automatically when auto-failover is enabled), TernaryCode switches to the next healthy account and resumes the same conversation without forcing you to re-explain the task from scratch.

What else shipped in v0.3.5

  • Slate UI redesign + live Overview (⌘0 / Ctrl+Shift+0): view every project's live terminal side by side in tiles and type straight into any of them.
  • Hook-backed attention queue (⌘J / Ctrl+Shift+J): Needs input, Running, Done, and Failed straight from each agent's hooks (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode; Antigravity CLI shows plain Active instead of guessing).
  • Embedded native browser (WebKit / WebView2 / WebKitGTK): agents drive it over MCP while you watch, plus in-place preview for PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, CSV, and images.
  • Local Wi-Fi phone companion: scan the QR code in Settings → Phone to view live output, approve/reject prompts, send follow-ups, and switch accounts from your phone using revocable per-device tokens.
  • Native Rust performance: built with egui/wgpu, alacritty_terminal, and wry — launches in ~0.2 s and idles at 0% CPU on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

Try it

  • GitHub: https://github.com/ilhamnadhif/ternarycode
  • Website & downloads: https://ilhamnadhif.github.io/ternarycode/

If you run multiple Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Antigravity CLI sessions — especially on Windows or Linux — I'd love feedback on where failover or hook detection can be sharper.

Disclosure: I'm the author of TernaryCode. This post was drafted with AI assistance from TernaryCode's source code and README, and verified against v0.3.5.

title: Building a 3D cinema kiosk on a shared ticketing engine
description:
I wanted the cinema demo to start with movie posters rotating in a projector beam. It gives the kiosk its own identity before anyone touches the screen. Once someone picks a screening, there’s a different job to do: make sure the seat they see is still available.

Separate the scene from the sale

I kept the 3D scene inside the kiosk UI. The shared engine handles the screening, seat availability, and reservations through its gRPC contract. This is the same engine the box office and online ticketing use. A kiosk can change the animation, layout, or rendering stack and still ask the engine the same questions.

A concrete flow

  1. Read the selected screening and its available seats from the engine.
  2. Draw the seating chart in the kiosk UI. When the customer chooses a numbered seat, request a hold from the engine.
  3. Show the result of the hold on the chart. If another register has already taken the seat, refresh availability so the customer can pick another one.

The important design choice is the third step. A blue seat on the screen is a display state. The hold recorded by the engine is what makes it unavailable at the other points of sale.

The demo uses a 3D attract screen, but the contract does not require that renderer. A team could build a kiosk in a 3D game engine if it can use a compatible gRPC client or connect through an adapter. That team can choose how the booth feels without rebuilding how a seat gets reserved.

See the actual kiosk and seat selection in the StillDeep Theater development post.

AI assisted with editing and translation.

title: Your 768px breakpoint is wrong on foldables — what the cover and inner screens actually report
description:
Almost every responsive layout is tested at two sizes: something around 390×844, and something wide. Then a foldable shows up, the user unfolds it, and the page does one of two things — stretches a phone layout across 750 px, or jumps to a two-column tablet layout with a vertical strip of dead space running down the middle of the text.

Neither is a rendering bug. Both are assumptions: that a device has one viewport, that width alone tells you the layout, and that the breakpoints you picked sit somewhere real.

A foldable is two viewports, not one

Here are the CSS pixel widths of the eight devices I keep in the test set (cover screen / unfolded inner screen):

Device Cover Inner
iPhone Duo 387 790
Galaxy Z Fold 7 412 750
Galaxy Z Flip 7 361 411
Mate X7 411 842
Pixel Fold 412 790
Find N5 412 824
Mate XT (tri-fold) 384 1080
Razr 60 Ultra 412 412

Two things fall out of that table immediately.

Cover screens are narrower than the phone you tested. The range is 361–412. If your layout is tuned at 390 and you have a breakpoint at 380 or a hard-coded min-width: 390px on a card grid, the smallest foldable cover lands just under it and gets the "narrow" treatment while a 412 px cover gets the other one.

There is a 338 px hole between 412 and 750. No phone occupies it. No tablet occupies it either — tablets start around 768. Every breakpoint you place between 412 and 750 is dead code that only ever fires on a device you did not think about.

Why 768 is the worst number in this range

Galaxy Z Fold 7 unfolded is 750 px. Your @media (min-width: 768px) does not fire. The user gets the single-column phone layout on a screen roughly the size of an iPad mini.

Mate X7 unfolded is 842 px. Same breakpoint fires. Two columns, desktop nav, everything.

So two people, same app, same OS version, comparing screenshots of "the foldable experience", see different products. The difference is 92 px of viewport width and no product decision behind it.

The fix is not "move the breakpoint to 720". There is no width that makes one layout correct for both a folded phone and an unfolded tablet, because those are different postures, not different widths. Width is a proxy for posture, and it is a bad one.

Ask the OS how many segments there are

Chromium exposes the Viewport Segments API. Instead of guessing from width, you ask whether the viewport is currently split into two panes and how wide each one is:

/* Structure changes only when there are actually two panes */
@media (horizontal-viewport-segments: 2) {
  .app {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns:
      env(viewport-segment-width 0 0)
      env(viewport-segment-width 1 0);
  }
  .pane-right {
    padding-inline-start: env(viewport-segment-left 1 0, 0px);
  }
}

env(viewport-segment-width 0 0) means "width of segment column 0, row 0". The last two numbers are column index, row index, which matters on a tri-fold where you can have three segments in a row — Mate XT at 384/1080 can present 2 or 3.

The point of using the API rather than a media query is that it keeps working when the OS changes its mind mid-session: unfold, fold, drag the app into split-screen, rotate. A width breakpoint has to be re-evaluated and re-designed for each of those. A segment query just asks again.

Where the API is not available, the honest fallback is not another width breakpoint. It is a layout that degrades gracefully in one column, with a max content width around 640 px, so a 750 px canvas shows a centered reading column instead of a stretched one.

Height breaks before width does

Every foldable in that table is 800+ px tall unfolded. Folded, the cover screen is about 850 px tall — and then the OS eats it:

  • keyboard open → dvh drops to roughly 450–500
  • split-screen with a video app → half the height
  • browser chrome on the cover screen → 60–90 px of the 850 gone before your CSS runs

height: 100vh on a hero section and position: fixed on a bottom bar are the two things that break first. The hero overflows, the bottom bar covers the last row of the form, and the user cannot scroll to the button because the bar is fixed over it.

.hero { min-height: 100svh; }        /* stable, ignores dynamic toolbars */
.screen { height: 100dvh; }          /* tracks the real dynamic viewport */
.cta-bar { padding-bottom: max(12px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)); }

Then test at 387×450, not just 387×850. That is the state where the keyboard is up and the user is trying to submit something.

The crease is a layout element

On a book-style foldable the hinge occupies a band in the middle of the inner screen. Content that crosses it is not broken — it is bisected. I have seen pricing tables where the middle column sat exactly on the seam and was unreadable in one orientation only.

The rule I use: structure may cross the crease, text may not. Two panes, a gutter, a divider line — fine. A paragraph, a table row, a button spanning both panes — no.

If you are not using segment queries, the cheap version is a centered gutter:

@media (min-width: 700px) and (max-width: 900px) {
  .content { padding-inline: 24px; column-gap: 40px; }
}

It is approximate. It costs nothing, and it prevents the worst case.

viewport-fit=cover is not optional anymore 

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover">

Without it, the browser letterboxes the page to avoid the rounded corners and the camera cutout. On a 387 px cover screen that costs you roughly 20 px per side — you are designing for 347 px and do not know it. With it, you own the edges and use env(safe-area-inset-*) to keep tap targets out of the corners.

The matrix I actually run

Sixteen to thirty-two viewports is not a lot of work if it is a checklist rather than a manual review:

  1. No horizontal scrollbar at any of the eight cover widths.
  2. No text crossing the 40 px band in the centre of the inner screen.
  3. Primary CTA reachable at 387×450 (keyboard-up state).
  4. Two-pane layout appears only when horizontal-viewport-segments: 2.
  5. No fixed bar overlapping form fields.
  6. Images not upscaled past 1× on the inner screen — a 790 px canvas showing a 400 px asset is a blurry hero.

Doing this by hand means resizing a browser window and lying to yourself about which device you are simulating — a 750 px window on a laptop is not a Z Fold 7, because the OS behaviour around segments, safe areas and posture does not come with it.

I built FoldCheck for exactly this: paste a URL, it renders the page inside faithful device frames at those eight widths, runs a 12-point foldable audit, and returns the offending selectors as a CSS patch you can drop into the bundle. It runs in the browser, no signup, and there is a CLI and a small SDK if you want the checks in CI.

The device shipped. The CSS did not get updated. Testing 390 and 1440 is not a matrix — it is a habit.

title: Build a required license-plate field that accepts common punctuation
description:
A required field should not reject data solely because the person used harmless punctuation. License plates are a useful example: users may know the characters but enter spaces, hyphens, periods, or slashes differently from the application’s preferred display.

The implementation separates three concerns. First, the field is explicitly required so omission is communicated by the browser and the form UI. Second, a client-side helper recognizes one documented plate layout: a short city-letter group, a second letter group, and a digit group. It accepts common separators between those groups rather than demanding one exact presentation. Third, every accepted value is normalized into a canonical form with uppercase letters and consistent spaces.

That means an entry such as b-ab/123 can be accepted and represented downstream as B AB 123. The feedback result also distinguishes an empty field from a malformed value. Empty input receives a direct required-field message; an invalid structure receives concise guidance about the expected groups and permitted separators; a valid entry confirms the normalized value. Connect that feedback to the control with aria-describedby so the guidance remains associated with the field.

The expected behavior is forgiving input without ambiguous storage or comparison. Search, deduplication, and later confirmation can use one predictable representation instead of handling several punctuation variants.

There are important limits. This is a narrow format rule, not a universal license-plate validator. Products serving multiple regions may need a region selector, different rules, or a less restrictive client hint. Also, browser validation and client-side messaging are usability aids, not a security boundary. The server must independently validate and normalize the submitted value before accepting it.

Working example 

// This client-side helper accepts the documented German-style plate groups:
// city (1–3 letters), letters (2–4), and digits (1–4).
// It tolerates spaces, hyphens, periods, and slashes between groups.
export const plateField = Object.freeze({
  label: 'License plate (required)',
  attributes: Object.freeze({
    required: true,
    // Suitable for an HTML pattern attribute; normalization still supplies the
    // canonical value used by the application.
    pattern: '[A-Za-z]{1,3}\\s*[-./ ]+\\s*[A-Za-z]{2,4}\\s*[-./ ]+\\s*[0-9]{1,4}',
    ariaDescribedBy: 'plate-feedback'
  })
});

const plateGroups = /^\s*([a-z]{1,3})\s*[-./ ]+\s*([a-z]{2,4})\s*[-./ ]+\s*([0-9]{1,4})\s*$/i;

/**
 * Returns a canonical, storage-friendly plate or null when the format is not
 * one of the supported group layouts.
 */
export function normalizePlate(value) {
  if (typeof value !== 'string') return null;

  const match = value.match(plateGroups);
  if (!match) return null;

  return `${match[1].toUpperCase()} ${match[2].toUpperCase()} ${match[3]}`;
}

/**
 * Produces concise inline feedback suitable for updating an aria-describedby
 * message while the person types. Server-side validation must repeat any
 * validation required for accepting a submission.
 */
export function validatePlateInput(value) {
  if (typeof value !== 'string' || value.trim() === '') {
    return {
      valid: false,
      normalized: null,
      feedback: 'Enter a license plate; this field is required.'
    };
  }

  const normalized = normalizePlate(value);
  if (normalized === null) {
    return {
      valid: false,
      normalized: null,
      feedback: 'Use 1–3 letters, 2–4 letters, and 1–4 digits, separated by spaces, hyphens, periods, or slashes.'
    };
  }

  return {
    valid: true,
    normalized,
    feedback: `Plate format looks good: ${normalized}.`
  };
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/validate-required-license-plate-field

title: Generate shell completions from the binary, with no new dependency
description:
New command-line tools keep arriving as single binaries, and shell completion is the small tax each one pays before it feels installed. Trendshift's weekly view, retrieved 24 November 2026 for the week of 23 to 29 November, lists the experimental google-gemini/gemini-api-cli at 503 stars gained that week. The cli tag on dev.to carried a run of independent tool releases on 22 and 23 November, among them a one-command repository readiness checker and a CLI profile manager with terminal OAuth approval. That is not evidence that completions are suddenly fashionable. It is evidence that small tools keep shipping, and that their users still have to wire them into a shell by hand.

Kolgrim33/broom#5 is one concrete way to pay that wiring cost without growing the dependency tree. It adds --completions <shell> to broom, a zero-dependency Rust utility for finding and sweeping stale build artifacts. The pull request was merged on 23 November 2026. I opened it and wrote its single commit, d7fce40e; Kolgrim33 merged it into their project. That split is worth stating plainly: the repository is theirs, the implementation is mine. The diff is 3 files, +348 and -0. The PR references broom issue #2, which is still open, so this is a step toward that request and not a claim that the request is finished.

The flag prints a script and stops

The intended use is a redirect into the shell's own completion directory:

broom --completions bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/broom
broom --completions zsh > ~/.zfunc/_broom
broom --completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/broom.fish

Three shells are supported: bash, zsh and fish. Parsing happens in src/cli.rs, where the new ParseOutcome::PrintCompletions(String) variant carries the generated text. In src/main.rs, that variant prints the string and returns ExitCode::SUCCESS before the path validation, scan or clean code runs. A completion request cannot touch a file on disk. That matters for a tool whose main job is deleting build artifacts.

The completion path reads the same option tables as the argument parser, so a new flag reaches the generated script without editing three generators by hand.

One table, three generators

The part I care about is where the script content comes from. Broom's parser already held the option descriptions in a shared table, with separate constants for the accepted --sort values (size, age, path) and the ecosystem IDs accepted by --type. The bash, zsh and fish generators read those same constants. They render the data into three different syntaxes: bash's COMPREPLY array, zsh's _arguments specs and fish's complete calls.

This is the whole design claim, and it is why the diagram above has a single source feeding three outputs. A completion script is a second description of the interface. When the two descriptions live in different files, they drift: a new flag is added to the parser, and the completion script quietly stops offering it. Generating from the parser's own table removes the second description. The generated text is never committed either, so there is no stale artifact in the repository to forget.

The new tests enforce exactly that. The unit test generates_completions_for_all_supported_shells loops over the three shells and asserts that every script contains each long flag, each sort value and each ecosystem ID. The integration test completion_scripts_cover_flags_and_values runs the compiled binary for all three shells and checks the same properties against its stdout. The tests fail if a generator lags behind the table.

The error path is a normal CLI path

An unsupported shell name goes through the same completion_script function. It lowercases the input, so --completions BASH works, and an unknown value produces unknown shell 'tcsh'. Supported shells: bash, zsh, fish on stderr with exit status 2. Status 2 is the same code broom uses for other argument errors, so a script can handle a bad shell name without a special case. There is no panic path and no partial output on that branch.

What the numbers actually are

The merged tree at d7fce40e contains 7 unit tests and 6 integration tests across the crate, 13 in total. The completion work added 276 lines to src/cli.rs, 4 lines to src/main.rs and a 68-line end-to-end test file. Cargo.toml has no [dependencies] table, before or after the change, so the completion feature adds no crate to the build. The PR's verification notes report cargo fmt --all -- --check, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings and cargo test --all-targets clean, plus bash -n, zsh -n and fish -n syntax checks on the generated scripts. The test counts above come from counting #[test] attributes in the merged source, not from trusting the PR prose.

The limit of this approach is worth naming. Hand-written generators are code, and code has to be maintained. A mature CLI with dozens of flags may prefer a maintained completion library, accepting a dependency in exchange for covering shell-specific edge cases such as quoting and nested subcommands. Broom has one command, a flat flag list and a hard zero-dependency constraint in its package description. For that shape, 348 lines buys completions that cannot silently fall out of sync, and the shell gets them from the binary it already installed.

Sources for the trend snapshot: Trendshift weekly, week of 23 November 2026 and dev.to cli tag, retrieved 24 November 2026.

title: The E2E test that built the wrong binary
description:
The merge request said "verified locally green" in its description, which in hindsight was asking for it.

It was the tail end of a big audit clean-up on go-tool-base, and one of the fixes came with a brand new end-to-end scenario: make sure generate add-flag doesn't throw away a command's aliases, shorthand flags and pre-run hooks when it regenerates. It passed on my machine. In CI, one scenario out of eighty-five fell over with this:

ERRO failed to load configuration: failed to load config: no configuration files found please run init, or provide a config file using the --config flag

Now that's a funny thing to be told by gtb... because gtb doesn't have an init command.

The star and the stunt double

go-tool-base builds two binaries from one repository, and only one of them ever ships. ./cmd/gtb is the real tool, the generator you install. ./cmd/e2e is a test rig: it switches on every optional feature the framework has, init and doctor and config and the rest, so the end-to-end suite can exercise framework behaviour that a downstream tool inherits. It's there so I don't have to bake weird test fixtures into the real binary.

If gtb's the star, the e2e binary is its stunt double. It looks like the star, it answers to the same name (both call themselves gtb, so they even read the same config paths), and it's built to do the dangerous scenes. You just don't put it in the close-ups.

And the test harness had put it in the close-ups. The old helper promised one thing in its comment and built the other:

// BinaryPath returns the path to the compiled gtb binary,
// building it on first call. The binary is placed in a temp directory
// and reused for all subsequent calls.
func BinaryPath() (string, error) {
    buildOnce.Do(func() {
        // ...
        binaryPath = filepath.Join(tmpDir, "gtb-e2e")
        cmd := exec.CommandContext(context.Background(), "go", "build", "-o", binaryPath, "./cmd/e2e")

"The compiled gtb binary", it says, right above the line that builds the other one! All of the generator scenarios had been running against the stunt double.

Why the double needed a config

The reason it mattered comes down to a rule in the framework. Whether a missing config file is fatal depends on whether the tool is able to create one. A tool with an init command is expected to have run it, so no config is an error. A tool without one is allowed to start empty. In the bootstrap it's one line:

allowEmpty := props.Tool.IsDisabled(p.InitCmd)

The real gtb disables init, so it runs happily with no config, same as in production. The stunt double enables init, so it demands one. And on my machine it found one. I have a perfectly real ~/.gtb/config.yaml from using the tool day to day. CI's clean runner had nothing of the sort.

The fix that would have hidden it

The first suggestion on the table was to give the scenario a config file of its own, the way another scenario already did. It would have gone green straight away. It would also have tested the generator with init switched on, which the real generator doesn't have, and buried the mismatch under a fixture.

What I typed back was "wait, what!!! the GTB binary should have the init FeatureCmd disabled and this not need a config file? is this the gtb binary or the e2e test binary". It was the e2e binary, naturally.

So the fix gave the generator scenarios the star. A second helper builds the real ./cmd/gtb, and the comment on it says why in more words than I'd normally allow, because this wasn't the first time I'd had that conversation and I didn't want a third:

// Generator scenarios must use this binary, not the e2e binary: the real
// gtb tool disables InitCmd (internal/cmd/root), so its bootstrap treats a
// missing config as allow-empty and the generate/regenerate/remove commands
// run without an external config file — exactly as they do in production.
func GeneratorBinaryPath() (string, error) {

The pipeline went green, the e2e binary got a proper explanation in its package docs, and that was that... for about two months.

My clean check wasn't clean

Looking back at it now, the local re-check that "proved" the fix proved rather less than I thought. It emptied XDG_CONFIG_HOME to simulate a clean machine, but gtb reads ~/.gtb/, not anywhere XDG points, so my config was there in plain sight the whole time. (The very first attempt at that re-check also finished in 0.013 seconds, because I'd forgotten the environment variable that switches the suite on, and every scenario skipped without a word.) The green CI pipeline was the real proof, and mine just happened to agree with it.

And I suspect there was always a bigger problem behind the first one. Picking the right binary fixed which tool the tests ran, and did nothing about whose home they ran in. The generator steps launched gtb with no environment of their own, so they inherited mine: my config, my caches, my AI provider settings, the lot.

August, and a dressing room of its own

In August that kind of bug came back for a second go. A docs-generation path behaved differently on my machine, which had an AI provider configured, than on CI, which didn't, and a hash bug sailed through a green local run and failed a merge request's pipeline. The fix finally gave the generator steps a home of their own, the way the CLI steps had always had, and its commit message says the thing I should have written in June:

'Green locally, so CI is flaky' was the wrong conclusion, twice.

Isolating HOME wasn't free, though. Done naively, with the Go and lint caches stranded in the old home, the generator suite went from 193 seconds to 809 (uncomfortably close to CI's fifteen-minute limit). Pinning the module, build and lint caches back to shared locations brought it down to 119, which is faster than it was before any of this!

So June sorted out which binary ran and August sorted out where it lived, and these days the star and the stunt double each get changed in their own dressing room instead of mine.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 24 November 2026.

title: Gamifying Customer Onboarding for Indian Apps: Mechanics That Work and Ones to Skip
description:
Most onboarding flows in Indian consumer apps already borrow from games: a progress bar on KYC, a scratch card after the first UPI payment, a streak counter on a learning app. Some of these genuinely help a new user get to their first useful action. Others just add noise, slow the flow down on a budget phone, or train people to chase rewards instead of learning the product.

This post is a practical sorting exercise for product and engineering teams in India who are planning (or cleaning up) a gamified onboarding flow. It's written from a game-design point of view: what each mechanic actually does to player behaviour, and where it tends to go wrong.

No benchmarks or conversion figures here on purpose. Your numbers depend on your audience, category and funnel. Treat each section as a hypothesis to test in your own analytics.

Start with the one action that matters

Before choosing mechanics, write down the single action that turns a sign-up into a real user. For a payments app it might be the first successful transaction; for an edtech app, finishing the first lesson; for an insurance or banking app, completing KYC.

Every mechanic below should be judged by one question: does it move the user closer to that action, or does it distract from it?

Mechanics that usually earn their place

1. Visible progress through a required flow

KYC, profile setup and permissions are tedious but necessary. A clear step indicator ("Step 2 of 4"), with each step saving progress, does two things: it tells people how much is left, and it lets them come back later without starting over. That second part matters a lot when users are switching between apps to fetch an OTP or photograph a document.

Watch out for: fake progress. If the bar jumps to 80% and then three more screens appear, people notice and trust drops.

2. A guided first win

Games teach by letting you do the thing in a safe space. The onboarding equivalent is a guided first action with low stakes: a sample portfolio, a practice quiz, a demo cart. The user learns the core loop before anything real is at risk.

Watch out for: tutorials that can't be skipped by returning users who reinstalled the app.

3. Small, predictable rewards tied to real milestones

A reward for completing profile setup or making a first transaction can work, as long as it's tied to a milestone that also benefits the user. Predictable rewards ("Complete KYC and unlock X") are easier to understand and explain than random ones.

Watch out for: rewards that cost you more in support tickets than they earn. If the terms are unclear, users will ask.

4. Gentle streaks for habit-forming products

For learning, fitness or savings apps, a short streak can help people come back during the first week. Keep the streak forgiving: allow a missed day, or a "freeze", so one bad day doesn't reset everything and push the user away.

Mechanics to skip (or use very carefully)

1. Leaderboards in onboarding

Competing with strangers on day one rarely helps someone learn a product. New users land at the bottom, which is discouraging. Leaderboards fit better later, among friends or within a cohort, once people know what they're doing.

2. Heavy animations and confetti on every tap

Celebration effects feel good on a flagship phone on Wi-Fi. On an entry-level Android handset on patchy mobile data, a large Lottie file or video celebration can add load time to exactly the screens where you can least afford it. Keep celebrations lightweight, cache them, and save them for meaningful milestones.

3. Random reward mechanics

Spin-the-wheel and mystery-box mechanics are tempting because they're exciting. They also raise questions you need to answer clearly: what are the odds, what are the terms, and could this look like gambling to a regulator or a parent? If you use them, get your legal and compliance team involved early, and don't make onboarding depend on them.

4. Badges with no meaning

A wall of badges for "Opened the app" and "Viewed settings" teaches nothing. If a badge doesn't mark a real skill or milestone, drop it.

Design notes specific to Indian audiences

  • Language: if your onboarding supports regional languages, make sure reward copy, terms and progress labels are translated too, not only the main screens.
  • Device range: test the full flow on budget Android devices with limited RAM. Gamified elements often carry the heaviest assets in an onboarding flow.
  • Data cost: keep downloadable assets small and avoid forcing large updates before the first action.
  • OTP and app-switching: design every step to survive the user leaving the app and coming back.

A simple review checklist

Before shipping a gamified onboarding flow, run through these:

  1. Is the one key action clearly defined, and does each mechanic support it?
  2. Does progress save between sessions?
  3. Can returning users skip tutorials?
  4. Are reward terms short and understandable in every supported language?
  5. Have celebration assets been tested on a low-end device and a slow network?
  6. Has compliance reviewed any random or monetary reward?
  7. Do you have events in analytics for each step, so you can see where people drop off?

Onboarding is only the first week, though. What keeps users around after that is a separate production problem, and I wrote about planning mobile retention work during production rather than after launch on our Substack.

If you're planning a gamified product or want a game-design review of an existing flow, our team at Juego Studios works on gamification design and development for apps and training products.

title: Building a Zero-Dependency, 60fps Image Comparison Slider in Vanilla TypeScript (Under 3KB)
description:
If you've ever needed a "Before & After" image comparison slider on a high-traffic landing page, you've likely faced the classic front-end dilemma:

You search NPM and find dozens of packages. You install one, and suddenly:

  • Your bundle size inflates by 45KB - 80KB.
  • It pulls in transitive dependencies you don't need.
  • Mobile touch dragging stutters on iOS Safari because it intercepts native scrolling poorly.
  • Your Google Lighthouse Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) score tanks because the container doesn't reserve the natural aspect ratio before images decode.

We decided to scrap the bloated libraries and build a zero-dependency, hardware-accelerated comparison slider in under 120 lines of clean TypeScript.

Here is the exact architecture, the CSS math, and how we solved the dreaded iOS touch-drag collision.

1. The Core Architecture: Why clip-path Beats Dual DOM Hierarchies

Old-school sliders duplicated the entire container or used two overlapping images with overflow: hidden on a nested div. That required synchronized width recalculations on every mousemove frame, triggering expensive layout reflows (Thrashing).

The modern, GPU-friendly way is CSS clip-path: inset():

<div class="diff-container" id="slider">
  <!-- Base Background Image (After) -->
  <img src="after.jpg" alt="After" class="diff-img diff-base" />

  <!-- Overlay Top Image (Before) -->
  <img src="before.jpg" alt="Before" class="diff-img diff-overlay" id="overlay" />

  <!-- Divider Line & Handle -->
  <div class="diff-handle" id="handle">
    <div class="diff-line"></div>
    <div class="diff-grip">↔</div>
  </div>
</div>

With clip-path: inset(0 (100% - X%) 0 0), the browser doesn't touch the DOM layout at all. It clips the pixel rasterization on the GPU compositor thread:

.diff-container {
  position: relative;
  overflow: hidden;
  user-select: none;
  touch-action: pan-y; /* Crucial for mobile UX */
}

.diff-img {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: auto;
  pointer-events: none;
}

.diff-overlay {
  position: absolute;
  top: 0;
  left: 0;
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  clip-path: inset(0 50% 0 0); /* Initial 50% split */
  will-change: clip-path;
}

2. The 60fps TypeScript Controller

To guarantee silky-smooth 60fps tracking even on budget Android devices, we decouple the coordinate capture from the DOM paint using requestAnimationFrame:

export class DiffSlider {
  private container: HTMLElement;
  private overlay: HTMLElement;
  private handle: HTMLElement;
  private isDragging = false;
  private currentPercent = 50;
  private ticking = false;

  constructor(containerId: string) {
    this.container = document.getElementById(containerId)!;
    this.overlay = this.container.querySelector('.diff-overlay')!;
    this.handle = this.container.querySelector('.diff-handle')!;

    this.bindEvents();
  }

  private bindEvents() {
    // Pointer Events API handles Mouse + Touch + Stylus simultaneously
    this.container.addEventListener('pointerdown', this.onPointerDown);
    window.addEventListener('pointermove', this.onPointerMove);
    window.addEventListener('pointerup', this.onPointerUp);
    window.addEventListener('pointercancel', this.onPointerUp);
  }

  private onPointerDown = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    this.isDragging = true;
    this.updatePosition(e.clientX);
    this.container.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
  };

  private onPointerMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    if (!this.isDragging) return;
    this.updatePosition(e.clientX);
  };

  private onPointerUp = () => {
    this.isDragging = false;
  };

  private updatePosition(clientX: number) {
    const rect = this.container.getBoundingClientRect();
    const rawOffset = clientX - rect.left;
    const clampedOffset = Math.max(0, Math.min(rawOffset, rect.width));
    this.currentPercent = (clampedOffset / rect.width) * 100;

    if (!this.ticking) {
      requestAnimationFrame(this.render);
      this.ticking = true;
    }
  }

  private render = () => {
    const rightInset = 100 - this.currentPercent;
    // GPU Compositor pass
    this.overlay.style.clipPath = `inset(0 ${rightInset}% 0 0)`;
    this.handle.style.left = `${this.currentPercent}%`;
    this.ticking = false;
  };
}

3. The 3 Mobile Gotchas We Solved

  1. The Mobile Scroll Hijack: If a user drags vertically across the slider, they expect the page to scroll. If they drag horizontally, they expect the slider to move. By specifying touch-action: pan-y; in CSS, the browser handles native vertical gestures natively without janky JS preventDefault() bugs.
  2. Zero Layout Shift (CLS = 0): We inject the intrinsic aspect-ratio into the container via CSS custom properties so the space is reserved before the images finish downloading over 4G connections.
  3. High-DPI Retina Alignments: Using sub-pixel CSS transforms (translate3d) prevents handle jitter on 3x display densities.

Conclusion & Live Tooling

By stripping away UI framework dogma and relying on raw modern web primitives (clip-path, PointerEvents, and requestAnimationFrame), we achieved a complete component weighing 2.8KB unminified, 0 dependencies, and 100/100 Lighthouse performance.

If you're building a landing page and need customizable before/after sliders without writing boilerplate code, we've packaged this entire architecture—along with responsive embed widgets, analytics triggers, and custom theming—into DiffSlider.

Feel free to inspect the DOM or try the interactive sandbox at DiffSlider!

How do you currently handle image comparisons in your production stack? Let me know in the comments below!

title: Go Video Checkout Alerts — Fix Missing Messages With Exact Channel Scope
description:
Giving a browser broader access can make a missing notification appear to be fixed while weakening the tenant boundary. Keep the boundary. Short answer: when realtime messages are not arriving, check that the issued token's scope includes the exact channel name the client subscribed to, read that channel back in the intended environment, and log the scope at issuance so the diagnosis rests on evidence. A tenant prefix difference is enough to break the match.

For an e-commerce video checkout room, the useful incident lesson is about admission: authorize the browser for the intended notification channel before treating an apparently healthy room as proof that order updates can arrive. Room participation and a notification subscription are separate things to verify. The W3C WebRTC 1.0 specification is a useful reference for the media connection; it does not establish the authorization contract of an application's notification service.

How do you debug token scope when realtime messages are not arriving?

Consider a hypothetical production incident, rather than a reported outage: a shopper enters a video room to discuss an order, the interface looks ready, and the expected in-app notification never appears. The subscription uses shop:amber:room:checkout-42, while the server's issuance record contains shop:amber-test:room:checkout-42. These are illustrative application names, not reserved provider syntax. The room suffix looks right to someone scanning a dashboard, but the tenant prefixes differ, and exact string matching makes that distinction decisive.

Nothing arrived.

Check the scope.

That observation alone cannot distinguish an authorization mismatch from other delivery problems. It can, however, justify a narrow first check: compare the actual subscribed name with the scope recorded when the token was minted. A mismatch can look silent from the client's point of view; that is a debugging observation about what the shopper sees, not evidence that access should have been granted. Reconnecting the same subscription with the same scope leaves the authorization mismatch intact.

The invariant is small: the channel selected by trusted application policy must be the same string used for scope issuance and browser subscription. Don't normalize away the difference during debugging. A convenient prefix substitution could erase the very tenant boundary the token is supposed to enforce.

If the strings agree, read the channel back in the environment where the application is running. Confirming existence in a developer environment does not establish existence in the checkout environment. Only after scope, subscribed name, and environment agree does it make sense to widen the investigation; this check is a starting point, not a universal explanation for dropped messages.

Make admission evidence part of the SLO

An availability graph for the video room is insufficient evidence for an in-app notification SLO. Define the user journey first: an authorized shopper can subscribe to the intended order-update channel and receive the expected application event. Choose delivery and timing objectives from the product requirement; no measured latency or uptime is implied here.

Record the authorized channel, the requested subscription channel, the environment, and the authorization decision together. These are proposed application log fields, not a vendor request or response schema. Log the scope you minted, but don't log the bearer token. Scope records can themselves reveal tenant or order identifiers, so give their access and retention deliberate treatment.

Capacity planning belongs here too. If the design mints a token whenever a browser enters a room, reconnect behavior becomes an input to issuance traffic as well as subscription traffic. Budget for the reconnect pattern you intend to support, then measure it under load; a connection count alone does not describe that demand. Repeated rejected admissions also need a bounded diagnostic path, or a single naming mistake can produce an unhelpful volume of duplicate records.

For illustration, a load plan might exercise 200 simultaneous checkout admissions and 3 reconnect attempts per browser. Those are proposed test inputs, not observed throughput or a provider limit. The acceptance condition is that no attempt gains a channel outside the server's authorization decision, and every rejected mismatch can be traced to its issuance record. Under that proposed plan, 200 initial admissions plus 600 retries give 800 admission decisions to account for; that arithmetic is a workload budget, not a throughput claim.

Count decisions, too.

Buy versus build starts at the trust boundary

A managed service can remove operational work, but the application still has to decide which shopper may enter which notification channel. Self-hosting moves more of the operational burden onto the platform team without supplying that business rule. The comparison below is an evaluation plan: questions to settle using each product's documentation and a small admission test, rather than a claim that their token formats or room models are interchangeable.

Option Buy versus build question for this checkout flow Boundary or limitation to evaluate
Ably Does its token authentication and capability model express the application's required channel authorization? Check channel resource names and permissions before translating the application's scope policy.
Pusher Channels Does its private-channel authorization flow fit a server decision made before browser subscription? Channel authorization is the relevant contract; don't assume another product's token shape applies.
LiveKit Does its room-token and grant model fit the video-room admission requirement? Evaluate the separate notification-channel requirement explicitly instead of inferring it from room admission.
PubNub Does its Access Manager permission model fit tenant-scoped checkout notifications? Review resource permissions and naming rules independently; room admission remains a separate requirement.
Application-owned service Is owning admission, subscription handling, and operations justified by the required control? The platform team must implement and operate the authorization boundary and its diagnostic evidence.

These are different evaluation surfaces: channel-oriented authorization is the question for the notification layer, while room admission is the question for the video workflow. A shared product label such as realtime should not collapse those decisions. Choose the candidate whose documented contract matches the boundary you actually need, then assess its operational burden and the effort required to change providers. A comparison of SDK convenience cannot settle that.

Infrai provides one key and one bill for an all-in-one backend, with unified billing and a single API key across 295 routes in 20 modules. Its self-describing REST API, public discovery, and runnable examples mean wiring a new capability starts with reading request and response schemas rather than learning another SDK. For checkout notification, storage, and observability integrations, credential consolidation reduces the separate keys the platform team must provision and rotate; a single invoice reduces billing reconciliation across those integrations. Keep the platform credential on the trusted server, while the browser receives only the scoped credential appropriate to its channel.

Discovery helps establish the contract. It doesn't choose the shopper's permissions.

Consolidated backend services are most useful when several integrations are actually on the platform roadmap. A team already operating a suitable notification service may gain little from another integration, and concentrating backend authority in one credential makes deliberate server-side handling particularly important. Evaluate the authorization contract first, then operational fit. Browser permissions still come from application policy.

Put the preventative check before token issuance

The following complete Go program checks the local admission invariant and reads the channel through the API without inventing a token payload. Save it as main.go and run it with Go; its optional first argument is the requested channel. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL in the trusted server environment, using the documented HTTPS API base ending in /v1. With no argument, the program checks the authorized channel. Passing shop:amber-test:room:checkout-42 rejects the mismatch with exit status 1 before any network request. It creates no room and issues no token.

The allowed channel is a fixed server-side fixture for this example; provision it in the target environment before running the diagnostic. In production, derive it from the authenticated shopper's authorized order and room, and use the checked value when constructing the documented token request. The program prints the proposed scope and decision, then surfaces the channel-read response without assuming undocumented response fields. An actual issuer must separately record the scope it successfully minted.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func readChannel(channel string) error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    target, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || target.Scheme != "https" || target.Host == "" ||
        target.User != nil || target.Path != "/v1" ||
        target.RawQuery != "" || target.Fragment != "" || key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set the trusted HTTPS API base ending in /v1 and API key")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            base+"/realtime/channel/get/"+url.PathEscape(channel), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 65537))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 65536 {
            return fmt.Errorf("channel response exceeded diagnostic size budget")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds diagnostic deadline")
                }
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("channel read HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("channel read retry budget exhausted")
}

type Decision struct {
    Environment string   `json:"environment"`
    Scope       []string `json:"proposed_scope"`
    Requested   string   `json:"requested_channel"`
    Allowed     bool     `json:"allowed"`
}

func main() {
    const authorized = "shop:amber:room:checkout-42"
    requested := authorized
    if len(os.Args) > 2 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: go run main.go [requested-channel]")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if len(os.Args) == 2 {
        requested = os.Args[1]
    }

    decision := Decision{
        Environment: "checkout-example",
        Scope:       []string{authorized},
        Requested:   requested,
        Allowed:     requested == authorized,
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(decision); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if !decision.Allowed {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "channel is outside the authorized scope")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if err := readChannel(requested); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The trap is letting a browser-supplied channel become its own authorization evidence. This example compares against a trusted fixture; replacing that fixture with a copy of requested would preserve the appearance of validation while removing the boundary. Trimming, lowercasing, or rewriting tenant prefixes here would likewise conceal a disagreement that should be resolved in the application's naming policy.

Fix the mapping.

Once the server has established the shopper's permitted channel, feed that same exact value into issuance and return the corresponding subscription instruction to the browser. Avoid independently reconstructing it in two places. Persist enough issuance evidence to compare the actual token scope against the browser's subscription later, without storing the bearer credential itself.

Where this incident lesson stops

This advice applies to missing in-app notifications associated with an e-commerce video room. It does not diagnose a media connection, establish that a publish happened, or prove that every authorized notification was delivered. Matching scope and channel names is necessary for this authorization check; it is not a delivery receipt.

When scope, environment, and channel existence all agree, move the investigation to evidence for the application's publish and receive path. Keep room admission and notification admission distinct in that investigation. Broadening browser permissions to make a symptom disappear leaves the original question unanswered: did this shopper receive exactly the authority the checkout workflow intended?

Sources

References for the media boundary and the competing authorization contracts discussed above:

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • Ably token authentication: https://ably.com/docs/auth/token
  • Ably capabilities: https://ably.com/docs/auth/capabilities
  • Pusher Channels authorization: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/server_api/authorizing-users/
  • LiveKit tokens and grants: https://docs.livekit.io/home/get-started/authentication/
  • PubNub Access Manager: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/security/access-control

title: Designing a Preview-First Custom Song Flow for Holiday & Milestone Gifts (2026 Notes)
description:
When shoppers compare personalized audio gifts before the holiday rush, two design choices decide whether a service feels trustworthy: letting people hear the result before paying, and keeping turnaround under a few minutes instead of a week.

Personalized Song Gift turns your story into an original song with their name in it — hear a free preview of both versions in minutes, keep it for $9.99 with an MP3, lyrics and a gift page.

Why Traditional Custom Song Workflows Create Drop-Off

In our earlier product build notes, we noticed that legacy custom song services typically ask for $150–$250 upfront, require a lengthy questionnaire, and deliver a single final audio file 4–7 days later. For buyers searching for a Songfinch alternative, paying upfront without knowing whether the vocal style or chorus fits the recipient is the #1 point of friction.

We documented the key differences across pricing, turnaround time, and preview models in our 2026 breakdown of the best custom song service landscape.

The Holiday Rush Test Case: Zero-Shipping Digital Keepsakes

December is the toughest test for any personalized gift flow. Shipping cutoffs close weeks before Christmas, yet people still want something that feels deeply personal rather than a generic gift card.

With a custom Christmas song, the flow stays lightweight:

  1. Story prompt: Add the recipient's name, shared holiday memories, and musical genre.
  2. Two free 60-second previews: Hear two distinct arrangements in minutes with no account signup required.
  3. One-time unlock ($9.99): Keep the preferred version (or $19.99 for a 3-song bundle) with full MP3 download, lyric sheet, shareable gift page, and a printable QR code to tuck inside a holiday card.

Key Takeaways for Building Consumer Gift Flows

  • Remove account walls before the aha moment: Letting visitors hear their recipient's name in the chorus before creating an account dramatically raises trust.
  • Offer two distinct takes: Giving buyers an A/B choice between two arrangements turns a passive wait into an active creative decision.
  • Deliver both digital and physical-ready formats: Pairing a shareable gift page with a printable QR code lets a digital gift sit cleanly inside a physical greeting card.

title: Your Downloaded Images Are Sideways: Parsing EXIF Orientation in JPEG, WebP and AVIF
description:
Every image collector eventually ships a bug report that reads like this: "the images I downloaded are rotated 90 degrees." And every developer answers it once with "that's just how the camera saved it", and then spends three hours discovering that it is not that simple.

The pixels on disk are not rotated. The file declares a rotation. Two different consumers — your browser, your image viewer, your design tool — disagree about whether to apply that declaration, and the one that disagrees with your pipeline is the one your user opens first.

This post is about where that declaration lives, byte by byte, in JPEG, WebP and AVIF, what browsers actually do with it, and why "just rotate it afterwards" is a trap that produces double-rotated images in production.

The photo was never sideways

A modern phone camera has a sensor that is physically landscape. When you hold the phone upright, the sensor still records a 4032 × 3024 landscape frame; the firmware then writes Orientation = 6 into the EXIF block, meaning "the viewer should rotate this 90° clockwise to display it correctly". The JPEG bitstream is untouched. Decode it with an orientation-unaware decoder and you get a correctly-exposed, correctly-colored, sideways photo.

That single integer is the entire problem. It is also, in practice, the most common metadata field in the world of image tooling that gets dropped, duplicated, or applied twice.

Where the flag lives: JPEG

JPEG is a marker stream. FF D8 (SOI) starts the file, then a sequence of segments, each introduced by FF plus a marker byte and, for most markers, a two-byte big-endian length that includes the length field itself.

EXIF rides in an APP1 segment (FF E1). Its payload begins with the six-byte signature 45 78 69 66 00 00 ("Exif\0\0"), followed by a TIFF structure:

  • a two-byte byte-order mark: II (0x4949) little-endian or MM (0x4D4D) big-endian
  • a two-byte magic 0x002A
  • a four-byte offset to the first image file directory (IFD0)

An IFD is a two-byte entry count followed by 12-byte entries. Each entry is tag (2 bytes), type (2 bytes), count (4 bytes), and a four-byte value-or-offset field. Orientation is tag 0x0112, type 3 (SHORT), count 1 — so the value lives in the first two bytes of the value field, and you have to read it with the endianness you detected from the II/MM mark.

That is roughly fifteen lines of parsing. The hard part is not parsing, it is knowing that you must:

  1. scan for APP1 rather than assuming it is the first segment after SOI (it usually is, but APP0 JFIF and APP2 ICC profiles can precede it),
  2. stop scanning at the first SOS marker (FF DA), because after that you are in entropy-coded scan data where FF bytes appear constantly and any marker-walking logic will start hallucinating,
  3. read the value with the correct endianness, because half the cameras in the world write big-endian and the rest write little-endian.

The eight defined values and their intended transforms:

1 = no transform (storage orientation)
2 = mirror horizontal
3 = rotate 180
4 = mirror vertical
5 = transpose (mirror horizontal + rotate 270 CW)
6 = rotate 90 CW
7 = transverse (mirror horizontal + rotate 90 CW)
8 = rotate 270 CW

Values 5 through 8 involve a transpose, which is why naive implementations that only special-case 1, 3, 6 and 8 quietly mangle every mirrored selfie.

WebP and AVIF do it differently, which is the part that bites

WebP is a RIFF container: RIFF, a four-byte size, WEBP, then chunks identified by four-character codes. If the file carries EXIF, it is in a chunk with the fourcc EXIF, and — this is the detail that trips up JPEG-trained parsers — the chunk payload starts directly with the TIFF header. There is no Exif\0\0 signature to skip. Read the chunk body, detect II/MM, walk IFD0, read tag 0x0112.

AVIF is not a metadata container at all. It is ISOBMFF, a tree of boxes, and orientation is expressed as a transformative property rather than a tag:

  • irot (image rotation): a one-byte angle field where the lower two bits hold the angle in anticlockwise units of 90°.
  • imir (image mirror): a one-byte axis field, 0 meaning the vertical axis, 1 meaning the horizontal axis.

Both boxes live inside meta → iprp → ipco, referenced from the item property association list. A file can carry an irot and an imir together, applied in order, and HEIF-derived encoders use clap (clean aperture) on top of that. So an AVIF pipeline that reads EXIF only will report "no orientation" for a file that is genuinely rotated, because the rotation was never in EXIF.

To make this worse, browsers apply AVIF irot/imir during decode with no CSS involvement at all. The displayed image is correct, the decoded pixels are correct, and your metadata-only reader is the only component in the chain that is wrong.

What the browser actually does

Here is the behavior that makes pipelines inconsistent:

  • <img src> applies orientation automatically. The CSS property image-orientation defaults to from-image, which means the browser reads the EXIF flag and rotates at paint time. Since Chrome 81 this has been the default across all major browsers.
  • createImageBitmap(blob) also defaults to imageOrientation: "from-image". Passing "none" gives you the raw, stored-orientation pixels — which is exactly what you want for a hash or a thumbnail you will rotate yourself, and exactly what you do not want if you forgot the option exists.
  • canvas.drawImage(htmlImageElement, ...) draws already-oriented pixels, because the element decoded them that way.
  • PNG has no orientation semantics. The eXIf chunk exists in the PNG extensions spec, but browsers do not apply it. Once you transcode a rotated JPEG to PNG, the rotation information is gone unless you baked it into the pixels.

That last point is the trap. A pipeline that says "read EXIF, rotate the image afterwards" works for JPEG and silently produces upside-down PNGs, because by the time the file is PNG the evidence has been re-encoded away. The correct order is: decode in stored orientation (imageOrientation: "none"), apply the transform to a canvas, then encode. Bake first, write second. Never write an EXIF flag you are not sure the next consumer honors.

And never do both. A surprising number of exported files carry Orientation = 6 and rotated pixels, because two stages of the pipeline each "fixed" it. The file looks right in a viewer that ignores EXIF and sideways in the one that honors it.

The cost of getting it right

Three practical costs, each of which shapes the design:

Byte access. EXIF for JPEG sits near the front of the file, usually within the first 64 KB, so a Range: bytes=0-65535 request is enough and you can skip the full download. But a SOS can arrive later than 64 KB on images with large embedded thumbnails, and some CDNs answer 200 and send the whole body anyway. So you stream, cap the buffer, and bail out with "orientation unknown" instead of downloading 8 MB to find one integer.

Re-encoding. Baking rotation means decoding to a bitmap, transforming, and re-encoding. For a 200-image export that is real CPU time and a real quality decision: re-encoding a JPEG at quality 92 costs you a generation of artifacts. Tools that care store the transform as an editing instruction and apply it once, at export.

Privacy. The same EXIF block that carries orientation also carries GPS coordinates, camera make and model, body serial number, lens serial, DateTimeOriginal, and often a thumbnail of whatever the photo looked like before it was cropped. A batch downloader that "keeps the metadata intact" is redistributing location data with every file. Stripping EXIF entirely is the safe default for anything leaving the machine; keeping it is a deliberate choice for archives that need provenance.

What OmniPic does with this

This is the layer OmniPic AI Studio Pro is built around, and it is the reason the export path looks more complicated than a zip of URLs.

When a full-site inspection finishes, every collected image has been through: header-based dimension and format detection, orientation resolution (EXIF tag 0x0112 for JPEG and WebP, irot/imir for AVIF), and a decision record for whether the transform must be baked. On export, rotated images are decoded in stored orientation, transformed on a canvas, and re-encoded — so what lands in your reference library is upright in every viewer, not just in the one you happened to test.

The parts that are already handled:

  • Full-site image inspection with classification — one pass over the page collects image elements, CSS backgrounds, srcset candidates and lazy-loaded sources, then groups them by source and type.
  • CDN original recovery — Alibaba OSS, Tencent COS and Qiniu thumbnail URLs are reverse-mapped to the original asset.
  • On-device AI reverse image search — a MobileNet backbone produces a 1024-dimension feature vector, accelerated with WebGPU; nothing leaves the browser.
  • pHash visual deduplication — perceptual hashing collapses near-identical variants into one entry before download.
  • Direct Eagle and Billfish integration — collected assets land in the reference manager you already use, upright and with sensible metadata.
  • Streaming ZIP export for 2,000+ images — a streaming archive writer keeps memory flat, so a huge export does not freeze the browser.
  • 100% local processing — decoding, rotating, hashing, embedding and packaging all run in your browser; no upload, no account.

The configuration surface for this — orientation baking, metadata policy, deduplication thresholds — looks like this:

And the export view, where the baked-in orientation and metadata policy decide what the ZIP actually contains:

OmniPic AI Studio Pro is available on all three major stores: Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. Install it here:

https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/omnipic-studio-pro/cokoeaaaglgcljahaffjeijomhmkljlc

If you are building your own collector, take the small piece even if you never install anything: read tag 0x0112 before you touch a pixel, decide whether the transform is baked or declared, and never do both. Orientation is fifteen lines of parsing and about four hours of debugging if you skip it.

title: SENTRIX: Turning Public Data into Attack Surface Intelligence
description:
An Advanced Passive Reconnaissance Platform Built with Go

In modern cybersecurity, understanding an organization's external attack surface begins with collecting and analyzing information scattered across multiple public sources. This is the challenge that inspired SENTRIX, an advanced passive reconnaissance and attack surface intelligence platform developed by MONSIF HMOURI (MONSTR MIND) under MONSTR MIND LABS.

Built entirely with Go, SENTRIX brings together five public intelligence sources: crt.sh, Wayback Machine, Common Crawl, urlscan.io, and AlienVault OTX. Instead of examining each source separately, SENTRIX consolidates their publicly available data into a unified intelligence workflow.

The platform collects discovered URLs and hostnames, normalizes records, removes duplicates, classifies endpoints, validates scope, and correlates observations across independent sources. It also assigns confidence levels based on source corroboration, helping researchers understand how strongly a finding is supported by available evidence.

SENTRIX includes project management, incremental rescanning, historical snapshots, filtering, backup and restore functionality, integrity checks, and structured reporting in JSON, CSV, TXT, and HTML formats.

Its built-in Scope Guard supports root domains, subdomains, exact hosts, URL prefixes, and exclusions, keeping research organized around explicitly defined boundaries.

Designed for authorized security research and bug bounty reconnaissance, SENTRIX is passive by design. It relies on information already available through public data sources and does not perform exploitation, credential testing, fuzzing, or direct vulnerability testing against target systems.

The objective is straightforward: transform scattered public information into organized, correlated, and useful attack surface intelligence.
