title: Why your MyBatis logs show question marks (and how to turn them into runnable SQL)
description:
When something breaks in production, the first thing I do is pull a SQL statement out of the logs and run it against the database myself.

What I actually get is this:

==>  Preparing: SELECT id, username, status FROM user WHERE username = ? AND status = ? AND created_at > ?
==> Parameters: tom(String), 1(Integer), 2026-11-20 10:00:00.0(Timestamp)

Three placeholders, three values, and I have to line them up by hand. Add quotes to the string, reformat the timestamp, strip the type annotations. Doing this once is fine. Doing it fifteen times a day is not.

So I wrote a tool to do it for me. I assumed it would be a weekend of regex. It turned into a description of what MyBatis log parsing actually involves, and I want to write down the six places it goes wrong — partly so I remember, partly because anyone else automating this will hit the same walls.

Trap 1: The parameters line often isn't there at all

Preparing: and Parameters: are two separate log statements at two different levels.

Preparing: is DEBUG. Parameters: requires TRACE.

Plenty of projects run at DEBUG for the mapper package, so you see the statement but never the values. No parsing tool can fix this — there is nothing to parse.

The check is one search: look for Parameters: in the log. If zero hits, it's a level problem, not a parser problem. Turn the mapper package up to TRACE in logback.xml or log4j2.xml.

There's a variant of this: the level is fine but another library owns the output. Add p6spy, or a log-shipping agent, and the line may be reformatted or dropped before you ever see it.

Trap 2: The prefix is not consistent

Depending on the environment, the version, and whatever wrapper is in play:

==>  Preparing: SELECT ...          # standard StdOutImpl
Preparing: SELECT ...               # bare form
==> Preparing: SELECT ...           # single arrow
[MyBatis] Preparing: SELECT ...     # framework prefix

Some teams prepend trace ids or tenant ids, which makes the prefix longer still.

One regex does not cover all of this. The reliable approach is to treat the prefix as optional noise: anchor on Preparing: and Parameters: and skip whatever comes before them. Do not try to match ==> specifically.

Trap 3: Batches don't line up

Single statements are easy. Batch inserts are not:

==>  Preparing: INSERT INTO log (a, b, c) VALUES (?, ?, ?)
==> Parameters: 1(Integer), 2(Integer), 3(Integer)
==> Parameters: 4(Integer), 5(Integer), 6(Integer)
==> Parameters: 7(Integer), 8(Integer), 9(Integer)

One statement, several parameter lines, each line a separate execution. If your parser takes "the last parameters line", you silently lose the first two rows.

The correct model: consecutive Parameters: lines belong to the same statement as repeated executions. Render them as one batch operation rather than three unrelated INSERTs, otherwise the reader can't tell what happened.

Trap 4: Values contain commas and parentheses

This is where a regex-based parser falls apart.

The parameters line is comma-separated, but values can contain commas:

==> Parameters: 张三,李四(String), 2026-11-20 10:00:00.0(Timestamp)

That is one string parameter, not two. Split on comma and it tears in half.

Parentheses are just as bad: a value containing () breaks the (Type) extraction. Quoted strings with escapes break naive regex immediately.

What worked for me was a small state machine: walk the line character by character, track whether you're inside a string and how deep the parentheses go, and only treat a comma as a separator when depth is 0 and you're outside quotes. It's not clever, but it's an order of magnitude more reliable than regex.

Trap 5: null and the string "null" look the same 

==> Parameters: null, null(String), null(Integer)

Three different things:

  • null — actually null
  • null(String) — the four-character string "null"
  • null(Integer) — shouldn't exist, but if it does, the type info is not trustworthy

Rendering the first as NULL and the second as 'null' gives completely different results, and neither throws. Silent wrong answers are worse than loud failures.

The only signal you have is whether a type annotation is present.

Trap 6: Strip the type, but keep the format

tom(String) becomes 'tom' — drop the type, add quotes.

But 2026-11-20 10:00:00.0(Timestamp) cannot just be type-stripped: it's a date and must become '2026-11-20 10:00:00'. The trailing .0 is Java's fractional-second placeholder; paste it into a client and some dialects reject it outright.

The same category of problem:

  • true(Boolean) → 1 or TRUE depending on dialect
  • byte[] parameters → logged as [B@1a2b3c, which is unrecoverable
  • Large text → truncated to ...(truncated) in the log

Each of these needs explicit handling, or an honest "this one can't be reconstructed" — not a best-guess SQL that happens to be wrong.

Two ways around all of this

Every trap above lives on the "reconstruct SQL from log text" path. You can avoid that path entirely:

Change the data source. Instead of parsing logs, intercept at the JDBC layer. A lightweight Java agent hooks PreparedStatement.execute* and gets the statement with parameters already bound, plus real timing, affected row count and the exception. No log format issues, no level requirements. The cost is that the application has to actually be running, and you authorize the agent once.

Change where you look. Instead of grepping in a terminal, read the SQL inside the IDE. I built an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that parses the console output into runnable SQL, clusters statements with the same shape, highlights slow queries, and jumps back to the source line. Once the app is running, the same plugin shows the JDBC-level capture: real parameters, milliseconds, rows affected, the original exception.

The part that matters day to day: the reconstructed SQL runs from inside the IDE. No copy-paste round trip through a database client.

Boundaries, stated plainly

This solves "turn what's in the log into something a human can use". It does not solve:

  • Missing parameters when the log level is too low (no data is no data)
  • byte[] and truncated values
  • Timing or row counts from the console path (the log doesn't contain them)
  • Static preview versus actual execution (static constants get inlined; pagination literals get evaluated)

The plugin is free and open source (Apache-2.0), requires IDEA 2024.3+, and is on the JetBrains Marketplace as MyBatis SQL Visualizer. Docs at sql-visualizer.jvtools.cn.

I'm the author of that plugin. All six traps are ones I actually hit while building the parser, not a generic list of "things that might go wrong". If you've written something similar, you've probably met a few of them — I'd be interested in the shapes I haven't seen yet.

title: Why one wallpaper crop cannot fit two screens
description:
A foldable phone is two screens with two different shapes, and almost every wallpaper you download assumes you have one.

The inner display is roughly square-ish (2670 × 1878 on the Duo), the outer display is tall and narrow (1398 × 2034). A photo cropped for Instagram fits neither. A photo cropped for the inner screen gets its subject sliced in half when it lands on the cover display.

The mistake is cropping once

Most people pick an image, set it as wallpaper, and then discover the outer screen shows the middle third of a face. The fix is not a better crop tool. It is deciding what each screen is for.

I use three rules now:

  1. Outer screen = identity. It is what you see 200 times a day, unlocked, in a hurry. It needs one clear subject and no text.
  2. Inner screen = scene. It is what you look at for a minute at a time. It can carry detail, depth and a horizon.
  3. Same photo, different crop. If the two screens show different images, the phone feels like two devices taped together.

Safe zones, not just aspect ratios

Even with the right ratio, the clock, the notification stack and the bottom gesture bar eat the edges. On the tall outer screen the top 12% and bottom 10% are effectively gone. On the inner screen the fold crease runs down the middle, and a face centred on it looks wrong.

So a wallpaper that works has:

  • a subject placed off-centre, away from the crease;
  • no important detail in the top or bottom 10%;
  • enough contrast at the top for a white clock to stay readable.

Resolution is not the same as sharpness

The inner screen is 2670 × 1878 at roughly 400 ppi. A 1080p image stretched to that looks soft, and JPEG artifacts become visible on gradients — skies are the worst case. Exporting at 3840 × 2700 gives the scaler room to work and survives the occasional zoom.

What I ended up building

I collect wallpapers that are already cut for both screens, with the two crops from one source image, at 4K. Best iPhone Duo has 135 of them, sorted by category (nature, abstract, city, space, night), plus a local cropping tool that runs in the browser and does not upload the photo anywhere.

The part I did not expect to care about: a download page that states the exact pixel dimensions and the file format for each wallpaper. Half the "4K" wallpapers on the web are 1080p upscales, and you only find out after you set one and look at the sky.

The general rule

Any device with two displays turns a single-image workflow into a two-crop workflow. The tools that win are the ones that treat the pair as one unit, not the ones that let you crop twice as fast.

title: I built Brokspace: local-first code search and context for AI coding agents
description:
I have a small confession: I'm much more comfortable building things than talking about the things I build. But after working on this project for a while, I figured it was time to leave my comfort zone and share it.

Meet Brokspace - a local-first tool that makes your development workspace searchable and ready for AI coding agents.

It started with a problem I kept running into

Around May 2026, I started building a small tool in Rust to help with my studies and day-to-day project work.

As AI became a bigger part of my development workflow, I found myself spending more time managing the surrounding chaos: prompts, MCP servers, skills, agents, project context, and all the little pieces needed to help an AI assistant understand a codebase.

And there was another problem: asking an LLM to understand a large repository often meant spending time collecting context, sending too much information, waiting for responses, and repeating the process in the next session.

I wanted something that could understand my workspace locally, find the relevant pieces of code, and make that context available to the tools and agents I already use.

So I started building it. With a little help from my friend Claudinho (Claude Code), the original study helper gradually became something much bigger.

I eventually decided to open source it. If it was helping me every day, maybe it could help another developer too.

So, what is Brokspace?

Brokspace gives your workspace a local index that can be used by the terminal, the editor, your LLM, and coding agents.

The goal is simple: let agents find and use relevant project context without having to ingest your entire codebase every time.

Today, the project includes a Rust-based CLI and runtime, a VS Code extension, an agent integration, an SDK for building extensions, and a shard template.

Some of the things you can do with it:

  • Search code by meaning or keywords across repositories and linked workspaces.
  • Ask questions about your code and get answers grounded in retrieved source references.
  • Expose workspace search and memory to coding agents through MCP.
  • Reuse engineering workflows through shareable SKILL.md skills.
  • Review local changes and generate commit messages from staged diffs.
  • Extend the workspace with small event-driven programs called shards.

A little bit under the hood

I wanted to make the project useful, but also interesting to build. A few implementation details:

1. Syntax-aware indexing

Instead of splitting source code into arbitrary text windows, Brokspace uses Tree-sitter-based parsing to create chunks around code structures such as functions, classes, and other definitions. That helps keep useful pieces of code together when building the index.

2. Hybrid search

Search combines two approaches:

  • BM25, for keyword-based retrieval.
  • Semantic search, using embeddings generated locally.

The rankings are fused so a result can be relevant by meaning even when it doesn't contain the exact words in the query, while still benefiting from precise keyword matches.

The current implementation uses a local embedding model through ONNX Runtime and stores index data in LanceDB or memory-mapped Arrow files. The index lives inside the workspace's .brokspace/ directory.

3. One local context layer for different tools

The CLI, VS Code extension, and coding-agent integrations share the same workspace index. Brokspace exposes tools through MCP, so compatible agents can search the project and use workspace memory without each integration building its own separate index.

4. An event bus and extensible shards

The runtime includes a local event bus. The default brok-agent shard tracks workspace changes and supports agent workflows such as grounded answers and reviews.

Shards are small, separate programs that subscribe to declared workspace events and publish their own events. The brok-sdk provides the protocol, manifest schema, and Rust client, while the wire protocol is documented for other implementations too.

This is one of the parts I'm especially excited about: instead of hard-coding every possible integration into the core, developers can build small extensions that react to what happens in a workspace.

Local-first means being deliberate about data

The index is created and stored on your machine. You can use a local model through Ollama or LM Studio, or choose a hosted OpenAI-compatible provider.

One important distinction: when you choose a hosted model, the relevant context included in a request is sent to that provider so it can generate an answer. Brokspace does not need to upload your entire repository to build its index, and the agent scrubs common secrets from context before sending it to a model. I prefer being explicit about this rather than calling something “private” without explaining the trade-offs.

A similar note applies to shards: their requested capabilities are declared and shown during installation, but filesystem and network restrictions are not yet enforced by an OS-level sandbox. As always, review what you install and trust the code you run.

Try it out

On macOS or Linux, you can install the CLI and initialize a workspace with:

curl -fsSL https://brokspace.org/install.sh | sh

cd /path/to/your/project
brok init
brok search "where do we validate access tokens?"

You can also use the VS Code extension or explore the getting started guide.

Why open source it now?

The core CLI has passed 300 downloads, and I've already received some early contributions from the community. That encouragement gave me the push to share the project more broadly.

Brokspace is still evolving. There are rough edges, things to improve, and probably a few bugs waiting for their moment to shine. That's part of why I'm opening it up: feedback from people using it in different workflows is incredibly valuable.

The project is dual-licensed under MIT or Apache-2.0. You can explore the code, open an issue, start a discussion, build a shard, or send a pull request.

  • 🌐 Website: brokspace.org
  • 🦀 Core project: github.com/brokspace/brok
  • 🧩 VS Code extension: github.com/brokspace/vscode
  • 💬 Discussions: Brokspace on GitHub

And that's Brokspace. The name is inspired by Brokkr, the master blacksmith from Norse mythology, and the forge where he worked. I liked the idea of a tool that helps developers forge better workflows. Apparently, naming things is still one of the hardest problems in software engineering.

Give it a try, tell me what breaks, suggest what should be better, contribute if something catches your eye , and constructive criticism is very welcome. And naturally, I'm always open to an invitation to grab a coffee.

Thanks for reading! ☕

title: How to Gate CPaaS Platforms in Go — 3 SMS Alert Checks
description:
Compare CPaaS platforms for a property-management SMS alert rollout by checking whether each integration preserves one signup verification intent through retries, expiry, and rollback. Record pricing against that tested workload. A successful send request alone is too weak a release criterion.

Short answer: compare CPaaS platforms for SMS alerts by implementing the same tenant-signup acceptance checks against each candidate, then recording the integration work those checks expose. Treat pricing as a workload worksheet, and separate signup verification from maintenance notices and urgent alerts: they have different deadlines and different consequences when a message arrives late.

This runbook uses three executable Go checks and a local transport stub. Its numbers are illustrative test inputs, not measured traffic or provider limits. The decision axis is integration effort: how much application code, operational ownership, and release coordination does each option require before a tenant can safely use a verification link?

Scope matters here. OWASP describes risks around SMS authentication, including SIM swapping, and advises considering alternatives for sensitive applications. Delivering an account-signup link should therefore establish only the assurance your signup design actually supports; it must not silently become proof that the recipient owns a property, holds a lease, or can authorize a payment.

What should an SMS platform comparison actually prove?

Start with the failure signal: the application cannot tell whether a tenant's pending verification request is eligible for another send. Perhaps the previous request timed out, perhaps a worker restarted, or perhaps a receipt arrived after the signup screen had already offered a resend. These are acceptance-test scenarios, not claims about a particular service.

Freeze the intent first.

For this design, one signup attempt has one internal verification intent, an expiry, and a record of submission attempts; an explicit resend policy decides when another attempt is allowed. Keep the verification token and its redemption state in the application, where the expiry and single-use decision can be enforced independently of the messaging integration. A transport receipt must never activate the account.

That boundary makes a comparison useful. Ask each candidate integration to satisfy the same contract: describe an ambiguous submission outcome, correlate later status information, and preserve enough evidence to avoid guessing during an incident. Mark an undocumented behavior as unverified and resolve it with documentation or a controlled test. Don't convert a missing answer into an assumed guarantee.

The buy-versus-build decision belongs beside that contract, because a shorter initial integration can move work into the on-call rotation.

Approach Integration work to record Operational ownership to assign
Managed verification workflow Map its token lifecycle, expiry rules, and resend behavior to the signup contract Who investigates an unsuccessful verification across application and service records?
Messaging transport with application-owned verification Implement token issuance, redemption, dispatch state, and status correlation The application team owns the verification state machine and recovery procedure
Self-operated dispatch worker around a transport Implement queue handling, concurrency limits, deployment, and replay controls in addition to verification The team owns worker capacity, backlog response, and safe rollback

These are architectural choices to investigate, not a feature matrix of named products. Count the work in each row before comparing quotes. A candidate that needs a custom status reconciler has a different integration burden from one whose documented lifecycle fits the application, even when both can submit the same SMS body.

For use cases, keep three separate worksheet rows: tenant signup links, scheduled maintenance notices, and urgent property alerts. Give each a deadline, expected burst, retry policy, and accountable team. Only the first row drives this runbook; sharing a transport does not justify sharing its release criteria.

Step 1: Budget the signup burst before connecting a transport

Make the load assumption executable. The following standalone program models 120 signup intents arriving together, a five-minute verification window, and an application dispatch limit of two submissions per second. Those values are proposed test settings. Replace them with measured arrival patterns, your chosen expiry, and a documented usable sending limit before making a production decision.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    const signups = 120
    const maxAttempts = 2
    const submissionsPerSecond = 2
    const validity = 5 * time.Minute
    const reserve = 1 * time.Minute

    submissions := signups * maxAttempts
    seconds := (submissions + submissionsPerSecond - 1) / submissionsPerSecond
    drain := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    eligible := drain+reserve < validity
    fmt.Printf("submissions=%d drain=%s reserve=%s eligible=%t\n",
        submissions, drain, reserve, eligible)
    if !eligible {
        panic("dispatch budget exceeds the proposed verification window")
    }
}

Save this block as a Go program and run it with the Go toolchain. It calculates 240 possible submissions and a two-minute drain budget, leaving the proposed one-minute reserve within the five-minute window. The pass condition is the strict inequality in the program; it does not demonstrate delivery performance.

That distinction is the trap. This arithmetic assumes the dispatcher continuously achieves the configured rate and ignores receipt delay, outages, and the tenant's time to open the link, so passing it only establishes that the proposed admission budget is worth testing. Define a separate signup SLO around completed verification before expiry, and observe dispatch latency as a supporting signal rather than substituting it for the user outcome.

For an initial rollout, require an explicit policy when the budget fails: reduce admitted signup traffic, reserve more dispatch capacity, or revisit the verification window through the security review. Increasing worker count without checking the usable transport limit is not a capacity plan.

The pricing worksheet should use this same workload. Request comparable quotes for destinations, message composition, expected attempts, and applicable charges, then record any assumptions that require confirmation. Do not compare a single advertised message price while leaving the retry workload undefined. Engineering time and on-call ownership belong in the decision record too, without pretending they can be reduced to an unsupported savings percentage.

Step 2: Exercise the verification intent with a local sender

Before introducing credentials or external calls, make the application prove its own dispatch boundary. This standalone example uses a fictional tenant intent, a reserved example-domain link, and an injected sender; it deliberately sends no SMS. It checks expiry before dispatch and records an accepted submission only after the sender returns successfully.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Intent struct {
    ID        string
    ExpiresAt time.Time
    Submitted bool
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(context.Context, string, string) error
}

type LocalSender struct {
    Calls int
}

func (s *LocalSender) Send(ctx context.Context, id, link string) error {
    if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    s.Calls++
    return nil
}

func dispatch(ctx context.Context, now time.Time, i *Intent, s Sender) error {
    if i.Submitted {
        return nil
    }
    if !now.Before(i.ExpiresAt) {
        return errors.New("verification intent expired")
    }
    if err := s.Send(ctx, i.ID, "https://tenant.example/verify"); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    i.Submitted = true
    return nil
}

func main() {
    now := time.Now()
    i := Intent{ID: "tenant-signup-001", ExpiresAt: now.Add(5 * time.Minute)}
    s := &LocalSender{}
    for n := 0; n < 2; n++ {
        if err := dispatch(context.Background(), now, &i, s); err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
    }
    expired := Intent{ID: "tenant-signup-002", ExpiresAt: now}
    if err := dispatch(context.Background(), now, &expired, s); err == nil {
        panic("expired intent was accepted")
    }
    if s.Calls != 1 {
        panic("unexpected dispatch count")
    }
    fmt.Println("repeat and expiry checks passed")
}

The decision criterion is concrete: two sequential dispatch requests for the first intent produce one local submission, and the expired intent produces none. The fixed link is a placeholder, not a verification-token implementation. A real application must issue and redeem its own token under the chosen security policy.

There is a substantial production boundary here. This in-memory example cannot coordinate concurrent workers or survive a restart, and a transport might accept a request before the application loses its connection or fails to persist the result. Persist the intent and attempt history, coordinate competing workers through durable state, and introduce an explicit unknown-outcome state; only automate another submission when the documented integration contract makes that action safe. The HTTP specification's treatment of retrying non-idempotent requests is relevant to that decision. Consider the controlled test where the remote side accepts an attempt and the local worker stops before saving its result: after restart, the application sees an unfinished attempt even though a message might already be on its way. A durable attempt record makes that uncertainty visible, but it cannot by itself prove remote acceptance. The adapter must either reconcile using documented evidence or leave the attempt unresolved under an explicit operator policy. That limitation is why the local sequential check is not suitable as proof of safe production retries.

Do not label an unknown outcome as a rejection.

When adapting a candidate, record how much code is needed to resolve that state, which identifiers remain available after a timeout, and how status updates are authenticated and correlated according to its documentation. Those are comparison results with consequences for integration effort. An interface with one method can still conceal several days of state-machine work.

Keep observability equally deliberate: count eligible intents, accepted submissions, unknown outcomes, expired intents, and completed redemptions; measure queue age separately. Use opaque correlation identifiers in operational events, and exclude verification links and tokens from routine logs. Otherwise a troubleshooting convenience becomes an additional place where signup credentials must be protected.

Keep tokens private.

Step 3: Verify the release gate and rehearse rollback

Make rollback stop new dispatch admission while preserving existing verification state. Deleting pending intents or automatically replaying them through another integration leaves the operator making a delivery decision with less evidence, precisely when the original outcome may still be unknown.

This final standalone program expresses a small release gate. Its 2,000 ms queue-age limit and zero tolerated unknown outcomes are illustrative canary criteria; choose production thresholds from the signup SLO and observed workload rather than inheriting these numbers accidentally.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func admit(enabled bool, queueAge time.Duration, unknown int) bool {
    return enabled && queueAge <= 2*time.Second && unknown == 0
}

func main() {
    cases := []struct {
        name    string
        enabled bool
        age     time.Duration
        unknown int
        want    bool
    }{
        {"healthy canary", true, time.Second, 0, true},
        {"queue over budget", true, 3 * time.Second, 0, false},
        {"outcome unresolved", true, time.Second, 1, false},
        {"rollback enabled", false, time.Second, 0, false},
    }
    for _, c := range cases {
        got := admit(c.enabled, c.age, c.unknown)
        if got != c.want {
            panic(c.name)
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s: admit=%t\n", c.name, got)
    }
}

Require all four cases to pass before wiring the gate into dispatch admission. This program verifies the predicate, not the production control plane: the deployment rehearsal must also show that workers observe the disabled setting, that in-flight attempts remain traceable, and that already-issued links retain their intended redemption behavior until expiry.

Then run controlled acceptance cases through the actual adapter: sequential duplicates, competing workers, expiry at the boundary, a timeout after possible acceptance, and delayed or repeated status updates where supported. Assign an expected state transition to each case before running it. A test without a defined outcome is an expensive demonstration.

Record the evidence.

During a canary, track completed signup verification against the SLO alongside dispatch and unknown-outcome signals. If the release criteria fail, stop new admission, preserve evidence, and reconcile pending attempts before resuming or switching transports. Tell the signup UI the actual pending state; do not offer an automatic resend that bypasses the policy being investigated.

Choose the integration whose documented behavior passes these checks with an amount of application and operational work the platform team can own. Keep the workload quote alongside that evidence. For tenant signup, a defensible comparison ends with a tested release decision and a rehearsed rollback path.

title: Why we made the staging list read-only during merges
description:
A few hours before a release, bugs we had already fixed came back, and features that were finished were missing from the branch. I spent an hour in the commit log before finding the commit where it happened: everything before it looked normal, and everything after it was missing a lot of code.

The author was one of our game designers. He had hit a conflict dialog and clicked discard on all the staged files. From where he stood, that was a reasonable decision: he had not written those files, and he was afraid that committing them would break the repository. The files were other people's commits from the previous days. Several more commits had landed on top, so a simple revert would have thrown away their work too. I spent another five hours walking the log and stitching code back together. What I ended up with looked complete, but I did not trust the foundation, so we moved the release date.

That's the exact situation I wanted a tool to remove. Not "make Git easier" in general — just that one click.

The click that made sense

A merge brings files into your staged list that you never wrote. To someone who does not know what those files are, Restore or Discard is not a dangerous button; it is the obvious button. Blaming the person who clicked it is easy and useless. The interface offered a tidy way out of a situation it had never explained.

So when we built Light Git, a small Windows Git GUI, we decided that during a merge that list would be read-only. No checkboxes, no context menu, nowhere for Restore or Discard to act. If a file came in from the merge, you can look at it, but you cannot discard it from that screen.

The tradeoff is real, and I want to be honest about it: while a merge is in progress, you can no longer hand-pick which files to commit. We took that ability away on purpose. The cost of keeping it was a colleague's work disappearing, and I had already seen what that costs in an afternoon.

The other half: one less button to forget

The same thinking shaped the commit flow. On the Changes page, you tick the files you want, write a short message, and click Commit once. The app commits, updates, and pushes in that order, and only the ticked changes go out. There is no second button to forget and no separate staging area to keep in sync — the staging area is read-only in daily use too.

The error path follows the same rule. When a push is rejected, the app distinguishes "the remote has new commits" from "you don't have permission to push here." The first tells you to update before pushing again; the second tells you to switch accounts. There is no force push button, because a one-click way to overwrite a colleague's commit is its own accident waiting to happen.

Conflicts without a "mark as resolved" button

Conflict handling has the same shape. Each conflict is handled hunk by hunk: choose the current branch, the incoming branch, both, or edit the code directly. Conflicted files stay pinned at the top of the list and cannot be hidden by a filter, and the UI shows how many hunks are resolved and how many remain.

There is no Mark as resolved button. On commit, the app checks the actual file contents: if no conflict markers remain, the file counts as resolved and goes into the commit. A forgotten click can no longer be the reason a commit is rejected. For spreadsheets there are no markers to look for, so the conflict card offers a cell-by-cell diff with a switch between ours/theirs, base/ours and base/theirs, then resolves with the usual Use mine / Use theirs buttons.

What we deliberately did not build

This is not a full Git client, and it is not meant to be. There is no interactive rebase, no squash, no force push. For those workflows, use the command line or a full-featured GUI. The read-only list applies during a merge; ordinary commits are unaffected, and the tick boxes work as you would expect.

Our designers and ops team use it now, including people who would rather not think about Git at all. The goal was never to cover every Git workflow. It was to remove a small number of high-cost mistakes from the paths people actually take.

If you have watched someone lose a day's work in a conflict dialog: would locking the staged list during a merge have helped, or would it just get in your way? I would especially like to hear from people who merge often and hand-pick files as part of their normal routine.

title: Avatar Upload Backend Storage — Large-File Throughput and Snapshot Recovery for EU/US Apps
description:
Short answer: keep avatar metadata in the database, keep the bytes in an object-oriented store, and treat local disk as a cache; for a fintech app that must restore tenant snapshots, measure large-file throughput and recovery time before choosing a layout.

I learned this from a backup drill, not a diagram. A tenant restore looked healthy because the database rows came back quickly, while the larger file set was still copying. The login path then served a mix of old and new avatars. Nothing crashed. The data was simply at two points in time, which is worse during an incident because it is easy to miss.

The invariant is simple: one database record names the immutable object version, and a restore changes the active pointer only after the corresponding bytes and checksum are verified. Local disk can accelerate a hot read, but it cannot be the source of truth for a multi-instance service.

Evaluating the split-brain avatar set after a restore

Start with a control-plane row. It needs a tenant identifier, an opaque object key, content type, byte length, checksum, snapshot identifier, and lifecycle state such as pending, active, or deleted. The client may send a filename for display, but it must not choose the storage key. A stable key also makes retries understandable: an upload attempt can be repeated without overwriting a different tenant's object.

The byte plane should support streaming writes, range reads, checksums, and lifecycle rules. Those are boring requirements. They are also the ones that decide whether a 400 MB restore is observable or just a spinner. Database blobs can give transactional coupling, but large values compete with indexes, replication, backups, and connection memory. Local disk has low latency until the process is rescheduled, the volume fills, or a second instance receives the request. During one drill, the metadata replay finished in seconds while the file copy was still running; an API process on another host then answered with the previous avatar version. The monitor saw 200 responses and called the test green. The restore report was wrong because it counted rows, not verified bytes, and nobody had recorded which snapshot each object belonged to. Since then, I treat the pointer switch as the recovery event and every earlier step as preparation.

For a small app in the EU and US, residency is a policy decision, not a country-code column. Place each tenant's objects in an allowed region, record that placement with the snapshot, and make a restore refuse a cross-region copy unless policy explicitly permits it. Your mileage may vary: the acceptable region set, retention period, and recovery objective belong in the service's written requirements.

Keep the transaction boundary narrow. The database transaction records pending; the upload happens outside it; a finalize step verifies size and checksum before setting active. If the worker dies after bytes arrive but before finalize, a reconciler can find the orphan by key and apply a retention rule. If finalize succeeds before the bytes are durable, reads must fail closed rather than silently falling back to an older version.

No shortcut.

Reliability signals from the restore worker

Throughput is end-to-end. A fast storage target cannot compensate for a single-threaded copy loop, a tiny HTTP connection pool, or a restore job that serializes every tenant. Measure at least four values: sustained write rate, sustained read rate, time to first byte, and time to restore a representative snapshot. Record p50 and p95, because a mean hides the slow tenant that keeps an on-call shift open.

I use bounded concurrency per tenant and a separate global limit. That keeps one customer's 2 TB restore from consuming every socket while still allowing independent tenants to make progress. Each object copy carries its snapshot ID and checksum. The destination is written under a new immutable key; only the metadata pointer is mutable.

Here is the core of that copy decision in Go. It is intentionally storage-agnostic so the same test can run against a local emulator and the production adapter.

package restore

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
)

type Object struct {
    Key      string
    Size     int64
    Checksum string
}

type Store interface {
    Copy(ctx context.Context, sourceKey, destinationKey string) error
    Stat(ctx context.Context, key string) (Object, error)
}

func CopyVerified(ctx context.Context, store Store, source Object, destinationKey string) error {
    if source.Key == "" || destinationKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("empty object key")
    }
    if err := store.Copy(ctx, source.Key, destinationKey); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    copied, err := store.Stat(ctx, destinationKey)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if copied.Size != source.Size || copied.Checksum != source.Checksum {
        return fmt.Errorf("snapshot verification failed for %s", destinationKey)
    }
    return nil
}

The restore coordinator should persist a per-object result and an idempotency key. A retry of CopyVerified may find the destination already present; the adapter should treat an identical verified object as success. Do not delete the old active key until the new snapshot is fully verified and the pointer switch is committed. That ordering gives operators a known rollback point.

Layout Large-file behavior Restore evidence Best fit
Database blob Transactional metadata and bytes, but backup and replication load grow with payload size Row commit plus database backup record Small files where one transactional backup domain is required
Local disk Excellent single-host latency; weak across replicas and replacement events Volume snapshot, if one exists Disposable cache or a single-node prototype
Object store plus metadata Parallel transfer and independent lifecycle controls Object checksum plus database snapshot pointer Multi-tenant production uploads and selected-snapshot restore

The table is a trade-off, not a ranking. A database blob is reasonable when files are tiny and the database backup system is the audited boundary. Local disk is reasonable when losing the file is acceptable and regeneration is guaranteed. Neither is suitable when a tenant must restore a selected snapshot after a host replacement without rebuilding bytes from another system.

The catch is operational ownership. Object storage shifts work into key design, lifecycle cleanup, region policy, checksums, and reconciliation. It does not remove backup testing. A lifecycle rule can expire noncurrent objects, but the application still needs to ensure that a metadata pointer never references an expired version; document those rules and test them against a staging bucket. The lifecycle model in the AWS S3 object lifecycle documentation is a useful standards reference.

How should a user avatar upload backend choose storage for recovery?

Before accepting an upload, enforce an allowlist of media types, a maximum byte length, and an authorization check for the tenant. Store the server-observed length and checksum, not only the browser's claims. On download, authorize the tenant first and send a disposition that matches the intended behavior: inline for a rendered avatar or attachment for a forced download. The MDN Content-Disposition reference documents that distinction.

During a restore, page on stalled progress, checksum mismatches, and a rising orphan count. A successful HTTP response is not proof that the selected snapshot is complete. The runbook should name the snapshot, count expected and verified objects, record bytes copied, and state whether the metadata pointer has switched. I first thought a checksum at the end was enough; later I found that per-object results were what made a partial restore explainable.

Three words: verify, then switch.

Do not choose this design when the application must run entirely offline, when policy requires all bytes inside a transactional database, or when the team cannot operate reconciliation and restore drills. In those cases, stick with a database-backed blob layout and accept its throughput ceiling, or choose a managed backup system whose audit contract you can test. The right answer is the one your team can restore at 03:00, not the one with the shortest upload handler.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: Networking and caching in enterprise apps: own the stale data
description:
This is part 3 of 8 of the free series Frontend system design for enterprise applications, first published on tt-tech.io.

A customer makes a transfer, goes back to the dashboard, and sees the old balance. The transfer worked. The dashboard read a cache that nobody told about the write. In a bank, that is a support call, and sometimes a second transfer.

Caching sits in this part, next to networking, because in an enterprise app they are one question: where does this data live, and when is it wrong? A cache without an owner is a bug with a delay.

One boundary to the backend

Components never fetch. One data-access layer per domain talks to the backend, and everything else reads from it. That gives you one place to add auth, one place to cancel, one place to invalidate.

When the screens need a shape the domain APIs do not have, put a backend-for-frontend (BFF) between them, owned by the frontend team. Do it for shape and for secrets, not to avoid talking to the API team.

The contract is generated, and required is the truth

Generate the types from the OpenAPI document instead of writing them by hand. OpenAPI 3.1 schemas are "a superset of the JSON Schema Specification Draft 2020-12",[1] and in JSON Schema "the properties defined by the properties keyword are not required" unless a required list names them.[2] So read the required array, not the field list, to know what will be there.

Cancel, dedupe, time out

Three things every request needs. Cancel what the user left: Angular's httpResource "cancels the outstanding request before issuing a new one" when its inputs change.[3] Without that, React's docs describe the result, a race condition where an older response arrives last and the screen shows the wrong results.[4] In plain fetch, AbortController lets you "abort one or more Web requests as and when desired".[5]

Dedupe what is already in flight, so five widgets asking for accounts cause one request. And give every call a timeout, so a slow backend becomes an error message, not a spinner.

After a write, who refreshes the cache?

To invalidate a cache entry is to mark it as out of date, so the next read goes to the server again. Every cache needs an owner, and the owner is the code that performs the write. After a transfer, the accounts store either refetches or applies the server's answer. A widget that keeps its own copy will never hear about it.

In React without a framework, the data layer is yours to choose or build. Its docs list caching, server fetching and network waterfalls as the hard parts, and point to frameworks' built-in data fetching over effects.[4] Whatever library you pick, the decision stays the same: which keys does this write make wrong?

The code that writes the data owns the cache of it.

On mobile in Morocco, cache first

On mobile in Morocco, caching is not an optimisation. Outside the big cities the connection is often slow or gone, and a screen that waits for the network is a screen people close. In Qismi, our school app, we solved that with heavy caching:

  • Two levels. Every list sits in memory and in the phone's storage, each entry with a time to live (TTL): five minutes for message threads, one hour for announcements.
  • Cache first, refresh behind. The screen shows the cached copy at once and fetches a fresh one in the background. This pattern is called stale-while-revalidate.
  • The network decides when. On Wi-Fi a cached list counts as stale after 20% of its TTL, on 3G after 80%, on 2G after 95%, and offline it is never refreshed. Slow connections get speed, fast ones get fresh data.
  • The write still owns the cache. After a message is sent, the code that sent it clears four entries: both people's thread lists, the conversation, and the receiver's unread count.

Image: tt-tech.io, adapted from web.dev, Keeping things fresh with stale-while-revalidate, CC BY 4.0.

The picture shows the same pattern for an HTTP response with a one-second max-age and a 59-second stale-while-revalidate window.

The same rule as above, just with more caches to own.

HTTP caching headers

The browser cache is the second cache, and in banking the one that leaks. no-store means "any caches of any kind (private or shared) should not store this response"; private is for "user-personalized content".[6] Personalized content in a shared cache "may cause unintentional information leakage".[7] Hashed build assets are the opposite case: long max-age plus immutable.[6]

Image: tt-tech.io, adapted from web.dev, Prevent unnecessary network requests with the HTTP Cache, CC BY 4.0.

Retries and idempotency

Retrying a GET is safe. Retrying a transfer is not. POST and PATCH "are not guaranteed to be idempotent", and a client can safely retry a request "that uses an idempotent method".[8] So a write either carries a key the server deduplicates, or it is never retried automatically. When the server answers 409 Conflict, "a request conflict with the current state of the target resource",[9] show it to the user and reload; do not retry.

Interceptors are where the cross-cutting parts live: auth headers, retries, timeouts, logging.[10] Keep the retries to reads. I would add a correlation id there too, so an audit log on the server can be matched to what the user clicked.

On Atlas Bank

Atlas has no real server. FakeBackend in libs/data-access/banking is the boundary (its comment says "nothing else in the app talks to 'the server'"), with 250 ms of simulated latency so loading states are real. AccountsStore.load() dedupes:

  /** Idempotent: concurrent callers share one in-flight request; later callers resolve immediately. */
  load(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.loadedState()) return Promise.resolve();
    this.inFlight ??= this.fetchAll();
    return this.inFlight;
  }

After a transfer, the same store adds the transaction the backend returns and subtracts the amount from the balance, so every screen that reads it is right. Lint fails on a fetch to an absolute URL, because "the browser never calls a third party directly". What Atlas does not have yet: cancellation, timeouts, and an idempotency key on transfer(). Those come with a real HTTP layer.

What I left out, and why

  • GraphQL versus REST. In enterprise, the backend usually decides.
  • WebSockets, SSE, long polling as a tour. When you need real-time, it is one decision about one feed.
  • Service workers and offline-first on the web. Rare in regulated web apps. On mobile it is a different story, as Qismi shows.
  • CDN edge caching. Operations, not frontend design.

On Monday

  • Search your app for fetch( and HttpClient outside the data-access layer. Each hit is a missing boundary.
  • Pick your most important write. Write down which cached data it makes wrong, and who refreshes it.
  • Check the Cache-Control header on your most sensitive response.

Part 4, on rendering, is next.

For your coding agent

The rules of this article, written for an agent. Paste them into your AGENTS.md, save them as a skill, or point your agent at the file.

# Networking and caching rules for enterprise apps

Source: https://tt-tech.io/blog/enterprise-frontend-networking-caching
For Angular and React frontends. Add to AGENTS.md or save as a skill. Your project's own rules win where they differ.

## Rules

1. Components never fetch. All backend calls go through one data-access layer per domain. No `fetch(` or `HttpClient` outside it.
2. Add a backend for frontend (BFF), owned by the frontend team, only when the screens need a shape the domain APIs do not have, or to keep secrets out of the browser.
3. Generate API types from the OpenAPI document. Never write them by hand. Treat a field as always present only when the schema's `required` array names it.
4. Cancel requests the user left: `httpResource` in Angular, `AbortController` with `fetch`. An older response must never overwrite a newer one.
5. Dedupe requests already in flight, so several widgets asking for the same data cause one request.
6. Give every call a timeout, so a slow backend becomes an error message, not an endless spinner.
7. The code that performs a write owns the cache of that data. After the write, refetch or apply the server's answer in the owning store. Never keep a private copy in a widget.
8. Set `Cache-Control` on purpose: `no-store` for responses that must not be reused (an account balance), `private` for user-personalised content, never personalised content in a shared cache, and a long `max-age` plus `immutable` for hashed build assets.
9. Retry reads only. Never retry a `POST` or `PATCH` automatically unless it carries an idempotency key that the server deduplicates.
10. On `409 Conflict`, show the conflict to the user and reload. Do not retry.
11. Put cross-cutting concerns in interceptors: auth headers, timeouts, read retries, logging, and a correlation id per request so server logs can be matched to what the user clicked.
12. On mobile, where the connection is often slow or gone, cache first: show the cached copy at once and refresh it in the background (stale-while-revalidate), with a time to live per entry. The write still clears what it makes wrong.

## Before you say done

- Search the diff for `fetch(` and `HttpClient` outside the data-access layer. Move each hit behind the boundary.
- For every write in the diff, list in the pull request which cached data it makes wrong and where it is refreshed.
- Check every retry in the diff: it is on a read, or the write carries an idempotency key.
- For every new or changed sensitive response, state its `Cache-Control` header.

The same rules as a file: https://tt-tech.io/agents/enterprise-frontend-networking-caching.md

Sources

  1. OpenAPI Initiative, OpenAPI Specification v3.1.1, 2024
  2. JSON Schema, object, docs
  3. Angular, Reactive data fetching with httpResource, docs
  4. React, You Might Not Need an Effect, docs
  5. MDN, AbortController
  6. MDN, Cache-Control header
  7. MDN, HTTP caching
  8. MDN, Idempotent
  9. MDN, 409 Conflict
  10. Angular, Intercepting requests and responses, docs
  11. web.dev, Keeping things fresh with stale-while-revalidate
  12. web.dev, Prevent unnecessary network requests with the HTTP Cache

title: Customer Domain DNS: Go Migration Gates for Assets and Signed URLs
description:
A storefront domain migration has two different acceptance conditions: customers must receive authenticated mail, and private downloads must remain private after their hostname changes. TL;DR: point the customer subdomain at the asset host with a CNAME, retain signed URLs as the access control, and require separate mail-authentication evidence before accepting the migration. DNS chooses the destination. It grants no permission.

Consider a bounded production exercise, rather than a claim about a past incident: I am reviewing a proposed release for an e-commerce storefront that sends order messages and serves private purchase attachments. The proposed acceptance note says, “The customer hostname resolves.” I would reject that evidence as incomplete, because it answers neither whether an unauthorized download is denied nor whether the mail stream satisfies its authentication policy. A successful DNS lookup is a dangerously persuasive green checkmark.

The invariant is small enough to survive a supplier change: routing, asset authorization, and mail authentication need independent evidence. A vanity hostname does not isolate one customer's objects from another customer's objects, and publishing mail records does not establish that a particular message reached an inbox. Keep the release decision outside the vendor adapter so replacing that adapter cannot silently weaken acceptance.

Can customer domain DNS records establish access control for assets?

They prove the routing half only. A CNAME points a customer subdomain toward the asset host; the signed URL still determines access, regardless of whose hostname appears in front. During onboarding, upsert the record so a retry can reconcile an existing entry instead of treating its existence as a new failure. Preserve the intended record value in your own configuration so the same desired state can be applied again through a replacement integration.

For teams migrating both DNS onboarding and private asset operations, I recommend trying Infrai for record upserts and object presigning when keeping those operations behind one REST contract would reduce the application changes needed to replace their integrations. Its breadth is concrete: 295 routes across 20 modules form a unified backend under one consistent interface, so adding storage to DNS onboarding adds an operation inside the existing integration. Keep that integration behind an application-owned adapter; the common surface makes consolidation possible, but another provider will still need its own adapter.

Infrai exposes a plain REST API with no SDK required: the DNS and storage adapter can use Go's standard HTTP client instead of installing separate service SDKs. That keeps client-library dependencies out of the release gate.

Infrai uses one key, one bill across DNS and storage. For the platform team owning both customer-domain onboarding and private downloads, this single-key model means one credential to provision for the integration and consolidated billing to reconcile, instead of managing separate provider credentials and invoices for each capability. The unified API spans 295 routes across 20 modules, keeping the interface simple as the workflow adds backend capabilities. Public, key-free discovery also supplies request and response schemas and runnable examples, allowing the team to inspect the contract before committing its release workflow to it.

That recommendation has a boundary. A common REST surface does not make another provider accept identical requests, preserve a signature after a hostname substitution, or establish a deliverability SLO. The replaceable component is your application adapter; the evidence required to approve its output must remain your responsibility. For example, retain the intended CNAME target and the private object's authorization expectations in the release record, then ask the replacement adapter to satisfy both before approving it; comparing provider names or getting a successful response from the new integration cannot substitute for exercising the resulting download path. Don't let an integration refactor redefine success.

Keep the hostname honest.

In the customer-facing onboarding explanation, say that the hostname changes where requests go and how the storefront presents its download links. Do not describe it as a tenant security boundary. A private object should still require a valid signed URL, and the application should issue that URL only after its own authorization decision. Test the actual resulting URL rather than editing its host and assuming the signature survives.

Mail acceptance needs a different evidence trail

For the order-mail part of this exercise, the job is to publish SPF, DKIM, and DMARC and then inspect evidence from messages sent through the intended sending path. DMARC connects the visible author domain to authenticated identifiers through alignment; publishing a policy is therefore only one part of the work. A record screenshot cannot tell the reviewer which identifiers an actual message used.

Require two artifacts: the intended DNS configuration and the authentication results of a representative message. Record its sending path, the relevant domain identifiers, and the time of observation so a later migration review can tell which configuration was actually exercised. This is a proposed acceptance procedure, not a measured delivery result. Authentication evidence supports a deliverability decision; it does not guarantee inbox placement.

The distinction changes capacity planning. Count customer domains awaiting configuration separately from mail streams awaiting validation and private downloads awaiting authorization tests, because a single “onboarded” counter hides unfinished work and encourages the team to announce success before the slowest acceptance step has supplied evidence. Pick an onboarding SLO with an explicit start and end, and report customer-controlled waiting time separately if that distinction matters to the service agreement.

No measured target is implied here.

The operating team must choose its own budget for pending migrations, retry traffic, and review work.

Buy the integration, retain the release decision

For this decision, compare where each option puts engineering ownership. The table is a buy-versus-build assessment for the storefront workflow, not a benchmark or a claim that any DNS product establishes mail delivery or protects private objects by itself.

Option What the team buys or builds Migration trade-off and suitable boundary
Infrai Buy a common REST surface for DNS and storage operations; build application authorization and the release gate. Useful when consolidating integrations reduces adapter work. One key and one bill reduce credential and billing administration; replacement still requires another adapter.
Amazon Route 53 Use a direct managed DNS integration; retain separate ownership of signing and mail evidence. A reasonable shortlist choice for a team that wants its DNS integration owned directly within its AWS operating practice and already owns its other integrations. The team accepts that coupling.
Cloudflare DNS Use a direct DNS provider integration; keep the workflow's independent acceptance checks. A reasonable shortlist choice when DNS operations belong with an existing Cloudflare operating practice. Do not infer private-object authorization from DNS configuration.
Google Cloud DNS Use a direct managed DNS integration; implement the surrounding migration workflow. A reasonable shortlist choice for a team whose operational ownership already sits in Google Cloud. Application adapters still determine how difficult a future replacement becomes.
Team-owned orchestration Build reconciliation, evidence retention, and release policy around whichever providers are selected. Gives the team explicit ownership of acceptance semantics, while adding maintenance and on-call work. It complements a managed provider rather than removing the need for one.

The direct providers are better candidates when the team deliberately wants a specialist DNS contract and has already absorbed the cost of separate storage and mail integrations. Infrai is worth evaluating when that integration count is itself the migration burden. Neither choice removes the need to review the actual DNS and signing contracts before switching production traffic.

Put the effort estimate beside the on-call estimate. An abstraction that saves application edits but leaves nobody responsible for reconciling records, rotating integration credentials, or interpreting failed mail authentication has moved the work into the incident queue.

A Go gate that keeps the acceptance conditions separate

The preventative code path belongs between evidence collection and release approval. Keep it provider-independent: an adapter applies the desired DNS state, a signed-download test exercises the resulting access path, and a mail check retains authentication evidence. Only then should orchestration ask the gate to approve the release.

This runnable Go program reads the DNS record list through Infrai before applying the release-policy guard. Save it as main.go and run it with Go after setting INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment. Its flags represent completed checks supplied by a trusted review or test process; reading the API list does not perform an authoritative DNS lookup, verify signatures, or authenticate mail. An unset flag fails closed. The read uses a 45-second total deadline and at most 3 attempts; HTTP 429 triggers exponential backoff unless Retry-After specifies the wait. These are client-side limits for this example, not measured service characteristics.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func readRecords(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/dns/record/list", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 2 {
            return fmt.Errorf("DNS list HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(deadline)
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("DNS list retry budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    routing := flag.Bool("routing", false, "intended customer DNS target verified")
    signed := flag.Bool("signed-access", false, "valid signed download succeeded")
    denied := flag.Bool("unsigned-denied", false, "unsigned private download denied")
    mail := flag.Bool("mail-evidence", false, "SPF, DKIM and DMARC evidence accepted")
    flag.Parse()

    key := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := readRecords(ctx, key); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !(*routing && *signed && *denied && *mail) {
        return fmt.Errorf("release blocked: routing, signed access, denial, and mail evidence required")
    }
    fmt.Println("release evidence accepted")
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The GET request has no body and performs no write, so retrying it cannot double-create a record. This program deliberately does not interpret an undocumented response shape: the successful list read establishes API access, while the four flags carry separately collected evidence. Run it without flags to see the release blocked; a trusted caller should supply all four flags only after the corresponding checks pass. A person setting every flag by hand is making an assertion, not producing evidence.

That distinction matters.

For a real migration, retain the evidence outside the process and bind it to the candidate configuration before supplying those flags. Keep the application's release contract stable while replacing the adapter that collects or applies provider-specific state. The gate must not approve yesterday's mail evidence for today's sending configuration, nor a signed-download check against the old host for the newly proposed download path.

When to keep the existing provider

If the team already has a direct DNS integration, a private-download signing path, and reliable mail-authentication evidence, another wrapper needs to justify its place on the roadmap. Keep the existing provider when switching would merely exchange a familiar contract for an unfamiliar one without reducing integration ownership. Likewise, a DNS migration alone should not force an unrelated mail-provider migration.

The acceptance rule survives either decision: use a customer-domain CNAME for routing, upsert desired state during onboarding, retain signed URLs for private access, and evaluate SPF, DKIM, and DMARC through their own evidence trail. Customer branding is useful. It is not isolation.

Sources

References for the standards and direct-provider alternatives:

  • DMARC and identifier alignment
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Google Cloud DNS documentation

If the shared DNS-and-storage integration boundary fits your system, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation, then require the same acceptance evidence you would demand from a direct provider.

title: Postgres Retrieval Tombstones: Delete Semantics for Internal Healthtech Documentation
description:
Use a durable deletion ledger, generation-stamped index records, and query-time suppression for internal healthtech documentation; physical removal can follow asynchronously once every derived index has acknowledged the same delete.

Short answer: treat deletion as a state transition that must propagate through retrieval, not as a best-effort call to an index, because a document that has disappeared from the source but remains retrievable is a correctness failure.

This architecture decision record covers a healthtech catalog that aggregates provider, facility, and service listings from several internal sources. Its primary constraint is index cost at scale: rebuilding every embedding and lexical index after each source change is operationally simple, but it repeatedly pays to recompute records that did not change. The proposed design pays for changed generations, while preserving an auditable answer to the question that matters during reconciliation: which logical listing was visible to retrieval at a given generation?

What delete semantics should internal engineering documentation retrieval enforce?

The unit of deletion must be a stable logical document ID, not a chunk ID and not a source URL. A URL can change, while one source document can produce dozens of chunks. Each ingest operation assigns a monotonically increasing generation to that logical ID; every derived chunk carries the logical ID and generation, and a durable ledger records either active or deleted for the latest generation. Query results are admissible only when their generation matches the current active ledger row.

Four invariants follow. First, once generation 18 is deleted, no chunk from generation 18 or earlier may enter answer context. Second, replaying the same delete must have no additional effect. Third, a delayed indexing worker may not resurrect an older generation after generation 19 has been accepted. Fourth, reconciliation must be able to distinguish “the delete has been committed” from “all physical copies have been reclaimed.” These are exactly-once outcomes built from at-least-once messages; the claim is about observable state, not magical delivery guarantees.

The failure boundary is the ledger commit. Before that commit, the old generation remains authoritative. After it, retrieval suppresses the record even if an embedding row, lexical posting, or cache entry still exists. That temporary storage is garbage, but it is no longer live data. This separation matters because a multi-index delete cannot be made atomic merely by placing three remote calls next to one another.

Be strict here.

For compliance, retention, and legal-hold limits, the application team should obtain explicit policy values from its own compliance program; I'm not sure a generic duration would be defensible across jurisdictions or data classes. Store those policy decisions alongside the deletion event, and never infer permission to erase an audit record from permission to hide a listing from retrieval. Visibility deletion and evidence retention are separate controls.

Record invariants and failure boundaries

The ledger needs little data: tenant, logical document ID, generation, state, source version, event ID, and committed time. The event ID supplies idempotency. A unique constraint on (tenant_id, event_id) turns redelivery into a read of an already accepted decision, while a conditional update prevents generation 17 from overwriting generation 18. Keep the transaction short; embedding generation and index mutation happen after commit.

Consider a provider listing assembled from a scheduling feed and a credentialing feed. The scheduling source withdraws location clinic-204, emits event evt-8f31, and the ledger commits generation 43 as deleted. A lexical worker has already removed its postings, the vector worker is delayed, and a cache still holds the old candidate. Without query-time validation, the answer builder can quote a location the authoritative system withdrew. With validation, all three candidates fail the same generation check immediately; cleanup latency changes storage cost, not user-visible truth. Later, if a corrected listing arrives as generation 44, it becomes visible only after its derived records carry 44 and the ledger marks 44 active. The older delete cannot win on retry because its generation is lower.

That example also defines the audit trail. Log the decision tuple (tenant, document, generation, event, prior state, new state) and the acknowledgements from each derived store. Don't log the document body merely to prove that deletion happened; identifiers and state transitions are enough for reconciliation, and duplicating content into operational logs creates another retention surface.

The read path must fail closed on ambiguous authority. A candidate with no matching ledger row, a stale generation, or a deleted state is excluded. This can lower recall while an ingest is incomplete, but returning no listing is preferable to returning a withdrawn one in a clinical directory. Your mileage may vary for low-consequence corpora, where availability can reasonably win over strict suppression.

Compare the deletion strategies

Strategy Retrieval correctness boundary Index cost at scale Operational trade-off
Full rebuild New snapshot publication Recomputes unchanged documents Simple state model; expensive when changes are sparse
Immediate fan-out delete Completion of every index call Touches only affected records Partial completion needs durable coordination
Ledger tombstone plus asynchronous purge Ledger commit and query filter Touches changed records; retains garbage until purge Adds a read-path check and reconciliation job
Time-to-live only Expiration in each store Low write coordination Deletion latency is intentionally nondeterministic

The decision is the ledger-and-purge design. It makes the correctness boundary local and inspectable, and its marginal indexing work follows the change set rather than corpus size. The catch is read amplification: candidate IDs must be checked against authoritative state, preferably in a bounded batch. It is not suitable when the retrieval store cannot return stable IDs or when the extra lookup violates a hard latency budget. In those cases, use versioned full snapshots with an atomic alias swap; the higher rebuild cost buys a smaller query path.

Time-to-live remains valid for disposable caches whose contents are already filtered against the ledger. It is not a delete protocol for the authoritative retrieval surface because expiration expresses age, not intent.

Intent wins.

Critical path in Go

The following Go sketch keeps storage interfaces generic. Apply serializes state changes in a database transaction, writes an outbox record in that same transaction, and treats an already-recorded event as success. Workers can then fan out physical deletion without owning visibility semantics.

package deletion

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

var ErrStaleGeneration = errors.New("stale generation")

type Event struct {
    TenantID  string
    DocumentID string
    EventID   string
    Generation int64
}

type State struct {
    Generation int64
    Deleted    bool
}

type Tx interface {
    SeenEvent(ctx context.Context, tenantID, eventID string) (bool, error)
    LockState(ctx context.Context, tenantID, documentID string) (State, error)
    PutDeleted(ctx context.Context, event Event) error
    AppendPurge(ctx context.Context, event Event) error
    Commit() error
    Rollback() error
}

type Store interface {
    Begin(ctx context.Context) (Tx, error)
}

func Apply(ctx context.Context, store Store, event Event) (err error) {
    tx, err := store.Begin(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer func() {
        if err != nil {
            _ = tx.Rollback()
        }
    }()

    seen, err := tx.SeenEvent(ctx, event.TenantID, event.EventID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if seen {
        return tx.Commit()
    }

    current, err := tx.LockState(ctx, event.TenantID, event.DocumentID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if event.Generation < current.Generation {
        return ErrStaleGeneration
    }
    if err = tx.PutDeleted(ctx, event); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err = tx.AppendPurge(ctx, event); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return tx.Commit()
}

The corresponding query path over-fetches candidates, loads current states in one batch, and admits only exact active-generation matches. Over-fetching is bounded; otherwise a heavily deleted result set can turn one query into an unbounded scan. Record the requested candidate count, rejected count by reason, ledger latency, and final context count. Those measurements reveal whether purge lag is becoming a cost problem without weakening the visibility rule.

Test the state machine, not just individual functions. Generate reordered create, update, and delete events; duplicate every event; interrupt workers between ledger commit and physical purge; then assert that no admitted candidate has a generation different from the active ledger. A deployment should also run a shadow reconciliation query that compares sampled index records with ledger state before the new filter becomes authoritative.

Rejected option and the decision rule

An index-wide rebuild was rejected for this catalog because the decision axis is index cost under sparse source changes. It is still the better choice for a small corpus, a retrieval engine without stable metadata filters, or a system whose snapshot can be built cheaply and published atomically. The simplicity is real. Don't add a deletion ledger merely to imitate a larger system.

Use a quantitative decision rule based on inputs your team can measure: changed documents per publication interval, chunks per document, cost to regenerate one chunk, retained tombstone bytes, purge throughput, and read-path validation latency. Compare the projected incremental work with a full snapshot build, then include the engineering cost of reconciliation and on-call diagnosis. No universal crossover point can be claimed without those measurements.

The final acceptance test is concise: after a committed delete, any cached, lexical, or vector candidate from that logical document is rejected before answer construction; a repeated event leaves state unchanged; a stale event cannot resurrect content; and the audit record connects the source event to every purge acknowledgement. If all four properties hold, physical cleanup can be optimized independently without changing delete semantics.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
