title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

title: Workflow SDK now writes over WebSockets on Vercel
description:
The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later.

Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on.

Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens:

Streams keep pace with AI output

In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second.

Fewer HTTP requests for event writes

Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery.

Get started

Read the Vercel World documentation to get started. If you're on 4.x, start with the upgrade guide, since v5 is a major release.

title: Vercel Container Registry now supports 2 GB compressed image layers
description:
Vercel Container Registry now supports compressed image layers of up to 2 GB each, up from 500 MB, the total image size limit stays 15 GB.

The registry works with standard workflows like docker push, docker pull, and docker tag, and pushing an image creates the repository on the fly.

Repositories can be made public for read-only pull access by any Vercel team, or shared with specific teams up to 100 from the dashboard or with vercel vcr permissions. The Vercel Managed Images that Vercel Sandbox runs on are served from ordinary public repositories, built with the same public-repository feature any team can use for its own images.

Manage repositories, images, and tags with the vercel vcr CLI commands in Vercel CLI v58.3.0 or later, and log CI workflows in from GitHub Actions with the vercel/vcr-action/login action using GitHub OIDC, which removes the need for long-lived registry credentials. title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max, with high as the API default.

Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2.

To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks. Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway, and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request.

Call it through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name:

This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format.

description:
You can now set a new project to expire when you deploy it with Vercel CLI. Expired projects are deleted automatically, so prototypes, demos, and test apps don't need cleaning up by hand.

Run vercel deploy with --delete-project-after and a duration:

Supported durations are 1h, 1d, 1w, 2w, and 30d, and the CLI prints the date and time when the project expires. The flag only applies when vercel deploy creates the project. If you deploy to an existing project with the flag, its expiration doesn't change and the CLI prints a warning.

To remove a project's expiration, run vercel project keep:

Update Vercel CLI to v65.12.0 or later to get started. Learn more in the vercel deploy documentation.

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

Read more

description:

When Token Pass credit runs out for the billing period, requests from a standard key or OIDC token fall back to your team's AI Gateway credits. Token Pass keys still stop until the next billing period.

Requests served through the Token Pass provider remain Zero Data Retention (ZDR). Fallback requests follow your team's setting. With team-wide ZDR enabled, they route only to ZDR providers.

Available now for Token Pass subscribers on Pro teams. If you created a Token Pass key during setup, switch to a standard API key or OIDC token to get fallback. Learn more in the Token Pass documentation.

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
description:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

title: Data Cache is moving to Runtime Cache
description:
Data Cache is exiting beta and moving to Runtime Cache. Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache will switch over on every version without code changes. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own Runtime Cache storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Once your team migrates, Data Cache reads and writes that were previously unbilled are charged at Runtime Cache pricing. Rates start at $0.40 per million read units and $4.00 per million write units, and vary by region.

Hobby teams get 1 million read units and 200,000 write units free each month across all projects. On Pro, usage draws from your $20 infrastructure credit each month, and anything beyond it is billed at regional rates. For Enterprise pricing, contact your account team.

Migration

Teams created on or after October 30, 2026 use Runtime Cache by default.

If your team already uses Data Cache:

  • Hobby: We’ll migrate your team on December 10, 2026.

  • Pro: We’ll notify you of your migration date and when billing changes take effect.

  • Enterprise: Your account team will contact you with migration details.

Before you migrate, review your project's Data Cache usage in Observability. To cut unnecessary reads and writes, follow the optimization guide or copy the agent prompt into your coding agent. In the Runtime Cache dashboard, you can also select Optimize with Vercel Agent.

Starting October 30, existing Hobby and Pro teams can opt in early from your team's CDN settings. Runtime Cache pricing applies as soon as you opt in.

You can also disable fetch and unstable_cache caching in CDN settings, which sends more requests to your data sources but doesn’t stop your migration.

Read about the architecture and recent improvements in the blog post.

title: Vercel MCP now supports MCP events
description:
Vercel MCP now publishes events, so agents can subscribe to Vercel platform events like deployment.succeeded and deployment.error and react to what happens on your projects instead of polling for changes.

An agent subscribes once, filtering by team, project, and environment, and Vercel MCP manages an ordinary expiring Vercel webhook behind it. Refreshes extend the subscription, an abandoned one expires on its own, and event webhooks run on their own per-team limit, so they don't count against your 40 account webhooks.

Deliveries are signed Standard Webhooks with Vercel's native webhook payload in data.

See the AI SDK cookbook Receive MCP Webhook Events to implement the receiving side.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.

title: A small delivery-state checklist for business text workflows
description:
A text appearing in an agent’s sent folder is not proof that the customer received it. For a business texting workflow, treat the sent message, provider acceptance, delivery receipt, and human follow-up as separate events. This distinction matters most after hours, when the person who sent the message may not be the person who sees a reply.

Model the message as a record

Give each outbound message a stable internal ID. Store the conversation ID, recipient, sender, submitted time, provider message ID, and current state. Keep the full message content only where your retention policy permits it. The provider ID is useful when a later status callback arrives.

A small state model might be queued → submitted → accepted → delivered, with branches for failed and unknown. An accepted event means a provider took the request; it does not prove delivery to a handset. A missing receipt should remain unknown until your documented timeout or reconciliation step runs.

Handle receipts defensively

  1. Verify that the status event came from the expected provider before changing a record.
  2. Match the provider message ID to one outbound message. Keep unmatched events for investigation.
  3. Make updates idempotent. Providers may retry a webhook, and duplicate events should not create duplicate tasks or customer notifications.
  4. Record the event time and processing time separately. A delayed callback can arrive after a newer staff action.
  5. Define which states can move forward. Avoid turning a confirmed failure into delivered merely because a stale event arrived.

Test the handoff, not just the API

Send a test message to a controlled number, inspect the provider event, and then have a second staff member open the shared conversation. Can that person see the latest state and know whether a reply needs an owner? Repeat the test with a simulated failed delivery and an after-hours reply. Document the expected owner, retry decision, and customer-facing language before production use.

The exact event names and delivery guarantees depend on the provider and channel, so check the provider’s current documentation. This checklist is a way to test the workflow around those events. Phone Clover is one example of a calling and texting app for HighLevel teams using Telnyx; evaluate its current behavior against your own routing and receipt requirements.

title: Alternativa offline a Descript y CapCut: quitar silencios, comprimir vídeos <10 MB y subtítulos con FFmpeg 9.1 y Whisper
description:
Si editas podcasts, tutoriales, gameplay o Shorts, seguramente ya conoces el peaje habitual de la nube: $20–$30 al mes en suscripciones como Descript, CapCut Pro o OpusClip, subidas lentas de archivos de varios gigas y marcas de agua si no pagas.

La buena noticia en 2026 es que FFmpeg 9.1 (ya con soporte nativo para whisper.cpp offline) permite hacer todo el trabajo pesado 100% en local a la velocidad nativa de tu PC, sin subir ni un byte a internet.

Aquí tienes las 4 recetas exactas listas para copiar y pegar, además de una Calculadora Exact-MB de Bitrate y Comandos FFmpeg 9.x gratuita (sin registro) para calcular los parámetros exactos de cualquier vídeo.

1. Comprimir un vídeo al tamaño exacto para Discord (<10 MB) o WhatsApp (15 MB) sin perder calidad

El error clásico al comprimir con CRF fijo es quedarse corto (calidad borrosa) o pasarse por 1 MB y que Discord rechace el archivo. La fórmula exacta de 2 pasadas (2-pass) usa todo el presupuesto de bits disponible:

bitrate_video_kbps = floor((objetivo_MB * 8192 * 0.94) / duracion_segundos) - bitrate_audio_kbps

# Ejemplo: vídeo de 60 segundos ajustado a 9.5 MB (audio 96k -> vídeo 1124k)
ffmpeg -y -i entrada.mp4 -c:v libx264 -b:v 1124k -pass 1 -an -f mp4 NUL && \
ffmpeg -y -i entrada.mp4 -c:v libx264 -b:v 1124k -pass 2 -c:a aac -b:a 96k salida_discord.mp4

En nuestras pruebas reales, un clip de 11,55 MB bajó a 0,62 MB exactos manteniendo el vídeo nítido. Puedes calcular el comando automático para cualquier duración en la Calculadora Exact-MB gratis.

2. Masterizar audio de podcast o vídeo a -16 LUFS sin recodificar el vídeo (-c:v copy)

La mayoría de editores re-renderizan todo el vídeo H.264 solo para subir el volumen de la voz. Con loudnorm y -c:v copy limpias graves (<75 Hz), eliminas ruido de fondo y clavas -16 LUFS (estándar de YouTube, Spotify y Apple Podcasts) en segundos y sin pérdida de imagen:

ffmpeg -y -i grabacion.mp4 -c:v copy -af "highpass=f=75,afftdn=nf=-25,loudnorm=I=-16:TP=-1.5:LRA=11" -c:a aac -b:a 192k master_16lufs.mp4

3. Reencuadrar vídeo 16:9 a formato vertical 9:16 (YouTube Shorts, Reels y TikTok) 

ffmpeg -y -i horizontal.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]scale=1080:1920:force_original_aspect_ratio=increase,crop=1080:1920,boxblur=24:6[bg];[0:v]scale=1080:-2[fg];[bg][fg]overlay=(W-w)/2:(H-h)/2" -c:v libx264 -crf 20 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -b:a 160k short_916.mp4

4. Subtítulos automáticos con IA 100% offline usando Whisper nativo en FFmpeg 9.1

FFmpeg 9.1 compila whisper.cpp directamente como filtro de audio, permitiendo generar archivos .srt sin pagar créditos ni APIs externas:

ffmpeg -i charla.mp4 -vn -af "whisper=model=ggml-base.bin:language=es:destination=subtitulos.srt:format=srt" -f null -

¿Prefieres una interfaz visual local sin recordar sintaxis de FFmpeg?

title: How to Compare Cloud Storage Providers for Direct Browser Uploads — Go
description:
Short answer: compare the tenant boundary before comparing upload latency. For a logistics receipt workflow, the browser should receive a short-lived upload URL for one server-selected object key, while the storage policy must prevent that URL from crossing tenants. S3, Cloudflare R2, and Wasabi can all be evaluated through that same contract because the important test is the trust boundary: who chooses the bucket, key, headers, and expiry, and what happens when a client retries?

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. Those alerts changed how I look at direct uploads. A successful HTTP response is not proof that the receipt is attached to the right shipment. A retry can create a second object, and a copied upload URL can expose another tenant's prefix. The provider comparison belongs after those cases are defined.

What can a browser upload safely?

The browser needs permission to send bytes, not permission to invent identity. The application authenticates the operator, resolves the tenant and shipment on the server, and creates an object key from trusted values. The response can contain an upload URL, an expiry, and the exact headers the browser must send. It should not accept a client-supplied bucket or an arbitrary key as an authority decision.

For example, the key can be derived from an internal tenant ID and receipt ID:

package upload

import "fmt"

func receiptKey(tenantID, receiptID string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("receipts/%s/%s/original", tenantID, receiptID)
}

That function is deliberately boring. Its input should already be validated identifiers, not a path copied from the browser. Keep the original file under a stable key, record the expected content length and media type in the database, and make the receipt ID idempotent. If the request is retried, the service returns the same pending upload record instead of creating a second logical receipt.

CORS is part of the browser contract, not an access-control substitute. The storage endpoint must allow the application origin and the required request method and headers, while the authorization decision remains in the signed request and storage policy. MDN's CORS guidance is useful here because a browser may block a response even when the server received the request; that is an operational failure mode worth testing separately.

Where did the tenant boundary fail?

The incident shape is easy to reproduce. Tenant A requests a receipt URL, then a worker or test tool changes the key to receipts/tenant-b/... before sending the request. A second case uses a valid URL after its intended expiry. A third sends a different content type than the one signed. These are not throughput tests. They answer whether the URL represents one narrow capability or a general storage credential.

I start with a matrix and keep the expected result explicit:

Test Expected result Why it matters
Valid key and signed headers Upload succeeds Confirms the normal browser path
Key changed to another tenant Rejected Tests tenant isolation
Signed URL after expiry Rejected Limits copied links
Same receipt request repeated Same logical receipt Prevents duplicate delivery records
Interrupted large upload resumed One finalized object Tests retry behavior

The last row deserves care. A multipart upload is a sequence, not one request. S3's multipart documentation describes separate initiation, part uploads, and completion, which means the application needs a cleanup policy for abandoned uploads. The browser can retry a part, but the service still needs to know which receipt owns that upload and when an incomplete upload should be removed.

Here is the server-side shape I use for the authorization decision. The signer is intentionally an interface, so the same test suite can exercise different S3-compatible backends without turning the article into a provider setup guide.

package upload

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Signer interface {
    PresignPut(ctx context.Context, bucket, key, contentType string, expires time.Duration) (string, error)
}

type ReceiptRequest struct {
    TenantID    string
    ReceiptID   string
    ContentType string
}

func CreateUpload(ctx context.Context, s Signer, r ReceiptRequest) (string, string, error) {
    if r.TenantID == "" || r.ReceiptID == "" || r.ContentType == "" {
        return "", "", errors.New("missing receipt identity or content type")
    }

    key := receiptKey(r.TenantID, r.ReceiptID)
    url, err := s.PresignPut(ctx, "receipts", key, r.ContentType, 10*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        return "", "", fmt.Errorf("presign receipt upload: %w", err)
    }
    return key, url, nil
}

The ten-minute value is an example policy, not a universal setting. Choose it from the expected upload duration, clock skew, and the consequences of a leaked URL. Persist the key and an upload state such as pending, complete, or expired; do not infer completion solely from the browser's callback. A worker can verify the object metadata, then atomically mark the receipt complete.

How should I compare cloud storage providers for direct browser uploads?

The protocol surface is similar enough to make a common test harness practical, but “S3-compatible” does not mean identical operations or identical operational behavior. S3 is the reference point for the multipart and lifecycle concepts in the supplied documentation. R2 exposes an S3-compatible API and documents presigned URLs, while Wasabi documents presigned URL workflows. For this use case, the difference to measure is the surrounding behavior: endpoint configuration, policy language, CORS controls, multipart limits, lifecycle cleanup, and the observability available to explain a rejected upload.

I would record the result as evidence rather than as a ranking:

Provider surface Check in the harness Decision signal
S3 API behavior Presigned PUT, multipart completion, lifecycle rule Does the workflow match the retention and cleanup model?
R2 S3-compatible endpoint Signature, endpoint, CORS, multipart behavior Are endpoint-specific settings explicit in deployment configuration?
Wasabi S3-compatible endpoint Signature, bucket policy, CORS, multipart behavior Can the same tenant-denial tests run without hidden exceptions?

No row answers tenant isolation by itself. A bucket policy can be carefully written and still be undermined by an application that signs the wrong key. Conversely, an application can derive the right key and still fail browser uploads because CORS does not allow the signed headers. Keep those layers separate in logs and tests.

Avoid making price the deciding argument. Storage and request economics change, and the receipt workflow has costs that a headline comparison misses: abandoned multipart parts, reprocessing, audit retention, cross-region movement, and the engineer-hours needed to diagnose a provider-specific rejection. A neutral comparison should carry those variables as measured inputs, not as a permanent cheapest-provider claim.

What should happen when the browser or worker retries?

A receipt has two identities: the business identity and the object identity. The business identity might be (tenant_id, receipt_id). The object identity is the server-derived key. Make the database uniqueness constraint match the first one, and make the key deterministic from it. That is the simplest guard against duplicate delivery records.

For completion, accept an event or callback only after checking the tenant, receipt ID, object key, size, and expected media type. Then use a compare-and-set transition so two workers cannot both perform the final side effect. The original file remains available for audit, while downstream processing can use a separate derived object or record.

A small state machine is easier to page on than a pile of booleans:

package upload

type State string

const (
    Pending  State = "pending"
    Complete State = "complete"
    Expired  State = "expired"
)

func CanComplete(current State, key, expectedKey string) bool {
    return current == Pending && key == expectedKey
}

The real implementation must perform the transition transactionally and verify object metadata through the storage API. This helper only makes the invariant visible: an expired or already-complete receipt cannot be completed by a late retry.

For large files, use multipart upload only when the reliability benefit outweighs the cleanup and state-management cost. The browser needs a resumable plan; the service needs an abort path and a scheduled check for stale uploads. S3's lifecycle documentation covers lifecycle management as a storage-side control, but the application still needs a receipt state and an audit trail. Storage cleanup cannot tell you whether a shipment's original was successfully processed.

The runbook I would ship

First, log a request ID, tenant ID, receipt ID, object key, provider label, and upload state. Do not log the signed URL. Second, alert on pending receipts older than the normal upload window, failed completions by tenant, and growth in incomplete multipart uploads. Third, keep a replay-safe reconciliation job that compares pending records with object metadata and makes no assumption that one notification arrived exactly once.

Before deployment, run the matrix against each configured endpoint from a real browser origin. Repeat it after changing CORS, signing libraries, bucket policies, or endpoint settings. Include clock skew in the test environment. A green unit test around key construction is valuable, but it cannot prove that a browser preflight, signature check, and storage policy agree.

The advice has a boundary. If receipts are tiny, uploads are infrequent, and the server already handles the file safely, a direct browser path may add more lifecycle work than it removes. The trade-off is operational: this design does not fit a team that cannot maintain upload state, validate object metadata, or operate cleanup for abandoned multipart work; choose a server-mediated upload when that control plane would be simpler. If an auditor requires immutable retention, add the relevant retention and deletion controls to the decision record; a presigned URL is an upload mechanism, not an audit policy.

The provider choice should be the final implementation detail. The durable decision is that a tenant can upload only the object the server assigned, retries preserve one receipt identity, and operators can explain every pending or rejected upload. That contract gives S3, R2, and Wasabi a fair test, and it keeps a storage outage from becoming an accounting mystery.

Sources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://docs.wasabi.com/docs/how-do-i-create-a-pre-signed-url

title: LIV Golf's Funding Drought: What's Next for the Controversial Golf League?
description:
LIV Golf's Funding Drought: What's Next for the Controversial Golf League?

The Saudi Funding Cliff: A Threat to LIV Golf's Survival?

LIV Golf, the controversial golf league founded by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), is facing a significant challenge. According to reports, PIF is set to stop funding the league after the 2026 season, leaving LIV Golf's future uncertain. In a recent statement, LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil acknowledged the funding cliff, but emphasized the league's commitment to delivering high-quality golf to its fans.

The PIF Funding Dilemma

PIF's decision to stop funding LIV Golf is not surprising, given the controversy surrounding the league's origins and the human rights concerns associated with Saudi Arabia's involvement. The league's launch in 2022 was met with widespread criticism, with many questioning the morality of accepting funding from a country with a questionable human rights record.

The PIF funding dilemma is a significant concern for LIV Golf, as it threatens the league's very existence. Without a stable source of funding, LIV Golf may struggle to maintain its current level of operations, let alone expand its reach and popularity. The league's reliance on PIF funding has been a major point of contention, with many critics arguing that LIV Golf's success is built on the back of Saudi Arabia's wealth.

The Impact on LIV Golf's Operations

The PIF funding cliff has significant implications for LIV Golf's operations. The league's ability to stage events, attract top talent, and maintain its current level of production quality is at risk. The uncertainty surrounding the league's future has already led to concerns about the stability of its staff, with some employees reportedly facing uncertainty about their job security.

The PIF funding cliff also raises questions about the league's long-term viability. Without a stable source of funding, LIV Golf may struggle to attract and retain top talent, ultimately impacting the quality of its events and the overall fan experience.

The Future of LIV Golf: What's Next?

So, what's next for LIV Golf? The league's CEO, Scott O'Neil, has emphasized the need for LIV Golf to adapt to the changing landscape, but the path forward is far from clear. The league may need to explore alternative funding sources, potentially through partnerships with other investors or sponsors.

However, finding a new source of funding will be a significant challenge, given the controversy surrounding LIV Golf's origins and the league's reliance on PIF funding. The league may also need to re-evaluate its business model, potentially shifting its focus from high-stakes, high-reward events to more sustainable, grassroots initiatives.

Key Takeaways

  • PIF is set to stop funding LIV Golf after the 2026 season, leaving the league's future uncertain.
  • The PIF funding cliff threatens LIV Golf's very existence, with significant implications for its operations and long-term viability.
  • LIV Golf may need to explore alternative funding sources, potentially through partnerships with other investors or sponsors.
  • The league may need to re-evaluate its business model, shifting its focus from high-stakes, high-reward events to more sustainable, grassroots initiatives.

Conclusion

LIV Golf's funding drought is a significant challenge, one that threatens the league's very existence. While the league's CEO has emphasized its commitment to delivering high-quality golf to its fans, the path forward is far from clear. The PIF funding cliff has significant implications for LIV Golf's operations, and the league will need to adapt quickly to survive. As the controversy surrounding LIV Golf's origins continues to unfold, one thing is clear: the future of LIV Golf is uncertain, and its very survival is at stake.
