title: Using JackedIN with AI agents
description:
Using JackedIN with AI agents

This article describes JackedIN 1.2.1, plus a safety rule being built for the next release. Human approval before any change is not in 1.2.1 yet. The canonical version is on the product site: Using JackedIN with AI agents.

JackedIN is an SSH, Telnet and serial terminal for Windows, Linux and Raspberry Pi. The same program is a desktop window, a command line, a local API, and a stdio MCP server. Built-in profiles for Junos, Cisco IOS/NX-OS, Arista, Nokia, MikroTik and more.

Use it only on devices you own or are allowed to manage. Examples use 192.0.2.10 and router1. Keep passwords out of the command line; set JACKEDIN_PASSWORD or a credential reference instead.

Human approval before any change (coming in the next release)

This is the safety rule being built for AI sessions, and it is not in JackedIN 1.2.1 yet:

  • Show-type commands run freely.
  • A command that changes something runs only after a human approves it.
  • The agent can never approve itself.

Until that ships, treat exec as able to send any command you allow it to run, and limit the agent by how you prompt it and which tools you enable.

The problem agents hit

If you pipe a command into a raw SSH/serial session, end-of-file often ends the session while the device is still paging, or after it printed an error the agent never read. The agent moves on as if the change landed.

JackedIN is built so that does not happen.

Wait for the prompt, then read the complete output

jackedin exec reads the whole command list first, sends one command, and waits until the device prompt is back before it sends the next. It pages through --More--, ---(more)---, ---(more 100%)---, and similar markers, then returns the complete output. A stdin pipe on connect also waits for the prompt after each line; after stdin ends, it waits for the prompt that follows the last line, then exits.

There is no --terminator flag. The device prompt, and those pager markers, are how JackedIN knows a command has finished. --prompt REGEX replaces the prompt JackedIN detects. --vendor NAME forces a profile; omit it and the prompt or banner picks one.

Pacing, when a slow console needs it:

  • --line-delay MS — gap between lines (serial defaults to 100 ms if you omit it)
  • --char-delay MS — pause between characters
  • --wait-for-echo — wait until the device echoes a line before sending the next
  • !sleep 500 in a command list — wait 500 ms and send nothing
  • --timeout SEC — cap each wait; omit it and JackedIN waits as long as the device needs

The same pacing fields on the API and MCP are lineDelayMs, charDelayMs, and waitForEcho.

--dry-run prints the plan and connects to nothing. Prefer exec over piping into connect.

jackedin exec --host 192.0.2.10 --user admin --trust-host-key \
  --json --timeout 8 --cmd 'show version'

JSON output

--json and --output json are the same flag. JACKEDIN_JSON=1 matches them. On exec, each command is returned as structured data: command, ok, output, prompt, matched_error, timed_out, duration_ms. ok is false if any command, timeout, or verify check failed. fleet and inventory sync also accept JSON output.

On Windows, capture that output with jackedin.com, not jackedin.exe.

MCP server

jackedin mcp is a stdio MCP server for the local API. It dials 127.0.0.1 only. It is not a public URL.

  1. Install JackedIN 1.2.1 from the download section (72-hour full trial; a license is needed after that).
  2. Turn the local API on in Settings. It stays off until you do. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only (port 47321 unless you change it) and requires a Bearer token.
  3. Leave the window open, or run jackedin headless (the API must still be enabled).
  4. Point the client at the stdio command: 
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "jackedin": {
      "command": "jackedin",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": {
        "JACKEDIN_API_TOKEN": "paste-the-token-from-settings",
        "JACKEDIN_API_PORT": "47321"
      }
    }
  }
}

The packaged examples include this snippet for generic clients, Cursor, and Claude Desktop. The token is JACKEDIN_API_TOKEN if that variable is set, otherwise the token saved in Settings.

Tools: list_sessions, open_session, send_session, exec, send_break, read_session, close_session, wait_for_output, scan_ports, ping_host, trace_host, read_events. Prefer exec. exec and send_break do not require the automationApi setting; wait, scan, ping, trace, and events do. scan_ports tells the caller to only scan devices they are allowed to test.

The local API, off by default

The same work is available over HTTP on the local machine: POST /v1/exec, POST /v1/sessions/{id}/exec, and the other routes in the packaged docs/openapi.yaml. The listener is off until you enable it, bound to 127.0.0.1, and token-protected. Do not expose it on a network.

Safe use

  • Only connect to or scan devices you are allowed to test.
  • Do not put secrets in argv, MCP config files you will share, or logs. Use environment variables and the credential store.
  • Prefer --dry-run and show commands until you are sure of the plan.
  • A changed SSH host key is refused in the background; --trust-host-key accepts a new key, not a changed one.

Coming in the next release: human approval before any change

The same rule as the headline above. It is being built for the next release and is not in 1.2.1: in AI sessions, show-type commands run freely; a command that changes something waits for a human; the agent cannot approve its own change.

Try it

  • Download: getpathprobe.com/jackedin/#download
  • Buy (launch price $19, after the 72-hour trial): getpathprobe.com/jackedin/#pricing
  • Release and SHA256SUMS: JackedIN 1.2.1 on GitHub
  • User's guide: JackedIN-Users-Guide.md

We build JackedIN. This article describes the current 1.2.1 app, and marks human approval before any change as coming in the next release.

title: A Risk Score Is Not a Decision: Building Smarter AML Workflows for Crypto Businesses
description:
AMLdark · Screen TRC20 USDT addresses for free

Live AML screening for Tron-based USDT addresses against OFAC designations, Tether's freeze list and darknet datasets. Free tier included.

amldark.com

What should your system do?

Reject the transaction? Freeze the account? Request additional information? Send it to a compliance analyst?

There is a problem with treating a risk score as a final answer: a number can describe a potential risk, but it cannot explain the entire situation.

This distinction becomes particularly important for businesses processing USDT, operating cryptocurrency exchanges, managing OTC transactions or building blockchain payment infrastructure.

As crypto adoption grows, companies need more than systems that simply identify suspicious addresses. They need systems that help them understand risk, prioritize investigations and make consistent decisions.

Let's explore how to build that kind of AML workflow.

  1. The Hidden Problem With Automated Risk Scores

Automated screening is useful because it can process information much faster than manual investigation.

However, automation introduces another challenge: false positives.

Consider three hypothetical situations.

Scenario A: Direct exposure

A wallet has a documented direct connection to an address associated with a sanctioned entity.

Scenario B: Indirect exposure

A wallet received funds from an address that interacted with a higher-risk service several transactions earlier.

Scenario C: Historical exposure

A wallet interacted with an address that was considered suspicious several years ago, but the available information does not establish a meaningful current connection.

All three situations might generate risk alerts.

But should they receive the same treatment?

Obviously not.

A responsible screening workflow needs to distinguish between direct and indirect exposure, consider transaction context and provide enough information for further investigation.

The objective should be better decisions, not simply more alerts.

  1. Why False Positives Are an Engineering Problem

False positives are often discussed as a compliance inconvenience.

In reality, they can become a serious operational problem.

Imagine a cryptocurrency exchange processing 10,000 deposits per day.

If its screening system generates hundreds of alerts that require manual investigation, the compliance team may struggle to keep up.

This creates several risks:

Legitimate customers experience unnecessary delays.

Analysts spend time investigating low-value alerts.

Important cases compete for attention with insignificant findings.

Operational costs increase.

Customer support receives more complaints.

Compliance teams may become less effective at identifying genuinely concerning activity.

This is why screening quality should not be measured exclusively by the number of detected addresses.

A useful system should help distinguish meaningful signals from background noise.

  1. Build a Risk Assessment Process Around Evidence

A better approach is to separate the detection stage from the decision stage.

Think about the process as four connected layers.

Layer 1: Detection

The screening system identifies relevant indicators, such as sanctions exposure, suspicious wallet connections or interactions with known high-risk services.

Layer 2: Context

The system provides additional information about the findings.

For example:

Is the exposure direct or indirect?

How many transaction hops separate the addresses?

Is the connection associated with USDT transfers?

When did the relevant interaction occur?

Is there more than one independent risk indicator?

Layer 3: Investigation

A compliance analyst evaluates the available evidence.

This stage may involve examining transaction history, customer information and additional external intelligence.

Layer 4: Decision

The business applies its documented risk policy.

Possible outcomes include standard processing, enhanced due diligence, additional information requests or escalation.

The important architectural principle is simple:

Detection should generate evidence. Decision-making should evaluate that evidence.

These responsibilities should not be confused.

  1. Transaction Graphs: Why One Wallet Is Never the Whole Story

Blockchain transactions create relationships between addresses.

These relationships can be represented as a graph.

Imagine a simple transaction chain:

Wallet A → Wallet B → Wallet C → Wallet D

If Wallet D receives USDT from Wallet C, looking exclusively at Wallet C may provide only a limited understanding of the available transaction history.

Additional analysis could reveal that Wallet C previously received funds from Wallet B, which had an earlier interaction with Wallet A.

This does not automatically make Wallet D suspicious.

It simply introduces additional information that may deserve attention.

When analyzing transaction graphs, several factors matter:

Hop distance

How many transfers separate the wallet being investigated from the identified risk source?

Transaction direction

Did the funds move from the risk-associated address toward the investigated wallet, or in the opposite direction?

Asset specificity

Was the relationship established through USDT transfers or through another asset?

Time relevance

How old is the connection?

Exposure concentration

Does the wallet have a single indirect connection or several independent relationships?

These distinctions are particularly important when investigating TRON-based USDT activity.

A transaction graph should help explain relationships, not create guilt by association.

  1. Why TRC20 USDT Screening Requires Its Own Perspective

USDT is available across multiple blockchain networks.

However, analyzing USDT on TRON is not necessarily identical to analyzing USDT on Ethereum or another blockchain.

The underlying infrastructure, transaction structure and operational characteristics differ.

For businesses working with TRC20 assets, a useful screening workflow should consider:

TRON address identification.

USDT token-transfer history.

Relevant sanctions information.

Tether freeze-list records.

Known fraud and darknet exposure indicators.

Connections between wallet addresses.

Risk information associated with transaction history.

Another important consideration is that native TRX activity and TRC20 USDT transfers are not interchangeable.

A system that only examines general blockchain activity may overlook information specific to the token being investigated.

This is why network-specific and token-specific analysis matters.

  1. Introducing Explainable AML: An Approach Worth Building Around

One of the most useful improvements a crypto business can make is moving from unexplained risk scores toward explainable risk assessments.

Consider the difference.

A basic screening interface displays:

Risk score: 78/100.

An explainable screening interface provides:

Overall risk assessment.

Relevant exposure categories.

Direct and indirect connections.

Supporting transaction information.

Relevant sanctions indicators.

Historical context.

Information requiring further investigation.

The second approach gives compliance professionals something they can actually work with.

It also makes it easier to document decisions and improve internal procedures.

For developers, this means thinking about AML data structures, reporting interfaces and investigation workflows from the beginning.

A good screening integration should not simply return a number and leave the rest of the work to the user.

  1. How AMLdark Fits Into This Workflow

This is an area where specialized cryptocurrency screening platforms become interesting.

AMLdark focuses on cryptocurrency AML analysis, particularly USDT TRC20 activity on the TRON network.

Its website describes several capabilities relevant to the workflow discussed above:

Wallet screening

Address analysis against sanctions-related information and other risk datasets.

Transaction graph analysis

Investigation of relationships between addresses through token-level transaction tracing.

Tether freeze-list checks

Screening against relevant Tether freeze-list information.

Risk categorization

Presentation of risk scores and individual exposure categories.

Additional network coverage

The platform also describes support for other blockchain networks, including TON and several additional ecosystems.

Developer-oriented functionality

API access, batch screening and webhook functionality are presented for businesses that want to incorporate AML checks into their operational workflows.

You can explore the platform and its available features here:

https://amldark.com

For development teams, the interesting question is not simply whether a screening service can return a risk score.

It is whether its underlying information provides enough context to support a meaningful investigation.

Before integrating any provider into production, evaluate its data sources, coverage, update frequency, API documentation, security controls and limitations.

  1. Designing an AML Workflow That Scales

A cryptocurrency business should not depend on individual analysts remembering how to handle every possible screening result.

The process should be documented and repeatable.

Here are five practical recommendations.

  1. Define risk categories clearly

Establish what low, medium and high risk mean within your organization's methodology.

Avoid treating a provider's numerical score as a universal legal standard.

  1. Document investigation decisions

Keep records of the evidence reviewed, the decision made and the person responsible.

  1. Establish escalation procedures

Define which findings require additional review and who is authorized to make the final decision.

  1. Review screening quality

Monitor false-positive rates, investigation time, unresolved cases and changes in data coverage.

  1. Reassess historical information

Risk intelligence changes. A result obtained months ago should not automatically be treated as a complete representation of current wallet risk.

These practices help transform AML from an isolated technical feature into a functioning operational process.

  1. The Future Is Not More Alerts. It Is Better Intelligence.

The cryptocurrency industry does not need systems that simply generate an endless stream of suspicious-wallet notifications.

It needs systems that help businesses understand why something was flagged, what evidence supports the finding and what should happen next.

This is especially important as stablecoins become increasingly integrated into payment infrastructure and international financial activity.

For developers, this creates an interesting engineering challenge.

The next generation of cryptocurrency applications will need to combine blockchain monitoring, risk intelligence, explainable analytics and human oversight.

The strongest solutions will not necessarily be the ones that produce the highest number of alerts.

They will be the ones that help organizations make better decisions with the information available.

title: AI SEO Agents: What They Can Publish Daily and Where Google Draws the Line
description:
Can an agent publish a blog post every day? Yes. Whether Google rewards it depends on one phrase in its spam policy.

I read the Google pages that decide this today. Here is what they say, and where I would draw my own line.

Free stuff: grab these first

  • The open source AI Employees (AI Employees). The page says "Open source, MIT licensed AI Employees. Free to hire." One of the eight is the SEO/AEO Employee: "Improves search content and answers your buyers' questions." The page lists 60 scheduled routines across the eight roles.
  • Google's spam policies (Spam Policies for Google Web Search). The section on scaled content abuse is the one that matters here.
  • Google's guidance on generative AI content (Using generative AI content). Short page. Read all of it.
  • Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content (Google Search Central). The standard your pages get measured against.
  • Google Search Console (search.google.com/search-console). Free. It shows whether your pages are getting impressions at all.
  • IndexNow (indexnow.org). A simple ping that tells participating search engines a URL was added, updated or deleted.

What Google actually says about AI content

Not "AI content is banned." It does not say that.

The generative AI page says generative AI "can be particularly useful when researching a topic, and to add structure to original content." Then the warning: using it to generate many pages without adding value for users may violate the policy on scaled content abuse.

The spam policy defines that term as many pages "generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users." It adds: "no matter how it's created."

The test is not who wrote the page. The test is whether the page helps the reader.

The same policy lists examples. A few that apply to agents:

  • Using generative AI tools to generate many pages without adding value for users.
  • Scraping feeds or search results to generate many pages.
  • Stitching content from different web pages together without adding value.
  • Creating multiple sites with the intent of hiding the scaled nature of the content.

If your agent does any of those on a schedule, it is not an SEO agent. It is a liability on a timer.

What an agent can safely do every day

Publishing daily is not the problem. What goes in each post is.

  • Research a keyword and read what already ranks. Reading is free and fast.
  • Draft a post with a point of view the other results do not have. One real number, one real example.
  • Pull sources and link to them. Authority links to real pages the reader can check.
  • Generate a hero image and the alt text. Google's page says to review metadata too, including title elements, meta descriptions, structured data and image alt text.
  • Add the URL to the sitemap and ping the engines. That is what Search Console and IndexNow are for.

What I would not hand to an agent

  • Fact-checking. Google's page is blunt: models "predict a likely sequence of words," outputs "may contain inaccuracies," and it is "critical to manually factcheck and review all AI-generated content" before publishing.
  • Claims about you or your clients. An agent will happily invent a case study. A human has to delete it.
  • The decision to publish ten near-identical pages. That is the scaled content example, word for word.

Tell readers how it was made

The generative AI page suggests giving readers context on how the content was created, "such as by providing more background information on how automation was used." I think that is good practice for trust, not only for Google. One line at the bottom of a post does it.

A realistic daily loop

  1. Pick one keyword from a list you wrote.
  2. Have the agent pull the top results and list what they all miss.
  3. Draft around the gap.
  4. You read it. You fix the facts. You cut anything you cannot stand behind.
  5. Publish, add to the sitemap, ping IndexNow.
  6. Check Search Console a week later. Keep what earns impressions, rewrite what does not.

Step 4 is the whole business. Skip it and you are on the wrong side of the policy page.

Where I would start

The SEO/AEO Employee in the open source library is built for the research and drafting half of that loop. It is free and MIT licensed. Install it, point it at one site, and read every draft before it goes live. If one post a day feels like too much to review, run one a week until it does not.

One small ask

If you run an agent that publishes for you, tell me in the comments what you check by hand before it goes out. I read all of them.

I run the Vibe Coding is Life community. Come say hi in the Facebook group or the free Skool community.

title: Shadow AI Discovery and Data Loss Prevention Playbook
description:
Shadow AI discovery is the part of AI governance that IT teams inherit without being asked. Nobody sends a memo announcing that the sales team pasted a customer contract into a chat tool, that an engineer connected a coding assistant to the production repository, or that finance trials four summarisation tools on last quarter's board pack. The usage simply exists, and the first question leadership asks is one nobody can answer from existing dashboards: how much of this is happening, and what data has left the building?

The comfortable answer, that the company has a policy and a list of approved tools, describes intent rather than reality. Discovery is a separate discipline with its own data sources, its own blind spots, and its own false positives. This playbook is the version I would run at a 100 to 1,000 person company with a small IT team and no enterprise SIEM: what signals to collect, what risks those signals reveal, and which controls are worth buying before the rest.

This sits inside the wider program described in the small business AI governance framework and the shadow AI risk overview. The written rules live in an AI acceptable use policy, and the vendor side of the problem, where a purchased tool overstates its controls, is covered in the AI washing vendor audit. The framework this article leans on is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, which treats inventory and measurement as prerequisites rather than afterthoughts.

How Do IT Teams Identify Shadow AI Usage across Enterprise Networks?

No single feed finds shadow AI. Six signals, combined, produce a defensible inventory, and each one has a specific blind spot you need to know before you trust the count.

Signal What it detects Blind spot
SSO application inventory and OAuth grants Tools that authenticate through your identity provider, and the scopes employees granted them Consumer tools reached with a personal login never appear
DNS and secure web gateway logs Domains resolved and requests made from managed devices Personal devices, mobile hotspots, and DoH resolvers inside apps
Browser extension inventory Assistant extensions with page-read permissions Extensions sideloaded outside management policy, and desktop apps
Expense and SaaS spend data Seats bought on corporate cards, including team-level purchases Free tiers and reimbursed personal subscriptions
Endpoint telemetry Local model runtimes, CLI assistants, and installers Web-only usage that leaves no process trace
Egress volume anomalies Unusual upload volume to newly seen destinations Small, repeated exfiltration that stays under thresholds

Three practical observations from running this.

Start with identity, because it is free and authoritative. Pull the SSO application report and the OAuth grant list for every user. Any assistant that asked for Drive, SharePoint, email, or repository scopes is an integration, not a chat session, and those grants are the highest-risk items in the inventory because they persist after the trial ends.

DNS logs are the best coverage-per-dollar signal for managed devices. A secure web gateway or filtered DNS provider gives you request volume by domain, which converts "someone might be using AI" into "these fourteen domains had traffic from these users this month". It will not see a personal phone on a cellular connection, and you should say so in the report rather than implying full coverage.

Expense data is the signal finance already owns. Card statements and reimbursement queues surface tools nobody would confess to buying. It lags by a month and misses free tiers, but it catches the purchases that create contractual obligations.

The output of discovery is not a list of names. It is a short register of four fields per tool: who uses it, what they do with it, what data classes can reach it, and whether it is sanctioned, tolerated, or prohibited. That register is what the rest of the program operates on.

What Are the Main Data Loss Prevention Risks of Employee AI Tools?

The risk is not that a model learns your secrets. It is that data leaves your boundary on a path you can no longer inspect, and the paths are predictable.

1. Prompt exfiltration. Employees paste customer records, contracts, source code, and HR documents into a chat box to get help. The data leaves with no inspection, no retention guarantee, and no record on your side. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications names this risk class directly as LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure, and it also applies to your own assistants when retrieval or logging puts data where it should not be.

2. Connector over-permission. An assistant that connects through OAuth to a drive, mailbox, or repository inherits broad read access, often with a scope the user did not read. The tool does not need to be malicious to be dangerous: a summariser that indexes everything the employee can see now holds a copy, and offboarding the employee does not revoke the tool's access to what it already indexed.

3. Retention and training posture. Consumer tiers frequently reserve the right to use inputs for improvement, while business tiers contractually do not. That distinction is a purchase decision, not a technical control, and it belongs in the register next to the tool name.

4. Generated content risk. Outputs can carry third-party IP, factual errors, or fabricated citations. An employee who pastes a generated paragraph into a customer proposal has introduced a risk that no firewall sees, which is why the copyright liability question belongs in the same policy as the data handling rules.

5. Insecure output handling. Generated text that lands in a ticket, a page builder, or a code path can carry instructions or markup that the downstream system executes. This is the same class of problem as prompt injection in web applications, arriving through a channel your security team never approved.

The pattern across all five is the same: the risk scales with the sensitivity of the data an employee can already reach, multiplied by the breadth of access the tool asks for. Rank tools by that product and the inventory becomes a prioritisation list.

How Do Mid-Market Companies Enforce AI Governance without Enterprise SIEM Budgets?

You do not need a SIEM to run this program. You need controls at three layers, in this order, and a decision about what you will not attempt to control.

Layer one: identity and policy, which cost nothing extra.

  • Publish an acceptable use policy that names sanctioned tools, prohibited data classes, and the approval path. Vague guidance produces workarounds.
  • Enforce SSO for sanctioned tools so revocation is one action and usage is attributable.
  • Review OAuth grants quarterly and remove scopes nobody uses. Start with mailbox and drive-wide read access, which is where most oversharing lives.
  • Turn on the identity provider's conditional access for unmanaged devices, at least as a reporting mode, so you can see what is connecting from where.

Layer two: network and browser controls, which cost a modest subscription.

  • Filter DNS and web traffic for unmanaged AI domains, and log rather than block in the first month. Blocking before you have data drives usage onto mobile hotspots.
  • Manage browser extensions by allowlist. Page-reading assistant extensions are the most under-reported data path in most companies.
  • Put an egress DLP policy on the one or two systems that hold the crown jewels, such as the CRM or the finance share, rather than trying to inspect all traffic.

Layer three: DLP and monitoring, where budget actually buys coverage.

  • Prefer DLP that can act at the browser or identity layer over network-only inspection, because most AI traffic is HTTPS to a small number of domains and network DLP sees only metadata.
  • Alert on volume and pattern, not on keywords. A single prompt containing "confidential" will generate noise; a user uploading 40 MB to a newly seen domain will not.
  • Keep a weekly review with a named owner and a 15-minute agenda: new domains, new OAuth grants, DLP hits above threshold, and open exceptions.

What to skip at this size: full CASB deployment, a custom model-monitoring platform, and formal data classification of every repository. Each is defensible later; starting there means the program stalls before it produces its first register.

A 30-Day Discovery and Control Sprint

Week one: assemble the register from data you already have. Export SSO applications and OAuth grants, pull 30 days of DNS or proxy logs for AI-related domains, list managed browser extensions, and pull the last two months of card and expense lines that look like AI subscriptions. Produce the four-field register and an honest coverage statement for each signal.

Week two: classify and prioritise. Tag each tool with the data classes it can reach this month and the access breadth it requested. Anything with mail or drive scope plus a consumer tier is a priority-one conversation, not a policy email.

Week three: publish and enforce the boundaries that matter. Ship the policy update with the sanctioned list, enable SSO for those tools, revoke grants nobody uses, and turn on logging for the domains you are not ready to block. Communicate the approval path so the answer to "can I use this" is a form, not a no.

Week four: baseline the metrics and pick the next control. Report sanctioned-tool share, unapproved-domain request volume, DLP events above threshold, and time to revoke. Then choose exactly one new control for next month, based on what the data says is the largest uncovered path.

Metrics That Show the Program Is Working

  • Sanctioned share of AI sessions. The portion of observed AI traffic going to approved tools. This is the number that moves when the program is healthy, because it measures migration rather than prohibition.
  • Unapproved domain requests per 100 managed devices. Trend, not absolute. A falling number means discovery and policy are working together.
  • OAuth grants with high-risk scopes. Count and age. A grant older than two quarters with mailbox access is a finding.
  • DLP events above threshold, and their disposition. Volume without disposition is noise; the useful metric is how many were investigated and closed.
  • Time from discovery to revocation. Target same business day for priority-one tools. If revocation takes a week, the program is documentation rather than control.

Five Failure Modes

Failure What it looks like Fix
Policy without telemetry A signed AI policy and no ability to say which tools are in use Run the six-signal discovery before the next policy revision
Block-everything rollout Usage moves to personal devices and mobile hotspots, invisible to you Log first, then block the highest-risk domains with a documented exception path
DLP that only logs Dashboards full of events nobody reviews Weekly review with a named owner and a disposition for every threshold hit
Broad OAuth grants left in place A summariser holds an indexed copy of a departed employee's access Quarterly grant review, least-scope re-consent, revoke with offboarding
No deprovisioning path Ex-employees keep AI tool access because the tool sits outside the identity provider SSO for every sanctioned tool, and an offboarding checklist that includes them

Conclusion

Shadow AI is not a discipline problem. It is an inventory and telemetry problem, and at mid-market scale the data already exists in four systems the company is paying for: identity, DNS or proxy, the browser, and the expense report. Combining them produces a register precise enough to argue about, which is a much better position than a policy that assumes compliance.

The sequence that works is unglamorous: inventory what you already have, classify by data reach, sanction a short list, make approval easy, and report a handful of metrics that leadership can read. The alternative, buying a control platform before you know what you are controlling, is how mid-market AI programs spend their first year's budget and still cannot answer the question the board actually asked.

title: Is It Safe to Delete ~/Library/Caches on a Mac? How to Clear Cache Safely
description:
Yes—most subfolders inside ~/Library/Caches are safe to delete on a Mac, as long as you quit running apps first, remove only the contents inside (never the Caches folder itself), and skip Apple system caches and sensitive tool data. Apps automatically recreate their cache files the next time you open them, so the only normal side effect is a slightly slower first launch or re-downloading cached assets.

What you should not touch are macOS's system-wide /Library/Caches and /System/Library/Caches folders—macOS manages those itself. Also keep expectations realistic: clearing cache reclaims disk space, not RAM or CPU performance; in fact, rebuilding caches can briefly use a little extra disk and network activity right after cleanup.

On one developer Mac we measured using CleanBit's scan engine, general App Caches inside ~/Library/Caches held 5.42 GB across 65 items, Chrome Disk Cache (~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome) held 4.37 GB, and dedicated developer caches living under ~/Library/Caches added over 1.2 GB more (including 575 MB for Swift Package Manager, 379.7 MB of Homebrew downloads, 261.7 MB of pip cache, and 24.1 MB of pnpm metadata). Even so, ~/Library/Caches was only a slice of the 124.29 GB scanned on that machine—far smaller than iOS DeviceSupport (24.1 GB du), CoreSimulator/Devices (43.0 GB du), Xcode DerivedData (15.3 GB du), and old node_modules folders (66.3 GB du). Always measure first so you know whether caches are actually where your storage went.

1. Check how much space ~/Library/Caches uses (read-only)

Before deleting anything, check the total size of your user cache folder and see which individual apps are taking the most space:

# Total size of your user cache folder (read-only)
du -sh ~/Library/Caches

# Top 20 largest folders inside ~/Library/Caches
du -sh ~/Library/Caches/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -20

If you also use web browsers with profile-level caches or developer tools that store caches outside ~/Library/Caches, you can inspect them read-only too:

du -sh \
  ~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome \
  ~/Library/Caches/Firefox \
  ~/Library/Caches/Homebrew/downloads \
  ~/Library/Caches/pip \
  ~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm \
  ~/Library/Caches/Yarn 2>/dev/null

Note: du reports total disk usage for a directory, not how much is safe to remove blindly. Some tools place virtual environments, downloaded browser binaries, or Apple system databases inside ~/Library/Caches, so always inspect folder names before deleting.

2. ~/Library/Caches vs. /Library/Caches: what is safe and what to leave alone

Location What lives inside Safe to clear? What happens after removal
~/Library/Caches/<third-party app> App thumbnails, HTTP/image caches, updater downloads Usually yes (quit the app first) App rebuilds the cache on next launch; first launch may feel slightly slower
Browser caches (~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome, Firefox, com.apple.Safari, plus profile Cache/Code Cache) Cached web pages, scripts, images, and shader caches Yes (quit the browser first) Websites re-download assets on next visit; cookies, history, bookmarks, and passwords stay intact
Developer caches in ~/Library/Caches (Homebrew/downloads, pip, Yarn, org.swift.swiftpm, CocoaPods, go-build) Downloaded package archives and build intermediates Yes (when no build or install is running) Package managers re-download archives next time you install or rebuild
Risky subfolders inside ~/Library/Caches (com.apple.FontRegistry*, com.apple.spotlight*, CloudKit*, com.apple.finder, pypoetry/virtualenvs*, ms-playwright*, pnpm/dlx*, JetBrains*) macOS system indexes/databases, Python virtualenvs, Playwright browser runtimes, IDE indexes No—skip these Deleting them can break font rendering, Finder/CloudKit sync, local Python virtualenvs, or test runners until rebuilt/reinstalled
~/Library/Containers/<bundle-id>/Data/Library/Caches Caches of sandboxed Mac App Store apps Usually yes (quit the app first) Sandboxed app regenerates its cache on next launch
/Library/Caches (root Library) System-wide caches shared across all user accounts and daemons Leave alone Requires admin privileges and can cause glitches in shared services; macOS prunes these itself
/System/Library/Caches Core macOS operating system caches (SIP-protected) Never touch Protected by System Integrity Protection; attempting to modify it risks system instability

3. How to clear cache on a Mac manually (Finder & Terminal)

You do not need any third-party app to clear ~/Library/Caches safely. Follow this conservative sequence instead of wiping the whole folder at once.

Step 1: Quit all running apps first

Deleting cache files while an app holds open file handles or writes to a SQLite cache database can cause the app to crash, lose transient state, or keep disk space occupied until the process exits. Quit your browsers, editors, chat apps, and Xcode (Command + Q) before cleaning.

Step 2: Inspect and clear specific folders in Finder

  1. Open Finder and press Shift + Command + G (Go to Folder).
  2. Type ~/Library/Caches and press Return.
  3. Switch to List view (Command + 2) and sort by Size (enable Calculate all sizes via Command + J if sizes are blank).
  4. Select specific large third-party app cache folders whose apps are not running—skipping com.apple.* folders, password managers, cloud sync apps, IDEs, and anything you do not recognize.
  5. Press Command + Delete to move those folders to the Trash (never delete the parent ~/Library/Caches folder itself).
  6. Relaunch your apps to verify everything opens normally, then empty the Trash to reclaim the disk space.

Step 3: Clear browser caches safely (without losing logins)

  • Safari: Open Safari → Settings → Advanced, check Show features for web developers, then press Option + Command + E (or click Develop → Empty Caches). This clears web cache without removing cookies, history, or passwords.
  • Chrome / Brave / Edge / Arc: Open Delete Browsing Data, check only Cached images and files (leave Cookies and Passwords unchecked), and confirm.
  • Firefox: Go to Settings → Privacy & Security → Cookies and Site Data → Clear Data, and check only Temporary cached files and pages.

Step 4: Clean developer caches with their official commands

When large folders inside ~/Library/Caches belong to developer tools, their built-in cleanup commands are safer than rm -rf:

# Clean old Homebrew download caches
brew cleanup --prune=all

# Purge pip's HTTP and wheel cache
pip cache purge

# Remove unused pnpm store packages (do not delete ~/Library/pnpm/store manually)
pnpm store prune

Warning: Avoid running rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/* blindly. Wildcard deletion hits caches of currently running apps and background services, wipes Apple subsystem caches like com.apple.FontRegistry, CloudKit, and com.apple.finder, and can accidentally destroy Poetry virtual environments (pypoetry/virtualenvs), Playwright browsers (ms-playwright), or JetBrains caches stored inside ~/Library/Caches. Always target specific verified folders—or move them to the Trash first.

What if ~/Library/Caches is only a few gigabytes?

On many Macs—especially developer or AI-coding machines—~/Library/Caches is not the main reason storage is full. If your disk is still tight after checking caches, check our dedicated guides on whether Xcode DerivedData is safe to delete, cleaning iOS DeviceSupport and Xcode Simulators, finding and deleting old node_modules folders, removing leftover Claude Code git worktrees, and tracking down Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex disk space.

4. How CleanBit handles ~/Library/Caches (and its sandbox boundaries)

I'm the developer of CleanBit, a sandboxed Mac App Store disk space cleaner for macOS 15+ (v1.0.1 now supports 9 languages and per-group Smart Scan cleaning). Because blind wildcard cleaning inside ~/Library/Caches causes unnecessary breakage, CleanBit applies multiple guardrails before anything can be removed:

  • Running-app blocking (checked twice): CleanBit checks currently running apps during scanning and locks their caches so they cannot be selected—then re-checks running apps again immediately before deleting each individual item, along with verifying the file path, symlink target, and file identity.
  • Protected Apple & third-party bundle lists: CleanBit refuses to delete the ~/Library/Caches folder itself, automatically skips com.apple.* and macOS subsystem prefixes (FontRegistry, Spotlight, CloudKit, Finder, Keychain, and more), excludes sensitive tool paths (pypoetry/virtualenvs, ms-playwright, pnpm/dlx, JetBrains), and skips over 300 protected third-party app bundle patterns during broad cache sweeps.
  • Dedicated rules with no double-counting: Browser caches (Safari, Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Vivaldi, Firefox—without touching cookies, history, or passwords) and developer caches (Xcode, Homebrew, pip, Yarn, SwiftPM, CocoaPods, Go) are handled by their own specific rules so nothing is counted twice.
  • Sandboxed App Caches (~/Library/Containers): If you optionally grant Full Disk Access, CleanBit can also inspect Data/Library/Caches and Data/tmp inside sandboxed app containers after verifying each container's containermanagerd metadata matches its bundle ID.
  • Clear deletion control & honest sandbox limits: Recommended caches are deleted permanently by default so disk space returns right away (or you can switch Recommended items to move to Trash in Settings), while Review items always move to the Trash. Because CleanBit runs inside Apple's App Sandbox with no root privileges and no background helper daemon, it never touches /Library/Caches, /System/Library/Caches, /private/tmp, APFS local snapshots, or iCloud Drive synced files.

Scanning and your first 2 cleans are free on the Mac App Store (with monthly, yearly, or one-time lifetime options).

Originally published at getcleanbit.app/guides/is-it-safe-to-delete-library-caches-mac/. Written by the CleanBit developer with AI assistance; all measurements were taken on a real developer Mac.

title: Your USDT Wallet Risk Score Is Not a Verdict: Building Better AML Checks for Blockchain Applications
description:
AMLdark · Screen TRC20 USDT addresses for free

Live AML screening for Tron-based USDT addresses against OFAC designations, Tether's freeze list and darknet datasets. Free tier included.

amldark.com

A blockchain transaction can be perfectly valid from a technical perspective and still deserve a closer look from a compliance perspective.

This distinction is becoming increasingly important for developers building cryptocurrency exchanges, payment gateways, wallet applications, P2P platforms, and Web3 infrastructure.

Consider a simple scenario:

A user deposits 5,000 USDT into a cryptocurrency application.

The transaction is confirmed. The tokens arrive. The smart contract behaves as expected.

From the blockchain's perspective, everything worked.

But what does the application actually know about the incoming funds?

Does it know anything about the sending address's previous activity? Has the address interacted with entities associated with sanctions, fraud, or other high-risk activity? Are there indirect relationships that deserve investigation?

A transaction hash alone cannot answer all these questions.

This is where blockchain analytics and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) screening become important engineering considerations.

In this article, we'll explore how developers can think about wallet risk assessment, why simplistic risk scores can be misleading, and how to design more transparent screening workflows for USDT transactions.

  1. Blockchain Validity and Financial Risk Are Different Layers

One of the most important architectural decisions is separating blockchain transaction validation from compliance analysis.

These processes answer different questions.

Blockchain validation asks:

Was the transaction included in the blockchain?

Did the transaction execute successfully?

Which addresses participated?

Which tokens were transferred?

What was the transaction timestamp?

AML analysis asks:

Is an address associated with known risk indicators?

Does it have relevant sanctions exposure?

Are there documented connections to fraudulent activity?

What does its transaction history reveal?

Is further investigation justified?

A successful transaction does not automatically establish the legitimacy of the funds.

Likewise, an address appearing in a risk dataset does not automatically establish criminal activity.

Developers should avoid combining these two layers into a single yes-or-no result.

A better system preserves the original blockchain facts while attaching a separate, explainable risk assessment.

  1. Why USDT on TRON Creates an Interesting Engineering Challenge

USDT is used across multiple blockchain networks, including TRON and Ethereum.

However, developers should never treat every USDT transaction as technically identical.

USDT on TRON uses the TRC-20 token standard, while USDT on Ethereum follows the ERC-20 standard.

The transaction structures, contract addresses, network infrastructure, and available analytical data differ.

For applications supporting TRC-20 USDT, the screening process should consider:

The correct TRON network.

The relevant token contract.

The sending and receiving addresses.

Transaction identifiers.

Token transfer events.

Available historical transaction information.

This is particularly important when applications support deposits from multiple networks.

A token symbol is not a sufficient identifier.

A reliable implementation should use network identifiers and verified contract addresses to prevent accidental cross-network assumptions.

  1. Address Screening Is Not the Same as Transaction Screening

This is one of the most important distinctions in blockchain analytics.

An address represents a blockchain account.

A transaction represents a particular movement of assets.

An address may have thousands of historical transactions, but the risk context of each transaction can be different.

For example, imagine an address that previously received funds from a service identified in a blockchain intelligence dataset.

A basic address-level screening system might return a warning.

However, a more detailed investigation should consider:

When did the interaction occur?

How many transactions separate the addresses?

What was the transferred amount?

Was the exposure direct or indirect?

Is the underlying attribution reliable?

Has the relevant information been updated?

The distinction matters because risk should be evaluated in context.

A single historical interaction should not automatically determine the status of every future transaction involving that address.

  1. The Problem With Treating AML Scores as Absolute Truth

Many blockchain screening systems use numerical risk scores.

These scores can be useful because they make large amounts of information easier to interpret.

However, developers should be careful about how they expose them.

Imagine two addresses:

Address A receives a high-risk classification because of a direct connection to a documented malicious service.

Address B receives a similar score because of several indirect interactions with addresses that have previously been flagged.

The numerical results might look similar, but the underlying circumstances are not necessarily equivalent.

A good screening interface should explain why a score was generated.

Ideally, it should distinguish between:

Direct exposure.

Indirect exposure.

Sanctions-related indicators.

Fraud-related indicators.

Mixer-related indicators.

Historical versus recent activity.

Confirmed information versus uncertain attribution.

The goal is not simply to generate a number.

The goal is to provide enough context for a human reviewer to understand the result.

  1. Designing a Practical AML Screening Pipeline

For developers building cryptocurrency applications, it helps to think about AML screening as a separate processing pipeline.

Here is one possible architecture.

Stage 1: Transaction ingestion

The application receives a blockchain event.

For a TRC-20 USDT transfer, the system should identify:

Transaction hash.

Sender address.

Recipient address.

Token contract.

Transfer amount.

Block information.

Transaction timestamp.

The original blockchain data should be preserved for future reference.

Stage 2: Data normalization

Different data providers may use different formats.

Normalize addresses, timestamps, network identifiers, token amounts, and entity references before performing further analysis.

This reduces inconsistencies across different screening sources.

Stage 3: Risk intelligence lookup

The system checks relevant information from available intelligence datasets.

Depending on the provider, this may include sanctions information, known scam addresses, fraud-related entities, darknet exposure, and other blockchain risk indicators.

The system should also record the source and timestamp of the information.

Stage 4: Relationship analysis

Direct address matching is only one part of blockchain investigation.

Graph analysis can help identify relationships between addresses.

However, developers should avoid assuming that every graph connection represents the same level of risk.

The distance between addresses, transaction amounts, timing, and nature of the relationship all matter.

Stage 5: Risk interpretation

Instead of producing only a single number, the application should return structured findings.

For example, an internal result might contain:

Overall risk classification.

Relevant risk categories.

Direct exposure indicators.

Indirect exposure indicators.

Supporting transaction references.

Data freshness.

Recommended review status.

Stage 6: Human review and decision-making

A screening result should support a decision rather than automatically replace every compliance procedure.

Depending on the business, potential outcomes may include additional verification, enhanced due diligence, escalation to a compliance team, or further investigation.

The appropriate action depends on the applicable legal and operational requirements.

  1. False Positives: The Hidden Cost of Poor Screening

A screening system that identifies every unfamiliar wallet as suspicious is not a useful screening system.

False positives can create serious operational problems.

Imagine a cryptocurrency payment application processing thousands of transactions daily.

If the system generates excessive warnings without sufficient context, the compliance team may spend most of its time investigating low-quality alerts.

This can result in:

Delayed deposits.

Unnecessary customer support requests.

Increased operational costs.

Poor user experiences.

Reduced attention to genuinely significant cases.

This is why screening quality should not be measured only by how many suspicious addresses a system identifies.

Developers should also evaluate:

The quality of underlying attribution data.

The accuracy of entity matching.

The treatment of indirect exposure.

The freshness of intelligence datasets.

The consistency of risk classifications.

The explainability of individual alerts.

A useful system should help analysts prioritize investigations rather than overwhelm them.

  1. API Integration: Turning AML Screening Into Infrastructure

For cryptocurrency businesses, manual wallet checks may become inefficient as transaction volumes increase.

This creates a practical opportunity for API-based screening.

A typical integration could follow this workflow:

A user initiates a deposit.

The application identifies the relevant blockchain address.

A screening request is submitted.

The screening provider returns available risk information.

The application evaluates the response according to its internal policies.

A compliance workflow handles cases requiring additional review.

Developers should pay particular attention to several technical considerations.

Response consistency

API responses should have predictable structures so applications can process them reliably.

Timeout handling

A screening service should not cause the entire payment infrastructure to become unavailable.

Caching

Repeated requests for the same address may be handled more efficiently with an appropriate caching strategy, provided data freshness requirements are respected.

Auditability

The application should preserve enough information to reconstruct why a particular decision was made.

Data privacy

Wallet addresses and transaction information should be handled according to the organization's privacy and security requirements.

AML screening should become a well-integrated component of the architecture, not an isolated tool that developers remember to use occasionally.

  1. Five Questions Every Developer Should Ask Before Integrating an AML Provider

Before choosing a blockchain screening solution, technical teams should investigate more than its advertised risk score.

Here are five useful questions.

  1. Which blockchain networks are supported?

A provider supporting Ethereum may not necessarily provide equivalent analytical coverage for TRON.

  1. Which risk categories are available?

Understand whether the provider covers sanctions, fraud, scams, mixers, darknet exposure, and other relevant categories.

  1. Can indirect exposure be explained?

A useful system should provide enough information to understand relationships between addresses.

  1. How fresh is the underlying intelligence?

Risk datasets can change. Developers should understand update frequency and information timestamps.

  1. Is the API suitable for production workloads?

Investigate documentation, authentication, response structures, error handling, rate limits, and integration requirements.

The right provider is not necessarily the one advertising the highest number of supported features.

It is the one whose data, methodology, and infrastructure fit the application's actual requirements.

title: Daily AI News Nov 24: Anthropic's Claude Ship Lets Agents Review and Approve Code
description:
Today's Storylines

Three Numbers That Belong on the Same Slide

The daily AI news for November 24 is about three capabilities arriving together: agents that can now approve code, sanctions that reshape chip supply, and a privacy shift that changes what models remember. Each moves the industry one step from demo to infrastructure.

The Five-Minute Version

  • Anthropic launched Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix and approve code changes in GitHub and GitLab.
  • US imposed sanctions on a Singaporean firm at the center of the Nvidia chip scandal, blacklisting Megaspeed.
  • Google Gemini now decouples chat history from AI training data, adding new user controls.
  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned after board reinstatement amid national security scrutiny.
  • Open source AI desktop app TheGitAI released for macOS, Windows and Linux.
  • Matching Sonnet 5.5 on medical chart review at 3% of the cost shows shrinking inference economics.

Anthropic Launches Claude Ship: Agents That Review, Fix and Approve Code

What Claude Ship Does

Anthropic announced Claude Ship on November 23, a new product that lets AI agents participate directly in code review workflows. The agents can read pull requests, suggest fixes, and now approve or request changes — the same actions a human reviewer takes.

The system integrates with GitHub and GitLab. When a pull request opens, Claude Ship agents analyze the diff, run tests in a sandbox, and post review comments. They can also apply fixes directly to the branch.

The Approve Button Changes the Workflow

Until now, AI code assistants stopped at suggestions. The human had to read, verify and click merge. Claude Ship adds the approve action, meaning an agent can now be the final gate before code lands.

Anthropic says the agent follows the same review standards the team configures: passing tests, style guides, security scans. The human sets the policy; the agent enforces it.

Why This Matters for Developer Velocity

Code review is often the bottleneck in shipping. Large teams wait hours or days for human reviewers. An agent that can approve routine changes — dependency updates, test additions, documentation fixes — removes that queue.

For risky changes, the agent requests human review. The workflow becomes: agent handles the 80% that are safe, humans focus on the 20% that need judgment.

Sources

  • TechCrunch: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix and approve code changes

US Sanctions Singapore Firm at Center of Nvidia Chip Scandal

Megaspeed Blacklisted

The US Commerce Department added Singapore-based Megaspeed to the Entity List on November 23. The company is accused of diverting Nvidia AI chips to China in violation of export controls.

Reuters reports the blacklist cuts Megaspeed off from US technology and banking. The move follows a Washington Post report that the Commerce Department approved 580,000 Nvidia chips for China in exchange for a revenue share.

The Singapore Connection

Megaspeed operated as a transshipment hub. Chips shipped legally to Singapore were re-exported to Chinese buyers. The firm's directors include individuals with ties to Chinese military procurement networks.

Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore sales in its latest earnings. The subpoena from California prosecutors and the Megaspeed blacklist suggest the channel was larger than previously acknowledged.

What This Means for Supply Chains

Companies buying Nvidia GPUs now face stricter due diligence on Singapore intermediaries. The Entity List designation means any US person or company dealing with Megaspeed needs a license — effectively a ban.

For AI labs planning compute purchases, the message is clear: the provenance of every GPU will be audited. Gray-market chains are being closed.

Sources

  • Reuters: US blacklists Megaspeed chip firm linked to Nvidia scandal
  • NY Times: Trump administration blacklists Megaspeed over Nvidia chip trade

Google Gemini Decouples Chat History from AI Training

New User Controls

Google announced updated controls for Gemini on November 23. Users can now choose whether their conversations are used to improve the model. The setting is off by default for new users.

Previously, chat history fed directly into training pipelines. The change separates the product experience (conversation continuity) from the model improvement loop.

Why the Default Changed

Regulatory pressure from the EU AI Act and US state privacy laws forced the shift. Google also faces a class action alleging unauthorized use of chat data.

The new architecture stores conversations in a user-controlled vault. Training pipelines pull from anonymized, aggregated datasets that users explicitly opt into.

Impact on Model Quality

Google says the quality impact is minimal because the opted-in corpus is still large. But the change sets a precedent: user data is no longer free training fuel by default.

Other labs will face the same pressure. The era of implicit consent for AI training data is ending.

Sources

  • Google Blog: Updated controls for Gemini app

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Reinstated Amid National Security Scrutiny

Board Overruled Management

Bloomberg reported on November 23 that Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO without consulting the management team. Huang had stepped aside temporarily amid a federal investigation into chip diversions to China.

The board's unilateral move is rare. It signals that Huang's control over the company's China strategy is seen as a national security matter, not just a governance issue.

Foreign Policy Calls It a Scandal

Foreign Policy published an essay calling Huang's return "the biggest national security scandal in US history." The argument: the CEO who oversaw the Singapore diversion channel is now back in charge of the company that supplies the chips.

Republicans in Congress are breaking with the administration over the reinstatement. The NY Times reports GOP members demand a full briefing on what the board knew.

Market Reaction

Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday, November 20, the day after the Anthropic IPO erased Nasdaq gains. The stock has not recovered. Short sellers who bet against Nvidia's China exposure were vindicated.

Sources

  • Bloomberg: Nvidia board reinstated CEO without consulting management
  • Foreign Policy: Huang's return is a national security scandal
  • NY Times: Republicans break with Trump over Jensen Huang

TheGitAI Desktop App Released for All Platforms

Open Source AI Coding Assistant

TheGitAI released its desktop application on November 23 for macOS, Windows and Linux. The app brings local AI coding assistance with Git integration, running models locally or via API.

The project is open source. Users can connect their own Ollama instance, LM Studio, or cloud API keys. The app handles context gathering from the repository, diff generation, and commit message drafting.

Why Local Matters

Enterprise policies often block cloud AI tools. A desktop app that runs entirely locally — model, context, diffs — satisfies compliance while delivering AI assistance.

The release adds to the growing local-first AI tooling ecosystem: Cursor, Windsurf, and now TheGitAI all offer varying degrees of local execution.

Sources

  • TheGitAI Desktop App

Matching Sonnet 5.5 on Medical Chart Review at 3% of the Cost

Propensity Labs Case Study

Propensity Labs published a case study on November 23 showing their Cortex Charts system matching Claude Sonnet 5.5 on medical chart review tasks at roughly 3% of the inference cost.

The system uses a smaller specialized model fine-tuned on de-identified clinical notes. It achieves comparable accuracy on ICD-10 coding, discharge summary quality, and comorbidity extraction.

The Economics Shift

Frontier model API pricing has been the ceiling for AI applications. A 97% cost reduction for a specific domain task changes the ROI calculation for healthcare AI deployments.

Hospitals and insurers running millions of chart reviews per year can now justify automated coding that was previously too expensive.

Sources

  • Propensity Labs: Cortex Charts case study

FAQ

What is Claude Ship and how does it differ from Copilot?

Claude Ship is an AI agent that participates directly in code review on GitHub and GitLab. Unlike Copilot which suggests code while you write, Claude Ship reviews pull requests after they are opened, runs tests, suggests fixes, and can approve or request changes — acting as an automated reviewer.

Did the US really blacklist a Singapore company over Nvidia chips?

Yes. The Commerce Department added Megaspeed to the Entity List on November 23 for diverting Nvidia AI chips to China. This follows reports that 580,000 Nvidia chips were approved for China sales with a revenue share arrangement.

Can I opt out of Gemini training on my chats?

Yes. Google added new controls on November 23 that let users choose whether conversations are used for model training. The setting is off by default for new users.

Why did Nvidia's board reinstate Jensen Huang without consulting management?

The board's unilateral move suggests Huang's role in China chip strategy is viewed as a national security matter. Foreign Policy called it "the biggest national security scandal in US history."

The Bottom Line

What to Watch Next

Watch whether Claude Ship's approve action becomes a standard CI gate. If agents can reliably approve routine changes, the code review bottleneck shrinks — but the liability question when an agent approves a bug remains open.

Watch the Megaspeed case for precedent. If Singapore transshipment hubs are systematically shut down, the gray market for AI chips contracts, and legitimate buyers face longer procurement cycles.

The Pattern Today

Three of today's stories are about control shifting to automated systems: agents approving code, export controls enforced via Entity List, and users controlling their training data. The industry is building the governance layer that was missing in the pure capability phase.

Keep Reading

This briefing is part of the daily AI news archive. The weekly AI news roundup publishes every Monday, and the monthly AI news recap publishes on the first of each month.

For the security thread running through this week, read our November 23 weekly roundup.

For yesterday's carbon and zero-day coverage, read the November 22 briefing.
