title: A Crypto Swap Is More Than a Button: What Really Happens When You Exchange Tokens on TRON?
description:
TronSeven — Non-Custodial Token Swaps on TRON Network

Swap TRC-20 tokens on TRON with self-custody and open-source smart contracts. Low fees, verifiable on TRONSCAN.

tronseven.com

Most people think a cryptocurrency swap is a simple operation.

Choose a token. Select another token. Enter an amount. Press Swap.

A few moments later, the new tokens appear in the wallet.

But this simple interface hides an interesting technical process. Behind every successful decentralized exchange, multiple components must work together: token contracts, wallet signatures, liquidity mechanisms, transaction execution, and blockchain resource management.

For developers and Web3 enthusiasts, understanding this process is much more valuable than simply knowing where the Swap button is.

Let's look beneath the interface and explore what actually happens when exchanging tokens on the TRON network.

  1. The Swap Interface Is Only the Beginning

A decentralized exchange interface is essentially a communication layer between a user and blockchain infrastructure.

When someone initiates a swap, the interface must translate a simple user request into operations that a smart contract can execute.

Consider a practical example:

A user has 100 USDT (TRC-20) and wants to receive TRX.

From the user's perspective, this looks like a single exchange.

Technically, several things need to happen:

The application identifies the selected tokens and their contract addresses.

It retrieves pricing and available liquidity information.

It calculates an estimated output amount.

It determines the transaction parameters.

The wallet requests the necessary authorization.

The transaction is signed and broadcast.

The smart contract executes the exchange.

The blockchain records the resulting state changes.

The interface makes these steps look simple, but each one has its own requirements and potential failure points.

This is why a reliable swap experience should be evaluated beyond its visual design.

  1. Why Token Contracts Matter More Than Token Names

One of the easiest mistakes in cryptocurrency is assuming that a token's displayed name or symbol uniquely identifies it.

It doesn't.

A token called USDT, for example, should always be checked against its official contract address on the relevant blockchain.

On TRON, fungible tokens commonly use the TRC-20 standard.

TRC-20 defines how compatible smart contracts expose token functionality, including operations such as:

balanceOf

transfer

approve

transferFrom

allowance

These functions are fundamental to many decentralized applications.

For example, a decentralized exchange may need permission to use a particular amount of a user's tokens before executing a swap.

This is where token approvals become important.

An approval is not the same as completing an exchange. It grants a smart contract permission to spend tokens within the approved allowance.

Developers should make this distinction clear in their interfaces.

Users should also understand what they are approving, which contract receives permission, and whether the allowance is limited or unlimited.

A good interface should never make users guess.

  1. Liquidity: The Invisible Component Behind Every Swap

Here is a question worth asking:

If someone wants to exchange a large amount of one token for another, where do the destination tokens actually come from?

The answer depends on the exchange mechanism.

Many decentralized exchanges use automated market makers (AMMs) and liquidity pools.

A liquidity pool contains reserves of different tokens. Users trade against these reserves rather than matching directly with another person placing an order.

One widely known AMM model uses the constant-product formula:

[
x \times y = k
]

Where:

(x) represents the reserve of one token.

(y) represents the reserve of another token.

(k) represents the constant product, ignoring fees and other adjustments.

When a trade changes one reserve, the relationship between the reserves changes the implied exchange price.

This creates an important consequence:

The size of a swap matters.

A small exchange may have relatively little influence on the pool price. A large exchange compared with available liquidity can create substantial price impact.

This is why developers should pay attention to:

Available liquidity.

Estimated output.

Price impact.

Slippage tolerance.

Trading fees.

Minimum acceptable output.

A displayed exchange rate is an estimate, not necessarily a guarantee of the final execution price.

  1. Slippage: Why the Final Amount Can Be Different

Imagine that an application displays an estimated output of 500 TRX.

The user reviews the quote and submits the transaction.

However, before the transaction executes, the pool price changes because another transaction has affected its reserves.

The final output may now be lower than the original estimate.

This is slippage.

A decentralized exchange generally uses transaction parameters to limit how much the execution outcome can differ from the expected result.

For example, a minimum-output condition can prevent a trade from executing if the received amount falls below the user's specified threshold.

Developers should understand the relationship between:

Expected output: The amount calculated when the quote is generated.

Minimum output: The lowest amount acceptable under the transaction parameters.

Actual output: The amount received after successful execution.

These values are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A thoughtful exchange interface should communicate them clearly before the user signs anything.

  1. TRON Has a Different Resource Model: Energy and Bandwidth

This is one of the most interesting aspects of building applications on TRON.

Developers familiar with Ethereum often expect blockchain transaction costs to follow a single gas-based model.

TRON uses a different resource structure.

Two important resources are Bandwidth and Energy.

Bandwidth

Bandwidth generally measures the size of transactions stored on the blockchain.

Energy

Energy measures the computational resources required to execute smart contracts in the TRON Virtual Machine (TVM).

A token swap involves smart contract interactions, so Energy can become an important part of the transaction cost.

Users can obtain resources through staking or delegation. When available resources are insufficient, TRX can be burned to cover the required costs under the network's rules.

This creates an important design consideration for decentralized exchange developers.

The application should help users understand the potential resource requirements before they authorize a transaction.

It should also avoid making misleading claims that every swap is automatically free.

For developers building on TRON, understanding this resource model is essential when designing a smooth user experience.

  1. What Happens Between Signing and Confirmation?

A wallet signature is not the same as a completed blockchain transaction.

This distinction deserves more attention.

When a user approves a transaction in a compatible wallet, the wallet signs the transaction using the user's authorization.

The signed transaction can then be broadcast to the TRON network.

But the application still needs to determine whether execution was successful.

A responsible transaction lifecycle should distinguish between several states:

Prepared: Transaction parameters have been generated.

Awaiting signature: The wallet is requesting user authorization.

Broadcast: The signed transaction has been submitted to the network.

Confirmed: The network has processed the transaction.

Execution result: The application checks whether the smart contract operation succeeded.

A transaction ID alone should not be treated as proof that a swap completed successfully.

Developers should inspect the transaction receipt and relevant contract execution results.

TRONSCAN can also help users independently examine transaction activity.

This separation between submission and successful execution is important for both application developers and everyday cryptocurrency users.

  1. Security Should Be Part of the Interface, Not an Afterthought

A decentralized exchange can have an excellent design and still expose users to unnecessary risks if its security model is unclear.

There are several areas worth examining.

Smart contract permissions

Users should understand which contracts they interact with and what permissions they grant.

Contract verification

Where source code is available, developers and technically experienced users should examine whether verified contract information matches the deployed implementation.

Token identification

Applications should use reliable token contract addresses rather than trusting symbols or logos.

Transaction simulation

Where supported, developers can simulate state-changing operations before broadcasting them. This can help identify execution problems, although simulation cannot guarantee that the final transaction will succeed under later blockchain conditions.

Transaction transparency

Users should be able to inspect the transaction ID and verify what happened independently.

No interface can eliminate every smart contract or market risk. Good engineering makes important information visible rather than hiding complexity behind a convenient button.

  1. Evaluating the User Experience of a TRON Swap Platform

Technical architecture is only one part of a decentralized exchange.

The other part is how effectively the application communicates with its users.

A useful swap interface should answer five questions:

Which asset am I exchanging?

Which asset will I receive?

What exchange rate and price impact should I expect?

What permissions and network resources are required?

How can I verify the completed transaction?

These questions provide a practical framework for evaluating any TRON swap application.

They are also useful when comparing different wallet-connected exchange interfaces.

For example, TronSeven is a project worth exploring when looking at the TRON swap experience:

https://tronseven.com

Rather than judging an exchange solely by its appearance, examine its supported assets, wallet compatibility, transaction information, and available contract documentation.

The same evaluation criteria should apply to every platform in this space.

  1. A Developer's Checklist Before Building or Using a Swap Application

Here is a practical checklist worth keeping:

Area

What to examine

Token contracts

Correct TRC-20 addresses

Wallet integration

Clear authorization requests

Pricing

Accurate quote calculations

Liquidity

Sufficient available reserves

Slippage

Minimum-output protection

Network resources

Energy and Bandwidth estimates

Execution

Transaction receipt verification

Security

Contract permissions and verification

User experience

Clear status and error messages

A decentralized exchange is not just a smart contract with a graphical interface.

It is a complete interaction between wallets, blockchain infrastructure, token standards, liquidity mechanisms, and users.

Missing even one of these components can create a frustrating experience.

title: Why max_connections=500 Killed Our DB: Production Sizing & Config Guide (PGSizer)
description:
Production Sizing Summary (PGSizer — Why max_connections=500 Killed Our DB): shared_buffers = 25% RAM | Pool via PgBouncer

  • Legacy Bottleneck: Managed RDS + OOM Spikes ($265/mo (3,000 IOPS Cap))
  • Right-Sized Target: Tuned KVM + PgBouncer ($19.99/mo (32GB NVMe))
  • Interactive Browser Calculator & 1-Click Config: PGSizer — Why max_connections=500 Killed Our DB

1. Real-World Incident Post-Mortem

At 02:14 UTC during a payroll batch, a 16GB PostgreSQL 17 primary vanished with kernel SIGKILL after max_connections=500 collided with work_mem=64MB across parallel hash joins.

Each analytical query spawned four parallel workers with three hash and sort nodes, so 65 active sessions allocated over 15GB of private heap and forced OOM-Killer onto postmaster.

Capping max_connections at 80 behind PgBouncer transaction pooling and lowering work_mem to 16MB stabilized p99 latency at 8ms on a $19.99/mo Hostinger KVM 8 NVMe server.

2. Audit Live Postgres Connection Heap, Temp Spills & Buffer Hit Ratio

Before resizing instances or migrating production workloads, run this baseline diagnostic sequence on your Linux host:

psql -U postgres -d app_prod -c "SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1;"
psql -U postgres -d app_prod -c "SHOW shared_buffers; SHOW work_mem; SHOW effective_cache_size;"
psql -U postgres -d app_prod -c "SELECT datname, temp_files, pg_size_pretty(temp_bytes) FROM pg_stat_database;"
psql -U postgres -d app_prod -c "SELECT round(100.0*sum(blks_hit)/nullif(sum(blks_hit+blks_read),0),2) AS hit_pct FROM pg_stat_database;"
grep -E "Out of memory|Killed process" /var/log/kern.log | tail -n 5
iostat -xz 1 3

Start by grouping pg_stat_activity by state: if idle sessions outnumber active queries ten-to-one, unpooled backend processes are wasting roughly 9MB of RSS memory apiece.

Next, check temp_bytes alongside iostat await: climbing temp_files means work_mem is spilling sorts onto NVMe, whereas kernel OOM entries prove per-node work_mem was set too high.

3. Production Reference Configuration & Guardrails

Core deterministic sizing equation used by PGSizer:

shared_buffers = 25% RAM | Pool via PgBouncer
01. work_mem multiplies per sort & worker
02. Set random_page_cost = 1.1 on NVMe
03. Cap max_connections at 80 behind pooler

Reference deployment snippet (pgsizer-audit.sh):

# Interactive vCPU/RAM Sizer & Config Generator: https://pgsizer.pages.dev/en/?src=auto_devto_pgsizer_c1
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# PostgreSQL 17 Memory, Temp Spill & IOPS Quick Audit — https://pgsizer.pages.dev/
DB_NAME="${1:-postgres}"
psql -X -U postgres -d "$DB_NAME" <<'SQL'
SELECT name, setting, unit FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('max_connections','shared_buffers','work_mem','hash_mem_multiplier','effective_cache_size','random_page_cost');
SELECT state, count(*) AS backends FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
SELECT datname, temp_files, pg_size_pretty(temp_bytes) AS spilled_to_nvme,
       round(100.0 * blks_hit / nullif(blks_hit + blks_read, 0), 2) AS cache_hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();
SQL

4. Four Critical Production Gotchas to Avoid

  1. PostgreSQL allocates work_mem per sort or hash node per parallel worker, and PG 17 defaults hash_mem_multiplier to 2.0, doubling hash table memory silently.
  2. Leaving random_page_cost at the legacy 4.0 spinning-disk default tricks the query planner into full sequential scans on fast NVMe; lower it to 1.1 immediately.
  3. PgBouncer pool_mode=transaction breaks session-level SET variables, LISTEN/NOTIFY channels, and unnamed prepared statements unless client drivers enable protocol-level support.
  4. Pushing shared_buffers past 40% of physical RAM creates double-buffering against Linux page cache and causes nasty checkpoint I/O stalls without checkpoint_completion_target=0.9.

5. Architecture Perspective: Vertical Headroom vs Premature Complexity

Paying $260/mo for managed RDS db.m6i.xlarge still caps baseline gp3 storage at 3,000 IOPS, whereas local AMD EPYC NVMe on Hostinger KVM or UltaHost VDS delivers raw 4K IOPS.

Doubling VPS RAM before deploying PgBouncer rarely fixes connection exhaustion; it simply gives hundreds of idle Postgres forks more memory to burn during context switches.

6. Zero-Downtime Cutover Checklist

  • [ ] Deploy PgBouncer in transaction mode on port 6432 and cap PostgreSQL max_connections between 60 and 120 based on physical vCPU cores.
  • [ ] Set shared_buffers to 25% of RAM, effective_cache_size to 75% of RAM, random_page_cost=1.1, and wal_compression=zstd in postgresql.conf.
  • [ ] Enable Linux huge_pages=try with explicit vm.nr_hugepages sizing so large shared_buffers avoid multi-gigabyte page-table TLB miss overhead.
  • [ ] Stream continuous WAL archives plus daily pgBackRest snapshots to off-box S3 object storage and rehearse point-in-time recovery before cutover.

7. Frequently Asked Engineering Questions

Why not set shared_buffers to 80% of RAM like MySQL InnoDB?

PostgreSQL relies heavily on the Linux OS page cache for compressed filesystem reads and sort spill files. Keeping shared_buffers near 25% avoids double-caching pages while leaving safe headroom for work_mem.

When should we step up from Hostinger KVM 8 to UltaHost VDS?

Once hot B-tree indexes exceed 24GB or sustained WAL write throughput demands zero CPU steal under 24/7 OLTP load, move to dedicated physical RAM and NVMe RAID on a 32GB or 64GB UltaHost VDS.

Model your exact workload concurrency, RAM headroom, and 36-month infrastructure TCO directly in the browser at PGSizer (pgsizer.pages.dev).

title: Stop Your Coding Agent From Cycling Through Refuted Guesses: Free-Text Monologue vs. a Structured Hypothesis Matrix (2.54x Faster)
description:
💡 AI Labo Benchmark Series — Experiment E27 (Structured Reasoning & Diagnostic Scratchpads)

This post is part of our empirical benchmark series testing AI coding agent harness patterns inside network-isolated Proxmox VMs against a hidden 20-case grading suite.

  • 🚀 View All 41 Benchmark Results & Master Ranking
  • 🛡️ Read How Our Proxmox & systemd Anti-Cheating Sandbox Works

Metadata & Experiment Identity

  • Experiment ID: E27 (Backlog Candidate C023)
  • Run ID: e27-20261029-vm231-01
  • Sandbox Environment: Proxmox Isolated VM VM231 (ai-e27-231, 0 NICs, PrivateNetwork=yes, NoNewPrivileges=yes, InaccessiblePaths, UID split labexp27 / labjudge27)
  • Model: gemini-3.8-flash (thinkingLevel: LOW, temperature=0.0)
  • Pattern Under Test: "Anthropic <think> Tool Research & SWE-agent Structured Diagnostic Scratchpad (Hypothesis Elimination Matrix)" — Unstructured Free-Text Monologue (FreeTextMonologueRunner) vs. Structured THINK.md Hypothesis Elimination Table (StructuredHypothesisTableRunner)

1. Executive Summary (TL;DR)

When debugging a multi-module pipeline with 7+ interacting defects, letting an AI coding agent reason via unstructured Free-Text Monologue ("Let me think... maybe the settlement total is off because of integer division? Or wait, did we check that earlier?") leads to Hypothesis Cycling: as tool logs grow across turns, the model loses track of which candidate root causes were already falsified and which boundary contracts remain unverified.

Inspired by Anthropic's <think> scratchpad research and SWE-agent diagnostic matrices, we tested replacing free-text debugging monologues with a mandatory Structured Hypothesis Elimination Table (THINK.md) inside isolated VM VM231 on the 3-module enterprise payment settlement pipeline (validator.py ➔ settlement.py ➔ statement.py):

  • Mode A (FreeTextMonologueRunner): Reasons through unstructured free-text monologue logs (92,463 tool output chars across Turns 1–2) before submitting on Turn 3.
  • Mode B (StructuredHypothesisTableRunner): Requires a fixed-schema Hypothesis Elimination Matrix (STRUCTURED_HYPOTHESIS_TABLE_MD) mapping Hyp ID ➔ Target Module ➔ Suspected Defect ➔ Diagnostic Probe ➔ Status (CONFIRMED/REFUTED) ➔ Canonical Fix before any code edit.

Key Result

Mode A missed validator_01 (19 / 20, 95.0%) after 3 turns (48,712 input tokens) because it over-constrained set(item.keys()) != required_keys instead of stripping extra keys into a clean 5-key dictionary. Mode B achieved a 20 / 20 (100%) pass in 1 turn, cutting LLM calls by -66.7% (3 ➔ 1), cumulative input tokens by -95.0% (48,712 ➔ 2,450 tokens—a 19.88x reduction), API cost by -83.6% ($0.0478 ➔ $0.0079), and running 2.54x faster (33.66s ➔ 13.28s, -60.6%).

Metric Mode A: Free-Text Monologue (FreeTextMonologue) Mode B: Hypothesis Matrix (StructuredHypothesisTable) Delta / Improvement
Hidden Grading Suite Score (labjudge27) 19 / 20 (95.0% — 1 failure) 20 / 20 (100% — Perfect) +5.0% accuracy (19/20 ➔ 20/20)
Hypothesis Cycling Traps (gotcha_traps_hit) 2 traps (Turns 1 & 2) 0 traps -100% (zero cycling)
LLM Calls (model_calls) 3 calls 1 call (1-shot) -66.7% (3 ➔ 1 turn)
Cumulative File Edits (file_edits) 5 edits 3 edits (1 per module) -40.0% fewer edits
Cumulative Tool Output (tool_output_chars) 92,463 chars 102 chars -99.9% (906.5x noise reduction)
Turn 1 Tokens (In / Out) 1,655 in / 18 out 2,450 in / 1,604 out +795 in for H-01..H-07 Matrix
Turn 2 Tokens (In / Out) 15,832 in / 1,333 out — (completed on Turn 1) Avoided monologue rambling bloat
Turn 3 Tokens (In / Out) 31,225 in / 1,641 out — (completed on Turn 1) Avoided secondary cycling bloat
Cumulative Input Tokens (promptTokenCount) 48,712 tokens 2,450 tokens -95.0% (19.88x efficiency)
Cumulative Output Tokens (candidatesTokenCount) 2,992 tokens 1,604 tokens -46.4% output reduction
Elapsed Execution Time (elapsed_seconds) 33.66 sec 13.28 sec -60.6% (2.54x faster)
Estimated API Cost (estimated_micro_usd) $0.0478 (47,755 micro-USD) $0.0079 (7,853 micro-USD) -83.6% (6.08x cheaper)

2. The Verified THINK.md Hypothesis Elimination Matrix (input-03.json)

Instead of rambling in prose, Mode B locked this 7-row structured diagnostic matrix (+795 tokens) before touching a single line of code:

Hyp ID Target Module Suspected Defect / Boundary Diagnostic Probe & Elimination Result Status Required Canonical Fix
H-01 validator.py ALLOWED_CURRENCIES missing "JPY" & empty list [] allowed validate_txns([]) did not raise; "jpy" rejected CONFIRMED Set ALLOWED_CURRENCIES = ("USD", "EUR", "JPY") and reject len(raw_txns) == 0
H-02 validator.py isinstance(True, int) passes in Python & cents <= 0 rejects $0 auth tx_count=True accepted; unit_cents=0 raised ValueError CONFIRMED Check isinstance(x, bool) before isinstance(x, int); enforce cnt > 0, cents >= 0, 0 <= bps <= 1000
H-03 validator.py In-place mutation item["merchant_id"] = ... & extra keys retained Caller dict mutated; "extra": 1 leaked into output CONFIRMED Construct a fresh 5-key dict (merchant_id, currency, tx_count, unit_cents, chargeback_bps)
H-04 settlement.py sorted(order) destroys first-seen merchant-currency order M-Z before M-A reordered to M-A, M-Z CONFIRMED Iterate for k in order: (never sorted(order))
H-05 settlement.py Chargeback reserve >= 300 vs strictly > 300 bps 300 bps charged 10% reserve instead of 0 CONFIRMED Charge (gross * 10) // 100 strictly when g["chargeback_bps"] > 300
H-06 settlement.py Tier discount > 15000 vs inclusive >= 15000 & rebate cap subtotal == 15000 missed discount; rebate > after_discount went negative CONFIRMED Use subtotal >= 15000 (GROWTH 10%/0%; ENTERPRISE 20%/10%) and min(fee_rebate, after_discount)
H-07 statement.py : separator and unsigned "0" on zero discount/rebate Output had M-1:USD and TIER_DISCOUNT: 0 CONFIRMED Format {merchant_id}#{currency} and always prefix -: TIER_DISCOUNT: -{batch['tier_discount']}

3. Why Free-Text Monologue Missed validator_01 (19/20)

In Mode A (freetext-monologue-bundle.json), without H-03 explicitly distinguishing "rejecting missing required keys" from "stripping unapproved extra keys into a fresh 5-key dict", Mode A wrote:

# ❌ Mode A (FreeTextMonologueRunner — Turn 3 Final validator.py, 19/20)
        required_keys = {"merchant_id", "currency", "tx_count", "unit_cents", "chargeback_bps"}
        if set(item.keys()) != required_keys:  # <-- BUG: Raises ValueError when caller passes {"extra": 1} instead of stripping it!
            raise ValueError("invalid keys")

Mode B, guided by row H-03 ("extra": 1 leaked into output ➔ Construct a fresh 5-key dict), extracted the 5 required fields and dropped extra keys cleanly without raising a false-positive ValueError.

4. Drop-In Implementation Recipe: HypothesisTableGate 

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class HypothesisRow:
    hyp_id: str
    target_module: str
    suspected_defect: str
    probe_result: str
    status: str  # "CONFIRMED" or "REFUTED"
    canonical_fix: str

class HypothesisTableGate:
    """Blocks code edits until all target modules have confirmed/refuted rows in THINK.md."""
    def __init__(self, required_modules: set[str]):
        self.required_modules = required_modules
        self.confirmed_rows: list[HypothesisRow] = []

    def register_table(self, rows: list[HypothesisRow]) -> str:
        covered = {r.target_module for r in rows if r.status in {"CONFIRMED", "REFUTED"}}
        missing = self.required_modules - covered
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(f"THINK.md table incomplete; missing modules: {sorted(missing)}")
        self.confirmed_rows = [r for r in rows if r.status == "CONFIRMED"]
        return f"THINK.md locked with {len(self.confirmed_rows)} confirmed root causes."

5. Practical Takeaway: Force Tabular State for Multi-Bug Debugging

  1. Replace unstructured CoT monologues with a fixed-column Markdown table (THINK.md) on multi-bug tasks: A 6-column table acts as an external working-memory register where every confirmed bug maps 1-to-1 to a required code change.
  2. Keep REFUTED rows visible: Recording why a hypothesis was ruled out (status: REFUTED) prevents the agent from re-trying the same failed guess three turns later.

🔗 Continue Reading the Series

  • 🛡️ Methodology & Sandbox Architecture: How to Benchmark AI Agents Without Eval Cheating or API Key Leaks: Designing a Proxmox & systemd Sandbox

  • 🔌 Next Sequential Post (E28): Breaking A➔B➔A Edit Oscillations in Coding Agents: Unguarded Retry Loops vs. a Loop-Detection Circuit Breaker (-94.9% Input Tokens)
  • 🌿 Related Context Hygiene Deep Dive (E19 — Rank #4): Why Keeping Failed Code Attempts in Chat History Poisons Your Coding Agent: Error-Trace Pruning vs. Accumulated History

The latest installment in the Call of Duty franchise, Modern Warfare 4, has been making waves with its innovative gameplay mechanics and gritty storyline. The latest addition to the series, DMZ (Designated Major Zone), is an extraction mode that promises to deliver a unique and intense experience for players. In this blog post, we'll dive into the details of DMZ, its gameplay, and what it means for the future of the Call of Duty franchise.

What is DMZ?

DMZ is a new extraction mode in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, designed to provide a more intense and realistic experience for players. The mode is set in a fictional city, where players must extract high-value targets (HVTs) from the city while avoiding enemy forces. The twist? The city is under siege, and players must navigate through the chaos to complete their objectives.

DMZ is built around a series of objectives, including extracting HVTs, securing key locations, and eliminating enemy forces. The mode features a variety of gameplay mechanics, including:

  • Stealth: Players can use stealth to sneak past enemy forces, eliminating the need for a full-on assault.

The first gameplay footage of DMZ has been revealed, giving us a glimpse into the mode's intense action and realistic gameplay. The introduction of DMZ marks a significant shift in the Call of Duty franchise, moving away from traditional multiplayer modes and towards a more realistic, tactical experience. The success of DMZ could signal a new direction for the franchise, one that emphasizes realism and strategy over fast-paced action. This could be a major departure from the franchise's traditional formula, but it could also lead to a more engaging and immersive experience for players.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ mode is an exciting addition to the franchise, offering a unique and intense experience for players. The mode's focus on extraction and stealth gameplay mechanics sets it apart from other Call of Duty modes, and its realistic graphics and environments are sure to impress. As the gaming community continues to evolve, it will be interesting to see how DMZ is received and how it shapes the future of the Call of Duty franchise.

title: How we keep a Laravel log ingest endpoint fast (Valkey buffer, batched ClickHouse writes)
description:
We're building a hosted log tool on Laravel 13, and the part that took the most thought was ingestion. Clients send logs in bursts, sometimes thousands of lines a second, and the endpoint can't sit waiting on a database while that happens.

The request does almost nothing

It checks the token, pushes the batch into Valkey (Redis-compatible) and returns a 202. There are no MySQL queries in that path and no queue job per line.

Drainers do the writing

Separate long-running drainer processes, one per buffer shard, claim a batch of 500 to 1000 lines, insert it into ClickHouse, and only acknowledge it after the insert succeeded. Popping first and writing second looks simpler, but it loses lines if the process dies in between.

Replays without duplicates

That raises the opposite problem: if a drainer dies after inserting but before acknowledging, the batch gets inserted again on restart. ClickHouse's insert_deduplication_token handles that. Every batch carries a token, and a repeat with the same token is ignored, so a replay doesn't create duplicates.

Reads start with source and time

Every query filters by source and time range first, because that's what the table's primary key is built on. Without that, ClickHouse has to scan far more than it needs to.

Live tail is the cheap part

After storing a batch, the drainer broadcasts it on a private Laravel Reverb channel and the browser appends the lines. Nothing extra is stored for it.

Happy to go deeper on any of this in the comments. If you want to poke at it, Tailcove is on DevHunt this week and has a free plan: https://devhunt.org/tool/tailcove

title: Hermes Agent + local Gemma(llama)
description:
Switching Between a Home LLM and a Free Cloud Model — Safely

A practical setup with llama.cpp + Tailscale + OpenRouter + Hermes Agent
By Matis atelier

About the date of this information
Everything here reflects the state of the software as of August 2026, when I read the Hermes Agent source code directly because I could not find this behavior documented. Official documentation has probably improved since then. Check the current docs first; treat this article as the "why it behaves that way" companion, not as the final word. Config key names may have changed.
All IPs, keys, hostnames and paths below are placeholders.

1. The goal

I run an LLM at home (llama.cpp, Gemma 4 12B) and an agent (Hermes Agent) on a VPS. I wanted:

Situation Behavior
Home server is up Use the home LLM
Home server is down Use a free cloud model (OpenRouter)
The free model also fails Retry, and surface an error if it still fails

Why bother? The home box is not on 24/7 (power schedule), and free cloud models are rate-limited when you need them most. Combining both is cheap and resilient.

 Telegram / cron
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐   Tailscale (encrypted)   ┌────────────────────┐
│ Agent (VPS)  │ ────────────────────────► │ Home LLM server    │
│              │   Bearer token required   │ llama.cpp          │
└──────┬───────┘                           └────────────────────┘
       │ if unreachable / failing
       ▼
  OpenRouter  (openrouter/free)

2. Step 1 — Lock down the local server first

A local LLM endpoint is an unauthenticated compute resource unless you protect it.

a) Require an API key in llama.cpp

llama serve -m <model.gguf> --host <bind-address> --port 8080 \
  --api-key <long-random-token>

Generate the token with openssl rand -hex 32. In systemd, remember the trailing \ on every continued ExecStart= line, or the flag is silently dropped. Then daemon-reload and restart.

b) Reach it over a private network, not the open internet

Use Tailscale (or WireGuard). Important: both ends need the client installed. I assumed the VPS side already had it; it did not, so every connection timed out until I installed it. Verify with tailscale status on both machines.

c) Don't bind more widely than you need

--host 0.0.0.0 listens on every interface. The API key is a good last line of defense, but prefer binding to the Tailscale address (or firewalling port 8080 to the Tailscale interface) and restricting who can reach it with Tailscale ACLs.

d) Keep secrets out of chat logs, tickets and screenshots. If a token ever lands somewhere public, rotate it.

3. Step 2 — Register the server in the agent (the gotcha that cost me hours)

The obvious config:

model:
  provider: custom
  base_url: http://<tailscale-ip>:8080/v1

plus OPENAI_API_KEY in the environment. Result: 401 Invalid API Key — while curl with the same key from inside the same container returned 200.

Reading the credential resolver showed why. For a bare provider: custom with a base_url, the generic OPENAI_API_KEY fallback was only used when the host was openai.com / openai.azure.com. For any other host the key was silently dropped and replaced by a "no-key-required" placeholder. This looks like a deliberate guard against leaking a generic key to arbitrary endpoints — sensible, but silent.

Fix: register a named custom provider with an explicit key_env:

model:
  default: <model-name-or-path>
  provider: "custom:home-llm"
  api_mode: chat_completions

providers:
  "custom:home-llm":
    base_url: http://<tailscale-ip>:8080/v1
    key_env: OPENAI_API_KEY        # name of the env var that holds the token
    default_model: <model-name-or-path>
    request_timeout_seconds: 120   # see "Unresolved" below

fallback_model:
  provider: openrouter
  model: openrouter/free

Named providers resolve the key through the explicit key_env lookup and skip the hostname gate. I used OPENAI_API_KEY as the variable name; the code suggests any name works, but I did not test other names.

Note the model name: llama.cpp reports the model's file path as its ID in /v1/models, so that is what you put in default.

4. Step 3 — The fallback

fallback_model takes a single provider/model (a list is also accepted for a chain). When the primary exhausts its retries on a connection or rate-limit error, the agent switches over automatically. I observed it working:

Max retries (3) exhausted — trying fallback...
Primary model failed — switching to fallback ...

Choosing the fallback model mattered:

  1. A specific model that was retired (HTTP 404: No endpoints found) → total failure.
  2. A specific free model that was busy (HTTP 429) → total failure.
  3. openrouter/free — OpenRouter's router that picks from currently available free models and filters for features your request needs → far more resilient.

Caveat: free-tier rate limits are account-wide, so openrouter/free reduces, but does not eliminate, 429s. If the free fallback also fails, the request errors out after its retries (it does not wait forever); a scheduled job simply tries again on its next run.

5. Pitfall checklist

Symptom Cause Fix
Timeouts to the home server Tailscale missing on one end Install and join on both machines
401 with a correct key Hostname gate on generic env key Named provider + key_env
.env change ignored docker restart does not reload env; compose had no env_file Add env_file: .env, then docker compose up -d --force-recreate
Key looks like it ends in \r docker exec -it pseudo-TTY adds it to output Re-check without -t; the value was fine
systemd flag has no effect Missing trailing \ in ExecStart= Fix continuation lines
Every request times out with long prompts Draft-model / speculative decoding overhead and small context I removed the draft model and raised -c to 65536

6. Step 4 — Don't wait minutes when the server is powered off

When the home machine is powered off, nothing answers the TCP SYN, so there is no quick "connection refused". Each attempt waited roughly 30 seconds, and with retries plus an extra primary retry round, switching took about 3 minutes. Painful for every message sent while the box is off.

(request_timeout_seconds did not seem to change this. See "Unresolved".)

A fixed-time schedule is fragile: boot takes a while before the model is ready, and shutdown (mine is triggered by a power-consumption watchdog) is not at a precise time. So instead of trusting the clock, health-check the server and let reality drive the switch.

The agent CLI can change config at runtime — no container recreation:

hermes config set model.provider "custom:home-llm"
hermes config set model.default  "<model-name-or-path>"

Both keys must move together; changing only the provider leaves a local file path as the model name, which the cloud provider rejects.

Watchdog (run from cron every 3 minutes):

#!/bin/bash
# home-llm-watchdog.sh
set -u
source /etc/home-llm-watchdog.env   # chmod 600; defines HOME_LLM_URL, HOME_LLM_KEY, LOCAL_MODEL
STATE_FILE=/var/lib/home-llm-watchdog.state
LOG_FILE=/var/log/home-llm-watchdog.log

CURRENT=dead
code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 3 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${HOME_LLM_KEY}" "${HOME_LLM_URL}/models" 2>/dev/null)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && CURRENT=alive

PREVIOUS=$(cat "$STATE_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
if [ "$CURRENT" != "$PREVIOUS" ]; then
  if [ "$CURRENT" = alive ]; then
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.provider "custom:home-llm" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.default  "$LOCAL_MODEL"    >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  else
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.provider "openrouter"      >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.default  "openrouter/free" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  fi
  echo "[$(date '+%F %T')] $PREVIOUS -> $CURRENT" >>"$LOG_FILE"
  echo "$CURRENT" >"$STATE_FILE"
fi

*/3 * * * * /usr/local/bin/home-llm-watchdog.sh

Design notes:

  • State file → only acts when the state flips; no log noise or needless writes.
  • Keep the built-in fallback too. If the server is supposed to be up but crashed, the watchdog still detects it, and the retry-then-fallback path remains a safety net in between checks.
  • The secret lives in a 600 file instead of the script. (The first version I ran had it inline; don't copy that.)

Verified end-to-end: the machine powered on by its timer, and within 3 minutes the agent switched back to the local model by itself.

7. Security checklist

  • [ ] API key required on the local server
  • [ ] Private network (Tailscale/WireGuard), installed on both ends
  • [ ] Bind address / firewall narrower than 0.0.0.0 on the open internet
  • [ ] Tailscale ACL limits which nodes can reach the port
  • [ ] Secrets in 600 files, never in scripts, chat logs or screenshots
  • [ ] Rotate any token that was exposed
  • [ ] Prefer explicit key_env per provider over a generic key that could be sent to the wrong host

8. Unresolved

  • request_timeout_seconds appeared to have no effect on the effective wait; I did not find the cause. Renaming the providers key to match custom:<name> did not change it. Newer versions may differ.
  • A harmless warning about missing endpoint credentials appeared from an auxiliary (non-chat) task; it did not affect normal conversations.
  • Selecting which local model (e.g. Gemma vs. Qwen) is a separate layer from this up/down switch; I kept this to liveness only.

Summary

  1. Secure the local server (token + private network), on both ends.
  2. Register it as a named custom provider with key_env.
  3. Use openrouter/free as the fallback.
  4. If the box is power-scheduled, add a health-check watchdog that flips config with hermes config set.

Hermes Agent behavior described here was observed in August 2026. Check current official docs before relying on it.

自宅のローカルLLMと無料クラウドモデルを安全に切り替える

llama.cpp + Tailscale + OpenRouter + Hermes Agent で作る実践構成
Matis atelier

この情報の時点について
本記事の内容は 2026年8月時点 のものです。公式ドキュメントに該当の記述が見つからなかったため、Hermes Agent のソースコードを直接読んで挙動を確認しました。その後、公式情報は充実している可能性が高いです。まず最新の公式ドキュメントを確認してください。 本記事は「なぜそう動くのか」を補う読み物として使い、設定キー名などは変わっている可能性がある点にご注意ください。
文中のIP・キー・ホスト名・パスはすべてダミーです。

1. 目的

自宅でLLM（llama.cpp / Gemma 4 12B）を動かし、VPS上のエージェント（Hermes Agent）から使います。やりたいことは次の通りです。

状況 動作
自宅サーバーが起動している 自宅のLLMを使う
自宅サーバーが止まっている 無料のクラウドモデル（OpenRouter）を使う
無料モデルも失敗した リトライし、それでもダメならエラーを返す

自宅サーバーは電気代節約のため常時起動ではなく、無料クラウドモデルは混雑すると429で弾かれます。両方を組み合わせると、安く、かつ止まりにくくなります。

 Telegram / cron
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐   Tailscale（暗号化）   ┌────────────────────┐
│ エージェント │ ──────────────────────► │ 自宅LLMサーバー    │
│   (VPS)      │   Bearerトークン必須    │ llama.cpp          │
└──────┬───────┘                         └────────────────────┘
       │ 到達できない／失敗したとき
       ▼
  OpenRouter（openrouter/free）

2. 手順1：まずローカルサーバーを守る

ローカルLLMのエンドポイントは、保護しなければ「誰でも使える計算資源」になってしまいます。

a) llama.cpp にAPIキーを要求させる

llama serve -m <model.gguf> --host <待ち受けアドレス> --port 8080 \
  --api-key <長いランダムなトークン>

トークンは openssl rand -hex 32 で生成します。systemdで複数行の ExecStart= を書く場合は、継続行の行末に \ が必要です。抜けると、そのオプションが黙って無視されます。編集後は daemon-reload と再起動を行ってください。

b) 公開インターネットではなく、閉じたネットワークで繋ぐ

Tailscale（またはWireGuard）を使います。重要なのは 両端にクライアントが必要 という点です。私は「VPS側にもTailscaleが入っている」と思い込んでいて、実際は未インストールでした。そのせいで接続がずっとタイムアウトしていました。両方のマシンで tailscale status を確認しましょう。

c) 必要以上に広く待ち受けない

--host 0.0.0.0 は全インターフェースで待ち受けます。APIキーは最後の砦として有効ですが、できればTailscaleのアドレスに限定するか、ファイアウォールで8080番をTailscaleインターフェースだけに絞ってください。TailscaleのACLで、到達できるノードも制限できます。

d) 秘密情報をチャットログ・チケット・スクリーンショットに残さない。 もし公開の場に出てしまったら、トークンを再発行してください。

3. 手順2：エージェントにサーバーを登録する（数時間ハマったポイント）

最初に書いた、ありがちな設定はこうです。

model:
  provider: custom
  base_url: http://<tailscale-ip>:8080/v1

これに加えて環境変数 OPENAI_API_KEY を設定しました。結果は 401 Invalid API Key。ところが、同じコンテナの中から同じキーで curl すると 200 が返ります。

認証情報を解決するコードを読んで理由が分かりました。provider: custom と base_url だけを書いた場合、汎用の OPENAI_API_KEY は ホストが openai.com / openai.azure.com のときにしか使われません。それ以外のホストでは、キーが黙って捨てられ、"no-key-required" というプレースホルダーに置き換わります。これは「汎用キーが無関係な接続先に漏れないようにする」ための意図的なガードだと思われます。理屈は妥当ですが、何も警告が出ない点が厄介です。

対処：key_env を明示した「名前付き」カスタムプロバイダーとして登録します。

model:
  default: <モデル名またはパス>
  provider: "custom:home-llm"
  api_mode: chat_completions

providers:
  "custom:home-llm":
    base_url: http://<tailscale-ip>:8080/v1
    key_env: OPENAI_API_KEY        # トークンを入れた環境変数の「名前」
    default_model: <モデル名またはパス>
    request_timeout_seconds: 120   # 後述「未解決」を参照

fallback_model:
  provider: openrouter
  model: openrouter/free

名前付きプロバイダーは key_env の明示的な参照でキーを解決するため、ホスト名によるガードを通りません。環境変数名は OPENAI_API_KEY を使いましたが、コード上は任意の名前で動きそうです（他の名前は未検証です）。

モデル名にも注意してください。llama.cpp は /v1/models でモデルの ファイルパスをそのままIDとして返す ので、default にはそれを書きます。

4. 手順3：フォールバックの設定

fallback_model には1組のプロバイダー/モデルを書きます（リスト形式でチェーンにもできます）。メインがリトライを使い切って、接続エラーやレート制限になると、自動で切り替わります。実際にログで確認できました。

Max retries (3) exhausted — trying fallback...
Primary model failed — switching to fallback ...

フォールバック先の選び方で、結果が大きく変わりました。

  1. 提供終了したモデルを指定 → HTTP 404: No endpoints found で全滅
  2. 特定の無料モデルを指定 → 混雑して HTTP 429 で全滅
  3. openrouter/free を指定 → OpenRouterのルーターが、その時使える無料モデルから、リクエストに必要な機能（画像入力やツール呼び出しなど）を満たすものを選ぶ。圧倒的に安定

注意点として、無料枠のレート制限はアカウント単位なので、openrouter/free でも429が完全になくなるわけではありません。無料フォールバックも失敗した場合は、リトライ後にエラーになります（永遠に待つわけではありません）。定期ジョブなら、次回の実行で再挑戦されます。

5. ハマりどころ一覧

症状 原因 対処
自宅サーバーへの接続がタイムアウトする 片方にTailscaleが未インストール 両方に入れてネットワークに参加させる
キーが正しいのに 401 汎用環境変数キーのホスト名ガード 名前付きプロバイダー + key_env
.env の変更が反映されない docker restart は環境変数を再読込しない／composeに env_file が無い env_file: .env を追加し、docker compose up -d --force-recreate
キーの末尾に \r が付いて見える docker exec -it の疑似TTYが出力に付けていた -t を外して再確認。値自体は正常だった
systemdのオプションが効かない ExecStart= の継続行の \ 漏れ 継続行を直す
長いプロンプトで毎回タイムアウト ドラフトモデル（投機的デコード）の負荷、コンテキスト不足 ドラフトモデルを外し、-c を65536に増やした

6. 手順4：電源が切れている間、何分も待たされないようにする

自宅マシンの 電源が落ちている と、TCPのSYNに誰も応答しないため、「接続拒否」がすぐに返ってきません。1回の試行で約30秒待たされ、リトライや追加のリトライラウンドも重なって、切り替わるまで約3分 かかっていました。電源が落ちている間は、メッセージを送るたびにこれが発生します。

（request_timeout_seconds はこの待ち時間に効いていないようでした。「未解決」を参照。）

時刻で固定的に切り替える方式は脆いです。起動後、モデルが使えるようになるまで時間がかかりますし、シャットダウンも（私の環境では消費電力監視で）ぴったりの時刻に行われません。そこで、時計を信用せず、サーバーの生死を実際に確認して、その結果で切り替えます。

エージェントのCLIには、実行中に設定を書き換えるコマンドがあり、コンテナの再作成は不要でした。

hermes config set model.provider "custom:home-llm"
hermes config set model.default  "<モデル名またはパス>"

2つのキーは 必ずセットで 変えます。プロバイダーだけ変えると、ローカルのファイルパスがモデル名として残り、クラウド側に拒否されます。

ウォッチドッグ（cronで3分おきに実行）：

#!/bin/bash
# home-llm-watchdog.sh
set -u
source /etc/home-llm-watchdog.env   # chmod 600。HOME_LLM_URL, HOME_LLM_KEY, LOCAL_MODEL を定義
STATE_FILE=/var/lib/home-llm-watchdog.state
LOG_FILE=/var/log/home-llm-watchdog.log

CURRENT=dead
code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 3 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${HOME_LLM_KEY}" "${HOME_LLM_URL}/models" 2>/dev/null)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && CURRENT=alive

PREVIOUS=$(cat "$STATE_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
if [ "$CURRENT" != "$PREVIOUS" ]; then
  if [ "$CURRENT" = alive ]; then
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.provider "custom:home-llm" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.default  "$LOCAL_MODEL"    >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  else
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.provider "openrouter"      >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.default  "openrouter/free" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  fi
  echo "[$(date '+%F %T')] $PREVIOUS -> $CURRENT" >>"$LOG_FILE"
  echo "$CURRENT" >"$STATE_FILE"
fi

*/3 * * * * /usr/local/bin/home-llm-watchdog.sh

設計のポイント：

  • 状態ファイルで、状態が変わったときだけ動作します。無駄な書き込みやログの増加を避けられます。
  • 標準のフォールバックも残す。 「起動しているはずの時間帯に落ちた」場合も、ウォッチドッグが検知しますし、検知までの間は従来のリトライ→フォールバックが安全網になります。
  • 秘密情報はスクリプトに直書きせず、600 のファイルに置きます。（私が最初に実行したスクリプトは直書きでした。真似しないでください。）

実機で確認できました。電源タイマーでマシンが起動し、3分以内にエージェントが自動でローカルモデルへ戻りました。

7. セキュリティチェックリスト

  • [ ] ローカルサーバーにAPIキーを要求させている
  • [ ] 閉じたネットワーク（Tailscale/WireGuard）を 両端 に入れている
  • [ ] 待ち受けを 0.0.0.0 のままにせず、バインドアドレスかファイアウォールで絞っている
  • [ ] TailscaleのACLで、到達できるノードを制限している
  • [ ] 秘密情報は 600 のファイルに置き、スクリプト・チャットログ・スクショに載せない
  • [ ] 露出してしまったトークンは再発行する
  • [ ] 誤った接続先に送られうる汎用キーより、プロバイダーごとの明示的な key_env を使う

8. 未解決の点

  • request_timeout_seconds が実際の待ち時間に効いていないように見えましたが、原因は特定できていません。providers のキー名を custom:<name> に合わせても変化はありませんでした。新しいバージョンでは挙動が違う可能性があります。
  • 補助タスク（チャット以外の処理）で「エンドポイントの認証情報が見つからない」という警告が出ましたが、通常の会話には影響しませんでした。
  • どのローカルモデル（GemmaかQwenか）を使うかは、今回の生死切り替えとは別のレイヤーです。今回は生死判定だけに絞りました。

まとめ

  1. ローカルサーバーを守る（トークン + 閉じたネットワーク）。しかも 両端 に。
  2. 名前付き カスタムプロバイダーとして key_env 付きで登録する。
  3. フォールバックには openrouter/free を使う。
  4. 電源スケジュールがあるなら、生死判定のウォッチドッグで hermes config set を使って切り替える。

本記事のHermes Agentの挙動は2026年8月時点で確認したものです。利用の際は最新の公式ドキュメントを確認してください。

title: Idempotency Ledger for Agent Tool Calls That Retry Blindly
description:
An agent retry is not a request repeat. It is a new request that looks identical. When a model re issues a tool call after a timeout, the downstream system sees two valid writes, two charged payments, or two created tickets. The failure is structural: the caller carries state in its prompt, the callee carries state in its database, and no key ties the two together.

Why prompt level retry logic breaks at scale

Most agent frameworks implement retry as a loop around the tool function. The loop lives in memory. A process restart, a context compaction, or a supervisor failover erases the attempt counter while the side effect survives. The result is at least once execution with no deduplication, which the operations team discovers through a duplicate invoice rather than a stack trace.

Measurement matters here. A 2026 study titled "Do LLM Agents Act Exactly Once?" measures idempotency violations under retries, which indicates that test suites never forcing a retry cannot surface this class of failure (doi 10.5281/zenodo.24166026).

The write ahead ledger contract

Before the tool executes, the agent writes a row keyed on a deterministic intent hash. The hash covers tool name, normalized arguments, tenant, and a caller supplied window id. The row stores three fields that matter: key, state, and result reference. State moves through reserved, executed, and settled. A retry with the same key reads the existing row instead of calling the tool again.

Stage aware retry plus idempotency plus exactly once semantics is not a novel pattern, it is a well documented pipeline property (doi 10.52783/jisem.v11i2s.14608). Agents fail it because the retry decision is made by a language model rather than by the pipeline.

Three states that prevent duplicate side effects

Reserved means the intent is claimed but the tool has not returned. Executed means the tool returned a reference and the row is no longer eligible for a fresh call. Settled means the downstream effect is confirmed by reconciliation. A retry that lands on reserved must wait, not re issue. A retry that lands on executed must return the stored reference. A retry that lands on settled is a pure replay.

Dead letter handling belongs in the same table. When a reserved row exceeds its lease without reaching executed, the row is released and the intent is parked for human review rather than retried forever, a strategy already standard in payment pipelines that combine idempotency with dead letter queues (doi 10.32628/ijsrst52310495).

What breaks when the key is derived by the model

Keys must be computed by code, never generated by the model. A model that writes its own key will produce a new key on retry because the prompt changed by one token, which defeats the entire mechanism. The safest design derives the key in the tool wrapper from the normalized payload, and treats any model supplied identifier as metadata only.

Research on counterfactual repair of LLM agent failures (doi 10.48550/arxiv.2605.25338) addresses attributing failures to specific actions, which presupposes that a failing action keeps a stable identity across attempts.

Verification checklist before production

Force a timeout after the tool returns but before the agent records success. Confirm the second attempt reads executed and returns the original reference. Kill the process mid flight and confirm the lease expiry releases the row without duplicating the downstream object. Count rows in the ledger against objects in the downstream system and require an exact match. Any mismatch is a duplicate, not a rounding error.

Canonical: https://rausalbahtiar.dev/blog/agent-tool-call-idempotency-write-ahead-ledger

title: Philippine Digital Banks Hold 22.4 Million Depositors and Less Than 1% of System Deposits
description:
The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas counted P138.5 billion in deposits across the country's digital banks at the end of 2025, spread over 22.4 million depositors (Source: Inquirer, 2026). The entire banking system held P22 trillion over the same period (Source: Inquirer, 2026). That is roughly one peso in every 160 of system deposits, for a sector that gets treated as if it already runs the country's money.

Growth Is Real; Balances Are Thin

Digital bank deposits rose 44% in 2025 while the depositor base jumped 81% (Source: Inquirer, 2026). Those rates look like a land grab until you divide them: P138.5 billion across 22.4 million depositors is about P6,200 per person. That is wallet money, not savings money. A deposit base that behaves like a wallet reprices overnight the moment a competitor runs a better promo.

The BSP Raised the Price of Looking Like a Digital Bank

Circular 1240, dated September 21, 2026, requires thrift, rural, and cooperative banks shifting to a digital business model to hold P1 billion in capital, the same floor as a digital bank license (Source: GMA News, 2026). Covered banks get six months to comply, and the requirement applies at the time of application. The BSP framed the rule as a level playing field, which is another way of saying it tired of small lenders marketing digital products while carrying small-lender risk. The licensing queue tells the same story: MariBank became the seventh licensed digital bank in July 2026, leaving three of the reopened slots unclaimed (Source: Inquirer, 2026).

One IPO Rewrote the Funding Math

Mynt, the parent of GCash, raised P60.9 billion in October 2026 in the largest IPO in Philippine history, listing with a market capitalization of P441.51 billion (Source: PSE, 2026). The detail worth studying is who bought: 140,725 GCash users invested about P1.1 billion through the app itself, many as first-time shareholders (Source: PSE, 2026). Distribution became capital formation. A fintech that already owns the daily transaction now also owns a channel into the same customer's investment account.

Payments Are Settled; Credit Is the Next Fight

Digital payments reached 64.7% of retail payments in 2025, up from 57.4% a year earlier, and QR Ph processed 2.47 billion transactions worth P1.16 trillion, passing cards for the first time (Source: GMA News, 2026). The payment layer is effectively won, which moves the fight to the balance sheet: credit, insurance, and wealth products. Underwriting there cannot lean on deposit collateral, because a P6,200 average balance secures almost nothing. Lenders will have to price risk from cash-flow data spread across wallets, payroll, and remittances instead.

Remittances Are the Quiet Rail Underneath

Cash remittances reached a record $35.63 billion in 2025 (Source: ABS-CBN News, 2026). September 2026 inflows rose 2.6% to $3.20 billion, the fastest growth in eight months (Source: GMA News, 2026). Full-year growth, though, may land as the slowest since 2020 (Source: BusinessWorld, 2026). For digital banks and wallets, that mix matters: remittance corridors remain the most reliable source of new money entering the formal system, and they are slowing.

What This Means for Builders

Compliance work is about to outrank feature work. When the capital floor rises and license slots run out, the differentiator stops being who ships a prettier app and becomes who can prove controls, reconcile ledgers, and document credit decisions. Yano.AI builds AI systems for document-heavy financial operations, and the questions lenders bring are consistent: how do you underwrite a borrower whose income evidence lives in three wallets, two payslips, and a remittance receipt? Teams that answer with auditable data will set the price of risk for everyone else.

FAQ

Q: How many digital banks are licensed in the Philippines?
A: Seven as of July 2026, with three license slots still unclaimed (Source: Inquirer, 2026).

Q: What capital does a digital bank need in the Philippines?
A: P1 billion. Circular 1240 now applies the same floor to thrift, rural, and cooperative banks that shift to a digital business model (Source: GMA News, 2026).

Q: Do digital banks hold a large share of Philippine deposits?
A: No. They held P138.5 billion against P22 trillion system-wide at the end of 2025, under 1% (Source: Inquirer, 2026).

Key Takeaway

The 2026 story is no longer about adoption. Payments crossed the halfway mark, digital bank deposits grew 44%, and the largest IPO in Philippine history belonged to a wallet company. What remains open is whether those 22.4 million wallet users become depositors who keep real balances, and whether a P1 billion capital floor makes that conversion easier or harder. If you run a wallet or lending product, what is your average balance per active user, and is it rising?

Sources

  • Philippine digital bank deposits reached nearly P139B in 2025
  • BSP sets P1-B capital requirement for banks shifting to digital models
  • Mynt, Inc. raises P60.9B in historic stock market debut
  • Digital payments accounted for 64.7% of total retail payments in 2025, says BSP
  • Philippines gets 7th digital bank as MariBank upgrades license
  • Cash remittances reach $35.63 billion in 2025
  • Cash remittances rose to $3.20B in Sept. 2026 - BSP
  • OFW remittances may grow at slowest pace since 2020
