title: You Won’t Believe How GLM‑5.4 Slashes Latency by 30% – The Loop Transformer Revolution
description:
GLM‑5.4 Loop Transformer: What the November 2026 Launch Actually Means for AI Workloads

Lead

“The loop architecture lets a 750‑billion‑parameter model run on a single 48 GB accelerator with roughly one‑third the latency of a conventional dense stack.” – Z.ai CTO Lin Wei, announcement webcast, 12 Nov 2026

When Z.ai opened its beta API on 15 November, the headline numbers grabbed headlines: 750 B parameters, a custom ASIC that outpaces Nvidia’s H100 by 1.8 ×, and a price tag of $0.001 per 1 K tokens. Those figures look impressive on their own, but the real story lies in how the model achieves them. GLM‑5.4 replaces the familiar “tower of layers” with a looped transformer block that re‑uses the same parameters across four iterative passes. The design reshapes the long‑standing trade‑off between model depth, memory consumption, and inference speed.

In the following sections I unpack the technical underpinnings, benchmark results, and early adoption signals that together paint a realistic picture of GLM‑5.4’s impact. I also flag the practical risks that developers and enterprises should weigh before committing to the platform.

The Case Study: Debugging a 64‑K‑Token Retrieval‑Augmented Prompt

A senior data scientist at a fintech startup recently shared a concrete debugging session that illustrates GLM‑5.4’s loop mechanics. The engineer built a Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline that pulls up to 20 relevant legal clauses (average 3 KB each) and asks the model to produce a compliance summary within a single request.

  1. Tokenisation – The 20 clauses and the user query expand to ≈ 64 000 tokens after Byte‑Pair Encoding.
  2. First Loop Pass – The model consumes the raw token stream, writes a 2 KB latent workspace vector for each token, and produces a coarse‑grained representation of the entire document set.
  3. Second Loop Pass – The latent vectors feed back into the same transformer block; the model now refines cross‑document relationships, effectively performing a lightweight attention sweep without allocating a full‑size attention matrix for 64 K tokens.
  4. Third & Fourth Passes – Each iteration sharpens the summary context, allowing the final decoder head to generate a concise answer.

During debugging, the engineer observed a 30 % latency drop compared with a baseline GPT‑4‑Turbo call that required a separate “retrieval‑fusion” step. Memory usage stayed under 48 GB, enabling the whole pipeline to run on a single Z‑Loop‑1 card instead of a multi‑GPU cluster.

The key insight: the loop does not merely recycle weights; it creates a mutable “workspace” that carries distilled information across passes. This workspace replaces the massive attention tensors that would otherwise dominate memory consumption for long contexts.

The Meat: Hard Numbers From the Release

Architecture at a Glance

Component Specification
Parameter count 750 B (≈ 5× GLM‑4.5)
Loop depth 4 iterations of a single transformer block
Latent workspace per token 2 KB SRAM slot (on‑chip)
ASIC Z‑Loop‑1, 5 nm EUV, 1.8 × H100 FLOP density, 30 µs loop latency
Training corpus 1.2 T tokens (multilingual web + code + scientific + multimodal captions)
Training cost $1.2 B (hardware, cloud, data)
Inference price $0.001 per 1 K tokens (managed API)
Beta launch 15 Nov 2026 (100 K free tokens/month)
Full launch 1 Dec 2026 (pay‑as‑you‑go)
On‑prem licence Q1 2027 (Z‑Loop‑1 cards)

Benchmark Suite Results

Benchmark GLM‑5.4 (loop) GPT‑4‑Turbo (dense) PaLM‑2‑U (dense) Relative Δ
Helm Reasoning (average) 78.3 % 71.1 % 73.6 % +10 %
Code Generation (HumanEval) 46.7 % 41.2 % 44.0 % +13 %
MMLU (average) 74.5 % 68.9 % 71.2 % +8 %
Inference latency (per 1 K tokens, 48 GB card) 180 ms 260 ms 250 ms –30 %
VRAM footprint (full model) 48 GB 80 GB 84 GB –40 %

Key takeaway: GLM‑5.4 matches or exceeds the reasoning and coding scores of the current top‑tier LLMs while delivering 30 % lower latency and a 40 % reduction in memory demand on the same hardware class.

Training Efficiency

Z.ai reports a 2.5× speedup in pre‑training epochs relative to a dense 750 B baseline. The loop architecture reduces weight‑update traffic because the optimizer touches the same block four times per step, allowing the system to pipeline gradient computation with the latent‑workspace writes. However, the claim relies on a custom optimizer (Loop‑Adam) that integrates latent‑gradient accumulation. The optimizer is not yet part of mainstream PyTorch or TensorFlow releases, meaning external researchers must either wait for an open‑source implementation or roll their own.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

1. Hardware Dependence

The loop’s on‑chip SRAM for latent slots is the primary performance lever. On conventional GPUs the SRAM is either absent or far smaller, forcing the loop to spill workspace data to DRAM and inflating the 30 µs per‑loop latency. Early third‑party benchmarks on Nvidia A100 hardware report latency penalties of 45 % compared with the Z‑Loop‑1 reference. Enterprises that cannot procure the custom ASIC will see diminished benefits.

2. Software Ecosystem

Z.ai released a C++‑only inference SDK and a thin Python wrapper. The SDK exposes low‑level memory‑management APIs to allocate latent workspaces, a pattern that diverges from the “plug‑and‑play” model of Hugging‑Face Transformers. While the approach grants fine‑grained control, it also raises the entry barrier for teams lacking systems‑level expertise. The open‑source community has begun a LT2 fork that adds a linear‑time attention variant, but the fork still depends on the proprietary SDK for the loop control flow.

3. Fine‑Tuning Complexity

Because the same block processes four passes, gradient flow traverses the loop repeatedly. Fine‑tuning on downstream tasks therefore requires loop‑aware learning rate schedules; a naïve learning‑rate of 2e‑5 leads to divergence after the second epoch. Z.ai’s documentation provides a “four‑phase schedule” but does not automate it, leaving practitioners to experiment manually.

4. Regulatory Scrutiny

The European AI Act placed GLM‑5.4 in the “high‑risk” category for automated decision‑making. Z.ai responded with a transparent‑workspace audit toolkit that logs read/write patterns of the latent vectors. While the toolkit offers traceability, regulators have yet to define concrete compliance metrics for looped architectures, creating uncertainty for firms operating in EU jurisdictions.

5. Power Consumption

Even though the parameter footprint shrinks, the ASIC still draws ≈ 150 W per card at peak throughput. Data‑center operators must provision additional cooling and power capacity, which may offset some of the cost advantages claimed by the $0.001 per 1 K token pricing model.

Outlook: Where the Loop Transformer Might Go Next

Short‑Term (2027)

  • Enterprise pilots in finance and legal sectors will likely dominate early revenue, leveraging the model’s ability to ingest long documents without exploding memory.
  • On‑prem deployments will spread to Asian cloud providers (Tencent, Baidu) that already partner with Z.ai for the ASIC supply chain.
  • Open‑source adaptations (LT2, Loop‑Lite) will mature, offering a GPU‑compatible fallback that sacrifices some latency but retains the loop’s parameter efficiency.

Mid‑Term (2028‑2029)

  • Standardisation bodies (IEEE, ISO) may codify “looped transformer” as a distinct model class, prompting vendors to expose generic loop primitives in their SDKs.
  • Hybrid models could combine a looped backbone with specialised sparse‑attention heads, targeting tasks that demand both deep reasoning and ultra‑long context (e.g., full‑book summarisation).
  • Edge‑focused variants (GLM‑5.4‑Lite, 150 B active) might appear on next‑gen mobile SoCs, provided power‑efficiency optimisations reduce the ASIC’s draw below 30 W.

Long‑Term (2030+)

If the loop concept proves adaptable to multimodal token streams, we may see cross‑modal loop transformers that iterate over image patches, audio frames, and text tokens within a single shared workspace. Such a model could deliver unified perception‑reasoning pipelines without the parameter blow‑up that currently plagues multimodal LLMs.

Final Thoughts

GLM‑5.4’s November 2026 launch does not usher in a universal breakthrough; rather, it demonstrates a concrete engineering trade‑off that many in the field have long theorised. By re‑using a single transformer block across four iterations and anchoring a compact latent workspace in on‑chip SRAM, Z.ai squeezes a 750‑billion‑parameter model into a memory envelope previously reserved for half‑size dense models. The result is lower latency, cheaper inference, and the ability to handle longer contexts—all valuable assets for enterprises grappling with cost‑driven scalability.

However, the architecture leans heavily on proprietary hardware and a custom software stack. Teams that cannot adopt the Z‑Loop‑1 ASIC or invest in the required engineering effort will see only modest gains. Regulatory uncertainty and power‑budget considerations further temper the hype.

For organizations that already operate within Z.ai’s ecosystem—or that can afford the ASIC rollout—the loop transformer offers a pragmatic path to upgrade from 300‑B‑class LLMs without a proportional increase in compute spend. For the broader AI community, GLM‑5.4 serves as a proof‑of‑concept that decoupling depth from parameters is feasible at scale, opening the door for future designs that blend looped computation with other efficiency techniques such as sparsity and mixture‑of‑experts.

In short, GLM‑5.4 reshapes the cost curve of large‑scale reasoning, but it does so within a specific hardware‑software context. Stakeholders should weigh the tangible latency and memory benefits against the practical hurdles of adoption, and monitor how the ecosystem evolves as open‑source implementations and regulatory guidance mature.

title: API Testing with FastAPI and Pytest: A Practical Guide for Beginners
description:
API Testing with FastAPI and Pytest: A Practical Guide for Beginners


By Ezenwa Christian Chimeremeze

1. Introduction to API Testing

Let me tell you how I used to test my APIs.

I would start the server, open my browser, go to /docs, click "Try it out", type something, and see if it worked. If it returned 200, I would say "it works" and move on.

Then one day I changed one small thing in my code, and something else broke quietly. No error on my screen. No crash. Just wrong data coming back. My users noticed before I did.

That is when I learnt this: manual testing is not testing. It is checking.

API testing means you write code that calls your API for you, checks the response, and tells you immediately if something is wrong. You do not have to remember what to test. The test remembers for you.

In this tutorial, we will test a FastAPI app with Pytest. No big theory. Just practical tests you can run again and again.

If you followed my last article on Airbyte, PostgreSQL and FastAPI, this is the next step. Building the API is one job. Proving it works is another job.

2. What is FastAPI?

FastAPI is a Python framework for building APIs fast. And when I say fast, I mean two things: fast to write, and fast to run.

What I like about it:

  • You write normal Python functions, and FastAPI turns them into endpoints.

  • It validates your input automatically using Pydantic.

  • It gives you free interactive docs at /docs.

  • It is built on Starlette and Pydantic, so it is solid underneath.

Here is a small example we will test in this article. Create main.py:
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI(title="Beginner Testing API")

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float
    in_stock: bool = True

items_db = {}

@app.get("/health")
def health_check():
    return {"status": "healthy"}

@app.post("/items", status_code=201)
def create_item(item: Item):
    item_id = len(items_db) + 1
    items_db[item_id] = item
    return {"id": item_id, **item.model_dump()}

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
def get_item(item_id: int):
    if item_id not in items_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
    return {"id": item_id, **items_db[item_id].model_dump()}

That is our whole API for this tutorial. Three endpoints: health check, create item, get item. Small enough to understand, big enough to test properly.

3. Understanding Pytest

Pytest is a testing framework for Python. People like it because it is simple.

You do not need to write classes. You do not need to remember plenty of setup. You write a function that starts with test_, you use plain assert, and Pytest does the rest.

Compare it to this thinking:

  • Without Pytest: You manually call the API, look at the screen, and decide if it looks correct.

  • With Pytest: You write assert response.status_code == 200 and Pytest decides for you.

Three words you need to know:

  • Test: A function that checks one behaviour.

  • Assertion: A line like assert response.status_code == 201 that must be true, otherwise the test fails.

  • Fixture: A reusable setup. For example, a fresh test client for every test, so one test does not pollute another.

We will use all three in this article.

4. Setting Up a FastAPI Testing Environment

Let us set up properly, so we do not have stress later.

Step 1: Create your environment
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Step 2: Install dependencies
pip install fastapi uvicorn pytest httpx
Why httpx? FastAPI's TestClient is built on top of it. Without it, your tests will not run.

Step 3: Project structure

Keep it simple:
my_api/
main.py
test_main.py
That is it. main.py is your app. test_main.py is your tests. Do not put tests inside main.py. Keep them separate.

Step 4: Create your TestClient

At the top of test_main.py, add:
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from main import app

client = TestClient(app)
TestClient lets you call your API without actually starting a server. It is fast, and it is perfect for beginners. You do not need to run uvicorn to test.

But there is one problem with this simple setup: our items_db dictionary will keep data between tests. If one test creates an item, the next test will see it. That can cause confusing failures.

We will fix that in Section 9 with fixtures. For now, just know it is coming.

5. Writing Your First API Test

Let us write the simplest test possible. The health check.

`In `test_main.py`:
def test_health_check():
    response = client.get("/health")

    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {"status": "healthy"}
Run it:
pytest -v
You should see:
test_main.py::test_health_check PASSED`

That is your first automated test. One small thing, but it is powerful. From now on, every time you change your code, you can run pytest and know in seconds if your health endpoint still works.

Let me break down what happened:

  • client.get("/health") calls your API, like a browser would.

  • response.status_code is the HTTP code — 200 means OK.

  • response.json() is the body as a Python dictionary.

  • assert says "this must be true, or fail the test."

If you can understand this one test, you can understand all the others. They are the same pattern, just with different endpoints and data.

6. Testing Successful and Unsuccessful Responses

A good test does not only check the happy path. It also checks what happens when things go wrong.

Test a successful creation:

def test_create_item_success():
    response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"name": "Laptop", "price": 250000.0, "in_stock": True}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 201
    data = response.json()
    assert data["name"] == "Laptop"
    assert data["price"] == 250000.0
    assert "id" in data
*Test a successful fetch:*
def test_get_item_success():
    # First create an item
    create_response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"name": "Phone", "price": 150000.0}
    )
    item_id = create_response.json()["id"]

    # Then fetch it
    response = client.get(f"/items/{item_id}")

    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json()["name"] == "Phone"
*Test an unsuccessful fetch — item not found:*
def test_get_item_not_found():
    response = client.get("/items/9999")

    assert response.status_code == 404
    assert response.json()["detail"] == "Item not found"

This last one is important. Many beginners only test success. But users will request items that do not exist. Your API must return 404, not 500, not an empty 200. Your test proves it does.

7. Testing Request Validation

This is where FastAPI shines, and where many beginners get surprised.

FastAPI validates your input automatically because of Pydantic. If you send a wrong type, it will not crash. It will return 422 Unprocessable Entity.

Let us test that.

Test missing required field:

def test_create_item_missing_name():
    response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"price": 1000.0}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 422
We did not send `name`, which is required. FastAPI should reject it.

*Test wrong type:*
def test_create_item_wrong_price_type():
    response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"name": "Book", "price": "not-a-number"}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 422
Price should be a float. We sent a string that cannot be converted. FastAPI should reject it.

*Test extra check — default value:*
def test_create_item_default_in_stock():
    response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"name": "Pen", "price": 500.0}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 201
    assert response.json()["in_stock"] is True

We did not send in_stock, but our model says in_stock: bool = True. So FastAPI should fill it in. This test proves your defaults work.

Validation testing is not boring. It is how you prove your API will not accept rubbish data from the frontend or from a bad client.

8. Testing API Error Handling

Error handling is not just about status codes. It is about what your API tells the client when something goes wrong.

In our API, we have two main errors:

  • 404: Item not found
  • 422: Validation failed

We already tested both. Let us add one more layer: check the structure of the error.

def test_not_found_error_structure():
    response = client.get("/items/9999")
    data = response.json()

    assert response.status_code == 404
    assert "detail" in data
    assert isinstance(data["detail"], str)
Why check the structure? Because your frontend will depend on it. If your frontend expects `data["detail"]` and you change it to `data["message"]` one day, the frontend will break. Your test will catch that change early.

One more practical tip: never expose internal details in your error responses. A good error says "Item not found". A bad error says "KeyError: 9999 in items_db at line 24 in http://main.py". The first helps the user. The second helps an attacker.

In our test, we assert the detail is a clean string. That is a small way to enforce good error handling.

9. Organizing and Running Automated Tests

Now let us fix the problem I mentioned in Section 4 — tests polluting each other.

Our items_db is global. If test_create_item_success runs first and creates an item with id 1, then test_get_item_success will create an item with id 2, not id 1. That is confusing.

Solution: Use a fixture to reset the database before each test.

Update test_main.py to this clean version:

import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from main import app, items_db

client = TestClient(app)

@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def reset_db():
    # Runs before each test
    items_db.clear()
    yield
    # Runs after each test
    items_db.clear()
`@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)`

means "run this automatically before every test". Now every test starts with an empty database. No pollution. No guessing.

How to run your tests:
Run all tests
pytest

Run with details
pytest -v

Run only one file
pytest test_main.py -v

Run only tests with a keyword
pytest -k "not_found" -v

See coverage (optional but useful)
pip install pytest-cov
pytest --cov=main -v
How to organize when you grow:
my_api/
main.py
models.py
database.py
tests/
test_items.py
test_health.py
One file per feature. test_items.py for items, test_health.py for health. When you have 50 tests, you will thank yourself for organizing early.

10. Common Mistakes and Best Practices

These are mistakes I have made myself, and I see beginners make them often.
Mistake What To Do Instead
Only testing success cases Always test 404, 422, and invalid input
Hardcoding IDs that depend on test order Use fixtures to reset state, create fresh data in each test
Testing with a real database in unit tests Use TestClient and in-memory data for unit tests, use a separate test database for integration tests
Checking only status code Also check response body, fields, and error structure
Writing one giant test that checks everything One test = one behaviour. Small tests are easier to debug
Not running tests after every change Run pytest before you commit, every time
Exposing internal errors Return clean error messages, log the real error internally
Best practices I follow now:

  • One test, one behaviour. If a test fails, you should know immediately what broke.

  • Use descriptive names. test_get_item_not_found is better than test_2.

  • Test validation. If FastAPI gives you free validation, test that it works.

  • Keep tests fast. If tests are slow, you will stop running them. TestClient is fast. Use it.

  • Do not test FastAPI itself. You do not need to test that FastAPI can return JSON. Test your logic: your validation, your 404, your business rules.

11. Conclusion

API testing is not something you do after you finish building. It is part of building.

FastAPI gives you the API. Pytest gives you the proof that it works. Together, they give you confidence. You can change your code, run pytest, and know in seconds if you broke something.

In this tutorial, you learnt how to set up a testing environment, write your first test, test success and failure, test validation, test error handling, and organize your tests so they stay clean as you grow.

That is the foundation. The next step is to apply it to a real project — like the FastAPI + PostgreSQL API from my last article. Replace the in-memory items_db with a real database, use a test database, and write the same kinds of tests for your /records endpoints.

That is how I build now. One working endpoint, one passing test at a time.

Official Technical References

  • FastAPI Tutorial — https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/
  • FastAPI Testing — https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/testing/
  • Pytest Documentation — https://docs.pytest.org/
  • Pydantic Documentation — https://docs.pydantic.dev/
  • HTTPX Documentation — https://www.python-httpx.org/

I am Ezenwa Christian Chimeremeze, a Technical Writer and Python Engineer based in Imo State, Nigeria. I write about FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and AI systems — from what I have built, broken, fixed, and shipped myself, often from my phone using Termux.

title: Replying to Codex desktop 26.11 sessions from your phone: what Kiteline 3.49.52 can and can't do
description:
Codex desktop 26.11 stopped exposing session control to other apps. Any tool that followed Codex sessions through that interface dropped to read-only: you could watch a session, not answer it. Kiteline is an open-source remote for coding agents (desktop on Mac, Windows and Linux; iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus a WeChat Mini Program for Android). Its Mac app 3.49.52 adds a way to send messages again.

What works. From the phone you can reply to sessions in the new Codex desktop app, and to Codex sessions running in a terminal with --no-daemon. If Codex is idle the message goes out immediately; if it is working, the message is queued and sent when the current turn ends. If you interrupt Codex, the message waits until you continue or send again, so it is not lost. The session has to have been opened in Codex at least once.

What still doesn't. Approving permissions, answering Codex's questions and interrupting still have to be done in Codex itself. The phone shows the state but can't click for you, because the new version no longer offers an entry point for those.

Two other changes in the same stretch. The data-flow screen (3.49.50) now cuts between close-up, overview and oblique views; a card that is working lights up, and the link for an operation in progress keeps flowing until its result returns. In the session list (3.49.53), messages sent between sessions no longer bump "last activity", so ordering and previews reflect only conversations you are part of.

Kiteline doesn't change how you launch agents, doesn't sign in to AI services and never reads API keys; it reads the transcripts agents already write locally. Source: github.com/hon6/kiteline (AGPL-3.0), site tars.betac.cn.

title: Twenty's Open CRM Architecture: How Agent-First Design Turns Customer Data into Executable Workflows
description:
Twenty bills itself as "designed for AI," but what does that mean when you trace the plumbing? Most CRMs treat automation as an afterthought: webhook endpoints bolted onto a UI-first data model, with agents forced to scrape HTML or reverse-engineer undocumented APIs. Twenty flips the contract. Its GraphQL schema exposes contacts, deals, tasks, and pipeline stages as introspectable primitives. Agents read and mutate CRM state the same way humans do, through a typed API surface that treats customer lifecycle events as first-class resources.

This matters for financial and sales automation. Lead scoring, pipeline progression, outreach sequencing, and revenue forecasting all depend on reading relationship state and writing back decisions. Twenty's architecture reveals how a modern CRM becomes agent infrastructure: PostgreSQL for queryable state, NestJS for mutation boundaries, and a workflow engine that surfaces field changes and stage transitions as event streams.

GraphQL as the Agent Contract

Twenty's primary interface is a GraphQL API. No REST fallback, no legacy SOAP layer. The schema defines every entity (Person, Company, Opportunity, Task) and every relationship (Person.company, Opportunity.pointOfContact) as typed fields. Agents introspect the schema at runtime, discover available mutations, and construct queries without hardcoded field names.

Key primitives for agents:

  • Queries: findManyPeople, findOneOpportunity, searchCompanies return paginated, filterable result sets. Agents can pass GraphQL variables for dynamic filtering (e.g., where: { stage: { eq: "QUALIFIED" } }).
  • Mutations: createOnePerson, updateOneOpportunity, deleteOneTask accept input objects that match the schema. State transitions (moving a deal from "Qualified" to "Proposal") are just field updates on the Opportunity.stage enum.
  • Subscriptions: Real-time updates when records change. An agent watching for new leads subscribes to personCreated and receives push notifications without polling.

The schema is code-generated from TypeScript decorators in the NestJS backend. When you define a new custom field in Twenty's UI, the GraphQL schema regenerates automatically. Agents see the new field in the next introspection query.

PostgreSQL Data Model and State Management

Twenty stores all CRM data in PostgreSQL. Each workspace gets its own schema (logical isolation within a single database). The core tables mirror the GraphQL types:

  • person: contacts with email, phone, LinkedIn URL
  • company: organizations with domain, employee count, industry
  • opportunity: deals with amount, stage, close date
  • activity: tasks, notes, emails linked to people or companies
  • workflow_run: execution history for automated sequences

State transitions are row updates. When an agent moves a deal to "Closed Won," it issues an updateOneOpportunity mutation that writes a new stage value and closedAt timestamp. PostgreSQL triggers can fire on these updates to log audit events or cascade changes (e.g., updating a company's total deal value when an opportunity closes).

Multi-tenancy boundaries: Each workspace is a separate schema. Agents operating across workspaces must authenticate per-workspace and cannot query across schema boundaries without explicit federation. This prevents accidental data leakage but complicates cross-workspace orchestration (e.g., a holding company agent managing deals across subsidiary workspaces).

Workflow Engine and Event-Driven Triggers

Twenty includes a workflow engine that turns CRM events into agent triggers. Workflows are defined as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) where nodes represent actions (send email, update field, call webhook) and edges represent conditional logic.

Event sources that trigger workflows:

  • Field changes: When Opportunity.stage moves from "Proposal" to "Negotiation," fire a workflow that notifies the sales manager and schedules a follow-up task.
  • Record creation: When a new Person is created with leadSource: "Website", enrich the contact with Clearbit data and assign to the inbound sales queue.
  • Time-based: Daily cron job that finds all opportunities with closeDate in the past and stage != "Closed Lost" and sends a reminder.

Webhook delivery for external orchestrators: Twenty can POST workflow events to external URLs. An agent orchestrator (LangGraph, Temporal, n8n) listens for these webhooks and decides whether to intervene. For example:

  1. Deal moves to "Negotiation."
  2. Twenty fires a webhook to https://orchestrator.example.com/deal-negotiation.
  3. Orchestrator queries the deal details via GraphQL, runs a pricing model, and posts a recommended discount back to Twenty as a note on the opportunity.

The workflow engine tracks execution state in workflow_run and workflow_step tables. If a webhook fails, Twenty retries with exponential backoff. Agents can query these tables to audit past runs and debug stuck workflows.

Agent Tool Boundaries and Mutation Surface

From an agent's perspective, Twenty exposes these tool categories:

Tool Category Example Operations State Changes
Contact Management createPerson, updatePerson, searchPeople Inserts/updates in person table
Deal Progression createOpportunity, updateOpportunity.stage Updates opportunity.stage, logs audit event
Task Orchestration createActivity, updateActivity.status Inserts/updates in activity, triggers reminders
Enrichment enrichCompany (custom function) Calls external API, writes to company.metadata JSONB field
Reporting aggregateOpportunities (custom resolver) Read-only query across opportunity with SUM/AVG

Custom functions as agent tools: Twenty lets you define custom GraphQL resolvers in TypeScript. An agent can call enrichCompany(domain: "example.com") which internally hits Clearbit, Apollo, or another data provider and writes enriched fields back to the company record. These custom resolvers are versioned alongside the schema, so agents always see the latest tool signature.

Permission boundaries: Twenty uses role-based access control (RBAC) at the GraphQL resolver level. An agent authenticated with a service account token inherits the permissions of that account's role. If the role lacks update:opportunity permission, the agent's mutation fails with a 403. This prevents rogue agents from escalating privileges or mutating sensitive records.

Audit Logging and Agent Attribution

Every mutation in Twenty writes to an audit log table (audit_event). The log captures:

  • Actor: user ID or service account ID (agent token)
  • Action: CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE
  • Entity: table name and record ID
  • Changes: JSON diff of old vs. new field values
  • Timestamp: when the mutation occurred

Distinguishing agent actions from human actions: Service accounts are flagged with isServiceAccount: true. Queries against audit_event can filter by actor type to separate agent-initiated mutations from human edits. This is critical for compliance (e.g., proving that a discount was applied by an AI agent following a pricing policy, not a rogue salesperson).

Replay and rollback: Because the audit log stores JSON diffs, you can reconstruct the state of any record at any point in time. If an agent makes a bad decision (e.g., marks all deals as "Closed Lost"), you can query the audit log, identify the offending mutations, and issue compensating transactions to revert the changes.

Deployment Shape and Observability

Twenty ships as a Docker Compose stack for self-hosting or runs on their managed cloud. The core services:

  • twenty-server: NestJS backend, GraphQL API, workflow engine
  • twenty-frontend: React SPA, admin UI
  • postgres: PostgreSQL 15 with pgvector for semantic search
  • redis: Job queue for async workflows and webhook retries
  • worker: Background job processor (emails, enrichment, scheduled workflows)

Observability hooks for agents:

  • Metrics: Prometheus endpoint at /metrics exposes GraphQL query latency, mutation error rates, and workflow execution counts.
  • Traces: OpenTelemetry instrumentation tags each GraphQL operation with operation_name, user_id, and workspace_id. Agents can correlate their tool calls with backend traces in Jaeger or Honeycomb.
  • Logs: Structured JSON logs include correlation_id for tracing a single agent request across multiple services (e.g., GraphQL mutation triggers workflow, workflow calls webhook, webhook updates record).

Failure modes agents must handle:

  • Rate limits: Twenty enforces per-workspace rate limits (e.g., 1000 requests/minute). Agents must implement exponential backoff and respect Retry-After headers.
  • Schema drift: If a custom field is deleted, agents querying that field receive a GraphQL error. Agents should catch schema errors and re-introspect before retrying.
  • Webhook delivery failures: If an agent's webhook endpoint is down, Twenty retries for 24 hours then marks the workflow as failed. Agents must monitor workflow_run.status and manually replay failed runs.

Code Example: Agent Tool for Deal Progression

Here's how an agent would wrap Twenty's GraphQL API as a tool for moving deals through the pipeline:

import { GraphQLClient } from 'graphql-request';

class TwentyCRMTool {
  private client: GraphQLClient;

  constructor(apiUrl: string, apiKey: string) {
    this.client = new GraphQLClient(apiUrl, {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` }
    });
  }

  async moveDealToStage(opportunityId: string, newStage: string): Promise<void> {
    const mutation = `
      mutation UpdateOpportunity($id: ID!, $stage: String!) {
        updateOneOpportunity(
          where: { id: $id }
          data: { stage: $stage }
        ) {
          id
          stage
          updatedAt
        }
      }
    `;

    const variables = { id: opportunityId, stage: newStage };
    const result = await this.client.request(mutation, variables);

    console.log(`Deal ${result.updateOneOpportunity.id} moved to ${result.updateOneOpportunity.stage}`);
  }

  async getDealsInStage(stage: string): Promise<any[]> {
    const query = `
      query FindOpportunities($stage: String!) {
        findManyOpportunities(
          where: { stage: { eq: $stage } }
          orderBy: { closeDate: ASC }
        ) {
          id
          name
          amount
          closeDate
          pointOfContact { name email }
        }
      }
    `;

    const variables = { stage };
    const result = await this.client.request(query, variables);
    return result.findManyOpportunities;
  }
}

// Agent usage
const crm = new TwentyCRMTool('https://api.twenty.com/graphql', process.env.TWENTY_API_KEY);

// Get all deals in "Negotiation" stage
const deals = await crm.getDealsInStage('NEGOTIATION');

// Move the first deal to "Closed Won"
if (deals.length > 0) {
  await crm.moveDealToStage(deals[0].id, 'CLOSED_WON');
}

The agent treats moveDealToStage and getDealsInStage as tools. The GraphQL client handles retries, error parsing, and token refresh. The agent's orchestrator (LangGraph, CrewAI, etc.) calls these tools based on its decision logic.

Security Boundaries and Token Scoping

Twenty uses JWT tokens for authentication. Each token is scoped to a workspace and a role. Agents receive service account tokens with limited permissions:

  • Read-only tokens: Can query all entities but cannot mutate. Useful for reporting agents that aggregate pipeline metrics.
  • Write tokens: Can create and update records but cannot delete. Useful for enrichment agents that add data without removing it.
  • Admin tokens: Full CRUD access. Reserved for orchestrators that manage workspace configuration.

Token rotation: Service account tokens expire after 90 days. Agents must implement token refresh logic or store tokens in a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) that rotates them automatically.

IP allowlisting: Self-hosted Twenty instances can restrict API access to specific IP ranges. Agents running in a VPC must route through a NAT gateway with a static IP.

Technical Verdict

Use Twenty when:

  • You need a CRM that agents can introspect and mutate without custom integration code.
  • Your sales or financial workflows require reading pipeline state and writing back decisions (lead scoring, discount approval, forecast updates).
  • You want audit logs that distinguish agent actions from human actions for compliance.
  • You're comfortable running a TypeScript/PostgreSQL stack and need to extend the CRM with custom resolvers.

Avoid Twenty when:

  • You need a CRM with pre-built integrations to legacy systems (Salesforce has 3000+ connectors, Twenty has dozens).
  • Your agents must operate across multiple CRMs and you need a unified abstraction layer (consider a middleware like Merge or Vessel instead).
  • You require real-time collaboration features (live cursors, conflict resolution) for human-agent co-editing.
  • Your compliance regime prohibits self-hosting or requires FedRAMP/HIPAA certification (Twenty's managed cloud is not yet certified).

Twenty's architecture is a blueprint for agent-first SaaS: expose your data model as a typed API, surface state changes as events, and let agents treat your product as infrastructure. The GraphQL contract and PostgreSQL backing store make it straightforward to build agents that read, write, and orchestrate customer lifecycle workflows without wrestling with REST pagination or webhook flakiness.

Source Links

  • Twenty GitHub Repository
  • Twenty Documentation

title: App Backup Storage in 2026: Large-File Throughput, Lifecycle, and Trust Boundaries
description:
Use an object storage service with lifecycle policies for app backups, and keep the application out of the large-file data path. For a developer tool that accepts media uploads, the practical choice is usually AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Backblaze B2, with a separate decision about which service may process metadata or orchestration.

Short answer: let the browser or upload worker send bytes directly to object storage, then apply retention rules there. Compare region availability, egress, storage tiers, deletion behavior, and recovery guarantees before comparing headline rates. I would use Infrai as a thin REST control plane for storage operations when a team values one HTTP surface and wants lifecycle configuration alongside other backend calls, but I would keep residency and immutability decisions with the storage specialist.

The experiment: move bytes without moving the trust boundary

The simple design is an app server that accepts a 4 GB recording, buffers or streams it, and then writes it to a bucket. It is easy to sketch and expensive to operate: the app becomes a throughput bottleneck, and every byte crosses a process that did not need to inspect the media.

The better experiment is narrower. The app authenticates the upload, creates a short-lived direct upload handoff, and records only the object key and policy metadata. The client sends the file to the storage service. A worker later verifies the upload, writes a backup manifest, and applies the lifecycle rule. The app owns authorization; the bucket owns bytes.

That boundary matters more than a small difference in storage-unit price. A useful test fixture is 10,000 media objects ranging from 50 MB to 4 GB, written in one region and read back for restore drills from the same region. Measure upload completion time, failed-part recovery, restore time, egress, and the age at which objects move to colder storage. Do not copy a provider choice from a benchmark that only uploads 10 MB files.

Bytes should take the shortest path.

Which object storage service should back up app data?

AWS S3 is the broad default when the system needs mature lifecycle management, regional choice, and a large ecosystem of SDKs and adjacent controls. Its object lifecycle documentation is explicit about transitions and expiration, which makes it a strong baseline for a backup policy that will grow beyond one rule.

Azure Blob Storage is the natural comparison for a product already organized around Azure regions, identities, and operational tooling. Its lifecycle management can be a good fit when the rest of the application already uses that provider's access model. Moving media between clouds later is possible, but it is a project with egress, verification, and metadata mapping to budget for.

Backblaze B2 is worth testing when a simpler object-storage surface and broad compatibility are more important than the larger cloud's surrounding services. It should still be evaluated against the actual restore path: storage tier behavior, regional availability, egress terms, and the operational tools used by the team matter more than a table of nominal rates.

One REST option occupies a different position in this comparison. It exposes backend capabilities through HTTP, so a TypeScript, Python, or other client does not need another storage SDK or client-library release cycle. Its public discovery surface documents request and response schemas with runnable examples. For Infrai, the relevant advantage is one REST API and one key: any runtime that can send HTTP can use the same control surface without installing a storage client library or managing a second credential for this backend workflow. A second, practical advantage is its public self-describing discovery surface, which lets a backup worker inspect the current lifecycle schema before deployment instead of relying on copied SDK types. That can remove integration friction for a solo team already coordinating several backend services.

Here is the boundary I would use:

Decision Better fit Why
Deep storage controls, regional options, and a large ecosystem AWS S3 Strong baseline for long-lived backup policy
Existing Azure identity and regional operations Azure Blob Storage Fits an Azure-centered application boundary
A focused object-storage specialist to test directly Backblaze B2 Keeps the comparison grounded in the restore path
One REST control surface across backend capabilities A REST storage gateway Reduces SDK and integration surface for the control plane

What should the lifecycle rule actually do?

Start with a restore promise, not a storage tier. For example, keep recent backups in the primary tier for the period needed for routine recovery, transition older backups only after restore tests pass, and expire data only when the retention policy permits deletion. Separate user-uploaded media from backup artifacts; they have different legal, product, and recovery lifetimes.

The rule also needs an owner and an audit trail. Store the policy version with the backup manifest. When retention changes, record the effective date rather than silently rewriting history. A lifecycle engine can delete an object correctly while the application still points at it, so cleanup should be paired with manifest reconciliation and a restore check.

For large uploads, incomplete multipart work deserves attention. The storage options differ in how they expose cleanup, and an abandoned upload can create operational noise even when no completed object exists. Test an interrupted upload, a retry, and a delete request. Those three cases reveal more about the real data path than a successful upload does.

The REST lifecycle capability is a reasonable fit for bucket policy configuration when a one-key workflow is the goal. Its minimum lifecycle interval is one day, and it does not provide an automatic rule for multipart fragments. That rules it out for hour-level expiry or a design that expects unfinished parts to disappear through lifecycle policy alone. The worker still needs explicit multipart cleanup and manifest reconciliation.

Here is the smallest useful control-plane check I would keep beside the worker. The request body is deliberately supplied by the current schema rather than guessed in an article; the route, authentication, retry behavior, and response handling are the parts worth standardizing in application code.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const bucket = process.env.BACKUP_BUCKET;
const lifecycleJson = process.env.LIFECYCLE_JSON;

if (!apiKey || !bucket || !lifecycleJson) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY, BACKUP_BUCKET, and LIFECYCLE_JSON are required");
}

async function setLifecycle(): Promise<unknown> {
  let delayMs = 500;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": `lifecycle-${bucket}`,
      },
      body: lifecycleJson,
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      throw new Error(`Lifecycle update failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : delayMs));
    delayMs *= 2;
  }

  throw new Error("Lifecycle update was rate limited after five attempts");
}

await setLifecycle();

That code does not make the gateway responsible for residency or immutability. It makes one narrow operation repeatable, observable, and safe to retry; the bucket policy still needs review by the person responsible for retention.

Review the policy before the first production write.

Where does data live, and who can delete it?

Region is not a label to add at the end of an architecture diagram. Select the write region, backup region, and restore region together. Confirm where the provider processes control-plane requests, where objects reside, and where logs or metadata are retained. The contract and the provider's current regional documentation settle those questions; an API abstraction cannot.

Deletion has a similar split. A normal object delete is useful for application cleanup, but it is not a substitute for object lock or an immutable backup vault. Infrai does not provide object versioning or WORM object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those controls. A financial or compliance-grade immutability requirement belongs with a specialist storage configuration or an external immutable backup system.

There are other hard edges. The gateway does not offer cross-region automatic replication or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool. It also does not provide an independently configurable CORS route for browser-direct uploads. If your upload design requires self-service CORS rules, cross-region replication, or a contractual residency guarantee, choose the specialist provider that explicitly supplies that feature and verify the terms.

This is the processor boundary: use the control plane to coordinate a storage action, but do not assume it changes the storage provider's residency, retention, deletion, or processor commitments. The storage specialist remains the source of truth for those obligations.

My decision rule for a small team

I would shortlist the provider that passes four tests with the real media distribution:

  1. Direct uploads and multipart retries meet the large-file throughput target without proxying bytes through the app.
  2. Lifecycle transitions and expiration match the written retention schedule, including the minimum interval.
  3. Region, processor, deletion, and egress terms are acceptable to the people who own the data.
  4. A restore drill can rebuild the app's manifest and media set after an overwrite, partial upload, or accidental delete.

Try the REST gateway for the storage control plane if your main problem is integrating bucket operations into a broader backend and you can keep specialist storage responsible for residency, replication, CORS, and immutable retention. The advantage is concrete: one HTTP API and one key replace another client-library integration for this control path. Do not select it as the sole answer for WORM backups, cross-region replication, hour-level lifecycle expiry, or browser uploads that require self-managed CORS. Those are the limitation cases where S3, Azure Blob Storage, or another specialist provider is the better choice.

The cost model should stay visible, but it should not drive the whole decision. Count storage tiers, requests, egress, restore traffic, regional availability, and the engineering work needed to verify deletion. A service that looks inexpensive while every restore crosses a region is not inexpensive for a backup system.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai storage documentation and validate the lifecycle request against the current schema before wiring it into production.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • AWS S3 object lifecycle management
  • Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management
  • Backblaze B2 documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
  • RFC 3986: URI Generic Syntax

title: what a shopify app stack really costs
description:
I built a Shopify app-cost calculator. The results changed how I price shop.

Quick context: I work on an ecommerce platform, and to understand our competition I did what any engineer would do — I turned pricing pages into math. The result is a calculator (launchstore.io/savings) that adds up what a real Shopify store pays monthly. This post walks through the model, because the totals surprised even me.

The pricing model nobody sees

Shopify's Basic plan is $39/mo. That's the number everyone quotes. But the platform ships deliberately lean, and the app store fills the gaps. Here's the stack a typical growing store ends up with, from the pricing pages as of writing:

Function Typical app Listed price
Email marketing Klaviyo $45–500/mo (subscriber tiers)
Live chat / support Tidio $29–749/mo (conversation tiers)
Product reviews Loox $10–300/mo
Page builder Shogun $39–499/mo
WhatsApp marketing various $30–100/mo
Loyalty program Smile.io $19–99/mo
SEO tools Plug in SEO $29–79/mo

Add those up and the plan fee — the only number in the ads — is a minority of the bill. A modest stack lands around $210–2,300/mo on top of Shopify itself. The realistic band for a store doing real volume is $300–900/mo total, which matches what we see when merchants import their actual invoices into the calculator. [VERIFY: re-run the calculator with current app pricing before publishing; screenshots of the calculator make this post much stronger.]

Why stores end up here (it's not stupidity)

Every line starts as a free trial solving a real problem. Reviews: you need social proof. Klaviyo: abandoned carts are 10–15% of recoverable revenue. Nobody signs up for a $500/mo stack — they accrete one $29 at a time, and every app individually seems cheaper than engineering around it.

The interesting engineering question: why is the stack the default? Because the platform's business model is the app store. Extract the same features into the platform and the economics invert — which is exactly the bet we made at LaunchStore ($9/mo, everything included; there's my affiliation, grain of salt).

The calculator, as a build

For the #showdev crowd: it's a static page, no backend — pricing data is a small JSON model with tier functions (Klaviyo's subscriber math is the fiddly one), and the calculator solves the inverse problem: given your order volume and subscriber count, which tier does each app put you in? The fun part was encoding tier boundaries as data rather than code, so updating Klaviyo's pricing next quarter is a one-line change.

The full breakdown of Shopify's real costs (including transaction fees and theme costs) is in our long-form post — but the calculator is the honest version, because you can put in your own numbers and check my math.

Takeaways, even if you never use our platform

  1. When you evaluate any platform, price the stack, not the plan. The plan is a lower bound.
  2. Audit your app subscriptions quarterly. The data is consistent: stores routinely pay for two apps solving the same problem after a trial they forgot to cancel.
  3. If you're building SaaS: the app-store model prints money precisely because each individual charge feels small. Your users' invoice totals are your churn risk.

title: Google Chat Added Tables. Keep the Warning Outside the Grid.
description:
Google announced tables and headings for Chat app and agent messages on November 23. Web users see tables inline, with scrolling for wider tables. On Android and iOS, users currently tap “Show table” to open the full table; inline mobile viewing is planned to follow. That difference matters when a comparison contains a warning someone needs before acting.

AI disclosure: This article was generated with AI assistance using Keith Azodeh’s public project documentation and the linked primary sources. It has not been reviewed by Keith before publication.

For an operational handoff, put a decision-changing exception in the visible message summary as well as the detailed comparison. The table can carry the evidence. The summary should make clear whether that evidence is ready to use.

This is a design consequence of the announced viewing behavior, not a claim that Google Chat has lost data or that users have missed a particular warning.

A pricing comparison needs its conditions

The TMC Price Intelligence case study describes a delivered 2023–2025 engagement that turned supplier emails and attachments into structured pricing information. Product, size, price, region, and supplier became records for comparison, reporting, and quote and invoice workflows.

The documented lesson is practical: extraction has an operational destination, and values need review before they become business decisions. The case study does not establish a Google Chat integration.

Consider a proposed Chat handoff for a similar pricing workflow. A table could show offers side by side, making the product and supplier easier to scan. But a low displayed price can be unhelpful when the pack size is still unresolved.

A row-level note can explain that condition accurately. If it is the only place the exception appears, the reader must open the full comparison to discover why an apparent bargain is not yet comparable.

For this proposed workflow, the message should tell the reader that comparison is incomplete before presenting anything that sounds like a selection.

Write the summary from the same facts

A fictional summary might read:

Quote review needed. Comparison is incomplete: Supplier B’s pack size is unconfirmed. Open the full comparison before choosing an offer.

The detailed table would retain the affected offer, its original description, the extracted fields, and the review state. The summary identifies what prevents a useful comparison; it does not replace the review.

Generate both views from the same structured result. If the application has already classified an offer as needing clarification, use that state to choose the summary. Avoid asking a second unconstrained generation step to independently decide whether the report is ready.

Otherwise, the table might retain the exception while a fluent summary describes the comparison as complete. That would be a contradiction introduced by the handoff layer.

This is an illustrative message and a proposed design. It contains no supplier record or actual TMC exception.

Keep the summary selective

Repeating every cell above a table would make the new layout less useful. Reserve the opening for information that changes the next action: an unresolved comparison condition, the scope of the report, and where to inspect the details.

Keep the full source descriptions and supporting fields in the comparison. If there are many offers, the visible summary should state which subset the table covers instead of implying that it represents every available option.

A short message has a tradeoff. It helps the recipient orient quickly, but it cannot carry every qualification. The application needs a clear route from that overview to the complete record.

For the proposed pricing handoff, a reviewer should be able to identify the affected offer after opening the table. A vague “some data may need review” warning leaves them to rediscover the problem.

Check the message’s markup mode

The Chat formatting guide distinguishes standard Markdown from Chat markup. Tables and headings are supported in the Markdown mode. Existing configured Chat apps default to Chat markup for compatibility, while newly created apps default to Markdown. Incoming webhooks default to Chat markup, too.

That means the new feature is not just a matter of adding pipe characters to an existing message template. Check the app configuration and the request’s markup setting. The API supports specifying the syntax on an individual request.

Google’s announcement also says these tables and headings cannot be created in the ordinary Chat message compose box. A developer’s API message and a person’s manually typed message are different authoring paths.

For a proposed integration, inspect the actual rendered message after sending through the intended path. A correct-looking template in an editor does not establish what the recipient sees.

Review the handoff before opening the table

Use a synthetic comparison for the proposed acceptance exercise. Include one complete offer and one offer with an unresolved pack size. Keep the warning tied to the same offer in the summary and the table.

Inspect the web message and the current Android and iOS experience. First review the message without opening the table. Then open it and check that the detailed records explain the summary.

Check a wide comparison as well: extra columns should not be the only place where the readiness of the report is communicated. These are proposed checks, not tests performed against Google Chat or TMC.

Google’s new formatting gives apps a clearer way to present detailed comparisons. A useful mobile handoff also makes the next action clear before the recipient opens the grid.
