title: Built in the open: four repositories, one rule — declare what's absent
description:
I'm a solo builder. Everything below is public on GitHub, free for non-commercial use with attribution under my Dual License Agreement v4.9. I'm not selling anything. This is a record of what exists, written for the people who judge work by running it.

The work's home on the web is https://www.livingphiphysics.com.

Living-Phi-Physics — the flagship proofs

https://github.com/pluscoder30-cpu/Living-Phi-Physics

Nine papers (P1–P9), committed August 19, 2026: phi-form laws with a classical limit (κ_φ → 0), including work on Navier–Stokes, Yang–Mills, and the Riemann hypothesis. The claim and the papers are dated by GitHub's own timestamps. Read them, check the dates, argue with the math — that's what they're there for.

Portable-XRF — the instrument package

https://github.com/pluscoder30-cpu/Portable-XRF

Software for a portable XRF spectrometer: 222 files, ~19,500 lines of Python, ESP32 firmware, ten papers. On a clean machine the test suite runs 236 passed / 9 skipped / 2 failed of 247 — both failures are the same self-declared absence (a vendor cross-check package that isn't public, named as absent in the code). Every reading carries a receipt with a verdict code — [VERIFIED] [REAL] [DECLARED] [PREDICTED] [SIMULATED] [ABSENT] — and Law 1347 keeps the core spectroscopy in exact classical form, enforced by a dedicated honesty test.

Omega_Field_GPU_Ultimate — the field processor

https://github.com/pluscoder30-cpu/Omega_Field_GPU_Ultimate

A self-defining field matrix processor with a holographic codec (real numpy encode/decode via pseudo-inverse). It ships with its own claim-checker: run VERIFY_CLAIMS.py and every check passes — the summary matches the README to the digit. Don't take the README's word; run the file that argues with it.

The-future-of-vehicles — the fleet

https://github.com/pluscoder30-cpu/The-future-of-vehicles

51 complete build packages — 1,138 files: priced parts lists from real suppliers, wiring and mechanical docs, assembly steps written so a 12-year-old can follow them, safety, and the physics for each. Total fleet cost ~$35,000 per the README. This one is a gift artifact: take a package and build the thing.

The rule that ties them together

Every package declares what it is and what it isn't. Verdicts are printed, absences are spoken, and the receipts are kept by third parties — GitHub's timestamps, hash chains — not by me. Judge it the way builders judge anything: clone it, run it, and see what holds.

— Christopher David Ayotte (pluscoder30-cpu)

title: The Agentic IDE Is an API: Building a Unified Tool Registry for Claude Code, Codex, and MCP
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Why One Registry?

Modern coding agents do not live inside a single IDE. They run as separate processes, connect to different model providers, and discover tools through incompatible mechanisms. Claude Code uses its own tool configuration. Codex operates within its own runtime. Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients connect to servers over stdio or HTTP. The result is a fragmented control plane where permissions, schemas, observability, and secrets are duplicated across every integration.

The architectural shift is simple: treat the agentic IDE as an API surface, not a collection of hardcoded tool menus. Every tool becomes a versioned capability with a schema, an authorization policy, an execution boundary, and a structured result. Claude Code, Codex, and MCP clients become consumers of that same registry.

This tutorial builds a runnable registry with a TypeScript control plane, a Fastify HTTP API, and an MCP-compatible adapter. You will expose a filesystem tool and a calculator, register both with explicit policies, and let multiple clients invoke them through the same endpoint.

Security note: The registry intentionally rejects arbitrary shell execution. Tool implementations run in a separate process with a restricted environment. In production, add container isolation, resource quotas, and a stronger identity provider.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Architecture Overview
  • 2. Prerequisites
  • 3. Project Setup
  • 4. Defining the Tool Contract
  • 5. Implementing the Tool Runtime
  • 6. Building the Registry API
  • 7. Adding Policy Enforcement
  • 8. Connecting MCP Clients
  • 9. Connecting Claude Code and Codex
  • 10. Adding Observability
  • 11. Production Hardening
  • 12. Testing the Registry
  • 13. Frequently Asked Questions

1. Architecture Overview

The registry sits between agents and tool implementations. Agents never receive direct access to credentials or the host filesystem. Instead, they submit a tool invocation to the registry, which authenticates the caller, authorizes the action, validates the arguments, executes the tool, and returns a normalized response.

┌───────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
│  Claude Code  │   │     Codex     │   │  MCP Client    │
└───────┬───────┘   └───────┬───────┘   └────────┬───────┘
        │                   │                    │
        │  OpenAI-style     │  MCP JSON-RPC      │
        │  function call    │                    │
        └───────────────────┴────────────────────┘
                            │
                    ┌───────▼────────┐
                    │ Tool Registry  │
                    │  • authn       │
                    │  • policy      │
                    │  • validation  │
                    │  • audit log   │
                    └───────┬────────┘
                            │
              ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
              ▼             ▼             ▼
        ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌────────────┐
        │ read_file│  │ calculate│  │ MCP Server │
        └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └────────────┘

Four layers matter:

  1. Contract layer. A registry entry contains a stable name, a JSON Schema for arguments, a version, and a capability tag.
  2. Policy layer. Every entry has an allowlist, a caller scope requirement, and optional argument constraints.
  3. Execution layer. Tool code runs behind an interface. The reference implementation uses a child process, but the interface permits containers, sandboxes, or remote workers.
  4. Adapter layer. Claude Code and Codex consume OpenAI-compatible function definitions. MCP clients consume JSON-RPC tools/list and tools/call methods.

The key invariant: all clients receive the same schema and the same authorization decision.

2. Prerequisites

You need:

  • Node.js 20 or later
  • npm 10 or later
  • A terminal and a text editor
  • Optional: an API key for Claude or OpenAI if you want to test with a live model

Verify your environment:

node --version
npm --version

3. Project Setup

Create the project and install dependencies:

mkdir agentic-tool-registry
cd agentic-tool-registry
npm init -y
npm install fastify @fastify/cors zod @modelcontextprotocol/sdk
npm install -D typescript tsx @types/node vitest

Create tsconfig.json:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "src"
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts", "test/**/*.ts"]
}

Set the package type to ES modules:

npm pkg set type=module
npm pkg set scripts.dev="tsx watch src/server.ts"
npm pkg set scripts.start="tsx src/server.ts"
npm pkg set scripts.test="vitest run"
npm pkg set scripts.typecheck="tsc --noEmit"

4. Defining the Tool Contract

A tool contract must be machine-readable and stable. Use JSON Schema for arguments because both OpenAI function calling and MCP understand JSON Schema conventions.

Create src/contracts.ts:

import { z } from "zod";

export type ToolContract = {
  name: string;
  version: string;
  description: string;
  inputSchema: Record<string, unknown>;
  requiredScopes: string[];
  allowedRoles: string[];
  timeoutMs: number;
  handler: (args: unknown) => Promise<unknown>;
};

export const ToolInvocationSchema = z.object({
  tool: z.string().min(1),
  arguments: z.record(z.unknown()).default({}),
  idempotencyKey: z.string().min(8).optional(),
});

export type ToolInvocation = z.infer<typeof ToolInvocationSchema>;

export type ToolResult = {
  ok: boolean;
  output?: unknown;
  error?: {
    code: string;
    message: string;
  };
  durationMs: number;
};

The ToolInvocationSchema validates the envelope. Each tool validates its own arguments with Zod, then translates that schema into JSON Schema for discovery. To avoid maintaining two definitions by hand, we can use zod-to-json-schema. Install it:

npm install zod-to-json-schema

Create src/tools.ts:

import { z } from "zod";
import { zodToJsonSchema } from "zod-to-json-schema";
import type { ToolContract } from "./contracts.js";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";

const ROOT = process.env.TOOL_ROOT ?? process.cwd();

const ReadFileArgs = z.object({
  path: z.string().min(1),
  encoding: z.enum(["utf8", "utf-8"]).default("utf8"),
});

const CalculateArgs = z.object({
  expression: z.string().min(1).max(200),
});

async function readFileTool(raw: unknown) {
  const args = ReadFileArgs.parse(raw);
  const resolved = path.resolve(ROOT, args.path);

  if (!resolved.startsWith(ROOT + path.sep)) {
    throw new Error("PATH_OUTSIDE_ROOT");
  }

  const content = await readFile(resolved, "utf8");
  return { path: resolved, content };
}

async function calculateTool(raw: unknown) {
  const args = CalculateArgs.parse(raw);

  if (!/^[0-9+\-*/().\s]+$/.test(args.expression)) {
    throw new Error("INVALID_EXPRESSION");
  }

  const tokens = args.expression.match(/\d+(?:\.\d+)?|[-+*/()]/g) ?? [];
  let position = 0;

  function parseExpression(): number {
    let value = parseTerm();
    while (tokens[position] === "+" || tokens[position] === "-") {
      const operator = tokens[position++];
      const right = parseTerm();
      value = operator === "+" ? value + right : value - right;
    }
    return value;
  }

  function parseTerm(): number {
    let value = parseFactor();
    while (tokens[position] === "*" || tokens[position] === "/") {
      const operator = tokens[position++];
      const right = parseFactor();
      value = operator === "*" ? value * right : value / right;
    }
    return value;
  }

  function parseFactor(): number {
    if (tokens[position] === "-") {
      position++;
      return -parseFactor();
    }
    if (tokens[position] === "(") {
      position++;
      const value = parseExpression();
      if (tokens[position] !== ")") throw new Error("INVALID_EXPRESSION");
      position++;
      return value;
    }
    const token = tokens[position++];
    const number = Number(token);
    if (Number.isNaN(number)) throw new Error("INVALID_EXPRESSION");
    return number;
  }

  const result = parseExpression();
  if (position !== tokens.length) throw new Error("INVALID_EXPRESSION");
  return { expression: args.expression, result };
}

export const tools: ToolContract[] = [
  {
    name: "read_file",
    version: "1.0.0",
    description: "Read a UTF-8 text file from the workspace root.",
    inputSchema: zodToJsonSchema(ReadFileArgs) as Record<string, unknown>,
    requiredScopes: ["files:read"],
    allowedRoles: ["developer", "agent"],
    timeoutMs: 5_000,
    handler: readFileTool,
  },
  {
    name: "calculate",
    version: "1.0.0",
    description: "Evaluate an arithmetic expression.",
    inputSchema: zodToJsonSchema(CalculateArgs) as Record<string, unknown>,
    requiredScopes: ["calc:execute"],
    allowedRoles: ["developer", "agent"],
    timeoutMs: 2_000,
    handler: calculateTool,
  },
];

The calculator uses a small recursive-descent parser instead of eval. It accepts only numeric literals and arithmetic operators, so the tool cannot execute arbitrary code.

5. Implementing the Tool Runtime

The runtime must enforce a timeout and normalize errors. A failed tool should never crash the registry or leak a stack trace to the client.

Create src/runtime.ts:

import type { ToolContract, ToolResult } from "./contracts.js";

export class ToolRuntime {
  private tools = new Map<string, ToolContract>();

  register(tool: ToolContract) {
    if (this.tools.has(tool.name)) {
      throw new Error(`DUPLICATE_TOOL:${tool.name}`);
    }
    this.tools.set(tool.name, tool);
  }

  list(): ToolContract[] {
    return [...this.tools.values()];
  }

  get(name: string): ToolContract | undefined {
    return this.tools.get(name);
  }

  async execute(name: string, args: unknown): Promise<ToolResult> {
    const tool = this.tools.get(name);
    const started = Date.now();

    if (!tool) {
      return {
        ok: false,
        error: { code: "TOOL_NOT_FOUND", message: `Unknown tool: ${name}` },
        durationMs: Date.now() - started,
      };
    }

    let timer: NodeJS.Timeout | undefined;

    try {
      const output = await Promise.race([
        tool.handler(args),
        new Promise((_, reject) => {
          timer = setTimeout(
            () => reject(new Error("TOOL_TIMEOUT")),
            tool.timeoutMs,
          );
        }),
      ]);

      return { ok: true, output, durationMs: Date.now() - started };
    } catch (error) {
      const code = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "TOOL_ERROR";
      return {
        ok: false,
        error: { code, message: "Tool execution failed" },
        durationMs: Date.now() - started,
      };
    } finally {
      if (timer) clearTimeout(timer);
    }
  }
}

Promise.race enforces a soft timeout. It does not terminate the underlying operation. For CPU-bound or runaway processes, run the handler in a worker thread or a container with a hard kill deadline.

6. Building the Registry API

The HTTP API exposes three operations:

  • GET /v1/tools returns the discovery catalog
  • POST /v1/invocations executes a tool
  • GET /healthz returns liveness status

Create src/server.ts:

import Fastify from "fastify";
import cors from "@fastify/cors";
import { ToolInvocationSchema } from "./contracts.js";
import { ToolRuntime } from "./runtime.js";
import { tools } from "./tools.js";
import { createMcpServer } from "./mcp.js";
import { authenticate } from "./auth.js";
import { authorize } from "./policy.js";

const app = Fastify({ logger: true });
const runtime = new ToolRuntime();

for (const tool of tools) runtime.register(tool);

await app.register(cors, {
  origin: process.env.ALLOWED_ORIGIN ?? "http://localhost:3000",
});

app.get("/healthz", async () => ({ status: "ok" }));

app.get("/v1/tools", async (request) => {
  const identity = await authenticate(request.headers.authorization);
  const visible = runtime.list().filter((tool) =>
    authorize(identity, tool).allowed,
  );

  return visible.map((tool) => ({
    name: tool.name,
    version: tool.version,
    description: tool.description,
    inputSchema: tool.inputSchema,
  }));
});

app.post("/v1/invocations", async (request, reply) => {
  const identity = await authenticate(request.headers.authorization);
  const parsed = ToolInvocationSchema.safeParse(request.body);

  if (!parsed.success) {
    return reply.code(400).send({
      ok: false,
      error: { code: "INVALID_REQUEST", message: parsed.error.message },
    });
  }

  const tool = runtime.get(parsed.data.tool);

  if (!tool) {
    return reply.code(404).send({
      ok: false,
      error: { code: "TOOL_NOT_FOUND", message: "Tool not found" },
    });
  }

  const decision = authorize(identity, tool);
  if (!decision.allowed) {
    return reply.code(403).send({
      ok: false,
      error: { code: decision.reason, message: "Tool invocation denied" },
    });
  }

  const result = await runtime.execute(tool.name, parsed.data.arguments);
  return reply.code(result.ok ? 200 : 422).send(result);
});

await createMcpServer(runtime, authenticate, authorize);

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 8787);
await app.listen({ port, host: "0.0.0.0" });

Notice that discovery is filtered by policy. A client never sees tools it cannot call. This prevents leaking internal capabilities through the catalog.

7. Adding Policy Enforcement

Authentication and authorization belong in separate modules so you can swap the identity provider without touching tool code.

Create src/auth.ts:

import { createHash, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

export type Identity = {
  subject: string;
  roles: string[];
  scopes: string[];
};

export async function authenticate(
  header: string | undefined,
): Promise<Identity> {
  if (!header?.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
    throw new Error("UNAUTHENTICATED");
  }

  const token = header.slice(7);
  const expected = process.env.REGISTRY_API_KEY;

  if (!expected) throw new Error("AUTH_NOT_CONFIGURED");

  const a = createHash("sha256").update(token).digest();
  const b = createHash("sha256").update(expected).digest();

  if (!timingSafeEqual(a, b)) {
    throw new Error("UNAUTHENTICATED");
  }

  return {
    subject: "local-agent",
    roles: ["developer", "agent"],
    scopes: ["files:read", "calc:execute"],
  };
}

The static API key is acceptable for local development. Replace it with OIDC token verification for production.

Create src/policy.ts:

import type { ToolContract } from "./contracts.js";
import type { Identity } from "./auth.js";

export type PolicyDecision = {
  allowed: boolean;
  reason: string;
};

export function authorize(
  identity: Identity,
  tool: ToolContract,
): PolicyDecision {
  const roleAllowed = tool.allowedRoles.some((role) =>
    identity.roles.includes(role),
  );

  if (!roleAllowed) {
    return { allowed: false, reason: "ROLE_NOT_ALLOWED" };
  }

  const scopesAllowed = tool.requiredScopes.every((scope) =>
    identity.scopes.includes(scope),
  );

  if (!scopesAllowed) {
    return { allowed: false, reason: "SCOPE_NOT_ALLOWED" };
  }

  return { allowed: true, reason: "ALLOWED" };
}

For real deployments, extend the policy function with argument-level constraints: maximum file size, allowed path prefixes, rate limits per subject, and approval requirements for destructive operations.

8. Connecting MCP Clients

The MCP SDK exposes a server implementation that speaks JSON-RPC over stdio. We will mount the same runtime behind it, so MCP clients inherit the registry's schemas and policies.

Create src/mcp.ts:

import { McpServer } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js";
import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js";
import { z } from "zod";
import type { ToolRuntime } from "./runtime.js";
import type { Identity } from "./auth.js";
import { authorize } from "./policy.js";

export async function createMcpServer(
  runtime: ToolRuntime,
  authenticate: (header?: string) => Promise<Identity>,
  authorizeFn: (identity: Identity, tool: any) => { allowed: boolean; reason: string },
) {
  const server = new McpServer({
    name: "unified-tool-registry",
    version: "1.0.0",
  });

  const identity = await authenticate(`Bearer ${process.env.REGISTRY_API_KEY}`);

  for (const tool of runtime.list()) {
    if (!authorizeFn(identity, tool).allowed) continue;

    server.registerTool(
      tool.name,
      {
        title: tool.name,
        description: tool.description,
        inputSchema: tool.inputSchema as any,
      },
      async (args: any) => {
        const result = await runtime.execute(tool.name, args);

        if (!result.ok) {
          return {
            isError: true,
            content: [{ type: "text", text: result.error?.message ?? "Tool failed" }],
          };
        }

        return {
          content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(result.output) }],
        };
      },
    );
  }

  await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport());
}

The MCP adapter uses the same runtime.execute path as the HTTP API. There is no separate authorization logic.

9. Connecting Claude Code and Codex

Both Claude Code and Codex support connecting to MCP servers. Create mcp.json in your workspace:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "unified-registry": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["tsx", "src/mcp.ts"],
      "env": {
        "REGISTRY_API_KEY": "your-local-development-key",
        "TOOL_ROOT": "/absolute/path/to/your/project"
      }
    }
  }
}\n```
{% endraw %}


Because the MCP server runs over stdio, it cannot share the HTTP server's port. Run it as a separate process:
{% raw %}


```bash
REGISTRY_API_KEY=your-local-development-key \
TOOL_ROOT="$PWD" \
npx tsx src/mcp.ts

In Claude Code, add the server with:

claude mcp add unified-registry \
  --env REGISTRY_API_KEY=your-local-development-key \
  --env TOOL_ROOT="$PWD" \
  -- npx tsx src/mcp.ts

For Codex, place the same server definition in ~/.codex/config.toml:

[mcp_servers.unified-registry]
command = "npx"
args = ["tsx", "src/mcp.ts"]

[mcp_servers.unified-registry.env]
REGISTRY_API_KEY = "your-local-development-key"
TOOL_ROOT = "/absolute/path/to/your/project"

Both agents now discover read_file and calculate through the registry contract. They see identical schemas regardless of which model provider generated the call.

If you prefer a direct HTTP integration, expose the discovery catalog as OpenAI-compatible function definitions:

export function toOpenAiTools(tools: ToolContract[]) {
  return tools.map((tool) => ({
    type: "function" as const,
    function: {
      name: tool.name,
      description: tool.description,
      parameters: tool.inputSchema,
    },
  }));
}\n```



Clients can fetch this catalog from `GET /v1/tools` and pass the resulting function calls to `POST /v1/invocations`.

## 10. Adding Observability

A registry without logs is impossible to audit. Record who called what, whether it succeeded, and how long it took. The `ToolResult` already includes `durationMs`. Fastify's logger captures HTTP-level metadata.

Add a structured audit event inside the invocation route:



```ts
app.log.info(
  {
    event: "tool_invocation",
    subject: identity.subject,
    tool: tool.name,
    version: tool.version,
    allowed: true,
    durationMs: result.durationMs,
    ok: result.ok,
  },
  "tool invocation completed",
);

For production, ship these events to OpenTelemetry, include a correlation ID from the client request, and record policy denials separately from execution failures. Denials often reveal misconfigured scopes or an agent attempting an unexpected action.

11. Production Hardening

The reference implementation is a starting point. Before deploying it:

Replace static keys with OIDC. Verify issuer, audience, expiry, and signature. Derive roles and scopes from verified claims rather than request headers.

Isolate tool execution. Run each tool in a container, gVisor sandbox, or dedicated worker with a read-only base image, a scoped filesystem mount, no network by default, and CPU and memory limits.

Add argument-level policy. Validate file paths against an allowlist of prefixes, cap file sizes, and require human approval for write or delete operations.

Version contracts. Include version in every registry entry. When a schema changes incompatibly, publish a new version and keep the old one available during migration.

Add rate limiting. Limit invocations per subject and per tool. A runaway agent loop should hit a quota rather than exhaust downstream resources.

Encrypt secrets. Use a secrets manager and inject credentials into the tool process at execution time. Never place secrets in the registry catalog or the MCP environment block in a shared config file.

Sign the catalog. If clients run in different trust domains, publish a signed manifest containing tool versions and schema hashes so clients can detect tampering.

Support idempotency. Store the idempotencyKey with a short TTL. If a client retries after a network timeout, return the original result instead of executing the tool twice.

12. Testing the Registry

Create test/registry.test.ts:

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { ToolRuntime } from "../src/runtime.js";
import { tools } from "../src/tools.js";
import { authorize } from "../src/policy.js";

describe("tool registry", () => {
  it("executes the calculator", async () => {
    const runtime = new ToolRuntime();
    for (const tool of tools) runtime.register(tool);

    const result = await runtime.execute("calculate", {
      expression: "2 * (3 + 4)",
    });

    expect(result.ok).toBe(true);
    expect(result.output).toMatchObject({ result: 14 });
  });

  it("rejects unsafe expressions", async () => {
    const runtime = new ToolRuntime();
    for (const tool of tools) runtime.register(tool);

    const result = await runtime.execute("calculate", {
      expression: "process.exit(1)",
    });

    expect(result.ok).toBe(false);
  });

  it("denies tools without the required scope", () => {
    const tool = tools.find((t) => t.name === "read_file")!;
    const decision = authorize(
      { subject: "test", roles: ["developer"], scopes: [] },
      tool,
    );

    expect(decision.allowed).toBe(false);
    expect(decision.reason).toBe("SCOPE_NOT_ALLOWED");
  });
});

Run the suite:

npm test
npm run typecheck

Start the server and verify the API:

REGISTRY_API_KEY=dev-key npm run start

In another terminal:

curl -s http://localhost:8787/v1/tools \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dev-key" | jq

curl -s http://localhost:8787/v1/invocations \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dev-key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tool":"calculate","arguments":{"expression":"10 / 4"}}' | jq

The calculation returns 2.5. The catalog lists both tools with their JSON Schemas.

13. Frequently Asked Questions

Why not let each agent connect directly to each MCP server?\n

Direct connections work for a prototype, but they multiply the trust boundary. With a registry, you get one audit trail, one schema source of truth, one policy engine, and one place to rotate credentials. Agents still reach MCP servers; they just do so through a governed adapter.

How do I handle tools with different authentication requirements?\n

Keep authentication inside the tool implementation. The registry authorizes whether a caller may invoke the tool. The tool then authenticates to its downstream service using credentials injected at runtime. This separation keeps the registry generic and prevents it from becoming a credential store.

Can multiple agents share one tool instance safely?\n

Yes, as long as the tool is stateless or uses per-invocation context. Pass the caller's subject and correlation ID into the handler context so downstream systems can enforce tenant isolation. If a tool holds mutable state, make that state keyed by subject or run the tool in an isolated process per invocation.

Final Result

You now have a single governed API that Claude Code, Codex, and MCP clients can all use. Tools are discovered through one catalog, authorized through one policy engine, executed behind one runtime, and audited in one place. The next step is to add a write tool with argument-level constraints and human approval, then move execution into containers before exposing the registry to remote agents.

title: Why UUIDv4 Causes PostgreSQL/InnoDB B-Tree Bloat — and How RFC 9562 UUIDv7 Fixes It
description:
Using random UUIDv4 values as database primary keys looks clean at 100k rows and turns painful past 20M rows. The bottleneck is not UUID size (16 bytes)—it is write locality inside B-Tree indexes.

1. What Random UUIDv4 Does to B-Tree Pages

Sequential keys append to the rightmost leaf page of a B-Tree, so hot index writes stay inside RAM (shared_buffers in PostgreSQL, innodb_buffer_pool in MySQL).

Completely random UUIDv4 keys scatter inserts across the entire index:

  • Half-full page splits inflate index size by 30–50% and drive random disk I/O.
  • In MySQL InnoDB, because the primary key is clustered and copied into every secondary index, random UUIDv4 keys degrade cache hit ratios across all indexes on the table.

2. How RFC 9562 UUIDv7 Keeps 16 Bytes and Restores Locality

UUIDv7 fits inside the exact same standard UUID column type, placing a 48-bit big-endian Unix millisecond timestamp in the first 6 bytes:

  • Bits 0..47: Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds
  • Bits 48..51: Version 7 (0111)
  • Bits 52..63: 12 bits of sub-millisecond monotonicity / randomness
  • Bits 64..65: RFC 9562 variant 10
  • Bits 66..127: 62 random bits

Because keys increase monotonically with time, inserts land at the rightmost leaf pages—and you can decode exact creation timestamps straight out of any UUIDv7 without touching the database.

3. Zero-Dependency CLI & Browser Inspector

I built a small MIT CLI (uuidv7-inspect, zero dependencies, node --test passing) to generate RFC 9562 UUIDv7s and inspect embedded timestamps, paired with client-side browser tools (0 bytes uploaded):

  • Open-Source CLI (uuidv7-inspect, MIT): https://github.com/JangYS0/uuidv7-inspect
  • Browser UUIDv7 / UUIDv4 Generator & Inspector: https://global-utils.com/en/uuid-generator
  • Unix Timestamp Converter: https://global-utils.com/en/timestamp-converter
  • UUIDv7 & Snowflake ID Suite: https://global-utils.com/en/assets/uuidv7-snowflake-high-throughput-id-suite

title: Export Python Stock Candles to CSV Without Losing the Query Context
description:
A stock candle CSV is easy to download and surprisingly easy to misread a week later. A file called AAPL.csv cannot tell you whether its bars are daily or minute, adjusted or raw, or whether the API returned the whole window. Export two files together: the candles as CSV and a manifest recording the request, the series actually returned, and the exact CSV bytes.

Record the request and the response separately

The request describes what you intended to download. Keep the full symbol, asset type, interval, price adjustment, limit and any requested time bounds. Store a UTC time for the capture, and don't send the API key to the browser or include it in the manifest.

The response says what you actually received. TickDB's Candlestick Data endpoint returns the applied symbol, asset type, interval, and adjustment alongside its bars. Compare these fields with the request before writing the export. If you asked for unadjusted daily bars and received adjusted minute bars, reject the export instead of silently naming it after the requested series.

Keep uncertainty visible

  • Window: Record row count and the earliest and latest returned labels. A request for ten records returning eight does not prove why two are absent, and a response returning ten does not prove complete coverage.
  • Time: Preserve the original integer millisecond labels in the CSV. Format times separately in the UI. A UTC timestamp does not, by itself, identify an exchange session or an exchange-local trading date.
  • Missing fields: A blank volume is not zero. Ignore neither the missing field nor the distinction when you import the file.
  • Finality: A recent candle can be provisional. If you cannot establish that a bar is final or that the window is complete, keep those states explicit rather than deriving them from row count or retrieval success.

A Python export you can check later

The sample requests ten unadjusted daily AAPL bars and writes a CSV plus a matching JSON manifest. The standard-library example needs a TickDB key in the server environment to make the request. The local checks below use synthetic payloads; they do not establish an account's permissions, the live feed's completeness, or an exchange timetable.

import csv, io, json, hashlib, os
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

ENDPOINT = "https://api.tickdb.ai/v1/market/kline"
QUERY = dict(symbol="AAPL.US", type="stock", interval="1d", adjust="none", limit=10)
FIELDS = ("time", "open", "high", "low", "close", "volume")

def export(payload, query, pulled_at):
    if payload.get("code") != 0:
        raise ValueError("provider returned a business error")
    data = payload["data"]
    applied = {k: data[k] for k in ("symbol", "type", "interval", "adjust")}
    if any(query[k] != v for k, v in applied.items()):
        raise ValueError("response series does not match export request")
    bars = data["klines"]
    times = [row["time"] for row in bars]
    if any(type(t) is not int for t in times) or len(times) != len(set(times)):
        raise ValueError("invalid or duplicate bar timestamps")
    f = io.StringIO(newline="")
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=FIELDS, lineterminator="\n")
    writer.writeheader()
    for row in sorted(bars, key=lambda r: r["time"]):
        writer.writerow({k: row.get(k) for k in FIELDS})
    content = f.getvalue().encode("utf-8")
    manifest = dict(request=query, applied=applied, queried_at_utc=pulled_at,
                    returned_rows=len(bars), first_ms=min(times, default=None),
                    last_ms=max(times, default=None), completeness="not established",
                    last_bar_finality="not established",
                    sha256=hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest())
    return content, manifest

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from pathlib import Path
    req = Request(ENDPOINT + "?" + urlencode(QUERY),
                  headers={"X-API-Key": os.environ["TICKDB_API_KEY"]})
    with urlopen(req, timeout=20) as response:
        payload = json.load(response)
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    content, manifest = export(payload, QUERY, now)
    Path("bars.csv").write_bytes(content)
    Path("bars.manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2)+"\n")

Verify the handoff

Treat the two files as a pair. Recompute SHA-256 over the CSV bytes and compare it with the manifest before importing the result. A mismatch means the files no longer correspond; a match proves byte identity, not market-data accuracy. Keep a distinct export ID for each capture in a production downloader rather than overwriting a prior pair.

In the synthetic checks, out-of-order rows are sorted, missing volume stays blank while an explicit zero survives, the row count and digest match, and a different adjustment, different interval or duplicate timestamp is rejected. An empty response exports only the header and records no returned time bounds. It does not assert that the market was closed.

For the downloader in a stock dashboard, the practical rule is simple: export the data and what you know about it, not just what the chart happens to show.

Source checked: TickDB REST API documentation, Candlestick Data and Latest Candlesticks.

title: I Wrote a Circuit Breaker and a Bitcask-Style WAL Engine for My Face Recognition API (With Real Code)
description:
A few weeks ago I shared what I learned building FaceMark, my facial-recognition attendance system (NestJS + Angular + a Python AI service). This post is the technical deep-dive I promised myself I'd write: the two components I built from scratch instead of pulling in a library, why I built them, and how they actually work.

Everything below is running code from the repo: ZiadtahaM/FaceMark.

Why build these myself?

Two reasons. First, both failure modes bit me in real testing: the AI service hanging froze my entire API, and restarting the Python service lost face embeddings stored as a pickle file that had corrupted once already. Second, I'm a junior developer, and I wanted to understand the patterns, not just import them. Both designs are straight out of Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann) - the circuit breaker from the reliability chapters and the storage engine from Chapter 3's Bitcask model.

Component 1: The circuit breaker (TypeScript, NestJS)

VisionService calls the FastAPI service over HTTP for every face registration and recognition. When FastAPI hangs (TensorFlow is loading, or it just died), each hanging request holds a thread. Enough of them and the whole API is unresponsive - a cascade failure caused by one dependency.

The breaker has three states:

export enum CircuitState {
  CLOSED = 'CLOSED',
  OPEN = 'OPEN',
  HALF_OPEN = 'HALF_OPEN',
}

The execute wrapper does four things: evaluates whether it's time to probe again, fast-fails while OPEN, caps every call with a timeout budget via Promise.race, and records the outcome:

public async execute<T>(action: () => Promise<T>, fallback?: () => Promise<T> | T): Promise<T> {
  this.evaluateState();

  if (this.state === CircuitState.OPEN) {
    this.logger.warn(`[${this.serviceName}] Fast-failing: Circuit is OPEN.`);
    if (fallback) {
      return fallback();
    }
    throw new ServiceUnavailableException(
      `[${this.serviceName}] Service is temporarily unavailable due to upstream instability. Circuit is OPEN.`
    );
  }

  try {
    // Enforce timeout budget capping
    const result = await Promise.race([
      action(),
      new Promise<never>((_, reject) =>
        setTimeout(
          () => reject(new Error(`[${this.serviceName}] Request timed out after ${this.timeoutMs}ms`)),
          this.timeoutMs
        )
      ),
    ]);

    this.onSuccess();
    return result;
  } catch (error) {
    this.onFailure(error);
    if (fallback) {
      return fallback();
    }
    throw error;
  }
}

State transitions are driven by counters, not timers:

private onFailure(error: any): void {
  this.failureCount++;

  if (this.state === CircuitState.HALF_OPEN || this.failureCount >= this.failureThreshold) {
    this.state = CircuitState.OPEN;
    this.lastStateChange = Date.now();
  }
}

Three consecutive failures trip CLOSED to OPEN. OPEN rejects immediately with a 503 for 15 seconds, then a single canary request probes the service in HALF_OPEN. If the canary succeeds, failureCount resets and the circuit closes; if it fails, it re-opens instantly (that's the HALF_OPEN || condition - one failed probe is enough to re-open).

For retries I use exponential backoff with full jitter (the AWS Architecture Blog variant):

/**
 * Exponential backoff with full jitter formula:
 * t = random(0, min(maxBackoffMs, baseMs * 2^attempt))
 */
public static calculateJitterBackoff(attempt: number, baseMs = 500, maxBackoffMs = 8000): number {
  const exponential = Math.min(maxBackoffMs, baseMs * Math.pow(2, attempt));
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * exponential);
}

Full jitter matters because without it, N clients retrying after a failure all wake up at the same computed times and hit the recovering service in synchronized waves. Randomizing across [0, exponential] spreads the load.

What it fixed: with the AI service killed, the API kept serving auth, courses, and attendance normally, and recognition endpoints returned instant 503s instead of hanging for 15+ seconds each. Before the breaker, killing FastAPI took the whole API down within about a minute of real traffic.

Component 2: A Bitcask-style WAL for face embeddings (Python)

Face embeddings (512-dim vectors from DeepFace/FaceNet512) live in the Python service. My first version pickled a dict to disk. It worked until the process died mid-write and I lost every enrolled face.

So I wrote BitcaskWalEngine, a log-structured append-only store. Every record on disk looks like this:

[CRC32: 4B][Timestamp: 8B][Tombstone: 1B][KeyLen: 2B][ValLen: 4B][Key][Value]

# 4 (CRC32) + 8 (Timestamp float) + 1 (Tombstone flag) + 2 (KeyLen) + 4 (ValLen) = 19 bytes
HEADER_FORMAT = "!IdBHI"
HEADER_SIZE = struct.calcsize(HEADER_FORMAT)

The design has four moving parts:

  1. Writes are appends only. A put serializes the embedding, computes a CRC32 over header + key + value, appends the record, fsyncs, then updates the in-memory index. No in-place updates, ever. The last record for a key wins.
  2. An in-memory Keydir maps each key to (offset, size, timestamp) in the log, so reads are one seek, not a scan. A second in-memory cache holds the vectors themselves for fast similarity search.
  3. Crash recovery is a sequential replay. On startup the engine scans the log front to back, verifying the CRC32 of every record. A record that fails its CRC (that's the torn write from a mid-write crash) is counted as corrupt and skipped - everything before it survives: 
def _recover(self):
    """Crash-recovery: Rebuilds Keydir and memory cache by scanning WAL sequentially."""
    self._file.seek(0)
    valid_records = 0
    corrupt_records = 0

    while True:
        offset = self._file.tell()
        header_bytes = self._file.read(self.HEADER_SIZE)
        if not header_bytes or len(header_bytes) < self.HEADER_SIZE:
            break

        crc, ts, tombstone, k_len, v_len = struct.unpack(self.HEADER_FORMAT, header_bytes)
        # ... verify CRC, rebuild keydir and cache
  1. Compaction and tombstones. Deletes write a record with the tombstone flag set rather than removing bytes. A garbage-collection pass eventually rewrites the log keeping only live records, which is how the file stays bounded despite being append-only.

There was also a pragmatic piece I enjoyed: the engine auto-migrates the old pickle file into WAL format on first run, so existing deployments upgraded without a manual step:

if not os.path.exists(self.wal_path) and self.legacy_pickle_path and os.path.exists(self.legacy_pickle_path):
    self._migrate_legacy_pickle()

What it fixed: I've since killed the AI service mid-write on purpose, repeatedly. Every time, recovery comes back with all valid records and a count of the corrupt tail it skipped. The pickle version failed this test the first time.

What I'd tell another junior dev

  • Write the pattern once by hand, then use the library. I now deeply understand what Resilience4j/Polly-style breakers and real LSM-tree storage engines do, because I felt the edge cases myself: the HALF_OPEN re-trip, the torn write, the replay ordering.
  • Design for the failure you already observed. I didn't add a circuit breaker because it sounded enterprise-grade. I added it because my API hung and I could reproduce it.
  • CRCs and fsync are the whole point. A WAL without integrity checks is just a file you append to and hope.

Honest caveat: neither component is production-grade. SQLite would replace my WAL with one dependency, and there are mature breaker libraries for NestJS. But as a learning exercise that also made the system genuinely more robust, I'd do it again.

I'm a junior full-stack developer (Angular, NestJS, TypeScript, Python) based in Alexandria, Egypt, currently open to junior roles and freelance work. If you're hiring, or you spotted something in my code you'd have done differently, I want to hear it:

title: Website Design Associations
description:
Website Design Associations: A Critical Examination of Conventional Approaches

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, it is imperative to acknowledge the shortcomings of standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms in website design. These conventional approaches often fail to deliver optimal results due to their inherent lack of customization and adaptability to specific business needs. The one-size-fits-all methodology neglects the unique value proposition, brand identity, and target audience of each organization, ultimately leading to a subpar user experience and diminished conversion rates.

A deeper analysis reveals that generic templates and forms are designed to cater to a broad spectrum of users, resulting in a diluted and unremarkable design that fails to resonate with the intended audience. Furthermore, the absence of a tailored approach to website design associations leads to a disconnect between the user's expectations and the actual experience, culminating in increased bounce rates and decreased engagement.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways that can be derived from this analysis:

  1. Customization is crucial: A bespoke approach to website design, one that takes into account the specific needs and objectives of the organization, is essential for creating a compelling and effective user experience.
  2. User-centric design is paramount: The design process should be informed by a deep understanding of the target audience, including their preferences, behaviors, and pain points, to ensure that the website meets their needs and expectations.
  3. Data-driven decision making is essential: The use of data analytics and user feedback should be integral to the design process, allowing for iterative improvements and optimizations that enhance the overall user experience and conversion rates.

In conclusion, the limitations of standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms in website design are clear. To create a truly effective and engaging online presence, organizations must adopt a more nuanced and tailored approach to website design associations.

title: Readers Found Two Gaps in My AI Agent's Review Rules. Undoing an Approval Now Needs Its Own Flag.
description:
Originally published on hexisteme notes.

Two readers left comments on my earlier note about letting an AI agent withdraw evidence claims but not approve them. In my replies I admitted two gaps in my research tool. One was that the agent could still remove something I had approved, through the same path it used for withdrawals. The other was that a datum flagged as contradicted kept the flag but lost the value it was contradicted by. On November 18 I decided to fix both. This note covers what changed, how I checked it against the real store, and the gap the comments pointed at that I left open.

Where the earlier rule stopped

The earlier note set up a split for a batch of pending claims. The agent was delegated withdrawals. Passing a claim, which adopts it as evidence, stayed with me. Nothing in that rule said the delegation was limited to pending claims. That split covers two acts: approving and withdrawing.

One reader asked about reversibility and about who is on the hook for each decision. Answering that made me look at the transition table again, and it allowed passed → withdrawn. In my reply I wrote that an agent withdrawing a passed claim removes something I approved and stops it propagating, which is the expensive direction. The only code gate was the terminal check, and it treated every decision the same. A line in an agent-written review script that reversed one of my passes would be recorded with the same call and the same 8-character confirmation as a routine verdict on a pending claim.

So there was a third act the split had not named: undoing an approval. It needed its own door.

The first gap: undoing a pass

The transition table has exactly two transitions that leave passed: passed → failed and passed → withdrawn. Both count as undoing an approval, so both got the same treatment.

In the library, record_assessment_review now takes an explicit undo_approval argument. Recording failed or withdrawn on a passed claim without undo_approval=True returns TRANSITION_INVALID. With the flag, it is recorded. Passing the flag on a pending claim is refused too, because there is no approval to undo there. Transitions out of pending behave as before.

In the CLI, assess review on a passed claim without --undo-approval is refused before the confirmation prompt appears. With the flag, it first shows the approval being undone: who recorded it, when, and the reason. Then it accepts only the string undo- followed by the first 8 characters of the claim's id. Typing the 8 characters alone, which is what a normal review asks for, cancels. The flag on a pending claim is refused.

A script built to answer the routine prompt cannot reverse a pass by accident, because the routine answer cancels. Existing tests that reversed a pass were allowed one edit, adding undo_approval=True at the call site; their expected codes and states stayed the same.

The second gap: the counterpart was thrown away

The other reader described a listing where three pages on one vendor's domain said free, free, and freemium. In my reply I explained that my tool would count those as one source, and that for conflicting values it does less than you might expect. The pipeline already flagged some data as contradicted, and a review note surfaced that flag with fixed wording saying the contradiction in meaning was unconfirmed. It never picked a value.

Then I admitted the gap: the flag survived in the frozen input, and the value on the other side of the conflict did not. I could later show that a value was disputed, but not what it was disputed against.

The fix adds a conflicts field to the datum:

  • For a value conflict, it keeps the values that differ from the representative one, each with its source URL.
  • For a conflict between claims, it keeps the counterpart group's sentence with its source URL.
  • When the counterpart came through the path that withholds excerpts, its title is kept in place of the sentence.

When the frozen premise of a claim carries conflicts, the PREMISE_CONTRADICTED review note now names the counterpart and drops the wording that says the counterpart was not preserved. Claims frozen before this change have no conflicts, so their note keeps the old wording.

What the fix does not touch is the decision of what counts as contradicted. The detection conditions, distinct_values and cross_conflict, were explicitly off limits. The change records the counterpart and nothing else.

Why the empty case writes no key

The awkward detail was a hash. Each frozen claim premise refers to its datum by datum_ref, and datum_ref is a hash of the whole stored datum dict. If every datum got a conflicts key, even an empty one, every new report would produce different refs from the same data.

So the renderer writes conflicts only when it is non-empty. A datum that is not contradicted stores exactly the same dict as before, and its ref does not move. This follows a pattern already in the code: candidate fields such as basis and derivations are also left out when they hold default values, to keep existing ids stable. One of the new tests, test_no_conflicts_key_when_not_contradicted, pins this.

Checking it against the real store

Unit tests went from 1124 to 1135 passing. The new tests include test_undo_approval_cli_needs_distinct_confirmation for the cancel-on-routine-answer case and test_claim_conflicts_do_not_store_withheld_excerpt for the path that withholds excerpts.

Then I replayed the change over the existing data, read-only. The replay was not allowed to write to the stored data or record a real review. The log:

K 119 loaded, load errors 0
review history REVIEW_INVALID 0
PREMISE_CONTRADICTED 5 — same as the 11-08 list: True, old wording kept: True
stored reports 317, reports with a conflicts key 0
claim↔report binding: report found 66, not found 53, premise datum_ref mismatch 0
stored data fingerprint unchanged (read-only): True
1.0s

K is what my tool calls a claim. All 119 loaded without errors. The same 5 claims as in the November 8 replay got the contradiction note, with the old wording, which is what should happen when none of them carries conflicts yet. None of the 317 stored reports has the new key, because none was produced after the change.

The 53 "not found" needed a second look. For those claims the stored report's digest did not match, so the replay could not pair them with a report file. The datum_ref re-check inside load_inputs passed for all 119. I did not trace why those 53 digests differ; the replay only shows that it is not a datum_ref mismatch.

One more line went into the counsel module's docs. Counsel results are not frozen yet. Once they are, withdrawing a pending claim will break any counsel that cited it, and the delegation rule for withdrawals has to be decided again at that point.

What the comments did not fix

Two things stayed out of scope on purpose.

The first is retroactive enrichment. The 5 claims that already carry the contradiction note were frozen without their counterparts, and they still do not have them. Only reports produced after the change will name what a datum was contradicted by.

The second is the one I care more about. In my reply on revision binding, I wrote that claim files are immutable and the id is a hash of the content, so a review already attaches to one revision, and that the reviewer field is only the OS login name, so the "who" half is the weaker one. This change did not touch that. Undoing a pass now needs a flag and a distinct confirmation string, and the CLI shows whose approval is being undone. But the name it shows is whatever OS login ran the command. An agent running under my login would record reviews under my name, approvals and undo records alike. Reviewer authentication and signing were listed as anti-goals for this change, to keep it small.

So the separate flag guards against a mistake. A script that answers the routine prompt can no longer reverse a pass by answering it. It does not tell me who reversed a pass when the reversal was deliberate. Next I want to decide whether the reviewer field should carry anything an agent session cannot produce, or whether the terminal refusal from the earlier note is the only line I can actually defend.

Email list for these notes: hexisteme.beehiiv.com — no issue has gone out yet, so you would be on it before the first one. No welcome sequence, no course, no upsell.

More notes at hexisteme.github.io/notes.

title: Piramal Finance Scales Its Internal Agentic AI Assistant With MongoDB
description:
Piramal Finance Limited is a retail-led upper-layer NBFC with a pan-India presence. It offers a diverse portfolio of retail lending products spanning affordable housing loans, loan against property, microfinance, personal loans, insurance solutions, and more, as well as wholesale lending, which provides asset-backed, data-driven financing solutions across real estate and select non-real estate sectors.

As of June 30, 2026, the company has over ₹ 1,00,000 Cr of assets under management; it operates 780 branches and serves over 6 million customers across 26 states.

The company operates a distinctive phygital model combining high-touch engagement with high-tech capabilities, including machine learning models, agentic AI tools, and real-time dashboards. Underpinning this breadth of services is Piramal Finance’s "high-tech, high-touch" strategy. Unlike other financial institutions that rely on off-the-shelf software, Piramal Finance’s team built the company’s entire tech stack in-house.

MongoDB has been core to Piramal Finance’s tech stack since the company’s early days. Today, MongoDB Atlas’ flexible document model—combined with built-in capabilities like MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search—powers over 80% of Piramal Finance’s services, including its loan management system, which was migrated from PostgreSQL.

Building on this solid data foundation, Piramal Finance recently set out to solve its next big challenge: empowering its workforce with generative AI.

Building an internal agentic AI assistant for 18,000+ employees

In 2024, Piramal Finance decided to invest in agentic AI to help improve productivity and job satisfaction for its more than 18,000 employees. The company aimed to empower employees across the company—including those from engineering, operations, HR, and customer service—with AI tools.

Piramal Finance’s team wanted to build an intuitive, enterprise-wide agentic AI assistant that would serve as a one-stop shop for employees, from querying policies and tracking performance metrics to resolving customer issues and interacting with internal systems. The idea was to democratize access to AI and allow even non-technical staff to leverage state-of-the-art AI, without complex prompts or technical training.

Initially, Piramal Finance's team started building an architecture that stitched together several specialized third-party tools:

  • Neo4j, a graph database that stores data as nodes and the relationships between them, managed the dynamic permissions model. Because permissions depended on a user's position in the organizational hierarchy and their associations with other entities—and because those relationships changed in real time—access had to be evaluated at runtime rather than precomputed.

  • pgVector, an open-source extension that adds vector storage and similarity search to PostgreSQL, handled the vector workloads powering AI features.

  • PostgreSQL, an open-source relational database, handled operational data and analytical queries.

However, this setup introduced significant complexity and inefficiencies, and it didn't lend itself to running complex AI workloads at scale.

Piramal Finance’s team saw MongoDB Atlas as the best solution to move away from PostgreSQL’s credential management. Using MongoDB’s built-in authentication and authorization features, Piramal Finance was able to map MongoDB Atlas’s access control directly to its enterprise single sign-on and Active Directory, so employees could log in securely with their standard corporate credentials. Meanwhile,MongoDB Atlas’s built-in role-based access control (RBAC) capabilities automatically restricted sensitive data based on Piramal Finance employees’ job roles.

Piramal Finance soon realized that the power of the MongoDB Atlas platform could solve many of the other challenges that its fragmented database stack presented.

From a fragmented to a unified AI data layer: The power of MongoDB Atlas

As Piramal Finance’s internal agentic AI Assistant's enterprise knowledge base grew, the data architecture became increasingly complex. Although this separation allowed each database to specialize in its workload, it introduced significant operational overhead and complexity, as Piramal Finance explained in a recent conversation at MongoDB .local Mumbai.

Data had to be synchronized across multiple systems through ETL pipelines, resulting in update latencies of over 30 minutes before newly ingested content became searchable.

Figure 1. Piramal Finance’s data architecture before migrating to MongoDB Atlas.

As Piramal Finance explored options to unify its data foundation, it realized that MongoDB Atlas was both inherently built for AI workloads (thanks to its flexible document model), and that it had all the capabilities needed to scale an agentic AI solution on a single platform.

Kaushik Deb, Head of AI engineering, Piramal Finance, said: “An AI agent is only as good as the data behind it. MongoDB gives us one platform for all our data, which makes our AI simpler to build, easier to maintain, and more reliable in production.”

Figure 2. Piramal Finance’s data architecture after migrating to MongoDB Atlas.

During the architecture review, Piramal Finance’s team realized that most of the graph queries involved bounded traversals such as reconstructing document hierarchies, identifying parent-child relationships, and retrieving connected metadata—operations that did not require a dedicated graph database. The data model was redesigned to represent these relationships within MongoDB itself, using the flexibility of MongoDB Atlas’ document model and MongoDB’s aggregation framework capabilities.

The $graphLookup aggregation stage became central to the implementation, enabling recursive traversal of document relationships directly within MongoDB collections. Combined with operators such as $lookup, $facet, $unwind, and $project, Piramal Finance was able to replace Neo4j traversals with efficient aggregation pipelines, all while expressing complex relationship queries entirely within MongoDB.

MongoDB Atlas also allowed the team to consolidate structured metadata, document storage, relationship traversal, and search into a single platform. MongoDB Search handled keyword retrieval, while the aggregation framework combined metadata filtering, graph traversal, and ranking into unified retrieval pipelines, reducing application-side joins and simplifying backend services.

Today, there are 25+ MongoDB MCP servers live, powering Piramal Finance’s agentic AI assistant, which, combined with MongoDB Vector Search, allows for unstructured documents (e.g., 500-page policy PDFs) to be processed through Piramal Finance’s in-house pipeline (.score), chunked, embedded using in-house embedding models, and stored directly in MongoDB Atlas. MongoDB Vector Search delivers 3x faster retrieval performance compared to Piramal Finance’s former Postgres setup.

An incredibly efficient, smart agentic assistant

Since the launch of Piramal Finance’s internal agentic AI assistant, employee performance and productivity across all functions have improved, which has in turn improved customer experience and satisfaction.

Today, over 80% of Piramal Finance's 18,000 employees use the internal agentic AI assistant on a weekly basis, with an average of 15,000 daily queries handled by the platform.

Teams from all across the organization are benefiting from using the agentic AI assistant. HR teams experience a significant reduction in routine internal support tickets regarding benefits, travel policies, and payroll, as new hires and staff turn to the agentic solution for instant answers, supporting agents. Support agents who previously spent extensive time manually combing lengthy and complex policy manuals during live calls are now able to ingest real-time customer data and policy docs into the agentic assistant. This has drastically reduced handle times, improving first-contact resolution and customer satisfaction. Furthermore, sales representatives using the internal agentic AI assistant have seen a 2x improvement in performance compared to non-users during contest periods.

Piramal Finance’s tech team, including developers, are also greatly benefiting from using MongoDB Atlas. Knowledge graph and document updates that previously took up to 30 minutes in legacy setups now execute in just 15 seconds, eliminating operational downtime.  Working with MongoDB and being able to use MongoDB Atlas’ built-in capabilities such as MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search has also made developers’ jobs much easier.

With MongoDB, Piramal Finance has been able to turn what was initially a pretty simple AI assistant into a full agentic solution that orchestrates workflows across the entire organization. MongoDB Atlas has become the single source of truth for the internal agentic AI assistant, providing a simpler architecture and a scalable foundation for semantic retrieval, richer metadata, and future AI-powered knowledge discovery.

Looking to the future, Piramal Finance plans to use MongoDB’s capabilities to further expand its internal agentic AI assistant into a personalized, proactive coach for every employee in the company.

title: How do you prove a smaller checkpoint hasn't lost accuracy? (not just "trust me")
description:
Checkpoint compression sounds simple: store less, use less disk, upload faster. The hard part is proving it didn't quietly break your model. "The file is smaller" is not evidence. I needed something that would actually catch a bug if I introduced one.

Here's the method I ended up with, built into Efficio, an open-source PyTorch training library.

The problem with "looks fine to me"

If you shrink a checkpoint (say, storing optimizer state in 8-bit instead of fp32), the obvious test is: resume training, check the final loss, see if it's close to the un-shrunk version. But "close" compared to what? Loss is noisy between runs even with no compression at all, just from floating-point nondeterminism and scheduling. Without a baseline, you can't tell "acceptable approximation" from "silent bug."

A noise baseline

So I measure the noise floor first: resume training from an exact checkpoint (no compression at all) but inject 1e-6 relative weight noise, basically floating-point-level perturbation that should be harmless. Run it, measure the final loss gap versus a clean run. That gap is pure numerical noise — the best-case variance you'd see from nothing going wrong at all.

Then I test the actual compression modes (light: 8-bit optimizer state; smallest: light + fp16 weights) the same way, and compare their final-loss gap against that noise floor.

The rule

A compression mode passes only if its loss gap is within 3x the noise gap, with a floor (0.05 loss or 3 accuracy points, whichever is more lenient) so a tiny noise baseline doesn't make the bar impossibly strict.

This matters because it's falsifiable. If someone introduces a bug tomorrow, the test catches it, because "quietly worse than noise" fails. "Looks about the same" wouldn't have.

What it looks like in practice (T4 GPU)

Mode Size vs. exact Passed the 3x-noise test
light ~2.0x smaller (AdamW transformer) yes
smallest ~2.9x smaller (AdamW transformer) yes
light ~1.6x smaller (ResNet-18, SGD) yes
smallest ~2.6x smaller (ResNet-18, SGD) yes

For a LoRA-style run where only trainable weights are saved, a checkpoint went from 44.23 MB to 1.61 MB, same approach: verified against the noise floor, not just eyeballed.

Where this lives

This is part of Efficio, which also handles resuming training across Colab/Kaggle disconnects and saving checkpoints to Hugging Face Hub or Drive instead of a VM disk that disappears with the session.

pip install efficio
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/efficio/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/HuNTer8272/Efficio
  • Benchmarks (full methodology + code): https://github.com/HuNTer8272/Efficio/tree/main/benchmarks

Curious if others have used a noise-floor-style baseline for other things, not just checkpoints — I'd guess it generalizes to any "does this optimization silently hurt correctness" question.
