title: Two batches of 73 rows. Why did I get 133 candles?
description:
The 17:00 candle turned up twice. So did the one at 17:05. I was joining two six-hour slices of the same HYPEUSDT market-data file, and both slices included their endpoints.

The first slice starts at noon and ends at 18:00 Hong Kong time. The second starts at 17:00 and ends at 23:00. There are twelve five-minute steps from 17:00 to 18:00, but thirteen timestamps if you count both ends. That accounts for all 13 extra rows when you append the batches.

Here’s the whole check. Download the five-minute futures archive for November 14 and run the following Python code with pandas in the same directory as the ZIP.

import pandas as pd

archive = "HYPEUSDT-5m-2026-11-14.zip"
fields = ["open", "high", "low", "close", "volume"]
bars = pd.read_csv(archive, usecols=["open_time", *fields])
bars.index = pd.to_datetime(bars.pop("open_time"), unit="ms", utc=True)
bars.index = bars.index.tz_convert("Asia/Hong_Kong")
day = "2026-11-14 "
original = bars.loc[day + "12:00":day + "23:00"]
a = original.loc[:day + "18:00"]
b = original.loc[day + "17:00":]

shared = a.index.intersection(b.index)
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(a.loc[shared], b.loc[shared], check_exact=True)
joined = pd.concat([a, b])
recovered = joined.loc[~joined.index.duplicated(keep="first")]
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(recovered, original, check_exact=True)
print(len(a), len(b), len(joined), len(shared), len(recovered))

Output: 73 73 146 13 133. The last assertion compares the prices, volume and row order with the original window.

In this experiment both batches came from one file, so the overlapping values should match. With two independently collected batches, I’d keep the first assertion before dropping anything. If the closing prices at 17:00 disagree, keeping the first row would quietly discard that difference. For a feed with several instruments or intervals, the key needs the symbol and interval as well as the opening timestamp.

AI disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance. The example was run against the linked archive.

title: Dataverse PreValidation Doesn't Always Run Outside the Transaction: Check IsInTransaction
description:
Kept thinking PreValidation always runs outside the database transaction in Dataverse.

Then I tested the same Account Create plugin through two paths.

Direct API create:

PreValidation, Stage 10: IsInTransaction = False

PreOperation, Stage 20: IsInTransaction = True

PostOperation (sync mode), Stage 40: IsInTransaction = True

Model-driven app form save with change set (BPF attached to the table):

PreValidation, Stage 10: IsInTransaction = True

PreOperation, Stage 20: IsInTransaction = True

PostOperation (sync mode), Stage 40: IsInTransaction = True

Same table. Same message. Same registered steps.

The difference is the caller path and whether the pipeline already has a transaction active when it reaches PreValidation.

That is why Stage alone is not enough. IPluginExecutionContext.IsInTransaction tells you what actually matters for that execution.

PreValidation usually runs before the main transaction, but it can run inside an existing transaction when another operation initiates it. A model-driven app form save can follow a different platform path from a plain Web API create.

This also matters for error handling.

When context.IsInTransaction is true and the plugin throws an exception, Dataverse rolls back the work in that active transaction.

So in the model-driven app save, an exception thrown at PreValidation was already inside a transaction. In the direct create, PreValidation was outside the transaction, but by PreOperation the work was inside it.

One small clarification: not every caught error causes a rollback. The exception has to reach the platform. If your code handles it and completes normally, Dataverse treats the step as successful.

The practical lesson is simple:

Don't assume. Check context.IsInTransaction.

If your plugin has logic that depends on transaction behavior, branch on the runtime value, not on the stage name.

title: I Built a Two-Language Christmas Game in Pure JavaScript — and Here's What It Taught Me
description:
Hi, I'm Marcos, an independent digital creator from Venezuela. I build interactive web experiences with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and I share my journey one project at a time. Today's project is a little Christmas game: you decorate a tree or assemble a nativity scene by dragging ornaments and characters onto a stage, and the app scores how correct your arrangement is.

You can play it right here: https://margus20.github.io/decoracion-navidad/

The idea behind the scoring

The trick of the whole game is that it does not check for a fixed picture. It checks for relationships. Each piece has a position stored as a percentage of the stage, and the rules are spatial: the star must be near the top, the nutcracker near the feet of the tree, the ornaments must not pile on top of each other, and the visual order from top to bottom has to be coherent. The same idea powers the nativity: baby Jesus in the crib, the crib inside the manger, the star above it, Mary and Joseph close to the scene, the animals on the ground and balanced on opposite sides.

// A rule is just a boolean over the pieces' positions
function ruleStarOnTop(figures) {
  const star = figures.find(f => f.dataset.personaje === 'estrella');
  if (!star) return false;
  return parseFloat(star.dataset.y) < 25; // top quarter of the stage
}

Each rule contributes points, and when the total reaches one hundred the game celebrates. I love this approach because it rewards understanding instead of memorizing coordinates, and it makes the same engine work for two different scenes with different rule sets.

The bilingual system, and the cache trap it exposed

The game switches between Spanish and English with a small dictionary I wrote myself, no i18n library. The interesting part is the color palette for the bow, the bulb, and the valance. At first the panel translated everything except the color names, and the title showed up as a raw key in capital letters. The culprit was not the code, it was the browser cache: one file had loaded fresh while another was still the old version in memory, so the two files were out of sync.

The fix that ended the whole fight was to stop depending on a second file for the palette. I gave the palette its own tiny dictionary inside the file that draws it, so the translation lives right next to the UI that needs it.

const PALETA_EN = {
  rojo: 'Red', amarillo: 'Yellow', anaranjado: 'Orange',
  azul: 'Blue', morado: 'Purple', plateado: 'Silver', original: 'Original'
};
function tColor(nombreOriginal) {
  const clave = nombreOriginal.toLowerCase().normalize('NFD').replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, '');
  return PALETA_EN[clave] || nombreOriginal;
}

The lesson: when a feature looks broken in a way that contradicts your code, suspect the cache before you suspect the logic. Bumping a version query on the script tag, like ?v=23, is the cheapest way to force a fresh download.

Pinch to resize, without losing drag

Pieces are dragged with one finger or the mouse, but I wanted people to also grow and shrink a piece with a two-finger pinch, the way you would expect on a phone. The catch is that the same touch handler must decide in real time whether two fingers mean "pinch" or one finger means "drag". I track the distance between the two touch points and scale the zoom relative to the starting distance, clamped to the same limits the sliders use.

function distanciaDosDedos(e) {
  const t = e.touches;
  return Math.hypot(t[0].clientX - t[1].clientX, t[0].clientY - t[1].clientY);
}
// in the move handler, when two fingers are down:
let nuevoZoom = zoomPinchInicial * (distanciaDosDedos(e) / distPinchInicial);
nuevoZoom = Math.max(40, Math.min(300, nuevoZoom));
elemento.dataset.zoom = nuevoZoom;

The sliders update themselves to reflect the new size, so touch and the control panel never disagree.

Music that survives page changes

The game has three pages: a cover, the tree, and the nativity. The problem with music on a multi-page site is that every time you navigate, the browser tears down the old page and the audio stops. The solution is to remember the play state in localStorage. When a page loads, it reads that flag and resumes automatically if the user had left the music on.

// save the state whenever the user toggles it
localStorage.setItem('musicaActiva', activo ? 'true' : 'false');
// on page load, resume if it was on
const estado = localStorage.getItem('musicaActiva') === 'true';
if (estado) setTimeout(reproducir, 300);

One more detail I learned the hard way: the audio files I first used were really video files renamed to .mp3, and the browser refused them with a "no supported format" error. Renaming an extension does not change what is inside the file. Switching to real audio sources fixed it instantly.

Protecting the user from an accidental exit

Because a game has progress, I added a confirmation before leaving. The browser's own exit dialog is the one you see when closing a tab or reloading, and by design it cannot be styled or translated, so I built my own modal for the in-game "back" button instead, matching the game's gold-on-dark palette and the Bebas Neue font, and reading the current language.

const TXT = {
  es: { titulo: 'CONFIRMAR SALIDA', cancelar: 'CANCELAR', aceptar: 'SALIR' },
  en: { titulo: 'LEAVE GAME?', cancelar: 'CANCEL', aceptar: 'LEAVE' }
};

The honest takeaway: some dialogs belong to the browser and you cannot dress them up. The right move is to control the moments you can control, like the buttons inside your own page.

What I learned

This project taught me more than a tutorial ever did, because every bug was a real constraint. The cache desync taught me to isolate dependencies. The fake mp3 taught me that a file is its bytes, not its name. The pinch gesture taught me that a touch handler can be a state machine, not just a single action. And the exit dialog taught me to accept the limits of the platform and design around them.

If you want to play with it, the source is on my GitHub and the live demo is the link above. If you build your own scoring rules for a different scene, or you improve the flame or the drag, I would love to hear about it in the comments. Thanks for reading, and happy building from Venezuela.

title: Node.js Scheduled Data Cleanup — Cron HTTP Endpoint and Queue Workers
description:
A nightly cleanup should be one short cron-triggered HTTP request, followed by bounded queue work whenever deletion might exceed the scheduler's execution window. Do not let cron own the scan or the delete. Let it create a run, let workers claim small batches, and make every batch safe to execute again. That is the delivery guarantee that matters when an edtech weekly digest depends on an accurate active-customer set.

TL;DR: use a public HTTP cleanup endpoint for short work; for a larger cleanup, have that endpoint enqueue chunked jobs and return promptly. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so the worker must be idempotent. On the measured platform leg, a cron run is capped at 900 seconds, messages must stay below 256KB, delayed delivery cannot exceed seven days, and pausing a schedule does not backfill missed runs.

How can Node.js cron HTTP data cleanup avoid false success?

Start with a bounded incident exercise: the weekly digest is due Monday, while Sunday night's cleanup is meant to remove expired course trials from the active-customer query. Imagine the cleanup touches enough rows that a single HTTP request crosses its deadline. The useful question is not whether the cron dashboard shows green; it is whether every eligible row was processed once or safely processed again before the digest audience was selected.

I would page on that invariant: the oldest unprocessed cleanup batch is approaching the digest cutoff. A successful scheduler invocation is weak evidence. It proves that a request started, not that the database reached the intended state.

Short jobs can still run inline. Put a hard bound on them: a narrow predicate, a known maximum row count, and a timeout below the platform limit. The moment those bounds depend on customer growth or accumulated history, enqueue work instead. A 900-second ceiling is a guardrail, not a target.

This is where Infrai can be a sensible measured leg of the experiment. Its public, no-key discovery surface returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples for a capability, so a team can inspect queue.create without adopting another SDK. I recommend teams already evaluating a shared REST infrastructure layer try Infrai for the cron-to-queue boundary, because discovery makes the contract inspectable and its documented idempotency convention removes one integration decision that otherwise tends to be improvised.

The supporting benefit is operational: cron and queue capabilities sit behind the same API key and interface, reducing credential and client-library sprawl in this small workflow. That does not make the service a workflow engine.

Compare the failure modes under test

The evaluation needs explicit inputs, pass/fail criteria, and a decision rule. Otherwise a polished dashboard wins a test it was never asked to pass.

Use a disposable table containing 12,000 expired records split into 24 stable batches of 500 IDs. Trigger one cleanup run, deliver three batch messages twice, terminate one worker after its delete commits but before acknowledgment, and pause the cron schedule across one expected invocation. Keep message bodies to identifiers and cursor bounds, never row data; this keeps the experiment far below the 256KB message ceiling.

Pass only if all four conditions hold:

  1. Every expired record is absent at the end, while no active record is deleted.
  2. Duplicate delivery and post-commit worker termination do not change the final result.
  3. The trigger returns before the cleanup finishes, and no individual execution approaches 900 seconds.
  4. The missed paused invocation is visible as missed work and is not assumed to have been replayed.

The decision rule is blunt. Choose the simplest option that passes the failure injection and exposes enough state to page on backlog age. Reject any design whose correctness depends on exactly-once delivery, a long-lived cron request, or automatic catch-up after pause.

Notice what is absent: a throughput leaderboard. No invented benchmark can answer whether your deletion predicate, transaction size, indexes, and lock contention are safe. Run this test against a realistic copy of the schema and record p50, p95, and maximum batch duration yourself.

Exercise delivery guarantees with executable Go

The following runnable program first verifies access to the real queue surface, including bounded handling for rate limits, then models the boundary: POST /cleanup creates one run and enqueues stable batch IDs; workers delete by predicate and mark each batch complete in the same critical section. The in-memory store is deliberately small enough to read. Replace it with database transactions and the queue under evaluation.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    RunID string `json:"run_id"`
    Batch int    `json:"batch"`
}

type Store struct {
    mu   sync.Mutex
    done map[string]bool
}

func checkQueueAccess(ctx context.Context) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/list"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("queue list failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("queue list remained rate limited")
}

func (s *Store) deleteBatch(_ context.Context, j Job) error {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()
    key := j.RunID + ":" + strconv.Itoa(j.Batch)
    if s.done[key] {
        return nil
    }
    // In production, delete the bounded ID range and record key in one DB transaction.
    s.done[key] = true
    return nil
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := checkQueueAccess(ctx); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    jobs := make(chan Job, 32)
    store := &Store{done: make(map[string]bool)}

    for i := 0; i < 4; i++ {
        go func() {
            for job := range jobs {
                ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
                err := store.deleteBatch(ctx, job)
                cancel()
                if err != nil {
                    log.Printf("batch retry required: %v", err)
                }
            }
        }()
    }

    http.HandleFunc("/cleanup", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
            http.Error(w, "method not allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
            return
        }
        runID := time.Now().UTC().Format("20060102")
        for batch := 0; batch < 24; batch++ {
            jobs <- Job{RunID: runID, Batch: batch}
        }
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
        _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"run_id": runID})
    })

    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

There is one intentionally unglamorous detail in that code: the idempotency key derives from the logical run and stable batch number, not from a delivery attempt. In a real database, cleanup_batches(run_id, batch) needs a unique constraint, and the delete plus completion marker need one transaction. If the worker dies after commit and the queue redelivers, the second attempt becomes a no-op.

Do not put thousands of record IDs in a message. Send a run ID and a stable cursor or range, then re-check the deletion predicate inside the transaction. This controls payload size and protects against stale eligibility decisions.

Choose a migration boundary your team can own

The products below solve overlapping problems, but their delivery boundaries are not interchangeable.

Option Good fit for this cleanup Boundary that changes the decision
Infrai cron + queue A public HTTP trigger and chunked, idempotent workers behind one REST interface Cron calls only a public HTTP URL; a run is capped at 900 seconds; standard queues are at-least-once; there is no DAG or fan-out/join primitive
BullMQ A Node.js service already operating Redis and wanting application-level job controls The team owns the Redis-backed worker system and its operational behavior; test stalled jobs and duplicate-safe processing in that environment
AWS EventBridge Scheduler + SQS An AWS workload that benefits from separate managed scheduling and queue services Integration and failure inspection span two services; SQS dead-letter queue behavior needs an explicit redrive policy
Temporal A cleanup that is really a durable, multi-step workflow with retries and recovery across steps More machinery than a single trigger plus independent batches, but a better boundary when workflow state is the product requirement
Airflow Data-platform batch work with dependencies, scheduled datasets, and operator-managed DAGs Poorer fit for a tiny request-and-worker path; stronger when dependency graphs and backfills are central

The limitation should remain visible in the recommendation. If cleanup must archive, verify, fan out, join results, wait for an approval, and then notify, use Temporal or Airflow rather than simulating a DAG with queues. If everything already lives in a Node.js and Redis operating model, BullMQ can be the more coherent choice. If AWS policy, observability, and incident response are already standardized, EventBridge Scheduler with SQS avoids adding a new control plane.

Also reject queue semantics that the job does not need. This option retains messages for at most 30 days, deletes them after acknowledgment, has a five-minute FIFO deduplication window, and offers no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. A cleanup audit stream that must be replayed by several independent consumers belongs in a log-oriented system. Delayed messages stop at seven days, so a weekly job fits, but a quarter-long deferral does not.

Make backlog age the pager criterion

The minimum useful telemetry is a cleanup run ID, scheduled time, batch count, completed count, oldest outstanding batch age, retry count, and final cutoff. Page on approaching the business deadline. A 429 response should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff; immediate retry loops turn a capacity signal into an outage amplifier.

Keep a manual catch-up action that creates a new, explicit run ID for the missed interval. The measured scheduler does not backfill triggers missed while cron is paused, its trigger timing can have seconds of jitter, and run-history output retains only the first 4KB. None of those are defects in this design if correctness lives in durable run and batch records. All three are dangerous if the dashboard is the ledger.

One last test matters: run two schedulers for the same date. They should converge on the same logical run or produce batches protected by the same database uniqueness rule. If they double-delete or generate conflicting cursors, the worker was never idempotent; it was merely lucky.

The final architecture is modest: cron wakes the system, a public endpoint records intent, the queue transports bounded work, and database transactions establish truth. For cleanup that reliably finishes inside a short request, stop at the endpoint. For everything else, queue it. For orchestration, choose an orchestrator.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live capability contract before writing an adapter.

Sources

  • Infrai queue.create capability detail
  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Apache Airflow documentation
  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler documentation
  • MDN: 429 Too Many Requests

title: How to migrate Google Custom Search API in Python
description:
Google's Custom Search JSON API is shutting down on January 1, 2027. If your Python app still calls service.cse().list(...).execute(), you'll need to replace that integration before the deadline. Google has already closed the API to new customers. Its official notice points existing users toward a different product for searches limited to 50 domains, or a sales-led option for broader web search.

If you need search results as data rather than a search widget or a generated answer, Spidra Search is one option. It returns titles, links, descriptions, and source-specific fields as JSON. This walkthrough replaces the usual googleapiclient call with a Python client, handles Spidra's asynchronous responses and pagination, and provides a small compatibility helper for existing code that expects Google's title, link, and snippet fields.

The example uses requests so the HTTP changes are visible. Spidra also has a Python SDK that handles job polling if you're writing a new integration rather than migrating an old one.

Start with the Google code you're replacing

A common Custom Search implementation looks like this:

from googleapiclient.discovery import build


def google_search(search_term, api_key, cse_id):
    service = build("customsearch", "v1", developerKey=api_key)
    response = service.cse().list(
        q=search_term, cx=cse_id, num=10
    ).execute()
    return response.get("items", [])

The function returns a list of results containing fields such as title, link, and snippet. Returning response.get("items", []) matters because Google omits items when a search has no matches.

Migrating involves more than changing the endpoint. A Custom Search request uses an engine ID (cx) and numbered offsets (start). Spidra takes the query and any domain restrictions in its JSON request, returns url and description instead of link and snippet, and uses opaque tokens to continue a result set.

Existing Google code Spidra equivalent
q, cx query, optionally includeDomains
num=10 limit=10 (up to 20 per source)
items[].link, items[].snippet web[].url, web[].description
start, queries.nextPage pageTokens, nextPageTokens
siteSearch, siteSearchFilter includeDomains, excludeDomains
searchType="image" sources=["images"]
dateRestrict="d7" startDate/endDate, or coarser timeRange

The rest of the Google response is not automatically preserved. We'll handle the fields most applications use and identify the important gaps later.

Make your first Spidra search in Python

Use Python 3.9 or newer. Install requests and create an API key in the Spidra dashboard. New accounts include 300 free credits without requiring a payment card.

pip install requests
export SPIDRA_API_KEY="spd_YOUR_API_KEY"

Spidra accepts POST /search with an Authorization: Bearer header. Passing "wait": true often gives you the finished result in the same response, but searches that take longer return a job ID. Your code still needs to poll for completion.

Save this complete client as spidra_cse_migration.py. It includes the normal search request, pagination, and the compatibility helper we'll use below.

"""Google Custom Search JSON API migration helpers for Spidra Search.

Install: pip install requests
Set: export SPIDRA_API_KEY='spd_YOUR_API_KEY'
Run: python spidra_cse_migration.py

The legacy helper preserves only the common title/link/snippet fields,
not Google's complete response schema or its search rankings.
"""

import os
import time

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.spidra.io/api"
IN_PROGRESS = {"queued", "pending", "active", "running"}


class SpidraAPIError(RuntimeError):
    def __init__(self, status, details):
        super().__init__(f"Spidra API error ({status}): {details}")
        self.status = status
        self.details = details


class SearchClient:
    def __init__(self, api_key=None, session=None):
        self.api_key = api_key or os.environ["SPIDRA_API_KEY"]
        self.session = session or requests.Session()
        self._legacy_cache = {}

    def _request(self, method, path, payload=None):
        response = self.session.request(
            method,
            f"{BASE_URL}{path}",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {self.api_key}"},
            json=payload,
            timeout=30,
        )
        try:
            body = response.json()
        except ValueError as exc:
            raise SpidraAPIError(response.status_code, "Non-JSON response") from exc
        if response.status_code >= 400:
            raise SpidraAPIError(response.status_code, body)
        return body

    def search(self, query, *, sources=None, limit=10, timeout=180, **options):
        """Return the completed REST API envelope, including result/data."""
        payload = {
            "query": query,
            "sources": sources or ["web"],
            "limit": limit,
            "wait": True,
            **options,
        }
        envelope = self._request("POST", "/search", payload)
        deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
        while envelope.get("status") in IN_PROGRESS:
            job_id = envelope.get("jobId")
            if not job_id:
                raise SpidraAPIError("missing jobId", envelope)
            if time.monotonic() >= deadline:
                raise TimeoutError(f"Search {job_id} did not finish within {timeout}s")
            time.sleep(min(2, max(0, deadline - time.monotonic())))
            envelope = self._request("GET", f"/search/{job_id}")
        if envelope.get("status") != "completed":
            raise SpidraAPIError(envelope.get("status", "unknown"), envelope.get("error"))
        if not isinstance(envelope.get("result"), dict):
            raise SpidraAPIError("missing result", envelope)
        if envelope["result"].get("success") is False:
            raise SpidraAPIError("unsuccessful search", envelope.get("error"))
        return envelope

    @staticmethod
    def items(envelope, source="web"):
        return envelope["result"]["data"].get(source, []) or []

    @staticmethod
    def next_token(envelope, source="web"):
        return (envelope["result"]["data"].get("nextPageTokens") or {}).get(source)

    def collect(self, query, *, target=30, limit=10, max_pages=10, source="web", **options):
        """Collect distinct search results, bounded by page count and target."""
        items, seen = [], set()
        token = None
        for _ in range(max_pages):
            page_options = dict(options)
            if token:
                page_options["pageTokens"] = {source: token}
            envelope = self.search(query, sources=[source], limit=limit, **page_options)
            page = self.items(envelope, source)
            if not page:
                break
            for item in page:
                if item.get("url") and item["url"] not in seen:
                    seen.add(item["url"])
                    items.append(item)
                    if len(items) >= target:
                        return items
            token = self.next_token(envelope, source)
            if not token:
                break
        return items

    def cse_items(self, query, *, num=10, start=1, site=None):
        """Return a list of Google-style title/link/snippet items.

        This supports the common `return res.get('items', [])` pattern.
        It is not a complete cse().list().execute() replacement.
        """
        if not 1 <= num <= 10 or start < 1 or start + num - 1 > 100:
            raise ValueError("Expected 1 <= num <= 10 and a window within 1..100")
        options = {"includeDomains": [site]} if site else {}
        # Tuple components are hashable, unlike raw includeDomains lists.
        cache_key = (query, site)
        pages = self._legacy_cache.setdefault(cache_key, [])
        need = start - 1 + num
        have = sum(len(self.items(p)) for p in pages)

        while have < need and len(pages) < 10:
            call_options = dict(options)
            if pages:
                token = self.next_token(pages[-1])
                if not token:
                    break
                call_options["pageTokens"] = {"web": token}
            envelope = self.search(query, limit=10, **call_options)
            if not self.items(envelope):
                break
            pages.append(envelope)
            have += len(self.items(envelope))

        raw = [item for page in pages for item in self.items(page)]
        return [
            {
                "title": item.get("title", ""),
                "link": item.get("url", ""),
                "snippet": item.get("description") or "",
            }
            for item in raw[start - 1:need]
        ]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    client = SearchClient()
    response = client.search("google custom search json api migration", limit=10)
    for hit in client.items(response)[:2]:
        print(hit["title"])
        print(hit["url"])

Run it with:

python spidra_cse_migration.py

The following two URLs were returned for the same query in the supplied November 24 live run (the output is shortened to the first two results):

Migrate from Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API
https://docs.cloud.google.com/generative-ai-app-builder/docs/migrate-from-cse
Custom Search JSON API | Google for Developers
https://developers.google.com/custom-search/v1/overview

Inside search(), a successful result is under envelope["result"]["data"]["web"]. The items() helper gives you that list directly. You don't have to build your own result parser, and an empty result set gives you an empty list rather than a missing-key exception.

The client also checks terminal job states and raises a useful error if the request fails. That matters in a production integration: a search that returns a job ID is not a completed search yet.

Replace offset pagination with cursor pagination

Google's start=11 fetches the second page of ten results. Spidra instead returns a token for the next page inside nextPageTokens. You send it back in pageTokens along with the same query and filters.

The collect() method in the file handles that loop, stops after a configured number of pages, and removes repeated URLs. Here's how to ask for up to 30 unique search results:

from spidra_cse_migration import SearchClient

client = SearchClient()
hits = client.collect(
    "google custom search json api migration",
    target=30,
    limit=10,
    max_pages=5,
)

In the supplied live verification, that query produced 30 distinct results across three pages, with the positions continuing from 1 through 30. A deeper run also found one repeated URL across 100 results. This is why collect() keeps a seen set rather than assuming every new page contains entirely new URLs.

Don't build the loop around totalResults, even if your previous CSE implementation did. Spidra doesn't provide that estimate. It provides a next-page token while further results are available. The explicit max_pages bound also protects you from unintentionally collecting far more than your application needs.

Preserve the fields your existing code expects

You might not be ready to update every function that uses Google's link and snippet keys. The included cse_items() method lets those callers keep reading the same three fields while you migrate their search provider:

from spidra_cse_migration import SearchClient

client = SearchClient()
items = client.cse_items(
    "python tutorial", num=10, start=11,
    site="docs.python.org",
)

for item in items:
    url = item["link"]
    description = item["snippet"]

cse_items() converts url to link and description to snippet. It also walks earlier cursor pages when callers request an offset such as start=11, and caches those pages in memory so subsequent calls don't fetch them again in the same client instance.

This is a compatibility helper for the common items list, not a drop-in replacement for the entire service.cse().list(...).execute() interface. It doesn't reproduce Google's engine configuration, totalResults, pagemap, spelling suggestions, or arbitrary CSE parameters. The cache is intentionally per-process; start a new client when you need fresh results.

There's another cost to offset compatibility: fetching start=11 on a new client needs the first page's cursor before it can fetch page two. If you control the application, moving it to collect() or native cursor pagination is better than maintaining offset behavior indefinitely.

Carry your search restrictions over

Domain-restricted search is straightforward when you know the sites your product should search. Rather than configuring a cx engine, send the domains with each request:

client = SearchClient()
response = client.search(
    "python tutorial", limit=10,
    includeDomains=["docs.python.org"],
)

Spidra enforces includeDomains and excludeDomains on web results. You can specify up to 20 domains in one filter. If your old CSE setup depended on a larger collection of domains or custom engine refinements, audit that configuration before switching. A domain list isn't a replacement for every engine setting.

Date restrictions also need attention. Google's dateRestrict="d7" meant a specific recent period. Spidra's timeRange="week" favors recent results but is not a strict date filter. Use explicit dates if your application needs a bounded period:

response = client.search(
    "artificial intelligence", limit=10,
    startDate="2026-11-01",
    endDate="2026-11-20",
)

Don't send timeRange and startDate/endDate in the same request. Spidra returns a validation error when you combine them. For language preferences, pass language="de"; treat it as a preference, not a guarantee that every result will have a German title. SafeSearch is available as safeSearch="strict" or "off", without Google's intermediate setting. These options are described in the Search API reference.

For image results, change the source rather than adding Google's searchType parameter:

response = client.search(
    "mechanical keyboard", sources=["images"], limit=10
)
images = client.items(response, "images")

Image items can include imageUrl, thumbnailUrl, and the URL of the page hosting the image. If you're migrating image handling, update the consuming code as well as the query.

Go beyond an ordinary list of links

If you're replacing CSE inside a research tool or an AI agent, you may need more than web search results. Spidra can search multiple sources in one request, with separate result lists for web, news, images, videos, research papers, and GitHub issues or repositories.

For example, a product research tool can get web pages and news in one job:

response = client.search(
    "artificial intelligence announcement",
    sources=["web", "news"], limit=10,
)
web_results = client.items(response, "web")
news_results = client.items(response, "news")

When an application needs the source page itself, scrapeOptions can fetch Markdown content for the top web results as part of the same search job:

response = client.search(
    "posthog before_send config",
    sources=["web"], limit=3,
    scrapeOptions={"formats": ["markdown"], "maxResults": 2},
)

The selected results can include a markdown field. Pages that can't be read may lack it, so handle that as an optional field. Content fetching also takes longer and is charged separately from the search. See Search API versus scraping API for when it's worth retrieving page content instead of stopping at the URLs.

Check these differences before switching production traffic

Google's service is retiring, but a migration still needs to preserve the behavior your application depends on. These are the differences I'd test against actual production queries:

  • Rankings won't match exactly. Spidra returns search results as data, not a copy of your old Google Programmable Search Engine configuration. Check result relevance on a representative set of queries.
  • No totalResults or Google pagemap. Page on tokens. For page content, request Markdown with scrapeOptions; structured page data is only available for some results, not a guaranteed replacement for pagemap.
  • Domain filters aren't engine definitions. They restrict results to the domains you send, but they don't reproduce Google's promotions or refinements.
  • Some options work only on certain sources. For example, sort="date" is for news; date filtering and SafeSearch support also vary by source. Inspect warnings if you combine sources and filters.
  • Search results can overlap across pages. Keep a URL deduplication step, especially for longer pagination chains.

One billing detail is easy to miss during testing. Spidra charges one credit per ten results per source, rounded up, and a source returning no results is free. Re-submitting the same search within five seconds can reuse its existing job ID. If you're reconciling search usage from response envelopes, deduplicate by job ID rather than counting the same job twice. The credit rules explain the underlying charges.

For a production cutover, run a sample of your existing queries through both providers while CSE is still available. Compare the fields your code reads, check the behavior of filters and empty result sets, and validate your cost assumptions. Switch the traffic only when the new responses meet the needs of your application.

You now have a Python client for Spidra Search, a bounded cursor paginator, and a compatibility helper for the most common Google result fields. If your application needs only search-result URLs and snippets, the migration can stay small. If it needs page content or additional search sources, the same API can support those workflows without a separate discovery step.

Create a free account at Spidra, set SPIDRA_API_KEY, and run the example against a query your application actually uses.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Google Custom Search JSON API shut down?

Google says existing customers must transition by January 1, 2027. The API is already closed to new customers. Google's published guidance points to Vertex AI Search for searches covering up to 50 domains, or a separate full-web search discussion for broader requirements.

Is Spidra Search a drop-in replacement for googleapiclient?

No. Spidra has a different HTTP request and response model, and it does not reproduce Google's cx engine or every response field. The cse_items() helper above adapts common result fields during migration, but broader integrations must be updated deliberately.

Can I retrieve more than Google's 100-result limit?

Spidra's cursor pagination can continue beyond 100 results when further results are available. The supplied live verification retrieved more than 100. Always set a maximum page count and deduplicate URLs in long-running collection jobs.

Can I migrate an image search or domain-restricted search?

Yes. Set sources=["images"] for image results or use includeDomains and excludeDomains for supported search sources. Image metadata and domain filtering aren't identical to Google's response and engine settings, so test the fields and restrictions your application uses.

title: Reading PDFs with no extractable text from a glyph table: AI drafts it once, then every run is free and identical
description:
When I analyze statistics as a hobby, the source numbers are often published only as PDFs from government offices: monthly reports that come out in the same layout every month. With a normal PDF, you can copy the numbers and paste them into a spreadsheet. But some PDFs read fine on screen and give you a string of symbols when you copy, or don't let you select any text at all.

They look the same, but the inside is different. A normal PDF contains data saying "the character 'S' is here." A PDF with no extractable text only says "a shape made of these lines is here"; the PDF itself does not know which character it is.

To read such a PDF, you usually render the page as an image and run it through OCR, or these days hand it to an AI model. But paying for AI every time you read a monthly report, and getting slightly different results each time, is a poor fit for hobby analysis.

This kind of PDF has one useful property: the same character is drawn with exactly the same shape every time. Unlike handwriting, a "5" is always the same "5". So if you build a table that says "this shape is 5" once, you should be able to read every later issue just by looking shapes up. I call this table the glyph table.

I built this method and compared it with OCR and with AI (four Claude models from Anthropic) under the same conditions. For test data I used samples I made myself and public data anyone may use (the monthly report "Population Estimates" from the Statistics Bureau of Japan).

Everything I built and every result is public: document-extraction-lab (topics/glyph-table/).

Build the table from the first month only; after that, just look shapes up

From the first month's PDF, collect every glyph shape. Put identical shapes into one group and decide which character each group is; that gives you the glyph table. AI models answer which character each group is, and a person checks only the groups where the models disagree (more on this below).

From the second month on, you only look shapes up in the table. No AI is used, so it costs nothing, nothing goes over the internet, and the same PDF always gives the same result.

The rule I cared about most: never make up a character it does not know. A shape that is not close enough to any shape in the table is not forced into a match; it comes out as "?". When different characters with similar shapes end up in the same group, that group also comes out as "?". A person who looks will notice a "?", but nobody notices a plausible wrong character.

I mixed in look-alike characters on purpose, the kind that fool people and AI

First I made 12 months of fictional monthly statements myself. The item-code column deliberately mixes look-alikes: capital I, small l and 1; O and 0; and in Japanese, katakana カ (ka) and the kanji 力 (power), the long-vowel mark ー and the kanji 一 (one), and so on. In the English font I used, I and l differ in height by only about 5%.

I made the same statements 17 ways: different fonts, Japanese text, ruled lines, tighter letter spacing, and so on. I built the table from January alone and read February to December.

What I counted is the silent error: a character read as a different one with no warning. A "?" does not count as an error.

Only the glyph table had 0 silent errors over 11 months

The glyph table had 0 silent errors in both English (5,259 characters) and Japanese (4,207 characters). In 16 of the 17 conditions it stayed at 0 for all 11 months.

OCR made 126 errors in English, reading O as 0 and I or l as 1, among others. In one month the amount "5,583" became "5,983". In Japanese it made 249 errors, 12 of them in digits, such as reading 0 as 9.

I told the AI models: "watch out for look-alikes, and you may write ? for a character you are not sure of." Even so, all four confidently picked between I and l, or between カ and 力, and got them wrong. Opus 5.5 made 11 to 15 errors in English; in Japanese every model made more than 190. When I had each model read the same page 3 times, only 0 to 2 of 11 pages came out the same all 3 times. The answer changes from read to read.

On the other hand, with a font where I and l look clearly different, the AI (Opus 5.5) also made 0 errors. What AI struggles with are strings like item codes, where the surrounding text gives no hint of what the character probably is.

The only errors the glyph table made, 25 characters, were in a condition built so that glyph shapes drift slightly on purpose. But in that condition, building the table already shows that "the same character does not have a consistent shape". In other words, you know the PDF is risky before you read it.

On a public statistics report: 0 silent errors, but the top AI models also had 0

Testing only on samples I made myself could turn into a test that suits me. So I also tested on a real document: 12 monthly issues of the Statistics Bureau of Japan's "Population Estimates". It is packed with small-print tables mixing kanji, Latin letters and digits.

These PDFs are actually normal PDFs you can copy from. So I made versions with the text information removed, leaving "only the shapes", and checked the results against the original text as the answer key. I built the table from the December issue alone and read the January to November issues of the following year, about 150,000 characters.

The glyph table had 0 silent errors here too. OCR made 4,145 errors, such as reading 人 (person) as "A", ＋ as 十 (ten), and 月 (month) as "4".

To be honest, the top AI models (Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2) also made 0 errors on this report. On an ordinary government document without confusing item codes, the glyph table does not win on accuracy.

The difference is elsewhere:

  • Cost: Opus 5.5 costs about $0.07 for every page it reads, about $690 a month for 10,000 pages. The glyph table uses AI only once, when the table is built
  • Same result every time: the glyph table always gives the same result for the same PDF
  • Whether the document leaves your machine: the glyph table reads entirely on your own computer

In the month the layout changed, it said "?" instead of misreading

In the January to October issues, about 3% of characters came out as "?", mostly characters that never appeared in the December issue the table was built from.

In the November issue this jumped to 77%. Looking into it, the size of the digits in the tables had changed slightly. Those sizes were not in the table, so the glyph table marked every November digit as "?" instead of misreading it. Once a person checks the new digit sizes and adds them to the table, it reads the following months again.

As someone who uses the data, I would much rather be told "I don't know" than be given a silent error.

An AI-drafted table repeats the same mistake every month unless it is checked

I also let AI decide "which character is this group" when building the table. Each group's representative glyph is shown inside the line where it was printed, with a red box around it, and the model answers which character it is.

For the 1,016 groups of the Population Estimates, Fable 5.2 answered 1,000 correctly. That is very good, but using that table without a check still gave 200 silent errors over 11 months. On the self-made statements, a single wrong entry (l answered as I) grew into 210 errors over 11 months. A wrong table repeats the same mistake every month.

Checking everything by hand is a lot of work, though. So I had four AI models answer independently, and a person looks only at the groups where their answers split. On the self-made statements, the person had to look at only 5 of 83 groups in English and 7 of 90 in Japanese, and every group where the majority vote was wrong was among them. On the Population Estimates, the person looks at 113 of 1,016 groups (about 1 in 10), and the corrected table had 0 silent errors.

The key is to mix different kinds of AI models. When I had the same model answer 3 times, it repeated the same mistake 3 times, so the answers never split and the mistake went unnoticed.

There was one place, though, where all four models made the same mistake (i answered as j). That character happened not to appear in later months, so it just didn't affect the results.

Tilted pages are straightened before reading; strongly tilted ones go to a person

When a page is rotated, the glyph orientations no longer match the table. When I tried reading pages turned upside down, silent errors appeared: n and u, and 6 and 9, turn into each other's exact shapes when flipped.

So before reading, the method measures the page's tilt and orientation and straightens it. In addition, pages where more than 30% of characters are "?", and pages tilted by more than 10°, are not read at all and go to a person as a whole.

I tested this after deciding and publishing "what counts as a pass" before running anything, so the criteria could not be changed afterwards to suit the results. Rounds 1 and 2 partly failed; round 3 finally passed everything. On the Population Estimates, all 66 tilted or rotated pages had their orientation and tilt corrected. The records of the failed rounds are kept as they are.

Summary

Within what I tested:

  • Using the fact that "the same character is the same shape", PDFs with no extractable text can be read for free with the same result every time. Unknown characters come out as "?", and there were 0 silent errors on 16 self-made conditions and on the public statistics report
  • AI is better used once, to draft the table, than to read every page. Comparing the answers of different kinds of AI models cut what a person has to check to about 1 in 10
  • On documents with few look-alikes, the top AI models are accurate enough too. The choice comes down not only to accuracy but to cost, whether the result is the same every time, and whether the document leaves your machine

I hope this helps anyone who collects statistics published in the same layout every month.

Appendix

Terms

  • Glyph table: a table of glyph-shape groups → characters
  • Silent error: a character different from the correct one, output with no warning
  • "?": a character not close enough to any shape in the table, or one in a confusable group. Not counted as an error
  • OCR: software that reads characters from a page image. Here OCRmyPDF 17.4.0 + Tesseract 5.3.4

How it works (for engineers)

  • Reads the filled shapes in the PDF (handles q/Q/cm) and drops long thin rectangles as ruled lines
  • Renders each glyph as a small black-and-white bitmap and measures similarity by overlap. If the width or height differs by more than a tolerance, it is a different character. Positions shifted by 1 pixel are also tried
  • The similarity threshold is set from the first month alone. If "the lowest similarity between same characters" is higher than "the highest similarity between different characters", the midpoint is used
  • Python standard library only. Reading takes 0.3–1.5 s per page (self-made statements) and about 10 s (dense tables of the Population Estimates)
  • Tilt is the median angle of the lines joining nearby glyphs of the same size

Conditions and caveats

  • Everything ran in the Claude Code cloud environment (x86_64)
  • The 17 self-made conditions: 4 fonts (Liberation Sans, Serif and Mono, DejaVu Serif), Japanese (IPAGothic), text turned into shapes by Ghostscript, each line merged into one shape, ruled lines touching glyphs, tight letter spacing, quotation marks, and 3 levels of coordinate jitter (±0.02 / ±0.05 / ±0.1 pt). Only the ±0.1 pt condition had errors
  • Population Estimates: pages 1–5 of the December 2025 to November 2026 issues (153,247 characters). Text was turned into shapes with Ghostscript 10.02.1 -dNoOutputFonts, and the original text was used as the answer key. These are not PDFs that were made of shapes to begin with. In the November issue the table digits changed from 7.5 pt to 7.14 pt and from 7.92 pt to 7.8 pt
  • I have not measured how much glyph shapes drift in real-world PDFs
  • The human check was simulated with the answer key. The real effort of a person checking 113 groups, and human misreads, were not measured
  • AI: only the four Claude models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.2); OCR: only Tesseract. The models saw 150 dpi page images with an instruction to watch for look-alikes. Costs are at list price
  • For all 3 rounds of the tilt and orientation work, the pass criteria were committed to the repository before testing (pre-registration). The angles used for judging were 0.3°, -4°, 9°, 95°, 25° and -60°
  • Vertical writing: one self-made condition only (0 errors, same as horizontal). Text in images embedded in the PDF is out of scope

Data source

Created by processing "Population Estimates" (Statistics Bureau of Japan) (https://www.stat.go.jp/data/jinsui/new.html), under the Public Data License (Version 1.0). Because the PDFs include font rights, the repository does not contain the PDFs; it holds only the download and conversion scripts and the reading results.

  • Japanese version: Zenn, Qiita

title: How UndoHaven encrypts snapshots so a host never sees file names
description:
I build UndoHaven; this post is about how it handles encryption.

UndoHaven is an unofficial third-party CLI for dsh, a local agent runtime. It takes an encrypted snapshot of a dsh home (plus AGENTS.md and skills/ under ~/.agents) and writes the files back after you quit dsh. Restore is a command, not a screen inside the app, so it does not run against a session that is still writing.

The default needs no account and no network. npx undohaven init (or undohaven snapshot later) writes ciphertext under $DSH_HOME/undohaven, or ~/.dsh/undohaven if DSH_HOME is unset. Storing the ciphertext next to the dsh home is intentional: the snapshot travels with that home. It is also the limit the homepage is explicit about. A full-permission agent can wipe a home directory, local backups included. The copy that survives that wipe is an export you take off the machine, a bucket you configure, or an upload after you log in.

The rest of this post is how those bytes are sealed, and what restore refuses to do.

A data key, wrapped twice

The client generates a 32-byte data key. It does not encrypt files with the passphrase itself. The passphrase is stretched with Argon2id (64 MiB of memory, 3 iterations, parallelism 1; the memorySize value is 65536 because hash-wasm counts kibibytes), and that wrapping key seals the data key with AES-256-GCM. A 24-word recovery code, in the BIP39 layout, is 32 bytes of entropy plus a checksum. It wraps the same data key a second time, but with HKDF-SHA256 over the entropy, not Argon2. The recovery code already has 256 bits of randomness. A human-chosen passphrase does not.

From the data key the client derives three more keys with HKDF-SHA256, each under a fixed info string: one to encrypt chunks, one to encrypt the manifest, and one to name chunks.

If you lose both the passphrase and the recovery code, there is no reset. init, a passphrase unlock, and a recovery-code passphrase change all write the unwrapped data key to local keys.json (file mode 0600, directory 0700) so later snapshots on this machine do not prompt every time. undohaven logout clears that field. chmod has no effect on Windows. keys.json sits in the same $DSH_HOME/undohaven directory as the ciphertext, so syncing or copying the whole home takes the key along. The encryption protects copies that leave this machine; it does not defend a machine that is already compromised. An export file and, if you log in, the server carry only the wrapped keys.

Content-defined chunks, keyed names, then padding

Each file is split with a normalized FastCDC cutter (Xia et al.). The gear table is a fixed SplitMix64 stream, so the same bytes cut at the same places on another machine. The defaults aim at a 1 MiB average chunk, with a 256 KiB floor and a 2 MiB cap, so a sealed chunk stays under a 4 MiB object limit.

A chunk id is not a plain hash of the plaintext. It is HMAC-SHA256 of the plaintext under the chunk-id key. Duplicate chunks still collapse for the same data key, which is what you want across one person's snapshots. A host that only sees the ids cannot confirm a guessed file the way it could with unkeyed SHA-256.

Each piece is optionally compressed with zstd if it is at least 32 bytes and the compressed form is actually smaller, then sealed: a version byte, a flag bit, a 12-byte nonce, AES-256-GCM ciphertext, and a 16-byte tag. On disk or in a bucket the sealed chunk is padded to a 64 KiB multiple (an UHVP header, the true length, then zeros). The stored chunk size is not the plaintext length, and it is not the exact ciphertext length either. Export files and the encrypted manifest are not padded that way.

Paths and per-file sizes live in the manifest, which is encrypted with the third derived key. The claim I will make about the hosted service is narrow: the server cannot see file contents or file names. That is spelled out on the encryption page.

What a snapshot refuses to pick up

The walker does not follow symbolic links or Windows junctions. It skips the undohaven data directory itself, node_modules, cache, common model-weight extensions, and any file larger than 64 MB. Credentials (.env, .credentials.yaml) stay out unless you pass --include-credentials. That flag is off by default. The free plan will still take a local snapshot that includes them if you opt in; it will not upload a snapshot that contains them.

Those cuts are practical. They also mean a snapshot is not a whole-disk image. Files that were never snapshotted cannot be invented later.

Restore runs after dsh has quit

undohaven restore --to SNAPSHOT_ID will not start if it thinks dsh is still up. UndoHaven itself listens on nothing; before restore it connects to 127.0.0.1 and ::1 on port 3999, plus UNDOHAVEN_DSH_PORT if set, to see whether the dsh desktop app is open. On Unix it checks session and desktop lock files through python3 flock or /proc/locks, and refuses the restore if neither method is available. On Windows it looks at tasklist for dsh.exe and at a named semaphore. The error is blunt: quit first, so a live writer cannot race the rollback. There is an escape hatch, UNDOHAVEN_ASSUME_DSH_STOPPED=1, which the code tells you not to set until dsh has actually exited.

If the home still has files, restore takes a safety snapshot first, tagged safety / before-restore, then writes the selected scope back. Files in that scope that are not in the snapshot are deleted; they are still in the safety snapshot. Scopes include all, sessions, storages, config, profile, scheduled tasks (--scope tasks), or a single session. For a full or config restore it also drops a removed tool-working-directory profile entry so a snapshot taken before dsh 0.2.2-rc.3 will still load on 0.2.2-rc.5. Session bytes, including workspace-root paths, are written as stored. dsh itself, not UndoHaven, moves the workspace root.

When dsh will not start at all, undohaven rescue --to SNAPSHOT_ID is narrower still. It does the same lock check and safety snapshot, then writes that profile's package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, and cordis.patch.yml back (--scope profile). It does not try to replay the whole home while you are still figuring out why the process will not boot.

The optional dsh-undohaven plugin can take snapshots on start, on a 6-hour timer by default, and when the plugin is disposed. The startup snapshot only runs when the local data key is already unlocked. If the installed dsh base package version has changed, startup pins the previous snapshot as pre-upgrade and also stores a storage-only snapshot. Restore still happens from the CLI after you quit, so it does not conflict with a session that is writing.

Try it

The CLI needs Node.js 24.9 or newer (undohaven-core itself accepts 22.19). As of 24 November 2026 (Asia/Shanghai), the published packages are undohaven 0.1.14, undohaven-core 0.1.15, and dsh-undohaven 0.1.12.

npx undohaven init
undohaven snapshot
undohaven list
# quit dsh first, including the tray icon
undohaven restore --to SNAPSHOT_ID --scope all

Write the 24-word recovery code down off the machine when init prints it. The crypto lives in the published undohaven-core package, in src/crypto.js, src/cdc.js, and src/byo.js.

Site: https://undohaven.com/

UndoHaven is an unofficial third-party tool compatible with dsh. It is not affiliated with DeepSeek.

title: CrowdStrike vai adquirir Zscaler por US$ 43,9 bilhões
description:
Operação recorde de US$ 43,9 bilhões

A CrowdStrike irá adquirir a Zscaler por US$ 43,9 bilhões, em uma operação recorde no mercado de cibersegurança. A conclusão está prevista para o segundo semestre de 2028, e o anúncio evidencia a preocupação crescente com as ameaças digitais.

Plataformas com frentes complementares

O acordo combina frentes diferentes de proteção: a CrowdStrike atua em computadores, servidores e outros dispositivos, enquanto a tecnologia da Zscaler protege o acesso de funcionários a aplicativos e dados. A proposta é reunir essas capacidades em uma plataforma mais abrangente para clientes corporativos e governamentais, cobrindo equipamentos e acesso a recursos digitais.

Reação do mercado e escrutínio regulatório

A resposta inicial das bolsas foi distinta para as duas companhias. As ações da Zscaler avançaram mais de 13% e chegaram a US$ 220,52, mas seguiram abaixo dos US$ 260,41 por ação implícitos na oferta. Já os papéis da CrowdStrike recuaram quase 12% nas negociações.

Essa distância entre a cotação da Zscaler e o valor implícito da proposta ocorre enquanto investidores avaliam a possibilidade de escrutínio regulatório. Como a transação reúne duas das maiores empresas do setor, essa análise está entre os pontos que o mercado acompanha.

Ameaças e resiliência digital

A procura por ferramentas de cibersegurança tem crescido porque empresas de todo o mundo enfrentam ataques cada vez mais sofisticados. A inteligência artificial amplia a pressão em duas frentes: facilita identificar e explorar vulnerabilidades de software e também aprimora as ferramentas criadas para detectar e conter ameaças.

Esse cenário de risco inclui interrupções recentes que afetaram companhias aéreas, bancos e órgãos governamentais. Também pesam vulnerabilidades de grande repercussão em softwares amplamente utilizados, entre eles Java e PHP. Esses episódios aumentaram as preocupações com a resiliência da infraestrutura digital crítica.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/crowdstrike-planeja-adquirir-zscaler-por-us-43-9-bilhoes/

title: Typed State Machines for React Email Verification
description:
Email verification looks like a small form feature: collect an address, send a code, wait for a message, and let the user continue. In a real product, it is an asynchronous workflow with several ways to get stuck.

The UI are not just waiting for a promise. It is waiting for a message that may arrive late, may be unreadable, or may belong to an older attempt. A typed state machine gives the React layer a small, explicit contract for those situations.

Why email verification needs explicit UI states

The usual implementation starts with three booleans: isSending, isWaiting, and hasError. That works until a user clicks resend during polling, changes the address, or opens a verification link in another tab. Then combinations appear that the product never intended to show, such as a success message beside an expired-code error.

Instead, model the meaningful states:

  • idle: no address has been submitted
  • sending: the request to create a verification attempt is in progress
  • waiting: the attempt exists and the client is waiting for a matching message
  • verified: the server accepted the code or link
  • expired: the attempt lease ended
  • failed: the user can retry after a recoverable error

This rules out accidental combinations. It also makes the copy, disabled buttons, and accessibility announcements easier to review together.

Model the flow as a discriminated union

TypeScript can make invalid rendering paths harder to write. Each state carries only the data that makes sense for it:

type VerificationState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending"; email: string }
  | { kind: "waiting"; email: string; attemptId: string; expiresAt: number }
  | { kind: "verified"; email: string }
  | { kind: "expired"; email: string }
  | { kind: "failed"; email: string; message: string; canRetry: boolean };

The attemptId is important. It prevents a late response from an older request changing the current screen. The expiry timestamp is useful too: the client can show a countdown, but the server must still enforce the actual lease.

I prefer a reducer for transitions because each event is visible in one place. A resend action should create a new attempt, clear the old polling task, and move back through sending; it should not quietly mutate a few unrelated flags.

Keep polling and inbox access behind a boundary

React should not know how a message is found. The component can call a small API such as waitForVerification(attemptId), while the service handles bounded polling, correlation IDs, and cleanup.

For staging and automated checks, an isolated disposable email generator can help inspect the message without mixing it with a personal inbox. It is test data, not proof that a production identity is trustworthy. Give each run a unique recipient and a short expiry.

The service boundary might look like this:

async function waitForVerification(
  attemptId: string,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<{ code: string }> {
  for (let tryNumber = 0; tryNumber < 12; tryNumber += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/verification/${attemptId}`, { signal });

    if (response.status === 200) return response.json();
    if (response.status === 410) throw new Error("verification expired");
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error("verification lookup failed");

    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1500));
  }

  throw new Error("verification timed out");
}

In production, the server should usually push a completion event or expose a carefully bounded endpoint. The loop is mainly useful as a simple adapter and for test environments. It need a cancellation path: when the address changes or the component unmounts, abort the old attempt.

If your workflow runs in CI, pair the adapter with an AWS deployment drift check so environment differences do not look like random email failures. For browser tests, inbox lease patterns for Cypress retries are a useful reminder that a retry needs a new, identifiable fixture.

Render useful React feedback

Keep the component focused on user decisions. In waiting, show the destination in a privacy-conscious way, offer “use a different address,” and provide a resend action only when the current attempt allows it. Do not expose the full verification token in the DOM or logs.

An aria-live="polite" region can announce “Verification email sent” and later “Code expired, request a new one.” Reserve space for these messages so the form does not jump around. A bit more clear copy usually beats a clever animation here.

People also search for phrases like temp gamil com when they are trying to find a temporary inbox. That typo can be useful in support analytics, but it should never become a label or a reason to weaken validation.

Testing the transitions

Test events and transitions, not just the final happy-path screenshot. At minimum, cover:

  1. A successful send moves from idle to waiting.
  2. A late response from an old attemptId is ignored.
  3. A 410 response renders the expired state and enables a new request.
  4. Aborting the request on unmount does not show an error toast.
  5. A matching code moves to verified, while an unrelated message is rejected.
  6. Keyboard users can reach resend and change-address actions in the right order.

The test don't need a real mailbox for every transition. Inject the verification service and return deterministic results. Reserve a smaller end-to-end suite for checking that the sender, inbox adapter, and application agree on the correlation contract.

Questions developers usually ask

Should the client poll forever?

No. Set a server-enforced expiry and a client timeout. “Try again” is more honest than a spinner that never ends.

Is a disposable temporary email safe for production accounts?

No. Use isolated test fixtures only, and never place recovery credentials or private customer data in them. A disposable inbox is a development tool with a narrow purpose.

Do I need a state machine library?

Not always. A discriminated union and reducer are enough for a compact flow. A library becomes more useful when verification is part of a larger process with parallel tasks, retries, and persisted transitions.

Final takeaway

Email verification becomes easier to ship when the UI treats it as a contract instead of a collection of flags. Define the states, correlate every attempt, bound the wait, and test the transitions that users actually see. The result is more predictable React code, cleaner TypeScript types, and fewer mysterious “the email never arrived” reports.

Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) X8i instances are available in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region. To get started, visit the AWS Management Console. X8i instances can be purchased via Savings Plans, On-Demand instances, and Spot instances. For more information visit X8i instances page.
