title: What Backup and Disaster Recovery Tools Don't Recover (2026): Configuration, Identity, DNS, and Secrets Gaps
description:
Backup and disaster recovery tools recover data and servers, but a business also needs its cloud configuration, identity, DNS, certificates, secrets, pipelines, and people working again before customers can use the service. The best cloud operations setup for business continuity and disaster recovery combines a platform such as Control Plane that keeps the application running in more than one location, a data protection tool for backups, configuration kept as code, and a tested recovery order for everything else. This guide maps eleven recovery layers against what the vendors’ own documentation says their tools restore, and sets out the order in which services should come back.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Backup and DR products restore data and server images and leave most of the operating environment to you.

  • Most backup and DR products leave cloud IAM, DNS records, TLS certificates, encryption keys, and CI/CD pipelines to you.
  • A complete business continuity posture covers eleven layers, from volumes and VMs through people and communication.
  • Recovery order decides whether restored data is reachable. Identity and DNS come before compute.
  • Every recovery path must be timed and tested, including configuration, identity, and user access in the recovery environment.
  • Control Plane keeps the application tier running across multiple locations and clouds so that a location failure needs no recovery launch, and its declarative resources make configuration exportable and re-appliable.

What is the difference between business continuity and disaster recovery?

Business continuity, disaster recovery, and high availability solve related problems at different scopes, and confusing them leads to plans that protect servers but leave the business offline.

Term What it keeps running Typical scope Owner
High availability A single system or service, through redundant components and automatic failover One application, usually across zones in a region, sometimes across regions Engineering and platform teams
Disaster recovery Information systems after a major, usually physical disruption, by relocating to an alternate site The information systems at an affected site IT operations and infrastructure
Business continuity The organization’s business processes during and after a disruption, including people, communication, and third-party dependencies The entire organization Executive leadership, with IT, legal, and operations

NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 draws the continuity and recovery lines explicitly. A business continuity plan sustains business processes during and after a disruption, a disaster recovery plan covers major disruptions that require relocating information systems to an alternate site, and an information system contingency plan recovers a single system. The same publication defines a business impact analysis as the process that maps a system to the business processes it supports, including interdependencies, and characterizes the consequences of a disruption. Without that mapping, a team can restore every database and still miss the payment gateway dependency that keeps revenue at zero.

What do backup and disaster recovery tools actually recover?

Backup and DR products are engineered for data and compute, and the vendors’ own documentation shows where each layer is left to you.

Layer What usually recovers it What it leaves to you
Data and volumes AWS Backup, Azure Backup, Google Cloud Backup and DR, Veeam, Commvault, Druva Verifying data integrity and application-level consistency after restore
Servers and VMs AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (block-level replication), Azure Site Recovery, restore from backup products Post-failover steps such as public IP assignment, load balancer attachment, and connection-string updates
Cloud network configuration (VPCs, subnets, security groups, load balancers) AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery network replication (VPC-level configuration, in-AWS networks only, through a CloudFormation stack), Azure Site Recovery network mapping, Commvault Cloud Rewind, infrastructure as code Public IPs, network security groups, and load balancers, which Azure Site Recovery leaves to recovery-plan scripts or manual steps; keeping definitions as code and checking parity between regions
Cloud IAM roles and policies Infrastructure as code, if the roles were codified; IAM is not on AWS Backup’s supported list Keeping role and policy definitions as code and testing them in the recovery account
Workforce identity (Entra ID, Active Directory, IAM Identity Center) Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery, Commvault IDRecover (Active Directory, Entra ID, Okta), Veeam Data Cloud for Microsoft Entra ID Hard-deleted and on-premises Active Directory-sourced objects when relying on Entra Backup and Recovery alone, Active Directory forest recovery when relying on Microsoft’s own process, and IAM Identity Center’s fixed primary Region
DNS records and failover Exported zone files or infrastructure as code; Route 53 hosted zones are not on AWS Backup’s supported list Failover through data-plane health checks, short TTLs on failover records, and restoring DNS before applications
TLS certificates Re-issuance or certificates provisioned in advance in the recovery region Provisioning each recovery region ahead of time, since AWS Certificate Manager certificates cannot be copied between Regions
Secrets and encryption keys Multi-Region replication you set up per secret or key, or vault backups Creating multi-Region KMS keys yourself; Azure Key Vault restores only within the same subscription and geography
Application configuration and deploy pipelines Infrastructure as code repositories and CI/CD definitions in version control Predeploying pipelines in every region and replicating DR plans, credentials, certificates, and scripts
Third-party dependencies (payments, email, SaaS APIs) Nothing in the backup stack Documenting API keys, OAuth tokens, webhooks, service principals, and partner allowlists of your egress IPs, and testing integrations from the recovery environment
People and communication Nothing in the backup stack Out-of-band communication channels, phone bridges, runbook distribution, and role assignments

AWS states that in addition to data, you must redeploy the infrastructure, configuration, and application code in the recovery Region, and AWS Backup’s saved EC2 metadata, such as instance type, VPC, security group, and IAM role, is only used when restoring to the same Region. Generating infrastructure as code from existing resources after the fact is unreliable. Microsoft says exporting an ARM template from the portal is not a reliable way to turn pre-existing resources into templates usable in production, and exported templates can miss password parameters and stop at 200 resources per resource group. Terraform’s configuration generation for imports is labeled experimental and produces a best guess. Google’s Terraform export of existing resources is Pre-GA, and some resource types are not supported. The AWS CloudFormation IaC generator works only for resource types the Cloud Control API supports and models up to 500 resources per template. Configuration that is not in code before the disaster has to be rebuilt by hand under pressure. The tools that keep it in code are compared in CI/CD and IaC tools for disaster recovery and self-healing.

Why do identity, DNS, and secrets break recovery?

Identity, DNS, and secrets sit near the bottom of the dependency stack, so data, compute, and traffic all wait on them.

Workforce identity is the first bottleneck. Microsoft Entra ID soft-deletes only users, Microsoft 365 groups, cloud security groups, and applications, for 30 days, and hard-deletes all other object types immediately. Microsoft calls recoverability a shared responsibility and tells customers to keep tenant configuration in an external versioned repository exported with Microsoft Graph. Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery became generally available in June 2026; the Standard plan keeps daily backups for 7 days, a 30-day Premium plan is in preview, and it cannot recover hard-deleted objects or objects managed in on-premises Active Directory. Active Directory forest recovery has no end-to-end automation and is more a logistical and organizational challenge than a technical one, according to Microsoft, which recommends regular domain controller backups over snapshot restore. On AWS, the IAM control plane runs in us-east-1, so creating or changing roles during an event depends on that Region, and AWS advises against relying on global-service control planes in recovery paths. IAM Identity Center runs in one primary Region; multi-Region replication exists but not for account instances or Active Directory-sourced identities, and the primary Region cannot be changed.

DNS, certificates, secrets, and encryption keys form the second set of hidden dependencies. The Route 53 control plane is in us-east-1 while DNS answering is global, and AWS says to use data-plane functions such as health checks for DNS failover. AWS calls a TTL of 60 or 120 seconds a common choice for failover records because resolvers cache answers until the TTL expires. AWS Certificate Manager certificates are regional and cannot be copied between Regions, so each recovery region needs its own certificates in advance. AWS never automatically creates or replicates multi-Region KMS keys. Azure Key Vault backups can be restored only within the same subscription and Azure geography, and Microsoft-managed Key Vault failover is best-effort and leaves the vault read-only. Data encrypted with a key that does not exist in the recovery region stays unreadable after the restore.

What order should you restore services in?

Recovery is sequence-dependent, and the wrong order leaves restored services idle while teams rebuild the prerequisites beneath them.

Step What to restore Why it comes here
1 Out-of-band communication and the incident bridge Teams need a coordination channel that does not depend on the systems being recovered; CISA’s incident response playbook calls for out-of-band communications and phone bridges
2 Break-glass access to cloud accounts and recovery tools Break-glass accounts do not depend on the failed identity provider, so the team can sign in and rebuild everything else
3 Network, then workforce identity and internal DNS Self-hosted domain controllers and identity servers need VPCs, subnets, routes, and security groups first, and Microsoft says you often need to recover Active Directory and DNS before other application components; time sync comes up here because Kerberos and certificate validation depend on it
4 Secrets, keys, and certificates Encrypted data is unreadable and TLS endpoints fail without them
5 Data Databases and volumes restore once keys and network paths exist
6 Compute and application tier Application code needs identity, networking, secrets, and data in place, plus container images, service quotas, and monitoring already available in the recovery region
7 Traffic cutover with health checks and short TTLs Users should reach the recovery environment only after the application passes health checks, and TTLs must already be short before the event because resolvers keep cached answers
8 Verify access, payments, and integrations Users must sign in, payments must clear, and third-party APIs must respond
9 Plan failback The recovery environment’s state is recorded and the return to the primary site is scheduled

Steps without a dependency between them run in parallel, and large data restores usually start as soon as keys and network exist because they set the RTO floor. Azure Well-Architected guidance says to replicate DR plans, credentials, certificates, and scripts across regions, keep offline copies, and predeploy CI/CD pipelines in every region. AWS Resilience Hub notes that even with backups copied to a fallback Region, you are still expected to maintain a restore procedure and test and time it. Keeping these artifacts in one region or one cloud account creates a single point of failure that no backup tool fixes.

What are the best cloud operations solutions for addressing business continuity and disaster recovery?

No single product covers all eleven layers, so the strongest setup combines solutions that each handle a distinct part of the problem.

  1. Control Plane keeps the application tier running across multiple locations and clouds. A workload runs in every location of its Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, which can span AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) regions, plus Kubernetes clusters you run yourself or that Control Plane runs for you. Each workload gets Control Plane’s canonical endpoint, one HTTPS URL that uses DNS to route clients to the nearest healthy location, and replicas in other locations take over when a whole location fails. Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to a workload running at least two replicas across at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers. Configuration is kept as declarative resources that export and re-apply. Custom domains get TLS certificates automatically, and org secrets are stored on multiple cloud providers, so a workload references the same secret wherever its GVC runs. The business continuity solutions for high availability across on premises and cloud roundup covers this layer in depth.
  2. Hyperscaler-native DR and backup handles server replication and data protection into one provider’s cloud. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates server volumes at block level, and AWS Backup covers its supported resource types. Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup provide VM replication and backup. Google Cloud Backup and DR covers workloads including Compute Engine, Persistent Disk, Filestore, Cloud SQL, and AlloyDB. The best cloud disaster recovery solutions for 2026 comparison scores them side by side.
  3. Data protection platforms provide backup, ransomware recovery, and identity backup. Veeam, Commvault, and Druva back up data across cloud and on-premises environments. Commvault IDRecover covers Active Directory, Entra ID, and Okta, and Veeam Data Cloud for Microsoft Entra ID backs up Entra ID. Commvault Cloud Rewind, now listed under Cloud Application Recovery, rebuilds cloud infrastructure and configuration along with data.
  4. Infrastructure as code and GitOps keep cloud configuration in version control so it can be reviewed and reapplied in a recovery account. Terraform, Pulumi, and CloudFormation define network, IAM, and security group state. The code has to exist and stay current before the disaster.
  5. A business continuity plan with a business impact analysis, out-of-band communication, and regular drills ties the technical layers to people and process. It covers third-party dependencies, communication channels, and decision authority.

Most companies need one solution from each of the first four types and a tested plan that ties them together. A backup product without codified configuration leaves identity and networking gaps, and a multi-location platform without data protection leaves backup and ransomware recovery gaps. The cloud vs on-premises disaster recovery guide covers where the recovery site itself should run.

How do you test that the whole business recovers?

AWS says the only error recovery that works is the path you test frequently, and a test that restores one database snapshot and declares success misses most of the recovery surface.

A complete drill rebuilds configuration and identity in the recovery account, applies the infrastructure as code, restores secrets and certificates, deploys the application, times the whole sequence against the RTO, and measures data loss against the RPO. Google’s DR guide says to test that permissions and user access work in the DR environment like they do in production. The drill should move traffic into the recovery DNS path with health checks and short TTLs, confirm that users can sign in, check that payment gateways and third-party APIs respond, and use the out-of-band communication channel. Every gap found becomes an action item with an owner and a deadline. Teams that skip the people and communication layer in drills find out during a real incident that the phone bridge was never set up. The steps for drilling without risking customers are in how to test failover without taking production down.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. When a location in a GVC fails, replicas in its other locations keep serving through the workload’s canonical endpoint. During the October 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, 20 percent of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their GVCs. According to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry, their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime. Teams use the same model to survive a cloud provider outage without a DR runbook for the application tier.

Every Control Plane resource, including GVCs, workloads, identities, secrets, policies, domains, and volume sets, is a declarative item reached through one API shared by the console, CLI, Terraform, Pulumi, and AI agents. Control Plane’s CLI command cpln apply creates or updates resources from YAML or JSON files, is idempotent, and applies related resources in dependency order. Existing resources export as re-appliable YAML or as Terraform HCL. The Control Plane console’s Export GVC action saves a GVC with its workloads, identities, and volume set definitions as one file for backup and restore. Org-level secrets, cloud accounts, and agents are handled separately, and secrets are not included in the export.

Control Plane ships Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the docs include CI/CD examples for GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and CircleCI, so it complements the infrastructure as code you already run. Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s identity for workloads, creates an IAM role, GCP service account, or Azure managed identity in your own account, so no long-lived AWS, GCP, or Azure keys sit in your code. Org secrets are envelope-encrypted and stored on multiple cloud providers in cloud hardware security modules, and workloads reference them by name. Custom domains get TLS certificates automatically and are DNS geo-routed to the nearest healthy location. Volume sets support on-demand and scheduled snapshots with a retention period and restoring a volume to a snapshot. For cross-region data, Control Plane’s Template Catalog includes replicating databases, such as the Postgres Multi-Location template, which promotes a replica automatically with three or more locations, and pgEdge, which runs active-active multi-master Postgres. Volume-set data itself is not replicated between locations, and a volume can be copied on demand to another location.

Inside an org, nothing is permitted until a policy grants it, and a tamper-proof audit trail records who did what across the org. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

It works alongside the backup and data protection tools a company already runs. Those tools keep protecting data copies, and Control Plane keeps the application serving from healthy locations.

FAQ

Short answers on backup gaps, recovery order, identity, and testing.

What are the best cloud operations solutions for addressing business continuity and disaster recovery?

Control Plane runs the application tier active-active across locations and clouds, so a location failure needs no recovery launch. Hyperscaler-native DR tools such as AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, Azure Site Recovery, and Google Cloud Backup and DR handle server replication and backups. Data protection platforms such as Veeam, Commvault, and Druva cover backup and ransomware recovery, and Commvault and Veeam extend to identity backup. Infrastructure as code and GitOps keep cloud configuration repeatable. A business continuity plan with a business impact analysis, out-of-band communication, and drills ties these layers to people and process.

What is the difference between business continuity and disaster recovery?

Business continuity sustains the organization’s business processes during and after a disruption, covering people, communication, and third-party dependencies as well as technology. Disaster recovery is the part focused on relocating and restoring information systems after a major disruption. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 draws this distinction and uses a business impact analysis to map systems to the business processes they support.

Is DRaaS enough for business continuity?

DRaaS covers servers and data by replicating workloads to a recovery site and automating failover. It typically leaves most cloud configuration, workforce identity, DNS, TLS certificates, encryption keys, CI/CD pipelines, third-party integrations, and people and communication to you. Business continuity needs tools and plans for each of those layers alongside DRaaS.

What does a backup not recover?

A backup typically does not recover cloud IAM roles and policies, workforce identity, DNS records and failover configuration, TLS certificates, encryption keys and secrets, CI/CD pipelines, third-party integrations, or communication channels. AWS Backup keeps EC2 metadata such as instance type, VPC, security group, and IAM role, but uses it only when restoring to the same AWS Region. IAM, Route 53 hosted zones, Secrets Manager, and KMS are not on AWS Backup’s list of supported resources.

How do I back up cloud configuration like IAM, DNS, and security groups?

Define cloud configuration in infrastructure as code before a disaster and store the code in version control outside the primary cloud account. Terraform, Pulumi, and CloudFormation can define IAM roles, DNS zones, security groups, and networks. Generating code from existing resources afterward is unreliable. The AWS CloudFormation IaC generator supports only Cloud Control API resource types and caps at 500 resources per template, Terraform’s import configuration generation is experimental, and Azure ARM template export can miss password parameters and stops at 200 resources.

How do I recover Microsoft Entra ID or Active Directory after a disaster?

For Entra ID, use Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery, generally available since June 2026, which keeps daily backups for 7 days on the Standard plan, with a 30-day Premium plan in preview. It cannot recover hard-deleted objects or objects managed in on-premises Active Directory, and Microsoft recommends keeping tenant configuration in an external versioned repository exported with Microsoft Graph. Microsoft says its Active Directory forest recovery process has no end-to-end automation and describes it as more a logistical and organizational challenge than a technical one. Commvault IDRecover and Veeam Data Cloud for Microsoft Entra ID provide third-party backup, with Commvault covering Active Directory, Entra ID, and Okta and Veeam covering Entra ID.

In what order should systems be restored after a disaster?

Start with out-of-band communication and the incident bridge. Restore break-glass access next, then the network, workforce identity, and internal DNS, followed by secrets, keys, and certificates. Restore data once encryption keys and network paths exist. Deploy compute and applications, cut traffic over with health checks and short TTLs, verify access and integrations, and plan failback.

How often should business continuity and disaster recovery plans be tested?

Test at least quarterly, which AWS recommends for Elastic Disaster Recovery drills, and again after significant infrastructure or organizational changes, because AWS states that the only error recovery that works is the path you test frequently. Drills should rebuild configuration and identity in the recovery environment, time the full restore against the RTO, verify user access and third-party integrations, and use the out-of-band communication channel.

How does Control Plane support business continuity and disaster recovery?

Control Plane runs each workload in every location of its Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, across regions and clouds. Each workload gets a canonical endpoint that routes requests to the nearest healthy location, and replicas in other locations take over when a location fails. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to a workload running at least two replicas across at least two locations. Every resource is declarative, and existing resources export as re-appliable YAML or Terraform HCL. Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s identity for workloads, keeps long-lived cloud keys out of code, org secrets are envelope-encrypted and stored in cloud hardware security modules on multiple providers, custom domains get automatic TLS certificates with geo-routing, and volume sets support on-demand and scheduled snapshots. Control Plane works alongside existing backup and data protection tools.

title: Alternatives to EKS, GKE, and AKS in 2026: What Staying Costs and What Changes When You Move
description:
The best alternative to EKS, GKE, or AKS depends on why you are leaving: cost, the operations work a cluster still needs, lock-in to one cloud, or control. Control Plane takes cluster operations off your team on one cloud or several. Serverless container services and the providers’ own managed modes remove most node work inside one cloud, smaller providers lower the control plane fee for teams that keep running Kubernetes themselves, and self-managed distributions give the most control for the most work.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Staying costs more in team time than in fees, and each alternative fits a different reason for leaving.

  • Cost of staying. The cluster fee is small. The real cost is the upgrade cycle, node management, and add-on maintenance your team still owns.
  • Managed modes. EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot, and AKS Automatic hand off node patching and scaling but keep you on one cloud. GKE Autopilot and AKS Automatic also run cluster-version upgrades; on EKS Auto Mode your team still starts them.
  • Alternatives by reason. Control Plane to take Day 2 operations and the cluster lifecycle off your team on one cloud or several, managed modes and serverless containers to reduce node work inside one cloud, smaller providers for a lower control plane fee, enterprise Kubernetes for governance, self-managed distributions for control, and Nomad or Swarm for non-Kubernetes simplicity.
  • What a move changes. Deployments and ConfigMaps move with few changes. Pod identity, ingress, persistent volumes, and image registry access are tied to one cloud and need a plan.
  • Control Plane. Handles Day 2 operations, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security, on Kubernetes clusters it orchestrates across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions. It converts Kubernetes manifests with its cpln convert command and offers a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas across at least two locations.

What does staying on EKS, GKE, or AKS cost and leave to your team?

EKS, GKE, and AKS each set a cluster fee and a version-support window, but the larger cost is the work your team still owns after the control plane is running.

Provider Cluster fee Version support What your team still does Managed mode that takes over nodes
Amazon EKS $0.10/cluster/hour standard; $0.60/cluster/hour extended support 14 months standard, then 12 months extended; a cluster not upgraded before extended support ends is auto-upgraded Start each upgrade one minor version at a time, update nodes, update VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy; deploy patched AMIs for managed node groups; configure Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter; own IAM, pod security, runtime security, network security EKS Auto Mode
Google GKE $0.10/cluster/hour; free-tier credit covers one Autopilot or zonal Standard cluster; $0.60/cluster/hour for Extended channel clusters in extended support 14 months standard; Extended channel adds ~10 months of security patches; GKE auto-upgrades all clusters over time Node pool sizing, autoscaling settings, security configuration, and add-ons on Standard clusters; Pod resource requests, VPC, and cluster configuration on Autopilot GKE Autopilot
Azure AKS Free tier (no SLA), Standard tier with uptime SLA, Premium tier for Long Term Support About 12 months of community support; Long Term Support (~24 months per version) requires Premium tier Node pools, upgrades (manual by default), networking, identity, and security on AKS Standard clusters AKS Automatic

Upstream Kubernetes supports each minor version for roughly 14 months and maintains the three most recent minor releases. On standard EKS your team starts each upgrade, one minor version at a time, and updates nodes and add-ons to match. On EKS, extended support is on by default, so a cluster that misses the standard window moves to six times the standard rate. GKE charges the same $0.60 only for clusters enrolled in its Extended channel and auto-upgrades the rest. AWS’s own pricing example shows a cluster that is never upgraded averages $0.33 per hour over 26 months. Node patching, autoscaler tuning, and security configuration add staff hours every month, a cost that weighs most on teams managing clusters without a platform team.

Why do teams look for alternatives to managed Kubernetes?

Four patterns explain most moves away from EKS, GKE, or AKS.

Cost. The cluster fee is predictable, but compute, storage, cross-zone data transfer, NAT gateways, and observability ingestion are billed separately and often exceed the cluster fee. Idle node capacity held for bursts and failover adds to it.

Operations work. With a managed control plane, your team still owns version upgrade planning and testing, node patching, autoscaler configuration, CNI and CSI add-on updates, ingress controllers, and security policies. Each provider handles upgrades, node pools, and add-ons differently, so a multi-cloud team needs a runbook for each.

Lock-in to one cloud. Pod identity, ingress, and persistent storage all tie a workload to a single provider. EKS Pod Identity maps an IAM role to a Kubernetes service account, GKE Workload Identity Federation grants Google IAM roles to Kubernetes entities, and AKS workload identity federates with Microsoft Entra ID. Teams looking to manage Kubernetes across multiple clouds without vendor lock-in hit these walls quickly.

Control. Some workloads must run on premises, at the edge, or on bare metal, outside any hyperscaler region. Regulated industries may need to own the full stack for audit and compliance reasons.

Should you switch to EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot, or AKS Automatic first?

The hyperscalers’ own managed modes take over node operations, while the cluster stays on one cloud and your team keeps the VPC and cluster configuration.

EKS Auto Mode uses Karpenter-based scaling, takes responsibility for node OS configuration, patching, and health, enforces a 21-day maximum node lifetime, and builds in pod networking, network policy, local DNS, GPU plug-ins, and EBS CSI storage. Customers keep responsibility for application containers, the VPC, and cluster configuration. Auto Mode adds a management fee per EC2 instance on top of the EC2 price, varying by instance type.

GKE Autopilot goes further. Google manages nodes, scaling, security settings, and upgrades of the control plane and worker nodes. General-purpose Autopilot pods are billed per second for the CPU, memory, and ephemeral storage they request, which removes idle-node waste but requires careful resource-request tuning.

AKS Automatic handles node management, scaling, security, and preconfigured settings, and automatically patches nodes and cluster components. It includes a financially backed 99.95% Kubernetes API server availability SLA.

All three managed modes take node patching and scaling off your team. GKE Autopilot and AKS Automatic also upgrade the cluster version through a release channel, and your team keeps workloads compatible with each new Kubernetes version. On EKS Auto Mode, your team still starts each control plane upgrade. None of them remove the VPC and cluster configuration work or the tie to a single cloud’s identity, ingress, and storage systems. A managed mode reduces node work on the cloud you already use, while the cluster itself, its configuration, and compatibility testing stay with your team.

What are the best alternatives to managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS)?

The right alternative maps to the reason you are leaving, whether you need the Kubernetes API, and how much work you want to own.

Option Examples Reason it fits Keeps the Kubernetes API What your team still runs Where it runs
Control Plane Control Plane Day 2 operations, total cost including staff time, and lock-in, on one cloud or several Yes on clusters joined through CPLN BYOK, Control Plane’s bring-your-own-Kubernetes option, or run by Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes; on built-in locations, manifests convert with cpln convert and a Kubernetes operator lets kubectl and Argo CD manage Control Plane resources Container images and workload settings AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions plus Kubernetes clusters you run or Control Plane runs for you, including on your own servers on premises
Managed modes of the same provider EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot, AKS Automatic Operations work, staying on one cloud Yes Apps, VPC, cluster configuration One cloud
Serverless containers Amazon ECS with Fargate, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps Operations work No Services, scaling settings, networking One cloud
Smaller managed Kubernetes providers DigitalOcean Kubernetes, Linode Kubernetes Engine, Civo, OVHcloud Lower control plane fee Yes Nodes, upgrades, add-ons That provider
Enterprise Kubernetes Red Hat OpenShift (including ROSA and ARO), SUSE Rancher for managing many clusters Governance across many clusters Yes The platform and its clusters, shared with Red Hat and the cloud on ROSA and ARO Several clouds and data centers
Self-managed lightweight Kubernetes K3s, Talos Linux Control, edge, bare metal Yes Everything including control plane and upgrades Anywhere
Non-Kubernetes orchestrator HashiCorp Nomad, Docker Swarm mode Simplicity, mixed workloads No The cluster, servers, and upgrades Anywhere

Control Plane takes Day 2 operations off your team and orchestrates hardened, security-isolated Kubernetes clusters across regions of the major clouds. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, lets you add a location to roll every workload out there and remove one to withdraw them. Locations can be AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions that Control Plane operates, plus Kubernetes clusters you run yourself or that Control Plane runs for you. cpln convert turns Kubernetes Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs, Secrets, ConfigMaps, PersistentVolumeClaims, and Ingresses into Control Plane workloads, secrets, volume sets, and domains. Control Plane also leads the wider list of best alternatives to Kubernetes, which compares Kubernetes and non-Kubernetes paths.

Managed modes reduce node work for a team staying on one cloud, while VPC and cluster configuration stay with that team.

Serverless containers remove the Kubernetes API from your team’s work. Amazon ECS has no additional charge for orchestration and Fargate bills per second with a one-minute minimum for Linux tasks. AWS App Runner is closed to new customers; AWS recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode instead. Google Cloud Run runs code as a service, job, worker pool, or instance, and a service with no incoming requests scales to zero. Azure Container Apps is powered by Kubernetes, Dapr, KEDA, and Envoy but does not provide direct access to the Kubernetes APIs. ECS, Cloud Run, and Container Apps each run on one cloud.

Smaller managed Kubernetes providers keep the Kubernetes API at a lower price. DigitalOcean Kubernetes includes the control plane at no cost and charges $40 per month for a high-availability control plane. Linode Kubernetes Engine includes the control plane at no additional cost, with its HA control plane starting at $60 per month per cluster depending on region. Civo says clusters launch in 90 seconds with an always-free control plane. OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes has a free plan and a Standard plan at $0.099 per cluster per hour. Your team still owns nodes, upgrades, and add-ons.

Enterprise Kubernetes targets governance across many clusters. Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS (ROSA) is jointly operated by Red Hat and AWS, and Azure Red Hat OpenShift (ARO) is jointly engineered by Red Hat and Microsoft. SUSE Rancher provisions clusters on hosted providers including EKS, GKE, and AKS, or imports existing clusters, and manages them; it does not replace them. Rancher and OpenShift also appear in the comparison of the best Kubernetes management platforms.

Self-managed lightweight Kubernetes gives the most control for the most work. K3s is a fully compliant Kubernetes distribution with SQLite as the default datastore, packaged as a single binary of less than 100 MB. Talos Linux is an immutable, API-driven OS for Kubernetes with no SSH, shell, or package manager. Both run anywhere, but your team owns everything including the control plane and upgrades.

Non-Kubernetes orchestrators suit teams that do not need the Kubernetes API. HashiCorp Nomad is a single binary for clients and servers with no external services for coordination or storage, and runs Docker, Java, Qemu VMs, and standalone binaries. Nomad 1.7.0 and later are under the Business Source License 1.1. Docker Swarm mode is built into Docker Engine; the older Classic Swarm is no longer actively developed. Both require your team to run the cluster, servers, and upgrades.

What changes when you move off EKS, GKE, or AKS?

Most Kubernetes objects are portable, but the integrations that connect a workload to cloud services are not.

What you have today Why it is tied to that cloud What a move takes
Deployments, StatefulSets, and CronJobs Standard Kubernetes API objects Copy manifests; adjust resource requests, node selectors, and tolerations that reference cloud-specific labels such as instance types or node groups
Container images in Amazon ECR, Artifact Registry, or Azure Container Registry Nodes pull images using that cloud’s IAM identity Grant the new environment pull access with registry credentials, or replicate images to a registry it can reach
ConfigMaps and Secrets Standard API objects, but values synced from a cloud secrets manager through External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI Driver depend on that cloud Point the sync at a secrets store the new environment can reach, or move values to the new platform’s secrets manager, without exporting plaintext Secrets
Ingress and load balancers AWS Load Balancer Controller creates ALBs; GKE creates Google load balancers from Gateway resources; Application Gateway for Containers is Azure’s managed L7 ingress Replace provider-specific annotations and controllers with the new platform’s ingress or Gateway API model; reissue TLS certificates held in the provider’s certificate service
Pod identity (EKS Pod Identity or IRSA, GKE Workload Identity Federation, AKS workload identity) Each maps a Kubernetes service account to that cloud’s IAM system Re-create identity bindings in the target cloud or use a cross-cloud identity layer
Persistent volumes An EBS volume and its instance must be in the same AZ; a zonal Persistent Disk is accessible only within one zone. Block volumes belong to one cloud. Copy data with file-level backups or database replication, since EBS and Persistent Disk snapshots restore only in their own cloud, or move it to a managed or replicated database first
Logging, metrics, and tracing CloudWatch Container Insights, Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, and Azure Monitor use each cloud’s agents and backends Move to OpenTelemetry or Prometheus-compatible collectors, or the target platform’s built-in observability, and rebuild dashboards and alerts
Network policies and private connectivity NetworkPolicy enforcement depends on the CNI, and AWS PrivateLink, Google Private Service Connect, and Azure Private Link are cloud-specific Re-create policies for the target CNI or platform; re-establish private paths and IP allowlists to databases and third-party services
Helm charts Portable if templates do not hard-code cloud-specific resources Audit templates for provider-specific storage classes, annotations, and service types
Operators and CRDs Portable unless they manage cloud resources, as AWS Controllers for Kubernetes, Google Config Connector, and Azure Service Operator do Test each operator on the target platform; replace operators that manage one cloud’s resources with the target cloud’s equivalent
GitOps with Argo CD Argo CD itself is portable; the manifests it deploys may not be Update repo manifests to target the new cluster; adjust secrets and image registries
Version upgrades Each provider sets its own support windows and upgrade mechanics Adopt the target platform’s upgrade cadence and tooling; plan for different extended-support terms

The safest approach is to move in steps. Set up workload identity in the target environment first and start replicating data early, because data takes longest to copy and its final cutover needs a write freeze or a replica promotion. Run old and new environments side by side behind weighted DNS records, with TTLs lowered well before cutover, so you can shift traffic gradually and roll back. Cut over one service, or one group of tightly coupled services, at a time, since calls between clouds add latency and egress charges, and budget for running both environments during the overlap. Decommission the old cluster only after the last service is stable and traffic to it has drained.

How do you choose an alternative to managed Kubernetes?

Five questions narrow the choice.

  1. Why are you leaving? Cost, operations work, lock-in, and control each point to a different category of alternative.
  2. Do you need the Kubernetes API, operators, or CRDs? If your CI/CD, observability, and deployment tooling depends on the Kubernetes API, eliminate serverless containers and non-Kubernetes orchestrators.
  3. How many clouds or regions do you need? Managed modes and serverless containers stay on one cloud, a platform that removes cluster operations works in one region as well as many, and a multi-cloud team needs a platform that spans providers.
  4. Who will run upgrades? If you do not have a platform team, choose an option that handles the upgrade cycle for you.
  5. Where does your data live? Persistent volumes and managed databases are the hardest things to move. Start your decision from the data layer.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security.

Control Plane is based on Kubernetes, works without in-depth Kubernetes knowledge, and augments and extends clusters you already run. Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s identity for workloads, creates an IAM role, GCP service account, or Azure managed identity in your own account, so no long-lived AWS, GCP, or Azure keys sit in your code.

CPLN BYOK, Control Plane’s bring-your-own-Kubernetes option, registers a cluster you already run as a location in a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC). It supports the three most recent Kubernetes minor releases and brings its own Istio-based service mesh. This lets a team keep an existing EKS, GKE, or AKS cluster in the same GVC as Control Plane’s cloud regions during a migration, so you can move services one at a time without a hard cutover. During the move, cpln convert maps Secrets to secrets, ConfigMaps to dictionary secrets, PersistentVolumeClaims to volume sets, and Ingresses to domains, and Universal Cloud Identity takes the place of pod identity bindings. Data on the old volumes is copied separately.

Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), Control Plane’s service that provisions and operates clusters for you, handles cluster creation, upgrades, and scaling across cloud platforms and private environments and is CNCF certified.

Workload types cover most production patterns: serverless (request-driven, scales to zero), standard (long-running services), stateful (stable per-replica identity and persistent storage), cron, and vm (a KubeVirt-backed virtual machine). Each workload gets a canonical endpoint, Control Plane’s per-workload HTTPS URL that uses DNS to route clients to the nearest healthy location.

cpln helm deploys Control Plane resources from Helm charts as versioned releases with rollback. The Control Plane Kubernetes Operator manages Control Plane resources from a Kubernetes cluster through CRDs, enabling GitOps with Argo CD. Control Plane’s Template Catalog installs over 80 open-source projects, including PostgreSQL, Redis, and Kafka, into a GVC as versioned releases you can upgrade or roll back.

Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to a workload running at least two replicas across at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. Teams that want the benefits of Kubernetes without a platform team run production workloads in one region or across several clouds without owning the cluster lifecycle.

FAQ

Common questions from teams evaluating a move off managed Kubernetes.

What are the best alternatives to managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS)?

Control Plane is the strongest fit for teams leaving because of operations work, on one cloud or several, because it handles Day 2 operations including autoscaling, observability, and security, takes the cluster lifecycle off your team, and removes the tie to one provider. Managed modes like EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot, and AKS Automatic reduce node work for teams staying on one cloud. Serverless containers like Amazon ECS with Fargate, Google Cloud Run, and Azure Container Apps remove the Kubernetes API from your team’s work but lock you to one provider. Smaller managed Kubernetes providers like DigitalOcean, Linode, Civo, and OVHcloud lower the control plane fee. Self-managed distributions like K3s and Talos Linux give full control. Nomad and Docker Swarm mode suit teams that do not need the Kubernetes API.

What are the best managed Kubernetes providers?

Control Plane operates the Kubernetes clusters behind its AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure locations, provisions and operates CNCF-certified clusters for you on your infrastructure through Managed Kubernetes, and joins clusters you already run through CPLN BYOK. Amazon EKS, Google GKE, and Azure AKS remain the largest providers with the broadest service ecosystems. DigitalOcean Kubernetes, Linode Kubernetes Engine, Civo, and OVHcloud offer lower-cost control planes for teams that want Kubernetes without hyperscaler pricing. The comparison of the top managed Kubernetes services covers the major providers in more detail.

Is EKS Auto Mode or GKE Autopilot an alternative to managed Kubernetes?

No. They are managed modes of EKS and GKE, so they reduce work inside managed Kubernetes and keep you on it. They take over node patching and scaling, and GKE Autopilot also runs cluster upgrades, but you still run a Kubernetes cluster on a single cloud with that cloud’s identity, ingress, and storage systems. They reduce operations work without addressing lock-in or multi-cloud requirements. On Control Plane’s built-in locations, Control Plane operates the clusters, so your team does not start or schedule Kubernetes version upgrades, in one region or across clouds.

How much does it cost to run EKS, GKE, or AKS?

EKS and GKE both charge $0.10 per cluster per hour in standard support. EKS charges $0.60 per cluster per hour in extended support, and GKE charges the same for clusters on its Extended channel once their version leaves standard support. GKE offers a free-tier credit covering one Autopilot or zonal Standard cluster. AKS offers a Free tier with no financially backed SLA, which Microsoft recommends for clusters under 10 nodes, a Standard tier with an uptime SLA, and a Premium tier required for Long Term Support. The cluster fee is a small part of the bill. Compute, storage, networking, observability, and engineering time for upgrades and security make up most of the total.

What is the cheapest alternative to EKS?

Control Plane is the strongest option when total cost includes staff time: it takes cluster upgrades and node management off your team, and Control Plane says customers see 30 to 50 percent lower compute costs compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. For the lowest control plane fee while keeping your own Kubernetes operations, DigitalOcean Kubernetes, Linode Kubernetes Engine, Civo, and OVHcloud all include the control plane at no cost or at a lower rate than EKS. DigitalOcean charges $40 per month for a high-availability control plane, Linode’s HA control plane starts at $60 per month depending on region, Civo offers an always-free control plane, and OVHcloud has a free plan. Compute costs and staff time for ongoing operations decide total cost, so the cheapest control plane is not always the cheapest overall.

Can I keep my Helm charts and operators if I leave EKS?

Yes, in most cases. Helm charts that produce standard Kubernetes objects move to another Kubernetes provider with changes only where templates reference cloud-specific storage classes, annotations, or service types. On Control Plane, cpln convert converts Kubernetes manifests into Control Plane resources, and cpln helm installs charts whose templates define Control Plane resources as versioned releases with rollback. Operators and CRDs that extend the Kubernetes API run on a Kubernetes cluster, which can be a cluster you join through CPLN BYOK or a Managed Kubernetes cluster that Control Plane operates on your infrastructure.

How do I migrate from EKS to another platform?

Start by inventorying AWS-specific dependencies: EKS Pod Identity or IRSA bindings, AWS Load Balancer Controller annotations, EBS-backed persistent volumes, images in Amazon ECR, and references to AWS services such as Secrets Manager or RDS. Set up identity in the new environment and start replicating data early, since data takes longest to move. Run the old EKS cluster and the new environment side by side behind weighted DNS with low TTLs, shift traffic service by service, and decommission the old cluster only after every service is validated. On Control Plane, CPLN BYOK can register the EKS cluster as a location in the same GVC as Control Plane’s regions while cpln convert turns each service’s manifests into workloads, and Universal Cloud Identity replaces Pod Identity or IRSA bindings with an IAM role in your AWS account.

What is the best alternative to EKS for running across multiple clouds?

Control Plane is the best fit. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, can span AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions, and a workload runs in every location of its GVC. CPLN BYOK lets you register an existing EKS cluster as a location in the same GVC, so you can migrate incrementally. Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s identity for workloads, creates the IAM role, GCP service account, or Azure managed identity in each cloud account, so a workload reaches services on all three with no long-lived keys in its code.

How does Control Plane compare to EKS, GKE, and AKS?

EKS, GKE, and AKS each manage a Kubernetes control plane on a single cloud and leave node operations, upgrade planning, identity, ingress, and security configuration to your team. Their managed modes take over node operations within that cloud, and GKE Autopilot and AKS Automatic also run version upgrades; identity, ingress, and VPC configuration stay with your team. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations, including autoscaling, observability, and security, on Kubernetes clusters it orchestrates in one region or across multiple clouds. Its 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas across at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers.

Talk to the Control Plane team to see how Control Plane takes over your cluster operations, or sign up free and deploy your first workload today.

title: Show DEV: MovieVerse — A Movie Discovery App I Built With React 19 and the TMDB API
description:
Live demo: https://film2027.netlify.app
Source code: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI/movieverse

MovieVerse is my flagship learning project — the app I built to go from knowing React to actually shipping something real with it. It is also the project I show recruiters when they ask what I can build.

What it does

  • Trending movies on the home page, loaded from the TMDB API
  • Search for any movie by title
  • Filters — release year and sorting (popularity, rating, date)
  • Detail pages for every movie, with full navigation via React Router
  • Favorites — save the movies you want to watch later
  • Dark mode and skeleton loaders while content is loading
  • Graceful error handling — when the TMDB API rate-limits, the app says so plainly instead of breaking

The stack

React 19, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, and the TMDB API. Deployed on Netlify.

What building it taught me

React Router in practice. Routing a real app with detail pages and filters is very different from reading about routes. (I wrote about the routing part in detail here: https://dev.to/wahib_el_khadiri_0/i-turned-a-single-page-react-site-into-a-real-multi-page-app-with-react-router-1n6b)

TypeScript catches the bugs you don't see. Typing the API responses forced me to understand the data shape instead of guessing — and the compiler caught mistakes before users did.

A real API means real failure modes. Loading states, empty results, rate limits, network errors — half the work of a "simple" movie app is handling everything that can go wrong between your UI and someone else's server. The skeleton loaders and the error messages are features, not polish.

Ship it, then show it. The demo is live, the code is public, and I'd rather get honest feedback on a real app than keep a perfect project on my laptop.

Try it, break it

Open the demo, search for a movie, save a favorite, switch to dark mode. If something breaks or feels wrong, tell me in the comments — that's exactly the feedback I'm here for. And if you're a junior dev building your own first real project: pick one API you like and build the whole thing around it. You learn more from one shipped app than from ten tutorials.

I'm Wahib El Khadiri, a junior full-stack developer from Kénitra, Morocco. I build with React, Node.js and Laravel, contribute to open source, and teach React in Darija on YouTube. Portfolio: https://wahib-portfolio.netlify.app — GitHub: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI

title: Object Storage for Browser Direct Uploads: Presigned URLs and Tenant Isolation
description:
Short answer: use private object storage with short-lived presigned URLs, keep tenant metadata in your database, and make multipart uploads the default for large media. For an edtech SaaS serving US and EU users, the least complicated choice is the provider whose region, CORS policy, and isolation model you can verify before launch. A single HTTP surface can reduce integration glue, but it cannot remove those checks.

The boundary that keeps your app out of the data path

The browser should upload bytes directly to storage. Your Node.js API authenticates the user, checks the tenant and object key, asks storage for a presigned upload URL, and returns that short-lived URL. The browser then sends the file to storage. Your app receives a completion event or records the object after a successful upload; it never becomes a media proxy.

That boundary matters for classroom video and large lesson recordings. A proxy ties bandwidth, timeout behavior, and failure recovery to your application fleet. Direct upload makes the storage service own those bytes while your database owns the facts about them: tenant ID, object key, course, uploader, size, and state.

This is where Infrai can fit early: its storage handoff uses one REST contract, so a Node.js service can call it with plain HTTP while the rest of a backend stays behind the same key.

The practical win is boring and useful: one REST API, one key, and no SDK install for this handoff. Any runtime that can send HTTPS can use the same contract, which keeps a small upload service from accumulating a second client library every time the product adds a backend capability. Infrai covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. The API is genuinely self-describing, with a public discovery surface and runnable examples, so the contract is inspectable before a key is issued.

Keep buckets private. Public-read URLs are unavailable in the storage capability described here, so this is not a fit for a permanent public file host, static website hosting, or an image CDN. Serve a fresh presigned download URL when an authorized viewer needs a file.

How should a SaaS app use presigned URLs for browser uploads?

Start with a tenant-scoped key such as tenant_42/course_8/lesson_3/video.mp4. The object key is not an authorization system by itself. Your API must derive or validate it from the authenticated tenant, and the database row should be the source of truth for ownership. Server-side metadata queries are limited: object listing supports prefix filtering, not arbitrary metadata search.

The API surface can stay small. The following TypeScript example shows the handoff shape with an explicit method and bearer token. In production, send the exact request fields documented by the discovery schema for your chosen expiry and content type; do not let a browser choose a bucket or tenant prefix. Before shipping, I would trace one complete upload on paper: the API authenticates a teacher, maps the request to tenant_42, writes an upload-intent row, issues a URL, and then waits for the browser's transfer result. If the browser retries, the object key remains stable and the database state machine decides whether the retry is allowed. If a student from another tenant guesses that key, the API refuses to mint a URL. That sequence is longer than a demo, but it exposes the exact place where isolation lives and prevents storage policy from being mistaken for application authorization.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function presignUpload(bucket: string, key: string) {
  const response = await fetch(
    `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/${bucket}/${key}`,
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({}),
    },
  );

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const waitMs = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "2") * 1000;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
    return presignUpload(bucket, key);
  }
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Presign failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  return response.json();
}

The retry is deliberately slow and bounded by your normal request deadline. For a create or publish operation, add an idempotency key; presigning itself should not be treated as proof that an upload completed. I started out assuming a storage listing could replace a media table. It cannot. Record the upload intent before issuing the URL, then mark it complete only after you have verified the object.

For a 2 GB lecture recording, use multipart upload. Create an upload, presign each part, upload parts from the browser, and complete the upload. A dropped connection then costs one part, not the whole file. Keep a cleanup job for abandoned multipart uploads because there is no automatic rule for deleting unfinished fragments.

Small files are different.

Which option fits isolation, regions, and setup?

There is no universal “best” bucket. The right answer depends on who controls tenant policy, where bytes must live, and how much provider-specific code you will carry.

Option Where it tends to fit Tenant-isolation trade-off
AWS S3 Teams that need the broadest mature storage controls and a large regional catalog Maximum policy surface also means more configuration and IAM to review
Cloudflare R2 Teams already operating at the Cloudflare edge and wanting an S3-compatible workflow Check regional and compliance requirements against your US/EU contract
Firebase Cloud Storage Mobile/web teams already using Firebase auth and rules Rules are convenient inside Firebase; a separate Node.js control plane adds another boundary
Infrai storage A SaaS that wants storage plus other backend modules behind one HTTP contract Validate CORS, region placement, and retention requirements before committing

Infrai's concrete advantage here is breadth behind a simple surface: one REST API and one key can cover storage alongside other backend capabilities, so adding a module does not require another SDK and credential flow. Its public discovery endpoint exposes request and response schemas with runnable examples, which is useful when I'm trying to get from zero to a first call without a configuration maze. Start by checking the storage discovery entry.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the storage handoff when your team values one HTTP contract and can keep tenant records and policy decisions in its own API and database. That is a developer-experience choice, not a claim that it wins every region or compliance review.

Where the simpler surface is the wrong tool

The catch is browser CORS control. There is no independent self-serve CORS route for this capability, so a flow that requires custom bucket CORS rules must validate compatibility first. A specialist with mature, user-managed CORS and policy tooling is safer when that control is non-negotiable.

Choose direct AWS S3 when you need object versioning, Object Lock (WORM), strict If-Match concurrency, cross-region replication, or bulk migration tooling. Those are explicit capability boundaries here, not small switches to flip. Firebase remains a sensible pick when Firebase Auth and Security Rules are already the center of your app. Your mileage may vary for US/EU residency: confirm the actual storage region and contract terms rather than inferring them from an API hostname.

Lifecycle policies have a one-day minimum, and there is no hourly expiry. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes. Plan a real billing path before production media lands in a bucket.

A decision rule you can test in one afternoon

Create two test tenants in the target US and EU deployment plan. Verify that tenant A cannot obtain a URL for tenant B's key, that an expired URL is rejected, and that a resumed multipart upload does not restart completed parts. Exercise a browser from the real origins you will ship; CORS behavior is part of the product, not a post-launch detail.

Then measure time-to-first-call, the number of credentials in CI, and the amount of provider-specific code in your upload service. I care about those numbers because they predict maintenance more reliably than a feature checklist. If the isolation tests pass and the single-contract benefit removes meaningful glue, Infrai is a reasonable fit. If a missing control blocks a requirement, pick the specialist and keep the boundary the same: your app authorizes, the browser transfers, and private storage holds the bytes.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://firebase.google.com/docs/storage
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS

Further reading

  • https://docs.infrai.cc

title: AWS Sign-In introduces configurable Sign-in duration of up to 90 days
description:
AWS Sign-In now enables developers and AI agents to stay authenticated for up to 90 days without frequent sign-ins or consent prompts. With this launch, administrators can configure Sign-in duration, which controls how long an OAuth Sign-in session remains active, for individual IAM users and roles.

This capability reduces authentication interruptions for long-running workflows and provides a more secure alternative to static access keys by using short-lived, renewable credentials. Existing session duration limits remain unchanged unless administrators explicitly configure longer durations.

Sign-In Duration supports AWS CLI (aws login), AWS MCP Server, and other OAuth-enabled applications. It does not affect AWS Management Console sessions. Customers can configure the setting using the IAM console, AWS CLI, or IAM API in all AWS commercial Regions.

To learn more, see the AWS Sign-In session management User Guide, Configure Sign-In duration on Role User Guide, Condition Key User Guide

title: new row violates check constraint on documents.source
description:
The short version

The documents table's source column had a CHECK constraint, documents_source_check, allowing only 'upload' and 'dropbox'. But the automated document-archiving feature inserts quote/invoice/application/receipt snapshots with source: 'system', and the Anyflow import feature inserts signed contracts with source: 'anyflow'. Neither value was allowed.

The result: the file upload to storage succeeded every single time, while the insert into the documents table failed every single time, with new row for relation "documents" violates check constraint "documents_source_check". Not one row of the automated document vault had ever been successfully created.

A failure designed to be swallowed silently

upsertDocument in document-archive.ts uploads the file to storage first, then upserts the documents row:

async function upsertDocument(
  admin: AdminClient,
  opts: { /* ... */ source: "system" | "anyflow"; /* ... */ }
): Promise<ArchiveResult> {
  const { error: upErr } = await admin.storage
    .from(BUCKET)
    .upload(opts.storagePath, opts.bytes, { contentType: opts.mimeType, upsert: true });
  if (upErr) return { ok: false, reason: `storage: ${upErr.message}` };

  // ...check for an existing row by external_ref...

  const { data: inserted, error } = await admin
    .from("documents")
    .insert({ ...fields, created_by: null })
    .select("id")
    .single();
  if (error) {
    // 23505 (uq_documents_external race) is handled separately above
    // ...
    return { ok: false, reason: `insert: ${error.message}` };
  }
  return { ok: true, documentId: inserted.id };
}

A CHECK violation (Postgres error code 23514) doesn't match the 23505 unique-violation race handled just above it, so it falls straight through to { ok: false, reason: "insert: new row for relation \"documents\" violates check constraint \"documents_source_check\"" }.

The function that calls this, archiveContractDocument, has a comment stating the intent directly:

/**
 * Automatically archives generated documents (quote/invoice/application/receipt)
 * to the document vault.
 * ...
 * - Callers (the signature webhook, invoice issuance) must not break, so every
 *   failure — including exceptions — is returned as an ArchiveResult instead of thrown.
 * ...
 */

archiveExternalDocument, which handles external imports, carries the same stated intent:

/**
 * Archives a signed file imported from outside (e.g. an Anyflow-signed contract)
 * to the document vault.
 * ...
 * - Failures are returned as an ArchiveResult so the caller (the webhook) is not broken.
 */

This was not an accident — it was the intended design. A document-archiving failure should never block the main flow, such as a payment-state transition or signature confirmation. Choosing to return a result object instead of throwing is reasonable on its own. The problem is that nothing downstream was actually reading that ArchiveResult.

Nobody was checking .ok

invoice-issue.ts looked like this:

// Auto-archive the invoice snapshot to the document vault.
// Runs before checking if the email can be sent, so the issued document is
// kept even without a registered email. Idempotent — failures are ignored.
const archived = await archiveContractDocument({ contractId, kind: "invoice" });

// ...resolve recipient...

const sent = await sendEmail({
  // ...
  text: [
    // ...
    "pdf" in archived && archived.pdf != null
      ? "The invoice (PDF) is attached to this email. ..."
      : "You can view and save the invoice as a PDF here (no login required):",
    // ...
  ].join("\n"),
  ...("pdf" in archived && archived.pdf != null
    ? { attachments: [{ filename: "invoice.pdf", content: archived.pdf }] }
    : {}),
});

Nowhere in the file is archived.ok ever read. Only archived.pdf (the PDF bytes for the email attachment) is used. Since dryRun isn't set, archiveContractDocument does attempt the real storage and DB writes, but PDF generation itself doesn't depend on whether the documents insert succeeded — so the email-sending path has no way to notice the archive is failing. Invoices kept issuing and sending normally while the document vault stayed empty underneath them.

The signing flow in contract-signed.ts has the same pattern, and says so in its own comment:

// 2b. Auto-archive the application snapshot to the document vault (ops spec §1).
//     A signature is frozen as proof of consent. Non-kimiteras contract types
//     are skipped inside archiveContractDocument. Idempotent — failures are swallowed.
try {
  const r = await archiveContractDocument({ contractId, kind: "application" });
  if (!r.ok) {
    console.error("[contract-signed] application archive failed:", r.reason);
  } else if (!r.skipped) {
    // ...signature evidence-anchor processing...
  }
}

This path does log the failure with console.error, but takes no further action. Without active log monitoring, this line filling up with CHECK violations never reaches anyone.

The fix was just widening the constraint

The fix, in migration 0074, only added 'system' and 'anyflow' to documents_source_check's allowed values:

alter table public.documents drop constraint if exists documents_source_check;
alter table public.documents add constraint documents_source_check
  check (source = any (array['upload'::text, 'dropbox'::text, 'system'::text, 'anyflow'::text]));

It's an additive, idempotent migration (drop constraint if exists then add constraint); since every existing row used 'upload', they all still satisfy the new constraint. No application code changed — upsertDocument and invoice-issue.ts were already correct code that only needed the constraint to let their rows through.

The hidden cost of "don't break the main flow"

Swallowing failures silently so the main flow never breaks is a reasonable design choice on its own. In fact, the payment-transition and signature-confirmation flows never stopped once, even while the CHECK violation went unfixed. The cost is that the assumption "the archive must be succeeding" accumulated for months with nothing ever verifying it. Multiple callers that never check archived.ok can't be caught by console.error logging alone — in practice, what surfaced this was literally counting the rows in the document vault. Choosing to swallow failures silently only works if the swallowed outcome (the count of ok: false results) is made visible somewhere else.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.

title: The Subset Font That Turned My Arabic Text Into Empty Boxes
description:
I was rendering product images for my shop: Arabic text, the brand name "STYLE POINT", and prices. Some words came out fine. Others came out as empty boxes. No error, no warning — just tofu where letters should be.

It took me a while to realize the bug wasn't in my code at all. It was in the font file.

The symptom: some words render, some don't

The broken words had something in common, but it wasn't obvious at first. "STYLE POINT" showed as boxes. Prices (digits) showed as boxes. The Arabic word "تشكيلة" showed as boxes — while other Arabic words rendered perfectly.

Three different kinds of text, all broken. That pattern was the clue: the problem wasn't the text, the layout, or the rendering library. It was the font itself.

The cause: a subset font

The font I was using, Cairo-Bold in .woff2 format, was a subset. A subset font is a font file with most glyphs stripped out to make it smaller — it only contains the characters the person who built it thought you'd need.

This one was missing:

  • Latin capital letters (so "STYLE POINT" became boxes)
  • Digits (so prices became boxes)
  • The Arabic letter ة in its final form (U+FE93) — so words like "تشكيلة" broke, even though other Arabic words were fine

That last one is the cruelest kind of font bug: it doesn't break all Arabic, just the words that happen to end in ة. Everything looks fine until exactly the wrong word shows up.

The fix: build one full font, and let the shaper do its job

I fixed it in two steps.

First, I built a complete font. Using fontTools, I merged the full Arabic and Latin versions of Cairo Bold (weight 700) into a single file, Cairo-Bold-full.ttf. One font file, every glyph I need, no more guessing which characters survived the subsetting.

Second, I stopped reshaping Arabic text by hand. I had been using a reshaping library to connect Arabic letters before drawing. I switched to letting Pillow do it natively, with proper shaping support (raqm/harfbuzz) and right-to-left direction:

from PIL import ImageFont, ImageDraw

font = ImageFont.truetype("Cairo-Bold-full.ttf", 84)
draw.text((x, y), "تشكيلة STYLE POINT 250",
          font=font, fill="white",
          direction="rtl", language="ar")

With the full font and native shaping, everything renders: Arabic, Latin capitals, digits, mixed text on the same line.

The lesson I now apply everywhere

Two rules I never break anymore:

  1. Never trust a font you didn't verify. A font file that works for your test words can still be missing the exact glyphs your real content needs. Check the full font, not the demo.
  2. Never rely on local() for Arabic fonts. In my YouTube pipeline I had the same class of bug: the system font wasn't guaranteed to exist. Now I always bundle a real Arabic .woff2 with @font-face (Cairo Bold for titles) — the font ships with the project, or it doesn't ship at all.

The bug looked like a rendering problem. It was a supply-chain problem: the asset I depended on was incomplete, and nothing told me so. The empty boxes were the only warning I got — and honestly, I was lucky to get even that.
