title: Node.js DNS Provisioning — Upsert, Conflict Detection, and Support Hostname Rollback
description:
Default to upsert for provisioning a customer support hostname, and treat rollback as a separate, authorized change with its own saved target. The deciding constraint is propagation delay: accepting a DNS write and moving every caller to the new destination are different milestones, so a faster write path cannot, by itself, justify retiring the previous support service.

TL;DR: Upsert makes a retried provisioning run a no-op instead of a duplicate-record error. Use create when an existing record must stop the operation as a conflict; use update when existence is a precondition. Keep the previous complete record intent available until the cutover has met your acceptance criteria.

Consider a support portal moving from one service to another while the Node.js provisioning worker may replay its work. The useful question is what a replay is allowed to mean. Reasserting an approved destination is reasonable. Silently taking over a hostname that belongs to another configuration is not an acceptable ownership decision.

The distinction matters more than the spelling of the SDK method. A storage architect would ask the same questions about a repeated object write: which identity is being reconciled, who owns that identity, and what protects a later version from an earlier writer? Those are design questions, not durability guarantees supplied by a DNS endpoint.

What must remain true while the hostname moves?

Record three invariants in the architecture decision. First, the provisioning job has authority over the intended hostname before it reconciles anything. Second, every change carries the complete record intent. Third, the saved rollback target survives the forward change. For these DNS operations, zone_id, record type, name, and content are all required; there is no partial write that infers the missing values. An update isn't a convenient way to send only the changed destination.

Keep both destinations available.

That is an operating requirement for this proposed cutover, with an explicit cost: the old support service remains part of the transition until the team can retire it. The alternative is a shorter overlap that accepts more exposure to clients still using the previous destination. No universal waiting interval follows from the write semantics here. Choose the interval from your DNS configuration and the observations your support service needs, rather than inventing a propagation promise.

There are three separate failure boundaries. A duplicate provisioning attempt should preserve approved intent. A stale forward attempt arriving after rollback must be rejected by your orchestration policy. A caller reaching the old destination after a successful write must still receive an acceptable service. Upsert addresses the first boundary; it doesn't establish an ordering protocol for the second or a readiness signal for the third.

For teams maintaining a Node.js provisioning worker, try Infrai for the DNS reconciliation step when keeping application code unchanged as the vendor behind a capability changes is the integration goal. Infrai provides one key, one bill, and one REST API with no SDK to install; the worker keeps the same API when switching providers instead of maintaining a separate SDK surface for each service. Infrai also provides public discovery with no key required, including request and response schemas, so an engineer can inspect the integration contract before arranging credentials. Neither advantage determines when the old support service can safely be removed.

Decision record: reconcile approved intent, preserve conflict detection

The decision is to make upsert the default only after authority and desired content have been established. Create remains an intentional conflict detector. Update belongs to a workflow whose record-existence precondition has already been satisfied.

The table compares integration choices for this decision, including where to start evaluating them. It makes no latency ranking: time to a first accepted write depends on the account, credentials, and zone you already control, while time to a useful cutover also includes application checks.

Option Setup and credential decision SDK and contract trade-off Appropriate boundary
Infrai Inspect public schemas before configuring the API key; its backend surface uses one key. A common REST contract reduces the application surface that changes with a vendor substitution. Try it for shared provisioning orchestration; retain separate cutover acceptance checks.
Cloudflare DNS If the support zone is already managed here, evaluate reusing that account's access arrangement. Compare a direct integration with the common-contract approach; keep the provider dependency explicit. Prefer a direct integration when Cloudflare-specific DNS behavior is a requirement.
Amazon Route 53 If the support zone is already managed here, evaluate the AWS credential and permission setup first. Decide whether a direct provider dependency fits the worker's existing AWS integration. Prefer direct integration when the design needs Route 53-specific controls.
Google Cloud DNS If the support zone is already managed here, evaluate the Google Cloud credential and permission setup first. Check whether another abstraction reduces work for an already Google Cloud-oriented worker. Prefer direct integration when Google Cloud DNS-specific controls drive the design.

These are alternatives, not interchangeable promises. Before selecting a direct provider, check its record identity and mutation semantics in its own documentation; an operation with a familiar name is insufficient evidence that replaying it has the same effect. The comparison leaves provider-specific conflict behavior unranked because this decision doesn't establish equivalence between those APIs.

Credential count is a poor standalone metric.

A common key reduces credential sprawl across integrations, but its permissions still need deliberate handling. Conversely, an existing direct-provider integration may have less setup work than introducing a new service. The relevant measure is how many contracts and access arrangements this particular worker must own, especially if a rollback needs to be executed by someone who didn't build the original integration.

Inspect the contract before putting a write on the critical path

The smallest safe integration example queries discovery and identifies the upsert capability by its published path. It uses Python's standard library, explicitly sets the method, checks HTTP failures, and retries rate limits. The discovery surface is public and requires no credential; this read-only example therefore needs no environment setup or API key. It prints the matching capability entry, rather than inventing an unverified write payload.

import json
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    if value is None:
        return 2 ** attempt
    try:
        return max(0.0, float(value))
    except ValueError:
        retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
        return max(
            0.0, (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
        )


def discover():
    request = Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
        headers={"Accept": "application/json"},
        method="GET",
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            delay = retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            time.sleep(max(2 ** attempt, delay))
    raise RuntimeError("Discovery retry budget exhausted")


manifest = discover()
matches = [
    capability for capability in manifest["capabilities"]
    if capability["path"] == "/v1/dns/record/upsert"
]
if len(matches) != 1:
    raise RuntimeError("Expected one upsert capability")
print(json.dumps(matches[0], indent=2))

This is contract inspection, not a cutover. The 30-second timeout and four-attempt retry budget are example client choices, not service limits or latency claims. The mutation adapter should take its path from discovery and its request fields from the capability schema. For authenticated writes, read the key from the environment and send Bearer authorization; keep error handling at least as explicit as in this read-only probe.

Before dispatching a mutation, persist the previous approved configuration and the proposed complete record intent. For an illustrative support hostname, that means retaining the old CNAME destination alongside the proposed new destination, together with the zone and name; those values must come from the actual configuration, rather than from a sample hostname copied into a worker. Printing a request or receiving a success response is not persistence of the rollback target.

Retries become subtle here. An identical upsert can be harmless while a delayed upsert containing an obsolete destination is harmful. Give the orchestration layer a way to reject stale intent before dispatch, and coordinate active workers when approving rollback. A generation check alone is insufficient if an already-dispatched forward write can still arrive afterward. Treat cancellation, in-flight work, and subsequent reconciliation as part of the rollback design.

Save intent first.

Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; request deduplication and desired-state reconciliation solve different problems. Reuse a request identity for retries of one approved mutation, and distinguish a new rollback mutation from that forward action. Don't turn the window into a claim that obsolete work remains safe forever. A fresh transport request can still contain stale application intent.

Rejected default: create on every provisioning attempt

Create is rejected as the default because a replay should not become a duplicate-record error merely because the first attempt already established the desired record. Update is also a poor onboarding default: it requires the record to exist. Neither choice supplies the ordinary reconciliation behavior that provisioning needs.

Create still has a valid and valuable use case. If an existing customer support hostname means another team configured it and automation must stop, treating presence as a conflict is exactly the desired behavior. Don't follow that conflict with an automatic switch to upsert; doing so would erase the ownership boundary that justified create in the first place. Resolve authority first.

The resulting decision rule is narrow: choose upsert for approved repeatable provisioning, create for mandatory conflict detection, and update for an established record whose existence is required. Choose a specialist or direct provider when its particular DNS controls are part of the requirement. Keep rollback intent and cutover acceptance in your own orchestration, because successful reconciliation alone cannot certify that every customer has reached the new support service.

References

  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Google Cloud DNS documentation

If the common-contract boundary fits your provisioning worker, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: I Built My First Real Website With React From Scratch
description:
In my earlier episodes, I learned React piece by piece — components, props, state. But everything was small examples. So I took the next step: I built a complete, real website — a landing page for a digital agency — and I want to show you exactly how. This is the written companion to my YouTube episode (React from Scratch #5, in Moroccan Darija): https://youtu.be/UCKbmOi8l4k

1. Start a new project, then clean it up

Create a fresh React project and run it locally to confirm everything works. Then delete the demo content you don't need and keep only the base you'll build on.

One thing to get right from the start: in React, you don't write the whole website in one file. You split it into small parts, and each part has one clear responsibility. That habit is what saves you later, when the project grows.

2. The Header

The header is the part at the top: the agency logo and the navigation links (Home, Services, Contact).

I made it its own component, in its own file — not inside the main file. Why? Because if I later want to change the header's color, add a link, or reuse the same header on other pages, the work is easy and organized.

Add some styling: logo on one side, links on the other, proper spacing — and the header is done.

3. The Hero section

This is the first thing a visitor sees after the header, so it has to be clear: a big title (something like "We help you build a professional digital presence"), a short description of what the agency does, a button ("Discover our services"), and an illustration.

The button shouldn't be decoration. I linked it to the Services section, so clicking it takes the visitor straight there.

Keep the hero simple: one clear title, one short description, one button that points to the next step. Don't overload it with text.

4. The Services section — where components prove their worth

Now the real lesson. The agency has three services: website design, app development, and digital solutions. Each one has a title, a short description, and the same card layout.

Should I write the same code three times? I could — but that's not organized. Instead, I built ONE ServiceCard component and used it three times, each time passing a different title and description as props.

<ServiceCard
  title="Website Design"
  description="Modern, fast websites that fit your business."
/>
<ServiceCard
  title="App Development"
  description="Mobile and web apps built to solve real problems."
/>
<ServiceCard
  title="Digital Solutions"
  description="Tools and strategies that grow your presence online."
/>

If I want to change the design of all the cards, I edit one component. That's the real power of React: reuse the same parts intelligently, without repeating code for no reason.

5. The Footer, and checking the phone

The last part is the footer: the agency name, a short line, and contact information. Then I put all the components together in the main file — Header, Hero, Services, Footer — and the code stays readable, because each part has its own file.

One more thing matters: the website has to work well on a phone. I shrank the screen and checked: the service cards that sat side by side on a computer stack on top of each other on a phone, and the links and buttons still work.

The result

A complete website, built from an empty page: header, hero, services, footer — organized into components, and working on computer and phone.

Your challenge: change the site's colors, add a new section about the agency, and give it its own component. If you can do that on your own, you're starting to understand how real websites are built with React.

In the next article, I take this same website and turn it into a real multi-page site with React Router: https://dev.to/wahib_el_khadiri_0/i-turned-a-single-page-react-site-into-a-real-multi-page-app-with-react-router-1n6b

I'm Wahib El Khadiri, a junior full-stack developer from Kénitra, Morocco. I build with React, Node.js and Laravel, contribute to open source, and teach React in Darija on YouTube. Portfolio: https://wahib-portfolio.netlify.app — GitHub: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI

title: [GUIA AWS CLOUD PRACTITIONER] #04 - ALCANCE GLOBAL
description:
A infraestrutura global da Amazon Web Services (AWS) permite que aplicações e serviços sejam implantados em diferentes partes do mundo, oferecendo recursos para melhorar a disponibilidade, reduzir a latência e atender a requisitos específicos de conformidade e custos.

Neste módulo, vamos explorar os principais componentes dessa infraestrutura, os critérios para escolher uma Região AWS e as ferramentas utilizadas para provisionar e gerenciar recursos.

1. Infraestrutura Global da AWS

A infraestrutura global da AWS é formada por diferentes componentes geográficos, cada um com uma função específica na entrega de serviços em nuvem.

Regiões AWS

As Regiões são áreas geográficas distribuídas pelo mundo que concentram a infraestrutura da AWS. Cada Região é composta por múltiplas Zonas de Disponibilidade.

A escolha da Região ou do conjunto de Regiões onde os recursos serão alocados depende de fatores como:

  • Demanda dos clientes.
  • Custos operacionais e de desenvolvimento.
  • Requisitos de conformidade.
  • Proximidade dos usuários finais.
  • Disponibilidade dos serviços necessários.

Zonas de Disponibilidade (Availability Zones — AZs)

As Zonas de Disponibilidade são locais isolados e independentes dentro de uma Região AWS.

Cada AZ possui infraestrutura própria de alimentação elétrica, rede e conectividade. Uma Zona de Disponibilidade pode ser composta por um ou mais data centers.

A separação entre as AZs permite distribuir recursos e reduzir o impacto de falhas localizadas em uma única zona.

Locais da Borda (Edge Locations)

Os Edge Locations são instalações menores, distribuídas estrategicamente pelo mundo, que armazenam conteúdo em cache próximo dos usuários finais.

Eles permitem entregar conteúdos, como imagens e vídeos, com menor latência, reduzindo a distância que os dados precisam percorrer.

Esses pontos de presença são utilizados pela rede de entrega de conteúdo (CDN) da AWS, principalmente por meio do Amazon CloudFront.

2. Principais Considerações ao Escolher uma Região AWS

A escolha de uma Região AWS deve considerar diferentes aspectos técnicos, legais e financeiros.

2.1. Conformidade

É necessário verificar as leis locais de proteção de dados e os requisitos regulatórios aplicáveis ao país ou à região onde os dados serão armazenados e processados.

Um exemplo é o RGPD (Regulamento Geral de Proteção de Dados), aplicado na União Europeia. Ele estabelece requisitos relacionados à coleta, ao acesso e à exclusão de dados pessoais, incluindo a necessidade de consentimento em determinadas situações.

2.2. Proximidade

A proximidade geográfica entre a Região escolhida e os usuários finais influencia diretamente a latência.

Selecionar uma Região próxima dos usuários reduz o tempo de percurso dos dados e pode melhorar o tempo de resposta das aplicações.

2.3. Disponibilidade de Recursos

Nem todos os serviços e recursos da AWS estão disponíveis em todas as Regiões.

Por isso, antes de escolher uma Região, é importante verificar se ela oferece os serviços necessários para a arquitetura planejada.

Um exemplo são as Regiões AWS GovCloud, que possuem controles específicos de segurança física, operacional e de pessoal para atender a determinados requisitos de agências governamentais dos Estados Unidos.

2.4. Preços

Os custos operacionais podem variar entre as Regiões AWS.

Entre os fatores que influenciam essas diferenças estão:

  • Alíquotas tributárias.
  • Incentivos fiscais locais.
  • Custos operacionais.
  • Leis de soberania de dados, que podem exigir que determinadas informações sejam armazenadas localmente.

Portanto, a Região mais próxima nem sempre será necessariamente a opção de menor custo.

3. Alta Disponibilidade, Agilidade e Elasticidade

Três conceitos importantes para compreender a infraestrutura global e a arquitetura em nuvem são alta disponibilidade, agilidade e elasticidade.

Alta Disponibilidade

É a capacidade de um sistema continuar operando sem interrupções significativas, mesmo diante da falha de componentes individuais.

Na AWS, uma das estratégias para alcançar alta disponibilidade é distribuir recursos entre múltiplas Zonas de Disponibilidade e, quando necessário, entre diferentes Regiões.

Essa distribuição reduz a dependência de uma única localização física.

Agilidade

É a capacidade de adaptar rapidamente a infraestrutura às mudanças nas necessidades do negócio ou do mercado.

A nuvem permite implantar, modificar e ajustar serviços de maneira mais rápida, sem depender exclusivamente da aquisição e instalação de equipamentos físicos.

Elasticidade

É a capacidade de aumentar ou diminuir automaticamente os recursos computacionais conforme a demanda.

Por exemplo, uma aplicação pode ampliar sua capacidade durante um período de grande acesso e reduzi-la quando a demanda diminuir.

4. Elementos-Chave da Infraestrutura Global da AWS

Os três principais elementos apresentados neste módulo são:

Elemento Características Finalidade
Regiões AWS Áreas geográficas compostas por múltiplas Zonas de Disponibilidade Distribuir recursos pelo mundo
Zonas de Disponibilidade (AZs) Locais isolados e independentes dentro de uma Região, compostos por um ou mais data centers Aumentar a disponibilidade e reduzir o impacto de falhas
Edge Locations Pontos de presença distribuídos geograficamente que armazenam conteúdo em cache Entregar conteúdo aos usuários com menor latência

Esses componentes trabalham em conjunto para permitir que aplicações sejam executadas em diferentes localidades e entreguem conteúdo de maneira eficiente aos usuários finais.

5. AWS CloudFormation e Infraestrutura como Código (IaC)

O AWS CloudFormation é um serviço que permite modelar e provisionar recursos da AWS por meio de arquivos de modelo, conhecidos como templates.

Essa abordagem é chamada de Infraestrutura como Código (Infrastructure as Code — IaC).

Em vez de criar e configurar cada recurso manualmente, é possível descrever a infraestrutura desejada em um arquivo e utilizar esse modelo para automatizar sua implantação.

Benefícios do CloudFormation

  • Automação: reduz a necessidade de configurações manuais.
  • Consistência: permite reproduzir configurações padronizadas.
  • Confiabilidade: reduz erros associados à implantação manual.
  • Escalabilidade: facilita a implantação de infraestruturas maiores.
  • Reprodutibilidade: permite utilizar o mesmo modelo em diferentes ambientes e Regiões.

Casos de Uso

O CloudFormation pode ser utilizado em diferentes cenários, como:

  • Automação de implantações em pipelines de CI/CD (DevOps).
  • Provisionamento padronizado de recursos.
  • Implantação de instâncias Amazon EC2.
  • Expansão de aplicações para múltiplas Regiões AWS.

A Infraestrutura como Código facilita o gerenciamento de ambientes complexos, permitindo que a infraestrutura seja versionada, reutilizada e implantada de maneira automatizada.

6. Formas de Interagir com as APIs da AWS

A AWS oferece diferentes maneiras de acessar e gerenciar seus serviços. As principais formas apresentadas são o acesso programático, o Console de Gerenciamento e as ferramentas de Infraestrutura como Código.

6.1. AWS CLI e SDKs — Acesso Programático

O acesso programático é indicado principalmente para desenvolvedores e profissionais técnicos familiarizados com programação e linhas de comando.

AWS CLI (Command Line Interface)

É uma interface de linha de comando que permite executar operações nos serviços AWS por meio de comandos e scripts.

Um exemplo de utilização é a automação de rotinas de backup de volumes Amazon EBS.

AWS SDKs (Software Development Kits)

São bibliotecas que permitem integrar as APIs da AWS diretamente ao código-fonte das aplicações.

Um exemplo é utilizar um SDK para implementar a gravação de arquivos no Amazon S3 a partir de uma aplicação.

6.2. Console de Gerenciamento da AWS

O Console de Gerenciamento da AWS é uma interface gráfica acessada pelo navegador.

É uma alternativa para iniciantes na computação em nuvem ou usuários que preferem gerenciar os serviços sem escrever comandos ou código.

Entre suas possibilidades de utilização estão:

  • Monitoramento visual dos recursos.
  • Consulta a painéis de faturamento e custos.
  • Gerenciamento de serviços por interfaces gráficas.
  • Acesso a serviços como Amazon QuickSight e Amazon Neptune.

6.3. Ferramentas de Infraestrutura como Código

Ferramentas como o AWS CloudFormation permitem descrever a infraestrutura de maneira declarativa e automatizar o provisionamento de ambientes completos.

Em vez de configurar cada recurso individualmente pelo Console, o usuário define o estado desejado em um template, que pode ser utilizado para implantar e reproduzir a infraestrutura.

7. Resumo do Módulo

Neste módulo, vimos como a infraestrutura global da AWS é organizada e quais fatores devem ser considerados ao escolher onde implantar recursos.

Os principais conceitos são:

  • Regiões AWS: áreas geográficas que concentram a infraestrutura da AWS.
  • Zonas de Disponibilidade: locais isolados dentro de uma Região, utilizados para aumentar a disponibilidade.
  • Edge Locations: pontos de presença que armazenam conteúdo em cache próximo dos usuários, reduzindo a latência.
  • Conformidade: atendimento às leis e aos requisitos regulatórios aplicáveis.
  • Proximidade: escolha de Regiões próximas dos usuários para melhorar o tempo de resposta.
  • Disponibilidade de recursos: verificação dos serviços oferecidos em cada Região.
  • Preços: consideração das diferenças de custos entre Regiões.
  • Alta disponibilidade: capacidade de continuar operando mesmo diante de falhas.
  • Agilidade: capacidade de adaptar rapidamente a infraestrutura.
  • Elasticidade: ajuste automático dos recursos conforme a demanda.
  • AWS CloudFormation: serviço de Infraestrutura como Código para automatizar o provisionamento.
  • AWS CLI e SDKs: ferramentas para acessar os serviços AWS programaticamente.
  • Console de Gerenciamento: interface gráfica para administrar e monitorar os recursos.

Conclusão

A infraestrutura global da AWS permite construir aplicações distribuídas, com maior disponibilidade e menor latência para usuários em diferentes partes do mundo.

Compreender a diferença entre Regiões, Zonas de Disponibilidade e Edge Locations é fundamental para planejar arquiteturas eficientes. Além disso, fatores como conformidade, proximidade, disponibilidade de serviços e custos devem orientar a escolha da Região.

Por fim, ferramentas como o AWS CloudFormation, a AWS CLI e os SDKs tornam o gerenciamento da infraestrutura mais automatizado, padronizado e reproduzível.

Esses conceitos formam a base para projetar e administrar soluções em nuvem que atendam às necessidades técnicas e operacionais de diferentes organizações.

title: Clean Architecture for Backend Services: When to Use It and How
description:
Many engineering teams fall into one of two architectural traps: they prematurely over-engineer simple microservices with complex abstraction layers, or they neglect architecture entirely until their core backend becomes an untestable monolith where business rules are entangled with database queries.

When you mix your framework, database, and business logic into a single unlayered codebase, swapping infrastructure components becomes a nightmare. Testing unit logic requires spinning up real database instances, and simple feature additions start breaking unrelated parts of the system.

Here is how to evaluate whether your project actually needs Clean Architecture, and how to implement it cleanly without adding unnecessary friction.

The Checklist: Do You Need Clean Architecture?

Before introducing multiple layers of abstractions, evaluate your domain against three questions:

  1. Does your domain contain complex business rules that will frequently evolve?
  2. Will multiple teams touch and extend this service over several years?
  3. Is unit testability without external dependencies (like DBs or external APIs) non-negotiable?

If you answered yes to these questions, Clean Architecture earns its keep. Your core domain stays isolated at the center, completely untouched by database migrations, framework updates, or external vendor swaps.

However, if you are building a straightforward CRUD application, a temporary prototype, or a narrow-scoped microservice, skip the overhead. A clean, single-file or basic module layout will ship faster and remain easy to manage.

Step 1: Define Core Entities and Interfaces

The innermost layer consists of your domain entities and repository interfaces. This layer has zero dependencies on web frameworks, ORMs, or database drivers.

Here is an example in Python defining a domain entity and an abstract repository interface using Protocol:

# domain/entities.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol, Optional

@dataclass
class Order:
    id: str
    total_amount: float
    is_paid: bool = False

    def mark_as_paid(self) -> None:
        if self.total_amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Cannot process payment for non-positive amount")
        self.is_paid = True


# domain/interfaces.py
class OrderRepository(Protocol):
    def get_by_id(self, order_id: str) -> Optional[Order]:
        ...

    def save(self, order: Order) -> None:
        ...

Notice how the Order entity enforces business rules (such as validating payment amounts) independently of how or where the order is stored.

Step 2: Implement Pure Application Use Cases

The next layer contains your application use cases. Each use case orchestrates the domain entities and abstract interfaces to execute a specific business operation.

# use_cases/pay_order.py
from domain.entities import Order
from domain.interfaces import OrderRepository

class PayOrderUseCase:
    def __init__(self, repository: OrderRepository):
        self.repository = repository

    def execute(self, order_id: str) -> Order:
        order = self.repository.get_by_id(order_id)
        if not order:
            raise ValueError(f"Order {order_id} not found")

        order.mark_as_paid()
        self.repository.save(order)
        return order

Because PayOrderUseCase relies on the abstract OrderRepository contract, you can test this entire flow using an in-memory mock repository without touching a live database.

Step 3: Implement Infrastructure Adapters

The outermost layer implements the concrete infrastructure components, such as database repositories, external API clients, and HTTP controllers.

# infrastructure/postgres_repository.py
from domain.entities import Order

class PostgresOrderRepository:
    def __init__(self, db_session):
        self.session = db_session

    def get_by_id(self, order_id: str) -> Order | None:
        record = self.session.query(OrderORM).filter_by(id=order_id).first()
        if not record:
            return None
        return Order(id=record.id, total_amount=record.total_amount, is_paid=record.is_paid)

    def save(self, order: Order) -> None:
        record = self.session.query(OrderORM).filter_by(id=order.id).first()
        if record:
            record.is_paid = order.is_paid
        self.session.commit()

If you ever need to replace PostgreSQL with MongoDB, DynamoDB, or an external third-party API, you only write a new adapter. Your use cases and domain entities remain completely unchanged.

Balance Abstraction with Pragmatism

Clean Architecture is a tool to manage complexity, not a goal in itself. For large-scale systems or core business services, isolating your business logic ensures longevity and testability. For simpler, single-purpose utilities, favor flat structures to maintain development speed. The real engineering skill lies in recognizing which approach the current problem demands.

About me

Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. Feel free to connect on LinkedIn.

title: Building a reading speed test that can't be gamed by skimming
description:
Our book review site needed a feature readers would actually use, and that other sites would want to link to. We settled on a reading speed test, then found that most existing tests share a flaw: skim the passage, press stop, and you're suddenly reading at 1,000 words per minute.

Here's how we built one that pushes back, in a single React client component inside a Next.js app.

The flow

The component is a small state machine with four stages: intro → reading → quiz → result.

const [stage, setStage] = useState<"intro" | "reading" | "quiz" | "result">("intro");

We wrote three original passages (about 300 words each), each with three multiple-choice questions. Original text matters: nobody has read it before, and there's no copyright question.

Timing with performance.now()

Date.now() can jump if the system clock changes, so we time with performance.now(). The visible timer updates four times a second, but the score uses the exact start and end values:

function finishReading() {
  const s = (performance.now() - startedAt) / 1000;
  if (s < 5) return; // nobody reads 300 words in under 5 seconds
  setSeconds(s);
  setStage("quiz");
}

const wpm = Math.round(words / (seconds / 60));

The "I'm done" button stays disabled for the first 5 seconds, so a reflex click can't produce a score.

Guarding against skimming

Two checks keep the result honest.

Comprehension questions. After reading, the passage disappears and three questions appear. The result shows the score, and if you got fewer than two right, we suggest retaking at a slower pace.

A credibility cap. Anything above 900 wpm is labelled "Too fast to measure" and isn't saved:

const MAX_CREDIBLE_WPM = 900;

if (score <= MAX_CREDIBLE_WPM) {
  try {
    localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, String(score));
  } catch {
    // storage may be blocked
  }
}

Why 900? A 2016 review of speed-reading research (Rayner and colleagues, Psychological Science in the Public Interest) found that comprehension drops sharply when people push far past normal reading speeds, so 900 is a generous ceiling. The baseline we compare against is Brysbaert's 2019 meta-analysis of 190 studies, which puts adult silent reading at about 238 wpm for non-fiction and 260 wpm for fiction.

Note the try/catch around localStorage: in some private browsing modes it throws, and the tool should still work there.

The book-time calculator

A speed on its own is a curiosity. "This book will take you 9 hours" is useful. The Open Library search API is free, needs no key and allows cross-origin requests from the browser, so we query it directly with a timeout:

const ctrl = new AbortController();
const t = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), 12000);
const res = await fetch(
  `https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}` +
    `&fields=key,title,author_name,number_of_pages_median&limit=6`,
  { signal: ctrl.signal }
);
clearTimeout(t);

Asking only for the fields we need keeps the response small. number_of_pages_median gives a sensible page count across editions. If the search fails, the user can still type a page count.

The maths is simple:

const totalWords = pages * wordsPerPage; // 275 by default
const minutes = totalWords / speed;
const days = Math.ceil(minutes / minutesPerDay);

What we'd do next

  • More passages, so repeat visitors get a fresh one
  • Separate averages for reading on a phone and on a desktop

You can try it here: Reading Speed Test

If you've built anything similar, I'd like to hear how you handled the skim problem.

title: I Turned a Single-Page React Site Into a Real Multi-Page App With React Router
description:
In my last project, I built a complete digital-agency website with React. Header, services, footer — everything looked right. But it was one single page. Clicking "Services" in the header just scrolled down. The URL never changed. It wasn't a real website yet.

So I turned it into a real multi-page site with React Router: Home, Services, About, and Contact — plus a 404 page. Here's exactly how, step by step. This is the written companion to my YouTube episode (React from Scratch #6, in Moroccan Darija): https://youtu.be/a0qK0ezaQ0w

1. Install the router

React on its own doesn't know about pages. It knows components. For navigation between pages, you need an external library:

npm install react-router-dom

After installing, check your package.json — the library should be listed there. Run the project again and confirm everything still works with no errors before moving on.

2. Define the routes

First, create one component per page, each in its own file — Home.jsx, Services.jsx, About.jsx, Contact.jsx — the same way I organized components in the previous episode.

Then wrap the whole app in BrowserRouter. It watches the URL and decides what to show:

import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';
import Home from './pages/Home';
import Services from './pages/Services';
import About from './pages/About';
import Contact from './pages/Contact';

function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/services" element={<Services />} />
        <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
        <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
      </Routes>
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}

Each Route connects a URL path to a page component. When the visitor goes to a path, the router renders the matching page — without reloading the whole site. Change the URL and watch the page swap in place.

3. Link vs a normal <a> — the beginner mistake I made

When I first built navigation, I used normal <a href> links. That's a big mistake inside a React app: every click makes the browser reload the entire page from the server. Everything unmounts and rebuilds from scratch. You lose all the speed React gives you.

The fix is the Link component that comes with the router:

import { Link } from 'react-router-dom';

<Link to="/services">Services</Link>

It looks like a normal link, but clicking it never reloads the page. The router just swaps the visible component, instantly. And the browser back button works properly, because the router records every page you visited.

The rule is simple: inside a React app, always use Link for internal navigation. Keep <a> only for links that leave your site.

4. One shared Layout, no repetition

Now the header and footer need to appear on every page. Copying them into each page would repeat code — exactly what we learned to avoid.

The answer is a Layout component: header on top, footer at the bottom, and an empty slot in the middle called Outlet:

import { Outlet } from 'react-router-dom';

function Layout() {
  return (
    <>
      <header>{/* navigation */}</header>
      <main>
        <Outlet />
      </main>
      <footer>{/* footer */}</footer>
    </>
  );
}

Then nest the four routes inside the Layout route in App.jsx. The router renders each page's content inside the Outlet, while the header and footer stay put. Change the header in one place, and it changes on every page.

5. Don't forget the 404 page

What happens when a visitor types a URL that doesn't exist? Without handling it, the router renders nothing — a blank page. That's not professional.

Add a catch-all route with path="*" pointing to a NotFound component: a big title saying the page doesn't exist, a short explanation, and a Link back to Home.

<Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />

Try a wrong URL now: the 404 page appears instead of a blank screen.

The result

The site is now a real multi-page website: four pages, instant navigation, a shared layout, and a proper 404 page.

Your challenge: add the Contact page with a form (name, email, message) that shows a thank-you message when submitted. If you can do that on your own, you're starting to understand how real React websites are built.

I'm Wahib El Khadiri, a junior full-stack developer from Kénitra, Morocco. I build with React, Node.js and Laravel, contribute to open source, and teach React in Darija on YouTube. Portfolio: https://wahib-portfolio.netlify.app — GitHub: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI
