title: Hardcharger Tops DB Olympics at 1 TB: Most Queries per Second, Lowest Cost, All 409 Answers Correct
description:
Philip Moore · 2026-11-23

Source: https://gizmodata.com/blog/dbolympics-hardcharger-1tb

DB Olympics is a new, open benchmark of 409 SQL queries asked by AI agents playing the staff of an online retailer. At 1 TB, Hardcharger 2.14.0 answered 4.74 queries per second, 1.85 times CedarDB and almost twice DuckDB, ran all 409 for $0.068, and is the only released database to answer all 409 correctly on every machine at every scale. Where we aren't first, the query that made us fork DuckDB, and the DuckDB Labs work it all stands on.

DB Olympics is a new, open SQL benchmark from Altan Birler and Tobias Schmidt of the database group at the Technical University of Munich. Instead of a fixed set of textbook queries, it simulates an online retailer, Tidewick Commerce, and lets AI agents play its people: the CEO, the CFO, data analysts, the security chief and more. Their questions became 409 SQL queries, which every system runs on AWS machines at four sizes, from 1 GB to 1 TB, with each answer checked against a reference result.

We submitted Hardcharger 2.14.0 on November 22, and DB Olympics ran it the next day. At 1 TB, Hardcharger has the highest throughput and the lowest cost of every system on the board, and it is the only released database that answered all 409 queries correctly on every machine at every scale.

Leaderboards move, and this one is only weeks old. We expect the other systems to catch up, some of them soon. But on November 23, at 1 TB, Hardcharger is on top, and we'll take it.

DB Olympics' Figure 1 at 1 TB: queries per second against the cost of all 409 queries, each system on its most efficient machine. Up and to the left is better. Hardcharger is listed as a variant of DuckDB, so to see it on the live chart, click the DuckDB row in the table below the chart to expand it. Screenshot of dbolympics.com, November 23, 2026.

The results at 1 TB

DB Olympics scores a system by the time it takes to run all 409 queries once after its last data load. Queries per second is 409 divided by that time, and cost is that time at the machine's AWS on-demand price. A query that runs past the timeout (30 seconds at 1 TB) counts as the full 30 seconds. This is every system on the largest machine, a c8a.24xlarge with 96 vCPUs and 192 GB of memory, each with its own storage format:

System Queries per second Cost of all 409 Slowdown Correct
Hardcharger 4.74 $0.124 1.40× 409
CedarDB 2.56 $0.229 1.35× 408
DuckDB 2.40 $0.244 1.58× 407
Hyper 1.70 $0.346 1.66× 404
ClickHouse 1.09 $0.538 4.20× 349
DataFusion (Parquet) 0.97 $0.605 4.84× 317
Firebolt 0.61 $0.959 4.39× 381

DB Olympics' Table 1 on the c8a.24xlarge. The site lists Hardcharger as a variant of DuckDB, the engine it builds on, and ranks only the base systems, so Hardcharger's row (highlighted) has no rank number of its own. Screenshot of dbolympics.com, November 23, 2026.

Hardcharger answers 1.85 times as many queries per second as CedarDB and almost twice as many as DuckDB, for about half the cost. The lowest cost on the board comes from a smaller machine: on a c8a.12xlarge (48 vCPUs, 96 GB), Hardcharger ran all 409 queries for $0.068, against $0.126 for DuckDB and $0.129 for CedarDB there. Its 4.31 queries per second on that machine are more than any other system managed on any machine.

Slowdown is DB Olympics' other measure: the geometric mean of how far each query is from the fastest system's time on it. It rewards the typical query rather than the total, and on the largest machine CedarDB is ahead on it, 1.35 to our 1.40. On the c8a.12xlarge and c8a.16xlarge, Hardcharger's slowdown is the lowest. CedarDB is faster than Hardcharger on more than half of the individual queries at 1 TB; Hardcharger wins on the total because it has no slow outliers. Its slowest query took 6.3 seconds. CedarDB's slowest answer took 16.6 seconds, and one more query timed out; DuckDB had two timeouts.

A note on what was measured. DuckDB runs embedded inside the benchmark program. Hardcharger runs as a server: the benchmark sent every query to hardcharger-server through the Hardcharger ADBC driver, over Chargewire on the same machine, and fetched every result. So Hardcharger's times include a client-server round trip that the embedded DuckDB entry doesn't pay.

All 409, everywhere

DB Olympics ran Hardcharger in 16 configurations: four scale factors (1 GB, 10 GB, 100 GB and 1 TB), each on three or four machine sizes. Hardcharger answered all 409 queries correctly in all 16, with no wrong result, no error and no timeout. The only other system to do that is Querybrew on ClickHouse, an experimental system from the DB Olympics authors in which their research database, Umbra, rewrites every query for ClickHouse; it isn't a released product, and at 1 TB it ran at about a quarter of Hardcharger's throughput. Among released systems at 1 TB, CedarDB answered 408 and DuckDB 407.

The query that started a fork

Query 318 was asked by the simulated Chief Information Security Officer:

"Since shopper accounts have 0% MFA, what actually stands in for a second factor today: are most shoppers authenticating through an OAuth provider (Google/Apple/etc., which carries its own security), or are they overwhelmingly raw password-only accounts with no backup at all?"

At its heart is a join of shoppers to their login attempts on the tenant and either the user ID or the email address:

join login_attempts la
  on la.tenant_id = s.tenant_id
 and (la.user_id = s.id or la.email = s.email)

The tenant is a weak key: it matches every shopper of a merchant to every login attempt of that merchant, and the or can't be used to look rows up, so an engine ends up checking a huge number of candidate pairs. At 1 TB on the c8a.24xlarge:

System Query 318 at 1 TB
Hardcharger 0.25 s
Querybrew on ClickHouse (experimental) 0.55 s
ClickHouse 6.15 s
Firebolt 7.29 s
CedarDB, DuckDB, Hyper, DataFusion (Parquet) and Hardcharger (Parquet) timed out at 30 s

Query 318 at 1 TB as DB Olympics shows it. Screenshot of dbolympics.com, November 23, 2026.

We'll be upfront: this is the query that made us fork. DB Olympics' first run of Hardcharger, version 2.0.0 on stock DuckDB 2.0.0 in late October, timed out on it at 10 GB and above, and the fix needed a change inside DuckDB's optimizer. So we started Hardcharger Engine, our performance fork of DuckDB, to ship and test such changes on Hardcharger's release schedule. Its first optimizer rule handles joins of this shape in general, not query 318 by name: for an eligible inner join under a DISTINCT, it builds two selective joins, one on tenant and user ID and one on tenant and email, and lets the existing DISTINCT remove the overlap. It applies only when it can prove the answer is unchanged, and it ships with its own regression tests. In our own test at 10 GB on a laptop, swapping stock DuckDB 2.0.1 for our engine took query 318 from 3.67 seconds to 19 milliseconds.

How Hardcharger Engine runs query 318's join. Left: stock DuckDB joins on tenant_id alone and checks the OR condition on every candidate pair. Right: Hardcharger Engine runs two selective joins and lets the query's own DISTINCT remove the overlap. An illustration, not to scale.

Two caveats, because they matter. Our Parquet configuration still timed out on query 318, so the rule doesn't help there yet. And at 100 GB, query 318 is what puts Hardcharger ahead: without it, CedarDB would be slightly faster on the c8a.12xlarge, 26.7 queries per second to our 25.1. At 1 TB the lead holds without it. Take query 318 out of every system's total on the c8a.24xlarge and Hardcharger still answers 4.74 queries per second, against 3.15 for CedarDB and 2.91 for DuckDB. At 10 GB and 1 GB, CedarDB leads outright.

One more: query 360

The simulated Head of Pricing and Promotions asked whether free deliveries going to customers whose subscription had already been canceled were "a slow-burning historical gap, steady, or accelerating". Here we don't win: at 1 TB on the c8a.24xlarge, CedarDB answered in 97.5 milliseconds and Hardcharger in 144. But stock DuckDB timed out at 30 seconds, and the next systems took from 0.9 to 2.5 seconds. The query joins orders to calendar days and exchange rates on a timestamp cast to a date, the shape another of our engine changes is aimed at: a better estimate of how many rows such a join produces. We haven't isolated that change as the reason (the DuckDB entry ran 2.0.0, a patch release behind our engine's base), so we'll just report the times.

Query 360 at 1 TB as DB Olympics shows it. Screenshot of dbolympics.com, November 23, 2026.

Standing on the shoulders of ducks

None of this exists without DuckDB. Hardcharger Engine 2.0.1 is DuckDB 2.0.1 with 14 performance commits on top, plus the hooks the Hardcharger server needs. The SQL, the execution engine, the storage and the database file format are DuckDB's, built by the incredible team at DuckDB Labs and DuckDB's many contributors, and released under the MIT license. Thank you. The 409 queries ran on your work.

One of those contributors, in a small way, is our founder, Philip Moore (prmoore77). Three of his pull requests are in DuckDB itself: the struct_insert function, HUGEINT support for bit_count and new information_schema views. Not many, but it means we've helped build the engine we know and love, not just build on it.

We'll take a little of the credit too. Our share of the result is:

  • The engine changes. Besides the join rule, the fork estimates timestamp-to-date joins better, applies integer range filters in one pass, reuses checks in filtered column scans, starts scan read-ahead sooner, and speeds up substring search and regular expression extraction. Each change is documented with its limits, its tests and what we measured.
  • The server around it. Hardcharger turns the engine into a multi-user server with sign-in, access control and an Arrow-native protocol, Chargewire, and it scored these numbers as a server, answering over the wire.

Thank you as well to Altan Birler and Tobias Schmidt for DB Olympics: an open benchmark where anyone can add a system, every result is checked, and the queries come from questions people would actually ask. Finding query 318 made our engine better.

And on ClickBench

We submitted Hardcharger 2.14.0 to ClickBench as well, and it was merged on November 22. On ClickBench's default combined score, as of November 23, Hardcharger places 6th of 93 entries on the c7a.metal-48xl and 6th of 91 on the c8g.metal-48xl, the highest-placed DuckDB-based system on both, behind Rayforce, CedarDB, ClickHouse and chDB. On the smaller c6a.4xlarge it is 9th of 102, a hair behind our own GizmoSQL entry from May. Cold runs, the first run of each query after a restart, are our weak spot there, and the next thing we want to improve.

The details

  • Hardcharger: version 2.14.0 on Hardcharger Engine 2.0.1 (DuckDB 2.0.1), queried through the Hardcharger ADBC driver 2.7.2. The DuckDB entry ran DuckDB 2.0.0.
  • Run: by DB Olympics' own runner on November 23, 2026, on AWS c8a machines (AMD EPYC), each system limited to the machine's cores and 80% of its memory, with data loaded from Parquet in five periods and the queries timed after the last load.
  • Numbers: computed from DB Olympics' published data with its own formulas (the site rounds them); prices are AWS on-demand, $2.5865 an hour for the c8a.12xlarge and $5.173 for the c8a.24xlarge.
  • See it for yourself: the results, query 318, the methodology and Hardcharger's entry in the DB Olympics repository. Hardcharger isn't one of the site's core systems: it is listed under DuckDB, so click the DuckDB row in the results table to expand it, and Hardcharger then appears in the table and on the chart.

Try Hardcharger

Start free with $25 of launch credit, applied automatically. No credit card needed. Run it on GizmoData Cloud, or install the open-source server on your own machine in a minute.

Install Hardcharger

Hardcharger™ and GizmoData™ are trademarks of GizmoData LLC. DuckDB is a trademark of the DuckDB Foundation; Hardcharger Engine is a fork of DuckDB maintained by GizmoData and is not affiliated with or endorsed by DuckDB Labs or the DuckDB Foundation. CedarDB, ClickHouse, Hyper, DataFusion, Firebolt and other names are trademarks of their respective owners. DB Olympics ran every system; the numbers above are computed from its published data.

title: Node.js Factors Influencing Lifecycle Policies for AI-Generated Property Image Storage
description:
Short answer: The factors that influence lifecycle policies are business state, private-link expiry, governance holds, regeneration or recovery value, and the throughput cost of moving large files. Use those signals together; file age alone is not a deletion policy.

A large AI-generated property image should live as long as its business purpose, access obligation, and recovery value justify. The least complex design is to give each object a retention state, keep the original immutable, create expiring download links on demand, and delete only after a recorded policy decision.

The useful signal is not "this object is old." It is "this object has no active lease, no legal or operational hold, and no recovery value left." That distinction keeps lifecycle automation from turning a quiet storage bucket into an incident.

The page is late.

No guessing.

Keep the deletion decision boring. The interesting part belongs in the evidence around it: which workflow owned the image, which lease was live, which hold was applied, and which policy revision made the transition eligible.

The page that arrives too late

The page fires when a resident cannot open a generated inspection image from a private portal. The on-call sees a 404 from the download service, a normal-looking object count, and a cleanup job that reported success overnight. Large files make this harder: a retry can consume worker bandwidth for minutes before anyone notices that the object was already deleted.

I start from the alert and work backwards. I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, and the useful lesson is consistent: the missing image is the final symptom. Earlier signals should have shown that an object moved from active to deletion_pending without a matching business event, or that a delete batch contained records whose download lease had not expired. A count of deleted objects is useful accounting; it is not proof that deletion was safe. Give the policy a revision such as 2026-01, record it with the decision, and keep the old rule available when an operator has to explain why a file was removed.

For a property-management workflow, the metadata record needs enough information to make the decision again: object identity, tenant or property scope, creation time, last authorized access, retention class, hold state, content digest, and the policy revision that made the object eligible. The image bytes and the decision record have different jobs. Keep them separate.

What factors influence lifecycle policies for AI-generated image storage?

The reader question sounds like a storage question, but the strongest inputs come from outside storage. AI-generated images may be intermediate renderings, published listing assets, resident-submitted documents, or evidence attached to a maintenance record. Those categories have different lifetimes even when their files are the same size and format.

A practical policy evaluates four gates:

  1. Business state: Is the image attached to an open work order, an active listing, or a closed record?
  2. Access state: Are there active sessions, download leases, or a pending export? An expiring link should be treated as a capability with a deadline, not as a permanent permission.
  3. Governance state: Is there a documented hold, privacy requirement, or retention class that prevents deletion? Security guidance for regulated data emphasizes defined safeguards and documented handling, so the policy should name its owner and evidence rather than hiding the choice in a cron expression.
  4. Recovery state: Can the image be regenerated deterministically, or would deletion remove the only useful artifact? A prompt, model configuration, source asset, and output digest are materially different from a recoverable copy of the rendered file.

The threshold is a policy decision, not a magic number. A short-lived preview can be deleted after its lease and workflow expire. A published image may need to remain while a listing is active. A record attached to a dispute may need a hold that outlives both.

There is a real trade-off here: keeping every original improves recovery, but increases the amount of private data that must be protected and the work a cleanup backlog can create. Deleting aggressively reduces that burden, but gives up forensic and regeneration options. The right boundary belongs to the record owner.

Why does large-file throughput change the design?

Large-file throughput changes what an operationally correct cleanup job looks like. Deleting metadata quickly while a transfer is still in flight creates a race. Rebuilding a full image to verify a digest consumes the same constrained path used by customer downloads. A queue that retries a timeout without an idempotency key can produce duplicate work, while a queue that retries a successful delete can produce a misleading error unless the delete operation is treated as convergent.

The worker should claim a small batch, re-read the decision fields, and make one idempotent transition. It should not stream the image merely to decide whether the object is eligible. This Go example shows the boundary; the storage adapter can use any object-store implementation that supports the required semantics.

type ImageRecord struct {
\tID             string
\tRetentionClass string
\tHold           bool
\tLeaseExpiresAt time.Time
\tDeleteAfter    time.Time
\tState          string
}

func EligibleForDelete(r ImageRecord, now time.Time) bool {
\tif r.Hold || r.State != "deletion_pending" {
\t\treturn false
\t}
\tif !now.After(r.LeaseExpiresAt) || !now.After(r.DeleteAfter) {
\t\treturn false
\t}
\treturn true
}

In production, the transition and the claim need a durable concurrency boundary. A worker that loses its lease should be safe to run again. The delete request should carry a stable operation identifier in logs, and the resulting state should distinguish deleted, already_absent, and blocked. Those outcomes support retries without pretending that every retry found a new failure.

Private delivery also needs a clean separation between authorization and transfer. The application checks the caller, records the intended object and expiry, then issues a link whose lifetime is bounded by the policy. The download path must not infer authorization from an object key that a caller can guess. A link that has expired should fail closed, while the record remains available for a controlled retry if the policy still permits it.

The instrumentation change that prevents the next page

I would instrument the policy evaluation before instrumenting the delete API. Emit a structured decision with the object class, policy revision, eligibility result, blocking reason, and age bucket. Do not log the private link or raw user data. Correlate the decision with the workflow event and the worker attempt.

The useful dashboard has three views: eligible objects waiting for work, blocked objects grouped by reason, and completed transitions grouped by outcome. Add transfer duration and bytes for downloads, but keep throughput separate from lifecycle correctness. A rising byte rate can be healthy; a rising mismatch between deletion_pending records and completed decisions is the earlier warning.

The alert should page on policy drift or an aging backlog, with a threshold based on the maximum tolerated delay for each retention class. A threshold set too low turns normal large-file retries into noise and teaches the on-call to ignore the page. A threshold set too high leaves a private delivery failure hidden. I would tune it against a replayable test set containing small previews, large originals, expired links, active holds, duplicate worker attempts, and objects that are already absent.

That test set matters because the dangerous bugs are temporal. Unit tests can prove the boolean rule; integration tests must prove that a lease expiring during a transfer, a policy revision, and a worker retry produce the intended final state. Run the same cases in a deployment check before changing the lifecycle worker.

A decision rule that survives change

Choose lifecycle behavior by evidence owned by the workflow, not by file age alone. Store the policy revision with the decision, make state transitions auditable, and require an explicit hold to override automatic cleanup. Keep original bytes immutable when their provenance matters, and use derived thumbnails or previews for high-volume access when the product permits it.

The design is portable because its contract is small: private object identity, bounded capability, durable metadata, idempotent transitions, and observable reasons. A storage backend can change without changing the policy question. The operational risk remains in the same place: deleting an object before the system has proved that nobody still needs it.

Further reading

  • NIST SP 800-66 Rev. 2, Implementing the HIPAA Security Rule: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/66/r2/final
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • W3C Trace Context: https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/

title: My laptop has 8 GB of RAM, so I made it borrow my VPS's
description:
So recently I started to realize that whenever I ran a full Rust build/test suite or anything heavy, my laptop froze to death, and then the OOM killer closed whatever I cared about most. Ig my 8 GB of RAM just isn't enough anymore for heavy builds plus Chromium, Zed and multiple Claude sessions all running at the same time, which is my basic daily workflow btw :( As I write this, free -h says 1.9 GiB is available. With nothing heavy running.

Meanwhile I have hermes. It's an Oracle ARM box with 2 cores and 12 GB of RAM. I mostly use it as my dev playground (running and learning things like SigNoz, k8s etc.), and most of the day it does basically nothing. It's so idle that I run a small ballast process on it so Oracle doesn't reclaim it for inactivity. Felt kinda dumb tbh: one machine dying, the other pretending to be busy.

So I made the laptop borrow it.

That's hopbox. You put it in front of the heavy command, and it copies your repo to the remote, runs the command there, streams the output back while it runs, and exits with whatever the command exited with. The last line tells you what happened:

hopbox: exit=0 source=remote host=hermes dur=41.8s

exit= is your command's real exit code, so a script, a CI step or a coding agent can treat a remote run exactly like a local one. It's out now: 1.0.0 is on crates.io and the AUR, and the code is on GitHub.

For eg. one of the things I've thrown at it is martin's test suite. 5802 tests, all green, 650 seconds on a cold first build on aarch64. Then I ran it again with nothing changed, and the whole hopbox run took 1.6 seconds, sync included. That second number is the one that convinced me rsync was fine and I didn't need anything clever.

why not just ssh in

Tbh, when I first asked Claude for a solution, that's what it suggested, and that's what I did for weeks: rsync the repo over, ssh in, run the thing, squint at the output. It works, and if you only do it twice a week, keep doing it.

Getting Claude to do the same thing took one line in my global CLAUDE.md. That part was easy. What broke it was the way I actually work now.

On a normal day I have two or three Claude sessions open, each started with claude --worktree, and they spawn subagents that often get worktrees of their own. So at any moment there can be four or five checkouts of the same repo sitting under .claude/worktrees/, and every one of them wants to run cargo test at some point.

With my one-liner, they all synced into the same folder on hermes. One agent's rsync would land in the middle of another agent's test run, and that agent would come back with a failure in code it never touched. Easy fix, I thought: one remote folder per worktree. Except every new worktree is a fresh checkout, so now each one starts with a cold Rust build. Three cold builds at once ate hermes exactly the way one ate my laptop, and took my Hermes agent down with it.

Then there's cleanup. A background command dies when the foreground subagent that started it finishes, and when I stop a stuck task from /tasks, Claude kills the local ssh. The build on hermes doesn't notice. It just keeps running, holding a few GB of RAM, for nobody.

And the obvious way to keep the output short, ssh hermes 'cd app && cargo test 2>&1 | tail -40', exits with tail's status. Which is 0. Red tests, green result, and an agent that happily moves on.

Every one of these has a known fix: separate folders, a lock, cgroup caps, pipefail, a trap that stops the remote job. Stack them all into one script, make it work for every project and every agent, and congrats, you've written a tool.

But yeah, like they say:

So I built the tool. Well, first I looked around. rr does rsync-and-run well, and it keeps a separate remote copy for each git worktree, an idea I stole. Offload keeps a warm daemon on the remote and routes test commands through a hook, which is fast. But both were missing things I cared about, which brings me to the rules.

Another way would be to use Herdr, treat my VPS as the main machine and run Claude Code there, so it can do whatever it wants. But my laptop is my main workstation. My project notes, skills, password manager and all the little workflows I've built live there, and I can't keep all of that in sync with a VPS that Oracle can reclaim any day they want. (I really need to build a homelab soon.)

the rules, and why each one exists

So I sat down for a grill me session and wrote four rules before writing any code, and they killed a bunch of features I really wanted.

nothing to install on the remote

If ssh box works, hopbox works. It needs rsync, bash and flock over there, which most Linux boxes already have, and that's it. A daemon would be faster, sure. It would also be one more thing to install, update and debug on every box, and I wanted to point this at any machine I can ssh into, including ones I don't own.

borrow, don't take over

hermes has a day job. It runs my Hermes agent in a 5 GB container, plus that ballast and some heavy part-time jobs. A runaway cargo build that eats all 12 GB takes everything down with it. So every job runs inside its own systemd scope with a memory cap (mine is 6G) and a lower CPU weight. During the martin build, hermes never dropped below 8.2 GiB available.

fail loudly

If hermes is down, hopbox stops and tells you why. It never quietly runs the job on your laptop instead. Offload falls back to local by default, and that's exactly what I didn't want: the whole point is that my laptop can't run the job.

money needs a human yes

hopbox can also rent a GPU box on vast.ai for you. It shows the price and waits for you to type yes, and every rental gets a deadline that the box enforces on itself, so a forgotten instance can't keep billing you while you sleep. Your agent can do this part too: it runs hopbox up, shows you the price, and waits for your yes before anything gets rented.

built for my claude code

This is the part I use the most. I built hopbox so my CC can run tests and builds freely while I keep working, without anyone waiting or worrying about the OOM killer.

The repo ships a skill that teaches the agent when to offload and how to read the result. Install it once:

npx skills add Itz-Agasta/hopbox --skill hopbox -g
# or as a Claude Code plugin:
claude plugin marketplace add Itz-Agasta/hopbox
claude plugin install hopbox@hopbox

Then three things change.

Long jobs go to the background. For a release build or a big test suite, Claude starts it with --bg and keeps working on other stuff, then collects the result when it's ready:

id=$(hopbox run --bg -- cargo build --release)
# ... Claude keeps working ...
hopbox wait "$id"     # exits with the build's exit code

The job keeps running on hermes even if I close the terminal or my laptop goes to sleep.

Subagents can build at the same time. Each git worktree gets its own copy on the remote, and every job runs in its own systemd scope with its own memory cap. So when I spawn a few subagents in separate worktrees, each one can run its own tests on hermes concurrently, isolated from the others. If one build blows up, the OOM kill hits that job only, and the other sessions (and my laptop) keep going. Two runs from the same worktree take turns instead of stepping on each other's files.

The output fits in context. hopbox run --tail 60 shows only the last 60 lines and points at the full log on disk, so Claude spends its context on the failure and never has to scroll past 5000 lines of passing tests. The status line has source=, so it can tell a real test failure (source=remote) from hopbox being unable to reach the box (source=hopbox). In the second case it tells me instead of quietly running the job on my laptop.

Yeah, I think this is where agents feel the RAM limit hardest: one agent is fine, but three agents each running cargo test on an 8 GB laptop is a slideshow. Moving the heavy part to a box that's sitting idle anyway fixed that for me.

try it 

cargo install hopbox     # or: paru -S hopbox-bin

Then tell it about a host in ~/.config/hopbox/config.toml. The ssh value goes straight to ssh, so your ~/.ssh/config, keys, jump hosts and Tailscale all just work:

default_host = "hermes"

[hosts.hermes]
ssh = "hermes"
memory_max = "6G"

hopbox doctor hermes     # checks ssh, rsync, the memory cap and PATH on the remote
hopbox run -- cargo test

Right now it runs from Linux and macOS laptops against Linux remotes. The code, docs are at github.com/Itz-Agasta/hopbox. If you point it at something and it breaks, open an issue and tell me how, and if it saves your laptop too, a star helps.

My laptop finally gets to just be a laptop, and Claude can test in the bg without me worrying about OOM errors.

Thanks for reading :)

title: Cloud Hygiene Without Production Changes: A Safer First Assessment
description:
Teams often ask an assessor for administrator access just to find out what is already in the cloud account. That request creates risk of its own, and unvalidated findings can push people into rushed changes.

This piece is adapted from a MeritSOLV™ Research & Insights guide on running a first cloud hygiene assessment with read-only evidence. The example below is illustrative, not a client report.

Why inventories fall behind

Cloud estates get hard to govern when inventories and architecture records lag. Start by writing the account boundary in one sentence: which subscriptions, projects or accounts are in scope, and which are explicitly out. Then list the read-only exports the owners can provide, such as resource inventories, policy settings and cost reports. Treat everything found as an observation until an owner confirms it, and keep change requests in a separate list.

A scope statement can be short:

In scope: the two product-team subscriptions.
Out of scope: the inherited test account.
Evidence: policy exports, resource inventory, cost categories, approved screenshots.
Access: time-limited, read-only. No administrator role.

A read-only review: evidence first, changes later

A small product team operates two cloud subscriptions and one inherited test account. Rather than handing an external assessor administrator rights, it provides policy exports, a resource inventory, cost categories and approved screenshots in a time-limited read-only collection. The assessment finds publicly reachable storage configuration, inconsistent tags and missing cost allocation on a shared subscription. The report separates observed configuration from a confirmed exploitable condition.

Finding Evidence Risk owner decision
Unknown public exposure Resource policy and network path evidence Request validation before a severity claim
Missing owner tag Inventory export Assign an owner and a remediation window
Broad role assignment Role-binding snapshot Review least privilege with the platform team
No recovery drill Backup policy only Plan a restoration test

Avoid the false promise of a "no-impact scan." Even read-only collection can expose sensitive metadata and consume API capacity. Agree on account boundaries, sensitive-data redaction, access expiration and approved collection methods beforehand. Any production changes should go later through the normal change process.

Five steps that keep the first assessment safe

1. Agree which accounts, subscriptions and environments are in scope. Get written approval naming each tenant or account, environment, data category and excluded resource before requesting any export or permission.

2. Gather approved read-only exports and architecture diagrams. Prefer a limited evidence pack with configuration snapshots, logging coverage, role bindings and architecture boundaries over unrestricted cloud console access.

3. Inventory resources, owners, environments and labels. Normalize tags and ownership. Mark shared resources, test subscriptions and orphaned cloud identities so recommendations address the actual operating footprint.

4. Document cost and configuration observations as hypotheses that still need validation. Label each observation as verified, suspected or outside scope, and separate cost optimization from security exposure so risk rankings stay accurate.

5. Rank findings by exposure, business impact, effort and decision owner. Propose validated follow-up steps with an owner, estimated effort and the required change authorization. Do not present evidence collection as production remediation.

What done should look like

You want a reviewed inventory and a prioritized cloud observations worksheet, with provenance, version, owner and outstanding exceptions visible. The sponsor should be able to see what was decided, what was not, and which actions remain. State the population, sampling method and limits of any review. A scoped example is not a full assurance engagement.

When the worksheet is ready, hand it to someone outside the delivery team. Can they find the latest version, name the accountable owner, explain the top unresolved issue and say what the next authorized action is? If any of that lives only in someone's memory, the handoff isn't finished.

The mistake that shows up most often

Changing cloud settings while performing what was meant to be documentation-only discovery. The fix is not more paperwork for its own sake. Keep the smallest set of artifacts that shows scope, evidence, review and the next decision. Automate only after the responsibilities and exceptions are clear.

Working checklist

  • Agree which accounts, subscriptions and environments are in scope.
  • Gather approved read-only exports and architecture diagrams.
  • Inventory resources, owners, environments and labels.
  • Document cost and configuration observations as hypotheses requiring validation.
  • Rank findings by exposure, business impact, effort and decision owner.
  • Confirm who approves the final output and how corrections will be handled.
  • Archive the approved version and record the next review or follow-up date.

If you want a first step this week, pick one real account, write the boundary in one sentence, and collect only the read-only exports the owners will approve.

Questions that come up

Can cloud hygiene begin read-only?

Yes. A properly scoped review can document observations without modifying production resources.

Is a configuration observation a verified vulnerability?

Not necessarily. Findings should identify the evidence, the assumptions and the validation still needed.

For deeper reading, the guide points to NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 on configuration and access controls, and to NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. This is general operational information, not legal, audit or certification advice. Review the cited standards and apply your organization's requirements.

The examples are illustrative, not reports of MeritSOLV™ client engagements.

Originally published at meritsolv.com.

title: How to Estimate Kubernetes CPU and Memory Requirements with a Free Online Calculator
description:
One thing I've noticed when working with Kubernetes is that deploying an application is only part of the job.

You also need to think about resources.

How much CPU does your container need? How much memory should you allocate? What happens when you increase the number of replicas?

These questions matter whether you're running a small development cluster or managing workloads in a larger environment.

Getting resource requests and limits wrong can lead to scheduling difficulties, unnecessary resource allocation, or containers running out of memory.

Let's look at why Kubernetes resource calculations matter and how an online calculator can make the process easier.

Understanding Kubernetes CPU and Memory

Kubernetes allows you to define resource requests and limits for containers.

  • CPU requests help Kubernetes decide which node can accommodate a workload.
  • CPU limits restrict how much CPU a container can consume.
  • Memory requests help Kubernetes schedule workloads based on memory requirements.
  • Memory limits define the maximum memory a container can use.

CPU is commonly measured in millicores:

CPU value Equivalent
100m 0.1 CPU
250m 0.25 CPU
500m 0.5 CPU
1000m 1 CPU

Memory is commonly represented using Mi and Gi:

Memory value Equivalent
128Mi 128 mebibytes
256Mi 256 mebibytes
512Mi 512 mebibytes
1Gi 1024Mi

Understanding these values makes it easier to estimate the resources required by your applications.

Why Calculate Resources Before Deployment?

Imagine you're deploying an application with four replicas.

Each replica requests:

  • 250m CPU
  • 512Mi memory

Your total requested resources would be:

CPU: 250m × 4 = 1000m (1 CPU core)

Memory: 512Mi × 4 = 2048Mi (2Gi)

This is a straightforward calculation, but when applications have multiple containers, different workloads, and varying replica counts, resource planning becomes more involved.

That's why having a convenient calculator can save time.

Try the Free Online Kubernetes Resource Calculator

If you work with Kubernetes, you can use the Free Online Kubernetes Resource Calculator from DevUtilityKits to help with resource calculations.

It's a handy online utility to explore when estimating CPU and memory requirements for Kubernetes workloads.

Instead of doing every calculation manually, you can use a dedicated tool as part of your planning workflow.

Tool link: Kubernetes Resource Calculator – DevUtilityKits

Practical Situations Where It Helps

Here are a few examples where Kubernetes resource calculations are useful:

  1. New deployments: Estimate the CPU and memory needed before deploying an application.
  2. Scaling applications: Understand how increasing replicas affects total resource requirements.
  3. Cluster planning: Compare planned workload requests against available cluster capacity.
  4. Learning Kubernetes: Get more comfortable working with CPU and memory units.
  5. Resource reviews: Revisit allocation figures when application requirements change.

One important point: calculated totals are estimates, not a guarantee that a workload will fit on a particular node. Kubernetes scheduling also considers available capacity, existing workloads, system reservations, and other constraints.

For production environments, review actual application usage and monitor workloads before finalizing resource requests and limits.

Explore More Cloud and DevOps Utilities

Resource planning is just one part of a developer's daily workflow.

Docker, Git, Linux, networking, CI/CD, and infrastructure configuration all involve repetitive technical tasks.

DevUtilityKits provides a collection of free online developer utilities for these areas.

Take a look at the Cloud and DevOps Tools collection to discover more useful tools.

Final Thoughts

Kubernetes resource planning doesn't have to be complicated, but it shouldn't be overlooked.

Understanding CPU requests, memory requests, limits, and replica counts helps you make more informed deployment decisions.

If you're working with Kubernetes, give the Free Online Kubernetes Resource Calculator a try.

title: SwiftPY 0.3.5 Beta: I Need Python Developers Who Will Try to Break It
description:
Most framework announcements say "try it". This one says something slightly different:

Please try to break it.

SwiftPY is an ASGI native, Eloquent style Python web framework I have been building for one reason. After more than ten years of backends with Laravel, and a recent stretch of AI projects on FastAPI, I wanted the async first speed of the Python ecosystem together with the structure, conventions and tooling I had learned to love. That framework did not exist, so I started building it.

SwiftPY is now at version 0.3.5, it is on PyPI, and it is still in beta. Before I call anything 1.0.0, I want people other than me to push on it.

GitHub: https://github.com/Obrainwave/swiftpy

Why beta testers matter more than any feature

I use SwiftPY on real projects, including its own documentation site (Next.js on the frontend, SwiftPY on the backend). Real use is the best bug finder I have, but it has a hard limit: it only exercises the paths I happen to take.

Every developer builds differently. You will name your models differently, nest your routes differently, deploy behind a different proxy and hit combinations I never imagined. That is exactly the information a 1.0.0 release needs.

The changelog shows what this loop looks like in practice. In 0.3.5 alone, the entries under "Fixed" include:

  • a comma separated trusted_proxies string that passed validation but later broke every request.ip() call
  • a scheduler loop that listed every schedule on each wake up instead of reading the earliest due time
  • overlap locks that could expire while a long running job was still executing

Each one is a small, specific, fixable problem. Finding them early, in public, is the whole point.

What is already in the box

SwiftPY is not a toy router. Over the last few weeks the beta has grown into a full framework:

  • An async Active Record ORM with typed models, eager loading, dirty tracking, HasMany, HasOne, BelongsTo and BelongsToMany, plus relationship existence queries such as has() and where_has()
  • A fluent query builder and migrations with Blueprint, pagination, group_by, having, and PostgreSQL advisory locks
  • Validation through FormRequest and validate(), failing closed before your handler runs
  • Authentication with JWT pairs, refresh token rotation, API keys, Auth.attempt(), remember me sessions, auth lifecycle events and built in login throttling
  • A native task scheduler with a strict five field cron engine, time zone support and a durable Redis store, driven by schedule:work
  • Queues, events, cache, storage, mail and WebSockets
  • A native AI subsystem for OpenAI and Anthropic: streaming, embeddings, vector stores, RAG, tool calling agents, and versioned prompt templates
  • A CLI that writes the boring code

A taste of the developer experience:

# Controller routing with per request dependency injection
router.get("/users", UserController.index)

# Credential login with throttling, events and optional remember me
await Auth.attempt({"email": email, "password": password, "active": 1}, remember=True)

# Update a model, respecting __fillable__ / __guarded__
await user.update({"name": "Alice"})

swiftpy new my_service
swiftpy make:model Post -m
swiftpy make:request CreateOrderRequest
swiftpy make:agent SupportAssistant
swiftpy make:prompt summarise.v2
swiftpy migrate
swiftpy db:seed
swiftpy schedule:work

Secure by default, and I want that tested hardest

Security is where outside eyes help most. These defaults already ship, and I would love you to attack them:

  • Mass assignment is denied unless a model declares __fillable__ or __guarded__
  • A WHERE less update() or delete() raises an error unless you opt in with .allow_all()
  • Client IP detection ignores forwarded headers unless you configure trusted proxies, and it resolves them right to left with strict bounds
  • Login throttling buckets IPv6 clients by /64, so rotating addresses inside one prefix cannot dodge a lockout
  • Scheduled tasks carry an HMAC signature, and tampered records are marked failed and never executed
  • Queue envelopes are signed before any class is imported
  • Production mode refuses weak secrets and never leaks tracebacks

If you find a hole, I want to hear about it. For anything security sensitive, please message me privately before posting it publicly.

How to get started

You need Python 3.12+, PostgreSQL and Redis. The scaffold ships with a Docker setup for the last two.

pip install swiftpy-framework
swiftpy new my_service
cd my_service
swiftpy migrate
swiftpy start --reload

The step by step guides live in the repository's documentations folder, and the full documentation site at https://swiftpy.net arrives with 1.0.0.

Five ways to help, from 15 minutes to a weekend

  1. Build something small. A blog API, a todo service, an auth flow, a job that sends email. Whatever you would normally build, build it with SwiftPY.
  2. Stress the risky corners. Try your real database schemas with the migrations, relationships you actually use with the ORM, the scheduler across multiple workers, or login throttling behind your own proxy.
  3. Try your own platform. Windows, macOS, Linux, Docker Desktop, a cheap VPS. Environment bugs are invisible to a single developer.
  4. Report what you find. Open an issue on GitHub with what you expected, what happened and how to reproduce it. "This confused me" is a valid bug report, because confusing documentation is a bug.
  5. Contribute. Tests, examples, documentation fixes and code are all welcome. You do not need prior open source experience.

What to expect

This is a beta, so expect rough edges and the occasional breaking change before 1.0.0. Every release lists what was added, changed, fixed and secured in the public changelog, so nothing changes quietly.

I am also not going to rush 1.0.0 just to have a stable looking number. It ships when I am confident the framework is stable, secure and reliable enough for production. Your testing is how I get there.

Join in

  • Star and explore the repo: https://github.com/Obrainwave/swiftpy
  • Open an issue for anything you find
  • Or send me a DM with "SWIFTPY TESTER" and I will help you get started

Building a framework is one thing. Building one other developers can trust is another. Help me earn that trust before 1.0.0.

SwiftPY: Building towards 1.0.0.

title: Your File Watcher Deleted the File You Just Saved
description:
The setup is about as simple as file-based automation gets: watch a folder, copy anything written there into a second folder, and — because a stale mirror is worse than no mirror — remove from the target whatever gets removed from the source. Four lines of chokidar and you're done.

Then someone hits Cmd-S in their editor, and the file vanishes from the target. Not corrupted, not half-copied. Gone. Sometimes it comes back a moment later; sometimes it doesn't. The source file is fine the whole time.

TL;DR: Most editors don't save into your file, they write a temp file and rename() it into place. A naive watcher sees unlink then add and, with delete-mirroring on, races itself into deleting the target. The fix is three ordered defenses: awaitWriteFinish so half-written files never get copied, a per-file debounce so a bundler's event storm becomes one copy, and a delay on every delete that gets cancelled the moment the path reappears. All three are in copy-watch, which is where the code below comes from.

Why Does Saving a File Look Like a Delete?

Because for a lot of software, it is one. An atomic save means the editor never leaves your file in a partially-written state: it writes the new content to a temporary file next to the original, fsyncs it, and then rename()s the temp over the target. rename() on the same filesystem is atomic, so a reader either sees the entire old file or the entire new one — never a truncated middle.

Excellent property. Terrible thing to watch naively. The kernel events you get are, in order:

unlink   notes.md
add      notes.md

Or, depending on the editor, a supporting cast of files you never asked about:

  • vim writes a probe file literally named 4913 into the directory to test whether it can create files there, then deletes it.
  • Some macOS editors stage the whole thing in a hidden .sb-a1b2c3d4 directory next to the file.
  • Copying onto exFAT or SMB volumes leaves AppleDouble siblings (._notes.md) carrying the resource fork.
  • iCloud Drive leaves notes.md.icloud placeholders for files that are visible in Finder but not actually on disk.

So a watcher that maps events one-to-one onto filesystem operations has already made two mistakes before any of your code runs: it will faithfully mirror junk, and it will faithfully mirror a delete that was never a delete.

Why Not Just Copy on Every Event?

Because add doesn't mean "this file is finished." It means "a directory entry appeared." A large asset written by a build step will fire add while it's still a few kilobytes of a few megabytes, and you'll copy the truncated version — with no error, because nothing failed. Truncated output that nobody reports is the expensive kind.

Chokidar's answer is awaitWriteFinish: don't emit until the file's size has stopped changing for a while.

const watcher = chokidar.watch(srcRoot, {
  ignoreInitial: !initial,
  usePolling: poll,
  interval,
  binaryInterval: interval,
  // Verhindert, dass halb geschriebene Dateien kopiert werden.
  awaitWriteFinish: {
    stabilityThreshold: stability,   // default 300ms
    pollInterval: Math.min(100, interval),
  },
  // ...
});

300ms is a compromise, not a law. It's the price of every copy — nothing is mirrored before it elapses — and it needs to be longer than the longest pause your writer takes mid-file. A bundler streaming output locally is comfortable at 300ms. A file arriving over a slow network mount is not; raise it there and accept the latency.

That handles one write. It does not handle the second problem: a bundler rewriting the same file four times in 200ms as it settles. Each of those is a legitimate, complete write, so awaitWriteFinish dutifully emits four events, and you do four copies where the first three are already garbage. Hence a second, separate timer — a per-file debounce, defaulting to 50ms:

const copyTimers = new Map();

const schedule = (map, key, delay, fn) => {
  clearTimeout(map.get(key));
  if (delay <= 0) {
    map.delete(key);
    fn();
    return;
  }
  map.set(key, setTimeout(() => { map.delete(key); fn(); }, delay));
};

Note the shape: keyed per path, and every new event for that path cancels the pending one. That's the primitive the delete fix needs too.

How Do You Make a Delete Safe?

You don't act on unlink when you receive it. You schedule the delete, and you let a subsequent add for the same path cancel it.

const deleteTimers = new Map();

const onWrite = (type) => (file) => {
  // Ein neu erscheinender Pfad annulliert eine noch offene Löschung.
  clearTimeout(deleteTimers.get(file));
  deleteTimers.delete(file);
  schedule(copyTimers, file, debounce, () =>
    run(type, file, (to) => copyFile(file, to, retries)),
  );
};

watcher
  .on('add', onWrite('copy'))
  .on('change', onWrite('update'))
  .on('unlink', (file) => {
    if (!deleteRemoved) return;
    clearTimeout(copyTimers.get(file));
    copyTimers.delete(file);
    schedule(deleteTimers, file, deleteDelay, () =>
      run('delete', file, (to) => rm(to, { force: true })),
    );
  });

Both directions cancel each other. An unlink drops any pending copy — no point copying a file that's gone. An add drops any pending delete — the atomic save's rename landed, so the "delete" was never real. The grace period (--delete-delay, default 400ms) is simply how long you're willing to wait to find out which of the two it was.

Pick it deliberately: too short and a slow rename slips through as a real delete, which is the original bug wearing a smaller hat; too long and genuinely deleted files linger in the mirror. 400ms covers a local rename() by three orders of magnitude and is imperceptible to a human deleting a file on purpose. Over SMB, raise it.

Worth being explicit about what this is not: it is not a correctness guarantee, it's a heuristic with a tunable window. There is no event that says "this was an atomic save." You are inferring intent from timing, and the honest thing to do is name the assumption in the flag's default rather than bury it.

What Should the Ignore List Actually Contain?

The tempting move, once you've seen 4913 and ._notes.md and .sb-a1b2c3d4 go past, is to ignore every dotfile and be done with it. Don't. That rule throws away .htaccess, .env, and the entire .well-known directory — for a folder being mirrored into a webroot, those are three of the files most likely to matter.

So the default list is deliberately narrow and enumerated:

export const DEFAULT_IGNORE = [
  /(^|[\\/])\.git([\\/]|$)/,
  /(^|[\\/])node_modules([\\/]|$)/,
  /(^|[\\/])\.DS_Store$/,          // macOS Finder-Metadaten
  /(^|[\\/])\.Spotlight-V100([\\/]|$)/,
  /(^|[\\/])\._[^\\/]+$/,          // AppleDouble Resource-Forks auf FAT/exFAT/SMB
  /\.icloud$/,                     // iCloud-Platzhalter
  /\.sb-[a-z0-9]+$/i,              // Atomic-Save-Verzeichnisse
  /~$/, /\.swp$/, /\.tmp$/, /\.crdownload$/, /\.part$/,
  /^4913$/,                        // vim-Testdatei beim Speichern
];

Every entry there is a name some piece of software chose for a file it intends to delete itself. That's the actual membership rule, and it's a much better filter than "starts with a dot."

Two more guards belong in the same category — cheap checks that turn a silent disaster into a startup error:

if (srcKey === destKey) {
  throw new Error('createCopyWatcher: "dest" darf nicht "src" sein');
}
if (destKey.startsWith(srcKey + path.sep)) {
  throw new Error(
    'createCopyWatcher: "dest" liegt innerhalb von "src" — das erzeugt eine Endlosschleife',
  );
}

A target nested inside the source is a feedback loop: every copy is a write inside the watched tree, which triggers another copy. It fills a disk in the time it takes to notice. And the comparison itself needs care on macOS, where the same path can arrive as NFD or NFC and comparisons are case-insensitive:

function normalizePath(p) {
  const normalized = path.resolve(p).normalize('NFC');
  return process.platform === 'darwin' || process.platform === 'win32'
    ? normalized.toLowerCase()
    : normalized;
}

Skip the normalize('NFC') and ~/Sites/Café compares unequal to itself depending on which program handed you the string.

What Doesn't This Replace?

rsync. If all you want is for B to look like A, this has been solved for decades and solved better:

rsync -a --delete ./dist/ ~/Sites/preview/

Pair it with fswatch and you have the same behaviour in two lines of shell, with none of the timing heuristics above — because rsync compares state instead of reacting to events, which sidesteps the entire atomic-save problem rather than defending against it.

A watcher earns its place only when something has to happen per file: purge a cache entry, trigger a reload, kick a deploy, transform the file on the way through. That's what the onEvent hook is for, and it's the only reason to accept the extra machinery.

It also doesn't preserve extended attributes, Finder tags, or resource forks — fs.cp copies content and mode, nothing more. Mirroring signed bundles or design files? Use ditto --rsrc --extattr. For build artifacts and source, it's irrelevant.

What's the Generalizable Lesson Here?

  • A filesystem event is a statement about a directory entry, not a statement about intent. unlink + add is one save operation about as often as it's two separate ones, and nothing in the event stream tells you which.
  • When you can't observe intent, encode the ambiguity as a tunable delay with a documented default — and say in the docs that it's a heuristic. A hidden 400ms assumption is a bug report waiting to happen; a documented one is a flag.
  • Use separate timers for separate concerns. Bundling repeat writes (debounce) and waiting out a possible rename (delete-delay) look similar and want different durations; merging them means one of the two is always wrong.
  • Make destructive operations cancellable and let the cheap signal cancel the expensive one. A pending delete that any new write annuls is strictly safer than a delete that has to be undone.
  • "Ignore all dotfiles" is the wrong abstraction for temp files. The real category is "files some program created and intends to remove itself" — enumerate those, and keep .env and .well-known working.

The other half of getting this tool to run at all — the sudo prompt, the macOS privacy dialog, and the EMFILE crash, none of which is actually about admin rights — is covered in the file watcher that looked like a permissions problem.

title: You Can't Eyeball a Geometry Library
description:
I have a side project whose entire purpose is to make letters look like a teenager went at them with a spray can. You type a word, it fattens into one connected outline, then a stack of warps shoves it around until it reads as graffiti. It is a deeply unserious project. So naturally I spent a weekend building a forensic area-diff tool to referee it, because that is apparently who I am.

Here's how the unseriousness turned serious. One step in the pipeline is a polygon offset — grow a closed shape outward by N pixels to draw the outline. Textbook geometry, and JavaScript has at least three grown-up libraries that do it. The sensible move is to pick the one with the nicest README and never think about it again.

I thought about it. Turns out two of the three produce byte-for-byte identical geometry, the third quietly fibs, and you cannot see any of that with your eyes. Which is the whole point.

The project in question. Deeply unserious. Note the two boring faces on the bottom — a plain serif and a monospace — because they end up mattering far more than they look.

TL;DR: Three JavaScript polygon-offset libraries, tested with a symmetric-difference-area diff instead of eyeballing the shapes. Two turned out to be geometrically identical (0.000% apart) and just a speed pick between them. The third — the popular, ergonomic one — quietly drifted up to 10% on delicate serif shapes, while also being 10–30× slower. The numbers:

Engine vs. reference (XOR area) speed
JS port of the reference 0.000% 1× (reference)
WASM build of the same 0.000% 2–4× faster
The charming third one 0.4–2.8% (display) · up to 10% (serif) 10–30× slower

Why Can't You Just Eyeball Two Outlines?

Geometry is where visual inspection goes to embarrass itself. Two offset outlines of the same word can look pixel-identical in the browser and differ by thousands of points under the hood. Or look identical and be off by a third of a unit — nothing, a rounding shrug — that then compounds through a boolean union into a genuinely wrong shape. Show me two outlines side by side and I will confidently tell you they match. I will be wrong, and I will be sure.

A screenshot diff would have blessed all three libraries. A point count would have told me they were different without telling me whether the difference was a problem or a personality. Neither is the question I actually had.

For filled shapes the honest metric is area — specifically the symmetric difference. Lay outline A over outline B, keep the bits that belong to exactly one of them (an XOR), and measure that leftover area as a percentage of the reference. Two engines that truly agree score zero. One that drifts tells you how far, in a number that means something.

So instead of choosing a library, I built a tiny courtroom. Same word, same font, same offset distance, run through each engine, then diff against Clipper as the reference:

areaXOR(a, b) / areaFill(a) * 100   // 0% = geometrically identical

Which Libraries Turned Out to Be Identical?

First verdict, and it's the comforting one: two of the three "different" libraries scored 0.000% against each other. Every font. No daylight between them at all.

Which is not luck — it's a fact I could only know because I checked. One is a pure-JavaScript port of a famous C++ geometry library; the other is that same C++ hauled into WebAssembly. Same DNA, two upbringings. You'd hope the port is faithful, but "hope" is not a test, and reimplementations drift for a living — an off-by-one in a fill rule, a rounding mode nobody documented, an edge case the port author simply never hit. A flat 0.000% XOR area across a pile of wildly different letterforms is what "faithful" looks like when you make it say a number out loud.

And once you know they're twins, the choice stops being about right-and-wrong and becomes a drag race. The WASM build ran 2–4× faster for identical output. Done: fast twin in the hot path, readable JavaScript twin kept around as the reference and for headless scripts. Easy call — but only easy because the geometry question got answered first, instead of being assumed away.

Which Library Quietly Drifted?

The third library is the popular, ergonomic one. Gorgeous API, wonderful at boolean ops, firm handshake, remembers your name. Against the reference it scored 0.4% to 2.8% on the graffiti display fonts. Small enough to wave off — "close enough, ship it" — especially since, again, the shapes looked fine.

Then I added the narcs.

I dropped two boring reference faces into the test set — a plain serif and a monospace, the typographic equivalent of a hall monitor — right next to the loud graffiti fonts. The drift on those didn't stay small. It jumped to around 6% on the monospace and 10% on the serif.

That jump is the actual lesson wearing a disguise. The library drifted worst exactly where the geometry was most delicate — thin serifs, hairline stems, tight little counters — which is, of course, precisely the case you can least afford to get wrong. On a fat spray-paint letter a 10% error has nowhere to hide and nothing to ruin. On a hairline serif it has the run of the place. If I'd only tested the "real" inputs — the display fonts the project is actually about — the 10% case would never have shown up, and I'd have happily shipped a subtly broken outline on the exact shapes that expose it. The most boring font in the drawer was the most useful witness in the room.

Grey is the reference offset. Top: the WASM engine (green) traces it exactly — 0.000%. Bottom: paper.js (red) floats a hair outside the true edge, everywhere at once. That gap is the drift — and notice you only spot it because someone drew both lines on the same shape. Left to their own panels, all three outlines look completely fine.

It was also 10–30× slower than the WASM engine, so it managed to be both wrong and last. The slowness I'd have caught on my own eventually, the way you notice a room's gotten cold. The geometric drift I would not have — not without pointing a diff at the right quantity.

Why Was the Measurement Tool Itself the Bottleneck?

One more finding, filed under quietly-embarrassing. To score "quality" I'd written a metric that counts self-intersections in an outline — the classic smell of a warp gone feral. First implementation was the obvious one: every edge against every other edge, O(n²). Correct. Honest. Fine.

It was also, once the comparison grid grew to a hundred-plus renderings each carrying thousands of points, the single slowest thing in the whole project — slower than all the actual geometry it was hired to evaluate. I had built a courtroom and the bailiff weighed more than the defendant. The fix was to stop hand-rolling it and let the geometry library resolve self-intersections with a sweep-line (SimplifyPolygon, O(n log n)) and compare the result. Same signal, a whole complexity class lighter.

Say it plainly, because it's easy to forget: the tooling you build to measure a thing is also code, and it is fully capable of being the bottleneck. A benchmark harness slower than what it benchmarks. A linter slower than the compile. A quality metric slower than the render. All the same joke, and it's usually on you.

What's the Generalizable Lesson Here?

  • "Drop-in replacement" is a claim about the API, not the output. For anything numeric or geometric, prove it with a diff before you trust it. Two libraries agreeing on function signatures tells you nothing about whether they agree on answers.
  • Pick a diff that speaks the domain. For filled outlines that's symmetric-difference area — not a point count, and for the love of god not a screenshot. The right metric turns "looks the same" into "0.000%" or "10%, exactly where it hurts."
  • Test the inputs most likely to break, not the flattering ones. The dull serif I almost didn't bother adding is the one that ratted out the drift. Boring, delicate, and adversarial cases carry more information than the happy path — invite them.
  • Settle correctness as a number and the rest of the decision falls out. Two engines proven identical collapse to a pure speed pick; one that's slower and wrong disqualifies itself. A good measurement doesn't just inform the argument, it ends it.
  • Watch the harness, not just the subject. Your quality metric can be asymptotically worse than the thing it's judging. Weigh the bailiff.

The whole rig — diff harness, warp pipeline, and the graffiti it was all secretly in service of — is open source if you'd like to poke at it: github.com/jhalitschke/warp-lab.

title: The rule that pays for a Chinese workplace injury lives in four documents
description:
I spent a morning trying to answer one question: what does an employer in China owe after a workplace injury? The short answer is a State Council regulation with four benefit bands. The longer answer is that three of the numbers people quote are not in that regulation at all, and one of them changes every January.

This is a note on how the chain fits together, and on the checks that caught my own misreadings.

The regulation is the easy part

The work injury regulation (State Council Order 375, rewritten by Order 586 in 2010) is a tidy document. Ten disability grades, a fixed number of months of the worker's wage for each, plus a monthly allowance for the top six. The wage it multiplies is not the salary in the contract: article 64 uses the average monthly contribution wage over the 12 months before the injury, then clamps it to 300% and 60% of the local average wage.

That clamp is the first place a hand calculation goes wrong. If a worker earns 30,000 a month in a city whose average wage is 8,000, the benefit is priced at 24,000. If a worker earns 3,500, it is priced at 4,800 — higher than what they actually earned. Both directions are in the same sentence, and the mechanism is contribution-based, so an employer that reported a low base produces a low payout.

A small function makes the rule testable:

GRANT = {1: 27, 2: 25, 3: 23, 4: 21, 5: 18, 6: 16, 7: 13, 8: 11, 9: 9, 10: 7}
ALLOWANCE = {1: 0.90, 2: 0.85, 3: 0.80, 4: 0.75, 5: 0.70, 6: 0.60}

def priced_wage(last12_avg, city_avg):
    lo, hi = 0.6 * city_avg, 3.0 * city_avg
    return min(max(last12_avg, lo), hi)

def one_off(grade, wage):
    return GRANT[grade] * wage

assert priced_wage(30_000, 8_000) == 24_000   # ceiling
assert priced_wage(3_500, 8_000) == 4_800     # floor
assert one_off(10, 10_000) == 70_000
assert one_off(1, 10_000) == 270_000

Number one that is not in the regulation: the death grant

Article 39 says a work-related death pays three items. Two of them are computed on figures that have nothing to do with the worker's wage: the burial grant is six months of the local average wage, and the one-off death grant is 20 times the previous year's national urban per-capita disposable income.

The 20 is in the regulation. The income figure is not. It arrives with the statistics bureau's January release. For deaths in 2026 the number is 56,502 CNY, so the grant is 1,130,040. For 2025 the figure was 54,188 and the grant was 1,083,760.

Two consequences worth writing down: the death grant is identical in every city, while the burial grant is not, because one uses a national income average and the other a local wage average. And if a death happens in the first weeks of January, before the release, a 2013 ministry opinion allows payment on the previous year's figure with a top-up later. A benefit table that hardcodes one year's number is wrong by the next January.

Checking is cheap here: recompute the prior year, subtract, and see whether the difference matches the published growth rate.

Number two: when the 48-hour clock starts

The regulation treats a sudden illness at work that kills within 48 hours as a work injury, and never says when the 48 hours begin. A 2004 ministry letter does: from the first diagnosis at a medical institution.

The interesting part is that this letter predates the 2010 rewrite, and part of it is visibly stale. One item still quotes the old commute clause, which covered motor vehicle accidents; the rewrite replaced it with any accident where the worker is not mainly responsible, across road, rail, ferry and train. So the letter is half-live: its 48-hour reading is still cited by the ministry, while its other items describe text that no longer exists.

That is the failure mode I keep running into with Chinese administrative law. An interpretive letter stays in force until something repeals it, even when the thing it interprets has been rewritten underneath it. The only reliable check is to read the letter and the current regulation side by side, and to note which items still map onto a live article.

Number three: the two subsidies only provinces can price

When the employment ends after a graded injury, two more payments appear: a medical subsidy from the fund and an employment subsidy from the employer. The regulation sets no amounts and hands them to each province.

Guangdong's statute gives grade 5 ten months of medical subsidy and fifty months of employment subsidy, down to grade 10 at one month and four months. At a 10,000 monthly wage, a grade 10 injury adds 50,000 to the 70,000 grant; a grade 5 adds 600,000 to the 180,000.

So "the compensation for a grade 10 injury" has no national answer. It has a national core plus a provincial tail, and the tail is larger than the core for low grades.

GD_MED = {5: 10, 6: 8, 7: 6, 8: 4, 9: 2, 10: 1}
GD_EMP = {5: 50, 6: 40, 7: 25, 8: 15, 9: 8, 10: 4}

def gd_termination(grade, wage):
    return GD_MED[grade] * wage, GD_EMP[grade] * wage

assert sum(gd_termination(10, 10_000)) == 50_000
assert sum(gd_termination(5, 10_000)) == 600_000

What I'd check first next time

Three questions, in this order, for any benefit that looks like a simple multiple:

  1. Is the multiplier applied to the worker's wage, a local average, or a national statistic? Article 39 uses all three in one paragraph.
  2. Is the base the wage paid or the wage contributed on? In China those diverge, and the benefit follows the contribution.
  3. Which document actually sets the amount? A regulation that says "the province decides" is a pointer, not an answer.

None of this is exotic. It is the ordinary work of reading a spec that is split across four files, where one file changes annually and one is older than the file it interprets.

I wrote the full version, with every article number and source date, at notebookfield.com.

Drafted with an AI assistant from my own reading of the primary documents; every clause number and link here was checked against the source.

title: How I built a SQL injection scanner for Java using ASTs (as a sophomore)
description:
I'm a CS sophomore at George Mason. This semester I wanted to understand how tools like CodeQL actually find bugs, so I built a small version myself. It's a GitHub Action that scans Java code for SQL injection and hardcoded secrets and marks the exact line on your pull request.

Here's what I learned building it.

Why regex isn't enough

My first idea was to just search for strings like "SELECT " +. That breaks fast. The SQL might be built in a variable three lines up, or split across a StringBuilder. Regex only sees text. It doesn't know what the code means.

What an AST is

An AST (abstract syntax tree) is the code turned into a tree of what it actually does: this is a method call, this is a string, this is a variable being added to a string. I used JavaParser to turn each Java file into a tree, then wrote "visitor" rules that walk the tree.

For SQL injection, the rule looks for a database call like executeQuery(...) where the query was built by gluing user input onto a string, instead of using a PreparedStatement with ? placeholders.

The hard part: false alarms

Finding secrets sounds easy: look for things like password = "...". But real code is full of fake ones, like test values, placeholders and example configs. My first version flagged way too much.

So I ran it on 31 open source projects (27,552 files) and went through the results by hand. I added rules to skip test folders, obvious placeholders and so on. False alarms on secrets went from 156 to 27, about 83% fewer, and every real secret in that survey was still caught.

That was the most useful part of the project. Making a scanner that finds stuff is easy. Making one people won't mute is hard.

Suggesting fixes with a local LLM

There's an optional step that sends a finding to a local model through Ollama to suggest a fix. I don't trust the output blindly. The fix gets parsed again to make sure it's valid Java before it's shown. There are 57 JUnit tests covering the rules.

Try it

It takes about 2 minutes. Create .github/workflows/security-scan.yml in your repo:

name: Security scan
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: noorhusaan302-png/ast-security-reviewer@v1.1.0

Then open the Actions tab. Any finding shows the file, the line and the problem.

I know CodeQL and Semgrep are way more complete. This was a learning project, but I'd love to make it useful for student and small projects. If you try it and hit a false positive, please open an issue.

title: When Routine Blood Tests Reveal More Than You Expect: Understanding Hyperparathyroidism
description:
Not every health problem starts with obvious symptoms. Sometimes, an ordinary blood test can reveal something that has been developing quietly for months or even years. Primary hyperparathyroidism is one example.

The condition occurs when one or more of the parathyroid glands produce too much parathyroid hormone (PTH). These four small glands sit behind the thyroid in the neck and help regulate calcium levels in the body. When they become overactive, calcium levels in the bloodstream can rise, potentially affecting the bones, kidneys, and other parts of the body.

Why the Condition Can Be Difficult to Recognize

One of the challenges with hyperparathyroidism is that its symptoms aren't always easy to connect to a single condition.

Some people experience persistent fatigue, muscle weakness, difficulty concentrating, mood changes, or general aches and pains. Others have no noticeable symptoms at all.

Because these issues can have many different causes, patients may spend considerable time investigating individual symptoms without realizing they could be connected.

Routine blood work can help identify the problem. Elevated blood calcium levels may prompt doctors to investigate further by checking parathyroid hormone levels and reviewing other relevant test results.

Why Looking Beyond One Test Matters

A diagnosis shouldn't depend on a single number in a laboratory report. Doctors consider calcium and PTH levels together, along with kidney function, vitamin D levels, and other clinical information.

Additional tests may include a 24-hour urine calcium measurement and a bone density scan. Kidney imaging may also be recommended to check for stones or other complications.

Imaging studies of the neck, such as ultrasound, sestamibi scans, or specialized CT scans, can help locate abnormal parathyroid tissue when surgery is being considered.

Understanding the Available Treatment Options

Treatment depends on the patient's overall health, laboratory results, symptoms, and whether the condition is affecting the bones or kidneys.

Some patients may be monitored with regular blood tests and bone density assessments. Others may benefit from medication or surgery.

Parathyroidectomy, which involves removing the overactive gland or glands, is the definitive treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism. The surgical approach depends on the individual case, including whether one gland or multiple glands are affected.

For people researching their diagnosis and possible treatment paths, HyperparathyroidMD provides educational information about parathyroid conditions, diagnostic testing, and surgical approaches.

The Importance of Asking the Right Questions

Receiving an unexpected blood test result can be confusing, especially when there are few obvious symptoms. Understanding what the results mean and discussing them with a qualified medical professional is an important first step.

Questions about calcium levels, PTH results, kidney health, bone density, and possible treatment options can help make consultations more productive.

The bigger lesson is that health problems don't always announce themselves clearly. Sometimes, paying attention to routine test results and looking at the bigger picture can make all the difference in identifying a condition early and understanding what to do next.
