title: Pretending to Delete
description:
Algorithms, a semester of SQL, and the slow realization that in real systems we mostly only pretend to delete.

A look back — long before any of the tools we argue about now.

This is the last of my memories of studying computer science — the database course, and the algorithms course that led up to it, closing out what I learned in school in the 1990s.

Algorithms

After data structures in my sophomore year, algorithms arrived as the course for learning to program "properly." The book was thick enough to be intimidating on its own. I worked hard at the front of it, held my breath through graphs, and somewhere around greedy methods and NP-hard and NP-complete I simply found it difficult. At first I took it for no more than a set of slightly cleverer ways to solve a given problem, but I kept turning back to it — in grad school, and later in working life — and for one reason or another it kept earning its keep. Ten years after graduating, when I set out to interview at Google, it was the book I gritted my teeth and opened again; what's left of it now is fragments.

INSERT / SELECT / DELETE

The database course came at the very end of my undergraduate years. There was a book, though it never quite felt like a textbook, and what I remember is SQL, all semester long. The sharpest thing that stayed with me — I can't reconstruct the exact tone — was a grad student who came in as our lab assistant and told us, "For the rest of your lives you'll need nothing else; just know SELECT." More than twenty-five years on, working with SQL that is still very much in use, I found myself thinking of him again.

There was the minor argument over whether SQL counts as a programming language, but it remains one of the most used, and by now whatever tool you pick probably supports it out of the box. Work on the backend and you'll get a fuller look; otherwise, the prophecy about SELECT has more or less come true. In the AI era, perhaps we'll be learning how to coax GPT into writing good SQL — a chain of person to GPT to SQL to database to machine that feels already half here.

is_deleted

In data structures and algorithms, the thing that took the most time was implementing delete — keeping the state from breaking, returning memory properly, holding everything together so that the far more frequent searches stayed fast. It was the part that gave me the worst headaches whenever I tried to build a system. In the database course, though, the most time went to a different question: how to make deletion recoverable. Real services carried the same worry — what happens when something deleted still needs to come back, and then what becomes of the backup — and the usual answer was to not actually delete anything, and only act as though you had.

It was a little deflating, honestly, how often adding an is_deleted field was all it took for a feature to work. Later I found the same idea already everywhere — page memory in the kernel, the way NAND flash behaves — less like rubbing something out with an eraser than throwing white paint over it. When a departed user signs up again, do you reuse what was there? And under certain laws, did you truly delete it? That one small question — "is it deleted?" — turns out to hold a great deal of room for misunderstanding.

P.S. On a single service it never shows, but once you meet scale, some things reveal enormous read performance the moment they're frozen read-only — and watching the same concerns come around again as domains and generations change, maybe there's something to the old line about none of it going to waste.

Adapted from my Korean essay on Brunch: brunch.co.kr/@chaesang/57

title: Go Recovery Security in 2026: Auditing SMS and Email OTP for SaaS
description:
Use SMS OTP as the managed verification path and treat email OTP as an application-owned fallback for short-expiry e-commerce password resets, with release approval tied to evidence that expired challenges cannot authorize a reset. The deciding constraint for a US/EU SaaS platform is whether the team can explain every authorization decision after delivery has been delayed or retried. A successful send is insufficient evidence.

TL;DR: choose the channel implementation your team can integrate and audit, retain application control over the reset deadline, and measure successful verification before that deadline. Neither an SMS delivery receipt nor an email open proves that the account owner completed verification; password recovery also needs its own security review rather than inheriting the assurance claims of a 2FA login flow.

How should SaaS teams audit SMS and email OTP security for recovery?

The operational signal is a gap between transport acceptance and a completed reset inside its validity window. A message can become useless while an application is waiting for delivery evidence, and automatically issuing a fresh challenge at that point can turn an apparent availability improvement into an authorization policy change. The relevant question is whether the application rejects the original challenge at the deadline and can reconstruct that rejection without storing the secret in its logs.

Expiration wins here.

For this runbook, use a proposed 300-second validity window, measured from challenge issuance rather than message arrival; that number is an example policy to review, not a vendor default or a compliance requirement. Record the issuance time, deadline, challenge identifier, reset purpose, selected channel, and decision reason in a controlled audit record. Keep raw OTP values and reset credentials out of that record. Review retention and access with the people responsible for the applicable US/EU obligations: an API feature list does not establish legal compliance, data residency, or a sufficient retention period.

For teams that want a managed SMS verification step behind an existing Go HTTP client, try Infrai for the SMS portion of this recovery workflow: its plain REST API avoids installing and maintaining another SDK. Public, unauthenticated discovery exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which gives a platform team a concrete way to review the integration contract before issuing credentials. Those are useful reductions in integration friction; they do not establish a delivery-latency SLO. Email fallback still needs application-owned code generation, storage, expiry, and verification around ordinary email sending.

Keep that ownership decision visible in the roadmap. Both channels expose delivery events through polling, so a fallback controller needs a deliberate observation interval and cannot assume immediate event notification. If voice, WhatsApp, or RCS recovery is a requirement, evaluate a specialist for that part of the workflow.

Infrai provides one key for SMS and email, so the fallback branch does not introduce a second provider credential to provision and rotate. This single key covers 295 routes across 20 modules; the practical benefit here is a smaller credential inventory for the two recovery channels. Its self-describing API also lets a reviewer inspect schemas without a key before approving that shared credential's use. Runnable examples in 10 languages include Go, which lets the owning team begin contract review in its existing stack rather than translating an SDK tutorial.

Don't skip review.

Buy versus build against the evidence requirement

A quick first send is a poor acceptance test for a recovery integration. Compare the first useful result instead: a challenge is issued, its transport outcome is correlated, an expired attempt is denied, and the evidence survives a retry. The following buy-versus-build table compares review boundaries, rather than implying that the products have interchangeable authentication guarantees.

Option Setup and integration surface Evidence and ownership trade-off
Infrai Plain REST with public discovery; managed SMS OTP send and verification, with custom email verification around email sending Reduces SDK surface; application retains recovery authorization, email challenge state, and polling orchestration
Twilio Verify Evaluate a verification-focused service and its channel configuration against the reset policy Prefer this specialist evaluation when verification-specific channel behavior is the procurement requirement; require evidence for the exact channels and regions selected
Amazon SNS Evaluate SMS messaging within an AWS integration and credential model Suitable to assess when the platform wants a messaging building block; explicitly assign ownership of the challenge lifecycle instead of treating publication as verification
Resend Evaluate a dedicated email API and sender setup for the email branch Suitable to assess when email delivery is the integration focus; require the application or a separate identity service to own the recovery decision
Amazon SES Evaluate an email-focused service within the AWS credential and sender-management model A reasonable email-branch candidate for an AWS platform; account recovery state and expiry still need an explicit application owner

Twilio Verify, Amazon SNS, and Resend are real alternatives at different layers. Their official documentation belongs in the review, but no latency ranking, regional compliance conclusion, or feature-equivalence claim follows from this comparison. If an existing identity platform already owns account recovery, extending its verified policy may create less on-call work than introducing a second challenge authority. That is the buy-versus-build question to resolve before writing an adapter.

Credential sprawl is also an operating constraint: count production secrets, rotation procedures, sender configurations, and incident owners for the actual combination you would deploy. A shared API credential can reduce integration inventory while increasing the importance of application-side access control. Do not equate fewer SDKs with fewer security responsibilities.

Implement the expiry boundary before connecting transport

Use five controls as the release boundary: an immutable issuance deadline, binding to the intended account and reset purpose, atomic single-use consumption, transport-independent audit evidence, and a fallback policy that preserves the original recovery deadline. These are application requirements. Do not infer their implementation from a provider accepting an SMS request.

Before wiring a send worker, inspect the API contract. This runnable Go program calls the read-only discovery surface, prints its JSON response, and needs only the standard library plus an INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable. Discovery itself is public; using the environment credential here demonstrates the HTTP authentication pattern without sending a reset or recipient data. Review the returned capability schemas before implementing SMS send or verify payloads.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY before running")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned invalid JSON")
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This request is read-only, so retrying it cannot issue duplicate challenges. Production write calls need their documented idempotency contract. Discovery success proves contract access, not delivery or verification success.

Keep authorization separate.

In production, reject the challenge at or after its deadline, check the intended account and purpose, validate the submitted secret through the appropriate verification path, then atomically consume the application challenge while rechecking expiry. A check followed by a separate update leaves room for two concurrent requests to pass. Enforce rate limits and define the behavior of concurrent challenges before exposing the reset flow to customers. A worker that resumes at second 305 of a 300-second window must discard that attempt, and a verifier receiving the correct code at second 300 must reject it; both decisions should have an audit reason that can be correlated to issuance without recording the code itself. These are policy examples to test, not reported production incidents.

The email branch deserves an explicit engineering estimate because the team owns its secret generation, protected storage, expiry, and verification. Sending an email is only one step. For SMS, keep the application's reset authorization separate from the managed OTP verification result so that the reset deadline remains enforceable even when the transport workflow completes later.

Verify the SLO with a capacity budget

Define a proposed journey SLO around eligible reset attempts that complete before their deadline, and report transport acceptance separately. Do not publish an achieved target until production evidence supports it. Segment the evidence by channel and the US/EU populations the service actually serves, while controlling access to recipient data; an aggregate success rate can conceal an unusable branch.

Polling consumes capacity.

For a planning example, 600 pending challenges checked every 10 seconds imply roughly 60 status checks per second if each challenge requires one check per interval, before resends, duplicate workers, or email fallback are counted. This is arithmetic for sizing a controller, not a measured throughput claim or a provider quota. If the queue wait plus observation delay consumes the remaining validity window, stop attempting the old challenge and return an explicit expired result. Never extend the deadline to make the delivery dashboard look healthier.

Verification should cover boundary times, duplicate submission, a worker resuming after expiry, a delayed delivery observation, and an email fallback attempted near the deadline. Require correlated records showing why each attempt was allowed or denied. For the email branch, review domain authentication against DMARC, and review the implications of Mail Privacy Protection before treating open telemetry as useful evidence. Neither source establishes that a particular reset reached its intended user.

Abuse controls belong in the same capacity review. Define business-layer geographic restrictions and country-level spending circuit breakers for SMS, plus per-account and per-origin request limits. Their thresholds should follow the application's threat model and traffic evidence. They are not substitutes for successful verification.

Roll back routing without reopening expired challenges

Release the channel decision behind an application-controlled routing setting, with one owner responsible for the challenge state and another explicitly assigned to transport operations if the responsibilities differ. Preserve request correlation and the original deadline across retries; for writes, use the documented idempotency mechanism and distinguish a transport retry from authorization to issue a new challenge.

If the rollout fails its journey SLO or cannot produce the required evidence, stop routing new attempts to that branch and return to the previously approved recovery path. Keep outstanding challenge state and audit records until the reviewed retention policy permits removal. Rolling back routing must not revive expired or consumed challenges, and stopping a worker must not be treated as recalling a message already in transit.

Approve the integration when the evidence chain is clear and the on-call ownership is affordable. Choose a specialist when its verification workflow or required channels remove more application responsibility than a common HTTP interface would.

References

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation
  • Resend introduction
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • DMARC specification
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with the API contract and discovery guidance in the Infrai documentation index.

title: Secure Database Access for AI Agents with db-mcp-gateway
description:
AI agents are useful when they can inspect data, but giving them direct database credentials creates a large security problem. A connection string in an agent prompt or a local environment variable is hard to rotate and easy to leak. db-mcp-gateway addresses this by acting as a self hosted MCP gateway between AI agents and databases. The agent sends a query request through MCP. The gateway checks identity and permissions before the database responds.

The repository is available at https://github.com/developerz-ai/db-mcp-gateway.

Credential isolation

The core rule is simple. Database credentials live only in the gateway. An AI agent receives query results, not connection strings. This removes the need to place a database URL on a developer laptop or inside an agent configuration file.

The gateway also avoids credential leakage in logs, errors, and responses. That matters because agents can produce verbose output, and debugging tools may capture more than expected. When the database password never enters the agent context, there is less to leak.

A typical request path looks like this. The AI agent calls an MCP tool. The gateway checks the caller identity and the grant. The gateway opens the database connection using its own credentials. The database returns rows. The gateway returns only the requested data to the agent.

Identity and SSO

db-mcp-gateway uses browser based SSO for authentication. Supported identity providers include Okta, Google Workspace, Entra, Authentik, and Keycloak. The agent does not need an embedded browser. The login flow happens through the user's normal browser session.

Every query can be traced from SSO user to group to grant to audit row. This gives security teams a clear attribution path. If an investigation asks who ran a query, the answer is not a shared service account. It is the identity that authenticated through SSO.

Group based permissions keep access manageable. A platform team can map an SSO group to a grant, and the grant can be reviewed like code.

Grants as code

Permissions are defined in YAML. There is no in band admin UI by design. This makes the permission model reviewable through pull requests and compatible with GitOps workflows.

A grant can specify the group, databases, actions, schemas, row limits, and whether a reason is required.

grants:
  - group: backend-devs
    databases: [production_postgres]
    actions: [query_read]
    constraints:
      schemas: [public, analytics]
      row_limit: 1000
      require_reason: true

This example allows the backend-devs group to run read queries against production_postgres. It limits the grant to the public and analytics schemas. It caps rows at 1000 and requires a reason for the query.

The gateway is read only by default. Writes are opt in per grant. Per database least privilege roles can be used, and statement timeouts and row caps are enforced at both the database and the gateway. Grants can also allow or deny schemas and define time windows.

Audit trail

Database access for AI agents needs an audit trail that is useful during an incident review. db-mcp-gateway records query history and stores gateway state and audit logs in PostgreSQL. The MCP tool surface includes get_query_history, which lets operators inspect prior queries.

The audit trail should answer who accessed a database and what query was run. It should also show which grant was used. This supports compliance efforts by providing access control and query logging. It does not make the project a certified compliance product, but it gives teams evidence they can review.

Deployment model

The gateway is distributed as a single Docker container. Configuration is one YAML file. PostgreSQL is used for gateway state and audit logs. The project targets PostgreSQL and MongoDB. MySQL and MSSQL are rejected at boot, which keeps the supported database surface explicit.

A basic run looks like this.

docker pull ghcr.io/developerz-ai/db-mcp-gateway:1.1.1
docker run -p 8080:8080 -v $(pwd)/config.yaml:/app/config.yaml ghcr.io/developerz-ai/db-mcp-gateway:1.1.1

This deployment style is small enough for a platform team to operate without a large control plane. The important operational control is the configuration file, because it defines grants and identity behavior.

MCP tool surface

The gateway exposes a small set of MCP tools. list_databases shows available databases. describe_schema returns table structure and relationships. sample_table previews data before a full query. run_query executes SELECT queries. explain helps with query analysis. get_query_history exposes the audit trail.

This tool surface is useful for AI agents because it gives them a safe way to explore data before running expensive queries. It also gives platform teams a narrow interface to monitor and restrict.

Who benefits

Platform and SRE teams get a way to enable AI agent database access without spreading credentials. Backend developers can query production data with their own SSO identity instead of a shared password. Security and compliance teams get centralized access control and query logging. They also get user attribution.

The main tradeoff is that the gateway becomes a required component for agent database access. That is usually acceptable when credential isolation and auditability are the goal.

Start with the repository

The project README includes the security model, grant examples, and deployment steps. Start by defining one read only grant for a non production database. Review the audit output. Then expand to production only after the identity and grant model is clear.

The repository is at https://github.com/developerz-ai/db-mcp-gateway. #MCP #DatabaseSecurity

title: Shared-schema multi-tenancy in Spring Boot + Hibernate: the reference code we actually run
description:
Shared-schema multi-tenancy in Spring Boot + Hibernate: the reference code we actually run

Multi-tenancy is one of those architectural decisions that looks deceptively simple until you start implementing it.

You add a tenant_id column, make sure queries are scoped to the current tenant, and assume you're done.

But what happens when a request has no tenant context? What happens when Spring Security hasn't populated the authentication context yet? What about native queries, background jobs, or writes that attempt to associate an entity with another tenant?

We ran into these questions while building our SaaS application, PresenceWave.

Rather than publish another theoretical explanation of multi-tenancy, I wanted to document the implementation we actually use: shared-schema, discriminator-based multi-tenancy with Spring Boot and Hibernate 6.

We've also extracted the relevant implementation into an open-source repository. It contains the tenant resolution filter, Hibernate integration, write-time validation, database schema and integration tests.

This isn't a library you can add to your build.gradle. It's reference code extracted from our production application, intended to be read alongside this article.

We've deliberately kept some of the rough edges and limitations in the implementation. They're often the most useful part of an engineering discussion.

Three kinds of requests

Before getting into the architecture, it helps to understand the different kinds of requests a multi-tenant application needs to handle.

There are three distinct scenarios:

  1. No tenant yet. Login, magic-link validation, health checks and other requests that happen before authentication. There's no tenant to scope the request to.
  2. A tenant from an authenticated session. A logged-in user working within their own tenant. This is the primary use case covered by our reference implementation.
  3. A tenant resolved from the request, without authentication. For example, a visitor accessing a customer's public blog, links page or embedded widget through that customer's custom domain.

Our TenantResolutionFilter handles the first two scenarios.

The third is also part of our production application, and probably accounts for the largest volume of requests. However, that uses host-based tenant resolution, which is product-specific and outside the scope of this repository.

It's also a somewhat different problem. Public pages are supposed to expose certain information across an anonymous request. The interesting security question there is ensuring that anonymous writes, such as form submissions, are still associated with the correct tenant.

That's worth a separate discussion.

The isolation model, and why we picked it

There are three common ways to isolate tenants in a relational database.

Model Isolation Operational cost
Database per tenant Strongest A connection pool and migration run per tenant. Cost grows with tenant count.
Schema per tenant Strong Requires a custom MultiTenantConnectionProvider and migrations per schema.
Shared schema + discriminator column Enforced in the ORM One schema, one migration path. Cheap to add tenants, but isolation depends on queries going through Hibernate.

We use the third approach.

Hibernate 6 supports discriminator-based multi-tenancy natively. We configure:

  • hibernate.multiTenancy=DISCRIMINATOR
  • @TenantId on the discriminator column.
  • A CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver implementation.

Hibernate then automatically appends a tenant predicate to queries against tenant-scoped entities and populates the discriminator column on inserts.

We don't need to add WHERE tenant_id = ? to every repository method or pass tenant identifiers through every service call.

The ORM handles that for us.

The honest trade-off is that the isolation guarantee depends on every relevant code path going through Hibernate.

The implementation and test suite are designed to make that boundary explicit.

Architecture

The complete request lifecycle looks like this:

[INSERT ARCHITECTURE DIAGRAM FROM ORIGINAL ARTICLE HERE]

Four components do most of the work:

  • TenantResolutionFilter runs once per request, after Spring Security, and determines whether the request has a tenant.
  • TenantContextHolder stores that decision using a pair of ThreadLocal variables.
  • CurrentTenantIdentifierResolverImpl connects Hibernate to the tenant context.
  • TenantAwareAspect addresses a gap that Hibernate's read-side filtering doesn't cover: writes.

Let's look at each component.

Resolving the tenant: a filter that runs after security, on purpose

The tenant resolution filter needs to know who is making the request.

For authenticated requests, it reads the authentication information from Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder and looks up the user's tenant membership.

A simplified version of the implementation:

// web/TenantResolutionFilter.java (trimmed)

private void resolveTenant(String path) {
    if (!path.startsWith(TENANT_SCOPED_PATH_PREFIX)) {
        // Not a tenant-scoped endpoint: public request,
        // Hibernate runs in root mode.
        TenantContextHolder.setPublicRequest(true);
        return;
    }

    Authentication auth =
        SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

    if (auth != null
            && auth.isAuthenticated()
            && auth.getPrincipal() instanceof UserDetails userDetails) {

        TenantUser membership = tenantUserRepository
            .findByUserEmail(userDetails.getUsername())
            .orElseThrow(() ->
                new IllegalStateException(
                    "Authenticated user has no tenant membership"
                )
            );

        TenantContextHolder.setTenant(membership.getTenant());

    } else {
        TenantContextHolder.setTenant(null);
        TenantContextHolder.setPublicRequest(true);
    }
}

Three outcomes come out of this method:

  • A non-tenant-scoped path.
  • An unauthenticated API request.
  • An authenticated API request.

Only the last one gets an actual tenant assigned.

There are two details here that are easy to get wrong.

1. Filter ordering is important.

Spring Boot registers its security filter chain at order -100.

We register our tenant resolution filter at order 1, after security, because it reads Authentication from SecurityContextHolder.

That authentication context doesn't exist until the security filter chain has run.

Interestingly, our production code used to have a comment saying the opposite: "keep before security".

It was wrong, and we corrected it while extracting the repository.

A stale comment pointing in the wrong direction on something this important is exactly the kind of thing worth checking in your own codebase.

2. The initial tenant lookup cannot itself be tenant-filtered.

When findByUserEmail runs, we don't know the tenant yet. That's precisely why we're running the query.

If it were a normal derived query against an entity annotated with @TenantId, Hibernate would append the tenant discriminator predicate using our fail-closed default tenant ID.

It would find nothing.

So we deliberately use a native query:

// tenant/TenantUserRepository.java (trimmed)

@Query(
    value = """
        SELECT tu.*
        FROM tenant_users tu
        JOIN users u ON tu.user_id = u.id
        WHERE u.email = :email
        """,
    nativeQuery = true
)
Optional<TenantUser> findByUserEmail(
    @Param("email") String email
);

Native queries bypass @TenantId entirely.

That's exactly what we need for this bootstrap lookup, but it's also why every other native query in a tenant-aware codebase needs to be reviewed carefully.

Hibernate's safety net only covers JPQL and derived queries.

Teaching Hibernate who's asking

The next component is CurrentTenantIdentifierResolverImpl.

Hibernate calls this resolver to determine the tenant identifier to use for the current operation.

Here's the relevant implementation:

// tenant/CurrentTenantIdentifierResolverImpl.java

public static final Long DEFAULT_TENANT_ID = -1L;
// Can never match a real row. Real IDs start at 1.

@Override
public String resolveCurrentTenantIdentifier() {
    try {
        if (TenantContextHolder.getCurrentTenantId() != null) {
            return TenantContextHolder.getCurrentTenantId();
        }
    } catch (Exception e) {
        return "" + DEFAULT_TENANT_ID;
    }

    return "" + DEFAULT_TENANT_ID;
}

@Override
public boolean isRoot(Object tenantId) {
    Boolean publicRequest =
        TenantContextHolder.getPublicRequest();

    return publicRequest != null && publicRequest;
}

Two decisions carry most of the design.

Fail closed, not fail open.

If a request forgets to set a tenant, it doesn't get access to all tenants' data.

It gets no data because -1 cannot match a real tenant ID.

The failure mode of a bug here is an empty result, not an accidental data leak.

isRoot() is the escape hatch.

When isRoot() returns true, Hibernate stops appending the tenant discriminator predicate.

We use this for public requests and background jobs that legitimately need to access data across tenants.

But we're not going to pretend this is a harmless switch.

It is the single riskiest part of this design because the ORM no longer provides automatic tenant isolation for those operations.

We register the resolver explicitly on the EntityManagerFactory, because we build it manually rather than relying entirely on Spring Boot autoconfiguration.

// config/PrimaryDataSourceConfig.java

return builder
    .dataSource(dataSource)
    .packages("com.example.multitenant")
    .persistenceUnit("primaryPU")
    .properties(Map.of(
        "hibernate.tenant_identifier_resolver",
        tenantIdentifierResolver
    ))
    .build();

Opting an entity in: one extends, two columns

We use a mapped superclass to make entities tenant-aware.

// tenant/TenantAwareEntity.java (trimmed)

@MappedSuperclass
public abstract class TenantAwareEntity {

    @Id
    @Tsid
    protected Long id;

    @ManyToOne
    @JoinColumn(name = "tenant_id")
    protected Tenant tenant;

    @TenantId
    protected String tenantIdFilter;

    @CreationTimestamp
    protected LocalDateTime createdAt;

    @UpdateTimestamp
    protected LocalDateTime updatedAt;
}

Notice that we have two tenant-related fields.

They serve different purposes.

  • tenant is a regular foreign-key relationship. It maintains relational integrity and can be used for joins.
  • tenantIdFilter is the discriminator column Hibernate uses for automatic tenant filtering.

The discriminator field is a String because that's what our resolver returns.

An entity opts into tenancy simply by extending this superclass.

For example:

// example/Project.java

@Entity
public class Project extends TenantAwareEntity {

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;
}

The repository doesn't need to know anything about tenants.

// example/ProjectRepository.java

public interface ProjectRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Project, Long> {

    List<Project> findByName(String name);
}

There is no tenant parameter in findByName.

Hibernate adds the discriminator predicate automatically.

That's the appeal of this approach: tenant isolation lives in one base class and one resolver, rather than being repeated across every repository method.

The gap Hibernate doesn't close: writes

@TenantId takes care of populating the discriminator column on inserts.

But it doesn't update or validate the tenant relationship.

Nothing inherently prevents application code from constructing an entity that points to another tenant, perhaps using an ID supplied by a client.

We address this with TenantAwareAspect.

The aspect intercepts save() and saveAll() calls across Spring Data repositories.

Here's the relevant code:

// tenant/TenantAwareAspect.java (trimmed)

@Before(
    "execution(* org.springframework.data.repository.CrudRepository+.save(..)) || "
    + "execution(* org.springframework.data.repository.CrudRepository+.saveAll(..))"
)
public void beforeSave(JoinPoint joinPoint) {

    if (!tenantAwareUtil.hasTenantContext()) {
        return;
    }

    Object entity = joinPoint.getArgs()[0];

    if (entity instanceof TenantAwareEntity tenantAwareEntity) {

        Tenant currentTenant =
            tenantAwareUtil.getCurrentTenant();

        if (tenantAwareEntity.getTenant() == null) {

            // New entity: stamp it from the current context.
            tenantAwareEntity.setTenant(currentTenant);

            tenantAwareEntity.setTenantIdFilter(
                "" + currentTenant.getId()
            );

        } else if (
            !tenantAwareEntity.belongsToTenant(currentTenant.getId())
        ) {

            // Entity points to a different tenant.
            throw new SecurityException(
                "Attempt to save entity with mismatched tenant"
            );
        }
    }
}

The intended behaviour is straightforward:

  • New entity without a tenant: assign the current tenant.
  • Existing entity belonging to another tenant: reject the operation.

We throw an exception rather than silently correcting the tenant relationship.

There is, however, a known limitation in this implementation.

The aspect only inspects joinPoint.getArgs()[0].

For save(entity), that argument is the entity itself.

For saveAll(collection), the first argument is a collection. The instanceof TenantAwareEntity check fails, and the call passes through without validation.

So saveAll() currently bypasses this aspect entirely.

We have deliberately left this limitation documented rather than quietly presenting the implementation as complete.

If your codebase relies on saveAll(), this needs to be fixed before adopting the pattern.

It's also a useful reminder that intercepting a repository method doesn't automatically mean you've handled every shape of its arguments.

Proving it, against a real database

Mocking the repository wouldn't prove much here.

The actual guarantee we're interested in is the SQL Hibernate generates and whether the database results respect tenant boundaries.

Our integration tests use Testcontainers to spin up a real PostgreSQL instance.

A simplified version of the tests:

// TenantIsolationIntegrationTest.java (trimmed)

@Test
void queries_AsAnotherTenant_DoNotSeeTheRows() {

    TenantContextHolder.setTenant(tenantA);

    Project alpha = projectRepository.save(
        Project.builder()
            .name("alpha")
            .build()
    );

    TenantContextHolder.setTenant(tenantB);

    assertThat(projectRepository.findAll()).isEmpty();

    assertThat(
        projectRepository.findById(alpha.getId())
    ).isEmpty();

    assertThat(
        projectRepository.findByName("alpha")
    ).isEmpty();
}

@Test
void queries_WithoutTenantContext_SeeNothing() {

    TenantContextHolder.setTenant(tenantA);

    projectRepository.save(
        Project.builder()
            .name("alpha")
            .build()
    );

    TenantContextHolder.clear();

    assertThat(projectRepository.findAll()).isEmpty();
}

@Test
void save_WithEntityOfAnotherTenant_IsRejected() {

    TenantContextHolder.setTenant(tenantA);

    Project foreign = Project.builder()
        .name("gamma")
        .tenant(tenantB)
        .build();

    assertThatThrownBy(
        () -> projectRepository.save(foreign)
    )
    .isInstanceOf(SecurityException.class)
    .hasMessageContaining("mismatched tenant");
}

These tests verify three different behaviours:

  1. Cross-tenant reads return no results, even when querying by an exact entity ID.
  2. A missing tenant context results in no data being returned.
  3. A write attempting to associate an entity with another tenant is rejected.

There's also a fourth test that deliberately sets publicRequest = true and verifies that it can see all tenants' rows.

That's an important test because root mode is a documented trade-off in this architecture.

A test suite that doesn't verify this behaviour would be hiding one of the most important parts of the design.

What we didn't smooth over

We left the limitations in the README rather than fixing everything before publishing.

These are useful considerations for anyone implementing this architecture.

1. Context doesn't automatically follow work onto other threads.

TenantContextHolder uses TransmittableThreadLocal.

However, that doesn't mean context propagation is automatically configured.

It requires TTL-aware executors or the TTL Java agent, neither of which is wired up in this reference repository.

A plain @Async method or @Scheduled job needs to set the tenant explicitly and clear it in a finally block.

Otherwise, it runs without a tenant context.

2. saveAll() bypasses the aspect.

As explained earlier, our aspect only inspects the first method argument as an entity.

A collection passed to saveAll() isn't inspected.

This needs to be addressed before relying on the aspect for collection writes.

3. Public requests are unfiltered.

When isRoot() returns true, Hibernate doesn't append the discriminator predicate.

There is no softer version of this behaviour.

Isolation for those requests depends on the application handler, not Hibernate.

4. Native queries are outside the safety net.

The initial tenant membership lookup deliberately uses a native query.

That's necessary because we don't know the tenant when performing the lookup.

But every other native query against tenant-scoped data needs to implement its own tenant restrictions.

5. The discriminator column needs an index.

The tenant discriminator should lead its own index.

Otherwise, tenant-scoped queries can end up scanning the table.

Our reference migration, V1__tenancy_core.sql, adds these indexes.

It's easy to overlook this when adding new tenant-aware tables later.

What's not here

This repository is intentionally scoped to the tenancy plumbing.

It doesn't include:

  • Resolving tenants from custom domains.
  • API-token authentication.
  • Tenant invitations and membership management.
  • Product-specific authorization rules.
  • Public visitor handling and anonymous form submissions.

Those are separate concerns from the narrower question of how Hibernate knows which tenant's rows it should return.

Try it, read it, take it apart

We've published the implementation as an open-source reference repository:

GitHub: https://github.com/JulioLabs/spring-boot-multitenant-starter

The README includes a suggested reading order:

  1. TenantContextHolder
  2. CurrentTenantIdentifierResolverImpl
  3. TenantAwareEntity
  4. Configuration
  5. TenantResolutionFilter
  6. TenantAwareAspect
  7. The isolation integration test

The docs/architecture.md file goes deeper into the request lifecycle and the implications of public-request handling.

We built this because we needed it for our own SaaS application, PresenceWave.

If you're evaluating shared-schema discriminator-based tenancy against schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant, hopefully seeing a real implementation — including its limitations — is more useful than another abstract description of the pattern.

I'd particularly welcome feedback from people who have implemented multi-tenancy with Hibernate:

  • Have you encountered other edge cases with @TenantId?
  • How do you handle tenant context propagation across asynchronous execution?
  • How do you enforce tenant consistency on bulk writes?
  • Have you found a better way to handle public or root-mode requests?

The intention here is to share something useful with the Java community and learn from people who have tackled the same problems.

Project setup

Third chapter of the "Fastify with TypeScript" series. Before writing a single line of business logic, you need a properly configured project: a package.json, two tsconfig files (one for type-checking, one for the production build), and a folder structure that scales. At the end of the chapter we'll run four commands to check that everything works.

Requirements: Node.js ≥ 22.19 (24 LTS recommended) and TypeScript 6.x. Type stripping runs flag-free from Node 22.19 / 23.6 / 24; on older 22.x you'd need --experimental-strip-types.

Initialization 

mkdir my-fastify-app && cd my-fastify-app
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install fastify
npm install -D typescript@6 @types/node
mkdir src test

package.json

npm init created a package.json for you. Open it and change three fields, main, scripts and engines, leaving everything else as it is (in particular the dependencies and devDependencies that npm just wrote):

{
  "name": "my-fastify-app",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "dist/server.js",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch --env-file-if-exists=.env src/server.ts",
    "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.build.json",
    "start": "node --env-file-if-exists=.env dist/server.js",
    "test": "node --test 'test/**/*.test.ts'",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"
  },
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=22.19.0"
  }
}

node --watch restarts the server on every file change and --env-file-if-exists loads a local .env when there is one, so the project never needs dotenv. start uses the same flag so you can run the built output locally; in production there is no .env file and the variables come from the real environment. Note that typescript is only a devDependency: in development Node runs the .ts files directly.

.env and .gitignore

Create the .env file now, even though it only holds one value for the moment:

echo "PORT=3000" > .env
printf 'node_modules\ndist\n.env\n' > .gitignore

Two reasons. The .env file will soon contain secrets, so it must never be committed: that's what the .gitignore line is for. And in watch mode Node also watches the .env file for changes, so on some versions npm run dev stops with an ENOENT error if the file isn't there.

tsconfig.json (type-checking)

This file is only used by tsc --noEmit and by your editor: the code is executed by Node with type stripping, no compilation involved.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2024",
    "lib": ["ES2024"],
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "types": ["node"],
    "rootDir": ".",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts", "test/**/*.ts"]
}

A few notes specific to TypeScript 6:

  • strict is now true by default, but we keep it explicit so the intent is obvious to anyone reading the file.
  • types is no longer auto-discovered (it defaults to []), so ["node"] is required or process, Buffer and friends won't exist.
  • rootDir is no longer inferred from your sources; set it explicitly.
  • erasableSyntaxOnly makes the compiler reject the TypeScript syntax that Node's type stripping can't handle (see the note below). This is the single most useful flag in this file.
  • verbatimModuleSyntax forces import type for type-only imports, which type stripping requires.
  • allowImportingTsExtensions + rewriteRelativeImportExtensions let you write import './app.ts' (what Node needs at runtime) and have tsc rewrite it to ./app.js in the build output.

tsconfig.build.json (production build) 

{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noEmit": false,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "declaration": true,
    "sourceMap": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}

A note on type stripping: Node removes type annotations without transforming code, so your source must avoid the TypeScript features that generate JavaScript: enum, namespace, constructor parameter properties (constructor(private x: string)) and import x = require(). With erasableSyntaxOnly: true, tsc reports an error on each of these, so you find out before Node does. Decorators are the exception: tsc accepts them, but Node can't run them, so the series doesn't use them. Finally, always use import type for types, and import local files with their .ts extension.

Check that it works

There is no application yet, so let's write a throwaway entry point just to try the four scripts. We'll replace it in the next chapter.

// src/server.ts — temporary: we replace it in the next chapter
const port: number = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

console.log(`Setup works. The server will listen on port ${port}.`);

npm run typecheck   # prints nothing: no type errors
npm run dev         # Setup works. The server will listen on port 3000.

npm run dev stays alive waiting for changes: edit the message, save, and it runs again. Stop it with Ctrl+C, then try the production path:

npm run build       # creates dist/server.js (plus .d.ts and source map)
npm start           # same message, this time from the compiled JavaScript

One last experiment, to see erasableSyntaxOnly earn its place. Add this line at the end of src/server.ts:

enum Color { Red }

npm run typecheck now fails with This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled, and Node itself refuses to run the file (TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode). Remove the line before going on.

Recommended project structure

This is where the project is heading over the next chapters:

src/
  app.ts               # builds the Fastify instance (no listen() here)
  server.ts            # entry point: imports app.ts and starts the server
  config.ts            # environment variables validated against a schema
  plugins/             # shared plugins (database, auth, security...)
  users/               # one folder per module, with everything that module needs
    users.route.ts       # the route plugin: routes + handlers
    users.schema.ts      # TypeBox schemas
    users.service.ts     # business logic and domain errors (chapter 13)
    users.repository.ts  # data access (chapter 13)
  auth/
    auth.route.ts
    auth.schema.ts
    auth.service.ts      # login rules (chapter 13)
test/
  helper.ts
  users.test.ts
  users.service.test.ts

The code is grouped by module, not by technical layer: there is no top-level routes/, services/ or repositories/ folder, and no modules/ wrapper either. Each module is a folder directly under src/: everything about users lives in src/users/, so working on a feature means working in one folder, and removing a feature means deleting one. plugins/ is the only folder that isn't a module: it holds the infrastructure shared by all of them.

Separating app.ts from server.ts is a very common convention in the Fastify ecosystem: app.ts exports a factory function that builds and configures the Fastify instance (routes, plugins, hooks) without ever binding to a network port; server.ts is the only file responsible for starting the listener. The main benefit is that in your tests you can import buildApp() from app.ts and use inject() without opening a TCP port (we'll cover this in the testing chapter).

⬅️ Previous chapter: Fastify core concepts · ➡️ Next chapter: Your first server (app.ts, server.ts, config.ts)

This article is part of the "Fastify with TypeScript" series — chapter 3 of 18.
