title: Risk-Tiered Checkout Friction: Routing Orders to AVS, 3DS, or Review
description:
Many card checkouts run every order through the same checks. One CVV rule, one AVS rule, one fraud score cutoff, and sometimes a 3-D Secure challenge on everything. That is simple to build. It also means your safest repeat customer gets the same friction as a first-time buyer shipping a gaming laptop to a freight forwarder.

The alternative is to match friction to risk. Low-risk orders pass with checks the buyer never sees. Medium-risk orders get a step-up challenge. Only the clearly suspicious ones get held or declined. The idea gets a brief mention in the broader discussion of eCommerce conversion optimization best practices. This article covers how to actually build it: the data flow, the decision logic, and the ways it tends to break.

The four outcomes

A risk-tiered checkout ends every order in one of four states:

Outcome Buyer experience Cost to you
Approve Nothing extra Fraud exposure if you're wrong
Step-up (3DS challenge) OTP, banking app prompt, or biometric Some buyers abandon
Review Order held, possibly delayed Analyst time, slower fulfillment
Decline Payment fails A lost sale if the buyer was legitimate (a false decline)

Every outcome has a cost. No single path is "safe." Your goal is to minimize total cost: fraud losses, chargeback fees, and the revenue lost to declines and abandonment.

Cheap signals vs. expensive signals

Sort your checks by who pays the friction cost.

Background signals. The buyer doesn't notice these.

  • AVS (Address Verification Service) result returned with the authorization
  • CVV/CVC match result
  • Device and browser fingerprint
  • Velocity, such as cards per device or orders per email in the last 24 hours
  • Account age and prior successful orders
  • Mismatch between IP geolocation, billing country, and shipping country
  • Order shape: basket value, resale-friendly SKUs, expedited shipping

Foreground signals. These add friction.

  • 3-D Secure challenge (EMV 3DS)
  • Manual review
  • Requests for extra documentation

The design principle: spend background signals freely, and spend foreground signals only where background signals leave real uncertainty.

Data flow: where each check actually happens

A common source of bugs is getting the order of operations wrong. AVS and CVV results come back with the authorization response. 3DS happens before authorization. So your decision logic has two phases.

Checkout submit
   │
   ▼
[Phase 1: pre-auth score]  ← device, velocity, account, order shape, geo
   │
   ├── score very high ──────────► Decline (no auth attempt)
   ├── score medium ─────────────► Request 3DS challenge
   └── score low ────────────────► Request 3DS frictionless or skip 3DS
   │
   ▼
Authorization (auth-only, no capture)
   │  returns: approval code, AVS result, CVV result
   ▼
[Phase 2: post-auth evaluation]  ← combine Phase 1 score + AVS/CVV
   │
   ├── clean ───────► Capture
   ├── ambiguous ───► Queue for review (keep auth open)
   └── bad ─────────► Void authorization

Two details matter here:

  1. Authorize first, capture later. If you capture immediately, a bad AVS/CVV result means issuing a refund instead of a void. Refunds cost more, and they can confuse the buyer's bank statement.
  2. The issuer has a say. With 3DS2, you send data to the issuer and it may decide to challenge or go frictionless regardless of your preference. Your code has to handle both responses on every path.

A decision table you can start from

AVS and CVV return codes vary by network and processor, so normalize them into a few categories first.

Pre-auth risk AVS CVV Action
Low Full / partial match Match Capture
Low Unavailable / not supported Match Capture
Low No match Match Review if high-value, else capture
Any Any No match Void (or step-up and retry)
Medium Any Match 3DS challenge before auth
Medium No match Match 3DS challenge + review
High Any Any Decline pre-auth or review

Note the second row. "AVS unavailable" is not a failure. AVS support is concentrated in a handful of countries. If you treat "unavailable" as "no match," you will decline a large share of your international customers.

Implementation sketch

Here is a minimal Python version of the two-phase router. Thresholds are placeholders. You tune them against your own data.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum

class Action(Enum):
    APPROVE = "approve"
    CHALLENGE = "challenge"
    REVIEW = "review"
    DECLINE = "decline"

class AvsResult(Enum):
    MATCH = "match"
    PARTIAL = "partial"
    NO_MATCH = "no_match"
    UNAVAILABLE = "unavailable"

@dataclass
class PreAuthContext:
    risk_score: float        # 0.0–1.0 from your model or rules
    order_value: float
    returning_customer: bool

LOW, HIGH = 0.3, 0.8
HIGH_VALUE = 500.0

def pre_auth_route(ctx: PreAuthContext) -> Action:
    if ctx.risk_score >= HIGH:
        return Action.DECLINE if not ctx.returning_customer else Action.REVIEW
    if ctx.risk_score >= LOW:
        return Action.CHALLENGE
    return Action.APPROVE  # still send 3DS data for frictionless if available

def post_auth_route(ctx: PreAuthContext, avs: AvsResult, cvv_match: bool,
                    authenticated_3ds: bool) -> Action:
    if not cvv_match:
        return Action.DECLINE  # void the auth
    if avs == AvsResult.NO_MATCH:
        if authenticated_3ds:
            return Action.APPROVE
        if ctx.order_value >= HIGH_VALUE or ctx.risk_score >= LOW:
            return Action.REVIEW
    return Action.APPROVE

In production, also persist the inputs and the decision for every order:

log_decision(order_id, phase="post_auth", inputs={
    "risk_score": ctx.risk_score, "avs": avs.value,
    "cvv": cvv_match, "3ds": authenticated_3ds,
}, action=action.value, rule_version="2024-06-01")

Without this log, you cannot tune thresholds later. You also cannot explain a decision when a customer or a dispute analyst asks.

Worked example: three orders, one router

Order A. Returning customer, $42, same device as the last five orders, AVS full match, CVV match. Pre-auth score 0.08 → no challenge requested. Post-auth: clean → capture. The buyer sees nothing extra.

Order B. New account, $310. The billing country differs from the IP country, and the shipping address is new. Pre-auth score 0.52 → request a 3DS challenge. The buyer approves in their banking app. Auth returns AVS no match, CVV match. Because 3DS authenticated, the router approves. This is the case a single strict AVS rule would have declined.

Order C. New account, $1,450, four different cards tried from the same device in ten minutes. Pre-auth score 0.91 → decline before authorization. You never send the auth, so the attempt doesn't show up against your authorization metrics.

That is three different levels of friction, each matched to the evidence.

Measuring whether it works

You need metrics per tier, not just overall totals:

  • Challenge rate and challenge abandonment rate. If abandonment is high, your medium band is too wide.
  • Review queue rate and review approval rate. If analysts approve nearly everything, those orders didn't need review.
  • Fraud/chargeback rate by tier. Chargebacks in the "approve" tier mean your low threshold is too loose.
  • Decline rate, plus an estimate of false declines. Track declined buyers who retry successfully with another card or contact support.

One trap is label delay. Chargebacks can arrive weeks or months after the order. If you tune thresholds on last week's data, the recent "approve" tier will look cleaner than it really is. Evaluate on cohorts old enough for disputes to have matured.

To estimate false declines directly, some teams use a small holdout: a tiny, capped slice of borderline orders that would have been declined goes to review instead. The approval outcomes show how many good buyers your decline rule was catching. Keep the slice small and the dollar cap strict.

Common mistakes and how to catch them

Treating AVS "unavailable" as a failure. Catch it by segmenting decline rate by billing country. A spike outside AVS-supporting regions is the tell.

Challenging everything with 3DS. This is safe but expensive in abandonment. Catch it by checking whether the challenge rate is close to 100% and whether conversion for challenged sessions trails unchallenged ones.

Capturing before evaluating AVS/CVV. You'll see refunds where voids should be. Audit for orders refunded within minutes of capture.

Ignoring issuer overrides. You asked for frictionless, but the issuer challenged anyway (or the reverse). Make sure both 3DS paths are covered by integration tests in your processor's sandbox.

Rules with no version. When fraud spikes, you need to know which rule set was live. Stamp every decision with rule_version.

Non-idempotent retries. A timeout on auth followed by a retry can create duplicate authorizations. Use your processor's idempotency key mechanism on every auth and capture call.

Optimizing one metric in isolation. Lowering the review threshold may cut chargebacks while quietly raising false declines. Always review fraud loss and declined revenue side by side.

Wrapping up

Risk-tiered friction isn't a single model or vendor feature. It's a routing problem with two decision points, pre-auth and post-auth, plus a feedback loop that matures slowly. Get the ordering right, normalize your AVS/CVV codes, log every decision with its inputs, and measure each tier on its own. Then the checkout gets easier for good buyers and harder for bad ones, which is the point.

title: npx -p playwright node script.mjs still threw ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. The fix was to stop trusting npx.
description:
I was taking screenshots of a website with a small Playwright script, written as an ES module, and ran it through npx. One of the commands I tried was this:

npx -p playwright node script.mjs

It ended in:

ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND

The reasoning looks airtight. -p playwright tells npx to make Playwright available, then run node script.mjs. The script imports Playwright. Playwright is available. Done.

It wasn't. After the second failure I stopped trying variations of the command and changed the approach entirely. This post is about why npx -p can't help an ES module find a package, what I did instead, why that kind of fix later broke on its own, and what I would do now.

The short version: npx puts things on your PATH. import never looks at your PATH. Those are two different lookup systems, and I was feeding the wrong one.

Failure, then failure again

I don't have a record of the exact first command I tried or its exact error, so I won't pretend I do. What I do have recorded is that npx -p playwright node script.mjs still ended in ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and that I changed approach after the second failure.

That second failure is where I stopped, and I want to explain why, because it's the part of this story I'd most like to keep.

When a command fails, the natural move is to try a slightly different command. Different flag, different order, quote something, clear a cache, try again. Each attempt is cheap, so it feels fine to keep going. But if the error is identical and the cause is identical, a third variation of the same shape is not a new experiment. It's the same experiment with a different spelling.

The rule I use now is simple: if the same operation fails twice for the same reason, don't run a third version of it. Find out why it fails, and switch to a different method. Retries for flaky things (timeouts, rate limits, a locked file) don't count. Two identical, deterministic failures do.

An honest note on sources: what I wrote down at the time was one line, "ESM can't resolve a package that npx provides," plus the workaround below. The fuller explanation in the next two sections comes from reading the npx and Node docs while writing this post.

What npx actually gives you

From the npm docs for npx, about --package:

"will be provided in the PATH of the executed command"

And about where it comes from, when the package isn't already in your project:

"installed to a folder in the npm cache"

[src:official:https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npx]

That's the whole contract. npx makes sure the package exists somewhere in the npm cache, and it puts that package's executables on PATH for the process it starts. That's what lets npx some-cli --flag work: your shell (or npx itself) looks up some-cli on PATH, finds the binary in the cache, and runs it.

Notice what's not in that contract: anything about where Node's module loader looks when your code says import 'playwright'. PATH is for finding executables. It's how a shell turns node into a file on disk. It has no role in resolving a bare specifier inside JavaScript.

So npx -p playwright node script.mjs did exactly what it promised. It put Playwright's CLI on PATH, then started node. My script never asked for the CLI. It asked the module loader for a package, and the module loader looked somewhere else.

Where import 'playwright' actually looks

Node's ESM documentation spells out the resolution algorithm. A bare specifier is a name like 'playwright' or 'some-package/sub', as opposed to a relative path or a URL. Bare specifiers go through a package lookup that, paraphrasing the spec's PACKAGE_RESOLVE step, does this:

  • Start at the folder of the module doing the import (the spec calls it parentURL).
  • Look for node_modules/playwright there.
  • If it's not there, move to the parent folder and look again.
  • Keep going until the filesystem root. If nothing is found, throw Module Not Found.

[src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html]

The anchor is the importing file's location. Not your current working directory, not PATH, not wherever npx happened to install something. If no folder above the script has node_modules/playwright, the walk reaches the root and fails. That's ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and it's the correct answer to the question an ES module asks when it imports a package by name.

"But NODE_PATH..."

If you've been writing Node for a while, you might remember NODE_PATH: an environment variable listing extra folders to search for modules. CommonJS still honors it. The modules docs say that if NODE_PATH is set, Node "will search those paths for modules if they are not found elsewhere" [src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/modules.html].

ES modules don't. The ESM docs have a short section titled "No NODE_PATH":

"NODE_PATH is not part of resolving import specifiers. Please use symlinks if this behavior is desired."

[src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html]

So even an approach that points NODE_PATH at the npx cache would not help an .mjs file. I didn't check whether npx sets NODE_PATH at all; for an ES module it wouldn't matter either way.

This is the gap in one sentence: npx extends the executable lookup, ESM uses the folder-walk lookup, and the only global escape hatch that used to bridge them (NODE_PATH) isn't part of ESM resolution.

What I did instead

Knowing what I know now, there are two directions: put Playwright somewhere on that walk, or stop using a bare specifier so there's no walk at all.

What I did at the time was the second one. ESM accepts absolute specifiers. The docs' example is 'file:///opt/nodejs/config.js', described as referring "directly and explicitly to a full path" [src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html]. An absolute specifier skips package resolution entirely. Node just loads that file.

Playwright was already on disk. npx had installed it into the npm cache at some point. I just needed to know where. I located the actual playwright package folder inside the npx part of the cache with find. I didn't save the exact invocation. The shape is a name search under the cache's _npx folder, something like this (illustrative, not the logged command):

find "<npm cache>/_npx" -type d -name playwright -path "*node_modules/playwright"

Then I imported Playwright by an absolute path into that folder, and it worked. No npx needed to make the package visible, which is what the title means: the fix was to stop relying on npx and point at the file directly.

I don't have that screenshot script's exact code in my notes. But the same day I wrote another small script, the one that renders cover images for these posts, and it uses the same pattern. This is its import line as it sits today, with my user folder and the cache folder's hash replaced:

import { chromium } from 'file:///C:/Users/<you>/AppData/Local/npm-cache/_npx/<hash>/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'

A detail worth knowing if you're on Windows: I used the file:///C:/... URL form rather than a bare C:\... path. The Node docs recommend converting paths with url.pathToFileURL when you import a path, because URL and path rules differ in places like percent-encoding [src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html]. The line above is a hand-written URL. Building it with pathToFileURL is what the docs suggest; I haven't tried that version.

Then the fix broke on its own

Some weeks later I went to make a cover image and the Playwright copy in the npx cache was gone. The cover script's import pointed at a path that no longer existed. I didn't fix it. I rendered the same HTML with headless Chrome another way and moved on. That's how this post's cover was made, too.

In hindsight this was predictable, and I should have written it down at the time I made the switch:

  • The npm cache is a cache. The npx docs describe it as the install location and don't promise anything about how long things stay there. Anything that clears or prunes the cache can remove the folder my script depended on.
  • The folder name was not chosen by me. The <hash> segment is something npm picks. I didn't look into what it's derived from, so I can't tell you when it would change. I only know I was hardcoding a name I didn't control.
  • The dependency was invisible. The repository the script lives in has a package.json at its root, but Playwright isn't listed in it today. Nothing declares "this script needs Playwright." The only record is a long string inside an import statement.

So the fix was real, and it worked, but it swapped one problem (Node can't find the package) for a quieter one (Node can find exactly one copy of the package, in a place that can disappear without warning). I'd call it a good diagnostic step and a poor permanent solution.

There's a smaller safety point too. A hardcoded import into a cache folder runs whatever is in that folder. And per the same docs, a missing package gets "installed to a folder in the npm cache" when npx runs, so that folder is filled by npx, not by anything I reviewed or pinned. For a screenshot script on my own machine, that risk is small. For anything that runs with real credentials in its environment, I wouldn't want to load code from a folder nothing in the project pins.

What I would try now (all untested)

Everything in this section is what I'd reach for next time. I have not tried any of these for this script, so treat them as options to evaluate, not results.

1. Make it a tiny project with a real dependency (untested here).
Install Playwright as a dev dependency in the folder's package.json. Then node_modules/playwright sits directly on the folder walk that the ESM resolver performs, a bare import 'playwright' works, and the dependency is written down in a lockfile. This is the boring answer, and it fixes both problems: resolution and invisibility. The cost is one more dependency to install and keep updated. Given what happened, that cost looks small.

2. createRequire anchored somewhere else (untested).
module.createRequire(filename) builds a CommonJS-style require whose lookup starts from the path you give it. The docs say the argument "Must be a file URL object, file URL string, or absolute path string" [src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/module.html]. In principle you could anchor it at a folder that does have Playwright in its node_modules. But that's still a hardcoded location; if the location is the npx cache, I'd have the same disappearing-folder problem with extra steps. I'd only consider it if the anchor were a stable, deliberately installed location.

3. A symlink, as the Node docs suggest (untested).
The "No NODE_PATH" section says to use symlinks if you want that behavior. A node_modules/playwright link next to the script, pointing at a real install, would put the package on the walk without copying it. Pointing it at the npx cache would inherit the same fragility, so this is only as good as the target.

4. Use the resolver itself as a diagnostic (untested).
Before changing anything, I'd like to have asked Node directly where it thinks 'playwright' resolves from the script's location. I haven't looked up or tried the API for doing that, so I won't name one or describe its output. The point is to get the answer from the resolver instead of from my mental model of the resolver, which is the thing that was wrong.

5. NODE_PATH: no.
Per the ESM docs quoted above, it isn't part of import resolution, so it isn't an option for an .mjs file at all.

The part I actually took away

The technical lesson is narrow and worth having: PATH resolves executables, the ESM loader resolves packages by walking up from the importing file, and npx only touches the first. If you remember that, npx -p some-lib node script.mjs will look wrong to you before you run it.

The process lesson is the one I use more often.

Stop at the second identical failure. I didn't keep trying variations; I stopped at the second failure and switched approach. The one-line note I kept was right, but it was a conclusion, not an explanation. Writing down which lookup was failing would have made the later breakage easier to see coming.

When you switch approaches, write down what the new approach depends on. This is the half I skipped. "Imports Playwright from the npx cache at this exact path" is a dependency with an expiry date. One line next to the import would have explained the later breakage immediately.

A workaround that works is still a workaround. "It runs now" is a fine place to stop only if you also write down what would make it stop running.

Checklist for ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND with npx

  • Is your code importing the package, or running its CLI? npx helps with the CLI. It doesn't change where import looks.
  • Where is the importing file? ESM looks for node_modules/<name> starting from that file's folder and walking up. Your working directory and PATH don't matter.
  • Is the file ESM? .mjs, or "type": "module" in the nearest package.json, means NODE_PATH is ignored for import.
  • Did the same error come back twice? Stop varying the command. Read what each tool actually promises.
  • If you hardcode a path to make it work, write down why and what it depends on. Especially if that path is inside a cache.
  • Prefer a declared dependency over a discovered one. A package.json entry survives cache cleanups. A path you found with find might not.

I'm building an AI code reviewer (getdevreview.com) that tries to point out the issues that matter instead of everything it can find. There's a free tier if you want to try it on a pull request. If you've hit the npx-versus-import gap and solved it in a cleaner way, I'd like to hear how.

title: Engineering Out Duplicate Charges: Idempotency, State, and Reconciliation
description:
Most chargeback advice is aimed at operations teams: write clearer descriptors, answer the phone, refund quickly. One category is mostly an engineering problem, though: the duplicate charge.

A customer who is billed twice for one order has a legitimate complaint. Card networks treat it as a processing error. Visa, for example, has a dispute condition for duplicate processing. These disputes are usually not worth fighting because the customer is right. The only good strategy is to make sure the second charge never happens, and to catch it yourself before the cardholder does.

The broader operational checklist is covered in this guide to preventing Visa disputes, which recommends reviewing transaction logs so each sale is submitted only once. This article looks at how to enforce that rule in code.

Where duplicate charges actually come from

Duplicates rarely come from one obvious bug. They come from retries that are reasonable on their own but unsafe together.

Source What happens
Client double-submit The user clicks Pay twice, or the mobile app retries on a flaky network.
Client timeout + retry The browser gives up after 30s, but the server finished the charge. The user tries again.
Server-to-PSP timeout Your backend calls the payment provider, the socket times out, and you retry. The first request had already succeeded.
At-least-once queues A job worker crashes after charging but before acking. The message is redelivered.
Webhook redelivery A payment succeeded webhook arrives twice and each copy triggers a capture or fulfillment step.
Batch resubmission A POS or batch file is re-sent after a partial failure, and settled items go through again.

All of these share one root cause: a network failure leaves the caller unsure whether the operation happened. The fix is to make retries safe, not to stop retrying.

Layer 1: Derive the idempotency key from intent

Many payment provider APIs accept an idempotency key, often sent as an Idempotency-Key HTTP header. The IETF HTTPAPI working group has a draft standardizing this header. The provider stores the first response for that key and returns it on repeats instead of charging again.

The common mistake is generating the key per request:

# WRONG: every retry gets a fresh key, so every retry is a new charge
key = str(uuid.uuid4())
psp.charge(amount, card, idempotency_key=key)

The key must identify the business intent, not the HTTP attempt. Derive it from data that is stable across retries:

def charge_key(order_id: str, attempt_group: int) -> str:
    # attempt_group increments only when the user deliberately
    # retries with a new card or amount after a decline
    return f'order:{order_id}:charge:{attempt_group}'

If the user's card is declined and they enter a new card, that is a new intent, so increment attempt_group. If the network dropped, it is the same intent, so reuse the key.

Also check how long your provider keeps idempotency keys. Retention windows are finite. A retry that happens days later, for example from a stuck queue, may not be protected by the provider at all. That is why you need the next layer.

Layer 2: Own the state locally

Never rely only on the provider for deduplication. Keep a payment record with a database-enforced uniqueness constraint and an explicit state machine.

CREATE TABLE payment_attempts (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id        TEXT NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  amount_minor    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  state           TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (state IN
                   ('pending','authorized','captured','failed','unknown')),
  psp_reference   TEXT,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- At most one successful capture per order
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_capture_per_order
  ON payment_attempts (order_id) WHERE state = 'captured';

The partial unique index is the important part. Even if application logic fails, the database will reject a second captured row for the same order.

The charge flow then looks like this:

def charge_order(order, attempt_group):
    key = charge_key(order.id, attempt_group)

    row = db.insert_or_get(
        'payment_attempts',
        idempotency_key=key, order_id=order.id,
        amount_minor=order.total_minor, currency=order.currency,
        state='pending')

    if row.state in ('authorized', 'captured'):
        return row                      # already done, return the same result
    if row.state == 'unknown':
        return resolve_unknown(row)     # never fire blind

    try:
        resp = psp.authorize(order.total_minor, order.currency,
                             idempotency_key=key, timeout=20)
    except (Timeout, ConnectionError):
        db.update(row.id, state='unknown')
        return resolve_unknown(row)

    db.update(row.id, state='authorized' if resp.ok else 'failed',
              psp_reference=resp.reference)
    return db.get(row.id)

The unknown state is the whole point

When a call times out, you do not know whether the money moved. Treating that as failed and letting the user retry with a new key is exactly how duplicates happen.

resolve_unknown should either retry with the same key, which is safe while the provider still remembers it, or look up the transaction using your own reference, such as the order ID in metadata. Only mark the attempt failed once you have confirmed it.

Layer 3: Make webhook handlers idempotent

Webhooks are typically delivered at least once. Your handler must accept the same event twice without side effects.

def handle_event(event):
    with db.transaction():
        inserted = db.execute(
            'INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (%s) '
            'ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING', [event.id]).rowcount
        if not inserted:
            return 200          # already handled
        apply_event(event)       # state transition, same transaction
    return 200

Recording the event ID and applying the state change in one transaction matters. If you mark the event processed and then crash before applying it, you lose the event. If you apply it and then crash before marking it, you apply it twice.

Also make apply_event a guarded state transition, for example UPDATE ... SET state='captured' WHERE id=%s AND state='authorized', so out-of-order events cannot move a payment backward.

Layer 4: Reconcile against settlement data

Prevention will not be perfect. A legacy integration, a manual terminal entry, or a resubmitted batch can still get through. Reconciliation is your detection layer, and it should run before the cardholder's statement arrives.

Pull the provider's settlement or transaction report daily and compare it to your ledger:

def find_suspected_duplicates(settled, window_hours=48):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for txn in settled:
        # card_fingerprint: a provider token for the card, never the PAN
        groups[(txn.card_fingerprint, txn.amount_minor, txn.currency)].append(txn)

    flagged = []
    for txns in groups.values():
        txns.sort(key=lambda t: t.settled_at)
        for a, b in zip(txns, txns[1:]):
            close = (b.settled_at - a.settled_at) <= timedelta(hours=window_hours)
            same_order = a.order_id and a.order_id == b.order_id
            if same_order or (close and not b.order_id):
                flagged.append((a, b))
    return flagged

Two checks are useful:

  1. Hard duplicates: two settled charges linked to the same order ID. This is almost always a bug, so auto-refund the second one and alert.
  2. Soft duplicates: same card, same amount, close together, with no distinct order behind the second charge. Send these to human review, since repeat purchases are legitimate.

Also check for orphans, meaning settled charges with no matching ledger row. Orphans often come from timeouts your system recorded as failures.

Decision table: what to do on each outcome

Outcome of charge call Local state Safe action
2xx, approved authorized Proceed to fulfillment
2xx, declined failed Allow retry with new attempt_group
4xx validation error failed Fix input; new intent if amount or card changes
409 / idempotency conflict unchanged Another request with this key is in flight or used different params; do not retry with a new key
Timeout / connection reset unknown Retry same key or look up by reference
5xx unknown Same as timeout; never treat as failure

Common mistakes and how to catch them

  • Random keys per attempt. Grep for UUID generation near charge calls. Keys should come from order data.
  • Treating timeouts as declines. Search your code for exception handlers around provider calls that set state to failed.
  • Disabling the Pay button as the only protection. That helps the UX, but a client-side guard is not a server-side guarantee.
  • Webhook handlers that fulfill without checking state. Send the same event twice in a test.
  • Capturing in two places. For example, both a webhook and a shipping job call capture. Pick one owner for the capture transition.

Tests worth writing 

def test_timeout_then_retry_charges_once(fake_psp):
    fake_psp.succeed_then_timeout()        # charge lands, response is lost
    with pytest.raises(PaymentPending):
        charge_order(order, attempt_group=1)
    charge_order(order, attempt_group=1)   # user retries
    assert fake_psp.successful_charges(order.id) == 1

def test_concurrent_submits_charge_once(fake_psp):
    run_in_parallel(lambda: charge_order(order, 1), n=10)
    assert fake_psp.successful_charges(order.id) == 1

The concurrency test often exposes read-then-insert races that a unique constraint would have prevented.

Summary

Duplicate charges come from ambiguity after failures, not from a single bug. Use four layers: intent-derived idempotency keys, a local state machine with database constraints, idempotent webhook handling, and daily reconciliation against settlement data. Together they turn "check your transaction logs" into a guarantee you can test.

title: The morning our app launch broke Postgres
description:
🚨 The morning it broke

It was the first morning of our marketing sale. We had launched our mobile app shortly before, and it had been running fine. Then the orders started pouring in. A truckload of them.

The first sign was an SOS from a teammate: browsing was slow. I opened our observability dashboards and the alerts were already firing. Lots of red. Not the festive kind. Database connections were pinned at their limit and new requests were being turned away. The website, the admin panel and the app were all failing with the same error: Database connection failed.

I was the support engineer on duty, and I was on my own. My honest first thought was: oh my. 😳 Customers were complaining, on the busiest morning we'd had.

What helped most wasn't technical. The rest of the team stayed calm. They spoke to customers kindly while I worked, which let me focus on the database instead of the noise. Shout-out to them.

What the app changed

Our database had handled the website for a long time without trouble. On a normal day, each request borrowed a connection from the backend's pool, ran its queries and gave it back quickly. Sale-day traffic plus the new app broke that rhythm in two ways.

  • Connections were held longer. The app's background sync and polling kept a steady stream of requests coming, and some code paths didn't give their connection back as soon as they should have.
  • It sent queries in bursts. Each time someone opened the app, it fetched their profile, notifications and telemetry all at once. Multiply that by a sale's worth of shoppers.

Our database plan (1 GiB of RAM) allowed only 22 connections. On a normal day that was enough. On sale day, with the new app, it ran out.

Fixing it, and making it worse

I started with the obvious moves. I scaled the database cluster to clear out stale connections and put PgBouncer, a connection pooler, in front of it. Then I upgraded the database to a bigger plan with 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB of RAM. DigitalOcean sets the connection limit by memory, so it jumped from 22 to 97.

With all that new room, I raised the app's connection limit to 90. It felt like the right call. More room, more connections, more speed. Right?

It wasn't. Database CPU shot to nearly 100%. Pages that had been slow were now crawling. My fix had made things worse. 🫠

Here's why. Think of a traffic jam: letting more cars onto the road doesn't get anyone home faster. A database with 2 CPUs can only truly run 2 queries at the same moment. Every other active query waits its turn, and the more queries are fighting for those 2 cores, the more time goes on juggling them. Some of ours were also hitting unindexed columns, which means scanning whole tables. Ninety of those at once pinned the CPU.

That was the lesson of the morning: a connection limit is not a target. It tells you how many connections the database will accept, not how many it can serve well. The real limit is the CPU behind it.

The fix that held

So I went the other way. I cut the app's limit to 20 and made sure PgBouncer was running in transaction mode. Fifteen minutes later, everything was back to normal. 😮‍💨 From the first refused connection to full recovery took about 75 minutes.

Three changes did the work together:

  1. All traffic goes through PgBouncer. The backend no longer connects to the database directly. The pooler shares a small set of real connections among many clients. Think nightclub bouncer: only so many inside at once, and nobody hogs the dance floor.
  2. Transaction mode. A connection goes back to the pool the moment a transaction finishes, not when the client disconnects, so the app's long sessions stop holding connections hostage.
  3. A pool sized to the CPU. Twenty works on 2 CPUs because most connections are idle at any given moment, waiting on the network or the app. A common starting point for truly active queries is about two per CPU core. If the backend scales to two containers, each gets 10, so the total stays at 20.

One catch with transaction mode: anything tied to a database session doesn't carry over between transactions. That includes session-level SET commands, advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY and, on older PgBouncer versions, prepared statements. Check your ORM or driver is configured for transaction pooling before you switch.

Database CPU now stays under 45% at peak, and average API response time is under 150 ms.

How I knew it worked

I watched two numbers on DigitalOcean's database metrics dashboard. Connections told me what was failing. CPU told me whether a fix was working.

I didn't call it resolved straight away. I kept the database on the 2-CPU tier for 48 hours and watched both graphs through a full traffic cycle first.

What I'd do differently

Looking back, this was a launch problem as much as a database problem. We planned the app's features and its release, but not what its traffic would do to a database sized for the website.

  • Load-test a new client before launch. A mobile app talks to the backend differently from a website. Test the pattern, not just the endpoints.
  • Put a pooler in front of the database from day one. It costs little and removes a whole class of outage.
  • Size the pool to the CPU, not the connection limit. Start small, measure, then raise it.
  • Release connections in code, every time, even when a query fails.
  • Find the slow queries. Missing indexes make every query hold its connection longer.

A launch isn't finished when the app ships. It's finished when the system behind it survives its first busy morning.

For the engineers: what I check now

Alert on the early signal, not the failure: connections above 80% of the limit, and database CPU above 70% for five minutes. And when something feels off, this shows what connections are actually doing:

SELECT state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database()
GROUP BY state;

The state to worry about is idle in transaction: a connection stuck inside an open transaction, holding a slot and often locks too. Behind PgBouncer, plain idle is normal; those are the pool's spare connections. In PgBouncer itself, SHOW POOLS; shows how many clients are waiting for a connection (cl_waiting).

The timeline

Minutes in What happened
0 Connections start climbing as sale traffic arrives.
75 Connections hit the limit of 22. The database starts refusing new ones.
90 Scaled the cluster to clear stale connections; started PgBouncer.
105 Upgraded to 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB of RAM; limit rises to 97.
120 Raised the app's limit to 90. CPU jumps to nearly 100%.
135 Cut the app's limit to 20; confirmed transaction mode.
150 Website, app and admin panel back to normal.

title: Nodus vs Spheron: which is better for running training?
description:
Nodus is the better way to run a training job you want finished: it lists the NVIDIA H100 at $2.60/hr against $2.65 to $2.98 for on-demand H100s on Spheron, and it restores your checkpoint on a new machine when one is lost. Spheron is the better pick when you want the cheapest reclaimable GPU and are happy to restart runs yourself, or when you want a bare-metal server or AMD hardware to manage by hand.

We build Nodus. Every Spheron fact below links to Spheron's own site or docs, the arithmetic is shown once, and one section covers where Spheron wins.

How do Nodus and Spheron compare at a glance?

They sell different things. Spheron says it "pools capacity from multiple providers and exposes it through a single API and dashboard" (Spheron overview). You pick an offer, get a VM or a bare-metal server, and run your training on it. Nodus takes a command or a training job, picks the machine, checkpoints your state directory and starts a replacement attempt if the machine goes away.

Spheron Nodus
What you launch A spot or dedicated VM, a bare-metal server, a container, or a reserved cluster A Job, TrainingJob, Workspace or Function that Nodus places for you
How prices work Live rates per GPU that follow partner supply Live quotes per machine, frozen when capacity is acquired
H100 listed rate $2.98 on-demand and $2.20 spot on the pricing page; $2.65 dedicated on the H100 page $2.60/hr
Billing Prepaid credits, billed per minute after a 20-minute minimum runtime Prepaid credits; each run shows boot, running and teardown cost
Spot capacity Reclaimed at any time with no warning; on the Spheron ES provider the spot price can change every 15 minutes Opt in per run with --interruptible; urgent checkpoint on a reclaim notice
After a reclaim or failure You redeploy and load your own checkpoint from a volume New attempt with your state directory restored
Coding agents MCP connector for Claude, ChatGPT and Codex CLI MCP server for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor
Multi-node Bare-metal clusters up to 80 x H100 (10 nodes); custom reserved clusters of 8 to 512+ GPUs Beta, up to 8 nodes
Hardware beyond NVIDIA AMD Instinct MI300X, Intel Gaudi2 NVIDIA only on the pricing page

Sources: Spheron pricing, Spheron H100 page, Spheron instance types, Spheron billing, Spheron AI connections, the Nodus pricing page, the Nodus usage and costs and multi-node training docs. Prices checked November 23, 2026.

Is Nodus cheaper than Spheron for an 8 x H100 training run?

On on-demand rates, yes, though the H100 gap is small. We priced the same job, 8 x H100 for 10 hours, which is 80 GPU-hours, from each company's public pages on November 23, 2026.

Option Rate per GPU-hour 80 GPU-hours
Nodus $2.60 $208.00
Spheron dedicated (H100 page) $2.65 $212.00
Spheron on-demand (pricing page) $2.98 $238.40
Spheron spot, no reclaim $2.20 $176.00

Prices checked November 23, 2026: Spheron pricing, Spheron H100 page and the Nodus pricing page. GPU rates only, no storage.


Nodus is 13% cheaper than Spheron's pricing-page on-demand rate; Spheron spot is cheapest if nothing is reclaimed.

Two Spheron numbers appear because Spheron's rates are live and its pages showed both on the same day. Its H100 page says the rates "move with partner supply". Nodus quotes are live too, so run nodus run --dry-run for your exact job instead of trusting any table, including this one.

The gap is wider on other cards. Spheron's pricing page lists the A100 80 GB at $1.43, the H200 at $4.80 and the L40S at $0.96 per GPU-hour on demand. The Nodus pricing page lists them at $1.09/hr, $3.593/hr and $0.793/hr. The B200 is the outlier: $11.06 on demand on Spheron against $5.50/hr on Nodus, though Spheron's B200 spot rate is $5.22.


On every card in this chart, the Nodus rate is lower than Spheron's on-demand rate.

When does Spheron spot stop being the cheaper option?

After about 1.8 hours of lost work on that run. Spheron spot instances "can be interrupted at any time" and are reclaimed "with no warning", so you lose everything since the last checkpoint your script wrote (Spheron instance types). A reclaim stops billing, so you pay for the hours the machine ran, and then pay again to redo the lost work.

Each lost hour on 8 x H100 spot costs 8 x $2.20 = $17.60 to redo. The spot run starts $32.00 below Nodus ($208.00 minus $176.00), and $32.00 / $17.60 = 1.82 hours. Here is how the total moves:

  • No lost work: $176.00
  • 1 hour lost: $176.00 + $17.60 = $193.60
  • 2 hours lost: $176.00 + $35.20 = $211.20
  • 3 hours lost: $176.00 + $52.80 = $228.80


Two lost hours of work make the spot run more expensive than the Nodus run.

That count is the floor, not the full bill. On Spheron ES the spot price itself can change as often as every 15 minutes and is capped at the dedicated price for the same machine, so $2.20 is the price at launch, not a promise. And every reclaim costs elapsed time while you notice, redeploy and reload data.

If you checkpoint every 30 minutes, two reclaims cost at most an hour of work and spot still wins. If your script saves once an hour, two badly timed reclaims can cost up to 2 hours and erase the saving.

Our rule: use Spheron spot for runs where your own restart script is already tested. Use Nodus when you want the restart handled and a cost estimate before you launch.

What happens to a training run when the machine is lost?

On Spheron, recovery is yours to build. Spheron's docs tell you to save checkpoints to a persistent volume and resume from them after a reclaim, with a torch.save example writing to /checkpoints (Spheron instance types). You then deploy a new instance, mount the volume and start your script again. Bare-metal and reserved instances can't be stopped or restarted from the dashboard at all (Spheron instance lifecycle).

On Nodus, your script writes its state to /nodus/state and loads it on start. When capacity gives notice that it is about to be reclaimed, Nodus asks your program for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement machine at the same time. A machine that stops sending heartbeats gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds and, on shared capacity, is declared lost after 60. The new attempt starts with your state directory restored, so a checkpointed run loses at most the work since its last committed checkpoint (attempts and recovery).

Neither platform resumes your training loop for you. Your program still has to read its last checkpoint when it starts. Our post on how to resume training after a spot preemption has the code.

What do you pay when a GPU sits idle?

On Spheron, a running instance bills until you stop or terminate it, after a 20-minute minimum runtime that applies even to a 5-minute job (Spheron pricing). Spheron gives you timers to limit the damage: stop an instance after 0.5 to 720 hours of running, or terminate it at a set time. A stop-when-idle timer exists too, but it needs GPU usage readings that only Agent GPU Sandbox instances report. A stopped instance still bills its disk at the provider's stopped rate (Spheron instance lifecycle).

On Nodus, a Job ends when your command exits. Nodus keeps the capacity warm for 60 seconds in case you launch again, and --no-warm releases it at once. --max-cost stops the run at a dollar cap you set (nodus run reference).

Spheron's timers are a sensible fix, but you have to set one on every instance. On Nodus, stopping when the work is done is the default.

Can you connect a Spheron account to Nodus?

No. Nodus can run work in some cloud accounts you already have, such as AWS, GCP, Azure and a list of API-key providers, but Spheron is not one of them (connect your cloud accounts). If you use both, you keep two accounts with separate credit balances.

Where is Spheron the better choice?

Pick Spheron in these cases:

  • You want the lowest price and handle restarts yourself. Spheron spot H100s are $2.20 per GPU-hour against $2.60/hr on Nodus, and B200 spot is $5.22 against $5.50/hr (Spheron pricing).
  • You need AMD or Intel hardware. Spheron offers AMD Instinct MI300X at $3.59 per GPU-hour on demand (Spheron pricing) and Intel Gaudi2 through one of its providers (Spheron instance types). The Nodus pricing page lists only NVIDIA GPUs.
  • You want bare metal. Spheron's Dedicated Bare Metal offers give you the whole server with no hypervisor, with NVLink or NVSwitch on SXM offers, and dedicated instances carry a 99.95% SLA (Spheron instance types).
  • You need a large InfiniBand cluster now. Spheron's H100 page lists bare-metal clusters of up to 80 x H100 across 10 nodes with 400 Gb/s InfiniBand, and Spheron sources custom reserved clusters of 8 to 512+ GPUs (Spheron H100 page, reserved GPUs). Multi-node training on Nodus is in Beta with a ceiling of 8 nodes, and public traffic between nodes is not encrypted in the Beta.
  • You want to pay in stablecoins, or keep credit indefinitely. Spheron takes USDC, and its credits never expire (Spheron billing).

How do you move a training script from Spheron to Nodus?

If your script already saves to a Spheron volume, change only the path. Keep /checkpoints as the fallback so the same script runs on both:

import os

# On Nodus this is /nodus/state; on Spheron, your mounted volume
STATE_DIR = os.environ.get("NODUS_STATE_DIR", "/checkpoints")

Then install the CLI, sign in, check the estimate and launch with a cap a little above it:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login
nodus run --dry-run --gpu H100:8 --expected-duration 10h -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 8 train.py
nodus run --gpu H100:8 --checkpoint /nodus/state --max-cost 230 -d -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 8 train.py

Add --interruptible to let Nodus use interruptible capacity for the same run, and check the dry-run estimate before you launch. If you are weighing other options too, our RunPod alternatives guide compares more platforms, and which GPU platforms checkpoint and resume training for you goes deeper on recovery.

FAQ

Is Spheron spot capacity cheaper than dedicated?

Spheron says spot is typically 30 to 60% cheaper than dedicated (Spheron instance types). On Spheron ES you can set a max price, and the instance stops automatically if the live spot price climbs above it, though that does not stop a reclaim.

Does a stopped Spheron instance keep its GPU?

Not always. Some Spheron providers release the hardware while an instance is stopped, so a start can be refused when that machine type is sold out (Spheron instance lifecycle). Nothing is lost when that happens; you try again when stock returns.

Does Nodus offer managed fine-tuning as well as raw jobs?

Yes, in Beta. Nodus TrainingJobs run managed runtimes for SFT with full, LoRA or QLoRA training, DPO, GRPO, distillation and continued pretraining, and a dry run prices the job before anything runs.

Is there a free tier on either platform?

Neither lists one. Spheron needs a minimum deposit of $15 by card (Spheron billing), and the public Nodus starter credit has ended, so new Nodus accounts add prepaid credit or use an approved promotional offer (Nodus credits).

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: CrowdStrike compra Zscaler em acordo de US$ 43,9 bilhões
description:
Acordo de US$ 43,9 bilhões

A CrowdStrike acertou a compra da Zscaler por US$ 43,9 bilhões, em uma operação totalmente em ações anunciada pelas empresas na segunda-feira, 23 de novembro de 2026. O valor fica próximo dos US$ 44 bilhões indicados no título do anúncio, e a transação ainda depende de aprovação regulatória.

As companhias esperam concluir o negócio por volta desta época no próximo ano, aproximadamente em novembro de 2027. Até lá, a aquisição permanece condicionada às autorizações necessárias; a conclusão é que permitirá a integração das plataformas descrita pelas empresas.

O foco de cada plataforma

Sediada em San Jose, na Califórnia, a Zscaler oferece produtos de cibersegurança em nuvem para cerca de 8 mil empresas. Entre eles está a tecnologia de confiança zero, que exige que funcionários se autentiquem a cada acesso a um sistema ou recurso interno da organização.

Essa exigência busca dificultar que invasores usem credenciais roubadas para conseguir acesso irrestrito à rede corporativa. A CrowdStrike, por sua vez, protege computadores, laptops, celulares e outros dispositivos conectados à rede de uma empresa por meio de software de proteção de endpoints.

Proteção combinada contra violações

Com a aquisição, a proteção de endpoints da CrowdStrike será reunida à plataforma de confiança zero da Zscaler. A combinação conecta a segurança dos dispositivos ligados à rede à verificação de quem acessa sistemas e recursos internos, duas frentes que as empresas pretendem integrar para defender clientes contra violações de dados.

As companhias afirmam que, juntas, as duas soluções poderão oferecer proteção superior aos clientes. Essa é a justificativa apresentada para unir os produtos: combinar capacidades que hoje estão em plataformas distintas e, segundo as empresas, reforçar a defesa contra o acesso indevido a dados corporativos.

Estratégia para a era da inteligência artificial

As empresas também associam a operação à adoção segura de inteligência artificial por seus clientes. Elas dizem que a integração das plataformas deve ajudar organizações a usar IA com segurança e que o acordo criará o “maior mercado endereçável individual” em cibersegurança, expressão usada para descrever a oportunidade comercial combinada.

A aquisição, portanto, tem duas justificativas declaradas: reunir tecnologias de segurança complementares e posicionar melhor as empresas para a era da IA. Essas metas dependem da conclusão do negócio e da integração das ofertas; por enquanto, o fechamento está previsto para cerca de um ano após o anúncio e sujeito à aprovação regulatória.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/crowdstrike-acordo-compra-zscaler-439-bilhoes/

title: CMYK to Pantone without false precision: what ΔE can and cannot tell you
description:
Most CMYK to Pantone converters return one confident code. That confidence is usually misplaced. A CMYK value is a process build; a Pantone number is a spot ink. Converting between them is not a formula — it is a nearest-neighbour search through a reference table, and the answer depends on assumptions most tools never show you.

Here is what is actually happening, and how to read the result without over-trusting it.

1. CMYK is not a colour; it is a recipe for a press

The same C40 M20 Y10 K0 build can look different on coated stock, uncoated stock, newsprint, or a digital press, because ink, substrate and profile change what reaches your eye. Without an ICC profile and a rendering intent, a CMYK number has no single absolute colour meaning.

Tools that skip the profile have to assume something: a generic coated assumption, or a simple arithmetic conversion from CMYK percentages to RGB. Both are approximations. The honest output is not "the Pantone for your CMYK" but "the nearest reference under these assumptions".

2. Nearest-match search is a distance problem

Once both sides are expressed in a perceptual space such as CIELAB, you can measure distance. CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) is the current standard for how different two colours look to a typical observer, and a searchable converter should use it instead of raw Euclidean RGB distance.

A useful match reports:

  • the nearest coated reference and the nearest uncoated reference, searched separately
  • the ΔE00 distance for each
  • a couple of runner-up candidates, so you can see whether the nearest match is isolated or in a crowded neighbourhood

If a tool only gives one code with no distance, you cannot tell whether it is a near-exact match or the least-wrong option in a sparse region.

3. Coated and uncoated are different libraries

A Pantone C and U pair with the same number are not the same colour. Uncoated stock absorbs ink differently, so the printed result shifts. Searching a single combined library and labelling the result "Pantone" hides that difference. Search each library independently; the nearest C match may be several ΔE away from the nearest U match, and that gap is real information.

4. Community digital references are not spectral measurements

Unless you license Pantone's own data, any web tool is working from community-sourced digital approximations — values transcribed from guides or derived by measurement, with their own error. They are useful for shortlisting and for communication, not for colour-critical sign-off.

The practical workflow:

  1. Shortlist two or three candidates with a converter, using the coated and uncoated libraries separately.
  2. Look at the ΔE00 values. Under ~2 is close; above ~3–4 you are choosing a nearby colour, not matching one.
  3. Pull a physical guide and compare under your actual lighting.
  4. Confirm with your printer before committing a spot ink to a production run.

5. What to ask any converter

When you evaluate a CMYK-to-Pantone tool, check whether it:

  • states its CMYK assumption
  • searches coated and uncoated separately
  • shows the distance metric
  • warns that matches are approximations
  • gives you a shareable result so a colleague sees the same candidates

I build HueConvert, a free converter that tries to meet those criteria: it converts HEX, RGB, CMYK and HSL, searches coated and uncoated references separately with CIEDE2000, shows the nearest distance and two alternatives, and publishes a guide on why CMYK to Pantone results differ. No account is required.

If your job depends on the colour, the final check is still a physical guide and a conversation with your printer. A converter should help you narrow the field and show its uncertainty — not pretend the uncertainty is not there.

title: Model Consolidation as a History of Membership, Not a List of Current Contents
description:
Picture a bag that left the hub this afternoon. This morning it held twelve customer packages. One was pulled for review before departure. Tonight a destination team wants to know what actually traveled, and a customer wants to know which handling fees apply to the package that stayed behind.

If the platform stores only the group's current contents, both answers may already be gone. The bag now looks as though the removed package was never there. Billing cannot tell a service performed on the package from a charge that belonged to the group. Customer status has nothing reliable to show.

This is the records problem behind consolidation at a multi-market hub. I have worked on a Caribbean cross-border forwarding platform for a Miami hub serving 9+ markets, where receiving, grouping, destination-specific charges, and handoffs have to remain explainable after the freight has moved. The design note below is a recommended model. It is not a dump of a client's production database.

GS1 identifies a logistics unit with an SSCC, and GS1 materials on shipping management describe relationships between units, shipments, and consolidated consignments. An SSCC should not be treated as interchangeable with a parcel carrier's tracking number. You do not need to adopt every identifier standard on day one. You do need identities that grouping cannot destroy.

Four identities, plus an event log

I would distinguish:

  1. The individual package the customer cares about.
  2. Any physical grouping (a bag, carton, pallet, or master unit).
  3. The onward dispatch or shipment that is supposed to leave the hub.
  4. External references: inbound tracking, an SSCC if you use one, a carrier tracking number for the onward movement.

The current membership of a group can be a view. It should not be the only table you have.

create table package (
  id                   bigserial primary key,
  customer_account_id  bigint not null,
  origin_reference     text,            -- inbound tracking or purchase ref
  destination_market   text not null,   -- a specific market, not a catch-all
  current_status       text not null    -- received, held, assigned,
                                        -- departed, arrived, exception
);

create table logistics_unit (
  id                      bigserial primary key,
  unit_type               text not null,  -- package, bag, carton, pallet, master
  sscc                    text,           -- optional; not a parcel tracking number
  carrier_tracking_number text,
  purpose                 text not null,  -- receiving, consolidation, onward_shipment
  created_at              timestamptz not null default now()
);

-- A package may also be represented as a logistics_unit of type 'package'.
create table package_unit (
  package_id  bigint primary key references package(id),
  unit_id     bigint not null unique references logistics_unit(id)
);

create table unit_membership_event (
  id              bigserial primary key,
  child_unit_id   bigint not null references logistics_unit(id),
  parent_unit_id  bigint not null references logistics_unit(id),
  event_type      text not null,   -- assigned, removed, held, handed_over, received
  occurred_at     timestamptz not null,
  actor_id        bigint,
  reason          text,
  location_id     bigint,          -- hub or destination office
  evidence        text
);

create table dispatch (
  id                   bigserial primary key,
  destination_market   text not null,
  master_unit_id       bigint references logistics_unit(id),
  planned_departure_at timestamptz,
  departed_at          timestamptz,
  arrived_at           timestamptz
);

-- A point-in-time list of what was expected or what actually moved.
create table dispatch_membership_snapshot (
  id               bigserial primary key,
  dispatch_id      bigint not null references dispatch(id),
  package_id       bigint not null references package(id),
  included         boolean not null,
  snapshot_at      timestamptz not null,
  snapshot_reason  text not null,  -- planned, departed, arrived
  unique (dispatch_id, package_id, snapshot_reason, snapshot_at)
);

Current contents can then be derived, instead of being edited in place:

-- Latest membership event per child/parent pair.
create view unit_current_membership as
select distinct on (child_unit_id, parent_unit_id)
  child_unit_id,
  parent_unit_id,
  event_type,
  occurred_at
from unit_membership_event
order by child_unit_id, parent_unit_id, occurred_at desc, id desc;

A package is in a group now only if its latest event for that parent is assigned or handed_over, not removed or held. That rule should be explicit in code. Do not infer it from a missing row.

Departed means "verified membership at the handoff," not "everyone who was ever assigned"

The bug I want to prevent is this: a package is assigned, then removed; the dispatch later departs; a report of "packages on dispatch X" is written as where dispatch_id = X against a current-contents table that no longer mentions the removal. The destination team cannot see the hole. Billing may still attach a group-level fee to a package that never left, or fail to bill a hold that did occur.

function removePackageFromDispatch(package, dispatch, actor, reason):
  parent = dispatch.master_unit
  child  = unit for package

  append unit_membership_event(
    child, parent,
    event_type = "removed",
    occurred_at = now(),
    actor, reason,
    location = current hub
  )

  set package.current_status = "held" or "exception",
      according to the reason

  mark any group-level checks as needing review
    (weight, piece count, documents, seal)

  do not edit earlier membership events
  do not assume destination charges or handling fees
    should move to the group or disappear

function closeDispatchForDeparture(dispatch, actor):
  members = packages whose latest event on dispatch.master_unit
            is an included type (assigned or handed_over)

  write dispatch_membership_snapshot(
    dispatch,
    every package ever assigned, with included = true/false,
    snapshot_reason = "departed",
    snapshot_at = now()
  )

  set dispatch.departed_at = now()
  set current_status = "departed" only for members actually included

  packages removed or held stay on their own status
  their history remains queryable against the same dispatch

Two billing rules fall out of the same model:

  • A service performed on the package (repacking, storage, a hold, a destination charge for that market) should reference the package, the account, and the time it was recorded.
  • A service charged to the group (a master-bag handling fee, a shared transport cost) should reference the dispatch and the snapshot that was in effect, not a later rewrite of membership.

If you only store the second kind of charge, and membership is a mutable list, you will not be able to explain either one.

Test a difficult dispatch, not only a clean bag

Walk the model through four cases before you trust a "add to consolidation" button:

  1. A normal consolidation that departs as planned.
  2. A package removed before departure, with a reason and an owner.
  3. A held item that never joins a dispatch.
  4. A destination discrepancy: the arrived snapshot does not match the departed snapshot.

For each case, ask:

  • Which record explains what was expected?
  • Which record confirms what was handed over?
  • Can staff trace the package without opening the group?
  • Can billing distinguish package-level services from group-level services?

Those questions are the requirements. The schema above is only useful if it can answer them after the freight has left the building.

This is the kind of exception that custom cross-border forwarding software has to hold if a corridor app only tracks the group that exists right now. Buy the existing product if it already preserves membership history, departed snapshots, and package-level charges. Extend or build when that history still lives in a spreadsheet.

This article is a rewritten engineering treatment of a subject I first discussed for operators, originally published on Consolidation Should Not Erase Individual Package History.

Hasnain Qureshi is co-founder of BlinkShift, which builds custom software for forwarding, consolidation, and destination-charge workflows.

title: Best tools for testing your own app's SMS and OTP flows (2026): cloud numbers, test numbers and SMS inboxes
description:
I work with DuoPlus, on the growth marketing side, so it's on this list and it sits near the top. Keep that in mind. Everything I say about the other five tools comes from their own websites and docs, which I opened again on 24 November 2026. I've left prices out. Pricing pages change too often to copy.

One more thing before the list. Everything here is about testing your own app: your signup screen, your password reset, your login code, your "we've sent you a text" step. None of it is about getting through someone else's phone verification. That's a different conversation and not one I'm having.

Why SMS flows are annoying to test

The bug reports always sound the same. "Code never arrived." "Code arrived but autofill didn't." "Worked in the US build, not the Brazil one." The usual fix is a teammate's personal phone, until that teammate is on leave or the test needs a country nobody lives in.

So the tools below split into roughly three kinds:

  • Fake numbers that never send a real SMS. Fast, free-ish, good for CI. They don't tell you whether a real message actually lands.
  • Real numbers that receive real SMS and expose them to your tests. Slower, but closer to what your users actually see.
  • A real Android device to read it on. Half the bugs are on the phone side: keyboard, autofill, the app killed in the background while the user checks Messages.

1. DuoPlus â€” for walking through the whole flow on a real Android device, in the country you care about

What it is: a cloud phone platform. You get real ARM Android cloud phones (Android 10, 11, 12 and 15) that you open in a browser, in the Windows or Mac client, or through the Android and iOS apps that control the cloud phone. The DuoPlus homepage lists a separate Cloud Number product, described as "online physical and virtual numbers for receiving SMS", next to the cloud phones.

Why it's on a list about SMS testing: the cloud phone itself doesn't have a real SIM, so when I'm walking through my own app's signup, I pair it with a DuoPlus cloud number that receives the code. The phone gives me the device side (install the APK, run the flow, see what the keyboard and autofill actually do) and the number gives me the message side.

Where it fits best:

  • Regional checks. The site lists location and SIM-card data settings for 150+ countries and regions. If your OTP copy, sender name or timing changes by market, you can sit in that market's environment instead of guessing from a VPN.
  • Handing a broken state to a teammate. Team collaboration is built in, so if the code arrives but the verify button hangs, I share the same cloud phone instead of writing a ten-step repro.
  • Version spread. One device on Android 10, one on 15, same build, same flow. That's usually where the "autofill works on my phone" bugs show up.
  • Batch setup. Bulk install, uninstall and launch, plus an API and ADB access if you want to spin devices up from a script. Root is available for the few test cases that need it.
  • Short sessions. Billing is per minute, which suits SMS checks; most of mine are fifteen or twenty minutes, not a full day.

Honest drawbacks:

  • It's Android only, and it won't place voice calls. If your app offers "call me with the code instead", you need something else for that path. iOS testing needs a different tool.
  • It's not an assertion library. If what you really want is for the SMS body to land inside a Playwright or Cypress test so your suite can check the code automatically, the next tool on this list is built for exactly that. DuoPlus is better at the "a human walks through it on a real device" side.

Link: duoplus.net. If you want to look around first, the DuoPlus market page is a decent starting point.

2. Mailosaur â€” for putting SMS codes straight into automated tests

Best known for email testing, Mailosaur also has an SMS product, and it's the most direct CI fit here. Their SMS page says you can test "using dedicated numbers across supported regions, without relying on phones or live SIMs", and that you can run "SMS OTP testing, verification code flows, and SMS notification tests" through their API with Cypress, Playwright, Selenium and others.

The docs show the pattern: assign a Mailosaur phone number to your test, trigger your app to send the SMS, then pull the message back in your test code and assert on it. They also mention project permissions for teams.

Where it fits: you want "receives code, enters code, gets in" to run on every build, not as a manual pre-release check.

What to watch: it tests the message, not the device. It won't tell you whether your Android autofill picks up the code. It also covers "supported regions", so check their list against your markets before you commit.

3. Firebase Authentication test phone numbers â€” free, fast, and fake on purpose

If you already use Firebase phone sign-in, start here. The Firebase docs let you set up fictional phone numbers and codes in the console. According to the docs, this lets you test without using your SMS quota, without sending an actual SMS, and without getting throttled when you run the same number over and over. It also works in an Android emulator without Google Play Services.

The limits are written down plainly: you can add up to 10 test numbers, they must be fictional (the docs suggest 555-prefixed US numbers), they go through the same format validation as real numbers, and Google recommends making the codes hard to guess and rotating them.

Where it fits: integration tests, app-review accounts, and days when you just need login to work.

What it can't tell you: whether a real SMS reaches a real phone in a real country. By design, nothing is sent.

4. Twilio test credentials and magic numbers â€” for testing the sending side of your code

If your backend sends codes through Twilio, their test credentials let you call parts of the REST API without being charged and without touching real phone numbers. The docs list what's supported: buying phone numbers, sending SMS, making calls, and Lookup. There are also "magic input" values that always produce a specific result, for example the number +15005550000 always returns a "number unavailable" error when you try to buy it, which is handy for testing your own error handling.

Two caveats from the same page. First, SMS sent with test credentials don't trigger status callbacks, so your delivery-status webhook path isn't covered. Second, and this one matters for new teams: Twilio now says you can't create test credentials in the new Twilio console. Credentials created in the legacy console keep working; otherwise they point you to a trial account.

Where it fits: backend tests for the "send code" call and its error paths. Not for checking what the user sees.

5. Telnyx Numbers â€” for buying real numbers by API in a lot of countries

Telnyx is a number provider rather than a testing tool, but some teams prefer to own a pool of real test numbers. Their numbers page lists local, national, toll-free and short code numbers across 130+ countries, a Numbers API to search, reserve and buy them, and "multi-function" numbers that handle voice, SMS, MMS and fax on the same number. They say they hold carrier licences in 30+ countries.

Where it fits: you want permanent test numbers in specific markets, managed in code, and you're fine wiring inbound messages to your own webhook.

What to watch: you build the "read the code" part yourself, and availability and paperwork differ by country.

6. Plivo phone numbers â€” a simpler number provider with a console

Plivo's numbers page says you can "instantly buy local, mobile, and toll-free numbers in more than 50 countries" through their API and console, with voice and SMS-enabled local and mobile numbers.

Where it fits: like Telnyx, for teams happy to handle inbound SMS on their own server, with a console for anyone who'd rather not script purchases. It lists fewer countries than Telnyx.

How I'd actually set it up

If I were starting fresh on a small app team:

  1. Firebase test numbers (or your provider's equivalent) for everyday dev and CI.
  2. Mailosaur, or a Telnyx/Plivo number wired to your own webhook, for one or two real end-to-end SMS tests that run on every release build.
  3. DuoPlus cloud phones plus cloud numbers for the human pass: one device per target market, Android 10 and 15 side by side, before a regional launch or a signup-screen change.
  4. Twilio test credentials only if you're already on Twilio and have legacy test credentials; otherwise, a trial account.

The fake numbers keep you fast. The real numbers keep you honest. And a real device in the right country is where you find out the code arrived fine but the screen didn't.

If you want to try the device side, DuoPlus is where I'd start, but I'm biased, so test it against your own flow before you take my word for it.
