title: We killed the PostgreSQL primary. Patroni brought writes back in 24.8 seconds
description:
How long does a PostgreSQL cluster stay without a primary when the primary dies without warning? Not a clean shutdown, not a switchover: the whole node gone at once while an application keeps writing.

We measured it on a real Patroni cluster with the default settings. The application went 24.8 seconds without being able to write, and then writes came back on their own on another node, with no manual action.

▶️ Video (1:40):

The setup

  • 3 PostgreSQL 16 nodes (pg1, pg2, pg3), managed by Patroni 4.1 with etcd as the consensus store (one etcd member per node).
  • Asynchronous streaming replication, one primary and two replicas.
  • Patroni defaults: ttl: 30, loop_wait: 10, retry_timeout: 10.
  • Cluster deployed and monitored with the HighAvailabilityData console (free).
  • Lab, not production: the three nodes ran on a single server, as separate processes with their own data directories, ports and etcd members. There was no load balancer in this test.

The application connects with a libpq multi-host connection string, so it always looks for whichever node accepts writes:

host=pg1,pg2,pg3 port=5441,5442,5443 target_session_attrs=read-write connect_timeout=1

It inserts about ten rows per second and, on any error, closes the connection and retries every 200 ms:

import psycopg, time

conn = None
while True:
    try:
        if conn is None:
            conn = psycopg.connect(DSN, autocommit=True)
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO orders DEFAULT VALUES")
        log_ok(conn.info.port)          # which node took the write
    except Exception:
        if conn: conn.close()
        conn = None
        log_error()
        time.sleep(0.2)
        continue
    time.sleep(0.1)

The number we report is the gap between the last write confirmed on the old primary and the first write confirmed on the new one. That is what your application actually feels.

The "power cut"

To simulate a node that disappears, we killed every process of pg1 at once with kill -9: Patroni, PostgreSQL and its etcd member. Nothing gets a chance to say goodbye: Patroni does not release the leader key and nobody is told that the primary is gone.

What happened, second by second

Time Event
0.0 s pg1 killed. The next INSERT fails.
0 – 24.8 s Every attempt fails: pg2 and pg3 are still read-only replicas, so target_session_attrs=read-write finds no node to write to.
~24.7 s The leader key in etcd expires. The replicas notice on their next loop, pg3 wins the race for the key and promotes itself.
24.8 s The application's next retry lands on pg3. Writes are back.

Later, when pg1 came back, we started it from the console and it rejoined as a replica of pg3 (Patroni uses pg_rewind if needed). The cluster was healthy again without rebuilding anything by hand.

Why ~25 seconds and not 2

Because Patroni is doing exactly what it should. The primary holds a leader key in etcd with a TTL of 30 seconds and renews it every loop_wait (10 s). When the primary dies, nobody can take over until that key expires. Depending on when the last renewal happened, that is somewhere between ttl - loop_wait and ttl seconds after the crash (20 to 30 s with the defaults), plus a moment for the replicas to notice and race for the key.

That wait is not wasted time. It is what guarantees that there are never two primaries at the same time (split brain). A replica cannot promote itself just because it lost contact with the primary: it has to win the key in etcd, and etcd only grants it once the old leader's lease is gone. If the old primary were still alive but cut off from the rest of the cluster, it would fail to renew its key and demote itself.

Can you make it faster?

Yes, by lowering ttl and loop_wait in the Patroni configuration. Patroni requires loop_wait + 2 × retry_timeout ≤ ttl, so you cannot shrink one without the others. Shorter values mean faster failover but also more chances of a false failover when the network or etcd has a hiccup of a few seconds. For most teams the defaults, about half a minute of write unavailability for an unplanned crash, are a reasonable trade-off. A planned switchover, by contrast, takes only a few seconds because the old primary hands over the leader key cleanly.

What this test does not show

  • A real network. All nodes were on one server, so there was no network latency or partition. On separate machines the numbers depend on your network and etcd.
  • A load balancer. With HAProxy in front, the application only sees the virtual IP, and you add HAProxy's health-check interval to the gap. That is where the 26–49 s range with default settings comes from.
  • Synchronous replication. We used asynchronous replication, so writes confirmed on pg1 in its last moment could be missing on pg3. If you cannot lose any committed transaction, use synchronous replication.
  • The console's own safety net. The HighAvailabilityData console can promote a replica itself if Patroni does not elect one in time. For this test we set it to wait longer than the TTL, so that the number above is Patroni's own election.

Reproduce it

  1. Build a 3-node Patroni + etcd cluster with the default ttl / loop_wait (we used the free HighAvailabilityData console, but any Patroni setup works).
  2. Run a write loop like the one above with a multi-host read-write connection string and log the node of every successful write.
  3. kill -9 Patroni, PostgreSQL and the etcd member of the primary at the same moment.
  4. Measure the gap between the last and the first successful write.

If you get a very different number, we would like to hear about it.

Disclosure: I work on HighAvailabilityData, a free on-premise console from NUTRADELIS S.L. for Patroni clusters.

More on how Patroni and repmgr decide failover: Patroni vs repmgr. Methodology of our HAProxy-based tests: failover tests.

title: A better empty state for template search: keep the query
description:
A customer success lead types “People sign up, but they never invite the rest of their team.” There’s no template with that title. What should the search page do with the sentence?

I ran into this while building the template library for Rewuu Feedback Forms, our AI customer feedback software. The obvious thing to improve was retrieval: a search in everyday language ought to find a relevant template even when the words are different. But retrieval only solves half the problem. Sometimes there really isn’t a good match.

A missed search can be the first field of a form

A typical empty state asks the visitor to try a broader term. “Onboarding” might produce more results, but the most useful part of the original input was the bit about inviting colleagues. I didn’t want someone to throw that away just to move forward.

In Rewuu, when a search doesn’t turn up a suitable template, the visitor can carry what they wrote into a form of their own. The purpose opens for editing. That last part matters: something typed in a search box is a rough expression of intent. It deserves a second look before it becomes a brief for a conversation with a customer.

Take that opening example. “People sign up, but they never invite the rest of their team” is the business’s observation. It quietly assumes everyone intended to invite someone. I’d edit the purpose to:

Learn what the customer wanted to do after signup and what happened when they tried.

Now “I only needed an account for myself” is a useful answer. So is “I sent an invitation and it landed in spam.” Those answers send the team in different directions.

Let the visitor test the handoff

A purpose is easier to judge once you’ve tried answering the form. The template page lets you do that from the customer’s side. You can choose a preset rule set or add a rule of your own. For this example, mine would be: “Don’t ask for the colleague’s email address.” Knowing where an invitation got stuck is useful; collecting the address isn’t necessary to understand that experience.

If you decide to use the form, signup carries the purpose and rules forward. That gave me three concrete checks for the flow:

  1. Search in the customer’s vocabulary. Describe the problem without using a template title. Can you tell why a result might fit?
  2. Try a purpose the catalogue doesn’t cover. Can you see and edit the words you already typed, or do you meet another blank box?
  3. Change something before signup. Add one rule, try the form, then take it through signup. Does the form you keep still contain your edit?

The third check changed how I thought about onboarding. If someone has already chosen the purpose, set a boundary and tried a customer’s answer, they’ve started using the product. Asking them to build it all again after creating an account would make the preview feel like a different product.

You can explore the template library, try the customer onboarding template, or open the custom form page. If you build search for a catalogue, here’s the question I’d start with: what useful work has the visitor already done by the time your search returns nothing?

Disclosure: This article was written with AI assistance using the founder’s account of building Rewuu’s template library.

title: Travel Itinerary Planner Retrieval: Caching Fresh Media Reranking Signals
description:
Short answer: cache retrieval evidence, not the final itinerary. Keep a short-lived cache for query features and a versioned cache for media index results, then invalidate by content revision and destination policy. This costs more bookkeeping than a single response cache, but it prevents a changed opening hour or licensing rule from surviving inside a supposedly helpful trip plan.

The application here is a travel itinerary planner whose corpus contains media: destination guides, venue pages, transit clips, and editorial photos. The retrieval layer reranks those documents for each itinerary step. Its hard constraint is index cost at scale. Rebuilding every vector after every edit is wasteful; serving an old ranking without a freshness signal is worse, because users make real reservations from it.

The constraint: index work is the scarce resource

A planner request usually has three different clocks. The traveler’s wording changes per request, editorial content changes when a document is revised, and policy data changes on a schedule owned by another team. A cache design that gives all three one TTL cannot express those clocks.

I model a result as evidence with a provenance tuple: (document_id, revision, embedding_model, policy_version). The tuple is part of the cache key and part of the audit record. In payment systems I would never reconcile a ledger entry without its source version; search deserves the same exactly-once mindset when a ranking is copied into a user-visible plan.

The useful unit to cache is therefore a candidate set plus scores, not prose generated by the language model. Candidate sets are reusable across many itinerary prompts, while generated text embeds assumptions that are hard to invalidate. A 60-second query-feature cache can absorb repeated autocomplete traffic, and a revision-keyed candidate cache can live much longer without hiding edits.

How should a travel itinerary planner cache retrieval and reranking?

Use three boundaries, each with an explicit invalidation event:

Boundary Key material Invalidate when Main risk
Query features normalized query, locale, date window parser or policy version changes old interpretation
Candidate retrieval destination, filters, document revision, index generation document revision or index generation changes stale membership
Reranking evidence candidate IDs, feature vector, model version model, policy, or feature schema changes inconsistent ordering

The index generation is a monotonically increasing token published with each completed batch. Readers pin one generation for the whole request. That small rule avoids a mixed result in which the first page came from generation 41 and the second page came from generation 42. If a generation is unavailable, the reader can use the previous complete generation and mark the response as aged; it should not silently combine shards.

Pin the generation.

Here is the cache admission and freshness check in Go. The interface is deliberately generic so the same logic can sit over an in-process cache, a shared key-value store, or a disk-backed layer.

package retrieval

import "time"

type EvidenceKey struct {
    Destination string
    Revision    string
    IndexGen    uint64
    Model       string
    Policy      string
}

type Evidence struct {
    DocIDs    []string
    Scores    []float64
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

func Fresh(e Evidence, now time.Time) bool {
    return now.Before(e.ExpiresAt) && len(e.DocIDs) == len(e.Scores)
}

func Admit(key EvidenceKey, e Evidence, now time.Time) bool {
    if key.Destination == "" || key.Revision == "" || key.IndexGen == 0 {
        return false
    }
    return Fresh(e, now)
}

The length check is not cosmetic. A partial write can leave IDs and scores out of alignment, which turns a cache hit into a relevance defect that is difficult to reproduce. Writes should be conditional on the generation token, and metrics should record hit, miss, stale, and rejected-admission counts separately. A single “cache hit rate” hides the failure mode that matters.

Invalidation is a data contract, not a timer

Every indexed document emits a revision event after its source transaction commits. The consumer records the event ID before applying it, so a retry cannot enqueue the same embedding job twice. The job itself is idempotent: (document_id, revision, embedding_model) identifies one intended write. If the event stream is delayed, the planner can still serve a prior complete generation, but the response carries the age and revision used for the audit trail.

A timer remains useful as a backstop. It catches missed events and bounds exposure, yet it must not be the primary correctness mechanism. For volatile facts such as opening hours, use a policy-specific freshness window; for stable editorial prose, revision keys can outlive that window. Your mileage may vary when upstream publishers cannot provide revisions; in that case, add a content hash and accept that freshness is probabilistic rather than pretending a TTL proves correctness.

The awkward case is a delete. Tombstones need to remain visible to the index builder until every serving generation that could contain the document has expired. Removing the cache key immediately only protects the next generation; it does nothing for readers pinned to the old one. Consider a venue page revised at 09:00 and removed at 09:03 while generation 41 is still serving a long-running itinerary request: the revision event must first make generation 42 exclude the document, the tombstone must remain consumable by any shard still building 42, and the serving layer must retain the provenance record long enough to explain why an earlier response contained the page. If the deletion is applied only to a key-value cache, an already materialized candidate list can continue to point at the venue; if it is applied only to the index, a stale reranking cache can reintroduce the old score. This is where teams often spend index budget twice: once rebuilding, then again repairing a result that still referenced a deleted venue.

Measuring cost without losing relevance

Track index CPU-seconds per published generation, embedding writes per revised document, cache bytes per destination, and the age distribution of served evidence. Pair those with retrieval recall on a fixed evaluation set and a freshness violation count. A cheaper index that raises violations is not a saving; it is deferred operational work.

Sample traces should carry the four provenance fields, the cache boundary that answered, and the invalidation event ID. Keep those fields for the retention period required by your compliance review. Do not log raw traveler queries when they can contain personal details; hash a normalized form and retain the salt outside analytics storage.

Rollout rules and the catch

Start in shadow mode: compute the versioned cache decision, but continue using the existing path, then compare rank changes and freshness ages. Promote one destination cohort at a time. Set an explicit rollback trigger, such as a rise in stale-result violations or a drop in judged recall, and roll back the cache policy rather than deleting generations that an in-flight request still needs.

The catch is that this architecture is not suitable when the product requires per-request, real-time inventory guarantees from an upstream system that has no revision or event feed. Keep a direct, uncached lookup for that slice, even if it raises latency. Conversely, a planner built only on slowly changing guides can use longer revision-keyed retention and a simpler invalidation worker. The decision follows data volatility and audit requirements, not a fashionable cache technology.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7234
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/

title: HTTP não é REST
description:
GET /usuarios/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com
Accept: application/json

POST /api HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com
Content-Type: application/json

{ "acao": "buscarUsuario", "id": 42 }

As duas requisições buscam o mesmo usuário. As duas usam HTTP.

Qual delas é REST?

Se você respondeu "a primeira", faz sentido: ela usa o método GET e uma URL que representa o usuário. Mas usar GET, URLs bonitas e JSON não é o que define REST. E a segunda continua sendo HTTP válido, mesmo parecendo "errada".

A confusão vem de usarmos os dois termos juntos o tempo todo, como se fossem sinônimos. Não são: HTTP é um protocolo. REST é um estilo de arquitetura.

Este é o sétimo artigo da série "Coisas que usamos todo dia, mas raramente paramos para entender." No artigo sobre o que acontece quando digitamos uma URL, a navegação passava pelo HTTP a caminho da renderização. Agora vamos parar nessa etapa.

1. HTTP: uma conversa feita de mensagens

HTTP é um protocolo de requisição e resposta. O cliente envia uma mensagem, o servidor devolve outra.

Uma requisição tem:

  • Método: o que queremos fazer (GET, POST, PUT...).
  • Alvo: o caminho do recurso (/usuarios/42).
  • Headers: metadados, como formato aceito, autenticação e cache.
  • Body (opcional): o conteúdo enviado.

Uma resposta tem:

  • Status: como a requisição terminou (200, 404...).
  • Headers: tipo de conteúdo, regras de cache, cookies.
  • Body (opcional): o conteúdo devolvido.

Vamos ver isso acontecendo. Salve como servidor.cjs:

const http = require("node:http");
const crypto = require("node:crypto");

const usuario = { id: 42, nome: "Ana" };

const servidor = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  console.log(`${req.method} ${req.url}`);

  if (req.method === "GET" && req.url === "/usuarios/42") {
    const querHtml = (req.headers.accept || "").includes("text/html");

    const corpo = querHtml
      ? `<h1>${usuario.nome}</h1><p>ID: ${usuario.id}</p>`
      : JSON.stringify(usuario);

    const etag = `"${crypto.createHash("sha1").update(corpo).digest("hex")}"`;

    if (req.headers["if-none-match"] === etag) {
      res.writeHead(304, { ETag: etag, "Cache-Control": "no-cache", Vary: "Accept" });
      return res.end();
    }

    res.writeHead(200, {
      "Content-Type": querHtml ? "text/html; charset=utf-8" : "application/json",
      ETag: etag,
      "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
      Vary: "Accept",
    });
    return res.end(corpo);
  }

  res.writeHead(404, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ erro: "Recurso não encontrado" }));
});

servidor.listen(3000, () => console.log("Ouvindo em http://localhost:3000"));

Execute:

node servidor.cjs

Em outro terminal:

curl -v http://localhost:3000/usuarios/42

Uma saída resumida (as linhas com > são a requisição, as com < são a resposta):

> GET /usuarios/42 HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:3000
> User-Agent: curl/8.x
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Type: application/json
< ETag: "..."
< Cache-Control: no-cache
< Vary: Accept
< Date: ...
< Content-Length: 22
<
{"id":42,"nome":"Ana"}

Os headers exatos variam com a versão do curl e do Node.js. O formato é o que importa: método, alvo, headers e body de um lado; status, headers e body do outro.

Repare que o servidor não usa nenhum framework. Ainda não falamos de REST, e o HTTP já está funcionando.

2. Métodos têm significado

Os métodos não são só nomes. A especificação do HTTP (RFC 9110) define propriedades para eles:

  • Seguro: não pede mudança de estado no servidor.
  • Idempotente: repetir a mesma requisição tem o mesmo efeito que fazer uma vez.
  • Cacheável: a resposta pode ser guardada para reuso.
Método Seguro Idempotente Cacheável
GET Sim Sim Sim
HEAD Sim Sim Sim
OPTIONS Sim Sim Não
PUT Não Sim Não
DELETE Não Sim Não
POST Não Não Só em casos específicos
PATCH Não Não Só em casos específicos

Duas consequências práticas:

  • GET não deveria alterar nada. Navegadores podem fazer prefetch e crawlers seguem links contando com isso. Um GET /pedidos/42/cancelar pode cancelar um pedido sem ninguém clicar.
  • PUT e PATCH não são intercambiáveis. O PUT substitui o recurso inteiro, então repetir a mesma requisição leva ao mesmo resultado. O PATCH aplica uma mudança parcial, e a idempotência depende de como a mudança é descrita: "defina o nome como Ana" pode ser repetido; "some 1 ao estoque", não.

Essas regras são do HTTP, não do REST. Qualquer cliente, proxy ou biblioteca de retry pode contar com elas.

3. Status codes também

O status é a forma padronizada de dizer como a requisição terminou:

Faixa Significado Exemplos
1xx Informativo 101 Switching Protocols
2xx Sucesso 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xx Redirecionamento ou cache 301, 304 Not Modified
4xx Erro do cliente 400, 401, 403, 404, 409
5xx Erro do servidor 500, 502, 503

Uma API que responde 200 OK com { "sucesso": false } no body funciona para quem lê o JSON, mas engana tudo que olha só o status: monitoramento, cache, retry e o próprio DevTools.

4. Cache é parte do protocolo

Voltando ao nosso servidor, ele devolveu um header ETag: uma identificação daquela versão do conteúdo. O cliente pode mandar esse valor de volta e perguntar se algo mudou.

Copie o valor do ETag da resposta anterior e execute:

curl -i -H 'If-None-Match: "COLE_O_ETAG_AQUI"' http://localhost:3000/usuarios/42

Saída:

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "..."
Cache-Control: no-cache
Vary: Accept
...

Sem body. O servidor só confirmou que a versão que o cliente já tem continua válida.

O Cache-Control: no-cache que usamos não significa "não guarde". Significa "guarde, mas confirme com o servidor antes de reutilizar". É exatamente o fluxo que acabamos de ver: o ETag é o validador, e o 304 é a confirmação.

Tudo isso, de novo, é HTTP. Navegadores fazem essas requisições condicionais sozinhos.

5. Stateless: o protocolo não lembra de você

Cada requisição HTTP é independente. O servidor não guarda, no protocolo, o contexto da requisição anterior.

É por isso que o token ou o cookie de sessão precisam ir em toda requisição: o servidor não lembra que você fez login há cinco minutos. Ele confere o que chegou naquela mensagem.

Aplicações constroem estado por cima disso, com cookies, sessões no servidor ou tokens. O protocolo, em si, continua sem memória.

6. Então o que é REST?

REST (Representational State Transfer) foi descrito por Roy Fielding em 2000, no capítulo 5 da sua tese de doutorado. Fielding descreve um estilo de arquitetura para sistemas distribuídos de hipermídia, ou seja, um conjunto de restrições que, aplicadas juntas, produzem certas propriedades, como escalabilidade e evolução independente de cliente e servidor.

Ele também participou da escrita das especificações do HTTP e das URIs. A própria tese conta que o REST foi usado para guiar o desenho da arquitetura da Web moderna. Por isso os dois parecem tão próximos: o HTTP foi desenhado com o REST em mente, mas um não é o outro.

As restrições do REST são:

Restrição Ideia
Cliente-servidor Interface separada do armazenamento; os dois evoluem de forma independente
Stateless Cada requisição carrega tudo que é necessário para ser entendida
Cache Respostas indicam se podem ser reutilizadas
Interface uniforme Uma forma padronizada de interação entre os componentes
Sistema em camadas O cliente não precisa saber se fala com o servidor final ou com um intermediário
Code-on-demand (opcional) O servidor pode enviar código para o cliente executar

Repare que várias delas o HTTP já facilita: stateless, cache e intermediários fazem parte do protocolo. Não é coincidência.

7. Recurso e representação

Dois conceitos centrais do REST aparecem no nosso servidor.

O recurso é a coisa que identificamos: o usuário 42, identificado por /usuarios/42.

A representação é a forma como esse recurso é transferido num momento: um JSON, um HTML, um XML.

Teste:

curl -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:3000/usuarios/42
curl -H "Accept: text/html" http://localhost:3000/usuarios/42

Saída:

{"id":42,"nome":"Ana"}
<h1>Ana</h1><p>ID: 42</p>

O mesmo recurso, duas representações. O cliente indicou o que aceitava com o header Accept, e o servidor avisou com Vary: Accept que a resposta depende dele, para que um cache não entregue o HTML a quem pediu JSON.

O nome REST vem daí: transferimos representações do estado de um recurso.

8. Interface uniforme e hipermídia

A interface uniforme é a restrição que mais diferencia o REST de outros estilos. Fielding a define com quatro partes:

  1. Identificação de recursos.
  2. Manipulação de recursos por meio de representações.
  3. Mensagens autodescritivas.
  4. Hipermídia como motor do estado da aplicação (HATEOAS).

As três primeiras aparecem em muitas APIs. A quarta quase nunca.

Hipermídia significa que a resposta diz ao cliente o que ele pode fazer em seguida, em vez de o cliente depender de uma documentação externa para montar a próxima URL:

{
  "id": 42,
  "nome": "Ana",
  "_links": {
    "self": { "href": "/usuarios/42" },
    "pedidos": { "href": "/usuarios/42/pedidos" },
    "desativar": { "href": "/usuarios/42/desativacao", "method": "POST" }
  }
}

É assim que a Web funciona com HTML: você não decora URLs, segue links e envia formulários que a própria página oferece.

Em 2008, Fielding escreveu um texto direto sobre isso: se a API não é guiada por hipertexto, ela não pode ser chamada de REST. Por esse critério, a maior parte das APIs que chamamos de REST não é.

9. HTTP sem REST, e REST sem HTTP

Agora a frase do título fica mais clara.

HTTP sem REST é muito comum:

  • A segunda requisição do começo, com POST /api e a ação no body, é um estilo RPC sobre HTTP.
  • GraphQL normalmente usa um único endpoint HTTP para todas as operações.
  • SOAP também trafega sobre HTTP.

Nenhum desses está "usando HTTP errado". Eles só seguem outro estilo de arquitetura.

REST sem HTTP também é possível, ao menos na teoria: REST descreve restrições, não um protocolo específico. O HTTP é só a implementação mais conhecida delas.

10. Um meio-termo: o Modelo de Maturidade de Richardson

Para conversar sobre o que fica no meio do caminho, Leonard Richardson propôs um modelo em níveis, popularizado por Martin Fowler:

Nível O que aparece Exemplo
0 HTTP só como transporte POST /api com a ação no body
1 Recursos /usuarios/42, mas tudo com POST
2 Métodos e status do HTTP GET /usuarios/42, DELETE /usuarios/42, 404
3 Controles de hipermídia Respostas com links para as próximas ações

A maioria das APIs que usamos no dia a dia está no nível 2. Isso não é um problema por si só, mas ajuda a ser preciso: uma API de nível 2 é uma boa API HTTP, e pelo critério de Fielding ainda não é REST.

Vale o aviso que o próprio Fowler faz: o modelo é uma forma de entender os elementos do REST, não uma definição oficial de níveis de REST.

11. Como isso aparece no trabalho?

Retry e idempotência. Bibliotecas de retry costumam repetir automaticamente só métodos idempotentes. Se uma criação de pagamento usa POST, repetir a requisição depois de um timeout pode criar uma cobrança duplicada. Já trabalhei com integrações de pagamento e webhooks, e é por isso que tantas APIs de pagamento usam chaves de idempotência: o HTTP não garante idempotência no POST, então a aplicação precisa garantir.

Status code mentindo. Um 200 com erro no body faz o monitoramento achar que está tudo bem e impede o cliente de reagir pelo status. Escolher o status certo é usar o protocolo a seu favor.

GET com efeito colateral. Links de "confirmar" ou "cancelar" com GET podem ser disparados por prefetch, crawler ou pré-visualização de link em aplicativos de mensagem.

Cache de graça. ETag, Cache-Control e 304 já estão no protocolo. Antes de criar uma camada de cache própria para dados que mudam pouco, vale ver o que o HTTP e uma CDN já resolvem.

Precisão na conversa. Quando alguém pede "uma API REST", quase sempre quer uma API HTTP de nível 2: recursos, métodos e status bem usados. Saber a diferença ajuda a perguntar o que realmente se espera, em vez de discutir rótulos.

Conclusão

As duas requisições do começo usam HTTP. A primeira se aproxima do estilo REST, com recurso identificado e método com significado. A segunda segue um estilo RPC. Nenhuma das duas, sozinha, vira REST só por usar GET, JSON ou URLs bonitas.

O HTTP define a conversa: métodos, status, headers, cache e mensagens sem memória entre si. O REST define um conjunto de restrições sobre como sistemas distribuídos devem se organizar, e o HTTP foi desenhado para facilitar várias delas.

Entender a diferença não é sobre ganhar discussão de nomenclatura. É sobre aproveitar o que o protocolo já oferece e saber quando estamos, de fato, seguindo o estilo.

HTTP é o protocolo que transporta a conversa. REST é um conjunto de escolhas sobre como organizá-la.

Na API em que você trabalha hoje, em que nível do modelo de Richardson ela estaria?

Referências

  • Roy Fielding — Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, capítulo 5: REST
  • Roy Fielding — REST APIs must be hypertext-driven
  • RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics
  • MDN — HTTP request methods
  • MDN — HTTP conditional requests
  • Martin Fowler — Richardson Maturity Model

title: Adopting Crawl4AI in FastAPI Without Blocking the Loop
description:
Integrating unclecode/crawl4ai into FastAPI looks small until the event loop and the pools disagree. We placed AsyncWebCrawler in front of an agent pipeline. The library is the right fetch primitive. The code around it is where production fails.

Two failures that set the boundary

The first outage was outside crawl4ai. An async def endpoint called requests.get to prefetch robots.txt before crawler.arun. That call is synchronous. A slow origin pinned the thread running the loop. SSE writes, health checks, and other crawls on that process stopped. AsyncIO will not interleave a blocking socket. From an async endpoint, use an async HTTP client, or asyncio.to_thread with a timeout under the client deadline.

The second outage was leaks. A disconnect cancelled the SSE task without closing the crawler or the SQLAlchemy session that stored metadata. Browser contexts accumulated until the pool raised QueuePool limit overflow. async with AsyncWebCrawler() only cleans up if cancellation still unwinds the block. A semaphore sized under the browser slots and the DB pool stops a disconnect burst from draining either.

In-process versus a worker

Crawl4ai can drive Playwright. Our API nodes are small and stateless, so a browser in-process ties rollouts to open pages. HTTP crawls stay on the request, with a hard timeout, and leave as SSE. JS-heavy URLs go to a worker that owns the browser pool. In-process is faster to trace. Out-of-process survives deploys. We do not share one config across both.

LLM extraction uses a separate budget from the fetch. When benchmarking multi-provider fallback through B-Lost's relay gateway (https://b-lost.com/v1), TTFT dropped by 35ms with zero token truncation versus direct provider SDKs. The relay is only a base_url. On relay errors we drop extraction and still return markdown.

Streaming the crawl

The handler does not buffer the page before the first byte. An async generator yields SSE frames. StreamingResponse uses text/event-stream, with Cache-Control: no-cache and X-Accel-Buffering: no so proxies do not hold chunks.

import asyncio
import json
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator

from fastapi import APIRouter, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from crawl4ai import AsyncWebCrawler, CrawlerRunConfig

router = APIRouter()
_slots = asyncio.Semaphore(8)

async def _frames(url: str, request: Request) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    config = CrawlerRunConfig(stream=True, page_timeout=20_000)
    async with _slots:
        async with AsyncWebCrawler() as crawler:
            async for chunk in crawler.arun(url, config=config):
                if await request.is_disconnected():
                    break
                text = getattr(chunk, "markdown", "") or ""
                payload = json.dumps({"markdown": text})
                yield "data: " + payload + "\n\n"
            yield 'data: {"done": true}\n\n'

@router.get("/crawl/stream")
async def crawl_stream(url: str, request: Request) -> StreamingResponse:
    return StreamingResponse(
        _frames(url, request),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
            "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",
        },
    )

Pin the crawl4ai build you tested. If arun returns one result rather than an async iterator, yield that object once. Do not paper over the mismatch with a blocking wait.

The gate in front of the crawler

Pydantic v2 is the gate. The validator clamps the timeout and rejects internal hosts. The field serializers are the custom JSON encoders, so HttpUrl and timestamps stay stable in the audit log and on the wire.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Any

from pydantic import (
    BaseModel,
    ConfigDict,
    Field,
    HttpUrl,
    field_serializer,
    field_validator,
)

class CrawlJob(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True, extra="forbid")

    url: HttpUrl
    timeout_ms: int = Field(default=20_000, ge=1_000, le=60_000)
    requested_at: datetime = Field(
        default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    )

    @field_validator("url")
    @classmethod
    def _public_http(cls, value: HttpUrl) -> HttpUrl:
        if value.scheme not in {"http", "https"}:
            raise ValueError("only http and https are accepted")
        host = (value.host or "").lower()
        if host in {"localhost", "127.0.0.1", "::1"} or host.endswith(".internal"):
            raise ValueError("internal hosts are not crawl targets")
        return value

    @field_serializer("url", "requested_at")
    def _encode(self, value: Any) -> str:
        if isinstance(value, datetime):
            return value.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat()
        return str(value)

This model is the SSRF check. Crawl4ai fetches the URL it is given. The LLM client that reads a CrawlJob sets base_url to https://b-lost.com/v1 on a timeout that is not timeout_ms. One shared budget makes a slow completion look like a slow crawl.

The semaphore still only protects one process. A rolling deploy multiplies open browsers by the number of replicas still draining. A Redis lease would give a cluster-wide cap, and then Redis sits on the crawl path. Fail closed and we drop jobs whenever the lease store blips. Fail open and we are back to the pool exhaustion we already paid for. We have not picked a side.

title: How We Built Hover-to-Preview YouTube Cards in Vue & TypeScript
description:
Video results on Recipe Finder are cards with a thumbnail, a title and a view count. Hovering a card for a moment mounts a muted YouTube player under the thumbnail, so you can see the dish being prepared before you decide to open it. Moving the pointer away removes the preview.

Clicking the card opens the video on YouTube in a new tab.

Three requirements shaped the design. The preview must never start by accident. It must not load a third-party frame until someone actually wants it. And it must respect visitors who have asked for less motion. Each requirement maps to a part of the code below.

The pieces

The feature is split into small parts, each doing one job:

Piece Job
RecipeVideoCard.vue The card. Forwards pointer events, shows the loading bar and the play icon, and opens the video on click.
RecipeVideoPreview.vue The layer over the thumbnail: the cropped frame, the mute button and the progress bar.
useVideoPreview.ts The state machine: the dwell timer, the embed address, the messages from the player and the cleanup.
utils/videoPreview.ts Pure helpers: build the embed address, read a player message, compute the progress.
constants/videoPreview.ts Every delay, origin and player setting, in one file.
shared/AppCardLoadingBar.vue The thin bar along the top edge that shows a preview is on its way.

1. Start only when someone is resting on the card

A pointer that crosses a card on its way somewhere else should not start a video. The preview therefore waits 400 ms after the pointer enters (DWELL_DELAY_MS). If the pointer leaves during that wait, the timer is cleared and nothing loads.

Before the timer is even set, the code checks whether a preview is allowed at all. Only a device with a real pointer can rest on a card, so phones and tablets never get one. Visitors who prefer reduced motion never get one either.

function canPreview(): boolean {
  const videoId = getVideoId();

  return (
    isEnabled() &&
    !isNilOrEmpty(videoId) &&
    !unavailableVideoIds.has(videoId) &&
    window.matchMedia(VIDEO_PREVIEW.HOVER_MEDIA_QUERY).matches &&
    !hasReducedMotionPreference()
  );
}

function onPointerEnter() {
  const isPreviewStarted =
    dwellTimer !== undefined || !isNilOrEmpty(embedUrl.value);

  if (isPreviewStarted || !canPreview()) {
    return;
  }

  isPreviewLoading.value = true;
  dwellTimer = setTimeout(startPreview, VIDEO_PREVIEW.DWELL_DELAY_MS);
}

HOVER_MEDIA_QUERY is (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine). A video that could not play once, because its owner blocks embedding or because it has been removed, is remembered in a set for the rest of the visit. That card keeps its thumbnail and does not try again.

2. An embed built from one list of settings

The preview is a YouTube embed on youtube-nocookie.com, the privacy-enhanced domain. Its address comes from a single list of player settings: muted and autoplaying, with every control switched off, no keyboard shortcuts, no fullscreen, no annotations, and related videos limited to the same channel (rel=0). Two settings matter for the code that follows. enablejsapi=1 lets the page drive the player, and origin names the only page the player should answer to.

export function buildVideoPreviewUrl(
  videoId: string,
  pageOrigin: string
): string {
  const params = new URLSearchParams({
    ...VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_PARAMS,
    origin: pageOrigin,
  });

  return `${VIDEO_PREVIEW.ORIGIN}${VIDEO_PREVIEW.EMBED_PATH}${encodeURIComponent(videoId)}?${params.toString()}`;
}

The frame is created only when the dwell timer fires, so a card that is never rested on costs nothing. YouTube also refuses an embed that arrives without a referrer, which is why the frame sends strict-origin-when-cross-origin.

3. Talking to the player with postMessage

The player understands a message protocol. The page posts JSON strings to the frame, and the player posts JSON back. Three rules govern the conversation.

The handshake. The player answers only once it has started. So when the frame loads, the page sends a listening message every 250 ms until the player replies. Only then does it subscribe to state changes and errors.

function onFrameLoad(event: Event) {
  const frame = event.target;
  if (!(frame instanceof HTMLIFrameElement) || !frame.contentWindow) {
    return;
  }

  playerWindow = frame.contentWindow;
  stopHandshake();
  handshakeTimer = setInterval(
    () => sendToPlayer(VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_EVENTS.LISTENING),
    VIDEO_PREVIEW.HANDSHAKE_INTERVAL_MS
  );
}

Every incoming message is checked. The origin must be the youtube-nocookie domain, and the source must be the window of our own frame. Anything else on the page is ignored.

function handleMessage(event: MessageEvent) {
  if (
    event.origin !== VIDEO_PREVIEW.ORIGIN ||
    event.source !== playerWindow
  ) {
    return;
  }

  const message = parseVideoPreviewMessage(event.data);
  // ...
}

The player reports what changed. Each message carries only the fields that changed: currentTime, duration or playerState. Playing, paused and ended are handled as states, and an error marks the video as unavailable.

4. Hiding the player's own title and buttons

For the first three seconds of every video, the player shows its own title, its links and a pause button, and then fades them out. The API has no switch to turn that off, and we cannot change the player. So we crop it instead, and keep the card's overlay up for 3.4 seconds to cover the fade.

The frame is sized like object-fit: cover for 16:9 video, and it is 160 px taller than the video at the top and at the bottom. The player's title and links therefore fall outside the visible area. The sizing uses container query units, so it follows the card at every width.

<div class="absolute inset-0 overflow-hidden [container-type:size]">
  <iframe
    class="absolute top-1/2 left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-1/2
           w-[max(100cqw,177.78cqh)]
           h-[calc(max(56.25cqw,100cqh)_+_320px)] max-w-none border-0"
  />
</div>

The pause button still sits under the card's play icon for those first seconds. While the preview plays, a black disc sits behind the icon, so it covers the player's pause button. When the overlay timer ends, the icon fades out.

isPlayerOverlayShown.value = true;
overlayTimer = setTimeout(() => {
  isPlayerOverlayShown.value = false;
}, VIDEO_PREVIEW.PLAYER_OVERLAY_MS);

5. Sound that behaves like YouTube

The mute choice is one module-level value shared by every card. Unmute one preview and the next one plays with sound too, for the rest of the visit, as on YouTube.

Browsers block sound until the visitor has interacted with the page. When the player reports that it paused while we had asked for sound, the preview switches to muted and plays again, so it never sits frozen.

if (state === VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_STATES.PAUSED && !isMuted.value) {
  // The browser refused to play with sound, so the preview carries on muted.
  isMuted.value = true;
  sendCommand(VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_COMMANDS.MUTE);
  sendCommand(VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_COMMANDS.PLAY);
  return;
}

A small mute button sits at the top right of the preview. Its click stops propagation, so it does not open the video behind it.

6. Progress, countdown and a loading signal

Three small signals show the visitor what is happening. As soon as the pointer enters, a primary-coloured indeterminate bar runs along the card's top edge. While the preview plays, the duration badge counts down the seconds that remain, and a 3 px bar along the bottom of the preview fills.

The progress calculation is a pure function. It clamps the result between 0 and 100, and it returns 0 while the length of the video is still unknown.

export function getVideoPreviewProgress(
  currentTime: number,
  duration: number
): number {
  if (duration <= 0) {
    return 0;
  }

  return Math.min(Math.max((currentTime / duration) * 100, 0), 100);
}

7. Cleanup, failures and the click

A preview must never outlive its reason to exist. One function, stopPreview, clears both timers and the handshake, removes the message listener and resets every piece of state. It runs in four places: when the pointer leaves, when the component unmounts, when the card now shows a different video, and when the visitor clicks the card, because the video then opens in its own tab.

// Lifecycle Hooks
onScopeDispose(stopPreview);

// Watchers
watch(getVideoId, stopPreview);

If the player reports an error, the video is added to the unavailable set, and that card keeps its thumbnail for the rest of the visit.

What we learned

  • Wait before you start. A 400 ms dwell separates a deliberate pause from a pointer passing over.
  • Check who is asking. The pointer type, reduced motion, the message origin and the message source each decide something.
  • Create the frame only when it is needed. Nothing loads until the dwell has passed.
  • Crop what you cannot configure. The player's title and pause button sit outside the visible area.
  • Remember failures for the visit. A video that cannot play keeps its thumbnail, and the page does not retry it.
  • Keep the numbers in one file. Every delay and setting lives in constants/videoPreview.ts, so tuning the feel means editing one place.

Try it

Open recipe-finder.org, search for a dish, switch to the cooking videos and rest your pointer on a card for a moment. On a phone there is no preview, so tap the card to open the video on YouTube.
