title: Internxt Drive audit: reproducing 13 vulnerabilities without touching production
description:
13 findings, 13 test files, 13 test logs. That was the most consequential decision in the whole audit, and it had nothing to do with the vulnerabilities.

When I started reading internxt/drive-server-wip in October 2026, I made one rule before writing a single assertion: nothing in this project would touch a production system, a real account, or a network service I did not own. The repository is public. The backend is a NestJS application with Sequelize, PostgreSQL, Valkey, a Bridge service for storage credentials, SendGrid for mail, and a fairly large e2e test harness already in the tree. All of that can be pointed at loopback. So every finding would be reproduced against a local checkout of a pinned commit, with synthetic users and disposable services, or it would not be reproduced at all.

That constraint shaped everything else. A security report is only useful if a maintainer can run it. If reproducing a finding needs a real account, a production dataset, or access to infrastructure the maintainer does not have, the report becomes an anecdote. So each finding got its own self-contained proof of concept, its own log, source references pinned to the audited commit 7d7a8be2 from 28 October, and a hash of the archive. A maintainer could run C07 without reading C08.

The first thing to build was the runner:

set -euo pipefail
case_id=${2:-}
if [[ ! "$case_id" =~ ^C(0[1-9]|1[0-3])$ || ! -f "$source_file" ]]; then
if [[ ! -f package.json || ! -x ./node_modules/.bin/jest || ! -d test/helpers ]]; then
target="test/security-poc-${case_id,,}.e2e-spec.ts"
if [[ -e "$target" ]]; then
cp -- "$source_file" "$target"
trap 'rm -f -- "$target"' EXIT
export NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules
export NODE_ENV=test
export RDS_HOSTNAME=127.0.0.1
export RDS_PORT=55432
export RDS_DBNAME=drive_audit
export RDS_USERNAME=audit
export RDS_PASSWORD=local_only_audit_password
export REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING=redis://127.0.0.1:56379
export REDIS_JOBS_CONNECTION_STRING=redis://127.0.0.1:56379
export PCREATED_USERS_PASSWORD=local_only_precreated_password
export NOTIFICATIONS_API_ENABLED=false
export SENDGRID_MODE_SANDBOX=true
./node_modules/.bin/jest --config ./test/jest-e2e.json --runInBand \
  --runTestsByPath "$target" --silent --forceExit

It takes a PoC source file and a case ID (C01 through C13). The first if rejects a bad ID or a missing file. The second refuses to run outside a checked-out repository with dependencies installed and a test/helpers directory. Then it refuses to overwrite an existing test file, copies the PoC to test/security-poc-<case>.e2e-spec.ts, and installs a trap that removes it again on EXIT. Every connection string is loopback: PostgreSQL on 55432 with TLS, Valkey on 56379. Every credential is synthetic and written into the report. NOTIFICATIONS_API_ENABLED=false and SENDGRID_MODE_SANDBOX=true exist so that no mail can leave the process even if a test path reaches the mailer by accident.

That trap line matters more than it looks. A PoC that leaves files behind changes the repository it claims to be testing. A PoC that overwrites an existing test can destroy evidence. A runner that happily executes against a non-loopback host turns a defensive test into something else entirely. These are small lines, and they are the difference between a reproducible report and a claim.

The installation step was equally deliberate, so that installing dependencies does not execute arbitrary package scripts or phone home, and 13 separate cases never share database state:

npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
./node_modules/.bin/jest --config ./test/jest-e2e.json --runInBand \
  --runTestsByPath "$target" --silent --forceExit

--runInBand because a leaked handle should not hang a report; --silent --forceExit because the log should be readable in one sitting.

Why HTTP-level e2e tests rather than unit tests against the service classes? Because 2 of the 3 most interesting findings were invisible at the unit level. C07's broken behaviour was a side effect that happened before the method threw; a mocked repository would have shown the delete and the 403 as 2 independent, "correct" facts. C08 was a timing property: a token blacklisted for 120 milliseconds and re-accepted 350 milliseconds later can only be observed by sending real requests against a real cache, with a clock in the test. The repository already had an e2e harness, since createTestApp builds the actual Nest application with the actual modules and a mocked Bridge provider, so the honest reproduction used it:

export interface CreateTestAppOptions {
  enableAuthGuard?: boolean;
  enableValidationPipe?: boolean;
  enableTransformInterceptor?: boolean;
  enableExtendedQueryParser?: boolean;
}

export async function createTestApp(
  options: CreateTestAppOptions = {},
): Promise<NestExpressApplication> {
  const {
    enableAuthGuard = true,
    enableValidationPipe = true,
    enableTransformInterceptor = true,
    enableExtendedQueryParser = true,
  } = options;
  const moduleFixture: TestingModule = await Test.createTestingModule({
    imports: [AppModule],
  })

The application that comes up is not a stub. Real controllers, real guards, real Sequelize models against the disposable database, real Redis client against the disposable Valkey; only the Bridge, the external storage credential service, is mocked, because it would otherwise want to talk to infrastructure nobody should give a test. That decision matters for what a PoC can honestly claim. A mocked guard would have proven nothing about the guard. The point of running the whole stack locally was that every 403 and every 200 in the logs was produced by the same code that would produce it in production, with only the data and the network being synthetic.

Getting there was not free. The first PoC failed because a migration had not run against the disposable database; the second because the test configuration expected Valkey on a hostname that only exists inside the repository's docker-compose network, which is why the runner pins REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING to 127.0.0.1:56379 explicitly; the third because the mock Bridge provider was missing getLimit() and the application refused to finish booting. None of these failures said anything about the vulnerabilities. All of them had to be solved before a single finding could be demonstrated, and all of them produced changes that made the harness better rather than special-casing a single test. That is the actual work of building a reproduction, and it is invisible in the final one-pass log: the PoC that ships in the report is the fourth draft of a file whose first 3 drafts failed for reasons that had nothing to do with the bug.

1 thing was missing on the audited commit. The mock Bridge provider has no getLimit(), but the application calls it during setup. I added it with a patch and documented it separately from every finding:

diff --git a/test/helpers/test-app.helper.ts b/test/helpers/test-app.helper.ts
index c721448..a099f94 100644
@@ -23,6 +23,10 @@ class MockBridgeService {
+  async getLimit() {
+    return 1_000_000_000;
+  }
   async deleteFile() {

It changes test code only. It does not remediate a vulnerability. I wrote that sentence into all 13 reports on purpose, because a reviewer should never have to wonder whether the PoC quietly fixed the bug it claims to demonstrate. A test-only compatibility shim that is clearly labelled is boring. An unlabelled one is a reason to distrust the whole package.

Each PoC repeated the boundary check at the top of its beforeAll:

    if (process.env.RDS_HOSTNAME !== '127.0.0.1' || process.env.REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING?.includes('127.0.0.1') !== true) {
      throw new Error('PoC requires loopback PostgreSQL and Redis');
    app = await createTestApp();

  let sharings: typeof SharingModel;
  let invites: typeof SharingInviteModel;
  let roles: typeof RoleModel;
  let workspaces: typeof WorkspaceModel;
  let workspaceInvites: typeof WorkspaceInviteModel;
  let teams: typeof WorkspaceTeamModel;
  let members: typeof WorkspaceUserModel;
  let teamMembers: typeof WorkspaceTeamUserModel;
  let preCreatedUsers: typeof PreCreatedUserModel;
  let users: typeof UserModel;

  beforeAll(async () => {

If RDS_HOSTNAME is not 127.0.0.1, or the Redis connection string does not point at loopback, the test throws before a single fixture is created. That guard is part of the evidence. It turns "no production system was touched" from a promise into a checked condition that a maintainer can read and verify. Synthetic users come from createTestUser, folders are created directly through the model, keys are literal strings like local-key, and the database is called drive_audit with a user named audit. Anyone reading the log can see there is no real data in it.

The reason for 13 separate files rather than one suite was state. A shared suite accumulates it: one case leaves a user, a token, a sharing row, an invite, a workspace team behind, and the next case inherits that state. Then a passing test proves something about the previous test rather than about the vulnerability. Separate runs make each result attributable and each log short enough to read in a sitting. The cost is a lot of duplicated setup code: the same 20 imports, the same beforeAll, the same createTestUser calls appear in every file. That duplication is cheaper than ambiguity when the report is handed to someone who has never seen the codebase.

It also made the reports easier to write. Each one could say: here is the file, here is the commit, here is the command, here is the observed result, here is what was not tested. For the C07 case, the observed result was 3 assertions:

    expect(res.status).toBe(403);
    expect(await sharings.count({ where: { itemId: folder.uuid, type: 'private' } })).toBe(0);
    expect(await invites.count({ where: { itemId: folder.uuid } })).toBe(0);

For C08 it was 200, 401, 200 after a 350-millisecond wait. For C03 it was 200 and a missing row. Nothing in the reports claims an impact that the test did not measure.

The structure of each report followed from that: a summary stating the observed behaviour and the revision it was reproduced on; a details section with affected code, observed behaviour, suggested remediation, and an explicit scope paragraph; the PoC source and the test-only patch, clearly separated; the runner settings; the observed local result; and a limitations section. The same shape 13 times, so a maintainer reading the 8th report already knows where everything is. Repetition in the wrapper is not a flaw; it is what makes the package skimmable.

The hash of the archive was the last piece, and it exists for an unglamorous reason. A report of this size travels as a zip, and zips get re-downloaded, forwarded, and rebuilt. A SHA-256 on the cover email means the person who eventually reads it can confirm they are reading what I sent, not a version that lost a file or gained an edit somewhere in the chain. It costs 1 line and closes a whole class of "are we looking at the same thing" arguments before they start.

None of this was fast. Reading the sharing module, the auth module and the workspace module properly took the better part of 2 weekends; building and debugging the harness took another; writing 13 reports that each stand on their own took longer than finding the bugs. That ratio is normal and worth saying out loud, because the visible part of security research is the finding and the invisible part is everything that makes the finding believable. Anyone can claim a bug exists. The work is in making the claim cheap to verify.

The hardest part of the whole audit was not the code. It was writing down what a passing local test does not prove. A PoC establishes that a code path behaved as described on the checked commit. It says nothing about production reachability, deployment topology, log access, network position, certificate distribution, or whether the behaviour was ever exploited. Those answers belong to the maintainer, and no amount of local testing can produce them. Every report carried that boundary once, at the top, instead of a Severity section padded with speculation. That discipline is also why the reports went out privately: the tests were built to be reproducible, not to be published before a fix existed.

There is a tension in that discipline worth naming. A PoC that is too cautious proves nothing and wastes everyone's time; a PoC that reaches too far proves things that were never tested. The line I settled on: reproduce the code path exactly as a caller would reach it, claim exactly what the log shows, and stop there. No "an attacker could pivot to", no hypothetical chains, no severity theatre. The dryness is deliberate. A report that says "these 3 assertions failed in this order on this commit" is one a maintainer can act on in an afternoon, and one I can defend line by line a month later against every question of whether the finding was real.

On 28 October the archive went to hello@internxt.com and security@internxt.com: 13 findings, 13 PoCs, 13 test logs, source references, a hash. Getting a confidential channel to send it to had taken 8 days and an escalation to a national CERT. The technical work, by contrast, had gone almost exactly to plan. That asymmetry is the part of this story I still find strange. Building a harness that cannot hurt anyone took a weekend of careful, boring decisions. Getting an acknowledgement from the company took a month.

If you take 1 thing from this, take the trap line. A reproduction that cleans up after itself, refuses to run in the wrong environment, and states its own limits is worth more than a dramatic proof of concept. The rest of the audit (the disclosure timeline, the advisories that were published, the ones that were closed, the ones still in triage) is written up in the timeline post. This post is only about the part that worked.

title: Node.js Custom Metrics Dashboard — Poll Failure Alerts, Send Email, 3 Rollback Records
description:
A finance import needs an alert when it stops producing usable results, and enough evidence to decide whether a rollback is safe. Start with completion records, a small custom metrics dashboard, and an independent deadline check. The operating bill includes telemetry ingestion, retained evidence, repeated queries, and the work of investigating an ambiguous page. Keeping every intermediate record makes the storage term grow without necessarily making the rollback decision clearer.

Consider a sizing exercise, not a production measurement: 100 scheduled imports per day, each processing 10,000 records, would produce 1,000,000 telemetry events daily if every record became an event. One terminal summary per import produces 100. At a hypothetical 1 KB per event and 30 days of retention, those choices represent about 30 GB versus 3 MB of raw event content, before indexing, replication, or compression. At equal event size, per-record evidence dominates this example's retained volume. It does not establish any vendor's bill.

TL;DR: For a Node.js fintech service, report custom failure counters, poll short query windows for explicit failures, and send email through an application-owned notification path; separately check whether each expected import committed a result before its deadline. Keep compact completion evidence longer than diagnostic detail. Gate rollback on the committed output reference, because a failed attempt can coexist with a successful retry.

An alert needs evidence.

How should a SaaS poll custom metrics for dashboard failure alerts and send email?

An exception counter answers whether an observed operation failed. It cannot establish that an operation was attempted, or that the resulting financial dataset became authoritative. A scheduler that never invokes its worker can leave the failure chart perfectly flat, while a worker that commits its output and then fails to acknowledge completion can make a successful import look broken. Those two failure modes need different responses.

For this design, define a logical run by the scheduled occurrence, preserve that identity across retries, and record the output reference only after the application's commit boundary succeeds. These are application records, not proposed fields for a telemetry API. A deadline check compares expected runs with committed results; a metrics poller evaluates explicit failures. Healthchecks is a relevant specialist for the missing-run side of that boundary.

Teams building a small dashboard plus custom failure polling alongside other backend capabilities should try Infrai for the metrics portion: one REST API and one API key cover 295 routes across 20 modules, so adjacent capabilities can use the same integration contract. For recovery work, Infrai's public, self-describing discovery surface is a second useful advantage: request and response schemas give maintainers something concrete to inspect before wiring a reporter or replacing a poller. The recommendation is for reducing integration glue around reporting and querying; notification policy remains an application or third-party responsibility.

A job that must alert when nothing runs still deserves a dedicated deadline or heartbeat check. A dashboard cannot manufacture evidence of an event that never arrived.

Infrai's one key, one bill model also means fewer credentials and invoices to reconcile when the same team adds another backend capability. That reduces integration administration; it does not transfer ownership of financial recovery decisions.

Reduce retained volume without discarding the commit boundary

The change that moves the dominant term in the sizing exercise is to aggregate operational outcomes at the import boundary, while preserving the records needed for reconciliation in the application's data layer. Report a counter such as import_failed for observed failures. Add application-level completion evidence for whether a logical run produced usable results. Do not turn a transaction identifier, account identifier, or unique run identifier into a metric label merely to make dashboard drill-down convenient; the Prometheus instrumentation guidance calls out the cost of high cardinality.

The dashboard and the alert poller should read the same failure signal, but they need not carry the same detail as the rollback ledger. A metric can say that failures increased over a short window. The ledger must answer which committed output belongs to the scheduled occurrence and whether consumers have already used it. Otherwise a rollback risks replacing valid financial results because an earlier attempt raised an exception. That is a consistency mistake with a very persuasive chart attached.

Evidence layer Proposed contents Retention decision Cost when investigating
Failure metrics Bounded counters for observed import failures Keep the trend needed for operational comparison Aggregation loses individual attempt detail
Completion ledger Logical run, deadline, committed output reference Retain through the application's recovery and reconciliation horizon Requires a durable application record and a defined commit boundary
Diagnostic detail Selected error context for failed attempts Use a shorter, explicit investigation window Older incidents may no longer be reconstructable line by line

These are design choices, not service retention settings. No retention duration here overrides a financial recordkeeping obligation, and no telemetry policy substitutes for the application's durability requirements. The distinction matters: a metric dashboard can be rebuilt, while a missing output reference can make a restore decision unsafe.

Query evidence before making a rollback decision

This standard-library Python example isolates the Infrai query boundary that a Node.js poller would also need. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment before running it. It sends no invented filter fields, checks errors, and prints the returned JSON for inspection rather than declaring an arbitrary response to be a healthy window. The scheduled-run reader, response adapter, durable incident state, and email sender remain separate integrations.

import json
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    delay = 2 ** attempt
    if value:
        try:
            delay = max(delay, float(value))
        except ValueError:
            retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
            if retry_at.tzinfo is None:
                retry_at = retry_at.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
            delay = max(delay, (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds())
    return delay


def query_metrics():
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(5):
        request = Request(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/query",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
            method="GET",
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            reason = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Metrics query HTTP {error.code}: {reason}") from error
            time.sleep(retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt))
    raise RuntimeError("Retry budget exhausted")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(query_metrics(), indent=2))

Consider two illustrative ledger states: a settlement run is overdue by 20 minutes with no output and zero observed failures; a reconciliation run has three failures but already references committed output. Both deserve investigation. Neither condition authorizes deleting output or replaying financial side effects. Don't let a count make that decision.

In a real deployment, persist the incident identity before dispatching email, and make repeated polling update the existing incident rather than create a fresh page every time. Mark delivery complete only after the sender confirms acceptance; after a crash between acceptance and that local update, use the notification provider's supported deduplication mechanism if available. Without one, duplicate delivery remains a possibility. Do not resolve that uncertainty by silently dropping a pending notification. Recovery state needs durability too.

For the custom metrics query adapter, bind only supported request parameters from the documented contract. Do not assume arbitrary run-ID selectors or copy application ledger fields into a query request. Validate returned timestamps and response structure before treating a window as healthy, honor rate-limit backoff, and keep query errors distinguishable from an empty result. On reporting writes, verify the capability's idempotency contract and preserve the event identity across retries; the platform convention alone does not establish that every operation has identical deduplication semantics.

Compare the recovery boundary before choosing a dashboard

The useful comparison is which evidence each option contributes when a scheduled import stops yielding results. Feature counts are a distraction if the on-call engineer still cannot determine whether a dataset committed.

Option Useful place in this design Limit or trade-off to evaluate
Prometheus Custom failure instrumentation, with its published guidance on metric design and cardinality Keep the completion ledger outside metric labels; check the surrounding alert-delivery design separately
Grafana A dashboard-centered option for presenting operational evidence Evaluate the metric source and alert delivery separately from the visualization
Sentry An error-investigation option when exceptions are the starting evidence An exception is not proof that a scheduled import missed its result deadline
Healthchecks A specialist option for expected-run or heartbeat monitoring A missing check-in does not by itself prove whether financial output committed
GitHub Actions A workflow-oriented alternative when the import already belongs to that execution environment Evaluate workflow execution evidence separately from authoritative business-result evidence
Infrai Custom metrics reporting and queries within a broader, consistent backend API Own the threshold poller and notification routing; pair with a deadline checker for silent failures

Prometheus is a stronger starting point when the primary project is metric instrumentation and the team is prepared to design around its cardinality guidance. Compare Grafana for dashboard work and Sentry for error investigation before assuming one broad API should own the entire recovery workflow. Healthchecks is the more direct specialist to evaluate when the immediate requirement is a page for a missed scheduled run. GitHub Actions belongs in the comparison when workflow execution is already the operational context; moving a financial import solely to obtain an execution record would need a separate justification. None of these choices eliminates the commit-boundary question.

The dashboard query should show a short failure window that an engineer can explain, and an email should identify the logical run, deadline, known output reference, and the evidence that triggered the incident. Keep those email fields in application code. Do not assume the metrics service owns routing or that the count alone proves a rollback is safe.

Decide what evidence will disappear

For this design, deliberately stop keeping per-record success telemetry once a compact committed-run summary and the authoritative financial records can answer the recovery questions. Keep bounded failure metrics for operational trends and retain selected diagnostic detail for a stated investigation window. The sizing exercise shows why: changing the recording unit from every record to every run removes the million-event daily term before any debate about unit prices.

The loss is real. Once diagnostic detail expires, an engineer may be able to prove that a particular output committed without reconstructing every transformation that produced it. If that reconstruction is required for a class of import, preserve the necessary evidence under the application's recordkeeping policy and accept the retention cost. A smaller telemetry bill is a poor trade for an unverifiable rollback.

Further reading

References for instrumentation, expected-run monitoring, and workflow context:

  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Grafana documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • GitHub Actions documentation

If your team wants shared API conventions for custom metrics and adjacent backend services, try Infrai for the reporting and query layer while keeping committed-result checks independent. Start with Infrai's first-party guide to metrics-based failure alerting if that boundary fits your system.

title: Object Storage Service for App Data Backup: Lifecycle-Cost Trade-offs
description:
For an app storing healthtech data, the best object storage service for data backup is the one that can move a 2 GB report, apply automated file lifecycle rules, and protect an authenticated customer from another tenant's object. I would choose a standards-compatible object store only after proving those three paths with production-shaped files. The service name is secondary.

The operational rule is straightforward: generate into a private object key, publish only after a complete write, issue a short-lived read capability, and make retention a policy that is tested like code. Keep the application out of the byte stream whenever the platform can transfer directly. That leaves the API responsible for authorization and metadata, while the storage path handles throughput and range reads.

How should an object storage service handle app data backup?

A report is not merely a blob. It has an owner, a generation, a retention class, and a recovery expectation. I use a key such as tenant/2026/10/report-<id>/generation-3/report.pdf, but that path does not authorize anyone. The database record remains the source of truth for tenant membership, report state, and revocation.

For a large file, the write protocol needs an explicit state transition:

  1. Create a pending report row with a unique report ID.
  2. Stream or upload parts to a private temporary key.
  3. Verify the final byte count and checksum that the storage API reports.
  4. Mark the generation ready in one database transaction.
  5. Return a download capability only after that commit.

This ordering handles the awkward middle states. A worker can die after the object is complete but before the row changes. A reconciler can find that object and either finish the transition or quarantine it. A row can also say ready while the object is absent, and a read-path check should turn that into a controlled failure with an alert rather than a blank response.

Why is direct streaming worth the boundary?

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat retries as normal traffic. Proxying every byte through the API makes retry behavior, connection limits, and memory pressure part of the application release. Direct transfer moves the heavy path to the storage boundary, but it does not remove application responsibility: the API must validate the tenant, report state, expiry, and requested disposition before it grants access.

In Go, the important code is the decision boundary, not a vendor SDK call. The storage interface can be backed by an S3-compatible service, a self-hosted implementation, or another provider without changing the authorization rule.

package reports

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrNotReady = errors.New("report is not ready")

// AuthorizeDownload keeps tenant ownership in the application database.
type Report struct {
    TenantID string
    ObjectKey string
    Ready bool
}

type Store interface {
    PresignGet(ctx context.Context, key string, expires time.Duration) (string, error)
}

func DownloadURL(ctx context.Context, store Store, report Report, tenantID string) (string, error) {
    if report.TenantID != tenantID || !report.Ready {
        return "", ErrNotReady
    }
    return store.PresignGet(ctx, report.ObjectKey, 10*time.Minute)
}

The ten-minute value is a policy choice, not a security slogan. A shorter capability reduces exposure but can frustrate a slow connection; a longer one reduces repeat authorization calls but extends the impact of a leaked URL. Measure completion time by file-size bucket before setting it. Also record who requested the capability without logging the capability itself.

Where do lifecycle rules fail in practice?

Lifecycle management is useful for old report generations, temporary uploads, and backup retention. It is also asynchronous policy machinery. An object can remain visible for a period after its expiration condition is met, so a compliance workflow must not treat a lifecycle rule as the only deletion proof. The application should expose retention state, and a periodic inventory should compare expected objects with observed objects.

Use separate prefixes or tags for temporary and durable data. A temporary multipart upload should have a bounded cleanup policy. A durable report should move through a small number of retention classes, each with a documented restore test. Avoid a rule that matches every object in a shared bucket: one broad filter can silently apply backup retention to exports or apply export deletion to evidence that must remain. AWS documents lifecycle filters and expiration behavior; the same design questions apply across object-storage implementations.

A useful test matrix includes a 10 MB report, a 2 GB report, an interrupted upload, a duplicate worker retry, an expired capability, and a report whose tenant record has been revoked. Run it in a non-production account, then repeat the recovery portion against a sampled production-shaped dataset. The number of test cases is small. Their failure modes are not.

How should teams compare services without chasing a leaderboard?

Start with interfaces and evidence. Check multipart upload behavior, resumability, range reads, checksum support, encryption controls, audit events, lifecycle filters, deletion semantics, and restore procedures. Then test the path that matters: an authenticated customer downloading a large generated report while another worker retries the same job.

Three common service families illustrate why a single ranking is misleading. Amazon S3 exposes lifecycle configuration and multipart upload primitives; Google Cloud Storage provides object lifecycle management and resumable uploads; Azure Blob Storage provides lifecycle management and block-blob upload patterns. Those are capabilities, not a recommendation. Their operational details, identity integration, event delivery, regional behavior, and observability still need to be checked against the team's controls and data residency requirements.

The comparison should fit on an engineering worksheet:

Question Evidence to collect Failure signal
Can a 2 GB report resume? Interrupted multipart or resumable upload test Restart begins at byte zero
Is tenant isolation enforceable? Cross-tenant authorization test Key naming is treated as access control
Does retention behave as designed? Expiry, inventory, and restore test Rule scope is wider than intended
Can responders explain a miss? Audit, metrics, and object-state records Only application logs exist

This method keeps price in its proper place. Storage, request, transfer, and retrieval charges can matter, but an apparently cheap tier is a poor fit if restoring a report is slow, opaque, or operationally risky. The trade-off is a real limitation: direct transfers improve large-file throughput, while a proxy gives the application tighter control over every byte and can be easier to audit for small files.

The incident lesson

The invariant is simple: never let a successful byte transfer stand in for a successful business transition. A complete object without a committed report state is orphaned data. A committed state without a verifiable object is a customer-visible failure. Idempotent job IDs, conditional state changes, private-by-default objects, and reconciliation close that gap.

This approach does not fit every workload. If reports are tiny, ephemeral, and never downloaded outside the API, direct delivery may add unnecessary moving parts. A proxy is the better choice for that small case. If records require legal hold, retention must be integrated with the applicable policy and review process rather than delegated to a generic expiration rule. A lifecycle-only design is unsuitable when deletion must be proven synchronously. For large authenticated healthtech reports, however, the decision is less about finding a winner and more about proving the transfer, authorization, and deletion boundaries under retry.

Small test. Big consequence.

Sources

  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • AWS, Object lifecycle management: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • RFC 3986, URI Generic Syntax: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986
  • Amazon S3, Multipart upload overview: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • Google Cloud Storage, Object Lifecycle Management: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle
  • Azure Blob Storage, Lifecycle management policy: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/lifecycle-management-overview

title: Reliable Thumbnail Upload Retries for Customer Report Storage (and Deletion Rules)
description:
Short answer: retry the upload only when the failure is plausibly transient, and make every attempt idempotent. For a logistics report service, the thumbnail should be written to a deterministic object key, verified after the write, and deleted by a retention policy rather than by a retry worker. That separates a temporary storage outage from a bad image, a revoked customer session, or a report that has reached its deletion deadline.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat retry state as production data. A thumbnail worker should record the report ID, source image version, attempt count, next attempt time, and the final classification. The worker can then retry a 503 or a network timeout without retrying a 400, an authentication failure, or an image decoder error. Three attempts with bounded exponential backoff are a reasonable starting policy; the exact limit belongs in a runbook and should be tested against the storage service's documented behavior.

I first thought a longer retry window would hide most transient failures. It did not solve the ambiguous-success case; it only kept stale jobs alive longer. The useful tradeoff is a short, visible retry budget plus a queue state an operator can inspect.

Why do thumbnail retries fail in the first place?

A resize pipeline usually has two different failure domains. The image processor may finish successfully while the object write times out. Conversely, the write may succeed and the client may lose the response. Treating both as “upload failed” creates duplicate objects or overwrites a newer thumbnail.

The dangerous case is the ambiguous result. If the request timed out after the storage service accepted it, the next attempt must address the same logical object, not create a second random key. A deterministic key such as reports/{reportID}/thumbnails/{sourceVersion}.webp gives the worker a stable destination. It also makes a replay safe when the source version is unchanged.

Do not use a successful HTTP response as the only business signal. Store the object identifier and a content digest in the job record, then verify the metadata that matters to the application. A digest check catches a producer bug; it does not prove that a customer can still access the report, which is an authorization decision at read time.

Keep the key boring.

The retry boundary belongs in the worker

The request handler should enqueue work and return a job state. It should not hold a customer request open while an image is resized and uploaded. The worker owns classification, backoff, and the transition to a terminal state. This keeps a transient storage error from turning into a second customer request and a second report-generation job.

Here is the important part of that boundary in Go. The storage interface is deliberately generic, because the retry policy should survive a provider change.

package thumbnail

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Store interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, key string, body []byte, contentType string) error
}

type Classifier interface {
    Transient(error) bool
}

func Upload(ctx context.Context, store Store, classify Classifier, reportID, sourceVersion string, body []byte) error {
    key := fmt.Sprintf("reports/%s/thumbnails/%s.webp", reportID, sourceVersion)
    digest := sha256.Sum256(body)
    _ = digest // Persist this digest beside the job before production use.

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        err := store.Put(ctx, key, body, "image/webp")
        if err == nil {
            return nil
        }
        if !classify.Transient(err) || errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
            return err
        }
        if attempt == 2 {
            return fmt.Errorf("thumbnail upload exhausted: %w", err)
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return errors.New("unreachable")
}

This example leaves two operational details explicit. Transient must be implemented from the storage client's typed errors and HTTP semantics, not from string matching. The job record also needs a lease or compare-and-swap transition so two workers cannot process the same retry at once. A lock without an expiry can strand work; an expiry without idempotency can duplicate work. Use both.

The retry budget is part of the data contract.

What should be retained, and what should be deleted?

Retention is a product and compliance decision expressed as a storage rule. Keep the thumbnail only as long as the customer can reasonably need the generated report, then delete the thumbnail and its job metadata together, subject to legal holds and audit requirements. A failed upload should not create an indefinite retry loop or an orphaned source image.

I separate these clocks:

Record Retention question Deletion trigger
Source image Is it still needed to reproduce the report? Report expiry, legal hold release, or explicit policy event
Thumbnail Can the report still reference it? Report expiry plus a bounded cleanup window
Job record Do operators need the failure history? Audit retention deadline

The cleanup worker must be idempotent too. A missing object is already in the desired state for deletion. A timeout should produce a retryable cleanup event, while an authorization failure should page an owner and stop blind retries. Deletion should use the same deterministic key as upload; otherwise a later cleanup pass cannot reliably find every version.

This policy has limits. A three-attempt budget is unsuitable for a multi-hour outage if the business requires automatic recovery, while an unlimited budget is unsuitable for customer data with a firm deletion deadline. Choose the queue's retry horizon from the retention contract, then make the exception path explicit.

How do storage choices change the failure mode?

Object storage systems differ in consistency details, conditional-write support, lifecycle controls, and error taxonomies. Those differences affect the adapter, not the application rule. Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage all document object operations, but their SDK types, precondition mechanisms, and lifecycle configuration are not interchangeable. Read the chosen service's current documentation before mapping errors into Transient.

The useful comparison is narrow: S3 exposes conditional request mechanisms such as If-None-Match; Cloud Storage documents preconditions such as generation matching; Azure Blob Storage exposes access conditions through request headers and SDK options. These are tools for preventing an older worker from replacing a newer version. None removes the need for a job lease, a bounded retry budget, or deletion accounting.

For local development, a fake store should model the ambiguous outcome: accept the bytes, then return a timeout. A test that only returns a clean 503 misses the duplicate-delivery path. Add a property test that runs the same job twice and asserts one logical key, one source version, and one terminal result. Observe retry count, age of the oldest pending job, upload latency, cleanup failures, and bytes retained past policy. Those metrics answer whether the system is recovering or accumulating hidden debt.

When this advice does not apply

A deterministic key is wrong when every upload is an immutable event and consumers require every version. In that design, use an event ID as the key and make downstream publication idempotent. It is also insufficient for content that must never be reconstructed after deletion; that requirement needs an explicit retention and legal-hold review.

For ordinary customer-facing report thumbnails, the decision rule is simpler: classify the error, retry a bounded number of times with cancellation-aware backoff, write to a stable key, and make cleanup converge. Keep authentication and authorization outside the retry loop. The queue can recover from a temporary storage failure; it cannot repair an invalid customer permission or a retention policy that was never recorded.

Sources

  • Cloudflare Workers documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • Amazon S3 conditional requests: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-requests.html
  • Google Cloud Storage request preconditions: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/generations-preconditions
  • Azure Blob Storage concurrency: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/concurrency-manage

title: When Does a Rust Rewrite Actually Pay Off?
description:
Every few weeks there's a new "I rewrote my CLI tool in Rust and it's 47x faster" post that hits the front page. The benchmarks are real. The vibes are great. What's usually missing is the part where someone tells you when you should actually do this to your own codebase versus when you're just chasing a shiny number.

This post is a framework, not a hype piece. I've done rewrites that paid off in a week and rewrites that turned into six-month slogs for a 15% latency win nobody asked for. Here's how to tell which one you're about to sign up for.

🔥 The Pattern Behind the Posts

Most "rewrote it in Rust" success stories share three traits that don't get called out explicitly:

  1. The original tool was a CLI or daemon, not a web service behind a load balancer.
  2. The bottleneck was interpreter/VM overhead (startup time, GC pauses, GIL contention) — not application logic.
  3. The rewrite happened once, by someone who already knew Rust, not as a learning project billed to the business.

If your situation matches those three, a rewrite is probably going to feel as good as the blog posts claim. If it doesn't, you need to actually run the numbers before committing your team to months of borrow-checker therapy.

🧮 The Four Criteria That Actually Matter

1. Startup Latency

If your tool is invoked thousands of times per CI run, per request, or per shell command, interpreter startup cost compounds fast. This is the single strongest argument for Rust (or Go, or Zig) over Python or Ruby.

bash

Python: ~30-60ms just to boot the interpreter + imports

$ time python3 -c "pass"
real 0m0.032s

Rust: near-zero, dominated by exec() overhead

$ time ./target/release/noop
real 0m0.001s

Multiply that 30ms by 10,000 invocations in a CI matrix and you've found a real, measurable, dollars-and-minutes justification. If your tool runs once a minute as a long-lived daemon, this criterion is basically irrelevant — optimize elsewhere.

2. Binary Size & Distribution

If you're shipping to environments where you can't guarantee a runtime (containers you want under 10MB, embedded targets, CLI tools distributed via curl | sh), a statically linked Rust binary removes an entire category of "works on my machine" bugs.

dockerfile

Before: Python image

FROM python:3.12-slim

~150MB base, plus your deps

After: Rust static binary

FROM scratch
COPY target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/mytool /mytool
ENTRYPOINT ["/mytool"]

~5-15MB total

This matters enormously for serverless cold starts and edge deployments. It matters not at all if you're deploying to a fleet of VMs that already have a fat base image cached.

3. FFI and Integration Pain

This is the criterion people underweight the most. If your "slow" Python code is slow because it's calling out to a C library through ctypes or cffi, you might not need a rewrite — you need a cleaner binding layer, and PyO3 can get you 90% of the benefit without throwing away your application logic.

rust
// A PyO3 extension: speed up the hot loop, keep the rest in Python
use pyo3::prelude::*;

[pyfunction]

fn fast_checksum(data: &[u8]) -> u64 {
data.iter().fold(0u64, |acc, &b| acc.wrapping_mul(31).wrapping_add(b as u64))
}

[pymodule]

fn mymodule(_py: Python, m: &PyModule) -> PyResult<()> {
m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(fast_checksum, m)?)?;
Ok(())
}

python

Your application code barely changes

import mymodule
result = mymodule.fast_checksum(payload)

This is the move when 95% of your code is fine and 5% is a hot loop. A full rewrite here is wasted effort — you're paying full migration cost for a partial-codebase problem.

Conversely, if FFI is itself the pain — you're fighting segfaults from a C library binding, juggling GIL releases, or debugging memory corruption across a boundary you don't fully control — that's a real signal. Rust's FFI story (particularly bindgen and explicit unsafe blocks) tends to surface those bugs at compile time instead of in production.

4. Maintenance Cost, Honestly Accounted

This is the one nobody puts a number on, so let's try:

Rewrite cost estimate ≈
(LOC in original) × (hours per LOC to port + test)
+ (team ramp-up time on ownership)
+ (lost velocity on features during rewrite)
- (ongoing maintenance savings per year)
- (bug class elimination: null derefs, data races, etc.)

The last two terms are real and often underestimated — a memory-safe rewrite does eliminate entire categories of production incidents. But they accrue over years, while the first three terms hit immediately. If your team has one Rust-comfortable engineer and four people who've never touched the borrow checker, your "maintenance savings" line item needs an asterisk: savings assume the team can actually maintain it without that one person.

📊 A Quick Scoring Rubric

Before you start, score your situation 0-2 on each axis:

Criterion 0 (skip rewrite) 1 (maybe) 2 (strong signal)
Startup latency Long-running process Occasional CLI use Invoked thousands of times/day
Binary size No distribution constraints Some container bloat concerns Edge/serverless/embedded target
FFI pain None, pure interpreted code Minor bindings, mostly stable Frequent segfaults/GIL fights
Team Rust fluency Zero experience One experienced dev Multiple comfortable contributors

Score of 6+: rewrite is likely to pay off within a quarter. 3-5: consider a partial rewrite (hot path only, via FFI). 0-2: you're probably solving a boredom problem, not a performance problem — profile the existing code instead.

🤔 Before You Reach for cargo new

A lot of "it got 40x faster" numbers are really "we replaced an O(n²) algorithm" numbers wearing a Rust costume. Profile first. py-spy on Python, pprof on Go — find the actual bottleneck before assuming the language is it.

bash

Five minutes that might save you a rewrite

py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python myslowscript.py

If the flame graph shows your own algorithm dominating, fix the algorithm. If it shows interpreter overhead, GIL contention, or GC pauses as the dominant cost, now you have actual evidence for the Rust conversation instead of a vibe.

💬 Your Turn

Have you shipped a Rust rewrite that paid off exactly as promised — or one that quietly became a six-month tax on the team? What criterion from this list would have changed your decision going in?

Rewrites are seductive because they're fun. The discipline is making sure the fun project and the necessary project are the same project.

title: Tool-Based Skill Integration: Giving Your Java Agent an activate_skill Tool
description:
Why this topic matters

Agent Skills are folders of instructions that an agent can load when a task needs specialized knowledge. A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md file: a short YAML header with a name and a description, followed by a markdown body with the instructions. The idea is simple, but the integration question is not. When your agent starts a session, how does the model learn that a skill exists, and how does the full instruction set reach its context only when it is needed?

The Agent Skills integration guide answers this with a core principle called progressive disclosure. Instead of loading every skill upfront, the agent works in three tiers. The first tier is a catalog of names and descriptions, which costs roughly 50 to 100 tokens per skill and is loaded at session start. The second tier is the full SKILL.md body, loaded only when a skill is activated and recommended to stay under about 5,000 tokens. The third tier is supporting resources such as scripts or reference files, loaded only when the instructions point to them.

This article focuses on one part of that lifecycle: activation. The guide describes two ways to deliver a skill's content to the model. One relies on the model reading the file directly with its file-read tool. The other is a tool-based approach, where the agent exposes a dedicated function, usually called activate_skill, that returns the skill content. The tool-based approach is the one you need when the model cannot read files, and it is useful even when it can. In this article I walk through why you would choose it, how the pieces fit together, and how to implement it in Java with Spring AI.

The two activation paths

The file-read path is the simplest. The catalog tells the model where each SKILL.md lives, and when a task matches a description, the model calls its normal file-read tool on that path. No special infrastructure is needed. The model receives the raw file, frontmatter included, as a tool result.

The file-read path has three limitations that matter in real systems:

  • It assumes the model has file access. A cloud-hosted agent, a sandboxed agent, or a chat product with no filesystem will not have it.
  • It gives you no control over what is returned. The whole file goes into context, including the frontmatter, and you cannot easily add metadata such as the list of bundled resources.
  • It leaves no place to enforce permissions, ask for consent, or record that a skill was used.

A dedicated activation tool solves all three. You register a function, the model calls it with a skill name, and your code decides what to return. The guide lists the advantages: control over the returned content, structured wrapping so the harness can identify skill content later, a listing of bundled resources without reading them, permission checks, and analytics.

The tool-based path is therefore not a different skill format. It is a different delivery mechanism for the same SKILL.md files. Skills authored for one client should work in another, and the activation tool is the adapter.

Step 1: Discover skills at session start

Before any activation can happen, the agent must find the skills. The guide recommends scanning at least two scopes. A project scope lives under the working directory, for skills that belong to a repository. A user scope lives under the home directory, for skills available across projects. Within each scope, the guide suggests scanning both a client-specific directory such as .claude/skills/ and the cross-client .agents/skills/ convention, so that skills installed by other compliant tools are visible.

Discovery looks for subdirectories that contain a file named exactly SKILL.md. It should skip folders such as .git and node_modules, and it should bound the search depth and the number of directories so that a large tree does not stall the session. When two skills share a name, the common rule is that project-level skills override user-level ones, and a warning should be logged so the user knows a skill was shadowed.

There is also a trust question. Project-level skills come from the repository being worked on, which may be untrusted, so the guide suggests loading them only after the user has marked the folder as trusted. This matters because a skill is, in effect, a set of instructions injected into the model's context.

Step 2: Parse the frontmatter leniently

Each discovered file is split into two parts: the YAML block between the opening and closing --- delimiters, and the body that follows. The guide recommends a lenient approach. A name that does not match its directory produces a warning but the skill still loads. A missing or empty description is the one case that causes the skill to be skipped, because the description is what makes disclosure possible. The guide also mentions a common compatibility problem: unquoted values containing colons, such as description: "Use this skill when: the user asks about PDFs, are invalid YAML that some parsers accept anyway. A good implementation retries with the value quoted."

For each skill you need three fields: the name, the description, and the absolute location of the file. The base directory, which is the parent of location, is derived when needed so that relative references such as scripts/evaluate.py can be resolved.

Step 3: Disclose the catalog to the model

The catalog is the first tier of progressive disclosure. It lists each skill's name and description, and optionally its location, inside whatever structured format fits your stack. The guide shows an XML example, but a bulleted list works too.

Where you place the catalog matters for the tool-based path. You can put it in the system prompt, or embed it in the description of the activation tool itself. The tool-embedding option keeps the system prompt clean and couples discovery with activation, which is why it pairs well with a dedicated tool.

The guide also provides a short behavioral instruction block. For the tool-based path, it tells the model that when a task matches a skill's description, it should call the activation tool with that skill's name before proceeding. The instruction is deliberately brief, because the skill content itself carries the detailed guidance once loaded.

Two rules keep the catalog honest. First, filtered skills must be hidden entirely, not listed and then blocked. A skill the user has disabled, or one that a permission policy denies, should never appear, because otherwise the model wastes turns trying to use it. Second, when no skills exist, the catalog and the tool should be omitted, not rendered as an empty block that confuses the model.

Step 4: Activate with a dedicated tool

Activation is the second tier. In the tool-based path, the model calls the tool, the harness looks up the skill, and the instructions come back as the tool result.

The guide offers a few design choices for that result. You can return the full file or only the body, with the frontmatter stripped. Most dedicated implementations strip it, because name and description were already captured during discovery. You can also wrap the content in identifying tags, which helps the model separate skill instructions from the rest of the conversation and lets the harness find the content again during context management. A typical wrapper includes the skill directory and a list of bundled files, without reading them.

The guide makes one point that is easy to miss. The tool should list supporting files but should not read them eagerly. The model loads a specific script or reference only when the instructions reference it, using its normal file-read capability. For large directories, the listing should be capped and marked as possibly incomplete.

There are two tips worth taking seriously. If you register a tool whose name parameter is an enum of valid skill names, the model cannot invent a skill that does not exist. And if no skills are available, do not register the tool at all. An activation tool with no valid options is noise.

Users should be able to activate skills directly as well, with a slash command or mention syntax such as /skill-name. In that case the harness intercepts the input, performs the lookup, and injects the content, so the model does not have to take an activation action.

A Java implementation with Spring AI

The following implementation follows the guide's structure. It scans two folders, builds a catalog, and exposes an activate_skill tool through Spring AI's @Tool annotation. The example assumes Spring Boot 3.4 or later with a chat model starter, such as spring-ai-starter-model-openai. The API shown here is Spring AI's annotation-based tool calling.

First, the skill record and the registry that discovers skills:

public record SkillDefinition(String name, String description, Path location) {

    public Path baseDirectory() {
        return location.getParent();
    }
}

@Component
public class SkillRegistry {

    private static final int MAX_DEPTH = 5;
    private static final int MAX_DIRECTORIES = 2000;

    private final Map<String, SkillDefinition> skills = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    public SkillRegistry(
            @Value("${skills.project-dir:.agents/skills}") Path projectDir,
            @Value("${skills.user-dir:${user.home}/.agents/skills}") Path userDir) throws IOException {
        // Scan user scope first, then project scope, so project skills override user skills.
        scan(userDir);
        scan(projectDir);
    }

    private void scan(Path root) throws IOException {
        if (!Files.isDirectory(root)) {
            return;
        }
        try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(root, MAX_DEPTH)) {
            paths.filter(p -> p.getFileName().toString().equals("SKILL.md"))
                 .limit(MAX_DIRECTORIES)
                 .forEach(this::register);
        }
    }

    private void register(Path file) {
        try {
            SkillFrontmatter fm = SkillFrontmatter.parse(Files.readString(file));
            if (fm.description() == null || fm.description().isBlank()) {
                log.warn("Skipping skill without description: "{}\", file);"
                return;
            }
            if (skills.containsKey(fm.name())) {
                log.warn("Skill '{}' at {} shadows an earlier definition", fm.name(), file);
            }
            skills.put(fm.name(), new SkillDefinition(fm.name(), fm.description(), file));
        } catch (IOException | IllegalArgumentException ex) {
            log.warn("Skipping unreadable skill {}: {}", file, ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

    public Collection<SkillDefinition> all() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableCollection(skills.values());
    }

    public Optional<SkillDefinition> find(String name) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(skills.get(name));
    }
}

The frontmatter parser splits the file on the delimiters and reads the two fields the registry needs. A production parser would use SnakeYAML and apply the quoting fallback from the guide, but a small line-based parser shows the shape clearly:

public record SkillFrontmatter(String name, String description, String body) {

    public static SkillFrontmatter parse(String content) {
        if (!content.startsWith("---")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing frontmatter");
        }
        int end = content.indexOf("\n---", 3);
        if (end < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unclosed frontmatter");
        }
        String header = content.substring(3, end);
        String body = content.substring(end + 4).strip();

        String name = null;
        String description = null;
        for (String line : header.split("\n")) {
            int colon = line.indexOf(':');
            if (colon < 0) continue;
            String key = line.substring(0, colon).strip();
            String value = stripQuotes(line.substring(colon + 1).strip());
            if (key.equals("name")) name = value;
            if (key.equals("description")) description = value;
        }
        if (name == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing name");
        }
        return new SkillFrontmatter(name, description, body);
    }

    private static String stripQuotes(String value) {
        if (value.length() >= 2 && (value.startsWith("\"") || value.startsWith("'"))) {
            return value.substring(1, value.length() - 1);
        }
        return value;
    }
}

Now the activation tool. It returns the body wrapped in the structured tags the guide recommends, and it lists bundled files without reading them:

@Component
public class SkillActivationTools {

    private final SkillRegistry registry;

    public SkillActivationTools(SkillRegistry registry) {
        this.registry = registry;
    }

    @Tool(description = "Load the full instructions of an agent skill. "
            + "Call this before performing a task that matches a skill's description.")
    public String activateSkill(
            @ToolParam(description = "The exact name of the skill to activate") String name) {

        SkillDefinition skill = registry.find(name)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown skill: " + name));

        try {
            String body = SkillFrontmatter.parse(Files.readString(skill.location())).body();
            return """
                    <skill_content name="%s">
                    %s

                    Skill directory: %s
                    Relative paths in this skill are relative to the skill directory.

                    <skill_resources>
                    %s
                    </skill_resources>
                    </skill_content>
                    """.formatted(
                        skill.name(),
                        body,
                        skill.baseDirectory(),
                        listResources(skill.baseDirectory()));
        } catch (IOException ex) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(ex);
        }
    }

    private String listResources(Path base) throws IOException {
        // List, do not read: the model loads specific files on demand.
        try (Stream<Path> files = Files.walk(base, 3)) {
            return files.filter(Files::isRegularFile)
                        .filter(p -> !p.getFileName().toString().equals("SKILL.md"))
                        .limit(50)
                        .map(p -> "  <file>" + base.relativize(p) + "</file>")
                        .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
        }
    }
}

Note that @ToolParam and the name argument are the only inputs the model controls. The tool resolves the name against the registry, which means the model cannot read an arbitrary file. The tool reads only files the registry discovered. That is a security property worth keeping: the activation tool is a lookup, not a file reader.

Finally, the catalog and the tool are wired into a ChatClient. The catalog goes into the system prompt, and the tool is registered as a default tool:

@Configuration
public class AgentConfig {

    @Bean
    ChatClient agentChatClient(ChatClient.Builder builder,
                               SkillRegistry registry,
                               SkillActivationTools activationTools) {

        String catalog = registry.all().stream()
                .map(s -> "- %s: %s".formatted(s.name(), s.description()))
                .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));

        String system = """
                You are a helpful engineering assistant.
                The following skills provide specialized instructions for specific tasks.
                When a task matches a skill's description, call activateSkill with the
                skill's name to load its full instructions before proceeding.

                Available skills:
                %s
                """.formatted(catalog);

        return builder
                .defaultSystem(system)
                .defaultTools(activationTools)
                .build();
    }
}

Two details in this wiring deserve attention. The catalog is built once at startup, which matches the guide's tier-1 behavior. And when the registry is empty, the wiring should skip both the catalog and the tool, as the guide advises. The version above omits that branch for brevity, but a production version should add it.

Context management

Once a skill is activated, its instructions sit in the conversation. Two problems follow. If the agent prunes or summarizes older messages to fit the context window, the skill can silently disappear, and the model keeps working without its instructions. The guide's answer is to protect skill content from pruning, either by flagging activation results or by recognizing the structured tags during compaction. The tags in the example above make that recognition straightforward.

The second problem is repetition. If the model activates the same skill twice, the instructions appear twice and waste tokens. A simple fix is to track activated skill names for the session and return a short acknowledgment instead of the full body on repeat calls.

The guide also mentions subagent delegation as an advanced option. Instead of injecting the skill into the main conversation, a separate session runs the skill and returns only a summary. This is useful for complex workflows that would otherwise flood the main context.

Security and trust

Three points deserve emphasis. The first is that a skill is untrusted instruction text. Project-level skills in a freshly cloned repository can steer the model, so loading them should depend on a trust decision by the user. The second is that the activation tool should resolve names against a known registry and never accept a path from the model. The example above does this by construction. The third is that bundled scripts are a separate permission question. If your agent can execute scripts from a skill directory, each execution needs the same scrutiny as any other tool call. The guide recommends allowlisting skill directories for reads so that the model does not trigger a permission prompt for every reference, but reads and executions are not the same risk.

When to choose each path

Use the file-read path when the model has a filesystem, the skills are local, and you have no need for permissions, analytics, or structured wrapping. It is the least code and the most portable across clients.

Use the tool-based path when the model cannot read files, when skills come from a remote registry or a database, when you need to enforce permissions or record activations, or when you want to shape the returned content. In a Spring application, it is the natural choice, because the registry, the permission checks, and the logging already live in your code.

Many agents support both. The guide notes that a dedicated tool is optional but useful even when the model can read files, which is a reasonable default if you are building a platform rather than a single script.

Key takeaways

  • Progressive disclosure keeps the base context small: names and descriptions at startup, full instructions on activation, and resources on demand.
  • The tool-based path is a delivery mechanism for the same SKILL.md files, useful when the model has no file access or when you need control over what is returned.
  • Discover skills in project and user scopes, let project skills override user skills, and gate project skills on trust.
  • Parse leniently, but skip any skill without a description, since the description drives disclosure.
  • Make the activation tool a registry lookup, not a file reader. The model should choose a skill name, not a path.
  • List bundled resources without reading them, and load them only when the instructions reference them.
  • Protect skill content from context pruning, and avoid re-injecting a skill that is already in context.

The guide is short, but it describes a complete lifecycle. If you are adding skills support to a Java agent, the tool-based path with Spring AI gives you that lifecycle in a few hundred lines, and the design decisions it forces, such as lookup over file access and tiered loading, are the ones that keep an agent predictable as the number of skills grows.

Sources

  • Agent Skills, "How to add skills support to your agent": https://agentskills.io/integrate-skills#integration-approaches
  • Agent Skills specification: https://agentskills.io/specification.md
