title: AWS Doubled the Timeout for Lambda Event Functions. Are You Still Paying for Speed You No Longer Need?
description:
Introduction

On November 19, 2026, AWS doubled the maximum timeout for on-demand Lambda Event Functions (previously known simply as Lambda Functions) from 15 to 30 minutes (announcement). Anyone would read that and think: great, longer jobs can run on Lambda Functions now. That was my first thought too. Then a second question hit me: if we suddenly have twice the time, are we still paying for speed we no longer need?

Here's what I mean. With Lambda Functions, a function with more resources usually runs faster, but it also costs more. When a job crept toward the 15-minute limit, a common quick fix was to give the function more resources so it finished in time. Now that the limit is 30 minutes, could those functions run on fewer resources and cost less? And more broadly, with this much more room on the timeout, how should we think about sizing our functions from now on?

To find out, I dug into AWS's pricing, its own benchmarks, and recent independent measurements. The answer is more interesting than yes or no: the same change, running a Lambda Function on fewer resources, reduce costs, save nothing, or make it more expensive. It all depends on what your function spends its time doing.

In this post, I'll start by covering three basics of running Lambda Functions (resources, pricing, and the time limit). Then I'll share how I used to handle the old 15-minute limit. After that comes the heart of the matter: where fewer resources save money, where they don't, and where they cost you more. Finally, I'll share a simple test to help you decide whether fewer resources are worth it for your own functions.

The basics: resources, pricing, and the time limit

Let's start with three ideas that make the rest of this post easy to follow, even if you've never worked with Lambda Functions before.

How resources are configured: you set the memory, the CPU follows

Unlike a regular server, a Lambda Function has no CPU setting. Instead, CPU comes with memory: the more memory you give it, the more CPU it gets (memory docs).

Memory CPU you get What it means
Below 1,769 MB A fraction of one vCPU, in proportion to memory Double the memory, double the CPU: work runs about twice as fast
1,769 MB One full vCPU The most a single-threaded function can use
1,769 to 10,240 MB Extra cores, up to 6 vCPUs (AWS News Blog) Only multi-threaded code gets faster; single-threaded code just costs more

That's why giving a function more memory often makes it faster, even when it never uses the extra RAM.

How Lambda Event Functions are priced: you pay for memory × time

Lambda Event Functions are billed by the GB-second: one gigabyte of memory held for one second (pricing).

Think of it like renting a room, priced by size and by the hour. A bigger room costs more per hour, and keeping it longer costs more in total. And you pay for the room you reserved, even if you only use one corner of it.

What you pay for is the product of memory and duration, not either number alone:

Memory Duration GB-seconds (memory × duration) Cost per 1,000 runs (EU Ireland)
1 GB 10 s 10 $0.17
2 GB 5 s 10 $0.17
512 MB 20 s 10 $0.17
4 GB 10 s 40 $0.67

The first three rows mix memory and time differently, but they cost exactly the same. The last one costs four times as much.

How long a function can run: you set the timeout, up to a hard ceiling

Every function also has a timeout: if it's still running when the timeout hits, it gets stopped. Until November 19, 2026, the highest timeout you could set was 15 minutes, and that limit shaped how we all designed our functions.

How I used to beat the 15-minute limit, and what it really cost

Whenever I built a new Lambda Function, I sized it for the job: enough memory for the work, and a timeout with room to spare. But jobs can grow and loads can change: a function that finishes in 4 minutes in its first weeks can creep toward 15 as its workload grows. When one got close to the 15-minute limit, or went past it, I had three kinds of fixes to choose from.

The fixes I had: redesign, optimize, or add memory

  • Structural fixes: rethink whether one Lambda Function should handle the whole job, split the work across several functions orchestrated with a workflow service like AWS Step Functions, or move it to a container-based service with Amazon ECS.
  • Code fixes: make the function itself faster, for example by profiling it, using a more efficient algorithm, running independent calls in parallel, or batching requests.
  • Resource fixes, the quick one: give the function more memory, so it gets more CPU, runs faster, and finishes under the limit.

Structural and code fixes take time to design, build, and test, so the quick fix was often the pragmatic first step. It works in some cases, not in others. Which case you're in depends on what the function is actually doing while the clock runs.

Working vs waiting: when the quick fix pays off, and when it backfires

A function spends its time in one of two states:

  • Working (CPU-bound): the processor is busy, so a faster CPU finishes sooner.
  • Waiting (I/O-bound): it depends on something outside it, like an API call, a database query, or an S3 upload, so a faster CPU barely helps.

Picture a kitchen. A skilled chef chops a mountain of vegetables faster, but doesn't make the delivery truck arrive any sooner.

And here's the key point: Lambda Event Functions bill wall-clock time, not CPU time. In other words, a second spent waiting costs exactly as much as a second spent working.

You can see this clearly in real measurements:

In the top diagram, the function is working, so the extra memory bought time at no extra cost.

In the bottom diagram, it's waiting on a download, so the extra memory bought nothing and multiplied the bill: download speed stayed flat at about 620 Mbps.

So for a job that mostly waits, the quick fix can't help: you need a structural or code fix instead.

Mixed jobs: the quick fix works, but at a price

To make this concrete, let's follow one example through the rest of this post: a nightly report, the kind of job almost every team runs. Every night, a Lambda Function:

  1. Calls external APIs to fetch the day's data. These APIs are slow and rate-limited, so most of this step is waiting.
  2. Processes the data and builds the report. That's working.
  3. Uploads the report to S3. Waiting again.

A single Lambda Function is a common, sensible home for a job like this while it's small.

Now, if you give this function more memory, only the working part gets shorter. The waiting part stays exactly the same:

For jobs that mix working and waiting, extra memory often does the trick, but at a price: the higher rate also applies to every second of waiting. Looking back now, that's the part I keep thinking about. With twice the time available, can those jobs lower their memory and stop paying that price?

The new opportunity: stop paying for speed you no longer need

With 30 minutes available, a job no longer needs extra CPU just to finish in time. That means any memory that wasn't making the function proportionally faster can go. There are two places to look:

  • Time spent waiting, which more memory never speeds up
  • Work that can't make full use of extra cores

Waiting time: stop paying the high rate to wait

Let's start with the main one. For a mixed job, lowering memory lets the working part take longer, while the waiting part stays the same. So the saving comes almost entirely from the waiting part:

GB-s saved per run≈memory removed (GB)×waiting time (s)

Back to the nightly report. Say it has grown to spend 9 minutes waiting on external APIs and needs 9 minutes of processing on one full vCPU (1,769 MB of memory). To keep things simple, I'm assuming the code can spread its work across several cores, so the working time depends on memory. At 4 GB (about 2.3 vCPUs) the processing takes about 3.9 minutes, and at 1 GB (about 0.6 vCPU) it takes about 15.5 minutes. Here's what happens when memory drops from 4 GB to 1 GB:

In numbers, using x86 pricing in EU (Ireland):

Setting Memory Runtime GB-s per run Cost per 1,000 runs
Old: fits under 15 min with headroom 4,096 MB 12.9 min 3,093 $51.55
New: fits under 30 min with headroom 1,024 MB 24.5 min 1,473 $24.55

That's 52% less. The working part costs about 933 GB-s in both cases, so the entire saving comes from the waiting part: 3 GB removed × 540 s = 1,620 GB-s.

Imperfect multi-core scaling: less memory, about 24% cheaper

The second place to look has nothing to do with waiting. Above 1,769 MB, extra memory buys extra cores, and many workloads can't use them all efficiently.

AWS's own PyTorch inference benchmark found that 5 GB cost the same as 1 GB while running 5x faster. At 10 GB, the function ran 7.6x faster but cost more: about $80 versus $61 per million invocations (AWS News Blog).

Now imagine a batch job that needed 10 GB to finish in 13 minutes. With the same ratios, it would take about 20 minutes at 5 GB: only possible under the new limit, and about 24% cheaper. One honest caveat: AWS measured short runs back in 2020, so I'm assuming the same ratio holds for longer jobs.

Not every function qualifies: when there's nothing to save

Of course, lowering memory isn't a free win. If a function is all work and no waiting, there's nothing to save: as the top diagram in “Extra memory buys time for working, but not for waiting” showed, dropping from 1,024 MB to 128 MB just makes the job 8x slower for the same cost. The idea also doesn't apply in these cases:

  • The memory floor. If the job needs the RAM, you can't drop it. And memory needs can vary: a busy night with more data, or a larger input file, may need far more RAM than a typical run. Only lower memory if you're confident about the peak requirement, and check Max Memory Used across your largest runs, not just an average one. Running close to the limit invites garbage-collection slowdowns or out-of-memory errors.
  • The free tier. Inside 400,000 GB-s a month, the saving is exactly $0. One 30-minute run at 1 GB uses 1,800 GB-s, so only about 222 such runs fit. In the nightly report example, 100 runs a month are free either way.
  • Other compute types. Lambda Managed Instances don't bill per-request duration at all, and Web Functions are billed on active CPU time and stay capped at 15 minutes (pricing).
  • Some event sources. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB, and Kafka mappings created before November 19, 2026 (unless in provisioned mode) remain limited to 14 minutes (announcement).

Going lower can backfire: when less memory ends up costing more

This is the part that's easy to miss: lowering memory can make things more expensive, either per run or in ways that never show up as GB-seconds.

A trap behind smaller sizes: the cost curve isn't a straight line

AWS's prime-number benchmark (Operating Lambda, part 2), shown in the top diagram of “Extra memory buys time for working, but not for waiting”, also tested two sizes in between, and both cost more than either end:

Going from 1,024 MB down to 512 MB would have raised the bill by about 9%. Measure, don't assume.

Synchronous callers: your savings, their extra cost

If another Lambda Function calls this one and waits for the answer, the caller is billed too, for every second it waits. So if your function now runs twice as long, the caller's cost doubles as well.

Longer runs: what you pay for outside the bill

Lower memory means longer runs, and longer runs bring costs that never show up as GB-seconds:

  • More concurrent executions
  • Slower stream processing
  • Longer queue timeouts
  • More work lost when a job fails late

AWS covers these in the “Considerations and best practices” section of its 30-minute timeout announcement, which is worth reading before you change anything.

How to tell which kind of function you have

So how do you know which kind of function you have? There's a simple way to get a first idea: halve its memory, run it again, and watch how the runtime reacts:

One rerun only points you in the right direction, though. Before changing anything for real, compare a few memory sizes on realistic inputs, including your biggest ones, keep headroom on both time and memory, and weigh the hidden costs of longer runs covered in “Going lower can backfire.”

Conclusion

The 30-minute limit is more than extra runway. It's a good moment to revisit how we size our Lambda Functions:

  • Memory buys CPU, not shorter waits. Before adding memory, check where the time actually goes.
  • Speed is now a choice, not a constraint. If a function spends much of its time waiting, you can trade a longer run for a smaller bill. If it's all work, there's nothing to trade.
  • Measure before you change anything. The cost curve has bumps, and longer runs bring costs that never show up as GB-seconds.

There's a broader lesson here about provisioning: faster isn't automatically better.

  • If nobody reads the results of a nightly Lambda Function until morning, a function that takes 25 minutes and costs half as much is the better design, even though "slower" sounds wrong.
  • If someone needs the result right away, the faster, pricier setting may be worth every cent.

The rule to remember: you save roughly memory removed × waiting time. Run the quick test before changing anything.

In the end, that's what engineering comes down to. Not the fastest setting, not the cheapest one, but the one that fits your specific need. Understand what your workload actually does, choose for that, and revisit the choice when the rules change, as they just did.

Sources

A quick note on the numbers: the measurements come from AWS and Classmethod, while the nightly report example is a model I built on AWS's published prices.

  • Announcing 30-minute timeout for on-demand AWS Lambda Event Functions, AWS Compute Blog, Nov 19, 2026
  • Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, AWS News Blog (where existing Lambda functions were renamed Event Functions)
  • AWS Lambda pricing
  • Configure Lambda function memory, AWS docs
  • New for AWS Lambda: Functions with up to 10 GB of memory and 6 vCPUs, AWS News Blog, 2020
  • Operating Lambda: Performance optimization, part 2, AWS Compute Blog
  • AWS Lambda scalable network bandwidth, AWS What's New, Aug 2026
  • Raising Lambda's network bandwidth to 3,000 Mbps, measured, Classmethod DevelopersIO, Sep 2026
  • Elastic Cloud Forwarder troubleshooting, Elastic docs

title: What a Farmers Market Website in Dubai Needs to Get Right on Market Day
description:
A farmers market in Dubai lives or dies on one morning a week. The website has one job: get the right people to the right place with the right expectations, before the stalls sell out. Most market sites we review fail at that job in the same three places.

1. Put this week's market first, not the market's history

Visitors open the site on Friday evening or Saturday morning. They want three facts: is it on this week, where exactly, and what time does it open. If those facts sit below a long story about the market's founding, the visitor leaves and asks on social media instead. The current date, the location, and the opening hours belong at the top of the page, updated every week without fail. A seasonal schedule page that lists every market date for the season earns the bookmark; a single static date does not.

2. Make every stall findable before arrival

A farmers market is not one shop, it is forty small businesses sharing a field. Shoppers come for a specific vendor — the cheese stall, the honey seller, the plant nursery. A stall directory with a short line per vendor, what they sell, and whether they take card payments turns browsing into a plan. When a vendor is absent for a week, say so on their listing. Nothing frustrates a regular more than arriving for a stall that never came.

3. Treat the vendor enquiry like a real application

Markets grow by adding good vendors, and good vendors apply through the website. A vendor enquiry page needs the honest questions up front: what do you sell, what space do you need, what power or refrigeration do you need, and which dates can you commit to. Collect it in one form, answer it within a couple of days, and keep a waiting list when the market is full. A market that answers vendors quickly gets first pick of the best stalls.

4. Design for a phone in one hand and a shopping bag in the other

Nobody browses a farmers market site at a desk. The visitor is standing in a car park, checking the location pin and the opening time. The map link, the parking note, and the WhatsApp enquiry route must work with one thumb and load fast on a weak connection. Big tap targets, short lines, and no image-heavy hero that delays the facts.

5. Let the season do the talking

Farmers markets change with the season, and the website should show it. A short weekly update — what is fresh this week, which stalls are new, what sold out last week — gives regulars a reason to return to the site instead of only to the market. Three lines and one honest photo beat a gallery of stock images every time.

6. Measure the Saturday, not the month

After launch, the number that matters is Saturday-morning behaviour: how many visitors checked the date and location, and how many tapped through to WhatsApp with a question. If enquiries spike on Friday evening, the schedule page is working. If they ask where the market is, the location section is not.

A farmers market website is a practical tool, not a brochure. It should answer the three questions every visitor asks, help vendors join, and stay current every single week. We build websites for Dubai businesses and booking apps for markets and events — if you run a market, start with the Saturday-morning test above and fix whatever fails it first. More about our work is on RapidBizz.

title: Model a Trust Boundary for OAuth Email Fixtures
description:
OAuth flows are often tested as if the inbox were a harmless test detail. It is not. An inbox that receives a verification code, magic link, or recovery message is a capability. Anyone who can read it may be able to move the flow forward.

That makes a test inbox part of your OAuth trust boundary. You can use a create temp mail workflow or a disposable email address generator for isolated fixtures, but the fixture still needs ownership, expiry, and audit rules. The goal is to make assumptions visible.

Why an inbox is an OAuth trust boundary

An OAuth test usually has several actors: the browser, the client application, the authorization server, and an email system. The email system is easy to forget because it sits outside the redirect flow, yet it can deliver a link that proves address control or resets a credential.

Treat that message as a short-lived capability, similar to a code or session token. A test inbox needs a clear owner and narrow purpose. It should never be a shared mailbox containing real customer messages, production reset links, or credentials copied from another environment.

This distinction matters: a disposable address is test data, not an identity guarantee. A passing test proves only that configured actors completed the flow.

A small threat model for email fixtures

Start with how a fixture can cross its intended boundary:

  • Cross-test reading: two parallel jobs use one inbox, so a code from one run is accepted by another. A shared fixture make this failure quiet.
  • Redirect confusion: the application accepts a redirect URI from a loose environment variable, allowing a token or link to land somewhere unexpected.
  • Log leakage: the full verification URL is printed by a failed test, a CI artifact, or a browser trace.
  • Long retention: old messages remain after the test. Cleanup is not a nice-to-have; it are part of the security control.
  • Account reuse: a fixture address is reused across branches, teams, or environments, making it hard to know which run created a message.

Some teams search for “tempail mail” when they are trying to find temporary test mail. The spelling is not the security issue; the important question is whether the mailbox can be isolated and deleted on a predictable clock.

Pair the fixture with a deletion clock for privacy-safe email tests. Deletion should be explicit, not a hope that a provider eventually removes old data.

Design the fixture boundary

Give every test run a fixture identity: run ID, environment, creation time, expiry time, and owner. Your application should still verify that the address belongs to the current run before accepting a message.

Make these rules explicit:

  1. One run, one fixture. Do not let parallel jobs poll the same address. If a provider cannot isolate it, add locking or use a different strategy.
  2. Short lease, enforced server-side. Store an expiry timestamp. Do not rely only on a CI timeout, because cancelled jobs do not always execute their final step.
  3. No production access. Keep test inbox credentials and OAuth client credentials in the test environment. Never make a test address a recovery route for a real account.
  4. Minimum message exposure. Extract the code or link, redact it from logs, and delete the message after the assertion.
  5. A dry-run path. Before sending, validate the recipient, environment, redirect URI, and lease. A dry-run contract for automation makes these checks repeatable.

This can feel over careful for staging, but staging often contains realistic configuration and copied data. A small boundary is cheaper than investigating a leaked token later.

Implement safer verification flows

Keep the email adapter behind a narrow interface. The test should ask for a message belonging to its run, not search a global inbox for the newest message:

async function waitForVerificationLink({ inbox, runId, expiresAt }) {
  const message = await inbox.waitForMessage({
    recipient: `oauth-${runId}@test.invalid`,
    after: new Date().toISOString(),
    until: expiresAt,
  });

  if (!message || message.runId !== runId) {
    throw new Error("verification message is outside the fixture boundary");
  }

  return extractVerificationLink(message.text);
}

The adapter should reject messages without the expected run correlation. If a test fail here, that is valuable evidence: the contract is incomplete or the system sent mail to the wrong place. Do not “fix” it by accepting the newest message from any recipient.

Validate the link before opening it: host, scheme, state, registered redirect URI, and the current browser session. Never print the complete link; log a hash or redacted route if debugging is needed.

Finally, make cleanup idempotent. A failed test, retry, and manual rerun should all call cleanup without turning a missing message into a second failure. The clean up step removes the mailbox or revokes its lease, then records only audit metadata.

A practical review checklist

Before merging an OAuth flow that depends on email, ask:

  • Is the test inbox isolated by run, environment, and owner?
  • Can one job read or consume another job’s verification message?
  • Are redirect URIs and state values checked before a link is opened?
  • Could a CI log, trace, screenshot, or artifact contain a token?
  • Does the fixture expire if the job is cancelled halfway through?
  • Is cleanup safe to run more than once?
  • Can an operator explain which messages existed without reading their contents?

Good audit data says what happened, when, and under which run ID. It does not preserve the secret that made the test pass.

Questions teams usually ask

Should temporary email be used for production authentication tests?

Use it for controlled test accounts and isolated environments, not as a substitute for identity verification. Production tests need synthetic data and monitoring that prevents a test account becoming a recovery path.

Is deleting the inbox enough?

No. Check application logs, CI artifacts, browser traces, provider logs, and caches too. A mailbox can be gone while its verification URL remains in a retained artifact.

What is the safest default when a message is ambiguous?

Fail closed. Require the exact run correlation, recipient, time window, and expected sender or message shape. A little extra polling is better than accepting an unrelated message.

Final takeaway

Email fixtures are part of the authentication system’s attack surface, even when they exist only for tests. Give each fixture a short lease, bind it to a run, validate every link before use, and remove both messages and derived secrets from retained artifacts.

The surprized result is usually positive: once the boundary is explicit, flaky OAuth tests become easier to debug as well as safer to operate. Security controls and reliable test design are pulling in the same direction here.

title: Why "the agent said so" isn't verification: signed receipts for agent calculations
description:
AI agents state numbers with total confidence: a sum, a percentage, a unit conversion, a date pulled from a document. When something goes wrong, the question is never "was the model smart?" but "can anyone show this was checked?" Today the answer is usually a log line nobody can replay.

Deterministic checks vs a second model

An LLM judging an LLM is fine for tone or summaries, but for arithmetic and quotations it adds a second thing that can be confidently wrong. For claims that have one right answer, recompute them with plain code. For "the contract says 30 days", check that the quoted text, number or date really occurs in the text you supplied.

What a receipt should contain

The claim, the inputs, the rule version, the result, a timestamp, and a signature. With an Ed25519 signature, a third party needs only the public key to confirm that this exact check was run and the result was not edited afterwards. The receipt is evidence of a check, not a guarantee that the underlying data is true.

What I built

AgentVerify is a small open-source (MIT) service and MCP server that does exactly this: https://github.com/Bencoombes23/agentverify-checks. There is a free demo (see DEMO.md in the repo for the shared key; it runs on a free host that sleeps, so allow a minute for the first call).

Honest limits

It's early. No SLA, no payments taken (an optional x402 paywall exists but is testnet-only and off by default), the replay store is in-process, and it only checks text you give it, never fetching URLs. It is run with an AI assistant and I say so up front.

Question for you

If you ship agents that produce numbers, has anyone ever asked you to prove a check happened? What would you need a receipt to prove? Tell me it's useless if it is.

title: How a desktop-only app's website can handle phone visitors, with no backend
description:
Originally published on claudictive.com.

A phone visitor on a desktop-only app's website is not a lost download if you give them a way to bring the link to their PC. On claudictive.com, a phone sees up to four buttons instead of the Windows download: email it to yourself, share it, a calendar reminder, and copy link. None needs a backend or collects anything new.

I build Claudictive, an in-game overlay for Claude Code, with Claude Code itself. It runs in games like World of Warcraft, League of Legends or Valorant, and it installs only on a Windows PC, through Overwolf. This is the short story of what we show people who find it on their phone, and why we skipped the obvious email form.

What happens when someone opens a Windows app's website on their phone?

They hit a dead end. The big button says download for Windows, a phone can't do anything useful with a Windows installer, and nothing on the page works on a phone.

I noticed it while looking at the site's own analytics and conversion. The write-ups I found solve the reverse problem: a desktop visitor and a mobile app. Branch recommends a "text me the app" page, and Mozilla's Send to Device widget is a form that emails a download link from a desktop browser to a phone. Both send the message from the site's side, through a server.

For our direction, phone visitor and desktop app, very little is written. The nearest thing is old redirect advice: in 2014 mobiForge quoted Google as saying "if there is no corresponding mobile page for a desktop page, then there should be no redirection at all". So the phone visitor stays on the real page, and the page has to offer them something.

Should you collect their email and send the link yourself?

That was option 2 in our decision record (ADR-031): collect an email address and mail the download link from our side. It looks like one form. Built safely, it is a lot more:

  • a transactional email provider and a verified sending domain;
  • abuse controls on a form that sends mail to any address someone types in, which means rate limits and a bot check;
  • a new section in the privacy page, because we would now hold email addresses;
  • a retention rule for how long we keep them.

Option 1 was to let the visitor send the link to themselves with the phone's own tools. I picked option 1. I wanted the method that would "reduce the privacy risks as far as possible", and I wanted something quick, relatively. An email form adds a new kind of data and a new thing to defend. The phone already has a mail app, a share sheet, a calendar and a clipboard.

How do you send a download link to your PC with no backend?

On a touch phone, each download button on the homepage, the use-case pages and the blog posts is replaced by a small panel. It reads: "On your phone? Claudictive installs on a Windows PC. Send yourself the link and grab it when you're back at your desk." The homepage hero swaps its download button for one that jumps to the panel in the download section.

The live download section at phone size (Chrome's phone emulation).

The panel picks phones with a media query, so a desktop with a mouse never sees it:

window.matchMedia('(hover: none) and (pointer: coarse)').matches

The buttons:

  • email_me_the_link: a mailto: link with no recipient. The visitor's own mail app opens with the subject and the link filled in, they type their own address and send it themselves. The address never touches our site.
  • share_to_another_app: the phone's share sheet (navigator.share), for sending the link to a notes app, a chat with yourself, or anything else.
  • remind_me_at_8pm: downloads a one-event calendar file (.ics) with the link in it and an alarm at the start time.
  • copy_link: copies the link to the clipboard.

Only the email button always shows. Share, the calendar reminder and copy appear only where the browser supports them. That matters, because a mailto: link needs a mail app set up on the phone, and on a phone without one, whichever of the other three the browser supports are still there.

The core of the email and the reminder is a few lines of plain JavaScript:

// mailto with no recipient: the visitor picks their own address.
'mailto:?subject=' + encodeURIComponent(TITLE) + '&body=' + encodeURIComponent(body)

// 20:00 local today, or tomorrow when it is already 19:00 or later.
var day = now.getHours() >= 19 ? now.getDate() + 1 : now.getDate();
return new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), day, 20, 0, 0);

The reminder uses floating local time, so it goes off at 8pm wherever the visitor is. I picked 8pm by thinking about my own routine and when I'm usually in front of the computer. From 7pm on, it is set for the next evening instead.

If the script fails for any reason, the page keeps its normal download button. Claude Code built the panel and the unit tests, which run it in a fake DOM and check the mailto and calendar-file builders. The parts only a real phone can prove, the mail app taking the mailto: and the calendar opening the reminder, I checked by hand on my own phone on the live site.

What do you count, and what stays on the phone?

We count the tap, and we don't count it as a download. The buttons send us nothing else. The privacy page says it this way: "On a phone this also covers the send-it-to-yourself buttons (email, share, calendar reminder, copy link): we only count the click. Your email address, your contacts and what you share stay in your own apps and never reach us."

That sentence was added to the privacy page in the same change as the panel. No new kind of data, no new storage, no new section.

When would we build the email form after all?

It is still an option. If the panel shows that people really want the link mailed to them, option 2 is written down with everything it needs. Until then, the phone's own tools do the job, and there is nothing new to protect.

title: How to test email invitations end to end
description:
Every app with teams has someone inviting someone else. The invitation is the person's first contact with the product, and it goes through three places: the inviter's screen, an inbox and the invited person's browser. That's why it usually goes untested, and breaks without anyone noticing: the email doesn't go out, the link lands on the wrong page, or the person joins a team that isn't theirs.

With a real inbox your test can read, the whole flow becomes an ordinary test. This guide uses Playwright and the saci.cc npm package, but the ideas apply to any tool.

What's worth testing

Seeing the email arrive isn't enough. A good invitation test checks that:

  • The invite reaches the address that was typed, saying who invited them and to which team. Nobody clicks an email from a sender they don't know.
  • The link opens the accept page with the email already filled in, and the account created there joins the right team with the right role.
  • The link works only once.
  • Resending or canceling an invite turns off the old link.
  • An invite for one address can't be used by an account with another address. This is the one that becomes a security hole: a forwarded or leaked link must not let a stranger into the team.

Set up the key and the inboxes

Create a free key on your account page, put it in SACI_API_KEY and install the client:

npm install --save-dev saci.cc

Each invited person is a new inbox, made with createInbox(). That way each inbox gets a single invite, and tests running in parallel don't get in each other's way. Inboxes created with your key are private, which matters here: an invite link gives access to a team.

The inviter is already signed in. In Playwright, that's usually a storageState saved by a setup project, so the test's page is already the team owner's account.

The full test

First, a function that sends the invite through your app's screen and returns the email. It notes the time before clicking, to skip emails that were already in the inbox:

import { test, expect, type Page } from "@playwright/test";
import { createInbox, type Inbox } from "saci.cc";

async function invite(page: Page, inbox: Inbox) {
  const invitedAt = new Date();
  await page.goto("/settings/team");
  await page.getByLabel("Email").fill(inbox.address);
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Invite" }).click();
  return inbox.waitForEmail({ subject: "invited you", after: invitedAt });
}

The test invites a new address, checks the email, opens the link in a browser with no session and creates the account:

test("an invited person joins the team", async ({ page, browser }) => {
  test.setTimeout(90_000);
  const inbox = await createInbox();

  const email = await invite(page, inbox);
  expect(email.text).toContain("Ana Souza"); // who invited
  expect(email.text).toContain("Acme"); // the team
  const link = email.links.find((url) => url.includes("/invite/"));
  expect(link).toMatch(/^https:/);

  // Someone else, in another browser, signed out
  const guest = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
  await guest.goto(link!);
  await expect(guest.getByLabel("Email")).toHaveValue(inbox.address);
  await guest.getByLabel("Password").fill("invited-password-123");
  await guest.getByRole("button", { name: "Join Acme" }).click();
  await expect(guest.getByRole("heading", { name: "Acme" })).toBeVisible();

  // The inviter sees them on the team
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole("row", { name: inbox.address })).toContainText("Member");
});

browser.newContext() is what makes the test count: without it, the link would open with the inviter's session, and the test would pass even with accepting broken.

Pick the link by its path

saci.cc finds the link to confirm an address, sign in or reset a password on its own, and returns it in the verificationLink field. A button like "Accept invitation" or "Join the team" is none of those, so don't count on that field for invites. Pick the link by its path, as in the test above, or with waitForLink inside invite():

const link = await inbox.waitForLink({ match: "/invite/", after: invitedAt });

Invitation emails usually have other links, like the logo, the privacy policy and "I don't know this person". Without match, waitForLink returns the verificationLink or, without one, the first link in the email, which is rarely the invite.

The link works only once

At the end of the previous test, open the same link in a new session. The app should refuse it:

const again = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
await again.goto(link!);
await expect(again.getByText("This invite was already used")).toBeVisible();

Resending and canceling

When an invite is resent, the old link should stop working. Otherwise each resend leaves one more valid link out there:

const first = (await invite(page, inbox)).links.find((url) => url.includes("/invite/"))!;

const resentAt = new Date();
await page.getByRole("row", { name: inbox.address }).getByRole("button", { name: "Resend" }).click();
const second = await inbox.waitForLink({ match: "/invite/", after: resentAt });
expect(second).not.toBe(first);

const guest = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
await guest.goto(first);
await expect(guest.getByText("This invite is no longer valid")).toBeVisible();

Canceling is the same test with the "Cancel" button and no second email.

Someone else's invite

Here the test needs two inboxes: the invited person's and someone who got hold of the link. The second person creates their own account and tries to use the invite:

test("an invite only works for the invited address", async ({ page, browser }) => {
  test.setTimeout(120_000);
  const [invited, other] = await Promise.all([createInbox(), createInbox()]);

  const link = (await invite(page, invited)).links.find((url) => url.includes("/invite/"))!;

  const intruder = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
  await signUp(intruder, other.address, "another-password-456"); // your sign-up
  await intruder.goto(link);
  await expect(intruder.getByText("This invite is for another email")).toBeVisible();

  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole("row", { name: other.address })).toHaveCount(0);
});

If your sign-up sends a verification code, signUp calls other.waitForCode() along the way, as in the Playwright guide.

Some apps invite with an open link that anyone can use until the seats run out. The saci.cc Team plan invite works that way. Then the test is a different one: the link expires on time, stops working when the team is full and turns off when a new one is made.

In short

  • One inbox per invited person, made with createInbox() and your key.
  • Open the link in a browser.newContext(), so you don't accept with the inviter's session.
  • Pick the link by its path, with links.find or waitForLink({ match }): verificationLink doesn't cover invites.
  • Also test what must not happen: a reused link, an old link after a resend, an invite accepted by another address.

I build saci.cc, temporary email inboxes for end-to-end tests and AI agents. The npm package is saci.cc and the client is open source on GitHub.
