title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports managed observability and user management extensions for Slurm clusters
description:
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports managed cluster extensions for Slurm clusters. You can install, configure, update, and remove managed features through the SageMaker AI console or API. The first two extensions cover observability and user management. Earlier, every observability or user management change for HyperPod Slurm clusters meant editing lifecycle scripts and then replacing or rerunning nodes. Now, HyperPod manages these features for you, and you keep lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs for your organization's own software.

For each extension, you declare a configuration. HyperPod validates it and applies it to every node, including nodes you add later. It then reports the extension's status and the health of each node. The observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), Slurm job, and Slurm cluster metrics. It sends them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and you can add Amazon Managed Grafana dashboards. The user management extension creates users and groups with the same IDs on every node. It also controls who can sign in with SSH and use sudo on each node type, with local users, Active Directory, or both.

Cluster extensions are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available. You pay only for the AWS resources you use. To learn more, see Cluster extensions in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide, read the launch blog, or visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page.

title: Node.js PDF Template Observability: Trace Invoice HTML Changes Through Support
description:
Keep invoice HTML in the repository when engineers own the layout; choose a stored template when finance needs to edit it without a deploy. For customer support teams turning scanned invoices into searchable text, that ownership decision should also determine where a layout investigation starts.

Short answer: a PDF template management API versus HTML in a repo is a choice about who changes the file. Git gives layout changes the application's review and rollback process. Stored templates allow changes independently of application deployment. Give each layout one owner, then carry that ownership into the records used to investigate support tickets.

Search needs context. A support agent who finds an invoice should be able to distinguish its extracted text from the layout used to produce a replacement invoice. OCR reads a scanned document. Rendering creates a document. Neither operation establishes who approved its appearance.

How should support trace PDF template changes to invoice HTML?

Before: scanned invoice → extracted text → search result. A result may answer which invoice mentions a disputed charge, but the trace says little about where to correct the layout of a replacement document.

After: scanned invoice → extracted text → searchable support record → replacement request → one recorded layout owner. The original scan remains the evidence for the customer's uploaded document; the replacement has its own layout reference. This distinction matters when a support agent sees an old address on a scan and finance has already changed the address used for newly generated invoices. A fresh render should not silently become the explanation for what the original scan contained.

Record the boundary.

For repository HTML, attach the revision selected by the application to its replacement request. For a stored template, attach the reference your application actually selected and whatever revision evidence the chosen service supports. Don't assume a template name identifies immutable content. Establish that in your service evaluation before relying on it during an investigation.

This is an observability design recommendation, not a claim that every template API supplies a revision history. The useful question is concrete: can support identify both the document it searched and the layout used for its replacement? Consider a synthetic ticket with two attachments: an uploaded scan and a newly generated replacement. They may share an invoice identifier while containing different addresses. Joining every event on that identifier alone would hide which document supplied the searchable text. Give the scan its own identifier and preserve the replacement's selected layout reference, so an investigation can follow the actual document relationship rather than infer it from matching invoice numbers.

A small Node.js example makes ownership visible

The following TypeScript example uses synthetic support data. It models the handoff after OCR has supplied text and before a renderer creates a replacement PDF. The output is escaped invoice HTML and a structured event; an actual OCR service, search index, and PDF renderer remain separate integration choices.

Copy it into a TypeScript file and run it with a TypeScript-capable Node.js setup. The example keeps one rendering branch deliberately: the selected owner is engineering, so the HTML lives with the application. Its revision is an explicit example label, not a fabricated Git commit.

type SupportInvoice = {
  ticketId: string;
  invoiceId: string;
  scanId: string;
  extractedText: string;
  replacementReason: string;
};

type RepoLayout = {
  kind: "repo-html";
  owner: "engineering";
  revision: string;
};

const invoice: SupportInvoice = {
  ticketId: "SUP-1042",
  invoiceId: "INV-208",
  scanId: "scan-17",
  extractedText: "Invoice INV-208. Support renewal.",
  replacementReason: "Customer requested a readable copy",
};

const layout: RepoLayout = {
  kind: "repo-html",
  owner: "engineering",
  revision: "example-layout-3",
};

function escapeHtml(value: string): string {
  return value
    .replaceAll("&", "&")
    .replaceAll("<", "<")
    .replaceAll(">", ">")
    .replaceAll('"', """)
    .replaceAll("'", "'");
}

function renderReplacement(record: SupportInvoice): string {
  return `<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Replacement invoice</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Invoice ${escapeHtml(record.invoiceId)}</h1>
  <p>Replacement requested through customer support.</p>
  <p>${escapeHtml(record.replacementReason)}</p>
</body>
</html>`;
}

const html = renderReplacement(invoice);
const event = {
  event: "invoice.replacement.prepared",
  ticket_id: invoice.ticketId,
  invoice_id: invoice.invoiceId,
  source_scan_id: invoice.scanId,
  layout_kind: layout.kind,
  layout_owner: layout.owner,
  layout_revision: layout.revision,
};

if (!html.includes(escapeHtml(invoice.invoiceId))) {
  throw new Error("Replacement HTML is missing its invoice identifier");
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(event));
console.log(html);

Notice what the event records: the source scan and the selected layout. The extracted text stays out of the event. These are application-defined fields, not parameters for a vendor's logging API. Feed the text into your search workflow under its own access rules; use identifiers to connect an investigation across the handoff.

There's a useful trap here. Logging a revision label doesn't preserve a layout. The repository must retain the corresponding content, or the stored-template workflow must provide equivalent evidence. Otherwise the event gives support a precise-looking identifier that cannot answer the question.

The example also avoids treating OCR text as authoritative replacement invoice data. A scanned phrase is useful for retrieval, but this demonstration doesn't validate financial amounts, addresses, or line items. That validation belongs before a production rendering request.

Compare candidates through the change path

Evaluate Puppeteer, DocRaptor, and PDFMonkey against the same invoice and the same ownership question. Their documentation provides starting points for browser-driven PDF rendering, HTML-to-PDF conversion, and managed document templates respectively. Those are different places to put the rendering boundary. A product name alone doesn't decide who should approve a layout change.

Candidate Ownership question to test Trade-off to examine
Puppeteer Can engineering keep the HTML and rendering setup under the repository's review process? Repository control also leaves the rendering setup with the engineering team.
DocRaptor Can the application submit the exact reviewed HTML needed for this invoice? A conversion service doesn't by itself establish who approves changes to the submitted HTML.
PDFMonkey Does the managed-template workflow let the intended editor make and review a change? Independent edits require a deliberate record of which template content produced a document.

These are evaluation boundaries, not benchmark results. Test 3 synthetic inputs: a long customer address, a multi-page invoice, and an OCR result containing a literal less-than sign. The first two probe the layout; the third probes how your application handles extracted text. Don't interpret successful PDF creation as proof that the invoice is searchable or that its text extraction is correct.

Infrai offers a plain REST API with a single API key and unified billing. An HTTP-capable application can call it without installing a vendor SDK. The same key spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so a support workflow evaluating OCR and PDF generation can keep credential handling together. Its public discovery surface also supplies request and response schemas for checking the contract. Evaluate its stored-template and PDF-generation workflow with the same ownership test. The integration style is useful; it doesn't select the layout owner for you.

Check the contract first.

Here is a separate, read-only contract check for that candidate. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service's documented HTTPS API base, including its version prefix, and INFRAI_API_KEY to your environment-managed key. Run this TypeScript in a Node.js setup with native fetch. Discovery is public and requires no key; the example uses the normal Bearer header to demonstrate the authenticated client's configuration without making a document write. It prints the discovery response for inspection before you implement template creation or rendering. No undocumented document fields are assumed.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY");
}
if (new URL(baseUrl).protocol !== "https:") {
  throw new Error("The API base must use HTTPS");
}

async function inspectContract(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl!.replace(/\/$/, "")}/discovery`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 2) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
      const seconds = retryAfter === null ? NaN : Number(retryAfter);
      const date = retryAfter === null ? NaN : Date.parse(retryAfter);
      const delay = Number.isFinite(seconds)
        ? Math.max(0, seconds * 1000)
        : Number.isFinite(date)
          ? Math.max(0, date - Date.now())
          : 1000 * 2 ** attempt;
      await response.text();
      await new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("Discovery retry limit reached");
}

inspectContract().then(
  (contract) => console.log(JSON.stringify(contract, null, 2)),
  (error: unknown) => {
    console.error(error);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  },
);

The deciding exercise is small. Ask engineering and finance to describe how a changed remittance address reaches the next replacement invoice. If both teams point to different editable copies of the same layout, resolve that ambiguity before selecting a renderer.

Does finance editing without a deploy weaken review?

It changes where review must happen. A stored template can be updated without an application deploy, which is useful when finance owns the content. That benefit needs an explicit approval process and enough retained evidence to explain a generated document. Check the candidate's actual editing and revision behavior rather than assuming it mirrors Git.

For engineer-owned layouts, Git review and rollback already travel with the code. That's a good reason to keep HTML in the repository. It's a poor fit if every routine finance edit then waits for an engineer to translate and deploy it. The right boundary follows the editor's job.

Pick one owner.

Can logs and alerts settle the choice?

They can expose an unclear boundary, but they can't appoint an owner. Start with structured records connecting the support ticket, source scan, replacement request, and selected layout. Then define an application check for missing ownership evidence before rendering; count failures and alert the team responsible for that handoff. Choose alert thresholds from the support workflow rather than inventing a universal number.

Keep separate signals for extraction and replacement generation. A generation success doesn't prove that OCR captured the original scan correctly, while a useful search result doesn't prove that finance approved the replacement layout. This separation gives an investigation a clear next step: inspect the scanned evidence, the extracted text, or the selected layout.

Choose repository HTML for engineering ownership and a stored template for finance ownership. Preserve the source scan relationship in either case. That makes the template decision useful to the support agent who must explain a document later.

References

  • PDF format standard, ISO 32000-2
  • Puppeteer documentation
  • DocRaptor documentation
  • PDFMonkey documentation

title: Spring AI's Model Layer: One API, Any Provider, Zero Rewrites
description:
Spring AI's Model Layer: One API, Any Provider, Zero Rewrites

If you have built an AI feature in Java, you have probably felt the same pain I did. You write the integration against one provider's SDK, the product works, and then a business decision, a price change, or a compliance requirement forces you to move to another model. Suddenly the code you thought was "done" is full of provider-specific request objects, response parsers, and retry rules.

Spring AI tackles this problem directly. Its model layer gives you a single, portable API for the kinds of models most applications use: chat, embeddings, images, audio, moderation, and decision models. Underneath, it connects to many providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google GenAI, Google Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock, Mistral AI, Ollama, DeepSeek, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

The practical promise is simple: you change configuration, not your application code. In this article I will explain how the model layer is organized, show how it fits with ChatClient, and walk through a small Spring Boot service that can switch providers without a single line of business logic changing.

The big picture

It helps to see Spring AI as a set of layers, each with a clear responsibility:

  • Models abstract the provider. You depend on a model interface such as ChatModel or EmbeddingModel, not on a vendor SDK.
  • ChatClient is the friendly, fluent entry point for talking to a chat model. It supports prompts, structured output, tool calling, and advisors that wrap each call.
  • Data and retrieval provide vector stores, document readers, and RAG building blocks, using one portable API across many vector databases.
  • Agents and protocols sit on top, for workflows that need planning, tools, and communication between agents.

This article focuses on the bottom layer, the model layer, because it is the foundation everything else depends on.

Six model APIs, one vocabulary

The model layer does not treat "AI" as a single thing. It defines one API per kind of model:

Model API What it does Typical use
Chat Text in, text out Assistants, summarization, extraction
Embedding Text in, numeric vector out Semantic search, RAG, clustering
Image Text in, image out Generating visuals, thumbnails
Audio Speech and audio processing Transcription, text to speech
Moderation Classify content for policy violations Filtering user input and output
Decision Choose among options with a model Routing and classification decisions

Each API has a consistent set of concepts: a model interface, options (such as the model name or temperature), and a response type. Once you learn one, the others feel familiar.

Why provider portability matters

Provider portability is more than a nice abstraction. It gives you concrete advantages:

  1. Cost control. You can route simple tasks to a cheaper model and reserve a premium model for hard ones.
  2. Resilience. If one provider has an outage or rate limits you, you can switch to another without a code release.
  3. Privacy and locality. You can run a local model with Ollama during development or for sensitive data, and use a hosted model in production.
  4. Evaluation. You can compare providers on the same prompts and pick the one that fits your quality bar.
  5. Negotiation and lock-in. Your architecture does not depend on one vendor's roadmap.

None of these advantages exists if your business code calls a vendor SDK directly. The abstraction is what makes them cheap to exercise.

Setting up the project

Start with a Spring Boot project and add the Spring AI starter for the provider you want to use first. Spring AI publishes a bill of materials (BOM), so you should manage the version through the BOM rather than hard-coding it on each dependency. The exact coordinates depend on the Spring AI version you target, so check the official reference documentation for the current setup.

With Maven, the shape looks like this:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-ai-bom</artifactId>
            <version>${spring-ai.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-ai-openai-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Notice that the starter is provider-specific, but the code you write against it is not. That distinction is the heart of the design.

Configuration decides the provider

Provider settings live in application.yml. Credentials come from environment variables, never from source code:

spring:
  ai:
    openai:
      api-key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY}
      chat:
        options:
          model: gpt-4o-mini
          temperature: 0.2

Switching to Anthropic is a configuration change, not a code change:

spring:
  ai:
    anthropic:
      api-key: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}
      chat:
        options:
          model: claude-sonnet-4-5
          temperature: 0.2

Model names change over time, so treat the values above as examples and check the current model list in each provider's documentation before you deploy.

For local development, you can use Ollama and keep everything on your machine:

spring:
  ai:
    ollama:
      base-url: http://localhost:11434
      chat:
        options:
          model: llama3.1

Spring profiles make this even cleaner. Keep application-local.yml pointing at Ollama, application-prod.yml pointing at a hosted provider, and select the profile at startup with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE.

A provider-agnostic service

Now the important part: the service code. Spring Boot auto-configures a ChatClient.Builder when a chat model is on the classpath. Your service depends only on that builder:

import org.springframework.ai.chat.client.ChatClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class SupportAssistant {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    public SupportAssistant(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        this.chatClient = builder.build();
    }

    public String answer(String customerQuestion) {
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        You are a concise support assistant for a digital bank.
                        Answer in the same language as the customer.
                        If you are not sure, say so and suggest contacting support.
                        """)
                .user(customerQuestion)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

This class does not mention OpenAI, Anthropic, or Ollama. Whichever provider is active at startup, the same code runs. That is the portability promise in practice.

Structured output: from text to Java objects

Free text is hard to use in a backend. Often you want a typed object. Spring AI can ask the model for JSON that maps to a Java record and convert the result for you:

import java.util.List;

public record TicketSummary(String category, String priority, List<String> keyPoints) {}

public TicketSummary summarize(String ticketText) {
    return chatClient.prompt()
            .system("Classify the support ticket and extract the key points.")
            .user(ticketText)
            .call()
            .entity(TicketSummary.class);
}

Structured output reduces brittle string parsing, which is one of the most common sources of production bugs in LLM integrations. It does not remove the need for validation. Treat the model's output as untrusted input: check ranges, enum values, and required fields before you act on it.

Embeddings: the other half of retrieval

Chat gets the attention, but embeddings are what make retrieval work. An EmbeddingModel turns text into a vector, and you store those vectors in a vector store. Here is a minimal example that embeds two texts and compares them with cosine similarity:

import org.springframework.ai.embedding.EmbeddingModel;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class SimilarityService {

    private final EmbeddingModel embeddingModel;

    public SimilarityService(EmbeddingModel embeddingModel) {
        this.embeddingModel = embeddingModel;
    }

    public double similarity(String first, String second) {
        float[] a = embeddingModel.embed(first);
        float[] b = embeddingModel.embed(second);
        return cosine(a, b);
    }

    private double cosine(float[] a, float[] b) {
        double dot = 0, normA = 0, normB = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            dot += a[i] * b[i];
            normA += a[i] * a[i];
            normB += b[i] * b[i];
        }
        return dot / (Math.sqrt(normA) * Math.sqrt(normB));
    }
}

In a real system you would not compare two texts on every request. You would embed your documents once, store them in a vector store such as PGVector, Redis, Elasticsearch, or Qdrant, and query by similarity. The point here is that the embedding code is the same regardless of which provider generates the vectors.

One caution: vectors from different embedding models are not compatible. If you switch the embedding provider, you must re-embed your corpus. Keep the embedding model choice as a deliberate decision, not a casual configuration tweak.

Testing without calling a real provider

Tests that call a live model are slow, expensive, and non-deterministic. Because your code depends on abstractions, you can test it with a fake. For example, a unit test can stub the model response and assert how your service builds the prompt and handles the answer. Keep a small number of integration tests that use a real or local model, and run them separately from your fast build.

This is also where the portability pays off in your test strategy: you can run the same integration suite against Ollama in CI and against a hosted provider in a nightly job.

Production concerns you should not skip

Switching providers is easy. Running them reliably is not. A few practices make a real difference:

  • Set timeouts and retries. Model calls can be slow. Define explicit timeouts and a bounded retry policy, and avoid retrying on errors that will not succeed on a second attempt.
  • Log carefully. Prompts and responses may contain personal data. Redact sensitive content and make logging levels configurable.
  • Track cost and latency per provider. Observability is part of the design. Spring AI exposes metrics and traces for the client, models, and vector stores, so connect them to your monitoring stack.
  • Control the prompt. Keep system prompts in version control and review them like code. A small wording change can alter behavior significantly.
  • Plan for model changes. Providers deprecate models. Pin the model name in configuration, and have a process for testing a replacement before you switch.
  • Guard the output. Use validation and, where needed, moderation models before you show or act on a response.

Common pitfalls

A few mistakes I see often:

  1. Leaking provider types into business code. If you import a vendor class into a service, you have lost portability. Keep provider-specific code in configuration.
  2. Assuming identical behavior. Providers differ in how they handle system prompts, token limits, and structured output. Test each provider you support.
  3. Mixing embedding models. Changing the embedding model silently breaks retrieval quality until you re-index.
  4. Hard-coding credentials. Use environment variables or a secrets manager.
  5. Skipping evaluation. Without a set of representative prompts and expected outcomes, you cannot tell whether a provider switch made things better or worse.

Where to go next

The model layer is the foundation, not the whole building. Once you are comfortable with it, the next steps are:

  • Add a vector store and build a small RAG pipeline with a document reader and a retrieval step.
  • Use advisors to add memory, logging, or safety checks around each call.
  • Introduce tool calling so the model can invoke your Java services.
  • Explore agent patterns such as chaining, routing, and orchestrator-workers when a single call is not enough.

Conclusion

Spring AI's model layer solves a problem that every Java team building AI features will eventually face: how to avoid being locked into one provider. By separating model APIs from provider implementations, and by letting configuration choose the provider, it gives you a clean path to switch models, control costs, run locally, and evaluate options without rewriting your business logic.

If you are starting an AI feature in a Spring Boot application, begin with the model abstraction, keep provider details in configuration, and invest early in tests and observability. Your future self, the one who needs to change providers on a Friday afternoon, will be grateful.

Have you already built an AI feature in Java? I would like to hear which provider you started with and what made you consider switching.

title: From AWS Cloud Practitioner to the Cloud Resume Challenge
description:
The cloud world has piqued my interest for a while and as the cliché goes, planning and not doing yields zero results. Rather than just watching multiple tutorials and not actually doing anything because of the fear of not being good enough, I decided to take the first step, which was getting the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification. It is the foundational level and it gave a broad understanding of the AWS services. One thing that really stood out was the shared responsibility model: how much AWS handles versus how much the customer handles. Shout out to the people I network with who not only advised me but shared resources to help me prepare for the exam, and yes, I passed!

It was a very interesting learning experience and the last thing I’d want is to lose this knowledge. In order for that not to happen, I'm putting it into practice through hands-on projects, continued learning, and hopefully more certifications soon. My end goal is to become a DevOps engineer, and I was advised to build a solid cloud foundation first, so that's where I'm starting.

Not sure where to go next, I came across the Cloud Resume Challenge, which looks beginner friendly. For each step I complete, I'll document what I learn as I’ve been told it is one way to get the knowledge to stick! Follow along on my journey if you are interested. Who knows, you may learn a thing or two as well.

title: SQL GROUP BY and HAVING: Find Your Top Customers and $3,000 Key Accounts in Eight Rows of Orders
description:
Before a quarterly review, someone usually gets asked two questions: who are our top three customers, and which accounts were worth $3,000 or more this quarter? The usual answer is a spreadsheet, a sort, and a lot of adding up by hand.

Both questions are four SQL keywords: GROUP BY, ORDER BY, LIMIT and HAVING. This walkthrough uses a made-up shop, Lakeside Office Supply, with eight orders. You can type all of it into DB Fiddle (free, no account needed, MySQL v9 selected).

Step 1: make the orders table

DB Fiddle has two boxes. The left one, Schema SQL, holds the table. Click inside it and type:

CREATE TABLE orders (
id INT, order_date DATE,
customer VARCHAR(40), amount INT);

Four columns: an id, the order date, the customer and the amount.

Leave a blank line and add the eight orders. Text goes in single quotes, numbers don't. Every row ends with a comma except the last one, which ends with a semicolon so the database knows the statement is finished:

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
(1, '2026-07-02', 'Maple Dental', 1250),
(2, '2026-07-15', 'Cobalt Legal', 860),
(3, '2026-07-28', 'Northside Realty', 2140),
(4, '2026-08-06', 'Cobalt Legal', 2310),
(5, '2026-08-19', 'Harbor Accounting', 640),
(6, '2026-08-27', 'Maple Dental', 980),
(7, '2026-09-09', 'Northside Realty', 1890),
(8, '2026-09-22', 'Cobalt Legal', 1270);

Four customers, eight orders, one quarter (July to September).

Step 2: total each customer with GROUP BY

In the right box, Query SQL, type:

SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer;

Click Run. GROUP BY customer collapses the eight rows into one row per customer, and SUM(amount) adds up that customer's orders. AS revenue names the new column.

You get four rows, but in no useful order.

Step 3: biggest first with ORDER BY

Delete the semicolon at the end of the last line, press Enter, and add:

ORDER BY revenue DESC;

DESC means descending, biggest first. Run it:

customer revenue
Cobalt Legal 4440
Northside Realty 4030
Maple Dental 2230
Harbor Accounting 640

Notice you can sort by revenue, the alias you just created. That works because ORDER BY runs after the totals are calculated.

Step 4: keep the top three with LIMIT

Remove the semicolon again and add one line:

LIMIT 3;

The full query now reads:

SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 3;

Run it: Cobalt Legal, Northside Realty, Maple Dental. That's question one answered.

One thing to watch: LIMIT without ORDER BY gives you three rows, but not necessarily the top three. Always sort first.

Step 5: key accounts with HAVING

Question two is different. It's not "the top N" but "everyone over a threshold". Replace the whole query (Ctrl+A, then type) with:

SELECT customer, COUNT(*) AS orders,
SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 3000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

COUNT(*) adds the number of orders next to the revenue. Run it:

customer orders revenue
Cobalt Legal 3 4440
Northside Realty 2 4030

Those are the two accounts that get a thank-you call. Change 3000 to any other number and the list updates.

Why HAVING and not WHERE

This is the part that trips up most beginners. It's tempting to write:

-- This does NOT do what you want
SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE amount >= 3000
GROUP BY customer;

WHERE filters single rows before they are added up. No single order in this table is $3,000 or more (the biggest is 2,310), so this returns nothing, even though two customers are clearly over $3,000 in total.

HAVING filters the totals after GROUP BY. "Customers worth $3,000 or more" is a question about totals, so it needs HAVING.

You can use both in the same query. WHERE first narrows which orders count (say, one month), then HAVING filters the totals:

SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-08-01'
GROUP BY customer
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 2000;

The order of the clauses

SQL is strict about the order you write things in:

SELECT  ...
FROM    ...
WHERE   ...   -- filters rows
GROUP BY ...  -- makes one row per group
HAVING  ...   -- filters groups
ORDER BY ...  -- sorts the result
LIMIT   ...   -- keeps the first N

If you get a syntax error on a query that looks right, check this order first.

Same table, new question

The table didn't change between question one and question two. Only the query did. That's the real shift from spreadsheets: at work the orders table already exists, and every new question from your manager is just a new query. GROUP BY works on any column: customer, month, region or salesperson.

Checklist

  • [ ] Every row in INSERT ends with a comma, the last with a semicolon
  • [ ] GROUP BY names the column you want one row per
  • [ ] ORDER BY ... DESC before LIMIT, or the "top three" is random
  • [ ] Thresholds on totals go in HAVING, thresholds on single rows go in WHERE
  • [ ] Clause order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT
  • [ ] One total checked by hand (Cobalt Legal: 860 + 2310 + 1270 = 4440)

Practice it

This is based on a free step-by-step lesson where you type every line yourself in a practice copy of DB Fiddle that checks your work as you go (14 steps, about 12 minutes): SQL: Top Customers and Key Accounts with GROUP BY and HAVING.

title: Azure Blob Storage vs Google Cloud Storage vs Amazon S3 Explained: 4 Receipt Trade-offs
description:
For storing user uploads, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, and Amazon S3 all look reasonable until a healthtech receipt must remain private, retrievable, and auditable. You are accepting a document, retaining the original for an audit, and later granting a controlled reader access to it. That makes access control the first constraint and delivery simplicity the second.

Short answer: choose Amazon S3 when multi-region durability and a deep API surface are the deciding factors. Choose Azure Blob Storage when the rest of the business already lives in Microsoft services. Google Cloud Storage is a sensible fit for very large datasets and pay-per-use operation. Infrai is worth trying when the team wants one self-describing REST surface and presigned storage access without adding another SDK, but it is not the right boundary for public assets, WORM retention, or self-managed browser CORS.

The effective bill is more than stored gigabytes. It includes egress, hot versus cool versus archive access, ingress assumptions, CORS work, retry logic, audit controls, and the number of vendor-specific integration paths someone must operate six months later.

What does the receipt workflow actually need?

For each receipt, the application should create an opaque object key, keep the original file private, and issue a time-limited signed URL to the intended reader. The metadata belongs in the application database: tenant, uploader, checksum, review state, retention date, and the object key. That split keeps storage useful for bytes and the database useful for business queries.

The hard boundary is auditability. If an employee overwrites receipts/acme/2026/10/24.pdf, a plain private bucket does not automatically give the reviewer the previous bytes. Infrai's storage caveats matter here: there is no object versioning or object lock, no If-Match conditional write, and lifecycle rules cannot expire objects more frequently than once per day. A financial-grade immutable record needs an external control or a specialist storage product.

Browser uploads add another trap. CORS has to be configured where the object service enforces it. Infrai exposes a bucket model with cors_rules, but there is no independent set-CORS route available for self-service configuration in this workflow. That makes a server-mediated upload, or a provider with the CORS controls you need, the cleaner choice for direct browser uploads.

The smallest useful implementation

The storage adapter should return a signed upload URL, never a public URL. This small adapter asks the self-describing REST storage surface for one. The browser sends the file to the returned URL; it does not receive the service credential.

type PresignResponse = Record<string, unknown>;

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

export async function createReceiptUpload(
  bucket: string,
  key: string,
): Promise<PresignResponse> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
      {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
      },
    );

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryAfter * 1000));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`presign failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return (await response.json()) as PresignResponse;
  }

  throw new Error("presign rate limit persisted after retries");
}

There are three deliberate details here. The object key is supplied by the application, the object is private by default, and the signed URL is short-lived. The upload endpoint is not an application download endpoint, and the application does not forward its authorization header to the returned URL. For a browser flow, validate file type and size before issuing the URL, then record the key only after the upload succeeds.

That is the whole game.

Keep it private.

A real receipt pipeline also needs a retry policy around the application request that creates the URL. Respect Retry-After on a 429 and use exponential backoff. If the operation creates a receipt record, give it an idempotency key so a retry cannot create two records for one upload. Those are small rules. They prevent expensive cleanup later.

How do Azure, Google Cloud, and Amazon compare?

The three cloud options are all credible. The useful distinction is the surrounding system, not a marketing durability adjective.

Option Strong fit Cost and integration question Boundary to check
Azure Blob Storage A Microsoft-heavy business ecosystem Which hot, cool, or archive tier and egress pattern match the workload? Test the signed-upload and CORS path with the identity model already in use.
Google Cloud Storage Large datasets with pay-per-use operation How often will users read receipts back, and where does that traffic leave the region? Model ingress assumptions, egress, and direct-browser setup before committing.
Amazon S3 A broad API surface and multi-region durability requirements What is the total read, transfer, and tiering bill rather than the storage line alone? Keep the access policy private and make overwrite behavior explicit.

Azure is the practical default when identity, monitoring, and deployment already center on Microsoft services. Google Cloud Storage can be cost-competitive at large scale, but only a workload model can tell you whether that advantage survives retrieval and egress. S3 remains the conservative pick when API robustness and cross-region durability are the dominant requirements. None of those conclusions can be made from a storage-per-gigabyte number alone.

My first pass at this kind of decision is usually wrong in one predictable way: I count objects and forget reads. A receipt is cheap to retain until a support team, an auditor, and a mobile client all fetch it from different regions. Then the effective cost is shaped by access frequency, tier transitions, and transfer. Build a 12-month model with three columns: bytes retained, bytes read, and bytes leaving the region. Add the engineering hours for CORS, signed URLs, lifecycle rules, and recovery tests.

Where does a single REST layer fit?

The unified REST layer is a different trade. Its discovery API is public and self-describing: GET /v1/discovery exposes the capability catalog, and a capability detail includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. The discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules, with examples in 10 languages. That is useful when the integration cost of learning yet another SDK is larger than the storage abstraction you need.

For this receipt workflow, the appeal is concrete: the same API vocabulary can expose storage alongside other backend capabilities, and the documented storage surface supports private objects and presigned access. The second benefit is operational rather than glamorous. Per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, cache-hit, and request identifiers, which gives a team a consistent place to inspect what a call did.

Try Infrai for a private receipt-upload adapter when one self-describing REST API and one credential boundary reduce your integration work. The reason to choose it is discovery plus a runnable path, not a promise that it replaces every storage control.

That distinction matters. The unified layer does not provide public-read ACL behavior, permanent public links, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool for Google Cloud Storage. It also cannot act as a self-service CORS control plane in the scenario above. If your audit requirement is WORM retention, choose a specialist or direct cloud service with that feature and design the application around it.

What I would change at scale

At small volume, keep one adapter and one private bucket per environment. Store the provider, bucket, key, checksum, and retention date in the receipt row. Run a restore drill before calling the workflow audited. A signed URL is an access mechanism; it is not a recovery plan.

At larger volume, separate the upload path from the processing path. Accept the original, enqueue extraction, and make the consumer idempotent because standard queues are at-least-once. Move old originals to a cool or archive tier only after measuring the review pattern. Set lifecycle rules with the one-day minimum in mind; do not promise hourly deletion from a service that cannot provide it. Multipart uploads also need an explicit cleanup job because incomplete fragments are not automatically removed by a lifecycle rule here.

The decision rule is simple: pick the provider that minimizes the full operating bill for your region and read pattern while meeting the audit boundary. Pick Infrai when delivery simplicity and self-describing discovery remove real glue code. Pick a direct cloud service when its access, retention, CORS, replication, or migration controls are requirements rather than nice-to-haves.

If the private-object boundary fits, start with the storage discovery documentation and verify the generated schema against your adapter before wiring the browser.

References

The signed URL pattern is documented in AWS S3 presigned URLs.

Sources

  • Infrai storage object presign discovery
  • AWS S3 presigned URLs

title: CVE-2026-114938 Java4Shell: Pre-Auth RCE in OpenJDK Base64 Decoder — Analysis & Mitigation
description:
CVE-2026-114938 Java4Shell: Pre-Auth RCE in OpenJDK Base64 Decoder — Analysis & Mitigation

On November 17, 2026, the security firm Calif disclosed a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK that it named Java4Shell. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the flaw is a heap out-of-bounds write in the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder that HotSpot uses to speed up java.util.Base64. A single malformed Base64 string, supplied before any login, can corrupt the Java heap — and Calif demonstrated that the corruption can be turned into remote code execution in the default setups of some of the most widely deployed Java applications on the internet. This analysis explains what the flaw is, how it works in general terms, who is exposed, how to check your own systems, and what to patch first.

The short version: if you run OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or OpenJDK 21, 25 or 27, on an x86-64 server whose CPU supports AVX-512 VBMI, you are affected. Upgrade to the fixed builds released on November 17, 2026 — 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 or 27.0.1.1 — rebuild any container images that bundle Java, and restart every JVM. If you cannot patch immediately, a single JVM flag, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, disables the vulnerable code path. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 are not affected.

What Is Java4Shell?

Java4Shell is a memory-corruption vulnerability in the OpenJDK Base64 decoder. Base64 is the encoding Java applications use constantly: HTTP Basic authentication credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, JSON Web Tokens, MIME attachments and API keys are all routinely Base64-decoded before a user is authenticated. That is what makes this flaw so dangerous — the vulnerable code runs on data an attacker controls, before any login check.

The bug lives in a hand-written, hardware-accelerated routine inside the HotSpot compiler. When the just-in-time compiler sees a hot Base64 decode loop on a capable CPU, it swaps the portable Java decoder for a vectorized native stub that uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions to decode many bytes at once. The flaw is in that stub, in the component OpenJDK lists as hotspot/compiler. Because the bug is in the JVM itself rather than in any application, no application code change can dodge it — every Java application running on a vulnerable JVM is exposed through the same path.

Calif found the flaw with AI assistance and reported it to Oracle ahead of the scheduled fix. The name Java4Shell follows the pattern of earlier landmark Java flaws: a single crafted input, no authentication, and a straight line to code execution. The vulnerable code was introduced as a performance optimization in OpenJDK pull request #4368, merged on June 25, 2021 — which means the flaw has been present in every affected release line for more than five years before anyone noticed it.

How CVE-2026-114938 Works

To understand the flaw, it helps to know how Base64 decoding works. Valid Base64 input comes in groups of four characters, each group decoding to three bytes, with = padding filling out the final group when the input length is not a multiple of three. The decoder computes how many output bytes a given input will produce, allocates a destination buffer of that size, and then writes the decoded bytes into it.

The bug is in how the accelerated decoder handles malformed padding. When the input ends with padding that should not be there — for example, a complete set of valid groups followed by a stray = — the decoder strips the padding with a subtraction that goes negative. That underflow produces a wrong output length, and the mask the decoder builds from it opens wider than the destination buffer. The vector write then lands past the end of the allocated buffer, corrupting adjacent memory on the Java heap.

At best, that corruption crashes the JVM, which is a denial of service. At worst, an attacker who controls the decoded data can overwrite heap structures — object headers, array lengths and pointers — in a way that eventually redirects execution to attacker-controlled code. That is how a decoding error becomes remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in the default setups of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and post-authentication code execution in Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Each target needs its own exploit chain, the attack is sensitive to network latency, and a failed attempt can crash the JVM — but the demonstrations prove the path from a malformed Base64 string to code execution is real.

Calif has published a bounded trigger that proves a JVM is vulnerable, and crash-level proof-of-concept code is public. The full application exploit chains are being held back by the researchers for now, which is the window defenders have: inventory and patch before those chains circulate. There is also a client-side route — a Java client that decodes Base64 from a malicious server over a TLS connection can be attacked the same way — so the exposure is not limited to servers.

Impact and Exposure

The exposure is large because Java is everywhere, but it is narrower than the headline suggests, and defenders should understand the two conditions that must both be true. First, the JVM must be a vulnerable build: OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or any release of the 21, 25 or 27 lines before the November 17 fixes, from any vendor — Oracle, Temurin, Corretto, Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat, Liberica, SapMachine or GraalVM. Second, the server must run on an x86-64 CPU that exposes the AVX-512 VBMI instructions — Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward, or AMD EPYC from Zen 4 onward, which includes common cloud instance types. ARM servers are not affected, and neither are older x86-64 CPUs without those instructions.

Both conditions must hold, and the application must also decode attacker-controlled Base64 — which, as noted above, most web applications do before login. Red Hat notes that HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens and MIME encoded words are routinely decoded before authentication, which is why internet-facing identity and collaboration software tops the priority list: Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate first, then Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker, and then every product, appliance or container image that bundles its own Java runtime.

Two facts keep the situation from being worse. First, as of late November 2026, the flaw has not been added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and Cisco and AWS have said they know of no malicious use. Second, fixed packages reached the major Linux distributions within days: by November 20, RHEL 8, 9 and 10, Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine and Amazon Linux had shipped fixed Java packages. That is not a reason to relax. A public crash proof of concept already exists, the full exploit chains are only being held back rather than impossible, and history says the window between disclosure and weaponization is short.

Who Is Affected

OpenJDK lineAffected versionsFixed build
1717.0.6 through 17.0.21.017.0.21.1
2121 through 21.0.13.021.0.13.1
2525 through 25.0.5.025.0.5.1
2727 through 27.0.1.027.0.1.1
18–20, 22–24, 26Every release (end-of-life lines)No fix — upgrade to a supported line
8 and 11Not affectedNo change needed

Two scoring disagreements are worth understanding, because they explain why different advisories quote different numbers for the same flaw. OpenJDK and the CVE record publish a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1, with a high attack-complexity metric, because exploitation needs both a vulnerable CPU and an application that decodes attacker-supplied Base64. Calif, the discoverer, scores it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Red Hat's preliminary score is 9.8. Atlassian also scores it 9.2. The gap is a judgement about how common the preconditions are, not a disagreement about the bug. For an internet-facing Java application, the preconditions are common enough that the higher scores are the honest ones to plan around — and this post carries both, so readers can see the full picture.

One trap deserves a warning. The Java version a server reports does not always tell you whether it is patched. Vendors ship fixed builds under the same feature version, and container images bundle their own JVMs, so checking java -version on the host is not enough. Check the exact build number, check the Java bundled inside every container image and appliance, and confirm against your vendor's advisory. A server that looks old but is actually fixed can be left alone, but a server that looks fine while its container still carries a vulnerable JVM is the one that gets compromised.

How to Detect It

Detection is harder than usual for this flaw, and defenders should know why before they start hunting. The attack traffic is an ordinary-looking request carrying a malformed Base64 value — a credential, a token, a SAML artifact — inside an encrypted TLS connection. Web access logs show almost nothing distinctive about an attempt, and the vulnerable code runs before authentication, so there is no failed-login trail to follow either.

Start with JVM stability, because a memory-corruption attempt usually leaves crashes behind before anything else. Look for JVM crashes, heap corruption errors and unexpected JVM restarts on Java services, and correlate them with inbound traffic. Repeated crashes on a Java service that decodes attacker-controlled Base64, especially alongside spikes in connections, should be investigated rather than dismissed as routine instability. A failed exploitation attempt can crash the JVM, so a cluster of crashes may be the first sign that someone is working through the exploit chain.

Next, inventory rather than hunt. The most reliable detection for this flaw is knowing where vulnerable JVMs run. List every Java runtime in the environment — hosts, containers, appliances and build pipelines — and record the exact build and the CPU it runs on. Anything on OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or on the 21, 25 or 27 lines before the November 17 builds, running on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, is exposed. Prioritize internet-facing identity and collaboration software first, then anything that decodes Base64 from untrusted input, then the long tail of bundled JVMs in appliances and images.

Then check processes and the network. A Java process that spawns a shell, or any unexpected child process running under the application user, is the loudest single signal of a successful compromise. Look for new or modified files under the application directory outside a change window, and for outbound connections from Java servers to unfamiliar hosts after a burst of requests. If the endpoint was reachable from the internet, check the host for compromise before patching over it — patching removes the hole, but it does not remove an attacker who already got in.

How to Fix It

Patching is straightforward, and the order matters. First, upgrade the Java runtime to a fixed build: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 or 27.0.1.1, or your Linux distribution's fixed package. Oracle's fixed releases shipped on November 17, 2026, and the major distributions followed within days. Rebuild every container image that bundles Java — patching the host JVM does nothing for a container that carries its own — and restart every JVM. A running JVM keeps using the old, vulnerable code until it restarts, so the restart step matters as much as the upgrade.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, disable the vulnerable code path with a single JVM flag: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. That turns off the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder and falls back to the portable implementation, which is not affected. Vendors confirm the flag has no meaningful performance impact for most applications, and it works on every affected version, so it is the right emergency mitigation while patching is scheduled. End-of-life lines — 18 through 20, 22 through 24 and 26 — have no fix at all and must be upgraded to a supported line.

After patching, verify rather than assume. Confirm the running build number on every JVM, including the ones inside containers, and re-run the exposure check. Calif's bounded trigger can prove whether a JVM is still vulnerable, which is more reliable than trusting a version string. Treat any internet-facing Java service that was reachable before the patch as potentially probed: review its logs and process history for the crash and compromise signals described above.

Lessons for Defenders

The first lesson is about where trust lives in a Java stack. Applications assume the JVM is a safe foundation, and most of the time it is — but Java4Shell is a reminder that the runtime itself is attack surface. A flaw in a standard-library decoder reaches every application that uses it, without a single line of application code being wrong. Runtime patching belongs in the same priority tier as application patching, and container images that bundle their own JVM need the same discipline as the hosts they run on.

The second lesson is about performance optimizations. The vulnerable code was a hand-written, hardware-specific fast path, introduced to make Base64 decoding faster on modern CPUs. Hand-written vector code is exactly the kind of code where a small arithmetic mistake becomes a memory-safety catastrophe, and it is also the kind of code that is hardest to review — the bug survived five years in one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world. When a fast path handles untrusted input, it deserves the same scrutiny as any parser.

The third lesson is about preconditions. Java4Shell needs a specific CPU, a specific JVM range and attacker-controlled Base64 — and yet it still reaches the most important Java applications on the internet, because those preconditions are ordinary in production. "It needs a modern server CPU" is not a meaningful defense when modern server CPUs are the default. Score a vulnerability by how common its preconditions are in your environment, not by how many conditions it has.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Java4Shell being exploited in the wild?

As of late November 2026, no exploitation in the wild has been reported, and the flaw is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Calif has demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in the lab and is holding back the full exploit chains. The absence of reported exploitation is a window, not a verdict.

Am I affected if my server uses an ARM CPU?

No. The vulnerable code only runs on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI instructions. ARM servers, and older x86-64 CPUs without those instructions, do not take the vulnerable path. Check your CPU flags before assuming either way.

Does Java 8 or Java 11 need patching?

No. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 do not contain the vulnerable code. Oracle's Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack has a fixed build, 8u513-perf, for the performance-pack variant only.

What does the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics flag do?

It disables the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder and makes the JVM use the portable Java implementation instead. That removes the vulnerable code path entirely, with no meaningful performance impact for most applications. It is the recommended emergency mitigation while patching is scheduled.

Why do different advisories show different CVSS scores?

OpenJDK and the CVE record score it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1, with high attack complexity, because exploitation needs a vulnerable CPU and an application that decodes attacker-controlled Base64. Calif scores it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 and Red Hat's preliminary score is 9.8, reflecting the view that those preconditions are common in production. Both scores describe the same flaw.

title: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports OpenSearch version 3.9
description:
You can now run OpenSearch version 3.9 on Amazon OpenSearch Service. OpenSearch 3.9 helps you reduce vector memory and storage, evaluate search quality with more large language model (LLM) providers, build more responsive AI agents, and control access to shared resources.

This release adds a new half-float vector type and a bf16 encoder, which store each vector dimension in 16 bits to reduce the memory and storage your vector indexes need. New 2-bit and 4-bit scalar quantization lets you choose the right balance of compression and recall for each workload. Base64-encoded vector ingestion makes request payloads smaller, which speeds up bulk loading. In addition, radial search now uses a redesigned graph traversal to improve both recall and throughput. In Search Relevance Workbench, LLM-as-a-Judge now works with Amazon Bedrock and other LLM providers through ML Commons connectors. You can also retry failed documents, edit ratings, and reuse earlier judgments to reduce repeated LLM calls.

OpenSearch 3.9 also adds gRPC streaming for model predictions and agent execution. Responses come back token by token, so your agentic applications can show answers as they’re generated. Finally, the new resource sharing and access control framework allows you to share resources such as anomaly detectors and machine learning models with specific users and roles without granting broad access.

OpenSearch 3.9 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Service is offered. To learn how to upgrade, see Upgrading Amazon OpenSearch Service domains in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

title: Go Backend API Evidence for React Native SMS OTP Recovery (3 Suppression Controls)
description:
Consider the page a property-management platform should be able to raise: a React Native mobile app completed SMS OTP administrator recovery, but its backend sent the security notice to an email address already marked invalid. The on-call needs the challenge identifier, notice identifier, destination version, and suppression decision together. A green SMS delivery indicator cannot explain why an invalid mailbox was selected.

TL;DR: use a server-owned SMS OTP challenge and a versioned suppression ledger, joined by one recovery event identifier. For a mobile app, autofill is a convenience; verification, resend eligibility, and evidence of the notice decision belong in the backend. The least complex useful design is an existing transactional database plus an outbox, with three explicit controls: challenge validity, recipient eligibility, and recorded dispatch authorization. Treat these as proposed controls, not evidence that a deployment already meets a legal obligation.

Preserve the evidence.

The property-management case makes the distinction practical: restoring access for a SaaS administrator may trigger a security notice, while that administrator's email address may have a previous permanent delivery failure. Suppressing that address must not silently mark the notice delivered, and an email bounce must not automatically invalidate the administrator's separately enrolled telephone number. Those are different destinations with different evidence.

What signal should have fired before the recovery page?

Work backward from that hypothetical page. The earlier signal is a notice authorized against an obsolete recipient decision, or an unprocessed delivery event old enough that the eligibility check cannot be trusted. Counting bounced messages alone misses both conditions, especially if no new send occurs after an address becomes invalid.

SMTP distinguishes temporary failures from permanent failures; enhanced status codes add a class, subject, and detail. RFC 5321 and RFC 3463 provide the vocabulary, but a broad permanent-failure class does not prove that a mailbox is nonexistent. A policy rejection and an invalid destination require different operational treatment. Persist the original status and its normalized interpretation, and make the rule that creates a suppression reviewable. Google's sender guidelines also make bounce handling and recipient hygiene relevant to deliverability, though those guidelines do not establish compliance for an administrator recovery workflow.

A useful proposed record links property account property-17, administrator admin-42, challenge challenge-8, notice notice-9, and email destination version 4. These are illustrative identifiers. Record the delivery event's source identifier, event time, ingestion time, classification rule version, and the resulting eligibility decision. Avoid putting the OTP or complete destination into logs; use an internal destination identifier and restrict access to the underlying contact record.

The evidence is the decision history. A dashboard total is only an index into it.

A compliance reviewer needs to distinguish a notice never requested, a notice deliberately suppressed, a submission accepted for delivery, and an outcome reported later. None of those states proves that the administrator read the notice. Define the retention period, access permissions, and correction process with the people who own the applicable obligations instead of treating an indefinitely retained log as inherently sufficient.

How should a React Native mobile app authorize SMS OTP recovery?

The mobile app can request a challenge, submit the entered code, and request a resend. Its UI should show the backend's retry time and a masked destination already enrolled for the administrator. React Native exposes text-input properties for OTP autofill, with platform-specific behavior documented in its TextInput reference. Autofill supplies input; it must travel through the same verification operation as a code typed by hand. Don't turn receipt of a message into automatic administrative access.

For a concrete backend API example, define three operations in prose: create a recovery challenge, verify a challenge, and request another delivery for that challenge. A successful create response carries an opaque challenge identifier, an expiry time, and a retry time. A verification request carries that identifier and the submitted code. A resend response updates the delivery state and retry time without extending the original recovery window. Keep account-existence responses generic, including the path where no eligible destination exists.

Use server time.

For this example, the challenge expires after five minutes, and a repeat SMS request must wait 60 seconds; validate both policies against delivery latency and the administrator support process. They aren't measured performance or universal safe defaults. NIST's authentication guidance treats PSTN-based out-of-band authentication as restricted and calls for controls including rate limiting and one-time acceptance; an organization must assess whether this channel is appropriate for privileged recovery at all. A lost-phone recovery route needs separate identity assurance and audit evidence. Allowing an unauthenticated caller to replace the enrolled number defeats the boundary.

The backend should generate codes with a cryptographically secure random source and protect the stored verifier against offline guessing; a keyed verifier with its key held separately is one possible design. Verification must atomically consume the challenge on success, reject expiration, and debit the attempt budget on failure. Resending must not reset that budget. Limit both verification and issuance across the account, destination, and network signals, because an attacker can distribute requests across challenge identifiers or IP addresses.

Make the three checks visible in the Go backend

The following Go example isolates the resend policy so its inputs can be logged as a decision. It assumes an authenticated internal caller has loaded the challenge and the eligibility of its enrolled SMS destination. Email suppression is evaluated separately when authorizing the recovery notice. The function neither verifies an OTP nor provides a complete abuse limiter.

package recovery

import "time"

type Challenge struct {
    ExpiresAt    time.Time
    NextSendAt   time.Time
    Consumed     bool
    AttemptsLeft int
    SendsLeft    int
}

type ResendDecision struct {
    Allowed bool
    Reason  string
}

func DecideResend(
    now time.Time,
    c Challenge,
    smsEligible bool,
    abuseAllowed bool,
) ResendDecision {
    switch {
    case c.Consumed:
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "challenge_consumed"}
    case !now.Before(c.ExpiresAt):
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "challenge_expired"}
    case c.AttemptsLeft <= 0 || c.SendsLeft <= 0:
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "budget_exhausted"}
    case !smsEligible:
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "destination_ineligible"}
    case now.Before(c.NextSendAt):
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "retry_later"}
    case !abuseAllowed:
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "abuse_limit"}
    default:
        return ResendDecision{Allowed: true, Reason: "authorized"}
    }
}

The dangerous gap is between returning authorized and submitting a message. Two workers can both pass this function against the same snapshot. In the real handler, serialize the challenge update, reserve the applicable abuse budgets, decrement the send budget, set the next retry time, and insert the outbound intent in one transaction or an equivalent coordinated reservation protocol. An outbox worker can then process that intent. Record the destination version and policy version used for authorization so a later reviewer can reconstruct the decision.

An outbox doesn't by itself create exactly-once external delivery. A timeout can leave submission ambiguous, so use transport idempotency where supported and otherwise retain an explicit unknown state for reconciliation. Blindly retrying an ambiguous SMS submission can deliver duplicates and spend the administrator's remaining patience.

Delivery feedback needs its own boundary: authenticate incoming events using the transport's documented mechanism, deduplicate by source event identity, and preserve both occurrence and receipt times. A delayed success must not erase a newer suppression decision merely because its webhook arrived last. Define precedence for conflicting events and retain corrections as new decisions. For an email recipient correction, verify the corrected address under the account's recovery policy before lifting suppression; repeating a failed send isn't verification.

Instrument evidence before choosing an operating model

Add a structured authorization event to each outbound intent, then connect it to subsequent delivery feedback. Measure the age of the oldest unprocessed feedback, the count of notices blocked by suppression, and the fraction of dispatch decisions with complete evidence. Keep account and challenge identifiers in access-controlled logs or traces rather than metric labels; unrestricted identifier cardinality makes capacity planning harder while exposing unnecessary detail.

A proposed evidence SLO is that 99.9% of recovery notice decisions become queryable with their policy and destination versions within 60 seconds. That is a design target, not a reported result. Define the denominator to include suppressed decisions and processing failures, or the system can appear healthy while the most interesting records disappear. Separately monitor delivery and successful verification. Evidence availability cannot stand in for either.

For capacity planning, estimate event ingestion from peak authorized sends multiplied by observed feedback events per send, then account for retries and replay. Size the backlog for an outage and measure the drain rate before adopting the SLO. The example's resend interval alone cannot bound traffic across a portfolio of properties or distributed attackers.

Operating choice Evidence boundary to verify On-call and ownership trade-off
Managed delivery with an application-owned ledger Submission identifiers, feedback authentication, retention and export guarantees Less transport work; the platform still owns suppression policy and reconciliation
Self-hosted delivery and an application-owned ledger Queue durability, delivery-status processing, retained decision history More control over raw events; transport operations and reputation become team responsibilities
Managed delivery with periodic evidence exports Export delay, missing-event detection, correction history Simpler ingestion initially; the evidence SLO is constrained by export behavior

Buy versus build starts with who can explain a missing notice during an audit. Evaluate operational staffing, integration maintenance, retention costs, and the ability to move the ledger without losing event meaning. No transport purchase transfers the application's responsibility for authorizing recovery.

Before deployment, replay synthetic duplicate, delayed, and out-of-order feedback; run concurrent resend requests; and verify the exact expiry boundary. Test that a permanently invalid email blocks the email notice without altering SMS eligibility, and that a suppressed notice still produces a queryable decision. Roll out classification changes against recorded events before letting them change recipient eligibility. A rule that increases suppression should be explainable by status category and reviewed examples.

Close the alert loop carefully. Page on an evidence gap that threatens the agreed SLO, while routing isolated suppression decisions into a review queue unless the business impact justifies waking someone. An aggressive bounce threshold can suppress valid contacts after temporary failures; an aggressive SMS abuse threshold can strand an administrator during recovery. Those false positives create manual identity checks and delayed access, so measure review volume and confirmed erroneous suppressions alongside the original alert. The threshold is acceptable only when the team can defend both the missed-event risk and the cost of blocking a legitimate administrator.

References

The SMTP specifications support delivery classification; the sender guidelines cover deliverability expectations. Authentication and client-input references support separate parts of the recovery flow. The transaction design, sample identifiers, intervals, and SLO above are proposed implementation choices.

  • Enhanced mail system status codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3463
  • Email sender guidelines: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126
  • Authentication and out-of-band requirements: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html
  • Mobile text input and autofill properties: https://reactnative.dev/docs/textinput

Further reading
