title: Bitmap: uma estrutura de dados com mais de 70 anos de história
description:
Bitmap é uma técnica de representação de dados que utiliza bits para armazenar informações de maneira compacta e permitir operações eficientes.

Embora o termo seja frequentemente associado a imagens e arquivos .bmp, seu uso na computação vai muito além dos formatos gráficos.

Representações baseadas em bits aparecem em sistemas operacionais, bancos de dados, mecanismos de busca, algoritmos de jogos e aplicações que precisam manipular grandes conjuntos de informações.

E o mais interessante: a ideia já era utilizada nos primeiros anos da computação digital, muito antes dos computadores pessoais.

Neste artigo, vamos entender sua história, seu funcionamento, suas aplicações e como utilizá-la em Java.

O que é um bitmap?

Um bitmap é uma representação de informações por meio de uma sequência de bits.

Cada bit pode assumir apenas dois estados:

  • 0: desligado, falso ou ausente.
  • 1: ligado, verdadeiro ou presente.

O significado desses estados depende do problema que queremos resolver.

Imagine que precisamos armazenar um conjunto contendo os números 1, 4 e 6.

Uma implementação convencional poderia utilizar um array:

int[] numbers = {1, 4, 6};

Em um bitmap, podemos representar o mesmo conjunto assim:

Posição:  0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
          ---------------
Bits:     0 1 0 0 1 0 1 0

Cada posição corresponde a um número.

Se o bit estiver ativado, o número pertence ao conjunto.

Assim, consultar o número 4 significa verificar diretamente o bit da posição 4.

Não é necessário percorrer os demais números.

Essa forma de representar pertencimento a conjuntos é conhecida como bitset, ou vetor de bits.

É importante distinguir os termos: bitmap é um conceito amplo de representação de informações por bits; bitset costuma designar especificamente uma estrutura utilizada para representar conjuntos.

Uma história que começa nos anos 1950

Não existe uma data universalmente reconhecida para a invenção do bitmap como estrutura de dados.

Entretanto, representações semelhantes aos bitsets atuais já eram utilizadas nos primeiros computadores digitais.

1952: o programa de damas de Christopher Strachey

Uma das aplicações históricas mais interessantes aparece no programa de damas desenvolvido pelo cientista da computação britânico Christopher Strachey.

Em 1952, seu programa já conseguia disputar partidas completas no computador Ferranti Mark 1, da Universidade de Manchester.

Um dos desafios era representar o estado do tabuleiro utilizando recursos computacionais extremamente limitados.

A solução empregava três palavras de 32 bits, utilizadas para identificar posições de peças pretas, peças brancas e damas.

Cada uma das 32 casas jogáveis do tabuleiro correspondia a uma posição de bit.

Ao ativar ou desativar determinados bits, o programa podia representar alterações no estado do jogo.

Essa técnica ficou conhecida como bitboard.

Em vez de armazenar cada casa como uma estrutura independente, era possível representar grande parte do estado do tabuleiro utilizando apenas algumas palavras de memória.

Essa abordagem também permitia aproveitar operações lógicas e deslocamentos de bits para trabalhar com posições e movimentos.

O projeto foi posteriormente reconstruído e documentado pela Computer Conservation Society.

1959: Arthur Samuel e o aprendizado de máquina

Outro exemplo histórico aparece no trabalho de Arthur Samuel, pesquisador da IBM.

Em 1959, ele publicou o artigo Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers.

O estudo apresentava um programa capaz de melhorar seu desempenho no jogo de damas a partir da experiência.

Para representar o tabuleiro, Samuel utilizava posições de bits dentro de palavras de memória do IBM 704.

Com essa representação, operações de deslocamento e operações lógicas podiam auxiliar nos cálculos relacionados ao jogo.

É interessante observar que técnicas de manipulação de bits já eram utilizadas em pesquisas pioneiras de inteligência artificial.

A lógica por trás da otimização continua relevante: representar dados adequadamente pode reduzir significativamente o trabalho necessário para processá-los.

Como um bitmap funciona na memória?

Para entender sua eficiência, precisamos olhar um pouco mais de perto para a representação binária.

Um byte contém oito bits.

Portanto, com apenas um byte, conseguimos representar oito condições independentes.

Por exemplo:

Bits:  1 0 1 0 0 1 1 0

Dependendo da aplicação, cada posição poderia representar uma permissão, um recurso ocupado ou a presença de determinado elemento.

Em Java, o tipo long possui 64 bits.

Isso significa que podemos representar 64 indicadores de pertencimento utilizando apenas um long.

long bitmap = 0L;

Inicialmente, todos os bits estão desligados.

Para ativar o bit da posição 5:

bitmap |= (1L << 5);

O operador << desloca os bits para a esquerda.

A expressão 1L << 5 cria uma máscara com o bit 5 ativado.

Já o operador |= realiza uma operação OR bit a bit, preservando os bits anteriormente ativados.

Para verificar se o bit está ligado:

boolean exists =
    (bitmap & (1L << 5)) != 0;

O operador & realiza um AND bit a bit.

Se o resultado for diferente de zero, significa que o bit consultado estava ativado.

Para desativar a posição:

bitmap &= ~(1L << 5);

E para alternar seu estado:

bitmap ^= (1L << 5);

Com essas operações conseguimos manipular conjuntos de informações diretamente sobre a representação binária.

Representando milhares de valores

Um único long consegue representar até 64 posições.

Mas e se precisarmos representar 10 mil valores possíveis?

Podemos utilizar um array de long:

long[] bitmap = new long[157];

Cada long possui 64 bits.

Portanto:

10.000 / 64 = 156,25

Arredondando para cima: 157 longs

Como cada long ocupa oito bytes:

157 × 8 = 1.256 bytes

Isso representa aproximadamente 1,23 KiB de dados, desconsiderando o cabeçalho do array e seu alinhamento na JVM.

Para ativar o bit correspondente ao valor 5411, primeiro precisamos encontrar a posição correta.

int value = 5411;

int wordIndex = value >>> 6;
int bitIndex = value & 63;

O resultado será:

wordIndex = 84
bitIndex  = 35

O deslocamento de seis bits equivale à divisão inteira por 64 para valores não negativos.

Já a operação & 63 equivale a obter o resto dessa divisão.

Agora podemos ativar o bit:

bitmap[wordIndex] |= 1L << bitIndex;

E consultá-lo:

boolean exists =
    (bitmap[wordIndex] & (1L << bitIndex)) != 0;

Assim, uma consulta encontra diretamente a palavra e o bit desejados, sem realizar uma busca sequencial.

Para um domínio numérico limitado e diretamente indexável, o custo da consulta é O(1).

Java já possui a classe BitSet

Não é necessário implementar manualmente todas essas operações.

A biblioteca padrão do Java disponibiliza a classe java.util.BitSet desde suas primeiras versões.

Ela oferece uma API para armazenar e manipular conjuntos representados por bits.

Veja um exemplo:

import java.util.BitSet;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BitSet numbers = new BitSet();

        numbers.set(1);
        numbers.set(4);
        numbers.set(6);

        System.out.println(numbers.get(4)); // true
        System.out.println(numbers.get(3)); // false

        System.out.println(numbers); // {1, 4, 6}
    }
}

O método set() ativa um bit.

O método get() verifica seu estado.

O método clear() permite desativá-lo.

A classe também disponibiliza outras operações:

Método Finalidade
set(index) Ativa um bit
get(index) Consulta um bit
clear(index) Desativa um bit
flip(index) Inverte um bit
cardinality() Conta os bits ativados
and(other) Interseção
or(other) União
xor(other) Diferença simétrica
nextSetBit(index) Encontra o próximo bit ativado

A documentação completa está disponível em java.util.BitSet — Java 21.

Um detalhe importante: BitSet é uma estrutura mutável e não é automaticamente segura para modificações concorrentes. Aplicações multithread precisam considerar sincronização, encapsulamento ou publicação de estruturas que não serão modificadas.

Operações entre conjuntos utilizando bits

Uma das características mais interessantes dos bitmaps é a possibilidade de combinar conjuntos por meio de operações bitwise.

Imagine dois conjuntos:

A = {1, 3, 5}
B = {3, 4, 5}

Suas representações binárias seriam:

Posição:  0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7

A:        0 1 0 1 0 1 0 0
B:        0 0 0 1 1 1 0 0

Se quisermos encontrar os elementos presentes nos dois conjuntos, basta utilizar AND:

A:        0 1 0 1 0 1 0 0
B:        0 0 0 1 1 1 0 0
          ---------------
AND:      0 0 0 1 0 1 0 0

O resultado representa o conjunto {3, 5}.

Em Java:

BitSet a = new BitSet();
a.set(1);
a.set(3);
a.set(5);

BitSet b = new BitSet();
b.set(3);
b.set(4);
b.set(5);

a.and(b);

System.out.println(a); // {3, 5}

Uma operação AND sobre palavras de 64 bits consegue combinar até 64 posições por palavra processada.

Isso é especialmente útil quando precisamos comparar ou combinar grandes conjuntos de informações.

Onde os bitmaps são utilizados?

A representação por bits aparece em diferentes áreas da computação.

1. Bancos de dados

Bancos de dados podem utilizar bitmap indexes para representar conjuntos de registros que atendem a determinadas condições.

Imagine uma tabela de usuários com informações sobre status e permissões.

Um bitmap pode representar os usuários ativos:

Ativos:     1 0 1 1 0 1

Outro pode representar usuários com determinada permissão:

Permissão:  1 1 0 1 0 1

Aplicando AND:

Resultado:  1 0 0 1 0 1

O resultado identifica os registros que atendem às duas condições.

Essa ideia é utilizada em mecanismos de indexação de bancos como o Oracle, especialmente em cenários analíticos e colunas com poucos valores distintos.

Os índices bitmap possuem características próprias e não substituem automaticamente índices B-tree.

Referência: Oracle Database — Bitmap Indexes.

2. Sistemas operacionais

Bitmaps podem representar recursos livres ou ocupados.

Por exemplo, um sistema pode utilizar bits para acompanhar a disponibilidade de blocos de armazenamento ou unidades de alocação.

Um bit indica que o recurso está livre; outro estado indica que está ocupado.

Isso permite representar grandes quantidades de estados utilizando relativamente pouca memória.

3. Controle de permissões e flags

Bits também podem representar permissões independentes.

Considere três permissões:

int READ    = 1 << 0;
int WRITE   = 1 << 1;
int EXECUTE = 1 << 2;

Podemos combiná-las:

int permissions = READ | WRITE;

E consultar uma permissão:

boolean canWrite =
    (permissions & WRITE) != 0;

Esse exemplo utiliza uma máscara de bits dentro de um único inteiro, em vez de um bitset extensível, mas o princípio de representação binária é o mesmo.

4. Mecanismos de busca e processamento analítico

Conjuntos de identificadores podem ser representados por bitmaps para acelerar operações de interseção, união e filtragem.

Uma família de estruturas especialmente interessante é a dos Roaring Bitmaps.

Ela combina diferentes representações internas, incluindo arrays e estruturas baseadas em bits, para lidar eficientemente com conjuntos de inteiros de diferentes densidades.

O objetivo é equilibrar consumo de memória e desempenho.

Mais informações: Roaring Bitmaps.

Bitmap, array ou HashSet?

Apesar das vantagens, bitmap não é necessariamente a melhor escolha para qualquer conjunto de valores.

Considere um problema de pertencimento:

Estrutura Busca Característica
Array não ordenado O(n) Simples, compacto para conjuntos pequenos
Array ordenado com busca binária O(log n) Pouca memória e busca por divisão
HashSet O(1) esperado Flexível para diferentes tipos de chaves
Bitmap diretamente indexado O(1) Eficiente para domínios numéricos limitados

Um bitmap diretamente indexado reserva posições de acordo com o domínio dos valores.

Se precisamos representar números de 0 a 9999, isso é relativamente barato.

Mas se os identificadores estiverem distribuídos por um domínio numérico extremamente grande, reservar um bit para cada valor possível pode ser inviável.

Por exemplo, um conjunto contendo apenas os números 1, 100 e 1.000.000.000 ocuparia pouquíssima memória em um array.

Já um bitmap diretamente indexado precisaria representar mais de um bilhão de posições, consumindo aproximadamente 125 MB apenas para três elementos.

Nesse caso, um array ou uma estrutura hash provavelmente seria mais apropriado.

É por isso que existem também estruturas de bitmap comprimido.

A escolha ideal depende da quantidade de elementos, da extensão do domínio numérico, da densidade do conjunto, das operações necessárias e do perfil de acesso.

Bitmap e performance

Uma característica importante dessa estrutura é que o espaço total reservado não corresponde à quantidade de memória acessada em cada consulta.

Um bitmap pode reservar milhares de bits, mas uma consulta individual normalmente precisa acessar apenas a palavra que contém o bit desejado.

Isso pode tornar verificações de pertencimento bastante rápidas.

Por outro lado, um bitmap grande pode ocupar mais espaço nos caches da CPU quando muitas estruturas diferentes são utilizadas.

Arrays pequenos, por sua vez, podem apresentar excelente localidade de memória e ser competitivos mesmo utilizando busca linear.

Portanto, não basta observar a complexidade O(1) do bitmap ou O(n) do array para determinar qual implementação terá menor latência real.

É necessário considerar custos constantes, layout de memória, distribuição dos dados, comportamento da CPU e resultados de benchmarks representativos.

Conclusão

Bitmap é uma técnica de representação de dados simples em sua ideia fundamental, mas com aplicações importantes em diversas áreas da computação.

Sua história remonta aos primeiros computadores digitais, passando por programas de jogos na década de 1950, sistemas de bancos de dados e aplicações modernas de processamento de informações.

Ao representar estados e conjuntos por meio de bits, podemos aproveitar diretamente operações lógicas oferecidas pelos processadores.

Entretanto, seu principal valor não está apenas na velocidade.

Está em permitir que determinados problemas sejam representados de uma forma mais adequada às características dos dados.

Antes de escolher um array, uma tabela hash ou uma estrutura mais sofisticada, vale compreender o domínio dos valores e as operações necessárias.

A maneira como representamos os dados pode ser tão importante quanto o algoritmo utilizado para processá-los.

Referências

  • Computer Conservation Society — Christopher Strachey's Draughts Program
  • Arthur Samuel — Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers (1959)
  • Oracle — java.util.BitSet
  • Oracle Database — Bitmap Indexes
  • Roaring Bitmaps

title: AWS WAF introduces simplified pricing
description:
AWS WAF now offers simplified pricing that follows what you protect instead of how you configure it. Previously, you paid separate charges for each web ACL, rule, rule group subscription, and capacity tier, making every security decision a billing calculation. Now, your bill follows three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply. This makes the cost-benefit trade-off easy to understand, and adding or changing rules no longer changes your rate.

The new model makes protection costs predictable before you deploy. Each web ACL now includes up to 2,500 WCU at no extra charge, up from 1,500, and you can add rules such as Bot Control common protections or the Anti-DDoS rule group without additional fees. You pay a resource fee for each protected resource, a base request fee for every request AWS WAF inspects, and a premium request fee only for traffic evaluated by advanced protections like Bot Control targeted protections, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security.

AWS WAF's new pricing is available today in all AWS commercial Regions, including Cape Town, Hong Kong, Hyderabad, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Zealand, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Thailand, Tokyo, Calgary, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain, Stockholm, Zurich, Tel Aviv, Sao Paulo, N. Virginia, Ohio, N. California, Oregon, as well as in AWS GovCloud, China Regions, and AWS Isolated Regions.

To learn more, visit the AWS WAF pricing page and review the AWS WAF Developer Guide as well as the blog post AWS WAF pricing now follows what you protect, not how you configure it.

title: AWS WAF announces automated discovery and protection for LLM, MCP, and A2A endpoints using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
description:
Automated AI endpoint discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover language model (LLM), Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent2Agent (A2A) endpoints behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF.

Discovery is available through the new API Gateway API Portal, which recognizes the AI endpoints among the APIs it discovers automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward. An undocumented, public-facing MCP server appears as a shadow API. For unprotected AI endpoints, customers can enable protection using WAF.

Protection is available through the new AWS WAF AI Security managed rule group, which protects your AI endpoints. AWS WAF implements protocol recognition and compliance checks to block malformed MCP and A2A messages. When you enable content inspection, the rule group calls Amazon Bedrock Guardrails InvokeGuardrailsCheck API to detect prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, harmful content in requests, and sensitive information in responses. You can use AI Security alongside other AWS Managed Rules or your own custom rules to protect your applications. Additional fees apply, and Amazon Bedrock charges separately for content inspection calls.

Together, API Portal and AI Security provide you a complete solution from discovery of all AI endpoints in your AWS environment to protecting them, without having to write any custom rules.

API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions. See the Amazon API Gateway FAQ for the list. AI Security is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Sydney).

title: Blobasaur and the 4th Cross way: how Zerodha's ~35-person tech team keeps shipping open source
description:
TL;DR: Zerodha just open-sourced Blobasaur, a sharded blob server written in Rust. It speaks the Redis Cluster protocol and stuffs everything into SQLite (yes, really). It serves chart layouts for about 20 million users at around 2 ms p99 on three small nodes. In this post I poke around how it works, meet the ~35-person team behind it, and then fall down the rabbit hole of side projects from the team and their CTO, Kailash Nadh.

🦖 A dinosaur that speaks Redis

On 19 November 2026, the Zerodha Tech blog dropped a post called "Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite" by engineer Sarat Chandra. It introduced Blobasaur:

  • a sharded blob server written in Rust
  • it speaks the Redis (Cluster) protocol
  • it stores everything in SQLite
  • a single binary, licensed AGPLv3
  • already in production behind Kite, Zerodha's trading platform

Redis is an in-memory cache. SQLite is an embedded file database. Seeing both in one sentence made me go "wait, what?" But the reasoning turns out to be pretty sensible, and it tells you a lot about how Zerodha builds software.

iamd3vil / blobasaur

A Blob store based on SQLite compatible with Redis protocol

Blobasaur

Blobasaur is a high-performance, sharded blob storage server written in Rust. It implements the Redis protocol for client compatibility and uses SQLite as the backend for each shard, providing a simple yet robust solution for storing and retrieving binary large objects (blobs).

Features

  • 🔄 Shard Migration: Built-in support for migrating data between different shard configurations with data integrity verification

The problem: 20 million people's chart layouts

Every Kite user customises something: chart layouts, indicator templates, drawings, and the multi-pane workspaces of the newer Terminal mode. Zerodha stores these preferences as blobs, mostly JSON, anywhere from a few KB to several MB each, for roughly 20 million customers.

The history of that store is a nice little lesson in trade-offs:

Store Why it was dropped
CouchDB Couldn't keep up with the throughput
SSDB Ran reliably for years, but was unmaintained, written in C++ outside their stack, and single-node. Large payloads hurt latency, which forced a 1 MB cap per blob

So the wishlist looked like this:

  • a simple key-value API
  • multi-MB blobs at bursty, market-driven throughput
  • horizontal scaling
  • good compression and low running costs
  • relaxed durability, because a lost chart layout is annoying but nowhere near as bad as a lost trade

What they ruled out

They did shop around before building anything:

Candidate Verdict
ScyllaDB, PostgreSQL Weak for large blobs
YugabyteDB, RocksDB Not built for multi-MB writes
Ceph Too complex to operate
SeaweedFS Closest fit, but disk growth under overwrites, no per-blob TTL, complex setup
S3 / MinIO Slow and expensive for small objects at this request rate
File-per-blob Would mean rebuilding atomic writes, batching and TTL indexing from scratch

Nothing fit, so they did the Zerodha thing and built their own.

How Blobasaur works

1. SQLite is the engine

SQLite hands you ACID transactions, crash recovery and decades of tooling for free. They picked Rust over Go to dodge CGo overhead and garbage-collector pressure from large buffers, and so they could ship one static binary.

2. Shards inside each node

SQLite allows only one writer per database file. The workaround is simple: each node splits its data across several SQLite files (shards).

  • Keys map to shards using multi-probe consistent hashing.
  • Each shard has a dedicated writer fed by a bounded queue that batches pending writes into a single transaction (group commit).
  • Reads go through a per-shard pool of read-only connections and run alongside writes.

In a 64 KiB benchmark, going from 1 to 16 shards:

Shards HSET throughput Median write latency
1 ~7,740 ops/s 8.2 ms
16 ~25,324 ops/s 2.1 ms

3. Redis Cluster on the outside

Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, so any cluster-aware Redis client just works. Routing happens at two levels:

key ──CRC16──▶ hash slot (1 of 16,384) ──▶ node
                                            │
                         consistent hash ──▶ SQLite shard on that node

If you're more of a pictures person, here's my rough sketch of the same thing:


My sketch of the two-level routing, based on the Zerodha post. Not an official diagram.

Nodes discover each other via gossip. For client code, this means you talk to it the way you'd talk to any Redis cluster:

# any cluster-aware client works; -c enables cluster mode in redis-cli
redis-cli -c -p <port> HSET layouts user:42 '{"panes": 4, "theme": "dark"}'
redis-cli -c -p <port> HGET layouts user:42

4. Compression and durability

  • Blobs are compressed before writing: zstd, lz4, gzip or brotli (production uses zstd).
  • Shards run in WAL mode with synchronous = NORMAL, so a power cut can drop the most recent commits but won't corrupt data.
  • An optional async-write mode acknowledges writes once they're in memory.

5. Resharding

Consistent hashing means going from 4 to 5 shards moves about 20% of keys, compared with about 80% with modulo hashing. Resharding is an offline CLI step with a verify option.

📊 The numbers in production

This is the part that made me sit up:

  • Cluster: 3 nodes, each with 4 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM. That's it.
  • Compression: an average ~63.6 KiB HSET payload lands on disk at ~5.5 KiB (~11x). At p99, 935 KiB shrinks to 59.3 KiB (~16x)
  • Latency over a full trading session: p99 around 2 ms on every node, p50 between 250 and 550 µs
  • Load: thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second, spiking with market volatility


The benchmark and compression numbers from the Zerodha post, charted.

A refreshingly boring migration

No big-bang cutover, no heroics:

  1. New workloads (Terminal mode) went to Blobasaur first.
  2. Existing services dual-wrote to both stores while a background job backfilled old keys.
  3. Reads tried Blobasaur first and fell back to SSDB.
  4. After a month of dual writes with zero discrepancies, SSDB was switched off.

For client code, the cutover was little more than swapping in a Redis Cluster client. Boring is good.

What they were honest about

The post doesn't pretend Blobasaur is perfect, which is a big part of why it's worth reading:

  • Slot assignment is static in config. There's no live rebalancing or automatic failover yet.
  • SQLite doesn't give disk space back by itself, so they enabled incremental auto-vacuum and added a vacuum subcommand.
  • Async writes need read-your-writes guarantees. Early versions could return stale data right after a queued delete. That's fixed now with an in-memory pending map that includes tombstones.
  • Large TTL cleanups caused latency spikes until deletes were routed through each shard's writer in chunks (1,000 rows by default).

The repo has been moving fast since release, with v0.7.x fixes for exactly these kinds of edge cases.

👥 The team behind it

Blobasaur is classic Zerodha Tech: a small group scratches its own itch and then publishes the result.

And the team really is small:

  • Kailash Nadh started the tech team in 2013.
  • In 2024 he said it had about 35 members, with only around five hires in four years and just two departures in a decade.
  • In 2020 he described how a roughly 30-person team, built over seven years, had built India's largest stockbroker.
  • CEO Nithin Kamath has credited Nadh with convincing him that adding people doesn't automatically solve more problems.

The team works out of Zerodha's HQ on 4th Cross, JP Nagar, Bengaluru. Their new project hub is named after that street: 4th Cross Labs (fourthcross.tech), which the Blobasaur post calls the home of the Zerodha.tech "hacker collective." I love that a street address became a brand.

🧰 Other projects from Zerodha Tech

The zerodha.tech/projects page lists 81 projects at last count, and each one was built and used internally first. For a team this size, that's a slightly ridiculous number.


The zerodha.tech projects page. It keeps scrolling for a while.

Here are the ones worth knowing.

Apps

  • listmonk: a self-hosted newsletter and mailing list manager, and their best-known project (24k+ ⭐). Go backend, Postgres, one binary
  • libredesk: a self-hosted customer support desk in one binary (3k+ ⭐)
  • whatomate: an open-source WhatsApp integration (1.7k+ ⭐)
  • logchef: a single-binary log analytics UI for ClickHouse
  • bureaucat: AI-native project management, pitched as an open alternative to Jira and Linear
  • oore.build: self-hosted CI and app distribution for Flutter, written in Rust
  • flowctl: a self-service workflow execution platform
  • linkpage: a self-hosted alternative to LinkTree

Services

  • hedwig: a minimalist, high-performance SMTP server in Rust
  • dungbeetle: a distributed job server for heavy async SQL reads on MySQL, Postgres and ClickHouse (1.2k+ ⭐). Think big report queries that you don't want hammering your main databases
  • kaf-relay: real-time Kafka topic replication between clusters, with failover
  • otpgateway: a standalone OTP and address verification server with pluggable providers
  • calert: pipes Prometheus Alertmanager alerts into Google Chat

Libraries and utilities

  • koanf: a lightweight Go config library (4k+ ⭐) and a popular alternative to viper
  • Tasqueue, fastglue, simples3, stuffbin: small, sharp Go building blocks
  • csvtotable: turns a CSV, TSV or Excel file into a searchable HTML page (1.1k+ ⭐)
  • hodor: an AI code reviewer for GitHub PRs and GitLab MRs, plus extensions for the pi coding agent (SRE incident mode, a PII privacy filter, web crawling)
  • autopilot: a Flutter QA test driver that doesn't need the app's source code
  • mvm: a CLI that spins up development microVMs from container images

A few that made me smile

  • terraform-provider-kite: manage your Kite stock portfolio with Terraform. Infrastructure as code, but for your investments 😄
  • A whole family of Nomad helpers (damon, nomctx, nomadboard, nomad-events-sink), which tells you what they run their workloads on
  • A bunch of Flutter plugins (flutter_displaymode, flutter_fgbg, flutter_curl) that look like they fell out of building the Kite mobile app

The trend is easy to spot: more Rust (Blobasaur, hedwig, oore.build) and a growing set of carefully scoped AI tools.

💸 Paying it forward with money as well as code

Shipping code is one thing. Writing cheques is another. In October 2024 Zerodha launched FLOSS/fund, which gives $1 million a year to open-source projects worldwide.

  • Year one went out in two tranches: $325,000 to nine projects (including Krita), then a final $675,000.
  • Another $1M is planned for 2026.
  • Its 2025 Open Source Pledge report also lists $500,000 to the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund and about $100,000 to the FOSS United Foundation, which Zerodha co-founded to grow open source in India.

🛠️ The CTO's side projects: Kailash Nadh's workshop

Kailash Nadh calls himself a hobbyist developer, and his project page backs that up. It's a long scroll. His first big FOSS project, the blogging platform boastMachine, dates back to 2002, and he has been shipping small, opinionated tools ever since. Grab a chai, this section got longer than I planned.

Oat (2026): a ~10 KB UI library

Oat (oat.ink) is a zero-dependency UI library of roughly 10 KB of CSS + JS combined, minified and gzipped.

The main idea is that semantic HTML should look right on its own. Buttons, forms, tables and other standard tags are styled directly, with no classes:

<!-- no utility classes, no framework, just HTML -->
<form>
  <label>Email <input type="email" required></label>
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

<table>
  <thead><tr><th>Symbol</th><th>LTP</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody><tr><td>INFY</td><td>1,512.40</td></tr></tbody>
</table>

The few interactive pieces, such as tabs, dropdowns and toasts, are WebComponents with minimal JS. There's no build step or toolchain: you include two files and start building.


The oat.ink homepage. Everything you see here is styled by about 10 KB of CSS and JS.

Nadh wrote it out of frustration with the bloat, dependency chains and sudden breaking changes common in JS UI libraries (relatable). It was released in January 2026 under MIT, has passed 5,000 ⭐, and reached v1 this autumn (v1.0.1 in late October, v1.1.0 on 1 November).

knadh / oat

Ultra-lightweight, zero dependency, semantic HTML, CSS, JS UI library. ~10KB min+gz.

Oat UI

Semantic, minimal, zero dependencies. ~10KB CSS and JS.

Oat is an ultra-lightweight HTML + CSS, semantic UI component library with zero dependencies. No framework, build, or dev complexity. Just include the tiny CSS and JS files and you are good to go building decent looking web applications with most commonly needed components and elements.

Semantic tags and attributes are styled contextually out of the box without classes, forcing best practices, and reducing markup class pollution. A few dynamic components are WebComponents and use minimal JavaScript.

I wrote this to use in my own projects after getting sick of the ridiculous bloat, dependencies, and rug-pulls in Javascript UI/component libraries.

See live demo and docs at oat.ink






View on GitHub


HUML (2025): YAML without the footguns

HUML (huml.io) is a strict, human-readable serialisation language for documents, datasets and config. It looks like YAML but is designed to avoid YAML's ambiguity, especially the way a single accidental indentation change can silently change a document's meaning. If YAML has ever ruined your afternoon, you'll get the appeal. It's still experimental, but community parsers have already appeared in other languages, including OCaml.

dns.toys (2022): a DNS server that does party tricks

This one is my favourite. dns.toys is a DNS server that bends the protocol to hand out small utilities. No app, no website, no API key. You just dig:

dig mumbai.time @dns.toys        # what time is it in Mumbai?
dig newyork.weather @dns.toys    # weather forecast
dig 42km-mi.unit @dns.toys       # unit conversion
dig 100USD-INR.fx @dns.toys      # currency conversion
dig ip @dns.toys                 # your public IP
dig 987654321.words @dns.toys    # numbers to words
dig excuse @dns.toys             # a random developer excuse

There's also pi, base conversion, a dictionary and more. It's written in Go, has around 2.7k ⭐, and exists mostly because it's fun.


dns.toys: every row is a tool you can call with one dig command.

listmonk (2019): the hobby project that got huge

listmonk started as a hobby project to fix Zerodha's own email problems. Today it's one of India's most-starred open-source projects, with 24k+ ⭐. The recipe is very Nadh: a Go backend, Postgres, a Vue dashboard, and the whole thing packed into a single binary you can self-host.

dictpress, Alar and Olam: dictionaries done properly

  • dictpress (dict.press) is a single-binary server for building dictionary websites in any language. All the data sits in one SQLite file (spot the pattern?), and search is pluggable, so you can plug in phonetic algorithms and find words by how they sound.
  • Alar is the open Kannada–English dictionary built on V. Krishna's four decades of work.
  • Olam is his English–Malayalam dictionary from 2010, which his project page says is used by over 2.2 million Malayalam speakers a month.
  • Around these sit the Indic language tools: phonetic algorithms for Kannada (knphone) and Malayalam (mlphone), the ml2en transliterator, and the Indic.page directory of Indic computing resources.

dont.build (2022): should you even build that feature?

dont.build is a tiny questionnaire for product people. You rate a feature idea on six things: how many users will use it, what it costs to build, how important those users are, how complex it is to run, how valuable it is, and how much risk it adds. Then it tells you whether to build it. It's opinionated and openly says so, but it's a great way to slow down before saying yes to everything.

funding.json (2023)

An open spec for projects to publish their funding needs as a simple JSON file. It sounds dull until you notice that FLOSS/fund uses it to take applications, which makes it a side project that helps move a million dollars a year.

tg-archive, Niltalk and dirmaker

  • tg-archive turns a Telegram group into a static website, like an old-school mailing list archive. It syncs messages into SQLite, then generates pages with media, polls, reply links and an RSS feed (1.2k ⭐). Heads up: he says he no longer actively maintains it.
  • Niltalk gives you disposable, password-protected chat rooms from a single Go binary. It can even run as a Tor hidden service.
  • dirmaker is a static site generator for directory websites. It's what powers Indic.page.

The tiny-library habit

Scroll his GitHub and you keep hitting libraries that are almost comically small:

  • autocomp.js: autocomplete in about 800 bytes
  • dragmove.js: draggable elements in about 500 bytes
  • tinytabs and tinyprogressbar: about 750 and 640 bytes
  • floatype.js, tinyrouter.js, highlighted-input.js: more of the same energy
  • On the Go side: koanf, stuffbin, smtppool, goyesql
  • And for fun: git-bars (commit activity as terminal bars), bigreddy (a pseudo-philosophical text generator) and a couple of Zig experiments

Once you've seen these, Oat stops looking like a one-off. It's what happens when the same person has been writing tiny libraries for 15 years.

2026 so far

  • ooru.space: an open-data directory of public community spaces in India
  • tinyi18n-rs: a small Rust i18n library
  • rconceptnet: a Rust CLI/server for ConceptNet on (of course) SQLite
  • tuwunel-admin: an admin UI for the tuwunel Matrix server
  • approve-pr-creation-from-issue: a GitHub Action that makes contributors get an issue approved before opening a PR. Very 2026

And way before GitHub

His project page also has a graveyard of 2000s web projects, and it's a fun read. Per that page, boastMachine once powered around half a million blogs, the blog ping service Pingoat was among the top 2,000 sites on Alexa, and his resume builder Cvmkr had 4M+ users before it shut down in 2023. The man has been shipping for a while.

Away from code, Nadh co-founded FOSS United, the Rainmatter Foundation (climate and ecology), the Indic Digital Archive Foundation, and the Samagata Foundation, which supports public commons and community spaces.

🧵 The common thread

Put Blobasaur, Oat and listmonk side by side and the same instincts show up:

  1. Solve your own problem first. Every project starts as something the team or Nadh actually needed.
  2. Keep it small. Single binaries, zero dependencies, and boring, proven foundations like SQLite and semantic HTML.
  3. Be honest about trade-offs. Relaxed durability, static slots, "sub-v1, expect breaking changes": the limits are written down.
  4. Give it back. Open-source the code, then fund the wider ecosystem too.

For a team of a few dozen people running infrastructure for millions of investors, that culture might just be the most interesting thing Zerodha has built.

Have you tried Blobasaur, Oat or listmonk? Got a favourite dns.toys command? Tell me in the comments. I'd especially like to hear from anyone running SQLite-backed stores in production. 👇

title: Don't Use Rust Unless You Really, Really Need It
description:
This happened in 2023 and 2024. The Rust ecosystem has moved since then, and I'll note what's changed where it matters.

My plan was simple, and I was quite proud of it.

I'd noticed a pattern in engineering blogs. A company builds its backend in Python, Ruby or Java. It grows. Then it rewrites the hot parts in C++ or Rust and writes a celebratory post about it. So I thought: why not skip the middle step? If I'll end up in Rust anyway, I might as well start there and never worry about a rewrite.

I needed a backend for my own apps, and I'd spent most of my career as a front-end and mobile developer. I'd built a few backends, but not many. Rust looked like the perfect excuse to level up. Every video I watched said the same things: it's as fast as C, it's memory safe, you can use it for anything, and it's the future.

So I bought the books, worked through the tutorials, and learned the basics. I knew the learning curve was steep, and I accepted it. Pay the cost once, I told myself, and the skills will pay for themselves for years.

I want to be clear about my attitude, because it matters for everything that follows. I wasn't a skeptic looking for reasons to hate Rust. I wanted to love it. I was ready for mistakes, ready for the hard parts, and ready to keep learning for as long as it took.

Fighting the compiler

The first friction came from the language itself. Pass a value to a function, and it's moved, so you can't use it on the next line. Take a reference instead, and the borrow checker starts asking about lifetimes. Then come trait bounds you don't understand, and .clone() calls sprinkled around until the code compiles.

Some of that was simply me being new, and I own it. Ownership is a real concept, and it does get easier with practice.

But I judged it wrong. I told myself the friction was temporary, a small adjustment in how I think. In reality, friction you feel on small code doesn't go away on big code. It compounds. And for a backend whose job is to move data between HTTP and a database, I was paying that price for protection against memory bugs I'd never have had in a garbage-collected language.

Choosing a database library

The first real decision was how to talk to the database, and Rust had no default answer. Diesel, SQLx and SeaORM were all reasonable, each with its own philosophy. The community advice was basically "pick whichever you like". That's fine for an experienced developer. As a beginner, I had no basis for liking anything.

Whichever one I picked, a lot ended up written by hand. Diesel migrations are plain SQL files. SQLx is raw SQL by design, checked at compile time. I don't mind SQL. Every backend developer should know it, and it will outlive most of the tools built on top of it.

But a backend is mostly CRUD, and writing every query and migration by hand doesn't scale. Sooner or later you write helpers to stop repeating the same SQL everywhere. At that point you're building a small, worse ORM of your own, which is exactly what I'd hoped a library would save me from.

Looking for Rails

That's when I changed my mind about something. I'd started out happy to learn everything from the ground up. Now I just didn't want to reinvent the wheel. I wanted what Django, Rails, Laravel or NestJS give you: run one command, and get routing, an ORM, migrations, validation, auth and a test setup that already fit together.

The Rust ecosystem was huge. There were crates for almost anything. But a batteries-included web framework barely existed. Axum and Actix are excellent, but they give you routing and middleware and leave the rest to you.

Loco, a framework openly modeled on Rails, had only just been released and was very young. The most ambitious project I found was Pavex, by Luca Palmieri, the author of "Zero to Production in Rust". It was in closed beta. You signed up, waited for an invite, and needed an activation key from the project's Discord just to run its CLI. And as I understood it at the time, the plan was to charge for using it rather than release it as ordinary open source.

I still remember the conference talk. The pitch was that this framework would finally make Rust mainstream for backend development. Then came the news that it wouldn't be freely available. (Pavex has since been released under the Apache 2.0 license, but back then it was a dead end for me.)

In hindsight, this was the biggest warning sign of all. Even Node, an ecosystem I'm not a fan of, has NestJS. When a language with that much enthusiasm behind it has no widely adopted, batteries-included web framework, it tells you who the community is building for. Rust's strongest communities work on infrastructure, tooling and systems software. CRUD apps aren't their priority, and that's a perfectly reasonable choice. It just wasn't a good sign for me.

The runtime nobody mentions

With no framework, I assembled the backend myself, from bits of "Zero to Production in Rust" and a lot of blog posts. Routing, configuration, logging, the database layer: all wired up by hand.

Then I ran into a problem I didn't know could exist. Rust has async and await, but no built-in runtime to run them. In JavaScript, Dart or Python, the event loop is simply there. In Rust, an async function returns a future that does nothing until an executor polls it, and the language doesn't ship one. You pick a runtime yourself, usually Tokio, sometimes async-std or smol.

That choice is bigger than it looks. Many libraries are written for one specific runtime, so your choice decides which libraries you can use. Mixing them can crash at runtime with an error like "there is no reactor running". Changing your mind later means touching a lot of code. I went with Tokio, like most people.

I also kept running into the advice that you don't need async at all unless you know what you're doing. Maybe that's true for a systems programmer. But after six to eight years of Dart and JavaScript, I couldn't picture a server without async, and nobody explained what the alternative looked like. The official async book was unfinished for years, so beginners pieced it together from blog posts.

Here's an opinion many experienced engineers will disagree with. I understand how an event loop works. I just don't think an application developer should have to care. Good abstractions exist so we can spend our attention on the product. Needing to understand executors, pinning and Send bounds to write a CRUD endpoint isn't a badge of honor. It's a cost.

Back to the database

Picking Tokio sent me straight back to the database. Diesel was synchronous at the time. Calling it inside an async handler blocks one of Tokio's worker threads, so you either wrap every query in spawn_blocking or add a separate diesel-async crate. SQLx was async, but you had to enable the right runtime through a feature flag, and getting it wrong meant those runtime panics again.

This is when I noticed the pattern that would define the whole project. Every decision was tied to another one. Every time I moved forward on one thing, I had to go back and redo something I thought was finished. One step forward, two steps back.

Writing tests

Once I had a database library that played nicely with Tokio, I could finally write my CRUD endpoints. Then came testing.

cargo test works, but it's minimal. There's no watch mode. I added cargo-watch to rerun tests on save and tried cargo-nextest as a faster runner. With tests running in parallel against a shared database, the watch setup never worked reliably for me.

Everything around the tests had to be built by hand: a separate test database, migrations before each run, transactions that roll back or tables cleaned between tests, fixtures, helpers for logged-in users. Frameworks in other ecosystems hand you all of this on day one. I found myself rebuilding things I hadn't had to think about in years.

Mocking was the hardest part. Say a handler calls a Google API, and I want to check that my code called it correctly without touching the network. In most ecosystems you put the service behind an interface and let a dependency injection container swap in a fake. Rust has no mainstream DI container. The usual approach is a trait, passed in either as a generic parameter or as a boxed trait object. Generics spread type parameters through every struct they touch. Trait objects bring their own lifetime and async headaches. Crates like mockall help, but add even more ceremony.

If you're reading this and have no idea what the hell I'm talking about, believe me, I felt exactly the same. That's the Rust way of doing things. Nothing is easy.

The result was code I couldn't trust. The compiler guaranteed memory safety, but memory safety was never my problem. Only tests can tell you whether your business logic is right, and tests were the most painful part of the whole stack.

There's a popular idea in the Rust world that a strong enough type system makes unit tests almost unnecessary: get the types right, and the compiler proves your logic is right too. In theory, maybe. In practice, encoding business rules that way takes a level of Rust wizardry very few people have. And even if I had it, I'd still take the simplicity of a plain unit test and TDD over a clever type.

Deploying

After weeks spent on features that would have taken days elsewhere, I rented a server and tried to deploy.

Rust compiles to native machine code, so you build for a specific target: a CPU architecture plus an operating system. As someone who had only ever deployed JavaScript, I first had to find out which architecture my server even used. Then came cross-compiling from my laptop to Linux, which needs extra toolchains and linker setup. Then glibc: a binary built against a newer C standard library refuses to start on a server with an older one. Then OpenSSL, which kept failing to build or link.

After a lot of configuration, I finally had something that installed. I started it.

It died.

No error message. No panic. No logs. The process was simply gone. After a lot of digging through system logs, I found two words: segmentation fault.

I'd spent my career on front-end and mobile code. I'd never written C, never built a desktop app or a game. I had never seen a segfault in my life. It's what happens when a program tries to touch memory it isn't allowed to, and the operating system kills it on the spot. It's the classic crash of C programs, and exactly the kind of bug Rust promises to prevent. Yet I met my first one in the language whose main selling point is memory safety.

I spent three evenings on it. Rebuilding, tweaking, reinstalling, searching. I never found the cause. The problem lived at a level of the stack my career had never asked me to touch. I just wanted to ship a backend, and I ended up counting bytes in my operating system.

For the curious: in hindsight, I still don't know my exact cause, but I've since learned how this usually happens. Safe Rust can't produce a segfault on its own. When a Rust program segfaults, the crash almost always comes from C code underneath: a system library, or a mismatch between where the binary was built and where it runs. Rust's guarantees stop at that boundary. And when the operating system kills a process for a segfault, Rust never gets the chance to print a panic or flush its logs. That's why there was nothing to read.

Docker

So I turned to Docker, hoping it would make the segfault go away. Isn't that its whole promise? Describe the environment once, and it runs anywhere.

I'd avoided it at first because I thought containers would cost me performance, and if I was using Rust, I wanted every bit of speed. That was wrong. On Linux, containers share the host's kernel, and the overhead is close to zero. Looking back, it was a perfect example of the mindset Rust had pulled me into: optimizing for performance I didn't need.

Docker helped, but much less than I expected. The image still had to be built for the right processor, so my old problems came right back. And when something didn't quite match inside the container, the app simply refused to start, again with no clear reason why.

Honestly, that still surprises me. Every problem I had came from the gap between my machine and the server, and closing that gap is the whole reason Docker exists. With Python or Node, you take the official image and move on. With Rust, my problems didn't go away. They just moved into the Dockerfile.

Up and running

Eventually, the Docker version worked. My backend was live and answering real requests.

That should have been the moment of triumph. Instead, it was the moment I lost interest. Every step had felt like walking through a minefield, and I couldn't face writing more code knowing the next mine was waiting somewhere. And remember, this was me at my most motivated, determined to love the language.

I spent the next couple of months looking for a batteries-included framework in another ecosystem, found one, and I've been building with it happily for about two years.

When Rust is worth it

Remember my clever plan to skip the rewrite? It had a flaw I couldn't see back then. Rewrite stories are memorable because they're rare. A typical backend spends most of its time waiting on the database and the network, not running its own code. When one server isn't enough, you add another. The companies that do move to Rust usually rewrite one proven bottleneck, years in, not the whole product before they have a single user.

Earlier I mentioned the advice that confused me so much: you don't need async unless you know what you're doing. My conclusion, it turns out, has the same shape. Don't use Rust unless you're absolutely sure you need top performance, or you work with something low-level, like microcontrollers. Otherwise, it's going to be a pain in the ass.

If you love the language, you don't have to give it up. Use it where it pays off. I still write Rust for scripts that have to be fast and for custom lint rules that run on every file in a codebase. And if your app hits a real bottleneck, you don't need to rewrite everything. Keep your main language, write that one hot path in Rust, and call it through FFI. Most ecosystems make this easy, with tools like PyO3 for Python or napi-rs for Node.

title: Curso gratuito de Node.js e APIs RESTful | IFRS
description:
Uma trilha de APIs com Node.js

Node.js é o ponto de partida desta formação básica, voltada a desenvolvedores iniciantes e intermediários que já conhecem o básico de JavaScript. Ele é oferecido pela IFRS. Ao longo de cinco módulos, a trilha avança da introdução ao ambiente Node.js para a construção de APIs RESTful e o uso do Express.js, conectando desenvolvimento de serviços, manipulação de dados e controle de acesso.

Uma API permite que aplicações troquem informações por meio de uma interface definida. Os fundamentos RESTful ajudam a organizar essa comunicação; depois, o desenvolvimento com Express.js leva o estudo à criação de APIs usando um framework associado ao ecossistema Node.js. Esses temas compõem o núcleo da formação, com carga horária total de 40 horas.

Dados e integração

A sequência inclui manipulação de dados e integração com bancos de dados. Esse tema amplia o trabalho com APIs para além da comunicação entre aplicações: os dados precisam ser tratados e conectados a uma fonte de armazenamento. O programa confirma essa integração como parte da trilha, sem especificar uma tecnologia de banco de dados ou um projeto final.

Autenticação e autorização

Autenticação e autorização encerram os tópicos listados. São responsabilidades distintas: a autenticação verifica quem está acessando, enquanto a autorização define quais ações esse acesso pode realizar. Em APIs, compreender essa diferença ajuda a pensar no controle de acesso aos recursos oferecidos pelo serviço. Esses assuntos completam o percurso ao lado de Node.js, RESTful, Express.js e integração com dados.

Público, formato e prazos

O curso é destinado a pessoas que desenvolvem software em nível iniciante ou intermediário e parte do conhecimento básico de JavaScript. Entre os requisitos informados estão compreensão de leitura em português e conhecimentos de informática e internet. O idioma do curso é português, e a metodologia é sem tutoria.

As inscrições ficam abertas até 31 de dezembro de 2026, sem necessidade de chave de inscrição. A conclusão deve ocorrer até 31 de janeiro de 2027. O prazo mínimo para obtenção do certificado é de seis dias a partir da inscrição. Com cinco módulos e 40 horas, a formação reúne os fundamentos de APIs modernas em Node.js em uma trilha que vai da construção do serviço ao tratamento de dados e ao controle de acesso.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/cursos/nodejs-introducao-ao-desenvolvimento-de-apis-modernas-turma-2026b/

title: Local AI Code Review and Security Scanning in VS Code with Ollama and Hushavyr
description:
I built Hushavyr because I wanted to review code and check for security issues inside VS Code while keeping my source code on my machine. It’s a free, open-source extension that combines static analysis with local AI code review through Ollama.

Hushavyr supports Java, Kotlin, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C#, PHP, and Ruby. I’m using Java in this demo because the JDBC example makes it easy to see what the scanner found and what the proposed fix changed.

From a security finding to a diff in VS Code

In the demo, a Java method looks up a customer by order ID. The method concatenates orderId into the SQL string, which creates a SQL injection risk. Hushavyr flags the line and proposes a PreparedStatement. I can inspect the diff in VS Code before applying the change.

Here’s the JDBC pattern behind the fix:

String sql = "SELECT customer FROM orders WHERE id = ?";

try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    statement.setString(1, orderId);

    try (ResultSet results = statement.executeQuery()) {
        return results.next() ? results.getString("customer") : null;
    }
}

The ? is a placeholder. setString binds the order ID separately as a value, so it can’t change the structure of this query.

I’d still check the full diff before applying it. Does the method return the same result when the order doesn’t exist? Does it close the statement and result set correctly? Those are the same questions I’d ask in a pull request review.

What runs locally

The built-in scanner can flag security issues and look for hardcoded secrets without loading an AI model. Optional analyzers such as Trivy and OSV-Scanner can check dependencies for known vulnerabilities.

Ollama runs the AI review on my machine. I can ask it to explain a finding in the context of the file or propose a code change. The security checks available for a file vary by language and installed analyzer.

Try it on your own code

  1. Install Hushavyr from the VS Code Marketplace.
  2. Open the Command Palette and run Hushavyr: Setup to choose a local model and any optional analyzers.
  3. Open a source file and run Hushavyr: Review Current File.
  4. If you request a fix, inspect the diff before applying it.

If you try it, tell me which language and local model you used. I’d especially like to hear about a finding you expected it to catch or a warning you’d dismiss. Those are concrete cases I can investigate.

Source code and issues on GitHub

This article was drafted with AI and prepared for publication by the project author.

title: Build an Offline-First Zakat & Nisab Calculator in React Using a JSON API
description:
Zakat calculators are a nice small project: a bit of state, a bit of math, and some real-world concerns like offline use, number formatting and right-to-left text. In this tutorial we build one in React, using the Zakat API from QuraniAPI as the data source.

Important: this is a coding tutorial, not a religious ruling. Please confirm rulings and your personal calculation with a qualified scholar.

What the API gives us

The Zakat endpoint is documented on its API page and in the docs. The slug is zakat and the request looks like this:

GET https://quranicapi.online/api/serve.php?slug=zakat&lang=en

Use lang=all for all 9 languages, or a code such as en, ur, fr, de, ru, tr, ms, zh-CN or ja. The sample response I saw on the page contains:

  • zakat_rate: 2.5
  • nisab: an array with entries for gold (87.48 grams, 7.5 tola) and silver (612.36 grams, 52.5 tola), each with a translations object
  • items: guideline entries with a category (for example cash) and a translation string

It is listed as a premium API. Check the pricing page for plans (at the time of writing: $20/mo, $100/yr, or a $900 one-time full dataset). The docs say to request a key; check the docs page for the exact way to send it, since I won't guess at it here.

Step 1: a local sample (offline-first)

Because the live response may need a key, we ship a clearly labelled local sample that copies the shape above. If the network fails, the app still works.

// zakatSample.js  -- LOCAL SAMPLE copied from the public sample JSON.
// Check the docs page for the exact live response.
export const ZAKAT_SAMPLE = {
  zakat_rate: 2.5,
  nisab: [
    { type: "gold", unit: "grams", value: 87.48, tola: 7.5 },
    { type: "silver", unit: "grams", value: 612.36, tola: 52.5 },
  ],
};

Step 2: a fetch helper with a cache 

// zakatApi.js
import { ZAKAT_SAMPLE } from "./zakatSample";

const URL = "https://quranicapi.online/api/serve.php?slug=zakat&lang=en";
const KEY = "zakat-cache-v1";

export async function loadZakat() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(URL);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);
    const data = await res.json();
    localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(data));
    return { data, source: "live" };
  } catch (e) {
    const cached = localStorage.getItem(KEY);
    if (cached) return { data: JSON.parse(cached), source: "cache" };
    return { data: ZAKAT_SAMPLE, source: "sample" };
  }
}

Order of preference: live, then last cached response, then the bundled sample. Showing the source to the user keeps things honest.

Step 3: the React component

The calculator does one simple thing: it takes a total of zakatable wealth, compares it to a nisab amount the user supplies in their currency, and multiplies by the rate from the API. Converting grams of gold or silver into currency needs a price that this API does not provide, so the user enters the current nisab value themselves.

import { useEffect, useMemo, useState } from "react";
import { loadZakat } from "./zakatApi";

export default function ZakatCalculator({ locale = "en", currency = "USD" }) {
  const [info, setInfo] = useState(null);
  const [wealth, setWealth] = useState("");
  const [nisabValue, setNisabValue] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => { loadZakat().then(setInfo); }, []);

  const fmt = useMemo(
    () => new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency }),
    [locale, currency]
  );

  if (!info) return <p>Loading...</p>;

  const rate = info.data.zakat_rate / 100;
  const gold = info.data.nisab.find((n) => n.type === "gold");
  const silver = info.data.nisab.find((n) => n.type === "silver");
  const w = parseFloat(wealth) || 0;
  const n = parseFloat(nisabValue) || 0;
  const reachesNisab = n > 0 && w >= n;
  const due = reachesNisab ? w * rate : 0;

  return (
    <section dir="auto">
      <p>Gold nisab: {gold.value} g. Silver nisab: {silver.value} g. (source: {info.source})</p>
      <label>Zakatable wealth
        <input type="number" min="0" value={wealth} onChange={(e) => setWealth(e.target.value)} />
      </label>
      <label>Nisab value in {currency}
        <input type="number" min="0" value={nisabValue} onChange={(e) => setNisabValue(e.target.value)} />
      </label>
      <p>{n === 0 ? "Enter a nisab value." : reachesNisab ? "Zakat due: " + fmt.format(due) : "Below the nisab you entered."}</p>
      <small>Confirm rulings with a scholar.</small>
    </section>
  );
}

Money math in floating point is fine for a display estimate, but for anything transactional use integer minor units.

Formatting and RTL tips

  • Intl.NumberFormat handles currency symbols and digits per locale. Try "ar-SA" or "ur-PK" with a matching currency such as SAR or PKR.
  • Set dir="auto" on text blocks so mixed Urdu/English content lays out correctly, or set dir="rtl" on the root when the whole UI is RTL.
  • Use CSS logical properties (margin-inline-start instead of margin-left) so one stylesheet works in both directions.
  • The API returns translations per language, so pass the lang parameter that matches your UI locale and read the matching key from the translations object.

Going further

Zakat is tied to a lunar year, so pairing the calculator with dates is natural. The Hijri Calendar API can help you build a reminder widget; check its page for the response shape. You can browse everything on the QuraniAPI home page, and the open repository is at sunnahsource-islamic-api on GitHub.

Wrap-up

We built a small component with a live, cached and bundled-sample data path, a simple 2.5% calculation using the API's rate, and locale-aware formatting. Next ideas: store the user's inputs locally, add a language switcher backed by the lang parameter, and show the guideline items text from the API under the result. Again, this is software only; please consult a scholar for your own zakat.

title: I Built Two AI Tools for Developers – Here's What I'm Learning Along the Way
description:
Building AI-powered tools sounds exciting, but turning an idea into something developers can actually use is a completely different experience.

I've been working on two projects as part of my development journey: Elite Article Engine and MakeYourUI.

Both solve different problems, but they share one goal: making AI more useful in real-world development workflows.

I wanted to share what I've been building, some of the challenges I've faced, and get honest feedback from the developer community.

1. Elite Article Engine – More Than Just an AI Writer

Most AI writing tools focus on generating text. But generating 2,000 words doesn't necessarily mean producing a useful technical article.

That's one of the problems I wanted to address with Elite Article Engine.

I'm building it around a research-driven content generation workflow.

Some of its features include:

  • Real-time research to provide relevant information before generation.
  • AI-powered article structure and topic-specific headings.
  • Technical explanations with practical examples.
  • Code playgrounds and working code examples.
  • Charts and visual elements where they make sense.
  • Automatically selected diagrams, including flowcharts, mind maps, timelines, and lifecycle diagrams.

One particularly challenging part is selecting the right diagram for each topic.

For example, a comparison between Java and Python needs a different visual structure from an article explaining a software development lifecycle.

I'm continuously improving the selection logic and content quality because I don't want the tool to generate visuals just for decoration.

Project: https://makemychance.com/elite-engine2/

2. MakeYourUI – Generate Frontend Code From Natural Language

My second project, MakeYourUI, focuses on frontend development.

The concept is simple: select your technology stack, describe the interface you want, and generate frontend code.

Some of its capabilities include:

  • Generate UI components from text prompts.
  • Support for different CSS and JavaScript frameworks.
  • Generate interfaces using Tailwind, Bootstrap, React, Vue, Next.js, Svelte, Angular, and more.
  • Upload an image or Figma screenshot as a reference.
  • Preview generated interfaces directly in the browser.
  • Inspect and copy the generated code.
  • Refine an existing design using additional prompts.
  • Test layouts at different viewport sizes.

I particularly wanted to make the generated output accessible to developers rather than limiting everything to a static visual result.

There is still room for improvement in code consistency, complex layouts, and maintainability, but that's part of the development process.

Project: https://makemychance.com/makeyourui/

3. What Building These Projects Has Taught Me

Working on both products has given me a different perspective on AI development.

A few things I've learned:

  • Better prompts alone don't guarantee better results.
  • Research and context are important for reliable AI-generated content.
  • Generated code should be editable, understandable, and reusable.
  • Visual quality and code quality are two different things.
  • Adding more features doesn't automatically make a product better.
  • Real user feedback is essential for improving an AI product.

One thing I've realized is that AI tools should help developers work more efficiently, not create another layer of complexity.

4. I'd Like Feedback From the Developer Community

These projects are still evolving, and I'd genuinely appreciate feedback from developers who work with frontend technologies, AI tools, and content generation.

I'm particularly interested in a few questions:

  1. What do you think is the biggest limitation of current AI article generators?
  2. When using an AI UI generator, would you prefer generating complete pages or individual reusable components?
  3. How important is screenshot-to-code functionality in your frontend workflow?
  4. What would make an AI-generated codebase easier to maintain?
  5. Which features would you actually use in tools like these?

You can explore both projects here:

  • Elite Article Engine: https://makemychance.com/elite-engine2/
  • MakeYourUI: https://makemychance.com/makeyourui/

I'm building these products and would rather receive honest technical criticism than generic praise.

If you've tried similar tools, I'd love to hear what worked, what didn't, and what you think is still missing.

title: Make your React/Vite SPA readable by AI crawlers without rewriting it
description:
Short answer: a React or Vite app sends an empty <div id="root"></div> and builds the page in the browser. AI crawlers don't run that JavaScript, so to ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity your site has no text. Pre-render it: build the HTML of each route at deploy time with a 15-line script, and React takes over in the browser as usual. You don't need to rewrite anything in Next.js.

When I audited 286 developer portfolios for an earlier study, 98 of them (34%) showed fewer than 20 words to a bot that doesn't run JavaScript. Most were React, Vue or Vite single-page apps. They look great to a person and blank to a crawler.

Check your site in 10 seconds

Ask for your page the way a crawler does and search for your main heading:

curl -s -A "GPTBot/1.1" https://yourdomain.com/ | grep -i "your main heading"

If nothing prints, AI crawlers can't see that text. You can also open view-source:https://yourdomain.com in the browser. If the body is a lone <div id="root"></div>, that's what the bots get.

The fix: 4 small changes

Vite can build your app twice: once for the browser and once for Node. The Node build can turn a route into an HTML string, and a short script saves one file per route. I tested this with Vite 8, React 19 and React Router 8.

1. Add a placeholder in index.html:

<div id="root"><!--app--></div>

2. Create src/entry-server.jsx, which renders a route to a string:

import { renderToString } from "react-dom/server";
import { StaticRouter } from "react-router";
import App from "./App.jsx";

export function render(url) {
  return renderToString(<StaticRouter location={url}><App /></StaticRouter>);
}

3. In src/main.jsx, change createRoot to hydrateRoot, so React reuses the HTML that's already there instead of building it from scratch:

import { hydrateRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { BrowserRouter } from "react-router";
import App from "./App.jsx";

hydrateRoot(
  document.getElementById("root"),
  <BrowserRouter><App /></BrowserRouter>
);

4. Add prerender.js at the project root and list your public routes:

import fs from "node:fs";
import { render } from "./dist-ssr/entry-server.js";

const routes = ["/", "/projects", "/about"];
const template = fs.readFileSync("dist/index.html", "utf8");

for (const url of routes) {
  const html = template.replace("<!--app-->", render(url));
  const file = `dist${url === "/" ? "" : url}/index.html`;
  fs.mkdirSync(file.replace("/index.html", ""), { recursive: true });
  fs.writeFileSync(file, html);
}

Then point the build script in package.json at the three steps:

"build": "vite build && vite build --ssr src/entry-server.jsx --outDir dist-ssr && node prerender.js"

Run the build and dist/projects/index.html now has your real heading, text and links. Run the curl again after you deploy and you should see it.

Things that break (and how to fix them)

  • window or localStorage at the top of a component. The Node build doesn't have them. Move that code into a useEffect, which only runs in the browser.
  • Different output in Node and in the browser. If something like Date.now() or Math.random() changes what's rendered, React warns about a hydration mismatch. Render the same thing in both places, and update it in a useEffect.
  • Routes with parameters. /blog/:slug isn't a list the script can guess. Build the list from your data (the same JSON or Markdown files your app reads) and add those URLs to routes.
  • The <title>. Every page still has the title from index.html. If you want one per route, replace it in the same loop, with a .replace() on the <title> tag.
  • Testing locally. vite preview returns the home page for /projects and the right file for /projects/. Static hosts like Vercel and Netlify serve dist/projects/index.html for /projects before applying the SPA rewrite, so it works when deployed.

When this isn't the right fix

If your content changes per visitor or every few minutes (a dashboard, prices in real time), pre-rendering at deploy time won't keep up. That's a job for server-side rendering, and at that point a framework like Next.js or React Router's framework mode is worth it. For a portfolio, a landing page or a small business site, pre-rendering is enough.

Don't want to touch your build?

If your site is a React or Vite SPA and you'd rather not deal with it, I can do it for you. I pre-render your public pages, check that AI crawlers can read them, and leave your app working exactly as it does now.
