title: What is an embedding, really? Building an AI agent from scratch in Java, part 2
description:
Not one word in common. No synonyms file, no tags, no LLM writing an answer. Just Postgres, a column of numbers, and an ORDER BY.

Some context first. This is part 2 of a series where I learn AI engineering by building everything by hand. In part 1 I wrote an MCP server, an MCP client and an agent loop in plain Java, with no AI frameworks, so a local Qwen model running in Ollama could read and write my notes file.

That agent has a catch, though. Its read tool hands the model the whole notes file, pasted into the prompt. Fine for a short to-do list. Point it at a wiki with hundreds of pages, and the prompt gets huge: slow, expensive, the model starts missing things, and eventually it doesn't fit at all. What the agent really needs is to pull in only the few paragraphs that matter for the question. To find those, it has to search by meaning.

That piece is the embedding, and it's the foundation under semantic search, recommendations and most of the "add your own data to AI" stuff.

Here's the plan for this post. We take a handful of short notes, turn each one into numbers with an embedding model, store them in Postgres, then search them by meaning instead of by exact words. No chat model, no MCP, no agent: just an embedding model and a database. By the end, things to buy finds Grocery list on your own machine.

To see why that's worth doing, start with how search usually works.

Keyword search matches words, not meaning

Classic search (SQL LIKE, MySQL FULLTEXT, Postgres full-text search, even Elasticsearch out of the box) works on words. Split the text into words, clean them up a bit (lowercase, calling → call), and find documents that contain the same ones.

That's great when you know the exact word. It falls over when you don't:

You search for The note says Keyword search
things to buy Grocery list: rice, lentils, ginger ❌ no shared words
reset my password Account recovery steps ❌
car my vehicle insurance renewal ❌

Humans read meaning, not spelling. To search the way humans read, we need a way to turn meaning into something a computer can compare. That's what an embedding is.

What an embedding is: text in, numbers out

An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. You get one by sending text to an embedding model.

I run mine locally with Ollama:

ollama pull nomic-embed-text

curl http://localhost:11434/api/embed -d '{
  "model": "nomic-embed-text",
  "input": "things to buy"
}'

The response, trimmed:

{
  "model": "nomic-embed-text",
  "embeddings": [[0.0123, -0.0456, 0.0331, 0.0718, -0.0092, ...]]
}

That inner list has 768 numbers. Every piece of text you send, whether it's three words or three paragraphs, comes back as exactly 768 numbers. That fixed length is what makes texts comparable.

  • An embedding model is not a chat model. It's a neural network, but a small one (nomic-embed-text is about 270 MB, versus 4.7 GB for the Qwen model I chat with). It can't write a sentence. Text goes in, numbers come out, and that's its entire job.
  • Nobody chose what the numbers mean. There's no "number 42 = food". The model invented its own 768 features during training. You can't read them, but you can compare them, and comparing them is the whole point.

Direction is meaning, length is "how much"

768 numbers are impossible to picture, so let's cheat. Pretend the model only produced 3 numbers, and each one meant a topic: [food, tech, travel].

Text Embedding
"pasta recipe" [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]
a 5-page article on Italian cooking [2.7, 0.3, 0.0]
"setting up Docker" [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]
"best ramen in Sapporo" [0.6, 0.0, 0.7]

Now picture each embedding as an arrow from the origin, pointing somewhere in that 3D space. Two things describe an arrow: which way it points, and how long it is.

  • Direction = what the text is about. "Pasta recipe" and the cooking article point the same way: mostly food, a bit of tech (recipe sites, I guess), no travel. "Setting up Docker" points somewhere else entirely.
  • Length = how much, not what. The article's numbers are three times bigger because it's longer and says more about food. It's not about a different topic, just more of the same one.
  • Mixed topics point in between. "Best ramen in Sapporo" sits between food and travel, which is exactly what it is.

That is what stood out for me: similar meaning = similar direction. Real embeddings work the same way, just in 768 dimensions with features nobody can name.

How close is close? Cosine

If meaning is direction, we need a number that says how alike two directions are. For text, that number is cosine distance. It measures only the angle between two arrows and ignores their length:

  • Same direction → distance 0 → same meaning.
  • Different direction → bigger distance → different meaning.

Why ignore length? Search "pasta recipe" and the 5-page cooking article points the same way, so cosine calls it a near-perfect match. A ruler-style distance would call it far away just for being longer, which is backwards for search.

Other measures exist (Euclidean, inner product) for other kinds of data, like map coordinates or recommendation scores. You don't have to pick: your embedding model's docs tell you which one it was trained for, and for text models that's almost always cosine. Just make sure you use the same model for what you store and what you search with.

Semantic search in Postgres with pgvector

You don't need a special vector database to try this. Postgres with the pgvector extension stores embeddings as a normal column type, and a search is a normal SELECT. The whole flow:

A chunk is a piece of a bigger document, roughly a paragraph, so each vector stands for one idea. In this post each short note is its own chunk.

I run the official pgvector/pgvector:pg17 Docker image. Setup:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE notes (
    id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title     text NOT NULL,
    body      text NOT NULL,
    embedding vector(768)          -- 768 must match the model's output
);

For each note, a small script asks Ollama for the embedding and stores it. pgvector accepts the vector as plain text:

INSERT INTO notes (title, body, embedding)
VALUES ('Grocery list', 'rice, lentils, ginger, chili', '[0.0123, -0.0456, ...]');

At search time, the request is embedded the same way, then:

SELECT title,
       1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS similarity      -- $1 = the query's vector
FROM notes
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1                      -- <=> is cosine distance
LIMIT 3;

    title          | similarity
-------------------+-----------
 Grocery list      |   0.71
 Dinner plans      |   0.48
 Ollama setup      |   0.39

That's it. Semantic search is an ORDER BY on a distance. The <=> operator is cosine distance (0 = same direction), so 1 - distance gives a similarity score where higher is better.

One honest note: results always come back sorted, even when nothing is relevant. Search for "quantum physics" in a grocery wiki and you'll still get three rows, so keep an eye on the scores.

What embeddings are bad at

Embeddings are fuzzy by design. That's perfect for "things to buy", but bad when the exact word matters: error codes (ERR_4021 vs ERR_4022 look nearly identical), invoice IDs, or "notes NOT about Docker" (Docker notes still rank first). Keyword search handles those, which is why real search systems often run both, called "hybrid search".

Wrap-up

The whole idea in five lines:

  1. An embedding model turns text into a fixed-length list of numbers, a vector.
  2. Think of each vector as an arrow. Direction is meaning; length is mostly noise.
  3. Cosine distance measures the angle between arrows. For text, it's the default.
  4. Use the same model for what you store and what you search with.
  5. Semantic search is just ORDER BY embedding <=> query LIMIT k. No chat model involved.

What clicked for me is how unmagical it is. "Understands meaning" turns out to be arrows and angles, and a database that can sort by an angle.

Next up

So far, nothing in this post talks back. It's just search. In part 3 the agent from part 1 finally gets to use it: I'll add a new search tool to my Java MCP server that embeds the question, runs this exact pgvector query and hands back the closest chunks. Then the agent can stop reading the whole notes file and just ask for the few paragraphs it needs.

Co-written with Claude, who patiently answered "but what does that mean?" about forty times.

title: Best Data Modeling Tools for Google BigQuery: SQLDBM, dbt, Dataform & Looker Compared
description:
Modeling data in BigQuery is a different beast than modeling in Postgres or SQL Server. You've got nested STRUCTs, repeated fields, partitions, clustering, and labels to think about. On top of that, most teams now layer dbt or Dataform for transformations and Looker for BI, which means your "modeling tool" has to play nicely with three or four other systems. Pick wrong and you'll be hand-writing YAML and copy-pasting DDL for months.

I spent a few weeks running the main options against real BigQuery datasets. I cared about three things: how well each tool handled BigQuery-native features, how much manual work it eliminated across the dbt and semantic-layer workflow, and whether a mixed team of architects, analysts, and business stakeholders could actually collaborate in it. Some tools nailed one of those and ignored the others. One tool did all three.

Here's how they stacked up.

How I Evaluated These Options

I connected each tool (or read through its docs and trials where a hands-on test wasn't possible) against a BigQuery project with a mix of nested schemas, partitioned tables, and clustered fact tables. I looked at BigQuery feature coverage, dbt/YAML integration, semantic-layer support, collaboration, governance features, and pricing. I also weighted how much of the end-to-end workflow a single tool covered, because stitching together three or four vendors adds its own cost.

1. SqlDBM - Best Overall

The only BigQuery modeling tool that visually designs your warehouse, generates your dbt YAML, and governs your semantic layer, all before you write a single line of code.

I tested every major tool in this roundup head-to-head on BigQuery, and SqlDBM is the one that actually ties everything together. The first thing that stood out was the native BigQuery integration. SqlDBM uses an in-house BigQuery parser, not a generic JDBC adapter, so STRUCTs, partitions, clustering, Labels, ARRAY/RANGE types, and primary/foreign key constraints all work out of the gate. I pointed a service account at a dataset, reverse-engineered the whole thing in seconds, and had a shareable ER diagram with no installs and no code.

The real differentiator for a dbt-and-BigQuery stack is how SqlDBM bridges visual modeling and transformation. It auto-generates dbt-compatible source and model YAML with column structures, descriptions, data types, tests, and freshness configs, then pushes it straight to your Git repo. That alone killed hours of manual YAML wrangling in my test. Mercadona, Spain's largest supermarket chain, uses the SqlDBM API to auto-generate dbt models deployed directly to BigQuery as part of its "Dato Unico" single-source-of-truth strategy, governing nearly 5,000 tables.

Then there's the semantic layer, which is where SqlDBM genuinely stands alone. Code-only semantic tools like dbt and Cube skip visual modeling. Traditional visual modelers like erwin skip the semantic layer. SqlDBM does both. You define semantic views that layer business context onto your physical BigQuery schemas, and those definitions automatically propagate when the schema changes. Your BI dashboards, dbt models, and AI pipelines all reference one governed definition of what the data actually means.

It's trusted by over 400,000 users globally, including DocuSign, Zendesk, Pfizer, and Hulu. It's a certified Google Cloud Partner listed on BigQuery Ready. PwC reported it cuts modeling time by 25 percent, and it won Database Modeling Solution of the Year at the Data Breakthrough Awards in both 2023 and 2024. Real-time multi-user collaboration means architects, analysts, and business users can work on the same model concurrently instead of emailing DDL scripts around.

Pros:

  • Native BigQuery parser with full support for STRUCTs, partitions, clustering, Labels, and ARRAY/RANGE types, not a bolt-on JDBC adapter
  • Auto-generates dbt-compatible source and model YAML and pushes directly to Git, eliminating manual YAML work for BigQuery dbt workflows
  • Only visual modeling platform that also includes a semantic layer, automatically propagating BigQuery schema changes to keep business definitions accurate
  • Proven at scale on BigQuery: Mercadona governs nearly 5,000 tables and auto-generates dbt models deployed to BigQuery via the SqlDBM API
  • Real-time multi-user collaboration so data architects, analysts, and engineers can work concurrently on the same BigQuery model

Cons:

  • The depth of features (semantic views, dbt YAML config, lineage) can present a learning curve for teams new to governed data modeling
  • Some niche BigQuery-only capabilities like BigLake or Omni could benefit from even deeper integration over time

Pricing: SqlDBM plans are quote-based and scale with team size, with enterprise packaging that layers in premium support, SSO, RBAC, and advanced security. There's a free tier to start modeling and explore BigQuery connectivity before you commit, with no credit card required. Contact sales for a tailored quote.

2. dbt (dbt Core and dbt Cloud)

dbt is the most widely adopted code-first transformation framework in the modern data stack. You write modular SELECT statements, and dbt compiles them into tables and views in BigQuery (or Snowflake, Databricks, and others). dbt Core is the free, Apache-2.0 CLI. dbt Cloud adds a browser IDE, job scheduling, CI/CD, a documentation and lineage catalog, a Semantic Layer for centralized metrics, and the dbt Copilot AI assistant.

On BigQuery, dbt supports partitioning, clustering, incremental models, and Git-based workflows. Built-in tests, auto-generated docs, and version control bring real software-engineering discipline to analytics. It's a strong fit for analytics engineers comfortable with SQL, Jinja, and Git.

The honest limitation: dbt is a transformation and logic layer. It doesn't do visual ER diagramming, conceptual/logical modeling, or forward-engineering of physical schemas. Many teams pair it with a dedicated modeling tool for that reason.

Pros:

  • Free, open-source dbt Core with a large community, package ecosystem, and talent pool
  • Built-in testing, documentation, lineage, and Git-based CI/CD
  • Warehouse-agnostic, so your BigQuery models stay portable
  • Semantic Layer and Copilot AI in dbt Cloud help standardize metrics

Cons:

  • No visual ER diagramming or conceptual/logical modeling
  • Per-seat dbt Cloud pricing adds up fast for larger teams, with BigQuery compute on top
  • Requires SQL, Jinja, and Git skills, which locks out non-engineers

Pricing: dbt Core is free and open source. dbt Cloud has a free Developer plan (1 seat, 1 project, around 3,000 models built per month). Starter is about $100 per developer seat per month with 5 seats and 15,000 models included. Enterprise and Enterprise+ are custom-quoted, with third-party sources estimating Enterprise at roughly $50,000+ per year. BigQuery compute is billed separately.

3. Dataform (Google Cloud)

Dataform is Google Cloud's managed ELT and transformation service, built right into the BigQuery console. You define tables, views, and incremental models in SQLX (SQL plus JavaScript), declare dependencies, add assertions for data quality, and schedule workflows. It plugs into GitHub and GitLab, and because it lives inside Google Cloud, it uses IAM, Cloud Logging, and Cloud Composer with no separate infrastructure or auth to set up.

For teams already running entirely on BigQuery, it's a low-friction alternative to dbt without adding another vendor or license. Documentation and dependency graphs are generated from your code.

Like dbt, though, it's a code-first transformation tool. There's no visual ER modeling, no reverse-engineering of warehouse schemas, and it supports BigQuery only. Teams that want multi-warehouse portability or a large package ecosystem will find it less mature than dbt.

Pros:

  • No license fee; you pay only for the BigQuery queries it runs
  • Native integration inside the BigQuery console with IAM, no extra infra
  • Dependency management, assertions, scheduling, and Git integration built in
  • Quick to adopt for teams already standardized on Google Cloud

Cons:

  • BigQuery only, no cross-warehouse portability
  • Smaller community and package ecosystem than dbt
  • No visual data modeling, ER diagrams, or conceptual/logical design

Pricing: Dataform is free. You pay BigQuery for the queries it runs, plus any adjacent Google Cloud services.

4. Looker (LookML)

Looker is Google Cloud's enterprise BI platform, and its real value lies in LookML, a code-based modeling language where you define dimensions, measures, joins, and business logic once in Git-versioned files. Every dashboard, explore, and API query then uses those shared definitions. Looker queries BigQuery live instead of extracting data, and it integrates tightly with the rest of Google Cloud.

It's a solid fit for large organizations that want one governed semantic layer shared across BI, embedded analytics, and AI use cases.

That said, Looker isn't a physical schema design tool. It won't draw ER diagrams, generate DDL, or reverse-engineer warehouse schemas. LookML takes specialist skills to write and maintain, which often creates a developer bottleneck. Cost is also real, which puts it out of reach for smaller teams. Most organizations pair Looker with a transformation tool like dbt or Dataform, and often with a dedicated modeling tool too.

Pros:

  • Strong governed semantic layer, metrics defined once and reused everywhere
  • LookML is Git-versioned, supporting code review and collaboration
  • Live querying of BigQuery and tight Google Cloud integration
  • Embedded analytics and API access for product workflows beyond dashboards

Cons:

  • High cost, platform fees starting around $60,000 per year before user licenses
  • LookML is proprietary and requires specialist skills, creating bottlenecks
  • It's a BI/semantic layer, not a physical modeling or DDL tool

Pricing: Quote-based through Google Cloud sales. Standard edition list price is about $5,000 per month (around $60,000 per year) and includes 10 Standard and 2 Developer users. Additional users are listed at $30 (Viewer), $60 (Standard), and $125 (Developer) per month. Enterprise and Embed editions are quote-only. AWS Marketplace listings run higher, with Standard around $66,600 per year. Looker Studio is a separate, free product.

5. erwin Data Modeler (Quest)

erwin Data Modeler, now owned by Quest Software, has been a standard enterprise data architecture tool for more than 30 years. It covers conceptual, logical, and physical modeling, with forward and reverse engineering, model comparison, complete-compare synchronization, and DDL generation. It supports 20+ platforms including Oracle, SQL Server, Snowflake, and BigQuery. Governance features include naming standards, model versioning, and a model repository for team collaboration.

It's aimed at data architects and large enterprises, especially regulated industries with heavily documented legacy estates. It's also the most traditional option in this roundup. It's a desktop application and feels heavier than browser-based modelers.

BigQuery support has historically been described as less complete than coverage for older relational platforms. I've seen reviewers say they were waiting for a newer release to get full BigQuery parity. If you're evaluating erwin specifically for BigQuery, verify current support for nested STRUCTs, partitioning, and clustering before you buy.

Pros:

  • Mature conceptual/logical/physical modeling with forward and reverse engineering
  • Broad database coverage, useful across hybrid or legacy-plus-cloud estates
  • Strong governance, standards features, and a large enterprise user base
  • Free trial available, some editions offer a free version

Cons:

  • Expensive subscription pricing, especially for larger teams
  • Desktop-centric and less collaborative than cloud-native modelers
  • BigQuery-specific features may lag behind native tools; verify your version

Pricing: Subscription-based and quote-driven through Quest. Third-party sources cite roughly $200 to $299 per user per month for standard cloud editions, around $399 per user per month for workgroup editions, and about $6,000 per seat per year for some term subscriptions. Free trial available. Confirm current pricing with Quest directly.

6. Vertabelo (Redgate Data Modeler)

Vertabelo, now marketed as Redgate Data Modeler, is a browser-based data modeling tool for visually designing database schemas. You get online ER diagramming, version history, team sharing, reverse engineering, and SQL generation, with no desktop install required. It's a lightweight, lower-cost option for small and mid-sized teams and solo designers who want visual modeling without enterprise licensing. It's also popular with educators and learners, with free access for academic and non-commercial use.

The strengths are ease of use and affordability. The trade-offs are that it isn't a BigQuery-specialized platform, and it's thinner on governance, data vault and data mesh support, and enterprise security than the heavyweight tools. Check which BigQuery data types and DDL options are supported before committing. It also doesn't do transformation or orchestration, so you'd still pair it with dbt or Dataform.

Pros:

  • Browser-based with no install, plus version history and sharing
  • Low entry cost and a free tier suited to small projects and students
  • Simple, approachable ER modeling with SQL generation and reverse engineering
  • Quick to learn compared with heavyweight enterprise suites

Cons:

  • Not specialized for BigQuery; verify support for nested/repeated fields, partitioning, and clustering
  • Lighter governance, standards enforcement, and enterprise security
  • No transformation or orchestration; needs to be paired with dbt, Dataform, or similar

Pricing: Third-party reviews report a free plan limited to 20 models, paid individual tiers of roughly $7 to $24 per month, and a team plan of about $83 per month for up to 5 users. 14-day free trial, and free for academic/non-commercial use. Pricing has shifted over time, so confirm with the vendor.

Final Verdict

If you're modeling for BigQuery, the honest reality is most of these tools solve one slice of the problem. dbt and Dataform handle transformations but skip visual modeling. Looker gives you a semantic layer but isn't a physical modeler. erwin and Vertabelo do visual modeling but leave the dbt YAML and semantic layer for you to figure out.

SqlDBM is the only tool I tested that covers visual modeling, dbt YAML generation, and a governed semantic layer in one platform, with a BigQuery parser that actually understands STRUCTs, partitions, and clustering. For most teams running BigQuery with dbt and Looker (or heading in that direction), it's the clear best overall pick. Start with the free tier, reverse-engineer a dataset, and see how much manual YAML you stop writing.

If you're a solo analytics engineer who lives in SQL and Git, dbt Core plus Dataform will get you a long way for free. If you're a large regulated enterprise with a legacy Oracle/SQL Server estate migrating to BigQuery, erwin is worth evaluating. And if you just need lightweight ER diagrams for a small project, Vertabelo is fine.

FAQ

Do I still need dbt or Dataform if I use SqlDBM?
Yes, most teams use them together. SqlDBM designs the physical schema and auto-generates the dbt YAML, then dbt (or Dataform) runs the actual transformations in BigQuery. SqlDBM eliminates the manual YAML work; dbt handles execution.

Does SqlDBM support BigQuery-specific features like STRUCTs and clustering?
Yes. SqlDBM uses an in-house BigQuery parser, not a generic JDBC adapter, so STRUCTs, ARRAY/RANGE types, partitions, clustering, Labels, and primary/foreign key constraints are all first-class.

What's the difference between a semantic layer and a data model?
A data model defines the physical structure of your tables (columns, types, keys, partitions). A semantic layer adds business meaning on top, defining what "revenue" or "active user" means so BI tools, dbt, and AI systems all use the same definition. SqlDBM lets you do both in one place.

Is Dataform really free?
The Dataform service itself is free. You still pay BigQuery for the queries it runs and for any other Google Cloud services (storage, scheduling, logging) you use alongside it.

title: De planilhas estáticas a Agent Skills: como estruturar BI e monetizar engenharia na Agensi
description:
Dados comerciais perdem valor estratégico quando ficam presos em planilhas estáticas e análises manuais. Ao mesmo tempo, pedir para um agente de IA gerar dashboards complexos do zero a cada sessão aumenta o risco de alucinação de estado, inconsistência visual e retrabalho estrutural.

O Inteligência de Vendas Atlas (insights-playground-52) foi projetado para resolver esses dois gargalos: transformar bases tabulares em painéis executivos interativos e empacotar essa solução como uma Agent Skill pronta para execução via protocolo MCP na Agensi.

Arquitetura da solução

Construída com React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS e Vite, a aplicação segue uma estrutura modular (src/, public/ e atlas-vendas.csv) acompanhada de especificações nativas em SKILL.md e AGENTS.md:

  • Indicadores executivos (KPIs): acompanhamento dinâmico de Receita Total, Lucro Bruto, Unidades Vendidas e Margem de Lucro, com comparativo anual (ex.: 2025 vs. 2024).
  • Filtros inteligentes: segmentação cruzada por ano de referência, categoria comercial e região geográfica.
  • Camada de dados e exportação: ingestão de dados tabulares estruturados, validação tipada e exportação limpa dos recortes filtrados em CSV.

Por que usar e publicar Skills na Agensi

Transformar código validado, regras de negócio e contratos de dados em uma skill muda a forma como soluções técnicas são distribuídas e executadas:

  • Para quem utiliza: agentes como Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, DeepSeek, Grok e Gemini CLI conectam-se via MCP e carregam uma arquitetura pré-configurada em vez de improvisar o scaffolding a cada prompt.
  • Para quem cria: padrões de engenharia e automações testadas deixam de ficar restritos a repositórios locais e ganham distribuição direta e monetização na loja de criador.
  • Governança e previsibilidade: instruções explícitas e verificação de segurança reduzem ambiguidades e elevam a confiabilidade das entregas técnicas.

title: Amazon Connect Customer now lets you test AI model version upgrades for automated evaluations
description:
Amazon Connect Customer now enables managers to test new AI model versions for automated evaluations before switching, so evaluation scores remain consistent through model upgrades. When a new version becomes available, managers can test how it would score the same contacts compared to the current version of the model. This lets managers catch scoring differences across models and adjust evaluation criteria before those differences affect agent performance results. Managers also have the flexibility to choose how evaluation forms handle model updates. They can automatically upgrade to the latest model version for ongoing accuracy improvements or stay on a specific version for consistent scoring.

This feature is supported in all AWS commercial regions where Amazon Connect Customer is offered. To learn more, visit our documentation and our webpage.

title: Amazon Connect Customer expands automated performance evaluations to 45 new languages
description:
Amazon Connect Customer now uses generative AI to automate evaluations of human and AI agent performance in 45 additional languages, such as Arabic, Dutch, Indonesian, and Polish. Managers define custom evaluation criteria in natural language and receive AI-generated evaluations with justifications in their preferred language. Performance evaluations also support cross-language evaluation and can complete assessments in English, even when the conversation is in another language. This enables multilingual contact centers to use a standardized evaluation framework across languages.

This feature is supported in all AWS commercial regions where Amazon Connect Customer is offered. For information about Amazon Connect pricing, please visit our pricing page. To learn more, visit our documentation and our webpage.

title: Amazon CloudFront is now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud
description:
Amazon CloudFront is now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Organizations with strict EU sovereignty requirements can now deliver websites, applications, and APIs with the performance, security, and scale of CloudFront, all within the EU. Until now, customers had to build and run their own delivery and TLS termination infrastructure to keep traffic and data inside the EU.

With CloudFront in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, content delivery, TLS termination, logs, and customer configuration stay within the European Sovereign Cloud boundary. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, and only EU-resident personnel operate it. This helps governments, healthcare, financial services and other regulated industries meet data residency and operational sovereignty requirements without trading away performance and scale. Customers use the same CloudFront APIs and console experience they already know making it easy to transfer over existing deployments and automations. If you plan to run media streaming or other high-volume workloads, contact your AWS account team and we can help you find the right solution, including options in AWS commercial Regions.

To get started, sign in to your AWS European Sovereign Cloud account and create a distribution in the CloudFront console. To learn more about available features and pricing, see the CloudFront Developer Guide and CloudFront pricing page in ESC.

title: Day Explained: A Rust Framework That Builds Native Apps for Every Platform
description:
Most cross-platform app frameworks make you choose between two things. You can share your UI code across platforms, or you can use each platform's real, native controls. Getting both usually means writing the interface more than once.

Day is an open-source framework that tries to give you both. You write your app once in Rust. On macOS it uses AppKit. On iOS it uses UIKit. On Android it uses Material Components. On Linux it uses GTK or Qt, and on Windows it uses WinUI 3. The buttons, text fields and menus your users see are the platform's own.

I have not built an app with Day. This breakdown comes from the project's website, documentation and GitHub repository. Anything about how well it works in practice is the project's own claim, not something tested here.

The short version

  • What it is: a framework for building desktop and mobile apps from one Rust codebase, using each platform's native UI toolkit.
  • Platforms: macOS, iOS and Android are the most supported. Linux and Windows are supported with less testing. Web and HarmonyOS are experimental.
  • Beyond UI: it includes localization, accessibility, a UI testing tool, packaging and app store preparation.
  • License: MPL-2.0, open source on GitHub.
  • Maturity: young. The repository was created in July 2026 and the CLI is at version 0.7.10. There is no hot reload, and the project tells you to test your hardest requirement first.

How it differs from other approaches

There are roughly three ways to build one app for many platforms:

  1. Draw everything yourself. The framework renders its own controls, so the app looks the same everywhere. You get full design control, but the controls are not the platform's own.
  2. Use a web view. You build the UI with web technology and show it inside a native window.
  3. Map to native controls. Your code describes the UI, and the framework creates the real platform widgets.

Day takes the third approach. Its own documentation is honest about what that means: "your interface will vary with the platform, and you will still need to test those differences." If you need pixel-identical screens and heavy custom animation everywhere, Day suggests that a framework with its own renderer "may give you more control."

The other point that sets Day apart is that the UI is shared, not just the business logic. In the project's words, "No bridging between disparate programming languages is required." Your layouts and event handlers are Rust, from the data model up to the buttons.

What the code looks like

Day calls a control, or a group of controls, a piece. You build screens with ordinary Rust functions that return pieces. State lives in signals, which update the UI when their value changes.

Here is the counter example from the docs overview:

use day::prelude::*;

pub fn root() -> impl Piece {
    let count = Signal::new(0i64);
    column((
        label(res::str::counter_value(count)).id(id!(counter_label)),
        button(res::str::add_one())
            .action(move || count.update(|n| *n += 1))
            .id(id!(increment_button)),
    ))
    .spacing(Space::M)
    .padding(Space::L)
}

A few things to notice:

  • It is declarative. You describe what the screen contains, and Day creates the widgets.
  • Updates are targeted. When count changes, Day updates the label. The docs say the whole root() function "does not run again."
  • Text is not hard-coded. res::str::counter_value and res::str::add_one come from translation files, which we will get to next.
  • Controls have stable IDs. The .id(...) calls are there so automated tests can find each control.

The pieces beyond UI

A framework that only draws controls still leaves you with a lot of work before release. Day tries to cover more of the path to shipping.

Localization. Translations use Mozilla Fluent files. Day generates typed Rust functions from them, so if a message expects an argument and your code does not pass it, the build fails. Translation mistakes become compile errors instead of bugs users find.

Accessibility. Because Day uses native controls, it starts from each platform's built-in screen reader and keyboard support. It adds a shared Rust API for labels, hints and changing values. The docs are clear that this is "a starting point, not a certification." On Android, accessibility support is listed as partial.

DayScript. This is Day's tool for testing and automation. You write a walkthrough that finds controls by their IDs and interacts with them. The same walkthrough can run on several platforms and in several languages, and take screenshots along the way. That makes it useful both for regression tests and for generating app store screenshots.

Packaging. The day CLI creates projects, checks that you have the right SDKs installed (day doctor), builds, launches, and packages your app with day pack. Depending on the platform, it produces .dmg, .ipa, .apk, .aab, .msix, Flatpak or AppImage files. It also prepares store listing metadata, but the actual store submission still uses each store's own tools and your credentials.

Optional add-ons. Extras are ordinary Cargo dependencies. The site lists web views, Lottie animations, text-to-speech, charts, camera, audio and video, OAuth and passkey sign-in, Bluetooth LE, local network discovery, push notifications, background tasks and crash reporting. Each has its own platform support notes.

Platform support, honestly

Day ranks each platform in a support tier. A tier describes how much testing and maintenance a target gets, not how complete its API is.

Tier 1, Supported:

  • macOS (AppKit), packaged as .dmg
  • iOS (UIKit), packaged as .ipa
  • Android (Material Components), packaged as .apk and .aab

Tier 2, supported with less testing:

  • Linux (GTK 4 or Qt 6), packaged as Flatpak and AppImage
  • Windows (WinUI 3), packaged as .msix and an installer

Tier 3, Experimental:

  • HarmonyOS (ArkUI), packaged as .hap
  • Web, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering real HTML elements

The platform page also includes small details that matter if you are planning a real project:

  • Apple builds need Xcode 27 or newer.
  • On iOS, daily development happens on the Simulator. The docs say physical-device debugging gets less use.
  • On Android, CI does not fail when the Android UI walkthrough fails. If the app process is killed, it restarts from scratch unless your app saves its own state.
  • On Windows, the docs say fewer apps have shipped than on the Apple, Linux and Android targets.

What is still missing

The docs keep a single list of gaps that apply across platforms. Some of the bigger ones:

  • No hot reload. Every code change means a rebuild and relaunch. A DayScript walkthrough can take you back to the screen you were working on, but the app still restarts.
  • Animation is partial. It works on AppKit, UIKit, Android, Web and ArkUI. On GTK, Qt and WinUI, changes apply instantly with no animation.
  • No automatic dark mode for custom colors.
  • No form validation framework. You build it yourself with signals.

The project's advice is direct: "Check this list before you adopt the framework."

Who is behind it

The repository belongs to a GitHub organization called Daybrite, which describes itself as "Stewards of Day." Almost all of the commits come from one developer, Marc Prud'hommeaux. His GitHub profile lists him as the founder of Skip, a tool for building iOS and Android apps from Swift. So this is not his first attempt at the cross-platform problem.

It also means Day currently depends heavily on one maintainer. As of November 23, 2026, the repository has 43 stars and 4 forks, and the day-cli crate on crates.io has about 10,900 downloads. Releases come out quickly: there have been 63 since the first one on August 13, including five in the past week. Fast releases are good for fixes, but they also mean the API may still change.

Is it a good fit?

Day's own features page is unusually clear about this. Based on it, Day looks like a good candidate if:

  • You want to write the whole app in Rust, or you already have Rust code you want to reuse.
  • You build "tools people use every day": settings screens, document windows, lists of records, where native controls feel right.
  • You are a small team that needs to ship on several platforms, and the built-in localization, testing and packaging save real work.

It is a weaker fit if:

  • Your team does not know Rust. The docs say learning the language "is part of the project."
  • Your design needs identical controls and heavy custom animation on every platform.
  • You depend on fast hot reload during UI work.
  • You need a large, mature ecosystem of third-party components today.

The project's suggestion for deciding is practical: build one screen from your own design, using the feature you are least sure about, and run it on every platform you plan to ship.

How to try it

You need stable Rust from rustup and the tools for your platform: Xcode 27+ on an Apple silicon Mac, Visual Studio C++ Build Tools and the Windows App Runtime on Windows, or GTK 4 and libadwaita on Linux. Then:

cargo install day-cli --locked
day --version
day doctor --toolkit gtk   # or appkit, winui

The first-app tutorial walks you through a small counter app in six lessons. The site also has a live browser demo of the same Rust UI code running through the experimental web target.

The takeaway

Day is an ambitious attempt to make one Rust codebase produce truly native apps, including the UI and not just the logic. Its best feature may be its honesty: the docs tell you what is stable, what is experimental, what is missing, and how to test whether it fits before you commit.

It is also very young and mostly built by one person. For a side project or an internal tool in Rust, it is worth an afternoon. For a production app, follow its own advice and prototype your hardest screen first.

Would you pick native controls that look different on every platform, or one custom look that is the same everywhere?

title: Evaluator-Optimizer with Spring AI: One Model Writes, Another Critiques
description:
Evaluator-Optimizer with Spring AI: One Model Writes, Another Critiques

Anyone who writes for a living knows the rhythm of revision. You draft something, reread it with fresh eyes, notice what is weak, and rewrite. The second draft is almost always better than the first, and the reason is not talent. It is the separation between producing a text and judging it. When the same mind does both at once, it tends to accept its own first answer.

The evaluator-optimizer pattern applies that rhythm to LLM systems. One model generates a solution. A second evaluation step judges it against explicit criteria and returns feedback. If the solution does not pass, the feedback goes back to the generator, and the loop continues until the evaluator accepts the result. Anthropic describes this workflow in its research on building effective agents, and the sample in the spring-ai-examples repository implements it with Spring AI.

This article walks through that sample: how the loop is built, what the prompts ask each model to do, and where the code needs guardrails before it is safe to run unattended. Some of those guardrails are missing from the sample, and I point them out, because the loop as written has no stopping limit.

Where the pattern fits

Anthropic's taxonomy separates workflows, where code decides the control flow, from agents, where the model decides its next action. Evaluator-optimizer is a workflow. The loop structure is fixed: generate, evaluate, and either return or retry. What changes from run to run is the content, and how many times the loop turns.

The pattern earns its cost when three conditions hold. First, you have criteria for what a good answer looks like, and you can state them in a prompt. Second, a critique can make the next attempt measurably better. Third, the first attempt is often close but not quite right. Translation with nuance, code that must meet a specification, and drafts that must follow a style guide all fit that profile. A simple factual question does not, because there is nothing for a critic to improve.

It is also a different shape from the other patterns in this series. Parallelization splits independent work and merges it. Routing picks one specialist. Orchestrator-workers plans subtasks at runtime. Evaluator-optimizer repeats the same work with feedback, which makes it the only one of the five that revisits its own output.

The sample task

The sample asks the model to implement a stack in Java with three operations: push, pop, and getMin, where all operations must run in O(1) time. The task also sets two style rules: inner fields must be private, and any use of a field must be prefixed with this..

The task is small, but it has the properties that make the pattern interesting. The O(1) requirement is easy to violate by accident: a naive getMin that scans the stack is correct but too slow. The style rules are easy to forget on a second draft. A critic that checks both is more useful than one that only checks that the code compiles.

The records

The pattern is described by three records in EvaluatorOptimizer:

public static record Generation(String thoughts, String response) {
}

public static record EvaluationResponse(Evaluation evaluation, String feedback) {

    public enum Evaluation {
        PASS, NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT, FAIL
    }
}

public static record RefinedResponse(String solution, List<Generation> chainOfThought) {
}

Generation is what the generator returns: a short statement of its approach and the proposed solution. EvaluationResponse is what the evaluator returns: a verdict from a fixed set of three values, and feedback in prose. RefinedResponse is what the caller receives: the final solution and the full history of generations, so you can see how the solution evolved.

The enum matters more than it looks. Because the verdict is a closed set, the code can branch on it. The loop in this sample only stops on PASS. NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT and FAIL both send the work back for another round, which is a reasonable choice for a demo but one you should revisit in production, since a FAIL often means the approach itself is wrong, not that it needs polishing.

The generator prompt

The generator prompt is unusual because it is almost entirely about format. Before it describes the task, it asks for a single line of valid JSON, with every newline and quote escaped:

Your response must be a SINGLE LINE of valid JSON with NO LINE BREAKS except those explicitly escaped with \n.
{"thoughts":"Brief description here","response":"public class Example {\n    // Code here\n}"}

This is a practical lesson. Code contains quotes, backslashes, and line breaks, and asking a model to put it inside a JSON string is a reliable source of malformed output. The prompt tries to prevent that with rules and an example. The rules help, but they are not a guarantee. The sample depends on Spring AI's structured output to parse the result, so a malformed response fails the whole run. The fix is not a better prompt alone. It is a retry on parse failure, which the sample does not have.

The generator prompt also tells the model to reflect on feedback from earlier rounds. That instruction is what turns a single call into a refinement step. Without it, each round would be a fresh attempt that ignores what went wrong before.

The evaluator prompt

The evaluator prompt is shorter, and it sets the criteria explicitly:

Evaluate this code implementation for correctness, time complexity, and best practices.
Ensure the code have proper javadoc documentation.
Respond with EXACTLY this JSON format on a single line:
{"evaluation":"PASS, NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT, or FAIL", "feedback":"Your feedback here"}
Use "PASS" only if all criteria are met with no improvements needed.

The criteria are concrete: correctness, time complexity, best practices, and Javadoc. A vague instruction such as "make sure it's good" gives the critic nothing to check, and its feedback becomes generic. The line "Use PASS only if all criteria are met" pushes the evaluator toward strictness, which matters because a lenient critic ends the loop too early.

This prompt is written for code. Change the criteria and you change the pattern's application. For a translation, the criteria would be fidelity, register, and idiom. For a summary, they would be coverage and length. The structure of the loop does not change; the evaluator's checklist does.

The loop

The core of the pattern is a short recursive method:

private RefinedResponse loop(String task, String context, List<String> memory,
        List<Generation> chainOfThought) {

    Generation generation = generate(task, context);
    memory.add(generation.response());
    chainOfThought.add(generation);

    EvaluationResponse evaluationResponse = evalute(generation.response(), task);

    if (evaluationResponse.evaluation().equals(EvaluationResponse.Evaluation.PASS)) {
        return new RefinedResponse(generation.response(), chainOfThought);
    }

    StringBuilder newContext = new StringBuilder();
    newContext.append("Previous attempts:");
    for (String m : memory) {
        newContext.append("\n- ").append(m);
    }
    newContext.append("\nFeedback: ").append(evaluationResponse.feedback());

    return loop(task, newContext.toString(), memory, chainOfThought);
}

Read it step by step. The generator produces a solution, which is recorded in memory and chainOfThought. The evaluator judges it. If the verdict is PASS, the method returns. Otherwise it builds a new context that lists every previous attempt and the latest feedback, and calls itself with that context.

The design choice to keep every previous attempt in the context is worth thinking about. It lets the generator see what it already tried, which helps it avoid repeating a mistake. It also means the prompt grows on every round. A third attempt carries two previous solutions and two rounds of feedback. For code, that growth is manageable. For a long document, it can become expensive quickly.

The missing stopping rule

This is the most important gap in the sample, and I would not run it without fixing it. The loop has no iteration limit. It only stops when the evaluator returns PASS. If the evaluator never passes the solution, because the criteria are too strict, or the generator cannot satisfy them, or the evaluator keeps finding something new to criticize, the recursion never ends. The most likely outcome is either an unbounded number of model calls or a StackOverflowError when the recursion gets deep enough.

A fix is simple. Pass a round counter, and stop after a fixed number of rounds:

private static final int MAX_ROUNDS = 4;

public RefinedResponse loop(String task) {
    List<String> memory = new ArrayList<>();
    List<Generation> chainOfThought = new ArrayList<>();
    String context = "";

    for (int round = 1; round <= MAX_ROUNDS; round++) {
        Generation generation = generate(task, context);
        memory.add(generation.response());
        chainOfThought.add(generation);

        EvaluationResponse evaluation = evalute(generation.response(), task);
        if (evaluation.evaluation() == EvaluationResponse.Evaluation.PASS) {
            return new RefinedResponse(generation.response(), chainOfThought);
        }
        context = buildContext(memory, evaluation.feedback());
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("No passing solution after " + MAX_ROUNDS + " rounds");
}

A loop also makes the control flow easier to read and easier to test than recursion. Whether you return the best attempt so far or throw an error when the budget runs out is a product decision. The important part is that the decision exists.

Other gaps

Three more issues are worth knowing about before you build on the sample.

The generator and the evaluator use the same ChatClient, so they are the same model. A model judging its own output shares its blind spots, and it may approve a solution it would have rejected from a different viewpoint. For high-stakes work, use a different model or a different prompt persona for the evaluator, and test whether the critic catches what the generator misses.

The FAIL verdict is treated like NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT. The evaluator is asked to say FAIL, but the code never uses that signal. In practice, FAIL should mean the approach is unsalvageable: stop, or switch strategy, instead of asking for polish.

The sample has no protection against a parse failure. Both entity(Generation.class) and entity(EvaluationResponse.class) throw if the model returns malformed JSON. Add a retry for those calls, separate from the refinement loop, so one bad response does not end the run.

The sample prints every generation and every evaluation to standard output. That is useful while you learn the loop and noisy in production. Replace the prints with a logger that records the round number, the verdict, and the length of the feedback. Log the full code only in a debug mode.

Testing the loop

The loop is straightforward to test, because EvaluatorOptimizer takes a ChatClient in its constructor. Use a stub client that returns a sequence of canned generations and evaluations. A good test set covers four cases:

  • The first generation passes, so the loop returns after one round.
  • The first evaluation fails and the second passes, so the final solution is the second generation and the chain of thought has two entries.
  • The evaluator never passes, so the loop stops at the round limit and does not recurse forever.
  • The evaluator returns malformed JSON, so the retry logic is exercised.

Testing the prompts is harder, and it is where most of the quality comes from. Keep a small set of tasks with clear acceptance criteria. Run the loop on each task, read the feedback the evaluator gives, and check whether the feedback is specific enough to act on. If the feedback is vague, tighten the evaluator's criteria before changing anything else.

When to choose this pattern

I use three questions. Can I write down what a good result looks like, in terms a critic can check? If not, the evaluator will be guessing. Does a second pass measurably improve the result? If the first answer is usually good enough, the extra calls are waste. Can I afford several rounds of latency and tokens, and can I bound them? If the answer to the last question is no, use a single well-written prompt and a cheaper check.

The pattern is also a good place to add a human. The evaluator can flag a solution for review when it reaches the round limit, instead of failing silently. That combines automated refinement with a person's judgment on the cases the loop cannot settle.

Running the sample

To run the sample you need Java 17 or later and a configured model. The project includes properties for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama. The sample configures gpt-4o for OpenAI, so set that key, or change the properties to the provider you use. Start the application with the Maven wrapper. The console shows each generation and each evaluation, and the final output prints the solution and the chain of thought.

Watch the first few rounds closely. You will see the evaluator's feedback become more specific as the generator fixes earlier problems, and you will also see the prompt size grow. Both observations are the pattern working as intended, and both are the reason the round limit matters.

Key takeaways

  • Evaluator-optimizer separates generating from judging, and loops feedback back into the generator until the evaluator accepts the result.
  • The pattern is worth its cost when criteria are explicit, a critique measurably improves the output, and the first attempt is often close.
  • The sample's loop has no stopping limit, so an evaluator that never passes can run forever. Add a round budget before you use it.
  • Use a closed set of verdicts, and decide what FAIL means in your system instead of treating it like a polish request.
  • Add retries for malformed structured output, and consider a different model for the evaluator when the stakes are high.

The full sample is in the spring-ai-examples repository under agentic-patterns/evaluator-optimizer. The pattern is described in Anthropic's research on building effective agents, alongside the other workflows covered in this series.

title: I graded 14 Go and Rust MCP servers without running a single one
description:
MCP servers describe their tools to the model: a name, a description, an input schema and a few hints like readOnlyHint and destructiveHint. The directories that list MCP apps check those descriptions, and clients use the hints to decide what to run without asking.

Most ways to check them start the server and call tools/list. That means installing it, giving it credentials, and trusting it enough to run. For a quick look at someone else's server, or a CI check on a pull request, that's a lot.

mcp-check 1.3 reads the tool list from the source instead. For Go it understands mark3labs/mcp-go, the official go-sdk and mcp-golang. For Rust it understands rmcp, rust-mcp-sdk and pmcp. It reproduces the tools as the SDK would list them, schemas included, and then grades them. TypeScript and Python were already covered.

The run 

npx @isokron/mcp-check --repo github.com/grafana/mcp-grafana

I ran that against 14 well-known open-source Go and Rust servers on 23 November.

Server Tools Spec Claude directory ChatGPT directory Hidden text Quality
github/github-mcp-server (exact) 149 A B C A B
grafana/mcp-grafana 136 A F D A A
containers/kubernetes-mcp-server 87 C C D A B
hashicorp/terraform-mcp-server 68 A A B A B
zerodha/kite-mcp-server 22 A D A A A
tuananh/hyper-mcp 20 D F D A A
mark3labs/mcp-filesystem-server 14 A D A A A
strowk/mcp-k8s-go 9 A F D A A
isaacphi/mcp-language-server 6 A D A A A
Roblox/studio-rust-mcp-server 6 A F F A A
apollographql/apollo-mcp-server 5 A C A A A
elastic/mcp-server-elasticsearch 5 A A D A A

Two weren't graded. genai-toolbox builds its tools from configuration at run time, so there's nothing in the source to read. The checker says that, names the four registrations whose names it couldn't resolve, and tells you to grade the live list. I'd rather have that than a confident F.

What came up

  • Missing titles (8 of 12). The Claude directory asks every tool for a human-readable title. A name like search_within_files isn't one.
  • Hints left unset (8 of 12). The ChatGPT app directory wants readOnlyHint, destructiveHint and openWorldHint set explicitly on every tool. Left out, a client has to guess, and the safe guess is "ask the human every time".
  • No hidden instructions anywhere. Every server graded A on that section.

None of this is a security hole. It's the difference between being listed and being bounced, and between a client that knows a delete tool deletes and one that has to ask.

Caveats

Grades from source are approximate. The reader can miss a tool built at run time, and a schema it can't work out is marked unreadable rather than graded as empty. A live list is exact:

npx @isokron/mcp-check -- ./your-server --stdio

In CI 

- uses: isokron-ai/mcp-check@v1

With no inputs, it reads your source, runs nothing, and writes a job summary. Add min-grade: B to gate on it.

If you maintain one of these servers and a grade looks wrong, open an issue on github.com/isokron-ai/mcp-check with the tool name. That's how the Go and Rust readers got this far.

title: Why Docker Silently Binds to 0.0.0.0 (And How to Trace Port Causality in Go)
description:
If you've spent any time working with Docker or Docker Compose, chances are high that you've written something like this:

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

It looks completely harmless. You just wanted to connect your local GUI database client (DBeaver, TablePlus, pgAdmin) to PostgreSQL.

Except you just exposed your database to your entire local network and every public interface on your machine.

The Silent Wildcard Footgun

When you declare "5432:5432" without an explicit host IP prefix, Docker defaults to binding to 0.0.0.0 (the wildcard address in IPv4) and :: (in IPv6).

That means:

  • If your laptop is on a coffee shop or office Wi-Fi, anyone on that subnet can reach port 5432.
  • If this runs on a cloud VM without a restrictive security group, port 5432 is open to the entire public internet.
  • iptables rules are automatically modified by the Docker daemon to bypass standard host firewalls (like UFW) unless specially configured.

To bind exclusively to your local machine, you have to remember to explicitly write:

ports:
  - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"

Yet across millions of repositories and development stacks, developers constantly forget the 127.0.0.1: prefix.

The Causality Black Box: ss and lsof Don't Help

When you suspect an unexpected port is open and run standard Linux diagnostic commands:

$ sudo ss -tulpn | grep 5432
tcp   LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:5432 0.0.0.0:* users:(("docker-proxy",pid=14205,fd=4))

All you see is docker-proxy.

  • You don't know which container owns it.
  • You don't know which docker-compose.yml file declared it.
  • You don't know whether it was intended as public or an accidental wildcard binding.
  • If you have 30 containers running across 5 microservices, you are left manually running docker inspect across every container or grepping your codebase.

Building Lantern: Tracing Configuration Causality

To solve this visibility gap, we built Lantern, an open-source, local-first CLI written in Go.

Instead of merely listing sockets, Lantern traverses the full causality graph:

[ Listening Socket ]
        ↓
[ OS Process / docker-proxy ]
        ↓
[ Docker Container ]
        ↓
[ Docker Compose Service & Source YAML Line ]
        ↓
[ Reachability Verdict (PUBLIC / LOCALHOST / DOCKER) ]

1. Instant Reachability Audit (lantern scan)

Running lantern scan audits all listening TCP sockets and classifies their exposure:

$ lantern scan
PORT    PROTO   BIND ADDRESS    REACHABILITY   PROCESS         CONTAINER / SOURCE
5432    tcp     0.0.0.0         PUBLIC         docker-proxy    my-project-db-1 (docker-compose.yml:8)
8080    tcp     127.0.0.1       LOCALHOST      node            api-gateway

Any wildcard binding (0.0.0.0 or ::) is immediately flagged with a high-contrast PUBLIC warning.

2. Root Cause Explanation (lantern why <port>)

If you want to know why a port is open, Lantern produces the exact causal chain:

$ lantern why 5432
Port 5432 (tcp) is bound to 0.0.0.0 (PUBLIC)
├─ Process: docker-proxy (PID 14205)
├─ Container: my-project-db-1 (ID 8a1b2c3d4e5f)
├─ Compose Service: db
└─ Defined in: /home/dev/projects/api/docker-compose.yml:8
   Recommendation: Change '5432:5432' to '127.0.0.1:5432:5432' to restrict access to localhost.

3. Real-Time Terminal Watch Mode (lantern scan -w)

Developers frequently start and stop containers. With -w, --watch:

lantern scan -w --interval 2s

Lantern renders a live terminal dashboard that triggers an [ALERT] the moment a new wildcard exposure occurs.

Enforcing Guardrails in CI/CD

Catching exposure on developer laptops is great, but preventing it from merging into production repositories is critical.

We built two native CI mechanisms into Lantern:

1. Zero-Exit Flag 

lantern scan --fail-on-wildcard --ignore-ports 80,443

If any container or process binds to 0.0.0.0 on a port other than 80 or 443, the command exits with code 1 and emits native GitHub Actions error annotations (::error::).

2. Official GitHub Action

You can drop Lantern into any repository workflow with a few lines:

name: Security Audit
on: [pull_request, push]

jobs:
  port-audit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Spin up test environment
        run: docker compose up -d

      - name: Audit Port Exposures
        uses: DhyaanKanoja11/lantern-action@v1
        with:
          fail-on-wildcard: 'true'
          ignore-ports: '80,443'

It automatically formats a rich Markdown report on your GitHub Actions Step Summary page.

How to Try It

Lantern has zero runtime dependencies and is distributed across major package managers:

# macOS / Linux (Homebrew)
brew tap DhyaanKanoja11/tap
brew install lantern

# Windows (Scoop)
scoop bucket add dhyaan [https://github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/scoop-bucket](https://github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/scoop-bucket)
scoop install lantern

# Go toolchain
go install [github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/Lantern/cmd/lantern@latest](https://github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/Lantern/cmd/lantern@latest)

Open Source & Getting Involved

The entire project is MIT-licensed and built with standard library principles in Go:

  • GitHub Repository: github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/Lantern
  • GitHub Action: github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/lantern-action

If you've ever had a container expose an unexpected port, give lantern scan a run and let us know what you think!

title: Ambient Mode – From Color Scheme to a Living Interface
description:
Originally published with interactive examples at lukiluki.me.

You open the same website at midday and late in the evening. The text stays familiar, but the light changes, the sky grows calmer and summer greens become winter outlines. Can an interface feel alive without making you learn new controls on every visit?

Ambient Mode adds atmosphere to light and dark reading colors: light, gradients, time of day or seasons change the background while content and controls stay dependable. This can give a website character and express personal preferences. Separate design layers, respect for system preferences and deliberate user control are essential. An attractive effect alone proves neither improved usability nor lower energy consumption.

Merksatz (Design principle):
Reading colors provide orientation, atmosphere sets the mood, and users decide how much change they want.

What changes between color scheme and atmosphere?

Dark and light modes first define which surfaces and text colors are readable together. Atmosphere can go further by borrowing light from content, representing a time of day or adding seasonal accents. Here, “Ambient Mode” is a design term, rather than the name of a single web standard.

A concrete product example is YouTube's Ambient Mode: video colors gently spread into the surrounding background. The effect complements the dark color scheme. A broader pattern follows: content or context supplies the mood, while the interface retains its purpose.

Three layers are useful for a digital garden:

  1. Reading: Text, reading surfaces, links and focus indicators need tested light and dark variants.
  2. Atmosphere: Sky, glow and landscape change; they convey no essential information.
  3. Meaning: Categories keep their colors, whether it is autumn or nighttime.

Colors and spacing are stored as design tokens (Named design values, such as text color, background, spacing or category accent, shared by components.). A warm evening sky can sit behind a clearly recognizable pink design tile. The season determines the surroundings; the category explains the content.

Who decides: the system, the clock or the person?

The system preference is a good starting point because people may already have chosen reading colors in their operating system or browser. The CSS query prefers-color-scheme exposes that preference. It says nothing about actual room lighting or the local position of the sun.

Mode What controls the interface? Suitable for Limitation
System The light or dark browser/OS scheme; the season follows the calendar. A respectful default without an additional decision. The system does not provide a time-of-day atmosphere.
Auto Local time and calendar determine reading colors and atmosphere. A page whose mood follows the day. Fixed times are not measured sunrise and sunset times.
Manual A chosen time and season determine the appearance. A personal mood independent of the actual date. This is a deliberate departure from the system preference.

Here in the garden, the page starts with System. Only Auto or Manual takes over control. Auto uses simple day boundaries of 06:30 and 18:30; the four seasons follow Northern Hemisphere meteorological months. This is a transparent design rule, rather than a location or weather sensor. The automatic season may therefore be unsuitable for visitors in the Southern Hemisphere.

Try Manual in the header, or Menu → Ambience on a phone: move the time from midday to night and switch from summer to winter. Sky, light and vegetation respond; navigation and categories stay familiar. Returning to System hands reading colors back to the browser and operating system. This experiment demonstrates the design; it does not measure energy savings.

How do transitions work with native CSS?

A convincing transition does not need a new background image for every hour. A few color stops and calculated intermediate values are enough for a calm progression through the day. In this garden, sky colors are mixed between such stops; sun, moon and seasonal shapes complete the scene. The reading scheme still switches between light and dark variants, rather than making every intermediate color a new text palette. Both variants and their actual backgrounds belong in the contrast check.

Native CSS provides useful building blocks for new interfaces: light-dark() chooses between two color values according to the active color-scheme; @property gives a custom CSS variable a type and enables interpolated animation. MDN lists the color variant of light-dark() as Baseline since May 2024, and @property since July 2024. That is useful compatibility guidance, rather than a guarantee for old browsers or embedded WebViews.

The following CSS is a small standalone recipe for an existing .reading-surface text area and a decorative .ambient-layer background. Both elements must exist, and the application must set data-time="evening" on the root element after an explicit time selection. Without that attribute, the initial state remains. The colors are examples, rather than a fully tested product palette.

@property --ambient-light {
  syntax: "<color>";
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: rgb(249 196 131 / 18%);
}

:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
}
.reading-surface {
  color: #172033;
  background: #faf8f4;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  .reading-surface {
    color: #e8edf5;
    background: #171c29;
  }
}
@supports (color: light-dark(white, black)) {
  .reading-surface {
    color: light-dark(#172033, #e8edf5);
    background: light-dark(#faf8f4, #171c29);
  }
}
.ambient-layer {
  pointer-events: none;
  background: radial-gradient(
    ellipse at 75% 15%,
    var(--ambient-light),
    transparent 65%
  );
  transition: --ambient-light 700ms ease;
}
:root[data-time="evening"] .ambient-layer {
  --ambient-light: rgb(147 123 221 / 18%);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .ambient-layer {
    transition: none;
  }
}

The reading surface stays opaque and follows the system; the glow has its own responsibility. Without light-dark(), the preceding colors and media query apply. Without @property, changing the custom variable may be abrupt, but the content remains readable. Gentle transforms and opacity changes are another option for continuous sun paths. Add a large blur or continuously running canvas scene only after checking performance.

What does OLED actually have to do with energy?

On OLED (Organic Light-Emitting Diode: Pixels emit their own light instead of being lit by a shared backlight.) displays, darker pixels need less energy. That explains a potential advantage of dark surfaces. This pixel-level saving does not directly carry over to a conventional backlit LCD (Liquid Crystal Display: A screen whose liquid crystal pixels are illuminated by a backlight.). Dark Mode also has design and personal motivations and cannot be reduced to a single historical purpose.

The 2021 Purdue study examined six Android apps on four OLED smartphones, each during 60 seconds of use. At 30–50 percent brightness, Dark Mode saved an average of 3–9 percent of total phone power; at 100 percent brightness, savings were 39–47 percent. These results describe the devices and workflows studied, rather than savings for every website or current hardware.

A glow is not evidence of energy savings
Bright backgrounds and additional animation can increase display and
computation costs. Ambient Mode can use less or more energy; without
measurement on the target device, the balance remains unknown.

Battery life between charges, battery lifespan and display aging are also different questions. Longer runtime between charges does not establish a longer device lifespan. Apple describes OLED burn-in as a possible result of high-contrast static images displayed for long periods at high brightness, and recommends automatic brightness and a short screen lock interval among other measures. An animated website offers no guaranteed protection; bright icons that remain in place in Dark Mode are still static image elements.

When does atmosphere help, and when does it distract?

A garden, portfolio or media site can gain a recognizable character from subtle changes in light. An administrative interface, long work form or focused reading view may be better served by a quiet background. This is a design hypothesis: whether atmosphere improves recognition, time spent or enjoyment must be tested with real users.

Readability matters between the attractive end states too. Version 2.2 of the WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: The W3C's guidelines for accessible web content.) requires at least 4.5:1 contrast for normal text and 3:1 for qualifying large text. Behind translucent surfaces, a moving glow can alter the actual visible background. Check intermediate states or use an opaque reading surface.

Motion is a separate decision. prefers-reduced-motion signals a preference for less nonessential animation. Sun and moon can remain still while selected colors and seasons continue to work. For a complete product, a separate control to disable decorative effects is also useful; a system preference alone does not cover every wish.

Four checks before using it

  • Respect the system: Without a saved, deliberate override, the page starts in the browser/OS scheme and follows changes to it.
  • Read intermediate states: Check midday, twilight, night and every season; text and focus indicators remain visible against their actual backgrounds.
  • Keep controls calm: Enable reduced motion and use sliders, mode selection and seasons by keyboard; decoration must not intercept clicks.
  • Measure the cost: On a less powerful target device, check CPU and GPU activity and smooth scrolling; energy claims also need appropriate hardware measurements.

Sources and next steps

Source research and verification in the original article: October 7, 2026. The Purdue figures explicitly come from 2021; the garden rules are an original implementation example.

  • YouTube: Ambient Mode – a concrete use in a media product.
  • MDN: prefers-color-scheme, light-dark() and @property – system preferences and native color features.
  • Purdue: Dark Mode measurements and original paper by Dash and Hu, MobiSys 2021 – method and limitations of OLED energy claims.
  • Apple: OLED displays – image persistence, burn-in and brightness.
  • W3C: Minimum contrast and MDN: Reduced motion – boundaries for comfortable design.

The Accessibility tile explores contrast and usability further. Explainable Text shows another kind of adaptation: readers choose the depth of information there, and the atmosphere here.
