title: How to continue a Claude Code task in Codex without re-explaining it
description:
If you use more than one AI coding agent, you have probably hit this. Claude Code stops at a usage limit halfway through a task. You open Codex to keep going, and it knows nothing: not the task, not what is done, not what you decided, not what is blocking. So you explain everything again from scratch.

I ran into this often, so I built pas-agent, a small open-source CLI that carries a task from one agent to the next. This post shows how to use it to move a task from Claude Code to Codex.

Why the next agent starts blank

Every AI coding agent keeps its own private session. When you switch agents, that session does not come with you.

But most agents read an instruction file when they start. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md. Codex, Cursor and OpenCode read AGENTS.md. Gemini CLI reads GEMINI.md.

pas-agent uses that. It keeps a small, local record of the task, the progress and the decisions in .pas-agent/session.json. When you switch, it writes that record into the file the next agent already reads at startup.

Install

pas-agent needs git on your PATH.

You can download a prebuilt binary for Linux, macOS or Windows from the latest release, or install it with Cargo (Rust 1.85+):

cargo install --git https://github.com/gfirik/pas-agent pas-agent-cli

Either way you get a single binary called pas-agent.

Step 1: start a session

In your project (any subdirectory works, the session lives at the git root):

pas-agent init --task "Add JWT auth"

Step 2: record progress as you go 

pas-agent update --completed "Login endpoint" \
                 --remaining "Token refresh" --remaining "Tests" \
                 --decision "Use jose, not jsonwebtoken, for edge runtime support" \
                 --next "Implement refreshToken()"

Flags can be repeated. You can also add blockers with --blocker.

Step 3: checkpoint 

pas-agent checkpoint "Login flow done"

A checkpoint snapshots the task, the git state and the changed files. pas-agent status shows the session with numbered lists, and pas-agent update --done 1 marks remaining item #1 as finished.

Step 4: hand off to Codex 

pas-agent export --to codex
codex

The export writes the session into AGENTS.md, and Codex reads it at startup. It now knows the task, what is done, what was decided and what comes next.

One thing to know: agents read their instruction file only when a session starts. So export before you launch the next agent. If it is already running, restart it or ask it to read AGENTS.md.

Let the agent keep it updated

You do not have to run these commands yourself. pas-agent is an ordinary command, so your agent can run it. Add something like this to your own part of CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md:

## Session handoff (PAS-Agent)
When you finish a piece of work, record it with
`pas-agent update --completed "..." --next "..."` (plus `--decision` / `--blocker` as needed).
At a milestone or before the session ends, run `pas-agent checkpoint "<summary>"`.

Your own files stay safe

export never overwrites a hand-written CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. It writes only inside a marked block (<!-- pas-agent:start --> to <!-- pas-agent:end -->) and leaves the rest of the file alone. Later exports replace only that block.

Which agents it supports

Right now export --to works for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Kiro CLI, Antigravity and Gemini CLI. Use --output <path> to write the context anywhere else.

Where the data lives

Everything is in .pas-agent/session.json at the project root. Commit it to carry the session across machines, or add it to .gitignore to keep it local. The CLI makes no network requests.

Since the session ends up in a file your agent treats as instructions, review changes to .pas-agent/ the same way you review changes to CLAUDE.md.

Status

pas-agent is in alpha. It works end to end, but the session format and commands may still change before 1.0. Next on the roadmap: shell hooks that update and export automatically when you switch agents.

It is MIT licensed. The code is on GitHub, and the docs are at gfirik.github.io/pas-agent. If you work with more than one AI coding agent, I would like to hear how it fits your workflow.

Originally published on fhsystems.dev. If you need a custom system or AI agent built for your business, send me a note.

title: MDX – Markdown Meets React Components
description:
Originally published with interactive examples at lukiluki.me.

You are writing technical documentation in Markdown. Plain text works until the reader needs a calculator, a live example or a reusable warning box. Copying HTML fragments across articles makes them harder to maintain. How can a document stay readable while using the same components as the application?

MDX combines Markdown with JSX, so documents can import and render React components. In the Next.js App Router, local MDX can participate in server rendering while interactive components live behind explicit client boundaries. This makes shared styling and focused interaction possible. The result still depends on the imported components: using MDX alone does not guarantee static output, type-safe metadata or zero client JavaScript.

Merksatz (Key takeaway):
Use Markdown for the learning path and components for tasks that need them. Keep interactive state in separate client components and check what reaches the browser.

How MDX works in the App Router

The MDX compiler turns a document into JavaScript that renders React elements. Headings and paragraphs become elements; imported components appear where they are used in the document. The MDX format guide explains the combination of Markdown, JSX, expressions and module imports.

With @next/mdx, Next.js processes local .mdx files through its build pipeline. An RSC (React Server Component: A component evaluated on the server whose rendered output can be composed with interactive Client Components.) can render the document and include client components where needed. Client components still need their JavaScript and hydration; importing one does not make the entire surrounding article a client component.

Document element Role What to verify
Markdown headings, paragraphs and lists Structure and readable explanations The rendered heading hierarchy and semantics
Shared component mapping Consistent design-system presentation Mapping does not introduce unnecessary client dependencies
Imported client component State, event handlers or browser APIs The interaction works and has accessible controls
Metadata and frontmatter Search, page titles and exports The project explicitly parses and validates the fields

Map standard elements to the design system

The App Router uses mdx-components.tsx to define component mappings. This allows a Markdown code fence or heading to reuse a styled application component. Next.js documents this setup, including the required mapping file and local MDX imports.

For example, a shared code component can provide syntax highlighting, a frame and a copy button for every article. Keeping that behavior in one place is easier to maintain than repeating styled HTML snippets. It also means the document inherits the behavior and client requirements of that shared component.

Frontmatter (Metadata stored at the start of a document, often as YAML between delimiter lines; parsing and validation must be configured by the application.) is not automatically a validated schema. In this garden, a build script parses metadata and checks it with Zod before generating the index. That is project infrastructure on top of MDX.

Keep interaction in a separate component

Before using this pattern, configure @next/mdx and the component mapping for your Next.js project. The example assumes an App Router application with an @/ source alias. The component file is ordinary TSX; the article imports it rather than defining hooks inside the MDX document.

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";

export default function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <button
      type="button"
      onClick={() => setCount((value) => value + 1)}
      className="min-h-11 rounded-lg border px-4 py-2"
    >
      Clicks: {count}
    </button>
  );
}

Save that component as src/components/Counter.tsx. The corresponding article can then contain:

import Counter from "@/components/Counter";

## Try the example

Activate the button by mouse or keyboard and watch the count change.

<Counter />

The expected result is a heading, an explanatory paragraph and a button whose count changes. Build the page, then test the interaction in the browser. A successful MDX compilation alone does not verify keyboard behavior, layout stability or the correctness of a larger interactive tool.

Use components where they improve the document

Markdown is a good default for explanations, lists and comparison tables. A reusable callout helps when it gives a warning a clear role. An interactive tool is useful when inputs change real data or behavior. A collection of preset comparisons can usually remain a table.

Keep large dependencies behind deliberate boundaries and load them when the reader needs them. Avoid placing client hooks directly in an article or importing an entire component catalog for one small example. Review the resulting bundle rather than assuming an island is free.

One design system, multiple reading depths
Shared components can keep documentation consistent with the application. UI Components discusses component libraries, while Explainable Text shows how optional explanations can stay in the reading flow.

MDX checklist

  • [ ] Put state, event handlers and browser APIs in separate client files.
  • [ ] Keep the page's H1 in its wrapper and use a coherent H2/H3 structure in the article.
  • [ ] Parse metadata explicitly and validate it against the page configuration.
  • [ ] Build the application, then test any imported interaction in a real browser.
  • [ ] Inspect the text export so important explanations survive without JSX.

Sources and next steps

  • MDX: What is MDX? – syntax, imports and embedded components.
  • Next.js: MDX guide – local integration and component mapping; check the guide for your installed version.

For shared UI choices, continue with UI Components. For optional depth within a paragraph, see Explainable Text.

title: Understanding public static void main(String[] args) in Java
description:
Introduction

In Java, public static void main(String[] args) is the traditional entry point of a Java application. When we execute a Java program, the Java launcher looks for a valid main method to start the application.

Let's understand each component.

1. Public

public is an access modifier. It allows the method to be accessed from outside its class. The Java launcher needs access to the main method to start the application.

2. Static

static is a keyword that makes a method belong to the class rather than an individual object.

The main method is static because the Java launcher needs to invoke it without creating an object of the class.

3. Void

void is a return type that indicates the method does not return any value.

For example:

void display() {
    System.out.println("Hello Java");
}

4. Main

main is the method name recognized by the traditional Java application launcher as the entry point of the program.

5. String[] args

String[] args is an array parameter used to receive command-line arguments. These arguments are passed when executing the program through the terminal.

Example:

class Student {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(args[0]);
    }
}

Execute:

java Student Abishek

Output:

Abishek

Here, args[0] accesses the first command-line argument.

How Does Java Execute the Main Method?

  1. We write Java source code.
  2. The javac compiler converts it into bytecode.
  3. The Java launcher starts the application.
  4. The JVM loads and initializes the required class.
  5. The launcher invokes the main method.
  6. The statements inside main are executed.

Conclusion

Understanding public static void main(String[] args) is essential for every Java programmer. It explains how a Java application starts, how the launcher invokes the main method, and how command-line arguments are passed to a program.

title: How to Schedule Storage for Saving User Documents: Throughput Signals
description:
Short answer: for saving user documents, compare storage adapters with interrupted multi-gigabyte uploads and duplicate retention jobs; select the integration whose recovery and audit boundaries fit the training pipeline.

The decision rule is straightforward: schedule retention from a durable manifest, and choose the storage adapter that keeps large training artifacts moving after an interrupted transfer. Small-document upload latency is not a useful proxy for this workload.

For a B2B SaaS training pipeline, I would test a 10 MB document, a 500 MB archive, and a multi-gigabyte artifact before committing to an integration. Record completed bytes, retry count, p50 and p95 upload time, and the time until the object is readable. Then make retention a versioned state transition rather than a nightly script that guesses what is safe to delete.

That approach answers the practical question behind comparing storage services for user documents. The service name matters less than the transfer boundary, authorization model, event behavior, and evidence available when a scheduled job runs twice. I used to treat the upload callback as the finish line; missed jobs and duplicate deliveries are why I now treat it as an input to reconciliation.

The scheduler is the boundary.

At first, I assumed a successful upload response was enough to start training. The failure appears later: a worker receives two completion events, one manifest write is delayed, and a retention pass sees a different state from the processor. That chain is why the verification record needs the object identity, byte count, policy revision, and downstream enqueue result together. When a 4 GB transfer fails near completion, those fields tell the on-call engineer whether to resume, inspect, or safely replay the job; without them, the team is left comparing timestamps and guessing which copy is authoritative.

How should storage handle saving user documents at scale?

An uploaded training artifact is both data and a future job. The bytes may be a compressed dataset, an evaluation bundle, or an exported notebook. The scheduler later decides whether that object is active, eligible for deletion, or already gone. Those decisions need a stable identity.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat an upload-complete notification as an at-least-once signal. It is not proof that the manifest was committed, the checksum was verified, or downstream processing succeeded. A worker must be safe to run twice. Boring retries are a design requirement.

Use a key that includes the tenant identifier, training-run identifier, artifact identifier, and schema version. Do not put an expiration date in the key. Retention rules change; object names tend to survive those policy changes. Keep the policy revision, checksum algorithm, byte count, and lifecycle state in a database manifest.

The object store owns bytes. The manifest explains why they should still exist.

How should the large-file path be measured?

Measure the failure path.

Start with a failure late in the transfer. Interrupt a 4 GB artifact after several gigabytes, retry with the same artifact identity, and compare resumed work with a second full upload. A happy-path benchmark hides the most expensive mistake: a retry that starts over while the first attempt still occupies bandwidth or storage.

The test harness should hold constant the region class, object sizes, concurrency, retry budget, checksum rule, and client/server path. Run direct client uploads separately from server-mediated uploads. Proxying a multi-gigabyte object through an application instance changes memory pressure, connection failure behavior, and throughput, so combining those measurements produces a misleading result.

I would record these fields for every attempt:

  • artifact identity and policy revision
  • attempt number and bytes acknowledged
  • checksum algorithm and final object generation
  • authorization result and time to readable state
  • event delivery delay and retention-deletion confirmation time

The comparison target is not a single upload speed. It is the amount of coordination required to make the result trustworthy. Supabase Storage documents an S3-compatible protocol and database-backed policy integration. Firebase Cloud Storage for Firebase uses Google Cloud Storage buckets with Firebase Security Rules. Amazon S3 exposes multipart upload primitives. Those are different integration boundaries, not a ranking.

Test each behind the same application interface. A useful result says which adapter resumes an interrupted transfer, how incomplete work is cleaned up, and which system owns the final authorization decision. It does not declare a universal winner.

Build the retention state machine before the worker

Keep the first state machine small: active, eligible, deleting, and deleted. The upload path creates an active manifest only after identity and size verification. A policy evaluation moves it to eligible with the policy revision that made the decision. A scheduled worker claims it, attempts deletion, and records the response. A retry can safely inspect the object and repeat the operation.

The application boundary should expose generic operations, not provider-specific calls. Here is a compact Go shape for a storage adapter and an upload verification step:

package retention

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
)

type ObjectStore interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, key string, body io.Reader, size int64) error
    Head(ctx context.Context, key string) (size int64, generation string, err error)
    Delete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

type Manifest struct {
    Key            string
    Size           int64
    Generation     string
    PolicyRevision string
    State          string
}

func VerifyUpload(ctx context.Context, store ObjectStore, key string, expectedSize int64) (Manifest, error) {
    gotSize, generation, err := store.Head(ctx, key)
    if err != nil {
        return Manifest{}, fmt.Errorf("inspect %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    if gotSize != expectedSize || generation == "" {
        return Manifest{}, errors.New("object identity check failed")
    }
    return Manifest{Key: key, Size: gotSize, Generation: generation, State: "active"}, nil
}

The adapter must define what generation means. It can be an object version, an opaque provider generation, or another documented identity. Do not compare unlike identifiers and call the result a checksum. For content integrity, use the storage system's documented checksum semantics and record the algorithm explicitly.

The worker needs an atomic claim in the manifest store. Two deliveries for the same eligible row should produce one logical deletion, even if both processes reach the provider. A lease or compare-and-swap claim can prevent concurrent work; idempotent delete behavior and an audit record handle a retry after a process crash. The exact mechanism is less important than making the state transition observable.

What does a fair storage comparison include?

Concern Test condition Evidence to retain
Large-file throughput 10 MB, 500 MB, and 4 GB artifacts at fixed concurrency p50 and p95 duration, completed bytes, retry count
Resume behavior Drop the connection after several gigabytes resumed bytes, duplicate objects, final generation
Authorization Repeat the same request for permitted and forbidden tenants decision latency and audit event
Retention Run two workers against the same eligible manifest one claim, repeatable delete, durable tombstone
Event handling Delay or duplicate completion notifications manifest state and downstream enqueue count

Supabase Storage, Firebase Cloud Storage for Firebase, and Amazon S3 can all be evaluated against this matrix, but their primitives do not remove the application work. A Firebase rules decision still needs to align with the tenant recorded in the manifest. S3 multipart work still needs a policy for abandoned uploads. An S3-compatible endpoint still needs a test for the exact features and checksum behavior used by the adapter.

That is the trade-off I would put in the review record: which boundary is simpler for the existing identity system, which one gives the training pipeline reliable large-file recovery, and which one leaves the clearest deletion evidence. Avoid turning a provider's client ergonomics into a proxy for operational correctness.

Verify rollout, then make rollback boring

Before enabling deletion, replay a fixture containing active artifacts, already-deleted artifacts, missing objects, expired policy revisions, and two workers claiming one row. The expected outcome is one durable state transition per artifact. Add a deliberate connection drop during a large upload. A test that never interrupts the stream is not exercising the incident path.

Use dry-run mode first. It should record the candidate key, policy revision, and reason without deleting bytes. Once deletion is enabled, keep the manifest tombstone and audit record for the period required by the data policy. Configure alerts for stuck deleting rows, abandoned multipart work where supported, repeated authorization failures, and a gap between an upload event and an active manifest.

Rollback should stop new deletion claims and leave existing object state untouched. Restoring a deleted artifact from backup is a recovery procedure, not a rollback button. If the policy logic is wrong, deploy a new policy revision and reconcile manifests explicitly; silently changing the meaning of an old revision makes the next postmortem much harder.

For cached responses, set directives deliberately. Cache-Control: no-store is appropriate when content must not be stored by caches. A bounded freshness policy can fit immutable, access-controlled artifacts served through a signed URL. Caching rules do not replace authorization or retention policy.

The final decision should fit in one review note: measured large-file behavior, failure recovery, tenant authorization, lifecycle evidence, and the operational work left to the team. If those facts are recorded, changing the storage adapter later is a controlled migration instead of a rewrite of the scheduler.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control
  • https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage
  • https://firebase.google.com/docs/storage
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html

title: AWS Partner Central expands analytics access with Partner Central Agents and Data Subscriptions
description:
AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers now have two new ways to access their analytics data in AWS Partner Central. Partner Central Agents answer questions in plain language, and Data Subscriptions deliver Partner Central data to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket every day.

Partner Central Agents answer questions about leads, marketing campaigns, opportunities and pipeline, and funding, without navigating dashboards or exporting to spreadsheets. AWS Marketplace sellers can also ask about usage, agreements and renewals, billing, collections, and disbursements. Partners can get the same answers in their own artificial intelligence (AI) assistants and agents through the Partner Central Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

Data Subscriptions deliver ready-to-use datasets to an S3 bucket daily, covering leads, marketing campaigns, partner account relationships, opportunities and pipeline, and AWS Marketplace usage, agreements, and renewals. Because the data lives in a partner's own S3 bucket, partners can connect it to the tools of their choice, such as a business intelligence (BI) tool, a customer relationship management (CRM) system like Salesforce or HubSpot, or a generative AI assistant, and build the reports they need.

Both features use existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and permissions, so partners see only the data they are already allowed to see, and exported data stays in their own AWS account.

These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Partner Central is available.

To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and ask an analytics question, such as "What are my top opportunities this quarter?" To set up Data Subscriptions, choose Settings, and then choose Data Subscriptions. To learn more, see Data Subscriptions in the Partner Central Guide.

title: Building Bilingual (Arabic + English) Shopify Themes: Practical RTL Lessons
description:
If you build storefronts for clients in the Gulf, sooner or later someone asks for an Arabic version of their Shopify store. Shopify Markets and the translation tools handle the words, but the theme has to handle direction. Right-to-left (RTL) support is where many otherwise solid themes fall apart: arrows point the wrong way, carousels slide backwards, prices wrap strangely and icons sit on the wrong side of their labels.

Here are the lessons that have saved us the most time when building bilingual themes.

1. Set the direction once, at the root

Do not sprinkle dir="rtl" across individual sections. Set it on the <html> element based on the active locale, so the whole document flips consistently:

{%- liquid
  assign rtl_locales = 'ar,he,fa,ur' | split: ','
  assign page_dir = 'ltr'
  if rtl_locales contains request.locale.iso_code
    assign page_dir = 'rtl'
  endif
-%}
<html lang="{{ request.locale.iso_code }}" dir="{{ page_dir }}">

With direction set at the root, the browser handles text alignment, table columns and form fields for you. Your job becomes fixing the places where the CSS fights the browser.

2. Replace physical CSS properties with logical ones

The single biggest improvement is moving from left/right to logical properties. Instead of:

.card__badge { left: 12px; }
.price { margin-right: 8px; text-align: left; }

write:

.card__badge { inset-inline-start: 12px; }
.price { margin-inline-end: 8px; text-align: start; }

margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, inset-inline-start, border-inline-start and text-align: start all follow the document direction automatically. One stylesheet now works for both languages, and you avoid maintaining a separate rtl.css file that drifts out of sync.

Browser support for logical properties is excellent in every evergreen browser, so there is little reason to avoid them on new builds.

3. Flip directional icons, not all icons

Arrows, chevrons and "back" icons should mirror in RTL. Search, cart, user and close icons should not. A small utility class keeps this explicit:

[dir="rtl"] .icon--directional { transform: scaleX(-1); }

Apply icon--directional only to icons that imply movement or reading order. Logos, product images and anything containing Latin text should never be flipped.

4. Watch out for sliders and JavaScript positioning

Carousel libraries often calculate positions with scrollLeft or translate values that assume left-to-right flow. Before shipping:

  • check whether your slider library has an RTL option and pass it based on document.dir,
  • test swipe gestures on a real phone, because swipe direction should feel natural for Arabic readers, and
  • check scrollLeft behaviour, since browsers report negative values in RTL containers.

A quick guard in your theme JavaScript helps:

const isRTL = document.documentElement.dir === 'rtl';
slider.init({ rtl: isRTL });

5. Handle mixed-direction content carefully

Product titles in Arabic stores often contain English brand names, model numbers or sizes. The Unicode bidirectional algorithm usually copes, but numbers and punctuation at the edges of a string can jump to the wrong side. Wrap user-generated or mixed values with <bdi>:

<span class="product-sku"><bdi>{{ variant.sku }}</bdi></span>

Prices deserve extra testing. Check how the currency code or symbol renders next to Arabic text, and make sure phone numbers in the footer stay readable in both directions.

6. Choose fonts that support Arabic properly

Many popular Latin web fonts have no Arabic glyphs, so the browser falls back to a system font and the store suddenly looks inconsistent. Pick a pairing with a proper Arabic companion, set it with a locale-based class, and increase the line height slightly. Arabic script generally needs more vertical space to stay readable.

[lang="ar"] body { font-family: 'Noto Kufi Arabic', system-ui, sans-serif; line-height: 1.8; }

7. Test the whole purchase path, not just the homepage

The homepage is usually fine after the steps above. Problems hide in the cart drawer, quantity selectors, filters, account pages and the order confirmation email. Walk through a complete order in Arabic on mobile before calling the job done.

Closing thoughts

RTL support is much easier when it is planned from the first line of CSS rather than patched at the end. Set the direction at the root, use logical properties, be deliberate about icons and sliders, and test real purchase flows. If you would rather hand the work to a team that does this regularly, a specialist Shopify Development Dubai studio can build bilingual themes from the ground up, and the same principles apply to any custom Web Design Dubai project that has to serve both Arabic and English audiences.

title: Build a Muslim Baby Names CLI and JSON Microservice in Go (stdlib only, cached, 9 languages)
description:
Name pickers are a common feature in Muslim parenting, family-tree and greeting-card apps. In this tutorial we build one in Go, using only the standard library:

  • a CLI that lists Muslim names filtered by gender and by a search term,
  • a disk cache so the data is downloaded at most once a day,
  • a small JSON microservice (GET /names?gender=female&lang=ur) that returns each name's meaning in the requested language, falling back to English,
  • unit tests with httptest, so the tests never touch the network.

The data comes from the public sample JSON of the SunnahSource Islamic Names API.

1. Look at the data 

curl -s https://sunnahsource.org/data/json/islamic-names.json

The response is a small document with an items array. Each item has an Arabic name, an English name, a gender and meanings in 9 languages (en, ur, fr, de, tr, ms, ru, zh-CN, ja):

{
  "title": "Islamic Names",
  "description": "Beautiful Muslim names for boys and girls with meanings",
  "is_free": false,
  "items": [
    {
      "name_ar": "عَلِي",
      "name_en": "Ali",
      "gender": "male",
      "translations": {
        "en": "High, elevated, noble",
        "ur": "بلند، عالی، شریف",
        "de": "Hoch, edel"
      }
    }
  ]
}

(Translations trimmed for space.) The public file is a sample with a handful of names. The full dataset is part of the paid API, see the pricing page. The code below works the same way with both, because the shape is identical.

2. Project setup 

mkdir names && cd names
go mod init names

Everything goes in one main.go. No third-party modules are needed.

3. Types that mirror the JSON 

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const sourceURL = "https://sunnahsource.org/data/json/islamic-names.json"

// Name mirrors one entry in the "items" array.
type Name struct {
    NameAr       string            `json:"name_ar"`
    NameEn       string            `json:"name_en"`
    Gender       string            `json:"gender"`
    Translations map[string]string `json:"translations"`
}

// Dataset mirrors the top-level JSON document.
type Dataset struct {
    Title       string `json:"title"`
    Description string `json:"description"`
    IsFree      bool   `json:"is_free"`
    Items       []Name `json:"items"`
}

translations is a flat map[string]string, so adding a new language on the server needs no code change.

4. Meaning with an English fallback, and filtering 

// Meaning returns the meaning in lang, falling back to English.
func (n Name) Meaning(lang string) string {
    if m, ok := n.Translations[lang]; ok && m != "" {
        return m
    }
    return n.Translations["en"]
}

// Filter returns names matching gender ("" = any) and a case-insensitive
// query against the English name or the meaning in lang.
func Filter(items []Name, gender, query, lang string) []Name {
    q := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(query))
    var out []Name
    for _, n := range items {
        if gender != "" && !strings.EqualFold(n.Gender, gender) {
            continue
        }
        if q != "" &&
            !strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(n.NameEn), q) &&
            !strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(n.Meaning(lang)), q) {
            continue
        }
        out = append(out, n)
    }
    sort.Slice(out, func(i, j int) bool { return out[i].NameEn < out[j].NameEn })
    return out
}

Searching the meaning as well as the name is what makes a name picker useful. A parent can type "noble" or "praised" and get matching names.

5. Download once, then cache on disk 

// Load reads the cache file if it is fresh, otherwise downloads and caches it.
func Load(url, cachePath string, maxAge time.Duration) (*Dataset, error) {
    if st, err := os.Stat(cachePath); err == nil && time.Since(st.ModTime()) < maxAge {
        if b, err := os.ReadFile(cachePath); err == nil {
            var d Dataset
            if json.Unmarshal(b, &d) == nil {
                return &d, nil
            }
        }
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    resp, err := client.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unexpected status %s", resp.Status)
    }
    var d Dataset
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&d); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if b, err := json.Marshal(d); err == nil {
        _ = os.WriteFile(cachePath, b, 0o644)
    }
    return &d, nil
}

Two details matter here. Always set a client Timeout, because Go's default client waits forever. And if the cache file is corrupt, the code just falls through and downloads a fresh copy.

6. The HTTP microservice 

type apiName struct {
    Arabic  string `json:"arabic"`
    English string `json:"english"`
    Gender  string `json:"gender"`
    Meaning string `json:"meaning"`
}

// Handler serves GET /names?gender=female&lang=ur&q=noble
func Handler(d *Dataset) http.HandlerFunc {
    return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        lang := r.URL.Query().Get("lang")
        if lang == "" {
            lang = "en"
        }
        res := []apiName{}
        for _, n := range Filter(d.Items, r.URL.Query().Get("gender"), r.URL.Query().Get("q"), lang) {
            res = append(res, apiName{n.NameAr, n.NameEn, n.Gender, n.Meaning(lang)})
        }
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8")
        w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=3600")
        _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]any{"count": len(res), "lang": lang, "names": res})
    }
}

Starting res as []apiName{} rather than nil means an empty result is encoded as [], not null. Front-end code will thank you.

7. Wire up the CLI 

func main() {
    gender := flag.String("gender", "", "male or female (empty = both)")
    lang := flag.String("lang", "en", "en, ur, fr, de, tr, ms, ru, zh-CN, ja")
    query := flag.String("q", "", "search the name or its meaning")
    serve := flag.String("serve", "", "listen address, e.g. :8080 (starts the HTTP API)")
    flag.Parse()

    d, err := Load(sourceURL, "islamic-names.cache.json", 24*time.Hour)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if *serve != "" {
        http.HandleFunc("/names", Handler(d))
        log.Printf("listening on %s", *serve)
        log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(*serve, nil))
    }
    for _, n := range Filter(d.Items, *gender, *query, *lang) {
        fmt.Printf("%-10s %-8s %-7s %s\n", n.NameEn, n.NameAr, n.Gender, n.Meaning(*lang))
    }
}

8. Run it 

$ go run . -gender female
Aisha      عَائِشَة female  Living, prosperous — wife of Prophet (SAW)
Fatima     فَاطِمَة female  One who abstains — daughter of Prophet (SAW)

$ go run . -lang ur -q yusuf
Yusuf      يُوسُف   male    اللہ بڑھاتا ہے — حضرت یوسف علیہ السلام

And as a service:

$ go run . -serve :8080
$ curl 'localhost:8080/names?gender=male&lang=de'
{"count":3,"lang":"de","names":[{"arabic":"عَلِي","english":"Ali","gender":"male","meaning":"Hoch, edel"},{"arabic":"مُحَمَّد","english":"Muhammad","gender":"male","meaning":"Gepriesener — Name des letzten Propheten"},{"arabic":"يُوسُف","english":"Yusuf","gender":"male","meaning":"Allah mehrt"}]}

(Arabic and Urdu are right-to-left. In a terminal the column alignment can look a little off. In a browser, wrap them in an element with dir="rtl".)

9. Tests without the network

httptest.NewServer gives the loader a fake upstream, so the tests check the cache logic and never call the real API:

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "path/filepath"
    "testing"
    "time"
)

var sample = []Name{
    {NameAr: "عَلِي", NameEn: "Ali", Gender: "male", Translations: map[string]string{"en": "High, elevated, noble", "ur": "بلند، عالی، شریف"}},
    {NameAr: "فَاطِمَة", NameEn: "Fatima", Gender: "female", Translations: map[string]string{"en": "One who abstains"}},
}

func TestFilterQueryMeaning(t *testing.T) {
    if got := Filter(sample, "", "noble", "en"); len(got) != 1 || got[0].NameEn != "Ali" {
        t.Fatalf("got %+v", got)
    }
}

func TestMeaningFallback(t *testing.T) {
    if m := sample[1].Meaning("ur"); m != "One who abstains" {
        t.Fatalf("fallback failed: %q", m)
    }
}

func TestLoadAndCache(t *testing.T) {
    calls := 0
    srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        calls++
        _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(Dataset{Title: "Islamic Names", Items: sample})
    }))
    defer srv.Close()
    cache := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "c.json")
    for i := 0; i < 2; i++ {
        if d, err := Load(srv.URL, cache, time.Hour); err != nil || len(d.Items) != 2 {
            t.Fatalf("load %d: %v", i, err)
        }
    }
    if calls != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 network call, got %d", calls)
    }
}

func TestHandler(t *testing.T) {
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    Handler(&Dataset{Items: sample})(rec, httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/names?gender=male&lang=ur", nil))
    var body struct {
        Count int       `json:"count"`
        Names []apiName `json:"names"`
    }
    if err := json.Unmarshal(rec.Body.Bytes(), &body); err != nil || body.Count != 1 || body.Names[0].Meaning != "بلند، عالی، شریف" {
        t.Fatalf("bad body %s", rec.Body.String())
    }
}

$ go test ./...
ok      names   0.006s

10. Going further

  • Add background for well-known names. Many Muslim names are names of prophets (such as Yusuf) or companions (such as Ali). You can show a short biography next to them with the Prophets Stories (Ambiya) API and the Sahaba API.
  • Names of Allah are a different list. If you also want the 99 Names (Asma ul Husna), use the Asma ul Husna API instead of mixing them into a baby-name list.
  • Deploy. The binary is a single static file. CGO_ENABLED=0 go build and copy it to any small VPS or container.

Source and links

  • SunnahSource Islamic Names API: https://sunnahsource.org/apis/islamic-names/
  • All SunnahSource Islamic APIs (Quran, Hadith, Duas, Prayer Times and more): https://sunnahsource.org/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/sunnahsourceofficial-droid/sunnahsource-islamic-api

If you build something with it, share it in the comments.

title: Best colour contrast checkers for WCAG text pairs
description:
Best colour contrast checkers for WCAG text pairs

Checking two colours against WCAG 2 contrast is a defined calculation: relative luminance of the lighter and darker colours, then (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). The tools that do that job are not interchangeable. Some only grade text. Some also cover the 3:1 bar for graphics and UI components in WCAG 2.1/2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11. Some add colour-vision simulations. None of the options below is an APCA checker, and none replaces a full accessibility audit of real components, focus states, or text inside images.

This article was written with the assistance of AI.

This compares five tools whose official pages are built around the same task: enter a foreground and a background, get a contrast ratio, and see WCAG-style pass or fail grades. It is not a hands-on benchmark and not a single “overall best” ranking. Pick by workflow — a quick hex pair in the browser, sampling colours off a PDF or a native window, or explaining who a failing pair may affect.

The same checks apply to each tool: the contrast model and whether non-text 3:1 is shown as its own result; hex, RGB, HSL or HSV, alpha, and eyedropper support; preview, font samples, reverse, saved pairs, shareable URLs, or an API; colour-vision simulations and how the vendor describes them; browser versus an installed app, plus published price; and only the data-handling claims the vendor actually states. Missing claims are marked unknown. Ratios were not re-computed here.

WebAIM Contrast Checker

WebAIM’s Contrast Checker is a free page from WebAIM, a non-profit service center at Utah State University that has published accessibility resources since 1999. You enter foreground and background colours as RGB hex, or use a colour picker; an alpha value can be set on the foreground, and lightness sliders let you nudge a failing pair toward a target ratio.

It reports AA and AAA for normal and large text, plus a separate WCAG 2.1 AA result for graphical objects and user interface components (the 3:1 non-text bar). Large text is defined on the page as 14 point (typically 18.66 px) and bold or larger, or 18 point (typically 24 px) or larger. Permalinks use fcolor and bcolor query parameters. Appending &api returns JSON with the ratio and pass/fail states. WebAIM also offers a bookmarklet and a companion link contrast checker for links distinguished by colour alone.

WebAIM’s terms say the organization will not sell or otherwise give personal information submitted to it to external parties. Colour values appear in the page URL. WebAIM pages use Google Analytics; treat any broader telemetry claim as unknown beyond those terms.

Best fit: a widely cited, no-install checker, including the non-text 3:1 row, a documented definition of “large text,” and an API or bookmarklet. Trade-off: no colour-vision simulation on this page, and it is not a system-wide eyedropper for a PDF or a native app.

TPGi Colour Contrast Analyser

The Colour Contrast Analyser (CCA), currently listed as version 3.5.5, is a free desktop app from TPGi / Vispero. The open-source repository describes Windows and macOS builds (Electron; GPL-3.0). The product page says it can be used on websites, app UIs, social graphics, PowerPoint, PDFs, and InDesign — anywhere you can point an eyedropper.

Documented features include swapping foreground and background; WCAG 2.0, 2.1, and 2.2 results; HEX, RGB, HSV, and HSL entry; alpha on the foreground; sliders to adjust a failing pair; short or long copy-to-clipboard result formats; a preview for text and non-text contrast; a colour-blindness simulator with eight vision-deficiency settings; and language plus theme preferences. The GitHub README notes that the colour picker is for Windows and macOS only, which matches the supported builds.

CCA is free, with the usual GPL “no warranty” language. A dedicated, CCA-specific privacy policy describing local sampling versus any app telemetry was not found on the product page — unknown. There is no shareable URL workflow, because this is an installed app.

Best fit: testers who need to sample real pixels from a document, a design file, or a running interface, with non-text contrast and a built-in colour-blindness simulator. Trade-off: it requires an install, and it is the wrong shape for “paste this permalink into the ticket.”

WhoCanUse

WhoCanUse is a free browser tool (open source, GitHub: CoreyGinnivan/whocanuse) that starts from a contrast ratio and then shows how that pair may look under several visual conditions. The site describes regular trichromatic vision, several red/green/blue deficiencies, achromatopsia, plus simulations for cataracts, glaucoma, low vision, direct sunlight, and Night Shift. Population percentages are attributed to colour-blindness.com and Vision Australia; the site itself warns that those estimates do not add up to 100% and do not cover every impairment.

The project says contrast comes from chroma.js, grades also consider font size and weight, and colour-blind simulations use the color-blind library. Cataracts, glaucoma, low vision, and the situational modes are described as personally created simulations — useful as illustrations, not clinical measurements. A failing grade is explained as a combination that “offers some visual strain” and “should be avoided if possible,” which is broader language than a strict WCAG table.

No price or account is mentioned. The homepage describes client-side libraries for the math and simulations; whether the hosted site also runs analytics is not stated there — unknown.

Best fit: critiques where the question is not only “does this pair pass AA?” but “who might struggle with it, and under what conditions?” Trade-off: the simulations are approximations; it is less of a token-handoff or audit-export tool than WebAIM or CCA.

colourcontrast.cc

colourcontrast.cc is a free Colour Contrast Checker by Alex Clapperton. The live page (verified 22 November 2026) shows pass/fail for AA Large, AAA Large, AA Normal, and AAA Normal; background and foreground fields; RGB and HSL slider tabs; copy-to-clipboard; reverse colours; a “Save colours” control; a “Select Google font” control; and large and normal example copy. Query parameters work as a share mechanism: https://colourcontrast.cc/?background=ffffff&foreground=000000 reloads those values in the inputs.

A dedicated non-text / UI-component 3:1 row was not present in the page UI reviewed for this article. Alpha inputs and a system eyedropper were also not found there. How “Save colours” is stored, and for how many pairs, is not documented on the page — unknown. Choosing a Google font implies a request to Google Fonts for preview.

Best fit: a clean, shareable pair checker with HSL controls and a font preview, without installing software. Trade-off: no documented non-text contrast row, and no documented colour-vision simulator.

Colour Contrast Analyser

The colour contrast analyser on Uwarp is a free browser tool for foreground and background pairs. The product page says it computes WCAG 2.x relative luminance, (Llighter + 0.05) / (Ldarker + 0.05), and lists pass/fail rows it describes as “above 3:1” (AA Large), “above 4.5:1” (AA normal and AAA Large), and “above 7:1” (AAA normal). Those “above” phrases are the page’s wording, not the standard. WCAG 2 uses at least: a ratio of 3:1, 4.5:1, or 7:1 meets the relevant criterion. Equality counts as a pass. Inputs are six-digit hex fields plus RGB and HSL sliders. You can reverse a pair, save up to six recent combinations in localStorage on that device, preview large and normal copy, optionally choose from a Google Fonts list (described as the top 50 by popularity), and reload a pair from background and foreground query parameters.

The page is explicit about scope: WCAG 2.x relative luminance, “not APCA, not print ink or window tint simulation.” Ratio math is described as client-side, with colours “not uploaded for analysis.” Optional Google Fonts previews, if used, would still request those font files from Google.

What it does not document, compared with some tools above: a separate non-text / UI-component 3:1 result, foreground alpha, a screen eyedropper, or colour-vision simulations. The saved-pair limit is six, locally, on that browser.

Best fit: a quick, shareable hex-pair check in the same browser style as colourcontrast.cc, with a clearly stated WCAG 2.x formula and a small local swatch history. Trade-off: it is not a substitute for CCA when you need to sample pixels off a PDF or a native window, and it is not a substitute for WhoCanUse when you need deficiency simulations.

Choose by the job, not by a composite score

Use WebAIM when you want the most widely referenced browser checker, including the non-text 3:1 row and an official API. Use CCA when the colours live on screen in a file or app, not already as hex tokens. Use WhoCanUse when the review needs simulations and a reminder that a ratio is about people, not only a badge. Use colourcontrast.cc or Uwarp when the workflow is “paste two values, preview type, share or save the pair.” Between those last two, the documented differences are practical: Uwarp publishes a six-pair localStorage cap and an explicit “not APCA” scope note; colourcontrast.cc exposes a working ?background=&foreground= share URL and the same hex/RGB/HSL plus font-preview pattern, but does not document a non-text row or a save-limit.

If the work is a design system or a production UI, use more than one of these for different questions — token contrast, on-screen sampling, and simulation — and still inspect the real component states. A passing pair in a checker does not guarantee that placeholder text, disabled buttons, or icons meet the same bar.

title: P2P Fraud Is a UX Problem: How One "Payment Confirmed" Button Empties Wallets
description:
A seller on a P2P marketplace recently lost his crypto to a classic case of P2P fraud — in a trade that looked completely normal.

The buyer tapped the button that marks a trade as paid. The interface updated. The trade screen showed the payment step as done. The seller, watching a countdown timer eat into his trade window, pressed "release."

His bank account was empty. It had always been empty. The "payment confirmed" state he trusted was never a confirmation of anything. It was the buyer's own claim, rendered by the interface with the same visual weight as a verified fact.

No hacking. No malware. Just one ambiguous button, one timer, and one moment of misplaced trust. This is how most P2P fraud actually works, and it is why I have come to see P2P fraud less as a security problem and more as a UX problem.

I work on community and growth at a mobile-first crypto project with a live P2P trading zone. I see these cases from the support side, and the pattern is almost always the same: the technology did not fail. The interface told a story that was not true, and the user believed the story.

The core bug: buyer-declared states wearing system-verified clothes

In most P2P trade flows, the payment step has two completely different events:

  1. The buyer declares "I have paid" (a self-reported claim)
  2. The seller verifies the money arrived in their own account (a checked fact)

Good interfaces keep these visually and structurally separate. Bad interfaces merge them into a single green checkmark.

When a buyer-declared claim is styled like a system verification — same color, same checkmark, same position in the progress bar — the UI is effectively lying. The seller reads "payment confirmed" and reasonably concludes the platform confirmed it. The platform confirmed nothing. It just recorded a tap.

This single design decision is behind a huge share of P2P fraud losses:

  • The "paid" button trick. The buyer marks the trade paid, sends a friendly message ("sent, please release"), and the seller releases against an empty account.
  • The fake screenshot. The buyer uploads an edited banking screenshot. Because the flow already trained the seller to accept in-app artifacts as proof, the image feels like one more confirmation.
  • Timer pressure. Trade windows count down. Verification takes a minute of opening a banking app. Releasing takes one tap. The interface rewards the fast, wrong action and punishes the slow, correct one.

None of these require the scammer to defeat any security system. They only require the scammer to understand the interface slightly better than the victim does.

What the fraud patterns teach us about design

Looking at real P2P fraud cases, the same design weaknesses keep appearing:

1. Proof is whatever the buyer uploads.
If your flow accepts a screenshot as evidence of payment, your flow accepts fiction as evidence of payment. The only trustworthy proof lives in the seller's own bank account, and the UI should say exactly that, at exactly the moment of release.

2. Reversible rails are treated like final ones.
Chargeback fraud works because a buyer can pay through a reversible method, receive the crypto, and then pull the payment back. Interfaces that display all payment methods as equally "safe" hide a real difference in risk. Method risk should be visible, not buried in a help page.

3. Leaving the platform feels like a shortcut, not an exit from protection.
Scammers constantly try to move the trade or the payment off-platform "to save fees." Users follow because nothing in the flow communicates that escrow and dispute protection end at the platform's border. The warning exists, but it appears once, early, in small text — not at the moment the user is about to step outside.

4. The dispute button is designed like an afterthought.
In too many trade flows, disputing is harder to find than releasing. Yet the dispute is the only action that freezes a bad trade while it can still be fixed. Once a trade completes, support teams, including ours, generally cannot reverse it. The safest button in the flow should not be the hardest one to reach.

Design fixes that actually reduce P2P fraud

If you are building or redesigning a P2P flow, these are the changes that matter most, in order:

Separate claim from verification in the state model.
Model the payment step as two states — buyer_claimed_paid and seller_verified_received — and render them differently. The claim can be neutral. Only verification gets the green checkmark. Never let a self-reported state borrow the visual language of a verified one.

Put the verification instruction on the release button itself.
At the moment of release, show: "Release only if the exact amount is visible in your own bank account. A screenshot or the buyer's message is not proof." This is not legal copy. It is the product working as intended.

Make dispute the path of least resistance.
When a trade is marked paid but the seller has not verified receipt, the dispute action should be at least as prominent as release. In our own P2P flow at UNC, the dispute option sits inside the trade itself, because a seller who cannot find it in ten seconds effectively does not have it.

Design timers that do not punish checking.
If your trade window expires while a seller is verifying a payment, your timer is a fraud feature. Pause the countdown when a payment claim is made, or extend it automatically while verification is pending.

Show counterparty risk where decisions happen.
Account age, completed trades, and verified-name matching between the platform profile and the payment sender should be visible inside the trade screen, not on a separate profile page the seller may never open.

Label payment methods by reversibility.
A small "reversible" tag on risky rails teaches users more than a blog post ever will.

The takeaway

P2P fraud is usually described as a user-education problem: "users should be more careful." But when the same mistake is made by thousands of different users, in the same place, in the same way, it is not a user problem anymore. It is a design signal.

The honest state model, the honest button label, the honest timer: these are small engineering choices, and they decide whether the next first-time seller keeps their money. Build the interface so that the truth is the easiest thing to believe.

Shahzad works on community and growth at UNC, a mobile-first crypto project built around verified human participation. Disclosure: the author is affiliated with UNC, whose P2P market is mentioned once above as an example of in-trade dispute placement.

title: Amazon CloudFront Announces HTTP/2 Support for Connections to Origins
description:
Amazon CloudFront now supports HTTP/2 connections to custom origins and VPC origins. HTTP/2 lets CloudFront send many requests over fewer connections to your origin. This means fewer connections and TLS handshakes for your origin to handle, which improves performance for API and agentic workloads, such as AI agents calling MCP servers or mobile and web apps calling backend APIs.

Until now, CloudFront connected to origins only over HTTP/1.1, which handles one request at a time per connection. When traffic spiked, for example when an AI agent made many tool calls at once, CloudFront had to open more origin connections. Each new connection added latency and load. With HTTP/2, those requests share connections, so your origin does less work and responds faster. HTTP/2 is also supported for WebSocket connections that support extended CONNECT. If your origin doesn't support HTTP/2, CloudFront automatically falls back to HTTP/1.1, so you don't need to change anything on your origin.

HTTP/2 to origins is available from all CloudFront edge locations. There is no additional cost for using HTTP/2 to origins. To learn more, visit Origin HTTP version in the CloudFront Developer Guide.

title: How to Use the Same Component on Multiple Websites (and Update It Once, Everywhere)
description:
Copies drift, npm packages make every site rebuild, and a hosted script can break the page. Component publishing keeps one versioned, isolated copy and delivers it to every site with one snippet.

There are four common ways to use one component on several websites: write a native Web Component, share an npm package (or a monorepo), embed an iframe, or load a hosted script.

If every site is built from the same codebase, by the same team, on the same framework, use a package or a monorepo. If the component can live in a fixed box, an iframe is enough. If the sites run on different stacks and the component has to be part of the page, you need a hosted script, which is safe only with three things in place: isolation, versions and a way back. A hosted script with all three is called component publishing, and that is what Taggor does.

What are the four ways, and where does each one fit?

1. A native Web Component, written by hand

How it works. You write a custom element with the browser's own APIs, put it in a .js file and load that file on each site.

Where it fits. A small element with no dependencies, on sites where you control the hosting.

Where it hurts. A Web Component is a format, not a delivery system. Where the file lives, how a new version reaches each site and how you go back are yours to solve. Copy the file into each project, and the original problem is back.

2. A shared npm package or a monorepo

How it works. The component lives in a package. Each site installs it, imports it and builds it into its own bundle.

Where it fits. One framework, one team, sites that have a build step. You get types, tests and code review. In this case it is the right answer.

Where it hurts. You publish the package, then every site bumps the version, rebuilds and deploys. Five sites are five deploys, and a site that skips one drifts. A WordPress theme has no npm install at all.

3. An iframe

How it works. You host the component as a small page of its own, and each site embeds that page with an <iframe> tag.

Where it fits. A self-contained widget that can live in a fixed box: a map, a video player, a booking calendar. Styles do not cross the frame in either direction, and one change to the hosted page reaches every site.

Where it hurts. The widget is a separate document. It does not grow with its content unless you write messaging code between the frame and the page, and it does not inherit the page's fonts and colors. An update overwrites the hosted page, with no versions and no way back unless you build them.

4. A hosted script (a remote embed)

How it works. The component is served from one address. Each site carries a script tag and the component's tag, and the component renders inside the page itself.

Where it fits. Sites on different stacks, or sites you cannot rebuild, when the component has to look and behave like part of the page. A single change reaches every site without a deploy on each.

Where it hurts. Reaching every site at once is also the risk, and the section after the diagram explains why. It is also the approach Taggor makes safe.

Why can a hosted script break the page?

Styles collide. The page's CSS reaches into your component, and your component's CSS leaks out into the page.

One error spreads. A script that throws can take other things on the page down with it, and a bad update does that on every site at once.

There is no way back. Say you overwrite widget.js. The old file is gone, and "undo" means fixing forward under pressure.

What is component publishing?

Component publishing is building a piece of a website as its own isolated, versioned unit and delivering it to any site with one snippet.

Here is how Taggor answers the three problems:

  • Isolation. Each component is mounted in a Shadow DOM inside the page, so styles stay on their own side, and an error boundary wraps it. What you write inside the component's tag is fallback content: the visitor sees it until the component loads, or permanently if it cannot load.
  • Versions. Every publish creates a version, and a version's code is immutable.
  • A way back. Sites do not point at a version. They follow a channel, Staging or Production, and a channel points at a version. Going back is moving the pointer.

The snippet is one async script tag per site. It loads a small loader that fetches only the components that site uses. The loader sets no cookies and uses no browser storage.

Taggor also covers the work around the script:

  • Checks before anything goes out. Every publish passes gates for types, size and security, and a file that looks like a secret stops the upload.
  • Your source is kept. Every publish stores the component's source, and npx taggor pull brings it back on any computer.
  • Forms have somewhere to go. A component can declare a collection, and Taggor stores what visitors submit, with anti-spam and export. The data is yours.
  • Your agent can write it. The docs have quickstarts for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor that publish a first component from one prompt.

What does it look like in practice?

The example is a signup form, signup-inline. The finished version in the picture comes from Taggor's own showcase: an email field and a button in one pill, storing each signup in a subscribers collection. The steps below use the starter that init generates, so you can follow them exactly on a new account and put your own form in later.

Sign in, create the project, preview the component and run the checks:

npx taggor login
npx taggor init --component signup-inline
cd <the folder init printed>
npm install
npx taggor dev
npx taggor check

init creates the project in ~/.taggor/projects/<workspace>/ and prints the path. The starter is one defineTaggorComponent call in components/signup-inline/src/index.tsx, with a single prop, headline. That file is where your form goes. dev serves it on a deliberately hostile test page with aggressive CSS, so collisions show up on your machine, not on a client's site. check runs the publication gates.

Create a test site and publish to it:

npx taggor sites create --name "Test site" --domain <test-hostname> --environment staging
npx taggor publish --site <site key>

sites create prints the site key and the snippet, and npx taggor sites snippet <site key> prints the snippet again whenever you need it. publish builds the component remotely, creates version 1.0.0, moves the Staging channel to it and attaches the component to the site. Paste the snippet once into the page, then write the component's tag where the form should appear:

<script async src="https://cdn.taggorcdn.com/s/<site-key>.js"></script>

<signup-inline headline="Join the list">
  <a href="mailto:hello@example.com">Write to us to join the list</a>
</signup-inline>

The link inside the component's tag is the fallback: with the CDN blocked, it is what stays on the page. The showcase form takes label in place of headline.

A client's live site is a Production site. Create it, attach the component, and paste that site's own snippet and the same component tag into its page. Then move Production to the version you just checked:

npx taggor sites create --name "Client A" --domain <client-a-hostname> --environment production
npx taggor attach signup-inline --site <site key>
npx taggor promote signup-inline --to production

Every further client is the first two commands again: per the docs, all Production sites show the version the Production channel points to. How many sites a workspace can have depends on its plan. On Free, sites create is refused above the plan's site limit; the pricing page has the numbers. The docs have platform guides for WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, Wix, Framer, Squarespace and more.

Update once, change everywhere

Now change the component and publish again:

npx taggor publish
npx taggor promote signup-inline --to production

publish creates a new version (1.0.1 in our run) and moves the Staging channel, so the test site shows it first while Production stays on 1.0.0. promote moves the Production channel, and every Production site follows. No page was edited and no site was rebuilt. The CLI says sites pick up the change within about 60 seconds; the docs allow up to about two minutes, because the loader is cached for a short time.

If the new version is wrong:

npx taggor rollback signup-inline --channel production
npx taggor versions signup-inline

rollback points the Production channel back to 1.0.0, on every Production site at once. versions lists each version and the channels that point to it.

When should you not use this?

  • One codebase, one framework, one team. A package or a monorepo does the job inside the tools you already have.
  • A fixed box is enough. For a widget that does not have to blend into the page, an iframe is simpler.
  • You need a different version on each Production site. In Taggor, two Production sites show the same version of a component. To show different versions, publish the component under another name.
  • You want to keep your existing framework components as they are. A Taggor component is written with the Taggor SDK and renders a Preact view, so existing ones have to be ported.

The short version

Copies drift, a package costs one deploy per site, and an iframe keeps the component in a box. A hosted script changes every site at once, so it needs isolation, versions and a way back.

Taggor gives you those three, plus the checks, the hosting and the form data, behind one snippet per site. If your sites are on different stacks, Taggor takes about ten minutes to try: the CLI quickstart goes from signing in to a component on a page of your own. Start at taggor.dev.

title: Lazy-Loading Images on Guide Pages Only — Never on Tool Pages
description:
I made a lazy-loading decision on ramrom.io that sounds backwards at first: the guide pages lazy-load their images, and the tool pages do not lazy-load anything at all. It is not an oversight. It is the one place where I deliberately do not apply a performance best practice, because on the tool pages it would make things worse.

The two kinds of page

The site has two kinds of page, and they behave very differently. A tool page is one job: paste a link, tap download, get the file. It has almost no images — a logo, maybe a small illustration in the 3-step guide, and that is it. A guide page is a long read, a couple of thousand words explaining how a downloader works or what to watch out for, with screenshots and diagrams scattered down the page.

That split is what drives the decision. Lazy loading exists to stop the browser downloading images the visitor may never scroll to. On a guide page that is a real win: most readers never reach the bottom, so why fetch every screenshot up front? On a tool page there is nothing below the fold worth deferring. Every image on the page is already visible, so lazy-loading it would only delay something the visitor needs right now.

What the guide pages do

On guide pages every content image gets loading="lazy" and decoding="async", and — this is the part people skip — explicit width and height attributes. The lazy attribute stops the download until the image nears the viewport. The width and height stop the page jumping when the image finally arrives, because the browser reserves the space before it knows the file.

That last point matters more than the lazy loading itself. I chased layout shift to zero on the tool pages and I am not about to reintroduce it on the guides. A page that reflows while you read is worse than a page that loads a fraction slower. So the rule on guides is: lazy, but with the box already reserved.

I also keep the first image on a guide page eager. It is usually the header illustration, it sits above the fold, and deferring it would delay the largest contentful paint for no benefit. The lazy attribute goes on everything from the second image down.

What the tool pages do instead

Tool pages carry no loading="lazy" at all. The logo and the 3-step visual guide are above the fold and part of the first paint, so the browser should fetch them immediately. Making them lazy would mean the logo pops in a beat after the rest of the page, which looks broken, and it would push the largest contentful paint later on the exact pages where speed matters most — the pages a visitor lands on, uses, and leaves in under a minute.

The deeper reason is that tool pages barely have images in the first place. The whole homepage stays under 100KB. There is no hero photograph, no carousel, no stock imagery. When a page has two small images, the optimisation is not lazy loading; it is not having a dozen images to defer. The performance budget is enforced by what I choose not to put on the page, not by clever attributes.

The check that keeps me honest

The rule is simple enough to test by hand. Open a guide page, watch the network tab, and confirm only the first image loads before scrolling. Open a tool page and confirm everything is there on first paint with no pop-in. If a new guide image ever ships without width and height, the layout shift shows up immediately in the field data, and that is the signal to fix it.

Lazy loading is a good default. It is just not a universal one. The question is never "should I lazy-load images" — it is "which images does the visitor actually need right now". On my site the answer splits cleanly down the middle: guides, yes, from the second image down; tool pages, no, because everything on them is already the job.

title: Tackling LLM Prompt Bloat: Building a Just-In-Time Context Router in Rust
description:
As autonomous agent frameworks grow in complexity, developers continually add rules, domain doctrines, coding style guides, and edge-case remediations.

The easiest path—and the most common anti-pattern—is simply appending every new rule to the global system prompt. Within a few months, the base prompt balloons from 500 tokens to 8,000+ tokens.

This phenomenon, known as Fatal Prompt Bloat, has severe consequences:

  1. Context Window Saturation: Drastically reduces available token space for real codebase context, compiler logs, and deep conversation history.
  2. Inference Latency & Cost: Every single turn incurs the quadratic attention overhead of parsing thousands of irrelevant static tokens.
  3. Reasoning Degradation (Attention Diffusion): When a model is bombarded with 50 disparate rules (e.g. Docker rules, Blender instructions, React best practices, and Git protocols simultaneously), its attention mechanism diffuses, leading to subtle instruction non-compliance.

When architecting the cognitive subsystem for Flowork OS, we outlawed always-on static prompts in favor of a Formula 5-3-3 Just-In-Time Sliding Window Router written in Rust.

The Zero-Bloat Mandate: 100% Conditional Directives

Under the Flowork OS system prompt architecture, the base prompt remains locked to a minimal anchor (~400 tokens covering identity and approval boundaries).

Every other domain instruction exists as a Passive Trigger (/opt/floworkos/system/system_promp/promps/triggers/) or a native compiled Rust rule checker (rules/.bin/*).

Directives are injected dynamically only when their environmental conditions match:

  • Not modifying an ISO build script? $ ightarrow$ The ISO build directive is completely absent from context.
  • Not working with Android APKs or Scrcpy? $ ightarrow$ The Android subsystem prompt is not loaded.
  • Not configuring Glass HUD compositing? $ ightarrow$ The HUD styling rules never enter the prompt envelope.

Sub-Millisecond Native Rule Evaluation

To ensure dynamic context injection introduces zero noticeable user latency, rule evaluation is executed natively in Rust (mrflow-rs/src/cognitive/mod.rs):

// Fast-path landmark and structural inspection (<50ms timeout)
let structural_checks = vec![
    (
        is_build_intent && (has_tool("compile_code") || has_tool("run_command")),
        "triggers/code_engineering.md",
    ),
    (
        is_search_intent && (has_tool("grep_search") || has_tool("glob")),
        "triggers/search_efficiency.md",
    ),
    (
        cwd.join("FLOWORK.md").exists() || cwd.join(".flowork/MEMORY.md").exists(),
        "triggers/memory_routing.md",
    ),
];

By keeping individual trigger directives dense and strictly under 250 words, the agent retains razor-sharp focus on the task at hand without suffering cognitive drift.

Explore the Codebase

The entire prompt router, native cognitive loop, and Landlock security sandbox are open-source.

  • Visit our project hub at floworkos.com
  • Read the architecture documentation on GitHub: flowork-os/flowork-os
