title: Gradle Under the Hood: Hybrid JPMS Process Isolation & Dynamic Module Reflection
description:
Over the first four articles of our Gradle Under the Hood series, we explored source-driven incremental tracking, network-immune classloader harvesting, compile-only dependency isolation, and our federated plugin architecture.

Today, in Part 5, we tackle one of the biggest friction points in modern enterprise Java builds: How do you run build-time JPA tooling—like bytecode enhancement, schema validation, and query linting—against modular Java applications (module-info.java) without forcing developers to weaken their module encapsulation?

Let’s look at how we engineered JPersist v1.9.0 to support hybrid JPMS execution, dynamic ModuleDescriptor reflection opens, and vendor-specific provider settings out of the box.

The JPMS Build-Time Tooling Wall

The Java Platform Module System (JPMS) provides strong encapsulation and reliable configuration. However, build-time persistence tools—especially Hibernate—rely heavily on deep reflection (Field.setAccessible(true)) to inspect entity classes, generate metamodels, and validate schemas.

When a project introduces a module-info.java descriptor, standard Gradle workers running on a flat classpath hit a wall:

  1. Encapsulation Blockades: Unless the user explicitly adds opens com.example.domain to io.github.jpersist.tools.hibernate.orm; inside their production module-info.java, Hibernate throws an InaccessibleObjectException during schema validation or query linting. Forcing developers to pollute production module descriptors just to satisfy build-time linters is an anti-pattern.
  2. Process Fork Overhead: Running every project inside a forked JVM process (processIsolation) guarantees modular boundaries, but adds unnecessary startup latency for traditional, non-modular classpath projects.

The Solution: Hybrid Execution Isolation (JPMSWorkerSupport)

To get the best of both worlds, we designed JPMSWorkerSupport—a hybrid execution router that inspects the target source set's compiled output directory at task execution time:

static boolean isModularProject(File classesDir) {
    return classesDir != null && new File(classesDir, "module-info.class").exists()
}

Depending on whether module-info.class is present, JPersist dynamically chooses the optimal Gradle WorkerExecutor isolation strategy:

  • Non-Modular Projects (Classpath): Executes in-process using fast classLoaderIsolation, avoiding any JVM fork overhead.
  • Modular Projects (JPMS): Switches automatically to hermetic OS-level processIsolation, placing the user's classes and dependencies onto --module-path while keeping Gradle's worker action bridge files on the bootstrap classpath.

Dynamic ModuleDescriptor Inspection & --add-opens Injection

To prevent users from having to manually open their entity packages in module-info.java, JPMSWorkerSupport reads the compiled module-info.class binary directly using Java's standard java.lang.module.ModuleDescriptor API before spawning the worker JVM:

private static void appendDynamicUserModuleOpens(File moduleInfoFile, List<String> jvmArgs) {
    try {
        byte[] bytes = Files.readAllBytes(moduleInfoFile.toPath())
        ModuleDescriptor descriptor = ModuleDescriptor.read(ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes))
        String moduleName = descriptor.name()

        descriptor.packages().each { String pkg ->
            jvmArgs.add('--add-opens')
            jvmArgs.add("\${moduleName}/pkg={HIBERNATE_MODULES}".toString())
        }
    } catch (Exception ignored) {
        // Safe fallback if module-info.class cannot be parsed
    }
}

At runtime, JPersist automatically constructs the exact --add-opens <userModule>/<package>=io.github.jpersist.tools.hibernate.orm,io.github.jpersist.tools.hibernate flags for the forked worker JVM. Production encapsulation stays completely intact, while build-time tools get temporary, scoped reflective access.

Dual-Layer SPI Resolution (ModuleLayer vs. ClassLoader)

Because workers can now boot either on a JPMS --module-path or a traditional ClassLoader, our underlying SPI resolution layer (PersistenceServiceResolver) adapts dynamically inside the worker process:

  • When ModuleLayer.boot() contains our io.github.jpersist.tools.api module, factories (NamedObjectParserFactory, SchemaValidatorFactory, EnhancerProvider) are discovered via ServiceLoader.load(ModuleLayer.boot(), serviceType).
  • Otherwise, it falls back seamlessly to Thread.currentThread().contextClassLoader.

Fine-Tuning Provider Behavior with Custom settings

Real-world enterprise schemas often rely on custom SQL dialects, specific default schemas, or strict JPA compliance flags. In v1.9.0, we also exposed @Input @Optional MapProperty<String, Object> getSettings() across both LinterExtension and ValidationExtension:

persistence {
    main {
        validation {
            settings = [
                'hibernate.default_schema': 'APP_CORE',
                'hibernate.physical_naming_strategy': 'org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy'
            ]
        }
        linter {
            settings = [
                'hibernate.dialect': 'org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect',
                'hibernate.jpa.compliance.query': 'true'
            ]
        }
    }
}

These properties are serialized cleanly across the Gradle Configuration Cache boundary and passed directly into the isolated worker's SPI factory initialization.

The Engineering Win

By combining hybrid worker isolation with bytecode-level ModuleDescriptor inspection, JPersist v1.9.0 removes the friction of adopting JPMS in enterprise persistence projects:

  1. Clean Production Descriptors: Zero need to pollute module-info.java with build-tool-only opens directives.
  2. Zero Overhead for Legacy Modules: Non-modular subprojects inside the same multi-module build continue running in-process without spawning extra JVMs.
  3. Full Vendor Control: Custom dialects, naming strategies, and compliance settings propagate cleanly into isolated worker sandboxes.

Are you adopting JPMS (module-info.java) in your enterprise Java builds, and what build-tool hurdles have you run into? Let's discuss in the comments below!

🔗 Explore the complete JPersist architecture on GitHub: https://github.com/jpersist/persistence

title: How a Sales Career at MongoDB Will Set You Apart
description:
A sales career at MongoDB means owning the entire sales cycle, from pipeline generation to close, in a team-based culture where peers share what works, and career advancement follows results. MongoDB sellers say being stretched by challenging projects and coached by leaders who roll up their sleeves and work deals alongside them is exactly what accelerates their growth.

Our sellers often describe MongoDB as “the MIT of sales” and a place where you’ll earn your “PhD in sales.” “MongoDB gives you a very unique opportunity to cover accounts that stretch you, continue to push you, and make you grow in ways that you never thought possible,” says Brett Baker, Strategic Account Director. The people who have built careers in MongoDB sales agree. The work is demanding, and the product is complex, but our sellers say that challenge is also the draw.

At MongoDB, you own the sales cycle, win alongside colleagues who share what they learn, and get promoted when you deliver—all while enabling global enterprises to build and succeed in the AI era. Here’s what sales leaders and account executives around the world say makes selling at MongoDB different.

A culture built on more than hitting your quota

As a workplace, MongoDB is known for high performance and rigorous standards. But the people who work here tend to lead with something else when they talk about what makes the company unique.

"I describe MongoDB sales culture in three words: excellence, teamwork, and recognition," said Charlotte Crété, a sales development manager in Barcelona. "Excellence, because you'll be surrounded by brilliant colleagues and leaders who will push you to become great at what you do. Teamwork, because at MongoDB, I've never seen anyone close a deal ontheir own. And recognition, because we make sure to celebrate each other's wins and contributions."

The importance of teamwork to MongoDB’s sales culture can’t be overstated. The sales motion at MongoDB is a team sport in the truest sense, with everyone from account development representatives, solutions architects, customer success, professional services, legal, and senior leadership all moving together on a deal.

What's equally striking is how openly team members talk about harder moments. Lukas Kowalski, a commercial growth account executive for the DACH region, put it plainly: "Sales is a roller coaster. No, you can't succeed all the time. You will lose some deals. You will have some difficult customer conversations." What matters, he said, is what happens next. "At MongoDB, you have people left and right who went through similar journeys, who have similar challenges, and everybody's here to help you succeed."

Owning the full sales cycle

Selling at MongoDB is not a handoff culture. Account executives own their deals from the first conversation to close, and that full-cycle ownership is something our team views as a genuine differentiator for professional development.

"At MongoDB, you truly own the entire sales cycle, from pipeline generation all the way to closing," said Woojoon Chu, an enterprise account executive in South Korea. "By focusing on working directly with developers and selling real technical value, you build the complete skillset needed for salespeople in the AI era."

Ella To, a senior enterprise account executive in Hong Kong who joined MongoDB after working at Microsoft and Google Cloud, explained the shift: "When I came to MongoDB, I realized that I needed to develop my own ability to incite interest for customers, tell the MongoDB story, and connect our value to the customer's priorities." The result, she said, has been a meaningful transformation. "MongoDB helped me grow from someone who was mainly experienced in cloud selling into a complete enterprise seller."

Peer learning as a daily practice

Formal training is a priority at MongoDB, from structured enablement programs, methodology frameworks, onboarding academies, and dedicated sales leadership development tracks. But the learning culture that our people describe most vividly is the informal kind: the peer-to-peer exchange that happens every day across teams and geographies.

"Whenever someone finds a new solution to a problem or a new way of including AI into our operating rhythm, it will be shared immediately," explained Kowalski. "We are creating our own development sessions within our teams, but also within the broader sales organization."

Navdeep Arora, a regional director for Asia-Pacific, described a culture she called the "teach-back" approach: "You take a concept or something you've learned and teach it back to your peers. It sounds simple, but it's incredibly powerful because when you teach something, you develop a much deeper understanding of it yourself. Experiences like this happen frequently at MongoDB and have helped me evolve beyond being a sales manager into a more strategic and impactful leader.”

Career progression that's real

MongoDB's BDR to CRO program gives our career progression philosophy a name, but what makes it feel real to the people inside it is how concretely it shows up in day-to-day conversations with leadership.

"The BDR to CRO program at MongoDB is a true testament to development. It is a structured framework that is transparent and performance-based, which supports the career aspirations of salespeople moving into multiple levels of leadership," said Arora. "The program also helps people upskill and gear up for opportunities to move between regions or even cross-functional teams, creating endless opportunities for their next career move."

Brett Baker, a strategic account director in the U.S., described how that looks from a rep's seat. "MongoDB is an extremely fast-growing company, which naturally creates a lot of growth opportunities for its employees," he said. "My manager and my VP spent a lot of time with me speaking about the future and identifying areas of opportunity to accomplish my goals and achieve the promotions I was after.”

The moment is now

The market context adds its own layer of motivation. MongoDB sits at the intersection of data modernization and AI adoption—two of the most significant technology shifts of the decade—and the people selling it know it.

"I am 100% sure that MongoDB will be a major winner in both the AI and agentic era," said Kowalski. "We’re not talking about AI alone anymore. We're talking about agents, independent systems that use AI and use your data to really do the work for you."

At MongoDB, our reps aren’t just selling a data platform. They’re sitting with engineering leaders and IT decision-makers at the exact moment that they're deciding on how they build for the next decade. Baker added a seller's perspective on why MongoDB's position in that moment is so strong: "The market opportunity at MongoDB is unmatched. As a seller, there's really no better place to be than at MongoDB in technology."

Sales at MongoDB can be demanding. The standards are high, the product is complex, and the expectations around performance are real. But what comes through most clearly from the people who have built careers here is that the challenge is the draw, not the deterrent. They stay because they’re surrounded by people who take their growth seriously, because they’re given real ownership from early on, and because the market they're operating in keeps getting more interesting.

In the AI era, sellers who understand the data layer will be the ones who shape what comes next for some of the world’s largest enterprises and most cutting-edge startups. For anyone looking for a sales career that builds something lasting, that combination is hard to find anywhere else.

title: Building Better Web Experiences with React: From Components to Full-Stack Integration
description:
Modern web applications require more than attractive designs. They need to be interactive, responsive, maintainable, and capable of communicating with backend services. React.js has become a popular choice for frontend development because it helps developers build dynamic user interfaces through a component-based approach.

As part of my software development internship at Valentius Kryptix, I worked on improving an existing portfolio web application by transitioning its frontend towards React. This experience helped me understand how frontend development works in practical projects and how individual technologies come together to create a complete web application.

Understanding React and Component-Based Development

React is a JavaScript library used to develop user interfaces. Its biggest advantage is component-based architecture. Instead of creating an entire website in one large file, developers can divide it into smaller, independent components.

For example, a portfolio application can contain separate components for navigation, project cards, login forms, dashboards, and project details. These components can be reused across multiple pages, reducing code duplication and making maintenance easier.

React also provides hooks such as useState and useEffect to manage application data and handle side effects. These features make it easier to build interfaces that respond to user interactions and changing information.

Technologies Behind a React Frontend

Building a functional frontend involves multiple technologies working together. React.js handles the user interface, while Vite provides a fast development environment. HTML and CSS define the structure and appearance, and JavaScript manages application logic.

React Router DOM helps implement navigation between pages without unnecessary full-page reloads. On the backend, Node.js and Express.js can provide APIs, while MongoDB stores application data.

Understanding how these technologies communicate is important for developing full-stack applications.

Connecting Frontend with Backend

A modern frontend should display real information rather than relying entirely on static content. API integration makes this possible.

For example, when a user opens a particular project page, React Router can extract its project ID using useParams. The frontend can then send a request to the backend and display the corresponding project information.

During development, handling loading indicators, errors, and successful responses is equally important. These details improve usability and make applications more reliable.

Challenges and Learning Outcomes

Working on an existing project introduced practical challenges, including organizing folders, correcting component import paths, implementing navigation, and connecting frontend components with backend APIs.

Debugging these issues helped me understand the importance of reading terminal errors, checking browser console messages, and testing API responses.

The experience strengthened my understanding of reusable components, state management, routing, asynchronous JavaScript, and frontend-backend communication.

Conclusion

React frontend development is not simply about creating visually appealing pages. It involves structuring applications, managing data, implementing navigation, integrating APIs, and providing a smooth user experience.

This internship project has helped me connect theoretical knowledge with practical development. It has also encouraged me to explore more advanced React concepts and continue improving my full-stack development skills.

Read the full article: https://valentiuskryptix.com/how-to-build-a-react-frontend-my-development-journey/

title: How to Use a Proxy in Go: net/http, HTTP_PROXY, and Why GOPROXY Is Something Else
description:
By Leo Lin, Product Manager at FlashIP (https://www.flaship.com/), Singapore. Disclosure: I work on FlashIP.

Go has two settings with "proxy" in the name. They do different jobs, and people mix them up all the time. HTTPS_PROXY is a network proxy that your traffic passes through. GOPROXY is a module mirror that go get downloads code from. If you're behind a corporate gateway and go mod download times out, changing GOPROXY won't help. If your company runs a private module mirror, setting HTTPS_PROXY won't point Go at it.

Below is how each one works, based on the official Go docs and a few tests I ran on Go 1.27 against a dead proxy at 127.0.0.1:9. Hostnames and credentials are placeholders.

1. net/http reads HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY

http.DefaultTransport, which http.Get and http.DefaultClient use, picks up its proxy from the environment through http.ProxyFromEnvironment. It reads HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY, or their lowercase versions, and chooses the proxy by the request's scheme:

export HTTPS_PROXY=http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080
export HTTP_PROXY=http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,.internal.example.com,10.0.0.0/8
go run .

Some details that trip people up:

  • The scheme decides. An https:// URL uses HTTPS_PROXY only. In my test, setting only HTTP_PROXY sent https://example.com direct (200 OK). With HTTPS_PROXY set, the same request failed with proxyconnect tcp: ... connection refused.
  • The value can be a full URL or just host[:port]. With host[:port], Go assumes http.
  • localhost is never proxied. ProxyFromEnvironment returns no proxy when the request host is localhost.
  • The environment is read once. In my test, calling os.Setenv("HTTPS_PROXY", ...) after the first request had no effect, and the second request still went direct. Set the variables before the process starts, or set the proxy in code (section 3).

2. NO_PROXY syntax in Go

According to the golang.org/x/net/http/httpproxy docs, NO_PROXY is a comma-separated list. Each entry can be:

  • an IP prefix (1.2.3.4) or a CIDR block (10.0.0.0/8)
  • a domain name, which matches the name and all its subdomains (example.com matches example.com and api.example.com)
  • a domain with a leading dot, which matches subdomains only (.example.com doesn't match example.com)
  • an IP or domain with a port (1.2.3.4:80)
  • *, which turns proxying off completely

Parsing is best effort and errors are ignored. A typo won't throw an error. Go just ignores that entry and proxies the request.

3. Set the proxy in code (including SOCKS5)

To use a proxy that doesn't depend on the environment, set Transport.Proxy:

proxyURL, _ := url.Parse("http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080")
client := &http.Client{
    Transport: &http.Transport{Proxy: http.ProxyURL(proxyURL)},
}
resp, err := client.Get("https://example.com")

Transport.Proxy supports the http, https, socks5 and socks5h schemes. If the scheme is empty, Go uses http. Go treats socks5 the same as socks5h. Username and password in the URL are sent in a Proxy-Authorization header. If Proxy is nil, Go doesn't use a proxy. So a Transport you build yourself without setting Proxy ignores HTTPS_PROXY entirely. To keep the environment behavior on a custom transport, set Proxy: http.ProxyFromEnvironment.

My test confirmed SOCKS5 works from both places: http.ProxyURL with a socks5:// URL and HTTPS_PROXY=socks5://127.0.0.1:9 both tried the dead proxy and failed.

4. GOPROXY is a module mirror, not a network proxy

GOPROXY tells the go command where to download modules. Its default value is:

https://proxy.golang.org,direct
  • direct means fetch from the version control repository, off means don't fetch at all, and the separator controls fallback. After a comma, Go tries the next entry only on a 404 or 410 response. After a pipe (|), it tries the next entry on any error, timeouts included.
  • GOPRIVATE=*.corp.example.com lists module path patterns that should never be requested from a proxy. It's the default for both GONOPROXY and GONOSUMDB.
  • A private mirror can take credentials in the URL: GOPROXY=https://user:pass@proxy.corp.example.com.

To save these settings, use go env -w GOPROXY=.... It writes to a config file in your user config directory, and GOENV changes where that file lives. go env -w only accepts Go's own variables, though. go env -w HTTPS_PROXY=... failed with unknown go command variable HTTPS_PROXY, so the network proxy still belongs in your shell or service environment.

The go command does honor HTTPS_PROXY when it talks to a module mirror. With a dead proxy in HTTPS_PROXY, go mod download failed with a proxyconnect error against proxy.golang.org. For direct fetches Go runs git, and Git has its own http.proxy setting. Its docs describe that setting as overriding http_proxy/https_proxy/all_proxy.

Quick triage

  • curl uses the proxy but your Go binary doesn't → check that HTTPS_PROXY is set for the process, and that a custom Transport sets Proxy.
  • An internal host still goes through the proxy → check NO_PROXY for typos. Remember the leading-dot rule.
  • go get is blocked by the network → set HTTPS_PROXY, not GOPROXY.
  • Private modules return 404/410 or fail checksum lookups → set GOPRIVATE.

If you're testing against an external proxy, FlashIP (https://www.flaship.com/) offers HTTP(S) and SOCKS5 endpoints with username:password or IP whitelist authentication. The URL formats above work for either type.

Sources

  • net/http package docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http
  • httpproxy package (NO_PROXY rules): https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/net/http/httpproxy
  • Go Modules Reference (GOPROXY, GOPRIVATE): https://go.dev/ref/mod
  • cmd/go (go env -w, GOENV): https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go
  • git-config (http.proxy): https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config

title: 116x Faster Is True. It Is Also the Wrong Number.
description:
The 116x number is not a lie. It is a measurement of the wrong thing. I ran the whole loop on my own fuzzy dedupe, a thousand names with typos, and the function really did get 110 times faster. The app got 48 times faster. Both numbers are from the same run, and the difference between them is the only thing worth writing about.

Fast-Anything does one thing: it profiles your app, finds the slowest function, has a coding agent rewrite just that function in Rust, proves the rewrite behaves the same on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. The headline number, 116x, comes from their fuzzy dedupe example: a Python dedupe of 700 names falling from 4.91 seconds to 42 milliseconds. I built my own version of the same job, 1,005 names with typos, 163 unique after dedupe, and ran the whole loop on it. My baseline was 2.61 seconds, then 2.57 on the repeat.

The scan took about seven seconds under the profiler and named the obvious suspect. dedupe was 99.9 percent of the run in a single call. Inside it, levenshtein ran 67,427 times and took 99.6 percent. The third function on the list was the typo generator, which the tool refused to port, correctly, because it calls random and no deterministic rewrite of a random function means anything. That refusal is the first thing the tool got right. A profiler that proposes porting your randomness is a profiler that has not understood your program.

The port step recorded one real call to dedupe and wrote a crate with a brief for the coding agent. I wrote the Rust myself, following that brief: the Levenshtein distance over characters, not bytes, because Python strings index by code point and a byte-based port would have failed on the first non-ASCII name. Then the tool replayed every recorded call plus the edge cases it derives, empty input, non-ASCII text, long inputs, against the Rust build. Thirty-five out of thirty-five came back identical. Per call, the function went from 2,536.8 milliseconds in Python to 23.1 in Rust. That is 110 times faster, measured, and close enough to the advertised 116 that the headline survives contact with my machine.

Then I ran the benchmark, which times the whole app, not the function. Five runs each, interleaved. Python: 2.60 seconds. Rust: 55 milliseconds. Forty-eight times faster end to end.

Forty-eight is the honest number and 110 is the true one, and they are different because the function is not the app. The app also generates a thousand names, prints a line, and starts a Python interpreter, and none of that got faster. The port moved the only part that was slow, and the slow part was 99.9 percent of the run, so the app still got dramatically faster. But the gap between 110 and 48 is the fixed cost of everything around the function, and no port touches that. A bigger app with more fixed cost would show a smaller end-to-end number from the same 110-times function. A smaller one would show a bigger number. The per-call figure belongs to the function. The end-to-end figure belongs to the app. Quoting the first as if it were the second is how a real speedup turns into a misleading one.

None of this makes the tool a gimmick. The loop worked exactly as described: scan found the hot function, the port was verified against real calls before anything was swapped in, and the swap is reversible. What it makes is a tool whose headline number needs a second number next to it, the one for the whole program. I would still port the hot function. I just would not tell anyone it made my app 116 times faster, because it made one function 110 times faster and my app 48 times faster, and the second number is the one a user feels.

What is the biggest gap you have seen between a function's speedup and the app's? I keep finding the fixed costs are larger than anyone admits before they measure them.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Kubernetes v1.38 Sneak Peek
description:
As we get closer to the release date for Kubernetes v1.38, the project develops and matures, features may be deprecated, removed, or replaced with better ones for the project's overall health. This blog post outlines some of the planned changes for the Kubernetes v1.38 release that the release team feels you should be aware of for the continued maintenance of your Kubernetes environment and keeping up to date with the latest changes. The information listed below is based on the current status of the v1.38 release and may change before the actual release date.

Deprecations and removals for Kubernetes v1.38

kubectl: WebSocket opt-out environment variables removed

kubectl has used WebSockets instead of SPDY by default for kubectl exec, attach and cp since v1.30, and for kubectl port-forward since v1.31. The KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS and KUBECTL_PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS environment variables let you turn that behavior off. These variables are going to be removed in v1.38. kubectl will then always try WebSockets first and fall back to SPDY when it needs to (the same as the current default behavior). If your scripts or CI environments set either of these environment variables, you can remove them since they will no longer have any effect.

To learn more, refer to KEP-4006: Transition from SPDY to WebSockets.

kubectl: name dropped from kuberc credential plugin allowlist entries

The kuberc file keeps kubectl user preferences separate from cluster credentials in the kubeconfig, including an allowlist of the credential plugins kubectl is allowed to run. In the beta kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 API, an allowlist entry can use name as an alias for command. The name field (not command) has been deprecated since v1.36.

With kuberc expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, the new kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1 API will not include name. If any of your allowlist entries use name, change them to command now.

To learn more, refer to KEP-3104: Separate kubectl user preferences from cluster configs.

Ongoing major changes

Future removal of cgroup v1 support

Support for cgroup v1 is being phased out. Since v1.35, the kubelet fails to start on nodes that use cgroup v1 unless you set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration. This option remains available in v1.38, but it should be treated as a short-term fix as support for cgroup v1 is planned to be removed in a future release. If you haven't already, please plan your migration to cgroup v2.

To learn more, refer to KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support.

Admission webhooks no longer receive authentication and authorization review requests

Since v1.37, the ExcludeAdmissionWebhookVirtualResources feature gate has been enabled by default. With it on, validating and mutating admission webhooks no longer receive requests for (virtual) writes to TokenReview, SelfSubjectReview, SubjectAccessReview, SelfSubjectAccessReview, LocalSubjectAccessReview or SelfSubjectRulesReview. Creating or updating a webhook configuration whose rules name one of these resources returns a deprecation warning, and the API server logs any existing configurations that are affected when it starts.

If you rely on a webhook to see these requests, you can turn the feature gate off for now, but note that the gate is planned to be locked on when the feature graduates to stable.

To learn more, refer to KEP-5793: Manifest Based Admission Control Config.

Breaking changes in Kubernetes v1.38

Container runtimes must report the cgroup driver

The kubelet in v1.37 and older supported releases provides a legacy mechanism to configure the cgroup driver. The modern way to do that is via the CRI RuntimeConfig RPC, which reports the cgroup driver that the container runtime recommends using. In v1.38, the kubelet defaults to not allowing the legacy configuration mechanism: it will be both deprecated and unavailable unless explicitly re-activated. As a result, v1.38 nodes will essentially require that your container runtime is running before the kubelet starts (to look up the expected cgroup driver); if the kubelet can't get the cgroup driver from the runtime even after retrying, it will exit with an error before even registering the node.

As part of this upcoming release, the cgroupDriver field in the kubelet configuration file will be deprecated. Not only is specifying that field going to be deprecated, the kubelet will actually reject it unless you reactivate the legacy mechanism by enabling the (temporary) LegacyCgroupDriverFallback feature gate. The kubeadm tool will also no longer set cgroupDriver to systemd by default, and its preflight checks will report an error if the runtime doesn't support the RPC. If any of your nodes run an older, incompatible container runtime, you should follow the instructions in the official v1.38 release notes about how to upgrade.

To learn more, refer to KEP-4033: Discover cgroup driver from CRI and kubernetes/kubernetes#136731.

Pod-level resources: swap behavior changes on LimitedSwap nodes

If you use pod-level resources on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2 and are configured with LimitedSwap, the kubelet in v1.38 will start applying swap limits based on the Pod's pod-level memory settings. This means that Pods whose pod-level memory request equals their memory limit will get no swap at all (both for the Pod and for every container in it), even if a container sets a memory request lower than its limit. Check any workloads that rely on swap before you upgrade, and be sure to read the official release notes for v1.38 for detailed advice.

To learn more, refer to KEP-2837: Pod Level Resource Specifications.

Featured enhancements of Kubernetes v1.38

The following list of enhancements is likely to be included in the upcoming v1.38 release. This is not a commitment and the release content is subject to change.

kubectl user preferences (kuberc) graduating to stable

kuberc, the separate kubectl configuration file for user preferences such as aliases, default options and a credential plugin policy, is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38.

To learn more, read Kubectl user preferences (kuberc) or refer to KEP-3104: Separate kubectl user preferences from cluster configs.

Pod-level resources graduating to stable

Pod-level resources, which let you set CPU, memory and hugepages requests and limits for a Pod as a whole, are expected to graduate to stable in v1.38. If you run Linux nodes with LimitedSwap, see the swap behavior change above before you upgrade.

To learn more, read Assign Pod-level CPU and memory resources or refer to KEP-2837: Pod Level Resource Specifications.

DRA support for partitionable devices graduating to stable

Partitionable devices let a Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver advertise a device such as a GPU both as a whole and as smaller partitions, and the scheduler allocates only combinations that fit within the physical device. The feature is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, and the DRAPartitionableDevices feature gate will then be locked on.

To learn more, read Partitionable devices or refer to KEP-4815: DRA: Add support for partitionable devices.

EvictionRequest API (alpha)

Evicting a Pod isn’t always as simple as terminating it. Some applications may be in the middle of important work, such as data migration or cleanup, and terminating them without giving them time to prepare can cause disruptions.

The EvictionRequest API introduces a more coordinated way to evict Pods. It gives applications and controllers time to prepare before a Pod is evicted. For example, when a node needs to be drained or a Pod needs to be moved to another node, a controller can create an EvictionRequest to signal that this Pod needs to be evicted.

The eviction request controller coordinates with the responders configured for the Pod. These responders can perform application-specific tasks such as completing ongoing work, cleaning up resources, or migrating data before the Pod is terminated.

If no custom responder is available or responders don't complete the process, Kubernetes can fall back to the existing API-initiated eviction mechanism, which continues to respect PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs). The EvictionRequest API does not replace PDBs. It gives applications a chance to participate in the eviction process.

As this is an alpha feature, you will need to enable the EvictionRequestAPI feature gate and the relevant alpha API group. Check the v1.38 release notes and documentation, once they're available, to confirm exactly what's required.

To learn more, refer to KEP-4563: EvictionRequest API.

Want to know more?

New features and deprecations are also announced in the Kubernetes release notes. We will formally announce what's new in Kubernetes v1.38 as part of the CHANGELOG for that release.

The Kubernetes v1.38 release is planned for Wednesday, December 16th, 2026. Stay tuned for updates!

You can see the announcements of changes in the release notes for:

  • Kubernetes v1.37
  • Kubernetes v1.36
  • Kubernetes v1.35

If you don't know where to start, join our monthly New Contributor Orientations where we teach the community how the project is structured, and we'll guide you on how to make your first contribution to the project.

title: AWS Global Accelerator now preserves client IPs for NLBs with TLS listeners
description:
AWS Global Accelerator now preserves the client IP address for traffic sent to Network Load Balancer (NLB) endpoints with TLS listeners. You can terminate TLS at your NLB and still see the original client IP address in your application. This means you can apply security groups, geo-blocking, rate limiting, fraud detection, audit logging, allowlists, and compliance controls based on the real client IP.

Previously, you couldn't add an NLB with a TLS listener to an accelerator that had client IP address preservation enabled. You had to choose between terminating TLS at the NLB and seeing the real client IP address. With this launch, you get both. This helps with workloads that need TLS termination at Layer 4, such as non-HTTP TCP protocols, applications that require static or Elastic IP addresses, and high-throughput traffic where a Layer 7 load balancer isn't a fit.

To enable this feature, add an NLB with a TLS listener as an endpoint to an accelerator with client IP address preservation setting turned on, the same way you add any NLB. No additional configuration is required! Client IP address preservation for NLBs with TLS listeners is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions. Standard Global Accelerator pricing applies.

To learn more, see Client IP address preservation in the AWS Global Accelerator Developer Guide and Create a listener for your Network Load Balancer in the User Guide for Network Load Balancers.

title: Amazon Aurora serverless for MySQL now supports up to 384 ACUs
description:
Amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use. 
 
 With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For new clusters, select a supported Aurora MySQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to update the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora MySQL versions 3.14 and 8.4.10, running on Platform Version 4. 
 
To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing.  To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console.

title: Announcing metal size for Amazon EC2 G7 instances

Customers can use the metal size of G7 instances to run physical AI simulations, deploy AI agent sandboxes, and accelerate graphics workloads that need direct access to bare metal infrastructure. title: Rust port: 177/177 match, 0.62x slower, 1 crash
description:
Rust port: 177/177 match, 0.62x slower, 1 crash

The leaf port matches 177 out of 177 recorded cases, runs slower than the Python it replaces, and enabling it as shipped crashes the app on launch. The tool knows about two of those three problems and says so in its own output. The third one it does not.

Yesterday I ran fast-anything on a fuzzy dedupe script: 10.06 seconds became 129 milliseconds, 78x faster, 34 out of 34 recorded calls matching. The same author shipped the bigger tool a week earlier — rust-anything, created 2026-11-16, 8,502 stars — and its pitch is the whole app, not the 5%: record what the app does, port it one piece at a time, prove each piece against the recording, and end with a pure Rust binary. I ran it on the exact same code to see what changes when the goal is the whole app instead of one hot function.

The setup

Same app as yesterday: 700 names, near-duplicates with typos, collapse within Levenshtein distance 2. Pure standard library, deliberately naive quadratic loop. Yesterday's clean baseline was 10.06s for dedupe(), with levenshtein called 151,315 times.

rust-anything 3.3.0, installed from npm. Its loop is: analyze -> bridge -> record -> port src/port.rs -> build -> diff -> gate, plus an app track (record / front-door / wire / lift) for moving the whole CLI.

go refuses the entry point

My first try was the one-command path, rust-anything go -- python3 dedupe.py. It ran the workload and then failed: no CPU profile was written: is the workload a node process? The profile step wants the repository root passed explicitly. With go . --lang python -- python3 dedupe.py it profiled fine — dedupe at 99% of the run, levenshtein at 98%, 151,315 calls, same shape as yesterday — and then refused:

error: every export of `dedupe.py` must stay in Python: levenshtein (not hot
in the profiled run; `go` ports one function), typo (not hot in the profiled
run; `go` ports one function), make_names (not hot in the profiled run;
`go` ports one function), dedupe (a command-line entry point: it stays in
Python, and `app front-door` takes the command line over when the whole app
moves)

This is the first real difference from fast-anything. The 5% tool ports whatever is hot, entry point or not. The whole-app tool will not port the function that owns __main__ — that belongs to the app track. So I ran the app track instead.

The front door: a Rust binary that runs Python

app record ran the CLI twice and stored 1 case (no-args), noting the timing line differs between runs and wildcarding it. app front-door scaffolded rust/app, a Rust binary with a clap parser that owns the entry point, and every command still runs the original Python underneath. Build and replay: 1/1 cases passed, fallback rate 100%.

That is the honest starting state of a whole-app migration: a Rust binary that is, for now, a launcher for the Python it will replace. The rest of the flow is supposed to drive the fallback rate to zero, one wired unit at a time.

analyze tripped over the tool's own install directory

One detour worth recording: analyze first reported the repo as TypeScript/JavaScript with 0 units. The cause was my own npm install rust-anything — the package.json and node_modules in the same directory made the language detector pick JS. Moving those out of the repo fixed it: the unit is dedupe.py, 69 lines, readiness 89, PyO3 bridge. The risk list it printed was accurate: string offsets and slicing, dynamic typing (3 places), clock and random numbers (make_names uses random.Random).

bridge ports the leaves, not the loop

bridge created rust/dedupe-rs for levenshtein and typo. dedupe and make_names stay in Python — again, entry points. So the unit to port is the two leaf functions, and the 151,315-call loop stays in Python, crossing into Rust once per call. The bridge has a --batch option for exactly this shape ("runs function over many param values kept in Rust"), which the profile output had hinted at, but the default bridge run does not apply it.

record: 177 cases, 143 of them throws 

Recorded 177 cases (143 threw) in rust/dedupe-rs/cases.jsonl
  levenshtein: 88
  typo: 89

The recorder feeds generated JSON values as arguments. For levenshtein that produces a genuinely interesting set: 34 cases return a value, 54 throw. The values include things like levenshtein(["a", 1], {}) == 2, levenshtein(null, null) == 0, levenshtein("x", []) == 1 — Python's duck typing doing its thing on lists and dicts. The throws are TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len(), KeyError: 0 (dict indexed by int), and friends.

For typo, all 89 cases threw. Every single one. The reason is structural: typo takes a random.Random object, and the recorder can only pass JSON values. All 89 errors are AttributeError: '<type>' object has no attribute 'choice' — dict, list, str, int, NoneType, bool. Not one recorded case exercises what typo actually does, because the input it needs cannot be expressed in the recording format. The tool's own docs suggest --pin-clock for random-dependent functions, but pinning the clock does not conjure a Random object into a JSON case either.

The port: Python-faithful, error for error

I wrote the port by hand (no agent is configured on this box, so go stops at TASK.md — same as yesterday). levenshtein reproduces CPython's semantics over JSON values: True == 1, len() TypeErrors with the exact message, dict KeyError: 0, "not subscriptable" for numbers and None, strings indexed by code point. typo reproduces the only behavior the recording covers: the AttributeError, with the type name filled in from the argument. That is a faithful port of the recording, and it is worth saying plainly what it is not: a port of typo.

$ rust-anything build rust/dedupe-rs
Built .../rust/dedupe-rs/python/dedupe_rs
$ rust-anything diff rust/dedupe-rs
177/177 cases match

fuzz — fresh inputs from a new seed, the check that is supposed to catch what the recording missed — was thin: 1/1 fresh cases match (1 round), and again 1/1 over two rounds with --cases 200 --time 60. One fresh case per round is not much of a net.

bench: the Rust is slower, and the tool says so 

function                  cases orig ns/call Rust ns/call   speedup
levenshtein                  88         1936         3446     0.56x
typo                         89         2349         3408     0.69x

Timed as callers call it, crossing included. Overall 0.62x (geometric mean);
0 of 2 functions at least 1.1x faster.
Do not ship this unit for speed: calling across costs more than the work
these functions do. Port a bigger unit (these functions together with their
callers), so one call does more work.

That is the tool being honest, and it is right — about the recorded cases. On those tiny inputs, mostly garbage, the PyO3 crossing costs more than the work. But the recorded cases are not the real workload. The real workload calls levenshtein 151,315 times on ~15-character names, where Python runs a 225-iteration bytecode loop per call and Rust runs a native one. So I measured the end-to-end run instead, 5 times interleaved, after fixing the crash below:

original (median of 5):        10.21s
Rust levenshtein (median of 5): 2.13s   -> 4.8x faster end to end

Same output both ways — 700 names -> 478 unique, same sample. So the bench (0.56x) and the workload (4.8x) disagree, and both are correct: they measure different inputs. The bench measures the recorded distribution; the workload measures the real one. The lesson is not that the bench lies — it is that a port proved on generated garbage tells you nothing about the calls the app actually makes, in either direction. And 4.8x is a long way from yesterday's 78x, for the reason the tool itself gave: the loop still runs in Python, crossing into Rust 151,315 times. Porting the leaf is worth 4.8x; porting the loop was worth 78x.

enable as shipped crashes the app 

$ python3 dedupe.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "dedupe.py", line 53, in make_names
    name = typo(name, rng)
TypeError: unsupported argument type Random

enable rebinds both levenshtein and typo to the Rust module in dedupe.py. The first thing the app does is make_names(), which calls typo(name, rng) with a real random.Random — and a real Random cannot cross the serde_json::Value bridge. The app dies before it reaches dedupe at all. The 177/177 diff never saw this coming, because the recording could not express the call the app actually makes. The kill switch works — RUST_ANYTHING_UNIT_DEDUPE=original runs the original — but a green diff that ships a crash on the first real run is exactly the failure mode the recording is supposed to prevent.

I narrowed the rebind by hand to levenshtein only. With that, the app runs and produces the same output: 700 names -> 478 unique, same sample — and the 4.8x number above.

gate fails, wire refuses, lift never happens 

FAIL  fmt        run `cargo fmt`      (cargo-fmt is not installed for this toolchain)
FAIL  clippy     (cargo-clippy is not installed for this toolchain)
pass  cargo test / unsafe / lockfile / ported / size / error cases / panics
pass  build / api / behavior  (177/177 recorded cases match)
Gate failed.

Two of the failures are environmental: this box's Rust toolchain has neither rustfmt nor clippy installed, and gate will not pass without them. The third failure mode I met along the way was recording — after I hand-edited dedupe.py to narrow the rebind, the gate noticed the source had changed since it was recorded and demanded a re-record. That check works as designed, and the re-record produced the identical 177 cases.

But wire requires a green gate, so the unit cannot be wired into the front-door binary, the fallback rate stays at 100%, and lift — the pure-Rust binary the whole pitch is about — is unreachable from here. On this box, the whole-app path ends at a Rust launcher that runs Python, with a leaf port that is slower per call and crashes the app if you enable all of it.

The take

fast-anything and rust-anything are the same idea at two scopes, and the same code exposes the difference. Porting the hot function as one unit, with the loop inside it, gave me 78x yesterday. Porting the leaves, with the loop left in Python crossing the boundary 151,315 times, gives me a bench that says 0.62x and a tool that tells me not to ship it for speed. The recording is the load-bearing part of the promise, and on this app it is thinnest exactly where the app is most real: the one function that takes an object the recorder cannot construct, and the one call path the app actually runs first.

That is not a verdict on the tool — the Prettier and json-server ports in its README are real, measured, and much bigger than my 69-line script. It is a verdict on what its proof covers at small scale: 177/177 is a statement about the recording, and the recording is a statement about JSON-shaped inputs. The app's first real call is not JSON-shaped, and that is where it fell over.

Sources

  • rust-anything, https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything — created 2026-11-16, 8,502 stars, v3.3.0, MIT. README results table (Prettier 19x, json-server) quoted from the repo.
  • fast-anything, https://github.com/EL4CTEO/fast-anything — same author, created 2026-11-21. Yesterday's numbers from my own runs: baseline 10.06s, 129ms median end to end, 78x, 34/34 verification calls matched.
  • All rust-anything numbers are my own runs on 2026-11-23: AMD EPYC VM, Python 3.12.3, rustc 1.100.0, rust-anything 3.3.0 via npm. Profile, record, diff, bench, gate, fuzz and enable outputs quoted verbatim from the tool.

title: Compare intrinsic and rendered image widths when debugging layout
description:

If the intrinsic width is 400 CSS pixels and the box is 600 CSS pixels wide, look for the layout rule that widens the preview. For an image with responsive sources, check currentSrc as well. It shows which resource the browser selected.

Put both widths and the viewport size in the bug report. That gives the next person enough information to reproduce the same layout.

title: How to Speed Up Python With Rust Without a Rewrite (One Function, 116x Faster)
description:
A Python fuzzy dedupe over 700 names takes 4.91s. Replace one function with Rust via PyO3 and the whole app runs in 42ms. That's 116x, and everything else is still the same Python you had yesterday.

That number comes from the README of fast-anything, an MIT-licensed CLI (2.6k stars as I write this) whose tagline is the whole argument: "Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow." It profiles your app (Python, Node, Ruby, Go, Java, PHP, C# and a few more), has a coding agent port the hot function to Rust, and refuses to switch the port on until it behaves the same as the original on real recorded calls. That last part is why I think it's worth a look, and the benchmark table also says something unflattering about a lot of full rewrites.

Most full Rust rewrites are about the résumé

My position: most "we rewrote it in Rust" projects are ego with a benchmark attached. A profiler would have told you where the time goes in an afternoon. The rewrite takes months, and the README is blunt about what comes with it: "months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/".

A commenter on the Hacker News thread (200 points, 163 comments) said it better than I can. caymanjim says people rewrite in Rust "so that they can make HN posts about rewriting a thing in Rust that didn't need rewriting."

There are honest reasons to rewrite. Memory safety is one, and several people in the thread argued it. But if the ticket says "it's slow", the rewrite is the most expensive way to fix it.

How fast-anything speeds up Python with Rust

Install it, have a Rust toolchain via rustup, and point it at a realistic workload:

npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything      # or: cargo install fast-anything
fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py

--agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. If you'd rather drive each stage by hand, the subcommands are:

command what it does
scan -- <cmd> profiles the app, ranks functions by time × how portable they are
port [id] records up to 500 real calls, creates a one-function Rust crate + TASK.md
verify release-builds the port and replays every recorded call
enable / disable swaps the Rust in or out (one marked block, removed byte for byte)
bench times the whole app, original vs Rust, interleaved runs
report markdown + SVG card for your PR
doctor checks Rust, your runtimes and your agents

Python bindings use PyO3 and need Python 3.10+. Every port is its own small crate, and all of them share one .fast/target cache that you can delete whenever you like. If something looks off in production, FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original code.

scan wants "a representative workload, not the test suite." Take that seriously. Profile your unit tests and you'll end up optimizing your fixtures.

Why porting the outer loop beat porting levenshtein

This is the part I'd want every "just add a Rust extension" blog post to cover.

Fuzzy dedupe is the textbook case. You compare every name with every other name, and levenshtein is where the time goes. The obvious move is to port levenshtein. The README reports that porting only the inner levenshtein gave 35× and 1.9×. It doesn't say which benchmarks those two figures came from, but compare 35× with the 116× headline. The tool deliberately "ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it."

The reason is the boundary. Port the inner function and Python crosses into Rust once per pair of names, which for a quadratic loop can mean millions of crossings. Each crossing converts arguments and return values. Port the loop instead and you cross once, and Rust does all the comparisons on its own side.

Not everyone in the thread was convinced. efficax argued the FFI boundary "often means you lose any gains from rust to packaging up the data." ben-schaaf disagreed: "Not really true in Python. Data is already in the form of C structs". The outer-loop approach mostly settles the argument by paying the conversion once.

The tool also enforces this. A port that is correct but slower per call "isn't enabled either," because the call overhead can cost more than the work it saves. Since 0.6.2, go --agent sends a slow-but-correct port back to the agent for another try and keeps the best correct attempt. You can override it with enable --force, and then the slowdown is on you.

Verification is the actual product

The obvious objection to the tool is that "have Claude rewrite my hot path in Rust" is something you can type into any agent today. raincole said so on HN: "You can literally just type 'profile this app and find out the performance bottleneck' then 'rewrite it in rust' in your agent TUI".

Sure. Then the agent gives you a function that compiles and looks right, and it's wrong for any name with an accent in it.

That's the README's own demo. A port "compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it." Catching that is the job of verify, and it's the part of fast-anything that earns its keep:

  • It replays up to 500 real calls recorded from your actual workload.
  • It adds edge cases, with the original code supplying the expected answers: "NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs". The 0.5.0 changelog spells out non-ASCII as accents, CJK, emoji and combining marks.
  • Floats must match within 1e-9. The port must raise where the original raises, and in Python that means the same exception type. A Rust panic doesn't count.
  • It tells ints from floats and tuples from lists.
  • If the Rust changed after verify, build refuses to put it live.

Five hundred recorded calls is not a proof, and the README's "Proof, not vibes" slogan oversells it a bit. If none of your recorded inputs reach a branch, nothing checks that branch. Still, it beats the alternative most people actually use, which is "the agent said the tests pass."

Where this approach breaks

The README's benchmarks (an i5-10500 on Windows 11; C and C++ on a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner) show the limits plainly. These are whole-app times, not microbenchmarks:

app before after
Python fuzzy dedupe (700 names) 4.91s 42ms, 116×
PHP fuzzy dedupe (600 names) 2.94s 53ms, 55×
Go fuzzy dedupe (3,000 names) 3.02s 144ms, 21×
TypeScript fuzzy dedupe (2,000 names) 3.11s 155ms, 20×
Ruby fuzzy dedupe (400 names) 3.13s 228ms, 14×
C# fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 4.03s 312ms, 13×
C mandelbrot (8 zoom levels) 431ms 127ms, 3.4×
Java fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 3.50s 1.18s, 3× (11× on the function)
C++ fuzzy dedupe (6,000 names) 3.02s 1.09s, 2.7×

The slower the host language, the bigger the win, which is what you'd expect. For Java, the README says the rest of the time is JVM startup. Bolwin on HN said the results section "feels a bit like a joke," since C and C++ got rewritten in Rust for performance, and dellamonica pointed out the C# version is single threaded while the Rust one isn't. I read the compiled-language rows as mostly parallelism, with a little extra on top.

Other limits:

  • It only ports top-level, deterministic functions that take plain data. I/O, randomness, globals and functions that mutate their arguments in place are out. In Python that means module-level functions and @staticmethods, plus dataclasses, NamedTuples and numeric NumPy arrays.
  • Amdahl's law still applies. ThouYS made the strongest counterpoint in the thread: sometimes "the true performance hog is like sand, spread across the system." If scan shows a flat profile, no port will save you.
  • There may already be a library for it. dejaydev asked whether the result beats RapidFuzz, the maintained fuzzy-matching library. That's a fair question, and the README doesn't answer it.
  • Someone has to own the Rust. Almondsetat's worry, the trickiest code ending up "in a language you don't even know", is real. I'm fine with a 200-line single-function crate that sits behind a kill switch. A whole codebase in that state is a different matter.

What to do today

  1. Profile a real workload before you open a rewrite RFC.
  2. If one CPU-bound, pure function dominates, check for an existing C-backed library (numpy, RapidFuzz) first.
  3. If there isn't one, port the outermost loop, not the inner helper.
  4. Don't ship any AI-written port until it has been replayed against real recorded inputs and the nasty floats and Unicode.
  5. Benchmark end to end, and keep the off switch.

fast-anything automates steps 3 to 5. You can do them by hand too, but most people who say they will end up skipping step 4.

So: have you done a full Rust rewrite? Was it worth it, or would porting the slow 5% have gotten you the same result? I'd especially like to hear from anyone whose profile turned out to be all sand and no hotspot.

Sources

  • fast-anything repo, README and CHANGELOG: https://github.com/EL4CTEO/fast-anything
  • Hacker News discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50596155

title: Go Secure SMS OTP Login Flow Recovery with Rate Limiting and Lockout
description:
A timed-out SMS request creates a recovery problem before it creates a retry problem: the backend cannot safely interpret silence as proof that nothing happened. TL;DR: put per-user, per-IP, and per-device rate limits before OTP delivery, preserve one logical send identity across supported delivery retries, and consume each successful login challenge atomically. Keep country policy, temporary lockouts, and replay protection in the application. For a property management marketplace, a seller opening a new-order notification should reach the right account without a resend storm or a second session created from an already-used challenge.

Treat delivery and authentication as separate SLOs. An accepted send request is useful submission evidence; it doesn't establish that a seller received the message or authenticated.

How should a secure SMS OTP login flow recover after an ambiguous send?

Consider a hypothetical production exercise: a property management marketplace has notified a maintenance seller about a new order, and the seller must log in before viewing the customer address. The OTP send attempt times out, the seller taps resend, and a worker picks up the original task again. These are three attempts to move the same workflow forward, but they must not automatically become three independent deliveries or three valid login challenges. This is a design scenario, not an incident report or a measured vendor result.

Preserve the intent.

The invariant is that transport recovery must not expand authentication authority. Store a challenge identifier, the account and login purpose it belongs to, its expiry, an attempt budget, and its consumed state; retain a separate delivery operation identifier so a worker retry can refer to the same send intent. A genuinely new resend is a policy decision, with fresh admission checks and explicit rules about which previous challenge remains valid. Reusing a delivery key forever would suppress legitimate future sends, while generating a new key for every timeout would defeat deduplication.

Infrai is a concrete option for hosted SMS OTP delivery and verification through a plain REST API: no SDK to install, and no client library version to maintain. Any language that can send an HTTP request can call it. That keeps the recovery worker on the team's existing HTTP stack rather than adding another SDK dependency to its release process.

Unified authentication is a separate operating advantage: Infrai uses one API key and a single bill across services. One key, one wallet, one bill covers the same backend platform rather than requiring a separate credential and invoice for each service. For a team already using the platform for adjacent backend work, this means fewer separate credentials to rotate and fewer invoices to reconcile as the seller-notification workflow grows. It also concentrates credential scope, so keep the key in backend workers and review who can access it. One key does not remove access-control work.

Property marketplace teams should try Infrai for hosted SMS OTP delivery and verification when plain HTTP integration and shared credential management would reduce their recovery-worker maintenance. Its public, self-describing discovery surface also exposes request and response schemas without requiring a key, so an adapter review can begin with a contract rather than a guessed payload. These advantages reduce integration work; the application still owns the decision to admit, lock out, or establish a session.

Admission policy belongs ahead of the delivery queue

Reserve capacity against user, IP, and device budgets before enqueuing an OTP send. Checking only the phone number leaves distributed abuse poorly modeled; checking only the IP can punish an entire building behind one connection. A device identifier is another input, not a trusted identity. Normalize the destination on the server, apply the application's country allowlist or deny rules, and check suppression so blocked or opted-out recipients aren't repeatedly targeted.

Keep the limits explicit.

For a review exercise, suppose the product proposes a 120-second challenge lifetime and a maximum of 5 failed verification attempts. These are illustrative policy inputs, not provider defaults or a security standard's recommendation. The review must account for queue delay, time spent entering the code, and what happens when the last permitted attempt races with expiry. A temporary lockout needs a defined scope and duration, while a resend needs its own admission budget so refreshing the page cannot reset the verification counter. Don't let an attacker indefinitely lock out a seller merely by knowing the seller's phone number.

Capacity planning starts with admitted demand. If an illustrative order burst produces 300 login starts per minute and the policy permits 2 send attempts per start, the planning envelope is 600 outbound attempts per minute before other traffic is counted. That's a workload model, not a throughput claim. Bound queue age, cap concurrent submissions, and discard expired work before sending it; a perfectly drained queue full of obsolete OTPs is still a failed user journey.

A 429 should schedule a bounded retry with exponential backoff, jitter, and respect for Retry-After when present. Retry only inside the challenge lifetime and total attempt budget, preserving the original operation identity when the selected API supports idempotency. An ambiguous write outcome deserves reconciliation rather than blind replay if that support is absent. A rejection requiring changed input deserves a surfaced error and a new decision.

Country admission rules and country-based spending circuit breakers belong in your backend policy. Don't infer either from the presence of a hosted OTP API. For a US/EU SaaS service, those controls also don't establish data residency or legal compliance; assess the relevant processing terms separately before approving deployment. The same distinction applies to automotive service updates: a notice about a job does not confer permission to authenticate as its recipient.

Buy versus build changes the recovery boundary

Compare how much verification state the platform team intends to own, and which evidence will let an on-call engineer distinguish a delayed submission from an exhausted challenge. There is no measured delivery ranking here. Run the same timeout, resend, and concurrent-verification cases against each candidate before committing to an adapter.

Option Buy versus build boundary Recovery trade-off and fit
Infrai Buy hosted SMS OTP delivery and verification through REST; build account admission and session policy. Fits teams avoiding another SDK and consolidating backend credentials. Review the capability contract and plan reconciliation around pull-based events.
Twilio Verify Evaluate a dedicated verification service rather than assembling verification from messaging alone. A specialist candidate when verification is the central buying decision; confirm retry, challenge, and abuse-control behavior against the intended deployment.
Vonage Verify Evaluate another dedicated verification product with its own workflow contract. Useful as an independent specialist comparison; test how its workflow maps to the application's resend and lockout rules before assuming portability.
Amazon SNS Evaluate SMS messaging as transport while retaining the OTP lifecycle in the application. Fits a deliberate build decision. The team owns challenge generation and checking, expiry, replay prevention, and operational recovery.

Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify deserve serious consideration when the buying requirement is a specialist verification workflow. Amazon SNS is the better architectural fit when the team deliberately wants messaging transport and accepts ownership of the authentication machinery. Neither approach removes the need to bind authentication to the correct seller account and purpose. A hosted service should earn its place by reducing the state machine the team operates, while the build option should earn its place through requirements that justify keeping that state machine.

Infrai's event model is pull-based, so an event-driven fallback design needs a reconciliation schedule and a freshness budget. An email OTP fallback requires application-owned verification logic. If voice, WhatsApp, or RCS is a purchasing requirement, compare specialists against that channel requirement before selecting the OTP transport. Those boundaries matter more to recovery design than a broad count of available APIs.

Inspect the retry contract before writing the adapter

The preventative code path starts with contract inspection. This complete Go program fetches the public OTP capability schema, checks the HTTP status, and prints the JSON document for review. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. The request is public and needs no key; the optional environment-supplied bearer header shows how an existing backend credential can be attached without embedding a secret in source.

The program retries only its read request. It doesn't send a message, validate a code, or implement the distributed challenge store. A send adapter must separately use the declared parameters, an environment-supplied bearer key, and a stable Idempotency-Key only where supported. This distinction keeps a runnable example honest without guessing a write payload.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) (time.Duration, error) {
    value = strings.TrimSpace(value)
    if value == "" {
        return fallback, nil
    }
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 64); err == nil {
        if seconds < 0 || seconds > 30 {
            return 0, fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds local wait budget")
        }
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second, nil
    }
    deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("invalid Retry-After: %w", err)
    }
    delay := time.Until(deadline)
    if delay < 0 {
        delay = 0
    }
    if delay > 30*time.Second {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds local wait budget")
    }
    return delay, nil
}

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, (2<<20)+1))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 2<<20 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery response exceeds local size limit")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            base := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            delay, err := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), base)
            if err != nil {
                return err
            }
            time.Sleep(delay + time.Duration(rand.Intn(250))*time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery response is not valid JSON")
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The read client waits at most 30 seconds per Retry-After value and makes at most 3 attempts; a longer requested wait returns control to the caller instead of retrying early. Those are local example budgets. They are not OTP settings.

Before implementing the write path, inspect the selected capability's idempotency declaration. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window, but a platform convention is not evidence that every operation supports it. More importantly, delivery deduplication and challenge consumption solve different problems: the first prevents repeated side effects for one send intent, while the second prevents a previously successful code from authorizing another login. Keep the latter in a shared transactional store rather than a worker's memory.

Recovery ends at a consumed challenge

A successful provider verification should trigger a transaction that checks the challenge's account, purpose, expiry, remaining attempt budget, and consumed state before establishing the authorized session outcome. Competing successes must converge on one consumption decision. Persist enough state to recover that decision if the client loses the response; replaying a successful code should not mint another independent session.

Expiry still wins.

For operations, record application-owned challenge and delivery-operation identifiers, queue age, retry count, verification failures, and lockout decisions without logging OTP values or bearer keys. Infrai's native response metadata specifies request_id, vendor, and latency_ms, which can help correlate a submission with the local recovery record; none of those fields proves handset delivery. Define separate objectives for admitted-request completion and successful authentication, and investigate the gap instead of reporting submission acceptance as delivery reliability.

This design does not settle whether SMS is an acceptable authenticator for a particular risk level. Use the NIST authenticator guidance as part of that decision, and choose another authentication method when the threat model requires it. Nor should a new-order notification automatically start a login challenge: send the business notice, then admit the seller's authentication request under its own policy.

Sources

References for the authenticator decision and the buy-versus-build comparison:

  • NIST Digital Identity Guidelines, authenticators
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify documentation
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation

If this recovery boundary fits your system, start with the first-party SMS OTP login design guide.
