title: Tools3000 v1.4.4: Building a Native 12-in-1 Windows Power-User Suite in C++20 & Rust (No Electron, ~15 MB Idle, GPL-3.0)
description:
Why I Built Tools3000

For years, my Windows system tray looked like a crowded parking lot: Everything for instant file search, Ditto for clipboard history, Snipaste/PixPin for screenshots and pins, Listary for Open/Save dialogs, PowerToys File Locksmith when a file refused to delete, WGestures for mouse gestures, a screen recorder, and endless disappointment trying to replace the discontinued Google Picasa Photo Viewer without ads.

Each of those apps is great on its own, yet running seven resident tools meant constant hotkey collisions, inconsistent High-DPI behavior, and multiple updaters. So I spent the past four months building and daily-driving Tools3000 — a free, local-first, GPL-3.0 open-source native Windows suite written in C++20, Rust, and Direct2D/Direct3D11 (no Electron).

We just shipped v1.4.4, incorporating early community feedback across memory modes, native file dialogs, offline multi-language OCR, and stability. Every module can be toggled independently, and my tray is finally down to one icon (~15 MB idle RAM).

What's Inside (12 Independently Toggleable Modules)

1. Instant Unified Search, QuickLook & 350 KB Rust CLI/MCP (Alt + Space)

  • Millisecond search across millions of NTFS files, installed desktop/UWP apps (app:), 37 Windows system tools (cmd:env, etc.), browser bookmarks with real site Favicons read offline from local caches (bm: / b:), and full-text document content (content: for Office, PDF, CAD, source code).
  • Live Watch updates, 3 RAM tiers (all the way down to 0 MB idle sleep), and Space QuickLook preview for docs, PDFs, ZIP/7Z/RAR archives, TTF/OTF fonts, and media.
  • Ships with tools3000-cli.exe — a 350 KB zero-dependency Rust CLI & native MCP server (tools3000-cli mcp) so AI coding agents can query your local file index cleanly.

2. Persistent Clipboard History (Alt + V)

  • Pure Rust persistence layer that survives reboots, supporting text, images, HTML/RTF rich text, custom groups, Alt + 1..9 instant paste, sensitive-app exclusion, and Shift / Ctrl click-order merge paste.

3. File Dialog Assistant & File Locksmith

  • File Dialog Assistant: Docks a Listary-style inline folder search bar onto Windows Open / Save As dialogs so you can jump to any directory in milliseconds without ever overwriting your Save-As filename.
  • File Locksmith: Right-click any stubborn file (optionally Shift + Right-click only) or pick it in Settings to inspect locking processes and unlock safely — 0 MB resident RAM, with automatic Explorer menu cleanup when disabled.

4. Screenshots, Scrolling Capture, Pin Groups & 8-Language Offline OCR / 1:1 Translation (F1 / F3)

  • Smart UI element snapping, dashed optical magnifier, one-click quick save, lossless head/tail trim on scrolling captures, and 120Hz color-grouped desktop pins.
  • Offline OCR auto-detects English, Simplified/Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Spanish, and Portuguese without manual switching — letting you select/copy/edit text directly on pinned screenshots or run clean 1:1 in-place translation with code-block protection and 0 ms original toggle.

5. Auto-Zoom Screen Recorder Studio, Mouse Gestures & Key Visualizer

  • Auto-Zoom Studio: Records screen and audio, then drops straight into a waveform trimmer with automatic cursor-follow zoom keyframes and one-click MP4 / GIF / WebP export.
  • Global Mouse Gestures: Pause-to-cancel misfire guard, smart window switching for Run App (including distinct multi-profile Chrome windows), Lua scripting support, plus screen-edge scroll for volume and real monitor hardware brightness (WMI / DDC/CI).

6. Optional < 2 MB Standalone Rust Classic Picasa Viewer

  • A standalone, zero-external-DLL Rust recreation of the classic Google Picasa Photo Viewer (even portable on its own).
  • Restores smooth cursor-anchored zooming and filmstrip navigation while adding native 4K High-DPI rendering and 41 image/RAW formats (WebP, AVIF, HEIC, SVG, PSD, CR2/NEF/ARW/DNG), using roughly 6–15 MB RAM on a 4 MP image.

Architecture Notes: Why C++20 + Rust Instead of Electron?

Rather than picking a single language dogmatically, I drew a clean boundary between OS shell integration and data-intensive/rendering engines:

  • C++20 + Direct2D / Win32 handles low-latency system hooks, window overlays, screen capture, hardware-accelerated annotation, and DPI-aware native surfaces.
  • 4 Pure Rust Engines power the pieces where memory safety, tight binary size, and zero-runtime-bloat shine:
    1. The NTFS MFT + live USN Journal search daemon
    2. The persistent clipboard storage engine
    3. The 350 KB CLI & MCP bridge (tools3000-cli.exe)
    4. The standalone < 2 MB D3D11/DirectComposition Picasa Photo Viewer
  • UI Layer: Only the configuration dashboard uses WebView2 (pre-installed on modern Windows), hibernating when closed so background memory stays tiny.
  • Privacy & Supply-Chain Transparency: 100% local-first core, zero telemetry, full non-ASCII install/user path support across 8 languages, plus signed releases with SHA256SUMS.txt and SBOM.spdx.json. Built-in diagnostics auto-redact usernames, paths, IPs, emails, and secrets locally before export.

Try It Out

  • GitHub Repository (source + 12 demo animations in 8 languages): https://github.com/yuan278501381/Tools3000
  • Latest Release v1.4.4 (Installer & Portable ZIP): https://github.com/yuan278501381/Tools3000/releases/latest
  • Scoop: 
  scoop bucket add tools3000 https://github.com/yuan278501381/Tools3000
  scoop install tools3000/tools3000

Which utility is still permanently pinned to your Windows system tray, and what would it take to replace it? I'd love to hear your thoughts and engineering feedback in the comments!

title: Best React Component Libraries in 2027 (Free and Paid)
description:
Picking from the best React component libraries is a decision you live with for years. Pick the wrong one and you spend months fighting its styles, its bundle or its license.

Most lists mix very different tools in one ranking. A headless primitive and a full design system don't solve the same problem.

This list groups 12 libraries by what they are for: headless primitives, full design systems and animated components. Each entry has the license and price as listed on the official site or npm in November 2026.

How do you choose a React component library?

Answer four questions before you look at screenshots:

  • Do you have a design already? If a designer hands you a custom look, use headless primitives and style them yourself. If not, a full design system gives you a finished look on day one.
  • How do you style? Tailwind projects fit shadcn/ui, HeroUI and the animated libraries. Mantine, MUI and Chakra UI ship their own styling systems.
  • Do you want the source in your repo? Copy-paste libraries (shadcn/ui and the libraries built on its CLI) put the code in your project. npm packages get updates for free but are harder to change deeply.
  • What does the paid tier cover? Several libraries are free at the core and charge for advanced components, blocks or templates. Check what you actually need before you budget.

Headless React component libraries

Headless libraries give you behavior, keyboard support and ARIA without styles. You bring the CSS.

1. Radix UI

Radix Primitives are unstyled, accessible components: dialog, popover, dropdown menu, tabs and more. They are MIT licensed and free. Many styled libraries build on Radix, including shadcn/ui. Best for teams who want proven primitives and full control of styling.

2. Base UI

Base UI is an unstyled React library from the team behind Radix, Floating UI and Material UI. It reached a stable 1.x release and is MIT licensed. shadcn/ui supports both Radix and Base UI. Best for new design systems that want an actively developed headless base.

3. React Aria

React Aria, from Adobe, offers over 50 components with behavior, adaptive interactions and internationalization built in, ready for your own styles. react-aria-components is Apache-2.0 and free. Best when accessibility and i18n are hard requirements, such as enterprise or government apps.

4. Ark UI

Ark UI is a headless library with 45+ accessible components powered by state machines (Zag.js). The same API works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte. MIT licensed. Best for teams that ship to more than one framework.

Full design system libraries for React

These give you styled components, theming and a consistent look out of the box.

5. shadcn/ui

shadcn/ui is not a package. Its CLI copies accessible, Tailwind-styled components into your repo, so you own and edit the source. It is MIT licensed and free. The CLI also installs from third-party registries, which is how many of the libraries below are distributed. Best for Tailwind projects that want a solid default they can fully change.

6. MUI (Material UI)

Material UI implements Google's Material Design and is one of the oldest React libraries still in heavy use. The core is MIT and free. MUI X adds advanced components like the data grid, date pickers and charts, with paid Pro ($299 per year per developer) and Premium ($599 per year per developer) plans at the time of writing. Best for data-heavy admin apps that need a mature data grid.

7. Mantine

Mantine is a full-featured React library with more than 120 components and 70 hooks, plus forms, dates and notifications packages. MIT licensed and free. Best when you want one library to cover most of an app, without Tailwind.

8. Chakra UI

Chakra UI is an accessible component system with a style-props API and strong theming. Version 3 is built on Ark UI. The library is MIT and free; premium components are sold separately. Best for product teams that like styling through props and design tokens.

9. HeroUI

HeroUI (formerly NextUI) offers free, accessible components for React and React Native, styled with Tailwind. The open source package is Apache-2.0. HeroUI Pro adds paid templates and extra tooling. Best for Tailwind apps that want a polished default look across web and mobile.

Animated React component libraries

These sit on top of a base library. Use them for landing pages, marketing sites and the parts of an app that should feel alive.

10. Magic UI

Magic UI has 150+ free, open source animated components built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion. It is MIT licensed and installs through the shadcn CLI. Magic UI Pro sells templates and landing page sections. Best for landing page effects like marquees, number tickers and animated backgrounds.

11. Aceternity UI

Aceternity UI offers 100+ free components built with React, Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion, aimed at landing pages. A paid All-Access license adds premium blocks, templates and full pages, sold as a one-time payment. Best for bold hero sections and visual effects on marketing sites.

12. beUI

beUI is a free, MIT-licensed library of animated components for React and Next.js, built with Framer Motion and Tailwind CSS. Components install through the shadcn CLI as @beui, since beUI is in shadcn's official registry directory. They handle keyboard focus and reduced motion, and the component catalog covers inputs, overlays, charts, AI agent UI and blocks like a command palette.

beUI also has React Native components built with Reanimated and Gesture Handler, and beUI Pro, a paid library of animated blocks, pages and templates for web and React Native. Best for product UI that needs motion with accessibility handled, on web and mobile.

Best React component libraries compared

Library Style License / price Best for
Radix UI Headless MIT, free Proven primitives you style
Base UI Headless MIT, free New headless design systems
React Aria Headless Apache-2.0, free Strict accessibility and i18n
Ark UI Headless MIT, free Multi-framework teams
shadcn/ui Tailwind, copy-paste MIT, free Owning your component source
MUI Material Design MIT core, paid MUI X Pro and Premium Data-heavy admin apps
Mantine Own styling system MIT, free One library for a whole app
Chakra UI Style props MIT, paid premium components Token-driven product UI
HeroUI Tailwind Apache-2.0, paid Pro Polished web and mobile defaults
Magic UI Tailwind + Framer Motion MIT, paid Pro templates Landing page effects
Aceternity UI Tailwind + Framer Motion Free components, paid All-Access Bold marketing sections
beUI Tailwind + Framer Motion MIT, free, paid beUI Pro Accessible animated product UI

Can you combine React component libraries?

Yes, and most teams do. A common stack is a headless base or shadcn/ui for forms, dialogs and menus, plus an animated library for the parts users notice. Because shadcn/ui, Magic UI and beUI all install through the same CLI and share Tailwind tokens, mixing them in one project stays consistent.

If you are comparing the animated options, the beUI vs Magic UI page goes into the differences in more detail.

FAQ

What is the best free React component library?

It depends on the job. shadcn/ui is the most flexible free starting point for Tailwind projects, Mantine covers the most ground as one package, and Radix UI or Base UI are the safest headless bases.

Is shadcn/ui a component library?

Not in the npm package sense. It is a set of components and a CLI that copies their source into your project, so you own the code and update it yourself.

Which React component libraries have paid tiers?

MUI (MUI X Pro and Premium), Chakra UI (premium components), HeroUI (Pro), Magic UI (Pro templates), Aceternity UI (All-Access) and beUI (beUI Pro) all keep a free core and sell extra components, blocks or templates.

What is the best animated React component library?

Magic UI and Aceternity UI are strong for landing page effects. beUI focuses on animated product UI with keyboard support and reduced motion built in, and also ships React Native versions.

Takeaway

Pick by the job, not the ranking. Headless if you have a design, a full system if you need one, and an animated library on top for the moments that matter. Most of these are free at the core, so try two in a branch before you commit.

Browse the free animated components at beui.dev and install your first one:

npx shadcn@latest add @beui/command-palette

title: Treat unavailable localStorage differently from an empty shortlist
description:
I build Riddle List, a daily-puzzle discovery directory with a browser-local shortlist. That makes a small UI distinction important: “there is nothing saved” and “the browser could not read storage” should not mean the same thing.

This is a standalone educational example, not a copy of the site's production storage format. Do not paste it over an existing application's keys or migrate real users without a separate compatibility plan. This article and example were prepared with AI assistance and reviewed and tested during the project work.

Four read states, not one empty array

A helper that catches every exception and returns [] is convenient until another effect writes that empty array back. A failed read can then look like an intentional empty shortlist. The same problem occurs if an old payload uses an unsupported schema version.

The reader below returns an explicit status:

  • missing: the key does not exist.
  • ok: the version and every ID are valid, including an intentionally empty array.
  • invalid: the key exists, but the data cannot be understood.
  • unavailable: accessing storage threw an exception.

Reading never writes, repairs or deletes the original value. The caller can show a recovery option for invalid data and keep the current in-memory list when persistence is unavailable.

// Standalone educational example, not Riddle List application source.
export function loadShortlist(storage, key) {
  let raw;
  try { raw = storage.getItem(key); }
  catch { return { status: 'unavailable', ids: [] }; }
  if (raw === null) return { status: 'missing', ids: [] };
  try {
    const value = JSON.parse(raw);
    if (value.version !== 1 || !Array.isArray(value.ids) ||
        !value.ids.every(id => typeof id === 'string' && id.length > 0)) {
      return { status: 'invalid', ids: [] };
    }
    return { status: 'ok', ids: [...new Set(value.ids)] };
  } catch { return { status: 'invalid', ids: [] }; }
}

export function saveShortlist(storage, key, ids) {
  if (!Array.isArray(ids) || !ids.every(id => typeof id === 'string' && id.length > 0)) {
    return { status: 'invalid' };
  }
  try {
    storage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify({ version: 1, ids: [...new Set(ids)] }));
    return { status: 'saved' };
  } catch { return { status: 'unavailable' }; }
}

Keep persistence out of the hydration effect

Load once into a result object. Do not immediately save result.ids on every result status. A missing key can initialize an empty list; an ok result can hydrate a list; an invalid or unavailable result needs a separate UI decision.

Likewise, the save function returns saved only after setItem succeeds. An app can continue working with an in-memory shortlist after an unavailable result, but should tell the user it could not persist the change. Silently displaying “saved” would promise durability the code has not established.

Deduplication preserves the first occurrence's order. It does not rename IDs or map them to a new catalog. Stable identity and route migrations deserve their own compatibility tests.

What I checked

The standalone module passed six Node test cases using fake storage objects: missing versus stored-empty, a blocked read, malformed/wrong-version/wrong-type payloads, ordered deduplication without overwriting bad data, a failed write, and valid-write round trips with invalid-input protection. These are unit checks of the example, not a claim that every browser storage policy was exercised.

To exercise the real UI, also check a reload in the same browser, an environment where persistence is unavailable, and the message shown when saving fails. Keep a disposable key for demonstrations. Never use another site's live storage as a test fixture.

The product boundary matters too

A directory bookmark and a game's progress are different records. Saving a game in Riddle List means adding it to that browser's shortlist. It does not save the publisher's puzzle attempt or create cloud synchronization. Keeping that boundary visible in the interface is as useful as catching the exception in code.

The MDN Web Storage API documentation explains availability checks and storage operations. Use the browser's actual behavior as the evidence for the message you display.

title: Build a hosting company homepage in Laravel, with plans and a billing snapshot
description:
Part 1 of Small Business Sites.

A hosting company homepage has one job: show the plans clearly enough that a visitor can pick one without opening a support ticket. Most small hosts I see either hard code their prices into the page, so every price change means editing HTML in four places, or they install a billing system built for a company ten times their size before they have ten customers.

This build sits between those two. The plans live in a database table, so the homepage reads them the way any Laravel page reads data. The price toggle switches between monthly and yearly without a page reload. A billing snapshot panel shows a signed in customer their invoices, due dates, and payment status, read only. Payments themselves stay outside this build, and I say where they would connect at the end.

Put the plans in a table first

Three plans are enough for a small host. The table needs the facts a buyer compares: name, disk space, bandwidth, email accounts, and the two prices. Store the monthly and yearly price as separate columns. Working the yearly price out from the monthly one inside the view sounds tidy and breaks the first time you run a yearly offer that is not a round multiple.

Schema::create('plans', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->string('name');
    $table->unsignedInteger('disk_gb');
    $table->string('bandwidth');
    $table->unsignedInteger('email_accounts');
    $table->decimal('monthly_price', 8, 2);
    $table->decimal('yearly_price', 8, 2);
    $table->boolean('featured')->default(false);
    $table->unsignedInteger('sort_order')->default(0);
    $table->timestamps();
});

Seed it with your real plans and your real prices. The names and numbers in my screenshots are sample data from my own template work, and yours should be the plans you can actually deliver. A plan card is a promise. If the disk figure on the homepage is larger than the disk you give the account, the page is lying in a way a customer will find in the first week.

The controller for the homepage stays small:

public function home()
{
    $plans = Plan::orderBy('sort_order')->get();

    return view('home', compact('plans'));
}

That is the whole point of the table. Adding a fourth plan next year is a row in the database, not an afternoon of HTML edits.

Draw the plan cards and the toggle

Each plan becomes one card. The card shows the name, the price, and the comparison rows in the same order on every card, so a visitor can read down one column and across the next. Keep the rows identical across cards. A row that appears on one card and not the next reads as a hidden limit, even when it was only a layout slip.

@foreach($plans as $plan)
    <article class="plan-card {{ $plan->featured ? 'featured' : '' }}">
        <h3>{{ $plan->name }}</h3>
        <p class="price">
            <span data-monthly="{{ $plan->monthly_price }}"
                  data-yearly="{{ $plan->yearly_price }}">
                ${{ $plan->monthly_price }}
            </span>
            <span class="per">/mo</span>
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>{{ $plan->disk_gb }} GB disk space</li>
            <li>{{ $plan->bandwidth }} bandwidth</li>
            <li>{{ $plan->email_accounts }} email accounts</li>
        </ul>
    </article>
@endforeach

The toggle is two buttons and a few lines of JavaScript. Both prices are already on the page inside the data attributes, so switching needs no request to the server and works even on a slow connection.

document.querySelectorAll('[data-cycle]').forEach(function (button) {
    button.addEventListener('click', function () {
        const cycle = button.dataset.cycle;
        document.querySelectorAll('[data-monthly]').forEach(function (el) {
            el.textContent = '$' + (cycle === 'yearly' ? el.dataset.yearly : el.dataset.monthly);
        });
        document.querySelectorAll('.per').forEach(function (el) {
            el.textContent = cycle === 'yearly' ? '/yr' : '/mo';
        });
    });
});

Check the cards at phone width before you call this section done. At 390px the cards stack in one column, the price stays on one line, and no card is wider than the screen. A pricing table that needs sideways scrolling on a phone loses the visitors most likely to be comparing plans away from their desk.

The billing snapshot panel

Once a visitor becomes a customer, the question changes from what does it cost to what do I owe and when. A snapshot panel answers that on one screen: the current plan, the invoices, each due date, and each status. It reads data. It does not take money, and it should not pretend to.

Invoices need their own small table: the customer, the plan, the amount, an issue date, a due date, and a status field that holds plain words like unpaid, paid, and overdue.

public function billing()
{
    $invoices = auth()->user()->invoices()
        ->orderByDesc('due_date')
        ->take(10)
        ->get();

    return view('billing', compact('invoices'));
}

In the view, show the status as text a person uses, with the due date next to it, and let overdue rows stand out by colour alone. Do not hide an unpaid invoice behind a tab. The panel earns its place the day a customer checks it instead of opening a ticket to ask when their renewal is due. When you later connect a payment gateway, it connects here: the gateway marks the invoice paid, and this panel keeps doing the same read it always did.

The domain box and the support section, kept small

A domain search box belongs on the homepage, as a front end form. Give it an input, a button, and an answer area. Until a real domain API connects to it, the honest version checks nothing and says so in the small print under the box, or stays off the page. A box that invents availability results is worse than no box.

The support section needs three things: the hours a person actually answers, a link to open a ticket or a contact page, and a status note the owner can edit by hand when something is wrong. One edited line that says the mail server restart finished at a real time builds more trust than a green all systems normal badge that never changes.

Trust sections that do not fake numbers

A new hosting company has no honest big numbers. It has no thousands of customers, no years of uptime record, and no wall of testimonials. Templates often ship with those numbers filled in, and leaving them in is the fastest way to make a real company look fake to anyone who reads closely.

What a new host can show is smaller and stronger. The exact plan limits, printed on the cards where the buyer compares them. The support hours it really keeps. How to reach a person, with a named page and a working form. The terms, privacy, and refund pages written as plain templates the owner has read. And the status note above, edited by hand. Each of those can be checked by a visitor, and a claim that can be checked is the kind that holds up.

Add the other numbers later, one at a time, when they are true. A first testimonial with a real customer name on it is worth more than a row of invented ones, and it cannot be taken apart in a comment thread.

What stays static and what goes dynamic

Keep the static parts static. The explanation of what shared hosting and VPS mean, the support hours text, the legal pages, and the company story do not change by the week, and plain Blade views with no queries keep them fast and hard to break.

Make dynamic only what changes or what belongs to a person: the plans and prices, because an offer or a new plan should not need a code edit; the status note, because it changes during an incident; and the billing panel, because it shows one customer's own invoices. That split is most of the maintenance story for a small host. The homepage stays quick, and the parts an owner edits from an admin screen are the parts that were going to change anyway.

Where this leaves you

With the plans in a table, the toggle on the cards, and the snapshot panel reading real invoices, a small hosting homepage in Laravel is a weekend of work and a short list of pages. If you would rather start from the finished version, HostNest is this homepage finished as a 10 page template. If you need the whole site and not only the homepage, it is $24 on Gumroad: https://mehedirafi.gumroad.com/l/hostnest

I am Mehedi Mansur Rafi, a freelance Laravel developer (B.Sc. in Computer Science & Engineering). I build hospital, clinic, and small business websites. My full store is at https://mehedirafi.gumroad.com/ and my site is https://mehedimansurrafi.online

title: Mechanics of AI Interface Feedback Loops: Capturing User Corrections Without Breaking UX
description:
You’ve just finished typing a prompt or tweaking an AI-generated suggestion, maybe correcting a label, adjusting a value, or rejecting a mistaken completion, and you expect the UI to instantly update, ready for your next move. But sometimes, the interface feels sluggish, or worse, your correction disappears, the AI’s response overwrites your input, and you think, “Why can’t this just behave like a normal app?”

That frustration hit me recently while working on a project with live AI-assisted forms. The core challenge? Capturing user corrections and feedback in real time without breaking the flow or introducing weird latency. Turns out, the mechanics of this feedback loop are subtle and surprisingly tricky.

Let’s break down what’s really going on under the hood when AI interfaces try to capture your input, handle your corrections, and update the UI smoothly.

The Feedback Loop: More Than Just Input and Output

At first glance, it seems straightforward: the user types or clicks, the AI responds, the UI updates. But that ignores a crucial reality, AI-generated content is often streaming in, partial, and probabilistic. Meanwhile, the user might be interacting with the UI, correcting or tweaking things mid-stream.

For example, imagine an AI autocomplete suggesting a phrase as you type. You spot a typo and try to fix it while the suggestion is still arriving. If the UI just blindly replaces the input with the latest AI output, your correction is lost. That’s a broken experience.

The key is managing two intertwined states:

  1. The user’s local input and corrections
  2. The AI’s generated response as it streams or updates

These have to coexist and merge carefully.

Event and State Management: Coordinating User Edits and AI Updates

How do interfaces keep your input intact while updating AI suggestions?

1. Local State vs Remote AI State

Typically, the UI maintains a local state reflecting your input and edits. Meanwhile, AI responses come asynchronously, often as partial streams. The interface needs to reconcile these two sources.

A common pattern is to treat user edits as authoritative until the AI finishes or the user signals completion. This means:

  • While you’re typing or correcting, your local input state overrides incoming AI updates.
  • The AI’s output is merged in only when it doesn’t conflict or after you pause.

This demands a nuanced event system that:

  • Detects user edits (input, selection, cursor position)
  • Temporarily suspends AI state updates that would overwrite user changes
  • Resumes syncing once the user stops typing

2. Debouncing and Throttling AI Updates

Since AI suggestions can stream rapidly, bombarding the UI with updates risks causing jitter or lost focus.

Throttling or debouncing AI updates helps:

  • Batch rapid AI output into manageable chunks
  • Avoid interrupting user input with constant overwrites

For instance, holding off AI state merges for 100-200ms after user input lets the user finish their edit before the AI response updates the UI.

3. Cursor and Selection Preservation

One subtle but critical piece is preserving cursor position during updates.

If the UI replaces text without maintaining cursor or selection, the user can lose their spot or type in the wrong place. This is especially tricky when AI updates insert or remove characters.

Many implementations track:

  • The cursor index before AI update
  • The diff between old and new text
  • Adjust cursor position accordingly

Failing to do this causes the cursor to jump unexpectedly, confusing users.

Design Tradeoffs: Balancing Latency, Responsiveness, and Clarity

Even with careful state management, tradeoffs remain.

Optimistic UI vs Consistency

Should the UI show AI suggestions immediately, or wait until the AI response is stable?

  • Showing suggestions early feels responsive but risks flicker or overwriting user edits.
  • Waiting for stable output reduces flicker but introduces latency.

A middle ground is incremental updates with clear UI cues (like loading spinners or subtle placeholders).

User Control: Letting Users Override AI

Good AI UX lets users override or dismiss suggestions without frustration.

Implementing undo, manual override, or explicit accept/reject actions helps prevent the AI from fighting the user.

Feedback Capture Without Interruptions

If the AI UI aggressively resets input on every model update, users get annoyed.

Instead, triggering AI updates only when the user pauses or via explicit action reduces interference.

Real-World Example: Live Code Completion Editors

I’ve seen these mechanics in action in live AI code editors:

  • The editor buffers your keystrokes locally.
  • AI completions stream in asynchronously.
  • The UI merges completions only if they don’t conflict with your edits.
  • Cursor position is preserved using diff algorithms.
  • Updates are throttled to avoid UI jank.

This orchestration creates smooth interactions where the AI assists but never steals control.

Wrapping Up

Building AI interfaces that capture user corrections without breaking UX requires juggling asynchronous AI streams, local user edits, and precise event coordination.

It’s a dance of state management and event handling, preserving your intent while letting the AI help.

Next time your AI UI feels smooth and responsive, you can thank the careful mechanics working quietly behind the scenes.

Helpful learning resources

  • W3C WAI accessibility guidance
  • W3Schools accessibility tutorials
  • MDN Web Docs Originally published at Under The Hood. Get the next deep dive in your inbox: subscribe to Under The Hood.

title: Why Rare-Answer Trivia Needs More Than Right or Wrong
description:
Open-ended trivia looks simple: a prompt, a text box, a clock. In practice it is nothing like a multiple-choice quiz. A prompt such as “name a sovereign country” has nearly two hundred valid answers. If every accepted answer is worth the same, the rational move is the first word that comes to mind. The game then rewards speed and popularity, not recall.

Krillion Unlimited is a free, no-login browser game built around that problem. You type answers to open-ended prompts. Valid answers are not equal. Common ones barely move you; rarer ones score more. This article is about that scoring ladder — why a rare-answer game needs more than right or wrong, and what a six-tier model changes for the player.

It is an independent game and is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by krillion.io.

A round, in brief

A standard expedition is seven prompts, with 25 seconds on each one. There are no multiple-choice buttons. You type an answer that fits the category. If the game does not accept it, the round does not end: the input is rejected and you can keep guessing until the timer runs out, or until a valid answer locks in. Minor spelling slips and some singular/plural variations on longer words are forgiven.

That loop is easy to learn and hard to play well. The tension is not “do I know anything in this set?” It is “can I find a valid member of the set that is not the one everyone else will type in the first two seconds?”

Six tiers, not one tick

On the official site, every accepted answer lands in one of six rarity tiers:

Tier Points Depth gained What it represents
Plankton 10 +100m The ultra-obvious first instinct
Too Clever 15 +150m A famous “smart” pick that thousands still guess
Schooler 30 +300m Solid mid-pack knowledge
Rare 60 +600m Sharper lateral recall
Deep Cut 85 +850m An abyssal pull almost nobody reaches under 25 seconds
One in a Krillion 100 +1000m Obscure, valid, and maximum depth

Each point is ten metres of depth, so a 100-point answer sinks you 1,000 metres, and a clean seven-prompt run can reach 7,000 metres.

The important design choice is not the metaphor. It is the spacing. A binary quiz only has to decide whether an answer belongs in the set. A rare-answer game also has to separate “everyone typed this,” “a lot of people thought they were being original,” and “almost nobody finds this in 25 seconds.” Without those bands, a player cannot tell a safe common answer from a genuine deep cut, and the prompt stops being a search problem.

The “Too Clever” trap

The 15-point band is easy to underestimate. When a prompt asks for an obscure country or a chemical element, a huge number of players reach for the same well-known “smart” example. It feels rare. It is not. The official site’s point is that those famous lateral picks belong in Too Clever, not in the 100-point trench.

That is useful as a scoring rule and as feedback. It tells the player: originality is not the same thing as the trivia-night favourite. The rarest valid answers are often quieter mid-sized members of the set, not the extreme everyone has already heard is “the obscure one.”

What this does to the 25-second clock

Because a wrong or misspelled guess does not end the round, the clock becomes a budget. You can spend seconds hunting for a deep cut. You can also spend them and leave with nothing. An expired clock scores no depth; even a 10-point Plankton answer still banks +100m.

The official guidance follows from that tradeoff:

  1. Skip the first one or two instincts. If an answer arrived in half a second, it is probably where the crowd is.
  2. Do not assume a famous “clever” pick is a 100-point answer.
  3. If an obscure spelling is rejected twice, lock in a guaranteed valid answer before the timer hits zero.

The game is not asking you to be obscure at any cost. It is asking you to be valid first, and then as rare as the remaining seconds allow.

An optional endurance mode, same ladder

The seven-prompt expedition is the standard shape. The official site also offers 3-Tank Endless Survival: you can descend past 7,000 metres for as long as three oxygen reserves hold. A tank is lost only when a 25-second round expires, or you skip, without a valid answer. A tank is refilled (+1, up to 3) only when you land a 100-point One in a Krillion answer.

That is a different pressure curve from the seven-prompt run, but it uses the same rarity ladder. The 100-point band is not just a high score; in survival it is also how you recover. I am describing the published rules here, not the implementation.

There is also a Pokémon-themed mode at https://krillionunlimited.co/pokemon, and you can play unlimited seven-prompt solo dives with no daily lockout and no account.

A note on independence — and on this article

Krillion Unlimited is independent. It is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by krillion.io.

This article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against the official site’s published rules before being prepared for publication. It does not describe the game’s internal implementation.

If you want to try the scoring ladder rather than read about it, the official game is here: https://krillionunlimited.co/.

title: Test GLM-5.4 on a 32px checkout overflow, with and without a screenshot
description:
A 352px Pay button stuck out of a 320px checkout panel. GLM-5.4 identified the right edge and returned box-sizing: border-box both times: once from the code alone and once with a screenshot attached. Applying each declaration to a separate copy in Chrome produced identical 320px buttons. Only the reply with the screenshot could read the order reference printed above the button. That reference wasn't in the prompt text.

At 10:07 UTC on November 23, 2026, both calls to POST /v1/chat/completions returned HTTP 200. The requested model was coding-glm-5.4; both responses reported glm-5.4.

Input Edge identified Order reference Input tokens Output tokens
Code only Right null 573 28
Code + screenshot Right TXA-B4M 743 66

The screenshot added 170 input tokens for this PNG with the same prompt text. The output counts are separate; neither call reported a cache hit.

Keep one file for the prompt and one for Chrome

The test page contains no customer data. The HTML and prompt in this example are shorter than the ones used for the recorded run: they reproduce the overflow, not the exact token counts. Save the HTML as checkout.html and leave the placeholder in the file you'll send to the model.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>Checkout</title>
<style>
  .panel { width: 320px; margin: 32px auto; outline: 2px solid #687f7a; }
  .pay {
    display: block; width: 100%; height: 48px;
    padding: 0 16px; border: 0; box-sizing: content-box;
  }
</style>
<main class="panel">
  <p>Order ref: {{ORDER_REF}}</p>
  <button class="pay">Pay $12.00</button>
</main>
</html>

Save the following as prepare.py. Run python3 prepare.py before each pair to put a fresh reference in the browser copy only. Open rendered.html in Chrome with a 390px-wide viewport at 100% zoom. Take a screenshot that includes the reference and the whole button, and save it as before.png next to checkout.html.

from pathlib import Path
from secrets import token_hex

template = Path("checkout.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
reference = token_hex(4).upper()
Path("rendered.html").write_text(
    template.replace("{{ORDER_REF}}", reference), encoding="utf-8"
)

Give both requests the same CSS

Use Python with the openai package (python3 -m pip install openai). Set AIHUBMIX_API_KEY to a key for a funded test account; the AIHubMix quick start covers client setup. Save this as compare.py and run python3 compare.py in the same directory.

import base64
import os
from pathlib import Path
from openai import APIStatusError, OpenAI

template = Path("checkout.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
if template.count("{{ORDER_REF}}") != 1:
    raise ValueError("Use the unfilled checkout.html template")
question = (
    "390px viewport. Which edge of .panel does .pay cross? Give one CSS "
    "declaration that keeps the button full width and both 16px paddings. "
    "Read the order reference only if visible in a screenshot, else use null. "
    "Return JSON with keys edge, property, value, order_ref.\n\n"
)
text = {"type": "text", "text": question + template}
png = base64.b64encode(Path("before.png").read_bytes()).decode("ascii")
image = {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64," + png}}
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://aihubmix.com/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["AIHUBMIX_API_KEY"],
    max_retries=0,
)
for name, parts in (("text", [text]), ("image", [text, image])):
    try:
        reply = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="coding-glm-5.4",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": parts}],
            max_tokens=1800,
        )
        print(name, reply.choices[0].message.content)
    except APIStatusError as error:
        print(f"{name}: HTTP {error.status_code}")

Both calls start a fresh conversation, use a 1,800-token output cap and leave temperature unset. Only the second gets before.png as an image_url part. The Coding Plan announcement describes vision on that plan. The AIHubMix channel guide lists image input without a verified vision flag. The exact transcription in this run is evidence for this particular PNG on this route.

Apply each proposed declaration to a clean copy

First check order_ref against your local browser copy. The text-only answer should contain JSON null. The image answer should match the fresh reference exactly. In the recorded run the text-only reply was plain JSON, but the screenshot reply wrapped its JSON in a Markdown code fence. Remove that fence before passing the reply to a JSON parser.

For the CSS check, start each candidate on its own copy of the broken rendered.html at 390px. Apply just the declaration from that reply. In the DevTools console, measure both edges with getBoundingClientRect():

const panel = document.querySelector(".panel").getBoundingClientRect();
const pay = document.querySelector(".pay");
const box = pay.getBoundingClientRect();
const style = getComputedStyle(pay);
console.log({
  edgesFit: Math.abs(box.left - panel.left) <= 1 && Math.abs(box.right - panel.right) <= 1,
  paddingIntact: style.paddingLeft === "16px" && style.paddingRight === "16px",
  labelIntact: pay.textContent.trim() === "Pay $12.00",
});

The repair passes if both edges line up within 1 CSS pixel, both paddings remain 16px, and the label is intact. Removing the padding would make the button fit but would fail this check.

On the recorded page, width: 100% with content-box gave all 320px to the button's content. Padding accounted for the extra 32px. Both replies put the padding inside the declared width with border-box. Chrome measured a 0px difference at each edge for each patch, with the original paddings and label intact. The model returned CSS; Chrome rendered the corrected page. The model didn't edit the PNG.

Keep that corrected screenshot out of your inputs. On this pair the code alone was enough to fix the layout, while only the screenshot supplied the reference. One page can't establish how often screenshots improve a repair.

Sources

  1. Original checkout and Chrome render after applying the model's CSS: same viewport and order reference.
  2. AIHubMix channel guide: request route and image-input status.
  3. Zixuan Li's Coding Plan announcement.
  4. MDN: box-sizing.
  5. MDN: getBoundingClientRect().

Keep reading

GLM-5.4: Debug a CSS overflow with a 320px test case

title: How to Add Interactivity to a Webpage Using JavaScript: A Beginner-Friendly Tutorial
description:
Have you ever clicked a button on a website and watched something happen instantly?

Perhaps a heading changed, a menu opened, a message appeared, or a counter increased without the entire webpage reloading.

Have you ever wondered how developers make these interactions possible?

The answer often involves JavaScript, a programming language that allows websites to respond to user actions and update content dynamically.

If you're learning web development, understanding JavaScript can feel much easier when you build something small and see the result for yourself.

You don't need to start with a complicated web application. You don't need hundreds of lines of code. You can begin with something as simple as a heading and a button.

In this tutorial, we'll build a small interactive webpage step by step. You'll learn how HTML, CSS, and JavaScript work together, and you'll practise important concepts such as variables, functions, DOM selection, event listeners, and updating text content.

By the end, you'll have a practical example you can experiment with and expand.

Let's get started! 🚀

What Are We Going to Build?

We'll create a webpage containing a heading and a button.

Initially, the heading will display:

Welcome to My Website!

When someone clicks the button, the heading will change to:

You just made this page interactive!

It may seem like a small project, but it introduces several important concepts used in frontend development.

Here's how the three core technologies will contribute:

HTML: Creates the heading and button.

CSS: Styles the button.

JavaScript: Detects the click and changes the heading.

Let's build it one step at a time.

Step 1: Create the HTML Structure

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It defines the structure and meaning of webpage content.

For our project, we need two elements: a heading and a button.

Create a file named index.html and add the following code:

<!DOCTYPE html>




My Interactive Webpage

Welcome to My Website!

Click Me

Let's understand a few important parts.

The

element represents the main heading on the page.

The element creates a button that users can click.

But what are id="heading" and id="changeButton" doing?

An id gives an HTML element a unique identifier within the document. JavaScript can use these identifiers to locate the specific elements it needs to work with.

For example, heading identifies our heading, while changeButton identifies our button.

At this stage, we have the structure, but the button doesn't yet change the heading.

That's perfectly fine. We'll add that behaviour shortly.

Step 2: Style the Button With CSS

Now let's improve the appearance of the button.

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It controls how HTML elements are presented, including their colours, spacing, borders, typography, and layout.

Create another file named style.css.

Add the following code:

body {
font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
text-align: center;
padding: 60px 20px;
}

h1 {
color: #2E2E2E;
}

button {
background-color: #800020;
color: white;
padding: 12px 20px;
border: none;
border-radius: 6px;
cursor: pointer;
font-size: 16px;
}

button:hover {
opacity: 0.9;
}

Here's what these styles accomplish:

font-family sets the font used on the page.

text-align: center centres the text horizontally.

padding creates space inside the button and around the page content.

background-color gives the button a burgundy background.

color: white makes the button text white.

border-radius rounds the button's corners.

cursor: pointer indicates that the button is clickable when using a mouse.

button:hover changes the button's appearance slightly when a mouse pointer hovers over it.

But there's one more thing to do.

We need to connect our CSS file to the HTML document.

Inside the element of index.html, add this line:

Your page now has a structure and a visual design.

However, the button still needs JavaScript to perform our intended action.

Step 3: Select the HTML Elements With JavaScript

Here's where things get interesting.

JavaScript allows us to access HTML elements and change their content, attributes, and other properties.

For this project, we need to select the heading and the button.

Create a file named script.js.

Add the following code:

const heading = document.getElementById("heading");
const button = document.getElementById("changeButton");

Let's break this down.

Understanding variables

A variable provides a name through which we can access a value.

In this example, we use const to declare two variables:

heading

button

The first variable stores a reference to the HTML heading element.

The second variable stores a reference to the HTML button element.

Why use const?

It declares a binding that cannot be reassigned to a different value. In this example, we don't need to reassign either variable.

Understanding DOM selection

DOM stands for Document Object Model.

The browser represents the HTML document as a structured model that JavaScript can access and modify.

The method document.getElementById() searches the document for an element with the specified ID.

For example:

document.getElementById("heading");

This retrieves the element whose ID is heading.

Because our HTML heading has that ID, JavaScript can now access it through the heading variable.

The same process allows us to access the button.

Why is this important?

JavaScript needs a way to identify the elements it should work with. DOM selection provides that connection between your JavaScript code and the webpage.

Step 4: Create a Function to Change the Heading

Now that JavaScript can access the heading, let's define what should happen when we want to change its text.

Add this code to script.js:

function changeHeading() {
heading.textContent = "You just made this page interactive!";
}

Let's examine the important concepts.

What is a function?

A function is a reusable block of code that performs a particular task when called.

Here, we've created a function named changeHeading.

The instructions inside the function tell JavaScript to update the heading's text.

Notice that defining the function doesn't automatically execute it. We still need to tell JavaScript when to run it.

What does textContent do?

The textContent property lets JavaScript read or update the text contained in an element.

This statement:

heading.textContent = "You just made this page interactive!";

replaces the heading's existing text with the new message.

Initially, the heading says:

Welcome to My Website!

After the statement executes, it says:

You just made this page interactive!

The heading element itself remains on the page. Only its text changes.

This is a simple example of DOM manipulation.

Step 5: Listen for a Click Event

We've created a function that changes the heading. Now we need to connect it to the button.

Add this line to script.js:

button.addEventListener("click", changeHeading);

Let's understand what this means.

What is an event?

An event is an occurrence that JavaScript can respond to.

Examples include:

A user clicking a button.

A user typing into an input field.

A form being submitted.

A keyboard key being pressed.

In our project, the event is a button click.

What is an event listener?

An event listener allows JavaScript to wait for a particular event and execute a function when that event occurs.

The addEventListener() method accepts the event type and the function that should run in response.

In our example:

button.addEventListener("click", changeHeading);

button refers to our HTML button.

"click" specifies the event we want to listen for.

changeHeading is the function that should execute when the click occurs.

Notice that we write changeHeading, not changeHeading().

We are passing the function itself as a callback so the browser can call it when the click happens.

If we wrote changeHeading() directly as the second argument, we would execute the function immediately rather than register it as the click handler.

This small distinction is important when learning JavaScript events.

Step 6: Connect JavaScript to HTML

We've written the JavaScript, but the browser needs to load the file.

Open index.html and add this script element just before the closing tag:

Placing the script at the end of the body in this example ensures that the heading and button have been parsed before the script tries to select them.

Your HTML file should now look like this:

<!DOCTYPE html>




My Interactive Webpage


Welcome to My Website!

Click Me

You now have three files:

index.html — the webpage structure.

style.css — the visual styling.

script.js — the interactive behaviour.

Make sure all three files are saved in the same folder, as shown in this example.

Step 7: Test Your Webpage in the Browser

It's time to see your code in action!

Open index.html in your browser.

You should see a heading that reads:

Welcome to My Website!

Below it, you'll see your styled button.

Now click the button.

The heading should change to:

You just made this page interactive!

Congratulations! 🎉 You've created a webpage that responds to a user's action.

Let's review the sequence:

The browser loads your HTML.

CSS styles the heading and button.

JavaScript selects the heading and button.

The browser waits for a click on the button.

When the click occurs, the event listener calls changeHeading().

The function updates the heading through textContent.

The browser updates the displayed text without requiring a full-page reload.

That's a simple but important example of JavaScript in action.

Step 8: Troubleshoot Common Problems

If your webpage doesn't behave as expected, don't panic. Debugging is part of programming.

Here are a few things to check.

The button does nothing

Make sure the script is connected correctly:

Check that the file is named script.js and is located where the HTML expects it to be.

The heading doesn't change

Check that the ID in your HTML matches the ID used in JavaScript.

Your HTML should contain:

Welcome to My Website!

Your JavaScript should use:

document.getElementById("heading");

Remember that spelling and capitalization matter.

The button isn't styled

Confirm that this line appears in the HTML's :

Also check the filename and folder location.

You're still stuck

If you're using a desktop browser, open the developer tools and inspect the Console for JavaScript errors. A message about a missing element or file can help you identify the problem.

If your browser reports that an element is null, check whether the element exists and whether the script runs after the element has been parsed.

Debugging isn't a sign that you're bad at programming. It's part of learning how your code works.

Step 9: Challenge Yourself With Small Improvements

Once the basic interaction works, try changing the project.

These small challenges will help you practise what you've learned.

Challenge 1: Change the message

Replace the existing message with something of your own.

For example:

heading.textContent = "Keep learning and keep building!";

Challenge 2: Change the button text

Can you also change the text displayed on the button after it's clicked?

Hint: The button element has a textContent property too.

Challenge 3: Create a counter

Instead of changing a heading, create a number that increases each time someone clicks a button.

This will help you practise variables and updating the DOM.

Challenge 4: Create a show-and-hide feature

Make a button that reveals additional text when clicked and hides it when clicked again.

This introduces the idea of changing an element's visibility and tracking its current state.

Challenge 5: Add a second button

Create another button that changes the heading back to its original message.

This will help you practise working with multiple events and functions.

You don't have to complete every challenge immediately. Start with one, make it work, and then move to the next.

Why This Small Project Matters

You might be thinking, "It's only a button that changes some text. Is that really useful?"

Yes—because the purpose of this exercise is not to create a sophisticated application. It's to understand the basic mechanism behind many interactive features.

The same fundamental ideas can contribute to much larger projects.

A shopping cart responds to button clicks and updates information.

A search interface responds to input and displays results.

A form can listen for submission events and provide feedback.

A dashboard can update its interface when new data arrives.

Larger applications introduce additional concepts, but understanding events, functions, DOM selection, and content updates gives you a foundation for learning them.

The best way to understand JavaScript is to connect what you learn with something you can build and test.

Conclusion: Start Small, Then Build Bigger

Adding interactivity to a webpage doesn't have to be complicated.

In this tutorial, you created an HTML heading and button, styled the button with CSS, selected the elements with JavaScript, defined a function, listened for a click event, and updated the heading's text.

Along the way, you practised five important concepts:

Variables.

DOM selection.

Functions.

Event listeners.

Updating text with textContent.

More importantly, you saw how these concepts work together to create a result you can observe in your browser.

Remember the roles of the three technologies:

HTML = Structure

CSS = Presentation

JavaScript = Behaviour

You don't need to master JavaScript before building your first project. You can start with one small interaction, learn from it, and gradually take on more challenging ideas.

Save your code. Experiment with it. Break something and figure out how to fix it.

Every experiment gives you another opportunity to learn.

Your Turn!

💬 If you could build your next JavaScript project, which would you choose?

A click counter.

A simple calculator.

A show-and-hide menu.

An interactive form.

Share your choice in the comments—and keep building!

title: I Stopped Hand-Tweaking shadcn/ui CSS Variables — Build the Whole Theme in Minutes Instead
description:
shadcn/ui gives you beautiful components and exactly one rite of passage: an afternoon inside globals.css, hand-tuning CSS variables, wondering why your primary color looks perfect in light mode and like a crime scene in dark mode.

--primary, --primary-foreground, --ring, --chart-3... every variable has a partner, contrast is a real constraint, and "just make it blue" turns into forty small decisions. There's a faster way to get a theme that's actually coherent.

🛠️ Free Tool: shadcn Theme Generator — WebToolsHub — pick colors visually, preview light and dark mode live, and export ready-to-paste CSS variables. Free, in-browser.

Why Hand-Tuned Themes Drift

A shadcn theme isn't one color. It's a system:

  • Backgrounds and foregrounds that must pair correctly
  • Primary, secondary, accent, and destructive — each with a foreground that stays readable on top of it
  • Border, input, and ring colors that harmonize instead of matching by accident
  • Chart colors that look like they belong to the same product
  • A radius that changes the entire personality of the UI

Change one value in isolation and the system quietly breaks somewhere else — usually the place a user finds first, like a disabled button nobody can read.

The Workflow That Respects Your Afternoon

  1. Start from intent, not hex codes. "Warm and trustworthy" or "sharp and technical" — pick the feeling, then the base color that carries it.
  2. Preview in both modes simultaneously. Dark mode is not inverted light mode. If you're only checking one, you're shipping the other on faith.
  3. Check the pairings, not the colors. Text on primary, text on destructive, muted text on background — contrast lives in pairs.
  4. Export and paste. The output should be the full variable block for globals.css, ready for Tailwind v4's @theme or the classic :root / .dark setup.

That's the whole loop the shadcn theme generator is built around: visual picking, live component preview in both modes, and a clean export you paste once.

Your Components Were Never the Problem

shadcn's components are consistent by design — which means when a UI looks "off," it's almost always the theme layer underneath. Fix the system once, and every button, card, and dialog you add inherits the fix.

Spend the afternoon building features. Let the theme take ten minutes.

title: Amazon SageMaker Studio now supports training job submission and model deployment for SageMaker HyperPod clusters
description:
Amazon SageMaker Studio now provides a native developer experience for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, enabling data scientists to submit distributed training jobs, deploy models, and monitor workloads through a visual interface on HyperPod clusters orchestrated with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). SageMaker HyperPod is a purpose-built infrastructure for distributed training and fine-tuning of foundation models at scale, designed to reduce infrastructure management overhead. Submitting training jobs and deploying custom models on HyperPod at scale requires familiarity with kubectl and authoring Kubernetes manifests, creating operational burden for data scientists who prefer to work in an interactive development environment.

With this launch, data scientists can now submit distributed PyTorch and Ray training jobs and deploy models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon S3, or Amazon FSx, through single-page forms with a live YAML preview in SageMaker Studio. Compute configurations in the forms provide reusable resource presets that data scientists select when submitting training jobs or deploying models, eliminating manual compute entry. Metrics and logs are embedded directly in the detail pages, powered by HyperPod Observability and Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, surfacing Kubernetes conditions and events, CloudWatch logs, and embedded metrics so data scientists can diagnose workloads without leaving their environment. For teams managing multiple workloads and using HyperPod task governance, Studio provides a unified queue view where users can see all pending tasks across training jobs and inference services, and adjust a task's priority class directly to optimize cluster utilization.

These updates are available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod and Amazon SageMaker Studio are currently supported.

To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod in Studio documentation.

title: Amazon Connect Customer AI agents now fill in step-by-step guides
description:
AI agents in Amazon Connect Customer can now populate fields of a step-by-step guide for contact center agents during live customer interactions. With step-by-step guides, managers can design forms and other user interfaces for common workflows, such as rebooking a trip or submitting a claim. Now, AI agents can fill in a guide when it first loads and suggest updates during live conversations, saving time and improving data accuracy.

When contact center agents speak to customers, they spend valuable time recording the information they need to solve the customer's problem in a step-by-step guide. For example, when a traveler calls an airline to change her flight, the agent might record her booking reference, dates of travel, and seat preferences. Now, Connect Customer's AI agents can automatically suggest and populate information like this, based on the context of the conversation. Human agents can review each suggestion, accept or reject suggestions individually or in bulk, and make any edits before submitting. The agent can focus on the customer and the problem at hand rather than on manual data entry.

You can use AI agents with step-by-step guides in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more and get started, see step-by-step guides in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

title: Amazon Inspector expands runtime reachability analysis for ECR and EC2 findings
description:
Amazon Inspector has expanded its vulnerability management capabilities with runtime reachability analysis for findings originating from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances. Previously, Inspector reported every vulnerability found in a resource, including packages that were never used by applications. Security teams had to manually assess which vulnerabilities actually posed risk in their deployed environments. Now, Inspector automatically identifies which vulnerabilities are potentially reachable by analyzing package placement in container images and process activity on EC2 instances.

With runtime reachability analysis, you can focus remediation efforts on vulnerabilities that matter most to your security posture. For container images, Inspector determines whether a vulnerable package is within your application's dockerfile paths defined by WORKDIR, ENTRYPOINT, or CMD instructions. For EC2 instances, Inspector identifies whether a vulnerable package was observed running as a process during the most recent scan. For EC2, customers must use the Inspector VM Scanner for agent-based scanning to get this capability. This helps organizations managing large container fleets or complex applications prioritize remediation by distinguishing between vulnerabilities that are potentially reachable versus those in unused dependencies, reducing noise and enabling development and security teams to work more efficiently. Newly generated findings will have runtime reachability analysis included, and backfill of existing findings will be completed over time.

Runtime reachability for Inspector findings is available at no additional charge and is available in all AWS Regions where Inspector is already available.

To learn more, visit the Amazon Inspector product page.

title: AWS CodeDeploy now supports suspending Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes
description:
AWS CodeDeploy can now suspend Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during EC2 in-place deployments to Auto Scaling groups. CodeDeploy is a fully managed service that automates application deployments to Amazon EC2 instances, on-premises servers, AWS Lambda functions, and Amazon ECS services. This launch helps prevent scaling activities from terminating or replacing instances while CodeDeploy is updating them, which can cause a deployment to fail.

You can choose to suspend any combination of these processes (Terminate, AZRebalance, InstanceRefresh, and ScheduledActions) on a deployment group, or on a single deployment. CodeDeploy suspends the processes you choose before it deploys and resumes them when the deployment succeeds, fails, or is stopped, so you don't need custom scripts to suspend and resume processes during deployments. A setting on the deployment group applies to every deployment in that group, including deployments that your existing pipelines start.

You can configure this feature by using the CodeDeploy console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. This feature is available in all AWS Regions, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions.

To learn more, see Suspending Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during deployments in the AWS CodeDeploy User Guide, or visit the AWS CodeDeploy product page.

title: API security with WAF
description:
Automated API discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover every API behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF.

Discovery is available through the new API Gateway API Portal, which identifies the APIs automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward. The API Portal classifies the APIs it finds, identifies zombie and shadow APIs, evaluates each API's security posture, and reports findings, including the ones that are missing WAF protections. For unprotected APIs, customers can enable protection using WAF.

Protection is available through the new AWS WAF API Security managed rule group, which protects your APIs against the most exploited API attack categories: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), where the attackers change record IDs in requests to read other users' data, Broken Authentication and Credential Stuffing, where the attackers forge tokens or try stolen passwords at scale, and API Reconnaissance and Enumeration, where the attackers map an API by guessing hidden routes and probing for exposed docs. The events detected by WAF are consolidated into the API Portal findings to provide a complete security picture of your APIs. You can use API Security alongside other AWS Managed Rules or your own custom rules to protect your applications.

Together, API Portal and API Security provide you a complete solution from discovery of all APIs in your AWS environment to protecting them, without having to write any custom rules.

API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions. See the Amazon API Gateway FAQ for the list. API Security is available in all AWS Regions where AWS WAF is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

To get started, see the following resources:

AWS WAF product page

AWS WAF API Security in the AWS WAF Developer Guide

API Portal Developer Guide

Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection blog post

title: AWS Systems Manager Automation now automates operational tasks in Azure and Google Cloud
description:
AWS Systems Manager Automation now lets you create custom workflows (runbooks) that can automate operational tasks across Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS resources. Automation helps you make changes safely at scale, such as remediating misconfigurations or cleaning up idle resources. Runbooks can roll out in controlled batches, pause for approval, and stop if errors pass a threshold. Instead of maintaining separate tools and credentials for each cloud, teams can now author and execute runbooks from a single place.

Six new runbook actions call Azure and Google Cloud APIs, check a resource's state, and wait for operations to finish without custom code. You can target Azure resources by subscription, region, resource group, resource type, and tag. Google Cloud resources can be targeted by project, zone, asset type, and label. For more complex logic, aws:executeScript now includes Azure and Google Cloud Python SDKs and gets short-lived credentials from your Systems Manager Cloud Connector, so you don't store secrets in runbooks. For example, you can stop tagged development virtual machines outside business hours or fix storage buckets that don't meet your security policy. To get started, use the AWS-provided runbooks that install the SSM Agent or the Amazon Inspector agent on your Azure or Google Cloud virtual machines, or create your own custom workflow.

title: GRACE: Controlled Evidence Interventions for Diagnosing and Improving Knowledge Integration in GraphRAG
description:
arXiv:2611.27350v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GraphRAG combines a language model's parametric knowledge with retrieved graph evidence, yet aggregate accuracy cannot show whether failures stem from missing paths, distractors, or conflicts with model knowledge. We introduce GRACE, a benchmark built by executing LC-QuAD 2.0 queries over Wikidata and applying four controlled interventions to each evidence subgraph: severing a support path, adding type-compatible distractors, attaching high-degree hubs, and replacing the supported answer with a counterfactual entity. Questions and option positions remain fixed across the five states. The validated benchmark contains 4,028 questions and 20,140 question-graph pairs. These comparisons reveal that question-only routing cannot distinguish evidence states, while relevance guidance can improve answerable states yet hurt when the support path is severed: relevant facts may not jointly suffice to answer. We propose QCFSE-SA, which combines typed local attention, global graph attention, and question-conditioned evidence guidance with a calibrated graph-support gate. With the factual context and generator held fixed, it improves controlled-state accuracy from 57.17% to 62.78% (+5.61 points; question-clustered 95% CI [+5.04, +6.17]) and broken-state accuracy from 55.41% to 67.85%. Over-abstention on semantic distractors remains an open challenge.

title: WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.27365v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.

title: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance
description:
arXiv:2611.27369v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.

title: ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2611.27372v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.

title: Evidence sufficiency assessment enables cost-effective review allocation in on-premise clinical AI agents
description:
arXiv:2611.27390v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-premise clinical AI agents must auto-accept high-confidence diagnoses, deferring others to clinician review, yet token probabilities and self-reported confidence miss errors, while more reliable five-run consistency incurs fivefold compute. We propose training-free decision-point evidence sufficiency assessment and a three-tier sequential triage protocol. Masking reasoning and diagnosis, the same 4B model scores sufficiency from objective evidence via prior-debiased probabilities over five ordered levels. Calibration freezes a nominal top-50% threshold, selecting single-run, five-run consistency, or full-deferral tiers by whether the one-sided 95% Wilson lower confidence bound of pass rate among accepted cases meets the 95% clinical target line.
