Retained notes have a limit: when a later event makes a note wrong, an agent without current reasoning responds little, while current reasoning makes the action follow the event. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. For Qwen3-8B, this holds also when that value has since been toggled. Without reasoning, state readouts are less reliable after toggles, and Qwen3-8B's answers about the state favor the outdated value. The state answer and the action also depend on different parts of the prompt. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step, where it makes the action respond to later events. The state that can be read out without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.

title: The Voice on the Line
description:
arXiv:2610.35272v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A transcriber listening through one microphone also hears everyone near it. We train causal voice isolators that keep only the caller for a speech recogniser: masking transformers with 20 ms of latency that enroll the caller from the call itself. Short evaluation windows hide two failures that real calls expose: forgetting the caller when another voice talks alone for a while, and damaging a caller who is alone. Long calls with turns, memory beyond the attention window and real headset crosstalk address the first, at a cost to the second. WavLM-Large's own weights, made causal and trained inside the model, move that trade, and training windows cut from longer calls remove most of a lone caller's cold start. The release (555M parameters) makes 16.13% word errors on 60 s AMI windows, against 23.66% for VoxLock, the strongest open isolator, and 14.77% on average over nine test sets, against 18.04%; it is level on Krisp's benchmark, and a caller who is alone still loses more words than with VoxLock. Distilled without WavLM into 22.1M and 9.8M parameters, it runs live on one CPU thread inside a LiveKit agent, at 12.5% and 8.5% of a core per call, with 10.66% and 10.99% error on our development sets (the release 10.49%). In an agent that talks back, noise interrupts it 0.54 times a minute of its speech behind our agent model, which gates its output on a caller-presence head, against 1.18 for VoxLock. We open-source the models, with a LiveKit plugin, at https://huggingface.co/collections/Scicom-intl/voice-isolator.

title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2611.12180v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.

title: When evaluation becomes intervention in clinical AI
description:
arXiv:2611.18297v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.

title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
description:
arXiv:2611.23651v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
description:
arXiv:2611.25086v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely. We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.

title: PGConf.dev 2027 Call for Proposals is Open
description:
PGConf.dev 2027 (May 11-14, 2027, Montréal, CA), aka PostgreSQL Developer Conference 2027, is the annual gathering of PostgreSQL community organizers, hackers, extension maintainers, and the developers who build on their work. Join us for four days of unconference sessions, workshops, hallway-track conversations, and talks that focus on building the future of PostgreSQL.

The call for proposals is open through January 12, 2027! We're looking for presentations (25 and 50 minutes), workshops, panels, posters, and other content focused on PostgreSQL development: patches and extensions, performance and architectural work, missing features and unmet user needs, lessons from production, research, community organizing, and more! A full list of ideas is available on the CFP page.

Community Discussion Sessions are interactive sessions where you can discuss ideas for PostgreSQL development and community in a meeting format. This year, discussion proposals are accepted in two rounds: the first round closes with the main CFP on January 12, 2027, and the second round closes on April 13, 2027. If you would like to present a poster, please let us know by March 15, 2027.

Have a topic you want to see at PGConf.dev? You can suggest it, or upvote other suggestions, through the Talk Solicitation Program.

Even if you've never presented at a PostgreSQL event before, we'd love to hear your ideas and can provide feedback on your proposal!

You can submit your content proposals here:

https://2027.pgconf.dev/program

PGConf.dev 2027 is not possible without the generous support of our sponsors. PGConf.dev is the premier worldwide gathering of PostgreSQL contributors, and is a chance to collaborate on upcoming PostgreSQL development. Your sponsorship helps directly with the ongoing development of PostgreSQL. To find out more about sponsorship opportunities, please visit the sponsorship page, or contact us at contact@pgconf.dev:

https://2027.pgconf.dev/sponsor

We look forward to seeing you in Montréal in May!

title: You can now copy data server-side between Amazon S3 buckets and Amazon FSx file systems with S3 Access Points
description:
You can now use Amazon S3 Access Points to copy or move data server-side between Amazon S3 general purpose buckets and Amazon FSx file systems within the same AWS Region, making it faster, lower-cost, and easier to move your data between S3 and FSx or across FSx file systems.

An S3 Access Point for FSx is an S3 endpoint that allows you to access the data on your Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems via the S3 API and from S3-based services and applications. You can also use S3 Access Points to transfer data to and from your file system without the need to mount it—for example, to copy data into your file system from an S3 bucket owned by a partner or to export job results into another team's bucket. Previously, S3 Access Points for FSx didn't support server-side copies, so transferring your data meant downloading and then uploading each object from a server you run. Starting today, you can now transfer data server-side using S3's standard CopyObject and UploadPartCopy operations, reducing the time, cost, and effort needed to move data between S3 and FSx or between FSx file systems.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where S3 Access Points for FSx are available. You can copy data with the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or S3-compatible tools to move and copy data. To learn more, see the FSx for ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS user guides, and visit the Amazon S3 Access Points page.
